units.tr: TO THE MOST SERENE KING OF ENGLAND AND FRANCE, LORD OF IRELAND, PRINCE OF WALES AND CORNWALL, DEFENDER OF THE CHRISTIAN faith, EDWARD the sixth of that name. Grace and peace from God the Father, through our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: CVM primum huic operi manum admouerem, Serenissime Rex, facile videbam, mihi non modo in scripturæ mysteriis explican-dis, verum etiam cum illis negotium fore, qui cū ipsi nihil laude dignum faciant vnquam, in aliorum laboribus insectandis nimium strenui & diligentes sunt. Etiam nunc mihi illos audire videor, qui me & imprudentiæ & temeritatis accusent. Impru-dens etenim videri possum, qui D. Ioannis epistolas post tot tantorumq; virorum labores ipse quoq; interpretari voluerim, operamq; inanem & superuacaneam mihi sumere: Temerarius vero, quòd Regiæ tuæ Maiestati meas lucubrationes offerre ausus sim. Sed facilis erit vtriusq; criminis excusatio apud eos, qui positis caecæ carnis affectibus remipsam æstimare voluerint. Nam scripturæ sacræ rationem omnem diligenter consyderanti, facile patebit, nullius boni labores & studia, quæ in huius explicatione versantur, vel superuacanea vel reprehensione digna videri debere. Tanta siquidem est huius agri fertilitas, tamq; inexhausta in hoc saluberrimarum frugum ubertas, vt si omnium hominum ingenia in eo excolendo laborent, nunquam tamen alicuius labor irritus & inanis erit, qui animum Christianae veritatis & ecclesiae studiosum attulerit. Quia enim æternæ sapientiæ spiritus scripturæ author est, in eius explicatione nullius hominis industria tantum mysteriorum exhauriet, vt reliquis omnem occasionem altiora & plura scrutandi præripiat. Semper etenim monstrabit benignus Dei spiritus (qui laboribus eiusmodi mirifice fauet) quod priores vel non obseruarunt, vel non necessarium duxerūt, in cuius tractatione multum laboris insumerent. Poterat hoc exemplis demonstrari, si verbis opus esset, vbi res ipsa loquitur. Quisquis ergo illorum labores damnat, qui pio sanctoq; studio in scripturarū explicatione versantur & post multorum aliorum interpretationes ea proferunt, quæ spiritu Christi adiuuante didicerunt: is mihi non tam homines accusare, quàm diuinæ sapientiæ atrocem iniuriam facere videtur: quasi huius vena tam sterilis tamq; exilis sit, vt paucorum hominum studijs tota inuestigari & exhauriri potuerit.
units.tr: When I first set my hand to this work, Most Serene King, I could easily see that I would have to deal not only with explaining the mysteries of Scripture but also with those people who, though they never do anything worthy of praise themselves, are exceedingly vigorous and diligent in attacking the labours of others. Even now I seem to hear them, accusing me both of imprudence and of rashness. I might seem imprudent, since I have chosen to interpret the epistles of St John myself after the labours of so many great men, and so I take on a vain and superfluous task; and rash, because I have dared to offer my studies to your Royal Majesty. But the excuse for both charges will be easy before those who, setting aside the blind passions of the flesh, are willing to judge the matter by itself. For anyone who carefully considers the whole method of Holy Scripture will readily see that the labours and studies of any good man engaged in its explanation ought to appear neither superfluous nor deserving of blame. So great is the fertility of this field, and so inexhaustible the abundance of most wholesome fruits in it, that even if all human talents laboured in its cultivation, the labour of anyone who brings to it a mind devoted to Christian truth and the Church will never be fruitless and empty. For since the Spirit of eternal wisdom is the author of Scripture, no human diligence will so exhaust its mysteries in the explaining that it snatches from others every opportunity of searching into deeper and more numerous things. The gracious Spirit of God, who wonderfully favours labours of this kind, will always show what earlier writers either did not notice or did not think necessary, and on which they would have spent much effort in treating. This could be demonstrated by examples, if words were needed, where the thing itself speaks. Whoever therefore condemns the labours of those who, with a devout and holy zeal, engage in the explanation of Scripture and, after the interpretations of many others, bring forward those things which they have learned with the help of the Spirit of Christ: such a man seems to me not so much to accuse human beings as to do a grievous injury to divine wisdom, as if its vein were so barren and meagre that it could be wholly investigated and exhausted by the studies of a few people.

units.la: Accedit huc, quòd cum hominum institutioni datæ sint sacræ literæ, illas obiter perstrinxisse, earumq; sensum aliquo modo adumbrauisse non sufficiet: sed pro locorum, temporum & personarum ratione eadem accommodari oportet, vt ea singuli inueniant, quæ ipsorum vel institutioni vel consolationi seruire possunt.
units.tr: Add to this that since the holy letters have been given for the instruction of mankind, it will not be enough to touch on them in passing and to sketch their meaning in some way; rather, the same must be adapted to the circumstances of places, times and persons, so that each may find those things which can serve either his instruction or his consolation.

units.la: Et huius interpretationis potissimā ratione Paulum habuisse constat, quiin mi-nistro dexteritate verbi Dei secandi potissimum requirit. Quæ sola ratio docere potest, omnium seculorum homines in scripturæ sacræ studijs versari debere, cum singulis seculis sui quasi peculiares morbi sint, quibus ecclesiæ ministros verbi Dei antidoto mederi oportet. Quì scopus, cum mihi in publico ecclesiæ ministerio versanti, propositus fuerit, si nō laudem aliquam mereor, saltem reprehensione & odio me indignum esse, pijs omnibus demonstrabit. Huius uero euentus mihi spem maximā facit, quòd uix alia sacræ scripturæ pars nostro seculo utilior est & magis necessaria cognitu, quàm Diui Ioannis epistolæ, quibus lucem aliquam inferre conatus sum. Vt enim his omnē Christianæ fidei & religionis ra-tionem comprehendit apostolus: ita omnibus ijs fidelissimè medetur, ad quæ multi non sine graui salutis iactura hodie impingunt, dum vel hominum authoritati nimium tribuunt, uel corruptis illorum moribus offenduntur, qui euangelij & Christi nomine falsò gloriari solent. Quos per se nutantes & rerum incertos non leui impulsu prosternūt ἀποβάται[?] quidam & noui Theologi, qui Veritate quandam hucusq; occultam prædicant, cuius cognitione absolutam ne apostolorum quidem temporibus ac primitiuæ ecclesiæ concedunt. Queruntur hi de nostri seculi dissensionibus, quas nec publici conuentus, nec tot annorum disputationes hucusq; dirimere potuerint. Expectant pacem & tranquillitatē, quam in terris hisce regno Christi à prophetis promissam esse dicunt. Eam quia nondum regnare vident, Veritatis cognitionem nullam adhuc habere contendunt. Sed quorsum illi spectent, facile hoc uno indicio patet, quòd in nullius doctrinam siue religionem inquiri & animaduerti uolunt. Periculū enim esse aiunt, ne dum rerum adhuc incerti, aliorum sententias damnare studemus, in ipsam ueritatem aliquando iniurij fuisse deprehendamur. Quod unum si regibus & ecclesijs persuaserint, mox eos & portenta errorum pariturosk & ceu Areopagitas aliquos ecclesijs praescripturos esse uidebimus. At si Ioannem audire libeat, quid nos facere conueniat, non obscurè patebit. Docet enim fidei & salutis rationè certam esse, nec circa obscuras & hucusq; incognitas speculationes uersari, sed in Christi Iesu cognitione, vera fide & vitæ innocentia cōsistere. De quibus & sufficienter disserit, & ad perseuerantiam in fide per apostolos tradita studiosè hortatur. Nec quosuis admitti uult, qui Dei spiritu se edoctos esse gloriantur: sed doctrinas, an ex Deo sint, probare iubet. Id quod Regibus quoq; & magistratibus dictū esse, nemo pius & sapiens negauerit. Quia enim horum curæ publica salus commissa est, doctrinæ potissimam rationem eos habere conuenit: quæ nisi uera & certa fuerit, & in Dei cultu perniciosè aberrabitur, & in diuersas opiniones distractus populus perpetuis dissidijs, non sine publico regnorum ac rerum pub. malo labo-rabit. Porrò ut apostolicæ doctrinæ veritatem & certitudinem contra falsos doctores Ioannes asserit[?]: ita & pseudochristianos, qui Christum ore profesi uita negant, seuere arguit: ubi de uitæ Christianæ officijs magna diligentia disputat. Adhæc contra mundi inimicitias, dissensionum & contentionum scandala nos fideliter præmunit, dum ex ipsa ecclesia, non contentiosos modò pertinacium disputationū authores, uerumetiam Antichristos prodire ostendit. Deniq;, quæcunq; ad fidei & vitæ Christianæ institutionem spectant, tanta perspicuitate dit, ut nemo, qui hunc non ofcitanter legerit, de Veritatis vel ignorantia uel incertitudine merito queri, & quid hoc tam contentioso seculo fieri debeat, gere possit. Consentiunt huius doctrinæ quæcunq; à prophetis & apostolis tradita habemus. Non est ergo, quòd uel nostri seculi dissensionibus, uel calumniis moueamur, qui inde occasione arrepta, euangelij doctrinā, quæ hodie singulari Dei beneficio ecclesijs restituta est, suspectā facere studeant. Persuasum sit nobis, apostolos Christi spiritu edoctos, de salutis ratione leges certas & omnibus numeris absolutas tradidisse. Tumultuatur quidem circa has infelix mundus: sed parua debet esse huius authoritas apud eos, qui Christo & ueritati derunt. Constat enim proprium hoc mundo esse, quòd ueritatis lucem satur & odit. Et scripturæ docent, Christum contradictionis signum fore, & dem scandali, ad quem multi offendant. Fatetur Paulus Apostolus, sectas omnino esse oportere, ut electi probentur. Imò ipse Christus contra omnem carnis pinionem, regnum suum de hoc mundo esse negat, & quo propius instat finis, eò maiores mundi turbas contra fidei & Veritatis doctrinam fore praedicit. Frustra ergo in terris sperant homines, quae in coelis repositá sunt, ubi πολίτευμα nostrum est, & unde saluatorem nostrum, Iesum Christum, expectamus. Nec tu-tius quicquam est, quàm in fidei & religionis causa apostolicae doctrinae formu-lam respicere, cuius authoritatem & certitudinem D. Ioannes tam studiose asse-rit. Altiora & hucusque incognita mysteria scrutentur, quibus diuina simplicitas sordet, & qui inextricabiles errorum Labyrinthos expeditae & salutari veritatis doctrinae praeferunt.
units.tr: And it is clear that Paul had this method of interpretation chiefly in view, who above all requires in a minister the skill of rightly handling the Word of God. This one principle can teach that men of every age ought to be occupied in the study of Holy Scripture, since each age has its own peculiar diseases, as it were, by which the ministers of the Church must be healed with the antidote of the Word of God. Since this aim was set before me, while I am engaged in the public ministry of the Church, if I do not merit some praise, at least I will show to all the godly that I am not worthy of reproach and hatred. The outcome of this gives me very great hope, because scarcely any other part of Holy Scripture is more useful for our age, or more necessary to know, than the epistles of St John, to which I have tried to bring some light. For just as the apostle comprehends in these the whole account of the Christian faith and religion, so he most faithfully remedies all those things into which many today stumble, not without grave loss of salvation, while they either place too much trust in the authority of men, or are offended by the corrupt morals of those who are wont to boast falsely of the Gospel and of Christ's name. Certain apostates and new theologians, who proclaim some hitherto hidden Truth, the knowledge of which they grant even to the times of the apostles and the primitive Church as not complete, overthrow with no slight push those who are wavering in themselves and uncertain of things. These men complain about the dissensions of our age, which neither public assemblies nor so many years of disputation have hitherto been able to settle. They look for peace and tranquillity, which they say was promised by the prophets to be in this earthly realm of Christ's kingdom. Because they do not yet see it reigning, they insist that they have as yet no knowledge of the Truth. But where those men are heading is easily made plain by this one sign: they do not want anyone's doctrine or religion to be examined and scrutinised. For they say there is a danger that while we are still uncertain of things and eager to condemn the opinions of others, we may at some point be found to have wronged the very Truth. If they once persuade kings and churches of this single point, we shall soon see them bringing forth monsters of error and, like certain Areopagites, prescribing laws to the churches. But if it pleases us to hear John, it will not be obscure what we ought to do. For he teaches that the method of faith and salvation is certain, and does not consist in obscure and hitherto unknown speculations, but in the knowledge of Christ Jesus, true faith and innocence of life. He discourses on these both sufficiently and with the aim of urging diligently perseverance in the faith handed down by the apostles. Nor does he wish to admit anyone who boasts that he has been taught by the Spirit of God, but bids us test the doctrines, whether they are from God. No godly and wise man will deny that this was said to kings and magistrates as well. For since the public welfare has been entrusted to their care, it is fitting that they have chiefly in view the soundness of doctrine: unless this is true and certain, men will go astray in the worship of God in a ruinous way, and the people, pulled apart into diverse opinions, will labour in perpetual discord, not without public harm to kingdoms and affairs of state. Moreover, just as John asserts the truth and certainty of the apostolic doctrine against false teachers, so he also severely rebukes the pseudo-Christians who profess Christ with their mouths but deny him by their lives, where he discusses with great care the duties of the Christian life. Besides this, he faithfully forewarns us against the enmities of the world and the scandals of dissensions and contentions, while he shows that from the Church itself there will come forth not only contentious authors of stubborn disputes but also Antichrists. Finally, whatever pertains to the instruction of faith and the Christian life he sets forth with such clarity that no one who reads this letter attentively could justly complain of ignorance or uncertainty about the Truth, and could grasp what ought to be done in this so contentious age. Whatever has been handed down to us by the prophets and apostles agrees with this doctrine. There is therefore no reason for us to be moved either by the dissensions of our age or by calumnies, by which men, seizing the opportunity, strive to make suspect the doctrine of the Gospel, which today by the singular benefit of God has been restored to the churches. Let us be persuaded that the apostles, taught by the Spirit of Christ, handed down certain laws concerning the way of salvation, perfect in every respect. The unhappy world indeed rages about these things, but the authority of the world ought to be small with those who yield to Christ and to the Truth. For it is clearly the nature of the world to hate the light of truth. And the Scriptures teach that Christ will be a sign of contradiction and a stumbling-block at which many will take offence. The apostle Paul confesses that there must be factions, so that the elect may be approved. Indeed Christ himself denies, against all fleshly expectation, that his kingdom is of this world, and the nearer the end draws, the greater tumults of the world against the doctrine of faith and truth he foretells. It is vain, therefore, for men to hope for on earth what is laid up in heaven, where our citizenship is, and whence we await our Saviour, Jesus Christ. Nor is anything safer, in a matter of faith and religion, than to look to the form of apostolic doctrine, whose authority and certainty St John so earnestly asserts. Let those who search out higher mysteries, hitherto unknown, for which the divine simplicity is held in contempt, and who prefer inextricable labyrinths of error to the plain and wholesome doctrine of the truth, do as they like.

units.la: Caeterum quòd Regiae tuae maiestati labores meos offerre ausus sum, nemo temeritati uel impudentiae tribuat. Nam ut hoc facerem, regiae dignitatis & potestatis munus, quod feliciter & magna totius orbis admiratione sustines, mo-uere potius quàm absterrere debuit. Quia enim per Christum reges regnant, quos hic suae ecclesiae nutritios esse voluit, issdem optimo iure labores suos offerre debent, quicunque ab eodem Christo in ecclesia docendi munus susceperunt. Nec quicquam in terris communi paci & tranquillitati seruandae utilius est, sancta & religiosa principum & ministrorum Verbi coiunctione: qua fit, ut unanimi studio & ardore ad gloriae Christi illustrationem, purioris doctrinae studium, & ecclesiae conseruationem magno & felici successu contendant. Quapropter minime au-diendi sunt, qui Reges ad altiora quaedam magisque necessaria uocatos esse clami-tant: cum uerbi diuini maiestate nihil altius fingi, nec eiusdem doctrina quicquam salutarius magisque necessarium excogitari possit. Per hanc enim Reges edocti, & sanctè & feliciter regnant: qui cum uel priuatos affectus, uel diuinae ueritatis hostes, in consilium admittunt, non sine publico malo & memorabili regnorum calamitate aberrare solent. Quae cum probè intelligas Serenissime Rex, ideoque regnum tuum syncerioris doctrinae & religionis asylum esse voluerís: minime mihi committendum putaui, ut inter eos, qui Regiae tuae Maiestati literaria dona offerunt, sanctisque coeptis tuis gratulantur, solus ego deessem. Nam praeter id, quòd Maiestatis tuae indolem, propter singulare pietatis studium, iustitiam san-ctam, & prudentiam aetate maiorem, amo & uenerur: Angliam tuam, quae me olim humanissime exceptum fauore summo prosecuta est, hoc officium abs me optimo iure postulare arbitrabar. Quapropter Regiae tuae Maiestati gratulor, quòd illam Deus ultimo hoc mundi ad extremum interitum uergentis seculo salutaris uerbi sui cognitione illustrare voluit. Qua factum est, ut Maiestas tua o-pus susceperit uere regium, ecclesiae nimirum reformationem & purioris doctri-nae restitutionem, quae iam seculis aliquot Antichristianis tenebris immersa late-bat. Fauit hucusque tam sanctis conatibus diuinum numen, eò quòd huius uerbi instituti tui formam & regulam esse voluisti. Nec deerit suo auxilio deinceps, si quod pio & felici auspicio coeptum est, constanter urgere & ad finem diuinitus praescriptum deducere pergas. Dei enim promissio est: Honore prosequar eos, qui me honore prosequuntur. Et exempla omnium seculorū probant, solos eos principes feliciter in regnorū suorū administratione esse uersatos, qui Christum Iesum, Regem & Sacerdotem ab aeterno destinatum, agnouerunt, & suae fidei commissum populum huic uni consecratum atque addictum esse voluere. Quod si Regia tua Maiestas seduló, ut coepit, facere pergat, studisq huius fructum immor-talem percipiet. Fauent conatibus istis omnes boni, & eosdem sanctis precibus apud Deum iuuare satagunt. Excitabit is per spiritum suum ubique locorum causae tam sanctae patronos, qui ore & calamo (quibus armis Christi regnum feli-cissimè propagatur) communem salutem iuuabunt. Inter quos, si & meum labo-rem aliquid profuisse sensero, Deo Opt. Max, me id debere agnosco, qui successum,quem unicè quæsivi,tribuit.Quòd si minus profecero, animi tamen studiū, quo in communi ecclesiæ Christi causa afficior, publicè testari volui, quod pijs & bonis omnibus puto nequaquam displicere posse. DOMINVS & saluator noster IESVS CHRITVS,Rex regum & Dominus dominantium,concedat Regiæ tuæ Maiestati spiritum sapientiæ, fortitudinis & constantiæ, idemq; regnum tuum regat,tueatur & conservet,Amen. Datæ Tiguro,primaria Helve-tiorum urbe. VIII.Januarij. Anno incarnati filij Dei M.D.LIII. Quando ante annos bis mille,ducentos & novem,Josias sanctissimus Judæorum rex, doctrinæ verae & religionis reformationem instituit: cuius studium spiritus sanctus æternæ memoriæ consecrauit, ac universis regibus commune ecclesiam reformandi exemplum esse voluit.
units.tr: Nor should anyone attribute it to rashness or presumption that I have dared to offer my labours to Your Royal Majesty. For the high office and power of a king, which you bear happily and to the great admiration of the whole world, ought rather to move me to do so than to deter me. For since kings reign through Christ, whom he willed to be the nursing fathers of his Church here, all who have received from the same Christ the office of teaching in the Church ought with the best right to offer their labours to them. Nor is anything on earth more useful for preserving common peace and tranquillity than the holy and religious alliance of princes and ministers of the Word, by which it comes about that, with united zeal and ardour, they strive with great and happy success for the glory of Christ, the pursuit of purer doctrine, and the preservation of the Church. Therefore those are by no means to be heard who cry out that kings have been called to higher and more necessary things, since nothing higher can be devised than the majesty of the divine Word, and nothing more salutary or more necessary than its doctrine can be thought of. For kings instructed by this reign both holily and happily; but when they admit to their counsel either private affections or enemies of the divine truth, they are wont to go astray, not without public harm and a memorable calamity to kingdoms. Since you understand this well, most Serene King, and have therefore willed your kingdom to be a refuge of purer doctrine and religion, I thought I must by no means be the only one lacking among those who offer literary gifts to Your Royal Majesty and congratulate your holy undertakings. For, besides the fact that I love and venerate the character of Your Majesty, on account of your singular zeal for piety, your holy justice, and your prudence beyond your years, I judged that your England, which once received me most kindly and followed me with the greatest favour, could with the best right demand this duty from me. Therefore I congratulate Your Royal Majesty that God has willed to illumine that country, in this last age of the world, which is tending to its final ruin, with the knowledge of his saving Word. By this it has come about that Your Majesty has undertaken a truly royal work, namely the reformation of the Church and the restoration of purer doctrine, which had for several centuries lain buried in Antichristian darkness. The divine power has hitherto favoured such holy endeavours, because you have willed the form and rule of this institution to be of his Word. Nor will it fail to help you further, provided that you persist in steadily pressing on with what has been begun under a pious and happy auspice and in bringing it to the end prescribed by God. For it is God's promise: "I will honour those who honour me." And the examples of all ages prove that only those princes have fared happily in administering their kingdoms who have acknowledged Christ Jesus, King and Priest appointed from eternity, and have willed the people committed to their trust to be consecrated and devoted to him alone. But if Your Royal Majesty continues to do this diligently, as you have begun, you will receive immortal fruit from these efforts. All good men favour these undertakings, and they take pains to help them by holy prayers before God. He will, through his Spirit, raise up everywhere defenders of so holy a cause, who will aid the common salvation by voice and pen (the weapons by which the kingdom of Christ is most happily propagated). Among these, if I shall perceive that my labour has been of some profit, I acknowledge that I owe this to God Best and Greatest, who grants the success which I have sought alone. But if I shall have profited less, I nevertheless wished to bear public witness to the zeal of mind with which I am moved in the common cause of Christ's Church, which I think can by no means displease all the pious and good. May our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, King of kings and Lord of lords, grant to Your Royal Majesty the spirit of wisdom, fortitude and constancy, and may he rule, protect and preserve your kingdom, Amen. Given at Zurich, the chief city of the Swiss, on the 8th of January, in the year of the incarnate Son of God 1553. When two thousand two hundred and nine years ago Josiah, the most holy king of the Jews, instituted the reformation of true doctrine and religion, a memory the Holy Spirit consecrated to eternal remembrance, and he willed his example of reforming the Church to be common to all kings.

units.la: CHRISTIANO LECTORI.
units.tr: TO THE CHRISTIAN READER.

units.la: LABOREM hunc non eo animo suscepimus, Christiane Lector, quasi eorum studia, qui ante nos D. Johannis epistolas interpretati sunt, improbemus. Veneramur enim & exosculamur omnes, qui in hoc scribendi genere pie & religiosè versantur, & aliorū lucubrationibus nos non parum adiutos esse, ingenuè fatemur. Quia tamen pleriq;, dum brevitati student, ita scripsere, ut doctioribus scripsisse videantur: non inanem operam me sumpturum putavi, si ipse mihi rudiores instituendos deligerem, qui fusiori rerum tractatione opus habent. Feci itaq;, quantum per domini gratiam licuit. Nihil ad ostentationem, nihil invidia vel odij causa, nihil lucri studio scripsimus. Neminem laedere, sed omnibus prodesse studuimus. Id si non assequor, solatio mihi est, quod nostra hæc nemini obfutura esse sat scio, cum ab orthodoxa & catholica prophetarum ac Apostolorum doctrina in fidei articulis nusquam deflexerim. Volui autē in duo posteria D. Johannis epistolia non Homilias proli-xiores dare, sed Homiliarum sylvam sive materiā proponere, quam quivis in literis mediocriter versatus latius diducat. Exhibemus illic nostrarum lucubrationum specimen, quibus & alios novi Testamenti libros illustrare conabimur, si primum hunc conatum nostrum pijs & bonis probari videamus.
units.tr: We undertook this labour, Christian reader, not with the intention of disparaging the efforts of those who before us have interpreted the Epistles of St John. For we honour and embrace all who devote themselves piously and devoutly to this kind of writing, and we freely confess that we have been not a little helped by the labours of others. Yet since most of them, while aiming at brevity, wrote in such a way that they seem to have written for the more learned, I thought it would be no wasted effort to take on the task myself of instructing those who are less learned and who need a fuller treatment of the matters. I have therefore done so, as far as the grace of the Lord has allowed. We have written nothing for display, nothing out of envy or hatred, nothing for the sake of gain. We have aimed to harm no one but to be of benefit to all. If I do not achieve this, it is a consolation to me that I know well that this work of ours will offend no one, since I have nowhere departed from the orthodox and catholic doctrine of the prophets and Apostles in the articles of faith. I have wished, however, in these two last Epistles of St John, to give not more expansive Homilies but to set forth a forest or store of Homilies, which anyone moderately versed in letters may spread out more widely. There we offer a specimen of our labours, by which we shall also try to illuminate the other books of the New Testament, if we see that this first attempt of ours is approved by the godly and good.

units.la: Tuum est Christiane Lector, ijs fauere, qui publicæ utilitati consultum volunt, & eorundem labores precibus iuvare apud Dominum. Vale.
units.tr: It is yours, Christian reader, to favour those who wish to serve the public good, and to help their labours by prayers before the Lord. Farewell.

units.la: IN EPISTOLAM D. IOANNIS APOSTOLI ET EVANGELISTAE CANONICAM I. RODOLPHI Gualtheri Tigurini Homiliae, CAPVT I. HOMILIA I.
units.tr: IN THE CANONICAL EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED JOHN THE APOSTLE AND EVANGELIST, HOMILIES OF RUDOLPH GWALTHER OF ZURICH, CHAPTER 1, HOMILY 1.

units.la: QVOD erat ab initio, quod audiuimus, quod uidimus oculis nostris, quod spectauimus, quod manus nostrae contrectauerunt de uerbo uitae [annunciamus vobis.]
units.tr: THAT WHICH WAS FROM THE BEGINNING, WHICH WE HAVE HEARD, WHICH WE HAVE SEEN WITH OUR EYES, WHICH WE HAVE LOOKED UPON, AND WHICH OUR HANDS HAVE HANDLED, CONCERNING THE WORD OF LIFE [we declare to you].

units.la: OLENT qui uel sacros uel prophanos libros exponere instituerunt, praefatio-nis loco authorum, qui eos scripserunt, laudes multis celebrare. At id mihi in praesenti superuacaneum uidetur. Notus enim est huius sanctissimi scripti author Ioannes Apostolus, dilectus ille Iesu Christi saluatoris nostri discipulus, cuius laudes si quis narrare uelit, dicendi finem non facile inueniet. Sufficiat nobis, quod à Christo unice dilectus fuit: quod in ultima coena super Christi discumbentis pectus recubuit: quod Christo morienti astitit, & salutiferi illius liquoris, qui ex mortui latere aperte promanauit, testis fuit oculatus: quod deniq; ipsi Christus moriens matrem Virginem commendatam esse voluit. Si cui enim haec minus suffecerint, eum nulla humanae eloquentiae uis adducere poterit, ut diuinum scriptorem admiretur, eiusq; scriptis fidem habeat. Nos potius occasionem, quae ipsum ad scribendum impulit, & totius epistolae argumetum explicemus.
units.tr: Those who have undertaken to expound either sacred or profane books are accustomed, by way of preface, to offer many praises of the authors who wrote them. But in the present case this seems to me unnecessary. For the author of this most holy writing, John the Apostle, is well known, that beloved disciple of Jesus Christ our Saviour, and if anyone wished to recount his praises, he would not easily find an end to speaking. It is enough for us that he was uniquely loved by Christ; that at the last supper he reclined upon the breast of Christ as he sat at table; that he stood by Christ as he died, and was an eyewitness of that saving fluid which flowed forth from the side of the dead man; and that, finally, Christ himself, dying, wished his Virgin mother to be commended to him. For if these things seem too little to anyone, no force of human eloquence will be able to lead him to admire the divine writer and to give credence to his writings. Rather, let us explain the occasion which prompted him to write, and the argument of the whole epistle.

units.la: Eadem uero Ioanni, quae & alijs apostolis, data fuit scribendi occasio: Errores nimirum uarij & multiplices, qui inter primordia ecclesiae, per pseudoapostolos, impostores & haereticos, non sine multorum scandalo & interitu disseminabantur. Si enim cum Apostolorum scriptis primitiae ecclesiae historiam conferamus, inuenire licebit, ipsis adhuc uiuentibus & commisso sibi munere fungentibus diligenter, horribiles haereses & sectas pullulauisse. Iam tunc enim operabatur iniquitatis mysterium satan in Simone Mago, qui praeter quam religionem sibi quaestum facere voluit, diuinos honores sibi conferri passus est, & Magna Dei uirtus à quibusdam appellabatur. Exorta quoq; iam erat Hebionis & Cerinthi uafania, qui Christum merum hominem praedicantes, eiusdem diuinam naturam prorsus abnegabant. Legem Euangelio miscebant Nazaraei, & legali iustitia gratuitam per Christi meritum iustificationem plane confundebant. Comitabantur corruptam doctrina & peruersa dogmata errores multi circa externos cultus. Inueniebantur enim qui à simulachris Deorum gentilium minus abhorrebant, imo qui & carnibus immolatitijs uesci consueuerant. Et quod apud Corinthios in Coena domini peccatum fuit, credibile est non apud illos duntaxat locum inuenisse. Adhaec tot & tam uarijs uitijs circa doctrinam fidei & religionis externae usum, effrenis eorum licentia accedebat, qui sub Christi merito & Christianae libertatis praetextu peccandi inpunitatem quaerebant: quorum improbitate fiebat, ut euangelij doctrina male audiret apud gentes, & uniuersum Christianae religionis negotium multis suspectum esset.
units.tr: The same occasion for writing was given to John as to the other apostles: namely, the various and manifold errors which, in the early days of the Church, were spread abroad through false apostles, impostors and heretics, not without the scandal and ruin of many. For if we compare the history of the primitive Church with the writings of the Apostles, we shall find that, while the apostles were still living and diligently discharging the office committed to them, dreadful heresies and sects were already springing up. For already then Satan was at work in Simon Magus, the "mystery of iniquity," who wished to make money out of religion and allowed divine honours to be paid to him, and was called by some "the great power of God." The folly of Ebion and Cerinthus had also already arisen, who preached Christ as a mere man and utterly denied his divine nature. The Nazarenes mixed the Law with the Gospel, and thoroughly confused justification freely given through the merit of Christ with legal righteousness. Accompanying this corrupt teaching and perverse doctrines were many errors concerning external worship. For there were those who did not greatly shrink from the images of the pagan gods, indeed who were accustomed even to eat meats offered to idols. And what was a sin among the Corinthians at the Lord's Supper is credibly believed to have found a place not among them alone. Besides these many and various vices concerning the doctrine of faith and the use of external religion, there was added the unbridled licence of those who, under the pretext of Christ's merit and Christian liberty, sought impunity for sinning; by whose wickedness it came about that the teaching of the gospel was ill spoken of among the nations, and the whole business of the Christian religion was viewed with suspicion by many.

units.la: His ergo malis praesenti epistola Ioanes medetur. Primo enim omnem nostrae salutis rationem, & summam fidei Christianae, paucis comprehensam proponit, docens quales nostrapte natura simus, & quid in Christo nobis collatum sit. Mox in ea stylum stringit, quae nos à salutis uia reuocare, uel in illa remorare possunt: qualia sunt mundi huius corrupti studium, & falsa uel Antichristianae doctrina. Tandem contra falsos Christiani nominis & fidei professores de uitae Christiana officijs, purificatione animorum, innocentia, fraterna charitate & alijs eius generis uirtutibus disserit: subinde tamen ea interserens, quae nos mysteriorum Christi admonere, & ad inuicta in uera fide constantiam adhortari possunt, quae singula suis locis uidebimus. Constat autem ex his, epistolae huius cognitionem nostro seculo cumprimis necessariam esse, quando & falsa de Christo & Christiana fide dogmata quotidie oriuntur, & omnis tam interna quàm externa religio friget, florentibus interim & regnantibus teterrimis uitijs & effreni scelerum licentia, quam multi fidei Christianæ prætextu uelare student.
units.tr: John therefore remedies these evils by the present epistle. First, he sets forth, in brief compass, the whole plan of our salvation and the sum of the Christian faith, teaching what sort of people we are by our own nature, and what has been bestowed upon us in Christ. Next, he turns his pen against those things which can call us back from the way of salvation or detain us in it: such as the pursuit of this corrupt world and false or Antichristian doctrine. Finally, against the false professors of the Christian name and faith, he discourses on the duties of the Christian life, the purification of souls, innocence, brotherly love and other virtues of that kind; yet he at times interposes things which can remind us of the mysteries of Christ and exhort us to unconquered constancy in the true faith, each of which we shall see in its place. It is clear from these things that knowledge of this epistle is especially necessary in our own age, when false doctrines concerning Christ and the Christian faith arise daily, and all religion, both inward and outward, grows cold, while meanwhile the most foul vices flourish and reign, and an unbridled licence of crimes, which many strive to cover with the pretext of the Christian faith.

units.la: Cæterum priusquam hinc digrediamur, operæpretium est obseruasse, quod cum superstites adhuc essent apostoli, ac docendi munus strenue obirent, hæc errorum portenta inter Christiani nominis professores oborta sunt. Adeo uerum est, quod Christus monet, dormientibus hominibus malignum illum humani generis hostem euangelico semini zizania & infelix lolium superseminare. Matth. 13. Non dormitarunt quidem in suo officio apostoli, quorum labores & studia pro ecclesiæ conseruatione satis nota sunt. Sed quia qui ab his instituebantur, oscitantiores fuerunt, non tantum proficere potuit apostolorum sedulitas, quantum illorum ignauia & socordia obfuit. Neminem igitur offendat, si hodie quoq; in ecclesijs errores horrendi, graues abusus & incurabiles ferè morbi oboriantur. Quin potus uigilemus omnes, ne & ipsi per incogitantiam inuoluamur. Intelligant ecclesiarum ministri, quantis curis & laboribus opus sit, si feliciter in hoc munere uersari uelint, & in hoc sint toti, ne quis ipsorum culpa pereat. Intelligant singuli, non sufficere ut in religione semel instituti sint, sed propter naturæ nostræ corruptione & hostis satanæ improbitate assiduas uigilias & preces, studium item indefessum, unà cum crebris admonitionibus requiri, siquidem ex Christiana religione fructu salutarem auferre cupiant. Possent hic nos erudire quotidiana exempla, nisi ad omnē mali sensu toti obsurduissemus. Sed his præmissis ad initium epistolæ explicandum accedamus. Sic enim hanc exorditur Apostolus.
units.tr: Moreover, before we depart from this point, it is worth observing that these monstrous errors arose among the professors of the Christian name while the apostles were still alive and vigorously discharging the office of teaching. So true is what Christ warns: that while men slept, that malignant enemy of the human race sowed tares and the unhappy darnel over the evangelical seed. Matt. 13. The apostles indeed did not sleep in their office, whose labours and zeal for the preservation of the Church are sufficiently well known. But because those who were trained by them were more sluggish, the zeal of the apostles could not profit as much as the idleness and carelessness of the others harmed. Let no one therefore be offended if today too there arise in the churches horrible errors, grave abuses and almost incurable diseases. Indeed, let us all the more keep watch, lest we ourselves be entangled through thoughtlessness. Let the ministers of the churches understand how great cares and labours are needed if they wish to conduct themselves successfully in this office, and how wholly they must be given to it, lest any perish through their fault. Let each one understand that it is not enough to have been once instructed in religion, but that, on account of the corruption of our nature and the wickedness of Satan the enemy, constant watchfulness and prayer, likewise tireless zeal, together with frequent admonitions, are required, if indeed they desire to derive a saving fruit from the Christian religion. Daily examples could instruct us here, were we not wholly deafened to every sense of evil. But with these things premised, let us proceed to explain the beginning of the epistle. For thus the Apostle begins it.

units.la: Quod erat ab initio, quod audiuimus, quod uidimus &c. Inest uerbis his primo intuitu quædam obscuritas, sed singula penitius inspicienti sensus facile patebit. Est enim hæc totius epistolæ proposi-tio, quæ ita resolui poterit: SCRibam de uerbo uitæ, hoc ipsum quod ab initio fuit à patre decretum, & cuius ipsi non auriti modo, sed oculati quoq; testes fuimus: cuius deniq; ueritas tam probe nobis constat, quàm eorum, quæ manibus nostris contrectantur. Duo igitur huius proposi-tionis membra sunt: primum, qua de re Ioannes scripturus sit, docet: alterum, quid de illa dicere uelit, pollicetur. Nos utrumq; paulò diligentius excutiemus.
units.tr: That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen, etc. At first sight there is a certain obscurity in these words, but to one who examines each part more deeply the meaning will readily become plain. For this is the proposition of the whole epistle, which can be resolved thus: I shall write concerning the Word of life, that very thing which was from the beginning, decreed by the Father, and of which we were not only hearers but also eyewitnesses; and finally, whose truth is as well established for us as are those things which are handled by our hands. Therefore there are two members of this proposition: first, he teaches what matter John is about to write about; second, he promises what he wishes to say about it. We shall examine both a little more carefully.

units.la: I. DE Verbo uitæ se scripturū dicit. Sunt, qui Verbum Hebraico more pro Causa, negotio siue ratione positum putent, ut idem sit ac si dixisset: De uniuerso uitæ & salutis negotio, ueraq; hanc consequendi ratione dicturus sum. Pius hic sensus est, nec à re præsenti omnino alienus. Sed simplicior & Ioannis institutio congruentior uidetur, ut per Verbum uitæ ipsum Christum Dei filium intelligamus, quem & in principio euangelicæ historiæ Verbum nominauit. Est enim is æternum illud & omnipotens Dei uerbum, per quod Deus omnia & iubet & facit. De hoc Dauid testatur: Verbo domini cœli facti sunt. Psal. 33. Et Apostolus hic nostram eam sententiam quasi explicans ait: Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, & sine eo factum est nihil, &c. Ioan. 1. Præterea, ut uerbum uel oratio animi index est, ita Christus dei filius expressa est substantiæ dei imago, in qua deus pater cognoscitur. Heb. 1. VERBum uitæ uero dicitur, quia (ut eodem loco Apostolus scribit) in quo uita est: & sic quidem, ut non ipse modo, quoad suam personam, uiuat, sed uitam omnibus alijs conferat. Porrò uitam hic dicimus, non animalem illam, quam in hisce terris uersantes agimus (quamuis & huius authorem Deum patrem per filium suum agnoscamus) sed eam quæ cum animarum salute coniuncta omnem hominis beatitudinem complectitur, & in æternum durat. Huius uitæ uerbum, id est, causa, author, largitor, uia & ratio unica est, Dei filius, qui propter nos homo fieri dignatus est, ut uitam hanc nobis conferre posset. Ipse enim tulit infirmitates nostras, et peccata, quæ à patris conspectu nos arcebant, in corpore suo pertulit super lignum, id est acerbo Crucis supplicio expiauit. Isa. 53. 1. Pet. 2. Idem resurrectione sua gloriosa mortem uicit, ne posthac nobis dominari posset, eandemq; transitu fecit in uitam æternam. Ioan. 5. Idem in cœlos euectus ad dextram patris consedet, ac inde in nos dona spiritus & uitæ conferens, simul etiam pro nobis intercedit, ut per illum ad thronum gratiæ nobis aditus pateat. Ephes. 4.1.Ioan.2.&c. Deniq; solus est, in quo pater omnes suæ gratiæ & salutis nostræ thesauros conclusit, sic ut extra hunc, iuxta Petri Apostoli testimonium, salus non sit aliqua. Act.4. Quid ergo maius & salutarius Ioannes polliceri poterat, quàm quod Christum Iesum, uitæ & salutis nostræ unicum authorem se descripturum dicit? Comprehendit hæc promissio non Croesi aut Midæ infelices diuitias, non incertam Solomonici regni gloriam, non tristes & sanguinarias contra homines uictorias: sed regni cœlorum beatissimas opes, & eiusdem nunquam intermorituram gloriam, lætamq; filij Dei contra omnem aduersariam potestatem uictoriam, & salutiferi de his triumphi lætum honorem complectitur. Quàm ergo chara nobis est salus nostra, tam chara & grata esse debet huius epistolæ meditatio, quæ bona hæc cœlestia nō modo in Christo ceu digito monstrat, sed & uiam hæc assequendi perspicue docet.
units.tr: I. He says that he will write concerning the Word of life. Some think that "Word," after the Hebrew manner, is put for cause, business or reason, so that it is as if he had said: I shall speak of the whole business of life and salvation, and of the true way of attaining it. This sense is pious and not altogether foreign to the present matter. But the simpler and more fitting reading of John seems to be that by the Word of life we understand Christ the Son of God, whom he also named the Word at the beginning of the gospel history. For he is that eternal and almighty Word of God, through whom God both commands and makes all things. David bears witness to this: "By the word of the LORD were the heavens made." Ps. 33. And the Apostle, as if explaining our opinion here, says: "All things were made by him, and without him was made nothing," etc. John 1. Moreover, as the word is the index of the mind, so Christ the Son of God is the express image of the substance of God, in whom God the Father is known. Heb. 1. He is called the Word of life, because (as the Apostle writes in the same place) "in him is life": and so indeed that he not only lives himself, as to his own person, but confers life on all others. Further, by life here we mean not that animal life which we lead while living in this earth (although we also acknowledge God the Father as its author through his Son), but that which, joined with the salvation of souls, embraces all human blessedness and endures for ever. The Word of this life, that is, its cause, author, giver, way and only reason, is the Son of God, who deigned to become man for our sake, so that he might be able to bestow this life upon us. For he himself "bore our infirmities and sins," which kept us from the sight of the Father, and "bore them in his body upon the tree," that is, he expiated them by the bitter punishment of the Cross. Isa. 53. 1 Pet. 2. The same by his glorious resurrection overcame death, so that it could no longer rule over us, and he made the passage into eternal life. John 5. The same, taken up into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and from there, bestowing on us the gifts of the Spirit and of life, at the same time also intercedes for us, so that through him access to the throne of grace lies open to us. Eph. 4. 1 John 2, etc. Finally, he alone is the one in whom the Father has enclosed all the treasures of his grace and of our salvation, so that outside him, according to the testimony of the apostle Peter, there is no salvation at all. Acts 4. What greater and more salutary thing could John promise than that he says he will describe Jesus Christ, the sole author of our life and salvation? This promise embraces not the unhappy riches of Croesus or Midas, not the uncertain glory of the kingdom of Solomon, not the sad and bloody victories over men; but the most blessed riches of the kingdom of heaven, and its glory which will never perish, and the joyful victory of the Son of God over every adverse power, and the joyful honour of such a saving triumph. Therefore, as dear to us as our salvation is, so dear and pleasing ought the meditation of this epistle to be, which not only points out these heavenly goods in Christ as with a finger, but also clearly teaches the way of attaining them.

units.la: QVID vero de Verbo vitæ, Christo Iesu, dicturus est? Sunt enim qui de rebus magnis & arduis sermones instituunt, sed ea dicunt, quæ vel manifeste falsa sunt, vel saltem ipsis minus comperta: quæ causa est, vt fidem minime mereantur. Sed nihil tale de Ioanne suspicandum erit. Dicit enim: Quod erat ab initio, quod audiuimus, quod vidimus oculis nostris, quod spectauimus, quod manus nostræ contrectauerunt, annunciamus vobis. Continent hæc verba insigne Apostolicæ doctrinæ dignitatem, quæ duobus argumentis, vetustate nimirum, & veritate siue certitudine commendatur. Vtrumq;, propter nostri seculi homines, qui doctrinâ de fide in Christum nouitatis & vanitatis accusant, non oscitanter inspicere conuenit.
units.tr: What then is he going to say about the Word of life, Christ Jesus? For there are those who undertake to speak of great and difficult matters, but what they say is either manifestly false or at least not well established to themselves, and this is the reason they deserve no belief at all. But nothing of that kind is to be suspected of John. For he says: "That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, which our hands have handled, we declare to you." These words contain the remarkable dignity of the apostolic teaching, which is commended by two arguments, namely antiquity and truth or certainty. It is fitting that we examine both of these carefully, on account of the people of our age who accuse the doctrine of faith in Christ of novelty and vanity.

units.la: Vetustatem exprimit, dicens: Quod erat ab initio. Sed initij vox ad Dei æternitatem, & æternum eiusdem de redemptione nostra consilium referri debet. Vt enim Iesus Christus, quoad divinam naturam, patri coæternus est: ita æternum hoc fuit Dei patris consilium, vt filius præfinito tempore incarnatus infelices homines à peccato & peccati pœna redimeret. Ideo D. Petrus ipsum præordinatum fuisse scribit, priusquam mundus hic conderetur. 1. Pet. 1. Sensus ergo verborum Ioannis est: De verbo vitæ, Iesu Christo redemptore & saluatore nostro, non noua & antehac inaudita, non item vel mea vel aliorum hominum figmenta tradere instituit: sed hoc ipsum, quod cœlestis pater ab æterno decreuit, quodque à prima mundi huius origine promisionibus & oraculis suis reuelauit, & tandem misso in mundum filio fidelissime præstitit. Quod si veteris testamenti scripturas cum Ioannis & aliorum Apostolorum doctrina conferas, verissimum esse videbis, quod hic pollicetur. Certe ipse Christus & Mosem & Prophetas & diuinos Psaltes de se testimonium tulisse, non semel fatetur. Luc. 24. Ioan. 5.
units.tr: He expresses antiquity when he says: "That which was from the beginning." But the word "beginning" must be referred to the eternity of God and to the eternal counsel of God concerning our redemption. For just as Jesus Christ is co-eternal with the Father as regards the divine nature, so this was the eternal counsel of God the Father, that the Son, incarnate at a appointed time, should redeem unhappy men from sin and from the punishment of sin. Therefore St. Peter writes that he was foreordained before this world was founded (1 Pet. 1). The sense, then, of John's words is this: he undertook to deliver not new things, unheard of until now, nor any inventions of his own or of other men concerning the Word of life, Jesus Christ our redeemer and saviour, but that very thing which the heavenly Father decreed from eternity, and which from the first origin of this world he revealed by his promises and oracles, and at last, having sent his Son into the world, most faithfully performed. And if you compare the Scriptures of the Old Testament with the teaching of John and the other apostles, you will see that what he promises here is most true. Certainly Christ himself, more than once, testifies that Moses and the Prophets and the divine Psalms bore witness concerning him (Luke 24; John 5).

units.la: Obseruanda autem est Ioannis fides in tradendis Christi mysterijs. Fuit is, vt antea diximus, Christo præ alijs omnibus familiaris, ab eodem tonitrui filius dicitur, adhæc omnium diutissime vixit & docuit in Christi ecclesia. Non tamen sibi tantum permittit, vt noua quædam de Christo & salutis nostræ negotio tradere instituat, vel quæ olim tradita erant aliquo modo inuertat & commutet. Quin æternum illud Dei patris de salute humani generis consilium, quale ab initio reuelatum est, syncerè prædicat. Eandem fidem in reliquis Apostolis est videre. Certè Paulus non veretur dicere: Etiamsi nos, aut angelus è cœlo prædicauerit vobis euangelium, præter id quod accepistis, anathema sit. Galat. 1. Et alibi nihil aliud se nouisse testatur, quàm Iesum Christum, & hunc crucifixum. 1. Corinth. 2. Conferantur cum hac Apostolorum fide, qui hodie illorum successores dici & haberi volunt, & quantum ab illis differant, luce clarius patebit. Non contenti enim nouos fidei articulos fingere, & in salutis negotio præter Iesum Christum multa alia comminisci, insuper in manifestis scripturæ oraculis, in expressis Christi præceptis, & antiquissimis ecclesiæ Christianæ & Apostolicæ doctrinæ Constitutionibus pro suo arbitrio dispensare, & illis contraria sub pœna excommunicationis & æternæ damnationis obtrudere audent. Quod si vero dilectis Christi discipulis non licuit alia, quàm quæ à Christo acceperant, tradere, multò minus hoc illis licere credemus, qui quotidianis vitijs & sceleribus satis declarant, quàm à Christi spiritu & Apostolorum fide alieni sint.
units.tr: Moreover, John's faithfulness in handing down the mysteries of Christ is to be observed. He was, as we said before, most intimate with Christ beyond all the others, is called by him a son of thunder, and moreover lived and taught in the Church of Christ longer than all. Yet he does not so far permit himself as to undertake to hand down some new things about Christ and the business of our salvation, or to overturn and change in any way what had been handed down long ago. Rather he sincerely preaches that eternal counsel of God the Father concerning the salvation of mankind, just as it was revealed from the beginning. The same faith is to be seen in the other apostles. Certainly Paul does not hesitate to say: "Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel other than what you have received, let him be anathema" (Gal. 1). And elsewhere he testifies that he knew nothing else than Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Cor. 2). Let these be compared with the faith of the apostles, those who today wish to be called and held their successors, and it will be clearer than light how far they differ from them. For not content to devise new articles of faith, and in the business of salvation to invent many other things besides Jesus Christ, they moreover dare, at their own discretion, to dispense with the plain oracles of Scripture, the express precepts of Christ, and the most ancient constitutions of the Christian and apostolic doctrine of the Church, and to impose things contrary to these under pain of excommunication and eternal damnation. But if the beloved disciples of Christ were not permitted to hand down anything other than what they had received from Christ, we shall believe much less that this is permitted to those who by their daily vices and crimes sufficiently show how far they are estranged from the Spirit of Christ and the faith of the apostles.

units.la: Alterum, quod ad huius doctrinæ veritatem & certitudinem pertinet, sic enunciat: Quod au diuimus, quod vidimus oculis nostris, quod spectauimus, quod manus nostræ contrectauerunt, annunciamus vobis. Omnium horum hæc sententia est, se non nisi cognita & modis omnibus comperta loqui, eamque esse suæ prædicationis certitudinem, vt nemo putare debeat, vel ipsos apostolos aliorum astu deceptos fuisse, vel alios astu & dolo fallere voluisse. Sed quàm diligenter hoc agit? Omnes fere sensus adducit, vt intelligant tam certo constare apostolis euangelij certitudinem, vt hanc non mente modò & ingenij speculationibus inuestigare, verumetiam externis sensibus deprehendere potuerint. Primùm, audiuimus inquit. Audiuerunt autem hæc salutis & Christi mysteria non ab hominibus dubiæ fidei, sed ab ipso Christo Dei filio, quo cum familiarissime aliquot annis conuixerunt. Pertinet huc quod alibi habemus: Deum nemo vidit vnquam: sed vnigenitus Dei filius, qui est in sinu patris, ipse enarrauit. Ioan. 1. Hunc concionantem audiuerunt apostoli. Idem doctrinæ suæ mysteria, quæ aliosiusto Dei iudicio cælabantur apostolis reuelare dignatus est. Matth. 13. Nec Christum modò sed Deum patrem de Christo concionantem audiuit Ioannes, voce cœlitus delata: Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi complacitum est: ipsum audite. Matth. 17. Quis ergo de illorum fide, ex quibus ista hauserunt apostoli, dubitet? Sed addit alterius quoq; sensus testimonium: Quod vidimus oculis nostris. Pleonasmo vti voluit, ne quid minus diligenter affirmasse videretur. Et quia multa obiter vident homines, & proinde visu falluntur, addit: Quod spectauimus, intus videlicet & in cute, vt illius veritas certò nobis pateret. Ve-rissime autem hoc dicit Ioannes. Viderunt enim Dei filium incarnatum apostoli. Viderunt eiu-s dem miracula certa diuinitatis ipsius testimonia. Viderunt eiusdem vincula. Vidit in Cruce suspensum Ioannes. Vidit moriente. Vidit in latere eius apertum vitæ & redemptionis nostræ fontem saluberrimum. Vidit euidentia Christi resuscitati in monumento indicia. Vidit deniq; à mortuis resuscitatum ambulare, edere et omnia ea obire, quæ ad corporis veritatē comprobandam pertinent. Vidit lætum ascensionis Christi spectaculum, & triumphum illum splendidissimum, quo excellentius orbis hic totus nihil vnquam habuit. Nec tamen, vt plures alij, hæc viderunt Apostoli, sed spectarunt non oculis modò, sed animis quoque intenti, vt qui in his salutis mysteria scrutabantur. At ne quis oculos illorum fascinatos & incantationum præstigijs delusos putaret, addit: Quod manus nostræ contrectauerunt. Infallibile veritatis argumentum communi ferè sensu homines ex manuum contrectatione capiunt. Quis enim de eo dubitare potest, quod manibus prijs contrectat? Id verò in Christo fecerunt Apostoli, quibus is nō modò mortale & mundi huius miserijs obnoxium corpus, sed illud ipsum clarificatum iam & omni corruptibilitate exutum contrectandum præbuit. Legantur quæ Luc.24. & Ioan.20. euangelica historia narrat, & certum habebis huius rei testimonium. Huc etiam referri debet, quod D. Petrus scribit: Non arte compositas fabulas secuti, notam vobis fecimus Domini nostri Iesu Christi virtutem & aduentum: sed qui oculis nostris aspeximus illius maiestatē, &c. 2.Pet.1. Prodest hæc diligenter obseruasse, cum omnibus seculis inuenti fuerint, qui Apostolicam doctrinam in dubiū vocare ausi fuerunt. Constat enim ex his, ipsos potuisse vera de Christo prædicare, cum omnium rerum oculati testes, imò etiam pars magna fuerint. De fide verò & integritate eorundem non dubitabit, qui cogitauerit, ipsos quæ ore & scriptis docuerunt, proprio etiam sanguine obsignauisse. Vitam enim potius deponere, quàm fidei veritatem, à se traditam, deserere voluerunt.
units.tr: The second point, which pertains to the truth and certainty of this doctrine, he states thus: "That which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, which our hands have handled, we declare to you." The meaning of all these words is that he speaks only of things known and in every way ascertained, and that this is the certainty of his preaching, so that no one ought to think either that the apostles themselves were deceived by the cunning of others, or that they wished to deceive others by cunning and trickery. But how diligently he does this! He brings forward almost all the senses, so that they may understand that the certainty of the gospel was so firmly established for the apostles that they could investigate it not only by the mind and by speculations of the intellect, but could also perceive it by the outward senses. First, he says, "we have heard." Now they heard these mysteries of salvation and of Christ not from men of doubtful faith, but from Christ himself, the Son of God, with whom they lived most intimately for some years. To this belongs what we have elsewhere: "No one has ever seen God; but the only-begotten Son of God, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him" (John 1). The apostles heard him preaching. He deigned to reveal to the apostles the mysteries of his teaching, which by the just judgment of God were hidden from others (Matt. 13). And John heard not only Christ but also God the Father preaching about Christ, when a voice came down from heaven: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him" (Matt. 17). Who then could doubt the faith of those from whom the apostles drew these things? But he adds the testimony of another sense too: "which we have seen with our eyes." He chose to use a pleonasm, lest he should seem to have affirmed anything less than carefully. And because men see many things in passing and are therefore deceived by sight, he adds: "which we have looked upon," that is, attentively and inwardly, and with a close gaze, so that its truth might be plainly certain to us. Now John says this most truly. For the apostles saw the Son of God made flesh. They saw his miracles, which are sure testimonies of his very divinity. They saw his bonds. John saw him hanging on the Cross. He saw him dying. He saw in his side the opened, most wholesome fountain of our life and redemption. He saw the plain signs of the risen Christ in the tomb. He saw, finally, the one raised from the dead walk, eat, and perform all those things which pertain to proving the truth of his body. He saw the joyful spectacle of Christ's ascension, and that most splendid triumph, than which this whole world has never had anything more excellent. Yet the apostles did not, like many others, merely see these things, but looked upon them not only with their eyes but also with their minds intent, as men who were searching out in these the mysteries of salvation. And lest anyone should think their eyes were bewitched and deluded by the tricks of enchantments, he adds: "which our hands have handled." Men take an infallible argument of truth from the handling of hands, by almost common sense. For who can doubt what he touches with his own hands? And this the apostles did in Christ, to whom he offered for handling not only his mortal body, subject to the miseries of this world, but that very body, now made bright and stripped of all corruptibility. Let the evangelical history which Luke 24 and John 20 narrate be read, and you will have sure testimony of this matter. To this also should be referred what St. Peter writes: "Not following cunningly devised fables, we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty, etc." (2 Pet. 1). It is useful to have observed these things carefully, since in every age there have been those who dared to call the apostolic doctrine into question. For from these things it is established that they were able to preach true things about Christ, since they were eyewitnesses of all the things, and indeed a great part of them. And whoever considers that they sealed with their own blood what they taught by mouth and in writing will not doubt their faith and integrity. For they chose to lay down their life rather than to forsake the truth of the faith handed down by them.

units.la: Præcipuum ergo huius tractationis nostræ Caput esto, vt de euangelij doctrina & eius dignitate recte iudicare discamus. Habet enim hæc omnia, quæ ad alicuius doctrinæ commendationem faciunt. Argumentum eius siue subiectum, circa quod versatur, Iesus Christus est, verbum vitæ, salutis nostræ author & largitor vnicus. Deinde non noua, sed omnium doctrinarum vetustissima est. Concepit enim hanc nostræ salutis rationem ab æterno suprema illa & æterna mens, eandemq; à primo mundi exordio & promissionibus & typis prophetarumq; oraculis reuelauit, & tandem Apostolorum prædicatione illustrauit perfectissime. Adhæc de Apostolorum, qui hac tradiderunt, fide nemini dubium esse potest. Ea enim tradiderunt, quæ ipsis fuerunt compertissima. Accedit omnibus istis, quod Christus Iesus iam mortem aditurus pro illis orat ardentissime: nec pro illis modò, sed & pro omnibus qui in ipsum iuxta illorum doctrinam crediderint, Ioan. 17. Amplectamur ergo æternæ veritatis verbum, vt vera fide Christo Iesu insiti, cum eodem viuamus, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: The chief point of this treatise of ours, then, should be this: that we learn to judge rightly the teaching of the Gospel and its worth. For it contains all the things that commend any doctrine. Its subject, the matter with which it is concerned, is Jesus Christ, the Word of life, the author and sole giver of our salvation. Next, it is not new but the most ancient of all doctrines. That supreme and eternal mind conceived this manner of our salvation from eternity, and from the very beginning of the world revealed it through the promises, the types and the oracles of the prophets, and at last illuminated it most perfectly through the preaching of the Apostles. Moreover, no one can doubt the good faith of the Apostles who handed these things down, for they handed down what was best known to themselves. To all this is added that Jesus Christ, about to go to death, prays most earnestly for them, and not for them only but also for all who, according to their teaching, believe in him (John 17). Let us therefore embrace the word of eternal truth, so that, grafted into Christ Jesus by true faith, we may live with him, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power forever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA II.
units.tr: Homily II.

units.la: ET uita manifestata est: & uidimus & testamur, & annuncia-mus uobis uitam illam, æternam inquam: quæ erat apud patrem, & manifestata est nobis. Quod uidimus & audiuimus, annuncia-mus uobis: ut & uos communionem habeatis nobiscum. Communio autem nostra est cum patre & cum filio eius, Iesu Christo, Et hæc scribimus uobis, ut gaudium uestrum sit plenum.
units.tr: "And the life was manifested, and we have seen and testify, and declare unto you that eternal life, which was with the Father, and was manifested unto us. That which we have seen and heard, declare we unto you, that you also may have fellowship with us. And our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ. And these things we write unto you, that your joy may be full."

units.la: DOminus noster & saluator Iesus Christus, cœlos ascensurus, discipulis suis ait: Vos eritis mihi testes, non solum Hierosolymis, verum etiam in Iudæa vniuersa & Samaria, denique vsque ad extrema terræ, Act. 1. Quibus verbis non illos modò sui officij admonere, verum etiam omnes homines docere voluit, quæ debeat Apostolicæ doctrinæ esse authoritas. Si enim iuratis testibus fides habetur, ijs inquam, quos in iudicijs nostri aduersarij legitimè sistunt, magna vtiq; est eorum temeritas & impietas, qui testibus filij Dei, qui es nostræ salutis ergò producit, contradicere audent. Animauit certe huius rei consyderatio ipsos Apostolos, qui nullis rationibus vnquam adduci potuerunt, quò minus Christo testimonium constanter & fideliter ferrent. Vidimus idem in principio huius epistolæ, quo D. Ioannes fui testimonij & totius Apostolicæ doctrinæ de Christo authoritatem & certitudinem, paucis quidem, sed solidis rationibus asseruit.
units.tr: Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, about to ascend into heaven, said to his disciples: "You shall be my witnesses, not only in Jerusalem, but also in all Judea and Samaria, and even unto the uttermost part of the earth" (Acts 1). By these words he wished not only to remind them of their duty, but also to teach all men what authority the apostolic doctrine ought to have. For if faith is given to sworn witnesses, namely to those whom our adversaries legitimately bring forward in lawsuits, then surely great is the rashness and impiety of those who dare to contradict the witnesses of the Son of God, who are put forward for the sake of our salvation. Certainly the consideration of this matter encouraged the Apostles themselves, who could never be induced by any arguments to bear witness to Christ less steadfastly and faithfully. We saw the same at the beginning of this epistle, where John, with few but solid arguments, asserted both his own testimony and the authority and certainty of the whole apostolic doctrine concerning Christ.

units.la: Cæterum quia de Verbo vitæ, qui Christus est, sermonem se instituisse dixerat, nunc de eodem clarius & copiosius disserit. Et primo quidem suæ doctrinæ rationem denuo reddens, ostendit, unde ipsi & aliis Apostolis huius verbi cognitio innotuerit. Deinde quæ nam & qualis hæc vita sit, explicat. Tertiò finem & scopum Apostolicæ prædicationis proponit. De his, quod Dominus dederit, ordine dicemus.
units.tr: But since he had said that he was treating of the Word of life, which is Christ, he now discourses about the same more clearly and at greater length. First, restating the ground of his doctrine, he shows whence the knowledge of this Word became known to himself and to the other Apostles. Then he explains what this life is, and of what nature. Thirdly, he sets forth the purpose and aim of apostolic preaching. We shall speak of these things in order, as the Lord shall grant.

units.la: Vita (inquit) manifestata est: & vidimus & testamur, & annunciamus vobis vitam illam, &c. Christum, quem antea verbum vitæ dixerat, nunc ipsam vitam nominat. Quia (ut in præcedenti sermone diximus) per ipsum viuimus, & solus ipse fidelium vita est. Christum enim, si auferas, morti & damnationi totus homo subiacet. Hoc rursum præsente, viuit & valet, imò exultat, qui antea desperationis telo quasi confossus iacebat. Rom.7. Idem quoque exemplum vitæ est, & virtus illa, per quam in Dei conspectu viuere & subsistere possumus. Cæterum Ioannes hisce verbis plenorem suæ doctrinæ de Christo & salutis negotio rationem reddit. Perinde enim est, ac si dicat: Iam olim quidem Deus omnem vitæ & salutis viam in filio suo conclusit, & eundem varijs promissionibus & typis, quasi per transsennam, spectandum proposuit. Plena tamen & absoluta cognitio temporis plenitudini & præfinito illi seculo reseruata fuit. Hoc igitur euoluto, vita illa manifestata est, id est, Verbum illud Dei caro factum est (sic enim ipse Apostolus interpretatur. Ioan.1.) & nobis discipulis suis sese manifestauit familiarius quàm reliquis, qui exhibitum minoris quàm decebat, æstimauerunt. Hunc quia nos vidimus operantem salutis mysteria, & sermones vitæ docentem audiuimus, & ab eodem rerum suarum testes sumus constituti, nō possumus non de illo testari, & salutis rationem ab ipso traditam, vobis exponere. Acto. 4. Faciunt verò & hæc ad Apostolicæ doctrinæ authoritatem afferendam, quòd Apostoli diuina & legitima dispensatione vel manuductione in filij Dei notitiam peruenerunt. Porro in hac prima huius loci parte quædam diligentius excutienda veniunt.
units.tr: "Life," he says, "was manifested; and we have seen and testify, and declare to you that life," and so on. Christ, whom he had earlier called the Word of life, he now names life itself. This is because (as we said in the previous sermon) we live through him, and he alone is the life of believers. For if you take Christ away, the whole man lies subject to death and damnation. Again, when he is present, the man who before lay as if pierced through by the dart of despair lives and is strong, indeed exults (Romans 7). He is also the example of life, and that power by which we are able to live and stand in the sight of God. But by these words John gives a fuller account of his doctrine concerning Christ and of the business of salvation. For it is just as if he were saying: Long ago God indeed shut up every way of life and salvation in his Son, and set him forth to be gazed upon through various promises and types, as through a lattice. Yet the full and complete knowledge was reserved for the fullness of time and that age appointed for it. This having unfolded, that life was manifested; that is, that Word of God was made flesh (for the Apostle himself so interprets it, John 1), and showed himself to us, his disciples, more familiarly than to the rest, who esteemed him less than was fitting. Since we have seen him working the mysteries of salvation and have heard him teaching words of life, and have been appointed by him witnesses of his affairs, we cannot but testify concerning him and set out for you the way of salvation delivered by him (Acts 4). Moreover, these things also serve to assert the authority of apostolic doctrine, namely that the Apostles came to the knowledge of the Son of God through a divine and lawful dispensation or guidance. Furthermore, in this first part of the passage certain things need to be examined more carefully.

units.la: Primum inquit: Vita manifestata est, vtique à Deo patre. Nec enim homines hanc proprij in genij viribus inuestigare poterant, cum (vt Paulus inquit) animalis homo non percipiat ea, quæ sunt spiritus Dei. 1.ad Corinthios, secundo capite. Sed & ipse Christus, Nemo (ait) venit ad me, nisi pater meus traxerit eum. Ioannis capite sexto. At quo officio Deum, vt nos trahat & illuminet, demerebimur, qui priusquam illuminemur, vitam non modò non cernimus, sed nec de illa aliquo modo fumus solliciti? Solidum ergo & merum est diuinæ gratiæ beneficium, Christi manifestatio & cognitio eiusdem. Nullam hic laudem vel ingenij nostri acumen, vel humanæ philosophiæ caliginosa lucernula, vel scholarū ambitiosæ disputationes merentur. Diuina luce opus est, & spiritus sancti afflatu, qui vbi vult spirare consueuit. Ioan.3. Patet verò hic paternus in nos Dei amor, qui salutis & vitæ donum non proponit modò, sed idem manifestat, & nos vt illius capaces simus, illuminat. Verè ergo is est, qui homines vult salvos fieri, & in veritatis cognitionem peruenire. 1.Tim.2. Nemo tamen hinc socordiæ & ofcitantiæ occasionem siue patrocinium quæret. Rari vult pro donis suis Dominus, & nostrum est, vt diuinarum rerum studio flagrantes, dato diuinitus talento rectè fœneremur. Clamemus ergo cum Dauide: Vias tuas mihi notas fac Domine & assuefacito me semitis tuis, &c. Psal.25. Et cum Apostolis dicamus: Domine, adauge nobis fidem. Luc.17. Hæc qui dignè expendunt, nec sibi insolenter arrogabunt salutis suæ & redemptionis gloriam, nec in eiusdem studio animos suos torpere patientur.
units.tr: First, he says: "Life was manifested," certainly by God the Father. For men could not search this out by the powers of their own nature, since (as Paul says) "the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God" (1 Corinthians 2). But Christ himself also says: "No one comes to me unless my Father draws him" (John 6). But by what service shall we merit that God should draw and enlighten us, we who, before we are enlightened, not only do not discern life but are not even at all concerned about it? The manifestation and knowledge of Christ is therefore a solid and pure benefit of divine grace. Neither the sharpness of our wit nor the dim little lamp of human philosophy nor the ambitious disputations of the schools deserve any praise here. What is needed is divine light and the breath of the Holy Spirit, who is accustomed to breathe where he wills (John 3). Here the fatherly love of God toward us is plainly seen, which not only offers the gift of salvation and life, but also manifests it, and enlightens us so that we may be capable of it. Truly, then, he is the one who wishes all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2). Yet no one should seek from this an occasion or pretext for sloth and drowsiness. The Lord wills his gifts to be rare, and it is our duty, burning with zeal for divine things, to make a sound return on the talent given us from above. Let us therefore cry out with David: "Make me to know your ways, O Lord, and teach me your paths," and so on (Psalm 25). And with the Apostles let us say: "Lord, increase our faith" (Luke 17). Those who weigh these things rightly will neither insolently claim for themselves the glory of their salvation and redemption, nor allow their minds to grow dull in the pursuit of it.

units.la: Secundò obseruandum, quòd licet Deus Christum communem humani generis saluatorem dederit, eundem tamen Apostolis potius quàm alijs primum manifestare, & illorum opera in eruendis alijs hominibus vti voluit. Quòd si Apostolos carnis & mundi iudicio æstimes, nihil in illis videbis, quod aliqua prærogatiua dignum censeas. Præter quàm enim pauperes fuerunt & contempti, rudes quoque & mysteriorum regni Dei tam ignaros fuisse constat, vt quantumuis assiduæ institutiones carnalem de terreno Christi regno opinionem illis vix excutere potuerint. Sed hoc sapienti Dei patris consilio factum est, qui per tales filij sui regnum propagare voluit, vt omnes hoc non humanum, sed diuinæ potentiæ opus esse intelligerent. Ideo Christus in euangelio ait: Gratias ago tibi pater, Domine cœli & terræ, quòd abscònderis hæc à sapientibus & prudentibus & reuelaris ea paruulis. Certè pater, sic fuit bona voluntas apud te. Matth.11. Et Paulus diuini consilij rationem planius exponens inquit: Videte vocationem vestram fratres, quòd non multi sapientes secundum carnem, non multi potentes, non multi nobiles vel generosi: verum quæ stulta erant secundum mundum, delegit Deus, vt pudefaceret sapientes: & quæ erant imbecilla in mundo, delegit Deus, vt pudefaceret ea quæ sunt robusta: & quæ ignobilia erant in mundo, delegit Deus, & ea quæ non erant, vt ea quæ sunt obliteraret: vt ne gloriaretur vlla caro coram ipso. 1.Corinth.1. Habes ergo quod illis respondeas, quibus hodie nimium insolens & absurdum videtur, si nobis & nostris hominibus, quorum nulla fere est apud mundum authoritas, veritatem in-notuisse dicamus, errantibus interim & in tenebris miserè palpantibus tot scholis, tot episcopis, tot principibus, quos propter insignem sapientiæ, eruditionis & potentiæ existimationem totus mundus admiratur. Nec enim ab hominum dignitate verbi Dei & regni cœlorum authoritas de-pendet. Imò si his rebus illud proveheretur, quis non illud humanum potius, quàm divinum o-pus esse crederet?
units.tr: Secondly, it should be observed that although God has given Christ as the common Saviour of the human race, yet he chose to manifest him first to the Apostles rather than to others, and willed to use their work in drawing other men out. For if you judge the Apostles by the judgment of flesh and the world, you will see nothing in them that you could think worthy of any special prerogative. For apart from being poor and despised, they are also known to have been rude and so ignorant of the mysteries of the kingdom of God that, however constant their instruction, they could scarcely shake off from themselves the carnal opinion of Christ's earthly kingdom. But this was done by the wise counsel of God the Father, who wished through such men to propagate the kingdom of his Son, so that all might understand that this was a work not of man but of divine power. Therefore Christ says in the Gospel: "I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little children. Yes, Father, for so it was well pleasing in your sight" (Matthew 11). And Paul, setting out the reason of the divine counsel more plainly, says: "Consider your calling, brethren, that not many wise according to the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble are called. But God has chosen the foolish things of the world to shame the wise, and God has chosen the weak things of the world to shame the strong, and God has chosen the base things of the world and the things that are despised, and things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are, so that no flesh should glory in his presence" (1 Corinthians 1).
