You have, therefore, an answer for those to whom it seems today too insolent and absurd if we say that the truth has become known to us and to our people, who have almost no authority in the world, while so many schools, so many bishops, so many princes, whom the whole world admires on account of their remarkable reputation for wisdom, learning and power, are meanwhile erring and miserably groping in darkness. For the authority of the Word of God and of the kingdom of heaven does not depend on the dignity of men. Indeed, if these things were put forward on such grounds, who would not believe it to be a human work rather than a divine one?

units.la: Tertio observemus, quod vitam à se & reliquis Apostolis prædicari, subinde repetit & inculcat. At per vitam Christum intelligi, modò diximus. Docet ergo hic locus in quo præcipuè omni-um ministrorum verbi functio versetur. Ut nimirum Christum Jesum, unicum vitæ authorem, adeoque ipsam vitam humani generis prædicent. Hunc ita prædicavit Joannes, ut illi nihil coniun-gat, quod cum Christo nostræ redemptionis gloriam communè habeat. Petr. eundem sic proponit, ut neget aliud nomen sub sole hominibus datum esse, per quod possint salvi fieri. Act. 4. Et Paulus se nihil præter Jesum Christum, & hunc crucifixum, novisse fatetur. 1.Cor.2. Peccant ergo contra Apostolorum exemplum, imò contra Christi præceptum, qui dum vitam in Christo prædicare debebant, ea proferunt, quæ animum hominis horribilibus conscientiæ terroribus occidût: qui ferè proprius omnium humanarum traditionū fructus est. Peccant item, qui vitam quidem pol-licentur, sed eandem alibi, quàm in Christo, monstrant. Sic enim miseros homines à fonte aquæ viventis ad cisternas vacuas abducunt. Jere.2. Imò illi ipsi (ut Apostolus ait) fontes sunt sine aqua, & nubes venti procella agitatæ, quæ salutarem illam doctrinæ & consolationis pluviam minimè afferût. 2.Pet.2. Sed hæc de prima huius loci parte dicta sufficiant. Transeamus ad secundam, qua explicatur qualis nam hæc vita sit, quam Apostoli prædicant. Sic enim ait:
units.tr: Thirdly, let us observe that John repeatedly declares and presses home that life is preached by himself and the other Apostles. We have just said that by "life" Christ is meant. This passage therefore teaches what the chief task of all ministers of the Word should be: namely, to preach Christ Jesus, the sole author of life and therefore life itself for the human race. John preached him in such a way that he joins nothing to him that could share with Christ the glory of our redemption. Peter sets him forth in the same way, when he declares that no other name under heaven has been given to men by which they may be saved (Acts 4). And Paul confesses that he knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Cor. 2). Those, then, sin against the example of the Apostles, and indeed against the command of Christ, who, when they ought to be preaching life in Christ, put forward things that crush the human spirit with the dreadful terrors of conscience, which is almost the chief fruit of all human traditions. Likewise they sin who promise life but show it to be elsewhere than in Christ. For in this way they lead wretched men away from the fountain of living water to empty cisterns (Jer. 2). Indeed, as the Apostle says, they themselves are "fountains without water, and clouds driven by the wind and storm," which bring none of that saving rain of doctrine and consolation (2 Pet. 2). But let these things suffice for the first part of this passage. Let us pass on to the second, in which it is explained what sort of life this is that the Apostles preach. For he says:

units.la: Vita erat apud patrem, & manifestata est nobis. Vult his non locum in quo Christus ante incarnationem fuerit, sed essentiam potius & divinam illius naturam, exprimere. Idem enim dicit, quod alibi: In principio erat verbum, & verbum erat apud Deum, & Deus erat illud verbum. Joan. 1. Illic enim principij vox, quia Deo tribuitur (qui nec principium nec finem habet) æternitatis, non ordinis, nota est: & in hunc modum Joannes argumentatur: Quicquid ab æterno est, Deus est. Christus est ab æterno. Ergo Christus Deus est. At Christum ab æterno fuisse, probatur per adiectam sententiam: Et verbum, id est Christus ille, erat apud Deum. Apud Deum enim esse dicitur, non ut angeli & sancti, qui in eius conspectu satietate gaudiorum fruuntur: sed quia cum Deo eiusmodi unione coniungitur, ut alter sine altero esse non possit. Relativa quippe sunt, pater & filius. Si enim pater ab æterno est Deus, ab æterno quoq; filium habeat, oportet. Huc illud Christi dictum pertinet: Credite mihi, quod ego in patre sum, & pater in me. Joan. 14. Et alibi: Ego & pater unum sumus. Joannis 10. Non temere autem Joannes tam in evangelica historia, quàm in hoc scripto Christi divinitatem asserit, id quod omnes & Apostoli & prophetæ magno studio faci-unt. Facit enim hæc ad demonstrandum fidei nostræ dignitatem. Contemnitur hæc à Judæis & Turcis hoc nomine, quòd nos Christo, quem illi nihil nisi hominem fuisse putant, fidamus: & ideo illud propheticum nobis obijciunt: Maledictus, qui confidit in homine. Jeremiæ 17. Sed si iidem agnoscerent, eum qui præfinito tempore in carne manifestatus est, ab æterno apud patrem esse, & proinde verum esse Deum, patri coæternum & consubstantialem, viderent maledictionem hanc nullo modo in nos competere. Quòd si vero Deus est, Jesus Christus, num de illius potestate quicquâ dubitabimus? Deo certè nihil impossibile esse Gabriel angelus fatetur. Luc. 1. At de eiusdem voluntate minus dubitare licebit, si eundem nullo nostro merito provocatum, nostræ salutis causa in carnem venisse, & in hac omnes huius mundi molestias, unà cum dira & infami Cru-cis morte subijsse, cogitemus. Est ergo unicum & invictum fidei nostræ fundamentum, hæc Chri-sti cognitio, qua illum & Deum & hominem esse certò credimus. De hac cognitione ipse loquitur: Hæc est vita æterna, o pater, ut cognoscant te solum Deum verum, & quem tu misisti, Jesum Chri-stum. Joan. 17. Porrò his expositis, Joannes prædicationis suæ & totius apostolicæ doctrinæ finem vel scopum subiungit, qui tertius huius tractationis locus est.
units.tr: "The life was with the Father, and was made manifest to us." By this he means not the place where Christ was before the incarnation, but rather his essence and divine nature. For he says the same thing as elsewhere: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1). There the word "beginning," since it is ascribed to God (who has neither beginning nor end), denotes eternity, not order. And in this way John argues: whatever is from eternity is God; Christ is from eternity; therefore Christ is God. That Christ was from eternity is proved by the added statement: "and the Word, that is, that Christ, was with God." To be "with God" is said not in the way that angels and saints are in his presence, enjoying the fullness of joys, but because he is joined to God by such a union that the one cannot exist without the other. For Father and Son are correlative terms. If the Father is God from eternity, he must also have the Son from eternity. To this belongs the saying of Christ: "Believe me, that I am in the Father, and the Father in me" (John 14). And elsewhere: "I and the Father are one" (John 10). Nor does John assert the divinity of Christ rashly, either in the gospel history or in this writing; all the Apostles and prophets do this with great zeal. For it serves to demonstrate the dignity of our faith. The Jews and the Turks scorn this on the ground that we trust in Christ, whom they think was nothing but a man; and therefore they throw in our faces that prophetic word: "Cursed is he who trusts in man" (Jer. 17). But if they acknowledged that he who was manifested in the flesh at the appointed time was from eternity with the Father, and therefore is the true God, co-eternal and consubstantial with the Father, they would see that this curse in no way applies to us. Yet if Jesus Christ is God, shall we doubt anything about his power? The angel Gabriel certainly affirms that nothing is impossible with God (Luke 1). And we may have even less doubt about his will, if we consider that he, provoked by none of our merits, came into the flesh for the cause of our salvation, and underwent in it all the troubles of this world, together with the dreadful and infamous death of the Cross. The only and unconquered foundation of our faith, therefore, is this knowledge of Christ, by which we firmly believe that he is both God and man. Of this knowledge he himself speaks: "This is eternal life, O Father, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent" (John 17). Having set these things out, John then adds the end or aim of his preaching and of the whole apostolic doctrine, which is the third point of this discussion.

units.la: Quod vidimus & audivimus, annunciamus vobis: ut & vos communionem habeatis nobiscum. Communio autem nostra est cum patre & cum filio eius, Jesu Christo. Et hæc scribimus vobis, ut gaudium vestrum sit plenum. Docet his Joannes, quid in doctrina Apostolorum maximè spectari & quæri debeat, simulque suæ prædicationi fidem conciliare studet. Quotquot enim unquam inter homines novarum religionum authores fuerunt, eas proprij emolumenti causa commenti sunt, ut vel ipsi maioris fierent apud posteros, vel in officio facilius retinerent, quos sibi subiectos esse volebant. Sic apud Romanos Numa Pompilius sibi cum Aegeria Nympha arcanos congressus esse dicebat, ut rudes & feroces animos, qui sub Romulo armis & sanguini assueuerant, sibi obsequentiores redderet. Et inter papisticarum superstitionum patronos multi sunt, qui persuasionibus variis opus esse aiunt, ad eos retinendos, qui alioqui nimium ferocirent. At quia fraudes eiusmodi diu latere non possunt, fit vt quicunque antehac inaudita & incognita docent, hoc nomine cuiuis cordato & prudenti suspecti sint. Hanc ergo suspicionem ab apostolica doctrina & Christiana religione longe remouet, quasi dicat: Si docendo vel vestras opes venarer, vel mundanæ gloriæ auram captarem, vel vllo alio modo priuati commodi studium præ me ferrem, merito quidem doctrina hæc mea vobis suspecta esse poterat. Sed longè alia mihi mens est, ô fratres. Tam enim abest, vt vestra quæram, vt potius vos eorum consortes esse cupiam, quæ nos possidemus. Non vestras opes nobis vendicare, sed cœlestes opes, quæ in nos collatæ sunt, vobis communicare studemus. Habemus nos cum Deo patre & eius filio communionem arctissimam. Nos enim pro filijs & hæredibus agnoscit. Nobis præparauit regnum in cœlis ab exordio mundi. Huius hæredes, vt & vos no biscum esse possitis, quærimus, & sic vestrum gaudium, vt & nostrum, plenum, fyncerum & perfectum sit. Sunt hæc Apostoli verba fideli meditatione dignissima, vt quæ multa continent ad no-stram institutionem & consolationem cumprimis necessaria.
units.tr: "What we have seen and heard, we declare to you, that you also may have fellowship with us. Our fellowship, moreover, is with the Father and with his Son, Jesus Christ. And we write these things to you, that your joy may be full." Here John teaches what ought chiefly to be looked for and sought in the doctrine of the Apostles, and at the same time he seeks to win credit for his preaching. For whoever among men has ever been the author of new religions has devised them for his own advantage: either that he himself might become greater among posterity, or that he might more easily keep in obedience those whom he wished to be subject to him. So among the Romans, Numa Pompilius used to say that he had secret meetings with the nymph Egeria, so that he might make more compliant those rude and fierce minds which under Romulus had grown accustomed to arms and bloodshed. And among the patrons of Papist superstitions there are many who say that various persuasions are needed to keep those who would otherwise be too unruly. But since frauds of this kind cannot remain hidden for long, it comes about that whoever teaches things previously unheard of and unknown is on this account suspected by every sensible and prudent person. John therefore removes this suspicion far from the apostolic doctrine and the Christian religion, as if to say: "If by teaching I were hunting after your wealth, or catching at the breath of worldly glory, or displaying in any way a concern for private gain, then indeed this my teaching could rightly be suspect to you. But my mind is far otherwise, brothers. For so far am I from seeking yours, that I would rather that you were partakers of those things which we possess. We are eager not to claim your riches for ourselves, but to share with you the heavenly riches which have been bestowed upon us. We have the most intimate fellowship with God the Father and his Son. For he acknowledges us as sons and heirs. He has prepared for us a kingdom in heaven from the beginning of the world. We seek to make you heirs of this, so that you may be with us, and thus your joy may be full, sincere and perfect, as ours is." These words of the Apostles are most worthy of faithful meditation, since they contain many things especially necessary for our instruction and consolation.

units.la: Primùm, in hoc est Ioannes, vt nos tam cum ipso, quàm cum omnibus alijs Apostolis, communionem habeamus. Est hoc argumentum synceræ charitatis, quà sancti Dei cultores erga omnes homines flagrant. Quia enim fide vera præditi sunt, quæ Dei gloriam omnium suarum actionum scopum sibi præfixum habet, non possunt non in hoc incumbere, vt in eius fidei consortium alios quoq; pertrahant, vt per ipsos etiam Dei gloria propagetur. Simul quoq; docemur, v-nam & eandem esse salutis rationem, tam Apostolis quàm nobis omnibus propositam. Vt enim salus in vno Christo comprehensa est: ita per Christum saluentur oportet, quotquot hanc asse-qui cupiunt. Ideo Christus omnes laborantes & oneratos, omnes esurientes, omnes sitientes ad se vocat. Matthæi vndecimo, Ioannis sexto & septimo capite. Et infra audiemus, Christum non modò pro Apostolorum, sed totius mundi peccatis mortuum esse. 1. Ioannis 2. Et Paulus apostolus, Deum sibi propitium & clementem ideo fuisse testatur, vt ijs exemplar proponeret, qui simili modo in ipsum credunt. 1. Timoth. 1. Non est ergo, quòd Apostolos quidem per Iesu Christi meritum saluatos esse, nos verò ipsorum meritis saluari oportere putemus. Nam & ipse Christus nos in salutis ratione cum Apostolis coniungit, quando pro illis orans, addit: Non pro eis tantum rogo, sed & pro ijs, qui crediturisunt per sermonem eorum in me. Ioannis capite decimoseptimo. Vt ergo Petrus, Ioannes, Paulus, Iacobus & omnes alij apostoli, per solius Christi meritum saluati sunt: ita nos in solo hoc salutem nobis repositam esse intelligamus. Vt Paulus & Ioannes vnum mediatorem inter se & Deum patrem agnouerunt. 1. Timoth 2. 1. Ioannis 2 ita nobis quoque nullum alium datum esse credamus. Vt Paulus in sola Christi cruce gloriatur, Galat. sexto capite: Ita nos in vna hac nostræ fidei gloriam & redemptionis spem sitam putemus. Vt vnicam corporis & sanguinis Christi hostiam, in ara Crucis pro peccatis mundi immolatam, agnouerunt Apostoli: Ita nos eadem contenti, nouas pro peccatis nostris satisfactiones minimè quæramus. Nec enim euacuari potest Christi meritum, nec ipse mutatur in horas, vt de suo Vertumno vel Proteo poetæ fabulantur. Sed idem est Christus heri, & hodie, & etiam in secula. Heb.13.
units.tr: First, John's aim is that we should have fellowship both with him and with all the other Apostles. This is a mark of the sincere love with which the worshippers of God burn toward all men. For since they are endowed with true faith, which has the glory of God set before it as the goal of all its actions, they cannot but labour to draw others also into the fellowship of this faith, so that the glory of God may be spread abroad through them as well. At the same time we are taught that there is one and the same way of salvation set before the Apostles and before all of us. For just as salvation is comprehended in Christ alone, so all who desire to attain it must be saved through Christ. Therefore Christ calls to himself all who labour and are burdened, all who hunger, all who thirst (Matthew 11; John 6 and 7). And below we shall hear that Christ died not only for the sins of the Apostles but for the sins of the whole world (1 John 2). And the Apostle Paul testifies that God was propitious and merciful to him for this reason, that he might set himself forth as a pattern to those who believe in him in the same way (1 Tim. 1). It is not, therefore, that we should think the Apostles were saved through the merit of Jesus Christ, but that we ourselves must be saved by their merits. For Christ himself joins us with the Apostles in the reckoning of salvation, when, praying for them, he adds: "I pray not for them only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word" (John 17). So just as Peter, John, Paul, James and all the other apostles were saved through the merit of Christ alone, so let us understand that salvation is laid up for us in this alone. As Paul and John acknowledged one mediator between themselves and God the Father (1 Tim. 2; 1 John 2), so let us believe that no other has been given to us as well. As Paul glories in the Cross of Christ alone (Gal. 6), so let us hold that the glory of our faith and the hope of redemption rest in this one thing. As the Apostles acknowledged the one and only sacrifice of the body and blood of Christ, offered on the altar of the Cross for the sins of the world, so let us, content with the same, by no means seek new satisfactions for our sins. For the merit of Christ cannot be emptied, nor is he changed from hour to hour, as the poets fable of their Vertumnus or Proteus. But Christ is the same yesterday, and today, and for ever (Heb. 13).

units.la: Secundò, quæ & qualis hæc sit communio, explicat. Merito enim de hac quærat aliquis, quando Apostolos Christi in hoc mundo miserrimos & calamitosissimos mortalium, & tanquam oues mactationi destinatas fuisse audit. Et ea est carnis nostræ natura, vt cum talibus communionem habere nequaquam cupiat, quos toti mundo exosos, & quorum amicitiam periculosam esse videt. Ostendit ergo quousq; extendatur ista communio siue societas. Ea (inquit) est cum Deo patre, & cum filio eius, Iesu Christo. Non ergo in ijs hærendum, quæ oculis nostris & reliquis corporeis sensibus offeruntur. Quia enim nos è mundo selectos sibi & patri suo consecrauit Christus, quicunq; in hunc credunt, non inter seipsos modò per fidei communionem vniuntur, sed in ferùtur Christo, vt eius corporis membra sint, cuius ipse caput est. In Christo manet, et Christus in ipsis. Ioan. 6. At quia Christus in patre manet, & pater in ipso, fieri nequit, quin Deo patri vniti & eius consortes sint, quicunq; per fidē Christo inserti sunt. Comprehendit hoc omniū bonorum, quæ in Christo sunt, promissione, adeoq; omnis boni, quod in Deo continetur, consortiū. Nobis enim omnipotens est Deus, vt nimirū nos sua illa omnipotentia tueatur & conseruet. Nobis bonus & misericors est, vt suæ gratiæ thesauros in nos conferat. Nobis verax est, vt promissiones sa-lutis impleat. Nobis iustus est, vt contra calumniatorem satanam protegat, & ex illius potestate liberet. Nobis sapiēs est, vt suo spiritu nos dirigat, & vias nostras in mūdi huius tenebris moderetur. Nobis diues & inexhaustus est, vt omniū nostrū votis possit sufficere. Similiter nobis iustitia à Deo patre factus est Christus, nobis factus est sapientia, satisfactio, sanctificatio & redemptio. 1. Corinth.1.Et hæc quidem non ad vnum modo & alterum,sed ad omnes ex æquo spectant. Omni bus fidelibus communia sunt. Non obest nobis eorum,qui ante nos huius communionis consor tes facti sunt,multitudo. Nam in domo patris mei (inquit Christus) mansiones multæ sunt.Ioan.14. Quis ergo non exclamet: O profunditatem diuitiarum Dei. O fontem perennem gratiæ & bonitatis. Debent vero hæc nostræ & consolationi & institutioni seruire. Docent enim,quid in apostolorum doctrina & fide Christiana quæri debeat:nimirum,non opes mundi huius,nō gloria huius seculi,non voluptatis carnalis illecebræ,non malesuadum otium,non infelix carnis secu ritas,sed communio hæc Christi,Dei patris & bonorum ipsius. Hanc qui vnicè quærunt,ijs quæ præsenti vitæ seruiunt,non deerunt vnquam.Matth.6. Habebunt ijdem consolationem in aduer sis omnibus.Quomodo enim paupertatis metu deijcientur,qui cum Deo opulentissimo se com munionem habere norunt,qui cum aperit manum suam,omnia implet benedictione, qui dat pe cori suapascua,& pullis coruorum inuocantibus se escam suam? Psal.145.&147.Quomodo mun di infamia terrebitur,qui in cœlis gloriæ Christi se confortem fore nouit? Luc.22.Cur exilium ti mebit,qui patriam in cœlis repositam habet,à qua nulla mundi tyrannis arcere poterit? Vel num mortis horrore se superari patietur,qui vitam suam in Christo abscònditam esse, & illius merito mortis vim omnem deuictam esse intelligit?2.Corinth.15.Harum rerum consideratione abreptus Paulus exclamat: Quis nos separabit à dilectione Dei? num afflictio? num angustia? num perse cutio? num fames? num nuditas? num periculum? num gladius? Imò in his omnibus superamus per eum,qui dilexit nos,&c.Rom.8.
units.tr: Secondly, he explains what this fellowship is and of what kind it is. Someone may well ask about it when he hears that the apostles of Christ were the most wretched and calamitous of mortals in this world, and were destined for slaughter like sheep. Such is the nature of our flesh that it does not at all desire to have fellowship with those whom it sees hated by the whole world and whose friendship it sees to be dangerous. He therefore shows how far this fellowship or society extends. "It is," he says, "with God the Father and with his Son, Jesus Christ." We must not, then, linger on those things which are offered to our eyes and to the other bodily senses. For Christ, having chosen us out of the world and consecrated us to himself and to his Father, not only unites those who believe in him among themselves through the fellowship of faith, but they are also joined to Christ, so that they are members of that body of which he himself is the head. "He abides in Christ, and Christ in them" (John 6). And because Christ abides in the Father, and the Father in him, it cannot but be that all who are grafted into Christ through faith are united to God the Father and are his partners. This embraces the promise of all the good things that are in Christ, and therefore the fellowship of every good that is contained in God. For God is almighty to us, so that he may indeed protect and preserve us by that his omnipotence. He is good and merciful to us, so that he may bestow on us the treasures of his grace. He is true to us, so that he may fulfil the promises of salvation. He is just to us, so that he may protect us against the calumniator Satan and free us from his power. He is wise to us, so that he may direct us by his Spirit and guide our ways amid the darkness of this world. He is rich and inexhaustible to us, so that he may be able to supply the wishes of all of us. Likewise, Christ has been made by God the Father our righteousness; he has been made our wisdom, satisfaction, sanctification and redemption (1 Cor. 1). And these things pertain not to one or another alone, but equally to all. They are common to all the faithful. The multitude of those who became partners of this fellowship before us does not stand in our way. For, as Christ says, "In my Father's house there are many mansions" (John 14). Who, then, would not cry out: "O the depth of the riches of God! O the perennial fountain of grace and goodness!" These things ought indeed to serve both our comfort and our instruction. For they teach what ought to be sought in the teaching and Christian faith of the apostles: namely, not the riches of this world, not the glory of this age, not the allurements of carnal pleasure, not idleness that corrupts, not the unhappy security of the flesh, but this fellowship with Christ, with God the Father, and with his good things. Those who seek this alone will never lack the things that serve the present life (Matt. 6). They will have consolation in all adversities. For how will those be cast down by fear of poverty who know that they have fellowship with the most wealthy God, who, when he opens his hand, fills all things with blessing, who gives their food to the beasts and to the young ravens that call upon him (Ps. 145 and 147)? How will the infamy of the world terrify those who know that they will be partners of Christ's glory in heaven (Luke 22)? Why will he fear exile who has a fatherland laid up in heaven, to which no tyranny of the world can bar the way? Or will he suffer himself to be overcome by the horror of death who understands that his life is hidden in Christ, and that through his death all the power of death has been overcome (2 Cor. 15)? Paul, carried away by the contemplation of these things, cries out: "Who shall separate us from the love of God? Shall affliction? Or distress? Or persecution? Or famine? Or nakedness? Or peril? Or the sword? No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us," etc. (Rom. 8).

units.la: Huc referri debet,quod de fine huius communionis Ioannes addit. Et hæc scribimus vobis, vt gaudium vestrum plenum sit.Varia sunt hominum in hoc seculo gaudia, & trahit sua quemq; voluptas.Sunt qui auaritia excæcati in pecuniarum aceruis gaudent, dum nummos contemplan tur in arca.Alij commessationibus gaudent & gulæ studio. Quosdam Veneris insana voluptas ex hilarat.Inueniuntur etiam belluini quidam,non hominum nomine digni,qui armis gaudét & san guine.Accedunt & alij, quos gloria & adulatorum ambitiosi applausus stulto gaudio quasi inebri ant.Sed nullum ex his gaudijs plenum,perfectum & syncerum dici potest.Quia enim illorū cau sæ instabiles & incertis fortunæ vicibus obnoxiæ sunt, certum & stabile gaudium esse nequit, quod illis nititur. Præterea, infiniti sunt casus, qui gaudia hæc doloribus acerbissimis inficiunt, quod experientia satis docet.At Christianis gaudium plenum,syncerum & omnibus numeris ab solutum Apostolus pollicetur. Huius fundamentum Christus est, qui cum peccatis nos liberet, cósscientiarum stimulos sedat,qui quoad nos pungunt,gaudij omnis causam plane auferunt.De hoc gaudio Christus loquitur:Iterum videbo vos,& gaudebit cor vestrum,& gaudium vestrum nemo tollit à vobis.Ioan.16.Et Paulus apostolus fideles semper gaudere iubet.Phil.4.Ea enim est fidei conditio, vt in afflictionibus quoque gaudeat, dum has gloriæ Dei seruire,& patienter eas dem ferentibus amplissimam in cœlis mercedem propositam esse nouit.Matth.5. Rom.5. Accedit his perpetua & æterna huius gaudij continuatio , quam nullus casus interrumpet. Isa. 64. & 66. Matth.25.&c.Felices certe sunt,qui pro hoc potius,quàm incerto mundi gaudio, laborare solent.
units.tr: To this belongs what John adds about the purpose of this fellowship: "And we write these things to you, that your joy may be full" (1 John 1). The joys of men in this age are various, and each person is drawn by his own pleasure. Some, blinded by avarice, rejoice in heaps of money while they gaze at the coins in their chest. Others rejoice in drinking parties and in the pursuit of gluttony. Some are cheered by the mad pleasure of lust. There are also certain brutal men, unworthy of the name of human beings, who rejoice in arms and in blood. Others too, whom glory and the ambitious applause of flatterers intoxicate, as if with a foolish joy. But none of these joys can be called full, perfect and pure. For since their causes are unstable and subject to the changing vicissitudes of fortune, that joy cannot be certain and stable which rests upon them. Moreover, there are countless accidents which stain these joys with the most bitter sorrows, as experience sufficiently teaches. But to Christians the apostle promises a joy that is full, pure, and in every respect complete. Its foundation is Christ, who, by freeing us from sins, calms the stings of conscience, which, so long as they prick us, altogether take away every cause of joy. Of this joy Christ speaks: "I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you" (John 16). And the apostle Paul bids the faithful always to rejoice (Phil. 4). For it is the condition of faith that it rejoices even in afflictions, since it knows that these serve the glory of God and that a very great reward in heaven is set before those who patiently endure them (Matt. 5; Rom. 5). To these is added the perpetual and eternal continuation of this joy, which no accident will interrupt (Isa. 64 and 66; Matt. 25, etc.). Certainly they are happy who are accustomed to labour for this joy rather than for the uncertain joy of the world.

units.la: Didicimus hucusq;,quid de filio suo Iesu Christo apostolis suis Deus pater manifestare digna tus fit.Audiuimus hunc esse vitam & salutem eorum,qui in ipsum credunt. Vidimus denique sa lutarem euangelicæ prædicationis scopum,communionem scilicet cum Deo patre & filio eius le su Christo.Comprehendit hæc in se omnes gratiæ & salutis nostræ thesauros.Leues facit omnes huius vitæ molestias.Et contra aduersariam potestatem armis insuperabilibus instruit. Hæc er go vera fide amplectamur,vt tam sanctæ & salutaris communionis membra facti, solido & æter no gaudio fruamur in eo,cui debetur benedictio,honor,gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: We have learned thus far what God the Father has deigned to make known to his apostles concerning his Son Jesus Christ. We have heard that he is the life and salvation of those who believe in him. Finally, we have seen the saving aim of the evangelical preaching, namely fellowship with God the Father and his Son Jesus Christ. This comprehends in itself all the treasures of our grace and salvation. It lightens all the troubles of this life, and it arms us with invincible weapons against the adverse power. Let us therefore embrace these things with true faith, so that, having become members of so holy and saving a fellowship, we may enjoy in him to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power forever, a solid and eternal joy. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA III,
units.tr: HOMILY III

units.la: E T hæc est promissio, quam audiuimus ex ipso, & annuncia mus uobis:quod Deus lux est,& tenebræ in eo non sunt ullæ. Si dicamus,quod communionem habemus cū eo, & in tenebris am bulamus,mentimur,& veritatem non facimus. Quòd si in luce am bulamus , sicut ipse est in luce,communionem habemus inter nos, & sanguis Iesu Christi,filij eius emundat nos ab omni peccato.
units.tr: And this is the promise which we have heard from him and announce to you: that God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all. If we say that we have fellowship with him and walk in darkness, we lie and do not practise the truth. But if we walk in the light, as he himself is in the light, we have fellowship among ourselves, and the blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, cleanses us from every sin.

units.la: EXposuit hucusque D. Ioannes ea, quæ ad Euangelicæ & Apostolicæ doctrinæ commendationem faciunt. Ostendit enim eius subiectum fiue argumentum esse Dei filium, Iesum Christum, quem verbum vitæ, imò ipsam vitam vocat, quia in ipso omnis nostræ salutis ratio cōfistit. Deinde eius veritatem & certitudinem multis argumentis, adductis etiam in eius testimonium externis sensibus, demonstrauit. Tandem lętissimum & salutarem eius finem siue scopum proposuit, communionem cum Deo patre & filio ipsius Iesu Christo, quę sola tā præsentis quàm futuræ vitæ bona vniuersa complectitur. Cæterum, licet hæc mera sint diuinæ gratiæ dona, & nullis nostrorum operum meritis acquiri possint (quid enim Deo, qui nostri minime indiget, exhibebimus, quod tantis ipsius beneficijs respondeat?) eam tamen à nobis gratiâ requirit, vt quoad fieri potest, voluntati diuinæ nos accommodemus, ne sua munera in indignos contulisse, vel facilitate sua & beneficentia impuram carnis licentiam & peccandi impunitatem plantauisse videri possit. De hoc igitur in præsenti loco diligenter Ioannes disserit. Primo enim argumento à Dei natura ducto docet, quam viuendi rationem hic ab illis requirat, quos per filium suos consortes fecit. Deinde falsos Christiani nominis professores arguit, qui vita Christum, quem ore profiten-tur, abnegant. Tertió vberrimos fructus & amplissima præmia eorum recenset, qui diuinæ naturæ & voluntati sese conformes reddere studet. Faxit Deus, vt in tanta nostri seculi licentia, de his cognitu perquàm necessarijs, vtiliter & multorum cum fructu disseramus.
units.tr: Up to this point John has set out those things which serve to commend the Gospel and apostolic teaching. For he shows that its subject or theme is the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom he calls the Word of life, indeed life itself, because in him lies the whole basis of our salvation. Then he demonstrated its truth and certainty by many arguments, also adducing in its witness the external senses. Finally he set forth its most joyful and salutary end or aim: fellowship with God the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ, which alone embraces all the good things of both present and future life. Moreover, although these are pure gifts of divine grace and cannot be acquired by any merit of our works (for what shall we offer to God, who has no need of us, that could match such great benefits of his?), nevertheless he requires of us that, as far as it can be done, we accommodate ourselves to the divine will, lest it seem that he has bestowed his gifts upon the unworthy, or by his readiness and bounty has planted an impure license of the flesh and impunity for sinning. Therefore John discusses this carefully in the present place. For first, by an argument drawn from the nature of God, he teaches what manner of life he requires here of those whom he has made his partners through the Son. Then he rebukes the false professors of the Christian name, who by their life deny Christ whom they profess with their mouth. Thirdly, he recounts the most abundant fruits and the greatest rewards of those who strive to render themselves conformed to the divine nature and will. May God grant that, in this great licence of our age, we may discourse usefully and with much profit about these things, which are most necessary to know.

units.la: I. Hæc est promissio, quam audiuimus ex ipso, & annunciamus uobis. Priusquam rem ipsam aggrediatur, hæc præfationis loco præmittit, quibus doctrinæ suæ certitudinem magis commendet. Quia enim fidei nostrę mille armis & artibus insidiatur Satan nullum studium nimium videri debet, quod huic confirmandæ & stabiliendæ tribuitur. Cæterum non ofcitanter prætereundum est, quòd doctrinam suam modò promissionem nominat. Euangelium ergo nō nuda rerum à Christo gestarum prædicatio est, sed quæcunq; in illo prædicat, nobis, propter quos ille missus est, pollicetur, vt ea nō à nobis aliena esse, sed cū primis ad nos pertinere intelligamus. Potest hoc facilè totius scripturæ testimonijs comprobari. Isa.53. Cognitione sui multos iustificabit seruus meus, &c. Isa.53. Quę verba manifestam promissionem habet. Taceo nunc quod promissiones patriarchis datæ, nihil aliud quàm Christi & mysteriorum ipsius descriptionem, adeoq; ipsissimum euangelium continent. Quòd si Christum concionantem audias, quid aliud quàm promissiones sonat? Venite (inquit) ad me qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego requiem vobis præstabo. Matth.11. Qui credit in me, habet vitam æternam. Ioannis 5. & 6. Si quis sitit, veniat ad me & bibat. Et quisquis biberit ex aqua, quam ego dabo ei, non sitiet in æternum, &c. Ioannis 7. & 4. Nec verò olim duntaxat, euangelicas promissiones, cum ipsius Christi ore proferrentur, ratas fuisse putabimus. Manent enim firmæ & solidæ in æternum ergà omnes, qui ipsas vera fide susceperint. Docent hoc Christi verba, qui docendi munus Apostolis commit-tens inquit: Ite in mundum vniuersum, & prædicate Euangelium omni creaturæ. Qui crediderit, & baptizatus fuerit, saluus erit. Mar.16. Et Baptista eandem promissionem vniuersalem facit, dicens: Pater diligit filium, & omnia dedit illi in manum. Qui credit filio, habet vitam æternam, &c. Ioannis 3. Similiter Petrus apud Cornelium Centurionem de Christo differens, ait: Huic omnes prophetæ testimonium ferunt, quod remissionem peccatorum accepturus sit, per nomen eius, quisquis crediderit in eum. Act.10. Sed quid testimoniorum multitudine opus est in re clarissima? Vsum potius huius nominis probè expendamus. Euangelium promissio vitæ & salutis est, ab ipso Christo per Apostolos tradita. Credamus ergo promissioni huic, ne in Christum iniurij & ingrati deprehendamur. Illam enim spreuisse & in dubium vocare, quid obsecro aliud est, quàm Dei filium mendacij insimulare?
units.tr: I. This is the promise which we have heard from him and announce to you. Before he approaches the matter itself, he premises these things by way of a preface, by which he may further commend the certainty of his teaching. For since Satan lays snares for our faith with a thousand weapons and devices, no zeal can seem excessive that is devoted to confirming and establishing it. Yet it must not be passed over carelessly that he now calls his teaching a promise. The Gospel, therefore, is not a bare proclamation of things done by Christ, but whatever it preaches about him, it promises to us, for whose sake he was sent, so that we may understand these things are not foreign to us but pertain to us above all. This can easily be proved by the testimonies of all Scripture. Isa. 53: "By his knowledge my servant shall justify many," etc. Isa. 53. These words hold a clear promise. I say nothing now of the fact that the promises given to the patriarchs contain nothing other than the description of Christ and his mysteries, and so the very Gospel itself. And if you hear Christ preaching, what else does he sound but promises? "Come to me," he says, "you who labour and are burdened, and I will give you rest." Matt. 11. "He who believes in me has eternal life." John 5 and 6. "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. And whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst again," etc. John 7 and 4. Nor indeed should we think that the evangelical promises were valid only at the time when they were uttered from the mouth of Christ himself. For they remain firm and solid for ever toward all who have received them with true faith. Christ's words teach this, who, committing the office of teaching to the Apostles, says: "Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature. He who believes and is baptized shall be saved." Mark 16. And the Baptist makes the same universal promise, saying: "The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand. He who believes in the Son has eternal life," etc. John 3. Likewise Peter, speaking about Christ to the centurion Cornelius, says: "To him all the prophets bear witness, that through his name whoever believes in him shall receive remission of sins." Acts 10. But why need there be a multitude of testimonies in a matter so clear? Let us rather weigh well the use of this word. The Gospel is a promise of life and salvation, delivered by Christ himself through the Apostles. Let us therefore believe this promise, lest we be found injurious and ungrateful toward Christ. For to despise it and call it into doubt, what, I beg you, is that other than to charge the Son of God with lying?

units.la: Videamus nunc quam viuendi rationem à nobis Deus exigat. Paucis hanc innuit Ioannes, & (vt diximus) argumento à Dei natura desumpto eandem nobis commendat. Deus (inquit) lux est, & tenebræ in eo non sunt ullæ. Quid verò hinc aliud sequetur, quàm in luce ambulandum, & opera lucis facienda esse ijs, qui cum Deo communionem habere volunt? Sic enim argumentum integrum constitues: Quicunque cum Deo communionem & consortium expetit, illius ingenio & naturæ sese accommodare & conformem reddere debet. At Deus lux est. Lucis ergo o-pera faciant, qui Dei consortes esse cupiunt. Lux verò dicitur Deus per comparationem. Vt enim luce nihil purius est: ita Deus ipsa est puritas & integritas in attributis suis omnib. Siue enim eius iustitiâ, siue bonitatem, siue sapientiâ, siue veritatem, aut alias virtutes inspicias, omnes illæ sine omni imperfectionis & pollutionis macula cōparebunt. Deinde, vt lux & ipsa videtur, & reliqua vt videri possint illustrat (est enim medium visus, sine quo is vim suam exercere non potest:) ita Deus solus est, qui vbi animis nostris innotuit, nos illuminat, vt quę salutis nostræ sunt, cernere possimus. Vnde apud Prophetam dicitur: In luce tua videbimus lucem. Psal.36. Rursum, vt lux animos serenat, & tristitiam propter tenebrarum caliginem obortam pellit: ita Deus, vbi nobis propitius affulget, ita animos recreat & exhilarat, vt nullis aduersis amplius concuti possint. Rectè igitur Dauid exclamat: Dominus lux mea & salus mea, à quo nam timerem? Psal.27. Præterea, vt lux gressus nostros dirigit & tutò nos facit incedere: ita Deus suo verbo & spiritu illuminatos ducit & regit, ne in densissimis mundi huius tenebris impingamus. Quare verbum eius lucernam pedum nostrorum Dauid appellare voluit. Psal.119. Talis ergo lux cum fit Deus, necessario vtique lucis opera ab ijs exiguntur, qui cum illo communionem habere desyderant. Quę vrò illa sint, collatione & aliquot scripturæ locis discemus.
units.tr: Let us now see what manner of life God requires of us. John hints at this in few words, and (as we have said) commends the same to us by an argument taken from the nature of God. God, he says, is light, and in him there is no darkness at all. What, then, will follow from this other than that those who wish to have fellowship with God must walk in the light and do the works of light? For you will set up the whole argument thus: whoever seeks fellowship and partnership with God must accommodate himself to God's disposition and nature and render himself conformed to it. But God is light. Therefore let those who desire to be partners of God do the works of light. Now God is called light by way of comparison. For just as nothing is purer than light, so God is purity and integrity itself in all his attributes. For whether you look at his justice, his goodness, his wisdom, his truth, or his other virtues, all of them will appear without any stain of imperfection or pollution. Then, just as light both is itself seen and illumines the rest so that they may be seen (for it is the medium of sight, without which sight cannot exercise its power), so God alone is he who, once he has become known to our minds, enlightens us so that we may discern the things that pertain to our salvation. Hence in the Prophet it is said: "In your light we shall see light." Ps. 36. Again, just as light calms the minds and drives away the sadness that arises from the darkness of shadows, so God, when he shines upon us favourably, refreshes and cheers our souls so that they can no longer be shaken by any adversities. Rightly, therefore, David exclaims: "The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?" Ps. 27. Moreover, just as light directs our steps and makes us walk safely, so God, by his word and Spirit, leads and guides those he has enlightened, so that we do not stumble in the thickest darkness of this world. Wherefore David wished to call his word a lamp to our feet. Ps. 119. Since God is such a light, therefore those who desire to have fellowship with him are necessarily required to do the works of light. What these are we shall learn by comparison and by several passages of Scripture.

units.la: Christus Ioan.3. de mundo dicit, quod tenebras dilexerit magis quàm lucem. Et addit rationem: Erant enim opera eius mala. Lucis ergo opera erunt, quæ malis opponuntur. Item Paulus apostolus Christianos sui officij admonens, Rom.13. scribit: Nox progressa est, dies autem appropinquat. Abijciamus ergo opera tenebrarum, & induamur arma lucis: tanquam in die compositè ambulemus, non in comessationibus & ebrietatibus, non cubilibus & lasciuijs, non contentione & æmulatione, sed induamini Dominum Iesum Christum. Et carnis curam ne agatis ad concupiscentias. Coniungit ergo opera tenebrarum cum carnis operibus apostolus, imò eadem facit. At idem carnis opera alibi per enumerationem plenius exponit, dicens: Manifesta sunt opera carnis, quæ sunt hæc: adulterium, fornicatio, immunditia, lasciuia, simulachrorum cultus, veneficium, inimicitiæ, lis, æmulationes, iræ, concertationes, seditiones, hæreses, inuidiæ, cædes, ebrietates, comessationes, & his similia, &c. Galat.5. Quæ omnia si in certos ordines distribuere velis, opera carnis & tenebrarum dices, quæcunque cum fidei & religionis puritate, cum vitæ & morum innocentia, cum veritate, cum temperantia & charitate fraterna pugnant. E contra lucis opera erunt, fides verò in Deum patrem per Christum Iesum, religio pura secundum Dei verbum instituta, vitæ puritas & sanctimonia, veritatis studium à fraude dolóq; alienum, Christiana vel fraterna Charitas, quæ sola totam legem implere dicitur. His ergo studeat oportet, qui vere Christianus & bonorum cœlestium consors censeri vult. Hæc enim per omnem scripturam exiguntur. Dauid certè communionem nostram cum Deo describens, Psalm.15. sic ait: Domine, quis habitabit in tabernaculo tuo? Quis in monte tuo sancto requiescet? Qui ambulat integer, & quod iustum est operatur, quiq; in corde suo veritatem loquitur. Non obtrectat lingua sua, nec malefacit proximo suo, nec sustinet probro indigne affici vicinū suum, &c. Et apud Isaiam cap.33. cum ardoribus æternis diuinæ iustitiæ habitaturus dicitur: Qui ambulat in iustitijs, & loquitur quæ recta sunt, &c. Etalibi externum cultum spiritus sanctus, ceu inutilem, damnans addit: Indicaui tibi homo, quid bonum sit, & quid à te requirat Deus: nempe facere iudicium, diligere benignitatem, & submissum ambulare cū Domino Deo tuo. Mich.6. Similiter Christus in euangelio inquit: Beati mundi corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt. Matth.5. Idem pedes, id est, affectus quotidie ablui vult, ne contra patris ipsius legem transuersi abripiamur. Ioan 13. Et Iacobus cap.1. dicit: Religio pura & immaculata apud Deum & patrem hæc est: Inuisere orphanos & viduas in afflictione sua, immaculatum seipsum seruare à mundo. Sed quid hisce testimonijs commemorandis immoror, cùm sacra legenti passim sint obuia? Imis animis potius Ioannis argumentum recondere decet, vt intelligamus, hæc non philosophorum placita, non humanarum traditionum figmenta, sed spiritus sancti inuiolabilia decreta esse, quæ nisi observauerimus, cum luce æterna communionem habere nunquam poterimus, sed tenebrarum filij in tenebras externas eijciemur. Et de his quidem in sequentibus Ioannes agit, quæ secunda huius loci pars est.
units.tr: Christ, John 3, says of the world that it loved darkness more than light. And he adds the reason: "For their works were evil." The works of light, therefore, will be those which are opposed to evil. Likewise the Apostle Paul, admonishing Christians of their duty, Rom. 13, writes: "The night is far spent, and the day is at hand. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armour of light; let us walk becomingly as in the day, not in revelling and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and jealousy, but put on the Lord Jesus Christ. And make no provision for the flesh, to fulfil its lusts." The Apostle therefore joins the works of darkness with the works of the flesh, indeed makes them the same. But elsewhere he sets out the same works of the flesh more fully by enumeration, saying: "The works of the flesh are manifest, which are these: adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness, idolatry, witchcraft, enmities, strife, jealousies, wraths, contentions, seditions, heresies, envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and the like," etc. Gal. 5. If you wish to distribute all of these into definite classes, you will call them works of the flesh and of darkness: whatever conflicts with the purity of faith and religion, with innocence of life and morals, with truth, with temperance and brotherly love. On the other hand, the works of light will be faith in God the Father through Jesus Christ, pure religion instituted according to the word of God, purity and holiness of life, a zeal for truth free from deceit and fraud, and Christian or brotherly love, which alone is said to fulfil the whole law. Therefore he who wishes to be considered a truly Christian and a partner in heavenly goods ought to be devoted to these things. For these are required throughout all Scripture. David, certainly, describing our fellowship with God, Ps. 15, speaks thus: "Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle? Who shall rest on your holy hill? He who walks uprightly, and works what is right, and speaks the truth in his heart. He does not slander with his tongue, nor does evil to his neighbour, nor bears reproach unworthily against his neighbour," etc. And in Isaiah chapter 33, where he is said to dwell with the eternal burnings of divine justice: "He who walks in righteousness and speaks what is right," etc. And elsewhere the Holy Spirit, condemning external worship as useless, adds: "I have shown you, O man, what is good, and what the Lord your God requires of you: namely, to do judgement, to love kindness, and to walk humbly with the Lord your God." Mic. 6. Similarly Christ says in the Gospel: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." Matt. 5. He likewise wishes his feet, that is, our affections, to be washed every day, lest we be drawn aside contrary to the very law of the Father. John 13. And James, chapter 1, says: "Pure and undefiled religion before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unspotted from the world." But why do I linger in recalling these testimonies, since they lie everywhere ready for the one who reads the sacred books? It is rather fitting to lodge John's argument deep in our hearts, so that we may understand that these are not the opinions of philosophers nor the fictions of human traditions, but the inviolable decrees of the Holy Spirit; and unless we observe them, we shall never be able to have fellowship with the eternal light, but the sons of darkness will be cast out into outer darkness. And John treats of these things in what follows, which is the second part of this place.

units.la: II. Si dicamus, quòd communionem habemus cum eo, & in tenebris ambulamus, mentimur, & veritatem non facimus. Si dicamus, nos cum Deo communionem habere, id est, si nomine Christi & filiorum Dei gloriemur, si nos Deo coniunctos esse, & regni cœlorum hæreditatem ad nos pertinere, contendamus: interim in tenebris ambulamus, id est, opera tenebrarum facimus, carnis & mundi studijs per omnia dediti, tam abest, vt prosit nobis hæc gloriatio, vt potius reos grauissimi peccati coram Deo faciat, & à regno ipsius in vniuersum excludat. Mendaces etenim nos esse, palàm testamur, & proinde non Dei, sed diaboli (qui in veritate non stetit. Ioan.8.) filij sumus. Quæ enim communio luci cum tenebris? 2. Corinth.6. Aut ergo tenebrarum opera deseramus oportet, aut frustra Dei & Christi ipsius nomine gloriabimur. Qui enim Christi sunt, carnem crucifixerunt cum affectibus & concupiscentijs. Galat.5.
units.tr: II. If we say that we have fellowship with him, and walk in darkness, we lie, and do not the truth. If we say that we have fellowship with God, that is, if we boast in the name of Christ and of the sons of God, and contend that we are joined to God and that the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven belongs to us, yet meanwhile we walk in darkness, that is, we do the works of darkness, given over in every way to the pursuits of the flesh and the world, then this boasting is so far from profiting us that it rather makes us guilty of the gravest sin before God and shuts us out altogether from his kingdom. For by our conduct we openly testify that we are liars, and therefore we are children not of God but of the devil, who did not stand in the truth (John 8). For what fellowship has light with darkness? (2 Cor. 6). Either we must therefore forsake the works of darkness, or we shall boast in vain in the name of God and of Christ himself. For those who are Christ's have crucified the flesh with its affections and lusts (Gal. 5).

units.la: Sunt hæc diligenti consyderatione dignissima. Licet enim omnes pro corrupto carnis ingenio quotidie peccemus, paucos tamen inuenire licet, qui non Dei cultores & amici haberi velint, Arbitrantur autem pleriq;, ad huius nominis gloriam externa symbola & fidei profesionem suf- ficere. Hinc fit, vt sub nominis Christiani praetextu, in omnem carnis licentiam abrepti, omnia ea faciant, quae olim falsos Israelitas sub templi & sacrificiorum velo fecisse legimus. Isa.1. Psal.50. Ie- re.7. &c. Est haec multorum & grauissimorum offendiculorum causa. Sic enim multis persuade- tur, euangelij doctrinam tantae licentiae & impuritatis causam esse, & qui honestatis morum pau- lo studiosiores sunt, ab hac doctrina, tanquam bonis moribus inimica, sibi abstinendum putant. Et qui eiusdem aperti hostes sunt, eo quod illis luce ipsorum arguitur improbitas, hinc occasione arrepta, in illam insana linguae rabie liberius grassantur. Nemini igitur leuiculum videatur, Christi nomen falso profiteri. Mendaces non fert, qui aeterna est veritas. Minus ergo eos feret, qui mendacijs suis & ipsius gloriae & multorum saluti officiunt. In hos stringi debet, quod Christus Matth. 7. ait: Multi dicent mihi in illo die: Domine domine, nonne per nomen tuum prophetauimus, & per nomen tuum daemonia eiecimus, & per nomen tuum multas virtutes praestitimus? At tunc confitebor illis: Nunquam noui vos. Discedite a me qui operamini iniquitatem, &c. Haec vtinam serio expenderent, qui Christianam libertatem carnalis licentiae praetextum faciunt.
units.tr: These things are most worthy of careful consideration. For although all of us sin daily through the corrupt nature of the flesh, yet one may find few who do not wish to be counted worshippers and friends of God. Most people, however, suppose that outward signs and a profession of faith are enough for the glory of this name. Hence it comes about that, under the pretext of the Christian name, carried away into every license of the flesh, men do all those things which we read that the false Israelites once did under the veil of the temple and the sacrifices (Isa. 1; Ps. 50; Jer. 7, etc.). This is the cause of many and very grave stumbling-blocks. For thus many are persuaded that the doctrine of the gospel is the cause of such great license and impurity, and those who are somewhat more earnest about the honesty of their morals think they must abstain from this doctrine as hostile to good morals. And those who are its open enemies, because their wickedness is exposed by its light, seize upon this occasion and rage more freely with that insane fury of the tongue against it. Let no one therefore think it a trifling matter to profess the name of Christ falsely. Eternal truth does not endure liars. Therefore he will endure less those who injure both his glory and the salvation of many by their lies. Against such people should be aimed what Christ says in Matthew 7: "Many will say to me on that day: Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and done many mighty works in your name? And then I will confess to them: I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity," etc. Would that those who make Christian liberty a pretext for carnal license would weigh these things seriously!

units.la: Interea habent hic, quo sese confirment simpliciores, dum propter multos licentiosius pec- cantes sub Christianae fidei praetextu, de huius veritate dubitare incipiunt. Nisi enim tales futu-ri fuissent, frustra contra hos per prophetas & apostolos pugnauisset spiritus sanctus, & frustra nos de illis admonuisset. Habes etiam quod illis respondeas, qui impuros hosce Epicuri de grege porcos nobis obijciunt, quasi talia scelerum portenta praedicatio gratiae Dei pariat. Sed eadem ratione illi Christū damnabunt, qui in suo coetu Iudam habuit, furem & proditorem impijssimum. Damnabunt omnem veterem ecclesiam, quam non modo prophani homines, carnis affectibus et flagitijs dediti, verumetiam haereticorum phalanges miserè vexauerunt. Sed stultum est, euange- lio paucorum licentiam acceptam ferre, cum nullus hominum ordo tam sanctus sit & integer, in quo non plures reperire liceat, qui carni & prauis cupiditatibus plus aequo indulgeant. Nos certum & infallibile axioma esse credamus, no Christianos & Dei filios, sed mendaces & diaboli pro-lem esse, qui Christiano nomine gloriantur, cum nihilominus in tenebris ambulent. Sequitur loci huius pars vltima, quae fructus & praemia eorum recenset, qui vitam Christiano nomine dignam & communioni diuinae respondentem viuunt.
units.tr: Meanwhile, here is something by which the simpler sort may be strengthened, when, on account of many who sin more licentiously under the pretext of the Christian faith, they begin to doubt the truth of it. For unless such people were to be, the Holy Spirit would have fought in vain against them through the prophets and apostles, and would have warned us about them in vain. You also have here an answer for those who throw in our faces these filthy swine from the herd of Epicurus, as if the preaching of the grace of God produced such monstrosities of crime. But by the same reasoning they would condemn Christ, who had in his company Judas, a thief and most wicked traitor. They would condemn the whole ancient Church, which was miserably harassed not only by profane men given over to the affections and disgraceful deeds of the flesh, but also by the battalions of heretics. But it is foolish to lay the license of a few at the door of the gospel, since there is no order of men so holy and sound in which one may not find several who indulge the flesh and depraved desires more than is right. Let us believe this to be a certain and infallible axiom: that those who boast in the Christian name, yet nevertheless walk in darkness, are not Christians and sons of God but liars and offspring of the devil. There follows the last part of this passage, which sets out the fruits and rewards of those who live a life worthy of the Christian name and corresponding to the divine fellowship.

units.la: III I. Quód si in luce ambulamus, sicut ipse est in luce, communionem habemus inter nos, & sanguis Iesu Christi, filij eius, emundat nos ab omni peccato. Duo pollicetur vere fidelibus & Christianis Ioan- nes. Primum est: Communionem habemus inter nos. Vbi non putabimus, communionis hu-ius iura inter homines tantum cōsistere. Quia enim fideles Christo insiti sunt, qui eosdem vnum facit cum patre, imo illis spiritum filiorum Dei largitur, ad ipsum Deum haec communio extendi-tur. Vult ergo dicere Apostolus: Si opera lucis sectemur, & vitam viuamus aeterna luce dignam, in communionem & consortium filiorum Dei vere adoptabimur, vt diuinae gratiae omniumque bonorum eius participes fieri possimus. Continet haec promissio, quaecunque ad veram hominis beatitudinem faciunt. Nihil etenim ei deesse potest, cui cum Deo, omnis boni fonte & copiae cor-nu, conuenit. Genef.17. Sed quia de hac communione supra multis egimus, eadem hic denuo in-gerere, superuacaneum est.
units.tr: III. I. If we walk in the light, as he himself is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, cleanses us from all sin. John promises two things to true believers and Christians. The first is: "We have fellowship with one another." Here we shall not suppose that the rights of this fellowship consist only among men. For since the faithful are engrafted into Christ, who makes them one with the Father, and indeed gives them the Spirit of the sons of God, this fellowship extends to God himself. The Apostle therefore means to say: If we pursue the works of light and live a life worthy of the eternal light, we shall truly be adopted into the fellowship and partnership of the sons of God, so that we may be made partakers of divine grace and of all its good things. This promise contains whatever contributes to the true blessedness of man. For nothing can be lacking to one who is joined with God, the fountain of every good and the horn of plenty (Gen. 17). But since we have treated this fellowship at length above, it is superfluous to repeat the same things here.

units.la: Alterum praemium est, quòd sanguis filij Dei, Iesu Christi, nos emundat ab omni peccato. Habet hoc turbatae conscientiae solatium. Licet enim per fidem Christo inferamur, & is spiritu suo innocentiae & sanctimoniae studium in nobis accendat, manent tamen peccati reliquiae, & cor-ruptae naturae ingenium: quod nunquam tam plenè reprimetur, quin vires suas proferat, & causa fit, vt iustus quoque in die cadat septies. Prouerb.24. Hic ergo, qui infirmior est, facilè tentabi-tur, vt se communione filiorum Dei excidisse, & omni spe coelestis haereditatis spoliatum putet. Huic tentationi occurrens Ioannes, in fidelibus, qui in luce ambulant, adhuc peccata superesse fa-tetur, quae emundatione opus habeant. Et quia emundationis meminit, eandemq; simul pollice-tur, docet eiusmodi infirmitatis nostrae lapsus vero fideli nequaquam officere posse. Est ergo hoc amplissimum vitae Christianae praemium, liberatio nimirum à peccato, cuius solius culpa fit, vt à regno Dei excludamur. Hoc sublato, quid restat, quàm vt filij Dei, regni eius haereditatem conse-quamur, vti pollicitus est?
units.tr: The second reward is that the blood of the Son of God, Jesus Christ, cleanses us from all sin. This gives comfort to a troubled conscience. For although we are joined to Christ through faith, and he by his Spirit kindles in us a zeal for innocence and holiness, yet remnants of sin remain, and the nature of corrupted man, which is never so fully restrained that it does not put forth its strength, and the cause is that the righteous man also falls seven times a day (Prov. 24). He who is weaker, therefore, will easily be tempted to think that he has fallen away from the fellowship of the sons of God and has been stripped of all hope of the heavenly inheritance. Meeting this temptation, John confesses that in the faithful, who walk in the light, sins still remain, which need cleansing. And because he mentions cleansing, and at the same time promises it, he teaches that the lapses of such weakness of ours can by no means harm a true believer. This, then, is the most ample reward of the Christian life, namely deliverance from sin, the sole fault of which is that we are shut out from the kingdom of God. If this is taken away, what remains but that, as sons of God, we obtain the inheritance of his kingdom, as he has promised?

units.la: Porrò, quod nam illud medium est, quo à peccatis emundamur? Sanguis filij Dei, Iesu Christi. Hunc quia nominat Ioannes, solum hunc emundationi nostrę sufficere, nec aliam peccatorum nostrorum expiationem vspiam extare, certò credamus. De ijs enim hic loquitur, qui veri filij Dei in luce ambulant, operibus lucis studeant, innocentiae & charitatis leges pro virili sectantur. Et ta-men illos, sanguine filij Dei emūdari & expiari, dicit. Quam ergo in suis operibus & meritis spem habebunt reliqui, si ad Christi meritum, qui reuera filij Dei sunt, relegantur? Quàm commo-dam hoc loco nostra opera & merita extollendi occasionem habuisset, fi illa aliquam in redemp-tionis nostræ causa laudem mererentur? Nam dicere poterat: Si in luce ambulemus, communio-nem cum sanctis & Deo habebimus, simulq; propter opera lucis, quæ à nobis fiunt, iustificati sa-lutem merebimur. Sed nihil tale cogitans, Sanguis (inquit) filij Dei nos emundat ab omni pecca-to. Et vt vnius sanguinis Christi meminit, ita vicissim omne peccatū nominat, ne alia quidè pec-cata sanguine Christi, alia verò nostris meritis expiari putaremus. Omnes ergo peccatorum expi-ationes, extra Christi meritum institutas, Ioannes breui hac & vere apostolica sententia iugu-lat. Quid enim homo faciat, qui ex semetipso non est idoneus, vt vel cogitet quod bonum est?2, ad Corinthios tertio. Stultum est ijs gloriari, quæ accepisti. At quid habes ô homo, quod non ac-ceperis? 1. ad Corinthios quarto. Dei opus est, quod abs te bene fit. Et cum illi mercedem pro hoc pollicetur, non meriti tui, sed gratiæ Dei hæc promissio est, qui opus suum in te coro-nare dignatur. Est hæc concors & vnanimis totius scripturæ doctrina. Apud prophetam Do-minus clamat: Ego ego ille ipse sum, qui deleo transgresiones tuas, ID QVE PROPTER ME, & peccatorum tuorum non recordabor. Isa.43.Item: Ego deleui transgressiones tuas, vt den-fas nebulas, & vt nubem peccata tua, &c. Isa.44. Et rursum: Ego ego sum dominus, & præter me nō est seruator. Isa.45. Similiter apud eundem prophetā: Ego dominus, & hoc est nomen meu, & gloriam meam alteri non dabo. Isa.42. At quomodo gloriam suam alteri non dat, si nos in nostræ redemptionis gloria locum aliquem obtinemus? Sensit idem Dauid, qui cum peccati à propria conscientia accusaretur, non ad sua opera, quæ plurima & sanctissima habebat, confugit, sed ad do-minum conuersus clamat: Laua me ab iniquitate mea, & à peccato meo munda me. Expia me hy-sopo, & mundus ero: laua me, & niue ero candidior, &c. Psal.51. Et hæc quidem veterum fuit sen-tentia, penes quos multus legis & sacrificiorum vsus erat. In nouo Testamento, primus eius mi-nister Christum digito monstrans diserte pronunciat: Ecce agnus ille Dei, qui tollit peccatum mun-di. Ioan.1. Si is tollit, quid nobis agendum superest? Et Petrus, Christum super lignum peccata no-ftra tulisse fatetur. 1.Pet.2. Idem in nullo alio salutem esse, constanter affirmat. Acto.4. Sed dies me deficeret, si quæcunq; in hanc sententiam dicuntur in sacris literis, recensere vellem. Nos prophe-tarum & apostolorum doctrinam secuti, solius Christi sanguine nos à peccatis ablui, credamus: qui & Petro dixit: Nisi ego lauero te, non habebis partem mecum. Ioan.13. Lauat autem in se cre-dentes, qua de re alibi copiosius dicendi locus dabitur.
units.tr: Furthermore, what is that means by which we are cleansed from sins? The blood of the Son of God, Jesus Christ. Since John names this alone, let us firmly believe that this alone is sufficient for our cleansing, and that there is no other expiation of our sins anywhere. For he here speaks of those who are true sons of God and walk in the light, who labour at the works of light and pursue as far as they can the laws of innocence and charity. And yet he says that these are cleansed and expiated by the blood of the Son of God. What hope, then, will the rest have in their own works and merits, if those who are truly sons of God are referred to the merit of Christ? How convenient an occasion for extolling our works and merits would John have had in this place, if they deserved some praise in the cause of our redemption! For he could have said: If we walk in the light, we shall have fellowship with the saints and with God, and at the same time, on account of the works of light which are done by us, we shall be justified and merit salvation. But thinking nothing of the kind, he says: "The blood of the Son of God cleanses us from all sin." And as he speaks of the blood of Christ alone, so in turn he names every sin, lest we should think that some sins are expiated by the blood of Christ and others by our merits. Thus by this brief and truly apostolic sentence John cuts the throat of all expiations of sins instituted outside the merit of Christ. For what can a man do who is not of himself sufficient even to think anything good? (2 Cor. 3). It is foolish to glory in those things which you have received. But what have you, O man, that you have not received? (1 Cor. 4). It is God's work that is well done by you. And when he promises a reward for this, the promise is not of your merit but of the grace of God, who deigns to crown his own work in you. This is the harmonious and unanimous teaching of all Scripture. In the prophet the Lord cries: "I, I am he who blots out your transgressions, FOR MY OWN SAKE, and I will not remember your sins" (Isa. 43). Likewise: "I have blotted out your transgressions like a thick cloud, and your sins like a mist," etc. (Isa. 44). And again: "I, I am the Lord, and there is no saviour besides me" (Isa. 45). Similarly, in the same prophet: "I am the Lord, and this is my name, and I will not give my glory to another" (Isa. 42). But how does he not give his glory to another, if we hold any place in the glory of our redemption? David also felt the same, who, when he was accused of sin by his own conscience, did not flee to his own works, which were many and most holy, but turned to the Lord and cried: "Wash me from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow," etc. (Ps. 51). And this indeed was the opinion of the ancients, among whom there was a great use of the law and of sacrifices. In the New Testament, the first minister of it, pointing to Christ with his finger, plainly declares: "Behold that Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world" (John 1). If he takes it away, what is left for us to do? And Peter confesses that Christ bore our sins upon the tree (1 Pet. 2). The same Peter constantly affirms that there is salvation in no other (Acts 4). But the day would fail me if I wished to recount all the passages of Holy Writ that are said to this effect. Following the teaching of the prophets and apostles, let us believe that we are washed from our sins by the blood of Christ alone, who also said to Peter: "Unless I wash you, you will have no part with me" (John 13). He washes, however, those who believe in him; a matter on which an opportunity for a fuller discussion will be given elsewhere.

units.la: Licet ex his æstimare quanta sit peccati atrocitas. Si enim peccata solius filij Dei sanguine emundari & expiari possunt, horribilem eorum culpam esse oportet, nisi Deum, vel imprudenter prodigum in filij sui sanguine fundendo, vel certe crudelem dicere velimus. Expendant hoc, qui peccati blanditias tam facilè admittunt, vt de omnibus flagitijs suis nimium leuiter pronuncient. Sed dic obsecro, quisquis es. Num Christum pro te passum, & in Cruce mortuum esse credis? Ita[?] teberis[?] scio, nisi te à regno Christi & salute alienum dicere velis. At quę causa est, vt propter te filius Dei in tam atrocem & diram mortem traditus sit? Non alia vtiq;, quàm peccata nostra. Sic enim scriptura pronunciat: Propter transgressiones nostras ipse vulneratus est, & attritus propter iniquitates nostras. Mulcta correctionis nostræ (id est, pœna, quæ nostris peccatis debeba-tur, & qua nos corrigi oportebat,) ei imposita est, &c. Isa.53. Tua ergo peccata, qualiacunq; tu illa æstimes, Christo tam acerbæ passionis causa fuerunt. Tua concupiscentia, tuo odio, tua libidine, tua fcortatione, tuis adulterijs, tuis vsuris & fraudibus, tuis dolis & mendacijs, tuis periurijs & blasphemijs, tuis homicidijs, tua idololatria, tua impietate, tuis denique transgressionibus, quæ abs te qualefcunq; contra Dei legem commisse sunt, factum est, vt tam crudele Crucis supplicium Dei filium subire oportuerit, cuius a'pectum nec Sol sustinere, nec eiusdem indignitatem perè ferre potuerunt. I nunc & tibijpfi blandire, quando ijsdem denuo te immergis, & omni admonitione ac pœnitentia spreta incurabilem te præbes pertinaciter.
units.tr: It is possible to judge from these things how great the atrocity of sin is. For if sins can be cleansed and expiated only by the blood of the Son of God, then their guilt must be horrible, unless we are willing to call God either imprudently prodigal in pouring out the blood of his Son or, at the very least, cruel. Let those consider this who so easily admit the enticements of sin, and who pronounce too lightly about all their crimes. But tell me, I beg you, whoever you are: do you believe that Christ suffered for you and died on the Cross? I know you do, unless you wish to say that you are alien to the kingdom of Christ and to salvation. But what is the reason that the Son of God was delivered up to so dreadful and cruel a death on your account? Surely none other than our sins. For thus Scripture declares: "He was wounded for our transgressions, and bruised for our iniquities. The chastisement of our peace (that is, the punishment which was owed to our sins, and by which we ought to have been corrected) was laid upon him," etc. (Isa. 53.) Therefore your sins, however great you judge them to be, were the cause of Christ's so bitter suffering. Your lust, your hatred, your wantonness, your fornication, your adulteries, your usuries and frauds, your deceits and lies, your perjuries and blasphemies, your murders, your idolatry, your impiety, and finally your transgressions, whatever sort they are that you have committed against the law of God: because of these it came about that the Son of God had to undergo so cruel a punishment of the Cross, whose appearance neither the Sun could bear to look upon, nor could they endure the indignity of it. Go now and flatter yourself, when you plunge yourself again into the same things, and, scorning every admonition and repentance, you stubbornly show yourself incurable.

units.la: Discamus fratres imis animis, quæ hucusque dicta sunt, recondere. Res magna & grauis est, Christiani nominis professio. Ea cum gloriari libeat, curemus ne falso & frustra hac gloriemur. Ambulemus in luce, & eius opera sectemur. Sic enim fiet, vt communionis cum deo & sanctis eius vere participes & sanguine filij Dei à peccatis abluti, cum eodem æternum viuamus, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Brothers, let us learn to store deep in our hearts what has been said up to this point. The profession of the Christian name is a great and weighty matter. Since we are pleased to glory in it, let us take care that we do not glory in it falsely and in vain. Let us walk in the light and follow its works. For thus it will come about that we truly become partakers of communion with God and his saints, and, washed from our sins by the blood of the Son of God, we shall live forever with him, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power forever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA IIII. SI dixerimus, peccatum non habemus : nos ipsos fallimus, &
units.tr: HOMILY 4. If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.

units.la: veritas in nobis non est. Si confiteamur peccata nostra, fidelis est & justus, ut remittat nobis peccata nostra, & emundet nos ab omni iniquitate. Si dixerimus, non peccavimus: mendacem facimus eum, & sermo eius non est in nobis.
units.tr: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just, that he may forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness. If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.

units.la: QVandoquidem Deo patri nostro visum fuit, nostrae salutis causa filium suum dilectū carne sumpta in mundum mittere, in eodem comprehensa esse voluit, quaecunq; ad salutem & redemptionem humani generis necessaria sunt. Sunt haec multa & eximia bona, in quibus explicandis scripturae crebro versantur. Joannes tamen, mirae & perspicuae brevitatis studiosus, omnia ea duobus generibus complectitur. Primo enim per Christum nobis communionem vel societatem cum Deo obtingere docet. At cui cum Deo convenit, qui omnis boni fons est vberrimus, ei nihil deesse poterit. Idem etiam contra omnem mundi & satanae tyrannidem satis munitus & instructus est. Si enim Deus nobiscum, quis contra nos? Rom. 8. Deinde, sanguine Christi nos à peccatis ablui dicit. In Christo igitur omnem salutis rationem monstrat. Nec enim aliud est quod à salute abstrahat, praeterquam peccatum, quod irae filios & Dei inimicos reddit. Verè ergo Paulus in Christo omnem plenitudinem, gratiae nimirum & salutis, habitare dicit. Col.1. Caeterū ubi haec praedicantur, duo prodeunt hominum genera, quae utraq; doctrinae huic inimica sunt. Primum hypocritarum est vel iustitiariorum, quales olim Pharisaei fuerunt. Quia enim isti propriis satisfactionibus & meritis nituntur, Christi sanguinem & meritum eius magnificare non possunt: imò praedicationem omnem de huius merito superuacaneam esse putant. Alterum filios huius saeculi habet, Epicureos, carnis & mundi studijs per omnia addictos homines. Hi, quia aut Deum esse, aut eundem mortalia curare negant, peccatorum atrocitatem non agnoscunt, nec tanta ipsis videtur, ut tā graui & pretiosa satisfactione opus fuerit. Rident[?] igitur quaecunq; de Christi mysterijs, de peccatorum emundatione, de satisfactione Christi, de poenitentia & reliquis piorum officijs dici audiunt. Utrisque in praesenti D. Joannes Apostolus mederi studet. Primò enim docet, omnes homines peccatores esse, & proinde gratia Dei per Christum collata opus habere, si salvari velimus. Secundò, quid nos facere deceat, exponit, ut à peccatis liberemur. Postremò repetit gravioribus verbis quod initio dixerat, quo & in hypocritis privatae fiduciae insolentiam reprimat, & alteris illis perniciosam illam carnis securitatem excutiat. De his quantum Dei gratia derit, in praesenti dicemus.
units.tr: Since it pleased God our Father, for the sake of our salvation, to send his beloved Son into the world, taking flesh, he willed that in him should be comprehended all that is necessary for the salvation and redemption of the human race. These are many and excellent goods, and the Scriptures frequently occupy themselves in explaining them. John, however, eager for a wonderful and clear brevity, embraces all of them under two heads. First, he teaches that through Christ we obtain communion or fellowship with God. Now whoever is in agreement with God, who is the most abundant fountain of every good, can lack nothing. He is also sufficiently fortified and equipped against all the tyranny of the world and of Satan. For if God is with us, who is against us? Rom. 8. Next, he says that we are cleansed from our sins by the blood of Christ. In Christ, therefore, he shows the whole manner of salvation. Nor is there anything else that could draw us away from salvation, except sin, which makes us children of wrath and enemies of God. Truly, then, Paul says that in Christ all fullness, namely of grace and salvation, dwells. Col. 1. Moreover, where these things are preached, two kinds of men come forward, who are both hostile to this doctrine. The first is that of the hypocrites or self-righteous, such as the Pharisees once were. For since these men rely on their own satisfactions and merits, they cannot magnify the blood of Christ and his merit; indeed, they think that all preaching about his merit is superfluous. The other kind has the sons of this age, the Epicureans, men wholly devoted to the pursuits of the flesh and the world. Since they deny either that God exists or that he cares for mortal things, they do not recognize the atrocity of sins, nor does sin seem to them so great that so heavy and precious a satisfaction was needed. Therefore they mock whatever they hear said about the mysteries of Christ, the cleansing of sins, the satisfaction of Christ, repentance, and the remaining duties of the godly. Against both of these, the Apostle John in the present passage takes pains to heal. For first he teaches that all men are sinners, and therefore that we have need of the grace of God offered through Christ, if we wish to be saved. Second, he sets out what it becomes us to do, that we may be freed from sins.
