Last, he repeats in weightier words what he had said at the beginning, by which he both restrains the arrogance of private confidence in the hypocrites and shakes off from the others that pernicious security of the flesh. How much of the grace of God these things require, we shall say in the present discussion.

units.la: I. Si dixerimus, peccatum non habemus: nos ipsos fallimus, & veritas in nobis non est. Coherent hęc praecedēti sententiae, & praeoccupationis specie habent. Dixerat enim, sanguis Jesu Christi emundat nos ab omni peccato. Quia vero emundatio ista, nec hypocritis proprię justitiae meritis nitentibus, nec mundi filijs securè peccātibus, necessaria videtur, hanc sententiā subiungit Apostolus, quasi dicat: Non temere factū est, quòd inter beneficia Christi, quae fide percipiuntur, emūdatio ni à peccatis primū quodammodo locū tribuit. Quia enim omnes peccatores sumus, ea omnibus est perquàm necessaria, nec quisquā hac se minus indigere putabit, qui vel peccati atrocitatē, vel propriae justitiae imperfectionem cōsyderare velit. Vehementiori aut dicēdi genere utitur, ut sententiā suā, nobis cognitu necessariam, magis commendet. Nec enim contentus est dixisse: Omnes peccatum habemus, & proinde indigemus gratia & merito Christi, qui nostra peccata abluat. Sed ait: Si alicuius ea fuerit praesumptio, cōfidentia, sive temeritas, ut se à peccato omni immunem & liberum dicere ausit, hic seipsum fallit. At omnis fallacia in salutis negotio damnabilis & exitiosa est. Addit verò & gravius quiddam: Veritas in eo nō est. Impossibile ergo, ut idem cum Deo, qui æterna veritas est, commercium habeat. Nemo autem solum Joannem in hac sententia esse existimet, quòd omnes nos peccatores simus. Est enim hęc cōcors totius scripturae doctrina. Deus certè, figmenta cordis humani ab ineūte ętate prava esse, dicit. Gen. 8. Dauid in peccātis se conceptū & genitū fatetur. Psal. 51. Quis verò tu es ô homo, qui Dauide, viro secundū cor Dei, te sanctiore esse censes? Propheta clamat: Omnes tanquā oves erravimus, unusquisq; in viā suam declinavit. Isa. 53. Sancti omnes orare cōsueuerunt: Ne ambules in ius cum servis tuis, quia nō justificabitur apud te ulla caro. Et si iniquitates observare velis, Domine, quis subsistet? Psal. 143. et 130. Paulus, per unum hominem peccatum & peccati poenā, mortem, in mundum introiisse, testatur Rom. 5. Sed & ipse Christus, nemine, praeter unū & solum Deū, bonū esse pronunciat. Matt. 19. Porrò rationes quoq; sunt, quibus hoc ipsum doceri potest. Peccatū est quicquid contra legem Dei fit. At contra legem Dei multa omnes nos facimus, nec aliquis reperitur, qui omnia legis capita se observasse gloriari possit, cū & animū totū Deus requirat, & concupiscentias in nobis repressas velit. Verè igitur Ioânes, nos omnes peccata habere affirmat. Verè etiam ueritatem in nobis esse negat, si nos peccatores esse negare audeamus. Quomodo enim ueritas in eo locum habere poterit, qui tot tamen perspicuis æternæ ueritatis oraculis contradicere nō ueretur? Sed priusquā hinc discere damus, quædam paulò diligentius excutienda sunt.
units.tr: I. "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us." These words cohere with the preceding sentence and have the appearance of an anticipated objection. For he had said: "The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin." Because this cleansing seems unnecessary, neither to the hypocrites who rely on the merits of their own righteousness, nor to the children of the world who sin without care, the Apostle adds this sentence, as if he said: It is not rashly done that, among the benefits of Christ which are received by faith, cleansing from sins is in a certain sense given the first place. For since we are all sinners, this is exceedingly necessary for all, and no one will think himself less in need of it who wishes to consider either the atrocity of sin or the imperfection of his own righteousness. He uses a more vehement manner of speaking, so that he may commend his statement, which is necessary for us to know, the more. For he is not content to have said: "We all have sin, and therefore we need the grace and merit of Christ, who may cleanse our sins." But he says: If there is anyone whose presumption, confidence, or rashness is such that he dares to say that he is free and immune from all sin, this man deceives himself. But every deception is damnable and destructive in the matter of salvation. He adds, moreover, something still more grave: "the truth is not in him." It is therefore impossible that the one who has no sin should have fellowship with God, who is eternal truth. Let no one, however, think that John stands alone in this statement, that we are all sinners. For this is the harmonious teaching of the whole of Scripture. God indeed says that the imaginations of the human heart are evil from youth. Gen. 8. David confesses that he was conceived and born in sins. Ps. 51. But who are you, O man, who think yourself holier than David, a man after the heart of God? The prophet cries out: "We have all gone astray like sheep; each one has turned to his own way." Isa. 53. All the saints are accustomed to pray: "Enter not into judgment with your servants, for no flesh will be justified before you. And if you should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand?" Ps. 143 and 130. Paul testifies, Rom. 5, that through one man sin and the punishment of sin, death, entered the world. But Christ himself also pronounces that no one is good except one, and that is God alone. Matt. 19. Moreover, there are also reasons by which this same thing can be taught. Sin is whatever is done against the law of God. But we all do many things against the law of God, and no one is found who can glory that he has observed all the heads of the law, since God requires the whole soul and wishes the desires within us to be restrained. Truly, therefore, John affirms that we all have sins. Truly also he denies that the truth is in us, if we dare to deny that we are sinners. For how can truth have a place in one who does not shrink from contradicting so many clear oracles of eternal truth? But before we allow ourselves to learn from this, certain matters must be examined a little more carefully.

units.la: Primò ordine, quo Ioannes in hac doctrina utitur, obseruare oportet. Dixerat in præcedentibus de Deo, qui lux est mera sine tenebris. Ostenderat itè, in luce ambulandum esse ijs, qui cū Deo communionem habere expetunt. His modò doctrinā eam subijcit, qua omnes nos peccati accusat & conuincit. Habes hic, qua via in tuijpsius cognitionem peruenire possis: quæ vt nobis perquàm necessaria, ita acquisitu difficilis est. Quare apud gentes olim præcipua sapientiæ pars iu dicata fuit, seipsum nouisse, & Chilonis illud γνῶθι σεαυτόν[?] in columna Delphica confecratū fuisse legimus. Quia enim philautiæ safcino excæcati sumus, nobisipsis mirè placemus, placet & quæcunque facimus. Et vt amatores deformia multa & turpes habitus in personis, quas amant, obseruare non possunt: ita nec nobis uitiosa apparent, quæ à nobis fiunt, licet uitiofissima sint. Accedit his, quòd aliorū de nobis iudicia indignè ferimus, & tam abest, ut aliorū uerbis uelimus argui, ut uerbum Dei eo nomine nobis exosum sit, quòd nostra corruptelam arguit. Vt ergo propria faciem nemo videt, nisi in speculo: ita nec nos nostræ naturæ imperfectione sine speculo aliquo unquam cognoscemus. Speculū hoc ipse Deus est, vel Dei cognitio. Vt primū enim animis nostris Deus innotescit, qui lux est pura & integra, mox quantæ in nobis tenebræ sint, animaduertimus. Vbi Dei voluntatem cernimus supremè sanctam & puram, quàm horribilis sit nostræ uoluntatis corruptio apparet. Sic cum Dei iudicia, quæ iustitia sunt & veritas, nobis ob oculos ponimus, mox fatebimur, nos coram isto iudice cõparere nullo modo posse, nisi aliena iustitia adiutos. In Dei ergo luce uidemus lucem. Psal. 36. Dei enim cognitio, quid nobis adhuc desit, & quid fieri à nobis conueniat, sola docere potest. Eadē, ut nobis ipsis displiceamus, facit, & studiū Deo placendi in nobis accedit. Ex hoc loco igitur de illis iudicare disce, qui corruptionē suá & uitia argui nolunt. Eacerte re euidens de se testimoniū ferunt, quòd in Dei cognitione nondū peruenerint, nec aliquo diuinæ illius lucis lumine perfusi sint, vtcunque cognitione Dei, eiusdē cultu, & uera fide gloriētur.
units.tr: First, we must observe the order in which John uses this doctrine. He had said above concerning God, who is pure light without darkness. He had also shown that those who desire to have communion with God must walk in the light. To these things he now adds the teaching by which he accuses and convicts all of us of sin. Here you have the way by which you can arrive at knowledge of yourself: a thing as necessary for us as it is difficult to acquire. Therefore among the nations of old, the chief part of wisdom was thought to be the knowledge of oneself, and we read that the saying "Know thyself" was engraved on the Delphic column. For since we are blinded by the fascination of self-love, we are wonderfully pleased with ourselves, and whatever we do pleases us. And just as lovers cannot notice many deformities and base habits in the persons they love, so the faults of what we do do not appear faulty to us, however faulty they may be. Add to this that we bear the judgments of others about us unworthily, and so far are we from wishing to be reproved by the words of others, that the word of God itself becomes hateful to us for this reason, that it reproves our corruption. Therefore, just as no one sees his own face except in a mirror, so we shall never know the imperfection of our nature without some mirror. This mirror is God himself, or the knowledge of God. For as soon as God, who is pure and whole light, becomes known to our minds, we notice how great the darkness in us is. When we perceive the will of God as supremely holy and pure, how horrible the corruption of our will is becomes apparent. Thus when we set before our eyes the judgments of God, which are justice and truth, we shall straightway confess that we can in no way appear before this judge, unless we are helped by a righteousness not our own. In the light of God, therefore, we see light. Ps. 36. For the knowledge of God alone can teach what is still lacking in us and what ought to be done by us. The same knowledge makes us displeased with ourselves, and a desire to please God comes upon us. From this passage, therefore, learn to judge those who are unwilling to have their corruption and vices pointed out. Indeed, by this very fact they bear clear witness against themselves, that they have not yet attained to the knowledge of God, nor been bathed in any light of that divine brightness, however much they may boast of their knowledge of God, the worship of him, and true faith.

units.la: Secundò vsum huius doctrinæ obseruemus, qui triplex est. Primò pharifaicâ propriæ iusti-tiæ & meritorū nostrorū fiduciam reprimit, id quod factu cumprimis est necessariū. Vt enim ne-mo non bonus haberi vult & talis sibijpsi videtur: ita operibus nostris coră Deo quoq; nitimur, quasi his illius beneficentiā mereri possimus. At quàm diu hæc nos inflat fiducia, tā diu Christi meritū, quo solo saluamur, nō amplestimur. Quare in salutis negotio nihil perniciofius est, quàm cæca hæc proprię iustitiæ gloriatio. Dementiæ enim esse uidetur, si extra nos quærere uellemus, quę penes nos putamus esse reposita. Vbi verò nos natura peccatores esse intelligimus, de nostra iustitia desperantes, iustitiā, quæ in Christo pponitur[?], cupidi apprehendimus. Hinc fit, quòd Paulus, quotiescunq; de iustificatione nostra sermonem instituit, tāto studio omnes homines peccati conuincit, vt tum alibi, tum in epistola ad Romanos cernitur. Quàm enim cum Christi merito pugnet propriæ iustitiæ fiducia, pharifæorum exemplo abunde docemur. Licet enim multorum inimicitia & insidijs Christus in terris agens oppugnatus fit, nullos tamē in hoc oppugnādo acerbiores & pertinaciores fuisse legimus, quàm pharifæos, quos propriæ iustitiæ fiducia demetabat.
units.tr: Secondly, let us observe the use of this teaching, which is threefold. First, it restrains the Pharisaic confidence in one's own righteousness and in one's own merits, which is especially necessary to be done. For just as no one does not want to be thought good and seems so to himself, so we also rely on our works before God, as if by them we could earn his kindness. But as long as this confidence puffs us up, we do not embrace the merit of Christ, by which alone we are saved. Therefore nothing is more destructive in the business of salvation than this blind boasting in one's own righteousness. For it would seem madness if we wished to seek outside ourselves what we think is stored up within us. But when we understand that we are sinners by nature, despairing of our own righteousness, we eagerly grasp the righteousness that is set forth in Christ. Hence it is that Paul, whenever he takes up the discussion of our justification, convicts all men of sin with such great zeal, as can be seen both elsewhere and in the Epistle to the Romans. For how the confidence in one's own righteousness fights against the merit of Christ we are amply taught by the example of the Pharisees. For although Christ, while living on earth, was assailed by the hostility and snares of many, we read that none were more bitter and obstinate in assailing him than the Pharisees, whom the confidence in their own righteousness made blind.

units.la: Deinde prodest nostrijpsius cognitio, ut peccandi desyderium nobis excutiat, & studiū uerę purificationis apud nos excitet. Vt enim lauari nō vult, nisi qui facie maculis & sordibus polluta esse nouit: ita de purificatione parū solicitus erit, qui quàm ea opus habeat, nondū intelle-xit. Et sanè hęc una causa est, quòd multos pertinaciter in peccatis pergere uidemus, quòd se peccare ignorāt, uel saltem peccata sua leuiora esse putant, quàm ut de his remouēdis multum laborare debeat. Exemplū huius rei Dauid est, qui tū demum de emendatione cogitat, & preces pro peccatorum remissione ad Deum fundit, quando ex Dei uerbo, se peccauisse audit. 2. Sam. 12.
units.tr: Next, the knowledge of ourselves is useful, so that it may shake off from us the desire to sin and stir up in us the zeal for true purification. For just as no one wishes to be washed unless he knows that his face is polluted with stains and filth, so he who has not yet understood how much he needs purification will be little concerned about it. And indeed this is one cause why we see many persist stubbornly in sins: because they are ignorant that they sin, or at least think their sins are too light for them to labor much to remove them. An example of this is David, who only then thinks of amendment and pours out prayers to God for the forgiveness of sins, when he hears from the word of God that he has sinned. 2 Sam. 12.

units.la: Postremus huius doctrinæ vsus circa consolatione versatur. Quia enim perfectionem à nobis exigit Deus, facilè terrebitur infirma conscientia, si se tot vitijs pollutum viderit. Erigitur tamen & cōfirmatur, si non se solum, sed vnà omnes homines, ab hac perfectione multis parafangis distare viderit. Audiet enim pro Dei amicis habitos fuisse olim plures, qui & ipsi multis in rebus impingere soliti fuerunt. Discet item, imperfectionem nostrā Christi perfectione curari, & in hoc nos incūbere debere, ut quando in uniuersum à peccato liberari non possumus, illud saltem non regnet in mortali nostro corpore. Rom. 6. Tam magnus ergo & multiplex cum fit huius cognitionis usus, non temere Ioannes tanta verborū vehementia illam inculcat. Discamus nos doctrinam hanc in ecclesijs retinere, vt vel priuatæ cōscientiæ testimonio conuincantur, quicūq; in sua iustitia aliquam salutis spem reponere incipiunt.
units.tr: The last use of this teaching concerns consolation. For since God requires perfection from us, a weak conscience will easily be terrified if it sees itself polluted by so many vices. Yet it is raised up and strengthened if it sees that not only itself but all men together are many miles distant from this perfection. For it will hear that in former times there were many regarded as friends of God who themselves were also accustomed to stumble in many things. It will also learn that our imperfection is healed by the perfection of Christ, and that we ought to strive in this, so that when we cannot be freed from sin altogether, it at least may not reign in our mortal body. Rom. 6. Therefore, since the use of this knowledge is so great and manifold, John does not rashly inculcate it with such vehemence of words. Let us learn to retain this doctrine in the churches, so that those who begin to place any hope of salvation in their own righteousness may be convicted either by the testimony of their private conscience or otherwise.

units.la: Restat, ut quod hic obijci potest, diluamus. Dicat enim quispiam: Ioannes, omnes nos pecca-tores esse, constáter affirmat. Idem vero infra à Christi cognitione & fide alienos pronútiabit, qui cunq; peccát. 1. Ioan. 3. Adhæc, Christianos homines populum sanctũ & immaculatũ dici legimus. Paulus enim de ecclesia loquens, uocat eã gloriosam, nõ habentem rugam uel maculam, sanctam item & irreprehensibilem. Ephes. 5. Et Petrus fideles genus electum, regale sacerdotiũ, & gentem sanctam nominat. 1. Pet. 2. Quid ergo ad hæc dicemus. Idem ne est peccare, & non peccare? Vel idem ne erit, peccatorem esse, & sanctum siue immaculatum censeri? Putant hæc multi paradoxa, & Apostoli sibijpsis contradicere videntur: sed penitius rem inspicientibus plana & perspicua sunt omnia.
units.tr: It remains that we dissolve what can be objected here. For someone may say: John plainly affirms that we are all sinners. Yet he will again declare that whoever sins is alien to the knowledge and faith of Christ. 1 John 3. Moreover, we read that Christian men are called a holy and unspotted people. For Paul, speaking of the Church, calls her glorious, not having spot or wrinkle, also holy and blameless. Eph. 5. And Peter names the faithful an elect race, a royal priesthood, and a holy nation. 1 Pet. 2. What then shall we say to these things? Is it the same to sin and not to sin? Or will it be the same to be a sinner and to be counted holy or unspotted? Many think these to be paradoxes, and the Apostles seem to contradict themselves; but to those who examine the matter more deeply, all things are plain and clear.

units.la: Porro quod Ioannis locum attinet, qui Christianos esse negat, eos qui peccant, quo sensu id accipi debeat, infra dicemus. Hic respondisse sufficiat, Christianos homines bifariam considerari debere: partim quidè, quoad homines sunt: partim verò quatenus Christo per fidè insi-ti dicuntur. Quatenus enim homines sunt, peccati naturâ sibi insitâ habent, qua interdū superantur, ut ex semetipsis iusti & mũdi nullo modo censeri possint. Quatenus verò Christiani, & Christi Iesu membra per fidem facti sunt, iusti, sancti, immaculati & irreprehensibiles dicuntur: nõ propria quidem iustitia, sed Christi, quæ propter fidem ipsis imputatur. Quotquot enim baptizati estis (inquit Paulus) Christum induistis. Galat. 5. Et alibi: Quis intentabit crimina aduersus electos Dei? Deus est qui iustificat: quis ille qui condemnet? Rom. 8. Licet ergo propter inhærentia naturæ nostræ vitia, merito & accusari & dânari possemus, Christi tamen iustitia & merito quasi tecti & velati, fumus irreprehensibiles. Vt ergo Christi meritum afflictas conscientias solatur, ne in desperationem inclinent: ita non obest, quo minus in peccatis fugiendis laboremus, & adhæren tes nobis sordes abluamus. Vtrumq; Christus completitur, quando discipulorũ pedes abluens inquit: Qui lotus est, non opus habet, nisi ut pedes lauet, sed est mundus totus. Ioan. 13. Lotos vocat omnes in se credentes, qui & propter fidem illam toti mũdi dicuntur. Quia tamen ijdem à carnis affectibus, quoad in carne viuunt, alieni esse non possunt, & mũdi conuersatione facilè & crebrò contaminantur, quotidiana pedum, id est, affectuũ & studiorũ ablutione opus habet. Sed hæc de prima huius loci parte dicta sufficiant. Tempus postulat, ut ad secundam transeamus.
units.tr: Further, as regards the passage of John, which denies that those who sin are Christians, in what sense this must be understood we shall say below. Here it will suffice to have answered that Christian men ought to be considered in two ways: partly indeed as far as they are men, partly as far as they are said to be grafted into Christ through faith. For as far as they are men, they have sin implanted in their nature, by which they are sometimes overcome, so that from themselves they cannot in any way be counted righteous and clean. But as far as they are Christians, and have been made members of Christ Jesus through faith, they are called righteous, holy, unspotted and blameless: not indeed by their own righteousness, but by that of Christ, which is imputed to them on account of faith. For as many of you as have been baptized (says Paul) have put on Christ. Gal. 5. And elsewhere: Who shall bring any charge against the elect of God? It is God who justifies; who is he who condemns? Rom. 8. Therefore, although on account of the vices inherent in our nature we could rightly be both accused and condemned, yet we are blameless, as if covered and veiled by the righteousness and merit of Christ. Thus, just as the merit of Christ comforts afflicted consciences, lest they incline to despair, so it does not hinder us from labouring to flee sins and washing away the filth that clings to us. Christ fulfils both when, washing the feet of the disciples, he says: He who is washed has no need except to wash his feet, but is clean all over. John 13. He calls washed all who believe in him, who on account of that faith are said to be clean all over. Yet since these same men cannot be alien to the affections of the flesh, as long as they live in the flesh, and are easily and often defiled by the conversation of the world, they need a daily washing of the feet, that is, of their affections and pursuits. But let what has been said of the first part of this passage suffice. The time demands that we pass on to the second.

units.la: II. Si confiteamur peccata nostra, fidelis est & iustus, ut remittat nobis peccata nostra, & emundet nos ab omni iniquitate. Docet quid à nobis fieri debeat, quando nos peccatores esse videmus, simul q; sui consilij siue præcepti fructum salutari promissione comprehendit. Præscribit verò peccatorũ nostrorum confessionem, qua ipsi nos peccatores esse testemur. Causa huius consilij, est nostrę salutis ratio. Vt enim de medicina non cogitant, qui se ægrotos esse ignorant: ita de peccatorum remissione soliciti non erunt, qui peccatis se laborare nesciunt. Itę ut medicum non admittunt, qui ægroti videri nolunt, & morbos dissimulare student: ita nec Christum admittent, nec ad salutarem euangelij medicinam confugient, qui animi morbos, peccata, dissimulare solent, ne pro peccatoribus habeantur. Huc illud Solomonis dicto pertinet: Qui transgressiones celat, huic non prospere cedet: qui verò confitetur & deserit, is misericordiam consequetur. Quâ ob rem ipse Christus se ægrotantium medicum esse dicit, & publicanis, qui se peccare fatebãtur, potius quàm pharisæis, familiarè sese facit. Matth. 9. Cæterũ, quia de Confessione peccatorum, multa hodie concertatio est, paucis quæ ad hunc locum pertinent, proferemus.
units.tr: II. "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (1 John 1:9) He teaches what ought to be done by us when we see ourselves to be sinners, and at the same time, by a saving promise, he includes the fruit of this counsel or precept. He prescribes the confession of our sins, by which we bear witness that we ourselves are sinners. The reason for this counsel is the consideration of our salvation. For just as those who know themselves to be sick do not think of medicine, so those who do not know that they are laboring under sins will not be anxious about the forgiveness of sins. And just as those who do not wish to seem sick, and strive to conceal their diseases, do not admit a physician, so they who are accustomed to conceal the diseases of the soul, their sins, lest they be held as sinners, will neither admit Christ nor flee to the saving medicine of the gospel. To this pertains the saying of Solomon: He who conceals his transgressions shall not prosper; but he who confesses and forsakes them shall obtain mercy. Prov. 28. For this reason Christ himself says that he is the physician of the sick, and he makes himself familiar with the publicans, who confessed that they sinned, rather than with the Pharisees. Matt. 9. Moreover, since there is today much contention concerning the confession of sins, we will set forth a few things that pertain to this passage.

units.la: Confessio, est peccati, cuius nobis probè conscij sumus, ingenua agnitio, qua Deo gloriã, nobis verò confusionem tribuimus, & culpam supplices deprecamur. Distribuitur hæc in priuatam & publicam. Priuata à singulis fit, quando se peccauisse agnoscunt, Deo id confitetur & remissionem postulant. Requirit hæc diligentem singulorum peccatorũ penitentiam, vt ardentius in nobis excitetur pœnitentiæ studium. Publica à toto cœtu fit, quando palàm in nobis peccata esse, nosq; diuina gratia per Christũ indigere testamur. Vtraq; autem soli Deo fieri debet, quia solus est, qui peccata remittit, quod & pharisæos, vtcunq; excæcatos, vidisse constat. Matth. 9. De confessione, quæ apud proximum fit, nihil hic dicimus, eò quòd hæc mutuæ amicitiæ & condonationis causa fit, non quòd gratiam aliquam coràm Deo mereatur. Comprehendit cõfesio hæc, quæcunq; ad pœnitentiam uerà & studiũ salutis pertinent. Oportet enim præcedat peccati agnitio, quia sine hac, quod confitearis, non habes. Peccati agnitionem cordis cõtritio sequitur. Qui enim fiat, vt nõ totus animo frangatur, qui in tã benignum patrę tot tamq; indignis modis sese peccasse cogitet? Non potest ab hac abesse certa & solida gratiæ Dei fiducia, quæ Christo nititur. Vt enim medico morbũ latentem nõ prodis, nisi huius arte te curari posse cõfidas: ita nec Deo culpã nostrã verè fatebimur, nisi eũ esse credamus, qui omnem culpã remittere & velit & possit. Quod enim Cainus, Iudas Iscariotes & alij eius farinæ homines sese peccauisse clamat, nõ tam Cõfesio, quàm propriæ cõscientię accusatio & animi in desperatione vergētis volûtaria dãnatio dici debet.
units.tr: Confession is a frank acknowledgment of a sin of which we are well aware, by which we give glory to God and confusion to ourselves, and humbly beg pardon for the guilt. This is divided into private and public. Private confession is made by individuals, when they acknowledge that they have sinned, confess it to God and ask for forgiveness. This requires a diligent repentance for each individual sin, so that the zeal for repentance may be more ardently stirred up in us. Public confession is made by the whole assembly, when we openly testify that sins are in us and that we need divine grace through Christ. Both, however, ought to be made to God alone, because he alone is the one who forgives sins, which it is certain the Pharisees, however blinded, also saw. Matt. 9. Concerning confession made to a neighbour we say nothing here, since this is made for the sake of mutual friendship and forgiveness, not because it merits any grace before God. This confession comprises whatever pertains to true repentance and zeal for salvation. For the acknowledgment of sin must come first, since without this you have nothing to confess. Contrition of heart follows the acknowledgment of sin. For how is it that a man's spirit is not wholly broken, who thinks that he has sinned in so many and such unworthy ways against so kind a Father? Certain and solid confidence in the grace of God, which rests on Christ, cannot be absent from this. Just as you do not reveal a hidden disease to a physician unless you trust that you can be cured by his skill, so we will not truly confess our guilt to God unless we believe him to be the one who both wills and is able to remit all guilt. For that cry of Cain, Judas Iscariot and others of that stripe, that they have sinned, ought to be called not so much confession as an accusation of one's own conscience and a voluntary condemnation of a mind sliding into despair.

units.la: Verae Confessionis exempla multa in scripturis proponuntur. Huc enim referri debet, quae Israelitae temporibus Iudicum fecerunt, quoties vndiq; vrgentibus malis edocti, peccata agnosce-re, eadem Deo fateri & remissionem postulare coeperunt. Eiusdem exemplar perfectu Dauid est, qui vt se à Nathan peccati conuictu videt, exclamat: Peccaui domino: nec breui hac formula contentus postea copiose omnem suam imperfectionem fatetur & deplorat. 2. Sam. 12. Psal. 51. Confitetur qui ad Ioannem Baptistam egressi poenitentiae doctrina & aduentus Christi praedicationem non ofcitatibus animis audiuerunt. Mar. 1. Idem vero faciunt, qui cum Petru apostolum concionantem audiuissent, totis animis copuncti consilium postulant. Act. 2. Confitetur publicè Ephesij, non verbis modo, verumetiam factis, dum libros magicos publicè exurunt. Act. 19.
units.tr: Examples of true Confession are set forth in many places in Scripture. To this belongs what the Israelites did in the times of the Judges: whenever, taught by the evils pressing on them from every side, they began to recognise their sins, to confess the same to God and to ask for forgiveness. A perfect example of this is David, who, when he sees himself convicted of sin by Nathan, cries out: "I have sinned against the Lord." Not content with this brief formula, he afterwards confesses and laments all his imperfection at length. 2 Sam. 12; Psalm 51. Those confess who came out to John the Baptist and heard the teaching of repentance and the preaching of Christ's coming with open minds. Mark 1. Those also do the same who, when they had heard the apostle Peter preaching, were pricked in their hearts and asked for counsel. Acts 2. The Ephesians confessed publicly, not only in words but also in deeds, when they publicly burned their magic books. Acts 19.

units.la: Cum his si Confessionem auricularem conferas, nihil simile videbis. Primo equidem nullo scripturae sacrae vel praecepto vel exemplo confirmatur. Quae enim aduersarij ex scripturis in hius defensionem proferunt, partim tam inepta sunt, vt risum potius quam confutatione mereantur: partim manifeste detorta, sic vt nemo nō dolū & temeritate videat. Deinde nō Deo fit, sed hominibus, à quibus quae solius Dei sunt petere, manifesto impietatis & apostasiae scelere nō caret. Praeterea nec vera peccati agnitione, nec cordis contritionem, & multo minus fidem sibi coniunctam habet. Si enim peccatum vere agnoscunt, qui ad hanc confugiunt, cur non vident eius atrocitatem maiorem esse, quam vt priuata alicuius authoritate remitti possit? Si animo vere contriti sunt, cur à Confessione eadem flagitia iterat, quod plerosq; facere videmus? Si fide solida Deo nituntur per Christum, cur ad homines potius, quam hunc, confugiunt? cur suis potius quam Christi meritis satisfactionis gloria tribuunt? cur deniq; horribiles conscientiae angustias sentiunt, & nouis satisfactionibus sese indies excruciant? Non est ergo, vt de ista Confessione vere hypocritica quicquam cogitemus. Eam Ioannes requirit, quae peccatorum agnitionem, cordis contritionem, emendationis studium & fidem in Iesum Christum, ceu fidas & indiuulsas comites, sibi coniunctas habet. Huius exempla in scripturis & primitiuae ecclesiae historijs pasim obuia sunt. Habet eadem amplissimos fructus, de quibus hic quoq; Ioannes loquitur.
units.tr: If you compare with these the auricular Confession, you will see nothing similar. In the first place, it is confirmed by no precept or example of holy Scripture. Those passages which our adversaries bring forward from the Scriptures in its defence are partly so silly that they deserve laughter rather than refutation, and partly so plainly distorted that everyone can see the deceit and rashness in them. Next, it is made not to God but to men, and to ask of men what belongs to God alone is not free from the crime of manifest impiety and apostasy. Moreover, it has neither a true recognition of sin, nor contrition of heart, and still less faith joined with it. For if they truly acknowledge sin who flee to this confession, why do they not see that its atrocity is too great to be remitted by the authority of any private person? If they are truly contrite in spirit, why do they repeat the same wickednesses in Confession, as we see most of them do? If they rest on God through Christ with solid faith, why do they flee to men rather than to Him? Why do they ascribe the glory of satisfaction to their own merits rather than to those of Christ? Why, finally, do they feel the terrible straits of conscience and daily torment themselves with new satisfactions? There is therefore no reason for us to think anything of that truly hypocritical Confession. John requires that Confession which has the recognition of sins, contrition of heart, the desire for amendment and faith in Jesus Christ joined to it as faithful and inseparable companions. Examples of this are everywhere to be found in Scripture and in the histories of the primitive Church. The same Confession has the most abundant fruits, of which John also speaks here.

units.la: Si (inquit) confiteamur peccata nostra, fidelis est & iustus, ut remittat nobis peccata nostra, & emundet nos ab omni iniquitate. Quid vero amplius polliceri poterat? Remittuntur peccata, quibus iram Dei in nos prouocauimus. Nec remittetur modo, sed accedet emundatio ab omni iniquitate. At vbi peccata remissa, imo deleta sunt, ibidem Dei irā cedere oportet, quae solis peccatis, ceu fomite quodā nutriri solet. Testatur idem Dauid, qui post multas & varias conscientiae suae dimicationes inquit: Vbi peccatum meum tibi notum feci, & iniquitatem meā non celaui, cūq; cogitarem: Fatebor cōtra me transgressione mea Domino: protinus remisisti iniquitatē peccati mei. Psal. 32. Hoc ipsum parabolis aliquot Christus illustrat. Seruo enim, qui debebat decem millia talentorum, nec erat soluendo, donatur omne hoc & remittitur, cum debitum confessus domini gratiam imploraret. Matth. 18. Et publicanus, qui in extrema templi parte oculos ad Deum attollere non audes dicebat: Domine, propitius esto mihi peccatori: iustior pharisaeo domum redit. Luc. 18. Non tamen ergo D. Ioannes tanta diuinae gratiae dona verè confitentibus pollicetur.
units.tr: "If," he says, "we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." What could he promise more? Sins are forgiven by which we have provoked the wrath of God against us. And they will not only be forgiven, but cleansing from all unrighteousness will follow. But when sins are remitted, nay, blotted out, God's wrath ought likewise to cease, which is wont to be nourished by sins alone, as by a kind of fuel. David bears witness to the same, who, after many and various struggles of his conscience, says: "When I made my sin known to You, and did not hide my iniquity, and thought: I will confess my transgression against me to the Lord; immediately You forgave the iniquity of my sin." Psalm 32. Christ illustrates this very point by several parables. For the servant who owed ten thousand talents, and was not able to pay, is granted all this and it is remitted, when, having confessed the debt, he begged the lord for mercy. Matt. 18. And the publican, who dared not lift his eyes to God in the furthest part of the temple, was saying: "Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner"; he returned home more justified than the Pharisee. Luke 18. Therefore John does not promise such great gifts of divine grace to those who merely profess their sins without true confession.

units.la: Verūtamen ratione firma & solida, à Dei natura siue ingenio desumpta, promissionem hanc confirmat, ne quid dubitemus. Deus (inquit) fidelis & iustus est. Remittet ergo peccataijs[?], qui se peccauisse confitentes suā misericordiā implorāt. Fidelem vero vocat Deū pro verace, qui promissis suis neminē fallat. Quare sensus est: Deus cū verax fit, promissa praestat. Promisit autem ad se cōfugientibus peccatorū omniū remissionē, quod scripturae omnes testantur. Nā apud Prophetam ait: Si peccata vestra fuerint vt purpura, supra niuem dealbabuntur: si rubent instar cocci, sicut natiua lana fient. Isa. 1. Item: Ego deleui transgressiones tuas, vt densas nebulas, & vt nubem peccata tua. Isa. 44. Et rursum: Ego ego ille ipse sum, qui deleo transgressiones tuas, idque propter me, & peccatorum tuorum non amplius recordabor. Isa. 43. Similiter: Conuertimini (ait) ad me, & ego conuertar ad vos. Zach. 1. Praeterea: Num desidero aut volo mortem peccatoris, dicit dominus Deus? Annon magis, vt conuertatur, & recedat à vijs suis, & viuat? Ezech. 18. An ergo Deum, qui ipsa est veritas, tot & tantis promissionibus suis defuturum putabimus? Non opinor.
units.tr: Yet he confirms this promise with a firm and solid reason, drawn from the nature or disposition of God, so that we may have no doubt. "God," he says, "is faithful and just. He will therefore forgive our sins, when we, confessing that we have sinned, implore His mercy." He calls God "faithful" in the sense of "true," who deceives none of those to whom He has made promises. The meaning therefore is: since God is true, He performs what He has promised. Now He has promised the forgiveness of all sins to those who flee to Him, as all the Scriptures testify. For in the Prophet He says: "If your sins are like purple, they shall be made white as snow; if they are red like scarlet, they shall become like natural wool." Isa. 1. Likewise: "I have blotted out your transgressions like a thick cloud, and your sins like a cloud." Isa. 44. And again: "I, I am He who blots out your transgressions, and for My own sake, and I will remember your sins no more." Isa. 43. Similarly: "Turn to Me," he says, "and I will turn to you." Zech. 1. Besides: "Do I desire or will the death of the sinner, says the Lord God? Is it not rather that he should turn and depart from his ways and live?" Ezek. 18. Shall we then think that God, who is truth itself, will fail in so many and such great promises of His? I think not.

units.la: Facit vero huc, quod iustitiam quoq; Dei allegat. Sed qua ratione (inquis) concludit Ioannes? Deus iustus est: Ergo remittet peccata nostra? Quis non potius, peccata puniturum dicat, cū iustus sit? Admirabilis sane ratio, sed plana & perspicua, si Christum solem iustitiae huic inferamus. Supra enim diximus, à Confessione vera fidem in Christum non posse abesse. At qui hanc habent, Christi merito iustificati sunt. Iustificatis ergo debetur iustitiae praemiū, gratiae nimirum diuinae haereditas. Adhaec filium suum in hoc dedit, vt per hunc reconciliaret sibi cuncta, pacificatis per sanguinem crucis eius per eundem siue quæ in terra sunt, siue quæ in cœlis. Col.1. Eos ergo, qui peccata sua agnoscentes per filium suum ipsi reconciliari cupiunt, non potest non recipere, nisi in filium suum iniustus fieri velit. Sed & filio suo omnem potestatem tradidit in cœlis & in terra. Matth.28. Inuitat vero hic ad se laborantes atq; oneratos, & venientibus requiem pollicetur. Eosdem ergo pater repellere non potest, nisi potestatem, filio iustè & legitimè traditam, iniusto modo eripiat. Qua enim culpa hac spoliari meruit, qui humiliauit se patri obediens factus usque ad mortem Crucis. Phil.2.
units.tr: Moreover, what he adds about the justice of God is also to the point. But by what reasoning (you will say) does John conclude? God is just: therefore He will forgive our sins? Who would not rather say that He will punish sins, since He is just? A wonderful reasoning indeed, but plain and clear, if we bring in Christ, the sun of righteousness, here. For above we said that true faith in Christ cannot be absent from true Confession. But those who have this faith are justified by the merit of Christ. To the justified, therefore, the reward of righteousness is due, namely the inheritance of divine grace. Moreover, He gave His Son for this, that through Him He might reconcile all things to Himself, having made peace through the blood of His cross, through Him, whether things on earth or things in heaven. Col. 1. He therefore cannot but receive those who, acknowledging their sins, desire to be reconciled to Him through His Son, unless He wishes to become unjust toward His Son. But He has also given all power in heaven and on earth to His Son. Matt. 28. And here He invites those who labour and are burdened to Himself, and promises rest to those who come. The Father therefore cannot repel the same persons, unless He takes away by an unjust means the power justly and lawfully given to His Son. For by what fault could He deserve to be deprived of this, who humbled Himself, becoming obedient to the Father even unto the death of the Cross? Phil. 2.

units.la: Sed ô stupendam Dei bonitatem. O admirabilem nostræ salutis certitudinem. O sapientiam diuinæ mentis inscrutabilem. Iustitia Dei ad mortem, ad damnationem, ad æterna inferorum supplicia omnes uocabamur. At Christi merito factū est, ut ideo nos exaudire & in gratiam recipere uelit, quia iustus est. Quid ergo ad hunc patrem accedere metuimus? Quid ô peccator trepidas? An deum tam tibi infensum credis, ut propter te in filium suum dilectū iniustus uideri & esse uelit? Imò ut huic quod debet exoluat, tibi benignus erit & propitius. Hæc tā admiranda salutis mysteria qui ignorant, eò cæcitatis deueniūt, ut nouis mediatoribus extra Christum opus esse exist-ment, & Confessione peccatorum, quę soli Deo debetur, non contenti, nescio quem scenicum ludum ex pœnitentia Christiana faciant. Sed copiosius de his dicendi locus fortasis alibi dabitur commodior. Reliquat adhuc postrema præsentis loci pars, quæ modo paucis absoluetur.
units.tr: But oh, the astonishing goodness of God! Oh, the admirable certainty of our salvation! Oh, the inscrutable wisdom of the divine mind! We were all called to the justice of God unto death, unto damnation, unto the eternal punishments of hell. But by the merit of Christ it has come about that He wishes to hear us and receive us into favour precisely because He is just. Why then do we fear to approach this Father? Why, O sinner, do you tremble? Do you believe God so hostile to you that for your sake He would wish to seem and be unjust toward His beloved Son? Rather, in order to pay to Him what He owes, He will be kind and gracious to you. Those who are ignorant of these so wonderful mysteries of salvation fall into such blindness that they think there is need of new mediators outside Christ, and not content with the Confession of sins, which is due to God alone, they make I know not what theatrical game out of Christian repentance. But perhaps a more suitable place for speaking of these things at greater length will be given elsewhere. There remains still the last part of the present passage, which will be finished in a few words.

units.la: III. Si dixerimus, non peccauimus: mendacem facimus eum, & sermo eius non est in nobis. Redit ad propositionem ante præmissam, ut penitius in nostræ infirmitatis cognitionem nos perducat. Non contentus autem eos, qui se peccatores esse negant, mendacij accusauisse, grauius iam loqui incipit. Duo enim absurda hinc sequi docet. Primum est: Si nos peccauisse negemus, mendace facimus Deum. Horribilis quidem, sed uera & certa sententia. Deus enim inquit: Figmenta cordis humani praua sunt ab ineunte ætate. Gen.8. Idem in filio suo omnes peccati arguit. Si enim non peccauimus, cur ille in mundum missus est? cur mulctam nostrę correctionis sustinuit? cur in crucę suspensus mortis genus Dei sententia maledictum subijt? Si non ægrotabamus, quid medicum mittere opus erat? Vides ergo non ueritatem modo Dei, sed & eiusdem iustitiam, & sapientiam periclitari, si nos peccatores esse negemus. Alterum absurdum est, quod uerbum eius in nobis esse negat. Verbum Dei enim clamat: Nos omnes tanquā ouis erravimus, unusquisq; uiā suam secta-tus est. Isa.53. Verbum Dei est, quod legitur: Dominus è cœlis super filios hominū prospexit, ut videret num sit, qui aut saperet, aut Dei studiosus esset. Sed cuncti defecerant, omnes pariter corrupti erant, nullus erat qui quod bonum est faceret, ne unus quidem. Psal.13. Verbum Dei inquā est: Omnes peccauerunt, & destituuntur gloria Dei, &c. Rom 3. Quis ergo uerbum dei in illo esse dicet, qui tam claris Dei sententijs & pronunciatis contradicere audit? At nisi sermonem ipsius in nobis manentem habuerimus, nec ipsum diligemus nos, nec ab ipso diligemur. Ioan.14.
units.tr: III. "If we say that we have not sinned, we make Him a liar, and His word is not in us." He returns to the proposition set forth before, in order to lead us more deeply into the knowledge of our weakness. Not content, however, to have accused of lying those who deny that they are sinners, he now begins to speak more severely. For he shows that two absurdities follow from this. The first is: if we deny that we have sinned, we make God a liar. A horrible saying indeed, but true and certain. For God says: "The imaginations of the human heart are evil from its youth." Gen. 8. He also accuses all men of sin in His Son. For if we have not sinned, why was He sent into the world? Why did He undergo the punishment of our correction? Why, hanged on the cross, did He undergo the kind of death under God's sentence of a curse? If we were not sick, what need was there to send a physician? You see, then, that not only the truth of God but also His justice and wisdom are imperilled if we deny that we are sinners. The second absurdity is that he denies His word is in us. For the Word of God cries out: "We all like sheep have gone astray, each one has turned to his own way." Isa. 53. It is the Word of God that reads: "The Lord looked down from heaven upon the sons of men, to see whether there was any who understood, or who sought after God. But all had turned aside, all were alike corrupted; there was none who did good, no, not one." Psalm 13. It is the Word of God, I say: "All have sinned, and come short of the glory of God," etc. Rom. 3. Who then will say that the word of God is in him who dares to contradict such clear sentences and declarations of God? But unless we have His word abiding in us, neither will we love Him, nor will we be loved by Him. John 14.

units.la: Iam ergo luce clarius constat, quas ob causas apostolus tam serio in hoc fit, ut nos peccatores esse demonstret. Qui enim hoc negant, non ipsi modò mendaces sunt, sed & Deum (quod dictu horrendum est) mendacij arguere conantur. Iidem seipsos à merito Christi & gratia Dei separant. Sternunt hæc uæsfanam Anabaptistarum insolentia, qui innocentia perfecta gloriari audent. Cadit, imò ruit, superba propriæ iustitiæ fiducia. Exploditur & exibilatur meritorum supererogationis diabolica gloriatio. Si enim peccatores fumus omnes, quo merito apud Deum gloriabimur? An uero nostri Deus indiget? Quæ uero insania est, in alios deriuare uel transfundere, quæ ipse feceris? An te plus præstitisse putare audes, quàm Deo debeas? Agnoscamus ergo fratres imperfectionem & infirmitatem nostram. Confiteamur peccata nostra domino, mente contrita & humiliata. Imploremus eiusdem gratiam. Sic enim fiet, ut remittat nobis peccata nostra, & emundet nos ab omni iniquitate nostra, per sanguinem & meritum Iesu Christi filij sui, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria, & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Now, then, it is clearer than daylight why the apostle is so earnest in showing that we are sinners. Those who deny this are not only liars themselves, but also try (which is dreadful to say) to charge God with lying. These same people separate themselves from the merit of Christ and the grace of God. The arrogance of the Anabaptists, who dare to boast of perfect innocence, scatters these things. The proud confidence in one's own righteousness falls, indeed collapses. The devilish boasting of works of supererogation is exploded and hissed off the stage. For if we are all sinners, on what merit will we glory before God? Surely God does not need what is ours? What madness is it to pass on or transfer to others what you yourself have done? Do you dare to think you have done more than you owe to God? Let us therefore, brothers, acknowledge our imperfection and weakness. Let us confess our sins to the Lord, with contrite and humbled minds. Let us implore his grace. For so it will come about that he forgives us our sins and cleanses us from all our iniquity, through the blood and merit of Jesus Christ, his Son, to whom blessing, honour, glory and power are due for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT II. HOMILIA V.
units.tr: CHAPTER II. HOMILY V.

units.la: FILIOLI mei, hæc scribo uobis, ne peccetis. Et si quis peccauerit, aduocatum habemus apud patrem, Iesum Christum, iustum. Et ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris: non pro nostris autem tantum, sed etiam pro peccatis totius mundi.
units.tr: MY little children, I write these things to you, that you sin not. And if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. And he is the propitiation for our sins; and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world.

units.la: VT homines externis Dei donis, quæ ad corporum incolumitatem seruandam pertinent, pro corrupto carnis ingenio ad suam perniciem crebro abutuntur: ita hoc ipsum in iis facere consueuerunt, quæ vt animarum saluti inseruiant, diuinitus data sunt. Possent exempli loco nobis esse Iudæi, qui templo & toto illo Leuitici sacerdotij cultu vrie abusi sunt, dum alij omnem salutis rationem in hoc consistere putauerunt, alij vero eundem omnium suorum scelerum & flagitiorum prætextum habuere. Sed quid opus est exempla longe petita producere, cum inter nos, qui Christi nomine gloriamur, idem quotidie fiat? Si enim per euangelij doctrinam vitæ innocentia, charitatis studium, & quæcunque alia fideles decent, exigantur: mox iustitiarij hypocritæ, vel pharisæi operum iustitiam asseri contendunt. Quòd si contra illos Christi meritum vrgeas, & nos omnes natura peccatores esse, ac solius Christi merito saluari prædices, statim cum huius seculi filijs dimicandum erit, qui hoc prætextu effrenem carnis licentiam quærunt. Non ignorarunt hoc Apostoli, qui magno studio doctrinam suam sic mode-rantur, vt neutra pars, quod inde venetur, habere possit. Est autem huic rei cumprimis accommodus præsens hic locus, quo quicquid in hac causa dici poterit, dilectus Christi discipulus summatim comprehendit. Primò enim, quia omnes nos peccatores esse dixerat, ne quis inde maiorem peccandi licentiam nobis concedi putaret, docet longè alium huius doctrinæ vsum esse, vt nimirum peccandi consuetudinem serio studeamus deponere. Deinde peccatoribus opem & salutem in Christo Iesu monstrat, cuius officium sufficienter describit. Nos de singulis, quantum spiritus domini dare dignatus fuerit, ordine dicemus.
units.tr: Just as men often abuse the external gifts of God, which pertain to preserving the health of the body, to their own destruction, through the corrupt nature of the flesh, so they have also customarily done the same with those things which were divinely given to serve the salvation of souls. The Jews could serve as an example for us, who abused the temple and the entire cult of the Levitical priesthood to their own harm: some thought that the whole method of salvation consisted in this, while others used the same thing as a pretext for all their crimes and vices. But why bring forth examples from far away, since among us, who glory in the name of Christ, the same thing happens every day? For if, through the teaching of the gospel, innocence of life, zeal for love, and whatever else befits the faithful are required, at once the self-righteous hypocrites, or Pharisees, insist that righteousness of works is being asserted. But if you press against them the merit of Christ, and proclaim that we are all sinners by nature and are saved by the merit of Christ alone, then at once you will have to contend with the children of this age, who seek under this pretext an unbridled license of the flesh. The apostles were not unaware of this, and with great care they so moderated their teaching that neither party could hunt out from it anything to use. Now this present passage is especially suited to this matter, since the beloved disciple of Christ briefly sums up whatever can be said in this cause. First, because he had said that we are all sinners, lest anyone think that a greater license to sin is thereby granted to us, he teaches that the use of this doctrine is quite different, namely that we should earnestly strive to lay aside the habit of sinning. Then he shows to sinners help and salvation in Christ Jesus, whose office he describes sufficiently. We shall speak of each of these, in order, as much as the Spirit of the Lord has deigned to grant.

units.la: I. Filioli mei, hæc scribo uobis, ne peccetis. Breuis quidem, sed perquàm necessaria admonitio. Dicat enim aliquis: Si confiteri debemus nos peccatores esse, agedum peccemus pro carnis arbitrio, vt quod confiteri possimus, semper nobis ad manum fit. Negat ergo hanc esse suæ doctrinæ consequentiam, nec ideo se illa dixisse, vt carni habenas laxaret: sed vt afflictis cõscientijs viam & medium salutis ostenderet. Adhæc cum peccatum præcipuam iræ Dei causam esse constet, per quam omnis generis calamitates, adeoq; ipsa mors, nobis imminent, quis non videt, nobis cum peccati accusamur, purificatione potius & emendatione, quàm nouis peccatis opus esse? Sed prodest singula verba, quibus hic vtitur, excutere.
units.tr: I. My little children, I write these things to you, that you sin not. A brief admonition indeed, but exceedingly necessary. For someone may say: If we ought to confess that we are sinners, come, let us sin at the will of the flesh, so that there may always be something at hand to confess. He therefore denies that this is the consequence of his doctrine, nor did he say those things so that he might loosen the reins for the flesh, but so that he might show afflicted consciences the way and means of salvation. Moreover, since it is established that sin is the chief cause of God's wrath, through which every kind of calamity, and indeed death itself, hangs over us, who does not see that when we are accused of sins we have need of purification and amendment rather than of new sins? But it is useful to examine the individual words which he uses here.

units.la: Filiolos suos vocat, quibus hæc scribit. Est hæc summi amoris vox, quo omnes pastores erga commissum sibi gregem affectos esse decet. Quia enim per ministros verbi Dei prædicatione generantur fideles, non immerito eorundem filij dici possunt. Sic Paulus Galatas suos filiolos nominat, quos denuo parturiat, donec in ipsis Christus formetur. Gal.4. Et Corinthios plures quidem pædagogos habere posse fatetur, patrem verò ipsorum se esse, quia per euangelium ipsos genuerit. I.Corinth.4. Neq; hoc cum Christi præcepto pugnat, qui ne patrem nobis in terra vocemus, prohibet. De ijs enim loquitur, qui sectas nouas profesi, ab hominibus, quos sibi tanquam patres salutis imitandos proposuerant, denominari volebant. Apostoli verò non nisi ministerij respectu patres haberi volunt, seq; regenerationis huius dūtaxat ministros agnoscunt, omnè verò eius virtutem & effectu æterno semini, verbo Dei, & spiritui sancto, qui illud in nobis viuificat, tribuūt[?]. I.Pet.1. Cæterū habent quod hic obseruēt tā ministri quàm qui ipsorū curæ cõmisi sunt. Vident enim ministri paterno affectu in ecclesia administranda opus esse, vt ab ouibus, perinde vt à filijs parentes, audiatur. Quo iure aut hoc ab ipsis postulabunt, si ipsi non fidi patres, sed scurræ, aut etiam tyranni, esse soleant? Discit populus, ministris eum amorem & reuerentia deberi, quem naturali & diuina lege parentibus nostris debemus. Quòd homines nati sumus, parentum ministerio factum est. At quòd regenerati in filiorum & hæredum Dei numerū adoptamur, præcipuè quidem diuinæ gratiæ & bonitatis opus est, sed eadem pastorum ministerio vtitur, quibus honore suum negare nō possumus, nisi in ipsum Deum, qui per hos nos regenerari voluit, iniurij esse velimus.
units.tr: He calls those to whom he writes these things his little children. This is a word of the highest love, with which all ministers ought to be affected toward the flock committed to them. For since the faithful are begotten through the preaching of the ministers of the Word of God, they can rightly be called their children. So Paul calls the Galatians his little children, whom he again brings forth in labor until Christ be formed in them. Gal. 4. And he confesses that the Corinthians may have many instructors, but that he is their father, because he begot them through the gospel. 1 Cor. 4. Nor does this conflict with Christ's precept, who forbids us to call anyone on earth our father. For he speaks of those who professed new sects and wished to be named after men whom they had proposed to imitate as fathers of salvation. But the apostles wish to be regarded as fathers only with respect to their ministry, and they acknowledge themselves to be only ministers of this regeneration, while they ascribe all its power and effect to the eternal seed, the Word of God, and to the Holy Spirit, who quickens it in us. 1 Pet. 1. Moreover, both the ministers and those committed to their care have something here to observe. For the ministers see that, in administering the Church, a fatherly affection is necessary, so that they may be heard by the sheep as parents are heard by their children. By what right will they demand this from them, if they themselves are not faithful fathers but are accustomed to be buffoons or even tyrants? The people learns that the love and reverence which we owe to our parents by natural and divine law are due to the ministers. That we were born as men came about through the ministry of parents. But that, having been regenerated, we are adopted into the number of the children and heirs of God is chiefly the work of divine grace and goodness, yet it uses the ministry of pastors, to whom we cannot deny their honor unless we wish to do injury to God himself, who willed that through these we should be regenerated.

units.la: Hæc scribo vobis. Apostoli ad prædicandum missi fuerūt. Christus enim illis ait: Ite in orbem universum, & prædicate Euangelium omni creaturæ. Marci 16. Non tamen adeo rigidi verbo-rum vel literæ observatores fuerunt, ut ore tantū prædicare, & à scribendo abstinere voluerint. Quin sui ministerij scopum diligenter observarūt, qui is erat, ut Christi cognitionem lōgè lateq; propagarent, de illo ubiq; testarentur, & eidem ex omnibus gentibus discipulos adducerēt. Actorum 1.Matth.28. Huic rei cum missas hinc inde literas cumprimis servire viderent, suo officio ne-quaquâ deesse voluerunt, sed scriptis suis fideles crebrò monuerunt de ijs, quæ diligentiori observatione indigebant. Deinde posteris quoque profuit, imò valdè necessaria fuit, hæc industria. Si enim tenebriones quidam, extantibus Apostolorum scriptis, infinitas nugas & constitutiones pla-nè impias ipsorum nomine ecclesijs obtrudere ausi sunt, quid non facturos putamus, si nulla apostolicorum scriptorum authoritate fuissent prohibiti? Nobis verò imitanda est hæc ipsorum sedulitas & industria, ut omnem viam ingrediamur, quæ euangelicæ doctrinæ propagationi servire potest. Nec enim audiendi sunt, qui nostro seculo nihil scribi volunt, eò quòd scriptis eiusmodi aduersariorum animi magis exacerbentur. An verò, ut paucorum gratiam venemur, aut iram declinemus, multorum fratrum, quorum infirmitas consolationem & institutionem exigit, salu-tem negligere convenit? Næ isti homines egregiè sapiunt, qui euangelium ita doceri posse putant, ut nemini bilem commoveat, cum nec ipsum Christum ea felicitate usum esse cōstet. Aut ergo Christum abnegent & euāgelium omne explodant, aut cum Christo & pro Christi gloria cru-cem & adversa ferre discant. Paulus quavis occasione Christum prædicari gaudebat. Phil.1. Idem opportunè & importunè instare jubet. 2.Tim.4. Et nos illud medium nobis eripi patiamur, quo euangelij doctrina omnibus seculis felicissimè disseminata est? Imò Apostolorum exemplo lin-guam, manus, pedes, omnia denique membra movere & omnes nervos intendere decet, ut quàm plurimos Christo lucrifaciamus.
units.tr: I write these things to you. The apostles were sent to preach. For Christ said to them: Go into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature. Mark 16. Yet they were not so strict observers of words or of the letter that they wished only to preach by mouth and to abstain from writing. Indeed they carefully observed the aim of their ministry, which was that they should spread the knowledge of Christ far and wide, bear witness of him everywhere, and bring disciples to him from all nations. Acts 1; Matt. 28. Seeing that letters sent hither and thither were especially serviceable to this end, they were by no means willing to be lacking in their office, but often admonished the faithful by their writings about those things which needed more careful observation. Moreover, this diligence was of benefit, indeed very necessary, to posterity as well. For if certain wretches, though the writings of the apostles are extant, have dared to thrust upon the churches endless trifles and utterly impious constitutions in their name, what do we think they would have done if they had not been restrained by the authority of the apostolic writings? We ought to imitate this zeal and diligence of theirs, so that we may enter upon every way which can serve the propagation of the evangelical doctrine. For those men are not to be heard who in our age wish that nothing be written, because the minds of adversaries are more exasperated by writings of this kind. Or is it fitting, in order to seek the favor of a few, or to avoid their anger, to neglect the salvation of many brothers, whose weakness demands consolation and instruction? Indeed, those men are wise in a remarkable way who think that the gospel can be taught in such a manner that it stirs anger in no one, since it is not established that Christ himself enjoyed such good fortune. Therefore either let them deny Christ and reject the whole gospel, or let them learn to bear the cross and adversity with Christ and for the glory of Christ. Paul rejoiced that Christ was preached on any occasion. Phil. 1. He likewise bids us press on in season and out of season. 2 Tim. 4. And shall we allow that means to be snatched from us, by which the doctrine of the gospel has been most happily spread abroad in all ages? Indeed, following the example of the apostles, it is fitting to move tongue, hands, feet, and in short all the limbs, and to strain every sinew, so that we may gain as many as possible for Christ.

units.la: Ne peccetis. Generale hoc præceptum est, quod omnibus scripturis præcipitur. Quia enim Deus non nisi cum sanctis & puris communionem habere potest, peccato autem prophanari so-lent homines, illud ubique impugnatur. Apud Isaiam certè peccata maceriam illam esse dicit, quæ inter Deum & nos erecta, ne ullo gratiæ ipsius fruamur, prohibet. Isa.59. Et alibi preces exaudiri negat, quòd manus sanguine pollutas ad ipsum extendant. Isa.1. Præterea, ut primis parentibus ob peccatum omnis generis miseriæ decernuntur, quales sunt, agriculturæ labores, sterilitas, mor-bi, dolores partus, curæ, solicitudines, paupertas, & si quæ alia sunt adversa: ita in lege sua domi-nus eadem mala transgressoribus mandatorum suorum nunquam non interminatur: gratiâ verò & beneficentiam iis promittit, qui præceptis eius obtemperaverint. Eodem referri debet, quod in euangelio dominus adulteræ, quâ à lapidationis supplicio liberaverat, Vade (inquit) & posthac ne peccaveris. Joan.8. Idem paralytico, quem à morbo annorum triginta & octo curaverat, ait: Ecce sanus factus es: ne posthac pecces, ne quid deterius tibi contingat. Joan.5. Ut ergo adulterâ non ideo liberat dominus, ut adulteriis novis sese polluat: nec paralytico medetur, ut peccandi studium rursus sectari possit, sed ab utrisque veram pœnitentiam & innocentiam requirit: Ita nec nos Christi sanguine ideo à peccatis abluimur, ut peccati sordibus denuo immersi polluamur, sed ut eam immunditiem, quam tanto tamque pretioso lavacro purgari oportuit, totis animis detestemur. Pertinet huc quæ Paulus scribit, Ro.6. Quid igitur dicemus? Manebimus in peccato, ut gratia abundet? Absit. Qui mortui sumus peccato, quomodo posthac viuemus in eode? An ignoratis, quòd quicunque baptizati sumus in Christum Jesum, in morte eius baptizati sumus? Sepulti igitur sumus una cum illo per baptismum in mortem: ut quemadmodum excitatus est Christus ex mortuis per gloriam patris, ita & nos in novitate vitæ ambulemus, &c. Infiniti sunt eius generis loci, qui hoc ipsum sedulò nobis commendant. Rectè ergo Joânes inquit: Filioli mei, hæc scribo vobis, ne peccetis. Cùm verò nos omnes peccare constet, sed & justus in die septies labatur, quis non videt perpetuam à nobis pœnitentiam exigi? Jugulat hæc sententia pseudoeuāgelicos nostri seculi, qui doctrinam Christia-nam & eius patrocinium professi, vitâ viuunt parum euāgelicâ, dum carni habenas ad omnem libidinem laxant. Quibus non immeritò illud obijci poterat: Quid tibi vis, quòd commemoras statuta mea? cur ore tuo fœdus meum jactas? Cū odio habeas disciplinam, & verba mea post te abijcias. Psal.50. Jugulat itè Papistas calumniatores, qui euāgelij prædicatione nos peccandi licentiam plantare dicunt. Christus equidem in suo nomine peccatorum remissione prædicari vult. Sed idem & pœnitentiam docere jubet. Luc.24. Et Joannes, qui antea dixerat: Sanguis filij Dei emundat nos ab omni peccato: idem nūc clamat: Filioli mei, hæc scribo vobis, ne peccetis. Non est ergo quòd ca-lumnias adversariorum multum moremur. In hoc potius toti sumus, ut vitæ nostræ conversatio juxta euāgelij doctrinam instituatur, ne aliquis hanc calumniandi occasionem habere possit.
units.tr: That you sin not. This is a general precept, which is enjoined in all the Scriptures. For since God can have fellowship only with the holy and pure, and men are wont to be profaned by sin, sin is everywhere opposed. In Isaiah, certainly, he says that sins are that wall which, erected between God and us, prevents us from enjoying any of his grace. Isa. 59. And elsewhere he denies that prayers are heard, because they stretch out hands polluted with blood. Isa. 1. Moreover, just as for our first parents every kind of misery was decreed because of sin, such as labors of tilling the field, barrenness, diseases, pains of childbirth, cares, anxieties, poverty, and whatever other adversities there are, so in his law the Lord always threatens these same evils to the transgressors of his commandments, but promises grace and blessing to those who have obeyed his precepts. To the same point should be referred what the Lord said in the gospel to the adulteress, whom he had freed from the punishment of stoning: Go, he said, and from now on sin no more. John 8. To the paralytic, whom he had cured of a disease of thirty-eight years, he said: Behold, you are made whole; sin no more, lest something worse befall you. John 5. Therefore, just as the Lord did not free the adulteress so that she might pollute herself with new adulteries, nor did he heal the paralytic so that he might again pursue the zeal for sinning, but from both he requires true repentance and innocence, so neither are we cleansed from sins by the blood of Christ so that we may again be plunged into the filth of sin and defiled, but so that we may detest with our whole souls that uncleanness which had to be purged by so great and so precious a laver. To this pertains what Paul writes in Rom. 6: What then shall we say? Shall we remain in sin, so that grace may abound? God forbid. We who have died to sin, how shall we live any longer in it? Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore together with him through baptism into death, so that just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life, etc. There are countless passages of this kind which earnestly commend this very thing to us. Rightly, therefore, John says: My little children, I write these things to you, that you sin not. But since it is certain that we all sin, and that the just man falls seven times a day, who does not see that a perpetual repentance is required of us? This sentence cuts the throat of the pseudo-evangelicals of our age, who, professing the Christian doctrine and its patronage, live a life hardly evangelical, while they loosen the reins of the flesh to every lust. To them it could rightly be objected: What do you mean by reciting my statutes, and by boasting of my covenant in your mouth? Since you hate discipline and cast my words behind you. Ps. 50. It likewise cuts the throat of the Papist calumniators, who say that by the preaching of the gospel we plant a license to sin. Christ indeed wills that remission of sins be preached in his name. But he also bids repentance be taught. Luke 24. And John, who had earlier said: The blood of the Son of God cleanses us from all sin, now cries out: My little children, I write these things to you, that you sin not. Therefore there is no need for us to linger long over the calumnies of the adversaries. Rather, let us be wholly intent on this, that the conduct of our life be ordered according to the doctrine of the gospel, so that no one may have the occasion of slandering it.

units.la: At dicat aliquis: Durum, imò intolerabile est, quod Ioannes præcipit. Quem enim mortalium dabimus, qui nō peccet? Figmenta cordis humani praua sunt ab ineunte ætate. Gene.8. Quid ergo dicemus, si in peccatis nos constitutos esse videamus? Num de Dei gratia desperabimus? Vel num ad nostrorum meritorum fiduciam conuersi proprijs satisfactionibus nitemur? Istis al-tera huius loci parte apostolus respondet, & neutrum fieri debere docet. Sic enim ait:
units.tr: But someone may say: this is harsh, indeed intolerable, what John commands. For who among mortals will we find who does not sin? "The imaginations of the human heart are evil from youth." Gen. 8. What then shall we say, if we see ourselves caught in sins? Shall we despair of the grace of God? Or, turning to confidence in our own merits, shall we strive by our own satisfactions? The apostle answers these things with the second part of this passage, and teaches that neither should be done. For he says thus:

units.la: I I. Et si quis peccauerit, aduocatum habemus apud patrem, Iesum Christum, iustum. Non ergo peccatum sic prohibet, quasi arbitretur, nos illud in vniuersum cauere posse. Sed deuotum peccandi studium vetare voluit, quod in Christianis hominibus locum habere non potest. Manent equidem in his peccati reliquiæ, & cum Paulo apostolo inueniunt legem peccati in membris suis, quæ non contradicit modò legi diuinæ, verumetiam inuitos rapit, vt ea faciant, quæ iuxta internum hominem detestantur. Rom.7. Hinc quotidiani illi lapsus & exorbitationes crebræ extra viam vitæ, quæ in scripturis proponitur. Pariunt eædem conscientiarum luctas & graues diuexationes, quas apud infirmiores satan excitat, vt propter delictorum suorum multitudinem vel atrocitatem de Dei gratia dubitare incipiant. Et multi cum Caino dicere incipiunt: Maior est iniquitas mea, quàm vt possit remitti. Genef.4. Multi rursum imperitiores adhuc, vel proprijs cogitationibus decepti, vel aliorum somnijs & impostoris seducti, nouas salutis vias, & nouos mediatores, quorum intercessione cum Deo in gratiam redire possint, sectantur. Hic ergo nos probè instituti esse conuenit, cum vtrinq; certissima & præsentissima salutis pericula instent, vt nisi mediam viam constanter sequare, tutus incedere non possis. Audiamus ergo Ioannem, qui instar altiuolantis aquilæ omnia humanæ rationis nubila superans, in æterna diuini Solis luce verum & infallibile salutis medium commonstrat. Si quis peccauerit (inquit) quod vtiq; omnibus contingit, habemus aduocatum apud patrem, &c. Hæc ipsissima est euangelij vox, quæ apud Deum peccatoribus quoq; gratiam monstrat. Sic enim dicere vult: Scio quidem à peccato immunem esse neminem, & quotidie in multis nos peccare & impingere. Sed nemo propterea desperet. Nemo quo-que vel propriæ rationis dictata, vel aliorum traditiones audiat. Ego salutis viam, adeoq; ipsam sa-lutem monstrabo fideliter. Quia peccatores sumus, & proinde rei transgressionis coram Dei tribunali consistimus, aduocato opus est, qui causam nostram agat, qui defendat, & à capitali æternæ damnationis sententia liberet. At non opus est oculos & mentem circumferre diutius, vbi nam locorum is inueniri possit. Iam nunc enim habemus aduocatum, qui causam nostram & vult suscipere lubens, & susceptam digne agere et tueri poterit. Aduocatum (inquam) habemus, nō aduocatos. Vnus enim est, non plures. Non ergo periculum erit, ne contemptis melioribus, ineptiorem aliquem aut minus gratiosum deligamus. Vnus est, qui & gratia valet apud patrem, quia filius: & iudicij illius rigorem sustinere potest, quia iustus est. Est is Iesus Christus, de cuius erga nos voluntate dubitare non licet, cum & homo pro nobis factus sit, & sanguinem proprium propec-catorum nostrorum emundatione fuderit. Ad hunc ergo confugite, qui vos peccasse sentitis. Huic conscientiæ vestræ dolores & angustias credite. Huius intercessionem expetite, & salus obtinget illico. Ipse enim clamat: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego requiem vobis præstabo. Matth.11. O lætam vocem & nullis diuitijs compensandam. O bonitatis diuinæ profunditatem inscrutabilem, quæ peccatoribus tam tutum & fidum salutis asylum præparare voluit. Quis in peccatis desperet amplius? Quis per auia humanarum traditionum potius errare, quàm breui hac & tuta via ingredi posthac volet? Quia vero ea est multorum cæcitas & amentia, ne quid grauius dicam, vt hoc aduocato & mediatore non contenti, alio confugiant, & salutem alibi quærant, huius rei tractatio altius paulò repetenda erit.
units.tr: "And if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous." He therefore does not forbid sin as though he thought we could guard against it altogether. But he wished to forbid a settled eagerness for sinning, which cannot have a place among Christian people. Indeed, remnants of sin remain in them, and with the apostle Paul they find a law of sin in their members, which not only contradicts the divine law but even against their will carries them off to do those things which they detest in the inner man. Rom. 7. Hence those daily slips and frequent wanderings outside the way of life which is set forth in the Scriptures. The same things produce struggles of conscience and grievous troubles, which Satan stirs up among the weaker ones, so that because of the multitude or atrocity of their offences they begin to doubt the grace of God. And many begin to say with Cain: "My iniquity is greater than can be forgiven." Gen. 4. Again, many who are still more unskilled, either deceived by their own thoughts or seduced by the dreams and impostures of others, pursue new ways of salvation and new mediators, through whose intercession they might be restored to favour with God. Here, then, it is fitting that we be thoroughly instructed, since on both sides the most certain and most present dangers of salvation threaten, so that unless you follow the middle way steadily, you cannot walk safely. Let us hear John, then, who, like a high-soaring eagle, rising above all the clouds of human reason, shows in the eternal light of the divine Sun the true and infallible means of salvation. "If anyone sins" (he says), which certainly happens to all, "we have an advocate with the Father," etc. This is the very voice of the gospel, which shows grace with God even to sinners. For he means to say thus: I know indeed that no one is free from sin, and that we daily sin and stumble in many things. But let no one therefore despair. Let no one listen either to the dictates of his own reason or to the traditions of others. I will faithfully show the way of salvation, and salvation itself. Because we are sinners, and therefore stand as guilty of transgression before the tribunal of God, we need an advocate who will plead our cause, who will defend us, and will free us from the capital sentence of eternal damnation. But there is no need to turn eyes and mind about for a long time, asking where such a one may be found. For now we have an advocate who both willingly wishes to take up our cause, and will be able to plead and maintain it worthily once taken up. We have an advocate (I say), not advocates. For there is one, not more. There will therefore be no danger that, having scorned the better, we choose some less suitable or less acceptable one. There is one who both prevails with the Father by grace, because he is the Son, and is able to sustain the rigour of his judgment, because he is righteous. This is Jesus Christ, concerning whose goodwill toward us it is not lawful to doubt, since he was both made man for us and shed his own blood for the cleansing of our sins. To him therefore flee, you who feel that you have sinned. Believe your conscience's pains and distresses in him. Seek his intercession, and salvation will be obtained at once. For he himself cries out: "Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will give you rest." Matt. 11. O joyful voice, to be repaid with no riches! O unsearchable depth of divine goodness, which wished to prepare for sinners so safe and faithful a refuge of salvation! Who would despair any longer in sins? Who would now prefer to wander through the trackless ways of human traditions rather than enter upon this short and safe way? But since such is the blindness and madness of many, not to say something harsher, that, not content with this advocate and mediator, they flee elsewhere and seek salvation somewhere else, the treatment of this matter must be taken up a little more deeply.

units.la: Aduocatum nos apud patrem habere dicit Apostolus, Iesum Christum. Paulus eundem inter nos & Deum mediatorem esse dicit. 1.Tim.2. Vnus vero & idem vtriusq; nominis sensus est. Aduocatus enim in iudicio requiritur, maximè cum reus is est, quæ nec innocentia sua tuto niti, nec propria prudentia & eloquentia causam suam tueri potest. Mediator non nisi inter eos, qui diuersis sententijs scisi inimicitias apertas exercent, locum habet. Si ergo mediator inter Deum & nos est, Christus Iesus, & idem aduocatus causam nostram agit, nos reos esse & cum Deo diffidere constat. Dissidij vero huius causa peccatum est. Quia enim peccauimus omnes, filij iræ facti sumus, & æternæ damnationis supplicio digni censemur. Et iudicio nobiscum contendit Deus. Ponit legem suam, & per hanc nos peccati conuincit. Accusat nos propria conscientia, & nonnunquam sic accusat, vt poenam commeritam nō sine graui & horribili terrore quasi in oculis nostris videamus. Hic nisi alius intercedat, actum est. Quem vero hic intercessorem dabimus? Partes contendentes sunt, Deus & homo. Intercessor ergo & mediator talis requiritur, quem & nostra infirmitas ferre, & qui vicissim diuinæ iustitiæ vim sustinere possit. Adhæc authoritate præditus sit, oportet, & tali quidem, quæ apud Deum alicuius momenti sit. Hæc quia in solo Christo sunt, solus etiam mediator vel intercessor dici debet.
