Solus enim hic verus Deus & homo est: Deus quidem ab æterno, homo autem propter nos factus, vt talem sciremus esse, qui nostris infirmitatibus posset condolere. Solus etiam inter homines iustus est, & proinde diuinæ iustitiæ rigorem nō timet. Solus naturalis ille filius Dei est, in quo patri complacuit, & proinde alijs quoq; eandem gratiam conciliare potest. Soli potestas in cœlo & in terris data est: quare nihil arrogantius facit vel ambitiosius, si causæ nostræ patrocinium suscipiat.
units.tr: The Apostle says that we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ. Paul says that the same is mediator between us and God. 1 Tim. 2. Indeed the sense of the two names is one and the same. For an advocate is required in a judgment, especially when the accused is one who can rely safely neither on his own innocence nor defend his cause by his own prudence and eloquence. A mediator has a place only among those who, divided by different opinions, carry on open enmities. If therefore Christ Jesus is the mediator between God and us, and the same is our advocate pleading our cause, it is plain that we are the accused and are at variance with God. The cause of this disagreement, however, is sin. For since we have all sinned, we have become children of wrath, and are judged worthy of the punishment of eternal damnation. And God contends with us in judgment. He sets down his law, and through this convicts us of sin. Our own conscience accuses us, and sometimes accuses us in such a way that we seem to see the deserved punishment, not without grievous and horrible terror, as if before our eyes. Here, unless another intercedes, the matter is finished. But whom shall we give here as intercessor? The parties in contention are God and man. An intercessor and mediator is therefore required, such as both our weakness can bear and who in turn can sustain the force of divine justice. Besides, he must be endowed with authority, and of such a kind as is of some weight with God. Since these things are in Christ alone, he alone ought also to be called mediator or intercessor. For he alone is true God and man: God indeed from eternity, but made man for our sake, that we might know him to be one who can sympathise with our infirmities. He alone also is righteous among men, and therefore does not fear the rigour of divine justice. He alone is that natural Son of God in whom the Father is well pleased, and therefore he can also obtain the same favour for others. Power in heaven and on earth has been given to him alone: wherefore he does nothing more arrogant or more ambitious if he takes upon himself the patronage of our cause.

units.la: Hinc est, quod in scripturis vnus hic & solus mediator proponitur. Nam vt veteris testamenti sanctos omittamus, qui in precibus suis ad vnctum illum domini semper respexerunt, ipse in euangelio, vt ante diximus, ad se solum inuitat. Et alibi inquit: Ego sum via & veritas. Nemo venit ad patrem, nisi per me. Ioan. 14. Ad patrem venire dicitur, qui illi reconciliatur, qui cum illo redit in gratiam. Id nemini cōtingit (ait Christus) nisi per me. Vnus ergo & solus inter Deum patrem & nos mediator sit, oportet. Et apostoli non alium nobis monstrauerunt vnquam. Paulus certè argumento à Dei vnitate ducto, dicit: Vnus est Deus, vnus etiam mediator inter Deum & homines, homo Christus Iesus. 1. Tim. 2.
units.tr: Hence it is that in the Scriptures this one and only mediator is set forth. For, to leave aside the saints of the Old Testament, who in their prayers always looked to that anointed one of the Lord, he himself in the gospel, as we said before, invites to himself alone. And elsewhere he says: "I am the way and the truth. No one comes to the Father except through me." John 14. To come to the Father is said of one who is reconciled to him, who returns into favour with him. This comes to no one (Christ says) except through me. Therefore there must be one and only mediator between God the Father and us. And the apostles never showed us any other. Paul, certainly, from an argument drawn from the unity of God, says: "There is one God, and one mediator also between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." 1 Tim. 2.

units.la: Arguunt hæ sententiæ eorum fabulas, qui intercessionis huius gloriam vel D. virgini, vel a-postolis aut alijs sanctis asignant. Quis vero Ioannem apostolum tam vel negligentem vel malignum D. virginis tutorem fuisse putet, vt eam hac gloria fraudare voluisset, si eam hac ornauisset filius? Quis Christum tam imprudentem dicat, vt matrem suam iam in Crucem affixus ei commendasset, cuius tantam negligentiam habuisset cognitam? Poterat sanè Ioannes & D. virginis commodè hoc loco meminisse, si aliquam huius rei gloriam ad hanc pertinere sciuisset. Sed quia tam ipsa quàm alijs sanctis omisisis, de solo Christo loquitur, ad solum hunc omnem gloriam pertinere docet. Facit huc, quòd HABEMVS, inquit, non HABETIS. Se ergo non eximit ab eorum numero, qui aduocato apud patrem opus habent: tam abest, vt se in huius locum substituere velit. Nec est, vt hoc modestiæ apostolorum tribuamus. Licet enim huius studiosissimi fuerint, nunquam tamen de sui ministerij dignitate humilius, quàm rei veritas postulat, loqui volue runt, quod ex Pauli epistolis facilè discet, qui eas non ofcitanter perlegerit. Adde his, quòd media torem & aduocatum agere non poterit, nisi qui omnium hominū arcana norit, & eorundem voces, imò & gemitus, exaudire queat. Id verò nemini hominum vnquam cōcessum fuisse legimus. Solus Deus corda & renes scrutatur. Solius Dei aures omnium vota & orationes penetrant. Ad solum Deū & suspiria & lachrymæ piorum pertingunt. Mediator ergo non erit, nisi qui idem & Deus sit, qui est Christus, qui est in omnibus Deus laudandus in secula. Rom. 9. Ita locum hunc D. Augustinus exposuit, cuius verba propter eos recitare volumus qui nos hodie scismatis in ecclesia excitati accusant, eò quòd Diuorum intercessionem improbamus. Sunt enim eiusmodi: Videte ipsum Ioannem seruantem humilitatem. Certè vir iustus erat & magnus, qui de pectore Domini mysteriorum secreta bibebat: ille ille, qui bibendo de pectore Domini diuinitatem ructauit: In principio erat verbum, & verbum erat apud Deum: ille talis vir, non dixit, Habetis: nec, Me habetis, dixit: nec, Ipsum Christū habetis, dixit: sed & Christū posuit, non se: & Habemus dixit, non Habetis: Maluit se ponere in numero peccatorum, vt haberet aduocatum Christum, quàm ponere se pro Christo aduocatum, & inueniri inter damnandos superbos. Fratres, Iesum Christum iu stum ipsum habemus aduocatum ad patrem, ipse propitiatio est peccatorum nostrorum. Hoc qui tenuit, hæresim non fecit: hoc qui tenuit, scisma non fecit. Vnde enim facta sunt scismata? Cū di cunt homines, nos iusti sumus: cum dicunt homines, Nos sanctificamus immundos, nos iustifica mus impios, nos petimus, nos impetramus. Ioa. autem quid dixit? Si quis peccauerit, aduocatum habemus apud patrem, Iesum Christum iustum, &c.
units.tr: These sentences refute the fables of those who assign the glory of this intercession either to the blessed Virgin, or to the apostles, or to other saints. But who would think that the apostle John was such a negligent or malicious guardian of the blessed Virgin that he would have wished to defraud her of this glory, if her son had adorned her with it? Who would say that Christ was so imprudent that, already fixed to the Cross, he would have committed his mother to him whose great negligence he had known? John could certainly have fittingly mentioned the blessed Virgin in this place, if he had known that some glory of this matter pertained to her. But since he has omitted her as well as the other saints, and speaks of Christ alone, he teaches that all the glory pertains to this one alone. What is relevant is that he says "WE HAVE," not "YOU HAVE." He therefore does not exempt himself from the number of those who have need of an advocate with the Father: so far is he from wishing to put himself in his place. Nor should we ascribe this to the modesty of the apostles. For although they were most eager for this, they never wished to speak of the dignity of their ministry more humbly than the truth of the matter requires, as one may easily learn from Paul's epistles, if he reads them not carelessly. Add to these that no one can act as mediator and advocate unless he knows the secrets of all men and is able to hear their voices, indeed even their groans. But we read that this has never been granted to any man. God alone searches the hearts and reins. The ears of God alone penetrate all the vows and prayers of men. The sighs and tears of the godly reach God alone. Therefore he will not be mediator unless he is also God, who is Christ, who is God to be praised in all ages over all. Rom. 9. Blessed Augustine expounded this passage thus, and we wish to quote his words on account of those who today, stirred up by a schism in the Church, accuse us because we disapprove of the intercession of the saints. They are as follows: "See John himself keeping humility. Surely he was a just and great man, who drank the secrets of the mysteries from the breast of the Lord: he, he, who by drinking from the breast of the Lord belched forth divinity: 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.' That man of such a kind did not say, 'You have,' nor did he say, 'You have me,' nor did he say, 'You have Christ himself,' but he put Christ, not himself; and he said 'We have,' not 'You have.' He preferred to place himself in the number of sinners, so that he might have Christ as advocate, rather than to place himself in Christ's stead as advocate, and be found among the proud who are to be condemned. Brethren, we have Jesus Christ the righteous himself as advocate with the Father; he himself is the propitiation for our sins. He who held this did not make a heresy; he who held this did not make a schism. For whence have schisms been made? When men say, 'We are righteous'; when men say, 'We sanctify the unclean, we justify the impious, we ask, we obtain.' But what did John say? 'If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous,' etc."

units.la: Prodest verò hic & modum intercessionis huius inspicere. Quia enim hunc ex communi homine minimum more æstimauerunt pleriq;, eò perducti sunt, vt plures mediatores fingerent. Alij enim Deum instar magni alicuius Imperatoris siue Regis imaginati sunt, ad cuius conspectum nemo admittatur, nisi qui vel prece vel pretio principes aulæ sibi propitios fecerit. Alij Christum semper iudicem fecerunt, qui nunquam non iratus fulmen indesinenter libret ad interitum humani generis. Eidem ergo astantem, vel etiam genibus aduolutam, finxerunt matrem virginem, quç & vbera monstret, & laborum omnium curarumq; maternarum memoriam refricet, quò iram conceptam remittere & animum commotum flectere dignetur. Sed vtinam isti homines dominū diligentè audirent: Cogitationes meæ non sunt cogitationes vestræ, neq; vt viæ vestrę sunt viæ meæ, Sed quemadmodum cœli terra sublimiores sunt, ita excedunt viæ meæ vias vestras, & cogitatio nes meæ cogitationes vestras. Isa. 55. Hæc cū verè dicat dominus, quæ vesania est, humanis ratioea de Deo fingere, quæ scripturæ de illo nusquam prædicant? Scimus equidem parabolas multas in euangelio contineri, quibus regni cœlorum mysteria adumbrantur. Sed quæ illis parabolis docemur, eadem disertis quoq; scripturæ locis alibi expressa sunt. Nec quia aliquibus parabolis spiritus sanctus uti voluit, nobis quoq; illico permissum est, nouas parabolas fingere, & Deum imaginari talem, qualem omnes scripturæ ignorant. Deum regem regum esse nemo negat. Sed idem regnum suum ipse administrat, nec male fidis vicarijs ut principes huius seculi, opus habet. Adhæc cum omnia ipse videat, omnia audiat, imò cordium quoq; & renum explorator sit, nemo illū fallere potest, nec alios vel prece vel pretio demereri opus est, quorum fauore in illius conspectum admittaris. Nam ipse ait: In die tribulationis tuæ clama ad me, & ego te exaudiam. Psal. 50. Præterea, cum Christus intercedere pro nobis dicitur, non forensem aliquam actionem animo concipere oportet, ut Christum fingas clauorum stigmata patri monstrare, meritum Crucis suæ allegare, lateris aperti fontem videndū exhibere, & alia multa in hanc sententiam facere. Sed meritū Crucis & mortis Christi respicere oportet. Hoc enim in conspectu patris semper recens est. Illius respectu idem nobis clemens & propitius est. Et pro nobis indesinenter Christus intercedere dicitur, quia perpetua & inexhausta est meriti ipsius apud patrem gratia & authoritas. Num vero aliquem dabis, cuius maior sit apud patrem authoritas, quàm filij huius dilecti? Num ex creaturis aliquam produces, quæ apud patrem, quod filius assequi non potest, impetret? Non opinor.
units.tr: Moreover, it is useful to consider here also the manner of this intercession. For many people, having esteemed him too little by treating him as an ordinary man, have been led so far as to invent several mediators. Some have imagined God as a great emperor or king, to whose presence no one is admitted unless he has won over the courtiers to himself, by prayer or by payment. Others have always made Christ a judge, who, never not angry, unceasingly hurls his thunderbolt for the destruction of the human race. To him, standing or even kneeling at his feet, they have then fashioned a virgin mother, who displays her breasts and revives the memory of all her labours and maternal cares, so that he may deign to lay aside the anger he has conceived and bend his stirred spirit. But would that these people listened carefully to the Lord: "My thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways my ways. But as the heavens are higher than the earth, so my ways exceed your ways, and my thoughts your thoughts." Isa. 55. Since the Lord says this truly, what madness it is to imagine about God by human reasoning things which the Scriptures nowhere proclaim of him! We certainly know that many parables are contained in the Gospel, by which the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven are shadowed forth. But what we are taught by those parables is also expressed plainly in other passages of Scripture. Nor, because the Holy Spirit has wished to use some parables, has it immediately been permitted to us also to invent new parables and to imagine God as such a one as all the Scriptures do not know. No one denies that God is King of kings. But he himself administers his own kingdom, and does not need, like the princes of this age, unfaithful deputies. Besides, since he sees all things, hears all things, and is indeed the searcher of hearts and reins, no one can deceive him, nor is it necessary to win others over by prayer or by payment, by whose favour you might be admitted into his presence. For he himself says: "In the day of your trouble call upon me, and I will hear you." Psal. 50. Furthermore, when Christ is said to intercede for us, one ought not to conceive in mind any kind of forensic action, such as imagining Christ showing the wounds of the nails to the Father, pleading the merit of his cross, exhibiting the fountain of his pierced side to be seen, and doing many other things to this effect. Rather, one ought to regard the merit of the cross and death of Christ. For this is always fresh in the sight of the Father. Out of regard for it, he is kind and propitious to us. And Christ is said to intercede for us unceasingly, because the grace and authority of his merit before the Father is perpetual and inexhaustible. Will you indeed name anyone whose authority before the Father is greater than that of this beloved Son? Will you bring forward any creature who could obtain from the Father what the Son cannot obtain? I think not.

units.la: Sed scio quid multi respondeant, qui Christum quidem unum & solum intercessorem apud patrem fatentur, interim verò apud Christum alijs mediatoribus opus esse dicunt, qui illius intercessionem nobis impetrent. Et hoc commentum infinitam illam mediatorum intercessionis cateruam nobis peperit, ut tot mediatores agnoscere oporteat, quot diui in cœlis esse creduntur. Quàm vana verò sit istorum hominum opinio, res ipsa demonstrat, & Joannes idem docet, qui quæ de Christo aduocato & intercessore dixerat probaturus, addit:
units.tr: But I know what many reply, who indeed confess Christ to be the one and only intercessor before the Father, yet meanwhile say that other mediators are needed with Christ, who may obtain his intercession for us. And this invention has brought forth that endless crowd of mediators for intercession, so that one must acknowledge as many mediators as there are saints believed to be in heaven. How empty the opinion of these men is, the matter itself demonstrates, and John teaches the same thing, who, about to prove what he had said of Christ as advocate and intercessor, adds:

units.la: Et ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris: non pro nostris autem tantum, sed etiam pro peccatis totius mundi. Quia Christum Jesum antea iustum dixerat, cogitaret quispiam: Hoc ipsum est, quod prohibet quò minus coram Deo comparere possim, quod ego peccator, ille vero iustus est. Quòd si & Christus, quem mihi aduocatum & mediatorem proponis, iustus est, iam ne in illius quidem conspectum tuto prodire datur, & nouis mihi apud hunc mediatoribus utendum erit. Docet ergo Joannes, se Christi iustitiam non in hunc finem allegauisse, ut nobis illa terrorem incutiat, sed ut intelligamus, ipsum intercessionis officio apud iustitiam patris rite fungi posse. Nobis verò, quoad infirmitatem nostram, aliud quoq; in Christo spectandum est. Hoc nimirum quòd nostra propitiatio factus est, quòd pro peccatis nostris sese tradidit, quòd pro ijsdem satis fecit, ut nocere amplius nō possint. Hoc unum si consyderes, vanissimum videbis quicquid nostri illi de intercessionis mediatoribus fingunt. Demus enim, esse aliquem, qui mihi obærato opes suas sponte offerat, apud creditores meo nomine non rogatus intercedat, pro me sponsorem agat: nonne insanus habebor, si illius bonitati adhuc diffidere, & aliorum intercessione hunc mihi demereri velim? Quid enim intercessores illi mei ab eo petent amplius, quod ille non iam ante præstiterit? Atqui eadem est hic ratio. Premebamur omnes ære alieno, peccatorum nimirum debitis implicati miserrime, & cum euangelico illo seruulo ad damnationem venundari merebamur, nec ipsi Deo patri satisfacere poteramus, nec erat qui causam nostram tueri posset alius. Atqui rationibus nostris omnibus tam intricatis, Dei filius sese sponte obtulit, homo & frater noster factus est, ut causam nostram suscipere posset, debita nostra in se transtulit, pro ijsdem in ara Cruci satisfecit, & ibidem expansis brachijs ad se inuitat omnes, alta voce clamás: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego requiem vobis præstabo. Quid ergo de illius in nos voluntate dubitamus? Quid illius iustitiam expauescimus? Quid nouis mediatoribus apud illum impetrabimus, quod non iam ante sua sponte nobis dederit? Num ut peccata nostra in se transferat? Atqui eius gratia in mundum venit. Num ut nostris infirmitatibus condoleat? Atqui hanc unam ob causam homo factus est. Num ut suæ mortis meritum nobis salutare esse velit? Atqui frustra mori haudquaquam voluit. Num ut causam nostram apud patrem agat? At priusquam mundus hic fundaretur, in hoc prædestinatus fuit. 1. Pet. 1. Quid ergo nobisipsis curarum & laborum authores fumus? Credeinte-sum Christum, illo intercessore & aduocato utere, & totus tuus est. Ipse inquit: Eum qui venerit ad me, non eijcio foras. Ioan. 6. Noli ergo immitem & inexorabilem fingere, qui omnes suæ gratiæ thesauros sponte tibi donare dignatus est.
units.tr: "And he himself is the propitiation for our sins; and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world." Since he had previously called Jesus Christ righteous, someone might think: this very thing prevents me from being able to appear before God, that I am a sinner, but he is righteous. But if Christ too, whom you set before me as advocate and mediator, is righteous, then I am not permitted to come forth safely even into his presence, and I shall have to use new mediators with him. John therefore teaches that he did not adduce the righteousness of Christ for this purpose, that it might strike terror into us, but so that we might understand that he is able to discharge the office of intercession properly before the righteousness of the Father. For us, however, with regard to our weakness, something else must also be looked at in Christ. This, namely, that he was made our propitiation, that he gave himself up for our sins, that he made satisfaction for the same, so that they can no longer harm us. If you consider this alone, you will see how most vain is whatever those men of ours invent about mediators of intercession. Let us suppose there is someone who, freely offering his riches to me, who am deeply in debt, intercedes with the creditors in my name without being asked, and acts as surety for me: would I not be considered mad, if I still distrusted his goodness and wished to win his favour for me through the intercession of others? For what more could those intercessors of mine ask of him, which he has not already given beforehand? Yet the reasoning here is the same. We were all weighed down by debt, indeed most wretchedly entangled in the debts of sins, and, like that servant in the gospel, we deserved to be sold into condemnation; nor could we ourselves satisfy God the Father, nor was there anyone else who could defend our cause. Yet, with all our affairs so entangled, the Son of God offered himself of his own accord; he became man and our brother, so that he could take up our cause; he transferred our debts to himself, made satisfaction for them on the altar of the cross, and there, with arms outstretched, invites all to himself, crying with a loud voice: "Come to me, all you who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." Why then do we doubt his will towards us? Why do we dread his righteousness? What could we obtain from him through new mediators, which he has not already given us of his own accord before? Is it that he should transfer our sins to himself? But he came into the world for this very grace. Is it that he should sympathise with our weaknesses? But he was made man for this one reason alone. Is it that he should wish the merit of his death to be salutary for us? But he was by no means willing to die in vain. Is it that he should act as our cause before the Father? But before this world was founded, he was predestined to this. 1 Pet. 1. What then are we to ourselves but the authors of our cares and labours? Believe in Christ, use him as intercessor and advocate, and you are wholly his. He himself says: "Him who comes to me I will not cast out." John 6. Do not, therefore, imagine him as harsh and inexorable, he who has deigned freely to give you all the treasures of his grace.

units.la: Sed videamus paulò attentius Joannis in hoc dicto diligentiam. Non contentus Christū propitiationem nostram dixisse, eum pro peccatis nostris propitiatione factum esse testatur. Nec hoc illi sufficit. Ne enim vel in sua duntaxat, vel Apostolorum omnium persona loqui videretur, addit: Non pro nostris tantum, verumetiam pro peccatis totius mundi. Mundi vocabulo vti voluit, ne aliquem à Christi merito exclusum putaremus, quemadmodum & ipse dominus inquit: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, vt filium suum vnigenitum traderet, &c. Ioan.3. Si mundum dilexit De-us, num nos odio habere poterit, quos è mundo filius ipsius selegit? Ioan.15. Si pro peccatis mundi sese filius Dei tradidit, num ad nos sanguinis sui meritum peruenire prohibebit, qui à mundo separari & ipsi totis animis vniri cupimus? Noli igitur desperare ô homo. Noli cum Caino dicere, Maior est iniquitas mea, quàm vt remitti possit. Christus enim pro peccatis tuis se tradidit. Christus in peccatorum tuorum ablutionem propriū sanguinem fundere dignatus est. Eius meritum non aspernabitur pater, qui illi testimonium coelitus tulit, dicens: Hic est filius meus dile-ctus, in quo mihi complacitum est. Matth.3. & 17. Caeterum priusquam sermoni finem imponamus, duo adhuc in hisce verbis obseruanda erunt.
units.tr: But let us look a little more carefully at John's diligence in this saying. Not content with having called Christ our propitiation, he testifies that he was made propitiation for our sins. Nor is this enough for him. Lest he seem to speak only in his own person or in that of all the apostles, he adds: "Not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world." He wished to use the word world, lest we should think anyone excluded from the merit of Christ, just as the Lord himself says: "So God loved the world, that he gave his only-begotten Son, etc." John 3. If God has loved the world, can he hate us, whom his Son has chosen out of the world? John 15. If the Son of God gave himself up for the sins of the world, will he prevent the merit of his blood from reaching us, who desire with all our souls to be separated from the world and to be united to him? Do not therefore despair, O man. Do not say with Cain: "My iniquity is greater than that it can be forgiven." For Christ gave himself up for your sins. Christ deigned to pour out his own blood for the washing away of your sins. The Father, who bore witness to him from heaven, saying, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased," will not disdain his merit. Matt. 3 and 17. But before we bring this sermon to an end, two things still remain to be observed in these words.

units.la: Primò docemur, Christum non particularem paucarum gentium, sed vniuersale totius mundi saluatorem esse. Hoc probè nouisse multum prodest. Vt enim de Iudaeis nihil dicamus, qui pro missum Mesiā ad se solos pertinere putat, multos ex Christiani nominis professoribus, ita tetari videmus, vt Christum quidem saluatorem esse fateantur, suū verò saluatorem agnoscere nolint, dū vel se eius merito ob peccatorum suorum atrocitatem indignos, vel Christi meritum tot tantisque peccatis eluendis minus sufficere posse existimant. Intelligant ergo isti homines, diuinae gratiae fontem, qui in filio Dei apertus fuit, inexhaustum esse. Nam bonus est dominus in omnes, & misericordia eius superat omnia opera ipsius. Psal.145. Nec putandum est, Dei gratiam & Christi meritum satanae armis & artibus superari posse. Nam apud prophetam inquit: Si peccata vestra fuerint vt coccus, niue reddentur albiora: si rubeant instar purpurae, sicut natiua lana reddentur. Ifa.1. Et eiusmodi promissiones ad vniuersos homines pertinere, tota scriptura probat. Licet enim Iudaeorum genti veteres promissiones datae sint, non tamen hoc ideo factum est, vt eas ad solam hanc pertinere putemus, sed in Iudaeis dominus demonstrare voluit, qualis erga omnes homines esse velit. Adhaec primam salutis promissionem de Christo, non Abrahae, sed primis parentibus, datam constat, vt illam ad omnem Adami posteritatem pertinere sciremus. Gen.3. Et Isaias propheta, cum dixisset: Nos omnes tanquam ouis errauimus, quisque viam suam sectatus: mox addit: Dominus autem effecit, vt incurreret in ipsum OMNIVM nostrum iniquitas. Ifa.53. Sed ipsum Christum audiamus, qui non modo fatetur, se alias quoque oues habere, quae ad Israelitici populi societatem externam non pertinent (Ioan.10.) sed quaecunque de redemptione nostra & suae mortis merito loquitur, vniuersalibus promissis confirmare solet. Ait enim: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, vt filium suum vnigenitum daret, vt OMNIS qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. Ioan.3. Quisquis biberit ex aqua, quam ego dabo, nō sitiet in aeternum. Ioan.4. Amen amen dico vobis, qui sermonem meum audit, & credit ei qui misit me, habet vitam aeternam, & in condemnationem non veniet. Ioan.5. Et rursum: Qui credit in me, habet vitam aeternam. Ioan.6. Vniuersales quoq; promissiones sunt: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego requiem vobis praestabo. Matth.11. Item: Si quis sitit, veniat ad me & bibat. Qui credit in me, sicut dicit scriptura: Flumina de ventre eius fluent aquae viuae. Ioan.7. Et iam morte aditurus, non pro Apostolis modo orat, sed etiam pro omnibus, qui per doctrinam Apostolorum in ipsum crediturí sunt. Ioan.17. Sed infinita sunt eius rei testimonia, quae sacra legenti passim occurrunt. Verè ergo Ioannes, Christum propitiationem esse dicit pro peccatis totius mundi. In quam sententiam & Baptista dixit: Ecce agnus ille Dei, qui tollit peccatum mundi. Ioan.1. Procul itaq; facessant cogitationes omnes, quae Christi meritum ad paucos modo extendi, & nos ab illo exclusos esse, persuadere conantur. Neminem enim Christus aspernatur, qui & hostium salutem quaerit, & madentem prophetarum sanguine Hierosolymam instar gallinae sub alas colligit, nisi quis ipsum fastidire, & propria diffidentia perditionis suae sibi author esse velit. Omnibus se-se offert, & quotquot ipsum recipiunt, dat eis vt possint filij Dei dici, &c. Ioan.1.
units.tr: Firstly, we are taught that Christ is not the Saviour of a few particular nations, but the universal Saviour of the whole world. It greatly helps to know this well. To say nothing of the Jews, who think the promised Messiah belongs to them alone, we see many of those who bear the Christian name so disposed that they confess Christ to be the Saviour, yet are unwilling to acknowledge him as their own Saviour, since they think either that they are unworthy of his merit because of the atrocity of their sins, or that Christ's merit is insufficient to wash away so many and so great sins. Let these people understand, therefore, that the fountain of divine grace, which has been opened in the Son of God, is inexhaustible. For the Lord is good to all, and his mercy is over all his works (Ps. 145). Nor should we think that God's grace and Christ's merit can be overcome by the weapons and arts of Satan. For the prophet says: "If your sins are like scarlet, they shall be made as white as snow; if they are red like purple, they shall become like white wool" (Isa. 1). And that such promises pertain to all men, the whole of Scripture proves. For although the old promises were given to the nation of the Jews, this does not mean that we should think they pertain to that nation alone; rather, in the Jews the Lord wished to show what kind of disposition he has towards all men. Moreover, it is clear that the first promise of salvation, concerning Christ, was given not to Abraham but to our first parents, so that we might know it pertains to the whole posterity of Adam (Gen. 3). And the prophet Isaiah, having said: "We all like sheep have gone astray, each one has turned to his own way," immediately adds: "But the Lord has caused the iniquity of us all to fall upon him" (Isa. 53). But let us hear Christ himself, who not only confesses that he has other sheep, which do not belong to the external fellowship of the Israelite people (John 10), but whenever he speaks of our redemption and the merit of his death, he is accustomed to confirm it with universal promises. For he says: "God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that EVERYONE who believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life" (John 3). "Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst for ever" (John 4). "Truly, truly I say to you, he who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and shall not come into condemnation" (John 5). And again: "He who believes in me has eternal life" (John 6). The promises are also universal: "Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will give you rest" (Matt. 11). Likewise: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly" (John 7). And now, about to go to death, he prays not only for the Apostles, but also for all who are going to believe in him through the teaching of the Apostles (John 17). But there are countless testimonies of this matter, which occur everywhere to the one who reads the sacred books. Therefore John truly says that Christ is the propitiation for the sins of the whole world. To this same effect the Baptist also said: "Behold that Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world" (John 1). Away, then, with all thoughts which try to persuade us that Christ's merit extends only to a few, and that we have been excluded from it. For Christ rejects no one, since he seeks the salvation even of his enemies, and gathers under his wings like a hen Jerusalem, which is drunk with the blood of the prophets, unless someone wishes to despise him and, by his own distrust, become the author of his own destruction. He offers himself to all, and to as many as receive him he gives the power to be called sons of God, etc. (John 1).

units.la: Secundo docet locus hic, regnum Christi nō vnius modò vel alterius populi finibus conclu-di, sed ad omnes gentes, vsq; ad extremos mundi cardines, extendi. Si enim meritum mortis ipsi-us ad omnes pertinet, illud ipsum vbiq; locorum praedicari oportet, vt in omnium gentium fidelibus verbo & spiritu suo regnare posit. Designati iam olim sunt isti termini. Nam per Dauidem spiritus sanctus loquitur: Recensebo decretum. Dominus dixit ad me: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Postula à me, daboq; gentes, vt sint haereditas tua, & terminos terrae, vt sint possessio tua. Psal.2. Et rursum: Imperabit à mari ad mare, & à flumine vsq; ad terminos terrę. Adorabūt eū omnes reges, omnes gentes seruient ei. Psal.72. Pertinet eodē & Nabuchodonozoris somniū q; lapidem fine manib. auulsum cadere, & statuā, quae monarchiarū typus erat, minutim conterere, ipsum vero crescere vidit in montem magnū, qui totum orbem impleuerit.Dan.2.Sed Christum audiamus, qui terras corpore suo relicturus ait: Data est mihi omnis potestas in coelo & in terra. Ite in orbe uniuersum, praedicate euangelium omni creaturæ, &c.Matth.28. Mar.16.Act.1.&c.Habet hæc regni Christi consyderatio eximiam consolationem. Quia enim omnium gentium rex est Christus, fideles suos ubique terrarum videt, curat, tuetur & regit. Nec aliquis in orbe angulus est, in quem eiecti extra Christi prouidentiam & protectionem constituti sint. Insaniat ergo mundus ut volet, non tamen quicquam efficiet aliud, quam quod Christus in bonum ecclesiæ fieri permittit, quam Cruce interdum exerceri oportet. Ipse interim ei præsens adest, usque ad consummationem seculi.Matth.28. Beati, qui hunc regem agnoscunt, & sub illius protectione mundi minas ridere & contemnere possunt.
units.tr: Secondly, this passage teaches that the kingdom of Christ is not confined within the limits of one or another people, but extends to all nations, to the furthest corners of the earth. For if the merit of his death pertains to all, it ought to be preached everywhere, so that he may reign by his Word and Spirit among the faithful of all nations. These boundaries were marked out long ago. For through David the Holy Spirit speaks: "I will declare the decree: the Lord has said to me, 'You are my Son, today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession'" (Ps. 2). And again: "He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth. All kings shall worship him, all nations shall serve him" (Ps. 72). To this also pertains the dream of Nebuchadnezzar, in which he saw a stone torn from the mountain without hands fall, and grind to powder the statue, which was a type of the monarchies, while the stone itself grew into a great mountain which filled the whole world (Dan. 2). But let us hear Christ, who, about to leave the earth in body, says: "All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature," etc. (Matt. 28; Mark 16; Acts 1, etc.). This consideration of Christ's kingdom holds an outstanding consolation. For since Christ is king of all nations, he sees, cares for, protects and rules his faithful people everywhere on earth. Nor is there any corner of the world in which they have been thrown and placed outside the providence and protection of Christ. Let the world therefore rage as it wishes; yet it will accomplish nothing other than what Christ allows to be done for the good of the Church, which must sometimes be exercised by the cross. Meanwhile he himself is present with them, even to the end of the age (Matt. 28). Blessed are those who acknowledge this King, and who under his protection can laugh at and despise the threats of the world.

units.la: Comprehendimus sermone hoc breue doctrinæ euangelicæ compendium. Audiuistis enim, Christianorum esse non peccare, sed iugem & perpetuam agere pœnitentiam. Didicistis, quo qui peccarunt, confugere debeant. Iesus Christus pro peccatis nostris propitiatio factus est. Idem aduocatus & intercessor pro nobis est apud patrem. Per hunc tendamus ad thronum gratiæ, ut cum eodem æternum uiuamus. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: In this sermon we have grasped a brief summary of evangelical doctrine. For you have heard that it is not the Christian's business to sin, but to undertake a continual and perpetual repentance. You have learned where those who have sinned ought to flee. Jesus Christ has been made the propitiation for our sins. The same is our advocate and intercessor with the Father. Through him let us press on to the throne of grace, so that with the same we may live eternally. To him be due blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA VI.
units.tr: Homily VI.

units.la: Et per hoc scimus, quod cognouimus eum, si præcepta illius observemus. Qui dicit: Noui eum: & præcepta eius non seruat, mendax est, & in eo veritas non est. Qui autem seruat sermonem eius, uere in illo charitas Dei perfecta est. Per hoc scimus, quod in ipso sumus. Qui dicit se in eo manere, debet, sicut ille ambulauit, & ipse ambulare.
units.tr: "And by this we know that we have known him, if we keep his commandments. He who says, 'I know him,' and does not keep his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him. But whoever keeps his word, in him the love of God is truly perfected. By this we know that we are in him. He who says that he abides in him ought himself also to walk just as he walked."

units.la: DOminus & saluator noster Iesus Christus Ioannis Baptistæ discipulis inquit: Beatus, qui in me non offenditur. Sententia hæc grauis & diligenti consyderatione digna est. Debet enim non de Cruce modo Christi & humilitatis specie, quam in terris hisce gestauit, uerumetiam de doctrina & tota salutis nostræ administratione, quam Christus obiuit, intelligi. Nam si carnis nostræ ingenium consyderemus, absurda plane & longe diuersa sunt illius circa fidem & religionem studia. Sunt enim hypocritæ iustitiarij, qui dum religionem in externa sanctimoniæ specie sitam esse existimant, quicquid in Christi doctrina traditur, eo rapiunt, ut Tragicum quendam cultum instituant & uana sanctimoniæ simulatione sese venditent. Ab his longe dissentiunt, qui peccandi licentiam sectantes, eius patrocinium sub Christi merito quærunt. Quia uero utriq; à religionis ueritate & salutis uia procul aberrant, utrisque diligenter sese opponunt apostoli, & inter hos Ioannes noster, qui subinde quasi ambabus manibus dimicat, ne alterutris fenestram sui erroris aperuisse uideatur. Etenim quæ hucusq; dicta sunt, fere ijs cohercendis seruiunt, qui externo cultu & simulatæ sanctimoniæ fiducia freti de Christo parum honorifice sentiunt, dum quæ ipsius sunt, quærunt alibi. Nunc vero ad eos sermonem dirigit, qui Christi sermonem dirigit, qui Christi nomen professi, parum Christianè uiuere consueuerunt. Et primo quidem summam suæ doctrinæ proponens, docet Christi notitiam & fidem, quæ euangelio traditur, minimè otiosam esse, sed observationem mandatorum Christi secum trahere. Mox illud ipsum argumento ab effectis sumpto probat. Cui mox aliud à Christi exemplo deductum subijcit. Faxit dominus, ut hæc non intelligamus modo, sed in eadem transformati vitam uiuamus nostra professione dignam.
units.tr: The Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ said to the disciples of John the Baptist: "Blessed is he who is not offended in me." This saying is weighty and worthy of careful consideration. For it ought to be understood not only of the Cross of Christ and the appearance of humility which he bore on this earth, but also of his teaching and of the whole administration of our salvation, which Christ accomplished. For if we consider the disposition of our flesh, the attitudes of men toward faith and religion are plainly absurd and widely different from his. For there are the hypocritical justiciaries, who, thinking that religion consists in an outward show of holiness, twist whatever is taught in Christ's doctrine so as to set up a kind of tragic worship, and to sell themselves by a vain pretence of sanctity. Far from these are those who, pursuing licence to sin, seek its defence under the merit of Christ. But since both wander far from the truth of religion and the way of salvation, the apostles oppose both carefully, and among them our John, who from time to time fights as if with both hands, lest he seem to have opened a window to error for either side. For what has been said so far serves chiefly to restrain those who, relying on outward worship and confidence in a feigned holiness, think little honourably of Christ, while seeking what is his elsewhere. Now, however, he directs his speech to those who have professed the name of Christ but are accustomed to live little like Christians. And first, setting out the sum of his doctrine, he teaches that the knowledge and faith of Christ which is delivered in the gospel is by no means idle, but carries with it the observance of Christ's commandments. Soon afterwards he proves this very point from an argument drawn from its effects. To this he then adds another, drawn from the example of Christ. May the Lord grant that we understand these things not only, but being transformed into the same, live a life worthy of our profession.

units.la: I. Per hoc scimus, quod cognouimus eum, si præcepta illius observemus. Qui dicit: Noui eum: & præcepta eius non seruat, mendax est, & in eo veritas non est. Summa huius doctrinæ istis verbis proponit, & habet propositio venustam antithesim, qua orationis figura Ioanes frequenter utitur, non tam perspicuitatis quam vehementiæ gratia. Per hoc scimus, quod cognouimus eum: id est, hoc argumento constat, nos vera Christi cognitione & fide in hunc esse præditos: si præcepta illius seruemus. Nec enim de historica Christi cognitione, quam & dæmones habent, loquitur, sed de saluifica illa, qua nos iustificari propheta testatur. Isa.53. Cæterum huic propositioni mox alteram opponit: Qui dicit se Christum nouisse, & præcepta eius non seruat, mendax est, & in eo veritas non est. Possunt hæc paucioribus verbis comprehendi ad hunc modum: Veræ cognitionis Christi & fidei argumentum est, præceptorum Christi observatio. Quisquis ergo sine hac Christi cognitione gloriatur, mendax est. Ex præcedentibus verò ista sic dependent: Dixi Christū Iesum nobis à Deo patre propitiationem pro peccatis totius mundi datū esse, & eo nos aduocato ac intercessore apud patrē uti debere. At ista nemo sic accipiat, quasi satis sit Christianū dici, historiam rerum à Christo gestarū memoria tenere, sacris ité à Christo institutis cōmunicare. Maius enim quiddam à nobis requiritur: Viua nimirū Christi Iesu cognitio, quæ spiritus sancti opus est. Ea Christo nos totos inserit, in illius admirationem & amorem rapit, ut nil perinde cupiamus quàm ipsi obedire. Accendit ergo studiū præceptorum ipsius, ut quæcunq; à nobis exigit, pro virili exequamur, nec unquâ desinamus ad proposita Christianæ perfectionis metâ tendere. Quis-quis hoc studium in se animaduerterit, is se veram Christi cognitionem iam assecutum esse cōfidat. Quis-quis autem ab hoc studio se adhuc abhorrere & alienum esse sentit, is Christi cognitione & fide gloriari desinat, ne palàm mendax & à veritate alienus deprehendatur. Et hic quidem verborum Ioannis sensus est. Insunt autem his quædam altiori consyderatione omnino necessaria.
units.tr: I. "By this we know that we have known him, if we keep his commandments. He who says, 'I know him,' and does not keep his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him." John sets out the sum of this teaching in these words, and the statement contains a graceful antithesis, a figure of speech which John often uses, not so much for clarity as for emphasis. "By this we know that we have known him": that is, this argument establishes that we are endowed with true knowledge and faith of Christ, if we keep his commandments. For he does not speak of the historical knowledge of Christ, which the demons also have, but of that saving knowledge by which, the prophet testifies, we are justified (Isa. 53.). Moreover, he soon sets against this proposition another: "He who says that he knows Christ, and does not keep his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him." These points may be summed up in fewer words thus: the observance of Christ's commandments is the mark of true knowledge and faith of Christ. Whoever therefore boasts of this knowledge of Christ without it is a liar. But from what precedes, these statements depend in this way: I have said that Christ Jesus has been given to us by God the Father as a propitiation for the sins of the whole world, and that we ought to use him as our advocate and intercessor with the Father. But no one should take this to mean that it is enough to be called a Christian by keeping in memory the history of the things done by Christ, and by sharing in the sacred rites instituted by Christ. A greater thing is required of us: namely, the living knowledge of Jesus Christ, which is the work of the Holy Spirit. This knowledge draws us wholly into Christ, carries us into admiration and love of him, so that we desire nothing so much as to obey him. It therefore kindles the desire for his commandments, so that we carry out, to the best of our strength, whatever he demands of us, and never cease to strive toward the goal of Christian perfection set before us. Whoever perceives this desire in himself may be confident that he has already attained true knowledge of Christ. But whoever still feels that he shrinks from this desire and is a stranger to it, let him cease to glory in the knowledge and faith of Christ, lest he be openly exposed as a liar and a stranger to the truth. This is indeed the sense of John's words. Yet there are in them some things which, on closer consideration, are altogether necessary.

units.la: Primò obseruandum venit, quòd sciendi & cognoscēdi verbis Ioānes utitur. Per hoc scimus (inquit) quòd cognouimus eū. Docemur ergo, verā & certam in nobis exoriri posse salutis nos-træ notitiā. Salutem enim fide apprehendi omnis scriptura testatur. Cum autē de fide nostra nos certos fieri posse Apostolus fateatur, imò eius certitudinis argumentū & notā infallibilem commonstret, fieri nequit, ut de salute sua fideles incerti sint. Arguit hoc impium & perniciosum sophistarū dogma, qui homine de salute sua semper dubitare docent, & impossibile dicūt, ut de hac quisquam dum hic viuit, certus reddatur. Et habēt isti homines, quo suū commentū velēt: quasi hæsitatio ista securitatem carnis pellat, & indefessum salutis studiū in nobis excitet. Interim ve-rò animaduertere nolunt, hæsitationem istam in desperationem declinare posse, quod horribiles multorum lapsus sæpe probauerunt. Iubet Paulus, ut cum timore & tremore salutem nostrā operemur. Phil.2. At idem de salute nuspiam dubitare, sed pios in fide firmos stare docet. Adhæc arrhabonem salutis nostræ spiritum sanctum nobis datum esse testatur, in quo clamemus, Abba pater. 2.Cor.1.&5. Ephef.1. Rom.8. Galat.4. Et Petrus Apostolus de maximo salutis periculo, diabolo nimirum, loquens, ubi illius improbum nobis nocendi studium descripsit, addit: Huic resistite solidi in fide. 1.Pet.5. At quomodo in fide solidi huic hosti resisteat, qui de salute sua dubitare edocti sunt? Prodit ergo se dogmate spiritus ille vertiginis, quo malignantium ecclesia regitur.
units.tr: First, it must be observed that John uses the words of knowing and knowledge. "By this we know," he says, "that we have known him." We are taught, therefore, that a true and certain knowledge of our salvation can arise in us. For all Scripture testifies that salvation is apprehended by faith. Since the Apostle declares that we can be made certain of our faith, and indeed shows the proof and infallible mark of this certainty, it cannot be that the faithful are uncertain of their salvation. This refutes the impious and pernicious dogma of the sophists, who teach that a man must always doubt his salvation, and say it is impossible for anyone to be made certain of it while he lives here. And these men have a pretext for their invention, as if this uncertainty drove out carelessness of the flesh and stirred up in us an unwearied zeal for salvation. Yet meanwhile they are unwilling to notice that this uncertainty can slide into despair, as the dreadful falls of many have often shown. Paul bids us work out our salvation with fear and trembling (Phil. 2.). But he nowhere teaches that the godly should doubt their salvation; rather, he teaches that they stand firm in faith. Moreover, he testifies that the Spirit given to us is the pledge of our salvation, by whom we cry, "Abba, Father" (2 Cor. 1 and 5; Eph. 1; Rom. 8; Gal. 4). And the Apostle Peter, speaking of the greatest danger to our salvation, namely the devil, and describing his wicked zeal for harming us, adds: "Resist him, steadfast in the faith" (1 Pet. 5.). But how can one resist this enemy steadfast in faith when he has been taught to doubt his own salvation? That spirit of giddiness, by which the church of the wicked is ruled, therefore betrays itself in its doctrine.

units.la: Secundo notā, ex qua veri Christiani agnosci possunt, diligenter obseruare decet. Christianū equidem fides facit. Sed quia hæc interdū latet, nec facile est de aliorū animis, in quibus fides se-dem suā habet, iudicare, externa nota fideles suos Christus agnoscere docuit. Est hæc præceptorum Christi obseruatio. Non autem perfecta illa & omnibus numeris absoluta debet intelligi, quam nemo carnis infirmitate circundatus unquam assequetur. Sed studium præceptorū Dei, quo fidelis anima flagrat, significatur, cuì tamē ex carnis corruptione imperfectio multa adhæret. Cæterū notā hanc Ioānes nō ex se finxit, sed à Christo ante tradita repetit. Is enim ait: Qui habet præcepta mea, & seruat ea, is est qui diligit me. Et rursum: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meū seruabit. Qui non diligit me, sermones meos nō seruat, Ioan.14. Alibi item: Vos amici mei estis, si feceritis quæcunq; ego præcipio vobis. Ioan.15. Sed & pater cœlestis, cū cœlitus pronūciauisset, Christum esse suum dilectum filium, in quo nobis reconciliatus est, nostri simul nos officij admonens subiungit: Ipsum audite. Matth.17. At audiendi verbo non hoc tantū exigit, ut auribus percipiamus quæ à Christo præcipiuntur, sed ut eadem factis exequamur. Beati enim ab ipso pronūciantur, qui audiunt sermonem Dei, & custodiūt illum. Lucæ 11. Ut ergo verè genuinus patris filius non dicetur, nisi qui patri placere studet: ita Christianum & Dei filium verè dicet nemo, nisi eū, qui præceptorum Christi obseruatione Deo patri sese approbare conetur.
units.tr: Second, we ought carefully to observe the mark by which true Christians can be recognised. Faith indeed makes the Christian. But since faith sometimes lies hidden, and it is not easy to judge the minds of others, in which faith has its seat, Christ taught that his faithful are to be recognised by an outward mark. This mark is the observance of Christ's commandments. This, however, must not be understood as the perfect observance which is complete in every respect, and which no one surrounded by the weakness of the flesh will ever attain. Rather, it signifies the zeal for God's commandments with which a faithful soul burns, though much imperfection from the corruption of the flesh still clings to it. Moreover, John did not invent this mark himself, but repeats what Christ had taught before. For he says: "He who has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me." And again: "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word. He who does not love me does not keep my sayings" (John 14.). Elsewhere likewise: "You are my friends, if you do whatever I command you" (John 15.). And the heavenly Father, when from heaven he had declared that Christ is his beloved Son, in whom we have been reconciled to him, at the same time reminding us of our duty, adds: "Hear him" (Matt. 17.). But the command to hear requires not only that we receive with our ears what is commanded by Christ, but that we also carry out the same by our deeds. For those are pronounced blessed by him who hear the word of God and keep it (Luke 11.). Just as no one will be rightly called a genuine son of the Father unless he strives to please the Father, so no one will rightly be called a Christian and a son of God unless he endeavours to approve himself to God the Father by observing Christ's commandments.

units.la: Imprimis verò obseruandum, quòd Christianos & verè fideles eos vocat, qui Christi præce-pta obseruauerint. Arguuntur hac sententia, qui Christianismum in humanarum traditionū ob-seruatione situm existimant, imò eius perfectionem in illa cōsistere palàm contendunt. Sic Franciscanus reliquis sanctior haberi vult, quòd regulam Francisci sequatur. Dominicanus & huic & Christianis omnibus sese præfert, eò quòd Dominici regulam profitetur. Eadem est multorum aliorum ratio. Sed Christianū solius Christi regula facit. Aut hac contentos viuere decet, aut demonstrandum erit, Franciscum, Dominicū, & alios eius farinæ homines, aliquid inuenisse & sanctius & perfectius iis, quæ à Christo nobis sunt tradita. Sed hoc demonstratu tam est facile, quàm Aethiopem dealbare, aut digito cœlum attingere. Quin, si quod verum est fateri velimus, Christianos esse negabimus, qui hominū potius traditiones, quàm Christi præcepta sequi voluerint. Quis enim verè Tigurinum dicet, qui Tigurinis legibus viuere detrectet? Christus certè disertè pronūciat: Frustra me colūt, docentes traditiones hominū. Et omnis plantatio, quam nō plātauit pater meus cœlestis,eradicabitur. Matt.15.Præterea D.Paulus Cephæorum, Apollonistarum & Paulinorū nomina pro factiosis ab ecclesia procul eijcit,& Corinthios carnales esse probat,quod istis nominibus in diuersas sectas scinderentur.1.Cor.1.&3.At hodie eò dementiæ processimus, vt eò perfectiores videri velint homines, si sacrosancto nomine Iesu Christi, in quo omne genu flectitur,abnegato,Franciscani, Dominicani, Bernhardini, Benedictini vel Augustiniani potius, q; Christiani dicatur. Sed vtvt illi suâ perfectione iactitent, & titulis vel Seraphicorū vel Cherubicorum turgeant,Christiani verè sunt & censebūtur, qui Christi præcepta seruare studuerint.
units.tr: Above all, it must be noted that he calls those truly Christians and faithful who have observed the precepts of Christ. By this sentence are refuted those who think Christianity consists in the observance of human traditions, and who openly maintain that its perfection lies in them. Thus the Franciscan wishes to be held holier than the rest because he follows the rule of Francis. The Dominican prefers himself both to this man and to all Christians, because he professes the rule of Dominic. The reasoning of many others is the same. But the rule of the Christian is Christ alone. Either we ought to be content to live by this, or it will have to be shown that Francis, Dominic and others of their sort have discovered something holier and more perfect than what has been handed down to us by Christ. But this is as easy to show as to whiten an Ethiopian or to touch the heavens with a finger. Indeed, if we want to confess what is true, we shall have to deny that they are Christians who have preferred the traditions of men to the precepts of Christ. For who would truly call a man a Zurich citizen who refuses to live under the laws of Zurich? Christ certainly declares plainly: "In vain do they worship me, teaching the traditions of men." And every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted (Matt. 15). Moreover, St Paul cast out the names of Cephas, Apollos and Paul as factious from the Church, and proved the Corinthians to be carnal because they were torn into different sects by these names (1 Cor. 1 and 3). But today we have come to such madness that men wish to be thought more perfect if, with the most sacred name of Jesus Christ, in which every knee bows, denied, they are called Franciscans, Dominicans, Bernardines, Benedictines or rather Augustinians, rather than Christians. But however much they boast of their perfection, and swell with the titles of Seraphic or Cherubic doctors, those are and will be counted truly Christians who have striven to keep the precepts of Christ.

units.la: At roget quispiam,quæ nam illa præcepta sint,quorum obseruatio tam necessaria est? Nam eos audias,quibus cū nobis hodie fidei & religionis cōtrouersia agitur, quæcunq; illi & faciūt, & aliis facienda obtrudunt, Christi præcepta esse clamitāt. At in huius causæ dijudicatione,non quid vel illi,vel quid nos dicamus,videndū erit,sed ipsius Christi verbum,quod in scripturis so-nat,audire conuenit. Nam vt Paulus testatur,Iesus Christus heri & hodie,idem est etiā in secula, Heb.13.Quæcunq; ergo olim seruanda tradidit,eorū authoritas & hodie valere debet. Adhæc cū ipsa sit Dei patris sapientia,& huic non ad mensuram spiritum suum pater dederit,sed ita vt de illius gratia nos omnes acceperimus,(Ioan.3.&1.) de præceptorum eius perfectione dubitare non potest,nisi qui & de ipsius Dei & spiritus sancti perfectione dubitare voluerit. Præterea cum in veteri testamento talem legem Deus dederit, cui quicquam vel addere vel adimere,piaculū erat: num nostram conditionem tempore correctionis deteriorem,& tam incertam putabimus,vt nouis assumentis quotidie opus sit? Adde his,quòd Christus ne Apostolis quidem liberum fecit,vt quæ ipsis salutaria videri poterant,traderent. Sed discipulos mihi facite (inquit) omnes gentes, docentes eos seruare,quæcunq; præcepi vobis. Matt.28.Et Paulus apostolus angelum anathema pronunciat,qui euangelium aliud prædicare ausit,quàm ab ipso prædicatum est. Galat.1.Noli er-go,quisquis es,Christi præcepta alibi quàm in scripturis quærere. At quæ nam illa sint,paucis dicendum erit.Possunt enim breuitatis & perspicuitatis ergo tribus ordinibus comprehendi.
units.tr: But someone may ask, what are those precepts whose observance is so necessary? For you will hear those with whom we are today in dispute over faith and religion cry out that whatever they do, and whatever they impose on others to do, are the precepts of Christ. But in judging this cause, we must look not at what they or we say, but hear the very word of Christ, which sounds in the Scriptures. For, as Paul testifies, "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and for ever" (Heb. 13). Therefore the authority of whatever he once handed down to be kept ought to hold good today also. Besides, since he is the very wisdom of God the Father, and God the Father did not give him the Spirit by measure, but so that we all have received from his fullness (John 3 and 1), no one can doubt the perfection of his precepts, unless he also wishes to doubt the perfection of God himself and of the Holy Spirit. Furthermore, since God gave such a law in the Old Testament, to which it was a sin either to add or to take away anything, shall we think that our condition in the time of correction is worse, and so uncertain that we constantly need new additions? Add to these that Christ did not even grant the apostles freedom to hand down whatever they might think salutary. But, he says, "make disciples of all nations, teaching them to keep whatever I have commanded you" (Matt. 28). And the apostle Paul pronounces anathema on any angel who dares to preach a gospel other than what has been preached by him (Gal. 1). Therefore, whoever you are, do not seek the precepts of Christ anywhere but in the Scriptures. But what those precepts are must be told in few words. For they can be comprehended, for the sake of brevity and clarity, under three heads.

units.la: Primus ordo eorum est,quæ fidem nostram instruunt. Præcipuum in his locū obtinet, quo in solum Deum credere iubemur,quod & in Decalogo primum ponitur. Maledictus enim qui fi dit in homine,& carnem fecerit brachium suum. Ierem.17. Proximum ab hoc est, quo is monstra tur,cuius merito & intercessione freti fiduciam & spem in Deum collocare audemus. Nisi enim eum homo videat,frustra illum ad Deum accedere iubebis,cum propriæ conscientiæ testimonio conuictus,se & peccatorem & filium iræ esse sentiat. Hic ergo Christus Iesus monstratur, quem mediatorem illum esse,proximo sermone didicimus. Et vt in se credamus,idem præcipit,dicens: Hæc est voluntas eius,qui misit me,vt omnis qui videt filium & credit in eum,habeat vitā æter nam. Ioan.6. Præceptum quoq; est,quod ait: Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis & onerati estis, &c.Matt.11.Item: Si quis sitit, veniat ad me, & bibat, &c.Ioan.7. Cæterū,quia fides non vana aut hominis persuasione concepta opinio est, sed certa & solida rerum, quæ in Christo proponuntur, apprehensio, Christus nobis hoc loco inspiciedus erit. Nisi enim talem agnoscamus,qualem se in scripturis cognoscendum præbet, fidei præceptum nunquam implebimus, vt nec hæretici fecerunt olim,qui alium Christum longè ab eo diuersum,qui scripturis traditur,finxerut. Poterit autem totus Christus duobus capitibus comprehendi,personæ nimirum & officij confyderatione.
units.tr: The first class is of those things which instruct our faith. The chief place among these is held by the command that we believe in God alone, which is also put first in the Decalogue: "Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm" (Jer. 17). Next to this is the one that shows us him by whose merit and intercession we dare to place our trust and hope in God. For unless a man sees him, you will bid him in vain come to God, since, convicted by the testimony of his own conscience, he feels himself both a sinner and a child of wrath. Here, therefore, Christ Jesus is pointed out, whom we have learned in the preceding sermon to be the mediator. And that we believe in him, the same one commands, saying: "This is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life" (John 6). There is also the command which says: "Come to me, all you who labour and are heavy laden," etc. (Matt. 11). Likewise: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink," etc. (John 7). Moreover, since faith is not an empty opinion conceived by human persuasion, but a certain and solid grasp of the things which are set forth in Christ, Christ must be looked upon here. For unless we acknowledge him as he presents himself to be known in the Scriptures, we shall never fulfil the precept of faith, as the heretics of old did not either, who feigned another Christ, far different from him who is handed down in the Scriptures. Now the whole of Christ can be comprehended under two heads, namely, by consideration of his person and of his office.

units.la: Persona Christi vna est & eadem,adeoq; indiuisa. Conueniunt verò in hac duæ naturæ,diuina & humana: quarum illa ab æterno eiusdem cum patre essentiæ & maiestatis consors,hæc verò præfinitis temporibus ex Maria virgine assumpta est. Conuenire has in vna persona,non misceri aut confundi,dicimus. Manet enim diuinitas,nec vlla humanæ infirmitatis macula violatur. Manet humanitas,nec diuinæ maiestatis gloria absorbetur. Et vt diuina natura perfecta est & omnibus numeris absoluta: sic humanam quoque perfectam & absolutam dicimus,vt quæ vero hominis corpore & anima humana constet. Extant vtriusq; clara in scripturis testimonia. De diuina enim prophetæ loquentes, Christum admirabilem,patrem æternitatis,coæqualem Deo, æternū, adeoq; ipsum dominum & Deum vocant. Isa.9.Zach.13.Iere.23. Rursus ijdem,dum ad humanam eius naturam respiciunt, eúdem furculum de stirpe Iesse, Dauidem, Dauidis filium, nouissimum virorum nominare consueuerunt. Isa.11.&53. In euangelio de diuinitate Christi dicitur: In principio erat verbum,& verbum erat apud Deum,& Deus erat illud verbum. Hoc erat in principio apud Deū. Omnia per ipsum facta sunt,& sine eo factum est nihil,&c.Ioan.1. At de eiusdē humanitate idem euangelista disserens, inquit: Verbum caro factum est: non diuinitatis mutationem, sed humanitatis assumptionem significans. Per expositionem enim addit: Et habitauit in nobis. Sed & ipse Christus in filij Dei persona loquens, ait: Ego & pater unum sumus.Ioan.10.Item: Antequam Abraham nasceretur, ego sum. Ioan.8. Idem vero in persona hominis loquens, dicit: Pater maior me est. Joan. 14. Infinita sunt eius generis testimonia, quę si omnia recensere vel lemus, dies nos deficeret. Sufficiat nobis, Christi præceptum esse, fidei nostræ cumprimis necessarium, ut Jesum Christum verum Deum & hominem in una indivisa persona esse credamus, naturis ita unitis, ut utriusque proprietates integræ permaneant. Qua naturarum & idiomatū communicatione fit, ut de toto Christo interdum dicatur, quod alterius duntaxat naturæ est. Id nisi observetur, errores parit horribiles & hæreses execrandas, ut in Arrio, Ebione, Marcione, Valentino, Nestorio & aliis euenisse legimus. Prodest etiam fidei nostræ fulciendæ hæc cognitio. Nec enim mediatorem agnoscere poterimus Christum, nisi & Deum & hominem esse credamus, ut supra dictum est, & infra quoq; patebit.
units.tr: The person of Christ is one and the same, and therefore undivided. In this person two natures, divine and human, meet: the former, from eternity, a partner of the same essence and majesty with the Father; the latter, assumed from the virgin Mary at appointed times. We say that these are united in one person, not mixed or confused. For the divinity remains, and is violated by no stain of human weakness. The humanity remains, and the glory of the divine majesty is not swallowed up. And just as the divine nature is perfect and complete in every respect, so we say the human nature too is perfect and complete, being made up of a true human body and a human soul. Clear testimonies of both are found in the Scriptures. For when the prophets speak of the divine nature, they call Christ "wonderful, the Father of eternity, equal to God, eternal, and indeed himself the Lord and God" (Isa. 9; Zech. 13; Jer. 23). Again, when they look to his human nature, the same prophets have been accustomed to name him the shoot from the stem of Jesse, David, the son of David, the last of men (Isa. 11 and 53). In the Gospel, of the divinity of Christ it is said: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made," etc. (John 1). But when the same evangelist speaks of his humanity, he says: "The Word was made flesh," signifying not a change of the divinity but an assumption of the humanity. For by way of explanation he adds: "And dwelt among us." But Christ himself, speaking in the person of the Son of God, says: "I and the Father are one" (John 10). Likewise: "Before Abraham was born, I am" (John 8). Yet he speaking in the person of a man says: "The Father is greater than I" (John 14). There are countless testimonies of this kind, which if we were to try to recount them all, the day would fail us. It is enough for us that it is a command of Christ, and especially necessary for our faith, that we believe Jesus Christ to be true God and man in one undivided person, the natures so united that the properties of each remain whole. From this communication of natures and properties it comes about that sometimes of the whole Christ is said what belongs to one nature only. Unless this is observed, it gives birth to horrible errors and execrable heresies, as we read happened in Arius, Ebion, Marcion, Valentinus, Nestorius and others. This knowledge also helps to strengthen our faith. For we shall not be able to acknowledge Christ as Mediator unless we believe him to be both God and man, as has been said above and will also be made clear below.

units.la: Officium Christi ipsis nominibus exprimitur. Cum enim divina providentia in multis hoc poetæ impleatur: Respondent fatis nomina sæpe suis: hoc ipsum in filio Dei, tot seculis expectato cumprimis fieri oportebat. JESV nomen Hebræum est, & illius officium generaliori significatione denotat. Saluatore enim vel seruatore sonat. CHRISTI vox Græca, specialius ipsum quoq; modum saluandi comprehendit. Quem enim Græci Christū dicunt, Hebræis Mesias, nobis vero Unctus appellatur. Ungebatur autem antiquitus divina ordinatione sacerdotes & reges, quos promisi saluatoris typos fuisse, nemo negare potest. Eius itaq; typi respectu saluator noster Christus, id est unctus dici debuit, non quod oleo externo delibutus fuerit, sed quod oleo lætitiæ (ut Psal. 45. habetur) spiritu sancto præ omnibus hominibus donatus, & in hoc consecratus sit, ut populi Dei summum atq; æternum tam sacerdotium quàm regnum susciperet. Quæ causa est, quod Baptista spiritum sanctum visibili specie super Christum descendere & manere vidit. Joan. 1. Cū ergo Dei filium Christum esse credimus & profitemur, eundem populi Dei, id est, ecclesiæ totius sacerdotem & regem agnoscimus. Agnoscenda itaq; sunt in eodem & sacerdotis & regis officia. Sacerdotes olim docebant populum & in lege Dei instituebant. Pro populo item orabant & sacrificabant. Eadem Christus plenissime præstat. Docuit enim iam olim in terris agens, & docet etiamnum hodie, dum verbum suum per ministros à se ordinatos ecclesiæ revelat, & spiritu suo in animis hominum vivificat. Imo solus & unicus ecclesiæ doctor cèseri debet, cum ministri externam duntaxat functionem obire, in hominum vero animis nihil operari possint. 1. Corint.3. Idem pro suis non modo in terris agens orauit, verumetiam hodie pro illis intercessor & aduocatus coram patre apparet, ut in præcedenti sermone vidimus. Præterea sacrificium obtulit, non qualia in veteri testamento offerri solebant, sed seipsum, corpus suum verum & sanguinem, quæ in ara Crucis pro nobis tradita peccati culpam expiaverunt & patrem nobis reddiderunt propitium. Cæterum non ea Christi sacerdotis ratio est, quæ in veteri testamento olim erat. Quia enim mortales erant illi, novis subinde successoribus opus fuit. At Christus cum immortalis sit, nec illi mors dominetur amplius, successore non indiget, ut nec vicario, cum officium sibi commissum minimè negligat. Ipsi enim dictum est: Tu es sacerdos in æternum, secundum ordinem Melchisedech. Psal. 110. Adhæc, cum sanguis boum & hircorum nō posset auferre peccata mundi, (Heb.10.) omniaq; veteris testamenti sacrificia nihil nisi typus essent sacrificij in Cruce immolandi, illa sæpius iterari oportuit. At Christus semel oblatus, nō in manufacta sancta ingressus est, sed in ipsum cœlum, ut appareat nunc in conspectu Dei pro nobis, non ut sæpius offerat semetipsum: sed unica sui corporis & sanguinis oblatione sufficientem & perfectam peccatorum nostrorum expiationem impetravit. Heb.9. Quisquis ergo in fidei causa Christi mandata servare vult, Jesum Christum verum, summum & æternum ecclesiæ sacerdotem esse credat oportet, qui verba vitæ æternæ solus habeat, qui pro nobis apud patrem solus intercedat, quiq; unico corporis & sanguinis sui sacrificio mundi peccata expiaverit. Sed regnum quoque Christi confyderemus.
units.tr: The office of Christ is expressed by the very names. For since divine providence fulfils in many things what the poet says: "Names often answer to their fates," this very thing ought especially to have come to pass in the Son of God, who was expected for so many ages. JESUS is a Hebrew name, and denotes his office in a more general sense. For it means Saviour or Preserver. CHRIST is a Greek word, and comprehends more specially the very manner of saving. For he whom the Greeks call Christ, the Hebrews call Messiah, and to us he is called the Anointed. Now, that by divine ordinance in ancient times priests and kings were anointed, who were types of the promised Saviour, no one can deny. In respect of this type, therefore, our Saviour Christ ought to be called the Anointed, not because he was smeared with external oil, but because he was endowed with the oil of gladness (as is said in Psalm 45) by the Holy Spirit above all men, and in this was consecrated, so that he might take up the highest and eternal priesthood as well as kingdom of the people of God. This is the reason why the Baptist saw the Holy Spirit descend upon Christ in visible form and remain (John 1). Therefore, when we believe and profess that Christ is the Son of God, we acknowledge the same to be the priest and king of the people of God, that is, of the whole Church. The offices of both priest and king must therefore be recognised in the same person. Priests of old taught the people and instructed them in the law of God. They also prayed and sacrificed for the people. Christ performs these same things most fully. For he taught already when he was living on earth, and still teaches today, while he reveals his Word to the Church through ministers ordained by himself, and quickens it by his Spirit in the hearts of men. Indeed he must be regarded as the sole and only teacher of the Church, since ministers can perform only the external function and can accomplish nothing in the hearts of men (1 Cor. 3). The same, while living on earth, prayed for his own, and today too he appears before the Father as their intercessor and advocate, as we saw in the preceding sermon. Moreover, he offered a sacrifice, not such as were wont to be offered in the Old Testament, but himself, his true body and blood, which, delivered for us on the altar of the Cross, expiated the guilt of sin and rendered the Father propitious to us. Yet the manner of Christ's priesthood is not that which existed of old in the Old Testament. For since those priests were mortal, new successors were needed from time to time. But Christ, since he is immortal, and death no longer has dominion over him, does not need a successor, nor a vicar, since he does not in the least neglect the office committed to him. For it was said to him: "You are a priest for ever, after the order of Melchizedek" (Ps. 110). Besides, since the blood of oxen and goats could not take away the sins of the world (Heb. 10), and all the sacrifices of the Old Testament were nothing but a type of the sacrifice to be offered on the Cross, those had to be repeated again and again. But Christ, once offered, entered not into holy places made with hands, but into heaven itself, to appear now before the face of God for us, not so that he might offer himself often; but by the one offering of his body and blood he obtained a full and perfect expiation of our sins (Heb. 9). Therefore, whoever wishes to keep the commands of Christ in the cause of faith ought to believe that Jesus Christ is the true, supreme and eternal priest of the Church, who alone has the words of eternal life, who alone intercedes for us with the Father, and who by the one sacrifice of his body and blood has expiated the sins of the world. But let us also consider the kingdom of Christ.

units.la: Regum officiū in populi incolumitate & publica pace conservanda præcipuè versatur. Huc spectat, ut sibi commissum populum bonis legibus instruant, secundum leges bonas gubernent, pro eius salute vigilent, judicium rectum administrent, suâ cuiq; tribui curêt, armis quoq; (si ita opus fit) eundem contra omnem injustam vim & tyrannidem defendant. At nihil horum Christo deest, si quæ scripturæ de illo tradunt, probè consyderaveris. Populi enim sui incolumitatem & pacem tâto studio quærit & provehit, ut pro hac sanguine proprium fundere dignatus fit. Leges tulit, quæ nō præsenti modo vitæ, verumetiā æternæ serviunt. Easdem tuetur, & obedientibus quidem benefacit, transgressores vero variè punit & coercet. Nec desunt illi arma, quibus regnum suū tueatur, & hostes devincat. Vicit iam olim omnis impietatis caput, fathanâ. Exarmavit peccatorū spicula, quibus is contra nos pugnare solet. Mortis quoq; tyrannidē oppressit, adeoq; portas inferorum contrivit. Pugnat adhuc quotidie verbo suo contra Antichristum & eius propugnatores, tyrannos. Jugulat illos spiritu oris sui. Imò horrenda in illos judicia sæpe exercet, dum fortunis omnibus spoliatos de gradu deijcit, tum honoribus exutos infamia sempiterna polluit, dum consilia eorum disipat, & omnes conatus euertit. Exempla eius generis infinita sunt, & ipse rerum euentus haec vera esse testatur. Quod enim regnū dabis, cuius leges, honor & maiestas tot seculis durarit, quot Christi regnum iam stetisse videmus? Deiecta & euersa iacet Assyriorum monarchia, quae primos mundi tyrannos fundatores habuit, vt ex illius magnificentia nihil, praeter nudam memoriam reliqui habeamus. Intercidit Persica tyrannis, & ita intercidit, vt nulla eius vestigia vspiam appareant. Idem euentus Graecorum Imperium sustulit. Quid Romae, quam aeterni tatis titulo tot assentatores ornauerunt, acciderit, res ipsa loquitur. Vt interim de aliis regnis, quae aliquando floruerunt, nihil dicamus, quorum vix nomina extant. At Christi regnum, vt ab ipsa mundi origine coepit, ita durat in hunc vsque diem, & vsque in cosummationem seculorum durabit. Et licet multis persecutionibus exagitatum fit semper, Christi tamen patrocinio sic defensum est, vt contra illud pugnauisse, nemini tyrannorum vnquam feliciter cesserit. Cōtra Christum enim, ne portae quidem inferorum praevalent. Matth.16. Talis ergo Christus agnoscendus erit, si iuxta ipsius praecepta in illum credere velimus. Cōprehendunt haec, quaecunque de illo in scripturis tradita habemus, eumq; vnicum & solum totius mundi saluatorem esse docent. Peccat ergo in praecipuū Christi praeceptū, quicunq; de eius vel persona vel officio aliter credunt, quàm ipse credere docuit. Peccant item, qui ista quidem se credere profitentur, non autem vno Christo contenti, quae ad redemptionis & salutis nostrae gloriam pertinent, vel proprijs meritis, vel aliis creaturis tribuunt. Vt enim Deus vnus est, qui solus adorari & coli vult: ita vnus est mediator Dei & hominum, Iesus Christus, qui & ipse zelotes cum sit, gloriam suam alteri non dat. 1. Tim. 2. Isa. 42. Ethaec quidem de primo praeceptorum Christi ordine dicta sufficiant.
units.tr: The office of kings chiefly concerns the preservation of the people's safety and public peace. To this end they equip the people entrusted to them with good laws, govern them according to good laws, watch over their welfare, administer right judgment, see that each receives what is his due, and, if need be, defend them by arms against all unjust violence and tyranny. Yet none of these things is lacking in Christ, if you carefully consider what the Scriptures tell us about him. For he seeks and promotes the safety and peace of his people with such zeal that he deigned to shed his own blood for them. He has given laws which serve not only the present life but also the eternal. He protects these laws, does good to those who obey them, and punishes and restrains transgressors in various ways. Nor does he lack arms by which to guard his kingdom and overcome its enemies. Long ago he conquered Satan, the head of all impiety. He has disarmed the darts of sins with which Satan is accustomed to fight against us. He has also overthrown the tyranny of death, and so has broken down the gates of hell.
