Every day he still fights, by his Word, against Antichrist and his supporters, the tyrants. He slays them with the breath of his mouth. Indeed, he often executes dreadful judgments against them: while he strips them of all their fortunes and casts them down from their rank, he also, once they are deprived of their honours, stains them with everlasting infamy, and he scatters their counsels and overturns all their attempts. Examples of this kind are endless, and the very course of events bears witness that these things are true. For what kingdom will you show whose laws, honour and majesty have lasted as many centuries as we see Christ's kingdom has already stood? The Assyrian monarchy, which had as its founders the first tyrants of the world, lies cast down and overthrown, so that of its magnificence we have nothing left but the bare memory. The Persian tyranny has perished, and has perished in such a way that no trace of it appears anywhere. The same fate has taken away the empire of the Greeks. What happened to Rome, which so many flatterers have adorned with the title of eternity, the thing itself speaks. Meanwhile, we say nothing of other kingdoms which once flourished, whose very names barely survive. But Christ's kingdom, as it began from the very origin of the world, so it endures to this day, and it will endure until the consummation of the ages. And although it has always been harassed by many persecutions, it has nevertheless been so defended by Christ's protection that to fight against it has never turned out well for any tyrant. For "the gates of hell shall not prevail against Christ" (Matt. 16). Such then must Christ be acknowledged, if we wish to believe in him according to his own precepts. These things comprise all that we have handed down about him in the Scriptures, and they teach that he alone is the one Saviour of the whole world. He therefore sins against the chief precept of Christ who believes anything about his person or office otherwise than he himself taught us to believe. Likewise they sin who profess to believe these things, but are not content with Christ alone, and ascribe to their own merits or to other creatures what pertains to the glory of our redemption and salvation. For just as God is one, who alone wills to be adored and worshipped, so there is one Mediator between God and men, Jesus Christ, who, being himself jealous, does not give his glory to another (1 Tim. 2; Isa. 42). And let these things said about the first order of Christ's precepts suffice.

units.la: Secundus ordo eorum est, quae ad cultum Dei, siue religionem externam spectant. Nā licet verus Dei cultus spiritualis sit, & in ijs potissimum versetur, quae de fidei praeceptis modo dixi-mus: nostrę tamen infirmitatis rationem habens Deus, externos ritus dedit, quibus fidem & religionem interna exerceamus. In ijsdem vero nostrae sapientiae petulantiā arctissimis terminis cir cūscripsit[?], ne eos cultus ipsi instituere-mus, qui nobis quidem pij & salutares uiderentur, cū Dei vero natura & gloria pugnarent. Et veteribus quidem innumera rituum moles praescripta fuit, quia promissum saluatore, qui legis finis est, varie adumbrari vtile erat. At quia is in mundū mis-sus correctionis tempus attulit, immenso illo Ceremoniarum pelago sublato, quaecunq; fidelem stram adiuuare & animorum deuotione excitare possunt, paucis capitibus comprehendit. Possumus hic primum locum coetibus sacris tribuere, propter promissionem à Christo datam, cum di-cit: Vbi duo vel tres congregati sunt in nomine meo, ibi sum in medio eorum, Matth.18. Atcoue-nisse[?] non prodest, nisi ea fiant, propter quae in nomine Christi conuenire decet. Hic ergo doctrina verbi requiritur, quòd Christus & syncere praedicari, & attentis animis cum fide audiri vult, sicut ea nota Dei filios à filijs diaboli dignoscere doceat. Ioan.8. Et Mariā eo nomine commendat, quod sorore hinc inde discurrente, ipsa pedibus ipsius assidens verbum docentis attenta audiret. Luc.10. Studio verbi preces coniungendae sunt. Nec enim coelestis illa sapientia cuiquā datur, nisi qui ipsam à patre luminum fideli oratione postulauerit. Iac.1. Ad Deum ergo fundendae preces, non ad Creaturas, & cum fide orandum, quae de Dei in nos voluntate & eiusdem praesentia dubitare prohibeat. Obseruandum hoc in omnibus precibus, tam priuatis quàm publicis, quę quàm gratę Deo sint, vel hinc colligi potest, quòd vbiq; nos ad precandum inuitat, & nominis sui inuocationem externis ritibus vniuersis praefert. Psal.50. Praecipuum aute in precibus est, vt & Dei voluntati nos totos subijciamus, & per Christū dominū nos exaudiri petamus. Quia enim toti corrupti & peccatores sumus, nec ipsi Deo quicquam arrogantius praescribere, nec sine Christo mediatore in illius conspectu turpi confidentia tendere debemus. Monet hoc ipse Christus, dū nos in nomine suo orare, & inter orandum dicere iubet: Fiat voluntas tua quemadmodum in coelo, sic etiam in terra. Ioan.16. Matth.6. Accedit his sacramentorum administratio & legitimus eorundem vsus, Baptismi nimirū & Coenae dominicae, quam Eucharistiam & Synaxin veteres dixerunt: in quibus magno studio huc incumbendū est, ne vel prophanentur, vel humanarū traditionum ad-ditionibus corrumpātur, quādo nec Paulum Apostolum sibi tantū permisisse legimus, vt in Coenae administratione per Christū instituta aliquid mutare ausus fuerit. 1. Cor.11. In his fere exter-num cultum consistere legimus, coetibus nimirum sacris, doctrina verbi, precibus & sacramētis, quae omnia & simplicissimè à Christo instituta, & à veteri ecclesia fideliter obseruata sunt. Qui his seruādis intenti sunt, mandata Christi sequuntur, sicq; declarat, se Christū vera notitia & fide apprehendisse. Si qui vero his omissis, nouos ritus ex sese fingunt, coetus sacros negligunt, verbum Dei contemnunt, humana cōmenta venerantur, preces ad Creaturas dirigūt, vel in illis alio mediatore quàm Christo apud patrem vtuntur, sacramentorum vsum peruertunt, insuper omnibus istis imagines addunt, suffitus, consecrationes nouas, imò & noua sacramenta comminiscuntur, ij Christi mandata seruare nequaquam dici poterunt, cũ hæc ab illo præcepta esse nemo probare possit.
units.tr: The second order of them concerns the worship of God, or external religion. For although true worship of God is spiritual, and lies chiefly in those things which I have just now spoken of as the precepts of faith, yet God, taking account of our weakness, has given external rites by which we exercise faith and inward religion. Yet in these matters he has confined within the narrowest limits our presumption of wisdom, so that we would not institute those forms of worship which seemed to us pious and salutary, but which were at odds with the nature and glory of God. Indeed, to the ancients a vast mass of rites was prescribed, because it was useful to foreshadow in various ways the promised Saviour, who is the end of the law. But since he, when sent into the world, brought the time of correction, that immense sea of ceremonies was taken away, and he has comprised in a few chapters whatever can help our faithful and stir up the devotion of souls. We may first assign the first place to sacred assemblies, on account of the promise given by Christ when he says: "Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them" (Matt. 18). But it does not profit to assemble unless those things are done for which it is fitting to come together in the name of Christ. Here therefore the teaching of the Word is required, for Christ wills that it be preached sincerely and heard with attentive minds and faith, as he teaches that by this mark the sons of God are distinguished from the sons of the devil (John 8). And he commends Mary on this account, that while her sister ran here and there, she herself, sitting at his feet, listened attentively to the word of the teacher (Luke 10). Prayers must be joined to zeal for the Word. For that heavenly wisdom is given to no one unless he has asked for it from the Father of lights in faithful prayer (James 1). Prayers are therefore to be poured out to God, not to creatures, and to be offered in faith, which forbids us to doubt the will of God toward us and his presence. This must be observed in all prayers, both private and public, and how pleasing they are to God can be gathered from this, that he everywhere invites us to pray, and prefers the invocation of his name to all external rites (Ps. 50). The chief thing in prayers, however, is that we submit ourselves wholly to the will of God and ask to be heard through Christ our Lord. For since we are wholly corrupt and sinners, we ought neither to prescribe anything more arrogantly to God himself, nor to approach his presence with shameful confidence without Christ the Mediator. Christ himself admonishes us of this, when he bids us pray in his name, and while praying to say: "Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven" (John 16; Matt. 6). To these is added the administration of the sacraments and their lawful use, namely of Baptism and of the Lord's Supper, which the ancients called the Eucharist and Synaxis. In these we must take great care that they are neither profaned nor corrupted by additions of human traditions, since we read that the Apostle Paul did not permit himself so much as to dare to change anything in the administration of the Supper instituted by Christ (1 Cor. 11). In these things we read that external worship chiefly consists: namely in sacred assemblies, the teaching of the Word, prayers and sacraments, all of which were instituted by Christ in the simplest way and were faithfully observed by the ancient Church. Those who are intent on keeping these things follow the commandments of Christ, and thereby declare that they have apprehended Christ by true knowledge and faith. But if any, leaving these aside, devise new rites of their own, neglect sacred assemblies, despise the Word of God, venerate human inventions, direct prayers to creatures, or in them use another mediator than Christ with the Father, pervert the use of the sacraments, and moreover add to all these images, incense, new consecrations, and even invent new sacraments, such persons can by no means be said to keep the commandments of Christ, since no one can prove that these things were commanded by him.

units.la: Tertio præceptorum Christi ordine, quæ ad conuersationem vitæ totius faciunt, continen-tur. Possent hæc tam latè diduci, quàm latè omnis vita nostra & eius actiones extenduntur. Sed tribus capitibus omnia hæc infra Cap.3. Ioannes comprehendet, quæ & nobis sufficere debent. Illic enim filijs Dei purificationem, iustitiam & fraternà dilectionem tribuit. Purificamur quidem solius Christi sanguine, ut supra didicimus. At qui ita purgati sunt, quotidie pedes suos abluere, id est, impuros carnis affectus, quibus ad peccandi studium rapiuntur, deponere debent. Ioan.13. Hoc enim nisi fiat, cũ Deo, qui ipsa est sanctitas, nobis conuenire nõ potest. Leuit.19. Ifa.33. &c. In sanctitiæ[?] vocabulo omnium præceptorum Dei obseruatio comprehenditur, ut nimirū tam Deo quàm singulis hominibus, ea tribuamus, quæ ipsis per nos diuino iure debentur. Dilectio siue charitas non iniurias modò prohibet, sed simul beneficentiá unicè cõmendat. Quia verò de omnibus istis infra copiosè disseremus, hæc paucula modò sufficiant. Hoc interim firmiter tenendum, nos Christi cognitione & fide frustra & falsò gloriaturos, nisi præceptorum Christi studio incensi, eadem legitima obseruatione exequi conemur. Sed video nos primæ huius loci parti diutius immoratos esse, quare tempus postulat, ut ad secundam transeamus.
units.tr: In the third order of Christ's precepts are contained those which pertain to the whole conduct of life. These could be spread out as widely as all our life and its actions extend. But John will comprise all these things under three headings, in chapter 3, and these ought to be sufficient for us. For there he assigns to the sons of God purification, righteousness and brotherly love. We are indeed purified by the blood of Christ alone, as we have learned above. But those who have been thus cleansed ought daily to wash their feet, that is, to lay aside the impure affections of the flesh by which they are carried away to the pursuit of sin (John 13). For unless this is done, they cannot agree with God, who is holiness itself (Lev. 19; Isa. 33, etc.). In the word holiness is comprehended the observance of all the precepts of God, namely that we render to God as well as to each man those things which are due to them by divine right through us. Love or charity not only forbids injuries, but at the same time commends beneficence alone. But since we shall treat all these things at length below, let these few words suffice for now. Meanwhile this must be held firmly: that we shall boast in the knowledge and faith of Christ in vain and falsely, unless, kindled by zeal for the precepts of Christ, we strive to carry them out by their lawful observance. But I see that we have lingered too long over the first part of this place, so time requires that we pass on to the second.

units.la: II. Qui autem seruat sermonem eius, uerè in illo charitas Dei perfecta est. Per hoc scimus, quòd in ipso sumus. Probat his, verè Christum nouisse & verè Christianos esse eos, qui Christi mādata seruat. Probat autè ab effectis, charitate nimirū siue dilectione Dei, quam Christi cognitio in nobis operatur. Argumentum tale est. Omnis qui Deū verè diligit, verè Christū nouit. At omnis qui Christi præcepta seruat, Deum verè diligit. Ergo qui Christi præcepta seruat, verā habet Christi notitiam, & verè Christianus est. Verè autè ad hunc modū argumentari Ioānem, non scriptura modò, sed & cõmunis sensus docet. Qua ratione enim fieri poterit, ut Deum diligat, qui eum nõ nouit? Nū in re ignota hærebit amor? At Deū nouisse non potest, qui Christū ignorat. Ipse enim est splendor gloriæ & expressa imago substantiæ illius. Heb.1. Et Deum nemo vidit unquam, sed filius, qui est in sinu patris, reuelauit nobis. Ioan.1. Plena ergo Christi cognitio præcedat oportet, maximè cum non frigida quædam amoris Dei professio sufficiat, sed hoc requiratur, ut illum super omnia diligamus, eidem soli fidamus, imò illius nomine relinquamus domum, parentes, coniugem, liberos, fratres, denique nos ipsos abnegemus. Matth.10.16. Marc.8. At rursum, tantus hic amor absque mandatorum Christi obseruatione nõ erit. Quia amoris proprium est, ei placere velle, quem amas. Sic filius parenti obediens est, nõ seruili timore, sed filiali amore adductus. Et Deus non alia de causa exigit, ut se diligamus ex toto corde & totis viribus, quàm quòd amor hic nos totos in Dei obseruantiam rapit, & mouet, ut nihil non facere parati simus, quò cũ hoc tanto bono, & tam valde à nobis amato, possimus coniungi. Cum ergo nec Dei amor sine Christi cognitione, nec idem sine præceptorum Christi obseruatione cõsistere possit, plenè & sufficienter præbuit Ioannes, Christianos reuera esse & Christi notitia verè gloriari, qui eius præcepta obseruauerint. Perfectam verò charitatem vocat, non quòd nobis aliquando, dum hic viuimus, ad summam illam perfectionem peruenire liceat, sed studium perfectionis commēdare vult, quo inflammati semper vlterius progredi conemur. Hoc enim qui facere negligunt, se nec Christum nouisse, nec Deum patrem à se diligi, satis apertè testantur.
units.tr: II. Whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of God is made perfect. By this we know that we are in him. John here proves that those who keep Christ's commandments truly know Christ and are truly Christians. He proves it from the effects, namely from the charity or love of God which the knowledge of Christ works in us. The argument runs thus: everyone who truly loves God truly knows Christ; but everyone who keeps Christ's precepts truly loves God; therefore whoever keeps Christ's precepts has true knowledge of Christ and is truly a Christian. That John reasons in this way is taught not only by Scripture but also by common sense. For how can someone love God if he does not know him? Can love take root in a thing unknown? But no one can know God who is ignorant of Christ. For he is the brightness of glory and the express image of his substance (Heb. 1). And no one has ever seen God, but the Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has made him known to us (John 1). Full knowledge of Christ must therefore come first, especially since a cold profession of love for God is not enough; what is required is that we love him above all things, trust him alone, and for his name leave home, parents, wife, children, brothers, and finally deny ourselves (Matt. 10; Mark 8). Again, such great love cannot exist without keeping Christ's commandments. For it is the nature of love to want to please the one you love. So a son obeys his father, moved not by servile fear but by filial love. And God requires us to love him with all our heart and all our strength for no other reason than that this love snatches us wholly into obedience to God and moves us to be ready to do anything, so that we may be joined to that great good, which we love so greatly. Since, then, neither the love of God can exist without the knowledge of Christ, nor the same without the keeping of Christ's precepts, John has fully and sufficiently shown that those who have kept his precepts are truly Christians and rightly glory in the knowledge of Christ. He calls it perfect charity, not because it is ever possible for us, while we live here, to attain that highest perfection, but because he wishes to commend the striving after perfection, by which, inflamed, we should always endeavour to press further forward. For those who neglect to do this sufficiently testify that they neither know Christ nor are loved by God the Father.

units.la: Indicat verò insignem huius studij fructum, quò magis nos cõmoueat & excitet. Ait enim: Per hoc scimus, quod in ipso sumus. Ea igitur Dei dilectio, quæ præceptorum Christi obseruationem in nobis gignit, argumento est, nos verè Christo esse insitos, & vel sola fidem nostram cõtra vacillantis carnis hæsitationem fulcire potest. Si enim in ipso sumus nos, illum in nobis esse oportet. Nam ipse inquit: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum seruabit, & pater meus diliget eũ, & ad eum veniemus, & mansionem apud eũ faciemus. Ioan.14. Non ergo Christum modo intra se habet, qui eum verè nouit, verè diligit, & eiusdem præcepta seruat: sed & pater cum illo mansionem facit, quæ certa hominis salus est, & gloriam parit, cui nulla mundi huius gloria æquari potest. Sic ubiq; Apostolus, Christi exemplū secutus, vehementissimos stimulos adhibet, quibus ad eorum obseruationem impellat, quæ persuadere conatur. At quia pleriq; ex eorũ numero videri volunt, qui Christo insiti sunt, & in quibus vicissim Christus maneat, inde occasione sumpta Ioannes ad institutum redit, & illos sui officij rursus admonet, quæ tertia loci, quę modo tractamus, pars est.
units.tr: He indicates the remarkable fruit of this striving, so as to move and stir us the more. For he says: By this we know that we are in him. Therefore that love of God which begets in us the keeping of Christ's precepts is a proof that we are truly grafted into Christ, and it alone can strengthen our faith against the wavering doubts of the flesh. For if we are in him, he must be in us. For he himself says: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our abode with him (John 14). Therefore he who truly knows Christ, truly loves him, and keeps his precepts not only has Christ within himself, but the Father also makes his abode with him, which is the sure salvation of man and brings forth a glory to which no glory of this world can be compared. So everywhere the Apostle, following the example of Christ, applies the most vehement goads by which he drives men to the observance of those things which he endeavours to persuade them of. But because many of their number wish to appear to be among those who are grafted into Christ, and in whom, in turn, Christ abides, John, taking occasion from this, returns to his purpose and reminds them again of their duty, which is the third part we are now treating.

units.la: III. Qui dicit se in eo manere, debet sicut ille ambulauit, & ipse ambulare. Argumentum est ei simile, quod Cap.1. de luce protulit. Qui cũ Deo societatem habere cupit, eius ingenio se accommomile, quod Cap.1. de luce protulit. Qui cũ Deo societatem habere cupit, eius ingenio se accommodare det, necesse est. Deus vero lux est, & tenebrae in eo sunt nullae. In luce igitur ambulet & operatur tenebrarum fugiat, qui cum hoc communionem expetit. Simili ratione hic docet, Christiani homines esse, ut Christi exemplum imitetur. Maior tamen huic argumento vis ex coniunctione, quae nobis cum Christo est, accedit. Fidei enim opus est, quod Christo inserimus, & vicissim ab illo spiritum ipsius accipimus, qui author est, ut in omni conversatione nostra vivum quoddam Christi exemplar conspiciatur. Ad hanc coniunctionem Paulus respiciens ait: Vivo non iam ego, sed vivit in me Christus. Gal.2. At quomodo fieri poterit, ut secus quam Christus ambulavit, ambulent, in quibus spiritu suo Christus vivit? Nec enim otiosus esse potest Christi spiritus, cum & regeneret, & carnis nostrae affectibus perpetuo resistat. Possent hic multa de Christi exemplo dici, quomodo nimirum ipse ambularit, & quam vitae rationem in terris agens, secutus fit. Sed quia vitam eius omnem ab euangelistis fideliter descriptam habemus, inde petant singuli, quae hic breviuscule traduntur. In Christo fidam cernimus obedientiam, qua patris sui voluntati se totum subiecit. Nam obediens factus est usque ad mortem, mortem inquâ Crucis. Phil.2. Eadem obedientia in omnibus apparet, qui Christum in se manentem habent. Christus nō sua, sed quae patris gloriae seruierunt, quae sivit unice, & illius nomen illustrari optavit. Ioan.12. Idem studium divinae gloriae prouehendae sectabuntur, quicunque in Christo manere cupiunt. Christus se totum & omnia sua hominum saluti impendit, imò & animam pro ouibus suis deposuit. Ioan.10. Eandem charitatem, & idem communis salutis studium ab iis exigit, qui ipsius discipuli censeri volunt. Ioan.15. & 13. Christus extremè humiliatus discipulorum pedes abluit. Ioan.13. Non possunt ergo nō humilitati studere, quicunque in Christo sunt. In Christo innocentia tam perfecta cernitur, ut pharisaeis dicere audet: Quis è vobis arguet me de peccato? Ioan.8. Idem ne falsis quidem testibus alicuius criminis convinci potest. Mar.14. Innocenter ergo & sanctè viuere studebunt, quicunque Christi nomine non frustra gloriari volent. Denique in Christo insigne omnium virtutum speculum, & exemplum omnibus numeris absolutum conspicitur, ad cuius imitationem sedulo accingi decet omnes eos, qui spiritus Christi & regni ipsius cofortes nō falso nomine dicuntur. Ad hoc exemplum, ceu Lydium lapidem, si examinentur, qui hodie Christi nomen profiteri audent, facilè videbimus, quàm pauci sint, qui professioni suae respondeant. Obedientiâ quidem Deo patri pollicemur, dum priuati cum modi ipes affulget: at vbi pro Dei nomine & gloria aliquid audendum est, vbi opum iacturam facere, voluptatum studia deponere, & carnis affectibus resistere iubemur, mox non inobedientes modò, sed murmuratores quoq; inuenimur. Gloriae Dei studium adeò non tangit nos, vt patientibus auribus & oculis ferre possimus, quae diuinam gloriam nō obiter modo lædunt, sed palam blasphemiae sunt & impiae. De innocentia, veritate, humilitate, dilectione fraterna, quid attinet dicere, cum vel caecus videat, quàm procul ab his disiuncti simus? Accedit omnibus istis caput malorum, effrenis admonitionum verbi Dei contemptus, & intolerabilis honestioris disciplinae fastidium, vt ea omnino secula agnoscere liceat, quae ante aduentum suum gloriosum fore Christus Iesus praedixit. Matt.24. Discamus ergo ô fratres, longè aliam veri Christianismi rationem esse, quàm quae nudis verbis & inanibus titulis absolui queat. Christum verè norunt, & reuera Christiani sunt, qui Dei patris charitatem in se perfectam habent. At haec sine praeceptorum Dei obseruatione non consistit. Eadem Christi exemplum imitari docet. Quisquis sine his Christi cognitione & fide gloriari audet, mendax est. Fugiamus itaque tam immane scelus, & Christi tam praecepta quàm exemplum secuti ex eorum numero nos esse testemur, qui cum Christo regnaturi sunt: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: III. He who says he abides in him ought himself also to walk as he walked. This is an argument similar to the one he put forward in chapter 1 concerning light. He who desires to have fellowship with God must necessarily conform himself to God's nature. God is light, and there is no darkness in him. Therefore whoever seeks fellowship with him must walk in the light and flee the works of darkness. In a similar way he teaches here that Christians ought to imitate the example of Christ. Yet this argument gains greater force from the union which we have with Christ. For it is by faith that we are grafted into Christ, and in turn we receive from him his Spirit, who is the author that in all our conduct a living pattern of Christ may be seen. Looking to this union Paul says: I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me (Gal. 2). But how can it happen that those in whom Christ lives by his Spirit walk otherwise than as Christ walked? For the Spirit of Christ cannot be idle, since he both regenerates and constantly resists the affections of our flesh. Much could be said here about the example of Christ, how he himself walked and what manner of life he led on earth and followed. But since we have his whole life faithfully described by the evangelists, let each one seek there what is here delivered very briefly. In Christ we see a faithful obedience, by which he subjected himself wholly to the will of his Father. For he became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross (Phil. 2). The same obedience appears in all who have Christ abiding in them. Christ sought not his own things but those of the glory of his Father, and he wished his name alone to be made illustrious (John 12). Those who desire to remain in Christ will pursue the same zeal for advancing the divine glory. Christ devoted himself wholly, and all that was his, to the salvation of men; indeed he laid down his life for his sheep (John 10). He requires the same love and the same zeal for the common salvation from those who wish to be counted his disciples (John 15 and 13). Christ, being most humble, washed the feet of his disciples (John 13). Therefore all who are in Christ cannot but strive after humility. In Christ such perfect innocence is seen that he dares to say to the Pharisees: Which of you will convict me of sin? (John 8). The same Christ cannot be convicted even by false witnesses of any crime (Mark 14). Therefore all who wish not to glory vainly in the name of Christ will strive to live innocently and holily. Finally, in Christ is seen the notable mirror of all virtues and an example complete in every respect, to whose imitation all those should diligently apply themselves who are not falsely called the fellows of his Spirit and kingdom. By this example, as by the touchstone, if they were tested, those who today dare to profess the name of Christ would easily see how few there are who answer to their profession. We promise obedience to God the Father while a private and comfortable condition shines upon us; but when something must be dared for the name and glory of God, when we are commanded to make loss of wealth, to put aside the pursuit of pleasures and to resist the affections of the flesh, we are at once found not only disobedient but also murmurers. Zeal for the glory of God so little touches us that we can bear with patient ears and eyes things which not merely lightly harm the divine glory but are openly blasphemous and impious. What need is there to speak of innocence, truth, humility, and brotherly love, when even a blind man can see how far removed from these we are? In addition to all these things there is the head of evils, unbridled contempt for the admonitions of God's Word, and an intolerable disdain for a more honourable discipline, so that one may recognise those times, which Jesus Christ foretold would come before his glorious coming (Matt. 24). Let us therefore learn, brothers, that the true Christianity is a very different thing from what can be settled by bare words and empty titles. They truly know Christ, and are really Christians, who have the perfect love of God the Father within them. But this does not stand without the keeping of God's precepts. The same love teaches us to imitate the example of Christ. Whoever dares to glory in the knowledge and faith of Christ without these things is a liar. Let us therefore flee so monstrous a wickedness, and, following both the precepts and the example of Christ, let us bear witness that we are among those who are to reign with Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA VII.
units.tr: Homily VII.

units.la: Fratres, nō præceptū nouum scribo uobis, sed præceptū uetus, quod habuistis ab initio. Præceptū uetus est sermo, quē audistis ab initio. Rursus, præceptum nouum scribo uobis, quod uerū est in ipso & in uobis: quia tenebræ præteriunt, & uerū lumen iam lucet.
units.tr: Brethren, I write to you no new commandment, but an old commandment, which you have had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word which you have heard from the beginning. Again, I write to you a new commandment, which is true in him and in you: because the darkness is passing away, and the true light now shines.

units.la: Divus Ioānes, Apostolus & euangelista, in eo loco, quem nuper tractauimus, dixit: Per hoc scimus, quod in ipso sumus. Qui dicit se in ipso manere, debet sicut ille ambulauit, & ipse ambulare. Comprehendit illis verbis absolutam vitae Christianae rationem, quae in duobus potissimum subsistit. Primum est, ut nos Christo simus insiti per fidem. Quia enim extra hunc salus non est aliqua, & in solo hoc patri complacitum est (Act.4. Matth.17.) frustra sine hoc in aliis rebus laborabimus, cum Deo sine fide quenquam placere impossibile sit. Heb.11. Alterum est, ut quemadmodum nos Christo sumus insiti, ita ipse vicissim in nobis fit, & in nobis spiritu suo operetur. Nam ex nobisipsis non sumus idonei, ut vel cogitemus quod bonum est: & ipse est, qui operatur in nobis & velle & perficere. 2. Cor. 3. Philip. 2. Idem ipse monet, cum inquit: Sine me nihil potestis facere, Ioan. 15. Ex duobus hisce finis Christianae vitae promanat, qui est, ut Dei similes reddamur, de quo iam semel & iterum Apostolus admonuit: eo quod impossibile est hominem saluari, nisi ad eam imaginem Dei, ad quam initio conditus fuerat, & unde sua culpa excidit, repetur. Porrò, cum haec doctrina in mundo, qui totus corruptus est, praedicatur, varia & peruersa de hac audiuntur hominum iudicia. Sunt enim, qui mandata haec non ardua modo, sed & noua, ac pinde[?] superuacanea esse existimant. Inter quos aliqui, dum suis affectibus nimium permittunt, totum euangelium Christi nouitatis insimulant. Illis ergo rursus respondet Ioannes. Et primò quidem, euangelij doctrinam omni nouitatis suspicione liberat. Quia tamen eadem nouum Dei fœdus, & nouum testamentum, nouam quoque legem continere interdum dicitur, secundo loco qua ratione illa dicantur, edocet. Adsit nobis spiritu suo Deus, ut veterem salutis doctrinam recte intelligamus, & ipsi in id quod recte intelleximus transformati, vitae nouitatem coram Christo domino nostro induamus.
units.tr: The divine John, Apostle and evangelist, in the passage which we lately treated, said: "By this we know that we are in him. He who says that he abides in him ought, just as he walked, himself also to walk." In these words he comprehends the whole rule of the Christian life, which chiefly consists in two things. The first is that we be grafted into Christ through faith. For since there is no salvation outside of him, and it has pleased the Father in him alone (Acts 4; Matt. 17), we shall labour in vain in other matters without this, since it is impossible to please God without faith (Heb. 11). The second is that, just as we are grafted into Christ, so he in turn is made in us, and works in us by his Spirit. For we of ourselves are not sufficient even to think anything good; it is he who works in us both to will and to perform (2 Cor. 3; Phil. 2). He himself admonishes this when he says: "Without me you can do nothing" (John 15). From these two things the end of the Christian life flows forth, which is that we be made like God, of which the Apostle has already admonished us once and again: because it is impossible for a man to be saved unless he is restored to that image of God in which he was created at the beginning, and from which he fell through his own fault. Moreover, since this doctrine is preached in a world that is wholly corrupt, various and perverse judgments of men are heard concerning it. For there are some who think these commandments not only hard but also new, and therefore superfluous. Among these, some, while they indulge their affections too much, accuse the whole gospel of Christ of novelty. John therefore answers them in turn. And first, he frees the doctrine of the gospel from every suspicion of novelty. But since the same is sometimes said to contain a new covenant, a new testament, and also a new law, in the second place he teaches in what sense those things are said. May God, by his Spirit, be present with us, that we may rightly understand the old doctrine of salvation, and, having ourselves been transformed into what we have rightly understood, may put on the newness of life before Christ our Lord.

units.la: I. Fratres, non præceptum nouum scribo vobis, sed præceptum vetus, quod habuistis ab initio. Præceptum vetus est sermo, quem audistis ab initio. Diserte & palam negat, quod de nouitate huius doctri-næ obijci poterat. Demonstrationis autem loco hoc ipsum euangelij verbum, quod ab initio prædicatum est, allegat. Sic enim loqui videtur: Scio quàm aduersa sint carni quæ tradimus, cum illa non aliud perinde quærat, quàm ut suis studijs impunè possit indulgere. Hinc multa & varia comminisci solet, quibus doctrinam, quam tradimus, inuisam & contemptam reddat. Et quia veteri corruptæ vitæ consuetudini ipsa assueuit, illico nouum esse clamat, quodcunque illi repugnauerit. Quod si rem ipsam consyderetis ô fratres, longè aliter sentietis. Quid enim aliud tradimus, quàm eam esse Dei voluntatem, ut cultores habeat sui similes? Dicimus enim: Deus lux est, & tenebræ in eo non sunt ullæ. Quòd si in luce ambulamus, sicut ipse est in luce, societatem inter nos habemus. Item: Qui dicit se in ipso manere, debet sicut ille ambulauit, & ipse ambulare. Quid vero aliud unquam requisiuit dominus? Conferte quæso, quæ olim veteribus dicta sunt, cū ijs quæ à Christo tradita habemus, & eandem utrinq; doctrinam haberi intelligetis. Abrahæ patri credenti dominus loquitur: Ego sum Deus omnisufficiens, ambula coram me, & esto integer. Gene. 17. In lege nunquam non inculcatur hæc sententia. Sancti estote, quia ego sanctus sum Dominus Deus vester. Leuit. 19.20. &c. Eandem doctrinâ in Psalm. & prophetis ubiq; invenire licet. Quòd si Christum audias, hoc ipsum non semel tradit. Nam in euangelio ait: Perfecti estote, quemadmodum pater vester, qui est in cœlis, perfectus est. Matth. 5. Et alibi: Deus est spiritus, & eos qui adorant eum, spiritu & veritate oportet adorare. Ioan. 4. Quibus certè hoc unum exigitur, ut diuinæ naturæ similes & conformes reddamur. Nec discrepat ab hoc communis humanæ rationis sensus. Quia enim salutis ratio non alia in re, quàm in societate cum Deo (qui summum bonum & unicus salutis fons est) consistit, & inter dissimiles studijs societas nulla esse potest, Dei similes reddamur oportet, si cum illo conuenire & salutem consequi velimus. Quoad ergo finem & scopum doctrinæ tam veteris quàm noui testamenti, discrimen planè nullum est. Quòd si medium inquiras, quo hæc Dei similitudo in nobis reparatur, utrobique idem inuenies. Adamo certè eo ipso die, quo ab imagine hac exciderat, semen mulieris promittitur, quod & caput serpentis conterere, & perditam hominis naturam instaurare debeat. Gen. 3. In lege idem & apertis oraculis & typis non obscuris adumbratur. Prophetarum testimonia & plura sunt & euidentiora, quàm ut illis commemorandis nos immorari necesse sit. Quæ ergo inscitia est (ne quid dicam grauius) nouitatis accusare, quod à prima mundi origine doceri coeptum, & progressu temporis per omnes Dei seruos omnibus seculis traditum est? Offertur hic latissimus dicendi campus, & in immensum extendi poterat oratio, si singulos salutis nostræ & fidei Christianæ articulos altius scrutari, & quæ de his tam in veteri quàm noua scriptura habentur, conferre vellemus. Sed diligentiorem omnium horum cõsyderationem pijs & fidelibus relinquimus, quibus occasionem & viam monstrauisse sufficiat. Sunt tamen alia quædam hic expendenda, quorum obseruatio hodie nec inutilis nec superuacanea est.
units.tr: I. Brethren, I write to you no new commandment, but an old commandment, which you have had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word which you have heard from the beginning. He plainly and openly denies what could be objected concerning the novelty of this doctrine. As a proof, however, he cites this very word of the gospel, which has been preached from the beginning. For he seems to speak thus: I know how hostile to the flesh is what we hand down, since the flesh seeks nothing else than that it may indulge its pursuits with impunity. Hence it is wont to invent many and various things by which it makes the doctrine we hand down hateful and despised. And because it has become accustomed to its old corrupt way of life, it at once cries out that whatever resists it is new. But if you consider the matter itself, brethren, you will think quite otherwise. For what else do we hand down than that it is the will of God that he should have worshippers like himself? For we say: God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all. But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another. Likewise: he who says that he abides in him ought, just as he walked, himself also to walk. What else, indeed, has the Lord ever required? Compare, I beg you, what was of old said to the ancients with what we have been handed down by Christ, and you will understand that one and the same doctrine is held on both sides. The Lord speaks to Abraham, the father, who believed: "I am God Almighty; walk before me, and be upright" (Gen. 17). In the law this sentence is never not inculcated: "Be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy" (Lev. 19, 20, etc.). The same doctrine may be found everywhere in the Psalms and the prophets. And if you hear Christ, he delivers this very thing not once. For in the gospel he says: "Be perfect, as your Father who is in heaven is perfect" (Matt. 5). And elsewhere: "God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and in truth" (John 4). Certainly this one thing is required of these, that we be made like and conformed to the divine nature. Nor does the common sense of human reason disagree with this. For since the reason of salvation consists in nothing else than in fellowship with God (who is the highest good and the only fountain of salvation), and there can be no fellowship between those who are unlike in their pursuits, we must be made like God if we wish to agree with him and obtain salvation. Therefore, as to the end and aim of the doctrine of both the Old and the New Testament, there is plainly no difference. But if you inquire into the means by which this likeness of God is restored in us, you will find the same on both sides. To Adam, certainly, on the very day on which he had fallen from this image, the seed of the woman is promised, who ought both to crush the serpent's head and to restore the lost nature of man (Gen. 3). In the law the same thing is shadowed forth both by plain oracles and by not obscure types. The testimonies of the prophets are both more numerous and more evident than that we need to dwell on recounting them. What folly, then (not to say anything harsher), is it to accuse of novelty what has begun to be taught from the very origin of the world, and in the course of time has been handed down through all the servants of God in all ages? Here a very broad field for speaking opens up, and the discourse could be extended immensely if we wished to examine each article of our salvation and of the Christian faith more deeply, and to compare what is held about these both in the old and in the new Scripture. But we leave the more careful consideration of all these things to the godly and faithful, to whom it is enough to have shown the way and the method. There are, however, certain other matters to be weighed here, the observance of which today is neither useless nor superfluous.

units.la: Primò Ioannem consyderemus, qui tanto studio doctrinam abs se tradita nouitatis suspicio-ne liberat. Egerat idem in ipso epistolæ huius principio. Non tamen ijs contentus, hoc ipsum in præsenti & repetit & plenius illustrat. Idem reliqui Apostoli faciunt. Nam & Paulus veteris scripturæ oraculis crebrò utitur, & Petrus nec se nec reliquos sui ordinis vel ab alijs deceptos, vel falsas sponte secutos fuisse, sed quæ ex ipso Christo & prophetarum scriptis hauserunt, ab ipsis tradita esse testatur.2.Pet.1.Imo ut ad Paulum redeamus, ea cura illum hic usum esse videmus, ut diserte inter ea, quae a Christo tradita noverat, & quae ipsi factu digna sine expresso Christiman-dato videbantur, distinxerit.1.Cor.7.&c.Eodem referri potest & debet, quod prophetę in suis o-rationibus nunquam non & praemittunt & repetunt: Haec dicit Dominus Deus exercituum. Nec hanc inanem vel superstitiosam curam fuisse putare quisquam debet. Nam in lege cauerat Deus, ne quis verbo suo vel adderet vel adimeret.Deut.4.&12. Et prophetis diserte mandatum fuit, ut verbum ex ore Dei, non proprio cerebro desumeret: quod videre est Jere.1.Ezech.3.&33.cap.Sed &Christus, cum apostolos praedicatum emitteret, inquit: Docete homines servare, quae ego vobis tradidi. Matth.28. Faciunt haec ad demonstrandum perfectionem & certitudinem doctrinae verbi divini, quae in scripturis continetur. Si enim nec Mosi, amico & collocutori supremi numinis familiarissimo, nec sanctis viris Dei prophetis, nec dilectis Christi apostolis permissum fuit a praescripta doctrinae forma discedere, & nova dogmata novosq; articulos proponere ecclesijs, eam perfectionem & certitudinem huius doctrinae esse constat, quae nec humanae sapientiae additionibus, nec humanae authoritatis approbatione sive testimonio opus habeat. Quę ergo (malū) vaesania est, doctrinam hanc in dubium vocare, dum vel multa addi oportere putamus, vel hominum authoritatem, qua approbetur, requirimus? Paulus se ipsum quoq; anathema pronunciat, si euangelium novum praedicet. Gal.1.Et nobis sua commenta impudenter obtrudent, qui nec eruditione nec pietatis zelo vel micam Paulini pectoris referunt?
units.tr: First, let us consider John, who with such zeal frees the doctrine he hands down from suspicion of novelty. He had done the same at the very beginning of this epistle. Yet not content with this, he both repeats it here and illustrates it more fully. The other apostles do the same. For Paul too frequently uses the oracles of the old Scripture, and Peter testifies that neither he nor the rest of his order had been deceived by others or had voluntarily followed false things, but that what they handed down they had drawn from Christ himself and from the writings of the prophets (2 Pet. 1). Indeed, to return to Paul: we see him take such care here that he expressly distinguishes between those things which he knew to have been handed down by Christ, and those which seemed to him worthy of being done without an express command of Christ (1 Cor. 7, etc.). To the same category can and should be referred what the prophets, in their orations, never cease both to prefix and to repeat: "Thus says the Lord God of hosts." Nor should anyone think that this was a vain or superstitious care. For in the law God had taken care that no one should either add to or take away from his word (Deut. 4 and 12). And the prophets were expressly commanded to take the word from the mouth of God, not from their own brain; as may be seen in Jer. 1, Ezek. 3 and chapter 33. But also Christ, when he sent out the apostles to preach, said: "Teach men to observe what I have delivered to you" (Matt. 28). These things serve to demonstrate the perfection and certainty of the doctrine of the divine word, which is contained in the Scriptures. For if neither Moses, the friend and most intimate interlocutor of the supreme deity, nor the holy men of God, the prophets, nor the beloved apostles of Christ, were permitted to depart from the prescribed form of doctrine and to propose new dogmas and new articles to the churches, then it is clear that this doctrine has such perfection and certainty that it needs neither additions of human wisdom nor the approval or testimony of human authority. What, then, is the madness (to put it bluntly), to call this doctrine into doubt, when we think either that many things ought to be added to it, or we seek the authority of men by which it may be approved? Paul pronounces even himself anathema if he preaches a new gospel (Gal. 1). And shall they impudently thrust their own inventions upon us, who do not bear even a crumb of the Pauline breast, neither in learning nor in zeal for piety?

units.la: Sed objiciat aliquis: Fatemur equidem euangelij doctrinam, sicuti olim per apostolos praedicata est, illis temporibus sufficisse. Sed additiones nostra tempora postulant, quae si a viris pijs sancto zelo & studio provehendae pietatis constituantur, non video cur vel amarulentius reprehendi, vel pro inutilibus negligi debeant. Habent eiusmodi objectiones aliquid momenti apud simpliciores homines, qui aliorum authoritatem suspicere consueuerunt. Sed maior apud nos divinae sapientiae authoritas esse debet, ne quid quod huic de detrahat, temere statuamus. Primo enim constat, hanc cum certa & immutabili veritate coniunctam esse. Nihil ergo statuit quod sibipsi pugnet, quales fere omnes sunt hominum traditiones, si ad verbi Dei regulam examinentur. Deinde scripturas non antiquis modo seculis, sed & nostris, adeoq; omnibus, datas esse constat, quae ad mundi consummationem usque evolui debent. Manet ergo earundem omnibus seculis firma & inviolata authoritas. Quoad vero illa manserit, consistere non possunt quaecunque cum scripturis pugnantia ab hominibus quantumuis doctis & devotis statuuntur. Si enim hoc asseramus, Dei sapientiam adeo imbecillem & imperfectam fingemus, ut quid omnibus seculis prosit & conveniat, videre non potuerit. Facit huc Pauli testimonium, qui de novissimi seculi impostoribus differens, ijsdem non aliud antidotum, quam scripturae sacrae authoritatem opponit, Timotheo suo scribens: At tu persistito in his, quae didicisti, & quae tibi concredita sunt: sciens a quo didiceris, & quod a puero sacras literas noveris, quę te possunt eruditum reddere ad salutem per fidem quae est in Christo Jesu. Quod si novissimo tempore novis traditionibus opus est, stulte & pernitiose monet Apostolus, qui ad solas scripturas relegat, & in illis persistere docet. At nec stultum nec perniciosum esse potest consilium, quodcunque Dei verbo obedire suadet. Stulti potius & perniciosi seductores censeri debent, qui certam salutis viam, in scripturis monstratam, relinquere, & ad incerta humanarum traditionum avia declinare iubent. Sunt & aliae rationes, quas diligenter observasse multum prodest, ut ingenij nostri insolentiam retundamus, qua suas nugas divinis legibus aequiparare audet. Nam ut modo diximus, ut primum nova fingunt homines, divina suspecta fiunt, quasi vel non sufficiant, vel tanquam inutilia abrogari debeant. Pugnat vero utrumque cum manifestis Dei oraculis. Christus enim in scripturis vitam aeternam contineri, & Paulus loco supra citato, eadem ad hoc servire dicit, ut hominem perfectu reddant &ad omne opus bonum praeparent.Joan.5. 2.Tim.3.Et apud Jsaiam propheta spiritus sanctus clamat: Verbum domini manet in aeternum. Jsa.40. Praeterea servitus non necessaria imponitur simplicio-rum conscientijs. Quia enim divina sufficiunt, humana illa superuacanea & inutilia sint oportet. Quare & Christus eadem sarcinis confert, quas falsi doctores imponant, ipsi vero eosdem ne digi-to quidem attingant.Matth.23.Tum Paulus indignum & absurdum esse iudicat, ut qui pretiolo Christi sanguine redempti sunt, servi hominum fiant.1.Corinth.7.Accedit omnibus istis, quod per humana praecepta a divinis abstrahimur. Sic enim natura comparatum est, ut foetuum nostrorum amantes simus nimium. Ut primum igitur humanae rationis statuta, pietatis & sanctimoniae fuco velata, cernimus, mox divina sordere incipiunt, & pro inutilibus vel superuacaneis negliguntur. Hinc illa in divinis praeceptis dispensandi audacia, quae quam Deo displiceat, infelix Saulis regis exemplum docet, quod qui videre cupit, historiam sacram legat, 1. Sam.13.&15. Non temere ergo factum putemus, quòd Dominus per Mosem loquitur: Ne peruertigetis post cor vestrũ, aut post oculos vestros, post quos scortari soletis. Quin memores sitis, & facietis omnia præcepta mea, eritisq; sancti Deo vestro. Numeri 15.
units.tr: But someone may object: "We grant that the doctrine of the Gospel, as it was once preached by the apostles, sufficed in those times. But our own times demand additions. If these are established by pious men with holy zeal and eagerness to advance piety, I do not see why they should be criticised more harshly, or neglected as useless." Objections of this kind carry some weight with simpler people, who are accustomed to look up to the authority of others. But the authority of divine wisdom must be greater among us, so that we do not rashly decide anything that detracts from it. For first, it is agreed that this wisdom is joined with certain and unchanging truth. It therefore lays down nothing that contradicts itself, which is nearly the case with all human traditions when they are tested by the rule of God's Word. Second, it is agreed that the Scriptures were given not only for ancient ages but also for ours, and for all ages, and that they must unfold until the end of the world. Therefore their firm and inviolable authority remains for all ages. As long as that authority remains, whatever is laid down by men, however learned and devout, that conflicts with the Scriptures cannot stand. For if we were to assert this, we would be imagining God's wisdom so feeble and imperfect that it could not see what would benefit and suit all ages. Paul's testimony bears on this. Speaking of the impostors of the last age, he opposes to them no other antidote than the authority of holy Scripture, writing to his Timothy: "But you, continue in the things you have learned and that have been entrusted to you, knowing from whom you learned them, and that from childhood you have known the holy letters, which can make you wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus." If in the last times new traditions were needed, the Apostle would be giving foolish and harmful advice when he refers people only to the Scriptures and teaches them to persist in them. But no advice can be foolish or harmful when it urges obedience to God's Word. Rather, those should be judged foolish and harmful seducers who bid us leave the certain way of salvation shown in the Scriptures and turn aside to the uncertain byways of human traditions. There are also other considerations, which it is very useful to observe carefully, so that we may repress the insolence of our own mind, which dares to equate its trifles with divine laws. For, as we have just said, as soon as men invent new things, the divine things become suspect, as though they were either insufficient or ought to be abrogated as useless. Yet both of these conflict with the clear oracles of God. For Christ says that eternal life is contained in the Scriptures, and Paul, in the passage cited above, says that the same Scriptures serve this purpose, that they make the man of God perfect and prepare him for every good work. (John 5; 2 Tim. 3.) And the Holy Spirit cries out through the prophet Isaiah: "The word of the Lord abides forever." (Isa. 40.) Moreover, an unnecessary servitude is imposed on the consciences of simple people. For since the divine things suffice, those human additions must be superfluous and useless. Hence Christ also lays on men the same burdens that false teachers impose, while they themselves will not so much as touch them with a finger. (Matt. 23.) Then Paul judges it unworthy and absurd that those who have been redeemed by the precious blood of Christ should become servants of men. (1 Cor. 7.) To all these things is added this: through human precepts we are drawn away from the divine. For it is so naturally ordered that we love our own offspring too much. Therefore, as soon as we see the statutes of human reason, veiled with the colour of piety and holiness, the divine things immediately begin to look contemptible and are neglected as useless or superfluous. Hence comes that audacity in dispensing with divine precepts, the displeasure of which God shows by the unhappy example of King Saul; whoever wishes to see this should read the sacred history (1 Sam. 13 and 15). Let us not think it happened by chance that the Lord speaks through Moses: "Do not go astray after your heart or after your eyes, after which you are accustomed to whore. But remember, and do all my precepts, and you shall be holy to your God." (Num. 15.)

units.la: Venit hic nobis deploranda infelix nostri seculi cæcitas, quæ quicquid de Christo, saluatore nostro, ex euangelij doctrina profertur, nouitatis crimine infamat & inuisum reddit. Si enim omnes doctrinæ, quam hodie ecclesijs nostræ fidei commisisis tradimus, articulos confyderes, non alios videbis, quàm qui & veteris & noui testamenti libris olim traditi sunt. His enim docemur Christum regem & sacerdotem esse æternum. His docemur, eundem ecclesiæ suæ caput esse vni cum. His docemur, vnum hunc pro peccatis nostris in ara Crucis expiationem factum esse, & semel immolatum corporis ac sanguinis ipsius hostiam pro totius mundi peccatis sufficere. Ex ijsdem sacrosanctam domini Cœnam, non sacrificium pro peccatis mortuorum & viuentium, sed sacrificij olim oblati commemorationem esse discimus. Christus eandem instituens, vtranq; speciem tradidit, & ex poculo omnes iusit bibere. Luc.22. Paulus quod à Christo acceperat, toti Corinthiorum ecclesiæ communicare ausus est. 1.Cor.11. Scripturæ vnum & solum Christum inter nos & Deum mediatorem vel intercessorem esse tradunt. Scripturæ omnibus afflictis in solo hoc pacem & refocillationem monstrant. Scripturæ non creaturas, sed Deum Creatorem per filium Christum inuocari debere docent. Scripturæ à solo Deo peccata nobis propter filij meritū remit ti prædicant. Christus Iesus clamat: Nemo venit ad patrem, nisi per me. Ioan.14. Petrus non aliud nomen, sub cœlo hominibus datum esse asserit, per quod saluari queant, præterquam nomen Iesu. Act.4. Christus cultum & adorationem certis locis alligare vetat. Ioan. 4. Christus hominis vires nullas esse, nec nos aliquid sine ipso posse, affirmat. Ioan.15. Christus Iesus omnes plantationes non plantatas à patre suo eradicandas esse prædicit. Matth.15. Christus pseudoprophetas esse docet, qui ipsum in syluis, in penetralibus, aut clausis receptaculis, monstrare audeant. Matth.24. Christi spiritu præmoniti Apostoli dæmoniorum doctrinas esse clamant, quibus & matrimonium vsus prohibetur, & ciborum discrimina introducuntur. 1.Tim.4. Col.2. In scripturis imagines illicitas & Deo exosas esse, spiritus sanctus acerrimè contendit. Scripturis edocemur, non proprijs operibus, sed sola fide in Christum propter illius meritum nos iustificari posse. Apostolus factiosa Paulinorum, Apollæorum, Petrinorum, & multò magis Franciscanorum, Dominicanorum, Benedictinorum, & si quæ alia sunt eius generis nomina, ab ecclesijs eijci debere monet.
units.tr: Here we are confronted with the lamentable, unhappy blindness of our age, which brands with the charge of novelty whatever is put forward about Christ our Saviour from the doctrine of the Gospel, and makes it hated. For if you consider the articles of all the doctrine that we today hand down to the churches committed to our faith, you will see none other than those that were once delivered in the books of both the Old and the New Testament. For from these we are taught that Christ is an eternal King and Priest. From these we are taught that he is the one Head of his Church. From these we are taught that this one, by his death on the altar of the Cross, was made the expiation for our sins, and that his body and blood, offered once, is a sacrifice sufficient for the sins of the whole world. From these same sources we learn that the holy Lord's Supper is not a sacrifice for the sins of the dead and the living, but a commemoration of the sacrifice once offered. Christ, instituting it, gave both kinds, and commanded all to drink from the cup (Luke 22). Paul dared to share with the whole congregation of the Corinthians what he had received from Christ (1 Cor. 11). The Scriptures teach that Christ alone, one and only, is the Mediator or Intercessor between us and God. The Scriptures show that in him alone peace and refreshment are found for all who are afflicted. The Scriptures teach that God the Creator, not creatures, must be invoked through the Son Christ. The Scriptures proclaim that sins are forgiven us by God alone, for the sake of the Son's merit. Christ Jesus cries: "No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14). Peter asserts that no other name under heaven has been given to men by which they may be saved, except the name of Jesus (Acts 4). Christ forbids binding worship and adoration to certain places (John 4). Christ affirms that man has no strength, and that we can do nothing without him (John 15). Christ Jesus foretells that every plant not planted by his Father shall be uprooted (Matt. 15). Christ teaches that they are false prophets who dare to point to him in the woods, in the inner chambers, or in closed storerooms (Matt. 24). Forewarned by the Spirit of Christ, the Apostles cry out that the doctrines are of demons, which forbid marriage and the use of foods and introduce distinctions among meats (1 Tim. 4; Col. 2). In the Scriptures the Holy Spirit most sharply contends that unlawful images are hateful to God. From the Scriptures we are taught that we are justified not by our own works, but by faith alone in Christ, on account of his merit. The Apostle warns that the factious names of the Paulines, the Apollonians, the Petrines, and much more of the Franciscans, Dominicans, Benedictines, and whatever other names are of that kind, must be cast out of the churches.

units.la: Attamen omnia hæc & quæcunque alia contra Romanæ sedis & communem errorem aliquot seculorum ex scripturis hodie traduntur, partim à simplicioribus & rerum imperitis, partim ab illis ipsis qui ecclesiarum & verbi antistites haberi volunt, nouitatis, imò & hæreseos accusantur. Noua ergo, siquidem hoc audiamus, Moses tradidit, & quicunque ante hunc viua Dei voce eruditi fuerunt. Noua ex suo cerebro prophetæ tradiderunt. Nouorum dogmatum Christus Iesus author fuit. Noua prædicarunt Apostoli, quorū scriptis & diserte & copiosè probari possunt, quæ modò diximus, omnia. Vide ergo, quisquis es, quid humanis traditionibus debeamus, quas per annos iam sexcentos aut quingentos egregij illi, si dijs placet, patres nobis obtrusere. Vetera dicuntur, quæ paucis seculis (nec tamen sine contradictione) in ecclesia durauerunt. Vicissim vero pro nouis & inauditis proscribuntur, quæ à prima mundi origine in hæc vsque tempora ab omnibus fidis Dei cultoribus & credita & obseruata fuerunt. Neminem sanè Turcarum esse arbitror, qui nouorum dogmatum prædicatorem dicat esse eum, qui doctrinam Mahometis ex Alcorano desumptam proponit. At inter Christianos eò cæcitatis deuentum est, vt pro veteribus non agnoscantur, quæ ipse Christus proprio ore locutus est, quæ ante hunc olim prophetæ, & post ipsius in cœlos ascensum, ex ipsius spiritu Apostoli tam prædicatione quàm scriptis tradiderunt. Eant nunc, & egregios suarum traditionum fructus prædicent, qui pietatem, vitæ innocentiam, religionis studiū, & alias præclaras virtutes his plantari dicunt. Illis enim verè opponetur, quod & omnem Christi doctrinam euertant, & ex Christianis ignaros ac cæcos hominum seruos faciant, qui nec veteres doctrinas amplecti, nec nouas fugere possint. Discamus itaque ex prima huius loci parte de doctrinæ & fidei vetustate, non ex paucis annorum centurijs ac hominum decretis iudicare, sed scripturas audiamus, quæ salutis nostræ ratione ab ipsa mundi origine deducunt.
units.tr: Nevertheless, all these things, and whatever else is today taught from the Scriptures against the Roman see and the common error of several centuries, are accused of novelty, and even of heresy, partly by simpler people and those inexperienced in affairs, and partly by those themselves who wish to be regarded as the leaders of the churches and of the Word. Therefore, if we listen to them, the new things are what Moses handed down, and all who were taught before him by the living voice of God. The prophets handed down new things from their own brain. Christ Jesus was the author of new doctrines. The Apostles preached new things; by their writings all the things we have just mentioned can be proved both clearly and abundantly. See then, whoever you are, what we owe to human traditions, which those outstanding men, if it pleases the gods, have foisted upon us over the past six or five hundred years. Things are called old that have lasted in the Church for a few centuries (and not without contradiction). Conversely, things that have been believed and observed by all the faithful worshippers of God from the first origin of the world down to these times are proscribed as new and unheard of. Surely I think there is no Turk who would call a preacher of new doctrines the man who sets forth the teaching of Mohammed taken from the Koran. But among Christians things have come to such blindness that those which Christ himself spoke with his own mouth are not recognised as old, nor those which the prophets of old taught before him, nor those which the Apostles, after his ascension into heaven, handed down from the Spirit of Christ both by preaching and by writing. Let them go now and proclaim the excellent fruits of their traditions, who say that piety, innocence of life, zeal for religion, and other splendid virtues are planted by them. For to them will rightly be opposed the fact that they overturn all the doctrine of Christ and make Christians into ignorant and blind slaves of men, who can neither embrace the old doctrines nor shun the new. Let us therefore learn from the first part of this place to judge of the antiquity of doctrine and faith not by a few centuries and the decrees of men, but let us hear the Scriptures, which trace the reasoning of our salvation from the very origin of the world.

units.la: Cæterum multos hic mouet noui fœderis & noui Testamenti appellatio, qua & ipse Deus vti voluit. Nam apud prophetam ait: Ecce dies venient, dicit dominus, & consummabo super domum Israel, & super domum Iuda, testamentum nouum, non iuxta testamentum, quod feci patribus illorum, &c. Iere.31. Quæ verba Paulus exponens inquit: Per hoc quod dicit nouum, antiquauit prius. Porrò quod antiquatur & senescit, in propinquo est, vt euanescat. Hebr.8. Adhæc ipse dominus & saluator Iesus Christus, cum in sacrosancta Cœna corporis sui pro nobis traditi, & sanguinis pro nobis effusi folennem & gratam commemorationè institueret,de poculo dicit:Hic est sanguis meus,qui est noui testamenti,&c.Matth.26. Eadem verba autem Paulus ad hunc modum reddidit: Nouum testamentum est in sanguine meo.1.Cor.11.Ex his multi nos fatis ineptos esse colligunt,quòd euangelicæ doctrinæ vetustate ex Mose & prophetis demonstrare conemur, cum ipse Dei filius totum hoc nostræ redemptionis negotiū, cuius ipse author & executor fuit, nouum appellet.Sed respondet his in ijs quæ sequuntur,hoc modo Apostolus:
units.tr: Moreover, the name "new covenant" and "new Testament," which God himself chose to use, troubles many people here. For through the prophet he says: "Behold, the days will come, says the Lord, and I will complete a new testament with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the testament that I made with their fathers, etc." (Jer. 31.) Paul, expounding these words, says: "In that he says 'new,' he has made the first one old. Now what is made old and grows aged is near to vanishing away." (Heb. 8.) Furthermore, the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ himself, when in the most holy Supper he instituted a solemn and pleasing remembrance of his body given for us and his blood shed for us, said of the cup: "This is my blood of the new testament, etc." (Matt. 26.) Paul, however, rendered the same words in this way: "The new testament is in my blood." (1 Cor. 11.) From these words many conclude that we are quite foolish, because we try to show the antiquity of the evangelical doctrine from Moses and the prophets, when the Son of God himself calls this whole business of our redemption, of which he was himself the author and executor, new. But the Apostle answers these objections in what follows:

units.la: I I. Rursus, præceptum nouum scribo uobis,quod uerum est in ipso & in uobis: quia tenebrae præte-reunt,& uerum lumen iam lucet. Concessionem habent hæc verba. Fatetur enim Ioannes,præce-ptum,quod modo vetus esse dixerat,nouum quoque dici, sed qua ratione sic dicatur, clare indi-cat.Obscuritatem vero huic loco vnica particula QVOD attulit. Quia enim hanc putarunt re-ferri ad præceptum,mire sese in hac sententia explicanda torserunt. At in Græca scriptura,alio e-am referri debere patet.Quod enim nos præceptum neutro genere dicimus,Græci ἐντολὴ[?] habent, quæ fœminini generis vox est,cui Relatiuum neutri generis minimè respondet. At fi hoc ad to-tum huius orationis contextum referas,mox sensus erit perspicacior.Sic enim Ioannes loquitur: Dixi me non noua,sed vetera scribere.Rursum verò, quia noui testamenti & nouæ legis vocabu-la vos objcitis,illa quoque repudiare nolo, sed nouum præceptum me scribere fateor: quod ve-rum est,id est,quod vere à me dici potest,non quidem quoad doctrinam, sed eorum respectu cir-ca quæ illa versatur.His iam cohærent sequentia, quibus euangelij præcepta duplici ratione no-ua dici tradit: partim nimirum in ipso Christo, id est, propter Christum:partim verò in nobis,id est,propter nos.Si enim quæ de substantia & summa salutis nostræ in euangelio traduntur,con-fyderes,eadem sunt cum ijs,quæ veteres scripturæ olim tradiderunt. Quòd fi verò ipsum Chri-ftum & nos,qui per hunc redempti fumus,inspicias,ijsdem nouitatis vocabulum non ineptè con-uenire videbis.Propter Christum enim nouum dici poterit,quia hic testamentum Dei, quod no-ftra culpa quasi obliteratum erat & abolitum,fui sanguinis merito instaurauit. Et vt pictura,cu-ius colores vetustate obscuriores facti sunt,fi à perito artifice instauretur, noua dicetur ob colo-res recenter induction,eadem tamen ob lineamenta veteris picturæ seruata,verè vetus est:ita Dei testamentum,quo salus nostra cotinetur,propter Christum reftauratorem nouum dicitur, cum reuera vetus fit, nec aliud comprehendat, quàm quod olim per Mosen & prophetas promissum fuit.Deinde quoad nos,vel propter nos,nouum dici potest quod traditur: quia tenebrae præterete-unt,& verum lumen iam lucet. Sunt qui per tenebras legem cum vmbris & typis suis intellexe-runt.Sed commodius videtur,vt regnum illud infelix tenebrarum accipiamus, quo totum mun-dum princeps tenebrarum,satan, ante Christum natum oppressit. De quo Paulus loquens, nos per Christum à potestate tenebrarum ereptos & liberatos dicit.Col.1. Notæ enim sunt diaboli il-lusiones, quibus per falsos & horrendos cultus, per mendaces oraculorum prædictiones, per ef-frenes libidines & omne genus flagitiorum infelices mortales multis seculis miserrimè seduxit. Quibus malis,per fe grauissimis,hoc multò grauius accedebat,quòd in tâ infelici & horrenda co-ditione salutem sibi homines pollicebantur.At Christus suo in mundû aduentu tenebrarum prin-cipem debellauit, tenebras discussit, & salutare cognitionis Dei lumen euangelij sui prædicatio-ne accendit,quo illuminati homines veram religionem sectari, verbi diuini regulas obseruare & peccatorum laqueos cauere didicerunt: quo factum est,vt nouam omnino mundi formam inue-ctam fuisse videamus.Verè ergo,quoad nos,dici potest nouum fœdus,nouum testamentum, no-uas leges,nouam deniq; politiam à Deo institutam esse.Consentit his Paulus apostolus,dum ait: Eratis quondam tenebrae,nunc autem lux in domino.Eph.4.Et rursum:Vos cum effetis mortui deliêtis & peccatis,in quibus aliquando ambulastis,iuxta seculum mundi huius,iuxta principem cui potestas est aeris,qui est spiritus nunc agens in filijs contumacibus, inter quos & nos omnes conuersabamur aliquando in concupiscentijs carnis nostræ,facientes quę carni ac menti libebat, & eramus natura filij irę,quemadmodum & cæteri. Sed Deus qui diues est in misericordia, &c. Eph.2.Fortasis & huc referri debet,quod alibi noster Apostolus,lucem Christi in tenebris luxi-fe dicit.Ioan.1.Sed ex omnibus istis loci huius sensum probè notemus, qui est,noui teftameti do-ctrinam per fe non nouam esse,sic vero dici,partim quidem propter Christum,qui salutis nostræ negotium nostra culpa obliteratum & antiquatum,instaurauit:partim vero propter nos, qui ex tenebrarum regno in lucem veritatis asserti & per Christū regenerati,noui homines facti sumus, nouam vitam viuimus,adeoq; totius mundi nouam formam in Christo agnoscimus.
units.tr: "Again, I write to you a new commandment, which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light already shines." These words contain a concession. For John admits that the commandment, which he had just called old, is also called new, and he clearly indicates for what reason it is so called. The obscurity of this passage, however, has been caused by the single word QUOD. For since people thought it refers to the commandment, they twisted themselves wonderfully in explaining this sense. But it is clear that in the Greek text it ought to be referred to something else. For what we call "praeceptum" in the neuter gender, the Greeks have [ἐντολή], which is a feminine noun, and a neuter relative pronoun does not correspond to it at all. But if you refer this to the whole context of this sentence, the meaning will soon be clearer. For John speaks thus: "I have said that I am writing not new things, but old ones. Again, however, because you object to the names of new testament and new law, I do not wish to reject those either, but I confess that I am writing a new commandment: which is true, that is, which can truly be said by me, not indeed with respect to the doctrine itself, but with respect to the things with which it is concerned." What follows is connected with these words, in which he teaches that the precepts of the gospel are called new in a twofold way: partly, namely, in Christ himself, that is, on account of Christ; and partly in us, that is, on account of us. For if you consider what is handed down in the gospel concerning the substance and sum of our salvation, these are the same as those things which the ancient Scriptures handed down long ago. But if you look at Christ himself and at us, who have been redeemed through him, you will see that the word "new" fits them fittingly. For on account of Christ he can be called new, because he, by the merit of his own blood, restored the covenant of God, which through our fault had been, as it were, blotted out and abolished. And just as a painting, whose colours have become duller with age, if it is restored by a skilled artist, will be called new on account of the freshly applied colours, yet, since the outlines of the old painting are preserved, it is truly old: so the covenant of God, in which our salvation is contained, is called new on account of Christ the restorer, although in truth it is old and comprises nothing other than what was once promised through Moses and the prophets. Next, with respect to us, or on account of us, what is handed down can be called new, because the darkness is passing away and the true light already shines. There are those who have understood the darkness to be the law with its shadows and types. But it seems more fitting that we take it as that unhappy kingdom of darkness by which Satan, the prince of darkness, oppressed the whole world before Christ was born. Speaking of this, Paul says that we have been snatched and freed by Christ from the power of darkness. (Col. 1.) For the deceptions of the devil are well known, by which, through false and horrible cults, through lying predictions of oracles, through unbridled lusts and every kind of wickedness, he miserably seduced unhappy mortals for many ages. To these evils, which were in themselves most grievous, this was added far more grievously: that in such an unhappy and horrible condition men promised themselves salvation. But Christ, at his coming into the world, overcame the prince of darkness, dispelled the darkness, and kindled through the preaching of his gospel the light of the saving knowledge of God, by which men, illuminated, learned to follow the true religion, to observe the rules of the divine word, and to beware of the snares of sins. As a result, we see that an entirely new form of the world has been brought in. Truly, therefore, with respect to us, it can be said that a new covenant, a new testament, new laws, and finally a new polity have been instituted by God. The Apostle Paul agrees with these things when he says: "You were once darkness, but now are light in the Lord." (Eph. 4.) And again: "You, when you were dead in your offences and sins, in which you once walked, according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who now works in the sons of disobedience, among whom we all once also lived in the lusts of our flesh, doing what pleased the flesh and the mind, and we were by nature children of wrath, as were the rest. But God, who is rich in mercy, etc." (Eph. 2.) Perhaps this too ought to be referred here, that elsewhere our Apostle says that the light of Christ shone in the darkness. (John 1.) But from all these passages let us carefully note the sense of this text, which is this: that the doctrine of the New Testament is not new in itself, but is called so partly indeed on account of Christ, who restored the business of our salvation, which through our fault had been blotted out and made old; and partly on account of us, who, having been asserted out of the kingdom of darkness into the light of truth and regenerated through Christ, have become new men, live a new life, and therefore acknowledge a new form of the whole world in Christ.

units.la: Obseruare hic conuenit veteris & noui Testamenti differentiam, quæ non in substantia,sed accidentibus hæret.Eadem enim vtrobiq; fides, eadem religio spiritualis fiue interna,eadem salus & salutis ratio.At in modo tradendi & tépore discrimen est.Illic enim promissiones & typi erant: nobis ipsa proponitur promissionum & typorum veritas. Illi saluatorem Christum venturū expectabant: nos eū venisse credimus, & eius aduentu nos scimus esse redemptos. At quia tā leues differentiæ rē ipsam turbare nō possunt, agnoscamus fidei & doctrinæ, quę vtrobiq; traditur, vni tatē, & vtriusq; scripturæ libris ad nostram institutionem, consolationem & ædificationē vtamur.
units.tr: It is fitting to observe here the difference between the Old and New Testament, which lies not in substance but in accidents. For the faith, the doctrine, and the spiritual or inward religion are the same in both, and the salvation and the manner of salvation are the same. But the difference lies in the mode of delivery and in time. For there the promises and types were present; to us the very truth of the promises and types is set forth. They looked for the Saviour Christ to come; we believe that he has come, and we know that by his coming we have been redeemed. But since such slight differences cannot disturb the thing itself, let us acknowledge the unity of the faith and doctrine that is delivered in both, and use the books of both Scriptures for our instruction, consolation, and edification.

units.la: Non oscitanter quoq; præterire conuenit, quòd nostris temporibus lucem tribuit. Facit hoc propter Christū, quem lucem gentium fore, olim prædictū erat. Ifa. 42. & 49. Simul tamen & nos officij admonet. Si enim lux oblata est, nos vt filios lucis, in luce ambulare & tenebrarū opera vita re decet. Monet hoc Christus dicens: Ambulate dum lucē habetis, ne quos tenebræ occupent. Et qui ambulat in tenebris, nescit quò vadat. Dum lucem habetis, credite in lucem, vt filij lucis sitis. Ioan. 12. Et Paulus: Nox progressa est, & dies appropinquat. Abijciamus igitur opera tenebrarum & induamur arma lucis, tanquam in die compositè ambulemus, nō in cōmessationibus, &c. Rom. 13. Sed longum foret recensere quæcunq; in hanc sententiam scripturis sacris passim traduntur.
units.tr: It is also fitting not to pass over carelessly what he attributes to our times, namely light. He does this on account of Christ, who was foretold long ago as the light of the Gentiles. (Isa. 42. and 49.) At the same time, however, he also reminds us of our duty. For if light has been offered, it becomes us, as sons of light, to walk in the light and to cast off the works of darkness. Christ admonishes this, saying: "Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you. And he who walks in darkness does not know where he is going. While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may be sons of light." (John 12.) And Paul: "The night is far gone, and the day is at hand. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armour of light; let us walk becomingly, as in the day, not in revelry, etc." (Rom. 13.) But it would be a long task to recount all that the holy Scriptures hand down everywhere to this effect.

units.la: Agnoscamus ô fratres, euangelicæ doctrinæ vetustatem, dignitatem & certitudinem. Huic firmiter inhærendo vitemus omnes eos, qui hanc in dubium vocare audent. Curemus autem, ne vana eius gloriatione decepti, quę nostri officij sunt negligamus. Si enim in ea, quę hac docemur, transformati fuerimus, pro filijs à Deo patre agnoscemur, qui nos regni sui consortes faciet, per Iesum Christum, filium suum dilectum, saluatorem nostrum, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Let us acknowledge, O brethren, the antiquity, dignity, and certainty of the evangelical doctrine. By firmly adhering to it, let us avoid all those who dare to call it into doubt. Let us take care, however, lest, deceived by its vain boasting, we neglect the things that belong to our office. For if we have been transformed into those things which are taught us here, we shall be acknowledged as children by God the Father, who will make us partakers of his kingdom, through Jesus Christ, his beloved Son, our Saviour, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory, and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA VIII.
units.tr: HOMILY VIII.
