units.la: Qui dicit se in luce esse, & fratrem suum odit, in tenebris est usque adhuc. Qui diligit fratre suū, in lumine manet, & offendiculū in eo non est. Qui aut odit fratre suū, in tenebris est, & in tenebris ambulat, & nescit quò eat: quia tenebræ obcæcauerūt oculos eius.
units.tr: "He who says he is in the light, and hates his brother, is in darkness even until now. He who loves his brother abides in the light, and there is no stumbling-block in him. But he who hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he goes, because the darkness has blinded his eyes."

units.la: Quæcunque ad hominis officium spectant, spiritus sanctus in scripturis duobus fere capitibus comprehendit. Primum ex his fides est, quæ vno & solo Deo per Christum Iesum nititur, & omnem religionem atque cultum in se comprehendit. Alterum totius vitæ & morum institutionem complectitur, quam secundum diuinæ legis formulam dirigi oportet. De vtroque Ioannes apostolus in epistola hac diligenter agit. Ad prius enim pertinent, quæ primo Capite audiuimus, vbi nos omnes peccatores esse docuit, purgari aut à peccatis & iustificari sanguine Chri sti,qui idem vnicus inter Deum & nos mediator existat. Alterum in plura membra diuidi potest. Nam & purificationem nostri, & vitæ innocentiam, & fraternam charitatem, & si quæ aliæ Chri stianorum virtutes sunt, comprehendit: de quibus singulis suo loco agetur. In præsenti verò Io-annes, occasione ex superioribus sumpta, de charitate paucis disserit, plura capite tertio & quarto dicturus. Primò enim docet, charitatem tam necessariam esse, vt frustra euangelicæ lucis cognitio ne glorientur, quicunq; hac destituti sunt. Deinde hoc ipsum ꝑ more suo eleganti collatione charitatis & odij explicat. Hæc, si precibus nostris benignus pater annuat, breuiter percurremus.
units.tr: Spirit of God in the Scriptures comprehends nearly all that pertains to the duty of man under two chief heads. The first of these is faith, which rests upon the one and only God through Christ Jesus, and comprehends within itself all religion and worship. The second embraces the whole instruction of life and conduct, which ought to be directed according to the form of the divine law. The apostle John treats diligently of both in this epistle. To the former belong the things we heard in the first chapter, where he taught that we are all sinners, and that we are cleansed from sins and justified by the blood of Christ, who is also the one mediator between God and us. The latter can be divided into several parts, for it comprehends both our purification, the innocence of life, brotherly love, and whatever other virtues Christians have, each of which will be treated in its place. At present, John, taking the occasion from what has gone before, discourses briefly on love, and will say more about it in the third and fourth chapters. For first he teaches that love is so necessary that those who lack it boast in vain of their knowledge of the light of the gospel. Then he explains this very point, by his customary elegant comparison of love and hatred. If our gracious Father grants this to our prayers, we shall briefly run through these things.

units.la: I. Qui dicit se in luce esse, & fratrem suum odit, in tenebris est usq; adhuc. Cohærent hæc superi oribus. Dixerat enim ijs, qui euangelij doctrinam amplexi sunt, verum lumen lucere, & eosdē ex tenebrarum potestate esse liberatos. At si hominum mores inspicias, luce hac multos gloriari vi debis, in quibus reuera adhuc tenebræ regnant: id quod tum alijs sceleribus, tū maximè fraternis odijs & inimicitijs testantur. Contra eos ergo orationem Ioannes instituit, & frustra luce gloriari dicit eos, qui opera tenebrarum nondum deseruerunt. Argumentum enim tale est. Qui tenebra rum opera faciunt, in tenebris sunt. Quicunq; verò fratres odiunt, opera tenebrarum faciunt. Er go qui fratres odiunt, in tenebris sunt. Probari potest consequentia hæc Christi verbis, qui tene brarum principem diabolum ab initio homicidam, & proinde humani generis osorem fuisse dicit. Ioan. 8. Et Paulus odium inter carnis opera numerat, quæ eadem cum tenebrarum operibus esse constat. Galat. 5. Sed prodest singulas huius sententiæ partes diligentius paulò expendere.
units.tr: I. "He who says he is in the light, and hates his brother, is in darkness even until now." These words cohere with what goes before. For he had said to those who embraced the doctrine of the gospel that the true light shines, and that they have been freed from the power of darkness. But if you look at the conduct of men, you will see that many boast of this light, in whom darkness truly still reigns; and this they attest both by other crimes and above all by brotherly hatreds and enmities. Against them, therefore, John directs his speech, and he says that those who have not yet forsaken the works of darkness boast of the light in vain. For the argument runs thus: those who do the works of darkness are in darkness. But those who hate their brothers do the works of darkness. Therefore those who hate their brothers are in darkness. This inference can be proved by the words of Christ, who says that the devil, the prince of darkness, was a murderer from the beginning, and therefore a hater of the human race (John 8). And Paul counts hatred among the works of the flesh, which are plainly the same as the works of darkness (Gal. 5). But it is useful to weigh each part of this sentence a little more carefully.

units.la: Primò ait: Qui dicit se in luce esse, id est, qui Christi cognitione & titulo gloriatur. Lucem ergo vocat Christi cognitionem, quæ sic dicitur, quia sine hac merę tenebrę sunt, quicquid homo vel nouit vel facit. Tenebrosa est omnis hominum sapientia, nisi Christi cognitione illuminetur, quod & gentium philosophi & Iudæorum Rabbini suo exemplo satis demonstrant. Illi enim dum ex semetipsis Dei naturâ altius cognoscere & scrutari cœperūt, in perniciosos errores et horribilē omnium flagitiorum sentinam prolapsi sunt. Rom i. Hi vero, dum diuini verbi oraculis non con-tenti nouas traditiones fingere ausi sunt, caeci caecorum duces facti, tam sibijpsis, quàm sectatoribus suis, interitus causa fuere. Matth.15. Sed quid exemplis longè petitis opus est, Teipsum inspice, & qualis olim, priusquam Christus animo tuo irradiaret, fueris, expendito: & fateberis, palpabiles quidem fuisse illas tenebras, te vero infelicem fuisse, qui eas deprehendere non potueris. Vt enim qui Labyrintho obscuro inclusi sunt, exire quidem cupiunt, sed quorsum tendere debeant, ignorant, & modo manus, modo caput & totum corpus parietibus illidunt, modo ad silices & truncos offendunt, saepe etiam in scrobes & foueas delabuntur: ita olim nos quidem inclusos & irretitos esse sentiebamus, viam vero liberationis & effugij nemo vidit, donec euangelij luce illata, multo longius nos a salutis via abfuisse vidimus, quàm aliquis nostrum putare poterat. Debet haec cogitatio animis nostris frequenter occurrere, vt eo maius in nobis accendatur erga tantam Dei benignitatem gratitudinis studium.
units.tr: First he says: "He who says he is in the light", that is, he who glories in the knowledge and the name of Christ. He calls the knowledge of Christ light, and it is so called because without it there is nothing but pure darkness, whatever a man either knows or does. All human wisdom is dark unless it is illumined by the knowledge of Christ, as both the philosophers of the Gentiles and the rabbis of the Jews sufficiently demonstrate by their example. For when they began to search out and know the nature of God more deeply from themselves, they fell into pernicious errors and into the horrible sewer of every wickedness (Rom. 1). Those others, not content with the oracles of the divine word, dared to devise new traditions, and, having become blind guides of the blind, were the cause of destruction both to themselves and to their followers (Matt. 15). But why need we far-fetched examples? Look at yourself, and consider what you were once, before Christ shone into your mind; and you will confess that those darknesses were palpable indeed, and that you were wretched, since you could not perceive them. For as those who are shut up in a dark labyrinth wish indeed to get out, but do not know where they ought to head, and now strike their hands, now their heads and whole bodies, against the walls, now stumble against flints and stumps, and often fall into pits and ditches: so we too once felt ourselves shut in and entangled, yet no one saw the way of deliverance and escape, until the light of the gospel was brought in, and we saw that we had been much further from the way of salvation than any of us could have supposed. This thought ought often to come to our minds, so that a greater zeal of gratitude for so great a goodness of God may be kindled in us.

units.la: Deinde cum de charitate & odio loqui velit, fratrum mentionem facit. Qui ergo fratres dicantur, inquirendum erit. Duplex autem est inter homines fraternitas. Carnalis nimirum vel naturalis, & Spiritualis. Carnalis fraternitas inter eos esse dicitur, qui ex ijsdem parentibus sunt progeniti. Spiritualis eorum est, qui vnum patrem spiritualem habent, cuius leges sequuntur, & eandem haereditatem spiritualem expectant. Quoad primam, fratres sunt omnes homines, quia ex ijsdem parentibus omnes originem trahunt, & omnes tandem in suum principium, terram vel pulverem, resoluuntur. Spiritualiter vero fratres sunt Christiani omnes, idque in Christo Iesu, qui ex Maria virgine homo nasci & frater noster fieri voluit. Inde est quod quicunque in Christum credunt, vnum & eundem habent adoptionis spiritum, vnum & eundem in coelis patrem inuocant, vno & eodem baptismo initiantur, vnam & eandem in coelis haereditatem sibi repositam adeunt. Vide de his Ephes.4. Quibus adde, quod omnes illi vnius & eiusdem corporis membra sunt, sub Christo vnico capite, cuius viuifico spiritu animantur. 1. Corinth.13. Ephes.1. Nulla ergo fraternitas arctior vel coniunctior excogitari potest, quàm ea, quam inter fideles in Christo esse dicimus. Ea enim nec temporum spatijs, nec locorum interuallis dirimitur: quia ad eandem pertinent, tâ qui olim à prima mundi origine crediderunt, quàm qui in posterum credituri sunt. Et in Christo Iesu non est Graecus vel Iudaeus, non circumcisio vel praeputium, non barbarus vel Scytha, nō seruus vel liber, non mas vel foemina, sed omnia in omnibus est Christus. Gal.3.Col.3. Docemur his, quantum peccent, qui ex semetipsis personarum discrimina fingunt, & sibi permissum putant, ali quos vel odisse, vel saltem contempsisse: quasi vero aliquod in externis hisce discrimen tanti momenti esse posit, propter quod fraternitatis huius vinculum longè arctissimum rumpi vel negligi debeat. Stultus certè, qui fratrem, quia peregrinus est, vel odit vel contemnit, cum eundem in coelestis haereditatis consortio ferre cogatur, nisi ipse à Deo abdicari velit. Infelix, qui ob egestatem vel conditionem minus splendidam fratres aspernatur, qui fortasis coram Deo maioris sint, & clariorem in coelis aliquando gloriam sortientur[?]. Horum memores fraternitatem hanc diligeter meditemur, quę sola omnes inuidiae & odij scintillas in animis nostris extinguere poterit.
units.tr: Then, since he wishes to speak of love and hatred, he makes mention of brothers. It will therefore have to be inquired who are called brothers. Now there is a twofold brotherhood among men: the carnal or natural, and the spiritual. Carnal brotherhood is said to exist among those who have been born of the same parents. Spiritual brotherhood belongs to those who have one spiritual Father, whose laws they follow, and for whom they look to the same spiritual inheritance. As to the first, all men are brothers, because all derive their origin from the same parents, and all at last dissolve into their common principle, earth or dust. But spiritually all Christians are brothers, and this in Christ Jesus, who willed to be born a man of the Virgin Mary and to become our brother. Hence it is that all who believe in Christ have one and the same Spirit of adoption, call upon one and the same Father in heaven, are initiated by one and the same baptism, and approach one and the same inheritance laid up for them in heaven. See on these things Eph. 4. To these add that all of them are members of one and the same body, under Christ the one head, by whose life-giving Spirit they are quickened (1 Cor. 13; Eph. 1). No closer or more intimate brotherhood can be imagined than that which we say exists among the faithful in Christ. For it is divided neither by spans of time nor by intervals of place, since it belongs equally to those who believed from the first origin of the world and to those who are going to believe in time to come. And in Christ Jesus there is neither Greek nor Jew, neither circumcision nor uncircumcision, neither barbarian nor Scythian, neither bond nor free, neither male nor female, but Christ is all in all (Gal. 3; Col. 3). We are taught by these things how greatly they sin who invent distinctions of persons for themselves, and think it permitted to them to hate or at least despise some; as if indeed any distinction in these external matters could be of such importance that for its sake the bond of this brotherhood, by far the closest, ought to be broken or neglected. Surely he is foolish who hates or despises a brother because he is a stranger, since he will be compelled to share with him in the fellowship of the heavenly inheritance, unless he himself wishes to be disinherited by God. Unhappy is he who spurns brothers on account of poverty or a less splendid condition, when they perhaps are greater before God and will one day obtain a more glorious renown in heaven. Mindful of these things, let us diligently meditate on this brotherhood, which alone will be able to extinguish all the sparks of envy and hatred in our minds.

units.la: Postremò obseruandum venit in hac sententia, quòd non ab atrocibus iniurijs, quibus proximo nocetur, sed de odio duntaxat, loquitur Apostolus. Nam ait: Qui fratrem suum odit, in tene-bris est vsq; adhuc. Est autem odium perpetua nocendi cupiditas, vt quidam non ineptè iram inueteratam esse dixerint. Quamuis interdum non ex ira, sed inuidiae affectu originem sumat. Vt primum enim priuati commodi studio excaecati, de aliena felicitate dolorem concipimus, doloris, si paulò diutius foueatur, nocendi cupiditatem & studium parit, ac tandem in affectu charitati planè contrarium, quem odium vocant, degenerat. Et quemadmodum cum charitate coiuncta sunt quaecunq; fratrum commodis inseruiùt, ac beneficentiâ exercent: ita odij comites indiuulsi sunt, quaecunq; proximi commodis obstare solent. Nunquam ab hoc separatur inuidia edax & liuida. Irae feruor quoq; leuissima quaq; occasione accenditur. Parit is cum iurgijs conuitia, probra, verbera, deniq; & vulnera. Vt enim leuis scintilla in ramentis delitescens proxima primum accendit, inde latius serpendo vires subinde acquirit, & tandem in ignem apertum erumpens horribili incendio omnia longè lateq; vastat: sic odij affectus, vtcunq; contemptibilis initio, vbi animi penetralibus conceptus moram trahit, serpere & augeri non definit, donec immanibus operibus contra charitatem & pacem publicam, magna cum multorum calamitate, grassetur. Exemplum huius rei euidens extat in Caino, primo diaboli mancipio. Is enim primum leui dolore ob fratris felicitatem permouetur, cum illi suae conditionis statum minus respondere videt. At vbi hunc non statim animo pellit, auctum maiori & nocentiori tabe serpere sentit. Quare & vultu toto concidit, fratrem nec rectis oculis intueri, nec amicè alloqui potest. Sed & hic affectus progressu temporis in pertinax odium exit, quod nec ipsius Dei verbis curari potuit. Odij tandem fructus infelix fuit parricidium. Atqui hoc ordine affectus hosce augeri & foueri, fatebuntur quicunque seipsos paulò attentius inspexerint. Non temerè igitur Ioannes contra eos, qui fraterno odio laborant, tam grauem tulit sententiam. Fontem enim & principium omnis mali monstrare & eundem obturare voluit. Quod si autem odij affectus cum Christiana professione tam pugnat, vt frustra hac glorientur, qui illud animis suis fouent, quid obsecro de illis iudicabimus, qui non contenti fratres odisse: sed odio, consultore pessimo, impulsi, fratrum famam cöuitijs vel obtrectationibus lædunt, opibus eorundem insidias struunt, & ipsa corpora quoq; armis petere audent? Licet qui dem illis inter deuotos huius seculi filios, vel hoc vel etiam splendidiori (si quis splendidior vspiam extaret) titulo gloriari, pro lucis tamen filijs coram Deo iudice nunquam agnoscentur. Disce ergo huius sententiæ meditationem inuidiæ & odij affectibus opponere, ne istos tanti momenti apud te esse patiaris, vt eum titulum & nomen tibi eripiant, sine quo aliquem saluari est impossibile. Sed Ioannem audiamus, qui ipse eleganti collatione sententiam hanc illustrat. Sic enim pergit:
units.tr: Lastly, it must be observed in this sentence that the Apostle speaks not of atrocious injuries by which a neighbour is harmed, but only of hatred. For he says: "He who hates his brother is in darkness even until now." Now hatred is a perpetual desire to do harm, which is why some not inaptly have called it an inveterate anger, although it sometimes arises not from anger but from the affection of envy. For as soon as we, blinded by the zeal for private advantage, conceive grief at another's happiness, that grief, if it is nourished a little too long, gives birth to a desire and zeal for doing harm, and at last degenerates into an affection completely opposed to charity, which they call hatred. And just as all things that serve the advantage of brothers and exercise beneficence are joined with charity, so the companions of hatred are inseparable, namely all things that are wont to stand in the way of a neighbour's welfare. Biting and livid envy is never separated from it. The heat of anger, too, is kindled by the slightest occasion. From this come quarrels, reproaches, insults, blows, and finally wounds. For as a slight spark lying hidden in the shavings first sets fire to what is nearest, then creeping more widely gathers strength, and at last breaking out into open flame lays waste everything far and wide with a dreadful conflagration: so the affection of hatred, however contemptible at the beginning, when conceived in the inner recesses of the mind and lingering there, does not cease to creep and grow until it rages with monstrous deeds against love and public peace, to the great calamity of many. A clear example of this exists in Cain, the first bondservant of the devil. For he was first moved by a slight grief at his brother's happiness, when it seemed to him that the state of his own condition answered less well to his. But when he did not at once drive this from his mind, he felt it creep on, enlarged by a greater and more harmful corruption. Therefore he collapsed in his whole countenance, and could neither look at his brother with a straight eye nor speak to him in a friendly way. But this affection too, as time went on, passed into a stubborn hatred, which could not be cured even by the very words of God. The unhappy fruit of hatred at last was parricide. Yet that anyone who examines himself a little more attentively will confess that the affections are increased and nourished in this order. John therefore did not rashly pronounce so grave a sentence against those who labour under brotherly hatred. For he wished to point out the source and origin of every evil and to stop it up. But if the affection of hatred so clashes with the Christian profession that those who nourish it in their minds boast of it in vain, what, I beseech you, shall we judge of those who, not content merely to hate their brothers, but impelled by hatred, the worst counsellor, injure the reputation of their brothers with insults and slanders, lay snares for their property, and dare to attack their very bodies with weapons? Indeed, such men may glory among the devoted sons of this age in this title, or even in a more splendid one (if any more splendid one existed anywhere); yet before God the judge they will never be acknowledged as sons of the light. Learn therefore to set the meditation of this sentence against the affections of envy and hatred, lest you suffer these to be of such importance in your eyes that they snatch from you that title and name without which it is impossible for anyone to be saved. But let us hear John, who himself illustrates this sentence by an elegant comparison. For he goes on thus:

units.la: I I. Qui diligit fratrem suum, in lumine manet, & offendiculum in eo non est. Qui autem odit fratrem suum, in tenebris est, & in tenebris ambulat, & nescit quò eat: quia tenebræ obcæcauerunt oculos eius.
units.tr: I I. He who loves his brother abides in the light, and there is no stumbling-block in him. But he who hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he goes, because darkness has blinded his eyes.

units.la: Conferuntur his fraternæ charitatis & odij fructus, vt eò euidentius appareat Christiani nominis titulo frustra gloriari eos, qui odij affectum animis suis fouent. Sed priusquam collatione hanc excutiamus, voces singulas, quibus de charitate loquitur, obseruare conuenit.
units.tr: The fruits of brotherly love and of hatred are set side by side with these words, so that it may appear more clearly that those who nurse the feeling of hatred in their hearts vainly glory in the title of Christian. But before we examine this comparison, it is fitting to observe the individual words by which he speaks of love.

units.la: Primò autè notabis, quòd de fratre dicens addit S V V M. Significat hæc vox, nostros esse, quicunque fratres dicuntur. Nostri autem sunt, quia ab eo nobis donati & commendati, cui tam in nos quàm in omnes alios ius est. At natura sic comparatum videmus, vt quæ nostra sunt, nec negligamus temere, nec à quouis perdi patiamur. Satis enim notæ sunt acres illæ de Meo & Tuo concertationes. At qui tuus est, quicunque per fidem in Christum frater Christi & cohæres factus est. Nec tamen ita tuus est, vt illum impune vel perdere, vel saltem negligere, liceat: sed vt prouincia tua vel depositum tuum dicitur, quod aliquando abs te requiret is, qui tibi istud credidit: ita tui fratres domino dante facti sunt omnes homines, qui eosdem de tuis manibus olim exiget, & se neglectum putabit, si illos neglexeris. Refutat hoc Cainorum confidentem proteruitatem, qui dicere audent: Num nos sumus custodes fratrum nostrorum? Talis vtique Cain videri & esse nolebat. Audit tamen de sua manu fratris sanguinem requiri. Sed ô dementiam nostri seculi, qua tam facilè eos negligimus, qui à tanto rege & iudice nobis, vt nostri fratres essent, donati sunt. Quo ore olim tuum fuisse negabis, quem Christus Iesus, qui necis & vitæ ius in te habet, tibi tradidit? Non æquum, non bouem, non canem, non fundum, qui tuus est, negligis: & cum negligere non pudet, qui non tuus modò, sed tuus frater & cohæres est? Quantò rectius Samuel, qui Saulem, licet reprobum, suum agnouit & pro illo lachrymas fundere dignatus est? 1. Samuelis decimoquinto & decimosexto capite. Sed & Paulus apostolus pro Iudæis, fratribus suis iuxta carnem, anathema fieri voluit, vt ipsi saluarentur. Roman. 9. Idem omnibus omnia factus est, vt multos Christo lucrifaceret. Idem animus & tibi erit, si quosuis obuios, & fratres & tuos esse, cogitaueris, &c.
units.tr: First, you will note that when he speaks of a brother he adds suum. This word signifies that all who are called brothers are ours. They are ours because they have been given to us and commended to us by him who has a right over them, both over us and over all others. We see that nature has so ordered things that we do not carelessly neglect what is ours, nor allow anyone at random to lose it. The sharp contests over Mine and Thine are well known enough. But he who is your brother is yours, whoever has been made a brother of Christ and a co-heir through faith in Christ. Yet he is not so yours that you may lawfully destroy him, or at least neglect him, with impunity. Rather, as a province or a deposit is called yours, which he who entrusted it to you will one day demand back from you, so all men have been made your brothers by the gift of the Lord, and he who will one day require them at your hands will consider himself neglected if you have neglected them. This refutes the bold insolence of the Cains, who dare to say: "Am I my brother's keeper?" Cain at any rate did not wish to seem or be such a man. Yet he hears that his brother's blood is required at his hand. But O the madness of our age, by which we so easily neglect those who have been given to us as brothers by so great a King and Judge! With what face will you deny that he was yours, whom Christ Jesus, who has the right of death and of life over you, has delivered to you? You neglect an ox, an ass, a dog, a field, which are yours, and are you not ashamed to neglect one who is not only yours but your brother and co-heir? How much more rightly did Samuel act, who acknowledged Saul as his own, although reprobate, and deigned to shed tears for him? 1 Samuel, chapters 15 and 16. Also the apostle Paul wished himself to be made accursed for the Jews, his brethren according to the flesh, that they might be saved. Romans 9. He became all things to all men, that he might gain many to Christ. The same mind will be yours too, if you consider every man you meet to be both a brother and yours, etc.

units.la: Deinde diligendi verbum obseruabis, quo quæcunque ad charitatem spectant comprehenditat. Est enim amor siue dilectio is affectus, quo animi nostri in aliquam vel rem vel personam totinclinant, vt ei bene esse & benefacere velint. Trahit secum illa animorum propensio omnem beneficentiam. Quia, vt infra capite tertio audiemus, misericordia viscera sibi coniuncta habet. Mouetur ergo alienæ miseriæ aspectu, & amatis nihil deesse patitur, siquidem ijs aliquo modo subuenire possit. Exhibet enim vbi opus est, externa officia omnia, dum famelicos cibat, potum præbet sitientibus, nudos vestit, ægrotos inuisit, captiuos vel alijs afflictionibus tentatos consolatur. Nec his quæ ad corpus spectant contenta, vlterius quoque progreditur. Quia enim communem hereditatem omnibus pijs in cœlo repositam nouit, in hoc versatur vt quàm plurimos huius con fortes faciat. Quoties ergo fratrem peccatorum illecebris deceptum, ceu bouem per auia cupiditatum hinc inde errare conspicit, pijs rationibus captum et ligatum, ad suum dominum, qui ipsum sanguine proprio mercatus est, reducit. Quò si eundem intolerabili peccatorum sarcina, instar asini, oneratum & tandem desperabundum succumbere videat, festinus accurrit, onus illud pijs ad monitionibus consolationibusque subleuat. Exod.23. Deuter.22. At si nihil horum possit, condolet saltem, & ardentibus precibus pro illis apud Deum intercedit, quos ad interitum vergere cernit. Nihil ergo habebunt quo glorientur, qui & inopiam fratrum, & morum vitæque corruptionem sine animi dolore & siccis oculis intueri possunt. Putant illi charitatis præceptum impleri,
units.tr: Next, you will observe the word diligendi (of loving), by which everything that pertains to charity is comprehended. Love, or affection, is that feeling by which our minds incline wholly toward some thing or person, so that they wish it well and wish to do it good. That inclination of the mind brings with it all beneficence. For, as we shall hear below in the third chapter, it has compassion joined to its very bowels. It is therefore moved at the sight of another's misery, and suffers nothing to be lacking to those it loves, provided it can in some way help them. For where there is need, it performs all external offices: it feeds the hungry, gives drink to the thirsty, clothes the naked, visits the sick, and comforts the captives and those tried by other afflictions. Nor, being content with what concerns the body, does it go further still. For since it knows that a common inheritance is laid up in heaven for all the godly, it labours to make as many as possible partakers of it. Whenever, therefore, it sees a brother deceived by the allurements of sin, wandering hither and thither like an ox through the trackless paths of desire, it brings him back, caught and bound by godly reasons, to his Lord, who purchased him with his own blood. And if it sees the same man, laden like an ass with the intolerable burden of sins and at last sinking down in despair, it hastens to him and lightens that burden with godly admonitions and consolations. Exodus 23; Deuteronomy 22. But if it can do none of these things, it at least grieves, and with burning prayers intercedes with God for those whom it sees heading toward ruin. Those therefore will have nothing in which to glory, who can look upon the poverty of their brethren and the corruption of their morals and lives without grief of heart and with dry eyes. They think the precept of charity is fulfilled

units.la: D si nemini noceant, vel etiam si omnibus bene esse cupiant, & nullius famam maledicentia lædant. At nemini nocuisse nō sufficit, nisi & omnibus pro virili prosis. Arguit ergo locus hic fœdam nostri seculi corruptionem, quæ tanta est, ut & domesticos fidei, & sanguine propinquos, imò & pro prios liberos, facilè negligamus. Sed videamus tandem dilectionis & odij fructus, quos in præsen-ti Ioannes confert.
units.tr: if they do harm to no one, or even if they wish well to all, and by slander injure no one's good name. But it is not enough to have harmed no one, unless you also help all as far as you are able. This passage therefore exposes the foul corruption of our age, which is so great that we easily neglect even the domestic members of the faith, our blood relations, and indeed our own children. But let us at length see the fruits of love and of hatred which John sets side by side in the present passage.

units.la: Qui diligit fratrem suum in lumine manet, & offendiculum in eo non est. Lumen pro vera Christi cognitione adeoq; ipsa fide accipi, supra diximus. Quia enim Christus lux mundi est (Ioan.1.&8.) in lumine non sunt, nisi qui in Christo manserint: quod per fidem fit. Primus ergo charitatis fraternæ fructus est, fidei nostræ testimonium certum & infallibile, quo tam nobisipsis quàm aliis constat, nos verè fideles, verè Christianos, & Christi cohæredes esse. Pertinent huc Christi verba: In hoc cognoscent omnes, quod discipuli mei sitis, si charitatem habueritis inter vos mutuâ. Ioa. 13. Sed quia de hoc plura alibi dicentur, hæc modò attigisse sufficiat.
units.tr: "He who loves his brother abides in the light, and there is no stumbling-block in him." We said above that light is taken for the true knowledge of Christ, and so for faith itself. For since Christ is the light of the world (John 1 and 8), only those are in the light who have remained in Christ, which is done through faith. The first fruit of brotherly love is therefore a certain and infallible testimony of our faith, by which it is evident both to ourselves and to others that we are truly faithful, truly Christians, and co-heirs of Christ. To this belong the words of Christ: "By this shall all men know that you are my disciples, if you have love one for another." John 13. But since these things will be said more fully elsewhere, it is enough for now to have touched on them.

units.la: Secundus fructus autem charitatis indicatur ab Apostolo, cum addit: Offendiculum in eo non est. Potest hoc bifariam intelligi, tam quod offendat neminem, quàm quod ipse non offendatur. Ab utroque enim charitatis ingenium alienissimum est. Quia enim nouit fidelis, quàm noceat vel facto vel dicto alijs peccandi occasionem præbuisse, in omnibus actionibus suis solicitè curat, ne quis ipsius exemplo fiat deterior. Imitatur & Pauli exemplum, qui carnibus in æternum potius abstinere voluit, quàm offendiculo esse fratri, pro quo Christus mortuus est. 1.Cor.8. Rursus quia charitas de omnibus bene sperat (1.Cor.13.) non facile aliorum factis offenditur: sed quæcunque ab alijs fiunt, in meliorem partem accipit, & operit multitudinem peccatorum, quæ à proximo committuntur. Prou.10.1.Pet.4. Nam procul abest ab ijs, qui charitatis igne calent, nocens illud & inuidum suspicionis malum, quo optima quæq; calumnijs & obtrectationibus arrodiso-lent. Quare, ut suspiciones temerariæ odijs & dissensionibus fomenta ministrant: sic charitas sua facilitate & pijs dissimulationibus concordiam mutuam fouet, & si quæ incidunt disidiorum scintillæ, eas illico extinguit & reprimit. Quàm ergo utilis & necessaria est ad hominum vitam conferuandam vera concordia, tam utilem & necessariam charitatem quoq; esse pronunciamus, sine qua hæc subsistere nequit. Similiter, quàm necessarium est Christiani nominis professoribus innocentiæ studium, tam necessaria erit charitas, quæ ne quem ipsi offendamus cauet, & obstat ne aliorum facta & dicta nos offendere possint. Opponamus nunc illi odium cum suis fructibus, ut quàm in felix sit eius seges euidenter pateat.
units.tr: The second fruit of charity is indicated by the Apostle when he adds: "there is no stumbling-block in him." This can be understood in two ways: both that he gives offence to no one, and that he himself is not offended. For charity is wholly alien to both. For since the faithful man knows how much harm it does to have given others an occasion of sinning, whether by deed or by word, he takes care in all his actions that no one be made worse by his example. He also imitates the example of Paul, who chose rather to abstain from meat forever than to be a stumbling-block to a brother for whom Christ died. 1 Corinthians 8. Again, since charity thinks well of all (1 Corinthians 13), it is not easily offended by the deeds of others, but takes whatever is done by others in the better part, and covers the multitude of sins committed by a neighbour. Proverbs 10; 1 Peter 4. For far from those who glow with the fire of charity is that harmful and envious evil of suspicion, by which the best things are gnawed at with calumnies and detractions. Therefore, just as rash suspicions supply fuel for hatreds and dissensions, so charity, by its ease and godly dissimulations, nurses mutual concord, and if any sparks of discord arise, it at once extinguishes and suppresses them. As true concord is therefore useful and necessary for preserving human life, so we declare charity also to be useful and necessary, without which concord cannot subsist. Similarly, as the pursuit of innocence is necessary for the professors of the Christian name, so charity will be necessary, which takes care that we offend no one, and prevents the deeds and words of others from being able to offend us. Let us now set hatred against it with its fruits, that it may be plainly seen how unhappy its harvest is.

units.la: Qui autem odit fratrem suum, in tenebris est, & in tenebris ambulat, & nescit quò eat: quia tenebræ obcæcauerunt oculos eius. Charitatis fructus duos exposuit, quorum alter fidei veritatem, alter vitæ institutionem spectat. His totidem ex odio profanantes opponit, qui & ipsi ad priora hæc genera referri debent. Primus est, quòd qui fratrem odit, in tenebris est, id est, Christi (qui solus vera & æterna lux est) cognitione & fide caret. Quia enim fidei indiuulsus comes est charitas, & per hanc fides operari solet (Galat.5.) fide careat oportet, quicunque charitate vacuus fraterno odio cotabescit. At quanta hominis pernicies sit, fide destitui, omnis scriptura indicat. Paulus certè peccatum esse fatetur, quicquid sine fide fit. Rom.14. Et idem impossibile esse dicit, ut aliquis Deo sine fide placeat. Hebr. 11. Ut enim fides Christum, & in Christo omnes scientiæ sapientiæ, bonitatis & iustitiæ diuinæ thesauros apprehendit: ita qui fide destituitur, idem & sapientia & bonitate & iustitia Dei destituatur oportet. Rectè ergo Ioannes alterum quoque odij fructum ex priori infert, & ait: In tenebris ambulat, & nescit quò eat: id est, certi habet nihil, & in omnibus actionibus suis regulam certam non habet. Qua ratione enim fieri potest, ut qui in obscuro loco sine lumine versantur, non in tenebris ambulent? At mundus hic totus caligine ignorantiæ tegitur, nec alia luce quàm Christo illuminari potest, quem fides apprehendit, quique non in aliorum, quàm fidelium, cordibus lucere solet. In tenebris ergo perniciosa caligine errant, quicunq; lucem hanc nondum apprehenderunt: quales esse iam probauimus, quotquot animos odio fraterno laborantes circumgestant. Quid igitur hos aliud manere potest, quàm quòd in tenebris ambulantes manet? Nesciunt illi quò vadant, via qua elabantur non norunt, & dum sese liberare volunt, magis implicantur. Videmus hoc in omnibus, qui odij cæcum affectum sequi solent. Sentiunt se miseros & infelices esse. Audiunt contra se propriæ conscientiæ testimonium, & cum Caino vident Dei favorem in alios translatum esse. Tenebroso tamen odij affectu sic excæcantur, ut in aliorum infortunijs suam felicitatem repositam esse putent, nec se felices fieri posse credant, nisi alios ante infelices viderint. Quæ causa est, quòd ad mendacia, simulationes, fraudes, impostura s, calumnias, obtrectationes, conuitia, rapinas & apertam vim conuersi, fratribus nocere studeunt, ut his oppressis ipsi magni & præclari fiant. At toto cælo errant. Tam enim abest, ut euentú, quem cupiunt assequantur, vt potius Dei irâ magis in se prouocent, poenas atrociores mereantur, quas tandem iusto suo iudicio dominus ab ipsis exigit. Exempla eius generis infinita sunt, sed prodest, vt singuli in se potius descendant, quàm vt alienis miserijs spectandis occupentur. Non alienum tamen ab instituto fuerit, si quid Christianae fidei & doctrinę persecutores faciunt, cōsyderemus: Hi enim quia charitatis affectum exuerunt, eò caecitatis adducti sunt, vt nullis Christianorū supplicijs, quantumuis atrocibus, exaturari possint. Et dum sanguinem fundunt eorum, qui Christi nomen & meritum ad salutem sufficere credunt, dum tormentis exquisitis eosdem excruciant, dum laqueis suspensos enecant, dum lentis ignibus non exurunt, sed torrent, & nihil nō inhumanitatis exercent, tum se beatos & felices fore sperant, vt qui Deo cultum offerant longè gratissimum. Interim non animaduertunt, sanguinem horum de terra pro vindicta clamare, & animas eorundem sub magno altari Dei iudicium exposcere. Apocal. 7. Idem in illis cernitur, qui vbi charitatem abiecerunt, vsuris & malis artibus rem domesticam augere studét: nec obseruant ijs rebus maledictionem conflari, quae omne genus calamitatum secum trahit.
units.tr: He who hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because darkness has blinded his eyes. John sets out two fruits of charity, one of which concerns the truth of faith, the other the instruction of life. Against these he sets the same number of fruits of hatred, which likewise ought to be referred to these two kinds. The first is that he who hates his brother is in darkness, that is, lacks the knowledge and faith of Christ, who alone is the true and eternal light. For since charity is the inseparable companion of faith, and faith usually works through charity (Gal. 5), whoever is empty of charity and wastes away with hatred of his brother must of necessity lack faith. And how great a ruin it is for a man to be deprived of faith, all Scripture shows. Paul certainly confesses that whatever is done without faith is sin (Rom. 14). And he says it is impossible for anyone to please God without faith (Heb. 11). For just as faith apprehends Christ, and in Christ all the treasures of wisdom, knowledge, goodness and the divine righteousness, so he who is destitute of faith must necessarily be destitute of the wisdom, goodness and righteousness of God as well. Rightly, then, John draws from the first the second fruit of hatred too, and says: He walks in darkness and does not know where he is going; that is, he has nothing certain, and has no sure rule in all his actions. For how can it be that those who dwell in a dark place without light do not walk in darkness? But this whole world is covered with the mist of ignorance, and it cannot be illumined by any light except Christ, whom faith apprehends, and who is accustomed to shine not in the hearts of others but of believers only. Therefore all those who have not yet apprehended this light wander in darkness with a deadly mist; and we have already shown that such are all who carry about in their minds the souls labouring under hatred of their brothers. What else, then, can await them than that they remain walking in darkness? They do not know where they are going, they do not know the way by which they might escape, and while they want to free themselves, they become more entangled. We see this in all who are accustomed to follow the blind passion of hatred. They feel that they are wretched and unhappy. They hear against themselves the testimony of their own conscience, and like Cain they see God's favour transferred to others. Yet by the dark passion of hatred they are so blinded that they think their happiness lies in the misfortunes of others, and they do not believe they can be made happy unless they first see others unhappy. This is why they turn to lies, pretences, frauds, deceits, slanders, detractions, reproaches, plunder and open violence, and eagerly seek to harm their brothers, so that once these are crushed they themselves may become great and illustrious. But they are wrong by the whole sky. For far from attaining the outcome they desire, they rather provoke the anger of God against themselves, and merit harsher punishments, which at last the Lord exacts from them by his just judgment. Examples of this kind are endless, but it is useful for each one to look into himself rather than to be busy gazing at the miseries of others. Yet it will not be out of place to consider what the persecutors of the Christian faith and doctrine do: for since they have cast off the disposition of charity, they have been led into such blindness that they can be satisfied by no punishments of Christians, however savage. And while they shed the blood of those who believe that the name and merit of Christ suffice for salvation, while they torture them with exquisite tortures, while they strangle those hanged on nooses, while they do not burn them with slow fires but roast them, and practise every kind of inhumanity, then they hope they will be blessed and happy, as though they were offering God a most acceptable worship. Meanwhile they do not notice that the blood of these men cries out from the earth for vengeance, and that the souls of the same men beneath the great altar of God demand judgment (Rev. 7). The same is seen in those who, having cast off charity, strive to increase their household wealth by usury and wicked arts; nor do they observe that a curse is being gathered upon such things, which drags every kind of calamity along with it.

units.la: Sed video me praesenti loco diutius, quàm statueram, immoratum esse. Non tamen inutilis esse potuit mora haec, cū satis constet, quàm difficulter sibi haec persuaderi patiatur caro nostra, si ne quibus nec fides in Christū, nec salutis ratio constare potest. Firmiter ergo teneamus ō fratres Christi nomine & luce euangelica frustra gloriari eos, qui in tenebris ambulant. Ambulant verò in tenebris, quicunq; odio potius indulgere, quàm charitatis studiū sectari volunt. Fugiamus ergo infelix tenebrarū regnum, ac abiecto odio charitati nos totos consecremus, vt hæc de fide nostra testimoniū ferre possit, & nos ex eorū numero esse olim deprehendamur, qui cū rege gloriae Iesu Christo coelestis regni haereditate sortientur: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: But I see that I have lingered in the present place longer than I had intended. Yet this delay has not been useless, since it is well established how hard our flesh finds it to be persuaded of these things, without which neither faith in Christ nor the way of salvation can stand. Let us therefore firmly hold, brothers, that those who walk in darkness boast in vain of the name of Christ and the light of the gospel. Now those walk in darkness who prefer to indulge in hatred rather than to pursue the practice of charity. Let us therefore flee the unhappy kingdom of darkness, and, casting off hatred, devote ourselves wholly to charity, so that it may bear witness to our faith, and we may be found at last to be among those who will share by lot with the King of glory, Jesus Christ, the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA IX.
units.tr: Homilia IX.

units.la: Scribo uobis filioli, quòd remittuntur uobis peccata propter nomen eius. Scribo uobis patres, quoniam cognouistis eū, qui ab initio est. Scribo uobis adolescentes, quoniam uicistis illū malum. Scribo uobis pueruli, quoniam cognouistis patrem. Scripsi uobis patres, quoniam cognouistis eum, qui ab initio est. Scripsi uobis adolescentes, quoniam fortes estis, & uerbum Dei manet in uobis, & uicistis illum malum.
units.tr: I write to you, little children, that your sins are forgiven you for his name's sake. I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, because you have overcome that evil one. I write to you, little children, because you have known the Father. I have written to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning. I have written to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome that evil one.

units.la: Quoniam mundus pro corrupto carnis ingenio euangelicæ doctrinæ lucem odit, multa comminisci solet, quibus hanc vel inuisam reddat omnibus, vel saltem in contemptum adducat. Inter alia verò duobus criminibus illam verè petit. Primò enim nouitatis accusat, quæ vt in alijs rebus grata, sic in religione nimis odiosa est, eò quòd nouam inducendo maiores damna re videmur. Deinde doctrinam hanc inutilem & superuacaneam esse persuadere conatur, & pro inde indignam, cuius nomine quisquam cum alio contendat atque altercetur. Et ea quidem opinione multos hodie infectos videmus, qui controuersiarum de religione æquisimi iudices videri volunt. Eò autem isti homines tandem deueniunt, vt doctrinam de religione nihil ad se pertinere existiment, dum alius ætatem, alius conditionem vitæ, alius ingenium, alij alias causas prætexunt. Non temere ergo fit, quod Ioannes noster in asserenda euangelicæ doctrinæ authoritate tanta di ligentia versatur:quod etiam in præsenti loco facit, quo ad vtraq; ea, quæ modo adduximus, firmis & solidis rationibus respondet. Prima enim parte summam euangelicæ doctrinæ comprehendens, se nihil tradere docet, quàm quod per omnes scripturas passim traditum extet. Inde doctrinam hanc omnibus ætatibus applicat, vt sic constet, eā & senibus & iuuenibus, imò & pueris conuenire. Et quia in hac re tá senes, propter priuatæ prudentiæ fiduciam, quàm iuuenes propter vehementiores suæ ætatis affectus, sibijpsis plus satis permittere audent, quæ de illis dixerat, denuo repetit & inculcat. Nostrum est, à patre luminum eam gratiam pijs precibus expetere, qua doctrinam hanc non modò ad nos pertinere intelligamus, sed in eandem tota vita transformemur.
units.tr: Since the world, out of the corrupt nature of the flesh, hates the light of the evangelical teaching, it is accustomed to devise many charges by which it makes this teaching either hateful to everyone or at least brings it into contempt. Among other things, it attacks it truly on two counts. First, it accuses it of novelty; and just as novelty is pleasing in other matters, so in religion it is excessively odious, because by introducing something new we seem to do great harm to our ancestors. Second, it tries to persuade people that this teaching is useless and superfluous, and therefore unworthy that anyone should contend or quarrel with another on its account. Indeed, we see many today infected with this opinion, who wish to be regarded as the most impartial judges of religious controversies. Yet these men finally come to think that the doctrine of religion has nothing to do with them, while one pleads his age, another his condition of life, another his temperament, and others other causes. It is therefore no accident that our John labours with such great diligence in asserting the authority of the evangelical teaching; and he does so in the present passage too, where he answers both of the objections we have just mentioned with firm and solid reasons. For in the first part, summing up the whole of the evangelical teaching, he teaches that he hands down nothing but what stands everywhere handed down throughout all the Scriptures. Then he applies this teaching to every age, so that it is clear it is suitable to old men and young alike, indeed even to children. And because in this matter the old, trusting in their private prudence, and the young, on account of the more vehement impulses of their age, dare to permit themselves more than enough, he repeats and impresses again what he had said about them. It is our task to seek from the Father of lights, with pious prayers, that grace by which we may understand that this teaching pertains not only to us, but that we may be transformed into it through the whole of our lives.

units.la: I. Scribo uobis filioli, quòd remittuntur uobis peccata propter nomen eius. Filiolos vocat, vt supra renatos per Christum. Sic autem dicit: Scio doctrinā nostrā multis eo nomine inuisam esse, quòd videamur maiorum fide & religione contempta, nouam salutis rationem comminisci. At iniuria nobis fieri, quando hac suspicione grauamur, res ipsa testatur. Quid enim aliud hucusq; docui & nunc scribo, quàm quòd peccata vobis remittantur propter nomen filij Dei, Iesu Christi, cui nos testimonium ferimus: Peccatores (inquam) esse trado omnes homines, & peccatorum remissionem non suis operibus & meritis cofequi, sed propter Christum, qui seipsum pro peccatis totius mundi in ara Crucis Deo patri suo victimam gratam & sufficiente obtulit. An verò primi vel soli nos sumus, qui ista docemus? An non eadem omnib. veteris testamenti libris traditur? An nō ipse Dei filius de his & Mosem & prophetas scripsisse affirmat? Ioan.5.Luc.24. Inquisiuerunt hanc salutis rationem omnes prophetæ, Christi spiritu ducti.1.Pet.1.2. Pet. 1. Iniquum ergo est nos nouitatis suspicione inuisos & exosos fieri, quando ad breuem hanc sententiam omnis nostra doctrina referri potest. Continetur his verbis non excusatio modò & apologia, verumetiam summa & compendium totius doctrinæ apostolicæ: quare singula verba penitius inspexisse proderit.
units.tr: I. "I write to you, little children, that your sins are forgiven you for his name's sake." He calls them little children, as those reborn through Christ above. He speaks thus: I know that our teaching is hated by many for this very reason, that we seem, having despised the faith and religion of our ancestors, to devise a new way of salvation. But that we are wronged by this suspicion, the thing itself bears witness. For what else have I taught hitherto, and what else do I now write, than that your sins are forgiven you for the sake of the name of the Son of God, Jesus Christ, to whom we bear witness: that all men, I say, are sinners, and that forgiveness of sins is obtained not by their own works and merits, but on account of Christ, who offered himself for the sins of the whole world on the altar of the Cross to God his Father as an acceptable and sufficient victim. Or are we the first or the only ones who teach these things? Is it not handed down in all the books of the Old Testament? Does not the Son of God himself affirm that Moses and the prophets wrote about these things? John 5; Luke 24. All the prophets, led by the Spirit of Christ, inquired into this way of salvation. 1 Peter 1:2. Pet. 1. It is therefore unjust that we should be made hateful and odious by the suspicion of novelty, when all our doctrine can be referred to this brief statement. Not only an excuse and defence, but also the sum and compendium of the whole apostolic doctrine is contained in these words; so it will be profitable to have examined each word more closely.

units.la: Primò ait: Remittuntur vobis peccata. Loquitur autem non de gentibus à fide adhuc alienis, sed de fidelibus qui iam per Christum renati erant, & proinde filioli ab ipso nominantur. Fatetur itaq; in Christianis peccata adhuc superesse, quæ remissionem postulant. Quòd si peccatis adhuc grauantur Christiani & Dei filij, quid de ijs dicemus, qui per fidem Christo nondum insiti sunt? Firmissimè ergo stabilitur hoc loco dogma, quo omnes homines pro corruptæ naturæ ingenio peccatores esse traduntur: in cuius demonstratione crebrò versatur scriptura, eò quod cognitio hæc homini cumprimis necessaria sit. Nisi enim hæc adsit, vel secuti de medico & medicina animarum nihil cogitamus, vel nostrarū virium & meritorū fiducia insolenter efferimur. Vtrumq; vero certum affert animabus nostris periculum. Celebres ergo sunt in scripturis sanctorum voces, quibus se peccauisse fatentur, & orant ne iudicio cum ipsis contendere Deus velit.
units.tr: First he says: "Your sins are forgiven you." He speaks not of Gentiles still alien to the faith, but of believers who had already been reborn through Christ, and therefore he names them little children. He thus confesses that sins still remain in Christians, which demand forgiveness. But if Christians and sons of God are still burdened with sins, what shall we say of those who are not yet grafted into Christ through faith? Therefore this doctrine is most firmly established in this place, by which all men are declared to be sinners by the nature of their corrupted nature; Scripture often dwells on the demonstration of this, because this knowledge is especially necessary for man. For unless it be present, we either think nothing of the physician and medicine of souls, or we are insolently puffed up by confidence in our own strength and merits. Both bring a certain danger to our souls. Therefore the voices of the saints in Scripture are famous, by which they confess that they have sinned, and pray that God would not wish to contend with them in judgment.

units.la: Deinde remedium quoque ostendit & exhibet Ioannes, quò nobis succurritur. Peccata (inquit) remittuntur vobis propter nomen ipsius. Remittendi verbum nobis omnem satisfactionis gloriā eripit. Est enim metaphora à creditoribus & debitoribus sumpta, quâ ipse Christus in euangelio explicat. Matth.18. Remittuntur debita ijs, qui soluendo non sunt. Cum igitur & nobis peccati debita remittat Deus, satis euidenti argumento probat, nihil in nobis esse, per quod iustitiæ ipsius satisfieri posit. Hoc ipsum alibi per delendi verbum exprimit, cum apud prophetam ait: Ego ego ille ipse sum, qui deleo transgressiones tuas. Isa.43. Et rursum: Ego deleui transgressiones tuas vt densas nebulas, & vt nube peccata tua. Isa.44. Possunt eodé & aliæ allegoriæ referri, vt cū Dauid nos peccatis exonerari, peccatū tegi, vel etiam nō imputari dicit. Psal.32. Siquidem omnia ea gratuitā remissionem siue condonationem significant. Quem enim tam forte & validum dabis, qui suis viribus damnationis sarcinam, quæ diuinæ iustitiæ legibus nobis impositā est, excutiat? Quis item peccata Deum celabit, qui & corda & renes scrutatur, cum ea rarissimè homines celare posimus? Vel quis sua authoritate efficiet, ne ipsi imputetur & vt debitum exigatur, quod contra Dei leges ab ipso commissum est? Vt ergo primus in iustificationis doctrina gradus est, no strę corruptionis notitia: sic secundo loco, nobis mera Dei gratia peccatorum remissionem obtinere, nouisse oportet.
units.tr: Then John also shows and offers the remedy by which help comes to us. "Sins," he says, "are forgiven you for his name's sake." The word remit snatches from us all glory of satisfaction. For it is a metaphor taken from creditors and debtors, by which Christ himself explains it in the Gospel. Matt. 18: debts are forgiven to those who are unable to pay. Since, therefore, God forgives us the debts of sin, he proves by a sufficiently evident argument that there is nothing in us through which the justice of God could be satisfied. He expresses the same thing elsewhere by the word blot out, when he says through the prophet: "I, I am he who blots out your transgressions." Isa. 43. And again: "I have blotted out your transgressions like a thick cloud, and your sins like a cloud." Isa. 44. Other allegories can be referred to the same thing, as when David says that we are unburdened of sins, that sin is covered, or even not imputed. Ps. 32. For all these signify free forgiveness or pardon. For who will give so strong and mighty a man who would shake off by his own powers the burden of damnation, which has been laid upon us by the laws of divine justice? Likewise, who will hide sins from God, who searches both hearts and reins, since we can very rarely hide them from men? Or who by his own authority will bring it about that it is not imputed to him, and that the debt, which he committed against the laws of God, is not demanded? Therefore, as the first step in the doctrine of justification is the knowledge of our corruption, so in the second place it is necessary for us to know that the forgiveness of sins is obtained by the sheer grace of God.

units.la: At quia Deum non misericordem modò, sed & iustum & seuerum peccati vindicem esse constat, causam aliquam esse oportet, propter quam peccata nobis remittat, quæ si in nobis non est, certè alibi eam inuenire opus erit, vt vel aliquo modo ad nos pertingat. Et cauendum, ne Dei gratiam sic afferamus, vt iustitia eiusdem, qua totum orbem regit & tuetur, extinguatur. Exprimit ergo causam hanc Apostolus, cum ait: Remittuntur vobis peccata PROPTER NOMEN EIVS. De Christo autem loquitur, vt primo capite & initio secundi vidimus. Quia enim is humana carne assumpta frater noster factus est, nostræ causæ patronus & vindex iure fieri potuit. Hanc ergo omnem in se transtulit, peccata totius mundi sibi imputari voluit, & pro ijsdē in Cruce immolatus satisfecit, deleto, quod aduersus nos erat, chirographo, & illud sustulit è medio affixum Cruci. Col.2. Ideo propheta dicit: Dominus effecit, vt incurreret in ipsum omniū nostrum iniquitas. Propter transgressiones nostras vulneratus est, & attritus propter iniquitates nostras. Et mulcta correctionis nostræ ei imposita est, &c. Isa.53. Verè ergo Ioannes dicit, propter Christi nomen peccata nobis remitti, cum is sit, qui pro illis satisfacere dignatus est. Consentiunt cum hac doctrina locupletissimi testes, quos pasim scriptura citat. Apud prophetam loco supra citato Deus clamat: Ego sum, qui deleo transgressiones tuas, idque propter me. Isa.43. Per seipsum verò Christum Iesum intelligit, qui patri consubstantialis & coæternus est. Idem in euangelio celeberrimam illam vocem bis repetit: Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi complacitum est. Matth.3. & 17. Baptista Christum digito monstrans: Ecce (inquit) agnus ille Dei, qui tollit peccatum mundi. Ioannis 1. Similiter ipse Christus omnes laborantes & oneratos ad se inuitat, & in se illis requiem fore pollicetur. Matth. 11. Apostolorum omniū hæc vna vox est, in solo Christo peccatorū remissionem & salutem contineri. Petrus enim hunc dicit in corpore suo peccata nostra pertulisse.1. Pet.2. Idem aliud nomen sub cœlo hominibus datum esse negat, in quo posint salui fieri,praeter nomen Iesu.Acto.4.Paulus Christum Iesum in mundum venisse scribit,vt peccatores saluos faceret.1.Tim.1.Idem nihil se nouisse fatetur, praeter Iesum Christum, & hunc crucifixum.1.Cor.2.Sed quid opus est testimonijs recensendis immorari, cum nullus vel veteris vel noui Testamenti liber sit,qui non multa huius farinę contineat? Patet ergo verisimam esse Ioannis sententiam, qua praedicationem Christi à nouitatis suspicione liberat. Caeterum vt haec insolentem nostrarum satisfactionum fiduciam deprimunt:ita officij quoque nos admonent. Quia enim eam esse videmus peccati atrocitatem, vt non nisi Christi morte expiari potuerit,nemo negabit, ardenti & vigilanti puritatis ac sanctimoniae studio opus esse ijs, quicunque in Dei conspectu versari cupiunt:nec putandum est,Christum ideo sanguinem suum fudisse, vt nobis impure viuendi licentiam impetraret.Pertinent huc quae habentur Rom.6.1.Corinth.6.1.Thessalon.4. Colost. 3.Tit.3.&c.Sed transeamus ad alteram huius loci partem,qua euangelij doctrinam omnibus aetatibus conuenire probat.
units.tr: But since it is established that God is not only merciful but also just and severe as an avenger of sin, there must be some cause for which he forgives us our sins; and if this cause is not in us, then surely we shall have to find it elsewhere, so that it may somehow reach us. And we must take care not to assert God's grace in such a way that his justice, by which he rules and preserves the whole world, is extinguished. The Apostle therefore expresses this cause when he says: "Your sins are forgiven you FOR HIS NAME'S SAKE." He is speaking of Christ, as we saw in the first chapter and at the beginning of the second. For since he, having taken on human flesh, became our brother, he could rightly become the advocate and avenger of our cause. He therefore transferred all this onto himself, willed that the sins of the whole world be imputed to him, and, being sacrificed on the Cross for them, made satisfaction, the handwriting that was against us having been blotted out, and he took it out of the way, fastened to the Cross. Col. 2. Therefore the prophet says: "The Lord caused the iniquity of us all to fall upon him. He was wounded for our transgressions, and bruised for our iniquities. And the chastisement of our peace was laid upon him," etc. Isa. 53. Truly, then, John says that sins are forgiven us for the sake of Christ's name, since he is the one who deigned to make satisfaction for them. The most abundant witnesses, whom Scripture everywhere cites, agree with this doctrine. In the prophet, in the passage cited above, God cries out: "I am he who blots out your transgressions, and that for my own sake." Isa. 43. But by himself he understands Christ Jesus, who is consubstantial and coeternal with the Father. The same thing, in the Gospel, he repeats twice in that most celebrated voice: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Matt. 3 and 17. The Baptist, pointing to Christ with his finger, says: "Behold that Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world." John 1. Similarly Christ himself invites all who labour and are burdened to come to him, and promises that he will give them rest in himself. Matt. 11. This is the one voice of all the apostles: that forgiveness of sins and salvation are contained in Christ alone. For Peter says that he bore our sins in his own body. 1 Pet. 2. The same denies that any other name under heaven has been given to men in which they can be saved, except the name of Jesus. Acts 4. Paul writes that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners. 1 Tim. 1. The same confesses that he knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified. 1 Cor. 2. But why should we linger in listing testimonies, when there is no book of either the Old or the New Testament that does not contain much of this kind? It is clear, then, that John's opinion is most true, by which he frees the preaching of Christ from the suspicion of novelty. Moreover, just as these things cast down the insolent confidence in our own satisfactions, so they also admonish us of our duty. For since we see that the atrocity of sin is such that it could not be expiated except by the death of Christ, no one will deny that there is need of an ardent and watchful zeal for purity and holiness in those who wish to live in the sight of God; nor is it to be thought that Christ shed his blood so that he might obtain for us a licence to live impurely. To this pertain the things found in Rom. 6; 1 Cor. 6; 1 Thess. 4; Col. 3; Tit. 3, etc. But let us pass to the other part of this passage, in which he proves that the doctrine of the gospel is suitable to all ages.

units.la: I I. Scribo uobis patres,quia cognouistis eum,qui ab initio est. Scribo uobis pueruli,quoniam cognouistis patrem. Tribus aetatibus omne hominum genus comprehendit. Nam cuiuscunque sint sexus,conditionis siue ordinis,aut pueri sunt,aut adolescentes,aut senes. Singulis vero praedicationem hanc conuenire docet, eo quod singuli ex ea discant,quod aetati ipsorum non vtile modo,sed & necessarium est. Exordium à senibus facit, quibus vitium hoc natura inhaeret,vt docentes impatientius ferant. Quia enim cum senili prudentia multorum annorum experientiam coniunxerunt, turpe putant,si alijs sese docendos praebeant. Dicit ergo:Scribo vobis patres,id est,ad vos pertinet ō senes,doctrina haec. Causa subijcitur: Quia ex hac eum agnoscitis,qui ab initio est.Quasi dicat:Multa quidem fert aetas, & de multis instruit diutina rerum experientia.Sed in salutis causa nihil illi deferendum est.Haec enim in vnigenito Dei filio Iesu Christo consistit,qui non tempore coepit,sed ab aeterno est, & in prima mundi origine humani generis redemptor & saluator promissus est.Tradit hunc euangelij doctrina,qua explicatur,vt quae olim praedicta fuerunt,per hunc impleta sint & praestita. Si ergo rerum vetustissimarum cognitio delectat,euangelium audite,& ex hoc Christum discite, cuius notitia nō inani modo voluptate pascit,sed aeternae salutis ministra est. Vtinam haec sententia senum animis esset commendatissima,qui vt prae caeteris sapere videantur, cum Terentiano sene sua narrant facinora,quae olim iuuenilibus cupiditatibus exceçati patrauerunt: quasi ex illis virtutis documenta,& non potius scelerum irritamenta,decerpi possint. Sic enim fit, vt nec ipsi de olim commissis flagitijs dignam poenitentiam agant,& iunioribus eadem audendi animum faciant. Discant ergo ad se per tinere euangelij doctrinam,ex qua filij Dei Iesu Christi cognitionem hauriat,& eidem, quicquid vitae tempus reliquum est,consecrare discant. Monet idem Paulus apostolus,qui senes vult sobrios esse,graues,modestos,sanos fide,charitate & patientia.Tit.2.Imitetur Simeonem, qui Christum puerum in vlnas suscipere & amplecti meruit.De hoc enim Lucas testatur,quod cum iustus ac pius esset,consolationem Israelis,id est,promissum orbis saluatorem ac fidelem populi Dei liberatorem expectarit, quod non aliud fuit, quam in eius cognitione versari, quem Ioannes hoc loco ab initio fuisse fatetur. At si nostri seculi senes inspicias,ita pleriq; viuunt, quasi mensuram libidinis iam demum implere velint, & Christi cognitionem nihil ad se pertinere existiment.
units.tr: I I. "I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning. I write to you, little children, because you have known the Father." He embraces the whole human race in three ages. For whatever their sex, condition or rank, people are either children, young men or old men. He teaches that this preaching suits each of them, because each learns from it something that is not only useful but necessary for their age. He begins with the old, who have a natural fault: they bear being taught with impatience. For having joined senile prudence to the experience of many years, they think it shameful to submit themselves to be taught by others. So he says: "I write to you, fathers"; that is, "this teaching concerns you, O old men." The reason follows: "because through it you have known him who is from the beginning." As if he said: "Long life brings much, and long experience of things teaches much. But in the matter of salvation nothing must be yielded to it. For salvation consists in Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, who did not begin in time but is from eternity, and who was promised in the first origin of the world as the redeemer and saviour of the human race. The doctrine of the gospel hands him down, by which it is explained that what was foretold long ago has been fulfilled and accomplished through him. If, then, the knowledge of the most ancient things delights you, hear the gospel and learn Christ from it, whose knowledge feeds you not with empty pleasure only, but is the minister of eternal salvation." Would that this saying were most commended to the minds of old men, who, in order to seem wise above others, recount with Terence's old man their wicked deeds, which they once committed while inflamed by youthful desires, as if from those tales the lessons of virtue, rather than incitements to crime, could be gathered. For thus it happens that they neither perform worthy repentance for the disgraceful acts once committed, nor give the younger ones the courage to dare the same things. Let them learn, then, that the doctrine of the gospel pertains to them, from which they may draw the knowledge of the Son of God, Jesus Christ, and learn to dedicate to him whatever time of life remains. The apostle Paul, who wants the old men to be sober, grave, modest, sound in faith, love and patience, also admonishes them (Titus 2). Let them imitate Simeon, who deserved to take the child Christ into his arms and embrace him. For Luke testifies of him that, since he was just and devout, he waited for the consolation of Israel, that is, the promised Saviour of the world and the faithful Deliverer of the people of God, which was nothing other than to dwell in the knowledge of him whom John here confesses to have been from the beginning. But if you look at the old men of our age, most of them live as though they wished to fill up at last the measure of their lust, and they judge the knowledge of Christ to have nothing to do with them.

units.la: Interim de certitudine euangelicae doctrinae hic locus admonet. Si enim Christus ab initio fuit,nec mutatur,sed vnus & idem est heri & hodie & vsq; in secula,(Heb.13.) certam & infallibilem esse oportet fidem & religionem, quae illo nititur.Porro, vt doctrinam hanc adolescentibus conuenire doceat,videamus.
units.tr: Meanwhile this passage gives a warning about the certainty of the evangelical doctrine. For if Christ was from the beginning, and is not changed, but is one and the same yesterday, today and forever (Heb. 13), then the faith and religion which rest upon him must be certain and infallible. Further, let us see how he teaches that this doctrine suits young men.

units.la: Scribo uobis adolescentes,quoniam uicistis illum malum. Adolescentum siue iuuenum hoc fere ingenium est,vt corporis robore & animi fortitudine elati,nil nisi pugnas & victorias spirent. Qua re eos tantum libenter audiunt,qui de his differere consueuerunt. Dicit ergo Ioannes:Licet ad se nes pertinere dixerim doctrinā hanc,qui iā otio & pace gaudent, eadem tamen non minus vobis seruit ō iuuenes,quos inter pugnas & certamina corporis & animi vires ostentare iuuat.Causa in promptu est:Quoniam vicistis illum malum. Vicistis vero ait pro vincetis, & praeterito vti maluit (qui scripturae sacrae mos est vsitatissimus) quo certitudinem & veritatem sui dicti melius exprimeret.Docet ergo,in euangelij doctrina pugnam longe pulcherrimam nobis proponi, & victoriam sperari non gloriosam modo,sed & ex omni parte felicem.Constat enim,humani generis hostem improbissimum esse satanam, qui quia nil nisi malum nouit & operatur, merito ille malus dicitur.Solet is circuire vt Leo rugiens,& subinde quaerit quem deuoret.1.Petr.5. Nec visibilibus armis pugnat,nec corpus modò nostrū impetit. Sed ānimis & cogitationibus nostris sese insinuans,ad ea nos solicitat,quæ nobis æterni interitus & damnationis causa sunt,& plerunque in hoc sæculo quoq; infelicissimos reddunt. Huius enim suggestione fit, quod Dei & verbi ipsius obliti,exemplum mundi potius,quàm salutis viam in scripturis propositam sequi malumus. Illo instigante verbo Dei contradicimus, nomè Dei sanctu blasphemo ore proscindimus, scortamur, mœchamur,cædes committimus,proximi fortunas furto,rapinis,usura alijsq; artibus illicitis nobis vendicamus:Deniq; huius suasu fit,ut nostra sponte peccati dominio nosipsos subijciamus, quæ servitus,ut carni iucunda est,ita omnibus modis infelices facit quicunq; illam serviunt. Peccati enim stipendium mors est.Rom.5. Nulla igitur pugna tâ necessaria homini, quàm quæ contra hoc hoste suscipitur. Nulla victoria tâ felix & læta,quàm quæ ab hoste tam improbo reportatur.Nec enim friuola huius mundi gloria & spolijs breui perituris decoratur,sed angelorum applausus sen-tit,triumphos in Dei conspectu lætos ducit,& æternæ vitæ præmijs compensatur.Hæc victoria multos ex Dei cultoribus longè celeberrimos fecit, cum ex hac apud posteros maiorem laudé re ferat,quàm vlli Alexandri,Scipiones,Marcelli,Cæsares ex sanguinolentis prælijs & gentibus sub iugatis retulerint. Celebratur quidem in prophanis scriptoribus Alexandri cōtinentia,qui Darij vxore & filiabus,cum captiuæ in suam venissent potestatem,abstinuerit. At quàm parum solida fuerit ista continentia,quam laudis studium potius,quàm vera pietas extorquebat, multa eius sa cinora alia testantur,& ipse nimis aperte prodidit,quando Persicas puellas oculorum dolores esse dicebat.At qui Christi spiritu animati vincunt,ipsis simul affectibus superiores fiunt,nec vllo vel oculorum vel aliorum sensuum dolore tanguntur, quos iam pridem per fidei obedientiam sub-egerunt : & ita victoriam reportant, quæ ipsis non apud homines modo, verumetiam apud Deum laudem parit immortalem. Hac potius Iosephi libidinis malum, quod feré iuuenibus indomitum videtur,deuicit,& coronam retulit immarcescibilé.Gen.39. Hac ipsa Dauid vindictæ cupiditatem repressit,cum Sauli,aperto hosti, potius parcere, quàm manus suas sanguine regis diuinitus vncti polluere maluit.1.Sam.24.& 25.Pro hac pugnarunt olim martyres,quos nullus tormentorum dolor,nulla carnificum sævities, nullæ tyrannorum minæ, nulla hominum ingratissimorum improbitas, nullæ amicorum preces, non denique coniugum & dulcissimorum pignorum aspectus superare potuit,quò minus pro Christo pulcherrimam mortem subire, & deuicto mundi principe,palmam æternam ac verè nobilem assequi cuperent. Nihil ergo habent quod de evan-gelij doctrina conquerantur,qui non otio,sed labore, non pace sed pugnis gaudent. Docentur enim seipsos vincere,quę victoria est longè pulcherrima. Cum eo etiam hoste committuntur,quem nisi Christo auspice vincamus,salvi fieri non possumus.
units.tr: "I write to you, young men, because you have overcome that evil one." The disposition of young men, or youths, is generally this: puffed up with bodily strength and courage of mind, they breathe nothing but battles and victories. Therefore they gladly listen only to those who are accustomed to speak about such things. John therefore says: although I have said that this doctrine pertains to the old men, who now rejoice in leisure and peace, it nonetheless serves you, O young men, no less, you whom it delights to display the strength of body and mind in battles and contests. The reason is at hand: "because you have overcome that evil one." He says "you have overcome" for "you will overcome," and preferred to use the past tense (which is a most common custom of Holy Scripture), so as to express the certainty and truth of his saying more clearly. He teaches, therefore, that in the doctrine of the gospel a most beautiful battle is set before us, and a victory is hoped for that is not only glorious but happy in every respect. For it is agreed that the most wicked enemy of the human race is Satan, who, since he knows and works nothing but evil, is rightly called that evil one. He is wont to go about like a roaring lion, and continually seeks whom he may devour (1 Peter 5). Nor does he fight with visible weapons, nor does he attack only our body. But insinuating himself into our minds and thoughts, he stirs us to those things which are causes of eternal ruin and damnation, and which in this age too often make us most unhappy. For it is by his suggestion that, forgetting God and his very Word, we prefer to follow the example of the world rather than the way of salvation set out in the Scriptures. At his instigation we contradict the Word of God, we tear the holy name of God with blaspheming mouths, we commit fornication and adultery, we commit murders, we claim for ourselves our neighbour's goods by theft, robbery, usury and other illicit arts. Finally, at his persuasion it happens that we of our own accord subject ourselves to the dominion of sin; and this slavery, however pleasant it is to the flesh, makes unhappy in every way all those who serve it. For the wages of sin is death (Rom. 5). No battle, therefore, is so necessary for a man as the one undertaken against this enemy. No victory is so fortunate and joyful as the one won over so wicked an enemy. For its glory is not adorned with the frivolous glory of this world and with spoils that will soon perish, but it is felt in the applause of the angels, it leads triumphs joyful in the sight of God, and it is rewarded with the prizes of eternal life. This victory has made many of the worshippers of God far most renowned, since from it they gain greater praise among posterity than any Alexanders, Scipios, Marcelli or Caesars have gained from bloody battles and nations brought under the yoke. Indeed, the continence of Alexander is celebrated among the profane writers, who abstained from the wife and daughters of Darius when they had come into his power as captives. But how little solid that continence was, which the desire for praise rather than true piety extorted from him, many other of his deeds bear witness, and he himself disclosed it too plainly when he said that the Persian girls were a pain to the eyes. But those who conquer, animated by the Spirit of Christ, become superior to the very passions themselves, and are touched by no pain either of the eyes or of the other senses, which they have long since subdued through obedience of faith. And so they win a victory which brings them immortal praise not only among men but also before God. Thus Joseph overcame the evil of lust, which seems almost untamable in young men, and won the crown that does not fade (Gen. 39). By this same faith David restrained his desire for revenge, when he preferred to spare Saul, an open enemy, rather than pollute his hands with the blood of the king divinely anointed (1 Sam. 24 and 25). For this faith the martyrs once fought, whom no pain of torments, no cruelty of executioners, no threats of tyrants, no wickedness of the most ungrateful men, no entreaties of friends, nor finally the sight of wives and dearest pledges could overcome, so that they did not desire to undergo a most beautiful death for Christ and, the prince of the world being conquered, to attain the eternal and truly noble palm. Therefore those who rejoice not in leisure but in labour, not in peace but in battles, have nothing of which to complain about the doctrine of the gospel. For they are taught to conquer themselves, which is by far the most beautiful victory. They also engage with that enemy whom, unless we conquer under the leadership of Christ, we cannot be saved.

units.la: Admonet itaq; locus hic,quàm errent,qui evangelium eo nomine amplectuntur,quòd otio & quiete se frui posse sperant,cum pugnæ indefinentes fidelibus propositæ sint. Non potest cum illis convenire mundus , cuius opera mala sunt & lucem veritatis fugiunt. Ioannis 3. & 15. Sed quid de mundo dico, non cum propria carne & sanguine conveniet tibi, ut primum Christi castra sequi coeperis. Armemur ergo spirituali armatura,cingamur baltheo veritatis, induamur thorace iustitiæ, calceati curramus in evangelio pacis,scutum fidei ignitis tentationum iaculis opponamus, galea salutaris tegamur, & gladium spiritus indesinenter vibremus, & succeßu fruemur felicissimo.Ephef. sexto .
