At omissis adolescentibus,Ioannes doctrinam suam puerili etiam ætati applicat.
units.tr: This passage therefore warns how greatly they err who embrace the gospel on the ground that they hope to enjoy leisure and quiet, when battles without end are set before the faithful. The world, whose works are evil and which flees the light of truth, cannot agree with them (John 3 and 15). But why do I speak of the world? Your own flesh and blood will not agree with you as soon as you begin to follow the camp of Christ. Let us therefore arm ourselves with the spiritual armour, let us gird our loins with the belt of truth, put on the breastplate of righteousness, run shod in the gospel of peace, hold up the shield of faith against the fiery darts of temptations, be covered with the helmet of salvation, and brandish without ceasing the sword of the Spirit, and we shall enjoy a most happy success (Eph. 6). But, having set aside the young men, John applies his teaching also to the age of childhood.

units.la: Scribo vobis pueruli,quoniam cognouistis patrem. Puerorum ea conditio est , ut alieno regimine & moderamine opus habeant . Quia enim per ætatem ratione minus firma & rudi adhuc præditi sunt,sua commoda nec ipsi prospicere,nec incommoda cauere possunt. Nisi ergo vel parentes,ex quibus geniti sunt,vel alios parentum loco fidos magistros & tutores habeant, facilè mala incurrunt grauissima.Evangelium ergo illis quàm maximè convenire dicit,eò quòd per hoc in eius cognitionem perducantur,qui unicus & verè fidelis omnium nostrum pater est, qui quos semel in suam tutelâ susceptos adoptauit,nûquam suo vel auxilio vel consilio destituere solet.Verè enim apud prophetâ ait: Num obliuioni tradit mulier infantem suum, quò minus misereatur filij uteri sui? Sed esto obliuiscatur illa,ego tamen tui non obliuiscar.Isa. 49. Prospicit autem ceu fidus parens suis non de ijs modò quæ corpori serviunt,verumetiâ illis quæ animarum salute promouet. Nam ut victum suppeditat,tuetur & conservat inter quotidiana pericula: sic spiritu suo animos illuminat,verbo suo docet, consolatur, mouet, hortatur, corrigit,& in via salutis æternæ dirigit. Extant etiam exempla, quibus probare voluit, quanta illi de pueris cura sit . Iacobum in vtero materno delitescentem se curare testatur, & eidem primatum ac primogenituræ prærogatiuam decernit. Genef. vigesimoquinto. Iosephum puerum adhuc prophetico spiritu instruit,& soler-tem facit somniorum interpretem.Genef. 37.40.& 41. Mosem quoque Nili fluctibus expositum hostili ōpera saluat,per filiam nimirū tyranni,qui tanti mali author fuerat. Exo.2. Pertinent huc, quæ de Samuele, Daniele & aliis habentur, quæ satis declarant,Deum puerilis ætatis patrem & tutorem esse fidelissimū.Qui hoc patre uti norunt,illis non parentum præmaturi obitus, nō hæredipetarum iniustę artes,non corrupta institutio, non praua cōmercia obesse poterunt:eo quòd ab omnibus istis clementissimus ille pater asserit. At hunc nobis patrem esse factum, non aliunde quàm ex euangelii doctrina discimus. Hæc igitur omnibus pulchre cōuenit, quicunq; patris regimine, disciplina & protectione opus habent, quo in loco cūprimis puerilem ætatem esse cōstat.
units.tr: "I write to you, little children, because you have known the Father." The condition of children is that they need the guidance and direction of another. For because they are, by reason of their age, still endowed with a rather weak and untrained understanding, they can neither foresee their own advantages nor guard against their disadvantages. Unless, therefore, they have either the parents from whom they were born, or other faithful teachers and guardians in the place of parents, they easily fall into the gravest evils. The evangelist therefore says that the gospel is most suitable for them, because through it they are led into the knowledge of him who is the only and truly faithful Father of us all, who, once he has taken those whom he has adopted into his protection, is never wont to abandon them, either by his help or by his counsel. For he says in the prophet truly: "Can a woman forget her infant, so as not to have mercy on the son of her womb? But even if she should forget, yet I will not forget you" (Isa. 49). Moreover, he cares for his own, like a faithful parent, not only for those things which serve the body, but also for those which promote the salvation of souls. For as he supplies food, and protects and preserves them amid daily dangers, so he enlightens their minds by his Spirit, teaches them by his Word, comforts, moves, exhorts, corrects them, and directs them in the way of eternal salvation. There are also examples by which he wished to prove how great his care is for children. He testifies that he took care of Jacob while he was still hidden in his mother's womb, and decreed for him the primacy and the prerogative of the firstborn (Gen. 25). While Joseph was still a boy, he instructed him with prophetic spirit and made him a skilful interpreter of dreams (Gen. 37, 40 and 41). He also saved Moses, exposed on the waters of the Nile, from the hostile hands of the tyrant's own daughter, who was indeed the author of so great an evil (Exod. 2). To this belong the things that are told of Samuel, Daniel and others, which sufficiently declare that God is the most faithful Father and guardian of childhood. Those who know how to use this Father will not be harmed by the untimely deaths of parents, by the unjust tricks of those who seek inheritances, by a corrupt upbringing, or by wicked dealings, because that most merciful Father protects them from all these things. But we learn that he has become our Father from nothing other than the doctrine of the gospel. This teaching, therefore, suits all those well who need a father's rule, discipline and protection, and in this respect especially childhood is evidently in need of it.

units.la: Docentur hoc loco parentes, quæ ipsorum circa liberorum educationem potissima cura esse debeat:hæc nimirum, ut illos Deū patrem à teneris agnoscere discant. Nam quo semel est im-buta recēs seruabit odorem Testa diu. Cerei sunt puerorum animi, & facilè illis quod lubet,inscribitur. Hoc ipsum verò usu & consuetudine cōfirmatum ita hæret,ut ex adamantina tabella citius aliquid expunxeris,quàm ex hominū cordibus euellas,cuius à pueris assueuerunt. Hinc Deum peculiaria de hac re præcepta dedisse videmus, quæ extant tum alibi, tum Deut.6.Exo.13.Psal. 78.&c.Et exempla sunt verè fideliū, quos magno studio in hoc incubuisse legimus, ut liberos in Dei cognitione & fide probè institutos haberent.In Abrahamo certè,patre credentiū,hoc ipsum Deus commédat,& ideo pœnam Sodomis imminentem illi ceu intimo amico reuelare dignatur. Nam scio(inquit)quòd mandaturus sit filijs suis & domui suæ post se,ut custodiant viam domini,&c.Gen.18.Hæc cura si omnium parentum animis insideret, iuuentutem sanctius institutam haberemus,& felicius succederent quæcunque ab illis vel priuatim vel publicè instituuntur. At quia suo se officio probè defunctos putant,si opibus congerendis inuigilent,si patrimonia ampla liberis relinquant,si de coniugijs opulentis & splendidis ptospiciant, nihil interim de fide liberorum & religione soliciti:permittit quidem Deus, ut ad tempus succedat quod instituunt,at tandem horrendis immissis cæsibus probat, quàm vana sint hæc omnia, nec quicquam prosint, nisi ipso patre & tutore utamur.
units.tr: Here the parents are taught what their chief care in the education of their children ought to be: namely, that they learn to acknowledge God as Father from their earliest years. For a jar keeps the scent of whatever was first steeped in it, fresh, for a long time. Children's minds are like wax, and whatever pleases them is easily stamped upon them. Indeed, once this has been confirmed by practice and habit, it sticks so firmly that you would sooner wipe something off an adamantine tablet than tear out of men's hearts what they have been accustomed to from boyhood. Hence we see that God has given special precepts about this matter, which exist both elsewhere and in Deuteronomy 6, Exodus 13, Psalm 78, and so on. And there are examples of truly faithful people who, we read, devoted great zeal to this, so that they would have their children well instructed in the knowledge and faith of God. Certainly in Abraham, the father of believers, God commends this very thing, and therefore deigns to reveal to him, as to an intimate friend, the punishment hanging over Sodom. For (he says) I know that he will command his sons and his household after him to keep the way of the Lord, etc. Genesis 18. If this care sat in the minds of all parents, we would have youth brought up more holily, and whatever is instituted by them, either privately or publicly, would turn out more happily. But because they think they have discharged their duty well if they labour to heap up wealth, if they leave ample inheritances to their children, if they provide for rich and splendid marriages, while meanwhile they are not at all anxious about the faith and religion of their children: God indeed permits what they establish to succeed for a time, but at last, by sending dreadful calamities, he proves how vain all these things are, and that none of them profits anything, unless we make use of the father and guardian himself.

units.la: Porrò priusquam ab hoc loco discedamus , illorum tyrannis producenda & confutanda est, qui omnes ferè hominum ordines à lectione scripturarū arcent,quibus doctrina hæc traditur. Periculum enim esse aiunt,ne imperiti & rudes ex his falsa dogmata haurientes hæresibus pestiferis implicentur. Improbum & malignum hominum genus,qui scripturis adeoq; spiritui sancto imputare audent,cuius ipsi authores sunt. Quia enim ipsi,cum ecclesiarum antistites haberi velint, docendi officium vel omnino negligunt,vel loco verbi Dei hominū traditiones docent, & sanioridoctrinæ locū omnino negant,sit ut imperiti homines,dum nec illis tutò credere,nec ex semet ipsis meliora videre possunt, varijs cogitationibus immersi in nouos & absurdos errores demergantur.Quòd si ipsi doctores veritatis synceri & fideles fuerint,populum ad scripturas sacras relegauerint, & easdem expo-suerint publicè,ut par est,breui sentient, euangelicæ doctrinæ mysteria,non humana modò philosophia turgidis, sed omnium ordinum hominibus, senibus,iuuenibus,pueris,fœminis & viris conuenire:imò hunc esse Dei morem,ut ea coram sapientibus huius mundi absconsa paruulis reuelet.Matth.11.Sed ad reliqua pergamus.
units.tr: Moreover, before we depart from this passage, the tyranny of those men must be brought forth and refuted, who bar almost all orders of men from reading the Scriptures, to whom this teaching is handed down. For they say there is danger that the unskilled and untaught, drawing false dogmas from them, will become entangled in pestilent heresies. A wicked and malignant kind of men, who dare to impute this to the Scriptures and even to the Holy Spirit, whose own authors they themselves are. For since they themselves, though they wish to be regarded as the leaders of the churches, either altogether neglect the duty of teaching, or teach the traditions of men in place of the Word of God, and altogether deny that there is a place for sounder doctrine, it comes about that unskilled men, since they can neither trust those men safely nor see better things for themselves, plunged into various thoughts, are sunk into new and absurd errors. But if the teachers themselves were sincere and faithful teachers of the truth, and had sent the people back to the holy Scriptures and expounded them publicly, as is fitting, they would soon perceive that the mysteries of the evangelical doctrine are suited not only to those puffed up with human philosophy, but to men of every rank: old men, young men, boys, women and men alike. Indeed, it is God's custom to reveal to little ones those things which are hidden from the wise of this world. Matthew 11. But let us proceed to the rest.

units.la: III. Scripsi vobis patres,quoniam cognouistis eum, qui ab initio est. Scripsi vobis adolescentes, quo-niam fortes estis,& verbum Dei manet in vobis,& vicistis illum malum. Repetit quæ de senibus & adolescentibus dixerat, quò minus de certitudine eorum, quæ dicta sunt,dubitemus. Indicat enim prioris membri repetitio indubitatam esse euangelij veritatem, & ab omni nouitatis suspicione alienissimam. Alterum verò membrum,quo de iuuenibus agit, doctrinam consolationi coniunctam habet. Quia enim pugnam illis proposuit, poterant aliqui illius metu succumbere,cum experientia doceat, quàm grauis & plena periculi res sit,cum hoste tam crudeli & versipelle cōgredi.Animum ergo illis addens,inquit:Fortes estis,& verbum Dei manet in vobis,& vicistis illum malum. Habent verba hæc rationes tres, quibus confirmentur. Primam ab ætatis huius ingenio desumit,quod est fortem esse & in periculis subeundis imperterritum.Quo fit,ut iuuenes interdum periculis sua sponte,nec magnam ob causam, sese obijciant.Quantò magis ergo hic pugnare & periclitari decet, ubi ignauia sempiternum affert interitum:' Secundò,auxilium monstrat,quo adiuti,pugnæ huius periculum sustinere possint. Verbū Dei (inquit) in vobis manet.Habet sua arma Satan,quibus infirmā carnem territat. Sed qui Christo sunt insiti,gladiū habent huic hosti formidabile planè,Verbum Dei scilicet,quod & technas illius patefacit & tela infringit,& pugnā di modum felicissimum monstrat. Idem animat & roborat, ut qui ex sese nihil poterant, omnia possint in Christo, Philip.4.Hoc qui cordibus suis impressum habent,in omnem euentum parati, nullis vel laboribus, vel periculis succumbunt. Tertiò ab anteactis ratiocinatur, dicens: Vicistis illum malum. Non iam demum vincendus erit hostis ille, sed iam olim deuictus est. Vicit hunc Christus, promissum illud semen mulieris, & caput eius contriuit. Gen. 3. Quæ victoria vestra est, cum hic caput vestrū fit, vosq; membra sua agnoscat. Quod ergo pugnas nouas ciet, non ea spe facit, quasi quicquam contra electos posse efficere, sed ingenij sui improbitati indulget, & permittit hoc illi Deus, quo sanctorum virtus, pugnis exercita, magis elucescat. Quare cū iuuentus per se intrepida fit, & verbum Dei indesinenter vos animet, cumq; hoste vobis res sit, quem & Christus olim vicit, & qua ratione vinci debeat docuit, posito timore strenuos vos præbete sub tanti ducis auspicijs milites. Videmus hoc loco fratres, vnde vires nobis suppetant contra salutis nostræ hostem Satanam. Ex Christo nimirum, si illi per fidem inserti verbo illius animemur. Is enim inuicta illa petra est, cui portæ inferorum non præualent. Matth. 16.
units.tr: III. I have written to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning. I have written to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome that evil one. He repeats what he had said about the old men and the young men, so that we may doubt less about the certainty of the things that have been said. For the repetition of the former clause indicates that the truth of the gospel is undoubted, and wholly free from any suspicion of novelty. But the other clause, in which he speaks of the young men, has its teaching joined to consolation. For since he has set a battle before them, some might have given way from fear of it, since experience teaches how grave and full of peril a matter it is to engage with an enemy so cruel and so crafty. Therefore, adding courage to them, he says: You are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome that evil one. These words contain three reasons by which they are confirmed. The first he takes from the disposition of this age, namely, that it is to be strong and fearless in facing dangers. Hence it happens that young men sometimes expose themselves to dangers of their own accord, and not for any great cause. How much more, then, ought one to fight and risk oneself here, where cowardice brings eternal destruction! Secondly, he shows the help by which, being aided, they can endure the danger of this battle. The word of God (he says) abides in you. Satan has his weapons, with which he terrifies the weak flesh. But those who have been grafted into Christ have a sword which is truly formidable to this enemy, namely the Word of God, which both lays bare his tricks and breaks his darts, and shows the most fortunate manner of fighting. The same word both encourages and strengthens, so that those who of themselves could do nothing can do all things in Christ, Philippians 4. Those who have this impressed on their hearts, being prepared for every outcome, do not give way to any labours or dangers. Thirdly, he reasons from what has gone before, saying: You have overcome that evil one. That enemy will not be overcome from now on, but has been already defeated long ago. Christ has conquered him, that promised seed of the woman, and has crushed his head. Genesis 3. This victory is yours, since he who is your head acknowledges you as his members. Therefore, the fact that he stirs up new battles is not done with the hope that he can accomplish anything against the elect, but he indulges the wickedness of his nature, and God permits this to him, so that the virtue of the saints, exercised by battles, may shine forth more brightly. Wherefore, since youth is by itself fearless, and the word of God encourages you without ceasing, and since you have to do with an enemy whom Christ once conquered, and whom he taught how he ought to be conquered, put aside fear and show yourselves valiant soldiers under the auspices of so great a leader. Here, brethren, we see whence strength is supplied to us against Satan, the enemy of our salvation: namely from Christ, if we are grafted into him by faith and are stirred up by his word. For he is that invincible rock against which the gates of hell do not prevail. Matthew 16.

units.la: Docuit hucusq; Ioannes Apostolus, quàm veneranda euangelicæ doctrinæ vetustas, & vtea dem omnibus ætatibus ac omnium ordinum hominibus non vtilis modo, sed & necessaria sit. Ac cendàt ista in nobis verbi studiū, vt huius cognitione instructi, hostem salutis vincere possimus, & sub Dei patris tutela securi viuamus, vsq; in eum diem, quâdo cū Christo capite nostro regna bimus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Thus far the Apostle John has taught how venerable is the antiquity of the evangelical doctrine, and how useful and indeed necessary it is for all ages and for men of every rank. May these things kindle in us a zeal for the word, so that, instructed in its knowledge, we may be able to overcome the enemy of our salvation, and live securely under the protection of God the Father, until that day when we shall reign with Christ our head: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA X.
units.tr: HOMILIA X.

units.la: Ne diligatis mundum, neque ea quæ in mundo sunt. Si quis diligit mundum, non est charitas patris in eo. Quoniam omne quod est in mundo, veluti concupiscentia carnis, & concupiscentia oculorum, & fastus vitæ, non est ex patre, sed ex mundo est. Et mundus transit & concupiscentia eius. Qui autem facit voluntatem Dei, manet in æternum.
units.tr: Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world. If any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For all that is in the world, as the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world. And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever.

units.la: VT mundus pro corrupto suo ingenio euangelicæ doctrinæ lucem odisse solet: ita si quando hanc recepisse & amplecti videtur, ferè sub eius prætextu carnis licentiam & peccandi impunitatem quærit. Exempla sunt, quibus hoc probari poterat, non modò nostri seculi hominū, sed Apostolorum temporibus idem accidisse, ipsorum scripta abunde docet. Magna ergo prudentia & circumspectione Ioannes apostolus doctrinam salutis per Christum partæ proponit. Nam de Christi merito, de redemptionis & fidei nostræ mysterijs ita disserit, vt subinde verè fideliū of ficia & vitæ Christianæ rationem simul commendet. Vidimus id nuper in ijs, quæ verba modo prælecta præcesserunt. Cum enim euangelij doctrinam singulis hominū ætatibus applicaret, quę de iuuentute dixerat, repetit, docens hac nos præparari, & instrui ad pugnam, quæ omnes homines manet, siquidem fidei laudem & coronam referre velint. Excutit hoc modo pestilentem carnis nostræ socordiam, quæ dum otio & quieti suæ indulget, improbis Satanæ tentationibus se totam exponit, quibus succumbens salutis iacturam facit nulla arte reparabilem. Cæterum, quia in pugna ista plurimum nobis obstat mundus hic, cuius splendore & blanditijs caro nostra facile capitur, Ioannes inde occasione sumpta aduersus mundi studiū sermone dirigit, primo quidem præcipiens quid pij facere debeat, mox vero præceptū suum firmissimis rationibus commendans.
units.tr: Just as the world, on account of its corrupt nature, is wont to hate the light of the Gospel doctrine, so, if at any time it appears to have received and embraced it, it commonly seeks under its pretext license for the flesh and impunity for sin. There are examples by which this could be proved, not only from men of our own age, but the writings of the Apostles themselves abundantly teach that the same thing happened in their times. John the apostle therefore sets forth the doctrine of salvation obtained through Christ with great prudence and circumspection. For he discourses on the merit of Christ and on the mysteries of redemption and of our faith in such a way that at the same time he commends, in turn, the duties of believers and the manner of Christian life. We saw this lately in those things which preceded the words just read. For when he applied the doctrine of the Gospel to the individual ages of men, having spoken of youth, he returns to it, teaching that we are prepared and instructed by these things for the battle which awaits all men, if they wish to win the praise and crown of faith. In this way he shakes off the deadly sloth of our flesh, which, while it indulges in leisure and quiet, exposes itself entirely to the wicked temptations of Satan, and by yielding to them suffers a loss of salvation that can be repaired by no art. Moreover, because in this struggle this world stands greatly in our way, by whose splendour and allurements our flesh is easily captured, John, taking occasion from this, directs his discourse against the love of the world, first indeed commanding what a godly person ought to do, and then commending his command by the firmest reasons.

units.la: I. Ne diligatis mundum, neque ea quæ in mundo sunt. Variè sumitur mundi vocabulum. Aliquando machinam hanc orbis totius, cœlum videlicet, terram & maria cū omnibus quæ his continentur, significat. Interdum verò pro negotijs vsurpatur, quæ dum in hoc mundo viuimus, non bis sunt obeunda. Sic enim Paulus, cum expositisset ea, quibus ferè in præsenti vita occupantur homines, subijcit: Præterit figura vel habitus mundi huius, &c. 1. Cor. 7. Plerunq; tamen, quando pijs & fidelibus opponitur, impijs & alienis à religione accipitur, quos alio nomine filios huius seculi scriptura vocat. Hoc sensu Christus dicit, lucem in mundum venisse, mundum verò magis dilexisse tenebras quàm lucem, eò quòd opera eius praua sunt. Ioan. 3. Et alibi spiritum suum discipulis pollicetur, quem mundus non potest accipere. Ioa. 14. Potest autem Ioannis præceptū ad omnes significationes hasce accomodari: Est enim Christiani homines, ne mūdi huius machinam visibilem aliter diligat, quàm vt eius contemplatione in cognitionem Creatoris Dei perducatur. Si enim in ea hærere velit nimium, ad eundem cū gentibus scopulum impingit, qui quod Creatori tribuendum erat, Creaturis tribuerūt. Rom. 1. Maximè tamen ad mūdi studia, & homines mundanos, vel seculi huius filios, præceptum hoc referri debet: quia vtraq; pijs etiā plurimum negotij facere solent. Quia enim mundi studia eiusmodi ferè sunt, vt in ijs in vniuersum abstinere nemo posit, possit, cum ad præsentis vitæ conuersationem necessaria sint, facilè illorum dulcedine irretimur, nisi illis in domino vtamur. Sic multis coniugium obfuisse constat, rem alioquin salutarem & necessariam, eò quòd cæco amoris affectu decepti, diuinæ gloriæ studium in vniuersum abiecerunt. Plurimos etiam cibus & potus perdit, dum gulæ potius & crapulæ quàm naturæ inseruiût. Alij circa contractus salutis iacturā faciunt, dum auaritia capti, insatiabile habendi studium sectantur. Eadem opum ratio est, honorum, amicitiarum, fœderum, valetudinis bonæ, licitarum voluptatum, & si quæ alia in huius vitæ curriculo nobis vsurpanda obueniunt. Deniq; nullum vitæ institutum est, quod nó exitio nobis esse possit, nisi diuini verbi regulam secuti, in omnibus Dei gloriam & proximi salutem quæsiuerimus. Monet ergo Ioannes, ne diligamus mundi studia, id est, ne totos nos illis consecremus, sed iuxta Pauli præceptum, meminerimus tempus contractum esse, & proinde qui vxores habent, sint tanquam non habentes: & qui plorát, sint quasi non plorent: qui gaudent, sint tanquá non gaudeant: qui emunt, sint quasi nó possideant: & qui vtuntur hoc mundo, sint tanquâ non vtantur. 1. Cor. 7. Præcipuè tamen circa amicitias filiorũ huius seculi præceptum hoc diligéter expendere oportet. Nec enim aliud est, quo facilius homines corrum pi possint, quàm exempla eorum, quibus cum viuimus: eò quod corrupta carnis natura quæuis occasio mali, vtcúq; in speciem leuicula, facilè incendit. Et corrúpunt mores bonos colloquia prava, quæ à malorũ commercijs abesse non possunt. 1. Cor. 15. Eò autem grauius est periculum, quò plura sunt, quæ amicitias eiusmodi nobis commendant. In mundo enim sunt, opum splendor, gloriæ maiestas, amicitiarum præsidia, verborũ blanditiès, voluptatum omnis generis illecebræ, victoriæ, triumphi, & infinita alia, quæ singula mille modis hominũ animos inescare, & à Dei commercio abstrahere possunt. Accedit his, quòd multi charitatis legem prætexunt, quasi ab hac alienum sit, eorum amicitias & conuersationem aspernari, qui in fide & religione à nobis dissentiût. Et sanè artificiosos & insignes charitatis præcones hodie audire licet, qui cum in contractibus, in matrimoniorum religione, in hæreditatibus appetendis, deniq; in omnibus quæ dicũt atq; faciunt, Christianæ fraternitatis ratione planè nullam habeat, hic tamen vel ipsum Christum dilectionis ardore vincere videntur, quando cum palàm impijs, vel priuati commodi vel etiâ voluptatis causa, commercium instituunt. Clamat igitur Ioannes: Ne diligatis mundũ. Quasi dicat: Nolo vos charitatis legem prætexere, quæ nõ eò extenditur, vt impios huius seculi filios tuæ vtilitatis gratia diligas, & eorum amicitijs delecteris. Christiana charitas exigitur, quæ non nisi inter eos esse potest, qui Christum norunt, & Christo inserti sunt. Nobis amicus esse non debet, quicunq; Dei inimicus est. Et amicitia huius mundi, inimicitia est cum Deo. Iac. 4. Nec est, quòd religionis studiũ prætexas. Alijs enim medijs plantatur veri Dei cognitio & cultus, quàm coniugijs, comessatio-nibus, voluptatum exercitijs, quæ ferè commerciorum eiusmodi præcipuæ causæ sunt. Imò potius euenire solet, vt piorum fides euertatur, religionis studiũ extinguatur, & in pietate languere incipiant, qui antea satis feruidi videbantur. Exempla sunt in primi mundi fidelibus, qui cũ filias hominum vxores ducerent, eò impietatis cũ tota sua prole delapsi sunt, vt horribilem diluuij pœnam mererentur. Gene. 6. Quantum Loto obfuerit gentis Sodomiticæ cõuersatio, extremæ inter illos noctis periculum, & incestæ filiarum nuptiæ, satis testantur. Gen. 19. Israelitas in Aegypto superstitionis semina imbibisse, vitulus, in deserto contra Dei præceptũ erectus, indicat. Exo. 32. Illis ipsis Moabiticarum feminarum conuersatio idololatriæ, & tandem funestæ cladis causa fuit. Num. 25. Samsonem virorum fortissimum Palæstini amores perdiderút. Iud. 14. & 16. Sed & Solomon mortalium sapientissimus, coniugijs exterarum deceptus, idololatriæ causam præbuit & excelsorum superstitionem inuexit, quæ nullis vnquam reformationibus tolli potuit. 3. Reg. 11. Non temere igitur factum est, quòd & olim in lege dominus peculiaria præcepta de vitandis impiorum commercijs tradidit, & eadem tum hoc loco, tum alibi repetuntur. Sed rationes, quibus Ioannes noster vtitur, videamus.
units.tr: I. Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world. The word world is used in various ways. Sometimes it signifies this frame of the whole universe, namely heaven, earth and seas, with all that is contained in them. Sometimes, however, it is used for the affairs which must be transacted while we live in this world. Thus Paul, after he had set forth those things with which men are for the most part occupied in the present life, adds: "The fashion of this world passeth away," etc. 1 Cor. 7. Yet most often, when it is opposed to the godly and faithful, it is understood of the impious and those alienated from religion, whom Scripture elsewhere calls the children of this age. In this sense Christ says that light came into the world, but that the world loved darkness rather than light, because its works are evil. John 3. And elsewhere he promises his disciples the Spirit, whom the world cannot receive. John 14. Now John's precept can be applied to all these meanings: for it is the duty of a Christian not to love the visible frame of this world otherwise than so that through contemplation of it he is led to the knowledge of God the Creator. For if he wishes to cling to it too much, he strikes upon the same rock as the Gentiles, who gave to creatures what was owed to the Creator. Rom. 1. Yet this precept ought to be referred most of all to the pursuits of the world and to worldly men, or the children of this age, since both of these are wont to cause the godly no small trouble. For since the pursuits of the world are of such a kind that no one can altogether abstain from them, since they are necessary for the conduct of the present life, we are easily ensnared by their sweetness, unless we use them in the Lord. Thus it is established that marriage has been a hindrance to many, although it is otherwise a salutary and necessary thing, because, deceived by a blind affection of love, they have cast aside altogether the pursuit of the glory of God. Food and drink also destroy many, while they serve gluttony and drunkenness rather than nature. Others suffer loss of salvation in their dealings, while, seized by greed, they pursue an insatiable desire to possess. The same reasoning holds for wealth, honours, friendships, covenants, good health, lawful pleasures, and whatever other things present themselves for us to use in the course of this life. Finally, there is no way of life which cannot be destruction to us, unless, following the rule of the divine Word, we seek in all things the glory of God and the salvation of our neighbour. John therefore warns us not to love the pursuits of the world, that is, not to devote ourselves wholly to them, but, according to Paul's precept, to remember that the time is shortened, and therefore those who have wives should be as though they had none; and those who weep, as though they wept not; those who rejoice, as though they rejoiced not; those who buy, as though they possessed not; and those who use this world, as though they used it not. 1 Cor. 7. Yet this precept must be weighed with especial care in regard to friendships with the children of this age. For there is nothing by which men are more easily corrupted than the examples of those with whom we live, because the corrupt nature of the flesh readily catches fire at any occasion of evil, however slight it may seem. "Evil communications corrupt good manners," which cannot be kept away from the company of the wicked. 1 Cor. 15. The danger is all the greater, the more numerous are the things which recommend such friendships to us. For in the world there are the splendour of wealth, the majesty of glory, the protections of friendships, the flatteries of words, every kind of enticement of pleasures, victories, triumphs, and countless other things, each of which can in a thousand ways allure the minds of men and draw them away from converse with God. To these is added that many put forward the law of charity, as though it were foreign to it to scorn the friendships and company of those who dissent from us in faith and religion. And indeed one may hear today skilful and notable heralds of charity who, while in their dealings, in the observance of marriage, in seeking inheritances, and finally in all that they say and do, have plainly no regard for the rule of Christian brotherhood, nevertheless seem to surpass even Christ himself in ardour of love when they enter into dealings openly with the impious, for private advantage or even for pleasure. John therefore cries out: Love not the world. As if he said: I do not want you to put forward the law of charity, which does not extend so far that for the sake of your advantage you should love the impious children of this age and take delight in their friendships. Christian charity is required, which can exist only among those who know Christ and are grafted into Christ. He who is an enemy of God should not be a friend to us. And friendship with this world is enmity with God. James 4. Nor is there any reason for you to pretend a zeal for religion. For the knowledge and worship of the true God are planted by other means than marriages, feastings, and the practice of pleasures, which are commonly the chief causes of such dealings. Indeed it is more often the case that the faith of the godly is overthrown, the zeal for religion is extinguished, and those who seemed fervent enough before begin to languish in piety. There are examples among the faithful of the first world, who, when they took the daughters of men as wives, fell with their whole offspring into such impiety that they deserved the dreadful punishment of the flood. Gen. 6. How much the company of the Sodomite people harmed Lot, the extreme danger of that night among them and the incestuous marriages of his daughters bear sufficient witness. Gen. 19. That the Israelites in Egypt had imbibed the seeds of superstition is shown by the calf set up in the wilderness against the command of God. Exod. 32. The company of the Moabite women was the cause of idolatry for those very people, and at last of a deadly disaster. Num. 25. The Philistines' loves ruined Samson, the strongest of men. Judg. 14 and 16. But Solomon too, the wisest of mortals, deceived by marriages with foreign women, furnished the cause of idolatry and introduced the superstition of the high places, which could never afterwards be removed by any reformations. 1 Kings 11. It was therefore not without reason that the Lord, both of old in the law, delivered special precepts concerning the avoidance of intercourse with the impious, and that the same are repeated both here and elsewhere. But let us see the reasons which our John uses.

units.la: II. Si quis diligit mundũ, non est charitas patris in eo. Quoniam omne quod est in mundo, ueluti concupiscentia carnis, et concupiscentia oculorũ, & fastus uitæ, non est ex patre, sed ex mũdo est. Et mundus trâsit, & concupiscentia eius. Qui autem facit uoluntatem Dei, manet in æternum. Diligens est in reddeda præcepti sui ratione spiritus sanctus, eò quòd magnam diligentiam exigit nostra corruptio. Sunt autem rationes duæ, quibus huius mundi dilectionem siue studium dissuadet: quarum prior docet, hoc ab ingenio filiorum Dei adeoque natura & proprietate Christianorum esse alienissimum: altera vero hoc ipsum vanum, friuolum, imò perniciosum esse demonstrat. Prior est: Qui di-ligit mundum, in eo non est charitas patris, id est, Deum patrem non amat, Deo non fidit, & proinde nec Dei filius, nec Christianus, siue fidelis, dici potest. Qui enim Dei filius est, Deum patrem amat, & sic quidé, vt nihil in rerū natura sit, quod ipsum à Dei dilectione possit abstrahere, Rom.8. Videtur autem sententiam hanc ex Christi verbis desumpsisse Apostolus, qui in euangelio ait: Nemo potest duobus dominis seruire: aut enim hunc habebit odio, & alterum diliget: aut huic adhærebit, & alterum negliget. Nō potestis Deo seruire & Mammonæ. Matth. 6. Quia enim inter Deum & mundi huius principem amicitia nulla est, Dei amicus esse non poterit, qui mundi studijs delectatur. Probat vero priorem hanc præcepti sui rationem enumeratione[?] studiorum huius mundi, quæ tribus generibus comprehendit. Ait enim: Quoniam omne quod est in mundo, veluti concupiscentia carnis, & concupiscentia oculorum, & fastus vitæ, non est ex patre, sed ex mundo est. Argumentum tale videtur: Quisquis quæ non sunt ex Deo patre, diligit, in eo non est charitas Dei. At qui mundum diligit, ea amat quæ ex patre non sunt: qualia sunt concupiscentia oculorum & vitæ fastus. Quisquis ergo mundum diligit, à Dei dilectione alienus sit oportet. Cōstat itaq; mundū cum studijs suis minimè diligi debere ab alijs, qui Dei filij & cultores haberi volūt.
units.tr: II. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For everything that is in the world, such as the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not from the Father, but is from the world. And the world passes away, and its lust. But he who does the will of God abides forever. The Holy Spirit is careful in giving the reason for his precept, because our corruption demands great diligence. There are two reasons by which he dissuades us from the love or pursuit of this world: the first teaches that this is most alien to the disposition of the sons of God, and so to the nature and character of Christians; the second shows that this very thing is vain, frivolous, and indeed destructive. The first is this: whoever loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him, that is, he does not love God the Father, does not trust in God, and therefore cannot be called a son of God, nor a Christian, or believer. For whoever is a son of God loves God the Father, and so truly that nothing in the nature of things can draw him away from the love of God (Rom. 8). The Apostle seems to have taken this sentiment from the words of Christ, who said in the gospel: No one can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will cling to the one and neglect the other. You cannot serve God and Mammon (Matt. 6). For since there is no friendship between God and the prince of this world, one who delights in the pursuits of the world cannot be a friend of God. He proves this first reason of his precept by enumerating the pursuits of this world, which he comprises under three kinds. For he says: For everything that is in the world, such as the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not from the Father, but is from the world. The argument seems to be this: whoever loves what is not from God the Father, has not the love of God in him. But whoever loves the world loves those things which are not from the Father, such as the lust of the eyes and the pride of life. Therefore whoever loves the world must be alien to the love of God. It is clear, then, that the world with its pursuits must not be loved by those who wish to be considered sons and worshippers of God.

units.la: Porrò obseruanda hic nobis veniunt mundi studia, ut his cognitis de nostri seculi hominibus iudicare possimus. Tria (ut diximus) illi tribuit. Primum est Cōcupiscentia carnis, qua ianatam[?] omnibus nobis naturæ nostræ corruptionem intelligit. Propriū enim carni est, quòd sua quærit, sibi bene esse vult, nulla interim vel gloriæ Dei vel salutis proximi ratione habita. Parit corrupta hæc natura effectus siue opera sibi conformia, quæ concupiscentiam oculorum vocat. Ut enim ignis scintillula delitescit quidem interdum, sed mox materia oblata idonea, sese diffundit & vires exerit: ita latet in carne nostra affectuū corruptio, & ita interdum latet, ut nec ipsi hos satis observemus: at ubi oculis nostris alijsq; sensibus externis obijcitur quod illos excitet, illico quasi euigilare & æstuari incipiunt. Sic qui natura ad libidinem pronus est, visa formæ præstantis mulieris, affectum libidinis quasi sulphure obiecto inflammari sentit, ut cum poeta dicat: Ut vidi, ut perij, ut me malus abstulit error. Ita auarus pecunia visa habendi cupidinem in se vehementiorem sentit. Iracundus eo magis furit, quo propius eum viderit, qui irae causam præbuit. Similiter qui odio & inuidia laborant, affectuū illorum stimulos duriores experiuntur, si coram videant, quos odio & inuidia prosequuntur. Coniunctus his est tertius gradus, quem fastum vitæ dicit, qui non affectus modo & cupidinum æstus, sed ipsa quoq;, quæ ex illis manat, opera praua complectitur. Ubi enim affectus diutina consuetudine in habitum transierunt, eò homines perducunt, ut nihil amplius penitus habeant, sed immani tam Dei quàm hominum contemptu ac fastu intolerabili elati, quiduis quod libet sibi licere existimant. Mox ergo laxatis affectuum habenis, aliena rapiunt, vindictam priuatam persequuntur, thoros alienos polluunt, linguâ ad conuitia, calumnias & obtrectationes soluunt, sanguinem fundunt, deniq; nemo mortalium eo loco & dignitate est, cui absque parci debere existiment. At quàm aliena hæc sint à Dei ingenio, quiuis perspicit. Is enim sanctus, purus & immaculatus, nos quoq; sanctos & immaculatos cultores habere cupit. Idem non inuidus bonorum suorum possessor est, sed in illorum comuunionem nos venire iubet, eamq; sponte offert. Tamq; abest à nostri contemptu, ut propter nos hominum contemptissimus fieri, & in carne infamem Crucis mortem subire voluerit. Sed & iustam iram, quæ quotidianis peccatis per nos provocatur, insigni bonitate & misericordia ineffabili temperare consueuit.
units.tr: Furthermore, the pursuits of the world must be observed here by us, so that, having known them, we may be able to judge the men of our age. He assigns three of them, as we have said. The first is the lust of the flesh, by which he understands the corruption of our nature innate in all of us. For it is proper to the flesh that it seeks its own, wishes itself well, with no regard meanwhile either for the glory of God or the salvation of a neighbour. This corrupt nature produces effects or works conformed to itself, which he calls the lust of the eyes. For as a spark of fire lies hidden at times, but soon, when suitable material is offered, it spreads itself and puts forth its strength, so the corruption of the affections lies hidden in our flesh, and it lies hidden at times so much that we ourselves do not sufficiently observe it; but when something is set before our eyes and other external senses that arouses it, at once they begin, as it were, to awaken and to glow. Thus one who is by nature prone to lust, having seen the form of an excellent woman, feels the affection of lust inflamed as if the object were sulphur, so that he says with the poet: "As soon as I saw, as soon as I was undone, as soon as that evil error carried me off." So the covetous man, having seen money, feels a stronger desire to possess it within himself. The angry man rages all the more, the closer he sees the one who provided the cause of his anger. Likewise those who labour under hatred and envy experience the harsher goads of those affections if they see face to face those whom they pursue with hatred and envy. Joined to these is the third degree, which he calls the pride of life, which embraces not only the affections and the heat of the desires, but also the wicked works that flow from them. For when the affections have passed into habit through long custom, they bring men to the point where they no longer have any restraint at all, but, puffed up with immense and intolerable contempt and pride both toward God and toward men, they think they may do whatever they please. Soon, therefore, with the reins of the affections loosened, they seize what belongs to others, pursue private revenge, defile the beds of others, let loose their tongues for reproaches, calumnies and slanders, shed blood, and finally there is no mortal in such a place or dignity whom they do not think they may assail without sparing. But how alien these things are to the nature of God, anyone can see. For He is holy, pure and spotless, and desires that we too have spotless and holy worshippers. He is not a grudging possessor of His goods, but bids us come into their fellowship, and offers it willingly. And He is so far from despising us that He was willing to become most despised of men for our sake, and in the flesh to undergo the infamous death of the Cross. Moreover, He is accustomed to temper His just anger, which is provoked daily by our sins, with remarkable goodness and ineffable mercy.

units.la: Hæc si cum nostri seculi moribus conferas, facilè videbis, qui & quales censeri debeamus. Inest omnibus naturalis corruptio, nec inest tantum, sed quauis occasione sese exerit, ut nō verbis modò, sed ipsis factis testemur, nos improbissima esse turpissimorum affectuum mancipia. Nota est omnibus effrenis scortandi licentia. Videtur passim impudens adulteriorum palæstra. Regnant usuræ, furta, rapinæ, impostura, & si quid aliud insatiabile auaritiæ malum parturire potest. Laxantur omnium ora, non in proximi famam modò, sed & in Dei optimi maximi patris ignominiam. Illius nomè prophano abusu polluitur. Nec melius apud nos Christus audit, cuiusacerba morte sumus redempti. Immani & barbaro fastu proximū quemq; cōtemnimus, dū in alio generis ignobilitatem, in alio vitæ conditionem, in multis patriâ & infinita alia friuolè reprehēdimus. Sed hæc ô fratres, non ex Deo, sed ex mundo sunt, cuius studia qui amat & sectantur, charitatem patris in se habent nullam. At quomodo pro Dei filijs censeri poterunt, qui à Dei dilectione alieni esse deprehenduntur? Quid aliud, si sic pergamus, quàm Dei iram, & iam olim commeritas pœnas expectare possumus? Porrò, quia pleriq; hominum in hisce studijs persequendis ideo constantiores & pertinaciores sunt, quòd durabilem & firmam certamq; felicitatē illis esse putát, Apostolus alteram rationem subijcit, qua illos vehementer falli demonstrat.
units.tr: If you compare these things with the morals of our age, you will easily see who and what sort of people we ought to be considered. Natural corruption is present in everyone, and it is present not merely, but it shows itself on any occasion, so that we bear witness not only by words but by the very deeds themselves that we are the most wicked slaves of the most base affections. The unbridled license of fornication is known to all. The shameless arena of adulteries is seen everywhere. Usury, thefts, robberies, deceit, and whatever else the insatiable evil of avarice can bring forth, hold sway. The mouths of all are loosed, not only against a neighbour's reputation but also against the dishonour of God, the best and greatest Father. His name is polluted by profane abuse. Nor does Christ, by whose bitter death we were redeemed, fare better among us. With savage and barbarous pride we despise each neighbour, while we censure in one the lowliness of birth, in another the condition of life, in many their country, and in countless other things we find fault in trifling ways. But these things, O brothers, are not from God but from the world, and whoever loves and follows its pursuits has no love of the Father in him. But how can those be counted as sons of God who are found to be alien to the love of God? What else, if we go on in this way, can we expect but the wrath of God and punishments long since deserved? Moreover, since most men are more constant and obstinate in pursuing these pursuits, because they think that they have a lasting, firm and certain happiness in them, the Apostle adds a second reason, by which he shows that they are gravely deceived.

units.la: Mundus transit & concupiscentia eius. Qui autem facit voluntatem Dei, manet in æternum. Bimembris est ratio, & eleganti antithesi figuratur. Confert enim inter se mundum hunc visibilem, & eum qui mundi studijs abnegatis, se totum voluntati Dei consecrauit. Mundus (inquit) & concupiscentia eius transit. Vocat autem concupiscentiam mundi, quicquid in mundo exoptabile habetur, & quod homines in sui amorem & desyderium rapere potest. Hæc omnia transeunt, id est, corruptioni sunt obnoxia, caduca sunt, & ad interitum vergunt. Manifestius hoc est, quàm ut longa demonstratione opus habeat. Quia tamen ea est hominum cæcitas, ut id videre & animad-vertere nolint, aliquid de rerum huius mundi instabilitate dicendum erit.
units.tr: The world passes away and its lust. But he who does the will of God abides forever. The reason has two members, and it is set forth by an elegant antithesis. For he compares this visible world with the one who, having renounced the pursuits of the world, has wholly consecrated himself to the will of God. The world (he says) and its lust pass away. He calls the lust of the world whatever is held desirable in the world, and which can draw men into love and longing for itself. All these things pass away, that is, they are subject to corruption, they are perishable, and they tend toward ruin. This is clearer than it needs any lengthy demonstration. Yet since such is the blindness of men that they are unwilling to see and notice this, something must be said about the instability of the things of this world.

units.la: Inspiciamus autem primum bona omnia, quæ homines expetere solent, quæ olim tribus generibus viri sapientes comprehendi posse putarunt, ut dicerent esse bona corporis, bona animi, & ea quæ extra hominem sunt, quæ multi bona fortunæ nominauerunt. Bona corporis sunt, valetudo integra, robur, agilitas, forma decora, sensuum omnium incolumitas, & si quæ alia eius generis habentur. Animi bona sunt, sapientia, prudentia, dexteritas in consiliis capiendis, fortitudo, eruditio, & imprimis mens sibi bene conscia, quæ stabilem animorum pacem parit. Externa bona dixerunt, quæcunq; non in ipso homine inveniuntur, sed aliunde illi accedunt: qualia sunt diuitiæ, fauor hominum, amicitiæ, gloria, fama celebris: quo & voluptates, & quæcunq; nos in mundo hoc delectant, referri possunt. Hæc omnia si ordine consyderes, quid in illis stabile & permanens inuenire licebit? Corpora certè tot morbis obnoxia, nec valetudinis, nec formæ, nec roboris sui durationem perpetuam sperare possunt. Videmus enim repentinis morbis frequenter omnia ista extingui. Et si cui ea valetudo obtingat, quæ corporis vires & formam diutissimè conseruet, obrepit tamen ta cito pede senectus, quæ ipsa morbus est, nec corporis modo bona imminuit, verùetiam animum oppugnans memoriam debilitat, intellectus lumen obscurat & extinguit, prudentiæ vires retundit, delirium affert, ut bis pueri senes merito dicamur. Omitto nunc infinita alia, quæ animi bona tollere possunt. Fuerunt, quibus tegula capiti incidens memoriam & intellectum omnem sustulit. Sunt qui panico terrore perciti, nec quid faciant ipsi videre possunt, nec bene consulentibus obtemperare audent. Inuenti sunt & inveniuntur quotidie, quibus ebrietas & scortandi rabies animum totum abstulit. Breuiter ea hominis conditio est, ut nihil vel in corpore vel animo eius stabile deprehendi possit. Quòd si ad ea oculos conuertamus, quæ extra hominem in mundo sunt, longè maiorem inconstantiam rerum deprehendes. Quid enim de opibus dicere attinet, quæ ita fluxæ sunt, ut interdum nobis quasi ignorantibus elabantur? Imò opulentissimos reges interdum harum præsidio, cum maximè illis opus erat, destitui videmus. Quid Croesus diuitiæ proverbio celebres profuerunt, quando rogum iam iam arsurus conscendens Solonis nomen alta voce sonabat? Quid Xerxes ex opibus suis auxilij habuit, cum piscatoria nauicula mare traijceret, qui paulò ante, quasi nouus in orbe terrarum Deus, maria nauibus ut ponte sternebat, flumina militum & iumentorum aquatione exiccabat, montes perfodere, adeoq; totam mundi faciem innouare conabatur? Eadem est gloriæ, fauoris, amicitiarum omniumq; voluptatum, quæ ex istis rebus capiuntur, conditio. Qui enim paulò ante omnium fauore elati cœlum digito contingere videbantur, eos mox inopinatus aliquis casus miserè præcipitatos in perpetuæ ignominiæ lutum deijcit. Sed ut omnia hæc firma sint & stabilia, vita tamen hominum instabilis & infirma est, nihilq; hora mortis incertius: ut nõ temere propheta, homine in imagine potius quàm reuera viuere, dixerit. Psal.39. Et ut illud videamus, quod extra omne fortunæ casum positum videtur, immensam videlicet mundi huius machinâ, eam quoq; corruptioni subiacere cõstat. Mutatur indies orbis facies, & modò maria esse cernimus, ubi paulò ante vrbes, vineta, agros & læta pascua videbamus. Modò ruinæ sunt, ubi ante pauca secula superbæ regum domus & mœnia inuicta habebantur. Imò iuxta prophetæ & ipsius Christi testimonia, cœli & terra inueterascent atque transibunt. Psal.102. Matth.5.&24. Quàm verè ergo iubente Domino propheta exclamat? Omnis caro fœnū, & omnis gloria carnis flos agri. Exaruit fœnum & flos decidit, &c. Isa.40. Et sapientissimus mortalium Solomon, cum omnia quæ in mundo sunt, magno cum iudicio & diligenter inuestigauisset, tandem pronunciat: Vanitas vanitatum, & omnia vanitas, &c. Eccle.1. Sequitur vero ex omnibus istis quod Ioannes hoc loco præcipit, mundum videlicet & ea quæ in mundo sunt, ab hominibus Christo consecratis minimè diligi debere. Quid enim stultius est, quàm ijs addici, quæ instabilia sunt & incerta? Maledictus (inquit propheta) qui facit carnem brachium suum, & cuius cor hominis confidit recedens à Deo. Ierem.17. Beatus verò cuius Deus Iehouah est, & qui spem habet in domino Deo suo. Psal.33. & 146. &c.
units.tr: Let us first consider all the goods that men are wont to seek. Wise men of old thought these could be grasped under three kinds: goods of the body, goods of the soul, and those that lie outside the man, which many have called goods of fortune. Goods of the body are sound health, strength, agility, a comely form, the soundness of all the senses, and whatever else is counted of this kind. Goods of the soul are wisdom, prudence, skill in taking counsel, fortitude, learning, and above all a mind conscious of its own good conduct, which brings a steady peace to the spirits. They called external goods whatever is not found in the man himself but comes to him from elsewhere: such as riches, the favour of men, friendships, glory, and renown; to these may be referred also pleasures and whatever else delights us in this world. If you consider all these things in order, what can you find in them that is stable and lasting? Bodies, indeed, are so liable to disease that they cannot hope for a perpetual duration of their health, their beauty, or their strength. We see that all these things are often snuffed out by sudden sicknesses. And if someone enjoys that health which preserves the powers and form of the body for the longest time, old age nonetheless creeps on with such swift foot, and old age is itself a sickness; it diminishes not only the goods of the body but also, assailing the mind, weakens the memory, dims and extinguishes the light of the understanding, blunts the powers of prudence, and brings dotage, so that we are rightly called old men twice over, as children. I now pass over the countless other things that can take away the goods of the soul. There have been those whom a falling tile struck on the head and robbed of all memory and understanding. There are those who, struck by panic terror, can neither see what they themselves are doing nor dare to obey those who advise them well. There have been, and daily there are, those whom drunkenness and the frenzy of lust have wholly taken away from their minds. In brief, such is the human condition that nothing, either in his body or in his mind, can be found to be stable. But if we turn our eyes to those things that lie outside man in the world, you will discover a far greater inconstancy of things. For what need is there to speak of wealth, which is so fleeting that at times it slips away from us, as if we did not know it? Indeed, we see even the most opulent kings sometimes deprived of its protection precisely when they most need it. What good did Croesus, famed in the proverb for his riches, do him, when, mounting the pyre about to be set alight, he cried out Solon's name in a loud voice? What help did Xerxes get from his resources, when he crossed the sea in a fishing boat, he who shortly before, like a new god on the earth, had bridged the seas with ships as with a pontoon, had dried up rivers by the watering of his soldiers and beasts, and had tried to dig through mountains and so renew the whole face of the world? The condition of glory, of favour, of friendships, and of all the pleasures that are gained from these things is the same. For those who a little while before, lifted up by the favour of all, seemed to touch the heavens with their finger, some unexpected accident soon casts down wretchedly into the mire of everlasting disgrace. But even though all these things may be firm and stable, the life of men is unstable and frail, and nothing is more uncertain than the hour of death; so the prophet did not rashly say that man lives in an image rather than in reality. Psalm 39. And that we may see what seems to lie beyond every chance of fortune: it is plain that the vast machine of this world is likewise subject to corruption. The face of the globe changes day by day, and now we see seas where a little while before we saw cities, vineyards, fields, and pleasant pastures. Now there are ruins where, a few centuries ago, the proud houses and unconquered walls of kings were standing. Indeed, according to the testimony of the prophet and of Christ himself, heaven and earth will grow old and pass away. Psalm 102. Matthew 5 and 24. How truly, then, does the prophet cry out at the Lord's command: All flesh is grass, and all the glory of flesh is the flower of the field. The grass withers and the flower falls, etc. Isaiah 40. And Solomon, the wisest of mortals, after he had investigated with great judgement and diligence all that is in the world, at last pronounces: Vanity of vanities, all is vanity, etc. Ecclesiastes 1. Yet from all these things there follows what John here enjoins: that men consecrated to Christ ought by no means to love the world and the things that are in the world. For what is more foolish than to devote oneself to things that are unstable and uncertain? Cursed (says the prophet) is he who makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from God. Jeremiah 17. But blessed is he whose God is Jehovah, and who has his hope in the Lord his God. Psalms 33 and 146, etc.

units.la: Alterum huius argumenti membrum est: Qui facit voluntatem Dei, manet in æternum. Voluntas Dei est, ut sanctificati[?] [illegible, ~5 letters]mur. Deus enim vult omnes homines saluos fieri, & in cognitionem veritatis venire. 1.Tim.2. At quia saluari non possunt nisi qui sanctificati fuerint, nos sanctos esse vult, & ut sanctificationi studeamus passim præcipit. 1.Thess.4. Impossibile autem est, ut seipsum sanctificet homo, qui in peccatis conceptus & genitus peccatorum sordes secum in mundum affert. Filium ergo suum Deus dedit, qui nostra sanctificatio fieret. 1.Cor.1.&5. Is sanguini suo peccata nostra abluit,nos q; sibi sponsam fecit carentem ruga & macula Et ijdem quotidie pedes abluunt, id est,affectus purgant,resistunt prauis concupiscentijs, & quicquid labis mundi exemplum & pollutionis plena in carne conuersatio aspergit, quotidiana & iugi poenitentia per fidem in Christum abstergunt. Ioan.13. Hoc ergo praecipuum diuinae voluntatis caput est,vt credamus nomini filij ipsius,Iesu Christi,de quo circa finem cap.5.huius epistolae pluribus dicetur. Quicunq; id fecerint,Christo inserti manent in aeternum.Manet enim in illis Christi verbum,quod coeleste & immortale est.Idem illud regenerationis semen est,quo filij Dei efficimur & haeredes Dei, cohaeredes autem Christi, vt iuxta promissionem ipsius,cum illo fimus in domo patris, vbi mansionem sempiternam sui sanguinis merito nobis impetrauit.Ioan. 14.&17. Haec vera hominis vita est, haec aeterna salus & nunquam intermoritura felicitas, quam nulla carnis sapientia inuestigare, nullae mundi vires acquirere, sed sola fides in Christum Iesum conferre potest.Haec quia non est in filijs huius seculi:qui spiritum veritatis accipere nō possunt, alienos à mundo fieri oportet,quicunq; in aeternum cum Christo manere cupiunt.
units.tr: The second member of this argument is: He who does the will of God abides for ever. The will of God is that we be sanctified. For God wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. 1 Timothy 2. But since they cannot be saved unless they have been sanctified, he wills us to be holy and everywhere commands us to strive after sanctification. 1 Thessalonians 4. Yet it is impossible for a man to sanctify himself, since he is conceived and born in sins and brings the filth of sins with him into the world. Therefore God gave his Son, who would become our sanctification. 1 Corinthians 1 and 5. He washed away our sins with his own blood, and made us a bride to himself, without spot or wrinkle. And the same Lord daily washes our feet, that is, cleanses our affections, resists evil lusts, and whatever stain the example of the world and a life of conversation full of pollution sprinkles upon us, he wipes away by a daily and continual repentance through faith in Christ. John 13. This, therefore, is the chief point of the divine will: that we believe in the name of his Son, Jesus Christ, concerning whom more will be said near the end of chapter 5 of this epistle. Whoever shall have done this abides in Christ for ever. For the word of Christ abides in them, which is heavenly and immortal. It is that same seed of regeneration by which we are made sons of God and heirs of God, and co-heirs of Christ, so that, according to his promise, we may be with him in the house of the Father, where he has obtained for us an everlasting dwelling by the merit of his blood. John 14 and 17. This is the true life of man, this is eternal salvation and happiness that never perishes, which no wisdom of the flesh can search out, no powers of the world can acquire, but faith in Jesus Christ alone can bring. Since this is not found among the sons of this age, who cannot receive the Spirit of truth, all who desire to remain with Christ for ever must become strangers to the world.

units.la: Firmum ergo & stabile est Ioannis praeceptum,quo mundi amorem & studiū prohibet.Constat enim, cum Dei natura & ingenio pugnare,quaecunq; mundus instituit & facit. Constat infelices esse,quicunq; mundum hunc instabilem & corruptioni obnoxiū diligunt: falli item spe sua, quicunque rebus huius mundi friuolis ac incertis nituntur.Rursus verò in aeternum felices fore constat, quicunq; Dei voluntatem fecerint, qui nos,depositis mundi & carnis nostrae studijs,filio suo consecrari vult. Huc igitur studium nostrum omne conferamus,& Christum Iesum amplexi ad coelestis regni haereditatem aspiremus,cuius ipse nos consortes reddidit.Ipsi debetur benedictio,honor,gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Firm and stable, therefore, is the precept of John, by which he forbids love and zeal for the world. For it is evident that whatever the world establishes and does is at odds with the nature and disposition of God. It is evident that those are wretched who love this unstable world, which is subject to corruption; likewise that those are deceived in their hope who rest upon the frivolous and uncertain things of this world. On the other hand, it is evident that those who do the will of God, who, laying aside the pursuits of the world and of our flesh, wills to consecrate us to his Son, will be blessed for ever. Therefore let us direct all our zeal to this, and, embracing Christ Jesus, strive after the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, of which he has made us partners. To him be blessing, honour, glory, and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XI.
units.tr: Homily XI.

units.la: Filioli,nouissima hora est: & sicut audistis quòd Antichristus uenturus sit,etiam nunc Antichristi multi facti sunt. Vnde scimus nouissimam horam esse. E nobis egressi sunt,sed non erant ex nobis. Nam si fuissent ex nobis, permansissent utiq; nobiscum. Sed ut manifesti fierent,quòd non sint omnes ex nobis.
units.tr: Little children, it is the last hour; and as you have heard that Antichrist is to come, even now many antichrists have arisen. Whence we know that it is the last hour. They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us. But that it might be made manifest that they are not all of us.

units.la: TEstatur in euangelio dominus noster Iesus Christus, quòd suos è mundo selegerit,sic ut de mundo esse non amplius censeri debeant. Admonet id nos nostri officij,quod est cauere,ne per mundi impuri & impij commercium denuo polluti,à communione Christi & filiorum Dei abstrahamur. Sunt autem in mundo duo ferè mala, quae salutem nostram euertere possunt. Primum est peccatorum immundities & variae eorundem illecebrae,quae tam mūdi exemplo,quàm carnis nostrae suggestionibus,nobis obijciūtur, & in homine naturaliter ad malum propensò plurimum possunt. Alterum, errores & seductiones sunt circa religionem, quibus vel superstitio & idololatria,vel Epicureismus & prophanus omnis religionis contemptus plantatur.De vtroque multus in sacris literis sermo est.Et Ioannes in ijs,quae proximè praecesserūt,diligenter monuit, mundi studia fugienda esse ijs, qui cum Christo aeternum viuere cupiant. Nunc autem de seductoribus agit, contra illorum tendiculas & errorum laqueos fideles praemuniens.Primò quidem temporis circumstantia probat,se non frustra de his admonere,sed instantis mali periculo moueri,ne in re valde necessaria officium suum negligat. Deinde cum seductoribus eiusmodi propius pedem conferens,docet,vnde isti prodeat,& offendiculis, quae inde ad simpliciores peruenire solent,medetur.
units.tr: Our Lord Jesus Christ testifies in the Gospel that he has chosen his own out of the world, so that they ought no longer to be counted as of the world. This reminds us of our duty, which is to take care lest, polluted again through the dealings of the impure and impious world, we be drawn away from communion with Christ and the sons of God. There are, however, in the world two evils, which can overthrow our salvation. The first is the filthiness of sins and their various allurements, which are set before us both by the example of the world and by the suggestions of our own flesh, and which have great power over a man naturally inclined to evil. The other is errors and seductions in matters of religion, by which either superstition and idolatry, or Epicureanism and the profane contempt of all religion, are planted. Of both there is much discussion in the sacred letters. And John, in the things that immediately preceded, diligently warned that the pursuits of the world are to be shunned by those who desire to live eternally with Christ. But now he deals with seducers, fortifying the faithful against their snares and the nooses of their errors. First, indeed, the circumstance of the time shows that he does not admonish about these things in vain, but is moved by the danger of a present evil, lest he neglect his duty in a matter of the greatest necessity. Then, approaching seducers of this kind more closely, he teaches whence they come, and remedies the stumbling-blocks which usually arise from them for the simpler folk.

units.la: I. Filioli nouissima hora est: & sicut audistis quòd Antichristus uenturus sit, etiam nunc Antichristi multi facti sunt. Vnde scimus nouissimam horam esse. Nouissima hora in scripturis dicitur omne illud tempus,quod post incarnationem & passionem Christi vsq; ad mundi consummationem euolui tur. Quia enim in Christo omnes prophetiae impletae sunt, nec aliud quàm nouissimus illius ad iudicium aduentus restat,merito nouissimam horam,vel vltimam mūdi ætatem,spiritus sanctus vocat illud tempus , quo praeter mundi finem & vltimum Christi aduentum, nihil aliud exspectare possumus.Praedixit autem de illis temporibus dominus, quòd plena seductionum & errorum futura sint. Nam surgent (inquit) pseudochristi & pseudoprophetae, & dabunt signa magna & prodigia,ita vt in errorem inducantur,si fieri possit,etiam electi.Matth.24.Et Paulus stolus scribit: Spiritus certò loquitur, quòd in postremis temporibus descíscent quidam à fide, at tendentes spiritibus impostoribus ac doctrinis dæmoniorum, per simulationem falsiloquorum, cauterio notatam habentium conscientiam, prohibentium cōtrahere matrimonium, iubentiū abstinere à cibis, quos Deus creauit, &c. 1. Tim. 4. Et alibi: Erit tempus, cum sanam doctrinam non sustinebunt, sed iuxta concupiscentias suas coaceruabunt sibi doctores, ij quibus pruriunt aures, &c. 2. Timot. 4. Sed & magnum illum Antichristum nouissimus diebus venturū esse, qui in templo Dei sedes effertur supra omne quod Deus dicitur & colitur, idem Apostolus disertè monet. 2. Thess. 2. Sic ergo à temporis circumstantia argumentatur Ioânes: Scitis filioli, nouissimos dies, propter falsos doctores, qui cateruatim insurgent, & apud homines veritatis impatientes locum inuenient facilè, periculosissimos fore, nec de illo quisquam dubitare debet, nisi de veritate oraculorum Christi dubitare velit. Cum itaque iam nunc euoluatur nouissimi temporis curriculum, necesse est vigilare, & magna cura seductionum & errorum laqueos cauere. Nec enim futura tantum pericula vos timere decet, sed præsentia iam sunt, quæ somnum ofcitatiæ vobis excutere debent. Prædixit quidem spiritus Dei, magnum illum Christi aduersariū venturum esse. Sed iam iam nūc, non vnus, sed multi Antichristi facti sunt, qui Christo & doctrinæ suæ sese opponere audent, & nunc operatur iniquitatis mysterium mendax ille & salutis humanæ hostis Antichristi spiritus. Loquitur autem de illorum temporum hæreticis, quales erat Simon Magus, Cerinthus, Hebion & qui horum castra sequebantur. Negabatur ab his diuina Christi natura. Nazaræi item erant, qui iustitiam legis stabilire, eam verò quæ ex fide in Christum Iesum est, exinanire cupiebant. Voluit autem satan eiusmodi initijs progredi, ut propter diuersitatem opinionum de Christo omne illius mysterii paulatim suspectum fieret, & Antichristo, suo tempore reuelādo, maior esset ecclesiam inuadendi occasio.
units.tr: I. Little children, it is the last hour; and as you have heard that Antichrist is to come, even now many antichrists have arisen. Whence we know that it is the last hour. In the Scriptures "the last hour" is called that whole time which runs on from the incarnation and passion of Christ until the consummation of the world. For since in Christ all prophecies have been fulfilled, and nothing remains but his final coming to judgment, the Holy Spirit rightly calls that time the last hour, or the final age of the world, in which, apart from the end of the world and the last coming of Christ, we can expect nothing else. Now the Lord foretold of those times that they would be full of seductions and errors. For (he says) false christs and false prophets will arise, and will give great signs and wonders, so that, if it were possible, even the elect would be led into error. Matt. 24. And the Apostle Paul writes: "The Spirit speaks expressly, that in the latter times some will fall away from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits and doctrines of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars, having their conscience seared with a hot iron, forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from foods which God created," etc. 1 Tim. 4. And elsewhere: "There will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own lusts will heap up for themselves teachers, having itching ears," etc. 2 Tim. 4. But the same Apostle also plainly warns that that great Antichrist will come in the last days, who will be exalted in the temple of God, above everything that is called God and worshipped. 2 Thess. 2. Thus, then, John argues from the circumstance of the time: You know, little children, that the last days will be most dangerous because of false teachers, who rise up in troops and easily find a place among men who cannot bear the truth; nor ought anyone to doubt this, unless he wishes to doubt the truth of the oracles of Christ. Since, therefore, the course of the last time is already running, it is necessary to be watchful, and with great care to beware of the snares of seductions and errors. For it is fitting that you fear not only the dangers that are to come, but those which are already present, and which ought to shake off the slumber of drowsiness from you. The Spirit of God indeed foretold that the great adversary of Christ would come. But already now, not one but many antichrists have arisen, who dare to set themselves against Christ and his doctrine; and now that deceitful one, the enemy of human salvation, the spirit of Antichrist, works the mystery of iniquity. Now he speaks of heretics of those times, such as Simon Magus, Cerinthus, Hebion, and those who followed their camps. The divine nature of Christ was denied by these. Likewise there were the Nazarenes, who desired to establish the righteousness of the law, but to empty out that which is through faith in Christ Jesus. Satan, moreover, wished that matters should advance from such beginnings, so that, on account of the diversity of opinions about Christ, the whole mystery of him should gradually become suspect, and that Antichrist, when revealed in his time, should have a greater occasion of invading the Church.

units.la: Obseruanda autem hic venit paterna pro nobis Dei cura, qui de salutis nostræ periculis & laqueis falsæ doctrinæ nos toties tamq; diligenter admonere dignatus est. Hinc enim patet, necessariam esse horum cognitionem, & in ecclesia frequenter inculcari debere, quæcunq; Antichristi & membrorum ipsius impietatem detegunt. Patienter ergo feramus eos, qui suum officium hac in re strenuè præstant, & lupos allatrare fidoq; indicio prodere student. Quia tamen plura cap. 4. dicentur, paucula hæc modo sufficiant. Cæterum, quia magni illius Antichristi Ioannes hoc loco meminit, quem & alibi scripturæ fidei & religionis nostræ summum prophanatoré, ac salutis per niciosissimum hostem fore, testantur, paucula de hoc dicenda erunt, quæ simplicioribus illum cognoscendum præbeant, quo facilius artes & arma ipsius effugere possint.
units.tr: Here the fatherly care of God for us must be observed, who has deigned to warn us so often and so diligently of the dangers of our salvation and of the snares of false doctrine. For from this it is plain that the knowledge of these things is necessary, and that whatever uncovers the impiety of Antichrist and of his members ought to be frequently inculcated in the Church. Let us therefore patiently bear with those who discharge their office vigorously in this matter, and who strive to bark at the wolves and to betray them by faithful indication. Because more will be said in chapter 4, let these few things suffice for now. Moreover, since John in this place makes mention of that great Antichrist, whom the Scriptures elsewhere also testify will be the chief profaner of our faith and religion, and the most pernicious enemy of salvation, a few things must be said about him, which may make him known to simpler folk, so that they may more easily escape his arts and weapons.

units.la: Antichristi vox Græca est, & Christi aduersarium vel æmulum significat. Antichristi ergo dici possunt, quotquot Christi doctrinæ & gloriæ, vel etiam redemptionis nostræ, per Christum acquisitæ, mysterio aduersantur. Quo sensu Ioannes multos Antichristos iam tum suo seculo factos fuisse dixit. At cū scripturę de singulari Antichristo verba faciunt, æmulū Christi velut intelligi, q, quę Christi sunt nō modo neget, sed ea in se transferre studeat. Et huc faciunt, quę de illo Paul. habet 2. Thes. 2. quando ἀντικείμενος[?] vocat, & eleuatū supra Deū. Possunt ex duobus hisce epithetis certissimæ notę deprehendi, ex quibus Antichristus facilè agnoscatur, quę non alibi, quàm in templo Dei, in ecclesia Christi sedē suā habituru esse, idē Paulus disertè testatur. Antichristus enim ille magnus erit, quicunq; Christo Iesu quasi ex diametro oppositus cum doctrina illius & vitæ exemplo pugnauerit, quiq; ea quæ solius Dei sunt, in se transferre ausus fuerit. Christi ergo vitam & doctrinam inspicere conuenit, ut ex ea Antichristum agnoscamus.
units.tr: "Antichrist" is a Greek word, and signifies an adversary or rival of Christ. Therefore, all who oppose the doctrine and glory of Christ, or even the mystery of our redemption acquired through Christ, may be called antichrists. In this sense John said that many antichrists had already arisen in his own age. But when the Scriptures speak of a single Antichrist, he is understood as a rival of Christ, who not only denies what belongs to Christ, but strives to transfer it to himself. And to this purpose are the things that Paul says of him in 2 Thess. 2, when he calls him "the one opposing" [ἀντικείμενος?], and exalted above God. From these two epithets, of the most certain mark, Antichrist can be easily recognized; and the same Paul plainly testifies that he will have his seat not elsewhere than in the temple of God, in the Church of Christ. For that great Antichrist will be whoever, as if diametrically opposed to Christ Jesus, has fought against his doctrine and the example of his life, and who has dared to transfer to himself those things which belong to God alone. It is fitting, therefore, to look into the life and doctrine of Christ, so that from them we may recognize Antichrist.

units.la: Christus Iesus, cum esset in forma Dei, formam serui assumpsit. Phil. 2. Quisquis ergo, cū homo fit, Deū se esse gloriari audet, & diuinos honores sibi vendicat, Antichristus censebitur. Christus in mundum venit, non ut illi inseruiretur, sed ut ipse inseruiret alijs. Matth. 20. Antichristus ergo erit, quisquis sub Christi prætextu omnium seruitia exigit, & omnibus dominari quærit. Christus eō humilitatis sese demisit, ut discipulorum pedes ablueret. Antichristus igitur non potest nō esse, qui suos pedes Christiani nominis professoribus, imō & regibus, deosculādos præbue rit. Christus coronam regni, cū offerretur, sumere detrectauit. Antichristus ergo est, quisquis sub falso Christi nomine coronas regnorū sibi vendicat. Christus circa gregis sui salutem occupatus fuit semper. Antichristus ergo est, qui gregis Christiani pastore sese professus, priuato potius cōmodo & opibus congerendis, quàm fidelium saluti inuigilat. Christus vendentes & ementes templo eiecit. Antichristus itaque est, quisquis eosdem in templa reducit, & ecclesiam domum mercatus constituit. Christus à legis seruitute suos liberat. Antichristus intolerabilia imponit humanarum traditionum onera. Christus matrimonia libera esse voluit, eaq; ad primam institutione reuocat. Antichristus ergo est, qui libertatem horum tollit, & tanquam impura prohibet. Christus ciborum discrimina sustulit. Antichristus igitur erit, quisquis illa reduxerit. Christi regnum non est ex hoc mundo, nec armis mundanis acquiritur & conseruatur. Antichristum ergo vere dici-mus, quisquis Christum praetexens mundi regna affectat, armis illa acquirit & retinet. Denique quicquid in Christi doctrina & vita cernitur, eius contrarium in Antichristo inuenire licebit.
units.tr: Christ Jesus, though he was in the form of God, took the form of a servant. Phil. 2. Whoever, therefore, being a man, dares to glory that he is God, and claims divine honours for himself, will be counted Antichrist.
