It is fitting that you hold fast to these and persevere in them with steadfast minds, and so there will be no danger from the Antichrists. He speaks, moreover, of the simple doctrine of salvation, which was revealed from the first origin of the world and was gradually made clearer and clearer, until, once the work of our redemption was accomplished through Christ, the Apostles preached it throughout the whole world among all nations. Let all those, therefore, persevere in it who in the controversies of our age are unwilling to suffer loss of salvation. The authority of this precept ought to be all the greater for us, because it is also prescribed to us elsewhere. For Christ Jesus too, when he had set out the various dangers of the last age, which threaten the faithful both from false doctrines and from other sources, commends constancy in the truth acknowledged as the one remedy against all these evils, saying: "He who endures to the end will be saved." Matt. 24. Paul likewise, warning Timothy about seducers, says: "But you, continue in the things you have learned and that have been entrusted to you, knowing from whom you have learned them, and that from childhood you have known the holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus." 2 Tim. 3. Therefore those are most shamefully mistaken who today think that, because of the various doctrines concerning the faith, a new kind of teaching is needed, and, turning to certain compromises, try to set up a form of doctrine of this sort which could be received and borne by all, provided only they cease to be stubborn. For since we see various and diverse dogmas sown concerning the faith, and men split into discordant opinions, there is therefore need of steadfastness of faith and of the acknowledged truth, with a persevering and unyielding zeal. For it is not within our right to change the Word of God, so that what is handed down in it may be altered at our discretion and shaped to men's pleasure. Moreover, since John refers us to that doctrine which was handed down from the very beginning and was preached by the Apostles when the churches were gathered, it will be worth our while to survey it briefly, summarized, so that, as in a mirror, we may see what we ought today to embrace and what to avoid.

units.la: Potest vniuersa Apostolorum doctrina duobus capitibus comprehendi, è quibus vtrumque in duas partes diuiditur. Primum salutis nostrae rationem tradit: alterum circa eorum officium versatur, qui redempti vel salui facti sunt. Quoad primum duo tradunt Apostoli. Docent enim omnes homines naturali corruptione infectos & peccatores esse, & proinde ex seipsis saluari non posse. Est haec doctrina perquam necessaria ijs, qui salutem cupiunt assequi. Nisi enim suae corruptionis sibi conscius fuerit homo, salutem penes seipsum quaeret frustra, neglecto interim eo, in quo solo omnis salus est. At quia caro nostra tam confidens est, ut nihil non sibi tribuere audeat, multum in hoc omnes scripturae versantur, ut innatam nobis corruptione ob oculos statuant. Nam ipse David testatur, figmentum cordis humani malum esse ab ineunte aetate. Gen. 8. Dauid vero ipsos fontes huius mali inuestigans, illud nobis haereditarium esse, & naturaliter inhaerere docet, cum inquit: En ego in iniquitate formatus sum, & in peccato concepit me mater mea. Psal. 51. In eandem sententiam propheta nos omnes ouium instar errauisse, & iustitias nostras foedas & abominabiles esse, fatetur. Isa. 53. & 64. Ut enim ex fonte infecto salubres riui duci non possunt: ita ex homine, qui peccati massam sibi innatam habet, opus aliquod omnibus partibus absolutum manare impossibi le est. Quare communis haec fuit fere sanctis omnibus vox: Ne ambules in ius cum seruo tuo Domine: nullus enim viuens coram te iustificabitur. Psal. 143. Item Psal.130 Si iniquitates obseruaueris o Deus, Domine quis subsistet? Hanc doctrinam ceu elementa prima Christianae institutionis, Apostoli tam constanter tradunt, ut cum hominis viribus & proprie iustitiae fiducia bellum irreconciliabile suscepisse videri possint. Quid enim primis capitibus praestantissimae illius ad Romanos epistolae Paulus agit, quam quod omnes homines, tam gentiles quam Iudaeos, peccatores esse grauissimis rationibus euincit? Idem adeo nos omni virtute spoliat, ut ad cogitandum quoque idoneos esse neget. 2. Cor. 3. Urgent vero hanc rem tam sedulo Apostoli, quia & poenitentiae seruit, quae prima euangelicae praedicationis pars est (Luc. 24.) & cogit vel inuitos nos, ut de proprijs viribus & humana iustitia desperantes, iustificationem & salutem extra nosipsos quaeramus.
units.tr: The whole doctrine of the Apostles can be comprehended under two heads, each of which is divided into two parts. The first sets out the manner of our salvation; the other concerns the duty of those who have been redeemed or made safe. Concerning the first, the Apostles teach two things. For they teach that all men, infected by natural corruption, are sinners, and therefore cannot be saved by themselves. This doctrine is most necessary for those who desire to attain salvation. For unless a man is aware of his own corruption, he will seek salvation in himself in vain, meanwhile neglecting that in which alone all salvation lies. But because our flesh is so confident that it dares to attribute nothing to itself, all the Scriptures labour much on this point, so that they set before our eyes the corruption innate in us. For David himself testifies that the imagination of the human heart is evil from its earliest age. Gen. 8. Yet David, investigating the very sources of this evil, teaches that it is hereditary for us and naturally inheres in us, when he says: "Behold, I was formed in iniquity, and in sin my mother conceived me." Ps. 51. To the same effect the prophet confesses that we all have gone astray like sheep, and that our righteousnesses are foul and abominable. Isa. 53 and 64. For just as healthful streams cannot be drawn from a polluted spring, so it is impossible that any work completed in every part should flow from a man who has within him a mass of sin innate to him. Therefore the common voice of almost all the saints has been this: "Do not enter into judgment with your servant, O Lord, for no one living will be justified before you." Ps. 143. Likewise Ps. 130: "If you, O God, should mark iniquities, Lord, who could stand?" The Apostles hand down this doctrine, as the first elements of Christian instruction, so steadfastly that they might seem to have waged an irreconcilable war against human strength and confidence in one's own righteousness. For what does Paul do in the first chapters of that most excellent Epistle to the Romans, except prove by the weightiest arguments that all men, Gentiles as well as Jews, are sinners? The same writer strips us so completely of all virtue that he denies we are even fit to think anything. 2 Cor. 3. The Apostles press this matter so diligently because it also serves repentance, which is the first part of the evangelical preaching (Luke 24), and it compels us, even against our will, to despair of our own strength and of human righteousness, and to seek justification and salvation outside ourselves.

units.la: Ne tamen peccatorem, qui corruptionem suam iam agnoscit, & de agnita dolet, diutius suspe sum teneant Apostoli, & conscientiae terroribus excrucient, Christum Iesum proponunt, in quo omnes gratiae diuinae thesauros & salutem vniuersam comprehendi docent. Hunc nobis iustitiam, sapientiam, sanctificationem, satisfactionem & redemptionem factum esse tradunt. 1. Corint. 1. Sed praestat singulorum de hoc testimonia audire, cum omnes in hoc misi fuerint, ut Christi testes essent. Acto. 1. Ioan. 15. Exordiamur autem à Petro, ut illis satisfaciamus, qui huius authoritate primatu quendam Persicum in ecclesia stabilire conantur. Is cum ingens auditorum multitudo à Christo deficeret, interrogatus: Num & vos vultis abire? respondet: Domine, ad quem ibimus? Verba vitæ æternæ habes. Et nos credimus & cognouimus, quòd tu es Christus filius Dei viui. Non videt ad quem relicto Christo eat Petrus, quia in solo hoc verbum & rationem vitæ æternæ ac salutis comprehensam videt. Idem coram senatu Hierosolymitano fidei & doctrinæ suæ rationem reddens, inter alia de Iesu Christo dicit: Hic est lapis ille, qui reiectus est à vobis ædificantibus, qui factus est caput anguli: nec est in alio quoquam salus. Non enim aliud nomen est sub cœlo datum inter homines, in quo oporteat nos saluos fieri. Actô 4. Et apud Cornelium de eodem sic ait: Huic omnes prophetæ testimonium ferunt, quòd remissionem peccatorum acceptur us sit per nomen eius, quisquis crediderit in eum. Actô. 10. Alibi rursus scribit: Christus peccata nostra ipse pertulit in corpore suo super lignum, quo peccatis mortui, iustitiæ viueremus. 1. Pet. 2. Et hæc quidem ex Petro adduxisse sufficiat. Ioannes verò, dilectus ille Christi discipulus, breui sententia quod alij multis dixerunt, comprehenditur dicës: In ipso vita erat. Item: Quotquot eum receperunt, dedit eis, vt liceret filios Dei fieri. Ioan. 1. Sed & supra cum omnes nos peccatores esse demonstrauisset, addit: Sanguis filij Dei emundat nos ab omni peccato. 1. Ioan. 1. Et paulò post: Si quis peccauerit, aduocatum habemus apud patrem, Christum Iesum. Et ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, non pro nostris autem tantum, sed pro totius mundi. 1. Ioan. 2. Et infra non alij doctrinæ credendum esse probabit, quàm quæ Iesum Christum nostræ salutis ergo in carnem venisse, & redemptorem nostrum factum esse, tradit. 1. Ioa. 4. Et si quis (inquit) ad vos venerit, qui doctrinam hanc non affert, illum ne in domum quidem recipite, & ne dixeritis ei, Aue, &c. 2. Ioan. 1. Habemus igitur duorum Apostolorum testimonia, quorum alter Christum præ cæteris dilexisse, alter à Christo præ aliis dilectus fuisse fertur. His si electû illud Christi organum & gentium doctorem Paulum coniungas, adeò nihil ab ijs quæ dicta sunt, diuersum inuenies, vt potius copiosè explicatum & firmissimis argumentis munitum vissurus sis, quod alij breuius docuerunt. Legantur ipsius epistolæ, eæ imprimis, quas ad Rom. Galat. & Ephesios scripsit, & verò dixisse deprehenderimur. In Synagoga Antiochena illum dixisse legimus: Notum sit vobis viri fratres, quòd per Iesum Christum vobis remissio peccatorum annunciatur, & ab omnibus, à quibus non potuistis per legem Mosi iustificari, per hunc omnis qui credit iustificatur. Actô 13. Idem alibi scribit: Certus sermo, & dignus quem omnibus modis amplectamur, quòd Christus Iesus venit in mundum, vt peccatores saluos faceret. 1. Timoth. 1. Et rursus: Vnus Deus, vnus etiam mediator Dei & hominum, homo Christus Iesus, qui dedit semetipsum pretium redemptionis pro omnibus. 1. Timoth. 2. Idem se non aliud nouisse testatur, quàm Iesum Christum, & hunc crucifixum. 1. Cor. 2. Præterea abesse (inquit) vt glorier, nisi in Cruce domini nostri Iesu Christi, &c. Galat. 6. Consentit hisce Apostolorum testimonijs primus noui testamenti præco, Ioannes Baptista, sanctissimus inter natos mulierum, qui Christum digito monstrans ait: Ecce agnus ille Dei, qui tollit peccatum mundi. Ioan. 1. Et ne hominum testimonijs niti videamur, Dei vocem allegare possumus, qui post tot promissiones patribus de Christo exhibitas, post typos legales, post prophetarum oracula, cœlitus de illo pronunciat: Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi complacitum est. Matth. 3. & 17. Et hæc quidem simplex & vnanimis est de salutis nostræ negotio Apostolorum doctrina, quanos[?] omnes peccatores esse, salutem verò in vno Christo contineri demonstrant.
units.tr: Yet lest the Apostles keep the sinner, who now recognises his corruption and grieves over what he has recognised, any longer in suspense, and torment his conscience with the terrors of guilt, they set before him Jesus Christ, in whom they teach that all the treasures of divine grace and all salvation are comprehended. They hand down that this Christ was made for us righteousness, wisdom, sanctification, satisfaction and redemption (1 Cor. 1.). But it is better to hear the testimonies of each one concerning this, since all were sent into the world to be witnesses of Christ (Acts 1.; John 15.). We shall begin with Peter, so that we may satisfy those who, on the authority of his words, try to establish in the Church a certain Petrine primacy. When a great crowd of his hearers fell away from Christ, and he was asked, "Do you also wish to go away?", he answered: "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life. And we believe and know that you are Christ, the Son of the living God." Peter does not see to whom he might go if he left Christ, because he sees the word and the reason of eternal life and salvation comprehended in this one alone. The same Peter, giving an account of his faith and teaching before the senate of Jerusalem, says among other things about Jesus Christ: "This is the stone which was rejected by you builders, which has become the head of the corner; nor is there salvation in any other. For there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved" (Acts 4.). And before Cornelius he speaks of the same in this way: "To him all the prophets bear witness, that through his name everyone who believes in him shall receive forgiveness of sins" (Acts 10.). Elsewhere he writes again: "Christ himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree, so that, being dead to sins, we might live to righteousness" (1 Pet. 2.). And let it suffice to have adduced these things from Peter. John, that beloved disciple of Christ, comprehends in a brief sentence what the others have said at length, saying: "In him was life." Likewise: "To as many as received him, he gave them the power to become sons of God" (John 1.). But also above, when he had shown that we are all sinners, he adds: "The blood of the Son of God cleanses us from every sin" (1 John 1.). And a little after: "If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ. And he himself is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but for the sins of the whole world" (1 John 2.). And further on he will show that no doctrine is to be believed except that which teaches that Jesus Christ came into the flesh for the sake of our salvation and was made our Redeemer (1 John 4.). "And if anyone," he says, "comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not even receive him into your house, and do not say to him, 'Hail,' etc." (2 John 1.). We have therefore the testimonies of two Apostles, of whom the one is said to have loved Christ above the others, and the other to have been loved by Christ above the rest. If you join to these the chosen instrument of Christ and teacher of the Gentiles, Paul, you will find nothing in him different from what has been said, so that you will see it rather explained at length and fortified with the firmest arguments, what the others taught more briefly. Let his epistles be read, especially those which he wrote to the Romans, Galatians and Ephesians, and you will find that he has indeed spoken truly. We read that in the synagogue at Antioch he said: "Let it be known to you, men and brethren, that through Jesus Christ forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is justified from all those things from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses" (Acts 13.). He writes elsewhere: "This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners" (1 Tim. 1.). And again: "There is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself a ransom for all" (1 Tim. 2.). He testifies that he knew nothing other than Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Cor. 2.). Moreover, he says: "God forbid that I should glory, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ," etc. (Gal. 6.). With these testimonies of the Apostles agrees the first herald of the New Testament, John the Baptist, most holy among those born of women, who, pointing to Christ with his finger, says: "Behold that Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world" (John 1.). And lest we seem to rely on the testimonies of men, we may adduce the voice of God, who, after so many promises given to the fathers concerning Christ, after the legal types, after the oracles of the prophets, pronounces from heaven concerning him: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Matt. 3. and 17.). And this is the simple and unanimous teaching of the Apostles concerning the business of our salvation: they demonstrate that all are sinners, and that salvation is contained in the one Christ alone.

units.la: Transfeamus nunc ad alterum apostolicæ doctrinæ caput, quo ea traduntur, quæ nostri sunt officij. Est & illud bimembre. Comprehendit enim ea quæ religionem spectant, & quæ ad vitæ sanctè morum institutionem pertinent. In religione primas obtinet fides in Iesum Christum, quæ nos illi inserit, & per hunc diuinæ gratiæ & regni cœlorum confortes reddit. Quæ causa est, quòd Apostoli docent, nos sola fide in Christum iustificari, eò quòd sola hæc Christum, qui iustitia nostra est, apprehendit. Et Paulus alibi, sine fide Deo neminem placere posse docet. Hebr. 11. Exigit hanc vbique Christus, cuius rei testimonia plura & luculentiora sunt, quàm vt multis ea recitari debeant. Ioannes certè, hanc causam finale euangelicæ prædicationis esse dicit, vt credamus, quòd Iesus est Christus ille filius Dei, & credentes habeamus vitam per nomen eius. Ioan. 20. Possent hic de fide in Christum multa dici, quæ omittimus, eò quòd commodior de illis dicendi locus inferatur. Manat ex fide hac spiritualis ille cultus Dei, quo totû sese Deo patri homo consecrat, de quo Christus Ioan. 4. & Apostolus ad Roman. 12. loquitur. Nec enim fieri potest, quin totus à Deo pendeat, totus Deo inseruiat, toto pectore Deum amet, quicunque Christum vera fi de amplexus in hoc diuinæ bonitatis excellentiam sentire cœpit. At qui totus Deo consecratus est, externa non curat, nec frigidarum Ceremoniarum obseruationem multum moratur. Quare ab apostolica doctrina vehementer alieni sunt, qui circa Ceremonias occupantur, quasi in his vniuersa diuini cultus ratio consistat. Qui fidem in Christum habet, & per hanc Deo vnitus verbo Dei ducitur, illo gubernatur, iuxta hoc sua omnia instituit, is Dei verus cultor solus habebitur. Christianæ vitæ conuersatio iuxta apostolicam doctrinam in duobus consistit, sanctimonia saimirum[?] vel puritate vitæ, & mutua dilectione. Quia enim nos Christi sanguine à peccatis ablu-tos docent, vitæ sanctimoniâ simul exigunt, vt in puritate ea maneamus, cuius nobis author Christus sua morte factus est. Hinc Paulus sanctificationem nostram Dei voluntatem esse dicit, & tum ab omni alia impuritate, tum à scortatione cumprimis dehortatur, quæ corpus Deo sacrum polluit. 1. Thessal. 4. 1. Corinth. 6. Idem nos in mortem Christi baptizari docet, vt cum illo ad vitæ nouitatem resurgamus. Roman. 6. Et sanè magnam Christo iniuriam faciunt, qui pretioso sanguinis sui lauacro mundati, peccatorum luto sese temere polluunt, quos idem Paulus Christi abnegatores esse dicit, eò quod vita negent eum, quem ore profitentur. Tit. 1. At quia multi vitæ puritatem tum se præstare putant, quando in solitudines profecti hominum commercia fugiunt & sibi solis viuunt, alterum Christianæ conuersationis ex Christi doctrina præceptum Apostoli tradunt, charitatem videlicet, qua nos totos fratribus impendere iubemur. Hanc non temere Christus verè fidelium tesseram facit, ex qua agnosci queant. Ioan. 15. Quia enim in Christo omnes nos eiusdem patris filij, imò vnius & eiusdem corporis membra facti sumus, eam inter nos charitatem esse conuenit, quam inter nostri corporis membra & fratres verè germanos videre licet. At cum de charitate in sequentibus multa dicturus sit Ioannes, quæ de ea dici poterant, in suum locum reseruabimus. Nostrum est, apostolicæ doctrinæ prima capita tenere, quibus nos peccatores esse, salutem verò in vno Christo contineri discimus, quæ nos fide amplecti decet, vt per hunc Deo vniti, illi seruiamus in spiritu & veritate, retineamus verò vitæ puritatem & dilectionem fraternam. In his nos manere iubet Apostolus. Hæc enim ab ipsa mundi origine tradita fuerunt, & vnanimi omnium Apostolorum consensu, iuxta spiritus sancti inspirationem, ecclesiæ præscripta sunt.
units.tr: Let us now pass on to the second head of apostolic doctrine, in which those things are delivered that belong to our office. This too has two parts. For it comprehends both what concerns religion and what pertains to the holy ordering of life and conduct. In religion, faith in Jesus Christ holds the first place, which engrafts us into him and through him makes us partakers of divine grace and of the kingdom of heaven. This is why the Apostles teach that we are justified by faith alone in Christ, because faith alone apprehends Christ, who is our righteousness. And Paul elsewhere teaches that without faith no one can please God (Heb. 11.). Christ requires this everywhere, and the testimonies to this are too many and too clear to need to be recited to many. John certainly says that this is the final cause of evangelical preaching, that we should believe that Jesus is that Christ, the Son of God, and that believing we might have life through his name (John 20.). Many things might be said here about faith in Christ, which we omit, because a more convenient place for speaking of them will be introduced. From this faith flows that spiritual worship of God, by which a man consecrates himself wholly to God the Father, of which Christ speaks in John 4. and the Apostle in Rom. 12. For it cannot be otherwise than that whoever has embraced Christ by true faith and has begun to perceive the excellence of divine goodness in this, should depend wholly on God, serve God wholly, love God with his whole heart. But he who is wholly consecrated to God does not care for outward things, nor dwell much on the observance of cold ceremonies. Wherefore they are very far removed from apostolic doctrine who occupy themselves with ceremonies, as if the whole manner of divine worship consisted in these. He who has faith in Christ, and through this is united to God, is led by the word of God, is governed by it, and according to this arranges all his affairs, he alone will be held to be the true worshipper of God. The conduct of Christian life, according to apostolic doctrine, consists in two things, namely holiness, or purity of life, and mutual love. For since they teach that we have been washed from our sins by the blood of Christ, they at the same time require holiness of life, that we remain in that purity of which Christ himself has become the author by his death. Hence Paul says that our sanctification is the will of God, and he warns us both from all other impurity and especially from fornication, which pollutes the body consecrated to God (1 Thess. 4.; 1 Cor. 6.). The same teaches that we are baptized into the death of Christ, so that with him we may rise to newness of life (Rom. 6.). And indeed they do great injury to Christ who, washed in the precious bath of his blood, rashly defile themselves with the mire of sins; the same Paul says these are deniers of Christ, because they deny by their life him whom they profess with their mouth (Tit. 1.). But since many think they show purity of life when they have gone off into solitudes and flee the company of men and live to themselves alone, the Apostles deliver the other precept of Christian conduct from the doctrine of Christ, namely charity, by which we are commanded to devote ourselves wholly to our brethren. Christ does not make this the token of true believers by which they may be recognised for nothing (John 15.). For since in Christ we have all been made sons of the same Father, indeed members of one and the same body, it is fitting that there should be among us that charity which can be seen between the members of our own body and true brothers. But since John is about to say many things about charity in what follows, which could be said about it, we shall reserve them for their own place. It is our task to hold to the first heads of apostolic doctrine, by which we learn that we are sinners and that salvation is contained in the one Christ, which it is fitting we embrace by faith, so that, united to God through him, we may serve him in spirit and truth, and maintain the purity of life and brotherly love. The Apostle bids us remain in these things. For these were handed down from the very origin of the world, and by the unanimous consent of all the Apostles, according to the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, have been prescribed to the Church.

units.la: II. Si in nobis manserit, quod audistis ab initio, & vos in filio & patre manebitis. Et hæc est repro-missio, quam ipse pollicitus est nobis, vitam æternam. Fructus perseuerantiæ exponit, & amplissima præmia ijs pollicetur, qui in doctrina per Apostolos tradita constanter manent. Primum est: Vos in filio & patre manebitis. Promittunt hæc nobis communionem cum Deo, de qua primo capite dictum est. Meminit huius & Christus in euangelio, cum ait: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum seruabit, & pater meus diliget eum, & ad eum veniemus, & mansionem apud eum faciemus. Ioannis 14. Comprehendunt hæc omnia, quæ ad hominis felicitatem spectant, quia impossibile est ei quicquam deesse, qui Deo, omnis boni fonte, tam familiari vtitur. Eadem verò & summam hominis dignitatem ostendunt. Quid enim de hoc excellentius dici poterat, quàm quòd eo honore illum dignatur Deus, vt ipsi non amicus modò & benefactor, verumetiam perpetuò præsens & contubernalis esse velit? Quòd si autem hoc honore eos dignatur Deus, qui in doctrina veritatis per Apostolos tradita perseuerant, satis euidenter patet, à Deo alienissimos fore, qui apostolicæ doctrinæ reclamant, ei aduersantur, vel nimium leues ab illa deficiunt. Docent idem & Christi verba ad Apostolos, quæ in euangelio habentur: Qui recipit vos, me recipit: & qui me recipit, recipit eum, qui misit me. Quicunque non exceperit vos, neque audierit sermones vestros, exeuntes ex ædibus aut ciuitate illa, excutite puluerem pedum vestrorum. Amen dico vobis: Tolerabilius erit terræ Sodomorum & Gomorrheorum in die Iudicij, quàm ciuitati illi. Matth. 10.
units.tr: II. If you remain in what you have heard from the beginning, you too will remain in the Son and in the Father. And this is the promise that he himself made to us: eternal life. He sets out the fruit of perseverance, and promises the greatest rewards to those who constantly remain in the teaching handed down through the Apostles. The first is: you will remain in the Son and in the Father. These words promise us communion with God, of which was spoken in the first chapter. Christ also mentions this in the Gospel, when he says: "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him." John 14. These promises include everything that pertains to human happiness, because it is impossible for anything to be lacking to one who enjoys such familiar fellowship with God, the fountain of every good. Yet they also show the supreme dignity of man. For what could be said that is more excellent than this, that God deigns to honour him so highly that he wishes to be not only his friend and benefactor, but also ever present with him and his fellow-dweller? But if God deigns to honour with this distinction those who persevere in the doctrine of truth handed down through the Apostles, it is quite plain that those will be utterly alienated from God who cry out against apostolic doctrine, oppose it, or fall away from it too lightly. The words of Christ to the Apostles, which are found in the Gospel, teach the same thing: "Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. Whoever does not receive you, nor hear your words, when you go out from that house or city, shake the dust off your feet. Amen I say to you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that city." Matt. 10.

units.la: Alterum, quod perseuerantibus in doctrina apostolica pollicetur, est vita æterna. Est verò secundum hoc prioris consequens. Quia enim Deus ipsa vita est, non potest non æternum viuere, quicunq; Deum in se manentem habet. Cæterum quò maior esset huius promissionis authoritas, non suo nomine hanc proponit Apostolus, sed Christum ipsum allegat huius promissionis authorem. Is enim iam Crucem aditurus pro omnibus illis orat, quicunq; iuxta Apostolorum sermonem in ipsum credunt. Ioan. 17. Et Apostolos in orbem emittens prædicatum, ait: Ite in mundum vniuersum, & prædicate euangelium omni creaturæ. Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, salus erit: qui verò non crediderit, condemnabitur. Mar. 16.
units.tr: The second thing promised to those who persevere in apostolic doctrine is eternal life. This is indeed a consequence of the former. For since God is life itself, whoever has God remaining in him cannot but live eternally. Moreover, so that the authority of this promise might be greater, the Apostle does not put it forward in his own name, but cites Christ himself as the author of this promise. For he, about to go to the Cross, prays for all those who believe in him through the word of the Apostles. John 17. And sending out the Apostles into the world to preach, he said: "Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature. He who believes and is baptized will be saved; but he who does not believe will be condemned." Mark 16.

units.la: Quoties ergo hodie de constantia fidei in solum Christum & perseuerantia in doctrina apostolica contendimus[?], non de lana caprina lis est, nec de rebus (vt multi putant) superuacaneis, sed de salute nostra & eius causis principalibus agitur. Nam Christo teste, qui euangelio per Apostolos prædicato crediderit, saluus erit: qui illi credere detrectat, condemnationi & morti æternæ subiacet. At grauius multò est & pœnam atrociorem meretur, fidem datam Christo negauisse, vel à veritate cognita desciuisse, quàm eius lucem nunquam voluisse admittere. Si enim quouis malo dignus est, qui fidem suam apud homines fallit, quantò horribilius peccat, qui Deo patri, qui filio Dei, cuius sanguine redemptus est, fidem in baptismo datā, & toties obstrictam, quoties cum fidelibus mensæ domini communicauit, fallere audet? Merito igitur de talibus Apostolus scribit: Facta sunt illis postrema peiora primis. Et satius fuisset illis, non cognouisse viam iustitiæ, quàm vbi cognouerunt, conuerti ab eo, quod illis traditum fuit, sancto præcepto. 2.Pet.2. Hæc qualim [?] non oscitantibus animis expenderūt sancti Dei martyres, qui corpora potius horribilibus tormentis excrucianda præbere, & cum sanguine animas ipsas profundere maluerunt, quàm à Christo & doctrina veritatis deficere. Horū exemplū nobis imitādum, pponamus. Felix ille dolor est, qui pro veritate defendenda sustinetur, & æternis regni cœlorum gaudijs terminatur. Reuera autem infelices & miseri sunt, qui breui perituram mundi pacem, & instabilem carnis voluptatem, æternæ beatitudinis iactura redimunt. Quid enim prodest homini, si totū mundum lucratus fuerit, animæ verò suæ iacturam fecerit? Aut quid dabit homo, cuius permutatione redimat animam suam? Matth.16.
units.tr: Whenever therefore today we contend about constancy of faith in Christ alone and perseverance in apostolic doctrine, the dispute is not about trifles, nor about things (as many think) superfluous, but our salvation and its principal causes are at stake. For, as Christ bears witness, whoever believes the gospel preached through the Apostles will be saved; whoever refuses to believe in him is subject to condemnation and eternal death. But it is far more serious, and deserves a much more terrible punishment, to deny the faith pledged to Christ, or to fall away from the truth once known, than never to have wished to admit its light. For if he deserves any evil who breaks his faith before men, how much more grievously does he sin who dares to break faith with God the Father and the Son of God, by whose blood he was redeemed, the faith given in baptism and bound so many times as often as he has communicated with the faithful at the table of the Lord? Rightly therefore the Apostle writes of such people: "The last state of those men has become worse than the first. And it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, having known it, to turn back from the holy commandment that was handed down to them." 2 Pet. 2. The holy martyrs of God, who considered these things with no sluggish minds, preferred to offer their bodies to be tormented with horrible torments and to pour out their very souls with their blood, rather than fall away from Christ and the doctrine of truth. Let us set their example before us for imitation. That suffering is happy which is endured in defence of the truth and ends in the eternal joys of the kingdom of heaven. But truly they are unhappy and wretched who, for the sake of the peace of the world which will soon perish and the unstable pleasure of the flesh, purchase the loss of eternal blessedness. For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and suffers the loss of his soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul? Matt. 16.

units.la: Hæc scripsi uobis de his, qui seducunt uos. Repetit periculi mentionem, ne frustra hæc monuisse & tanto studio inculcauisse videatur. Nisi (inquit) essent, qui vestræ salutì insidias struunt, qui à via salutis ad auia perditionis abducere studeant, facilè hoc meum studium omittere & animum tam solicita cura liberare poteram. Sed cum seductores multi sint, & iam nunc agere incipiat iniquitatis mysterium perditionis filius Antichristus, hæc non potui non scribere, nisi mercenarium me præbere, non bonis pastori officio defun-gi, voluissem. Admonet hæc Ioannis cura omnes dominici gregis pastores, ut lupos obseruent diligenter, ut falsas doctrinas arguant, seductores accusent, deniq; in hoc toti sint, ne quis ipsorum negligentia & incuria impostoribus eiusmodi præda fiat. Nec enim illi audiendi sunt, qui hunc laborem superuacaneum esse putant, & interdum seditionum authores esse dicunt eos, qui in erroribus arguendis fidelem operam nauant. Sunt hi stolidarum ouium instar, qui pericula potius incurrere quàm vitare malunt, quorum stoliditati prudens pastor non cedere, sed potius fideli industria occurrere debet.
units.tr: "These things I have written to you about those who lead you astray." He repeats the mention of the danger, lest it seem that he had warned and urged these things with such zeal in vain. Unless (he says) there were those who lay snares for your salvation, who strive to lead you away from the way of salvation into the pathways of destruction, I could easily have omitted this concern of mine and freed my mind from such anxious care. But since there are many seducers, and already the mystery of iniquity, the Antichrist, the son of perdition, is beginning to work, I could not but write these things, unless I wished to show myself a hireling, not discharging the good office of a shepherd. The care of John admonishes all the ministers of the Lord's flock to watch carefully for wolves, to refute false doctrines, to accuse seducers, and finally to be wholly intent on this, lest through their negligence and carelessness any such impostors become prey. For those men are not to be heard who think this labour superfluous, and sometimes call those who faithfully labour to refute errors the authors of sedition. They are like foolish sheep, who prefer to run into dangers rather than avoid them; and a prudent shepherd ought not to yield to their folly, but rather meet it with faithful diligence.

units.la: Didicimus hoc sermone, fratres, inter controuersias de fide & religione tutissimum asylum esse perseuerantiam in doctrina primitiuæ ecclesiæ per Apostolos tradita. Audiuimus in quibus illa versetur, & quàm ampla huius constantes obseruatores præmia maneant. Suspectos itaq; habeamus omnes eos, qui ab huius simplicitate nos auocant. Christi solius vocem sectemur, quod ouium ipsius proprium est. Sic fiet, ut omnibus errorum laqueis exempti, Deo patri tuto seruire possimus, æternæ vitæ coronam olim recepturi ab eo, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Brethren, we have learned from this discourse that, amid controversies about faith and religion, the safest refuge is perseverance in the doctrine of the primitive Church handed down through the Apostles. We have heard in what it consists, and how great are the rewards that remain for its steadfast observers. Let us therefore hold all those suspect who call us away from its simplicity. Let us follow the voice of Christ alone, which is the proper mark of his sheep. Thus it will come about that, freed from all the snares of error, we may serve God the Father safely, destined in time to receive the crown of eternal life from him to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XIIII,
units.tr: HOMILY XIIII,

units.la: Et unctio, quam vos accepistis ab eo, manet in vobis. Et non necesse habetis, ut quisquam doceat vos: sed sicut ipsa unctio do-cet vos de omnibus, & verax est, & non est mendacium. Et sicut docuit vos, manete in eo. Et nunc filioli, manete in eo, ut cum apparuerit, habeamus fiduciam, et non pudefiamus ab eo in aduentu e-ius. Si scitis quòd iustus est, scitote, quòd omnis qui facit iustitiam, ex ipso natus est.
units.tr: "And the anointing which you have received from him abides in you. And you have no need that anyone teach you; but as the same anointing teaches you concerning all things, and is true, and is not a lie. And as it has taught you, abide in him. And now, little children, abide in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not be ashamed before him at his coming. If you know that he is righteous, know that everyone who does righteousness has been born of him."

units.la: OVamuis multa sunt corruptionis nostræ argumenta, quibus illa facilè agnosci potest, eui [?] dentissimè tamen seipsam prodit in causa religionis & salutis nostræ negotio. Cum enim Christus Iesus omnem salutis rationem breui & dilucido compendio proponat, iugumque eius (vt ipse fatetur) sit suaue & facile, ea tamen est ingenij humani peruersitas, vt contempta simplici Christi traditione, & relicta salutis via plana & facili, ad ea conuertamur totis animis, quæ nec esurientes animas pascere, nec sitientium æstum restinguere possunt: imò relicto fonte aquæ viuentis cisternas vacuas & pertusas nobis effodimus. Ier.2. Meretur tanta ingratitudo, vt succes-sum aliquem falsis doctoribus Deus permittat, vt efficacem illusionem sentiant, qui veritatis amorem amplecti noluerunt. 2.Thess.2. Quia tamen idem ille suorum curam habet, & eisdem patet no animo semper prospicit, frequenter de falsis doctoribus & erroneis doctrinis admonet, & erudit, vt harum laquei caueri possint. Sunt eius argumenti tam in veteri quàm nouo Testamento infiniti loci, quibus postrema huius Capitis pars, quæ de Antichristianis doctoribus agit, adnumerari debet. Comprehendit hæc plenissimè quæcunque de hac causa dici possunt. Docuit enim fos doctores agnoscere, & vt in simplici apostolicæ doctrinæ veritate constanter perseuerent, monuit. Pertinet ad admonitionem hanc & præsens hic locus, quo doctrinam apostolicā aliquot argumentis commendat, illius certitudinem & omnibus numeris absolutam perfectionem describens, vnà cum amplissimo præmio, quod eius sectatores in nouissimo die recipient. Tandem locum hunc concludens ad sequentem tractationem commodè transit. Nos singulas huius loci partes, qua fieri poterit breuitate, percurremus.
units.tr: Although there are many signs of our corruption by which it can easily be recognized, it reveals itself most clearly in matters of religion and the business of our salvation. For when Christ Jesus sets forth the whole account of salvation in a brief and clear summary, and his yoke (as he himself says) is sweet and easy, yet such is the perversity of the human mind that, despising the simple tradition of Christ and abandoning the plain and easy way of salvation, we turn with all our hearts to those things which can neither feed hungry souls nor quench the heat of thirsty ones. Indeed, having abandoned the fountain of living water, we dig for ourselves empty and broken cisterns. Jer. 2. Such ingratitude deserves that God should permit some success to false teachers, so that those who refused to embrace the love of truth feel a powerful delusion. 2 Thess. 2. Yet because that same God cares for his own, and always looks upon them with an open and kindly mind, he frequently warns and instructs them about false teachers and erroneous doctrines, so that they may guard against their snares. Of this kind there are countless passages in both the Old and New Testaments, to which the last part of this chapter, which deals with antichristian teachers, must be added. It comprehends most fully whatever can be said on this subject. For he taught them to recognize such teachers, and admonished them to persevere constantly in the simple truth of the apostolic doctrine. To this admonition belongs also the present passage, in which he commends the apostolic doctrine by several arguments, describing its certainty and its perfection, absolute in every respect, together with the very great reward which its followers will receive on the last day. Finally, concluding this passage, he passes conveniently to the following discussion. We shall run through the individual parts of this passage as briefly as possible.

units.la: I. Et unctio, quam uos accepistis ab eo, manet in uobis. Et non necesse habetis, ut quisquam doceat uos: sed sicut ipsa unctio docet uos de omnibus, et uerax est, & non est mendacium. Et sicut docuit uos, manete in eo. Comprehendit his verbis apostolicæ doctrinæ certitudinē & absolutam perfectionē, quę duo ad doctrinarū cōmendationem plurimū faciunt. Quis enim incerta dogmata vel amplecti, vel eadem cum vitæ periculo tueri, velit? Quis ité eam doctrinā magni faciat, cui multa adhuc deesse videt, quę ad eius perfectionē necessaria sunt? Vtrumq; aūt eo testimonio probat, quo nullū & plenius est & irrefragabilius, spiritus sancti nimirum, quē fideles singuli intra animos suos testificari de sua sentiunt. Hunc enim vnctionis vocabulo intelligi, ex superioribus patet. Sic ergo dicere vi detur Apostolus: Si ea doctrina recipi & retineri meretur, quæ & certa & absoluta est: præ omnibus alijs retineri debet constantissimè, quâ de Christo per Apostolos tradita habemus. Hac enim nihil certius & absolutius est. Nec longè huius argumenta petantur. Vos enim ipsos appello, & cōscientiarum vestrarum testimonia audire cupio, quibus Christi spiritus inest, quē is fidelibus suis promisit, & promissum liberalissimè largitur. Is quid credi à vobis debeat, vos edocet. Idem in cultu tam externo quàm interno vos instruit. De niq; de omnibus, quæ saluti seruiunt, sic instituit, vt nullo alio doctore vobis opus sit. Vnus siquidem hic plus præstat, quàm nemo hominū præstare possit. Colligantur. n. in vnū Rhetores eloquentissimi, Dialectici acutissimi, Philosophi sapientissimi, profundissimi Theologi, & iungantur his quicunq; aliqua authoritate in mundo valent: nunquam tamen omnes illi efficient, vt hominis animus, in salutis causa fluctuans, tutū fidei portum inueniat. Solius spiritus Dei hoc opus est. At si hunc consulatis, nostræ doctrinæ omnino astipulabitur. Agnoscet enim Christi vocē, cum Christi spiritus sit. Et de salutis vestrę ratione, quę per nos traditur, tá certos faciet, vt nullis nouis traditionibus, nec alicuius generis additionibus vobis opus sit. Est hæc singularis euangelicæ doctrinæ dignitas, & admirabilis fidei in Christum Iesum virtus, quam soli sentiunt, qui ea non frigidis modo verbis gloriantur, sed eandē in animis suis viuâ & vegetâ apprehenderunt. Cum hac si conferas omnes aliarū religionum doctrinas, eas nullius precij & momenti esse videbis. De omnibus enim, qui in religione humanæ sapientiæ traditiones sequuntur, verissimè dicitur, quod Samaritidi respōdet dominus. Vos adoratis quod nescitis. Ioan. 4. Cum enim cor hominis sit imperuestigabile, nō possunt non fluctuari & dubij hære re, quicunq; cordis humani placitis nituntur. Soli Christiani adorant quod sciunt, eò quòd fidei suę & religionis fundamentū habent, Iesum Christum, super quo ipsi viui lapides in domū spiritualem ædificati sunt. 1. Pet. 2. Quamobrem rationibus hisce Ioannes præceptum interserit, vt nimirum in eo constanter maneant, quod vnctione, id est, spiritu sancto docentur. Sunt tamen hic quædam paulò diligentius nobis excutienda, priusquam ad reliqua transeamus.
units.tr: I. "And the anointing which you have received from him abides in you. And you have no need that anyone teach you; but as the same anointing teaches you concerning all things, and is true, and is not a lie. And as it has taught you, abide in him." In these words he comprehends the certainty and absolute perfection of the apostolic doctrine, two things which contribute greatly to the commendation of doctrines. For who would wish to embrace uncertain dogmas, or defend them at the risk of life? Who would hold in high regard a doctrine which he sees still lacking many things necessary for its perfection? He proves both by that testimony than which none is fuller or more unanswerable, namely the Holy Spirit, whom individual believers feel testifying within their own hearts. For that this is understood by the word anointing is clear from what comes before. So the Apostle seems to say: if that doctrine deserves to be received and retained which is both certain and complete, then above all others the doctrine which we have from Christ delivered through the apostles ought to be held most constantly. For nothing is more certain or more complete than this. Nor need we seek the arguments from afar. For I appeal to you yourselves, and I wish to hear the testimony of your consciences, in which the Spirit of Christ dwells, whom he promised to his faithful ones and bestows his promise most generously. He teaches you what is to be believed. He instructs you likewise in outward and inward worship. Indeed, concerning all things which serve salvation, he so provides that you have need of no other teacher. For this one does more than anyone among men could ever do. For let the most eloquent rhetoricians be gathered together, the sharpest dialecticians, the wisest philosophers, the most profound theologians, and let there be joined to them all who hold any authority in the world: they will never bring it about that the mind of a man, wavering in the matter of salvation, finds the safe harbour of faith. This work belongs to the Spirit of God alone. But if you consult him, he will wholly agree with our doctrine. For he will recognize the voice of Christ, since he is the Spirit of Christ. And he will make you so certain about the way of your salvation, which is delivered through us, that you have no need of any new traditions or additions of any kind. This is the singular dignity of the evangelical doctrine and the admirable power of faith in Christ Jesus, which only those perceive who not merely boast of it in cold words, but have apprehended the same in their souls living and vigorous. If you compare with this all the doctrines of other religions, you will see that they are of no worth or weight. For concerning all who in religion follow the traditions of human wisdom, what the Lord answered the Samaritan woman is most truly said: "You worship what you do not know." John 4. For since the heart of man is unsearchable, those who rely on the pleasures of the human heart cannot but waver and be doubtful in their belief. Only Christians worship what they know, because they have as the foundation of their faith and religion Jesus Christ, upon whom they themselves, as living stones, are built into a spiritual house. 1 Pet. 2. Wherefore John inserts this precept by these reasons, namely that they should constantly abide in what they are taught by the anointing, that is, by the Holy Spirit. There are, however, certain matters here which we must examine a little more carefully before we pass on to the rest.

units.la: Primò dicit Ioannes: Non necesse habetis, vt quisquam doceat vos. Quę verba nonnulli eò torserunt, quasi verbi ministerium quod Christus in ecclesia instituit, euertant. Sed falli eos, si nō alijs argumentis, saltem Christi exemplo probari potest, qui per euangelij prædicationem homines ad fidē & salutis cōmercium adduci vult. Et iam discessurus à suis inquit: Oportet prædicari sub nomine meo pœnitentiam & remissionē in omnes gentes. Luc. 24. Et Paulus ait: Quomodo credēt ei, de quo non audierunt? Quomodo autē audient absq; prædicante? Rom. 10. Et alibi Christum Iesum ecclesiæ suæ dare dicit apostolos, prophetas, euangelistas, pastores & doctores ad instaurationem sanctorum. Eph. 4. Errant itaq;, qui hac Ioannis sententia ecclesiæ ministerium & docēdi munus abrogari putant. Nouas potius traditiones oppugnat apostolus, quibus fideles nequaquā opus habere dicit. Quia enim in Christo data sunt nobis, quæcunq; ad nostram institutionē & salutem faciunt, ineptū est, illis aliquid adsuere velle. Quid enim humana ratio excogitabit, quod diuinis mandatis conferri queat? Aut nū illa imperfecta putabimus, & humanarum traditionum assumento indigere? Itàne hominē Deo non æquabimus modo, verumetiā præferemus? Christus nobis à Deo patre sapientia factus est. 1. Corinth. 1. In Christo omnes sapientiæ & scientiæ thesauri recōditi sunt. Col. 2. Hunc ergo audiamus, nec extra hunc aliquos admittamus doctores, qui nobis fidei articulos cōdūt, & via salutis, quā fidei nostrę antecessores ignorauerūt, mōstrare audēt.
units.tr: First, John says: "You have no need that anyone teach you." Some have twisted these words as if they overturned the ministry of the Word, which Christ instituted in the Church. But they can be shown to be mistaken, if not by other arguments, at least by the example of Christ, who wills that men be brought to faith and to fellowship in salvation through the preaching of the gospel. And, about to depart from his own, he says: "Repentance and forgiveness of sins must be preached in my name to all nations." Luke 24. And Paul says: "How will they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without a preacher?" Rom. 10. And elsewhere he says that Christ Jesus gave to his Church apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers for the building up of the saints. Eph. 4. Those therefore err who think that by this saying of John the ministry of the Church and the office of teaching are abolished. Rather, the apostle attacks new traditions, which he says the faithful have no need of at all. For since everything that serves our instruction and salvation has been given to us in Christ, it is foolish to want to add anything to these things. For what will human reason devise that could be compared with the divine commands? Or shall we think these imperfect, and in need of the support of human traditions? Shall we not only make man equal to God, but even prefer him? Christ has been made wisdom to us from God the Father. 1 Cor. 1. In Christ all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. Col. 2. Let us therefore hear him, and let us not admit any teachers beyond him who compose for us the articles of faith and dare to show a way of salvation which our forefathers in the faith did not know.

units.la: Deinde ait Apostolus: Sicut vos docuit, manete in eo. Præcipit perseuerantiam, de qua in præcedēti sermone satis dictum est. Obseruandus verò hic est perseuerantiæ modus & regula, quam nisi obserues,sub perseuerantiæ Christianæ prætextu pertinax eris & impiè rebellis:quales mul-ti hodie sunt,qui ne leues videantur, olim conceptos errores deponere nolunt, nec à maioribus acceptam superstitionem exuere. At Ioannes nos in Christo manere iubet, nec id simpliciter, sed sicut (inquit) spiritus vos docuit, sic manete in eo. Falluntur ergo, qui in ea fide et religione perseuerare volunt, quam spiritus in scripturis non docuit, nec in animis ipsorum suo testimonio probat. Falluntur etiam, qui Christum fingunt alium, quàm qui scripturis traditur: vt qui saluatorem quidem fatentur, non autem soli tribuunt quę salutis nostrę sunt, sed infinita cōminiscuntur, quę Christi defectus suppleant, & ipsius imperfectioni succurrant. Sunt tales qui vnà cum Christo aliōs habent apud Deum aduocatos, iustitiæ Christi suorum operum iustitiam coniungunt, sacrificium Christi nouo Missæ sacrificio perficiunt, & alia eius generis commenta pertinaciter reti-nent. Aut enim nullus Christus habendus est, aut talis, qualem scripturę tradunt, credendus erit. Hæc autem non saluatorem modò, sed vnicum saluatorem esse tradunt. In his non mediator modò inter Deum & homines, sed vnicus mediator esse dicitur. Spiritus illum non immolatum modò in ara crucis esse docet, sed victimam illam semel duntaxat oblatam, & sufficientem expiatio-nem esse affirmat pro peccatis totius mundi. Simili ratione vnicus populi sui rex, vnicus & æter-nus sacerdos, vnicus ecclesiæ suæ sponsus, vnicum sui corporis caput nobis describitur. Vni & soli redemptioni nostræ gloria cedere debet. Vni & soli debetur suæ ecclesiæ regimen. Talem ergo agnoscamus, & in agnito constanter perseueremus. Id qui faciunt, doctrinam sequuntur verè apo-stolicam, cuius certitudinem [?] spiritus sancti testimonium demonstrat, & cuius perfectio tam ab-soluta est, vt nulla aliarū traditionum additamenta ferre possit. Iugulantur his verbis omnes huma-næ traditiones quocunq; fuco & prætextu ornentur. Quia non necesse habemus, vt quis alia nos doceat, quàm quæ spiritus tam in scripturis quàm animis nostris testatur, & talem nos Christum firmiter retinere decet, qualem idem spiritus in scripturis tradit.
units.tr: Then the Apostle says: "As it has taught you, abide in him." He enjoins perseverance, of which enough has been said in the preceding sermon. But the manner and rule of perseverance is to be observed here, which unless you observe, you will be stubborn and impiously rebellious under the pretext of Christian perseverance, as are many today who, lest they seem fickle, are unwilling to lay aside errors once conceived, nor to cast off the superstition received from their elders. But John bids us abide in Christ, and not simply so, but "as," he says, "the Spirit has taught you, so abide in him." They are therefore mistaken who wish to persevere in that faith and religion which the Spirit has not taught in the Scriptures, nor proves in their hearts by his testimony. They are also mistaken who fashion a Christ other than the one delivered in the Scriptures: those who indeed confess him as Saviour, but do not ascribe to him alone what belongs to our salvation, and devise endless inventions which supply the defects of Christ and come to the aid of his imperfection. There are such people who have other advocates before God alongside Christ, who join the righteousness of their own works to the righteousness of Christ, who complete the sacrifice of Christ with the new sacrifice of the Mass, and who obstinately retain other fictions of this kind. For either Christ must be held to be none, or he must be believed to be such as the Scriptures deliver. But these Scriptures teach that he is not only Saviour but the only Saviour. In these passages he is called not only mediator between God and men, but the only mediator. The Spirit teaches that he was not only sacrificed on the altar of the cross, but that he is affirmed to be that victim offered once only, and a sufficient expiation for the sins of the whole world. In a similar way he is described to us as the only king of his people, the only and eternal priest, the only spouse of his Church, the only head of his body. To him alone and to his redemption glory must be given. To him alone belongs the governance of his Church. Let us therefore acknowledge him as such, and constantly persevere in what we have acknowledged. Those who do this follow the truly apostolic doctrine, whose certainty the testimony of the Holy Spirit demonstrates, and whose perfection is so complete that it can bear no additions of any other traditions. By these words all human traditions are overthrown, however they may be adorned with any colour or pretext. For we have no need that anyone teach us anything other than what the same Spirit attests both in the Scriptures and in our hearts, and it becomes us to hold firmly to such a Christ as the same Spirit delivers in the Scriptures.

units.la: II. Et nunc filioli,manete in eo,ut cum apparuerit,habeamus fiduciam,& nō pudefiamus ab eo in ad-uentu eius. Est hæc altera apostolicæ doctrinæ commendatio, quæ fine lętisimum & amplisimum præmium continet, quod eius sectatores expectant. Ideo (inquit) manendū in Christo, qui vo-bis per euangelij prædicationē traditus est, quia qui in hoc manent, illius aduentum certa fiducia sustinere poterunt, nec in illo cum alijs impijs pudefient. Loquitur autē de aduentu Christi ad iu-dicium, in quo fratres suos & cohæredes agnoscet eos, qui ipsum vera & cōstanti fide retinuerunt & coram hominibus liberè cōfessi sunt. Rursum verò fratres suos esse negabit, nec in regni sui cō-fortium admittet, quicunq; mūdi huius degeneris & adulteri authoritatē tanti fecerint, vt ipsum negare, & à fidei veritate declinare ausint. Vide de hoc Matth.10. & Marc.8. Sunt hæc diligenti cō-syderatione digna. Nec enim ea erit eius iudicij ratio, quam in nostris sæpe seruari videmus, vbi actorem multis modis fallere, iudicē detrectare, testes reijcere, causas in aliud tempus protrahere, locum iniquū causari, & infinita alia cōminisci possumus, quę causam iniquam aliquo modo iuua-re possunt. Hic enim necessariò omnes sistemur ad tribunal Christi, qui in gloria patris sui veniet, vt reportet vnusquisque ea, quæ in corpore suo designauit, siue bona, siue mala. Rom.14.2.Cor.5. Accusatorē habebimus illo tempore, non diabolum, qui & ipse tunc finalē suæ damnationis sentētiam recipiet, sed propriam conscientiam quæ mille testiū loco est, quam fallere nunquā licebit. Iudex erit, qui non ex aliorum verbis de causa præsenti pronunciabit, sed quæ ipse vidit. Vidit autē omnia, cum scrutator sit cordiū & renum. Psal.7. Hic causam nostrā sustinere & tueri solus Christus poterit, qui & iudex est. Quos enim hic pro suis agnouerit, eos illi cohæredes esse volet Deus pater. Quos idē reiecerit, in ignem infernalē cum diabolo & angelis ipsius æternum cruciandi detrudentur. Pro suis autē agnoscet Christus, quicunq; euangelio per Apostolos prędicato crediderunt, & sermonē Apostolorum, ceu fidei sui regulā infallibilem, secuti sunt, & propter nomen ipsi-us affligi potius, quàm illud abnegare, voluerunt. Testatur hoc, cum se nō pro Apostolis modò orare dicit, sed pro omnibus ijs, qui in se credunt, iuxta doctrinā per Apostolos traditā. Ioan.17. Hius diei conditionē quicunq; diligenter expenderit, intelliget quātum bonum fit, quod hoc loco Ioannes pollicetur: sentiet quoq; q infelix & horribilis futura sit illorum confusio qui Christū ab-negare, cōtemnere, doctrinā et mēbra eius persequi ausi sunt. Nam vt sapiens inquit: Prodibunt pauidi peccatorū suorum reputatione, fuisq; sceleribus coràm conuincentur. Tunc iustus coram oppressoribus suis laborumq; suorū vituperatoribus magna cum audacia stabit: quo illi viso, gra-ui pauore percelletur, & præinopinata salute stupescet. Pœnitētia tāsti, & præ angustia spiritus ge-metes, sic apud se dicēt: Hic est ille, quē risui quondā habuimus, puerbioq; cōtumeliōso. Stulti vi-tā eius existimabamus vssania, & exitū eiusdē ignominiosum. Itàne vnà cū filijs Dei adnumera-tus est, & suā inter sanctos sortem adeptus? Aberrauimus vtiq; à via veritatis, lumen iustitiæ non fulsit nobis, nec intelligentię sol est exortus. Itinerib. iniustitię & interitus affatim vsi fumus: peruasimus inuia deserta, via vero domini ignorauimus. Quid profuit nobis superbia? diuitię fastuo sę quid nobis contulerunt? Tanquam umbra nunciusq; transcurrens illa prǣterierunt omnia, & in modum nauis fluctuosas aquas permeantis, cuius elapsę vestigium non inuenias, &c. Vide locum Sap.5.cap. & elegantem videbis confusionis, quę impios manet, hypotypofin.
units.tr: II. And now, little children, abide in him, that when he shall appear, we may have confidence, and not be ashamed before him at his coming. This is the second commendation of the apostolic teaching, which holds out the most joyful and magnificent reward that its followers await. Therefore (he says) we must abide in Christ, who was delivered to you through the preaching of the gospel, because those who abide in him will be able to await his coming with sure confidence, and will not be put to shame before him along with the other ungodly. He speaks here of the coming of Christ to judgment, in which he will acknowledge as his brothers and fellow heirs those who held fast to him in true and steadfast faith and openly confessed him before men. Conversely, he will deny that they are his brothers and will not admit into the fellowship of his kingdom those who have valued the authority of this base and adulterous world so highly that they dare to deny him and turn away from the truth of the faith. See on this Matt. 10 and Mark 8. These matters are worthy of careful consideration. For the manner of that judgment will not be like the one we often see observed in our courts, where we can deceive the plaintiff in many ways, challenge the judge, reject witnesses, postpone the case to another time, plead an unfair venue, and devise endless other devices that can somehow help an unjust cause. For there we shall all necessarily be brought before the tribunal of Christ, who will come in the glory of his Father, that each one may receive what he has done in his body, whether good or evil. Rom. 14; 2 Cor. 5. At that time we shall have no accuser but the devil, and he too will then receive the final sentence of his damnation; rather, we shall have our own conscience, which takes the place of a thousand witnesses, and which it will never be permitted to deceive. The judge will be one who will pronounce on the present case not from the words of others but from what he himself has seen. He sees all things, since he is the searcher of hearts and reins. Ps. 7. Christ alone, who is also the judge, will be able to sustain and defend our cause here. For those whom he shall acknowledge here as his own, God the Father will wish to be their fellow heirs. Those whom he rejects will be thrust into the infernal fire to be tormented forever with the devil and his angels. Christ will acknowledge as his own all who believed the gospel preached through the Apostles, followed the word of the Apostles as the infallible rule of their faith, and preferred to be afflicted for his name rather than deny it. He bears witness to this when he says that he prays not only for the Apostles but for all who believe in him through the teaching handed down by the Apostles. John 17. Whoever carefully weighs the condition of that day will understand how great a good it is that John promises here; he will also perceive how unhappy and terrible the confusion will be of those who have dared to deny Christ, despise him, and persecute his teaching and his members. For as the wise man says: They will come forward trembling at the reckoning of their sins, and will be convicted by their own wickedness. Then the righteous man will stand with great boldness before those who oppressed him and disparaged his labors; when they see him, they will be struck with deep fear and will be stunned by his unexpected salvation. Groaning with repentance and with anguish of spirit, they will say to themselves: This is he whom we once held in derision and as a reproachful proverb. We considered his life madness and his end dishonorable. How is it that he is numbered among the sons of God and has obtained his lot among the saints? We have certainly strayed from the way of truth; the light of righteousness has not shone upon us, nor has the sun of understanding risen. We have wearied ourselves plentifully with the paths of iniquity and destruction; we have gone through pathless deserts, but the way of the Lord we have not known. What has pride profited us? What have riches and boasting brought us? All those things have passed away like a shadow and a fleeting message, like a ship cutting through the waves, of which no trace can be found after it has passed... etc. See the passage in Wisdom 5 and you will see an elegant sketch of the confusion that awaits the ungodly.

units.la: Docent hæc quanta fidei in Christum Iesum præstantia sit, quæ tum iuuat, quando omnia huius mundi suos cultores fallunt, & præsidio suo destituunt. Nec enim in illo die aliqua erit diui tiarū vtilitas, vt quę vno incendio vnā cū elementis consumptę erunt. 2.Pet.3. Non ꝑderit insana mundi gloria, quę nulla omnino supererit. Non iuuabūt eloquentia & prudētia humana simul cū iunctę, quia non verbis nec humanis rationib. sed diuinę iustitię sententia irrefragabili lis illa termi-nabitur. Non clientū & amicorū fauore siue patrocinio defendi poterimus, eo quod omnes ab eo dē iudice iudicandi sunt. Sola fides in Christū ea nos iustitia vestire potest, quę iudicē nobis non ęquū modo & beneuolū, verumetiam fratrē facit. Hac qui carent, veste nuptiali carent, sine qua ę-terni gaudij nuptijs interesse nō licet. Matth.22. Allegabunt quidē multa, quibus cœli cōmercium se meruisse dicēt: sed dicetur illis: Nō noui vos. Discedite à me ꝓcul operarij iniquitatis. Matth.7.
units.tr: These things teach how great is the excellence of faith in Christ Jesus, which helps us when all the things of this world deceive its worshippers and leave them without support. For on that day there will be no usefulness in riches, since they will be consumed together with the elements in one fire. 2 Pet. 3. The mad glory of the world will not help, since none of it will remain at all. Human eloquence and prudence, though joined together, will not help, because that dispute will be ended not by words or human reasons but by the irrefutable sentence of divine justice. We cannot be defended by the favor or patronage of clients and friends, since all of us are to be judged by the same judge. Only faith in Christ can clothe us with that righteousness which makes the judge not only just and kind to us but even a brother. Those who lack it lack the wedding garment, without which it is not permitted to take part in the wedding feast of eternal joy. Matt. 22. Indeed, they will allege many things by which they will say they have earned the fellowship of heaven, but it will be said to them: I do not know you. Depart from me, you workers of iniquity. Matt. 7.

units.la: Habemus hoc loco ingens piorum & impiorū discrimen. Pij fiducia habent in aduentu Chri-sti, imo in hoc sperant, illum auidi expectant, huius spe quæuis aduersa fortiter & patienter sustinent. Norunt enim, Christū tunc quoq; ipsis saluatore fore. Et cum ea, quæ die aduentus Christi præcessura ipse prædixit, euenire vident, non animis suis pauidi consternantur, nō desperant, sed iuxta præceptū Christi, attollunt capita sua, eo quod die redemptionis suæ instare nouerunt. Luc. 21. Sic fortissimus ille patientię miles Iob, maximū consolationis argumentum ex nouissimi diei consyderatione sumit, cū ait: Noui & ego, quod vindex meus viuit, & nouissimo tempore adhibebit suā vim pulueri. Postquā vero circumdederint hoc mea cute, spectabo Deū è carne mea. Quē ego mihi cotemplabor, & oculi mei videbunt, & non alius: quod vnicū meum est desyderiū. Iob. 19. Eadem mente prædictum [?] legimus Paul. Apostolum, qui cū sub Nerone tyranno truculentissi-mo captiuus in singulas horas carnificis ensem expectaret, magna cum animi fiducia scribit: Ipse iā immolor, & tempus meę resolutionis instat. Certamen bonū decertaui, cursum consummaui, fidem seruaui. Quod superest, reposita est mihi iustitię corona, quā reddet mihi dominus in illo die, qui est iustus iudex: non solum aut mihi, sed & omnibus, qui diligunt aduentum ipsius. 2. Tim. 4. Cum his si impios & à fide Christi alienos conferas, longè alios videbis. Quia enim cœlestia ignorant, terrenis solis inhærent, in his voluptuantur & sperant, nihil illis molestius incidere potest, quàm nouissimi diei mentio. Sentiunt enim in animis suis conscientię stimulū, quæ illos tanti iu-dicis conspectū minimè sustinere posse docet. Ne tamen cogitatio hæc ipsos omni gaudio & volu-ptate spoliet, multis artibus illā eludunt, & argumenta fingunt, quibus vel reclamante propria cō-scientia, omnē de aduētu Domini doctrinā in dubiū vocent. Nā vt Petrus illorū sermones describit, feré dicunt: Vbi est pollicitatio aduentus eius? Siquidē ex quo die patres dormierunt, sic omnia permanent vt ab initio conditionis 2. Pet. 3. Ab anteactis enim falso argumentantur, & quia mundū hunc per annos plus quinquies mille durauisse, nec vnquā interitum sensisse vident, nullam omnino eius consummatione fore dicūt. Deinde & patres accusant, qui & ipsi vana spe ducti, finem mundi frustra expectarint. At omnia hæc eò tendunt, vt sibijpsis animum faciant, ne mole-sta cogitatione rei, quā maximè oderunt, infestati rerum mundanarū voluptatem amittant. Eiusdem rei gratia & sacras cōciones deuitant, quibus cogitationes istæ excitantur, & cōpotationibus potius indulgent, cumq; fui similibus conuersantur, quò facilius omnem harū rerum memoriam excutere possint. Sed sequitur illos infelix, de qua paulò ante diximus, cōfusio, cuius prǣludia in-terdum in hac quoq; vita sentiunt, dum morte præmatura circumuēti, sibi ē mundo migrandum esse vident, nec aliqua futuri seculi cognitione instructi, nihil præter horribiles desperabundę mē-tis terrores experiuntur. Hæc vtinam obseruarent, quibus hodie volupe est omnem salutis doc-trinam ridere, religionem omnem in dubium vocare, & Christum lusum iocumq; ducere. Sed tandem vltima huius loci verba, quibus tractationem hanc concludit, videamus.
units.tr: Here we have a great distinction between the godly and the ungodly. The godly have confidence in the coming of Christ; indeed, they hope for it, eagerly await it, and by that hope bear whatever adversity with courage and patience. For they know that Christ will then also be their Savior. And when they see those things come about which Christ himself foretold would precede the day of his coming, they are not dismayed in their minds, they do not despair, but, according to the command of Christ, they lift up their heads, since they know that the day of their redemption is near. Luke 21. Thus that most valiant soldier of patience, Job, draws the greatest argument for consolation from the consideration of the last day, when he says: I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last time he will exert his power upon the dust. And after they have destroyed this skin of mine, I shall see God from my flesh. Whom I shall behold for myself, and my eyes shall see, and not another: this is my only desire. Job 19. We read that the Apostle Paul, with the same mind, while a captive under the most savage tyrant Nero, expecting hourly the executioner's sword, wrote with great confidence of spirit: I am already being poured out as an offering, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day; and not only to me but to all who love his appearing. 2 Tim. 4. If you compare the ungodly and those who are alien from the faith of Christ with these, you will see them to be far different. For because they do not know heavenly things and cling only to earthly things, they take their pleasure and hope in these, and nothing can befall them more unpleasant than the mention of the last day. For they feel in their minds the goad of conscience, which teaches that they cannot endure the sight of so great a judge. Yet, lest this thought strip them of all joy and pleasure, they evade it by many devices and invent arguments by which, even though their own conscience objects, they call the whole teaching about the Lord's coming into doubt. For, as Peter describes their words, they roughly say: Where is the promise of his coming? For since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they have from the beginning of creation. 2 Pet. 3. For from past events they argue falsely, and because they see that this world has lasted more than five thousand years and has never felt an end, they say that there will be no consummation of it at all. Then they also accuse the fathers, who, led by vain hope, expected the end of the world in vain. But all these things tend to this: that they may persuade themselves, lest, troubled by the disquieting thought of a thing they most hate, they lose the pleasure of worldly things. For the same reason they also avoid sacred sermons, in which such thoughts are stirred up, and rather indulge in drinking parties, and associate with those like themselves, so that they may more easily shake off all memory of these things. But that unhappy confusion of which we spoke a little earlier follows them, the first signs of which they sometimes feel even in this life, when, surrounded by premature death, they see that they must depart from the world, and, not instructed by any knowledge of the age to come, they experience nothing but the horrible terrors of a despairing mind. Would that they would take heed of these things, those who today take pleasure in mocking all the teaching of salvation, call all religion into doubt, and treat Christ as a plaything and a jest. But let us at last look at the final words of this passage, with which he concludes this discussion.

units.la: III. Si scitis quòd iustus est, scitote, quòd omnis qui facit iustitiam, ex ipso natus est. Videtur illis oc-currere velle, qui fidē in Christum ꝓfesi [?], apostolica doctrina gloriātur, cū interim sub huius prę-textu carnis licentiā quærant, & eius prauis desyderijs indulgeant turpissimè. Sic enim vult dice-re: Cum iubeo vos manere in Christo, velim vos simul cogitare quis ille fit. Est is iustus, adeoque ipsa iustitia vere dicitur. Ex hoc igitur nati non videbuntur, nisi qui & ipsi iustitiam fecerint. Est aut iustitiā facere, idē quod iustitiæ studere, & illius officiū præstare, tā in ijs quæ Deo, quàm quę proximo debentur. Memorabilis omnino sententia, quæ sit tā diligenter expenderetur, quàm frequens est Christiani nominis & apostolicæ doctrinæ professio, minus in Ecclesia offendiculorū, plus autem pietatis & profectus in fide haberemus.
units.tr: III. If you know that he is righteous, know also that everyone who does righteousness has been born of him. This verse seems to be aimed at those who profess faith in Christ and boast of apostolic teaching, yet under the pretext of faith seek licence for the flesh and shamefully indulge its depraved desires. For John means to say this: when I bid you remain in Christ, I want you to consider who he is. He is righteous, and so he is rightly called righteousness itself. Therefore only those who have themselves done righteousness will appear to be born of him. To do righteousness is the same as to strive after righteousness and to perform its duty, both in what is owed to God and in what is owed to our neighbour. It is a memorable saying, and if it were weighed as carefully as the profession of the Christian name and of apostolic doctrine is frequent, we would have fewer stumbling-blocks in the Church and more piety and progress in faith.

units.la: Obseruandus hic nobis est nostræ iustificationis ordo, ex quo & salutis nostræ certitudo & officia Christianæ vitæ dependent. Primum in hoc locō obtinet regeneratio, qua filij Dei nasci-mur. Nisi enim homo renatus fuerit è supernis, nō potest videre regnū Dei. Ioan.3. Sed vt nō est humanarū viriū, nec arbitrij humani, naturalis nostra generatio, qua homines mortales nascimur, ita multò minus nostri arbitrij & virtutis erit, vt filij Dei nascamur. Confertur aūt nobis ex mera gratia per Iesum Christum, quē vbi fide amplexi fuerimus, ipsi inserimur. Hic enim dat omnib. qui ipsum recipiunt, vt possint filij Dei fieri: qui non ex sanguinibus, neq; ex voluntate carnis, neque ex voluntate viri, sed ex Deo nati sunt. Ioan.1. Porrò cū Christus iustitia nostra à Deo patre factus fit, necessariò iustificatur quicūq; illi per fidē inserti sunt. 1.Cor.1. Nam ideo ille pro nobis peccatū factus est, vt nos efficeremur iustitia Dei per illum. 2.Cor.5. Quid vero iustificati aliud q̄ opera iustitiæ facient? Siquidē qui exercet iustitiā, iustus est. 1.Ioan.3. Naturali ergo ordine inter se cohærent, regeneratio ex gratia, iustificatio fidei per Christū, & iustitiæ veræ studiū, quod opera verè bona coplećtitur. Arguit hoc illorum impudentia, qui fidei doćtrina peccandi licentia plátari clamāt. Fatemur quidē plures esse, qui Christo & iustitia ipsius turpiter abutuntur: sed num propter impuros aliquos Epicuri de grege porcos, doćtrinā Christi inuertere & corrumpere fas est? Vsum potius verum & finem iustificationis per Christum factæ respiciamus, qui est, vt abnegata impietate & mundanis concupiscentijs, sobriè & iustè & piè viuamus in præsenti seculo, expectantes beatam illam spem, & apparitionem gloriæ magni Dei, & seruatoris nostri Iesu, qui dedit semetipsum pro nobis, vt redimeret nos ab omni iniquitate, & purificaret sibijpsi populum peculiarem, sećtatorem bonorum operum. Tit.2.
units.tr: Here we must observe the order of our justification, on which both the certainty of our salvation and the duties of the Christian life depend. In this place regeneration comes first, by which we are born as children of God. For unless a man is born again from above, he cannot see the kingdom of God. John 3. But just as our natural generation, by which we are born as mortal men, is not a matter of human strength or human will, so much less is it in our power or virtue that we are born as children of God. It is bestowed upon us from pure grace through Jesus Christ, and once we have embraced him by faith, we are grafted into him. For he gives to all who receive him the power to become children of God, who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God. John 1. Moreover, since Christ is made our righteousness by God the Father, necessarily all who have been grafted into him by faith are justified. 1 Cor. 1. For he was made sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him. 2 Cor. 5. But what else will the justified do than works of righteousness? For he who practises righteousness is righteous. 1 John 3. Therefore these things cohere with one another in a natural order: regeneration from grace, justification by faith through Christ, and the pursuit of true righteousness, which embraces truly good works. The shamelessness of those who cry out that the doctrine of faith provides a licence for sinning proves this. We admit that there are indeed many who shamefully abuse Christ and his righteousness; but is it right, on account of some impure swine from Epicurus' herd, to overturn and corrupt the teaching of Christ? Let us rather look to the true use and end of justification effected through Christ, which is that, having renounced impiety and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, justly and godly in the present age, awaiting that blessed hope and appearing of the glory of the great God and our Saviour Jesus, who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity and purify for himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works. Titus 2.
