units.la: Constat ergo ex his, quę hucusq; dićta sunt, apostolica doćtrina, qua fides in solū Iesum Christum, vnicū mundi saluatorē traditur, certa & irrefragabile esse, vtpote quæ ipsius spiritus sancti testimonio in animis hominū obsignatur. Constat eandē & omnibus numeris esse absoluta, nec vllo nouarum traditionū additamento indigere. Vidimus insigne præmiū, quod illius sećtatoribus Deus pater proposuit. Eam itaq; fide syncera amplećtamur, sancta constantia retineamus, & secundum illius præscriptionem instituamus omnia nostra, vt in aduentu glorioso filij Dei fiducia habere & cum illo in regno patris sui viuere possimus: cui debetur benedićtio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: It is therefore clear from what has been said so far that the apostolic doctrine, by which faith is delivered in Jesus Christ alone, the only Saviour of the world, is certain and unshakeable, inasmuch as it is sealed in the hearts of men by the testimony of the Holy Spirit himself. It is clear too that the same doctrine is complete in every respect and needs no addition of any new traditions. We have seen the remarkable reward which God the Father has set before its followers. Let us therefore embrace it with sincere faith, hold it fast with holy constancy, and order all our affairs according to its prescription, so that we may have confidence at the glorious coming of the Son of God and may live with him in the kingdom of his Father, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT III. HOMILIA XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER III. HOMILY XV.

units.la: VIDETE quantam charitatem nobis dedit pater, ut filij Dei nominemur. Propter hoc mundus non novit vos, quia non novit eum. Charissimi, nunc filij Dei sumus, & nondum innotuit, quod futuri sumus. Scimus autem, quòd cum apparuerit, ipsi similes erimus: quoniam videbimus eum, sicuti est. Et omnis, qui habet hanc spem in ipsum, purificat se, sicut et ille purus est.
units.tr: SEE what love the Father has given us, that we should be called the sons of God. For this reason the world does not know you, because it did not know him. Beloved, now we are the sons of God, and it has not yet been revealed what we shall be. We know that when he appears we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is. And everyone who has this hope in him purifies himself, just as he is pure.

units.la: Vamuis[?] Deus, pater misericordię, in filio suo dilećto, domino & saluatore nostro Iesu Christo, quæcunq; ad humani generis salutem spećtant, paucis & sufficienter comprehensa nobis proponat: ea tamen est multorū peruersitas, vt vnico hoc saluatore nō contenti, salutem extra hūc, vel in proprijs vel aliorum meritis quærant. Euenit his, quod Israelitis olim euenisse legimus, qui derelićto fonte aquæ viuentis, cisternas vacuas & pertusas sibi foderūt. Iere. 2. Quicunq; enim aquā proprijs viribus haustā biberit, sitiet iterū. Solus Christus aquā dat, quę semel hausta, facit ne sitiamus in æternū. Ioan.4. & 7. Contra eos igitur, qui alio con fugiunt, hucusq; Ioan. multis disputauit. Docuit enim, nos, quoad naturā nostrā, peccatores esse, & tales quidē, qui cū Deo, ęterna luce, cōmunionem habere non possimus. Rursum vero ostēdit, sanguine filij Dei nos à peccatis ablui: qui idē noster apud patrē aduocatus & intercessor fit, si quā do carnis infirmitate superati denuo peccemus. Simul quoq; monuit, vt in simplici hac euangelij doćtrina, per Apostolos tradita, perseueremus: cū reuera impostores & Antichristi sint, quicunq; Iesum hunc Christū esse negare audent, & redemptionis nostræ gloriā alio transferunt. At cum hęc doctrina proponitur, aliud prodit hominū genus, quibus non minori studio occurrere oportet. Sunt hi carnales & mundi studio dediti. Hi enim facilè sibi persuaderi sinunt, ut Christū unicum saluatoré & unicam pro peccatis nostris satisfactione agnoscant: sed sub huius prætextu carnis licentiam venando, ita viuunt, ut Christum (quem ore profitentur) factis & rebus ipsis abnegent. Tit.1. Cū his ergo in sequentibus sermone instituit Apostolus, multa de vitæ Christianæ officijs, maximè aut de vitę puritate & fraterna charitate differēs: quę singula suis locis videbimus.
units.tr: Although God, the Father of mercies, sets before us in his beloved Son, our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, all the things that pertain to the salvation of the human race, briefly and sufficiently comprehended, yet such is the perversity of many that, not content with this one Saviour, they seek salvation outside him, either in their own merits or in those of others. There happens to them what we read happened of old to the Israelites, who, having forsaken the fountain of living water, dug for themselves empty and broken cisterns (Jer. 2). For whoever drinks water drawn by his own strength will thirst again. Christ alone gives water which, once drunk, makes us never thirst forever (John 4 and 7). Therefore, against those who flee to another refuge, he has disputed at length up to this point in John. For he taught us that, as to our nature, we are sinners, and such that we cannot have fellowship with God, who is eternal light. Again, however, he showed that we are washed from our sins by the blood of the Son of God, who is also our advocate and intercessor with the Father, should we at any time, overcome by the weakness of the flesh, sin again. At the same time he also warned us to persevere in this simple doctrine of the gospel, delivered through the Apostles, since those who dare to deny that this Jesus is the Christ are in truth impostors and Antichrists, and they transfer the glory of our redemption to another. But when this doctrine is set forth, another kind of men comes forward, whom we must meet with no less zeal. These are carnal men, given over to the pursuit of the world. For they readily allow themselves to be persuaded to acknowledge Christ as the only Saviour and the only satisfaction for our sins; but under the pretext of this, hunting for license for the flesh, they live in such a way that they deny by their deeds and actions the Christ whom they profess with their lips (Titus 1). Therefore, against these men the Apostle, in what follows, instructs them with a discourse on many duties of the Christian life, treating especially of purity of life and brotherly love, which we shall see one by one in their places.

units.la: Status siue primaria totius tractationis propositio est: Qui habet spem vel fidem in Deum, purificet seipsum, sicut & ille purus est. De hoc in præsenti loco sic agit. Primo à diuinæ bonitatis commendatione orditur, ut illius consyderatio in nobis studium Deo obediendi & eidem placendi excitet. Deinde offendiculo occurrit & medetur, quod ex corrupto de nobis mundi iudicio & assiduis tribulationibus oboritur. Tandē statum, cuius modò meminimus infert. Et de his modò pro gratia diuinitus data ordine dicemus.
units.tr: The main proposition, or primary point, of the whole treatment is this: whoever has hope or faith in God purifies himself, just as he is pure. He deals with this in the present place as follows. First he begins from the commendation of divine goodness, so that the consideration of it may arouse in us zeal for obeying God and pleasing him. Then he meets and remedies the stumbling-block that arises from the corrupt judgement of the world about us and from constant tribulations. Finally he introduces the state of which we have just spoken. And with God's grace, given from above, we shall speak of these things in order now.

units.la: I. Videte quantam charitatem nobis dedit pater, ut filij Dei nominemur. His fundamentum propositæ disputationis iacit, diuinæ erga nos bonitatis consyderationem ob oculos nobis statuens. Non contentus verò, Dei bonitate prædicasse, nos ut illam consyderemus, adhortatione excitat. Similis locus in Psal.34. extat, ubi sic legitur: Gustate & videte, quàm bonus sit dominus: felix ille vir, qui sperat in eum. Poterat autem multa diuinæ erga nos bonitatis et beneficentiæ argumenta producere, utpote quòd ex gratia nos condidit, cum nostri minimè indigeret: quòd propter nos omnem hanc mundi machinam fieri voluit, cum ijs quæ hac continentur: quòd nos pascit, tuetur & omnis generis bonis quotidie accumulat. Sed quia hęc corpori ferè seruiunt, & caduca sunt ac temporaria: summi beneficij, quod in nos extat, meminit: eius nimirum, quòd nos filios suos vocari voluit. Vocari autem idem est quod Esse. Quę enim Deus vocat, talia reuera sunt, qualia ab ipso vocari solent: quia verax est, nec quenquam inanibus titulorum fucis & præstigijs ludit. Comprehendit hic titulus, quæcunque de hominis æterna felicitate dici possunt. Si enim filij Dei sumus, utique & hæredes. Hæredes quidem Dei, cohæredes autem Christi. Rom.8. Et sic impletur, quod in primo fœderis diuini articulo comprehensum est, dum Deus se nostrum Deum, & nostram o-mnisufficientiam, fore pollicetur. Genef.17. Exod.20. Ierem.31. Indicant hęc singularem in Deo erga nos amoris affectum, qui tum luculentior erit multò, si circumstantias, quę hic incidunt, simul omnes consyderaueris. Obseruabis ergo eas hoc ordine.
units.tr: I. See what love the Father has given us, that we should be called the sons of God. With these words he lays the foundation of the proposed discussion, setting before our eyes the consideration of God's goodness toward us. Not content, however, with having preached the goodness of God, he stirs us by exhortation to consider it. A similar passage is found in Psalm 34, where it is read thus: Taste and see that the Lord is good; blessed is the man who trusts in him. He might indeed have produced many proofs of God's goodness and beneficence toward us: that out of grace he created us, when he had no need of us; that for our sake he willed this whole machinery of the world to be made, together with the things contained in it; that he feeds us, protects us, and daily heaps upon us every kind of good. But because these things serve mostly the body and are perishable and temporary, he recalls the greatest benefit which exists toward us: namely, that he willed us to be called his sons. Now to be called is the same as to be. For those whom God calls are truly such as they are wont to be called by him, since he is truthful and deceives no one with the empty colourings and tricks of titles. This title comprehends whatever can be said of man's eternal happiness. For if we are sons of God, then surely also heirs: heirs indeed of God, and joint heirs with Christ (Rom. 8). And thus is fulfilled what is contained in the first article of the divine covenant, while God promises that he will be our God and our all-sufficiency (Gen. 17; Exod. 20; Jer. 31). These things indicate a singular affection of love in God toward us, which will be far more striking if you consider together all the circumstances that arise here. You will therefore observe them in this order.

units.la: Primò personæ proponuntur, Deus & homo, quæ sibi inuicem collatæ admirabilem huic cō syderationi diuinę bonitatis lucem inferunt. Deus, quoad essentiam eius, æternus est, immortalis, incorruptibilis, & extra omnem mundi huius fortunam constitutus. Attributa eius & propria sunt, quòd est æterna sapientia, infallibilis veritas, iustitia perfecta, lux inaccessa, insuperabilis potentia, gloria ineffabilis & maiestas immensa. His si hominem conferas, tam eum cum illo dissidere videbis, quàm album à nigro differt. Nam quoad essentiam hominis, creatura est, initium & finem habens: mortalis siquidem est, & quamdiu hic viuit, tot ærumnis & fortunæ casibus obnoxius, ut arenas citius quàm, quæ humano generi incidunt, calamitates numeraueris. Propria homini sunt ob innatam naturæ nostræ corruptionem, stultitia, qua excæcatus non percipit ea quæ sunt spiritus Dei. 1.Cor.2. Mendacium, quo & seducit & seducitur. Psal.116. Peccatum, quod omnes nos iræ filios, & æternę mortis reos facit. Rom.3. Tenebrę excæcationis & vertiginis, quas & diligit, ne ipsius opera praua arguantur. Ioan.3. Infirmitas carnis, quæ nec peccati illecebris for-titer resistere, nec huius pœnas patienter ferre potest. Ignominia & dedecus sempiternum, si iustitiæ suę potius seueritatem, quàm clementiæ facilitatem Deus sequi velit. Quis ergo non stupore dignam censebit eam bonitatem Dei, quæ ipsum, ut ad tam infelices creaturę communionem sese demittat, nosq; non amicorum modò, verumetiā filiorum & hęredum loco habeat, cōmouet. Clementię singularis laude principes ferunt, qui subditos vel salutare, vel familiarius alloqui dignantur. Sed nihil vel in vulgari homine, imò non in parente quidem, fingi poterit, quod non hęc Dei bonitas longè superet.
units.tr: First, the persons are set forth, God and man, which, when set side by side, bring an admirable light to this consideration of divine goodness. God, as to his essence, is eternal, immortal, incorruptible, and established beyond all the fortune of this world. His attributes and properties are that he is eternal wisdom, infallible truth, perfect justice, unapproachable light, invincible power, ineffable glory and immense majesty. If you compare man with these, you will see him as far at odds with God as white differs from black. For as to the essence of man, he is a creature, having a beginning and an end; he is indeed mortal, and as long as he lives here he is subject to so many troubles and the chances of fortune that you could count the calamities that befall the human race more quickly than the grains of sand. The properties of man, because of the innate corruption of our nature, are: folly, by which, blinded, he does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2); lying, by which he both deceives and is deceived (Ps. 116); sin, which makes us all children of wrath and guilty of eternal death (Rom. 3); the darkness of blindness and giddiness, which he also loves, lest his evil works be exposed (John 3); the weakness of the flesh, which can neither bravely resist the allurements of sin nor patiently bear its punishments; and everlasting shame and disgrace, if God should wish to follow the severity of his justice rather than the kindness of his clemency. Who, then, will not judge that the goodness of God is worthy of astonishment, which stirs him to lower himself to fellowship with creatures so unhappy, and to hold us not only in the place of friends, but of sons and heirs? Princes are praised for singular clemency when they deign to address their subjects, whether in greeting or in a more familiar way. But nothing can be imagined, either in an ordinary man or indeed in a parent, which this goodness of God does not far surpass.

units.la: Secundò medium inspiciendū venit, per quod eò dignitatis euecti sumus. Quia verò est hominis conditio, qualem modò descripsimus, nihil certè in ipso inuenies, quod eum in tam altum dignitatis gradū extollere possit. Hic ergo Christus prodit, unigenitus ille & dilectus Dei filius, patri coæternus, consubstantialis & coæqualis per omnia. Quia enim quoad nos, omnis & salus & salutis spes amissa erat, hunc hominem ex Maria virgine nasci, & fratrem nostrum fieri Deus voluit: ut sic nostram causam suscipere, nosq; cōfratres suos, Dei filios & hæredes facere posset. Nec enim aliud erat medium, quod hoc præstaret. Solus Christus is est, qui fide apprehensus nos sibi ita unit, vt nos in ipso simus, & ipse in nobis. Ioah. 6. & 15. Et huc referri debent, quae Ioan. 1. legi-mus: In sua venit, & sui eum non receperunt. Quotquot autem receperunt eum, dedit eis, vt licer ret filios Dei fieri: videlicet his, qui crediderunt in nomen ipsius. An vero Deum patrem filio suo tam iniquum putabimus, vt huius incarnatione & morte nos saluare, & in filiorum numerum ac censere voluerit, si vlla alia superesset eius dignitatis consequendae ratio? Quis ergo hanc Dei er ga nos beneficentiam satis admirabitur? Laudantur, & merito quidem, qui aere suo captiuos vel ex carceribus vel e triremibus redimunt, & in libertatem asserunt: cum ijdem fere in eo beneficen tiae gradu quiescant, nec bonorum suorum haeredes faciant, quos semel redemerunt. At Deus non auro & argento, corruptibilibus bonis, sed sanguine filij sui nos redimere dignatus est. 1. Pet. 1. Nec hic quieuit ipsius beneficentia, sed redemptos filij sui consortes & coheredes esse voluit.
units.tr: Second, the means must be considered, through which we have been raised to so high a dignity. But since man's condition is such as we have just described, you will certainly find nothing in him that could lift him to so high a degree of dignity. Here, therefore, Christ appears, that only-begotten and beloved Son of God, co-eternal with the Father, consubstantial and co-equal in all things. For since, as far as we are concerned, all our salvation and hope of salvation was lost, God willed that this man should be born of the Virgin Mary and become our brother, so that he might thus take up our cause and make us his co-brethren, sons and heirs of God. For there was no other means that could accomplish this. Christ alone is the one who, apprehended by faith, so unites us to himself that we are in him and he in us (John 6 and 15). And to this must be referred what we read in John 1: He came to his own, and his own did not receive him. But as many as received him, to them he gave the power to become sons of God, namely to those who believed in his name. Shall we indeed think God the Father so unjust toward his Son that he would not have willed to save us through his incarnation and death, and to enrol us in the number of his sons, if any other way of attaining this dignity had remained? Who, then, will sufficiently marvel at this beneficence of God toward us? Men are praised, and rightly so, who with their money redeem captives from prisons or from galleys and set them at liberty; yet these same men usually stop at this degree of beneficence and do not make heirs of their goods those whom they once redeemed. But God has deigned to redeem us not with gold and silver, corruptible goods, but with the blood of his Son (1 Pet. 1). Nor did his beneficence rest here, but he willed that those redeemed should be fellow-heirs and co-heirs with his Son.

units.la: Tertio causam efficientem huius rei confyderafse iuuabit. Hic enim humana ratio, Deu vel nostrae opis indigum, vel nostris meritis prouocatu fuisse putabit, vt tanta in nos beneficia confer-re voluerit. Sed Ioannes vnica charitatis voce vtrumq; negat. Videte (inquit) quantam charitatem nobis dederit Deus. Charitatem dedit, non retributionem accepti a nobis beneficij. Eadem enim verba ipse infra exponet, dicens: In hoc est charitas Dei, non quod nos dilexerimus Deum, sed quod ipse dilexerit nos, & misit filiu suum, &c. 1. Ioan. 4. In eandem sententiam & Christus loquitur: Sic Deus dilexit mundu, vt filium suum vnigenitu traderet, &c. Ioa 3. Et ideo MVNDI vocabulo (quod plerunq; in mala partem sumitur) vti voluit, vt merá diuinae gratiae bonitatem assereret. Eodem faciunt, quae a temporis circumstantia, imo ab aeternitate, in huius causae assertio nem argumenta proferuntur. Nam Petrus Apostolus, Christum antequa mundus hic conditus esset, prae ordinatu fuisse dicit, vt ipsius merito redempti filij Dei efficeremur. 1. Petr. 1. Et Paulus nos priusquam mundi fundamenta iacerentur, electos scribit. Ephes. 1. Nec est quod dicamus, Deu prae uidisse quales futuri eramus, & meritis, quae praeuidebat, hanc gratia ab aeterno praeparauisse. Contra has enim argutias & superbas philautie nostre ratiocinationes omnis scriptura coclamat. Isaias dicit: Omnes tanqua ouis errauimus. Isa. 53. Dauid se in peccatis conceptum & genitum fatetur. Psal. 51. Deus figmenta cordis humani ab ineunte aetate praua esse, testatur. Gene. 8. Solomon iustum in die septies labi, affirmat. Prou. 24. Paulus, Omnes (inquit) peccauerunt, ac destituuntur gloria Dei. Iustificantur autem gratis per illius gratiam, per redemptionem, quae est in Christo Iesu, &c. Rom. 3. Item, Conclusit Deus omnia sub incredulitatem, vt omnium misereretur, Rom. 11. Si ergo gratis iustificamur, non vtiq; ex merito. Nec enim meritum cum gratia conuenire potest. Si item nostri miseretur Deus, non est in nobis, quo iustitiae ipsius rigorem emollire & grati am demereri possimus. Omnis igitur hic euertitur nostrorum meritorum & operum fiducia, vt ne cestario cu sanctis orare cogamur: Domine: ne intres in ius cum seruo tuo: quoniam coram te non iustificabitur omnis caro. Psal. 143. Haec est immensa illa Dei charitas, in cuius consyderationem Ioannes nos abripit, tantam innuens, vt nullis humani ingenij viribus satis inuestigari, nec vllis hominum linguis pro merito praedicari posit: quae & sola nostrae salutis origo est & colophon.
units.tr: Thirdly, it will help to consider the efficient cause of this matter. Human reason would suppose that God, who lacks nothing from us, or who was moved by our merits, wished to confer such great benefits upon us. But John denies both with a single word of love: "See," he says, "what love God has given us." He gave love; he did not give a return for a benefit received from us. For John himself explains the same words later on, saying: "In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son," etc. (1 John 4.) Christ speaks to the same effect: "God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son," etc. (John 3.) And so he chose the word WORLD (which is usually taken in a bad sense) in order to assert the pure goodness of divine grace. Arguments drawn from the circumstance of time, indeed from eternity, in support of this cause point the same way. For the Apostle Peter says that Christ was foreordained before the world was made, so that we might become children of God through his merit redeemed (1 Pet. 1). And Paul writes that we were chosen before the foundations of the world were laid (Eph. 1). Nor can we say that God foresaw what kind of people we would be, and prepared this grace from eternity on account of the merits he foresaw. For all Scripture cries out against these subtleties and against the proud reasonings of our self-love. Isaiah says: "We all went astray like sheep" (Isa. 53). David confesses that he was conceived and born in sins (Ps. 51). God testifies that the imaginations of the human heart are evil from youth (Gen. 8). Solomon affirms that the just man falls seven times a day (Prov. 24). Paul: "All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God; but they are justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus," etc. (Rom. 3). Likewise: "God has shut up all under unbelief, that he might have mercy on all" (Rom. 11). If, then, we are justified freely, it is certainly not by merit. For merit cannot agree with grace. Likewise, if God has mercy on us, there is nothing in us by which we might soften the rigour of his justice and earn his favour. All trust in our merits and works is therefore overthrown here, so that we are compelled to pray with the saints: "Lord, enter not into judgment with your servant, for in your sight no flesh will be justified" (Ps. 143). This is that immense love of God, into the contemplation of which John carries us, indicating it to be so great that it can be sufficiently searched out by no powers of human intellect, nor praised as it deserves by any human tongue; and it is both the sole origin and the crown of our salvation.

units.la: Sed quorsum (inquis) tâ diligens gratiæ & bonitatis Dei consyderatio feruit? Magni & salutares huius fructus sunt. Nam praetequam superbam noftrarū virium & meritorum fiducia noce tissimum salutis nostrae impedimentu, reprimit, praesenti etiā Ioannis instituto mire cōuenit. Primo enim officij nostri nos admonet, & studiu excitat obedientiae, qua Deo, qui ita dilexit nos, placere posimus. Sed de hoc postea suo loco dicetur. Deinde, consolatione affert admirabilem, quae sola omnes mundi molestias leuare, & animos in desperationis praecipitiū vergentes, reuocare potest. Si enim filios suos nos fecit Deus, seq; patre noftrū profitetur, vtiq; nostri memor esse & nostri cura gerere vult, quod patres fidos maximè decet. Testatur hoc ipse de se apud prophetam dicēs: Num obliuioni tradit mulier infante fuū, quo minus miseretur filij vteri sui? Sed esto, obliuiscantur illae, ego tamen tui non obliuiscar. Ecce in manib. istis ambabus insculpsi te, &c. Ifa. 49. Hoc ergo nobis in animo ob oculos versetur, quoties vel propter paupertate, vel morborū pertinaces & diutinos dolores, vel infamē contemptū & dedecus, vel exiliū, vel conscientiae horribiles tétationes, vel alia quaecūq; nos vexāt aduersa, de Dei in nos beneuolētia dubitare incipimus. Sic enī vna hęc Apostoli sententia plus cōsolationis afferet, qꝯ oīs totius mūdi maiestas polliceri queat.
units.tr: But (you ask) to what purpose does such a diligent consideration of the grace and goodness of God serve? Its fruits are great and salutary. For, apart from the fact that it restrains the proud trust in our own strength and merits, which is a most harmful impediment to our salvation, it also fits remarkably well with John's present purpose. For first, it reminds us of our duty and stirs up a zeal for obedience, by which we may please God, who has so loved us. But this will be said about later in its proper place. Second, it brings an admirable consolation, which alone can lift all the troubles of the world and recall minds that are tending toward the precipice of despair. For if God has made us his sons, and professes himself our Father, then certainly he wishes to be mindful of us and to take care of us, as faithful fathers ought most of all to do. He himself testifies to this concerning himself through the prophet, saying: "Can a woman forget her infant, so as not to have compassion on the son of her womb? But even if those women forget, yet I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you on both of my hands," etc. (Isa. 49). Let this therefore be kept in mind and before our eyes whenever, either because of poverty, or the stubborn and lasting pains of diseases, or infamous contempt and disgrace, or exile, or the dreadful temptations of conscience, or whatever other adversities harass us, we begin to doubt God's goodwill toward us. For this single saying of the Apostle will bring more consolation than all the majesty of the whole world could promise.

units.la: Sed obijciat hic aliquis: Si filij Dei sumus, & pro talibus agnoscit pater, cur non idem ille effi cit, vt totus mundus nos tales esse intelligat? Cur permittit, vt tanquam hostes Dei & ecclesiae i-psius desertores contemnamur & conuitijs omnium proscindamur? Cur nos omni malorū gene re ab impijs peti & obrui patitur? Est haec frequens admodū tentatio, quę ob carnis infirmitatem multum negotij facit infirmis adhuc & simplicioribus. Ea enim carnis natura est, vt ex praesenti-bus rebus veritatis fidei & salutis aeternae argumenta petat: quare non potest non vehementer offendi, si videat ijs, qui fidem in Christū profitentur, & euangelicæ doctrinæ sese regendos præbuerūt, omnia aduersa cōtingere. Huic igitur offendiculo in sequentibus Ioānes occurrit dicēs:
units.tr: But let someone object here: If we are sons of God, and the Father acknowledges us as such, why does he not also bring it about that the whole world understands us to be such? Why does he permit us to be despised as enemies of God and deserters of his Church, and to be torn apart by the reproaches of all? Why does he allow us to be attacked and overwhelmed by the impious with every kind of evil? This is a very frequent temptation, which, on account of the weakness of the flesh, causes much trouble for the weak and rather simple. For it is the nature of the flesh to seek proofs of the truth of the faith and of eternal salvation from present circumstances; hence it cannot but be greatly offended if it sees that all adversity befalls those who profess faith in Christ and have submitted themselves to be guided by the evangelical doctrine. John therefore meets this stumbling-block in what follows, saying:

units.la: II. Propter hoc mundus non novit vos, quia non novit eum. Charissimi, nunc filij Dei sumus, & nondum innotuit, quod futuri sumus. Scimus autem quòd cum apparuerit, ipsi similes erimus: quoniam videbimus eum sicuti est. Duobus argumentis hic vtitur Apostolus, quorum alterum à mundi ingenio, alterum ex futura fidelium Christi conditione desumit. Prioris sensus est: Si mundus hic Deū noscet, vtique & vos novissetis huius esse filios. Sed mundus hic Deū ignorat. Licet enim eius cognitione glorietur, Dei nomen frequenter in ore habeat, vana tamen est omnis hæc gloriatio, quia Christum nō amplectitur, sine quo nemo venit ad patrem. Ioan.14. Fieri ergo nequit, vt vos pro Dei filijs agnoscat & reuereatur. Potest etiā aliud ex his argumentū duci, ad hunc modū. Mundus eos novit, id est, obseruat, amat & magnificat, qui de mundo sunt, & eius studia sequūtur. Vos de mundo non estis, sed Christus de mundo selectos patri suo, ceu obedientes filios, consecrauit. Ioan.15. Ergo mundus hic vos nec amare nec magni facere potest. Adde his & tertiū. Mundus hic veritatis lucem odit, quia opera eius mala sunt, nec eos ferre potest, qui vt hæc luceat authores sunt. Ioan.3. Ergo nec vos ferre vnquā poterit. Obseruemus in his diligēter, quid pij & fideles, dū hic viuunt, de mundo sibi polliceri debeant. Crucem nimirū perpetuā, & assiduos omnis generis aduersitatū fluctus. Christus enim inquit: Si quis vult post me venire, abneget semetipsum, tollat crucem suam, & sequatur me. Matth.16. Alibi item: In mūdo afflictione habebitis, Ioan.16. Rursus: Si me persecuti sunt, & vos persequentur. Ioan.15. Quorū probè memor Paulus, ait: Omnes, qui volūt piè viuere in Christo Iesu, persecutione patientur. 2. Tim.3. Quid ergo ô fratres offendimur, quando ea eueniunt, quæ Christus nobis euentura prædixit? Etenim stultissimi sunt mortalium, qui Christianam fidem & religionem profesi, Cruce & aduersis offenduntur, quos Christus suorum indiuulsos comites esse voluit. Quin potius ad exempla sanctissimorum hominum respicimus, qui iam olim similibus casibus sunt exercitati. Primus ex Adamo natus Dei cultor fraterni odij sæuitiā & parricidales manus expertus est. Quid Noe, quid Abraham, quid Lot, quid Isaac, Iacobus & reliqui fideles perpesi sint, partim historia sacra docet, partim ex illorum temporū conditione & impurissimarum gentiū, quibus cōuersati sunt, corruptissimis moribus facilè conijci potest. An ergo nostram conditionē illorum præstantiorem esse volumus? Memi-nerimus nos Dei filios & hæredes, hostes vero nostros duntaxat diuinæ irę seruos, & iudiciorū Dei, quæ carnis nostræ infirmitas meretur, executores esse. Sæuiūt interdum in heriles filios nequam serui. Sed vbi hero visum fuerit, eijciuntur domo, cum filijs integra reposita sit totius patrimonij hereditas. Ideo Paulus pijs & fidelibus hoc quasi proprium tribuit, quòd in afflictionibus quoque glorientur. Rom.5. Et ipse non in excellentia reuelationum alijsque donis, quæ mundo quoque præclara videntur, sed in infirmitate & aduersis, pro Christo exhaustis, gloriari solet. 2. Cor.11. & 12. Qui hoc facere norunt, eos nulla mūdi infamia ex fidei gradu unquā deijcere poterit.
units.tr: II. For this reason the world does not know you, because it did not know him. Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet been made known what we shall be. But we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. The Apostle uses two arguments here: one he draws from the disposition of the world, the other from the future condition of the faithful in Christ. The sense of the first is this: If this world knew God, certainly you too would have been known to be his children. But this world is ignorant of God. For although it boasts of its knowledge, often has the name of God on its lips, yet all this boasting is empty, because it does not embrace Christ, without whom no one comes to the Father (John 14). Therefore it cannot be that it should acknowledge and reverence you as children of God. Another argument may also be drawn from these words, in this way: The world knows, that is, favours, loves and magnifies, those who are of the world and follow its pursuits. You are not of the world, but Christ has set you apart from the world as obedient sons to his Father (John 15). Therefore this world can neither love you nor hold you in esteem. Add to these a third: this world hates the light of truth, because its works are evil, and it cannot bear those who are the authors of that light to shine (John 3). Therefore it will never be able to bear you either. Let us observe carefully from these things what the pious and faithful ought to expect from the world while they live here: namely, a perpetual cross and constant waves of adversity of every kind. For Christ says: "If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me" (Matt. 16). Elsewhere likewise: "In the world you will have affliction" (John 16). Again: "If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you" (John 15). Paul, well mindful of this, says: "All who wish to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution" (2 Tim. 3). Why then, brothers, are we offended when those things happen which Christ foretold would happen to us? Indeed, the most foolish of mortals are those who, professing the Christian faith and religion, are offended by the cross and by adversities, when Christ wished his own to be inseparable companions. Rather, let us look to the examples of the most holy men, who long ago were exercised in similar trials. The first man born of Adam, a worshipper of God, experienced the savagery of brotherly hatred and the murderous hand of a parricide. What Noah, what Abraham, what Lot, what Isaac, Jacob and the other faithful endured, sacred history teaches in part, and in part it can easily be inferred from the conditions of those times and from the most corrupt morals of the most impure nations among whom they lived. Do we then wish our condition to be more excellent than theirs? Let us remember that we are sons and heirs of God, but that our enemies are only servants of the divine wrath, and executors of the judgments of God which the weakness of our flesh deserves. Wicked servants sometimes rage against the sons of their master. But when it seems good to the master, they are cast out of the house, while the inheritance of the whole patrimony remains reserved intact for the sons. Therefore Paul attributes this as something peculiar to the pious and faithful, that they glory even in afflictions (Rom. 5). And he himself is wont to glory not in the excellence of revelations or other gifts, which seem splendid even to the world, but in weakness and adversities endured for Christ (2 Cor. 11 and 12). Those who know how to do this, no infamy of the world will ever be able to thrust down from the rank of faith.

units.la: Alterum argumentū à futura fidelium conditione desumptū sic enunciat: Charissimi, nunc filij Dei sumus, & nondum innotuit quod futuri sumus. Scimus autem quòd cū apparuerit, ipsi similes erimus, quoniam videbimus eum sicuti est. Ratio argumenti talis videtur. Quicunq; sta-bilem felicitatem & immarcescibilem gloriam sibi repositam norunt certò, præsentis vitæ incerta & instabili fortuna minimè affici vel concuti decet. Atqui nos scimus quàm ampla conditio, quæ gloria & felicitas in Christi aduentu parata sit. Quid ergo ob huius seculi aduersa de patris erga nos voluntate dubitamus? Cæterum quod paucis dici poterat, propter consolationem nostram paulò fusius explicat. Charissimi (inquit) iam nunc filij Dei sumus. Quasi dicat: Non ex incerta spe pendemus, nec dubia est nostræ salutis conditio. Ad hæc non expectandum nobis, quando post molestam diuini temporis moram à Deo in filiorū locum adoptemur. Sed iam nūc Dei filij reuera sumus. Quòd autem nec mundus tales agnoscit, nec nostræ carni id semper persuadetur, hinc est, quòd nondū innotuit publicè ea, quæ nos sub Christi aduentum manet, gloria. Interea certò scimus nos, quæ illa futura sit. Nam Christo similes reddemur, qui (vt Paulus ait) transfigurabit corpus nostrū humile, vt cōforme reddat corpori suo gloriosō, secundū potentiā, qua potest sibi subijcere omnia. Phil.3. Coprehendit verò hac locutione Ioānes, quæcūq; ad corporū & animarū perpetuam felicitatē spectāt. Vt enim Christus in morte nō mansit, sed tertio die resuscitatus est: ita nec nos à morte æternum detinebimur, sed virtute resurrectionis Christi resurgemus & nos. Vt Christus illo ipso corpore, quo in Cruce pro mundi peccatis oblatus & acer bos mortis dolores perpessus est, resurrexit, clarificato tamen & ab omni corruptibilitate libero: ita & hæc nostra corpora, quæ modò esuriunt, sitiunt, algent, laborant, & infinitis periculis vndi-que imminentibus subiacent, resuscitabuntur, sed clarificatione excoēta[?], quæ omnem ex peccato corporibus obortam molestiam absorbet. De hac Paulus scribes inquit: Seminatur in corruptio-ne, resurgit in incorruptibilitate: seminatur in ignominia, resurgit in gloria: seminatur in infirmi-tate, resurgit in potentia. Item: Oportet corruptibile hoc induere incorruptibilitatem, & mortale hoc induere immortalitatem. 1.Corinth.15. Præterea vt Christus nunc in gloria patris sedens re-gnat, nec regni eius erit finis: ita fideles eiusdem cum illo gloriæ & regni consortes cernetur. Ipse enim dixit: Vado paraturus vobis locum. Iterum veniam, & assumam vos ad meipsum, vt vbi ego sum, & vos sitis. Ioan.14. Et alibi: Ego dispono vobis sicut disposuit mihi pater meus regnum, vt edatis & bibatis super mensam meam in regno meo. Luc.22. Item: Pater, quos dedisti mihi, volo vt vbi sum ego, & illi sint mecum, &c.Ioan.17. Non ergo Apostoli Ioannis, sed Christi verba agno-scamus, quibus hæc nobis promittuntur. Sed addit & causam huius glorificationis nostræ: Quia videbimus eum sicuti est. Videbunt & impij Deum in iudicio. Videbunt Christum, in quem pu-pugerunt.Ioan.19. Sed quia conscientiæ terroribus illos concutiet tam seueri iudicis iustitia, non inde gloriam & gaudium, sed confusionem & dolorem reportabunt. Pij vero patrem cernent, pa-terni pectoris largissimas indulgentias experientur, conscientiæ fiducia erigentur, & ita in cõspe-ctu Dei stabunt semper, in quo est satietas gaudiorum perpetuò.Psal.16.
units.tr: Next, John sets out a second argument, drawn from the future condition of believers: "Beloved, now we are the sons of God, and it has not yet been made known what we shall be. But we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, since we shall see him as he is." The reasoning of this argument seems to be this. Those who know with certainty that a stable happiness and an unfading glory are laid up for them ought not to be affected or shaken by the uncertain and unstable fortune of the present life. But we know how great the condition is, and what glory and happiness is prepared at the coming of Christ. Why, then, do we doubt the Father's will towards us because of the adversities of this age? Moreover, what could have been said in a few words, he explains at somewhat greater length for our consolation. "Beloved," he says, "we are now the sons of God." As if he said: We do not hang on an uncertain hope, nor is the state of our salvation doubtful. Nor must we wait for the time when, after a tedious delay of God's time, we shall be adopted by God into the place of sons. Rather, we are already truly the sons of God. But that neither the world acknowledges such people, nor is this always persuaded to our flesh, is why the glory which awaits us at the coming of Christ has not yet been made publicly known. Meanwhile we know for certain what that glory will be. For we shall be made like Christ, who (as Paul says) "will transform our lowly body, that it may be made conformable to his glorious body, according to the working by which he is able to subject all things to himself." Phil. 3. Moreover, by this expression John comprehends whatever pertains to the perpetual happiness of both body and soul. For as Christ did not remain in death but was raised on the third day, so neither shall we be held by death for ever, but we too shall rise by the power of Christ's resurrection. As Christ rose in that same body in which he was offered on the Cross for the sins of the world and suffered the bitter pains of death, yet clarified and free from all corruptibility, so also these bodies of ours, which now hunger, thirst, grow cold, labour, and lie open to infinite dangers threatening on every side, will be raised, but with a clarification that swallows up all the discomfort that has arisen for bodies from sin. Of this Paul writes: "It is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption; it is sown in dishonour, it is raised in glory; it is sown in weakness, it is raised in power." Likewise: "This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality." 1 Cor. 15. Furthermore, as Christ now sits in the glory of the Father and reigns, and of his kingdom there will be no end, so the faithful shall be seen to be partners of the same glory and kingdom with him. For he himself said: "I go to prepare a place for you. I will come again and take you to myself, that where I am, you may be also." John 14. And elsewhere: "I appoint to you, as my Father has appointed to me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom." Luke 22. Likewise: "Father, those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me," etc. John 17. Let us therefore acknowledge these words as the words of Christ, by which these things are promised to us, rather than the words of the Apostle John. But he also adds the cause of this glorification of ours: "Because we shall see him as he is." The wicked too will see God in judgement; they will see Christ, whom they pierced. John 19. But since the justice of so severe a judge will shake them with terrors of conscience, they will bear away from it not glory and joy but confusion and sorrow. The godly, however, will see the Father; they will experience the most abundant indulgences of a fatherly heart, they will be lifted up by the confidence of a good conscience, and so they will stand always in the presence of God, in whom is fullness of joys for evermore. Ps. 16.

units.la: Vnde verò hæc Ioanni fiducia, quòd hæc tam constanter affirmat? Quòd non credendi aut sperandi, sed sciendi verbo vtitur. Scimus, inquit, quòd ei similes erimus. Operatur hoc in animis fidelium spiritus Christi, qui arrhabo salutis & adoptionis nostræ, indesinenter in animis nostris nos Dei filios esse testatur. Plura de hoc apud Paulum videre est. Ephef.1.2.Cor.1. & 5. Rom.8. Gal.4. Et est hæc magna fidei & salutis nostræ tam certitudo quàm gloria, quòd non nostris opi-nionibus, non hominum stipulationibus, non angelorum promissis, sed ipsius spiritus sancti testi-monio intra animos nostros obsignatur.
units.tr: Whence, then, does John have this confidence, that he affirms these things so constantly? It is because he uses the word not of believing or hoping but of knowing. "We know," he says, "that we shall be like him." The Spirit of Christ, who is the pledge of our salvation and adoption, works this in the hearts of the faithful, continually testifying in our hearts that we are the sons of God. Much more on this may be seen in Paul: Eph. 1; 2 Cor. 1 and 5; Rom. 8; Gal. 4. And this certainty, as much as the glory, of our faith and salvation is great, because it is sealed within our hearts not by our opinions, not by the stipulations of men, not by the promises of angels, but by the testimony of the Holy Spirit himself.

units.la: Cęterum, quod huius loci caput est, probè obseruemus: vt de nostra & omnium fideliū Chri-sti fide & beatitudine, non ex præsentis vitæ conditione, sed præparata illis in futuro seculo glo-ria iudicare discamus. Incredibile di-ctu, quantum hic erretur cæco hominum iudicio, qui dum præsentis vitæ commoda vnicè quærunt, ex eius conditione de fide & religione pronunciant. At si eius iudicij aliqua debet esse authoritas, iam nemo erit sanctorum, quotquot à prima mūdi hu-ius origine extiterunt, quem non damnari oporteat. Imò nec ipse Christus sententiam hanc tam præcipitem effugere poterit. Is enim post infinitos labores & horrenda pericula in crucem inter latrones medius affixus est, vt iuxta prophetæ sententiam ex eorum numero videri posset, qui di-uino iudicio damnati scelerum pœnas exoluunt.Isa.53. Cogitemus igitur in cœlis patriâ nostram esse, in qua cœlestis hæreditatis thesauri nobis repositi sunt, quos nulla fortunæ iniquitas, nulla diaboli ferocia, nulla etiam principum tyrannis eripere poterit. Cogitemus aliud superesse iudi-cium, ad quod filius Dei in gloria patris venturus palàm monstrabit, quantum discrimen sit in-ter iustum & iniustum, contemptorem Dei & eiusdem fidum cultoré.Malach.3. Cogitemus mi-rabilem rerum vicissitudinem, quam tunc videbimus. Qui enim hic propter Christum & veritā-tis studium afflicti sunt, pro filijs Dei dilectis agnoscentur: confusi autem & reprobi stabunt, qui totius mundi fauore & applausu muniti, illos persequi ausi fuerunt. Lege in libro Sapientiæ cap.5. & plenam huius retaliationis cognitionem auferes. In hanc qui animi oculos conferunt, & de aliorum conditione iudicaturi illorum fidem ex verbo Dei æstimant, nunquam fallentur, vtvt mundus hic sursum & deorsum perturbet. Sed statum huius loci videamus, quem omnibus istis infert ad hunc modum.
units.tr: Moreover, what is the chief point of this passage we should carefully observe: that we may learn to judge concerning our own and all the faithful's faith and blessedness in Christ, not from the condition of the present life, but from the glory prepared for them in the future age. It is incredible to say how greatly people go wrong through the blind judgement of men, who, while they seek only the advantages of the present life, pronounce upon faith and religion from its condition. But if any authority ought to belong to that judgement, then there will be no one of the saints, as many as have existed from the first origin of this world, whom it would not be necessary to condemn. Indeed, not even Christ himself could escape this so hasty sentence. For after endless labours and dreadful dangers, he was fixed to the cross between thieves, so that according to the prophet's saying he could be seen to be among the number of those who, condemned by divine judgement, pay the penalties of their crimes. Isa. 53. Let us therefore consider that our homeland is in heaven, in which the treasures of a heavenly inheritance are laid up for us, which no unfairness of fortune, no ferocity of the devil, and not even the tyranny of princes will be able to snatch away. Let us consider that another judgement remains, to which the Son of God, coming in the glory of the Father, will openly show how great a difference there is between the just and the unjust, the despiser of God and his faithful worshipper. Mal. 3. Let us consider the wonderful reversal of things which we shall then see. For those who here are afflicted for Christ's sake and for zeal for the truth will be acknowledged as beloved sons of God; but those who, fortified by the favour and applause of the whole world, dared to persecute them will stand confused and rejected. Read in the Book of Wisdom, chapter 5, and you will take away a full knowledge of this retribution. Those who turn the eyes of their mind to this, and who, about to judge the condition of others, estimate their faith by the word of God, will never be deceived, however much this world may be thrown into confusion, up and down. But let us see the state of this passage, which he brings to bear on all these things in the following manner.

units.la: III. Et omnis, qui habet hanc spem in ipsum, purificat se, sicut & ille purus est. A fidei ingenio argumentum ducens fideles sui officij admonet. Ingenium fidei est, ei se quoad fieri potest, con-formem reddere, cui nititur. Nititur autem vni Deo, qui purus, immaculatus & sanctus est. Puri-ficationi ergo, sanctificationi ac innocetiæ & ipsa studet. Potest etiam à fine vel præmio fidelium argumentum formari, vt præcedentibus sic cohæreat: Quicunq; olim in glorioso Christi aduen-tu Dei similes fieri cupiunt, eos dum hic viuunt, Deo se conformes facere oportet. Impossibile e-nim est vt ad Dei similitudinem vnquam pertingamus, nisi eius studium in hac vita suscipiamus, quando defunctis nulla superest quicquam operandi occasio. Hic ergo purificationis nostræ ini-tium faciamus, vt coram Deo puro & sancto in die iudicij subsistere possimus. Nihil vero hic exi-git Ioannes, quàm quod vnanimi totius scripturæ consensu præscribitur. Fœderis cum Abraha-mo facti caput est: Ego sum Deus omni sufficiens: ambula coram me, & esto integer.Gene.17. In lege idem dominus dicit: Sancti estote, quia ego sanctus sum Dominus Deus vester.Leuit.19. & 20.&c. Eodem totus Psalmus 15.referri debet, hanc ipsam felicitatis consequendæ viam common strans. Et apud prophetam spiritus sanctus clamat: Quis ex nobis habitabit cum igne devorante? Quis habitabit cum ardoribus æternis? Qui ambulat in iustitijs, & loquitur quæ recta sunt: qui abhorret ab emolumento per vim & calumniam quæsito, qui excutit manus suas, ne munus contrectent: qui aures suas obturat, ne audiat sanguines: & oculos suos comprimit, ne intueatur malum. Isa. 33. Atqui omnibus istis veram sanctimoniâ & puritatem vitæ quasi per partes vel species describit. Huc dictum Christi pertinet: Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt. Matt. 5. Et alibi pedes, id est, affectus carnis, quibus ceu pedibus in viam malitiæ & impuritatis ferimur, abluere docet. Ioan. 13. Ad eundem modum D. Paulus scribit: Hæc est voluntas Dei, sanctificatio vestra, ut abstineatis à fornicatione, & sciat unusquisque vestrum vas possidere cum sanctificatione & honore, non cum affectu concupiscentiæ, quemadmodum gentes, quæ non noverunt Deum. 1. Thess. 4. Sed tempus me deficeret, si omnes locos, qui sanctificationis & puritatis studium nobis commendant, recensere vellem. Illud observasse sufficiat, non posse leviculum & nullius momenti esse, quod tot ac tam diligentibus utriusq; scripturæ testimonijs non modo commendatur, sed ut supremè necessarium exigitur. Consyderemus ergo diligenter, quæ ad purificationem istam pertinent.
units.tr: III. "And everyone who has this hope in him purifies himself, as he also is pure." From the nature of faith he draws an argument and reminds the faithful of their duty. It is the nature of faith to make itself conformable, as far as can be, to the one on whom it rests. But it rests on God alone, who is pure, unspotted and holy. It therefore also strives after purification, sanctification and innocence. The argument can also be framed from the end or reward of the faithful, so that it coheres with what precedes thus: Whoever desires in the future, at the glorious coming of Christ, to become like God, must make himself conformable to God while he lives here. For it is impossible that we ever attain to the likeness of God unless we take up his zeal in this life, since to the dead no opportunity of working remains. Let us therefore make a beginning of our purification here, so that we may be able to stand before the pure and holy God in the day of judgement. Yet John here demands nothing except what is prescribed by the unanimous consent of all Scripture. It is the heading of the covenant made with Abraham: "I am God all-sufficient; walk before me and be blameless." Gen. 17. In the Law the same Lord says: "Be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy." Lev. 19 and 20, etc. The whole of Psalm 15 must be referred to the same thing, showing this very way of attaining happiness. And in the prophet the Holy Spirit cries out: "Who among us will dwell with the devouring fire? Who will dwell with eternal burnings? He who walks in righteousnesses and speaks what is right; he who abhors gain gotten by force and calumny, who shakes his hands so that they do not handle a bribe; who stops his ears lest he hear blood, and closes his eyes lest he look upon evil." Isa. 33. Yet by all these things he describes true holiness and purity of life, as it were part by part or in its kinds. To this belongs the saying of Christ: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." Matt. 5. And elsewhere he teaches us to wash the feet, that is, the affections of the flesh, by which, as by feet, we are carried into the way of malice and impurity. John 13. In the same way Paul writes: "This is the will of God, your sanctification, that you abstain from fornication, and that each of you know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour, not in the affection of lust, like the Gentiles who do not know God." 1 Thess. 4. But time would fail me if I wished to recount all the passages which commend to us the zeal for sanctification and purity. It is enough to have observed this: that what is not only commended by so many and such diligent testimonies of both Scriptures, but is required as supremely necessary, cannot be trivial or of no moment. Let us therefore consider carefully what pertains to this purification.

units.la: Primùm, quid purificari oporteat, inquirendum erit. Ubi totus homo sese offert, qui quàtus est, pollutus & contaminatus est. De omnibus enim dicitur, quod de semetipso fatetur Dauid: Ecce in iniquitate formatus sum, & in peccato concepit me mater mea. Psal. 51. Ad omnes similiter pertinet, quod Deus ipse loquitur: Figmentum cordis humani malum est ab adolescentia sua. Gen. 8. Adde quòd apud prophetam pij clamant: Fuimus omnes nos veluti immundum, & tanquâ vestis centonum sordidorum omnes iustitiæ nostræ. Isa. 64. Omnibus enim naturaliter insidet & hæreditario primæ transgressionis iure adhæret totius naturæ corruptio. Excæcata peccati illecebris & mundi tenebris ratio nostra, non videt nec percipit ea quæ sunt spiritus Dei. 1. Cor. 2. Rationem corruptam non potest non sequi voluntas corruptissima, quam improbissimi affectus sic exagitant, ut ex nobis ipsis ne cogitare quidem possimus quod bonum est. 2. Cor. 3. An verò impura opera deesse possunt tam improbæ voluntati, cum tantæ nos undique circumstent malè operandi occasiones? Nullus hominis sensus est, qui non & provocetur ad peccandum quotidie, & peccet. Peccant oculi rerum huius mundi & illicitarum concupiscentia. Peccant aures vel voluptate audiendi quæ impura sunt, vel nimia patientia in ijs audiendis, quæ diuinæ gloriæ & honestati officiunt. Peccat gustus, totumque corpus helluationis & crapulæ mancipium reddit. Peccat tactus tot modis, quot sub cœlo hoc nobis offeruntur peccatorum species. Quæ ergo hic salutis & communionis cum Deo, spes esse poterit, nisi totus homo, quàtus est, purificetur? Huc ita-que, quæ alibi monemur, referri debent. Christus Nicodemo ait: Amen dico tibi, nisi quis natus fuerit è supernis, non potest videre regnum Dei. Ioan. 3. Eam igitur purificationem requirit, quæ totum hominem quasi regeneret, & novum vel alium faciat. Rursum idem Christus nostri abnegationem ijs necessariam dicit, qui ipsius discipuli haberi velint. Matt. 16. Et Paulus membra hæc terrestria mortificare, & depositò veteri homine novum nos induere iubet. Col. 3. Ephef. 4. Idem in Christi mortem sepultos cum eodem ad vitæ novitatem resuscitari vult. Rom. 6. Nihil itaque in se homo esse existimet, quod vel purum vel tolerabile coram Deo videri possit, sed se totum purificatione opus habere intelligat.
units.tr: First, we must inquire what needs to be purified. Here the whole man presents himself, who, however great he is, is polluted and contaminated. For what David confesses of himself is said of everyone: "Behold, I was formed in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me" (Ps. 51). Likewise, what God himself says pertains to all: "The imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth" (Gen. 8). Add that in the prophet the godly cry out: "We are all become as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags" (Isa. 64). For corruption of the whole nature naturally dwells in all, and clings to them by the hereditary right of the first transgression. Our reason, blinded by the allurements of sin and the darkness of the world, does not see or perceive the things of the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2). A corrupt reason cannot but be followed by a most corrupt will, which such wicked affections so stir up that of ourselves we cannot even think what is good (2 Cor. 3). Indeed, can impure works be lacking to so wicked a will, when such great occasions of doing evil surround us on every side? There is no human sense that is not provoked to sin daily, and does not sin. The eyes sin by the lust of the things of this world and of forbidden things. The ears sin, either by the pleasure of hearing what is impure, or by excessive patience in hearing those things which offend the divine glory and honour. The taste sins, and makes the whole body the slave of gluttony and drunkenness. The touch sins in as many ways as the kinds of sin that are offered to us under this heaven. What hope, then, of salvation and communion with God can there be here, unless the whole man, however great he is, is purified? Hence, those things which we are warned of elsewhere must be referred to this. Christ says to Nicodemus: "Verily, verily, I say unto thee, unless one is born from above, he cannot see the kingdom of God" (John 3). He therefore requires that purification which, as it were, regenerates the whole man and makes him new or other. Again, the same Christ says that self-denial is necessary for those who wish to be called his disciples (Matt. 16). And Paul bids us mortify these earthly members, put off the old man, and put on the new (Col. 3; Eph. 4). The same apostle wills that those buried with Christ in his death be raised with him to newness of life (Rom. 6). Let no one, then, think there is anything in himself which can seem either pure or tolerable before God, but let him understand that he has need of purification in his whole being.

units.la: Secundò purificationis huius fines aut modos, intra quos consistat, aut quousque progredi debeat, novisse oportet. Circumscribit hos Ioannes dicens: Purificet se, sicut & ille purus est. De Deo autè hic loquitur, cuius puritatem nostræ purificationis modū, limitè vel regulam esse vult. Sed ô difficilem, imò impossibilem modum. An verò carnis nostræ infirmitas ad hanc metā, tam à nobis remotam, ut nec oculis cerni, nec metis & ingenij acumine satis investigari possit, unquâm pertinget? Num homo impura carnis mole grauatus ad tam altum diuinæ puritatis gradū subuolabit? Nunquam profectò id fiet, utut vel meditando, vel operando sese conficiat. Cur ergo quod factu impossibile est, exigit dominus? Annon hoc modo de salute nos desperare cogit? Minimè gentium. Imò hoc nostræ saluti cumprimis seruit. Sic enim de nostris viribus & meritis desperare, & ad Dei gratiam, quæ sola per Christi meritum succurrit, confugere discimus. Confutantur ergo, qui ut primum vitæ puritatem & quæ ad hac spectant, exigi audiunt, ex operibus hominem iustificari & salvari clamant. Exigitur quidem puritas & innocetia, sed talis, ad quam nemo hominum unquam peruenire possit. Nemo igitur ex eadem iustificari poterit. Ad hæc studium purificationis indefessum & indefinens hæc diuinæ puritatis meta nobis commendat. Facilè hic delassatur caro nostra, & ut primùm aliquoufque se progressam videt, sibijpsi applaudit, & hunc profectum ad salutem sufficere credit. Sed quoad nos ab eius puritatis perfectione, quæ in Deo est, abesse videmus, tam diu nobis pergendum est. Et cum Paulo apostolo unum illud agamus, vt ea quæ à tergo sunt obliuiscentes, ad ea quæ à fronte sunt enitamur, & iuxta præfixũ signum assequamur palmam supernæ vocationis Dei per Iesum Christum. Philip.3.
units.tr: Second, we ought to know the limits or measures of this purification, within which it must stand, or how far it ought to advance. John sets these limits, saying: "Let him purify himself, even as he is pure" (1 John 3). But here he speaks of God, whose purity he wills to be the measure or rule of our purification. But oh, what a difficult, indeed impossible, measure! Will our frail flesh ever reach this goal, so remote from us that it can be neither seen by the eyes nor sufficiently investigated by the keenness of mind and wit? Will a man weighed down by the impure mass of the flesh fly up to such a high degree of divine purity? Certainly it will never happen, however much he prepares himself by meditating or by working. Why then does the Lord require what is impossible to do? Does he not, in this way, compel us to despair of salvation? By no means. Rather, this especially serves our salvation. For thus we learn to despair of our own strength and merits, and to flee to the grace of God, which alone helps through the merit of Christ. Those therefore are refuted who, as soon as they hear that purity and innocence of life, and what pertains to these, are required, cry out that man is justified and saved by works. Purity and innocence are indeed required, but such as no man can ever attain. No one, therefore, can be justified by them. Besides, this goal of divine purity commends to us an unwearied and unceasing zeal for purification. Our flesh is easily wearied here, and as soon as it sees itself advanced thus far, it applauds itself and believes this progress is sufficient for salvation. But as long as we see that we are far from that perfection of purity which is in God, we must press on. And with the apostle Paul let us do this one thing: forgetting the things which are behind, let us strive toward those which are before, and according to the set mark, pursue the prize of the heavenly calling of God through Jesus Christ (Phil. 3).

units.la: Postremò purificationis huius organum vel instrumentum habere conuenit. Atqui purifica-mur quidē à peccatis & omni corruptione merito sanguinis Christi. Sed hic de eo organo inqui-rendum, quod in nobis fit oportet, vt ad purificationē Christi pertingere possimus. Mõstrat hoc nobis D.Petrus Apostolus, qui de gentibus legis sarcina non grauandis loquens, fide corda illorū purificata esse dicit. Act.15. Fidem verò nominamus firmum illum & certum assensum, qui verbo Dei à nobis præbetur. Hac nos purificari multis argumentis constat. Primò enim per hanc solam Christum & meritum ipsius apprehedimus, in quo vno nostra iustitia, sanctificatio, satisfactio & redemptio consistit, 1.Cor.1. Qui enim in hunc credit, eidem insitus, omnium quę in hoc sunt bonorum consors redditur. Et vt extra hūc salus nulla est: ita nec purificatio aliqua esse potest, quæcunque non cum fide in hunc coniuncta fuerit. Præterea, fides hæc Dei verbo viuo & efficaci ni-titur, quod non viam modò purificationis monstrat, sed eiusdem studium accendit, & eandē pro sua natura operatur. Est enim acutus ille gladius, qui penetrat vsque ad diuisionem animæ simul & spiritus, compagumque & medullarum. Heb.4. Per hunc resecantur superfluæ affectuum no-strorum cogitationes. Hoc reprimitur luxurians cupiditatum seges. Eodem abscinduntur & ef-fodiuntur membra, quæ nobis sunt offendiculo. Mar.9. De hoc Christus loquitur, Apostolis di-cens: Iam vos mundi estis, propter sermonem, quem locutus sum vobis. Ioan.15. Adhæc fides cha-ritatem sibi perpetuò coniunctam habet, per quam efficax est & operatur, Gal.5. Nec enim fieri potest, vt non amet Deum, quicunque Christi beneficio ab hoc collato totus innititur. Quomo-do enim filij censebuntur qui patrem non amauerint? Malach.1. Quod si patrem diligimus, vtiq; & homines diligemus, quos apud illum tanto in pretio esse videmus, vt & filium suum vnigeni-tum pro illis dederit. At charitas legem implet, quod clarius est, quàm vt multa demonstratione opus habeat. Rom.13.1.Corinth.13.
units.tr: Lastly, it is fitting that this purification have an instrument or means. Yet we are indeed purified from sins and all corruption by the merit of the blood of Christ. But here we must inquire about that instrument which must be produced in us, so that we may be able to attain to the purification of Christ. The apostle Peter shows us this, who, speaking of the Gentiles, that they should not be burdened with the yoke of the law, says that their hearts were purified by faith (Acts 15). By faith we mean that firm and certain assent which is given by us to the Word of God. It is clear from many arguments that we are purified by this. For first, through this alone we lay hold of Christ and his merit, in whom alone our righteousness, sanctification, satisfaction and redemption consist (1 Cor. 1). For he who believes in him, being grafted into him, is made a partaker of all the good things that are in him. And just as there is no salvation outside him, so there can be no purification of any kind which is not joined with faith in him. Moreover, this faith rests upon the living and effective Word of God, which not only shows the way of purification but kindles the zeal for it, and works the same according to its own nature. For it is that sharp sword which penetrates even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow (Heb. 4). Through it the superfluous thoughts of our affections are cut away. By it the luxuriant crop of desires is restrained. By the same, the members which are a stumbling block to us are cut off and dug out (Mark 9). Of this Christ speaks, saying to the apostles: "Now you are clean, through the word which I have spoken to you" (John 15). Besides, faith always has charity joined to it, through which it is effective and works (Gal. 5). For it cannot be that he who wholly rests upon the benefit of Christ conferred on him should not love God. For how will they be counted sons who have not loved the father? (Mal. 1). And if we love the Father, we will surely love men also, whom we see to be of such great worth in his eyes that he gave his only-begotten Son for them. But charity fulfils the law, which is clearer than that it needs much demonstration (Rom. 13; 1 Cor. 13).

units.la: Habemus ergo hic fratres, in quibus & examinemus & exerceamus fidem nostram. Prodest hic multum diuinæ in nos bonitatis & beatitudinis, quę in cœlis nobis repositæ est, consyderatio: quæ facit, vt mundi de nobis iudicium susque deq; feramus. Interim annitendum nobis, vt puri-ficationis studio accensi, dum hic viuimus, quoad fieri potest, Deo sancto & puro conformemur, vt in magno illo die iudicij, quando omnis caro iudicabitur, Dei filij comparere, & in cœlestis pa-trimonij hæreditatem ingredi possimus, cum Iesu Christo, saluatore & redemptore nostro, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Here, brethren, we have something in which we may both examine and exercise our faith. Much profit comes from considering the divine goodness and blessedness toward us, which is laid up for us in heaven, which makes us regard the judgment of the world as nothing. Meanwhile we must strive, kindled with zeal for purification, that while we live here, as far as can be done, we may be conformed to the holy and pure God, so that in that great day of judgment, when all flesh shall be judged, we may be able to appear as children of God, and enter into the inheritance of the heavenly patrimony, with Jesus Christ, our Saviour and Redeemer, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XVI.
units.tr: HOMILIA XVI.

units.la: Omnis qui committit peccatum, idem & iniquitatem committit: & peccatum est iniquitas. Et scitis, quòd ille apparuit, ut peccata nostra tolleret, & peccatum in eo non est. Omnis qui in eo manet, non peccat: omnis qui peccat, non vidit eum, nec cognouit eum.
units.tr: Everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity, and sin is iniquity. And you know that he appeared to take away our sins, and in him there is no sin. Everyone who abides in him does not sin; everyone who sins has not seen him, nor known him.

units.la: Magna extat in nos diuinæ beneficentiæ argumenta: maximum tamen est, quòd sanctus ille & omnipotens Deus, infelices nos, qui propter peccatum iræ & dânationis filij censeri merebamur, per filium suum Iesum Christum, ex mera gratia, in filiorum suorum numerum & regni sui hæreditatem adoptare dignatus est. Postulat autem à nobis optimo iure Deus pro tanto beneficio, vt vita viuamus, quæ filios tam sancti patris deceat, quæq; in ipsius gloriâ redundet. Matth.5. Rectè ergo Ioannes, cùm Dei beneficium exposuisset nuper, subjicit: Qui habet hanc spem in ipsum, purificat se, sicut & ipse purus est. Et quia diuinæ puritatis exemplar imitandum proponit, perpetuo & indefinenti purificationis studio opus esse docet, cum ad huius perfectionem nobis, quoad hic viuimus, peruenire fit impossibile. Cæterum in hac causa plurimum nobis obest cæcum & corruptum carnis de peccatis iudicium. Quia enim natura peccatores sumus, mi-rificè nobisipsis inter peccandum blandimur. Et sunt, qui quicquid agunt, quantumuis iniustum & iniquum, per carnis infirmitatem excusare student. Habent etiam exempla sanctorum, quibus impudenter & perniciosè abutuntur. Sic ebrius Noæ & Loti vinolentiam sibi patrocinari putat. Et adulter Dauidis peccatum suæ impuritatis prætextum facit. Sunt rursum alij, qui hoc nomine se iustos censent, nec pro peccatoribus haberi volunt, quòd à grauibus illis & enormibus flagitijs,quæ ipse mundus quoque abominatur,immunes sint. Hinc fit,vt cum pœnitentiam à se flagitari audiunt,mox respondent,se nec fures,nec raptores, nec sicarios, nec veneficos esse, quos ista doctrina obtundi oporteat. Tantæ ergo pesti, qua non alia purificationis studio nocentior est, in præsenti Ioânes medetur,vt euincat necessariam esse omnibus hominibus purificationem, quam antea tradiderat. Primò enim de peccato rectè iudicare docet,vt fucatæ iustitiæ laruam nobis detrahat. Deinde solidis argumentis probat, peccandi studium à verè Christianis & fidelibus alienissimum esse debere. Tandem conclusionem infert,ex qua omnes homines facilè agnoscemus, quales censeri debeant. Et de his quidem,si suo spiritu nobis adsit dominus,modò dicetur.
units.tr: There are great proofs of God's kindness toward us, but the greatest is this: that the holy and almighty God, who deigned to adopt us, wretched as we were, who by reason of sin deserved to be counted children of wrath and damnation, through his Son Jesus Christ, out of pure grace, into the number of his sons and the inheritance of his kingdom. God rightly demands from us, in return for so great a benefit, that we live a life fitting for the children of so holy a Father, and one that reflects on his glory. Matt. 5. Rightly, then, John, having just set forth God's benefit, adds: Whoever has this hope in him purifies himself, just as he is pure. And because he sets before us the pattern of God's purity to be imitated, he teaches that there is need of a constant and unceasing zeal for purification, since it is impossible for us to attain its perfection while we live here. Moreover, in this matter our blind and corrupt judgment of sins does us great harm. For since we are sinners by nature, we flatter ourselves wonderfully when we sin. And there are those who, whatever they do, however unjust and iniquitous, strive to excuse it by the weakness of the flesh. They also have the examples of the saints, which they abuse shamelessly and to their own ruin. Thus the drunkenness of Noah and Lot, they think, defends their own intemperance; and David's adultery they make a pretext for their impurity. There are again others who think themselves righteous on this account, and do not want to be regarded as sinners, because they are free from those grave and monstrous crimes which the world itself abominates. Hence it happens that when they hear that repentance is demanded of them, they straightaway reply that they are neither thieves, nor robbers, nor murderers, nor poisoners, the kind of people this teaching ought to rebuke. John, therefore, heals this great plague, more harmful than any other to the zeal for purification, and he proves that the purification which he had taught earlier is necessary for all men. For first he teaches us to judge rightly about sin, so that he may strip from us the mask of counterfeit righteousness. Then by solid arguments he proves that the pursuit of sinning ought to be most alien to true Christians and believers. Finally he draws a conclusion by which we will all readily recognise what sort of people we ought to be considered. And about these things, if the Lord is present to us by his Spirit, we shall speak presently.

units.la: I. Omnis qui committit peccatum,idem & iniquitatem committit: & peccatum est iniquitas. Obscura multis visa est Apostoli sententia, dum nescio quod discrimen peccati & iniquitatis anxiè inquirunt,cum tamen Ioannes hæc eadem esse diserte testetur. Sed fefellit hos, partim quòd in Græca voce expendenda fuerunt ofcitantiores,dum vulgari translationi nimium inhærent. Ioannis consilium est, docere,vt de peccato iudicari cõveniat,& contra eos potissimũ (vt paulo ante diximus) sermonem dirigit, qui sibijpsis blandientes, purificationis præceptũ nihil ad se pertinere putabãt. Docet ergo nullum peccatũ tam leuiculum esse,in quo deponêdo nõ laborare debeât homines. Id verò probat per definitionê peccati, quod dicit ἀνομίαν esse. Est quidê ἀνομία iniquitas Latinis, latius tamê Græca vox patet,& omnem legis transgressionê, vel quicquid contra legem fit, significat. Sic ergo Ioânes argumentari videtur: Omnis qui legem Dei trâsgreditur, iram Dei & maledictionê incurrit. (Moses enim ait: Maledictus, qui non implet verba legis huius,vt faciat ea,& dicet vniuersus populus, Amen. Deut.27.) Omnis verò, qui peccat,legem trâsgreditur. (Quia peccatum est quicquid contra legem fit.) Ergo quisquis peccat,quocunque peccati genere, legis transgressor factus, iræ Dei & maledictioni subiacet. Nec tamen hinc quisquam colligat, Ioannem stoli-dam Stoicorum sententiam sequi,qui omnia peccata paria esse dicebant. Manet enim peccatorũ discrimé,vt alia alijs graviora sint, licet in suo genere, quod est legis transgressio, omnia cõveniát. Et Ioannes eorum refellit stultitiam,qui quę ab ipsis fiebant, parui facientes, nulla emendationis cura tenebãtur: quasi dicat: Quid prodest ô viri fratres, in peccatis vestris defensionem inutilem quærere? Scio quidem alium alijs grauius peccare. Qualiacunque tamen vestra peccata sint,legis transgressiones sunt. Licet igitur nemo accusset,accusabit tamen lex,per quam & iudicabimini. Quin ergo abiecto vanæ defensionis studio, culpam agnoscite,& vobis quoque necessariam putate purificationem, de qua modo dixi,ne dum illam negligitis,pœnam sentiatis tandem, quæ peccatis diuino iure debetur.
units.tr: I. Everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity, and sin is iniquity. The saying of the Apostle has seemed obscure to many, while they anxiously inquire into some distinction between sin and iniquity, although John plainly testifies that these are the same. But what deceived them was partly that they were too careless in weighing the Greek word, since they clung too much to the common translation. John's purpose is to teach that we must agree about judging sin, and, as we said a little earlier, he directs his speech chiefly against those who, flattering themselves, thought the command of purification did not apply to them. He therefore teaches that there is no sin so trivial that people should not labour to put it away. He proves this by the definition of sin, which he says is anomia [ἀνομία]. Indeed anomia is "iniquity" in Latin, but the Greek word has a wider range, and signifies every transgression of the law, or whatever is done against the law. John thus seems to argue as follows: Everyone who transgresses the law of God incurs the wrath and curse of God. (For Moses says: Cursed is he who does not fulfil the words of this law, so as to do them; and all the people shall say, Amen. Deut. 27.) But everyone who sins transgresses the law. (For sin is whatever is done against the law.) Therefore whoever sins, by whatever kind of sin, having become a transgressor of the law, is subject to the wrath and curse of God. Yet no one should infer from this that John follows the foolish opinion of the Stoics, who said that all sins are equal. For there remains a difference of sins, so that some are more grievous than others, although within their own kind, which is the transgression of the law, they all agree. And John refutes the folly of those who, making light of their own deeds, took no care for amendment; as if he said: What good, O brothers, does it do to seek a useless defence for your sins? I know indeed that one sins more gravely than another. Whatever your sins are, however, they are transgressions of the law. Therefore, although no one accuses you, the law will accuse you, by which you also will be judged. Why then, putting aside the vain pursuit of defence, do you not acknowledge your guilt, and regard as necessary for yourselves also that purification of which I have just spoken, lest, while you neglect it, you at last feel the punishment which is due to sins by divine right.

units.la: Non temere autem peccatum legis transgressionem esse definit hoc loco. Sic enim docet,vt de omnibus actionibus nostris iudicare debeamus. Non vtique secundum cæcum & corruptum carnis nostræ iudicium, sed secundum legem diuinitus datam. Ideo enim Hebræis lex Thorah, id est,regula siue norma dicitur. Regulæ verò vsus non modò in ædificando est, sed etiam in eo, vt per hanc opus iam absolutum probetur. Ad hanc itaque examinemus quæcunque à nobis fiunt tâ in religione,quàm in totius vitæ nostræ conuersatione. Sic enim videbimus,in multis nos grauiter peccare, in quibus extra omnem culpam nobis constituti videbamur. Quædam tamen exempli loco inspiciamus, vt huius examinis formam aliquam simpliciores habeant.
units.tr: Nor does John define sin here as a transgression of the law without reason. For he teaches us thus, so that we ought to judge all our actions, not by the blind and corrupt judgment of our flesh, but according to the law given by God. For this reason the Hebrews call the law Torah, that is, rule or standard. The use of a rule is not only in building, but also in this, that by it a work already finished is tested. Let us therefore examine by this standard whatever we do, both in religion and in the whole course of our life. For so we shall see that in many things we sin gravely, in which we seemed to ourselves to stand free of all fault. Yet let us look at some things by way of example, so that they may give some more simple form to this examination.

units.la: In religione eaferè est mundi huius sententia,vt quáuis religionis formam Deo placere posse[?] existiment. Habent quo suum illud commentum probent, Deum videlicet animum hominis, non externos ritus inspicere. Probari ergo ei animâ cultus sui studio flagrantem,vtcunq; ipsius præscriptionibus externæ Cerimoniæ nõ per omnia respondeant. Plausibilis sanè sententia,& huius seculi filijs valde commoda, quibus absurdũ videtur, de religione & fide sic contedere,vt propter has mutua amicitia & cõcordia interrũpatur. Et multos videre est, qui nec Turcas nec Iudęos in religionis causa à quoquam damnari velint. Hinc fieri videmus,vt facilè nouos fidei articulos & nouos cultus admittamus, nec quicquâ in religione certi & firmi habeamus. At si hoc factũ ad legis regulam examines, longè aliam Dei sententiam videbis. Is enim per Mosem inquit: Ne peruertigetis post cor vestrum, aut post oculos vestros, post quos scortari soletis. Quin memores fitis,& facietis omnia præcepta mea, eritis q; sancti Deo vestro. Num.15. Et apud prophetá eorum religionem damnat, qui hominum præceptis inhærebant. Isa.29. Sed & ipse Christus eandẽ prophetæ sententiã citans, addit: Omnis plantatio, quá non plantauit pater meus cœlestis, eradicabitur. Matt.15.
