Confirmantur hæ sententiæ innumeris diuinorũ iudiciorũ exéplis, quæ in illos edidit Dei iustitia, qui cõtra facere ausi sunt. Igne cœlitus immisso perdûtur Aaronis filij, quòd igne alienû in sacra intulissent. Leuit.10. Saulé regé magiæ & incantationis accusat Samuel, quòd ex ijs[?] sacrificare vellet, quæ dominus excindere iusserat.1.Sam.15. Corinthios pesse mulctatos author est, quòd sacram domini Cœnam nouis additamentis peruertere ausi fuissent. Hæc ergo & alia his similia consyderantibus, facilè patebit, non tam leuem culpâ esse quàm carnis iudicio videtur,in religione & cultu aliquid contra Dei præceptum instituere.
units.tr: In religion the opinion of this world is almost always that any form of religion may be pleasing to God. They have a pretext by which they defend this invention of theirs, namely that God looks at the heart of man and not at outward rites. Therefore, they say, a worship that burns with zeal for him is pleasing to him, even though its external ceremonies do not in every respect correspond to his prescriptions. It is indeed a plausible opinion, and very convenient for the sons of this age, who think it absurd to contend about religion and faith in such a way that mutual friendship and harmony are broken by them. And one may see many who do not wish either Turks or Jews to be condemned by anyone in the matter of religion. Hence we see that we easily admit new articles of faith and new forms of worship, and have nothing certain and firm in religion. But if you examine this by the rule of the law, you will see a very different judgment of God. For he says through Moses: Do not go astray after your own heart or after your own eyes, after which you are wont to play the harlot. Rather be mindful and do all my commandments, and you shall be holy to your God. Num. 15. And through the prophet he condemns the religion of those who clung to the precepts of men. Isa. 29. But Christ himself, quoting this same saying of the prophet, adds: Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up. Matt. 15. These sayings are confirmed by innumerable examples of divine judgments which the justice of God executed on those who dared to act against him. The sons of Aaron were destroyed by fire sent from heaven, because they had brought strange fire into the sacred rites. Lev. 10. Samuel accuses King Saul of magic and enchantment, because he wished to sacrifice with those things which the Lord had commanded to be destroyed. 1 Sam. 15. The author says that the Corinthians were punished with death because they had dared to pervert the Lord's sacred Supper with new additions. Therefore, considering these and other things like them, it will readily be clear that to institute something against God's command in religion and worship is not so slight a fault as it seems to the judgment of the flesh.

units.la: Idem in totius vitæ conuersatione obseruemus ô fratres,& quàtum carnis iudicio fallamur, facilè patebit. Leue multis videtur vitium diuini nominis abusus, quem vel propria vel vulgari aliorum consuetudine pleriq; excusari posse existimant. Sed si ijdem legem Dei dicentem audiant: Non impunitum dimittet dominus eum, qui nomen ipsius vanè sumpserit. Vitium hoc longè atrocius esse intelligent, quàm vulgo æstimetur: maxime cum olim diuino mandato lapidatus fuisse legatur, qui in nomen Dei blasphemus fuerat. Similiter scortationis & adulterij scelera mundus pro leuiculis æstimat,imò his deditos ferè risu iocisq; prosequitur. Sed si his diuinæ legis regulam applicemus, illa cum hac ex diametro pugnare videbimus. Lex Domini enim est: Ne mœcheris. Exod. 20. Et rursum: Ne fit scortum de filiabus Israel.Ad-hæc Paulus Apostolus nec scortatores,nec adulteros regni Dei hæredes fore,diserte pronunciat. Sed & mortis supplicium diuina lex adulteris statuit. An ergo leuiculum censeri debet,quod Deus morte multari vult, & quod à regno cœlorum excludere consueuit? Ita qui militiam mercenariam sequuntur,sanguinis effusionem leuem culpam esse iudicant. Imò plures inuenire est, qui summam viri fortis laudem & gloriam in hac sitam existiment. Sed longè aliter iudicare discent,si diuinæ legis sententiam audierint.Hæc enim ita pronunciat: Qui effundit sanguinem hominis,eius sanguis per hominem effundetur: quia in imagine Dei homo factus est. Item:Sanguis facit vt terra fallat,nec potest terra à sanguine, qui in ea effusus est,expiari, nisi per sanguinem illius qui sanguinem fudit. Adde his solenne illam & publica totius ecclesiæ approbatione confirmatam sententiam.Maledictus,qui accipit munus, vt percutiat animam sanguinis innocentis, & omnis populus dicet,Amen. Nec desunt exempla priuata & publica, quibus docemur,sanguinis studium & effrenem bellandi rabiem nemini vnquam feliciter cesisse. Væ enim ei qui ædificat ciuitatem in sanguinibus, vt propheta exclamat. Sed longum foret,de singulis peccatis dicere.Hæc exempli loco dicta sint,vt hinc discamus actiones nostras omnes ad legis diuinæ amusim examinare, peccatorum abominabilem atrocitatem agnoscere,eadem horrere,& purificationis studium,ceu vnice necessariū, sequi. Huc enim pertinent,quæ Ioânes secunda huius loci parte subiungit:
units.tr: Likewise, my brothers, we should observe this in the whole course of our life, and it will easily become clear how far we are deceived by the judgment of the flesh. Many people think the abuse of the divine name is a light fault, which they believe can be excused by their own habit or by the common custom of others. But if they hear the law of God saying: "The Lord will not leave unpunished the one who takes his name in vain," they will understand that this sin is far more atrocious than it is commonly reckoned, especially since we read that the man who blasphemed the name of God was stoned by divine command. In the same way, the world regards the crimes of fornication and adultery as trifling, and indeed it usually greets those given to them with laughter and jokes. But if we apply to these the rule of the divine law, we will see that the world's view is in direct conflict with it. For the law of the Lord is: "You shall not commit adultery" (Exod. 20.). And again: "Let there be no whore among the daughters of Israel." Moreover, the Apostle Paul plainly declares that neither fornicators nor adulterers will be heirs of the kingdom of God. Divine law also appoints death as the punishment for adulterers. Can, then, a thing be considered a small matter when God wills it to be punished with death, and when he is accustomed to exclude from the kingdom of heaven those who commit it? So too those who follow the mercenary soldier's trade judge the shedding of blood to be a light fault. Indeed, one may find many who regard the highest praise and glory of a brave man as resting in this. But they will learn to judge quite differently if they hear the sentence of divine law. For it pronounces thus: "Whoever sheds the blood of a man, by man shall his blood be shed, because man was made in the image of God." Likewise: "Blood defiles the land, and the land cannot be cleansed of the blood that has been shed in it, except by the blood of him who shed it." Add to these the well-known sentence, confirmed by the solemn and public approval of the whole Church: "Cursed is he who takes a bribe to strike down the soul of innocent blood; and all the people shall say, Amen." Nor are there lacking private and public examples by which we are taught that the pursuit of bloodshed and the unbridled rage of war have never turned out well for anyone. For woe to him who builds a city with bloodshed, as the prophet cries out. But it would be long to speak of each individual sin. These things have been said by way of example, so that from them we may learn to examine all our actions by the rule of the divine law, to recognise the abominable atrocity of sins, to shudder at them, and to pursue purification as the one thing truly necessary. To this pertains what John adds in the second part of this passage:

units.la: II. Et scitis quòd ille apparuit,ut peccata nostra tolleret,& peccatum in eo non est. Probat Ioânes,peccandi studium à Christianis alienissimum esse debere. Sunt autem huius demonstrationis rationes duæ,vtræque à Christi exemplo desumptæ, cuius authoritas apud Christianos merito maxima esse debet.Prima est: Christus ideo apparuit,id est,carne sumpta in mundum venit,vt peccata nostra tolleret. Tollendi verbo autem non expiationem modò peccatorum in ara Crucis sanctam comprehendit, qua fit, vt pœna peccati à nobis non exigatur, qui per fidem Christi iustitiæ confortes reddimur:sed eam quoque liberationem intelligit,qua Christus peccata sic sustulit,ne amplius in nobis regnare,& satanæ mancipia,quæ æternum damnentur, constituere possint.Huc enim pertinet,quod infra sequetur, Christum venisse vt opera diaboli,inter quæ primatum peccata facilè obtinent, dissoluat. Sic ergo argumentatur Ioânes: Non decet,vt Christiani iis se inuoluant & implicent, quæ Christus suo in mundum aduentu remouit & planè è medio sustulit: imò propter quæ tollenda ille homo factus est.Constat verò præcipuâ incarnationis Christi causam fuisse, vt peccata nostra tolleret. Nam propheta clamat:Infirmitates nostras ipse portauit, & dolores nostros ipse baiulauit.Et ipse eodem quasi alludens: Venite (inquit) ad me,qui laborati & onerati estis,& ego requiem vobis præstabo. Et Petrus eodem sensu Christū nostra peccata super lignum tulisse scribit . Quis ergo non videat,rem Christiano nomine indignissimam esse, si peccatorum studio nos ipsos denuo consecremus? Annon hoc erit,Christi meritum contemnere,& vniuersum incarnationis mysterium quasi pedibus conculcare? Paulus certè non immerito,tales Christum denuo sibijpsis crucifigere & ludibrio exponere dicit. Reprehenduntur rectè, qui aliorum beneficentia ære alieno liberati,eodem se denuo prodigalitate sua implicant,imò indigni censentur,quibus succurratur.At eadem omnium ratio,qui Christo satisfactore redempti,peccatorum sarcinis scientes & volentes se rursus aggrauant.Admonet simul locus hic, vbi liberatio à peccatis & redemptio quæri debeat. Apud Christum scilicet,qui (vt Paulus inquit) in mundum venit, peccatores saluos facere. Quia enim hic sese omnibus vniuersalem seruatorem offert, turpe est aliam extra hunc salutem quærere. Sed cum de hoc supra semel atque iterum dixerimus,eadem hic fusius repetere,superuacaneum foret.
units.tr: II. "And you know that he appeared to take away our sins, and in him there is no sin." John proves that the pursuit of sinning ought to be most alien to Christians. There are two reasons for this demonstration, both taken from the example of Christ, whose authority among Christians ought rightly to be greatest. The first is this: Christ appeared, that is, he came into the world having taken on flesh, in order to take away our sins. By the word "take away," however, he understands not only the expiation of sins on the holy altar of the Cross, by which the punishment of sin is not exacted from us, since through faith in Christ we are made partakers of righteousness; he also understands that deliverance by which Christ so removed sins that they could no longer reign in us, nor make us slaves of Satan, who are to be damned eternally. To this pertains what follows below, that Christ came to destroy the works of the devil, among which sins easily hold the first place. John therefore argues thus: it is not fitting that Christians should entangle and involve themselves in those things which Christ, by his coming into the world, has removed and has plainly taken out of the way; indeed, it was for the sake of removing them that he became man. Now it is certain that the chief cause of the incarnation of Christ was that he might take away our sins. For the prophet cries out: "He himself has borne our infirmities, and carried our sorrows." And he himself, as if alluding to the same thing, says: "Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will give you rest." And Peter, in the same sense, writes that Christ bore our sins upon the tree. Who, then, does not see that it is most unworthy of the Christian name, if we consecrate ourselves anew to the pursuit of sins? Will this not be to despise the merit of Christ and to trample the whole mystery of the incarnation underfoot? Paul rightly says that such people crucify Christ again for themselves and expose him to mockery. Those are rightly reproached who, having been freed from debt by the kindness of others, involve themselves again in the same debt by their own prodigality; indeed, they are judged unworthy to be helped. Yet the reasoning is the same for all those who, having been redeemed by Christ as satisfaction, knowingly and willingly load themselves again with the burdens of sins. This passage also reminds us where deliverance from sins and redemption ought to be sought: namely in Christ, who (as Paul says) came into the world to save sinners. For since here he offers himself as the universal Saviour to all, it is shameful to seek salvation apart from him. But since we have said this above once and again, to repeat the same things here at greater length would be superfluous.

units.la: Christus tollit peccata. Alteram rationem, qua Ioannes à peccandi studio dehortatur,his verbis comprehësam proponit:Peccatum in eo non est.Argumentatur verò vt supra:Qui Deo inseri & bonorû ipsius cófors fieri cupit,debet sicut ipse lux est,in luce ambulare.Sensus ergo præsentis loci est: Quotquot Christi fratres & membra dici volunt, Christo similes esse studeant. In Christo peccatû non est. Nam propheta inquit:Iniquitate non fecit,nec inuentus est dolus in ore eius.Isa.53.Et in euangelio acerrimis hostibus dicere audet:Quis ex vobis arguet me de peccato?Ioâ.8.Decet ergo vt qui huic inseri cupiunt, à peccandi studio alieni & immunes sint. Si enim bonus & virtutis amâs pater filios bonos & virtutis amantes habere cupit, Deum patrem eo ingenio prædituʼ[?] putabimus, qui cū ipse sanctisimus sit,peccatis & vitijs addictos filios ferre velit?Quê enim virum bonû dabis,quê turpis sodalitij nô pudeat,cum tales vulgo putemur,quales sunt quibus cum versamur? An ergo Christus feret,vt ipsius fratres & membra dicantur,qui omni scelerum labe polluti sunt? Ipse certè in euangelio ait:Ego sum vitis vera,& pater meus agricola est.Omnem palmitem in me non ferentem fructum,tollit:& omnem,qui fert fructum, purgat, vt fructum copiosiore afferat.
units.tr: Christ takes away sins. The second reason, by which John dissuades us from the pursuit of sinning, he sets forth in these words: "In him there is no sin." He argues, however, as above: whoever desires to be grafted into God and to become a partaker of his goods must, just as he himself is light, walk in the light. The sense of the present passage, therefore, is this: all who wish to be called brothers and members of Christ should strive to be like Christ. In Christ there is no sin. For the prophet says: "He did no violence, neither was any deceit found in his mouth" (Isa. 53.). And in the gospel he dares to say to his most bitter enemies: "Which of you will convict me of sin?" (John 8.). It is fitting, therefore, that those who desire to be grafted into him should be alien to, and free from, the pursuit of sinning. For if a good father who loves virtue desires his sons to be good and to love virtue, shall we think that God the Father, who is himself most holy, would wish to bear sons given over to sins and vices? For what good man will you give, or who is not ashamed of a foul fellowship, when we are commonly thought to be such as those with whom we associate? Will Christ then bear that those be called his brothers and members who are polluted with every stain of wickedness? He himself certainly says in the gospel: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in me that bears no fruit he takes away, and every one that bears fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit."

units.la: Item:Qui manet in me,& ego in eo,hic fert fructum multum.Ioan.15.Quis verò dubitet,Christū de verae fidei fructibus, innocentia nimirum & charitate, loqui,cum hos vbique tam anxiè requirat?Sed videamus præsentis loci conclusionem,quam ex ijs,quæ hucusque dicta sunt,infert.
units.tr: Likewise: "He who abides in me, and I in him, the same bears much fruit" (John 15.). Yet who would doubt that Christ speaks of the fruits of true faith, namely innocence and love, since he so anxiously requires these everywhere? But let us see the conclusion of the present passage, which he draws from what has been said so far.

units.la: III. Omnis qui in eo manet,non peccat. Omnis qui peccat,non vidit eum,nec cognouit cum[?]. Bimembris est hæc Conclusio. Familiaris enim hic Ioanni mos est, vt sententias suas antithesi ornatas pro ponat,vt contraria sibi inuicem oppositâ magis elucescant. Primum membrum est: Omnis qui in Christo manet,non peccat. Alterum: Omnis qui peccat,non vidit eum,nec cognouit eû. In Christo manere dicuntur,qui in Christum credunt. Fides enim vnicum illud medium est, per quod il li inferimur. Ipse enim inquit: Qui edit meam carnem,& bibit meum sanguinem,in me manet & ego in illo.Ioan. 6. At Christum fide comedi & bibi ad vitam æternam, manifestius est, quàm vt vt longa demonstratione opus habeat. Facit etiam huc quod in oppositomembro dicitur. Cum enim dicere debuisset: Omnis qui peccat, non manet in eo:potius dicere voluit:Non vidit eum, nec cognouit eum:quæ vtraque non nisi ad fidei sensum referri debent. Prioris ergo membri sententia hæc est.Quicunque in Christum verè credit & eidem vera fide insitus est,nô peccat. Huic alterum membrum sic opponitur:Quicunque peccat,in Christum nô credit, nec ei vera fide adhuc insitus est. Sunt hæc paradoxa & valde absurda primo intuitu. Dicat enim aliquis: Quicúque in Christum credit,non peccat. Peccamus autê omnes.(Nam & iustus in die septies labitur. Prouerb.24.) Ergo nemo hominum in Christum credit. Sed peccandi verbum aliter hoc loco , quàm alibi soleat,accipitur. Nec enim de corrupta hominis natura vel carnis infirmitate Ioannes loquitur,quasuperati quotidie peccamus:sed de peccandi studio, quo impij excæcati absque omni pœnitentiæ sensu affectuum habenis laxatis in omne nefas effrenes feruntur. Peccare igitur hic idem est,quod peccato seruire & eidem omni studio addictum esse. Hoc à verè pio & fideli alienissimû est. Peccant quidem fideles,& iustus in die septies labitur:sed idem septies quoque resurgit, & in peccati luto non hæret,cum ideo nos à peccato per Christi meritû sciat redemptos esse , ne illud posthac regnet in corpore nostro mortali, Rom.6. Sic peccauisse Dauidem legimus.Sed idê peccatum suum verę pœnitentiæ lachrymis & contritione prosecutus est, cauens sibi ne ad eundem lapidem denuo impingeret.Et Christus in euangelio pœnitentiam doceri vult,cuius prædicatione opus non esset,si peccata in pijs locum non habérent.Valeant ergo phanatici Anabaptistarum & Libertinorum spiritus,qui hoc & alijs similibus locis decepti,se peccatores esse negant,& mirabilia quædam atque inaudita suorum operum discrimina fingunt, ne peccatores esse conuincantur.Quæcunque enim ab ipsis improbè & turpiter fiunt,ea carnis opera esse dicunt,non sua. Carnem verò nihil ad se pertinere,cum illi iam olim valedixerint,& toti spiritu regantur.Sed ô callidi-tatem homicidæ diaboli. Itâne homini persuades, perfidisime quadruplator, vt quæ proprijs sensibus & membris committit,& ad quæ proprijs affectibus impellitur,nihil ad se pertinere exi-stimet?Fugiamus ô fratres hasce verborû præstigias, & diabolicam sanctimoniæ gloriationem esse certò credamus, si nos ab omni peccato liberos esse iactemus. Agnoscamus potius cum Dauide,nos in peccatis conceptos esse & genitos.Pfal.51.Teneamus Ioannis sententiam, qui supra dixit:Si dixerimus nos peccatum non habere,nosipsos fallimus,& veritas in nobis nô est:imô men dacij arguimus Deum,& verbum eius non est in nobis.1.Ioan.1.
units.tr: III. "Everyone who abides in him does not sin. Everyone who sins has not seen him, nor known him." This conclusion has two members. For it is John's familiar custom to set forth his statements adorned with antithesis, so that opposed things may stand out more clearly by being set against each other. The first member is: everyone who abides in Christ does not sin. The second: everyone who sins has not seen him, nor known him. Those are said to abide in Christ who believe in Christ. For faith is the one means by which we are brought into him. For he himself says: "He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him" (John 6.). But that to eat and drink Christ by faith unto eternal life is too evident to need a long demonstration. What is said in the opposed member also bears on this. For when he ought to have said, "Everyone who sins does not abide in him," he preferred to say, "has not seen him, nor known him": and both of these ought to be referred only to the sense of faith. The meaning of the first member, therefore, is this: whoever truly believes in Christ and is truly grafted into him by true faith does not sin. The other member is set against this: whoever sins does not believe in Christ, nor is he yet grafted into him by true faith. These statements seem paradoxical and very absurd at first sight. For someone may say: whoever believes in Christ does not sin. But we all sin (for even the righteous man falls seven times a day, Prov. 24.). Therefore no one believes in Christ. But the word "sin" is taken in this passage otherwise than it commonly is elsewhere. For John is not speaking of the corrupt nature of man or the weakness of the flesh, by which we sin daily even though we are overcome; he is speaking of the pursuit of sinning, by which the ungodly, blinded and without any sense of repentance, are carried off, with the reins of their passions loosened, into every wickedness unbridled. To sin here, then, is the same as to serve sin and to be devoted to it with every effort. This is most alien to one who is truly pious and faithful. Believers do indeed sin, and the righteous man falls seven times a day; but he also rises seven times, and does not cling in the mire of sin, since he knows that he has been redeemed from sin through the merit of Christ, so that sin may no longer reign in our mortal body (Rom. 6.). Thus we read that David sinned. But he pursued his sin with the tears and contrition of true repentance, taking care not to stumble against the same stone again. And Christ in the gospel wishes repentance to be taught, which would be unnecessary to preach if sins had no place among the godly. Let the fanatical spirits of the Anabaptists and the Libertines, then, be gone, who, deceived by this and other similar passages, deny that they are sinners, and invent certain marvellous and unheard-of distinctions in their works, so that they may not be proved to be sinners. For whatever they do wickedly and shamefully, they say is the work of the flesh, not theirs; and that the flesh has nothing to do with them, since they have long since bidden it farewell and are ruled wholly by the Spirit. But oh, the cunning of the murderous devil! Do you so persuade men, most treacherous deceiver, that they should think nothing pertains to them of what they commit with their own senses and members, and to which they are driven by their own passions? Let us flee, my brothers, these juggling tricks of words, and firmly believe that boasting of holiness is diabolical if we pride ourselves on being free from all sin. Let us rather acknowledge with David that we were conceived and born in sins (Ps. 51.). Let us hold to the sentence of John, who said above: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us; indeed, we make God a liar, and his word is not in us" (1 John 1.).

units.la: Obseruemus aut singulari diligentia posterius conclusionis huius membrû: Omnis qui peccat,id est,peccandi studio addictus est,peccato feruit & nulla tangitur pœnitentiæ cura, is Christum nec vidit nec cognouit. Negatur hac propositione in Christû credere, vel Christianus esse, quicûq; peccatis addictus est.Quàm multos ergo inuenire licebit,qui Christi nomine frustra gloriantur: & quàm rursus pauci sunt,quos verè Christianos dicere possis? Excommunicatur enim hac sententia quotquot scortationis & adulteriorum finem facere nolunt, vtvt per Dei verbum crebrò & diligenter admoneantur. Excommunicantur sanguinarij milites,qui cædibus superbi-unt,& hoc suo quæstu,ceu omnium honestissimo,gloriantur. Excommunicantur ebrij & vino-lenti cömessatores,impœnitentes gulæ & ventris serui.Excommunicatos dicere oportet incura-biles vsurarios,quos nullæ verbi Dei admonitiones,nullæ leges politicæ,nulla pauperum angu-stia adducere potest,vt peccati fui atrocitatem agnoscere & pœnitere velint. E Christianorû numero remouentur,quotquot in odijs & inimicitijs persequendis pertinaces charitatem omnem excludunt.Publicani & ethnici censentur, quotquot auaritiam secuti, in opibus spem omnê re-ponere pergunt. Denique Christiano nomine indignos, à Christo & regno ipsius alienos Ioânes pronunciat, quotquot non contenti peccasse,in peccatis improbè pergunt, pœnitentiæ studium rident,admonitionum impatientes sunt,& curari nolunt. Nec est quod illorum clamores audia-mus,quibus se & Christianos & Dei cultores esse urgent. Nam respondet illis Christus, dicens: Non omnis,qui dicit mihi: Domine domine, introibit in regnum meum, sed qui fecerit voluntatem patris mei,qui in cœlis est.Matth.7. Non etiam iuvabunt hos sacramenta,quæ cum verè Christianis communia habent.Nam & olim multos ex Israelitis circumcisos fuisse legimus, quibus tamen dicitur, quòd in fœdere Dei non permanserint. Iere.31. Similiter eosdem frequenter sacrifi-cavisse & adoleuisse constat,idq; iuxta ritum diuinitus præscriptum:quibus tamen dominus di-xit:Ad quid mihi multitudo sacrificiorum vestrorum.Holocausta arietum & adipem saginatorû fastidio, boum sanguinem, taurorum & hircorum non amo. Item:Cum expanderitis manus vestras,abscondam oculos meos à vobis : etiamsi multiplicaueritis orationem,non exaudiam : quia manus vestræ plenæ sunt sanguinibus.Isa.1.Similia his videre est & Psal.50. Itë Ier.4.&7. Mich. 6.Hose.6.Concludimus ergo cum Ioanne, à fide Christiana & consortio regni Christi alienos esse,quotquot pœnitere nescij peccatis seruiunt, nec magis profuturâ his Christiani nominis professionem,baptismum, Cœnam domini, preces & quæcunq; huius generis sunt, quàm olim Iudæis profuit,quòd peculium Dei & filij Abrahami dicebantur,quòd templo gloriabãtur,& in eodem quotidie sacrificabant atque adolebant. Quia enim Christus Iesus veritas est, populum requirit verè sanctum,non talem,qui falso sanctitatis titulo sese venditet.
units.tr: We should observe with particular care the last part of this conclusion: whoever sins, that is, who is devoted to a zeal for sinning, burns with sin and is not touched by any care for repentance, has neither seen nor known Christ. By this proposition, whoever is given over to sin is denied to believe in Christ or to be a Christian. How many, then, will one be able to find who boast in vain of the name of Christ? And how few, on the other hand, are there whom you could truly call Christians? For this sentence excommunicates all who are unwilling to make an end of whoredom and adultery, although they are frequently and diligently admonished through the Word of God. Excommunicated are the bloodthirsty soldiers, who take pride in slaughter and glory in this their gain, as though it were the most honourable of all. Excommunicated are the drunkards and the wine-bibbing revellers, the unrepentant slaves of gluttony and belly. We must call excommunicated the incurable usurers, whom no admonitions of the Word of God, no civil laws, no distress of the poor can bring to recognise the atrocity of their sin and to wish to repent. Removed from the number of Christians are all who, persistent in pursuing hatreds and enmities, shut out all charity. Tax collectors and heathens are reckoned as those who, following avarice, continue to place all their hope in riches. Finally, John declares unworthy of the Christian name and alien from Christ and his kingdom all who, not content to have sinned, persist wickedly in their sins, mock the zeal for repentance, are impatient of admonitions, and are unwilling to be healed. Nor should we listen to their clamours, by which they insist that they are both Christians and worshippers of God. For Christ answers them, saying: "Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into my kingdom, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven." Matth. 7. Nor will the sacraments help them, which they have in common with true Christians. For we read that long ago many of the Israelites were circumcised, yet it is said of them that they did not remain in the covenant of God. Jer. 31. Likewise it is well known that these same people often offered sacrifices and burned incense, and did so according to the rite divinely prescribed; yet the Lord said to them: "What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me? I am weary of the burnt offerings of rams and the fat of fed beasts; I do not delight in the blood of bullocks, lambs and goats." Likewise: "When you stretch out your hands, I will hide my eyes from you; even if you multiply prayer, I will not hear, for your hands are full of blood." Isa. 1. Similar passages may be seen in Ps. 50. Likewise Jer. 4 and 7, Mic. 6, Hos. 6. We conclude therefore with John that all who serve sins and do not know how to repent are alien from the Christian faith and from fellowship in the kingdom of Christ; and that the profession of the Christian name, baptism, the Lord's Supper, prayers, and whatever is of this kind, will profit them no more than it once profited the Jews, that they were called God's own people and sons of Abraham, that they boasted of the temple, and that they daily offered sacrifices and burned incense in it. For Jesus Christ is the truth, and he requires a people that is truly holy, not one that falsely puffs itself up with the title of holiness.

units.la: Porrò ex his docemur quoque,quàm iniqui nobis sint,quicúque euangelij doctrina & gratuita remissionis peccatorum prædicatione bona opera prohiberi, simulq; securitatem & carnis licentiam plantari dicunt. Atqui bona opera totum euangelium vbiq; exigit,& Christus eum palmitem resecandum dicit,qui fructum non tulerit.Ioan.15.Opera autem requirit, non quæ nobis bona videntur,sed quæ iuxta Dei præscriptum facta,ipsius iudicio pro bonis haberi possunt.Carnis licentiam adeò non plantat euangelij prædicatio,vt nos Christianos esse neget,nisi carne mortificauerimus, abnegauerimus,crucifixerimus.Coloss.3.Matth.16.Galat.5.Sed hæc est mundi & principis eius astutia,qui eiusmodi calumnijs euangelij doctrinâ inuisam facere conatur cum eandem non alio nomine magis oderit, quàm quòd luce sua opera praua arguit, & dignos pœnitentiæ & fidei fructus requirit.Ioan.3. Nostrum est,fratres,præsentem hunc locum diligenter observare,vt de peccatis verè iudicare possimus. Eadem tamen agnouisse non sufficit, nisi illa fugiamus,& perpetuum pœnitentiæ studium secuti, fidem in Christum innocentiæ & charitatis studio exprimamus. Sic enim cum illo viuemus & regnabimus, cui debetur benedictio,honor,gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, from these things we are also taught how unjust are those who say that the preaching of the gospel and the proclamation of the free forgiveness of sins forbid good works, and at the same time plant security and license for the flesh. Yet the whole gospel everywhere requires good works, and Christ says that the branch which does not bear fruit must be cut off. John 15. But it requires works not which seem good to us, but which, done according to God's prescription, can be held good by his judgment. The preaching of the gospel does not so much plant licence for the flesh that it denies us to be Christians unless we have mortified, denied and crucified the flesh. Col. 3; Matth. 16; Gal. 5. But this is the cunning of the world and of its prince, who try to make the doctrine of the gospel hateful by such calumnies, since they hate it for no other reason than that its light exposes their evil works, and it requires fruits worthy of repentance and of faith. John 3. It is our task, brothers, to observe carefully this passage, so that we may judge truly concerning sins. Yet to recognise them is not enough, unless we flee from them, and, pursuing a continual zeal for repentance, express our faith in Christ by a zeal for innocence and charity. For thus we shall live and reign with him, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XVII.
units.tr: HOMILIA XVII.

units.la: Filioli, nemo vos seducat. Qui facit iustitiam,iustus est,sicut & ille iustus est. Qui facit peccatum, ex diabolo est: quoniam ab ini-tio diabolus peccat. In hoc apparuit filius Dei,vt opera diaboli dissoluat. Omnis, qui natus est ex Deo, peccatum non facit: quia se-men eius in ipso manet, & non potest peccare, quia ex Deo natus est.In hoc manifesti sunt filij Dei & filij diaboli.
units.tr: My little children, let no one deceive you. He who does righteousness is righteous, just as he is righteous. He who commits sin is of the devil, for the devil has sinned from the beginning. For this purpose the Son of God appeared, that he might destroy the works of the devil. Everyone who is born of God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him, and he cannot sin, because he is born of God. In this the children of God and the children of the devil are made manifest.

units.la: PErquàm memorabilis est spiritus sancti sententia, quam Psal.49.pronunciat:Homo cum in honore sit & pretio,non intelligit:similis ergo erit iumentis,quæ prorsus intereunt. Vt enim munere sibi commisso nunquâ digne fungitur, qui illius dignitatem nô expendit: ita impossibile est, eum hominem vitam suam coram Deo, ut par est, instituere, qui dignitatem nostræ conditionis, in quam divina gratia evecti sumus, non probè consyderat. Quamobrem cū Ioannes de vita Christiana & Christianorum officijs sermonem instituisset, prudenter inde exordium fecit, ut ostenderet, quàm excellens sit eorū, qui Christo insiti sunt, conditio. Docuit autē nos à Deo in filiorum numerum adoptatos esse, ut cum filio Dei Iesu Christo, cui olim coformes reddemur, in novissimo die, regni cœlorum hæreditatem consequamur. Quid vero præstantius dici poterat? Superat enim hoc omnem regum huius mundi honorem & gloriam. Cæterum ex his ea colligit Ioannes, quæ ad vitæ nostræ institutionem faciunt. Si enim filii Dei sumus, & in eius communione permanere cupimus, decet ut puritatem & sanctimoniam, quæ in Deo est, nostris moribus & vita exprimamus. Rursum, si Christi fratres & coheredes dici volumus, minimè convenit, ut eorum studijs teneamur, propter quæ tollenda & propulsanda Christus in mundum venit. Venit autem, ut peccata è medio auferret, quæ nos à Dei facie repellebant. Christianos ergo pro virili peccatis abstinere oportebit: imò pro Christianis minimè habendi sunt, qui semetipsos illis consecrauerunt. Sunt hæc argumenta gravia, & quæ merito authoritatis magnæ apud nos esse debent. Quia tamen ea est nostra corruptio, ut facilè admittamus peccatorum illecebras, multi quo que indies exurgât, qui scurrilibus dicteriis animis nostris peccati horrorem & divini iudicii me tum excutere solent, plura ad hanc causam pertinentia Apostolus subiungit. Et primò quidè breui admonitione contra seductores eiusmodi nos instruit. Mox eleganti antithesi inter se committit filios Dei, verè fideles scilicet, & pœnitere nescios diaboli filios. Finis huius collationis est, ut utrorumque mores agnoscere, & horum quidem exemplum cavere, illorum verò studia imitari possimus: id quod argumentis firmis & solidis nobis persuadere studet. Adsit nobis spiritus suo do minus, ut non sine fructu, quæ ad filiorum Dei institutionem pertinent, proferantur.
units.tr: How memorable is the saying of the Holy Spirit in Psalm 49: "Man, though he is in honour and esteem, does not understand; he is therefore like the beasts that perish." For as one who does not weigh the dignity of an office entrusted to him never discharges it worthily, so it is impossible for one who does not rightly consider the dignity of our condition, into which we have been raised by divine grace, to order his life before God as he ought. Therefore, when John had begun to speak about the Christian life and the duties of Christians, he wisely made his beginning from this point, to show how excellent is the condition of those who have been grafted into Christ. He taught us that we have been adopted by God into the number of his sons, so that, together with the Son of God, Jesus Christ, to whom we shall one day be made conformed, we may obtain the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven on the last day. What could be said that is more outstanding? For this surpasses all the honour and glory of the kings of this world. Moreover, John draws from this those conclusions which bear upon the ordering of our life. For if we are sons of God, and desire to remain in his fellowship, it is fitting that we express in our morals and our life the purity and holiness that are in God. Again, if we wish to be called brothers and co-heirs of Christ, it is by no means fitting that we be occupied with those pursuits for the sake of which Christ came into the world to remove and drive away. He came, indeed, that he might take away from the midst the sins which were driving us from the face of God. Christians, therefore, ought to abstain from sins as far as in them lies; indeed, those who have consecrated themselves to sins are by no means to be regarded as Christians. These are weighty arguments, and they ought rightly to carry great authority with us. Yet, because our corruption is such that we easily admit the allurements of sin, and there are many today who are wont to shake off in our minds the horror of sin and the fear of divine judgment with scurrilous jests, the Apostle adds several things pertaining to this cause. And first, he instructs us against such seducers with a brief warning. Soon afterwards he sets over against one another, in an elegant antithesis, the sons of God, namely those who are truly faithful, and the sons of the devil, who know not how to repent. The aim of this comparison is that we may recognise the morals of both, and beware of the example of the one, while being able to imitate the pursuits of the other; this he strives to persuade us of by firm and solid arguments. May the Lord, his Spirit, be with us, so that what pertains to the instruction of the sons of God may be set forth not without fruit.

units.la: Filioli, nemo vos seducat. Breuis quidem, sed fidelis & paterna admonitio. Filiolos vocat, paterni pectoris pro salute ipsorum solicitudine exprimens. Addit: Nemo vos seducat. Quibus verbis non tam alijs, quam illis ipsis, quid facere debeant, præscribit. Perinde enim est ac si dixisset: Vestrum est cavere, ne aliorum dolis aut blanditijs seducamini. Et quia de hoc admonet, satis testatur, fideles, quoad in mundo viuunt, extra seductionis periculum non fore. De ijs autem seductoribus hic loquitur (ut ex toto sermonis contextu conijcere licet) qui vitæ & morum integritati insidiantur, dum peccata extenuant, illorum atrocitatem tegunt, Deum ista abominari & iudicijs suis punire negant, ut hoc modo omnem Dei timorem pellere, & quiduis agendi securam audaciam in hominum animis plantare possint. Habuerunt eius generis seductores omnia sæcula. Apud Isaiam enim væ illis imprecatur dominus, qui bonum malum, & è contra malum bonum dicere audent. Isa.5. Et alibi in eos gravissimè invehitur, qui puluillos & ceruicalia consuebant, id est, qui alijs securè peccandi adeoq; peccatis indormiendi authores erant. Ezech.13. Diligenter verò observandum, quod has pestes novissimo sæculo maximè grassaturas scripturæ prædicunt. Christus certè homines eorum similes fore dicit, qui temporibus Loth & Noæ vixerunt, securos nimirum in peccatis suis, admonitionum & minarum Dei contemptores, quiq; indies peccando proficiant. Matt.24. At Petrus Apostolus tanti mali fontem demonstrans, venturos dicit illusores, qui quæcunque de Christi aduentu, de extremo iudicio & præmio peccatorum dicuntur, in dubium vocat. 2.Pet.3. Quid enim in homine superesset quo peccandi licentia & scelerum audacia frænari possit, quando divini verbi authoritas contempta iacet, & iudiciorum Dei metus explosus est? Num verò nostris sæculis tales sint, videre operæpretium est. Securitatem certè peccandi regnare passim, nemo negabit. Unde verò hæc orta est? Nimirùm ex ijs animis, quos multi verbis palàm produnt. Audiùtur enim, qui cum Nabal dicunt, vel Deum omnino nullum esse, vel certè eundem non curare mortalia. Psal.14. Sunt, qui de peccatis leviter iudicant, dum vel veteris consuetudinis præextextu[?], vel multitudinis peccantium authoritate, vel carnis natura & ingenio, atrocissima quæq; flagitia excusare audent. Allegant exempli loco felices impunè peccantium successus, & quæcunque alia in hanc sententiam adduci possunt. Capiuntur horum sermonibus multi, maximè cum exemplis quotidianis, quorum maxima est authoritas, simul oppugnentur. Sed Ioannes brevi sententia, ne hos audiamus, monet. Causa est, quia seductores sunt. Quis in via ambulans eum audire & sequi velit, quem seductorem esse, & manifesta devia monstrare videat? Atqui hoc illi faciunt, & perniciosius multò seducunt, quàm si quis ad immania ferarum lustra, ad præcipitia horrenda, ad latronum stationes, denique in præsens mortis periculum abduceret. Abducunt enim à via iustitiæ & præceptorum Dei, quæ sola ad vitam potest perducere. Authores sunt, ut post carnis cupiditates ambulemus, quæ in mortiferos peccatorum laqueos trahunt. Pacem pollicentur & incolumitatem rerum omnium sectatoribus suis, cum nihil horum præstare possint. Nec enim in ipsorum manu sunt Dei iudicia, qui suo tépore tam ipsos quàm sectatores ipsorū horribiliter puniet. Discamus ergo fratres, suspectos habere omnes, quicunq; peccatis nostris blandiuntur, & eorū sermonibus aures nō præbeamus. Beatus enim, qui in eorū via non stetit, nec in cōsessu eiusmodi illusorum sedit. Psal. 1. Sed ad collationem piorum & impiorum, quæ præsentis loci caput est, trāseamus.
units.tr: My little children, let no one deceive you. A brief but faithful and fatherly warning. He calls them little children, expressing the solicitude of a fatherly heart for their salvation. He adds: let no one deceive you. By these words he prescribes what they themselves ought to do, rather than what others should do. For it is just as if he had said: It is your task to take care that you are not seduced by the cunning or flattery of others. And in warning them of this, he sufficiently testifies that the faithful, so long as they live in the world, will not be free from the danger of seduction. He speaks here, however (as may be gathered from the whole context of the discourse), of those seducers who lay snares for the integrity of life and morals, while they minimise sins, cover up their atrocity, deny that God abhors them and punishes them by his judgments, so that in this way they may drive out all fear of God and plant in the minds of men a secure boldness to do whatever they please. Seducers of this kind have existed in every age. For through Isaiah the Lord pronounces woe upon those who dare to call evil good and good evil. Isa. 5. And elsewhere he inveighs most severely against those who sew cushions and pillows, that is, who were the authors of securely sinning for others, and thus of lulling them to sleep in their sins. Ezek. 13. Moreover, it must be carefully observed that the Scriptures foretell that these plagues would especially rage in the last age. Christ indeed says that men will be like those who lived in the times of Lot and Noah, namely secure in their sins, contemners of God's admonitions and threats, and who advance daily in sinning. Matt. 24. But the Apostle Peter, pointing out the source of so great an evil, says that there will come scoffers who call into doubt all that is said about the coming of Christ, the final judgment and the reward of sinners. 2 Pet. 3. For what would remain in a man by which the licence to sin and the boldness of wickedness could be restrained, when the authority of the divine word lies despised and the fear of God's judgments has been cast out? Whether such men are in our own age, it is worth the trouble to see. That security in sinning reigns everywhere, no one will deny. But whence has this arisen? Assuredly from those minds which many openly betray by their words. For there are heard those who, like Nabal, say either that God does not exist at all, or at least that he does not concern himself with mortal affairs. Ps. 14. There are some who judge lightly of sins, while under the pretext either of ancient custom, or the authority of the multitude of sinners, or the nature and disposition of the flesh, they dare to excuse even the most atrocious crimes. They adduce, as examples, the happy and unpunished outcomes of those who sin, and whatever else can be brought forward to this effect. Many are captured by their words, especially when, at the same time, daily examples, whose authority is very great, are set against us. But John, by a brief sentence, warns us not to listen to these men. The reason is that they are seducers. Who, walking on a road, would wish to hear and follow one whom he sees to be a seducer and to point out manifest pitfalls? Yet this is what they do, and they seduce far more perniciously than if someone were to lead a man into the monstrous dens of wild beasts, to horrible precipices, to the posts of robbers, finally into the immediate danger of death. For they lead men away from the way of righteousness and of the commandments of God, which alone can bring us to life. They are the authors of our walking after the lusts of the flesh, which draw us into the deadly snares of sins. They promise peace and safety in all things to their followers, although they can provide none of these things. For the judgments of God are not in their hand; in his own time he will punish both them and their followers in a dreadful manner. Let us learn therefore, brethren, to regard with suspicion all who flatter our sins, and let us not lend our ears to their words. For blessed is the man who has not stood in their way, nor sat in the seat of such scoffers. Ps. 1. But let us pass on to the comparison of the godly and the ungodly, which is the chief point of the present passage.

units.la: II. Qui facit iustitiam, iustus est, sicut & ille iustus est. Qui facit peccatum, ex diabolo est: quoniam ab initio diabolus peccat. Primo loco de filijs Dei, qui vere fideles & justi sunt, agit. Sic vero sermonē instituit, ut eos arguere videatur, qui cum a justitiæ studio alieni sint, fideles tamen & justi haberi volunt. Sic enim vult dicere: Noui equidem multos justitiæ titulo gloriari, qui se Christi merito justificatos & sanctificatos esse dicunt. Sed minimè putādum est, quòd nudi tituli gloriatio quen quam coram Deo justum efficiat. Christus patrem suum nobis imitandum proponit, dicēs: Perfecti estote, sicut pater vester in cœlis perfectus est. Matth. 5. Atqui is non dicitur tantummodo justus in scripturis, sed reuera justus est, & justitiam suam in omnibus suis judicijs & operibus conspiciendam profert. Quisquis ergo idem studiū secutus fuerit, ut opera justitiæ edat, is vere justus dici poterit, Argumentū, si libet, sic formare licebit. Qui Dei justitiā imitari studet, justus est. Deus justitia non modò gloriatur, sed justitiam facit. Ergo, qui justitiam facit, justus est. Breuis hæc, sed diligenti consideratione digna sententia. Nam docemur, Christianorum justitiam non in titulorum splendore, non in externo fuco vel hypocrisi, sed in ipsa re consistere. Justitiā hic voco, non eam quæ propter fidem in Christum imputatur nobis, quę sola coram Dei judicio nos defendit: sed eius effectus, quos in externa vitæ cōuersatione profert. Quia enim fides verè Christo insert, & viuos facit illius vitis palmites (Joan. 15.) minimè otiosa est, sed fructus Christo & eius cōmunione dignos operatur, non clam, sed in propatulo, ut ex fructibus fides nostra dijudicari possit. In hanc sententiam Christus loquitur: Vos estis lux mundi. Non potest oppidū abscondi supra montē situm: neq; accendūt lucernā, & ponunt illam subter modiū, sed super cādelabrum, & lucet omnibus, qui sunt in domo. Sic luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videāt vestra bona opera, glorificentq; patrē vestrum, qui in cœlis est. Et paulò post: Nisi abūdauerit justitia vestra plus quàm scribarum & pharisæorū, nō poteritis ingredi in regnum cœlorum. Matt. 5. Eodem Jacobum respexisse videmus, qui cōtra vanos fidei & justitiæ fidei gloriatores disputās, ait: Ostende mihi fidem tuam ex factis tuis, & ego ostendā tibi ex factis meis fidem meam. Jac. 2. Qui loci satis evidenter docent, fidei quidē deberi justitiæ & salutis nostræ gloriam, sed viuæ & veræ fidei, quę nō vana & inanis est gloriatio, siue verborum fucus, sed certus & efficax animi assensus, quem spiritus sanctus in nobis excitat, & per eundem nos Christo inserit, ut & salutis in illo consortes, & eidē, quoad sanctimoniam & puritatem conformes reddamur. Firma ergo & solida stat Joannis sententia, justum & filium Dei veręq; fidelem eum esse & reuera dici, qui justitiæ studium, juxta exemplar in Deo propositum, secutus fuerit.
units.tr: II. He who does righteousness is righteous, just as he is righteous. He who commits sin is of the devil, for the devil has sinned from the beginning. In the first place he treats of the sons of God, who are truly faithful and just. He so arranges his discourse that he seems to be censuring those who, while they are strangers to the pursuit of righteousness, nonetheless want to be held faithful and just. For he wishes to say: I know indeed that many glory in the title of righteousness, who say that they have been justified and sanctified by the merit of Christ. But it must by no means be thought that the mere boasting of an empty title makes anyone righteous before God. Christ sets his Father before us to be imitated, saying: Be perfect, as your Father in heaven is perfect. Matt. 5. Yet he is not called righteous merely in the Scriptures, but is truly righteous, and displays his righteousness to be seen in all his judgments and works. Whoever therefore has followed the same pursuit, so as to produce works of righteousness, may rightly be called righteous. We may, if we like, frame the argument thus: He who strives to imitate the righteousness of God is righteous. God not only glories in righteousness, but also does righteousness. Therefore, he who does righteousness is righteous. This sentence is brief, yet worthy of diligent consideration. For we are taught that the righteousness of Christians does not consist in the splendour of titles, nor in external paint or hypocrisy, but in the thing itself. By righteousness I do not here mean that which is imputed to us on account of faith in Christ, which alone defends us before the judgment of God, but its effects, which it produces in the external conduct of life. For since faith truly engrafts us into Christ, and the branches of his vine are made alive by him (John 15), it is by no means idle, but works fruits worthy of Christ and of communion with him, not secretly but openly, so that our faith may be judged from its fruits. Christ speaks to this effect: You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden; nor do men light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, and it gives light to all who are in the house. So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven. And a little after: Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. Matt. 5. We see that James also had regard to the same thing, who, disputing against the empty boasters of faith and righteousness, says: Show me your faith by your works, and I will show you my faith by my works. James 2. These passages teach quite clearly that the glory of our righteousness and salvation is due to faith, but to a living and true faith, which is not an empty and vain boasting, nor a mere display of words, but a certain and effective assent of the mind, which the Holy Spirit stirs up in us, and through which he engrafts us into Christ, so that we may be partakers of his salvation and be made conformed to him in holiness and purity. Therefore John's sentence stands firm and solid: that he is truly just and a son of God and a truly faithful man, and is really so called, who has pursued the pursuit of righteousness according to the pattern set forth in God.

units.la: Alterū antithesis membrum impios & à fide alienos cōprehendit. De his sic loquitur: Qui facit peccatū, ex diabolo est. Obseruandum verò (quod & supra monui) Joannem peccādi vel peccati vocabulis nequaquā carnis nostrę corruptam naturā & infirmitatem & quæ inde promanant delicta, cōplecti. Quia si hanc speciēs, omnes peccata facimus, & in multis labimur omnes. Jac. 3. Sed & Joannes supra mendacē eum esse dixit, qui se peccatū nullum habere, gloriari ausit. 1. Joan. 1. Quam ob rem de deuoto peccandi studio Apostolum loqui sentiamus, & eos intelligere, qui nihil nisi peccant, qui semel lapsi resurgere nolunt, qui peccatorū luto gaudent, & absq; omni pœnitentia & doloris sensu in eo obstinati perseuerāt. Quos alibi seruos peccati scriptura vocare solet. Joan. 8. 2. Pet. 2. Qui talis est (inquit Joannes) tam abest ut Christianus, vel Christi membrū, filius & hæres Dei dici mereatur, ut potius diaboli filius dici debeat: nō quidem generatione (nec enim quenquam diabolus generat, nec inter principia Manichaico errore collocari debet) sed imitatione. Id quod argumento subiecto declarat. Addit enim: Quia ab initio diabolus peccat. Initiò quidem bene conditus erat, ut minister esset divinæ majestatis, ad salutem eorum, qui electi sunt. Sed in veritate non stetit. Joan. 8. Et ubi semel excidit, non contentus peccavisse, Deo & voluntati ipsius obstinato animo sese pertinaciter opposuit. Mox enim primos parentes mendacijs seduētos in nassam perditionis illexit. Nec cessat etiamnum hodie, sed semper ceu leo rugiens obambulat, quaerens quem devoret. 1. Petr. 5. Tales vero non sunt boni angeli. Tales non sunt sancti & fideles Dei cultores. Sed ut primum illi per carnis infirmitatem & mundi blanditias superati peccant, mox admoniti peccatum agnoscunt, fatentur, dolent, pœnitent, & à lapsu per Dei gratiā resurgunt. Nota sunt Davidis, Ezechiæ, Petri Apostoli, peccatricis, & multorum aliorū exempla, quæ omnes pij sedulò imitantur. Quis ergo non ab horum moribus & ingenio alienos, & diaboli potius quàm Dei filios dicat, qui non contēti peccasse, toti sese peccatis cōsecrant, admonitiones omnes contemnunt, & peccata peccatis pœnitere nescij accumulant, imò alijs quoque nunquam non peccatorum authores sunt? Verè ergo argumentatur Joannes: Quicunque diaboli mores & ingenium imitantur, ex diabolo, non Deo, nati esse censeri debent. At diaboli mores & ingenium imitantur, qui peccatis addicti, in ijs deuoto animo pergunt. Diaboli ergo, non Dei filij existimandi sunt. Argumento hoc tam libere & audacter Joannes utitur, quia eodem Christus quoq; usus erat. Nam cum pharisæis, patris Abrahami titulo gloriantibus, disputans ait: Si filij Abrahami estis, opera Abrahami faceretis. Nunc autem quæritis me interficere, hominem, qui veritatem vobis locutus sum, quam audivi à Deo. Hoc Abraham non fecit. Vos facitis opera patris vestri. Vos ex patre diabolo estis, & desyderijs patris vestri vultis obsequi. Ille homicida erat ab initio, & in veritate non stetit, &c. Joan. 8. Finis ergo & scopus huius collationis est, ut intelligamus, Christianos & filios Dei esse, qui fide in Christum viva animati, justitiæ studium sectantur: rursus, diaboli filios esse & censeri debere, qui deuoto animo & pœnitere nescij peccatis indulgent. Dura quidem sententia, & quam molles filiorum huius seculi aures difficulter admittunt: vera tamen & inviolabilis, quia Dei verbo nititur, & dictante spiritu sancto scripta est. Applicemus hanc nostri seculi hominibus, & facilè patebit, quos pro domesticis fidei agnoscere, & quos publicanorum & ethnicorum loco habere debeamus. Patebit inquam, quorum mores imitari cōveniat, & quorum commercia cāne peius & angue odisse oporteat.
units.tr: The second member of the antithesis takes in the impious and those alien to faith. Of these he speaks thus: "Whoever commits sin is of the devil." It must be observed (as I also noted above) that John, by the words "to sin" or "sin," does not embrace the corrupt nature and weakness of our flesh and the faults that flow from it. For if we take sin in this sense, "we all commit sins, and we all stumble in many things" (James 3). Yet John also said above that the one who dares to boast that he has no sin is a liar (1 John 1). Wherefore let us understand that the Apostle speaks of a devoted zeal for sinning, and means those who do nothing but sin, who, once fallen, refuse to rise again, who delight in the mire of sins and persist obstinately in them without any repentance or sense of grief. Scripture elsewhere is accustomed to call such people "slaves of sin" (John 8; 2 Peter 2). John says that one of this kind is so far from deserving to be called a Christian, or a member of Christ, a son and heir of God, that he ought rather to be called a son of the devil. Not indeed by generation (for the devil begets no one, nor ought he to be placed among the first principles with the Manichaean error), but by imitation. This he declares in the argument that follows. For he adds: "because the devil has sinned from the beginning." At the beginning, indeed, he was well created, to be a minister of the divine majesty for the salvation of those who are elect. But "he did not stand in the truth" (John 8). And once he had fallen, not content with having sinned, he obstinately and stubbornly opposed himself to God and his will. Soon he enticed our first parents, seduced by lies, into the snare of destruction. Nor does he cease even today, but always prowls like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour (1 Peter 5). Such are not the good angels. Such are not the holy and faithful worshippers of God. But as soon as those others are overcome through the weakness of the flesh and the flatteries of the world and sin, straightway, when admonished, they acknowledge their sin, confess it, grieve, repent, and rise again from their fall by the grace of God. The examples of David, Hezekiah, Peter the Apostle, the sinful woman, and many others are well known, and all the godly diligently imitate them. Who then would not say that those who are alien to the manners and disposition of these men, and are sons of the devil rather than of God, are those who, not content with having sinned, consecrate themselves wholly to sins, despise all admonitions, and, ignorant of how to repent of sins, heap sin upon sin; nay, who are always the authors of sins for others as well? John argues truly: whoever imitates the manners and disposition of the devil ought to be judged born of the devil, not of God. But those who, given over to sins, persist in them with a devoted mind, imitate the manners and disposition of the devil. Therefore they are to be considered sons of the devil, not of God. John uses this argument so freely and boldly because Christ also used the same argument. For when, disputing with the Pharisees, who gloried in the title of Abraham their father, he said: "If you were the children of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham. But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth, which I heard from God. Abraham did not do this. You do the works of your father. You are of your father the devil, and you want to fulfil the desires of your father. He was a murderer from the beginning, and did not stand in the truth," etc. (John 8). The aim and purpose of this comparison, therefore, is that we should understand that those are Christians and sons of God who, animated by a living faith in Christ, pursue zeal for righteousness; and conversely, that those are and ought to be counted sons of the devil who indulge in sins with a devoted mind and do not know how to repent. A harsh sentence indeed, and one which the soft ears of the sons of this age admit with difficulty; yet it is true and inviolable, because it rests on the word of God and was written under the dictation of the Holy Spirit. Let us apply this to the men of our own age, and it will easily become clear whom we ought to acknowledge as members of the household of faith, and whom we ought to regard in the place of tax collectors and Gentiles. It will become clear, I say, whose manners it is fitting to imitate, and whose company we ought to shun worse than a dog or a snake.

units.la: Admonet item hic locus, ut in ecclesia doctrinæ antistites de palàm sceleratis & pœnitere nescijs, tum judicare tum loqui debeant. Hic enim si mundi judicium audiamus, modestiæ nos admonebit & charitatis, cum interim ipse nulla vel modestiæ vel charitatis cura tangi soleat. Quasi ve-rò modestiæ lex sit, immodestam quiduis patrandi licentiam plantare, & charitas præcipiat, ne cui peccandi modum & limites præscribamus. Longè aliter spiritum sanctū, qui & modestiæ & charitatis spiritus est, judicare & loqui videmus. Nam in lege, cum voluntatis suæ capita exposuisset Deus, contra illorum transgressores sententiā proferens, maledictos & execrabiles pronunciat: nec alicui mortalium copiam facit aliter de his judicandi. Maledictus (inquit) qui fecerit sculptile, opus manuum artificis: & respondebit omnis populus, Amen. Maledictus, qui maledicit parentibus suis: & omnis populus respondebit, Amen, &c. Deut. 27. Publico totius ecclesiæ testimonio suas sententias dominus probari vult. Quæ ergo temeritas fuerit, easdem sub modestiæ & charitatis prætextu inuertere, Deumq; quasi rigidior & crudelior æquo fuerit, insimulare? Inter prophetas certè neminem tam confidentem fuisse legimus, qui vel jubentibus regibus & toto populo, aliter loqui ausus fuerit, quàm dominū loqui audiuisset. Legātur sermones illorū, Jsaiæ imprimis, Jeremiæ & Ezechielis, & quam docendi ratione secuti fuerint, facilè constabit. Nec est quòd eos audiamus, qui noui Testamenti mitiore spiritu fingūt. Unus & idè tà veteris quàm noui testamenti spiritus est. Nam spiritus sancti impulsi locuti sunt prophetæ. 2. Pet. 1. Una igitur & eadem quoq; est utrobiq; de peccatis & flagitijs loquēdi ratio. Primus certè noui testamenti minister, Baptista, pharisæos & scribas progeniem viperarū vocare, & eosdem filios Abrahami esse, negare audet. Matt. 3. Christus Jesus, quo cū nemo opinor modestiæ & mansuetudinis certamē facilè fusce perit, eosdem nō modo rapaces lupos, cæcos cæcorū duces, devoratores viduarum sepulchra dealbata & hypocritas, sed diaboli filios, fures & latrones vocare cōsueuit. Joan. 8. & 10. Matth. 21. Quid ergo dicemus? Num vel Christum Jesum immodestiæ accusabimus, vel illos his titulis dignos fuisse fatebimur? Similis Apostolorum doctrina est. Petrus, cum primâ Hierosolymis concionem haberet, de populi peccatis non adulatorio more loquitur, sed ait: Deus patrum nostrorum, glorificavit filium suū Jesum, quē vos tradidistis, & negastis in conspectu Pilati, cum ille judicasset esse absoluendum. Vos autē sanctum & justum negastis, & postulastis, ut virum homicidam donaret vobis, authorē verò vitæ interfecistis, &c. Act. 3. Quæ verba si probè examinentur, nescio quid grauius, immanius, atrocius & horribilius dici possit. At digni erat (inquis) quibus hæc obijcerentur, ob immane illud proditi & occisi filij Dei facinus. Sed heus tu, annon eadem severitate dignos censebis, qui effreni peccandi licentia sanguine filij Dei prophanant, & eundem (quantum in ipsis est) denuo crucifigunt? Heb. 6. Cur ergo tales à Joanne diaboli filij dicuntur, quo nullum fingi & excogitari potest convitiū grauius? Cur eosdem à regno cœlorum Paulus excludit? 1. Cor. 6. Aut ergo veterem corripiendi & increpandi libertatem retinere oportet, aut demonstrandum erit, nostro seculo eam esse morum sanctimoniā, eam vitæ integritatem, tam ardens synceræ religionis studium, ut hac opus non sit. Id verò si quis affirmare audet, eum Christus mendacij arguit, qui nouissimo seculo iniquitatem abundaturā, fidem verò & charitatem quasi intermoritu-ras prædixit. Matt. 24. Luc. 18. &c. Contradicet eidem totus mūdus, si nō verbis, factis certè, quod testimoniū est longè locupletius. Friget ubique fidei & religionis amor. Extincta iacet charitas. Iam olim terras Aftræa reliquit. Expulsa, apud Garamatas fortasse, vagatur vitæ innocentia. Exulant pudor, temperantia, honestas, cum toto aliarum virtutum choro. Subiere in horum locū impietas, inconstantia, leuitas, odia, inuidia, æmulationes, vsuræ, rapinæ, furta, doli, impostura, iniquitas, iudiciorum corruptela, impuritas, libido, scortatio, adulteria, incestus, impudentia, luxus, ebrietas, omnis denique vitiorum caterua, quam olim ex imo Acheronte profusam poetæ finxerunt. Et adhuc in ministris modestiam requirimus, dum ista accusant? Ingens profecto periculum est, ne plures hic eo nomine accusari possint, quod in hominum gratiam canes muti fiunt, & stulti speculatores venientem gladium prædicere nolunt. Imitandi potius prophetæ, & inter hos Ionas cumprimis, qui intra quadragesimum diem orbi tot scelerum sarcinis onusto interitum minitetur. Imitandus Christus, & cum hoc Ioannes noster, vt libere diaboli filios dicamus, quicunque pœnitere nolunt. Eæ enim sunt scelerum blanditiæ, vt nisi illis fucum detrahas, neminem illorum pœnitere possit. Vidit hoc Cato, homo ethnicus, qui apud Saluftium omnis corruptelæ causam dicit, quod rerum nomina vera & propria iamdudum amisissent. At indignè fert mundus, qui fata sua non vult argui. Ioan.3. Quid tum postea? Verbum Dei intonare vel inuitis oportet, etiam si fractus illabatur orbis. Hunc qui audire nolunt, tandem hostium clamores, armorum strepitus, cornuum bombos exteri militis horribiles & non intellectas minas, bombardarum tonitrua, & ruentium turrium fragores, & si quid aliud belli alea parturit, audire, cogetur. Sed longius quam instituera, progressus sum. Redeamus ad Ioannem, qui hinc occasione sumpta, firmissimis argumentis, quod dixit, denuo confirmat, sic tamen vt ijsdem ad innocentiæ & integritatis studium Christianos homines adhortetur.
units.tr: This passage also admonishes that in the Church the teachers of doctrine ought both to judge and to speak concerning those who are openly wicked and do not know how to repent. For if we listen to the judgment of the world, here it will admonish us to modesty and charity, while itself is usually untouched by any care for modesty or charity. As if indeed it were a law of modesty to plant an unbridled license for committing any kind of deed, and charity commanded that we prescribe no bounds or limits to anyone's sinning! We see the Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of both modesty and charity, judging and speaking in a far different way. For in the law, when God had set forth the heads of his will, pronouncing sentence against their transgressors, he declares them cursed and accursed, and he gives no mortal leave to judge otherwise about them: "Cursed is he who makes a graven image, the work of the hands of the craftsman; and all the people shall answer, Amen. Cursed is he who curses his parents; and all the people shall answer, Amen," etc. (Deuteronomy 27). The Lord wills that his sentences be confirmed by the public testimony of the whole Church. What rashness, then, would it be to overturn these same sentences under the pretext of modesty and charity, and to accuse God of being more severe and cruel than is right? Among the prophets we certainly read of no one so bold as to dare to speak otherwise than he had heard the Lord speak, even when kings and the whole people commanded it. Let their sermons be read, especially those of Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel, and it will easily be clear what method of teaching they followed. Nor should we listen to those who feign a gentler spirit of the New Testament. There is one and the same spirit of the Old Testament and of the New. For the prophets spoke, moved by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1). Therefore there is also one and the same manner of speaking about sins and crimes in both. Certainly the first minister of the New Testament, the Baptist, dares to call the Pharisees and scribes a brood of vipers, and to deny that they are sons of Abraham (Matthew 3). Christ Jesus, with whom, I think, no one could easily contend and be defeated in modesty and meekness, was accustomed to call the same men not only ravening wolves, blind guides of the blind, devourers of widows, whitened sepulchres and hypocrites, but also sons of the devil, thieves and robbers (John 8 and 10; Matthew 21). What then shall we say? Shall we accuse Christ Jesus of immodesty, or shall we confess that they were worthy of these titles? The teaching of the Apostles is similar. Peter, when he gave the first sermon at Jerusalem, speaks of the sins of the people not in a flattering manner, but says: "The God of our fathers has glorified his Son Jesus, whom you delivered up and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had judged him to be released. But you denied the Holy and Just One, and asked that a murderer be granted to you, and killed the Author of life," etc. (Acts 3). If these words are weighed rightly, I do not know what could be said more grave, monstrous, atrocious and dreadful. But, you say, they deserved to have these things thrown at them because of that monstrous deed of betraying and killing the Son of God. But look here: will you not think worthy of the same severity those who profane the blood of the Son of God by unbridled license to sin, and (so far as in them lies) crucify him anew? (Hebrews 6). Why then are such people called sons of the devil by John, than whom no more grievous reproach can be imagined or devised? Why does Paul exclude them from the kingdom of heaven? (1 Corinthians 6). Therefore either we must retain the old freedom to correct and rebuke, or it must be shown that in our age there is such sanctity of manners, such integrity of life, and so ardent a zeal for pure religion, that there is no need for it. But if anyone dares to affirm this, then Christ, who foretold that in the last age iniquity would abound and faith and charity would almost die out (Matthew 24; Luke 18, etc.), is convicted of falsehood. The whole world will contradict this same man, if not in words, certainly in deeds, which is a far richer testimony. Everywhere the love of faith and religion grows cold. Charity lies extinct. Long ago Astraea left the earth. Expelled, perhaps among the Garamantes, innocence of life wanders. Shame, temperance, honesty are in exile, together with the whole choir of the other virtues. In their place have come impiety, inconstancy, levity, hatreds, envy, rivalries, usury, plunder, thefts, deceits, fraud, iniquity, the corruption of judgments, impurity, lust, fornication, adulteries, incest, impudence, luxury, drunkenness, in short the whole rout of vices which the poets once fabled to have poured forth from the depths of Acheron. And do we still require modesty in ministers while they denounce these things? There is certainly a great danger that many may be accused on this account, that for the sake of men's favour they become dumb dogs, and foolish watchmen refuse to foretell the sword that is coming. Let us rather imitate the prophets, and among them especially Jonah, who threatened destruction to the world, laden with so many burdens of crimes, within forty days. Let us imitate Christ, and with him our John, so that we may freely call those the sons of the devil who refuse to repent. For such are the flatteries of sins that unless you strip off their paint, none of them can be brought to repentance. Cato, a Gentile, saw this, who, in Sallust, names the cause of all corruption as this: that men had long since lost the true and proper names of things. But the world takes it very ill that it is not allowed to have its fate argued against (John 3). What then? The Word of God must be thundered forth even against the unwilling, even if the broken world should fall in ruins. Those who are unwilling to hear it will at last be compelled to hear the clamours of enemies, the clash of arms, the blare of trumpets, the terrible and unintelligible threats of a foreign soldier, the thunder of bombards, the crash of falling towers, and whatever else the hazard of war brings forth. But I have advanced further than I intended. Let us return to John, who, taking occasion from this, confirms again by the strongest arguments what he has said, yet in such a way that he exhorts Christians by the same arguments to a zeal for innocence and integrity.

units.la: III. In hoc apparuit filius Dei, ut opera diaboli dissolvat. Omnis qui natus est ex Deo, peccatum non facit: quia semen eius in ipso manet: & non potest peccare, quia ex Deo natus est. Pertinent hæc ad priorem antithesis membrum, quod duobus argumentis probat vel confirmat. Habent tamen & exhortationem, ut qui fideles siue Christiani haberi volunt, innocentiæ & sanctimoniæ studeant, eò quod impuritas & peccandi libido cum natura & ingenio Christianismi planè pugnent. Primum argumentum à fine incarnationis Christi sumitur. Filius Dei ideo apparuit & homo factus est, ut diaboli opera dissolvat. Nam in paradyso serpenti dictum fuerat: Ponam inimicitias inter semen mulieris & inter te. Ipsum conculcabit tibi caput, & tu insidiaberis calcaneo ipsius. Gene.3. At inter opera diaboli primas obtinet peccatum. Per hoc primi parentes seducti sunt. Per idem hodie in filiis inobedientiæ diabolus regnat. Per illud quoque letiferum illud mortis venenum in omnem Adami posteritatē transfusum est. Unde sequitur principalem incarnationis Christi causam fuisse, ut peccatum dissolueretur, ne per illud in nobis ad interitum nostrarum animarum satan regnare posset. Atqui id, cuius gratia Christus venerat, perfecit. Nam & ipse principem huius mundi foras eiectum & iudicatum esse testatur. Ioan.12.&16. Adhæc, cum mortem, quæ peccati pœna est, gloriosa sua resurrectione deuicerit, peccati vires dissolutas & eneruatas esse oportet. 1. Corinth. 15. Ex his autem evidenti demonstratione colligitur, quod Ioannes probare instituit. Fideles nimirum & verè Christianos iustitiam facere, & peccatis abstinere. Sic enim argumentabimur: Qui Christo per fidem insiti sunt, ea sectari non possunt, quæ Christus suo in carnem aduentu dissoluit. At Christus venit, ut dissolveret peccatum, quod præcipuum diaboli opus, & diabolicæ tyrannidis quasi caput est. Indignum ergo & planè absurdum fuerit, si huius studium sectari velint qui Christum profitentur.
units.tr: III. In this, the Son of God appeared, that he might dissolve the works of the devil. Whoever is born of God does not commit sin, for his seed remains in him; and he cannot sin, because he has been born of God. These words belong to the first member of the antithesis, which John proves or confirms by two arguments. Yet they also contain an exhortation: those who wish to be regarded as faithful, that is, as Christians, should strive for innocence and holiness, since impurity and the lust of sinning are plainly at odds with the nature and character of Christianity. The first argument is taken from the purpose of Christ's incarnation. The Son of God appeared and was made man so that he might dissolve the works of the devil. For in Paradise it was said to the serpent: "I will put enmity between the seed of the woman and your seed; he shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for his heel." Gen. 3. Among the works of the devil, sin holds the first place. Through sin our first parents were seduced; through it the devil still reigns today over the sons of disobedience; and through it that deadly poison of death has been passed on to all the posterity of Adam. Hence it follows that the chief cause of Christ's incarnation was that sin should be dissolved, lest Satan could reign through it in us to the destruction of our souls. Now he who came for this purpose has accomplished it. For he himself testifies that the prince of this world has been cast out and judged. John 12 and 16. Moreover, since he has overcome death, which is the penalty of sin, by his glorious resurrection, the power of sin must be broken and enfeebled. 1 Cor. 15. From these things, by clear demonstration, there follows what John set out to prove: namely, that the faithful, and those who are truly Christians, practise righteousness and abstain from sins. For we shall argue thus: those who have been grafted into Christ through faith cannot pursue those things which Christ dissolved by his coming in the flesh. But Christ came to dissolve sin, which is the chief work of the devil and as it were the head of diabolical tyranny. It would therefore be unworthy and altogether absurd if those who profess Christ wished to pursue its cause.

units.la: Alterum argumentum à fidelium persona sumit, adeoq; à causa efficienti, per quā isti creantur. Omnis qui natus est ex Deo, peccatū non facit. Probat hoc: Quia semen eius in ipso manet. Deinde hoc ipsum explicat per amplificationē: Non potest peccare, quia ex Deo natus est. Priusquam verò argumenti formā inspiciamus, de quo semine loquatur, videndum erit. Docet id Petrus Apostolus, qui de Christianis loquens ait: Renati nō ex semine mortali, sed ex immortali per verbum Dei viuum & manens in æternum. 1. Pet. 1. Immortale hoc semen esse dicit Petrus. Quia si mortale esset, immortales creare non posset. Idem verò, quasi digito demonstrans, verbum Dei esse dicit, quod apud prophetam in æternum manere legimus. Isa.40. Et sanè non aliud regenerationis, per quam filij Dei nascimur, semen constitui potest, cum ipse Christus feminis parabola eius naturam exponere voluerit. Matth.13. Luc.8. Per hoc enim intellectus hominis, qui non capit ea quæ sunt spiritus Dei, illuminatur, & quasi alius efficitur, ut regni cœlorū mysteria videre & intelligere possit. Per illud ipsum, ubi animis nostris cœceptum & spiritu viuificatu fuerit, voluntas nostra reformatur, ut diuinæ voluntati obtemperare cupiat. Hoc ipso animatus homo vires nouas cœcipit, quibus ea faciat & exequatur, quæ dominus præcipit, quibus ité à lapsu per gratiam Dei resurgat: ut merito regeneratus vel nouus homo factus dici possit. Ad hæc igitur alludes Apostolus,sic argumentatur: Quicunque ex Deo natus est,feminis fui naturam & ingenium referit. At Christiani ex Deo nati sunt. (Nisi enim hoc demus, Christiani nequaquam dici poterūt. Nam Christus inquit: Nisi quis natus fuerit è supernis, non potest videre regnum Dei. Ioan.3.) Christiani ergo sui feminis,quod est verbum Dei,naturam referre debent. Quę autem verbi Dei natura est? quod ingenium? Idem haud dubie,quod & ipsius Dei est. Si enim in homine animi in dex sermo est,multo magis in Deo hoc dicendum erit,qui cum ipsa veritas sit,ab omni simulatio ne & dolo alienissimus est. Vt ergo Deus purus est & sanctus,ita verbum eius purum sanctumq; sit oportet. Vnde Dauid exclamat: Eloquia domini,eloquia munda: vt argentum excoctum in ca tino terreo,defecatum septies. Psal.12. Deinde vt Deus non ipse modo purus & sanctus est,sed & alios sanctificat. Ezech.20. & 37. ita verbum Dei sanctificare solet omnes,qui illud rite amplexan tur. Consumit enim quæcunque in nobis terrenam originem sapiunt, & acutior quouis gladio an cipiti,penetrat ad compages ossium & medullas intimas. Heb.4.
