Quomodo ergo impuritate pec catorum polluetur,qui ex hoc renatus fuerit? Imo peccare deuoto animo non potest,quicunque per hoc semen ex Deo natus est. Si enim communis sensus & quotidiana experientia dictat,impos sibile esse vt vrticæ aut cardui semen rosam generet,aut è contra,ex rosæ semine vrtica nascatur: qua ratione fieri poterit,vt ex puro, sancto & immortali semine verbi Dei homo nascatur impu rus,pphanus,peccatis deditus,& pinde mortis æternæ reus? Fortes creatur fortibus, inquit poe ta. Et nos è Deo natos p verbū ipsius ęternū,nō Dei, sed diaboli potius ingeniū referre dicemus?
units.tr: The second argument is taken from the person of the faithful, and so from the efficient cause through which they are created. "Whoever is born of God does not commit sin." He proves this: "because his seed remains in him." Then he explains the same thing by amplification: "He cannot sin, because he has been born of God." Before we look at the form of the argument, we must consider what seed he is speaking of. The apostle Peter teaches this, speaking of Christians: "You have been born again not of mortal seed, but of immortal, through the living and abiding word of God forever." 1 Pet. 1. Peter says that this seed is immortal, because if it were mortal it could not produce immortal beings. And he says that it is the word of God, which, as we read, remains forever in the prophet. Isa. 40. And indeed no other seed of the regeneration through which we are born as sons of God can be appointed, since Christ himself, in the parable of the seed, wished to expound its nature. Matt. 13; Luke 8. For by this the human understanding, which does not grasp the things of the Spirit of God, is enlightened, and as it were made another person, so that it can see and understand the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven. By the same word, once it has been conceived in our minds and quickened by the Spirit, our will is reformed, so that it desires to obey the divine will. Animated by this, the man begins to have new powers by which he does and carries out what the Lord commands, and by which he rises again from his fall through the grace of God; so that he can rightly be called regenerate, or made a new man. With these things in mind, the apostle alludes and argues thus: whoever has been born of God bears the nature and character of his seed. But Christians have been born of God. (For unless we grant this, they cannot be called Christians at all. For Christ says: "Unless someone is born from above, he cannot see the kingdom of God." John 3.) Christians therefore ought to bear the nature of their seed, which is the word of God. But what is the nature of the word of God? What is its character? Undoubtedly the same as that of God himself. For if in man the word of the mind is sincere, much more must this be said of God, who is truth itself and utterly free from all pretence and deceit. Therefore, just as God is pure and holy, so his word ought to be pure and holy. Hence David cries out: "The words of the Lord are pure words, like silver tried in a furnace of earth, refined seven times." Ps. 12. Then, just as God not only is pure and holy himself but also sanctifies others (Ezek. 20 and 37), so the word of God is accustomed to sanctify all who receive it rightly. For it consumes whatever in us savours of earthly origin, and it pierces more keenly than any two-edged sword, even to the division of joints and the innermost marrow. Heb. 4. How then can someone who has been born again through this be polluted by the impurity of sins? Indeed, whoever has been born of God through this seed cannot sin with a devoted mind. For if common sense and daily experience teach that it is impossible for the seed of a nettle or a thistle to produce a rose, or conversely for a nettle to spring from the seed of a rose, by what reasoning could it happen that from the pure, holy and immortal seed of the word of God a man should be born impure, profane, given over to sins, and therefore liable to eternal death? "Brave men are born of brave," says the poet. And shall we say that we, born of God through his eternal word, bear the character not of God but rather of the devil?

units.la: Sunt hæc magno studio nobis meditanda ô fratres. Vt enim de ingenio filiorum Dei nos erudiunt:ita quàm atrox flagitium sit docent,si, qui filij Dei nati sumus, peccatorum luto temere denuo inuoluimur. Sunt qui hoc leuiculum & venia dignum existiment, quòd sibiipsis peccent, & sibijpsis duntaxat noceant. Sed hæc Ioannis verba expendenti longè aliud videbitur. Sic enim peccamus in ipsum Deum,qui nos ex se renasci voluit. Peccamus in verbum Dei,cuius semé animis nostris fuerat insitum. Peccamus in ipsum Christum,cuius incarnationem & passionē, quantum in nobis est, irritam facimus. Viros bonos filiorum pudet, quos præter officium multa iniquè & impudenter designare vident,& illos abdicare consueuerunt. An ergo Deum tam facilem putabimus, vt filios ferre possit tam ingratos, & tot modis in se, in verbum suum & in filium Iesum Christum iniquos? Sed audiamus tandem huius loci epilogum.
units.tr: These things, brothers, we must ponder with great care. For just as they instruct us about the character of the sons of God, so they show how atrocious a crime it is, if we who have been born as sons of God rashly entangle ourselves again in the mire of sins. There are those who think this a trifling matter and deserving of pardon, because they sin only against themselves and harm only themselves. But to one who weighs the words of John this will appear quite otherwise. For in this way we sin against God himself, who willed to beget us again from himself. We sin against the word of God, whose seed had been implanted in our minds. We sin against Christ himself, whose incarnation and passion we render, as far as lies in us, void. Good men are ashamed of their sons when they see them committing many wrongs and shameless acts beyond their duty, and they are accustomed to disown them. Shall we then think God so easygoing that he could bear sons so ungrateful, and so wrongful in so many ways towards himself, towards his word and towards his Son Jesus Christ? But let us at last hear the epilogue of this passage.

units.la: In hoc manifesti sunt filij Dei, & filij diaboli. Finem & scopum eorum, quæ dixit hucusque,indicat. Est is,vt inter filios Dei & filios diaboli discernere discamus,ne vel ipsi nobis falsi tituli gloria tione imponamus,vel corrupto filiorū diaboli exéplo seducamur. Notas verò manifestas esse dicit, ex quib.vtriq; agnosci possint. Quis n.non dignoscat iustitię studiū à deuota & effreni peccādi libidine? Quisqs ergo fallitur,sciēs volēsq; fallitur,nec habet quo ignorantiā vel errore suo excusetur.
units.tr: In this the children of God are manifest, and the children of the devil. He indicates the aim and purpose of what he has said so far. It is this: that we may learn to distinguish between the sons of God and the sons of the devil, so that we neither impose upon ourselves the boast of a false title, nor are led astray by the corrupt example of the devil's sons. He says, moreover, that the marks by which both may be recognised are plain. For who does not distinguish the pursuit of righteousness from the devoted and unbridled lust of sinning? Whoever therefore is deceived, knowingly and willingly deceives himself, and has no excuse of ignorance or error.

units.la: Obseruemus autem locutionem,qua Ioannes vti voluit. Poterat dicere: In hoc vel per hoc fumus filij Dei, & filij diaboli. Sed sic operibus iustitiæ tribuere videri poterat, quasi per illa filij Dei efficeremur. Cauere ergo volens periculosum illud propriæ fiduciæ præcipitium,In hoc manifesti sunt (inquit) filij Dei,& filij diaboli:vt intelligamus opera hæc nequaquam nos iustificare coram Deo,sed fidei iustificantis esse signa & indicia. Signa verò hæc certa sunt & infallibilia. Fieri ergo nequit,vt fides,quæ spiritum sanctum sibi perpetuò coniunctū habet,otiosa quiescat. Quà obrem, vt nostrorum operum meritis salutis gloriam tribuere non debemus, ita vicissim cauendum erit,ne fide gloriemur falso,dum peccandi studio nos totos addiximus. Nec enim mendaces sui nominis professores fert,qui ipsissima est veritas. Suspecta ergo nobis sint, quæcunq; suis blanditijs persuadere caro studet. In timore & tremore operemur salute nostram. Denique in hoc vnum incumbamus, vt purum illud sanctumq; semen, quo renati sumus, in vniuersa vitæ nostræ conuersatione conspici possit, vt germani Dei filij, cum Christo Iesu viuamus,cui debetur benedictio,honor,gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Let us observe, however, the manner of speaking which John chose to use. He could have said: "In this, or by this, we are the children of God, and the children of the devil." But in that way he might seem to ascribe to works of righteousness what belongs to the grace of God, as though by them we became the sons of God. Wishing therefore to guard against that dangerous precipice of self-confidence, he says: "In this are manifest the children of God and the children of the devil," so that we may understand that these works do not justify us before God, but are signs and indications of justifying faith. These signs, moreover, are certain and infallible. It is therefore impossible that faith, which has the Holy Spirit joined perpetually to itself, should lie idle. Wherefore, just as we ought not to attribute the glory of salvation to the merits of our works, so conversely we must take care not to glory falsely in faith while we have given ourselves wholly to the pursuit of sinning. For he who is the truth itself does not bear those who are liars about their own name. Let those things, then, be suspect to us which the flesh eagerly tries to persuade us of with its flatteries. "Work out your salvation with fear and trembling." Finally, let us devote ourselves to this one thing: that that pure and holy seed by which we have been born again may be seen in the whole course of our life, so that as true children of God we may live with Christ Jesus, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power forever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XVIII.
units.tr: HOMILIA XVIII.

units.la: Omnis qui non facit iustitiam, non est ex Deo, & qui non dili-gīt fratrem suum. Quoniam hęc est annunciatio, quam audistis ab initio, ut diligamus nos invicem. Non sicut Cain ex illo malo erat, & occidit fratrem suum. Et propter quid occidit eum? Quia ope-ra eius mala erat, fratris autem eius iusta. Ne miremini fratres mei,
units.tr: Everyone who does not do justice is not of God, and neither is he who does not love his brother. For this is the message you heard from the beginning, that we should love one another. Not like Cain, who was of the evil one and slew his brother. And why did he slay him? Because his works were evil, but his brother's were righteous. Do not be surprised, my brothers,

units.la: si odit vos mundus. Nos scimus, quòd transivimus ex morte in vitam, quia diligimus fratres.
units.tr: if the world hates you. We know that we have passed from death into life, because we love the brethren.

units.la: MVltæ & graues sunt regni Iesu Christi in hoc mundo remoræ, multa quoque communis salutis nostræ hostis satan quotidie comminiscitur, quibus illud turbet, nosq; ab eius communione abstrahat. At nulla hic tam noxia sunt obstacula, quàm quæ ab ijs struuntur, qui Christi nomen & fidem falsò iactant. Ex illorum enim numero seductores & antichristi (vt præcedenti capite vidimus) emergunt, qui & Christi regnum & omnem salutis nostræ rationem humanarum traditionum tenebris obscurare student. Ex illis etiam sunt, qui Christum priuati commodi gratia profitentur, sacris Christianorum communicant, interim vero Christū & fidem factis (vt Paulus inquit Tit.1.) negant. Est hoc hominum genus cumprimis noxium & detestabile. Quia et infirmiores suo exemplo offendunt, & apertis Christi hostibus occasionem præbent, qua fidem & doctrinam Christi calumnientur, quasi hæc libidinis & licentiæ peccandi vnica causa fit. Non temere ergo fit, quòd de vita Christiana & eius conuersatione tam diligenter Ioannes disputat. Non contentus enim purificationem nostri nobis commendauisse, & ad hanc tam ipsius Dei patris quàm Christi exemplo instigauisse, eleganti antithesi filios Dei & filios diaboli inter se committit, & firmis argumentis probat, non Dei, sed diaboli filios esse & censeri debere, quicunq; purificationis studio abiecto, peccandi licentiam sequuntur. Scopus vero omnium hic est, vt qui filij Dei censeri cupiunt, puritatis studium amare, & deuotam peccandi consuetudinem abominari discant. Eodem & hic locus referri debet, qui simul alterum quoq; Christianæ conuersationis partem, siue notam, proponit. Primò enim repetit quæ ante dixerat de discrimine filiorum Dei & filiorum diaboli. Deinde, quia charitatis fraternæ meminerat, docet, hanc quoque germanam filiorum Dei notam esse. Tertio loco consolationem subijcit, qua illis medetur, qui dum charitati student, omnium inimicitijs & odijs subiacent. Et de his quidem, pro gratia à patre luminum concessa, ordine disseremus.
units.tr: The obstacles to the kingdom of Jesus Christ in this world are many and grave, and Satan, the enemy of our common salvation, devises many more every day, by which he may disturb it and draw us away from its fellowship. Yet none of these hindrances is so harmful as those put in place by men who falsely boast of the name and faith of Christ. For from their number come the seducers and antichrists (as we saw in the previous chapter), who strive to darken both the kingdom of Christ and every account of our salvation with the shadows of human traditions. Among them too are those who profess Christ for the sake of private advantage, take part in the sacred rites of Christians, and yet in their deeds deny Christ and the faith (as Paul says, Titus 1). This kind of man is especially harmful and detestable, because by his example he offends the weaker brethren and gives the open enemies of Christ an occasion to slander the faith and doctrine of Christ, as if these were the sole cause of lust and license to sin. It is therefore no accident that John disputes so carefully about the Christian life and its conduct. For not content to commend to us the purifying of ourselves, and to urge us to it by the example of God the Father himself and of Christ, he sets the sons of God and the sons of the devil over against one another in a elegant antithesis, and proves by firm arguments that those who cast off the zeal for purity and follow a license to sin are not, and ought not to be counted, sons of God but sons of the devil. The aim of the whole passage is this: that those who wish to be counted sons of God should learn to love the zeal for purity and to abhor the habit of sinning. To this same point this passage must also be referred, which at the same time sets forth the other part, or mark, of Christian conduct. For first he repeats what he had said before about the distinction between the sons of God and the sons of the devil. Then, because he had mentioned brotherly love, he teaches that this too is a genuine mark of the sons of God. Third, he adds a consolation, by which he heals those who, while they pursue charity, are exposed to the enmities and hatreds of all. Concerning these things, by the grace granted from the Father of lights, we shall discourse in order.

units.la: I. Omnis qui non facit iustitiam, non est ex Deo, & qui non diligit fratrem suum. Dependent hæc ex præcedentibus. Dixerat eos, qui ex Deo nati sunt, non peccare, imò peccare non posse: quia semen Dei, verbum scilicet regenerationis, in illis fit. Ex illis ergo contrarium infert: Omnis qui non facit iustitiam, id est, omnis qui peccat, ex Deo non est. Est hæc vera consequentia, quam nemo negare poterit, si ad hunc modum proponatur. Omnis qui ex Deo natus est, non peccat, eò quòd semen Dei in ipso manet. Omnis autem, qui non facit iustitiâ, peccat. Ergo omnis qui non facit iustitiam, non est ex Deo. Minor facilè probatur. Peccatum enim est, quicquid contra officium facimus, quod à Deo iustis & æquis legibus nobis præscriptum est. Cæterum, quia de hac Christianismi nota prius satis copiosè disputauit, in præsenti alteram quoque, charitatem fraternam nimirum, adijcit. Possumus ergo ex hac Ioannis sententia duas notas constituere, ex quibus tam filios Dei quàm filios diaboli dignoscamus. Quicunq; enim iustitiâ faciunt & fratres suos diligunt, ex Deo sunt, & Dei filij censeri debent. Rursus, qui non faciunt iustitiam, & fratres non diligunt, ex Deo non sunt. Diaboli ergo filij sint, necesse est. De vtraque nota fusius paulò differendum est, tam vt alios homines internoscere, quàm vt nostri officij magis memores esse possimus.
units.tr: I. Everyone who does not do justice is not of God, and neither is he who does not love his brother. These words depend on what goes before. He had said that those who are born of God do not sin, indeed cannot sin, because the seed of God, namely the word of regeneration, is in them. From this he draws the contrary conclusion: everyone who does not do justice, that is, everyone who sins, is not of God. This is a true consequence, which no one will be able to deny if it is set out in this form: Everyone who is born of God does not sin, because the seed of God remains in him. But everyone who does not do justice sins. Therefore everyone who does not do justice is not of God. The minor premise is easily proved. For sin is whatever we do contrary to the duty prescribed to us by God through just and equitable laws. But because he had already disputed at sufficient length about this mark of Christianity, he now adds the other, namely brotherly love. From this saying of John we can therefore establish two marks by which we may distinguish the sons of God and the sons of the devil alike. For whoever does justice and loves his brethren is of God and ought to be counted a son of God. Again, whoever does not do justice and does not love the brethren is not of God. Therefore he must be a son of the devil. Each of these marks must be discussed somewhat more fully, both so that we may recognise other men and so that we may be more mindful of our own duty.

units.la: Prima filiorum Dei nota est, ex qua fides illorum & spiritus adoptionis agnoscitur, facere iustitiam. Iustitiæ vocabulum latius hic extendimus, quàm vulgò soleat. Comprehendit enim omnium præceptorum Dei obseruationem. Nam iustitia (vt à philosophis & iurisperitis definitur) virtus est, quæ vnicuique quod suum est tribuit. Vnde iustitiam facere Ioannes dicit eū, qui vnicuiq;, tam Deo quàm hominibus, tribuit quod illis diuino iure debetur. Hic ergo & Deus & homines nobis consyderandi veniunt, vt quid singulis debeatur, videamus.
units.tr: The first mark of the sons of God, by which their faith and the spirit of adoption are recognised, is to do justice. Here we extend the word "justice" more broadly than is customary. For it comprehends the observance of all the commandments of God. For justice (as philosophers and jurists define it) is that virtue which gives to each what is his own. Hence John says that he does justice who gives to each, both to God and to men, what is due to them by divine right. Here, then, both God and men come before us for consideration, so that we may see what is owed to each.

units.la: Inter ea quæ Deo debentur, primatum fides obtinet: vt nimirum talem agnoscamus, qualis reuera est, omnemq; fiduciam & spem in ipso solo habeamus repositam. Exigit hoc ipse suo iure, dum inquit: Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus: Ne sint tibi Dij alieni coram me. Exod.20. Debetur eidem amor, & tantum quidem, vt à nobis diligatur super omnia, ex toto corde, ex tota anima et toto viribus. Deuter.6. Matth.22. Cohæret his cultus, tam internus quàm externus, cuius iustitia in hoc erit, vt secundum ipsius præscriptum institutus sit. Quisquis igitur ex Deo natus est, iustitiam hanc facit, vt Deo nihil neget eorum, quæ ille suo & optimo iure à nobis exigit, cum pater sit & benefactor liberalissimus. Regnabit in illo homine certa & syncera in vnum Deum fiducia, nec animum suum post Creaturas fornicari patietur. Non opes, non voluptates, non mundi studia, non coniugem, non liberos, non corpus suum, non ipsam vitam pluris faciet quàm Deum, sed hunc amabit super omnia, quæ in mundo amari solent. Idem animum totum Deo consecrabit, vt illum colat in spiritu & veritate. Ioan.4. Quæcunque verò in externa religione diuinitus instituta sunt, sancte obseruabit, vt ab illis ne latum vnguem discedat. Et hæc quidem iustitia est, quam in ijs quæ Deo debentur, præstant Dei filij. His si contrarium opponas, qui nam Dei filij non sint, mox patebit. Quisquis enim fiduciam & spem suam in Creaturis aut etiam proprijs operibus sitam habet: quisquis mundi huius studia præ Deo diligit, & propter illa obedientiam, quæ Deo debetur, negligit: quisquis labijs ad Deum appropinquat, spiritualem verò cultum, quo is vnicè delectatur, omittit: quisquis in externo cultu tantum sibi permittit, vt pro suo arbitrio quicquam adijciat, auferat, mutet vel inuertat, iustitiam non facit, & proinde ex Deo non est, quantumuis splendido titulo glorietur.
units.tr: Among the things owed to God, faith holds the first place: namely, that we acknowledge him as he truly is, and place all our trust and hope in him alone. He himself demands this by his own right, when he says: "I am the Lord your God; you shall have no other gods before me" (Exod. 20). Love is owed to him too, and indeed so much that he is loved by us above all things, with the whole heart, the whole soul and all our strength (Deut. 6; Matt. 22). Worship, both inward and outward, is bound up with these, and its justice will consist in this, that it is instituted according to his own prescription. Whoever is born of God therefore does this justice, giving God nothing less than what he demands from us by his own most just right, since he is Father and most generous benefactor. In such a man a sure and sincere trust in the one God will reign, and he will not suffer his mind to play the harlot after creatures. He will not esteem wealth, pleasures, worldly pursuits, wife, children, his own body, or life itself more than God, but will love him above all the things that are commonly loved in the world. He will likewise consecrate his whole mind to God, to worship him in spirit and in truth (John 4). And whatever has been instituted by divine authority in the external religion he will observe faithfully, so as not to depart from them by a hair's breadth. This indeed is the justice which the sons of God practise in what is owed to God. If you set the opposite of this before them, it will soon be clear who are not sons of God. For whoever has his trust and hope placed in creatures or even in his own works; whoever prefers the pursuits of this world to God, and on their account neglects the obedience that is owed to God; whoever draws near to God with his lips but omits the spiritual worship in which God alone takes delight; whoever permits himself in external worship so much that he adds, takes away, changes or overturns anything at his own discretion, does not do justice, and therefore is not of God, however much he may boast of a splendid title.

units.la: Sed ad homines quoq; transeamus, inter quos varia sunt vocationum & conditionum discrimina, quæ singula eum inspicere oportet, qui iustitiam facere voluerit. Habent hic primum locum parentes & liberi, & quicunque parentum loco sunt, vtpote doctores, pædagogi & magistratus. Debent parentes liberis educationem honestam, religionis & morum institutionem, eruditionē, correptionem, omnia denique, quæ corporum & animarum saluti inseruire possunt. Ephes.6. Debent vicissim his liberi obedientiam spontaneam, dilectionem, reuerentiam, alimenta quoque & quæcunq; sunt vitæ subsidia, si hos egere conspexerint. Præstabunt hæc vtrinq;, qui iustitiam facere & Dei filij censeri voluerint. Similiter magistratus est populum Deo adducere, ius dicere ex iustitia & æquitate, vindicare afflictos, seruare pauperes, iniustitiä & vim prohibere, vsuris obstare, pacem publicam defendere, plantare denique, quæcunque Dei gratiam populo conciliare possunt, excindere autem & è medio auferre, quæcunque eiusdem iram & meritas pœnas prouocât. Psal.72. Pro istis autem officijs subditi obedientiam debent voluntariam, amorem, reuerentiam, timorem, censfus, tributa, vectigal, & si quæ alia sunt eius generis. Hæc qui vtrinq; præstant, iustitiam faciunt & verè filij Dei sunt. Eodem modo mutua coniugum officia recenseri possent, & quæ heri seruis debent, quæq; ab his vicissim iure exiguntur, sed breuitatis studio illa omittimus. Possunt enim quæ dicta sunt sufficere, vt erga omnes ea exequi studeamus, quæ diuina & naturali lege nos illis debere intelligimus. Et vt ad omnes hominum ordines hæc iustitia extenditur: ita in omnibus vitæ nostræ actionibus locum habet, ex quibus nullæ sanctæ erunt, nullæ Deo placere, nullæ etiam filios Dei decere poterunt, nisi iuxta huius iustitiæ regulam administrentur. Ob oculos ergo versetur in iudicijs, in foro, in contractibus, in coniugijs, in agricultura, in artibus discendis & exercendis, in bello, in pace, in re domestica, omnibus denique negotijs: & sic nihil tam leuiculum erit, in quo non Dei filium à filio diaboli dignoscere possis.
units.tr: But let us also pass on to men, among whom there are various distinctions of callings and conditions, each of which must be considered by anyone who wishes to do justice. Here parents and children have the first place, and all who stand in the place of parents, such as teachers, tutors and magistrates. Parents owe their children an honourable upbringing, instruction in religion and morals, learning, correction, and in short everything that can serve the welfare of body and soul (Eph. 6). In turn, children owe their parents willing obedience, love, reverence, and also food and whatever else is needed for life, if they see them in want. Those who wish to do justice and to be counted sons of God will perform these things on both sides. Likewise the office of the magistrate is to bring the people to God, to dispense law in justice and equity, to vindicate the afflicted, to protect the poor, to prohibit injustice and violence, to resist usury, to defend public peace, and in short to plant whatever can win the favour of God for the people, and to root out and remove whatever provokes his wrath and deserved punishments (Ps. 72). In return for these duties, subjects owe voluntary obedience, love, reverence, fear, the census, taxes, tolls, and whatever other things are of that kind. Those who perform these duties on both sides do justice and are truly sons of God. In the same way the mutual duties of husbands and wives could be listed, and what servants owe to their masters and what in turn is rightly demanded from them; but for the sake of brevity we omit these. What has been said may be enough for us to strive to carry out towards all people those things which we understand we owe them by divine and natural law. And just as this justice extends to all orders of men, so it has its place in all the actions of our life, none of which will be holy, none pleasing to God, none able to be fitting for sons of God, unless they are administered according to the rule of this justice. Let it therefore be before your eyes in judgments, in the forum, in contracts, in marriages, in agriculture, in learning and practising the arts, in war, in peace, in domestic affairs, in short in all business; and thus there will be nothing so trivial in which you cannot distinguish the son of God from the son of the devil.

units.la: Altera filiorum Dei nota est, fraterna dilectio. Fratres qui sint, octauo sermone diximus. Comprehenduntur eo nomine omnes omnium locorum homines, imprimis tamen, qui per fidē & spiritum adoptionis nobis in Christo fratres facti sunt. Omnibus ergo dilectionem debemus, nec aliquem excludere licebit, nisi eundem & hominem esse, negare possimus. Si quis enim homo est, frater sit oportet, cum ex vno patre omnes simus progeniti. Quod si idem & Christianus fuerit, duplici fraternitatis vinculo nobis obstrictus, magis diligi debet. At in dilectionis vocabulo multum à multis erratur. Sunt enim, qui philautia & carnis iudicio exceptati, tunc se fratres diligere arbitrantur, si neminem laedant vel dicto vel facto. Sed hæc nō magis dilectio dici poterit, quàm lux dicetur, cui fulgor & splendor omnis abest, aut ignis, qui calore omni careat. Dilectio enim is in homine affectus est, qui animum totum in rem amatam inclinat & propensum reddit, vt ei bene velit, & proinde bene de illa loquatur, benefaciat eidem, nec quicquam omittat eorum, quæ ad eius incolumitatem faciunt. Quia enim amoris ea vis est (quod vulgò cernitur) vt animum totum ab ripiat, & quasi auferat desyderio, quo cum re vel persona amata coniungi cupimus, ab eodem bene volentia & beneficentiæ studium abesse non poterit. Testantur hoc Christi verba, qui in dilectione Dei & proximi totam legem consistere dicit. Matth.22. Et Paulus de eodem loquens ait: Nemini quicquam debeatis, nisi hoc vt inuicem diligatis. Nam qui diligit alterum, legem impleuit. Roman.13. At ridiculum foret, dilectionem legis impletionem dicere, si illa in frigido carnis affectu ac quiesceret, nec voluntate & beneficijs suam vim testaretur. Vehementer ergo eos falli dicimus, qui cum abs se neminem vnquam laesum esse, vel adhuc laedi dicere possunt, eo nomine sic sibi placent, vt vlterius progrediendum esse non arbitrentur. Christus certè Deum patrem nobis imitandum proponit. Matth.5. Is verò non ita diligit, vt ab iniuria tantummodo & malefactis abstineat, sed simul benefacit, & quæcunque in se habet bona, hominibus communicare studet. Quod studium quicunque negligunt, neglectæ charitatis ab ipso Christo accusantur. Docet hoc parabola, quæ Lucæ decimo capite describitur. Licet enim miserum illum & saucium, nec Leuita nec sa[?] cerdos spoliauissent, proximum tamen dilexisse negantur, quòd opem egenti non tulerunt. Samaritanum vero imitari iubemur, qui ad saucij aspectum misericordia motus, vulnera eius abluit, iumento impositum deduxit, hospiti commendauit. Adde his, quòd in nouissimo die nô de ijs conqueretur dominus, qui vestem eius abstulerint, qui victum rapuerint, corpus pulsarint, famam lę[?]serint, occiderint denique: sed famelico cibum, sitienti potum, nudo vestem non praebuisse, & captiuum vel aegrotum non visitauisse, ad aeternae damnationis iudicium sufficiet. Matth.25. Satis enim nocet, qui egenti opem, quam ferre posset, denegat. Annon per te frater moritur, dum fame perit, nec abs te victum vllis precibus impetrat? Annon vestem negando conficis eum, qui frigore vel mox deficit, vel in morbum incidit incurabilem? At quomodo fratrem diligit, qui ista fieri patitur? Desinamus ergo nobisipsis adulari o fratres, & operibus testemur charitatem, quae germana filiorum Dei nota est. Per hanc enim fides operari dicitur. Galat.5. Nec fieri potest, quin proximum diligat, qui Deum verè nouit, & in illo omnem salutis spem repositam habet. Qui principis aut opulenti alicuius fauorem demereri student, eius filios & domesticos diligere & colere cô sueuerunt. Et tu Deo te gratum fore putas, si homines diligere recuses, quos ille ex gratia condidit, quos pro filijs agnoscit, quos filij vnigeniti sanguine redemit? Recte ergo Ioannes, Dei filios esse negat, quicunque fratres non dilexerint. Sed vtinam in his confyderandis ingenij vires & totos animos magis intenderemus, & mox insanum illud iniuriarum pelagus, & horribiles priuatae vindictae furias, procul cedere videres. Fugerent quoque, imò euanescerent, doli, impostura, iniquitas & quicquid tandem malorum insatiabile priuati commodi studium peperit. Si enim neglectae charitatis rei sunt, & aeternae damnationis sententiae subiacent, qui opem non ferunt egenti, quid de illis futurum putabimus, qui hac animorum duritia non contenti, insuper nocent? Damnatur qui nudum non vestit, & tu impune te laturum speras, qui vestes aufers alienae pecuniae emptas? Damnatur qui victum egenti negauit. Quid ergo de te fiet, qui domum vi diripis, qui segetes proculcas, nec contentus praesentia abstulisse, spem anni in herba extinguis? Accusatur à Christo, qui peregrinum in domum propriam non suscipit. Tune ergo accusari non debes, qui domum alienam, mercenarius miles, incendis? qui vsura, fraudulentis contractibus, impostu-ris & omni iniuriarum genere tuae opis indigos auitis & paternis sedibus extrudis? Qui captiuum, cum potest, non consolatur, damnationi subiectus est. Quae igitur in te statuetur poena, qui calumniis & falso testimonio circumuentos vincula ferre cogis? qui vsurarijs artibus illectos ęre alieno gravas, & grauatos cum soluendo non sunt, carceribus mancipas? Haec haec peccata illa sunt fratres, quę in coelum clamare legimus. Hic ille Abeli sanguis est, qui vindictam postulans à Deo auditur. Ad hanc regulam si eos examines, qui hodie Christiani dici volunt, quàm exilis sit illorum numerus, videbis. Regnant enim passim, quaecunque charitate pugnant, vitia. Et eo peruentum est, vt bonus haberi possit, qui à notorijs iniurijs, violentia & dolo malo abstinet, licet charitatis officia omnibus deneget. Quid ergo Dei nos punientis iram miramur? Mendacium non fert qui ipsa est veritas. At quod nam mendacium tam detestabile, quàm in Dei conspectu filium Dei te dicere, cum omnis vita & actiones vniuersae diaboli filium loquantur? Si Dei filij censeri, & imminens nobis excidium vitare volumus, iustitiam facere & fratres diligere conueniet. Nobisipsis blandiri & hominum iudicia fallere possumus: Deum vero, qui corda scrutatur & renes, fallere non possumus.
units.tr: The second mark of the sons of God is brotherly love. We said in the eighth sermon who are brothers. That name embraces all men in every place, but above all those who through faith and the Spirit of adoption have become our brothers in Christ. We owe love to everyone, and no one may be excluded unless we can deny that he is even a man. For if someone is a man, he must be a brother, since we are all born of one Father. But if he is also a Christian, bound to us by the double bond of brotherhood, he ought to be loved all the more. Yet many go wrong about the word love. There are those who, judged by self-love and by the judgement of the flesh, think they love their brothers if they harm no one by word or deed. But this cannot be called love any more than light can be called light when it has no brightness or splendour at all, or fire when it has no heat. For love is an affection in a man that inclines his whole mind toward the thing loved and makes him disposed to wish it well, and therefore to speak well of it, to do it good, and to leave undone nothing that serves its welfare. For this is the power of love, as is commonly seen: it seizes the whole mind and, as it were, carries it away with the desire by which we long to be joined to the thing or person loved, so that goodwill and zeal for doing good cannot be absent from it. Christ's words bear witness to this, when he says that the whole law rests on the love of God and of neighbour (Matt. 22). And Paul, speaking of the same thing, says: "Owe nothing to anyone except to love one another; for he who loves another has fulfilled the law" (Rom. 13). But it would be absurd to call love the fulfilling of the law if it lay idle in a cold affection of the flesh and did not show its strength in goodwill and in benefits. We therefore say that those are greatly deceived who, because they can say that they have never harmed anyone, or do not harm anyone now, are so pleased with themselves on that account that they do not think they need to go any further. Christ certainly sets God the Father before us as the one to be imitated (Matt. 5). And God does not love in such a way that he merely abstains from injury and wrongdoing, but at the same time does good, and eagerly shares with men whatever good things he has. Whoever neglects this zeal is accused by Christ himself of neglected charity. The parable described in Luke chapter ten teaches this. For although neither the Levite nor the priest had robbed that wretched and wounded man, they are nevertheless said not to have loved their neighbour, because they did not bring help to the needy man. We are commanded to imitate the Samaritan, who, moved with pity at the sight of the wounded man, washed his wounds, set him on his beast, led him away, and commended him to the innkeeper. Add to these things that on the last day the Lord will not complain of those who have stripped his clothing, seized his food, struck his body, damaged his reputation, or finally killed him; but it will be enough for the sentence of eternal damnation that they did not give food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the naked, and did not visit the captive or the sick (Matt. 25). For he who withholds help from a needy man, when he could give it, does harm enough. Is a brother not dying through you when he perishes of hunger and does not obtain food from you by any entreaty? Do you not, by refusing clothing, bring to ruin the one who either soon faints with cold or falls into an incurable sickness? But how does he love his brother who allows these things to happen? Let us therefore cease to flatter ourselves, brothers, and let us bear witness to charity by our works, which is the true mark of the sons of God. For faith is said to work through love (Gal. 5). Nor can it be that he who truly knows God, and has all hope of salvation placed in him, does not love his neighbour. Those who strive to win the favour of a prince or of some wealthy man are accustomed to love and cherish his sons and household. And do you think you will be pleasing to God if you refuse to love men whom he created by grace, whom he acknowledges as his sons, and whom he redeemed by the blood of his only-begotten Son? John rightly says that those who do not love their brothers are not sons of God. But would that we would direct the powers of our minds and our whole souls more intently to considering these things, and you would soon see that that mad sea of injuries and the dreadful furies of private revenge recede far away. Deceit, trickery, iniquity, and whatever evil the insatiable pursuit of private advantage has produced would also flee, indeed vanish. For if those who do not bring help to the needy are guilty of neglected charity and are subject to the sentence of eternal damnation, what shall we suppose will become of those who, not content with this hardness of heart, go further and actively harm others? He is condemned who does not clothe the naked, and do you hope to go unpunished, you who take away garments bought with another's money? He is condemned who denied food to the needy. What then will become of you, who plunder a house by force, trample down the crops, and, not content with carrying off what is present, extinguish the hope of the year in the blade? He is accused by Christ who does not receive the stranger into his own house. Should you not then be accused, you who, a hired soldier, set fire to another's house? You who, by usury, fraudulent contracts, deceptions, and every kind of injustice, drive out of their ancestral and paternal homes those who are in need of your help? He who does not console the captive when he can is subject to damnation. What punishment then will be laid upon you, who force men entangled in false accusations and false witness to bear chains? You who consign to prison those whom usurious arts have enticed into heavy debt, and who, when they are unable to pay, are burdened the more? These, brothers, are the sins that we read cry out to heaven. This is the blood of Abel, which, demanding vengeance, is heard by God. If you examine by this rule those who today wish to be called Christians, you will see how slender their number is. For wherever vices fight against charity, they reign. And things have come to such a point that a man may be thought good if he abstains from notorious injuries, violence, and evil deceit, even though he denies all the duties of charity to everyone. Why then do we wonder at the anger of God who punishes us? He who is truth itself does not bear lies. But what lie is so detestable as to call yourself a son of God in God's sight, when your whole life and all your actions speak of you as a son of the devil? If we wish to be counted as sons of God and to avoid the destruction hanging over us, it will be fitting to do justice and to love our brothers. We can flatter ourselves and deceive human judgements; but God, who searches hearts and reins, we cannot deceive.

units.la: II. Quoniam haec est annunciatio, quam audistis ab initio, ut diligamus nos inuicem. Non sicut Cain ex illo malo erat, & occidit fratrem suum. Et propter quid occidit eum? Quia opera eius mala erant, fratris autem eius iusta. Est haec secunda huius loci pars, quae demonstrationem habet, qua fraternam dilectionem, filiorum Dei germanam & propriam notam esse probatur. Quia enim natura philauti-fumus, & priuato commodo studemus, difficulter nobis persuaderi patimur, quod nostris affectibus aduersatur. Vtitur autem duobus argumentis, quorum alterum à pronunciatis desumptum Christi testimonio nititur, alterum exemplo constat.
units.tr: II. "For this is the message that you heard from the beginning, that we should love one another: not as Cain, who was of the evil one and slew his brother. And why did he slay him? Because his own works were evil, and his brother's righteous." This is the second part of this passage, which contains a demonstration by which it is proved that brotherly love is the true and proper mark of the sons of God. For since by nature we are self-loving and pursue private advantage, we are slow to be persuaded of what runs against our affections. He uses two arguments, one of which rests on the testimony of Christ's sayings, the other is established by an example.

units.la: A pronunciatis sic argumentatur: Verę Christianorum vel filiorum Dei notae sunt, quas Christus ab illis exigit. At fraternam dilectionem à suis vbique Christus requirit. Eadem ergo vera & germana filiorum Dei nota est. Nec nouum est, quod nunc dicimus. Ab initio enim praedicationis euangelicae haec audiuistis. Etenim Christus inimicos diligere iusit, & idem, vt nobis exemplo esset, pro ijs orat, à quibus crucifigebatur. Matth.5. Luc.23. Quomodo igitur vel nouum vel absurdum videbitur, si fratres diligere iubeamur? Addam & aliud testimonium multò luculentius. In vltima coena Christum discipulis dixisse legimus: Praeceptum nouum do vobis, vt diligatis vos mutuò, sicut dilexi vos. In hoc cognoscent omnes, quod discipuli mei sitis, si charitatem habueritis inter vos mutuam. Ioan.13. Si ex mutua charitate discipuli Christi esse agnoscimur, charitas eorundem nota fit,oportet. Sed idem postea hoc ipsum repetens,inquit: Hoc est præceptum meum, vt diligatis vos inuicem,sicut dilexi vos. Et rursum: Hæc præcipio vobis, vt diligatis vos mutuo. Ioannis 15. At quid testimonijs hisce recensendis immoramur, cum illa scripturas legenti, passim occurrant?
units.tr: He argues from the sayings thus: the true marks of Christians or of the sons of God are those which Christ requires of them. But Christ everywhere requires brotherly love of his own. Therefore the same is the true and genuine mark of the sons of God. Nor is what we now say new: for you have heard this from the beginning of the preaching of the gospel. Indeed Christ commanded us to love our enemies, and he himself, to be an example to us, prayed for those by whom he was being crucified (Matt. 5; Luke 23). How then will it seem either new or absurd if we are commanded to love our brothers? I will add another testimony, far more clear. We read that at the last supper Christ said to his disciples: "A new commandment I give you, that you love one another, as I have loved you. By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another" (John 13). If we are recognised as disciples of Christ by mutual love, it must be that the love of the same people becomes a mark. But he afterwards repeating this very thing says: "This is my commandment, that you love one another, as I have loved you"; and again: "These things I command you, that you love one another" (John 15). But why do we linger in listing these testimonies, when they meet us everywhere as one reads the Scriptures?

units.la: Alterum argumentum exemplo constat, quod ex prima fere mundi origine producit. Vide-tur enim à contrarijs vel oppositis argumentari, hoc modo: Filiorum diaboli perpetua nota, ab ipso statim mundi exordio, fuit odium contra fratres. Ergo perpetua filiorum Dei nota semper fuit fraterna dilectio. Antecedens exemplo Caini probat. Fuit is ex illo malo, id est, diabolo: non quidem generatione (nam ex Adam & Eua nō minus quàm Abel natus fuit) sed imitatione, adeoq; diaboli primogenitus dici potest, cum primus sit ex vniuerso mortalium genere, qui se huic per omnia regendum subiecerit. Quæ vero eius fuerunt studia? Vno facto ea declarantur, quòd nimirum fratrem suum occidit. Pessima ergo illius studia & plena odij fuisse constat. Nec enim alia eius parricidij causa allegari potest, quàm Caini improbitas, & Abelis simplicitas, & syncerū iustitiæ studium. Patet hoc, si historiā, quæ Gen. 4. habetur, diligenter perlegeris. Qua ratione enim Cainū odio fraterno laborauisse negabimus, cum diuinum fauorem & felices rerum successus illum fratri inuidisse constet? Quia enim ad Abelis sacrificium respexerat dominus, iratus est Cain (inquit scriptura) vehementer, & cecidit vultus eius. Vt igitur in Caino peruersi animi & plane diaboli nota fuit fraternum odium: ita ex eadem nota, quales sint, dignosci poterunt, quicunq; odio fratrum ringuntur. Ad huius probationem multum facit temporis circumstantia. Quia enim in exordio mundi in primis Adami filijs ista indicia sese protulerunt, non dubiū est, quin eadem apud omnem posteritatem duratura sint. Caini enim, qui diaboli primogenitus est, ingenium sequentur quicunq; ex diabolo nati sunt: Abelis autem, qui primus ex Adamo Dei filius natus est, mores referent, quicunq; Dei spiritu & verbo regenerantur. Porrò memorabile cumprimis est exemplum hoc, propter multa quæ inde edoceri possumus, quæ obiter inspicienda sunt.
units.tr: The second argument rests on an example and proceeds from almost the very origin of the world. It seems to argue from contraries or opposites, in this way: the constant mark of the children of the devil, from the very beginning of the world, has been hatred of brothers. Therefore the constant mark of the children of God has always been brotherly love. The antecedent is proved by the example of Cain. He was of that evil one, that is, of the devil: not indeed by generation (for he was born of Adam and Eve no less than Abel was), but by imitation; and so he may be called the firstborn of the devil, since he was the first of the whole human race who submitted himself to be ruled by him in everything. What, then, were his pursuits? They are shown by one deed, namely that he killed his brother. It is clear, therefore, that his pursuits were most wicked and full of hatred. Nor can any other cause be alleged for his murder than Cain's wickedness, Abel's simplicity, and his zeal for righteousness. This is plain if you read carefully through the history recorded in Genesis 4. For on what grounds shall we deny that Cain was afflicted with hatred of his brother, since it is evident that he envied his brother God's favour and his happy successes? For when the Lord looked upon Abel's sacrifice, Cain (Scripture says) was exceedingly angry, and his countenance fell. Just as hatred of brothers was a mark of a perverse mind and of the devil himself in Cain, so from the same mark may be recognised what sort of people those are who are consumed with hatred of their brothers. A circumstance of time contributes much to this proof. For since these signs first appeared among the first sons of Adam, at the beginning of the world, there is no doubt that they will last among all posterity. For all who are born of the devil follow the disposition of Cain, the firstborn of the devil; and those who are regenerated by God's Spirit and Word bear the manners of Abel, who was the first son of God born of Adam. Moreover, this example is especially worthy of note, on account of the many things we may be taught from it, which should be considered in passing.

units.la: Primò enim admonemur, non sufficere externam fidei gloriationem & religionis externę, fesionem, nisi animus vera fide & syncero religionis studio imbutus sit. Nam si Cainum & Abe-lem conferas, quoad professionem fidei & externum cultum, nihil discriminis inuenies. Vnum & eundem Deum, mundi Creatorem vterq; agnouit. Vni Deo & eidem vterq; sacrificauit. Promissionem quoq; seminis illius salutiferi tam Caino quàm Abeli notam fuisse, verisimile est. Nec propter sacrificij materiam Deum Caino iniquiorem fuisse dicere possumus, cum nec pecudum sanguine nec frugum manipulis ipse opus habeat. Quid igitur in Abele fuisse dicemus, quod ipsius sacra Deo commendauit? Apostolum respondentem audi, qui inquit: Per fidem Deo vberiore hostiam obtulit Abel, quàm Cain, per quam testimonium meruit, quòd esset iustus, testimoniū perhibente de donarijs illius Deo, & per hàc mortuus adhuc loquitur. Heb. 11. Fide factū audis, quòd Abel Deo placuit. Quia enim hac fuit præditus, non agnū modò, sed seipsum obtulit, & in hoc fuit, vt innocentiæ & charitatis studio sese Deo patri approbaret. Eadem quia caruit Cain, dum sacrificat, non Dei gloriā, sed priuatum commodum quærit, cuius studio inuidia in fratrē, inde odium, & tandē immane parricidij scelus procreatur. Misere ergo falluntur, qui ptopter externos cultus se Deo placere existimant. Is enim quia spiritus est, spiritu & veritate coli vult. Ioan. 4. A veritate autē alienissimi sunt, qui dum Deo cultū præstare videri volunt, sua potius quærunt, quàm ea quæ Dei sunt: & in illos dicitur, quod apud prophetam dominus pronuciat: Populus iste ore suo mihi appropinquat, & labijs suis me honorificè prædicat: cor autē eius longè abest à me. Isa. 92. &c.
units.tr: For first we are reminded that an outward boasting of faith and an outward confession of religion are not enough, unless the mind is imbued with true faith and sincere zeal for religion. For if you compare Cain and Abel in respect of profession of faith and outward worship, you will find no difference. Both acknowledged one and the same God, the Creator of the world. Both offered sacrifice to the one and same God. It is also probable that the promise of that saving seed was known to Cain as well as to Abel. Nor can we say that God was less favourable to Cain on account of the matter of the sacrifice, since he has no need of the blood of cattle or of handfuls of fruits. What, then, shall we say was in Abel that commended his sacrifice to God? Listen to the Apostle answering: By faith Abel offered to God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, through which he obtained the testimony that he was righteous, God bearing witness to his gifts; and through it he being dead still speaks (Heb. 11). You hear that Abel pleased God by faith. For since he was endowed with this, he offered not only a lamb but himself, and in this he took care to approve himself to God the Father by his zeal for innocence and love. Because Cain lacked this, when he sacrificed he sought not God's glory but his own private advantage; from this zeal there arose envy of his brother, then hatred, and at last the monstrous crime of murder. Those therefore are wretchedly deceived who think they please God by outward worship. For since he is a Spirit, he wills to be worshipped in spirit and truth (John 4). But those are very far from the truth who, while they wish to seem to render worship to God, seek their own things rather than those that are God's; and of them is said what the Lord pronounces through the prophet: This people draws near to me with its mouth, and honours me with its lips, but its heart is far from me (Isa. 29), etc.

units.la: Secundò, causa obseruanda venit, ob quâ impij pios perpetuo odio prosequuntur. Quare (inquit) fratrem suũ Abelem occidit Cain? Num ea fuit Abelis morositas & contumacia, vt cū illo conuenire non potuerit? Vel num ab iniurijs & aperta vi sese hoc modo tueri coactus est? Nihil horum dicit Ioannes. Sed quia opera Caini mala erant, fratris aut iusta, ideo ipsis non potuit conuenire inter sese. Quæ enim natura disident, in vnū cōuenire nequeunt. At quid magis disidet q; Deus & Belial, Dei filij & filij diaboli, opera deniq; filiorū Dei & filiorū diaboli opera? Hęc enim praua sunt & verbo Dei prorsus contraria. Illorum aut opera Dei spiritū & verbū per omnia referunt. Quàm ergo difficile est, aquà igni miscere aut tenebris luce coniungere, tâ difficile erit pio-rum & impiorū studia inter se cociliare. Accedit his alia causa, cuius saluator noster Ioan. 3. ca. meminit. Quia mundi huius opera mala sunt, lucè ferre nō potest, qua illorū turpitudo arguitur. Nā licet corruptus sit mundus, nec aliud quàm peccare potest, idē tamē ambitiosus est, & sanctimoniæ simulator egregius. At quia apud Dei filios veritatis lux fulget, quæ res omnes arguit, & peccata deterso fuco quasi nuda in hominum conspectum protrahit, non possunt non Dei filij mundo exosi esse. Atqui hinc originem suam, à primo mundi exordio, habuerunt acres illæ & inde finentes pugnæ impiorum cum pijs & fidelibus. Vt enim Abeli cum Caino non conuenit: itanec Noe cum Nephilim ante diluuij tempus conuenire potuit. Exosus est apud Sodomitas Lot, pius Dei cultor. Isaacum Ismael ridet & persequitur. Iacobum Esau à pueris oppressum voluit. Fratres suos ob iustitiæ studium hostes habet Ioseph. Quid multis? Non prophetis cum impijs regibus, non Baptistæ cum Herode incesto, non Christo cum scribis & sacerdotibus, nec cum ijsdem Christi Apostolis vnquam conuenire potuit. Stultissimi ergo mortalium merito dicuntur, qui cunque & Dei cultores haberi, & mundi huius amici esse cupiunt. Verè enim Apostolus dicit, amicitiam mundi huius esse inimicitiam cum Deo. Iac.4. Et Christus de eodem admonet, dicens: Si de mundo essetis, mundus quod suum est diligeret. Quia verò de mundo non estis, sed ego selegi vos de mundo, propterea odit vos mundus. Ioan.15. Cuius dicti Paulus memor, de mundi amicitia adeò parum solicitus fuit, vt sic potius argumentari voluerit: Si hominibus placerem, Dei servus non essem. Galat.1.
units.tr: Second, we must note the cause for which the wicked pursue the godly with perpetual hatred. Why (it says) did Cain kill his brother Abel? Was it because Abel was so surly and stubborn that he could not get along with him? Or because he was forced to defend himself in this way against injuries and open violence? John says none of these things. But because Cain's works were evil and his brother's righteous, therefore they could not agree among themselves. For things that differ in nature cannot come together into one. But what differs more than God and Belial, the sons of God and the sons of the devil, and finally the works of the sons of God and the works of the sons of the devil? For these are wicked and utterly contrary to God's Word. But the works of the others reflect God's Spirit and Word in every respect. How hard it is, therefore, to mix water with fire or to join darkness with light, so hard will it be to reconcile the pursuits of the godly and the ungodly with one another. To these is added another cause, which our Saviour mentions in John chapter 3. Because the works of this world are evil, it cannot bear the light, by which its wickedness is exposed. For although the world is corrupt and can do nothing but sin, it is nevertheless ambitious and an excellent pretender to holiness. But since the light of truth shines among the sons of God, which exposes all things and drags sins, stripped of their false colouring, into the sight of men, the sons of God cannot but be hated by the world. And indeed from this beginning, from the very origin of the world, those bitter and never-ending struggles of the ungodly against the godly and the faithful have had their source. For as Abel could not agree with Cain, so Noah could not agree with the Nephilim before the time of the flood. Lot, a godly worshipper of God, was hated among the Sodomites. Ishmael mocks and persecutes Isaac. Esau wished to oppress Jacob from boyhood. Joseph has his brothers as enemies on account of his zeal for righteousness. Why say more? The prophets never could agree with wicked kings, nor the Baptist with the incestuous Herod, nor Christ with the scribes and priests, nor with the same Apostles of Christ. Those of mortals are rightly called most foolish who wish both to be counted worshippers of God and to be friends of this world. For the Apostle truly says that friendship with this world is enmity with God (James 4). And Christ warns of the same, saying: If you were of the world, the world would love what is its own. But because you are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hates you (John 15). Mindful of this saying, Paul cared so little about friendship with the world that he preferred to argue thus: If I still pleased men, I should not be a servant of Christ (Gal. 1).

units.la: Cæterum cum hæc traduntur, varias secum rationes init caro nostra. Quia enim pacis & otij natura appetentes sumus, multi longè consultissimum esse existimant, si fidem in Christum dissimulent, si de religione cum nemine mortalium contendant, si denique omnium moribus & studijs sese accommodent, ne hominum odia morositate sua in se cocitauisse videantur. Alios rursum est videre, quos perpetua Crux & assiduæ piorum persecutiones adeò offendũt, vt propter has de fidei veritate dubitare incipiant. Istis ergo mederi studens Apostolus, institutæ tractationi de fraterna charitate breuem consolationem interserit, quæ vltima huius loci pars est.
units.tr: Moreover, while these things are being taught, our flesh devises various reasons against them. For since we are by nature inclined to peace and quiet, many think it far the wisest course to conceal their faith in Christ, not to contend about religion with anyone, and finally to accommodate themselves to everyone's manners and pursuits, lest by their surliness they seem to have stirred up the hatred of men against themselves. On the other hand, one sees others whom the constant Cross and the unceasing persecutions of the godly so offend that on account of these they begin to doubt the truth of the faith. The Apostle, therefore, eager to heal these, inserts into the discussion of brotherly love a brief consolation, which is the last part of this passage.

units.la: III. Ne miremini fratres mei, si odit vos mundus. Nos scimus, quod transiuimus ex morte in vitam, quia diligimus fratres. Ex præcedentibus ista concludit. Sic enim vult dicere: Cum ea filiorum Dei sors sit, vt perpetuis in mundo hoc tribulationibus subiaceant, quæ sors in Abele initio sumpto ad omnem piorum posteritatem deriuata est: non mirum aut nouum vobis videri debet, si tale quid & vobis contingat. Num enim tot Dei cultoribus, qui à mundi exordio in hæc vsque tempora vixerunt, vos meliores & lætiori fortuna dignos putabitis? Num melius vos, qui serui & discipuli estis, tractari vultis, quàm dominum & magistrum vestrum, Iesum Christum, tractatum fuisse legimus? Quin ipsum loquente audite: Non est seruus maior domino suo. Si me persecuti sunt, & vos persequentur. Ioan.15. Sed & Paulus scribit: Omnes qui volunt piè viuere in Christo Iesu, persecutionem sustinebunt. 2.Tim.3. Simili ratione Petrus fideles monet, ne mirentur dum per ignem explorantur, quasi nouum aliquod ipsis obtingat: sic nimirum innuens, perpetuam hanc piorum in mundo conditionem fore. 1.Pet.4.
units.tr: III. Do not be surprised, my brothers, if the world hates you. We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brothers. John draws these things as a conclusion from what has gone before. For he means to say this: since it is the lot of the sons of God to be subjected to perpetual tribulations in this world, a lot which, beginning with Abel, has been passed down to all the posterity of the godly, it should not seem strange or new to you if something of the kind happens to you as well. For will you think that you are better and worthy of a happier fortune than so many worshippers of God who have lived from the beginning of the world down to these times? Or do you wish to be treated better than your Lord and Master, Jesus Christ, whom we read was treated? Indeed, hear him speaking himself: "The servant is not greater than his lord. If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you" (John 15). Paul also writes: "All who wish to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution" (2 Tim. 3). In a similar way Peter warns the faithful not to be astonished while they are tested by fire, as if something new were happening to them, thus clearly indicating that this will be the perpetual condition of the godly in the world (1 Pet. 4).

units.la: At Ioannes in præsenti consolationem insignem, à fine vel præmio desumptam, subijcit. Nos scimus (inquit) quod transiuimus ex morte in vitam, quia diligimus fratres. Sciendi verbo huius fiduciæ & spei certitudinem denotat. Consistit hæc partim in nota fidelium, charitate scilicet, de qua modò dictum est: partim verò in Christi promissionibus. Ipse enim inquit: Pater volo, vt vbi ego sum, ibi etiam sint quos dedisti mihi. Ioan.17. Similia & eadem habentur Ioan.12. & 14. At qui charitati fraternæ student (vt modò audimus) ex Deo sunt, & proinde Christo dati sunt. Cum Christo igitur erunt, & de morte in vitam transierunt (præterito pro futuro siue præsenti vtitur, vt certitudo præmij magis elucesçat) sicuti Christum ex morte in vitam & gloriam patris transiisse constat. Phil.2. Habet hæc sententia insigne charitatis elogium, quo vix aliud extat præstanti us. Nam per hanc nos de salute nostra certos fieri dicit. Quod tamen non ita accipiendum est, quasi per hanc vel iustificemur vel saluemur. De signo enim, nō de causa efficiente salutis, Ioannes loquitur, & charitatem infallibile signum esse docet, quo deprehendere possumus, fidem in nobis et se veram, nosq; in filiorum Dei numero censeri debere. Vt enim ignem adesse deprehendimus ex calore & lumine: ita fidei præsentis argumentum est charitas.
units.tr: But John, in the present passage, adds a remarkable consolation drawn from the end or the reward. "We know," he says, "that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brothers." By the word "know" he indicates the certainty of this confidence and hope. It rests partly on the mark of the faithful, namely love, of which we have just spoken; and partly on the promises of Christ. For he himself says: "Father, I wish that where I am, there also may be those whom you have given me" (John 17). Similar and the same things are found in John 12 and 14. Now those who devote themselves to brotherly love (as we have just heard) are of God, and therefore have been given to Christ. They will therefore be with Christ, and have passed from death to life (he uses the past tense for the future or present, so that the certainty of the reward may shine more clearly), just as it is established that Christ passed from death to life and to the glory of the Father (Phil. 2). This sentence contains an outstanding commendation of love, and scarcely anything else exists more excellent than it. For through it he says that we are made certain of our salvation. This, however, is not to be understood as if we were justified or saved through it. For John speaks of the sign, not of the efficient cause of salvation, and teaches that love is an infallible sign by which we can perceive that faith is true in us and that we ought to be counted among the number of the sons of God. For just as we perceive that fire is present from its heat and light, so love is the evidence of present faith.

units.la: Præcipuum verò huius sententiæ caput est, vt Crucis & afflictionum, quæ propter Christi nomen accidunt, dignitatem agnoscere discamus. Consistit hæc in duobus argumentis, quæ merito maximi apud nos ponderis esse debent. Primum est, quod inde constat, nos non ex mundo hoc, sed Dei filios esse. Alterum est, quod amplissimi præmij spem nobis habemus propositam. Nam si commorimur, & conuiuemus: si sufferimus, & conregnabimus. 2.Tim.2.
units.tr: The chief point of this sentence, however, is that we learn to recognise the dignity of the cross and of the afflictions which befall us on account of the name of Christ. This rests on two arguments, which ought rightly to carry the greatest weight with us. The first is that it is evident from this that we are not of this world but sons of God. The other is that the hope of a most ample reward is set before us. For "if we die with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him" (2 Tim. 2).

units.la: Docemur hic etiam, quàm vani & irriti sint huius mundi conatus, quibus filijs Dei nocere studet. Occisos hos cupit & deletos. Sed illi transeunt de morte in vitam, Christo dicente: Amen amen dico vobis, qui sermonem meum audit, & credit ei qui misit me, habet vitam æternam, & in condemnatione non veniet, sed transiuit à morte in vitam. Ioan.5. Quid ergo turbamur o fratres? Num in vita transire graue est? Num Christo in cœlis cohabitare detrectamus? At scio quid multi respondeant, qui non de mortis acerbitate, sed calumniis queruntur, quibus mundus hic piorum memoriam apud posteros infamem facere studet. Sed cogitandum erat, dominum esse, qui impio-rum memoriam excindit, ossa autem iustorum conseruat. Psal. 34. Prophetas & Apostolos vide, qui & ipsi calumniis circumuenti, haereseos & seditionis accusati sunt. Regnat tamen hodie & flo-ret celebris eorundem in ecclesia Dei memoria.
units.tr: We are taught here also how empty and vain are the attempts of this world, by which it strives to harm the sons of God. It desires them killed and destroyed. But they pass from death to life, Christ saying: "Amen, amen, I say to you, he who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and will not come into condemnation, but has passed from death to life" (John 5). Why then, O brothers, are we troubled? Is it a hard thing to pass into life? Do we refuse to dwell with Christ in heaven? But I know what many answer, who complain not of the bitterness of death but of the slanders by which this world strives to make the memory of the godly infamous among posterity. But we ought to have considered that it is the Lord who cuts off the memory of the wicked, but preserves the bones of the righteous (Ps. 34). Look at the prophets and apostles, who were also beset by slanders and accused of heresy and sedition. Yet today the celebrated memory of them still reigns and flourishes in the Church of God.

units.la: In hoc igitur totis viribus incumbamus, ut viua in nobis fides sit, quae iustitiae & dilectionis studio se prodat. Hac animati non curemus quaecunque contra nos mundi princeps molitur, qui dum nocere studet, ut plurimum prodest. Nam è valle lachrymarum liberat, facitq; ut a morte in vitam translati cum Jesu Christo viuamus, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Therefore let us in this strive with all our strength, that faith may be living in us, showing itself in the pursuit of righteousness and love. Encouraged by this, let us not care about whatever the prince of this world devises against us, who, while he strives to do harm, for the most part does good. For he frees us from the vale of tears and makes us, translated from death to life, live with Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XIX.
units.tr: Homily XIX.

units.la: Qui non diligit fratrem, manet in morte. Omnis qui odit fratrem suum, homicida est. Et scitis, quod omnis homicida non habet vitam aeternam in se manentem. In hoc cognouimus charitate, quod ille animam suam pro nobis posuit: & nos debemus pro fratribus animas ponere. Qui vero habuerit substantiam mundi, & viderit fratrem suum egentem, & clauserit viscera sua ab eo, quomodo charitas Dei manet in illo?
units.tr: He who does not love his brother abides in death. Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer. And you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him. By this we have come to know love, that he laid down his life for us; and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers. But whoever has the goods of the world, and sees his brother in need, and shuts up his heart against him, how does the love of God abide in him?

units.la: QVemadmodum tantae in nos bonitatis est Deus, pater clemens & misericors, ut non bona tantummodo sua nobis fruenda offerat, sed simul se totum, qualis & quantus est, nobis donet, quos filiorum loco habere dignatur: ita vicissim optimo iure a nobis eam vitae conversationem exigit, quae ipsius beneficiis respondeat, & quae tanti patris filios decere possit. Huius rationem & modum Joannes Apostolus tribus capitibus siue articulis comprehendit. Primo purificationem praecepit, qua peccati sordes deponimus, affectus prauos & cogitationes prophanas excutimus, & sancti atque irreprehensibiles fieri studemus. Quia enim in peccatis concepti & geniti non possumus non quotidie inquinari & pollui, quotidiana quoq; purificatione nobis opus est, si cum Deo sancto & immaculato communionem habere velimus. Secundo iustitiam praescribit, eam nimirum, qua & Deo & hominibus singulis, quod ipsis debetur, praestamus. Comprehendit haec fidem, & quaecunq; ad cultum Dei pertinent, simulq; per omnem vitam nostram ad omnes actiones & universos hominum ordines extenditur. Tertium locum fraternae charitati tribuit, quam totius Christianismi ratio exigit. Sumus enim eiusdem patris filij, quem in spiritu adoptionis invocamus. Una & eadem omnium haereditas in coelis est. Decet igitur ut fraterno amore coniuncti, per hunc probemus nos Dei unius filios esse. Caeterum, quia cum charitate corrupta carnis nostrae natura ex diametro pugnat, quae philautiae malo excaecata subinde quaerit & invenit quod charitatis legibus obganniat: magno studio & feruore hanc causam Joannes tractat. Primo enim iis, qui odia, contentiones, pugnas & caedes diutina consuetudine excusari posse existimant, Caini exemplum, ex ipsis mundi primordiis desumptum, opponit: quo fatetur quidem verum esse quod isti dicunt, sed haec ipsa certa & infallibilia argumenta esse dicit, satanae filios esse, qui his student. Deinde, quia ingratitudine mundi plures absterrentur a charitatis officiis, illis quoque medetur. Pluris enim facere docet charitatis fructum, quae filiorum Dei & haeredum vitae signum est, quam infelicis mundi amicitiam vel inimicitiam. Sunt tamen infinita alia, quibus caro nos obturbat, quae singula in sequentibus diluuntur. Et in praesenti quidem loco haec agit Apostolus. Principio contra illos disputationem instituit, qui charitatis studium adiaphoron esse putant, quod vel sequi vel negligere, salua hominis salute, liceat. Docet enim hoc necessarium esse, eo quod sine illo nec mortem effugere, nec vitam consequi possimus. Mox limitibus certis charitatem circumscribit, ut intelligamus quousque illa extendi debeat. Tandem illos arguit, qui & Christiani haberi volunt & charitate gloriantur, cum interim vel infima charitatis officia plane negligant. Utinam Deus, qui lux est, animis nostris suo spiritu affulgeat, ut haec non sine fructu tractasse & audivisse videamur.
units.tr: As God is so good to us, a Father gracious and merciful, that he not only offers us his goods to enjoy, but also gives us himself, wholly and in whatever way and greatness he is, us whom he deigns to have in the place of sons; so in turn, by the best right, he requires of us that manner of life which answers to his benefits and which may befit the sons of so great a Father. The Apostle John comprehends the reason and manner of this in three heads or articles. First, he enjoins purification, by which we put off the filth of sin, shake off depraved affections and profane thoughts, and strive to become holy and blameless. For since we, conceived and born in sins, cannot but be daily stained and polluted, we need daily purification too, if we wish to have communion with the holy and spotless God. Second, he prescribes righteousness, that righteousness by which we render to God and to each man what is owed to them. This comprises faith and whatever pertains to the worship of God, and at the same time it extends through our whole life to all actions and all the orders of men. Third, he assigns the place to brotherly love, which the whole rule of Christianity requires. For we are sons of the same Father, whom we invoke in the Spirit of adoption. One and the same inheritance of all is in heaven. It is fitting, therefore, that joined by brotherly love, we prove through this that we are sons of the one God. Moreover, since the nature of our flesh, corrupted, fights directly against charity, and being blinded by the evil of self-love, seeks at every turn and finds what runs counter to the laws of charity, John handles this cause with great zeal and fervour. For first, to those who think that hatreds, quarrels, fights and slaughters can be excused by long custom, he opposes the example of Cain, taken from the very beginnings of the world; by which he indeed admits that what they say is true, but says that these very things are sure and infallible arguments that those who pursue them are sons of Satan. Then, since many are deterred from the duties of charity by the ingratitude of the world, he also remedies this. For he teaches that the fruit of charity, which is the sign of the sons of God and heirs of life, is to be valued above the friendship or enmity of this unhappy world. There are, however, infinite other things by which the flesh troubles us, each of which is refuted in what follows. And in the present passage the Apostle deals with these things. First, he conducts a disputation against those who think that the pursuit of charity is a matter of indifference, which one may follow or neglect, the man's salvation being safe. For he teaches that this is necessary, because without it we can neither escape death nor obtain life. Soon after he circumscribes charity within certain limits, so that we may understand how far it ought to extend. Finally, he rebukes those who wish to be held Christians and boast of charity, while meanwhile they utterly neglect even the lowest duties of charity. May God, who is light, shine upon our minds by his Spirit, so that we may seem to have handled and heard these things not without fruit.

units.la: I. Qui non diligit fratrem,manet in morte. Omnis qui odit fratrem suum, homicida est. Et scitis,quod omnis homicida non habet vitam aeternam in se manentem. Docet quàm necessarium sit fraternae dilectionis studium. Argumentum sumit à contrario, indicans, quæ eius conditio sit, qui charitate vacuus est. Ait enim: Qui non diligit fratrem, manet in morte. Ergo nisi in morte manere velimus, fratres diligamus oportet. Est autem hæc sententia grauis adeoq; horribilis, si quàm exiguus sit eorū numerus consyderes, qui fratres syncerè diligunt. Non contentus enim vitâ negauisse, eum in morte manere dicit: quo dicto etiam spes vitæ negatur ei, qui fratrem non diligit. Sed non curat eius modi minas caro nostra, imò pro somniis & pfafforum deliramentis habet. Dictum itaq; suâ[?] breui demonstratione cõfirmat, cuius propositiones si inuertas, syllogismum habebis integrum, hoc modo: Nullus homicida habet vitam æternam in se manentem. Omnis qui odit fratrem, est homicida. Ergo nullus qui odit fratrem, vitam æternam in se manentem habet, sed manet in morte. Vides hic Ioannem pro vno & eodem ducere, si quis fratrem non diligat, & si eundem odio prosequatur. Satis enim odit, qui non diligit, nec iuuat cum potest. Rursum, quod dixit: Manet in morte: exponit per id quod est, vitam æternam nõ habere in se manentem. Hanc enim si auferas, quid obsecro in homine superesset, quàm mors? Sed ad argumentum Ioannis reuertamur, cuius veritatem nisi probè afferamus, difficulter nobis hic mundus consentiet. Nullum homicidam in se habere vitam æternam, omnis scriptura testatur. Psal.5. Dominus virum sanguinarium auersari dicitur. Quomodo autem vitæ consors erit, quem dominus auersatur, in quo solo vita est? Apud prophetam item Deus preces se exaudire negat, qui manus sanguine plenas ad illum extendant. Isa.1. Nec ignoramus per sanguines ibi quæuis atrociora flagitia designari. Sed cum hæc sanguinis nomine notare velit spiritus sanctus, utiq; inter hæc longè atrocissimum est sanguinis effusio. Paulus quoq; inter ea scelera, quæ à regni cœlorum hæreditate excludunt, homicidium non postremo loco nominat. Gal.5. Sed & Iesus Christus in reuelatione sua, homicidas cum canibus, scortatoribus, veneficis, & alijs id genus hominibus, per portas cœlestis illius Hierufalé ingressuros negat. Apo.22. Sed quid hæc adducere opus est, quando nec præsenti hac vita dignos iudicat Deus, qui sanguine effuso sese polluerunt? Notæ enim sunt de his ipsius Dei sententiæ, quas qui volet, legat Gene.9. Numer.35. Abunde ergo probata est maior Syllogismi huius propositio, utut diuersum fere huius seculi filijs videatur. Minorem itaq; videamus, cuius veritatem multò minus carnis nostræ excæcatum iudicium perspicit.
units.tr: I. He who does not love his brother abides in death. Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer. And you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him. He teaches how necessary is the pursuit of brotherly love. He takes the argument from the contrary, indicating what the condition is of one who is empty of charity. For he says: He who does not love his brother abides in death. Therefore, unless we wish to abide in death, we ought to love our brothers. This saying, however, is grave and indeed dreadful, if you consider how small is the number of those who sincerely love their brothers. For not content with denying him life, he says that he abides in death; by which saying hope of life is also denied to him who does not love his brother. But our flesh does not heed threats of this kind; nay, it holds them to be dreams and the delirium of priests. The saying, therefore, he confirms by a brief demonstration, whose propositions, if you invert them, you will have a complete syllogism, in this way: No murderer has eternal life abiding in him. Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer. Therefore no one who hates his brother has eternal life abiding in him, but abides in death. You see here that John regards as one and the same the one who does not love his brother and the one who pursues him with hatred. For he who does not love, and does not help when he can, hates enough. Again, what he said, abides in death, he explains by what it is, not having eternal life abiding in him. For if you take this away, what, I pray, would remain in a man but death? But let us return to John's argument, whose truth, unless we bring it forward well, the world will hardly agree to here. That no murderer has eternal life in him, all Scripture testifies. Ps. 5. The Lord is said to abhor the bloodthirsty man. But how will he be a partaker of life whom the Lord abhors, in whom alone is life? Likewise in the prophet God denies that he hears prayers from those who stretch out hands full of blood to him. Isa. 1. Nor are we ignorant that by bloods there are designated any atrocious crimes whatever. But since the Holy Spirit wishes to mark these by the name of blood, surely among these the effusion of blood is by far the most atrocious.
