Paul too, among those crimes which exclude from the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven, does not name murder in the last place. Gal. 5. But also Jesus Christ, in his Revelation, says that murderers, with dogs, fornicators, sorcerers, and other men of that kind, will not enter through the gates of that heavenly Jerusalem. Rev. 22. But why is it necessary to adduce these things, when God does not even judge worthy of the present life those who have polluted themselves by shedding blood? For God's own sentences concerning these are well known; let whoever wishes read Gen. 9. Num. 35. The major premise of this syllogism, therefore, has been sufficiently proved, though it seems almost contrary to the sons of this age. Let us see, then, the minor premise, whose truth the judgment of our flesh, blinded, perceives far less.

units.la: Qui odit fratrem suum homicida est. Si ex seipso hoc dixisset Ioannes, nimium audaculus & confidens videri poterat. Sed habet qui ipsum omni culpa liberat, Christum Iesum, patris sapientiam & verum diuinæ legis interpretem. Is enim Matth.5. ait: Audistis quòd dictum sit veteribus: Non occides. Quisquis autem occiderit, obnoxius erit iudicio. At ego dico vobis, quòd quisquis irascitur fratri suo temere, obnoxius erit iudicio. Igitur Christo teste in Dei conspectu homicidij reus ducitur, quicunq; in fratrem irascitur. At multò grauior odij quàm iræ culpa est, siquidem odium (ut reuera est) iræ inueteratæ affectum, adeoq; iram pertinacem dicere velimus. Quis ergo Ioannem accusset, quòd homicidam eum vocat, qui fratrem odit, cum Christus iræ hanc ipsam culpam inurat? Dei filium ergo in ius vocet, cui hæc durius dicta videntur. Sed nec Christi sententia displicebit, si re ipsam ad viuum resecemus. Constat equidem, Deum qui spiritus est, spiritu coli velle. Ioan.4. Animum ergo requirit, quem suo ingenio conformem vult, vnà cum actionibus, quæ animo propriæ sunt, quales sunt, affectus & voluntas. Quomodo enim animũ Deo consecratum dicemus, qui affectibus & voluntatibus, à Dei natura & voluntate alienissimis, distrahitur? Quia ergo voluntates nostræ totusq; animus Deo debetur, Deus destinata hominis voluntatem merito punit. Adhæc, cum destinata voluntas actionum quasi parens fit, hæ si non sequantur, aliunde obstaculum accedat oportet. Alioqui, quoad nos, quicquid voluntas nostra semel decreuit, ad finè perductum cupimus. Impossibile ergo, ut non ipsius facti culpa coram Deo imputetur iis, qui eius voluntatem destinatã animo conceperunt. Quis autem ab odio nocendi voluntatem abesse dicat? Qui odit, perditum vult quem odit. Quòd à perdendo abstinet, inde fit, quòd vel timore diuinitus immisso, vel publicis legibus, vel alijs rebus impeditur. An verò ipsius probitati imputandum quòd non nocet, cum non propria voluntate & ratione, sed aliena vi, nocere prohibeatur? Imò potius culpa, quæ in ipso hæret, facti pœnam meretur, cum ab ipso facto, nisi prohibitus, non abstineret. Quòd si ad hanc regulam nosmetipsos examinemus, mox videbimus quo loco simus apud Deum. Quem enim dare poteris, qui non legis transgressor & mortis reus iudicari debeat? Omnes ergo ad Dei gratiam confugere oportet, nec possibile est, ut proprijs meritis confisi coram Deo appareamus. Sed hæc est alterius loci tractatio, de qua suo tempore agetur.
units.tr: Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer. If John had said this from himself, he might seem too bold and confident. But he has one who frees him from every fault, Christ Jesus, the wisdom of the Father and the true interpreter of the divine law. For he says in Matt. 5: You have heard that it was said to the ancients: You shall not kill. Whoever kills shall be liable to judgment. But I say to you that whoever is angry with his brother rashly shall be liable to judgment. Therefore, with Christ as witness, whoever is angry with his brother is held guilty of murder in the sight of God. But the guilt of hatred is much graver than that of anger, since hatred (as it truly is) is the affection of an inveterate anger, or we might say an obstinate anger. Who then would accuse John, because he calls a murderer the one who hates his brother, when Christ brands this very fault of anger? Let him therefore summon the Son of God to court, to whom these things seem said too harshly. But neither will the saying of Christ displease, if we cut it down to the quick in the matter itself. It is certainly agreed that God, who is spirit, wishes to be worshipped in spirit. John 4. He therefore requires the mind, which he wills to be conformed to his own nature, together with the actions that are proper to the mind, such as affections and will. For how shall we call a mind consecrated to God, which is pulled apart by affections and wills most alien to the nature and will of God? Since, therefore, our wills and our whole mind are owed to God, God rightly punishes the intended will of man. Besides, since the intended will becomes, as it were, the parent of actions, if these do not follow, some obstacle must have arisen from elsewhere. Otherwise, as far as we are concerned, whatever our will has once decided, we desire to bring to completion. It is impossible, therefore, that the guilt of the deed itself should not be imputed before God to those who have conceived its intended will in their mind. Yet who would say that the will to harm is absent from hatred? He who hates wishes the one he hates to perish. That he refrains from destroying comes from this, that he is hindered either by fear sent from God, or by public laws, or by other circumstances. Or is it to be imputed to his uprightness that he does not harm, when he is prevented from harming not by his own will and reason, but by another's force? Nay rather, the guilt that clings to him deserves the punishment of the deed, since, were he not prevented, he would not refrain from the deed itself. But if we examine ourselves by this rule, we will soon see in what position we stand before God. For whom can you name who ought not to be judged a transgressor of the law and liable to death? All of us therefore must flee to the grace of God, nor is it possible that we should appear before God trusting in our own merits. But this is the treatment of another place, which will be discussed in its own time.

units.la: Obseruemus hic, fratres, q; mísera sit eorū conditio, qui à charitatis studio alieni sunt. Quid.n. de homine grauius dici poterat, quàm illũ in morte manere, & non habere in se manentem vitam æternam. Subiacent autem huic sententiæ, vt modò demonstrauimus, quicunq; animos charitatis vacuos habent. Non est ergo, quòd aliunde periculum metuant. Ipsi enim sibi maximè miseriæ & calamitatis, qua non alia maior est, authores sunt. Quid enim de opum, honorum adeoq; ipsius vitæ iactura conqueri opus est, cum ipse te cœlesti vitâ, quæ sola vitæ nomen meretur, & æternis regni cœlorum thesauris ac honoribus spolies? Vtinam horum memores essent, qui odio pertinaci contabescunt. Gloriosum illis videtur & magni animi indicium, si quis in ira remittenda aduersarium non præueniat, nec ab illo veniam roget, sed rogari potius velit. At magno constat hæc gloria, ô fratres. Nam interea temporis, dum inimico nocere studes, tibi ipsi maximum damnum infers. Cor enim tuum, quo nihil habes excellentius, pertinaci vindictæ desyderio excrucias & confi-cis: vt non temerè à maioribus nostris dictû fit, neminem hominum cibis delicatioribus, vel pre-ciosioribus[?] vesci, quàm eum qui odio laborat irreconciliabili. Cor quippe exedit proprium, & quan-tum in se est, vitæ suæ dies abbreviat. Sed tolerabilis esset hæc iactura, nisi maior, de qua modò di-ximus, illi accederet. Qua enim ratione probabimus, eū vita æterna se nequaquâ spoliare, qui odium pertinax & inueteratum animo suo occulit, cum proprijs precibus diuinæ iustitiæ vindictam in se prouocet? Christo iubente oramus: Remitte nobis debita nostra, sicuti nos remittimus debitoribus nostris. At penes te remissio debitorum proximi locum non habet, sed in illum immitis durus & odij tenax es. Quid ergo aliud à Deo postulas, quàm vt in te quoq; talis esse velit, & in-iurijs, quibus illum offendisti, minus ignoscere? O duram conditionem. Aut non dicenda diuina illa & consolationis spei q; plena oratio, qua Deum sub dulci patris nomine inuocamus: aut sic dicenda, vt in damnationis iustæ te stimoniû dicenti cedat. Pertinet enim hoc parabola, quæ à Christo Matth.18. proponitur, quam in præsenti breuitatis studio omittimus. Sequamur itaque Pauli consilium, qui monet, ne Solem super iram nostram occidere patiamur. Eph.4. Id enim si fiat, ferè eius diuturnitas in odium degenerare consueuit.
units.tr: Let us observe here, brothers, how wretched the condition is of those who are estranged from the zeal of charity. For what could be said of a man more grievous than that he remains in death and does not have eternal life abiding in him? Moreover, as we have just shown, all who have minds empty of charity lie under this sentence. There is therefore no need for them to fear danger from elsewhere. For they themselves are the authors of their own misery and calamity, which is no greater than this. For why should one complain about the loss of wealth, honours, and indeed of life itself, when you yourself strip yourself of the heavenly life, which alone deserves the name of life, and of the eternal treasures and honours of the kingdom of heaven? Would that those who waste away with stubborn hatred were mindful of these things. It seems glorious to them, and a sign of a great spirit, if someone does not anticipate his adversary in remitting anger, nor asks pardon from him, but would rather be asked. But this glory costs dearly, brothers. For in the meantime, while you are eager to harm your enemy, you inflict the greatest damage on yourself. For you torment and wear out your heart, than which you have nothing more excellent, with the desire of stubborn revenge; so that it is not without reason that our forefathers said that no one among men eats more delicate or more precious food than the one who labours under implacable hatred. For it consumes its own heart, and as far as it is in its power, it shortens the days of its life. But this loss would be tolerable, were it not joined by that greater loss of which we have just spoken. For by what reasoning shall we prove that he does not in any way strip himself of eternal life who hides in his mind a stubborn and inveterate hatred, while by his own prayers he provokes the vengeance of divine justice against himself? Commanded by Christ we pray: Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. But in you the remission of debts to your neighbour has no place; rather you are harsh and cruel toward him, and tenacious of hatred. What else, then, do you ask of God than that he likewise be such toward you, and forgive less the injuries by which you have offended him? O hard condition. Either that divine prayer, so full of consoling hope, by which we call upon God under the sweet name of Father, should not be spoken at all, or it should be spoken in such a way that it becomes a testimony against you, as you speak it, of your just condemnation. For this bears on the parable which Christ sets forth in Matthew 18, which in the present zeal for brevity we omit. Let us therefore follow the counsel of Paul, who warns us not to allow the sun to go down upon our anger. Eph. 4. For if this happens, its prolonged duration is usually wont to degenerate into hatred.

units.la: Nemo tamen putet, eos duntaxat à charitate alienos esse, qui odio proximi laborant. Vt enim charitas, quæ legis impletio est, omnes ferè virtutes in sese complectitur: ita contra hanc varie peccari solet. Huc enim & auari pertinent, qui à charitatis affectu tam procul absunt, vt illum cum auaritia coniungere impossibile sit. Huic enim debemus dolos, impostoras, furta, rapinas, vsu-rariorum mille artes, & eas quidem inextricabiles, quibus omnibus in charitatem palàm peccatur, quare & omnia hæc diuinis legibus prohibita sunt. Imprimis verò hic aures arrigere velim immi-tes vsurarios & monopolas, qui aliena egestate & publica victualium inopia gaudent & exultant, eò quòd inde quæstus ad ipsos redit vberior. Tunc enim venenatos morsus ijs inferunt, quos opibus suis iuuare debebant: dum artibus suis irretitos eò adducunt, vt tandem auitis sedibus & agris cedere cogantur. Hi sunt, qui onus frumenti accipiunt à paupere. Amos.5. Hi sunt, quorum iniu-stis exactionibus terra grauatur, vt cultores suos nec alere nec sufferre possit. Gemit & clamat con-tra hos afflicta pauperum turba, cuius voces non potest negligere Deus, qui se patronum horum passim in scripturis profitetur. Audiant illi quæso non mea vel alterius hominis, sed Dei domini verba, qui apud prophetam Babylonicæ captiuitatis & horrendi illius suæ gentis excidij causas commemorans, inter ait: Fœnus & excessum accepisti, & emolumentum tuum promoui-sti cum iniuria proximi tui, atque mei es oblita, dicit dominus Deus. Et ecce ego percussi manum meam super auaritia tua, quam exercuisti, & super sanguines tuos, qui fuerunt in medio tui. Ezechielis 22. Quòd si in terra tâ vbera, quæ ob felicissimam fertilitatem lacte & melle fluere dicitur, intolerabilis visa est Deo vsura, non dubium est, quin illa eidem multò intolerabilior videatur in nostra terra, quæ & maiori molestia atque sumptu colitur, & agricolarum laboribus minus liberaliter respondet. Intolerabilius ergo, quàm priores illi, in charitatem peccant auari vsurarij, quia & se vita æterna spoliant, & publicarum calamitatum authores sunt: quamobrem ceu publicas pestes communibus omnium suffragijs illos exibilari oportebat.
units.tr: Let no one, however, think that only those are estranged from charity who labour under hatred of their neighbour. For just as charity, which is the fulfilment of the law, embraces almost all the virtues within itself, so on the contrary, it is customary to sin against it in various ways. For here belong also the covetous, who are so far removed from the affection of charity that it is impossible for them to join it with avarice. To this vice we owe deceits, frauds, thefts, robberies, and the thousand arts of usurers, and indeed inextricable ones, by which charity is openly violated in all these ways; for this reason all these things are forbidden by divine laws. Above all, here I would like to prick up the ears of the cruel usurers and engrossers, who rejoice and exult in another's want and in the public scarcity of provisions, because their profit thereby returns more abundant. For then they inflict venomous bites on those whom they ought to help with their wealth, while by their arts they entangle them and bring them to the point where at last they are compelled to yield their ancestral homes and fields. These are the ones who take a burden of grain from the poor. Amos 5. These are the ones by whose unjust exactions the land is burdened, so that it can neither nourish nor bear its tillers. Against these the afflicted crowd of the poor groans and cries out, whose voices God cannot disregard, he who everywhere in the Scriptures professes himself their patron. I beg those men to hear not my words or those of another man, but the words of God the Lord, who, recounting through the prophet the causes of the Babylonian captivity and of that dreadful destruction of his people, says: You have taken usury and excess, and you have increased your gain by the wrong done to your neighbour, and you have forgotten me, says the Lord God. And behold, I have struck my hand upon your covetousness, which you have practised, and upon your bloodshed, which has been in your midst. Ezekiel 22. But if in that land, which is said to flow with milk and honey on account of its most happy fertility, usury seemed intolerable to God, there is no doubt that it appears to him much more intolerable in our land, which is cultivated with greater trouble and expense and responds less generously to the labours of the farmers. Covetous usurers therefore sin against charity more intolerably than those earlier ones, because they both strip themselves of eternal life and are the authors of public calamities; wherefore, like public plagues, they ought to be hissed down by the common votes of all.

units.la: Obseruent hæc etiam Cares nostri, venalis mercenariorum militum turba, qui præcipuam vi-ri laudem in effusione sanguinis collocant, & numo conducti ad bellum, cuius causas sæpius ignorant, tanquam ad lætum conuiuium concurrunt. Habent illi rationes varias, quibus hoc suum studium tueantur. Belli omnem culpam, si illud iniustum sit, in eius authore recidere dicunt, se enim hoc tantum facere, ad quod data mercede conducantur. Quasi verò idem fit, ad iugulandos homi-nes & mactandas pecudes conduci. Sed & publicam vtilitatem allegant, dum necessarium esse di-cunt, vt respub. viros habeat rei militaris peritos, quorum opera in propulsandis hostibus, si quan-do opus fit, vti queat. Sunt qui egestate & inopia se tuentur, & honestius censent, hanc militia mer-cenaria subleuare, quàm furtis aut alijs inhonestioribus artibus. Illorum enim iudicio honestius est, hominem vbi illum spoliaueris domumque eius exusseris, insuper mactare in coniugis & liberorum conspectu,quàm simplici furto rem alienam eripere. Sed mirum est,eò deuenisse homines,vt nullam se fuosq; alendi rationem superesse norint, quàm furta & bellum, quod omnium scelerum & scholam & palaestram esse constat. Apud ethnicos olim vulgari prouerbio notabantur Cares,quod ad quoquis bella sese conduci paterentur. Hodie inter Christianos,qui hoc faciunt seq; sponte offerunt,primam laudem sibi vendicant. At rationes illorum non multum moramur; cum vnus hic Ioannis locus ipsis confutandis sufficiat. Aut enim probent, sanguinis effusionem & alia quae militiâ comitantur facinora, charitatis opera esse: aut se à charitate alienissimos esse fateri cogetur, & proinde vitam eternâ in se manente non habere. At prius illud nunquâ probabût. Posterius ergo illud in ipsis haereat oportet,iuxta Dei sententiam, dicentis: Maledictus,qui accipit munus,vt percutiat animam sanguinis innocentis: & dicet vniuersus populus,Amen. Deute. 27. Discant itaque omnes,non moueri caecae carnis rationibus,quae odij,auaritiae,ambitionis & superbiae[?] affectibus superata in charitatem peccare docet. Firma enim & in aeternum rata manet spiritus sancti sententia: Omnis,qui non diligit fratrem suum,manet in morte.
units.tr: Let our Carians also take note of these things, the venal crowd of mercenary soldiers, who place the chief praise of a man in the shedding of blood, and who, hired for money to war, the causes of which they often do not know, rush to it as to a joyful banquet. They have various reasons by which they defend this their pursuit. They say that if a war is unjust, all the blame falls back upon its author, for they do only this, to which they are hired for a set wage. As if it were the same thing to be hired to slaughter men and butcher cattle! But they also plead public utility, saying that it is necessary for the commonwealth to have men skilled in military affairs, whose work it can use to repel enemies whenever there is need. There are some who defend themselves by poverty and want, and think it more honourable to relieve their lack by this mercenary soldiering than by thefts or other more dishonourable arts. For in their judgement it is more honourable, after you have despoiled a man and burned his house, then to slaughter him besides in the sight of his wife and children, than by simple theft to snatch away another's property. But it is a wonder that men have come to such a point that they know of no means of supporting themselves and theirs except theft and war, which is well known to be the school and wrestling-ground of all crimes. Among the heathen of old the Carians were marked by a common proverb, because they allowed themselves to be hired for any wars whatever. Today among Christians those who do this and offer themselves willingly claim the first praise for themselves. But we shall not dwell long on their reasons, since this one passage of John is enough to refute them. For either they must prove that the shedding of blood and the other crimes that accompany soldiering are works of charity, or they will be compelled to confess that they are most alien from charity, and therefore do not have eternal life abiding in them. But they will never prove the former. The latter, then, must cling to them, according to the sentence of God, who says: Cursed is he who takes a bribe to strike down the soul of innocent blood; and all the people shall say, Amen. Deut. 27. Let all therefore learn not to be moved by the reasons of blind flesh, which, overcome by the affections of hatred, covetousness, ambition and pride, teaches them to sin against charity. For the sentence of the Holy Spirit remains firm and ratified for ever: Everyone who does not love his brother abides in death.

units.la: Porrò hic multos audire est,qui sibijpsis mirificè placent,& charitatis officia abs se nequaquam negligi existimant. Dicunt enim: Nemo est mortalium, quem odio prosequamur, aut quem alias ob causas vellemus perditum. Scientes & volentes nemini iniuriam facimus. Fratrum concordiâ non turbamus, quin potius disidentes sibi inuicem reconciliari cupimus. Nullius bonis vel per vsuram vel alias artes illicitas inhiamus,sed nostris contenti viuimus. Linguam ita frenamus,ne alicuius famâ & honor laedatur. Manus quoq; abstinemus, ne cuiquam mortalium iniuriam faciamus. Quis ergo nos charitatis vacuos dicet? Annon haec secundum charitatis leges fiunt? Sed alteram duntaxat charitatis partem isti homines consyderant,quę monet ne quem laedamus. At ne mini nocuisse non sufficit,sed vt omnibus prodesse studeamus,exigitur. Quam ob rem Ioannes sequenti sententia charitatis limites describit,vt quousq; illa extendatur,intelligamus. Sic enim ait:
units.tr: Furthermore, here one may hear many who are wondrously pleased with themselves, and who think that the duties of charity are by no means neglected by them. For they say: There is no mortal whom we pursue with hatred, or whom we would wish to be lost for any other reason. Knowingly and willingly we do no one an injury. We do not disturb the concord of brothers; rather we desire that those who are at odds with one another be reconciled. We do not covet anyone's goods, either by usury or by other unlawful arts, but we live content with our own. We so curb the tongue that no one's reputation or honour is harmed. We also abstain from our hands, so that we do injury to no mortal. Who, then, will say that we are empty of charity? Are not these things done according to the laws of charity? But these men consider only the one part of charity, which warns us not to harm anyone. But it is not enough to have done no harm to anyone; we are required to strive to benefit all. Wherefore John, in the following sentence, describes the limits of charity, so that we may understand how far it extends. For he says:

units.la: I I. In hoc cognouimus charitatem, quòd ille animam suam pro nobis posuit: et nos debemus pro fratribus animas ponere. Christi exemplum commendat,& hunc nobis imitandum proponit. Quia enim priuati commodi studium omnibus charitatis legibus plurimum aduersatur, nunquam ea abs se impetrari pateretur caro quae hic exiguntur, nisi aliquem suo exemplo praeiuisse videat, quê sper nere non possit. At quis eò audaciae & impudentiae procedat, vt Christi exemplum contemnere velit? Sic ergo Ioannes argumentatur: Christianae charitatis termini sunt, quos Christus suo exemplo praefixit. Christus vero nos amando eoufq; procesit,vt animam quoq; pro nobis posuerit. Ergo quicunque vere diligunt fratres,pro ijsdem animas ponere parati sunt. Ne quis tamen Apostoli sententiam humani ingenij figmentum putet,obseruandum est,hoc ipsum Christi verbis asseri. Nam in euangelio inquit: Hoc est praeceptum meum, vt diligatis vos inuicem, sicut dilexi vos. Maiorem hac dilectionem nemo habet,vt quis animâ suam ponat pro amicis suis. Ioan. 15. Dicit haec Christus pro vulgari hominum consuetudine. Inter hos enim quidâ inuenti sunt, qui pro amicis morte obire dignati sunt. At Christus pro inimicis mori sustinuit,cuius exemplo nemo vnquam eorum imitatus est,qui extra huius cognitionē sunt versati. Docemur itaq; hoc loco,charitatem totum hominem requirere,nec satis esse, si nemini noceas, sed omnibus pro virili prosis oportet. Imò non sufficit,opes,ingenium,vires,eloquentiam & quaecunq; habes bona,ad proximi salutem & emolumentum contulisse,nisi & vitae tuae iactura illius incolumitatē redimere paratus sis. Monet hoc Christi exéplū,qui vt nō sibi sed nobis, & propter nos homo natus est: ita propter nos in terris vixit, propter nos docuit,propter nos miraculis claruit,propter nos capi,dânari,cōspui, flagellari & tandem crucifigi voluit, cū ipse omnibus istis minimè opus haberet. Imitati sunt hunc, quotquot ipsius spiritu verè animati fuerunt. Inter alios enim Mosem vide, qui enormi Israelitarum ingratitudine & atrocissimis iniurijs superari non potuit,quin in extremo ipsorū periculo suam vitam apud Deum interponeret,ne illi,vt meriti erant,delerētur. Nam ait: Nunc remitte peccatum hoc eorum:aut si non vis,expunge me quęso ex libro tuo,quę scripsisti. Exod.32. Eodem animo Dauidè praeditum legimus: qui cum angelū in Israele funesta lue grassari videret, exclamat: Ego peccaui,ego iniquè egi:oues autê istae quid fecerunt? Sit quaeso manus tua contra me, & contra domum patris mei.2.Sam.24. Quid de Paulo dicemus? Is certè post graues cotumelias & iniurias iniquissimas,à Iudaeis sibi illatas,non veretur dicere: Optarim ego ipse anathema esse à Christo pro fratribus meis,pro cognatis meis secundū carnem,qui sunt Israelitae,&c. Rom.9. Et alibi, quàuis sibi conducibile videat,dissolui & esse cū Christo, mauult tamen diutius vitae huius aerumnis & calamitatibus exerceri,q; suo auxilio ecclesias destituere. Phil.1. Non est ergo,vt confiliū, non praeceptum,esse putemus quod hic traditur:cum certò constet, fidelissimos quoq; Dei cultores iuxta hoc Christi exemplum & viuere & mori voluisse,vt multorum saluti consulerent. Cæterum nemo hęc ita accipiat, quasi Christus velit nos pro quouis fure aut latrone mortis supplicium subire, & illorum vitam nostra morte redimere. Nec enim nostræ mortis idem meritum est, quod mortis Christi fuit. Is vt æternam vitam miseris hominibus impetraret, morte sub ijt. At nemo nostrum, vel millies moriedo, alicui mortalium salutis cœlestis author fuerit. Soli quip pe Christo hæc debetur gloria, qui torcular calcauit solus, nec aliquem in huius laudis cófortium admittit. Isa.42.63. Adhęc, idem ille politicas leges, quibus manifesta scelera puniuntur, nequaqua sustulit. Nam & latronem, qui ex electorum numero erat, crucifigi, non alterius innocentis morte à supplicio liberari voluit. Et Paulus magistratui gladium datum esse docet, vt hoc boni defendantur, puniantur autem iniusti & improbi. Rom.13. Sed & Deus lege cauit, ne propter patres filij occidantur, aut filiorum culpam parentes luant. Deut.24. An ergo Deum velle putabimus, vt alio rum culpa & poena grauentur, qui illis nullo necessitudinis vinculo coniuncti sunt? Sano igitur sensu charitatis termini intelligendi sunt, vt quoties fratrum salus periclitatur, omnia nostra, vitam quoque, pro ijs impendere parati simus, salutis tamen legibus diuinitus latis, sine quibus publicam salutem & pacem consistere, est impossibile. Restat vltima huius loci pars, quam paucis absoluemus.
units.tr: I. "By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers." Christ's example commends this and sets it before us for imitation. For since the pursuit of private advantage is most opposed to all the laws of love, the flesh would never allow these things to be obtained from it unless it saw someone who had gone before with his own example, which it cannot despise. But who would proceed to such audacity and impudence as to wish to despise Christ's example? John therefore argues thus: the limits of Christian love are those which Christ set by his own example. Christ, however, loved us to such an extent that he also laid down his soul for us. Therefore, whoever truly loves the brothers is ready to lay down their lives for them. Lest anyone think the Apostle's saying is a figment of human wit, it must be observed that this same thing is asserted in Christ's own words. For in the Gospel he says: "This is my commandment, that you love one another, as I have loved you. Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends." John 15. Christ says this according to the common custom of men. For among men there have been some who thought it worthy to die for their friends. But Christ endured to die for his enemies, and no one of those who lived outside the knowledge of him has ever imitated his example. We are taught, therefore, in this place that love requires the whole man, and that it is not enough if you harm no one, but it is necessary to benefit all to the best of your power. Indeed, it is not sufficient to have contributed your wealth, talent, strength, eloquence and whatever other goods you have to the salvation and advantage of your neighbour, unless you are also ready to redeem his safety at the loss of your own life. Christ's example admonishes this, who, not for himself but for us and on account of us was born a man; so on account of us he lived on earth, on account of us he taught, on account of us he shone with miracles, on account of us he willed to be seized, condemned, spat upon, scourged and at last crucified, although he had no need of any of these things. All who were truly animated by his Spirit have imitated him. Consider Moses among others, who, overcome by the enormous ingratitude and most atrocious injuries of the Israelites, could not refrain from putting his own life before God in the extreme danger of theirs, so that they would not be destroyed as they deserved. For he says: "Now forgive this their sin; or if you will not, I beg you, blot me out of your book which you have written." Exod. 32. We read that David was endowed with the same spirit: when he saw the angel raging among Israel with deadly plague, he cries out: "I have sinned, I have done wickedly; but what have these sheep done? Let your hand, I beg you, be against me and against my father's house." 2 Sam. 24. What shall we say of Paul? He certainly, after grievous insults and most unjust injuries inflicted on him by the Jews, does not hesitate to say: "I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites," etc. Rom. 9. And elsewhere, although he sees that it is more advantageous for him to be dissolved and to be with Christ, he nevertheless prefers to be exercised longer by the troubles and calamities of this life, rather than to leave the churches destitute of his help. Phil. 1. It is not therefore to be thought that what is here delivered is a counsel and not a command, since it is certain that the most faithful worshippers of God also wished, according to this example of Christ, both to live and to die, so that they might provide for the safety of many. However, let no one take these things in such a way as if Christ wished us to undergo the punishment of death for any thief or robber whatever, and to redeem their life by our death. For our death does not have the same merit as the death of Christ had. He underwent death in order to obtain eternal life for wretched men. But none of us, even by dying a thousand times, would be the author of heavenly salvation for any mortal. To Christ alone this glory is due, who alone trod the winepress and admits no one as a partner in this praise. Isa. 42; 63. Moreover, that same one by no means abolished the political laws by which manifest crimes are punished. For he also willed that the robber, who was among the number of the elect, be crucified, and not be freed from punishment by the death of another innocent person. And Paul teaches that the sword has been given to the magistrate, so that the good may be defended and the unjust and wicked be punished. Rom. 13. But God also decreed by law that children should not be put to death for their fathers, nor parents bear the guilt of their children. Deut. 24. Shall we then think that God wills that men be burdened with the guilt and punishment of others, who are bound to them by no tie of kinship? The limits of love are therefore to be understood in a sound sense: that whenever the safety of the brothers is in danger, we should be ready to expend all that is ours, our life too, for them, yet within the laws of salvation given by God, without which public safety and peace cannot stand. There remains the last part of this place, which we shall finish in a few words.

units.la: III. Qui vero habuerit substantiam mundi, & viderit fratrem suum egentem, & clauserit viscera sua ab eo, quomodo charitas Dei manet in eo? Quoniam docendi ratio in his potissimum consistit, vt homines & quid sit officij ipsorum intelligant, & videant quantum ab ipsis peccatum fit, tum qua in re emendatione opus habeant: opportunè Ioannes, postquam charitatis modum & limites constituit, eos iam apertè arguit, quorum supra quoque mentio facta est, qui charitatis nomine gloriantur eo quod nemini vim & iniuriam inferunt, cum interim vel infima charitatis officia negligant. Sic enim vult dicere: Audio quidem sermones vestros, quibus vestram innocentiam prædicatis: quasi satis sit neminem suis possessionibus eiecisse, neminem dolis & vsurarijs artibus circumuenisse, neminem per vim spoliasse, & pulsauisse neminem. Sed toto cœlo erratis, si hoc putatis. Charitas enim vt ab iniurijs abstinet, ita benefacit quoties potest: & cum vires benefaciendi desunt, saltem to-tis viscera-bus commouetur ad alienæ calamitatis conspectum, nec alium dolorem grauiorem sentit, quàm quod periclitanti & laboranti subuenire non potest, cum non fortunas modo, sed & vitam (vt modo diximus) pro fratribus deponere parata sit. Quid ergo charitate gloriari iuuat o homo, qui habes substantiam mundi, qui opibus affluis & abundas, ijs autem securus frueris, tibi soli viuis, nec aliena tangeris miseria? Vides famelicum, nec cibas. Vides sitientem, nec potum præbes. Vides nudum & algentem, nec vestis. Vides incertis vagari sedibus fratrem, nec in domum colligis. Vides morbis afflictum, nec vlla ope subleuas. Imo postulantes opem surdis auribus præteris. Cur vero hæc omnia abs te officia negliguntur? Nonne quod viscera clausa habes & indurata, in quæ nullus alienæ miseriæ sensus penetrare potest? Qua enim causa alia te impediri dices? Inopiam & priuatam necessitatem allegare nequis, quia opibus abundas. Non igitur facultas, sed voluntas deest. At quia hæc animi motus est, animum tibi à charitatis affectu alienum esse constat. Define igitur falso titulo gloriari. Define tibi ipsi imponere. Define Deo illudere, qui nullo titulorum & verborum splendore fascinatur, nulla simulatione fallitur, sed cordis affectum videt, & opera charitatis, non falsam gloriationem, requirit. Hic mihi verborum Ioannis sensus videtur, in quibus duo non indiligenter obseruanda veniunt.
units.tr: III. "But whoever has the substance of the world, and sees his brother in need, and shuts up his bowels against him, how does the love of God abide in him?" Since the method of teaching consists chiefly in this, that men understand what their duty is, and see how great a sin they commit, and then in what matter they need correction: John, opportunely, after he has fixed the measure and limits of love, now openly rebukes those of whom mention was also made above, who glory in the name of love because they do no violence or injury to anyone, while in the meantime they neglect even the lowest duties of love. For he wishes to say: I indeed hear your words, by which you proclaim your innocence, as if it were enough not to have driven anyone from his possessions, not to have circumvented anyone by deceit and usurious arts, not to have despoiled anyone by force, and to have struck no one. But you are wholly mistaken if you think so. For love, as it refrains from injuries, so it does good whenever it can; and when the powers of doing good are lacking, at least its bowels are moved at the sight of another's calamity, and it feels no greater grief than that it cannot help one who is in danger and in trouble, since it is ready to lay down not only its fortunes but also its life (as we have just said) for the brothers. Why, then, does it help you, O man, to boast of love, you who have the substance of the world, who abound and overflow in riches, and who enjoy them without concern, living for yourself alone, and are not touched by the misery of others? You see a hungry man, and you do not feed him. You see one thirsting, and you offer no drink. You see one naked and shivering, and you do not clothe him. You see a brother wandering with no fixed dwelling, and you do not take him into your house. You see one afflicted with diseases, and you relieve him with no help. Nay, you pass by with deaf ears those who ask for help. But why are all these duties neglected by you? Is it not because you have closed and hardened bowels, into which no feeling of another's misery can penetrate? For what other cause will you say hinders you? You cannot plead poverty or private need, since you abound in wealth. Therefore it is not the means that is lacking but the will. But since this is a motion of the mind, it is plain that your mind is alien to the affection of love. Cease therefore to glory under a false title. Cease to impose upon yourself. Cease to mock God, who is not charmed by any splendour of titles and words, is not deceived by any pretence, but sees the affection of the heart and requires the works of love, not a false boasting. Here the meaning of John's words seems to me to be, in which two points are to be observed with no little care.

units.la: Primum est, quod charitati viscera tribuit. Facit hoc Hebraica phrasi. Hebræis enim viscera dicuntur naturales amoris affectiones, quas Græci σπλάγχνα vocant, quales sunt parentum erga liberos, & horum vicissim erga parentes, fratrum item & consanguineorum in se mutuo. Docet igitur hac voce, charitatem non opera modo & officia habere externa, sed illorum originem in animo hominis esse ex compassione & condolentia, qua homo ob alienam miseriam afficitur. Arguit hoc hypocritas, qui charitatem exercere se putant, quando eleemosynas largiuntur & variè subueniunt egenis, cum interim hæc faciendo, vel priuatam gloriam quærant, vel maiora beneficia inde à Deo se accepturos sperent. Faciunt hi quidem illa ipsa, quæ charitas facere solet, sed quia non ex charitatis affectu promanant, non charitatis, sed ambitionis potius aut etiam auaritiæ opera dici merentur. Contra hos Christus loquitur: Attendite, ne eleemosynam vestram præstetis coram hominibus quo spectemini ab illis. Alioqui præmium non habetis apud patrem vestrum, qui est in cœlis. Sed cum eleemosynam præstas, nesciat sinistra tua quod facit dextra tua, &c. Matth.6. Per dexteram enim syncerum illum charitatis affectum intelligit, à quo omnis sinistra cupiditas procul abesse debet. Huc quoque Paulus respicit, dum scribit: Si insumam in alimoniam omnes facultates meas, & si tradam corpus meum vt comburar, charitatem autem non habeam, nihil vtilitatis capio. 1.Cor.13. Præterea feruit hoc nobis in illum finem, vt nosipsos dijudicare & probare disceberorum conspectu, quàm simplici furto rem alienam eripere. Sed mirum est, eò deuenisse homines, vt nullam se fuosq; alendi rationem superesse norint, quàm furta & bellum, quod omnium scelerum & scholam & palæstram esse constat. Apud ethnicos olim vulgari prouerbio notabantur Cares, quod ad quoquis bella sese conduci paterentur. Hodie inter Christianos, qui hoc faciunt seq; sponte offerunt, primam laudem sibi vendicant. At rationes illorum non multum moramur, cum vnus hic Ioannis locus ipsis confutandis sufficiat. Aut enim probent, sanguinis effusionem & alia quæ militiâ comitantur facinora, charitatis opera esse: aut se à charitate alienissimos esse fateri cogetur, & proinde vitam æterna in se manente non habere. At prius illud nunquâ probabût. Posterius ergo illud in ipsis hæreat oportet, iuxta Dei sententiam, dicentis: Maledictus, qui accipit munus, vt percutiat animam sanguinis innocentis: & dicet vniuersus populus, Amen. Deute. 27. Discant itaque omnes, non moueri cæcæ carnis rationibus, quæ odij, auaritiæ, ambitionis & superbiæ affectibus superata in charitatem peccare docet. Firma enim & in æternum rata manet spiritus sancti sententia: Omnis, qui non diligit fratrem suum, manet in morte.
units.tr: The first is that he attributes bowels to love. He does this in the Hebrew manner. For the Hebrews call by the name of bowels the natural affections of love, which the Greeks call σπλάγχνα, such as those of parents towards children, and of these in turn towards parents, likewise of brothers and kinsmen towards one another. By this word, therefore, he teaches that love has not only outward works and duties, but that their origin lies in the mind of man, arising from compassion and sympathy, by which a man is moved at another's misery. This rebukes hypocrites, who think they exercise love when they bestow alms and in various ways help the needy, while in doing these things they either seek private glory or hope to receive greater benefits from God for them. These indeed do the very things that love is accustomed to do, but because they do not spring from the affection of love, they deserve to be called works not of love, but rather of ambition or even of avarice. Against such people Christ speaks: "Take heed that you do not give your alms before men, to be seen by them; otherwise you have no reward with your Father who is in heaven. But when you give alms, let not your left hand know what your right hand does," etc. Matt. 6. For by the right hand he means that sincere affection of love, from which every left-handed desire ought to be far removed. Paul also looks to this when he writes: "If I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give up my body to be burned, but have not love, I gain nothing." 1 Cor. 13. Moreover, this serves us to this end: that we may judge and prove ourselves, and learn how much of a simple theft it is to snatch away another's property. But it is astonishing that men have come to such a point that they know of no means of supporting themselves and their families except thefts and war, which is well known to be the school and training ground of all crimes. Among the heathen of old, the Carians were marked by a common proverb, because they allowed themselves to be hired for any wars whatever. Today among Christians, those who do this and offer themselves willingly claim the first praise for themselves. But we shall not dwell long on their reasons, since this one passage of John is sufficient to refute them. For either let them prove that the shedding of blood and the other crimes that accompany soldiering are works of love, or they will be compelled to confess that they are most alien to love, and therefore do not have eternal life abiding in them. But they will never prove the former. The latter, therefore, must cling to them, according to God's judgment, who says: "Cursed is he who takes a bribe to strike the soul of innocent blood." And all the people shall say, Amen. Deut. 27. Let all therefore learn not to be moved by the reasonings of blind flesh, which, overcome by the affections of hatred, avarice, ambition and pride, teaches them to sin against love. For the saying of the Holy Spirit stands firm and remains fixed for ever: "Whoever does not love his brother abides in death."

units.la: Porrò hic multos audire est, qui sibi ipsis mirificè placent, & charitatis officia abs se nequaquam negligi existimant. Dicunt enim: Nemo est mortalium, quem odio prosequamur, aut quem alias ob causas vellemus perditum. Scientes & volentes nemini iniuriam facimus. Fratrum concordiâ non turbamus, quin potius disidentes sibi inuicem reconciliari cupimus. Nullius bonis vel per vsuram vel alias artes illicitas inhiamus, sed nostris contenti viuimus. Linguam ita frenamus, ne alicuius famâ & honor laedatur. Manus quoq; abstinemus, ne cuiquam mortalium iniuriam faciamus. Quis ergo nos charitatis vacuos dicet? Annon hæc secundum charitatis leges fiunt? Sed alteram duntaxat charitatis partem isti homines confyderant, quæ monet ne quem laedamus. At ne mini nocuisse non sufficit, sed vt omnibus prodesse studeamus, exigitur. Quam ob rem Ioannes sequenti sententia charitatis limites describit, vt quousq; illa extendatur, intelligamus. Sic enim ait:
units.tr: Moreover, here one must listen to many people who are wonderfully pleased with themselves and think that they by no means neglect the duties of love. For they say: "There is no one among mortals whom we hate, or whom we would wish to be ruined for any other reason. Knowingly and willingly we do no one an injury. We do not disturb the harmony of the brethren; rather, we desire that those who disagree with one another be reconciled. We do not covet anyone's goods, either by usury or by other unlawful arts, but we live content with what is ours. We so bridle our tongue that no one's reputation or honour is harmed. We also refrain our hands, so that we do injury to no mortal. Who, then, will call us empty of love? Are not these things done according to the laws of love?" But these men have considered only one part of love, the part which warns us not to harm anyone. Yet it is not enough to have done no harm to me; we are required to strive to benefit all. Therefore John, in the following sentence, describes the limits of love, so that we may understand how far it extends. For he says:

units.la: II. In hoc cognouimus charitatem, quòd ille animam suam pro nobis posuit: et nos debemus pro fratribus animas ponere. Christi exemplum commendat, & hunc nobis imitandum proponit. Quia enim priuati commodi studium omnibus charitatis legibus plurimum aduersatur, nunquam ea abs se impetrari pateretur caro quæ hic exiguntur, nisi aliquem suo exemplo præiuisse videat, quæ speranere[?] non posit. At quis eo audaciæ & impudentiæ procedat, vt Christi exemplum contemnere velit? Sic ergo Ioannes argumentatur: Christianæ charitatis termini sunt, quos Christus suo exemplo præfixit. Christus vero nos amando eoufq; processit, vt animam quoq; pro nobis posuerit. Ergo quicunque verè diligunt fratres, pro ijsdem animas ponere parati sunt. Ne quis tamen Apostoli sententiam humani ingenij figmentum putet, obseruandum est, hoc ipsum Christi verbis asseri. Nam in euangelio inquit: Hoc est præceptum meum, vt diligatis vos inuicem, sicut dilexi vos. Maiorem hac dilectionem nemo habet, vt quis animâ suam ponat pro amicis suis. Ioan. 15. Dicit hæc Christus pro vulgari hominum consuetudine. Inter hos enim quidâ inuenti sunt, qui pro amicis morte obire dignati sunt. At Christus pro inimicis mori sustinuit, cuius exemplo nemo vnquam eorum imitatus est, qui extra huius cognitionē sunt versati. Docemur itaq; hoc loco, charitatem totum hominem requirere, nec satis esse, si nemini noceas, sed omnibus pro virili prosis oportet. Imò non sufficit, opes, ingenium, vires, eloquentiam & quæcunq; habes bona, ad proximi salutem & emolumentum contulisse, nisi & vitæ tuæ iactura illius incolumitate redimere paratus sis. Monet hoc Christi exéplu, qui vt nō sibi sed nobis, & propter nos homo natus est: ita propter nos in terris vixit, propter nos docuit, propter nos miraculis claruit, propter nos capi, dánari, cófpui, flagellari & tandem crucifigi voluit, cū ipse omnibus istis minimè opus haberet. Imitati sunt hunc, quotquot ipsius spiritu verè animati fuerunt. Inter alios enim Mosem vide, qui enormi Israelitarum ingratitudine & atrocissimis iniurijs superari non potuit, quin in extremo ipsorū periculo su am vitam apud Deum interponeret, ne illi, vt meriti erant, delerētur. Nam ait: Nunc remitte peccatum hoc eorum: aut si non vis, expunge me quæso ex libro tuo, quæ scripsisti. Exod. 32. Eodem anno Dauide præditum legimus: qui cum angelū in Israele funesta lue grassari videret, exclamat: Ego peccaui, ego iniquè egi: oues autè istæ quid fecerunt? Sit quæso manus tua contra me, & contra domum patris mei. 2. Sam. 24. Quid de Paulo dicemus? Is certè post graues cōtumelias & iniurias iniquisimas, à Iudæis sibi illatas, non veretur dicere: Optarim ego ipse anathema esse à Christo pro fratribus meis, pro cognatis meis secundū carnem, qui sunt Israelitæ, &c. Rom. 9. Et alibi, quàuis sibi conducibile videat, dissolui & esse cū Christo, mauult tamen diutius vitæ huius ærumnis & calamitatibus exerceri, q; suo auxilio ecclesias destituere. Phil. 1. Non est ergo, vt consilij, non præceptum, esse putemus quod hic traditur: cum certò constet, fidelissimos quoq; Dei cultores iuxta hoc Christi exemplum & viuere & mori voluisse, vt multorum saluti consulerent. Cæterum nemo hęc ita accipiat, quasi Christus velit nos pro quouis fure aut latrone mortis supplicium subire, & illorum vitam nostram morte redimere. Nec enim nostræ mortis idem meritum est, quod mortis Christi fuit. Is vt æternam vitam miseris hominibus impetraret, morte sub ijt. At nemo nostrum, vel millies moriędo, alicui mortaliū salutis cœlestis author fuerit. Soli quip pe Christo hæc debetur gloria, qui torculare calcauit solus, nec aliquem in huius laudis cōsortium admittit. Isa.42.63. Adhęc, idem ille politicas leges, quibus manifesta scelera puniuntur, nequaquā sustulit. Nam & latronem, qui ex electorum numero erat, crucifigi, non alterius innocentis mor te à supplicio liberari voluit. Et Paulus magistratui gladium datum esse docet, vt hoc boni defen dantur, puniantur autem iniusti & improbi. Rom.13. Sed & Deus lege cauit, ne propter patres filij occidantur, aut filiorum culpam parentes luant: Deut.24. An ergo Deum velle putabimus, vt alio rum culpa & pœna grauentur, qui illis nullo necessitudinis vinculo coniuncti sunt? Sano igitur sensu charitatis termini intelligendi sunt, vt quoties fratrum salus periclitatur, omnia nostra, vi tam quoque, pro ijs impendere parati simus, saluis tamen legibus diuinitus latis, sine quibus pu blicam salutem & pacem consistere, est impossibile. Restat vltima huius loci pars, quam paucis absoluemus.
units.tr: II. "By this we have known love, that he laid down his life for us; and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren." He commends the example of Christ and sets it before us as one to be imitated. For since the pursuit of private advantage is most opposed to all the laws of love, flesh would never allow these things that are here required to be obtained from it, unless it saw that someone had gone before it with his own example, which it cannot hope for. But who would proceed to such audacity and impudence as to wish to despise the example of Christ? Thus John argues: the limits of Christian love are those which Christ set down by his own example. But Christ, by loving us, went so far as to lay down his life for us also. Therefore whoever truly love the brethren are ready to lay down their lives for them. Lest anyone, however, think that the Apostle's saying is a figment of human wit, it must be observed that this very thing is asserted in the words of Christ. For in the Gospel he says: "This is my commandment, that you love one another, as I have loved you. Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends." John 15. Christ speaks these words according to the common custom of men. For among men there have been some who deemed it worthy to die for their friends. But Christ endured to die for his enemies, and no one of those who have lived outside the knowledge of him has ever imitated his example. We are taught therefore in this place that love requires the whole man, and that it is not enough if you harm no one, but you must benefit all to the best of your power. Indeed, it is not sufficient to have contributed your wealth, talent, strength, eloquence, and whatever other goods you have, to the salvation and advantage of your neighbour, unless you are also ready to redeem his well-being at the cost of your own life. The example of Christ admonishes this, who, not for himself but for us and on account of us, was born a man; so on account of us he lived on earth, on account of us he taught, on account of us he shone with miracles, on account of us he willed to be seized, condemned, spat upon, scourged, and at last crucified, although he had by no means need of any of these things. All who have been truly animated by his Spirit have imitated him. Among others, consider Moses, who, although the enormous ingratitude and most atrocious injuries of the Israelites overcame him, could not refrain from interposing his own life before God in their extreme peril, so that they might not be blotted out, as they deserved. For he says: "Now forgive their sin; but if not, I beg you, blot me out of your book, which you have written." Exod. 32. We read that David, in the same spirit, when he saw the angel raging with deadly plague in Israel, cried out: "I have sinned, I have done wickedly; but what have these sheep done? Let your hand, I beg you, be against me and against the house of my father." 2 Sam. 24. What shall we say of Paul? He, certainly, after grievous insults and most unjust injuries inflicted on him by the Jews, does not hesitate to say: "I myself would wish to be anathema from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites, etc." Rom. 9. And elsewhere, although he sees it to be more advantageous to be dissolved and be with Christ, he nevertheless prefers to be exercised longer in the troubles and calamities of this life than to forsake the churches by withdrawing his help. Phil. 1. It is not therefore to be thought that what is here delivered is a counsel and not a precept, since it is certain that the most faithful worshippers of God also, according to this example of Christ, were willing both to live and to die, that they might provide for the salvation of many. Yet let no one take these things as if Christ wished us to undergo the punishment of death for any thief or robber whatever, and to redeem their life with our death. For the merit of our death is not the same as the merit of Christ's death. He endured death so as to obtain eternal life for wretched men; but none of us, even by dying a thousand times, would become the author of heavenly salvation for any mortal. For this glory is due to Christ alone, who alone trod the winepress and admits no one into fellowship of this praise. Isa. 42, 63. Moreover, the same Christ did not at all abolish the civil laws by which manifest crimes are punished. For he willed that the thief, who was of the number of the elect, be crucified, and not be freed from the punishment by the death of another innocent person. And Paul teaches that the sword has been given to the magistrate, so that the good be defended and the wicked and the dishonest be punished. Rom. 13. But also God has provided by law that children not be put to death for their fathers, nor parents bear the guilt of their children. Deut. 24. Shall we then think that God wishes others to be burdened with the fault and punishment of those who are bound to them by no tie of kinship? Therefore the limits of love are to be understood in a sound sense: that whenever the salvation of the brethren is in peril, we should be ready to expend all that is ours, even our lives, for them, yet with the divinely given laws kept safe, without which public safety and peace cannot possibly stand. There remains the last part of this place, which we shall finish in a few words.

units.la: III. Qui vero habuerit substantiam mundi, & viderit fratrem suum egentem, & clauserit viscera sua ab eo, quomodo charitas Dei manet in eo? Quoniam docendi ratio in his potissimum consistit, vt ho mines & quid sit officij ipsorum intelligant, & videant quantū ab ipsis peccatum sit, tum quia in re emendatione opus habeant: opportune Ioannes, postquam charitatis modum & limites constitu it, eos iam apertius arguit, quorum supra quoq; mentio facta est, qui charitatis nomine gloriantur eo quòd nemini vim & iniuriam inferunt, cum interim vel infima charitatis officia negligant. Sic enim vult dicere: Audio quidem sermones vestros, quibus vestram innocentiam prędicatis: quasi satis sit neminem suis possessionibus eiecisse, neminē dolis & vsurarijs artibus circumuenisse, ne minem per vim spoliasse, & pulsauisse neminem. Sed toto cœlo erratis, si hoc putatis. Charitas e nim vt ab iniurijs abstinet, ita benefacit quoties potest: & cum vires benefaciendi desunt, saltē to tis visceribus commouetur ad alienæ calamitatis conspectum, nec alium dolorem grauiorem sen tit, quàm quòd periclitanti & laboranti subuenire non potest, cum non fortunas modo, sed & vi tam ( vt modò diximus ) pro fratribus deponere parata sit. Quid ergo charitate gloriari iuuat ô homo, qui habes substantiam mundi, qui opibus affluis & abundas, ijs autem securus frueris, tibi soli viuis, nec aliena tangeris miseria? Vides famelicum, nec cibas. Vides sitientem, nec potum præbes. Vides nudum & algentem, nec vestis. Vides incertis vagari sedibus fratrem, nec in do mum colligis. Vides morbis affliĉtum, nec vlla ope subleuas. Imò postulantes opem surdis auri bus præteris. Cur verò hæc omnia abs te officia negliguntur? Nonne quod viscera clausa habes & indurata, in quæ nullus alienæ miseriæ sensus penetrare potest? Qua enim causa alia te impe diri dices? Inopiam & priuatam necessitatem allegare nequis, quia opibus abundas. Non igitur facultas, sed voluntas deest. At quia hæc animi motus est, animum tibi à charitatis affeĉtu alie num esse constat. Define igitur falso titulo gloriari. Define tibijpsi imponere. Define Deo illude re, qui nullo titulorum & verborum splendore fascinatur, nulla simulatione fallitur, sed cordis affeĉtum videt, & opera charitatis, non falsam gloriationem, requirit. Hic mihi verborum Ioannis sensus videtur, in quibus duo non indiligenter obseruanda veniunt.
units.tr: III. "But whoever has the substance of the world, and sees his brother in need, and shuts up his bowels against him, how does the love of God abide in him?" Since the method of teaching consists chiefly in this, that men may understand what their duty is and see how great a sin they commit, and also because they need correction in this matter, John rightly, after he has set out the measure and limits of love, now more openly accuses those whom we mentioned above as well, who boast in the name of love because they do violence and injury to no one, while meanwhile they neglect even the lowest duties of love. For he wishes to say this: "I indeed hear your words, by which you proclaim your innocence, as if it were enough to have driven no one from his possessions, to have cheated no one by fraud or usurious arts, to have despoiled no one by force, and to have struck no one. But you are wholly mistaken if you think so. For love, as it abstains from injuries, so it does good whenever it can; and when the powers of doing good are lacking, it is at least moved in all its bowels at the sight of another's calamity, and feels no greater grief than that it cannot help one who is in danger and in trouble, since it is ready to lay down not only its fortunes but also its life, as we have just said, for the brethren. Why, then, does it please you to boast of love, O man, who have the substance of the world, who abound and overflow with riches, yet enjoy them securely, live for yourself alone, and are not touched by another's misery? You see the hungry man and do not feed him. You see the thirsty and do not give him drink. You see the naked and shivering and do not clothe him. You see a brother wandering in uncertain dwellings and do not gather him into your house. You see him afflicted with diseases and do not relieve him with any help. Indeed, you pass by those who ask for help with deaf ears. Why, however, are all these duties neglected by you? Is it not because you have closed and hardened bowels, into which no sense of another's misery can penetrate? For what other cause will you say hinders you? You cannot plead poverty and private necessity, since you abound in riches. Therefore it is not ability that is lacking, but will. And since this is a motion of the mind, it is clear that your mind is alien to the affection of love. Cease, therefore, to boast under a false title. Cease to impose upon yourself. Cease to mock God, who is not charmed by any splendour of titles and words, is not deceived by any pretence, but sees the affection of the heart and requires the works of love, not a false boasting. Here, to me, appears the sense of John's words, in which two points are to be observed not carelessly."

Hebræis enim viscera di cuntur naturales amoris affeĉtiones, quas Græci σπλάγχνας vocant, quales sunt parentum erga liberos, & horum vicissim erga parentes, fratrum item & cōsanguineorum in se mutuo. Docet igitur hac voce, charitatem non opera modo & officia habere externa, sed illorum originem in animo homi nis esse ex compassione & condolentia, qua homo ob alienam miseriam afficitur. Arguit hoc hy pocritas, qui charitatem exercere se putant, quando eleemosynas largiuntur & varie subueniunt egenis, cum interim hæc faciédo, vel priuatam gloriam quærant, vel maiora beneficia inde à Deo se accepturos sperent. Faciunt hi quidem illa ipsa, quæ charitas facere solet, sed quia non ex chari tatis affeĉtu promanant, non charitatis, sed ambitionis potius aut etiam auaritiæ opera dici meren tur. Contra hos Christus loquitur: Attendite, ne eleemosynam vestram præstetis coràm homini bus quò speĉtemini ab illis. Alioqui præmium non habetis apud patrem vestrum, qui est in cœ lis. Sed cum eleemosynam præstas, nesciat sinistra tua quod facit dextra tua, &c. Matth.6. Per dex teram enim syncerum illum charitatis affeĉtum intelligit, à quo omnis sinistra cupiditas procul abesse debet. Huc quoque Paulus respicit, dum scribit: Si insumam in alimoniam omnes faculta tes meas, & si tradam corpus meum vt comburar, charitatem autem non habeam, nihil vtilitatis capio.1.Cor.13. Præterea seruit hoc nobis in illum finem, vt nosipsos dijudicare & probare difcamus,num verè in nobis locum habeat charitas. Si enim viscera tua commoueri,id est alienæ miseriæ sensu te affici & studium iuuandi in te accendi sentias, germanus hic veræ charitatis affectus est,qui quò magis exercetur beneficentia,eò maior fit & ardentior. Quòd si verò talem te esse deprehendis, quem nulla tangit fratrum miseria, & qui siccis oculis ac sine gemitu aliorum labores & angustias cernere potes,scias te à charitatis sensu adhuc alienissimum esse.
units.tr: First, he attributes the bowels to charity. He does this in the Hebrew manner. For the Hebrews, "bowels" means the natural affections of love, which the Greeks call σπλάγχνα [splanchna], such as those of parents towards children and of children in turn towards parents, and likewise those of brothers and relatives towards one another. By this word, then, he teaches that charity does not consist only in external works and services, but that their origin lies in the heart of a person, arising from compassion and sympathy, by which a person is moved at another's misery. The hypocrites refute this, who think they practise charity when they hand out alms and help the needy in various ways, while in doing so they are seeking either private glory or hope to receive greater benefits from God in return. These people do the very things that charity usually does, but because they do not spring from an affection of charity, they deserve to be called works not of charity but rather of ambition or even of greed. Christ speaks against such people: "Take heed that you do not give your alms before men, to be seen by them; otherwise you have no reward with your Father who is in heaven. But when you give alms, let not your left hand know what your right hand does," etc. (Matt. 6.) By the right hand he means that sincere affection of charity, from which all left-handed desire must be kept far away. Paul also has this in view when he writes: "If I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I hand over my body to be burned, but have not charity, I gain nothing." (1 Cor. 13.) Moreover, this serves us for the purpose of learning to examine and test ourselves, whether charity truly has a place in us. For if you feel your bowels stirred, that is, if you sense that you are moved by the feeling of another's misery and that the zeal to help is kindled in you, this is the genuine affection of true charity, which grows greater and more ardent the more it is exercised in beneficence. But if you find that you are such a person that no misery of your brothers touches you, and you can look upon the labours and distresses of others with dry eyes and without a groan, know that you are still most alien to the sense of charity.

units.la: Deinde quis verus opum huius seculi vsus fit,hisce verbis docet Ioannes,quem vel hoc nomine diligenter expendisse prodest,quòd circa has à plerisq; in charitatem peccari cõstet. A charitate Dei,id est,ea quam Deus in suis operatur,& quæ ad Dei exemplum formata est, alienum dicit, qui cum opes possidet,egentis fratris miseria nõ afficitur. Opum ergo legitimus vsus est, aliorum egestatem subleuare ac laborantibus succurrere. Patebit hoc,si omnem harum rationem penitius inspicias. Dei enim donum esse opes,scriptura docet. Quòd si has cum tua persona conferas, non alijs vsibus tibi seruire poterunt,quàm vt tuæ necessitati inseruiant,dum victum,amictum, hospitium & alia ad corporis curam pertinentia largiuntur. Præter hæc ex opibus,etiam amplissimis,nihil ad te redire potest. Nam vt Paulus inquit: Nihil inferimus in mundum,nec quicquam efferre possumus:sed habentes alimenta & quibus tegamur,contenti simus.1. Tim.6. Cum ergo ad te ex opibus non aliud redeat,quàm quod necessitas exigit,qui fit,vt multis tantas opes concedi videamus,quantæ multis alijs alendis sufficerent,interim verò multis ea quoque desint, quibus natura carere non potest? An Deum tam imprudentem bonorum suorum dispensatorem dicemus, vel affectibus humanis regi,qui aliorum quidè fortunis gaudeat, aliorum verò infortunijs delectetur? Nequaquam. Sed inæqualitate hac,ceu arctissimo necessitatis vinculo,charitatem nobis commendare voluit. Siquidem si omnes quibuscunque indigent in se haberent,charitas locum inter homines non inueniret. Quis enim alterius opem non indigus expeteret? Quis eam non indigenti,nec etiam poscenti,vltrò deferret? Charitatis loco,quæ humiles,modestos,faciles & beneficos reddit, mox insolentiam, proteruiam, morum asperitatem & intolerabile priuati commodi studium regnare videremus. Quare vt omnibus istis malis vno pharmaco mederetur, inæqualitatem hanc inuexit Deus,vt pauperiores quidem opulentioribus,quorum ope indigent, honorem & obsequium iustum deferrent:hi verò ipsa opum affluentia sui officij admonerentur, & intelligerent, eam aliorum inopiæ & egestati subuenire debere. Admonet de his pulchre Paulus apostolus,dum Timotheo in priori epistola cap.6.scribit: His qui diuites sunt in præsenti seculo, præcipe, ne elato sint animo,neq; spem ponant in diuitijs incertis,sed in Deo viuente, qui præbet nobis omnia affatim ad fruendum,vt benefaciant,vt diuites sint operibus bonis,vt faciles sint ad impartiendum: liberiter communicantes,recondentes sibijpsis fundamentum bonum in posterū,vt apprehendant vitam æternam. Et Christus dominus iubet nos nobisipsis amicos facere ex mammone iniusto,vt cum defecerimus,recipiant nos in æterna tabernacula. Luc.16. Nec omittendum illud Iacobi apostoli,qui auri & argenti repositi eruginem diuitibus iustæ damnationis testimonium fore dicit.Iacob.5. Sic enim patet,benefaciendi facultatem ipsis non defuisse,sed voluntatem. Sed quantum, proh dolor,in his peccatur hodie. Si omnes quotquot Christi nomen profitentur inspicias,aut opibus per fas & nefas accumulandis inhiant,aut easdem luxu & libidine turpiter dilapidant. Quo fit, vt à prioribus illis pauperes opprimantur & expilentur miserè: ab alteris verò non sine turpi nominis Christiani ignominia negligantur,qui opes in scorta potius,aleam,comessationes,vestes libidinis instrumenta, sumptuosas domus, quàm in pauperes Christi ,viua spiritus sancti templa & membra Christi impendere volunt. Hæc igitur cum fiant passim, nū charitas Dei in nobis est? Vos appello ô diuites,num vnquam de his cogitetis serio? Si id facitis,nec emendatis,corda vos saxis duriora habere dicam. Vos appello ô magistratus,an vnquam tantis malis & maculis ecclesiæ remedium adhibere studeatis? Peccant hic,& diu peccarunt omnes hominum ordines,nec dubium est,Deum charitatem neglectam atroci iudicio puniturum, nisi maturè & breui emendemur. Hæc animis imis recondamus ô fratres,& abiectis odij,superbiæ & philautiæ affectibus,cõsultoribus prauissimis, charitatem sectemur, vt Christi exemplum imitati cum eodem in cœlis viuamus,cui debetur benedictio,honor,gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Next, John teaches by these words what the true use of the riches of this world is, and it is useful to weigh this carefully, not least because it is clear that many people sin against charity in this matter. He says that someone who possesses wealth but is not moved by the misery of a needy brother is alien to the charity of God, that is, to the charity that God works in his people and that is formed after God's example. Therefore the lawful use of wealth is to relieve the poverty of others and to come to the aid of those in distress. This will be clear if you examine the whole reckoning of these matters more closely. For Scripture teaches that riches are a gift of God. But if you compare them with your own person, they can serve you for no other purpose than to supply your need, while they provide food, clothing, shelter and the other things pertaining to the care of the body. Beyond these, nothing can come back to you even from very great riches. For, as Paul says: "We brought nothing into the world, and we cannot carry anything out; but having food and clothing, let us be content." (1 Tim. 6.) Since, then, nothing more returns to you from riches than what necessity requires, how does it happen that we see great riches granted to some, sufficient to feed many others, while at the same time many lack even those things which nature cannot do without? Shall we say that God is so imprudent a steward of his goods, or that he is ruled by human passions, rejoicing in the fortunes of some and taking delight in the misfortunes of others? By no means. But by this inequality, as by the closest bond of necessity, he wished to commend charity to us. For if all had in themselves whatever they lacked, charity would find no place among men. Who would seek another's help if he did not need it? Who would willingly offer it to one who did not need it, nor even asked for it? In place of charity, which makes people humble, modest, affable and beneficent, we would soon see arrogance, insolence, harshness of manners and an intolerable zeal for private advantage reigning. Therefore, in order to heal all these evils with one remedy, God introduced this inequality, so that the poorer would indeed render due honour and service to the wealthier, on whose help they depend, and so that the wealthy, by the very abundance of their riches, would be reminded of their duty and understand that it ought to relieve the want and poverty of others. Paul the apostle admonishes about these matters admirably, when he writes to Timothy in the first epistle, chapter 6: "Charge those who are rich in this present age not to be haughty, nor to set their hope on uncertain riches, but on the living God, who gives us all things richly to enjoy; that they do good, that they be rich in good works, that they be ready to give, willing to share, laying up for themselves a good foundation for the future, that they may lay hold on eternal life." And Christ the Lord bids us make friends for ourselves by means of unrighteous mammon, so that when we fail, they may receive us into eternal dwellings. (Luke 16.) Nor should we omit that saying of the apostle James, who says that the rust of stored gold and silver will be a testimony of just condemnation against the rich. (James 5.) For thus it is plain that the rich did not lack the ability to do good, but the will. But alas, how much is sinned in these matters today! If you look at all who profess the name of Christ, they either lust to amass wealth by every means, fair or foul, or they shamefully squander the same in luxury and lust. The result is that the poor are oppressed and wretchedly plundered by the former, while they are neglected, not without shameful disgrace to the Christian name, by the latter, who prefer to spend their riches on harlots, dice, carousing, clothes as instruments of lust, and sumptuous houses, rather than on the poor of Christ, the living temples of the Holy Spirit and members of Christ. Since these things happen everywhere, is there then the charity of God in us? I address you, O rich: do you ever think about these things seriously? If you do so and do not amend, I shall say that your hearts are harder than stones. I address you, O magistrates: do you ever strive to apply a remedy to such great evils and stains of the Church? Here they sin, and all orders of men have long sinned, nor is there any doubt that God, whose charity is neglected, will punish with a dreadful judgment unless we are amended soon and quickly. Let us lay these things up in our innermost hearts, brothers, and, casting off the affections of hatred, pride and self-love, those most wicked counsellors, let us pursue charity, so that imitating the example of Christ we may live with him in heaven, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XX.
units.tr: HOMILY XX.

units.la: Filioli mei,ne diligamus sermone,neq; lingua,sed opere & veritate. Et per hoc cognoscimus, quòd ex veritate sumus: & coram ipso persuadebimus cordibus nostris. Quòd si condẽnet nos cor, maior est Deus corde nostro, & nouit omnia. Charissimi, si cor nostrum non condemnet nos, fiduciam habemus erga Deum: & quicquid petierimus, accipimus ab eo: quoniam praecepta eius custodimus, & ea quae sunt placita coram eo, facimus.
units.tr: My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue, but in deed and truth. And by this we know that we are of the truth, and we shall persuade our hearts before him. But if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things. Beloved, if our heart condemn us not, then have we confidence toward God; and whatsoever we ask, we receive of him, because we keep his commandments, and do those things that are pleasing in his sight.

units.la: Quamuis infelix hominum genus in huius vitae curriculo nihil vel salutarius vel magis necessarium habeat, fraterna charitate, quae pacem, concordiam, & quaecunque hanc sequuntur, ex sese gignit: ea tamen est nostri ingenij corruptio, ut propter innatam carni philautiam & priuati commodi studium, nihil perinde atque hanc auersemur. His enim excaecati, odijs & inimicitijs potius scindi, quam nostra sorte contenti pacifice viuere volumus. Quae causa est, quod Ioannes Apostolus, vbi in charitatis mentionem incidit, non obiter modo de ea admonet, sed omnem mouet lapidem, ut eius studium nobis persuadeat. Et multa quidem in praeceden tibus dixit, quae longum foret repetere. Omnibus tamen illis non contentus, praesentem locum subijcit, in quo & describit verae charitatis ingenium, & fructuum eiusdem enumeratione ad eius studium nos excitat. Orandus Deus, ut meam linguam sic moderetur spiritu suo, ut hoc ipsum animis vestris persuadere, & cunctantes impellere possim.
units.tr: Although the unhappy race of men has nothing in the course of this life more wholesome or more necessary than brotherly love, which of itself begets peace, concord, and all the things that follow these; yet such is the corruption of our nature that, on account of the self-love innate in the flesh and the pursuit of private advantage, we turn away from it almost entirely. Blinded by these, we prefer to be torn apart by hatreds and enmities rather than to live peacefully, content with our lot. This is why the Apostle John, when he comes to mention love, does not merely remind us of it in passing, but turns over every stone to persuade us to pursue it. And indeed he has said many things in the preceding verses, which it would be tedious to repeat. Yet not content with all those things, he adds the present passage, in which he describes the nature of true love and, by listing its fruits, stirs us up to pursue it. May God be prayed to moderate my tongue by his Spirit, so that I may be able to persuade this very thing to your minds and to move you when you hesitate.

units.la: I. Filioli mei, ne diligamus sermone neque lingua, sed opere & veritate. Sententiam hanc ijs opponit, qui de charitate multis & splendide loquuntur, amicis item verbis quosuis compellant, officia vero eius plane negligunt. Regnauit hoc hominum genus omnibus seculis, & hodie sic regnat, ut totius orbis dominium longe lateque obtinere dici possit. Verborum autem Ioannis sensus est: Cum charitate exigo, o filioli, nemo me blandos sermones, promissiones beneficas & quae alia sunt eius generis humanitatis officia, exigere putet. Est equidem aliquid, animi benevolentia verbis contestari, anxium & afflictum consolari, & indigo opem polliceri. Sed nō in his germana & perfecta charitas subsistit. A verbis enim vlterius ad opera quoque progreditur, & beneficia non modo pollicetur, sed re ipsa praestat. Eo igitur & vos anniti velim, ut charitatis affectum non verborum duntaxat blanditijs, sed ipsis operibus & animi syncéritate[?] palam demonstretis. Habent haec verba non inelegantē verae charitatis descriptionem. Docent enim hanc in duobus potissimum consistere, ipsis nimirum operibus & veritate: de quibus sigillatim dicendum erit.
units.tr: I. My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue, but in deed and in truth. He sets this sentence against those who speak much and eloquently about love, and who likewise address everyone with friendly words, but plainly neglect its duties. This kind of men has reigned in every age, and today it so reigns that it may be said to hold dominion over the whole world, far and wide. The sense of John's words is this: "I require love, O little children; let no one think that I demand flattering speeches, promises of kindness, and other such offices of humanity. It is indeed something to attest goodwill of mind by words, to console the anxious and afflicted, and to promise help to the needy. But true and genuine love does not stop at these. For it goes further from words to deeds as well, and it not only promises benefits but actually bestows them in fact. Therefore I would have you strive for this too: to show your affection of love openly, not merely by the flatteries of words, but by the works themselves and by sincerity of mind. These words contain no inelegant description of true love. For they teach that it consists chiefly in two things, namely in deeds themselves and in truth; of which things we shall have to speak one by one."

units.la: In charitate opera requiri ex praecedentibus patet. Illic enim viscera commiserationis illi tri buit. Est autem commiseratio motus animi, quo aliena miseria sic afficimur, ut eius dolor ad nostrum quoque animum pertingat.
