At cui aliena dolet miseria, eam ope aliqua subleuatam vellet, nec in ea voluntate subsistit, sed opem suam pro virili cofert: quod clarius est, quam ut multa demonstratione opus habeat. Quia ergo in charitate commiseratio est, ab eadem opera subuentionis nullo modo abesse possunt, siquidem aliqua fit subueniendi facultas. Exemplum huius in Samaritano, quem fraternae dilectionis typum facit, Christus proponit, Luc.10. Is cum saucium & spoliatum iacere videret, hominem sibi alias ignotum, mox misericordia motus est. Vides igitur charitatem, quae misericordiae affectu sese prodit, nec rigidis oculis alienam calamitatem intuetur. Sed num in commiseratione illa Samaritanus subsistit? Num contentus est verba protulisse condolentis animi indicia? Num consolatione, vel consilio quoque nonnihil recreatum deserit? Minimè. Imo quia non verbis, non querelis, non consolationibus, neque consilijs, sed auxilio hunc indigere videbat, sese totum ad hoc ferendum, disponit. Descendit enim ex iumento, quo vehebatur. Humi iacentem subleuat. Vulnera vino & oleo, quę ad manum erant, abluit. Iumento impositum in hospitium vehit, pro illo satisfacit hospiti, simul & in posterum pro illo fidem suam interponit. Hunc qui imitantur, non verbis & lingua, sed reipsa fratres diligunt. Arguuntur igitur hoc loco, qui cum praesenti ope proximus indiget, ad consilia vertuntur, quidq; agendum censeant multis exponunt, vel eundem ad alios ablegant, & de aliorum beneficentia splendide illi pollicentur, cum ipsorum esset opem, quam ferre poterant, non negare. Nemo tamen haec ita accipiat, quasi sana & fida consilia, quae amicis dantur, improbemus. Haec enim in loco & tempore adhibita saepe plus prosunt, quam splendidissima alioqui opera, imo inter amicitiae officia prima collocari debet. Sed tergiuersatores taxamus, qui cum opem praesentem necessitas postulat, charitatis officium verbis exequi student.
units.tr: That love requires works is clear from what goes before. For there he attributes to it the bowels of compassion. Now compassion is a movement of the mind by which we are so affected by another's misery that its grief reaches our own mind as well. But one whom another's misery grieves wishes that person to be relieved by some help, and does not rest in that wish, but contributes his own aid as far as he is able; this is clearer than that it needs much demonstration. Since, therefore, compassion is part of love, the works of relief cannot in any way be absent from it, provided there is some ability to help. An example of this is set before us by Christ in the Samaritan, whom he makes a type of brotherly love, Luke 10. When he saw a wounded and robbed man lying there, a man otherwise unknown to him, he was at once moved with mercy. You see, then, that love, which shows itself by the feeling of mercy, does not look upon another's calamity with hard eyes. But does the Samaritan stop at that compassion? Is he content to have uttered signs of a sympathetic mind? Does he leave the man refreshed somewhat by consolation, or even by counsel? By no means. Indeed, because he saw that the man needed not words, not complaints, not consolations, nor counsels, but help, he disposed himself wholly to bearing it. For he got down from the beast on which he was riding, raised up the man lying on the ground, and washed his wounds with wine and oil, which were at hand. Placing him on the beast, he carried him to an inn, satisfied the innkeeper on his behalf, and at the same time pledged his own faith for him in the future. Those who imitate him love their brothers not in word and tongue, but in fact. Therefore those are rebuked in this place who, when a neighbour needs present help, turn to counsels, lay out at length what they think ought to be done, or send him away to others, and splendidly promise the beneficence of others, when it was their duty not to refuse the aid they were able to give. Yet let no one take this as if we condemned sound and faithful counsels given to friends. For these, applied in the right place and time, often profit more than otherwise splendid works, and indeed ought to be placed first among the offices of friendship. But we censure the shirkers who, when necessity demands present help, labour to discharge the duty of love with words.

units.la: Alterum in charitate veritas est. Refertur haec ad animum & ab operibus charitatis omnem priuatum affectu excludit. Sunt enim qui & verbis & operibus egentes iuuant, sed animo ficto, qui longe alio quam charitatis affectu mouetur. Nam aut famae suae metuunt, si opem postulatam non ferant: aut popularis gloriae auram venantur, ut de pharisaeis Christus loquitur. Sed & alij sunt, quos priuati commodi studium excitat. Quia enim Deum remuneratorem esse audiunt eorum, qui pauperes ope sua subleuant, paucula quaedam conferunt, ut cū fœnore à Deo illa recipiant. Habent horum opera charitatis speciem, sed non ea charitas in illis regnat, quam Paulus ex puro corde manare testatur.1.Timoth.1. Hanc igitur Joannes commendat, dum veritatem exigit, ut verbis & operibus ipsa quoque hominis mens & syncerus affectus respondeant. Nec enim patitur Deus, officia quae à nobis postulat, aliquo fuco simulationis pollui, cum ipse ęterna & pura sit veritas.
units.tr: The second thing in love is truth. This refers to the mind, and it excludes all private affection from works of love. For there are some who help the needy both in words and in deeds, but with a feigned mind, moved by a feeling quite different from love. For they either fear loss of their reputation if they do not supply the aid requested, or they hunt for the breath of popular glory, as Christ speaks of the Pharisees. But there are also others, whom the pursuit of private advantage stirs. For since they hear that God is the rewarder of those who relieve the poor with their help, they contribute small amounts so that they may receive them back from God with interest. The works of these men have the appearance of love, but that love does not reign in them which Paul testifies flows from a pure heart, 1 Timothy 1. John therefore commends this love when he requires truth, so that the very mind of the man and his sincere affection correspond to his words and works. For God does not allow the duties he requires of us to be polluted by any veneer of pretence, since he himself is eternal and pure truth.

units.la: Hæc si cum nostri seculi moribus conferantur, facilè patebit, quàm rarum hodie fit fraternæ charitatis studium. Ut enim de illis modò nihil dicamus, qui odijs ringuntur, & apertas inimicitias exercent, eos saltem inspice, qui charitatis studiosi videri poterant. Quotus quisque illorum est, qui non verbis potius quàm reipsa amorem testetur? Audiuntur passim blandæ voces & promissiones magnificæ, quàm rara verò beneficia has sequantur, non sine dolore sentiunt qui opis alienæ sunt indigi. Quid, quod prouerbio dicitur, nobilium esse multa polliceri, eadem vera præstare, rusticanum putatur. Rusticus ergo illis hominibus Joannes dicetur, qui opera, non promissiones exigit. Sed & illos vide, qui operibus quoque charitatem testari videntur, paucos tamē inuenies, qui illis veritatem coniunctam habeant. Paucissimi siquidem sunt, qui non alio potius quàm charitatis affectu, ad benefaciendū permoueantur. Et si ipsè maioris lucri auferas, frustra ad beneficentiam hortaberis eos, qui hodie illam exercere videtur. Quid ergo aliud dicemus, quàm ea esse tempora, de quibus Christum prophetauisse legimus, cùm charitatem extinctum iri, & fidem penes homines, aut nullam aut perquam exiguam, fore dicit? Admonet ergo nos locus hic quanto emendationis studio & quàm assiduis precibus opus sit, ut huic malo gratia sui spiritus Deus subuenire velit. Cæterum, ut mentes hominum philautiæ fascino excæcatas[?] & priuati com modi studio indormientes, excitet, charitatis syncerę fructus amplissimos Joannes enumerat, quæ altera huius loci pars est.
units.tr: If these things are compared with the manners of our own age, it will easily be plain how rare the pursuit of brotherly love has become today. For to say nothing for the moment of those who are caught up in hatreds and carry on open enmities, look at least at those who might seem eager for love. How few of them are there who attest their love by words rather than in fact? Pleasant voices and magnificent promises are heard everywhere, but how rarely do benefits follow them! Those who are in need of another's help feel this with no small pain. What of the proverb that it is the mark of nobles to promise much, and to perform the same things truly is thought rustic? So John will be called a rustic by those men, since he requires works, not promises. But look also at those who seem to attest love even by works; yet you will find few who have truth joined with them. Indeed there are very few who are moved to do good by any affection other than that of love. And if you take away the prospect of greater gain, you will urge in vain to beneficence those who today seem to practise it. What, then, shall we say, except that these are the times of which we read that Christ prophesied, when he said that love would be extinguished and faith would be found among men either not at all or in very small measure? This place therefore admonishes us how great a zeal for amendment is needed, and how constant prayers, so that God may be willing to come to the aid of this evil by the grace of his Spirit. Moreover, so that he may rouse the minds of men who are blinded by the charm of self-love and drowsing in the pursuit of private advantage, John enumerates the very ample fruits of sincere love, which is the second part of this passage.

units.la: I. Per hoc cognoscimus, quòd ex veritate fumus, & corā ipso persuadebimus cordibus nostris. Quòd si condemnet nos cor, maior est Deus corde nostro, & nouit omnia, &c. Fructus charitatis tres principales proponit, quorum spe huius studium nobis persuadere nititur. Primus est, cuius supra quoq; mentionem fecit obiter. Ait enim: Per hoc cognoscimus, quòd fumus ex veritate, id est, ex Deo, qui ipsa est veritas. Charitatem ergo signum esse dicit, ex quo tam alij quàm nos ipsi deprehendimus nos Dei filios & heredes esse. Est hic fructus amplior quàm verbis exponi posit. Ut enim homini nulla maior calamitas accidere potest, quàm si de salute sua dubius sit: ita hæc hominis consolatio & lætitia summa est, si salutis suæ certitudine sibi verè persuasam habeat. Est autem huius argumentū infallibile, si nos Dei filios esse agnoscamus. Quis enim pater filios suos, quando juvare potest, negligat? At syncerus charitatis affectus, nos verè Dei filios esse probat. Idè igitur de salute certos reddit, & solus efficere potest, quod nulla eloquentia, nullæ principum pollicitationes, nulla rerum huius mundi excellentia efficere possent. Sed ut clarius cernatur fructus hic, totum Joannis argumentum nobis consyderādum proponamus, quod tale videtur. Qui Dei ingenium referunt, reuera Dei filij sunt. Qui verè & syncera mente fratres diligunt, Dei ingeniū referunt. Ergo qui verè diligunt, veri sunt Dei filij. Maior ex se satis clara est. Quia enim Dei filij ex spiritu & verbo Dei generamur, non alio quàm Dei ingenio præditi esse possumus. De minori nemo dubitat, quicunque beneficia Dei in nos collata observaverit. Deus enim nō verbis modò opem pollicetur, sed eandem reipsa præstat. Salutem non modò promisit, sed promissam (cū alia ratione conferri non posset) in filio suo Jesu Christo contulit. Afflictos & anxios non fucatis verbis fallit, non alio ablegat, sed efficacibus spiritus sui dictatis consolatur & ad se unicum boni fontem invitat. Deus item non aliâ ob causam nobis benefacit, quàm quòd nos suæ opis & gratiæ indigos videt: nec ipse nostri indiget, ut qui Deus ab æterno sit, & cui nihil unquam deesse potuit. Quis ergo Dei filios negabit, quos hæc, superato philautiæ carnis ingenio, facere viderit. An tu ipse te ex Deo natum esse dubitabis, qui tam evidentia divinę naturæ & indolis signa in teipso vides & observas? Certè Christus dominus in novissimo judicij die non alio signo se suos agnituru dicit, quàm syncerę dilectionis operibus. Vide locum Matth.25. & huius argumenti confirmationem habebis certissimam.
units.tr: I. "By this we know that we are of the truth, and we shall persuade our hearts before him. If our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things," etc. John lists three principal fruits of charity, and by hope of these he strives to persuade us to take up this practice. The first is the one he also mentioned in passing above. For he says: "By this we know that we are of the truth," that is, of God, who is truth itself. He therefore says that charity is a sign by which both others and we ourselves recognise that we are sons and heirs of God. This fruit is greater than words can express. For just as no greater calamity can befall a man than to be doubtful about his own salvation, so this comfort and joy of a man is supreme if he has truly persuaded himself of the certainty of his salvation. Now the infallible proof of this is if we acknowledge that we are the sons of God. For what father neglects his sons when he is able to help them? But sincere affection of charity proves that we are truly sons of God. It therefore makes us certain of salvation, and alone can accomplish what no eloquence, no promises of princes, no excellence of the things of this world could accomplish. But so that this fruit may be seen more clearly, let us set before ourselves the whole argument of John, which seems to be this. Those who reflect the disposition of God are truly sons of God. Those who truly and with a sincere mind love the brethren reflect the disposition of God. Therefore those who truly love are true sons of God. The major premise is clear enough in itself. For since we are born as sons of God by the Spirit and the Word of God, we can be endowed with no other disposition than that of God. No one doubts the minor premise, whoever has observed the benefits of God bestowed upon us. For God does not only promise help by words, but actually gives the same in deed. He has not only promised salvation, but, since it could not be conferred in any other way, has bestowed it promised in his Son Jesus Christ. He does not deceive the afflicted and anxious with feigned words, nor send them away elsewhere, but comforts them by the effective dictates of his Spirit and invites them to himself, the one fountain of good. God also does good to us for no other reason than that he sees us to be in need of his help and grace; nor does he himself need us, since he is God from eternity and nothing could ever be lacking to him. Who then will deny that those are sons of God whom he sees making these fruits, having overcome the self-love of the flesh? Or will you yourself doubt that you were born of God, you who see and observe such evident signs of the divine nature and disposition in yourself? Certainly Christ the Lord says in the last day of judgment that he will acknowledge his own by no other sign than the works of sincere love. See Matthew 25, and you will have a most certain confirmation of this argument.

units.la: Admonet autem præsentis sententiæ consideratio, ut eiusdem oppositum vel contrariū expendamus. Si enim syncera charitas infallibile filiorum Dei signum est, quid de illis dicemus, qui charitatem fallacibus verbis simulant? Qui (ut veteri adagio utamur) altera manu panem ostentant, altera verò lapidem in fratris interitum librat? Annon illos ex veritate esse negabimus? Dei certè filios nemo dicet, nisi qui ex Deo & Dei spiritu filios degeneres nasci posse asserat. Sed absurdum[?] fuerit ei calamitati & infortunio Deum subijcere, quo non aliud magis dolet pijs & probis parentibus. Diaboli igitur filij sunt, quotquot amicitiam ore profesi, animis suis odij & inimicitiæ vel simultatis venenum insidiose cælant. Hoc enim diaboli ingeniū esse, primum illius stratagema, quo Euam oppugnauit, perspicuè probat. Huic enim æternitatè & diuinos honores pollicitus, eidem mortem & interitum sempiternum struit. Idem fecerunt, quotquot eius filij in scripturis proponuntur, ex quibus solum Judam, infelicem illum perditionis filium, produxisse suffi-ciat. Is enim Christum dominum amicè exosculans & præceptoris nomine salutans, eundem hostibus prodit. Judæ ergo osculum est, subdola amicitiæ simulatio. Judæ salutatio est, blanda & fallax officij promissio, & eundem cum Juda exitum meretur. Deus enim virum fraudulentum & linguam mendacem odit. Psalmo 5. Prouerbiorum 6. In horum meditatione ut inam maiori cura versarentur, qui hodie linguas suas sic assuefecerunt, ut nihil nisi simulatum & fictum loqui possint: quo fit ut minus concordiæ, plurimum verò discordiæ & simultatis inter omnes hominum ordines pasim regnet.
units.tr: Moreover, the consideration of the present sentence urges us to weigh its opposite or contrary. For if sincere charity is an infallible sign of the sons of God, what shall we say of those who feign charity with deceitful words? Who (to use the old proverb) show bread in one hand, but in the other weigh a stone for the destruction of their brother? Shall we not deny that they are of the truth? Certainly no one will call them sons of God, unless he asserts that degenerate sons can be born of God and of the Spirit of God. But it would be absurd to subject God to such a calamity and misfortune, which grieves godly and upright parents above all else. Therefore all who have professed friendship with their mouths, but secretly conceal in their minds the poison of hatred, enmity or grudge, are sons of the devil. For that this is the disposition of the devil, and his first stratagem by which he assailed Eve, is plainly proved. For he promised her eternity and divine honours, and in return he planned for her death and everlasting destruction. The same have done all of his sons who are set forth in the Scriptures, of whom it is enough to mention only Judas, that unhappy son of perdition. For he, kissing the Lord Christ warmly and greeting him with the name of teacher, betrayed him to his enemies. The kiss of Judas is therefore a deceitful pretence of friendship. The greeting of Judas is a flattering and treacherous promise of service, and it deserves the same end as Judas. For God hates a deceitful man and a lying tongue. Psalm 5; Proverbs 6. If only those who today have so accustomed their tongues that they can speak nothing but pretence and feigned words would meditate on these things with greater care! The result is that concord is scarce, and discord and grudges reign everywhere among all orders of men.

units.la: Secundum fraternæ dilectionis fructum his verbis comprehendit: Coram ipso perfuadebi-mus cordibus nostris. Est hic prioris consequens. Significat enim pacatæ & tranquillæ conscientiæ statum, quo de salute nostra cōtra omnes tentationes certi sumus. Nam cordibus nostris persuadere, quid aliud est, quàm animos nostros, qui peccatorū conscientia fluctuant, certos & quasi securos facere, ut de salute amplius non dubitent? Poterat autem hoc idem cum priori videri. Siquidem qui se Dei filium, & ex veritate genitum esse nouit, se & Dei hæredem fore sperat. Sed manent in nobis, etiam regeneratis: humanæ infirmitatis reliquiæ, quæ tentationibus crebris exa-gitantur, & interdum cogunt, ut cum Davide & Christo clamemus: Domine quousq; mei obli-uiscēris? Quare me dereliquisti? Atqui verus quidem & fidelissimus in ista animorum fluctuatione consolator est, spiritus Christi, quem is ideo paracletum vocat. Quia tamen carnis ingeniū est externis potius inhærere quàm internis niti, consolationes aliquas extrinsecus accedere non inutile est. Eas ex fraterna dilectione efficacissimas manare, Joannes hoc loco docet. Primò enim hanc infallibilem filiorum Dei notam esse audiuimus. Habet igitur ex ea spiritus sanctus, quo de adoptione & regeneratione certos faciat. Deinde, cum propter ea plerunq; tumultuemur animis non stris, quæ ab hominibus impijs & verbi Dei oforibus, ingratis item & improbis, immittuntur, magna inde conscientiæ fiducia fumi potest, si nos de hostibus nostris meliora commeritos esse sciamus. Inde enim certo colligere licet, Deum qui innocentium assertor & ingratitudinis acerrimus vindex est, nobis nequaquam defuturum: cum è contra, qui sibi malè conscij sunt, & odijs, simultatibus, calumnijs aut etiam manifestis iniurijs se hominum inimicitias prouocauisse norunt, nihil aliud sperare posint, quàm quòd eadem mala iusto Dei iudicio in ipsos quoq; decreta sint. Nūquam non enim Christi sententia animis illorum occurrit: Qua mensura metimini, eadem metientur vobis alij. Matth.7. Adhæc quasi in oculis positos vident, quoscunque contra charitatis leges iniquis & iniustis modis læserunt. Obuersantur illorum cogitationibus per vim oppressi orphani, proculcatæ viduæ, afflicti peregrini, dolis, sycophantijs & vsuris circumuenti fratres, qui omnes vna voce Dei iustitiā contra hos implorare videntur. Sentiunt in conscientijs suis clamantem contra se pro vindicta effusum sanctorum sanguine. Cogitant de pauperum clamoribus & querelis, quas surda aure aliquando neglexerunt. Nec quicquam hic proficiunt vel consolationes vel promissiones quorumuis hominum. Nam propriæ cōscientiæ testimonium mille testium loco est, ut prouerbio dicitur. Et hæc quidē grauissima hominis miseria est, qua nulla alia atrocior excogitari potest. Quid enim infelicius, quàm hostem & accusatorem habere, tam familiarem, ut in animi penetralibus resideat, tamq; importunū, ut & vigilantibus & dormientibus, & quocunq; tandem negotio occupatis, ea ogganniat, quæ omnem lætitiæ sensum auferunt? Utriusq; exemplum in eximio Rege & propheta Davide cernitur, si eius animum quando sub Saule persecutiones sustinebat conferas cū eo, quem in Absolonica seditione habuit. Licet enim & grauior & diuturnior esset calamitas, quæ à Saule inferebatur (nā patrio solo cedere, infensissimis hostibus sese coniungere, & mille mortis pericula, ceu publicus patriæ & regni hostis, subire coactus fuit) animum tamen eius infractum & lætum cernimus. Quippe sibi bene cōscius, ut qui nullum fidei & charitatis officium erga Saulem & patriam intermisisset, causam suā intrepidus Dei iudicio com-mendare audet. Hinc voces illæ consolationis plenæ: Domine Deus meus, in te confisus sum: serua me ab omnibus qui me persequuntur. Item: Domine Deus meus, si istuc commisi, si est peruersitas in manibus meis. Si ei qui pacis fœdere mihi iunctus fuit, malum rependi, imò si destitui infe-stantem me sine causa: Persequatur hostis animam meã, &c. Et paulò post: Dominus judicet populos, me quoq; judica ô Domine, secundum justitiam meam, & secundum integritatem meā, quæ est in me, &c. Psal.7. Et alibi: Iustus dominus iustitias diligit, rectum vultu suo intuetur. Psal.11. Sed longum foret omnes huius generis sententias recensere. At si eundem Dauidem in Absolo-nica persecutione consyderes, quam propter violatas charitatis leges, adulteriū scilicet & cædem Vriæ iniustam, sibi immitti agnoscebat, longè alium videbis. Tunc enim non Dei iustitiam appel-lare audet, sed anxius multitudinem miserationum Dei implorat. Psal.51. Nec recentis modò faci-noris memoria excruciatur, sed occurrunt cum hoc, quæcunque à pueris perperam facta erant. Quare alibi ait: Peccatorum adolescentiæ meæ ac scelerum meorū ne fis memor. Memor autem mei fis iuxta benignitatem tuam, &c. Psal.25. Hæc si ipse tecum conferas, & in propriæ conscien-tiæ penetralia descendas, ô homo, facilè videbis, quàm amplus & excellens hic fraternæ dilectio-nis fructus sit.
units.tr: He comprehends the second fruit of brotherly love in these words: "we shall persuade our hearts before him." This follows from the former. For it signifies the state of a pacified and tranquil conscience, in which we are certain of our salvation against all temptations. For what else is it to persuade our hearts than to make our minds, which are tossed by the consciousness of sins, certain and as it were secure, so that they no longer doubt about their salvation? This same thing, however, might seem to be identical with the former. For whoever knows that he is a son of God and born of the truth also hopes that he will be an heir of God. But there remain in us, even in the regenerate, remnants of human weakness, which are harassed by frequent temptations and sometimes compel us to cry out with David and Christ: "Lord, how long wilt thou forget me? Why hast thou forsaken me?" Yet the true and most faithful consoler in this tossing of minds is the Spirit of Christ, whom for this reason he calls the Paraclete. Nevertheless, since it is the nature of the flesh to cling to external things rather than to strive after internal ones, it is not useless for some consolations to come from outside. John teaches in this place that these come most effectively from brotherly love. For first we have heard that this is the infallible mark of the sons of God. The Holy Spirit therefore has from it a means by which he makes us certain of adoption and regeneration. Then, since we are often disturbed in our minds on this account by the things which are sent against us by impious men and enemies of the Word of God, and likewise by the ungrateful and wicked, great confidence of conscience can be drawn from this, if we know that we have deserved better things from our enemies. For from this one may certainly conclude that God, who is the defender of the innocent and the most severe avenger of ingratitude, will by no means fail us. On the other hand, those who are conscious of wrongdoing, and know that they have provoked the enmity of men by hatreds, quarrels, slanders or even manifest injuries, can hope for nothing else than that the same evils have been decreed against them too by the just judgment of God. For the saying of Christ never fails to come to their minds: "With what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again." Matthew 7. Besides, they see as if placed before their eyes all whom they have harmed against the laws of charity by unfair and unjust means. The orphans oppressed by force, the trodden-down widows, the afflicted strangers, the brethren circumvented by fraud, slander and usury, all of whom seem with one voice to implore the justice of God against them, come before their thoughts. They feel in their consciences the blood of the saints poured out crying out against them for vengeance. They think of the cries and complaints of the poor, which they once neglected with a deaf ear. Nor do the consolations or promises of any men avail here at all. For the testimony of one's own conscience is in place of a thousand witnesses, as the proverb says. And this is indeed the most grievous misery of man, than which no other more atrocious can be devised. For what is more unhappy than to have an enemy and accuser so familiar that he sits in the innermost parts of the mind, and so troublesome that, whether waking or sleeping, and occupied in whatever business, he murmurs those things which take away every sense of joy? An example of both is seen in the excellent king and prophet David, if you compare his mind when he endured persecutions under Saul with that which he had in the rebellion of Absalom. For although the calamity inflicted by Saul was both heavier and more long-lasting (for he was forced to leave his fatherland, to join himself to most bitter enemies, and to undergo a thousand dangers of death as a public enemy of his country and kingdom), yet we see his mind unbroken and cheerful. Indeed, being conscious to himself, as one who had omitted no duty of faith and charity towards Saul and his country, he dares fearlessly to commend his cause to the judgment of God. Hence those words full of consolation: "O Lord my God, in thee do I put my trust: save me from all them that persecute me." Again: "O Lord my God, if I have done this, if there be iniquity in my hands; if I have rewarded evil to him that was at peace with me, yea, if I have delivered him that without cause is mine enemy: let the enemy persecute my soul," etc. And a little later: "The Lord shall judge the people: judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness, and according to my integrity that is in me," etc. Psalm 7. And elsewhere: "The righteous Lord loveth righteousness; his countenance doth behold the upright." Psalm 11. But it would be too long to recount all sentences of this kind. Yet if you consider the same David in the persecution of Absalom, whom he acknowledged to be unjustly sent against him on account of his violations of the laws of charity, namely adultery and the murder of Uriah, you will see him quite otherwise. For then he does not dare to appeal to the justice of God, but anxiously implores the multitude of God's mercies. Psalm 51. Nor is he tormented only by the memory of a recent crime, but whatever had been done wrongly from boyhood comes to mind along with this. Therefore he says elsewhere: "Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my transgressions. But according to thy mercy remember thou me," etc. Psalm 25. If you, O man, compare these things with yourself and descend into the innermost parts of your own conscience, you will easily see how ample and excellent this fruit of brotherly love is.

units.la: Sed ut hæc magis commendaret, breui demonstratione docet, quanta eorum sit infelicitas, quos mens sibi malè consci-a exagitat: vicissim verò quàm felices sint, quos nulla conscientiæ in-festatio exercet. Sic enim subijcit: Quòd si cõdemnet nos cor, maior est Deus corde nostro, & no-uit omnia. Charissimi, si cor nostrum non condemnet nos, fiduciam habemus erga Deum. Prius membrum comparationem habet minoris & maioris. Sic enim dicere videtur: Si ea est peccati a-trocitas, vt corda nostra, quæ alioqui cæca sunt & sibijpsis in sceleribus blandiri solent, eius con-scientia infestare possit, quid de illo Deus iudicabit, qui & maior est corde nostro, & omnia no-uit? A corde quidem nostro non multum timendum est, quia potestatem vel in nos vel in alios nullam habet. Deus verò is est, qui vno momento damnare & ad inferos detrudere potest. Ad-hæc corda nostra sæpe multa latent, quæ à nobis contra Dei leges facta sunt, dū ad carnis & mun-di iudicium potius quàm ad Dei tribunal respicimus. At Deus sua sapientia omnem creaturam penetrat, omnia videt, omnia audit, est denique scrutator renum & cordium. Psal.7. Ier.11.17.20. &c. Quid ergo coram hoc iudice poterimus? Quam afferemus excusationem? Quo prætextu il-lius seueritatem eludemus, qui ne proprij cordis accusationem possumus effugere? Annon hæ-rebit animus & trepidabit quoties de Deo cogitat? Quòd si verò res nostras sic instituerimus, vt nullius destinatæ malitiæ nobis simus conscij, intrepida nobis esse poterit per Iesum Christũ di-uinæ gratiæ fiducia. Nam licet multas labes peccatorum nostra nobis aspergat infirmitas & natu-ralis corruptio, eas tamen Christi merito ablui certò norunt & credunt, qui deuoto peccandi stu-dio non tenentur.
units.tr: But to commend these things more strongly, he shows in a brief demonstration how wretched are those whom a guilty mind torments, and conversely how happy are those whom no disturbance of conscience troubles. For he goes on thus: "If our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knows all things. Beloved, if our heart do not condemn us, we have confidence toward God." The first clause contains a comparison of less and greater. He seems to say: If the enormity of sin is such that our hearts, which are otherwise blind and are wont to flatter themselves in their wickedness, can trouble us with their accusation, what will God judge of him who is both greater than our heart and knows all things? Indeed we need not fear our heart greatly, since it has no power either over us or over others. But God is he who can damn and thrust down to hell in a single moment. Moreover, our hearts often conceal many things that we have done against God's laws, while we look to the judgment of flesh and world rather than to the tribunal of God. But God by his wisdom penetrates every creature, sees all things, hears all things, and is in short the searcher of the reins and hearts. Ps. 7; Jer. 11, 17, 20, etc. What then shall we be able to do before this judge? What excuse shall we offer? By what pretext shall we elude the severity of him whom we cannot escape even by accusing our own heart? Will not the mind cleave to itself and tremble whenever it thinks of God? But if we so order our affairs that we are conscious of no deliberate malice, a fearless confidence in divine grace through Jesus Christ will be open to us. For although our infirmity and natural corruption sprinkle many stains of sins upon us, those who are not held by a devoted zeal for sinning know with certainty and believe that these are washed away by the merit of Christ.

units.la: Docet hic locus, quàm referat conscientiæ sensum non extinguere, vel reprimere violenter. Nam quosdam inuenire licet, qui vt liberius & maiori cum voluptate peccare possint, toti in hoc sunt, vt contra proprij animi dictata securum Dei & iudiciorum ipsius contemptum sibi perfua-deant: ijs similes, qui apud Psalmistam dicebant: Dominus non videt, neque Deus Iacob intelli-git. Sed quid ijsdem propheta respondet? Intelligite stupidi in populo, & stulti quando demum sa-pietis? Is qui aurem condidit, quomodo non audiret? qui oculum finxit, quo pacto non videret? Qui totas gentes corripit, quique homines scientiam docet, vos non argueret? Nouit dominus cogitationes hominum vanas esse, &c. Psal.94. Nemo igitur falsa persuasione sibijpsi illudat. Infe-lix enim finis est eorum, qui Deum nihil videre & nihil iudicare persuasi, in omnem peccandi li-centiam efferuntur. Non dormitat Deus, qui conscientiæ stimulos suo tempore in animis eorum excitat, vt qui cum Caino Deo impudenter obloqui audebant, tandem dicant: Maior est iniqui-tas nostra, quàm vt remitti possit. Cogitemus potius, nos in Dei conspectu ambulare, qui tam bo-ni quàm mali remunerator est, coram cuius tribunali omnes quoque nos sisti oportet, vt repor-tet vnusquisque in corpore suo iuxta id quod fecit, siue bonum siue malum. 2. Corinth.5. Sed ad Ioannem redeamus, qui tertium fraternæ dilectionis fructum his verbis exprimit.
units.tr: This passage teaches how important it is not to extinguish the sense of conscience or to suppress it by force. For one can find some who, in order to sin more freely and with greater pleasure, devote themselves entirely to persuading themselves, against the dictates of their own mind, that God is secure and that his judgments are despised. They are like those who, in the Psalmist's words, said: "The Lord does not see, neither does the God of Jacob understand." But what does the prophet answer them? "Understand, you stupid among the people, and you fools, when at last will you be wise? He who formed the ear, shall he not hear? He who fashioned the eye, shall he not see? He who chastises whole nations, and who teaches man knowledge, shall he not rebuke you? The Lord knows that the thoughts of men are vain," etc. Ps. 94. Let no one therefore deceive himself by a false persuasion. The end of those who, persuaded that God sees nothing and judges nothing, are carried away into every license of sinning, is unhappy. God does not sleep: in his own time he stirs up the goads of conscience in their minds, so that those who with Cain dared shamelessly to speak against God at last say: "Our iniquity is greater than that it can be forgiven." Let us rather consider that we walk in the sight of God, who is the rewarder of good and evil alike, before whose tribunal we must all also be brought, so that each one may receive in his body according to what he has done, whether good or evil. 2 Cor. 5. But let us return to John, who expresses the third fruit of brotherly love in these words.

units.la: Et quicquid petierimus, accipimus ab eo: quoniam præcepta eius custodimus, & ea quæ sunt placita co-ram eo, facimus. Infigne bonum est, quod pollicetur, & quo vix aliud hominibus magis necessa-rium. Vt enim vita hæc nostra miseriarum plena & quasi lachrymarum vallis est: ita in miserijs vni-ca salutis anchora & asylum est Deus, ad quē per pias & fideles preces confugitur, iuxta id quod ipse præcipit: In tempore tribulationis inuoca me, & eripiam te, tu vero glorificabis me. Psal.50. At quia multa occurrere possunt, quæ precantes remorantur, ne certa fiducia Deum inuocent, il-los confirmari omnino necesse est, cum non exaudiatur, qui sine fide orat. Et hic quidem primum locum merito obtinere debent promissiones ab ipso Deo nobis exhibitæ, quibus opem suam in-uocantibus se pollicetur, quales in scripturis passim obuias habemus. Sed quia in homine est quod fidem eius oppugnat, prodest in illo ipso monstrare quo eadem confirmetur. Facit hoc ad-optionis spiritus, in quo clamamus, Abba pater. Ne vero ita clamates illud audiamus, quod apud prophetam Israeli obijcitur: Si ego pater vester sum: vbi honor est quem mihi impenditis? Mal.1. alio rursum fulcro animos nostros confirmari oportet, quod in charitate nobis monstrat Apostolus. Si (inquit) hac instructi fuerimus, accipiemus à Deo, quicquid petierimus. Simul autem huius dicti causam subijcit: Quoniam præcepta eius custodimus, & ea quæ placita sunt coram eo, faciemus. Argumentum tale est: Quicunq; Dei præcepta custodiunt & ipsi placere student, exaudiuntur à Deo in suis precibus. Scribitur enim: Oculi domini inteti sunt super iustos, & aures eius ad preces eorum. Psal.34. Quicunque verò charitatem fraternam exercent, Dei præcepta faciunt & illi placent. (Nam & charitas legis impletio est. Rom.13. & Christus hoc suum præceptum primū, & quasi vnicum, esse dicit, quo reliqua omnia comprehendantur, vt nos inuicem diligamus, sicut ipse dilexit nos. Ioan.15. & 13.) Quid ergo hinc aliud colligemus, quàm illorum preces certò exaudiri, qui animos charitate instructos habent? Est hic locus diligenti consyderatione propter duo, quæ hinc disci poterunt.
units.tr: "And whatever we ask, we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do the things that are pleasing in his sight." What he promises is an outstanding good, and there is hardly anything more necessary to men than this. For as this life of ours is full of miseries and is, as it were, a valley of tears, so in miseries God is the only anchor of salvation and refuge, to whom we flee through pious and faithful prayers, according to what he himself commands: "In the time of trouble call upon me, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me." Ps. 50. But because many things can arise that delay those who pray, so that they do not invoke God with sure confidence, it is altogether necessary that they be confirmed, since he who prays without faith is not heard. And here indeed the promises which God himself has offered us, by which he pledges his help to those who call upon him, rightly ought to hold the first place; such promises we find everywhere in the Scriptures. But because there is in man something that assails his faith, it is useful to point out in that very thing the means by which the same faith is confirmed. This is the work of the Spirit of adoption, in whom we cry, "Abba, Father." Yet lest we cry thus while hearing what is objected to Israel through the prophet: "If I am your father, where is the honor that you give me?" Mal. 1. Our minds ought to be strengthened by another prop, which the Apostle shows us in charity. "If," he says, "we are instructed in this, we shall receive from God whatever we ask." At the same time he adds the reason for this saying: "because we keep his commandments and do the things that are pleasing in his sight." The argument is this: whoever keeps God's commandments and strives to please him is heard by God in his prayers. For it is written: "The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayers." Ps. 34. Now whoever practices brotherly love does God's commandments and pleases him. (For love is the fulfilling of the law, Rom. 13; and Christ calls this his first and as it were only commandment, in which all the rest are comprehended, that we love one another as he loved us. John 15 and 13.) What else then shall we gather from this, than that the prayers of those who have minds furnished with charity are certainly heard? This passage deserves careful consideration on account of two things that may be learned from it.

units.la: Primò enim admonemur, qui fiat quòd interdum preces nostræ minus exaudiuntur. Eam nimirum ob causam, quòd à charitate fraterna alieni, aliorum miserijs nec commouemur, nec illorum precibus quicquam à nobis impetrari patimur. Quid enim tam iustū est, quàm vt irritos clamores ipsi quoque fundant, quos nulli egentium fratrum clamores commouere possunt? Quare spiritu sancto dictante Solomon pronunciauit: Qui obturat autem suam ad clamorem pauperis, clamabit & ipse, & non exaudietur. Prou.21. Quò & illud Iacobi referri potest, qui contra priuati commodi studiosos & æmulatores inuidos scribens ait: Concupiscitis, & non habetis: inuidetis & æmulamini, & non potestis adipisci: pugnatis & bellatis, nec habetis, propterea quòd non postulatis. Petitis, & non accipitis, eo quòd male petatis, vt in voluptatibus vestris insumatis. Iac.4. Quæ tamen omnia non in eum sensum rapi debent, quasi charitatis operibus meritum ascribamus, & hæc faciamus salutis nostræ causam. Ex ijs enim, quæ hucusque dicta sunt, satis patet, charitatem fidei fructum, & filiorum Dei externam esse tesseram. Quicquid ergo charitati tribuitur, propter fidem fit, quæ eius quasi parens & fons est.
units.tr: First, we are admonished why it happens that our prayers are sometimes less heard. The reason, no doubt, is that we are estranged from brotherly charity, and are not moved by the miseries of others, nor do we allow anything to be obtained from us by their prayers. For what is so just as that those should themselves pour out futile cries whom the cries of no needy brethren can move? Wherefore Solomon, speaking by the Holy Spirit, declared: "He who stops his ear at the cry of the poor shall himself cry out, and shall not be heard." Prov. 21. To this also can be referred the saying of James, who, writing against those zealous for private advantage and envious rivals, says: "You covet, and you do not have; you envy and strive, and you cannot obtain; you fight and war, yet you do not have, because you do not ask. You ask and do not receive, because you ask amiss, that you may spend it on your pleasures." James 4. Yet all these things ought not to be carried off to such a sense as if we ascribed merit to the works of charity and made these the cause of our salvation. For from what has been said so far it is sufficiently clear that charity is the fruit of faith and the outward token of the sons of God. Whatever therefore is attributed to charity is done on account of faith, which is as it were its parent and source.

units.la: Secundò docet locus hic, qui homines Deo placere possint. Ait enim Apostolus: Præcepta eius custodimus, & ea quæ sunt placita coram ipso facimus. Deo igitur placent, quæ iuxta præce pta ipsius fiunt: eidem verò displicent, quæcunque præceptis ipsius sunt contraria. Nec enim ex nostro arbitrio & zelo cultus Dei dependet, sed ex ipsius voluntate, quam verbo suo nobis reuelauit. Et vt is seruus nobis placere solet, qui nostris præceptis obtemperat, non sui animi dictata sequitur: ita Deo placebimus nos, si quæ ipse præcepit, exequi studeamus. Iugulantur hic humanæ traditiones, de quibus iam olim pronunciauit Dominus: Frustra me colunt, docentes doctrinas hominum. Ifa.29.
units.tr: Second, this passage teaches how men can please God. For the Apostle says: "We keep his commandments and do the things that are pleasing in his sight." Therefore those things please God which are done according to his precepts, and those things displease him which are contrary to his precepts. For the worship of God depends not on our own judgment and zeal, but on his own will, which he has revealed to us in his word. And just as that servant usually pleases us who obeys our commands and does not follow the dictates of his own mind, so we shall please God if we strive to carry out the things he has commanded. Here human traditions are overthrown, concerning which the Lord long ago pronounced: "In vain do they worship me, teaching the doctrines of men." Isa. 29.

units.la: Quod si duo hęc probè expendamus ô fratres, nō mirabimur pertinaces & diutinas nostri se culi calamitates, de quibus multi querūtur, qui tamen in causis illarū expendendis toti cęcutiunt. Num enim melior & lætior illorū sors esse potest, qui nec in precibus suis exaudiri meretur, nec Deo placere possunt in suis actionibus? At nostro seculo charitatis scintillæ omnes in animis hominum ita extinctæ sunt, vt nulla fratrum nostrorum calamitas tam atrox esse posit, quæ animos nostros aliquo commiserationis affectu commoueat. Et qui reliquis sanctiores haberi volunt, illorum sanctitas in nuda & frigida simulatione consistit, quæ & ipsa tamen non iuxta diuinæ legis præcepta, sed secundum hominum traditiones instituitur. Nisi ergo hæc emendemus, melioris status & fortunæ spes esse non poterit. Quare quę Ioannes monet, animis nostris sic re-condamus, vt in vita & moribus nostris synceræ charitatis affectus, & ardens præceptorum Dei studium, eluceat. Hinc enim fiet, vt in hoc seculo pro germanis Dei filijs certò agnosci, & cum Iesu Christo iuxta ipsius promisionem æterno regno frui possimus, cui debetur benedictio, gloria, honor & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: If we weigh these two things carefully, brothers, we will not be surprised at the stubborn and lasting calamities of our age, about which many complain, yet who are utterly blind when it comes to examining their causes. For can the lot of those be better and happier who do not deserve to be heard in their prayers, and cannot please God in their actions? But in our century all the sparks of charity have been so extinguished in people's hearts that no calamity of our brothers can be so atrocious as to stir our minds with any emotion of pity. And those who want to be regarded as holier than the rest, their holiness consists in bare and cold pretence, which is itself also established not according to the precepts of the divine law, but according to the traditions of men. Unless therefore we amend these things, there can be no hope of a better state and fortune. Wherefore let us so store up in our hearts what John admonishes, that in our life and conduct the feelings of sincere charity and an ardent zeal for God's precepts may shine forth. For thus it will come about that in this age we may be surely recognised as the true sons of God, and may be able to enjoy the eternal kingdom with Jesus Christ, according to his promise, to whom belong blessing, glory, honour and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXI.
units.tr: HOMILY XXI.

units.la: Et hoc est præceptum eius, vt credamus nomini filij eius, Iesu Christi, & diligamus nos mutuò, sicut dedit præceptum. Et qui ser uat præcepta eius, in illo manet, & ipse in eo. Et per hoc scimus, quòd manet in nobis, è spiritu, quem dedit nobis.
units.tr: And this is his commandment, that we should believe in the name of his Son, Jesus Christ, and love one another, as he gave commandment. And he who keeps his commandments abides in him, and he in him. And by this we know that he abides in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us.

units.la: MVlta hucusq; de fraterna dilectione dixit Apostolus, & illius studium multis, ijsque so-lidis & firmis, rationibus comendauit. Fuit inter has nouissima, quòd nos à Deo precibus nostris impetraturos dixit quæcunque petierimus, si nos mutuò diligamus. Est hæc insignis & cumprimis magnifica promissio, eoque maiore authoritate digna, quod argumento euidenti confirmatur. Additur enim, nos ideo accepturos quæ petimus, quia præcepta Dei obseruamus & quæ illi placent facimus. Possunt hæc breui ratiocinatione comprehensa facilè intelligi. Constat enim oculos domini intentos esse super iustos, & domini aures illorũ precibus patere, qui legem eius audiunt & obseruant. Psal.34. At vicissim constat, legis diuinæ obseruationem maximam partem ex dilectione dependere. Nam Christus de Lege interrogatus respondet: Diliges dominum Deum tuum ex corde tuo, & in tota anima tua, & in tota mente tua. Hoc est primum & magnum mandatum. Secundum autem est simile huic: Diliges proximum tuum, perinde atque teipsum. In his duobus mandatis tota lex & prophetæ pendent. Matth.22. Et Paulus ait: Qui diligit alte-rum, legem expleuit. Rom.13. Quid ergo hinc aliud sequetur, quàm à Deo patre benigniter exau-diri eorum preces, qui dilectionis studio flagrant? Cæterū, quia Apostolus hac occasione in mentionem præceptorum Dei & obseruationis eorundem inciderat, commodè absolutiorem eius locitractationem subijcit, quam non ofcitanter inspexisse multũ proderit. Primò autem omnia legis diuinæ præcepta, quæ in infinitas species diduci poterat, duobus capitibus principalibus comprehendit. Mox ad eorum obseruationem incitat, dum insignes fructus, qui hanc sequuntur, proponit. Tandem omnia ista irrefragabili spiritus sancti testimonio confirmat. Oremus hûc, vt animis nostris huius doctrinæ certitudinem sic persuadeat, vt feruenti præceptorũ Dei studio excitati, tam insignis præmij fructum assequamur.
units.tr: Hitherto the Apostle has said much concerning brotherly love, and has commended its practice by many reasons, and those sound and firm. Among these, the last was that he said we would obtain from God whatever we ask in prayer, if we love one another. This is a remarkable and especially magnificent promise, and all the more worthy of credit because it is confirmed by a clear argument. For it is added that we shall receive what we ask because we observe God's commandments and do what pleases him. These things, set out in a short chain of reasoning, can easily be understood. For it is agreed that the eyes of the Lord are fixed upon the righteous, and that the ears of the Lord are open to the prayers of those who hear and keep his law (Ps. 34). And conversely, it is agreed that the observance of the divine law depends for the most part upon love. For Christ, when asked about the Law, answers: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like it: You shall love your neighbour as yourself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets" (Matt. 22). And Paul says: "He who loves another has fulfilled the law" (Rom. 13). What then follows from this, except that the prayers of those who burn with the zeal of love are graciously heard by God the Father? Moreover, since the Apostle on this occasion had come to mention God's commandments and their observance, he conveniently adds a fuller treatment of them, which will be greatly profitable if we examine it carefully. First, he comprehends all the precepts of the divine law, which could be spread out into endless kinds, under two principal heads. Then he urges their observance, while setting forth the remarkable fruits that follow it. Finally, he confirms all these things by the unfailing testimony of the Holy Spirit. Let us pray that he may so persuade our minds of the certainty of this doctrine that, roused by a fervent zeal for God's commandments, we may attain the fruit of so remarkable a reward.

units.la: I. Et hoc est præceptum eius, ut credamus nomini filij ipsius, Jesu Christi, & diligamus nos mutuò, sicut dedit præceptum. Unum praeceptum Dei proponit, non multa: quia una duntaxat salus, & uni-ca eius origo est. Quia autem nos circa multa occupamur, unicum hoc praeceptum variis rebus accommodatum, multiplex fit & in species varias scinditur. Sed has omnes duobus capitibus Johannes complectitur, fide nimirum & dilectione: & hac quidem quaecunque ad vitae huius couersationem ac morum institutionem faciunt comprehendit: illa vero religionem & cultu Dei vniuersum contineri docet. Nostrum est, quid de vtraque dicatur, totis animis considerare.
units.tr: I. "And this is his commandment, that we should believe in the name of his Son, Jesus Christ, and love one another, as he gave commandment." He sets forth one commandment of God, not many, because there is only one salvation and one source of it. But since we are occupied with many things, this one commandment, adapted to various matters, becomes manifold and is divided into various kinds. But John embraces all of these under two heads, namely faith and love; and the first comprehends whatever pertains to the conduct of this life and the ordering of morals, while the second teaches that the whole of religion and the worship of God is contained in it. It is ours to consider with all our souls what is said of each.

units.la: Præceptum fidei est, vt credamus nomini filij Dei, Iesu Christi. Consentiunt huic sententiæ, quæ ipse Dei filius alibi dicit: Hæc est voluntas eius qui misit me, vt omnis qui videt filiũ, & credit in eum, habeat vitam æternam. Item hoc est opus Dei, vt credatis in eum, quem ille misit. Ioa. 6. Est hoc ipsissimum salutis præceptum. Quia enim per Christum ad patrem peruenitur. (Ioan. 14.) qui vna & vera salus est, non potest non saluari, quicunque huic per fidem insitus fuerit.
units.tr: The commandment of faith is that we should believe in the name of the Son of God, Jesus Christ. The Son of God himself agrees with this sentiment when he says elsewhere: "This is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life." Likewise: "This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent" (John 6). This is the very essence of the command of salvation. For since through Christ we come to the Father (John 14), who is the one and true salvation, whoever has been engrafted into him by faith cannot but be saved.

units.la: Prodest vero obseruasse Joannis verba, quibus hoc praeceptum enunciat. Cum enim simpli-citer dicere potuisset, praeceptum Dei esse, ut credamus in filium Dei, Jesum Christum: dicere ma-luit: Hoc est praeceptum Dei, ut credamus nomini filij eius, &c. Est haec prioris definitio. Docet enim quid sit credere in filium Dei: hoc ipsum scilicet, quod credere ipsius nomini, id est, ea de fi-lio Dei credere quae nomine eius significantur. Exemplo res clarior fieri poterit. Exhibetur tibi ab hortulano vel aliquo medicinae studioso herba vel planta aliqua, quam ille Serpillum esse di-cet. Credes tu illius nomini, si serpillum esse assentiaris, eaque illi tribuas, quae historiae naturalis scriptores serpillo tribuere consueuerunt. Eadem erit gemmarum, arborum, animalium, rerum denique aliarum omnium ratio. Sic nomini filij Dei credere dicuntur, qui talem esse agnoscunt, qualis suo nomine describitur. Sunt enim nomina rerum notae, ex quibus illarum natura, proprietas & conditio dignosci solet. Hic ergo nomen filij Dei inquirendum erit: ubi nec circa Ju-daeorum Schem ham phoras nos occupari oportet, nec ea sigillatim excutere, quae passim à pro-phetis & Apostolis illi tribuuntur. Sed generalissimum illud, quo ceu proprio in scripturis appel-lari solet, & ex quo nos quoque appellationem traximus, debet inspici, quod est, JESVS CHRISTVS. Hoc enim illud sanctum & vere salutare nomen est, in quo omne genu flectitur, in quo salus omnis datur, in quo miracula fiunt, in quo denique totius humani generis conseruatio sub-sistit. Sed quia de hoc quaedam in secundo capite dicta sunt, breuius in praesenti singula perstrin-gi poterunt.
units.tr: It is indeed profitable to observe John's words by which he states this commandment. For when he could simply have said that it is God's commandment that we believe in the Son of God, Jesus Christ, he preferred to say: "This is the commandment of God, that we should believe in the name of his Son, etc." This is a definition of the former. For it teaches what it is to believe in the Son of God, namely this very thing: to believe his name, that is, to believe those things concerning the Son of God which are signified by his name. The matter will become clearer by an example. A gardener, or some student of medicine, shows you an herb or some plant, which he says is wild thyme. You will believe his name if you assent that it is wild thyme, and attribute to it those things which the writers of natural history are accustomed to attribute to wild thyme. The reasoning will be the same for gems, trees, animals, and indeed all other things. Thus those are said to believe in the name of the Son of God who acknowledge him to be such as his name describes him. For names are the marks of things, from which their nature, property and condition are usually known. Here, then, the name of the Son of God is to be inquired into; and here we ought not to occupy ourselves with the Jewish Shem hamphoras, nor to examine individually those things which are attributed to him scattered throughout the prophets and Apostles. Rather, that most general name by which he is customarily called in Scripture as his proper name, and from which we too have taken our appellation, ought to be examined, which is JESUS CHRIST. For this is that holy and truly saving name, in which every knee bows, in which all salvation is given, in which miracles are done, in which finally the preservation of the whole human race subsists. But since some things about this were said in the second chapter, the individual points may be touched upon more briefly in the present one.

units.la: JESV nomen filio Dei incarnato proprium fuisse constat. Nam ab angelo illud inditum fuit, priusquam in utero conciperetur, & postea in Circumcisione, solenni usu confirmatum. Matt. 1. Luc.1. Hebraeis vero à salute dicitur, ut & Jehofua: cuius rei locupletissimus testis est angelus, qui Josepho in somnis ait: Vocabis nomẽ eius Jesum: Is enim saluum faciet populum suum à peccatis suis. Jesu ergo saluatore significat, quod nomen filio Dei proprie conuenit, cum non aliud nome sub coelo hominibus datum sit, in quo salui fiat. Act.4. Et nomini filij Dei verè credet, quicunque huic saluatore esse agnoscunt, cuius beneficio è peccatorū luto asserti, & eorundē poenis liberati sumus. CHRISTUS filij Dei cognomen est,quod ex officio impositū,viam & ratione omnem,qua per ipsum saluati sumus, comprehendit. Græcis enim Christus dicitur, quem Hebræi Messiam nominant. Nobis utrumque Unctum sonat. Quia autem antiquitus Reges & Sacerdotes oleo sacro inungi solebant,ijdem etiam uncti domini dicebantur. Nulli tamen illorum nomen istud magis convenire potuit,quàm filio Dei pro nobis incarnato, qui & Rex populi Dei unicus & eiusdem Sacerdos æternus factus est.Illi enim ab æterno dictū legimus:Ego constitui regem meum super Zion montem meum sanctum.Psal.2.Et rursus:Tu es sacerdos æternus juxta ordinē Melchizedæch. Psal.110. Et sanè diligenter in eius consyderatione versanti, nullum in illo, vel regis vel sacerdotis officium,deesse patebit. Nam regis boni instar leges fert & jura verè sancta constituit. Idem omne judicium à patre sibi commissum habet, & olim in tremendo illo die judicij extremam sententiam feret super omnem carnem.Joan.5.Matt.25. Adhæc pro suis jam olim pugnauit,cum communi nostro hoste satana cōgressus, peccatum aboleuit,mortem deuicit,inferorum portas confregit,& omnem adversariā potestatem pedibus suis gloriosus victor contriuit. Adest quoque suis indesinenter, eosdem defendit, nec aliquem ex suis sibi eripi patitur. Et cum talis tantusq; rex sit, suis tamen minimè onerosus est, cum ipse sibi sufficiat, & beneficia potius conferre quàm exigere norit. Neminem ergo exactionibus grauat, neminem tributis exhaurit, nemini vectigalium postulatione molestus est,nullius terreno regno inhiat, non opes alienas affectat,sed regni cœlorum thesauros continua & inexhausta liberalitate profundit,propter nos olim in terris pauper factus,ut nos æternis opibus ditaret. Quòd si eundem & sacerdotem videre cupis,quæ sacerdotum fuerunt olim considera. Versabatur illorum munus in docendo, orando & sacrificando. At quia mortales erant, crebris successoribus erat opus. Adhæc,quia non verę expiationis,sed umbrarum duntaxat ministri erant, illorum sacra omnia crebrò iterari oportebat. At Christus,verus ecclesiæ sacerdos,quia æternus est,successores vel vicarios nullos agnoscit,& perfectæ redemptionis antistes,sacrificij sui repetitione non habet opus. Nam sacrificio corporis & sanguinis sui,semel in ara Crucis oblato, perfecta expiatione pro peccatis totius mundi satisfecit,& æterna redemptione impetrata, carnem & sanguinem,quæ ex nobis assumpserat,in cœlos subuexit,ut certi redderemur & nostra corpora eodē subuchenda esse. Idem & in terris ages magna cum authoritate docuit, & hodie per ministerium ecclesiæ, abs se institutum, docet, simulq; hominum animis spiritum suum inserit, qui eos illuminat & veritatis capaces reddit. Eodem modo & olim,cum in mundo versaretur,pro nobis orauit, & hodie in cœlis intercessor & mediator noster coram Deo patre apparet.Hunc ergo Sacerdotem esse negabit nemo,nisi qui lucem tenebras dicere audeat. His vero in unum collatis, patet eos nomini ipsius credere, qui hunc regem ecclesiæ unicum & æternum agnoscunt,qui ut judicem observant,qui ut redempto ri fidunt, qui ut munificum largitorem amant: adhæc qui sacerdotem agnoscentes,docente audiunt,intercessione eius firmiter niituntur, & in unica sacrificij per ipsum oblati satisfactione ac quiescunt. Comprehendunt hæc quæcunque de Christo Jesu in scripturis passim habentur,quæ omnia ad duos hosce Regis & Sacerdotis titulos referri debent. Quotquot itaque hęc in Christo vel omnino non agnoscunt, vel alios in horum participatum intrudunt, dum quæ Christi regis & sacerdotis sunt,alijs tribuunt,nomini filij Dei non credunt,& proinde primum hoc & summū Dei præceptum impia temeritate transgrediuntur.
units.tr: That the name JESUS was proper to the Son of God made flesh is agreed. For it was given by an angel before he was conceived in the womb, and afterwards confirmed by the solemn custom at the circumcision (Matt. 1; Luke 1). Among the Hebrews, indeed, it means salvation, as does Jehoshua; the angel who said to Joseph in a dream is a very rich witness of this matter: "You shall call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins" (Matt. 1). Jesus therefore signifies Saviour, which name properly belongs to the Son of God, since there is no other name under heaven given to men in which we must be saved (Acts 4). And whoever acknowledges him to be this Saviour truly believes in the name of the Son of God, by whose benefit we have been drawn out of the mire of sins and freed from their punishments. CHRIST is a surname of the Son of God, which, imposed from his office, comprehends the whole way and manner by which we have been saved through him. For he is called Christ by the Greeks, whom the Hebrews call Messiah. Both mean "Anointed" to us. But since in ancient times kings and priests were accustomed to be anointed with holy oil, the same were also called "anointed lords." Yet that name could befit none of them more than the Son of God made flesh for us, who has been made both the sole King of the people of God and its eternal Priest. For we read that of him it was said from eternity: "I have set my king upon Zion, my holy mountain" (Ps. 2); and again: "You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek" (Ps. 110). And indeed, to one who diligently dwells upon his consideration, it will be plain that no office of either king or priest is lacking in him. For like a good king he brings laws and establishes truly holy rights. He also has all judgment committed to him by the Father, and will in that dreadful day of judgment at last pronounce sentence upon all flesh (John 5; Matt. 25). Moreover, he has already fought for his own, when he engaged with our common enemy Satan, abolished sin, conquered death, broke the gates of hell, and as a glorious victor crushed under his feet every hostile power. He is also ever present with his own, defends them, and suffers none of his to be snatched from him. And though he is so great and so high a king, he is nevertheless in no way burdensome to his people, since he is sufficient for himself and knows how to confer benefits rather than to demand them. Therefore he burdens no one with exactions, drains no one with taxes, troubles no one with demands for tribute; he covets no earthly kingdom and seeks no foreign wealth, but pours out the treasures of the kingdom of heaven with continual and inexhaustible liberality, having once for our sake been made poor on earth, that he might enrich us with eternal riches. But if you wish to see him also as priest, consider what the priests of old did. Their office consisted in teaching, praying and sacrificing. But because they were mortal, they needed frequent successors. Furthermore, since they were ministers not of true expiation but only of shadows, all their sacred rites had to be repeated often. But Christ, the true priest of the Church, because he is eternal, acknowledges no successors or vicars, and as the bishop of perfect redemption has no need to repeat his sacrifice. For by the sacrifice of his body and blood, once offered on the altar of the Cross, he has made satisfaction for the sins of the whole world by perfect expiation, and having obtained eternal redemption, he has carried up into heaven the flesh and blood which he had taken from us, so that we might be assured that our bodies too are to be carried up thither. The same, both on earth, he taught with great authority, and today he teaches through the ministry of the Church, instituted by himself, and at the same time he implants his Spirit in men's minds, who enlightens them and makes them capable of the truth. In the same way, too, when he was in the world, he prayed for us, and today in heaven he appears before God the Father as our intercessor and mediator. No one will deny that he is this Priest, unless he dares to call light darkness. When these things are gathered together into one, it is plain that those believe in his name who acknowledge him as the sole and eternal King of the Church, who observe him as Judge, who trust in him as Redeemer, who love him as the bountiful giver; and besides, those who, acknowledging him as Priest, listen to his teaching, rest firmly on his intercession, and find their rest in the one satisfaction of the sacrifice offered through him. These comprehend whatever is found everywhere in the Scriptures concerning Christ Jesus, all of which must be referred to these two titles of King and Priest. Therefore, as many as either do not acknowledge these things in Christ at all, or thrust others into a share of them, while they attribute to others what belongs to Christ as King and Priest, do not believe in the name of the Son of God, and so with impious rashness transgress this first and highest commandment of God.

units.la: Alterum magni illius & principalis præcepti caput est: Ut diligamus nos mutuò, sicut dedit præceptum.Poterat simpliciter dilectionem mutuā requirere,sed eius modum & regulam, quoque monstrat,quę est præceptum Christi.Quia enim hic caput nostrū,rex & sacerdos ecclesię est unicus,omnes nostras actiones juxta ipsius præscriptum institui oportet. Excludit hoc omnem simulationem & fucum,quo in dilectione plerique utuntur. Nam multos inuenire est,qui proximum diligere videntur, & dilectionis officia cumulatim cōferunt, dū bene de illo loquuntur,famam eius defendūt,prosunt etiā ubicunq; datur occasio. Sed quia hęc omnia non nisi priuati cōmodi gratia faciunt,dum maiora beneficia ab illis,quos amare videtur,vel recipiunt,vel saltè spe rant, certè non proximū,sed seipsos diligere dici debent. Aufer enim illis omnem cōmodi spem, & quicquam ad illos ex proximi commodis utilitatis peruenire nega, mox tepidos & languentes videbis, qui in amore toti feruere videbantur. Rursum alij sunt,qui verbis quidem amant,opera autem dilectionis omnino nulla exercent, quos tinnienti cymbalo non ineleganter confert Paulus apostolus.1.Cor.13. At si Christum audias,illius præcepto omnem hunc fucum procul arceri senties. Is enim quia hostes diligere & ijs benefacere iubet, qui & verbis & factis in nos iniurij sunt,nullum priuato affectui in dilectione locum relinquit.Matt.5.Adhæc,dum suo exemplo animas pro fratribus deponere præcipit,dilectionē nullo modo in verbis cōsistere, sed factis eoufq; extendi vult, vt nec sanguini proprio parcamus, si hunc proximi salus exigat. Ioan.15. Vides ergo non temere factum, quod dilectionis regulam, Christi praeceptum, Apostolus proponit. Sed quia de hac in praecedentibus multa dicta sunt, plura etiam sequenti Capite subijcienur, hæc modò pauca sufficiant.
units.tr: Another head of that great and principal command is this: that we love one another, as he has given us the command. He could simply have required mutual love, but he also shows its manner and rule, which is the command of Christ. For since this Head of ours, who is the sole king and priest of the Church, is unique, all our actions ought to be ordered according to his prescription. This excludes all pretence and sham, which many use in love. For one may find many who seem to love their neighbour and heap up acts of kindness: they speak well of him, defend his reputation, and help him wherever an occasion is given. But since they do all this only for the sake of private advantage, while they either receive greater benefits from those whom they seem to love, or at least hope for them, they should rightly be said to love not their neighbour but themselves. Take away from them all hope of gain, and let nothing come to them from their neighbour's advantage, and you will soon see lukewarm and sluggish people who seemed to burn wholly with love. Again, there are others who indeed love in words, but perform no works of love at all; the apostle Paul aptly compares them to a tinkling cymbal (1 Cor. 13). But if you listen to Christ, you will feel that this sham is far removed by his command. For since he bids us love our enemies and do good to those who wrong us in word and deed, he leaves no place for private feeling in love (Matt. 5). Moreover, by his own example, when he commands us to lay down our lives for the brethren, he wills that love does not consist in words at all, but extends to deeds, so that we do not spare even our own blood if the salvation of a neighbour requires it (John 15). You see, then, that it was not without reason that the apostle set forth Christ's command as the rule of love. But since much has been said about this in the preceding chapters, and more will be added in the following chapter, let these few things suffice for now.

units.la: Priusquam tamen ab hoc loco discedamus, rationem inspicere oportet, propter quam fidei & dilectionis praeceptum coniungantur. Hanc dum aliqui minus observant, inter fidem & dilectionē ita distinguunt, quasi vna abs; altera homini adesse posit, & fidem dilectione perfici fingunt. Quo errore decepti eò delabuntur, vt contra Apostolicā doctrinam fidei iustificationē negent, & omnem iustificationis gloriā in opera transferant. Obseruādum ergo duo hæc naturali-ter coniungi, nec alterū sine altero posse subsistere. Nec enim fieri potest, vt Christo fidat, qui illum non diligit. At quomodo Christum diliget, qui illum fide nondū apprehendit & nouit? Rursus qui Christum diligit, eiusdem membra diligat oportet, à quibus ille separari nō potest. Quoties ergo fidei dilectio coniugitur, vel fides per dilectionē operari dicitur (vt Gal.5.legimus) non eo sensu id accipi debet quasi fides absq; dilectione subsistere posit, ea autē vbi libet ceu instrumento vtatur: sed dilectionē naturalem & ingenitā fidei vim esse intelligamus, qua sese operibus declarat. Quæ causa est, quòd opera quæ fiunt, ad fidem potius quàm dilectione referri debent, si proprie loqui velimus. Nā quæ per se dilectionis opera videri poterant, si absq; fide fiant, peccati potius quàm bonorum operū nomen merentur. Rom.14. Et Christus pharisæorū eleemosynas eò nomine damnat, quòd ambitione fascinati, præmiū ex hominibus sperarent, nō autem fide ad Deum remuneratorem respicerent. Matth.6. Exempla sunt & similia in rerum natura, quæ hoc ipsum pulchre illustrant. Ignis & calor inter se distincta videri possunt, & nominibus verè distinguuntur. Sed quia natura sic coniuncta sunt, vt nec ignis sine calore, nec hic sine illo esse queat, caloris effectus ad ipsum igne, qui hunc naturaliter gignit, referuntur. Quoties ergo sophistæ fidem sine operibus nobis obijciunt, & opera dilectionis ita extollunt, quasi per ea fides absoluatur, impio & scelerato dolo simplicium animis laqueos tendunt. Fides enim, quæ dilectione caret, non magis fides est, quàm cadauer mortuum homo dici poterat. Et Apostoli dum fide nos iustificari docent, non de mortua & inani fidei gloriatione loquuntur, sed viuū illum & certum assensum animi intelligunt, qui operatione spiritus sancti generatus, Christum totum amplectitur, hominem totum in Christi communionem rapit, vt iam non homo ex se, sed in homine Christus & homo in Christo viuat. Gal.2. Sed tēporis angustia monet, vt ad secundam huius loci partē transeamus.
units.tr: Before we leave this place, however, we must consider the reason why the command of faith and the command of love are joined together. While some pay less attention to this, they so distinguish between faith and love as if the one could be present in a man apart from the other, and they imagine that faith is completed by love. Deceived by this error, they go so far as to deny justification by faith, contrary to apostolic teaching, and transfer all the glory of justification to works. We must therefore observe that these two are naturally joined, and that the one cannot subsist without the other. For it cannot happen that a man trusts in Christ who does not love him. But how can he love Christ who has not yet grasped and known him by faith? Again, whoever loves Christ must love his members, from whom he cannot be separated. Therefore, whenever love is joined to faith, or faith is said to work through love (as we read in Gal. 5), this ought not to be understood as if faith could subsist without love and then use love as an instrument wherever it pleases; rather we should understand that love is the natural and inborn power of faith, by which it declares itself in works. This is why works that are done ought, to speak properly, to be referred to faith rather than to love. For works which might seem by themselves to be works of love, if they are done without faith, deserve the name of sin rather than of good works (Rom. 14). And Christ condemns the alms of the Pharisees on this very ground: that, bewitched by ambition, they hoped for reward from men, and did not look to God as rewarder with faith (Matt. 6). There are examples and similar things in nature which beautifully illustrate this very point. Fire and heat may be seen as distinct, and they are truly distinguished by their names. But because they are so joined in nature that neither can exist without the other, the effects of heat are referred to the fire itself, which naturally produces it. Therefore, whenever the sophists object to us faith without works, and so extol the works of love as if faith were completed through them, they spread snares with an impious and wicked deceit for the minds of simple people. For faith that lacks love is no more faith than a dead corpse could be called a man. And when the apostles teach that we are justified by faith, they do not speak of a dead and empty boasting of faith, but understand a living and certain assent of the mind, which, begotten by the working of the Holy Spirit, embraces Christ wholly and draws the whole man into communion with Christ, so that now it is no longer man who lives from himself, but Christ in man, and man in Christ (Gal. 2). But the shortness of time bids us pass to the second part of this place.

units.la: II. Et qui seruat praecepta eius, in illo manet, & ipse in eo. Breuis inest verbis hisce ad obseruationem praeceptorum Dei exhortatiuncula. Explicant enim & pollicentur amplissimū fructum ijs, qui ista obseruauerint. Qui Dei praecepta seruat, in illo manet, & Deus manet in eo. Describit sic communionem, quæ est inter Deum & praeceptorum eius obseruatores, de qua Cap.1. dictum est. Meminit eiusdem ipse Christus, ex cuius ore Ioānes omnia sua desumit. Ait enim ille: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meū seruabit, & pater meus diliget eum, & ad eum veniemus, & mansionem apud eum faciemus. Ioan.14. Comprehendit promissio hæc omnem hominis felicitatem, tam futuri quam præsentis seculi: quia fieri nequit, vt ei quicquam desit, qui cum Deo omnis boni fonte, communione tam familiari fruitur. Non patiuntur parentes liberis suis ea deesse, quæ ipsorum saluti seruiunt. At longè fidelior est cœlestis pater, qui nec immorigeris & palàm impijs Solis lucem & pluuiam negat, eo argumento declarans, quàm prompto animo, quàm benefico in eos esse velit, qui in præceptis suis ambulare studunt.
units.tr: II. "And he who keeps his commandments abides in him, and he in him." In these words there is a brief exhortation to the observance of God's commandments. For they both explain and promise the most ample fruit to those who have kept these things. He who keeps God's commandments abides in him, and God abides in him. In this way he describes the communion which exists between God and the keepers of his commandments, of which it was said in chapter 1. Christ himself, from whose mouth John takes all his material, also mentions it. For he says: "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him" (John 14). This promise comprehends all human happiness, both of the age to come and of the present age, because it cannot happen that anything should be lacking to him who enjoys communion with God, the fountain of every good, in such a familiar way. Parents do not allow their children to lack those things which serve their welfare. But the heavenly Father is far more faithful, who does not deny the light of the sun and the rain even to the unruly and openly wicked, thereby declaring by this argument how ready and how beneficent his mind is toward those who strive to walk in his precepts.

units.la: Est ergo memorabilis omnino hæc sententia. Tradit enim absolutissimā veræ felicitatis consequendæ rationem, quæ in obseruatione præceptorum Dei versatur. Consentiunt huic quęcūq; in scripturis de hac traduntur. Deus certè cū Abrahamo fœdus pangens, & omnem in seipso sufficientiā pollicens, hanc vicissim ab illo postulat, dicés: Ambula coram me, & esto integer. Gen.17. In lege nihil tam frequens & vulgare est, quàm quòd præceptorū Dei obseruatoribus omnis generis bona promittuntur, eorundem verò transgressores minis horrendis territantur. Lege Leuit.26. Deut.28. &c. Prophetarum scripta hoc ipsum nusquam non inculcant. Nec exempla desunt, quibus ista confirmentur. Vnicus profectò Iudicum liber hic nobis prolixi Commētarij loco esse potest, qui Israelitarum graues & intolerabiles calamitates narrat, quibus impliciti fuerunt, quotiescunq; à Dei præceptis discedere ausi sunt. Vt primum verò in viam obedientiæ reuersi, præceptis Dei paruerūt, libertatis vindices & assertores Deus excitauit, qui hostium tyrannidem infringerent. Debebat horū cōsyderatio hodie esse frequentior, quādo multi pertinaces nostri seculi calamitates admirantur, famem nimirū & penuriam rerum diuturnā, incognita ante & noua morborum genera, seditiones, bella intestina, exteros hostes, ciuitatū excidia, rerumpublicarū oppressiones, & quæcunque alia infelicem terrarum orbem hodie miserè diuexant. At iuste admirationis locus nullus est, si quæ publicè & impunè apud omnes fiunt, consyderes.
