Quem enim populum dabis, quam rempub. quæ in magni huius & verè salutaris præcepti observatione seriò versetur, vel illud saltem ad se pertinere putet? Fides in unigenitum Dei filium, Iesum Christum, non à Turcis modò & Iudæis, verum etiam ab ijs maximè, nō negligitur, sed proculcatur, qui Christianissimi vi deri volunt. Licet enim hunc & Iesum & Christum esse fateantur, negant tamen quæcunq; hisce nominibus comprehensa sunt. Nam & salutis gloriam in Creaturas transferunt, & noua fingunt ecclesiæ capita, & quasi Christus ea deserta apud Aethiopes cum Ioue Homerico conuiúetur, vicarios pro suo arbitrio constituunt: alios item doctores sequuntur, in quorum nomina, contempto & neglecto Christi nomine, iurare ipsis graue non videtur: mediatores & intercessores alios quærunt, satisfactiones pro peccatis nouas indies excogitant, sacrificium Christi iterare audent, quasi vel non perfectum fuerit, cū ipse se in ara Crucis offerret, vel illius virtus, ut plantæ alicuius emortuæ, consumpta sit & abolita. Et hæc non modò faciunt stulti homines, sed & alios eadem facere cogunt, & regum potentia ad suæ impietatis defensionem abutuntur. Taceo nunc infinitos abusus, quos istorum hominum audacia, contra fidei præceptum, in ecclesiam inuexit. Taceo falsa dogmata, sacrorum nundinationes & quæcunq; alia sunt eius generis, quibus cōmemorandis totus hic dies non sufficeret. Quòd si vero nos videas, qui euangelij notitia gloriamur, nihilo his meliores inuenies. Auditur quidem in ecclesijs nostris vera Christi saluatoris doctrina. Uendicatur illi constanter omnis nostræ salutis gloria. Prædicatur Iesus, id est, saluator esse unicus. Prædicatur Christus, id est, rex & sacerdos. Sed quotus quisque est, qui huic prædicationi credat? Si enim saluatorem credimus, cur non amamus, & pro illo fortunas nostras deponimus? Cur ab illo nos patimur abstrahi? Cur mundi amicitiam & voluptates carnales illi præferimus? Si regem agnoscimus, cur non obedimus? Cur non iudicium eius expauescimus? Cur non pro illo pugnamus? Cur ipsum pro nobis pugnantem nō strenui sequimur? Cur ipsius protectioni diffidimus? Si sacerdos & doctor veritatis nobis est unicus, cur nō credimus doctrinæ, quæ ab ipso docetur? Cur virtutes cōmendantem nō audimus? Cur vitia dissuadentę negligimus, ridemus, imò conui tijs proscindimus? An verò hęc omnia à nobis fieri negabimus? Neminem certè hoc vel posse vel velle arbitror. Clamat enim & testatur contra nos vita nostra. Accusant nos fidei hostes, qui nos ipsis nihilo sanctiores esse verè dicunt, & propter nostrę vitæ coscelerationem euägelij doctrinâ exosam habent. Costat ergo fidei præceptum passim negligi ab illis ipsis, qui Christi nomine gloriantur. De dilectione quid attinet dicere, cū passim regnent quæ cū huius legibus ex diametro pugnát? Iamne ergo amplius calamitates, tā graues & diuturnas, nostri seculi mirabimur, aut illa rum causas vanis speculationibus inquiremus? Cū hęc ubiq; fiant, cū Deo cōmunionem habere nō possumus, & proinde à spe melioris cōditionis sumus exclusi. Una salutis via est, ad Dei præce pta reuerti & illorū observationi studere. Peccatis cessantibus, cessabūt & horum poenæ. Reuertimini ad me (clamat apud prophetam dominus) & ego reuertar ad vos. Zach. i. Ier. 3. & 31. &c.
units.tr: This saying is therefore altogether memorable. For it delivers the most complete method of attaining true happiness, which lies in the observance of God's precepts. Whatever is handed down about this in the Scriptures agrees with it. God, certainly, when he makes a covenant with Abraham and promises all sufficiency in himself, in turn demands this from him, saying: "Walk before me, and be upright" (Gen. 17). In the law nothing is so frequent and common as that every kind of good is promised to the observers of God's precepts, while the transgressors of the same are terrified with dreadful threats. Read Lev. 26, Deut. 28, etc. The writings of the prophets urge this same thing everywhere. Nor are there lacking examples by which these things are confirmed. The book of Judges alone may serve us in place of a lengthy commentary, which narrates the grievous and intolerable calamities in which the Israelites were entangled whenever they dared to depart from God's precepts. But as soon as they returned to the way of obedience and obeyed God's commands, God raised up deliverers and champions of liberty who broke the tyranny of their enemies. The consideration of these things ought to be more frequent today, when many stubborn people of our age wonder at the calamities, namely the long-lasting famine and scarcity of goods, kinds of disease unknown before and new, seditions, civil wars, foreign enemies, the destruction of cities, the oppression of commonwealths, and whatever else today miserably harasses the unhappy globe. But there is no ground for just wonder if you consider what is done publicly and with impunity among all. For what people will you point to, what commonwealth which seriously applies itself to the observance of this great and truly saving command, or at least thinks that this command pertains to itself? Faith in the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, is neglected and trampled underfoot not only by the Turks and Jews, but above all by those who wish to be seen as most Christian. For although they confess that this is both Jesus and Christ, they deny all that is comprehended under these names. For they transfer the glory of salvation to creatures, invent new heads of the Church, and, as if Christ were forsaken there, feast with the Homeric Jove among the Ethiopians, and appoint vicars at their own pleasure. Likewise they follow other teachers, in whose names they think it no serious matter to swear, the name of Christ being despised and neglected. They seek other mediators and intercessors, devise new satisfactions for sins every day, and dare to repeat the sacrifice of Christ, as if it were either not perfected, though he offered himself on the altar of the Cross, or his power had been consumed and abolished, like that of some dead plant. And these things foolish men not only do, but they also compel others to do the same, and they abuse the power of kings to defend their impiety. I now pass over the countless abuses which the audacity of these men has introduced into the Church, against the command of faith. I pass over false doctrines, the trafficking in sacred things, and whatever else is of that kind, which would not suffice to recount even if this whole day were given to it. But if you look at us, who boast of the knowledge of the gospel, you will find ourselves no better than these. The true doctrine of Christ the Saviour is indeed heard in our churches. The whole glory of our salvation is constantly claimed for him. Jesus is preached, that is, that the Saviour is one alone. Christ is preached, that is, king and priest. But how few are there who believe this preaching? For if we believe him to be Saviour, why do we not love him, and lay down our fortunes for him? Why do we allow ourselves to be drawn away from him? Why do we prefer the friendship of the world and carnal pleasures to him? If we acknowledge him as king, why do we not obey him? Why do we not dread his judgment? Why do we not fight for him? Why do we not eagerly follow him fighting for us? Why do we distrust his protection? If he is our sole priest and teacher of the truth, why do we not believe the doctrine which he teaches? Why do we not listen when he commends virtues? Why do we neglect, laugh at, or even tear apart with reproaches those who dissuade us from vices? Or shall we deny that all these things are done by us? I think no one can or wishes to do this. For our life cries out and bears witness against us. Our enemies of the faith accuse us, who rightly say that we are in no way holier than they, and because of the wickedness of our lives they hold the doctrine of the gospel in hatred. It is therefore clear that the command of faith is everywhere neglected by those very people who glory in the name of Christ. What need is there to speak of love, when everywhere reign things that fight directly against its laws? Shall we then wonder any further at the calamities, so grievous and long-lasting, of our age, or shall we seek their causes in vain speculations? Since these things are done everywhere, we cannot have communion with God, and therefore we are excluded from hope of a better condition. There is one way of salvation: to return to God's precepts and to strive to observe them. When sins cease, their punishments will cease too. "Return to me," the Lord cries through the prophet, "and I will return to you" (Zech. 1; Jer. 3 and 31, etc.).

units.la: Sed dicat aliquis: Magna & splendida quidem hæc promissio, quòd Deū in se manentem habiturus sit, & ipse quoq; in Deo mansurus sit, qui ipsius præcepta observat. Quo autem teste de re tanta certior reddi poterit homo? Quis animum fluctuantem cōfirmabit? Nec enim hic aliqua esse potest humani testimonij authoritas. Nisi propria hominis mens huic promissioni cōsentiat, frustra vniuersus orbis hanc auribus ingeret. Ne quid ergo dubij superesset, testem producit locupletissimum Ioannes, quo nemo & maior & fide dignior produci poterat. Sic enim ait:
units.tr: But someone may say: this promise is indeed great and splendid, that the one who keeps God's precepts will have God abiding in him, and will himself abide in God. But by whose witness can a man be made more certain of so great a matter? Who will steady a wavering mind? For here no authority of human testimony can count for anything. Unless the man's own mind agrees with this promise, the whole world will pour it into his ears in vain. So that nothing doubtful may remain, John produces a witness most weighty, and no one greater or more trustworthy could be produced. For he says:

units.la: III. Et per hoc scimus, quòd manet in nobis, è spiritu, quem dedit nobis. Sensus verborū est: Magna sunt & præclara quæ promisimus ò homo, & scimus dubitationes de his non exiguas in animis hominum oboriri posse. Sed non est, quòd ad nostram vel quorumuis aliorum authoritatem respicias. Intra teipsum huius rei testem irrefragabilem senties, ut primum præcepto huic Dei te totum addixeris. Christus Iesus enim ijs, qui in se credunt, spiritum suum pollicitus est, quem nō possunt non habere quicunque Christi sunt. Ioan. 14. 16. Rom. 8. Is inter alias functiones & hac habet, quòd arrhabo & pignus est salutis nostræ, quemadmodum Apostolus prædicat. 2. Cor. 1. & 5. Eph. 1. Sicut enim Christus carnè è nobis assumpsit, eamq; in cœlos subuexit, ut pignus nostrum in cœlis esset, quo cōstaret & nostram carnem eodem iuxta illius promissionem subuehi debere: ita vicissim de spiritu suo nobis dedit, ut eiusdem rei pignus in animis nostris haberemus. In hoc spiritu clamamus, Abba pater, eō quòd adoptionis & filiorū Dei spiritus est. Rom. 8. Gal. 4. Hunc spiritum sentiunt, quicunq; fidem habēt in se veram, cuius testimonium tam est efficax, ut solum contra totius mundi clamores sufficiat. Licet enim omnes philosophorum scholę, omnes patres, omnia Concilia, omnes reges & principes, omnes deniq; omniū ordinū homines vni ex fidelibus contradicant, & uno ore hæreticum & damnatum esse pronuncient, irrita tamen erit omniū hō-rum authoritas, & in animo fidelis murus aheneus erit spiritus hic, quo ita confirmatur, ut si fractus illabatur orbis, impauidum feriant ruinæ. Exempla huius rei in Apostolis sunt & martyribus, qui nec tantæ contradicentium authoritati resistere, nec tot minis tamq; atrocibus supplicijs sufficere potuissent, nisi maiori cœlestis spiritus virtute fuissent confirmati.
units.tr: III. And hereby we know that he abideth in us, by the Spirit which he hath given us. The sense of the words is this: Great and glorious are the things we have promised, O man, and we know that no small doubts about them can arise in men's minds. But there is no reason for you to look to our authority, or to that of anyone else. Within yourself you will feel an irrefutable witness of this matter, as soon as you have devoted yourself wholly to this precept of God. For Christ Jesus has promised his Spirit to those who believe in him, and those who belong to Christ cannot fail to have him. John 14:16; Rom. 8. This Spirit has among his other offices this one as well: that he is the earnest and pledge of our salvation, as the Apostle proclaims. 2 Cor. 1 and 5; Eph. 1. For just as Christ took our flesh from us and raised it into heaven, so that we might have a pledge in heaven, by which it is assured that our flesh too must be raised up after it, according to his promise, so in turn he has given us of his Spirit, so that we might have a pledge of the same thing in our minds. In this Spirit we cry, Abba, Father, because he is the Spirit of adoption and of the sons of God. Rom. 8; Gal. 4. Those who have true faith in themselves feel this Spirit, and his testimony is so effective that it alone suffices against the clamours of the whole world. For although all the schools of the philosophers, all the Fathers, all the Councils, all kings and princes, and finally men of every rank should contradict one believer and pronounce with one voice that he is a heretic and condemned, yet the authority of all these will be empty, and this Spirit will be a bronze wall in the faithful man's soul, by which he is so strengthened that, even if the world should fall in pieces and collapse upon him, the ruins would strike him without fear. Examples of this are found in the Apostles and martyrs, who could neither have resisted the so great authority of their opposers, nor endured so many threats and such atrocious punishments, unless they had been strengthened by the greater power of the heavenly Spirit.

units.la: Patet in his excellens nostræ fidei dignitas & gloria, quæ & tantis promissionibus nititur, & tanti testis authoritate stabilitur. Iactitent alij suorum placitorum authores, glorientur patribus, Concilijs, pontificibus, Imperatorum maiestate, regum & principum splendore: nobis hic testis sufficit, qui nullius contradictione confunditur, nec aliorum clamoribus cedere novit. Hic animos nostros de veritate cognita tam certos reddit, ut dubitare nō possint. Illorum aut animi non possunt nō fluctuare, quoties principum ruinas & instabilem mundi huius conditionē intuentur.
units.tr: In these things the excellent dignity and glory of our faith is evident: it rests on so great promises and is established by the authority of so great a witness. Let others boast of the authors of their opinions, let them glory in the Fathers, the Councils, the popes, the majesty of emperors, the splendour of kings and princes: for us this witness suffices, who is confounded by no one's contradiction and knows not how to yield to the clamours of others. He makes our minds so certain of the truth once known that they cannot doubt. But the minds of those others cannot help wavering whenever they look upon the ruin of princes and the unstable condition of this world.

units.la: Admonet nos officij locus hic. Si enim spiritum suum animis nostris Christus inseruit, nos spiritus sancti templa & hospitia esse constat. Decet ergo, ut puritati & sanctimoniæ studeamus, ne contristetur in membris nostris spiritus Christi, qui cum impuris habitare nescit. Refer huc quæ à Paulo dicuntur 1.Corinth.6.cap.
units.tr: The place of duty admonishes us here. For if Christ has implanted his Spirit in our minds, it is clear that we are temples and dwelling-places of the Holy Spirit. It is fitting, therefore, that we should strive for purity and holiness, lest the Spirit of Christ, who cannot dwell with the impure, be grieved in our members. Refer here what Paul says in 1 Corinthians, chapter 6.

units.la: Vidimus hucusque, fratres, breve eorum quæ saluti nostræ serviunt compendium. Docuit Ioannes quæ præceptorum Dei summa sit, quæ fidei ratio, & totius vitæ nostræ conversatio esse debeat. Promisit studij tam sancti fructus uberrimos, & promissionis suæ teste adduxit, quem contemnere nemo potest, nisi qui animo proprio credere nolit. Agnoscamus ergo Dei bonitatē, qui nec præceptis nimijs nos grauare, nec salutis incertos esse voluit. Servemus præcepta eius, ut in huius vitæ curriculo communionem cum illo habeamus, æternum regnaturi cum filio eius Iesu Christo, cui debetur benedictio, gloria, honor & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: We have seen thus far, brethren, a brief summary of those things which serve our salvation. John has taught what is the sum of God's precepts, what is the rule of faith, and what the whole conduct of our life ought to be. He has promised the most abundant fruits of so holy a pursuit, and as a witness to his promise he has brought forward one whom no one can despise, unless he is unwilling to believe with his own mind. Let us therefore acknowledge the goodness of God, who has willed neither to burden us with excessive precepts nor to leave us uncertain of salvation. Let us keep his precepts, so that in the course of this life we may have fellowship with him, destined to reign eternally with his Son Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, glory, honour and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT IIII. HOMILIA XXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 4. SERMON 22.

units.la: DILECTI, ne cuiuis spiritui credatis: sed probate spiritus, an ex Deo sint. Quoniam multi pseudoprophetæ exierunt in mundum. Per hoc cognoscite spiritū Dei. Omnis spiritus, qui confitetur Iesum Christum in carne venisse, ex Deo est. Et omnis spiritus, qui non confitetur Iesum Christum in carne venisse, ex Deo non est. Et hic est ille spiritus Antichristi, de quo audistis, quod venturus sit, & iam nunc in mundo est.
units.tr: Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are from God. For many false prophets have gone out into the world. By this know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is not from God. And this is the spirit of Antichrist, of which you have heard that it is coming, and it is now already in the world.

units.la: Vidimus nuper circa finem capitis tertij omnem fidei & salutis nostræ rationem breviter quidem, sed perspicuè, ab Apostolo comprehensam. Docuit enim omnia Dei præcepta impleri fide in filium Dei Iesum Christum, & mutua dilectione. Simul verò exposuit amplissimos fructus, quos consequi solet, quicunque hæc Dei præcepta observaverit. Nam is cum Deo communione fruitur, quæ omnis boni causa & origo est. Ne tamen de promissione tam liberali & magnifica aliquid dubitaret nostræ carnis infirmitas, eiusdem testem producit irrefragabilem, spiritum Christi, quem is animis nostris immittit, ut salutis nostræ arrha-bo sit, & nutantes in fide animos quotidie suffulciat & confirmet. Est hæc doctrina simplex & facilis, quam quivis & intelligere & sequi potest, cuius animus à religione & veritatis studio minus abhorret. Sed ea semper fuit hostis satanæ improbitas, ut simplicem veritatis doctrinam fuco errorum & superstitionis obscurare conatus sit: nec eorum modo opera ad eam rem utitur, qui manifesti nominis Christi hostes sunt, sed illorum quoque, qui Christi nomine gloriantur, & spiritu Christi se duci & impelli simulant. Quam ob rem ne illorum insidijs nostra pateret simplicitas, nos contra illos hoc loco præmunit Apostolus. Nā primò, à fidelibus prudentiā requirit, qua usi nō facilè ample-ctatur quoduis doctrinæ genus, sed singula probè examinata ad iudicium veritatis revocent. Deinde ut hoc fieri possit, breviter docet. Utrobiq; autem rationes interserit, quæ id necessarium factu esse, demonstrent. Faxit Deus, ut inter tā graves & perniciosas nostri se-culi de doctrina controversias, de re omnium utilissima dignè & cū multorum fructu disseramus.
units.tr: Recently, near the end of the third chapter, we saw the whole method of our faith and salvation summed up briefly but clearly by the Apostle. For he taught that all the commandments of God are fulfilled by faith in the Son of God, Jesus Christ, and by mutual love. At the same time he set out the very great fruits which he who observes these commandments of God usually obtains. For he enjoys communion with God, which is the cause and source of all good. Yet lest the weakness of our flesh should doubt anything about so generous and magnificent a promise, he brings forward as its unfailing witness the Spirit of Christ, whom he sends into our souls as the pledge of our salvation, and who daily supports and strengthens minds wavering in faith. This teaching is simple and easy, and anyone can understand and follow it, whoever has a mind that shrinks little from religion and the pursuit of truth. But it has always been the wickedness of Satan, the enemy, to try to obscure the simple teaching of truth with the paint of errors and superstitions; and he uses for this purpose not only the work of those who are open enemies of the name of Christ, but also of those who glory in the name of Christ and pretend that they are led and driven by the Spirit of Christ. Therefore, lest our simplicity lie open to their snares, the Apostle here forearms us against them. For first, he requires of the faithful a prudence by which they do not readily embrace every kind of doctrine, but have each one carefully examined and brought back to the judgment of truth. Then he teaches briefly how this can be done. In both places, moreover, he inserts reasons which show that this is necessary to do. May God grant that, amid the so grave and pernicious controversies over doctrine of our age, we may discuss this most useful of all matters worthily and to the profit of many.

units.la: I. Dilecti, ne cuiuis spiritui credatis, sed probate spiritus, an ex Deo sint. Quoniam multi pseudoprophetæ exierunt in mundum. Proponit his verbis summam suæ admonitionis. Spiritus vero vocat vel doctrinas vel doctores, qui spiritu se præditos esse gloriantur: quo sensu & illud Pauli dicitur: Spiritus prophetarum prophetis subijciuntur. 1. Cor. 14. Sensus ergo verborum Apostoli est, non temere omnibus credendum esse, qui doctrinæ suæ spiritus sancti authoritatem prætexunt. Requiri enim examen, quo doctrinæ omnes ad veritatis regulam probétur, ne falsa pro veris, & pro salutaribus Dei præceptis perniciosas & noxias hominum traditiones recipiamus. Subijcit vero rationem, qua hoc & vtile & necessarium esse probet, cum inquit: Quoniam multi pseudoprophetæ exierunt in mundum. Sic enim vult dicere: Si non alij quàm synceri veritatis doctores essent, nec alia dogmata quàm quæ cum simplici veritate faciunt, in mundo spargerentur, superuacaneum videri poterat quod moneo, meaque hæc cura plane esset inutilis. Sed oberrant hinc inde falsi doctores veris intermixti, qui virus suum partim clàm inspirant simplicioribus, partim aperto Marte fidem veram oppugnant. Facilè igitur fieri potest, vt in tales incidamus, & mendaciorum tendiculis capiamur, si temere cuiuis docenti fidem adhibere libeat. Necessarium ergo est quod moneo, hæc nisi ab illis contemni potest, qui suæ salutis rationem habent nullam. Sunt hæc nobis diligenter meditanda o fratres, nostro seculo, quando vbique terrarum noua quotidie dogmata sparguntur, eaq; tam inter se pugnantia, vt simul subsistere nullo modo possint. Excutiamus itaq; singula, quæ hic dicuntur, paulò diligentius.
units.tr: I. Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are from God. For many false prophets have gone out into the world. In these words he sets out the sum of his admonition. By "spirits" he means either doctrines or teachers who boast that they are endowed with the Spirit; in this sense also that saying of Paul is used: "The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets." 1 Cor. 14. The sense of the Apostle's words, therefore, is that one must not believe rashly everyone who puts forward the authority of the Holy Spirit for his teaching. For a test is required by which all doctrines are approved by the rule of truth, lest we receive false things for true, and perverse and harmful traditions of men for the salutary commandments of God. He then adds the reason by which he proves that this is both useful and necessary, when he says: "For many false prophets have gone out into the world." For he wants to say this: if there were none but sincere teachers of the truth, and no doctrines in the world except those which agree with simple truth, what I admonish might seem superfluous, and this my care would be plainly useless. But false teachers, mixed in with true ones, wander here and there; some of them secretly breathe their poison into the simpler folk, and others openly attack the true faith in open battle. It can therefore easily happen that we fall into such people and are caught in the snares of lies, if we are willing to give rash faith to every teacher. What I admonish is therefore necessary, and it can be despised only by those who have no concern for their salvation. These things, brothers, we must diligently consider in our age, when new doctrines are scattered every day throughout all lands, and these so mutually at odds that they can in no way stand together. Let us therefore examine each of the things that are said here a little more carefully.

units.la: Priusquam vero reliqua attingamus, generalem illam curam spiritus sancti obseruare conuenit, qua fidissimi patris instar cauet, ne fides nostra impostorum falsis dogmatibus subuertatur. Adhibuit hanc omnibus seculis tanto studio, vt nullum vel veteris vel noui Testamenti librum inuenias, qui non hac in re nos probè instruat. Extant enim in Lege nõ contemnendi Canones, quibus pseudoprophetas à veris dignoscamus, quos videre est tú alibi, tum Deute. 13. cap. In prophetarum scriptis passim obuia sunt, quæ ad hanc causam faciunt. Nec enim tantum cõtra sui seculi seductores pugnant, sed etiam de venturis vaticinantur, & eosdem agnoscere docent. Legantur quæ huc pertinent, Ezech. 34. Dan. 7. & 11. Zachar. 5. & 11. &c. In novi Testamenti libris vt omnia alia, ita & hæc euidentius multò tradùtur. Christus clamat: Cauete vobis à pseudoprophetis, qui veniunt ad vos vestiti pellibus ouium, intus autem sunt lupi rapaces. Ex fructibus illorum agnoscetis eos. Matt. 7. Idem monet, vt cæcos cæcorum duces deuitemus, qui neglectis Dei præceptis hominum traditiones prædicant. Matth. 15. Alibi fures & latrones esse pronunciat, quicunque per aliud ostium, quàm ipse est, ingredi conantur, & extra Christum aliam salutis viam monstrare audent. Ioan. 10. Nec contentus eos impugnauisse, qui illo tempore populum seducebant, eos quoque depingit, quos nouisimo seculo venturos esse nouerat. Matth. 24. Ait enim: Si quis vobis dixerit: Ecce hic Christus, aut illic, nolite credere. Surgent enim pseudochristi & pseudoprophetæ, & dabunt signa magna, & prodigia, ita vt in errorem inducantur, si fieri possit, etiá ele cti. Ecce prædixi vobis. Si ergo dixerint vobis: Ecce in deserto est: nolite exire. Ecce in penetralibus: nolite credere, &c. Exemplum Christi imitati Apostoli, eadem magno serio vrgent & inculcant. Facit id Paulus Acto. 20. 1. Tim. 4. 2. Tim. 3. & 4. 2. Thess. 2. &c. Nec circa hoc negligens est Petrus, qui 2. cap. epistolæ suæ posterioris omnia, quæ de pseudoprophetis nostri seculi dici possunt, satis copiosè exponit. Idem in Ioanne supra cap. 2. vidimus, qui tamen eadem (ne quid omittat) hic repetit, plura & in secunda epistola post dicturus. At magnas & graues esse oportet huius diligentiæ spiritus sancti causas, vt reuera sunt. Sicuti enim vera doctrina in hominum animis fidem plantat & alit, Christo inserit & in viam salutis deducit: ita falsis doctrinis fides subuerti, à Christo homines abstrahi, & in viam vel barathrum perditionis abripi consueuerunt. Non igitur superuacanea videri debet eorum diligentia, qui hodie in hoc incumbunt, vt falsis doctoribus negotium faciant. Si enim olim hæc prædici oportuit, quid nunc factu opus est, quando lupi illi in grege Christiano grassantur, quando Christus monstratur hinc inde, & totus quantus est vnà cum anima & diuinitate in sacramento altaris, vel etiam ædicula sacramenti siue Cibo-rio esse dicitur? Quando item falsis doctrinis ecclesiam Christi in varias sectas scissam, & stupendis superstitionibus pollutam, cernimus? Hic certè totis viribus inflari debet verbi diuini tuba, ne quis nostra socordia pereat: nec audiendi sunt, qui vt omnibus commodi videatur, omnes religiones probant, & omnibus doctrinis assentiri & blandiri solent. Vt enim de hoc periculo taceamus dicere, alij quoque non poenitendi huius studij fructus sunt.
units.tr: Before we touch on the rest, however, it is fitting to observe that general care of the Holy Spirit, by which, like a most faithful father, he guards against our faith being overthrown by the false doctrines of impostors. He has applied this care in all ages with such zeal that you will find no book, either of the Old or the New Testament, which does not instruct us well in this matter. For in the Law there are not negligible rules by which we may distinguish false prophets from true, which one may see both elsewhere and in Deut. 13. In the writings of the prophets, passages that bear on this cause are found everywhere. For they fight not only against the seducers of their own age, but also prophesy of those to come, and teach us to recognize the same. Let those passages that pertain here be read: Ezek. 34. Dan. 7 and 11. Zech. 5 and 11, etc. In the books of the New Testament, as in all other things, so in this the matter is set out much more plainly. Christ cries out: "Beware of false prophets, who come to you clothed in sheep's skins, but inwardly are ravening wolves. By their fruits you will know them." Matt. 7. He likewise warns us to avoid the blind leaders of the blind, who, neglecting the commandments of God, preach the traditions of men. Matt. 15. Elsewhere he declares that all who try to enter by another door than himself, and dare to show another way of salvation apart from Christ, are thieves and robbers. John 10. Nor is he content to have attacked those who at that time were leading the people astray; he also depicts those whom he knew would come in the last age. Matt. 24. For he says: "If anyone says to you, 'Behold, here is Christ, or there,' do not believe it. For false christs and false prophets will arise, and will show great signs and wonders, so that, if it were possible, they would lead even the elect into error. Behold, I have told you beforehand. If therefore they say to you, 'Behold, he is in the desert,' do not go out; 'Behold, he is in the inner rooms,' do not believe it," etc. The Apostles, imitating the example of Christ, press and impress the same with great earnestness. Paul does so in Acts 20, 1 Tim. 4, 2 Tim. 3 and 4, 2 Thess. 2, etc. Nor is Peter negligent in this matter, who in the second chapter of his second epistle sufficiently and fully sets out everything that can be said about the false prophets of our age. The same we saw above in John, chapter 2, who nevertheless here repeats the same things (lest he omit anything), and is going to say more in the second epistle afterward. But the reasons for this diligence of the Holy Spirit must be great and weighty, as indeed they are. For just as true doctrine plants and nourishes faith in men's souls, joins them to Christ and leads them into the way of salvation, so false doctrines are accustomed to overthrow faith, draw men away from Christ, and snatch them into the way of perdition or the abyss. The diligence of those who today devote themselves to giving trouble to false teachers ought therefore not to seem superfluous. For if these things had to be preached of old, what must now be done, when those wolves rage in the Christian flock, when Christ is shown here and there, and is said to be whole and entire, together with his soul and divinity, in the sacrament of the altar, or even in the little shrine of the sacrament or tabernacle? When we see also the Church of Christ split into various sects by false doctrines, and polluted with astounding superstitions? Here certainly the trumpet of the divine Word must be blown with all our strength, lest anyone perish through our sloth; nor are they to be listened to who, in order to seem agreeable to all, approve all religions, and are accustomed to assent to and flatter all doctrines. For, to say nothing of this danger, other fruits of this zeal are not to be regretted.

units.la: Docent enim tam fidæ Christi & Apostolorum de seductoribus admonitiones, ne offenda-mur si quando falsa dogmata seminari, & sectas pestilentes excitari cernimus. Nihil enim hic nouum fit, sed quod futurum spiritus sanctus prædixit. Et est hæc perpetua euangelij conditio, vt huic in animos nostros seminato per sua organa infelix lolium superseminet improbus generis humani hostis, dū homines dormiūt, &c in salutis negotio securiores sunt, quàm par erat. Matt.11.[?] Permittit aut ea iusto iudicio Deus, partim vt probentur electi (1.Cor.11.) partim vt impij digno supplicio pereant. Quid enim tam iustum est, quàm vt mendacijs ad perditionem & interitū sempiternum seducantur, qui veritatem diuinitus oblatam amplecti & sequi nolunt? Vide hac de re Paulum scribentem 2.Thess.2. & impostorum nostri seculi felices successus minus miraberis.
units.tr: For the teaching of the faithful Christ and of the Apostles about seducers likewise warns us not to be offended when we see false doctrines sown and pestilent sects stirred up. Nothing new happens here, but what the Holy Spirit foretold would come to pass. This is the constant condition of the gospel: after the good seed has been sown in our minds through its instruments, the wicked enemy of mankind oversows the unhappy tares while men sleep and are more secure in the business of salvation than they ought to be. Matt. 11.[?] God permits these things by his just judgment, partly so that the elect may be proved (1 Cor. 11.), partly so that the ungodly may perish with due punishment. For what is more just than that those who refuse to embrace and follow the truth divinely offered should be seduced by lies to destruction and eternal ruin? On this matter see Paul writing in 2 Thess. 2., and you will marvel less at the happy successes of the impostors of our age.

units.la: Admonemur praeterea, errores nulla vetustate & consuetudine aut longi temporis praescriptione defendi posse, cum & olim errores multi fuerint, & qui hodie sunt, prophetarum oraculis praedicti sint, vtrosque autem iam olim spiritus sanctus damnauerit. Quod si aliquot secula ad doctrinae & religionis alicuius, per homines introductae, defensionem sufficere putamus, eadem ratione & gentilismum totumque illud gentilitiae idololatriae chaos probabimus, quod multis seculis omnes nostri seculi errores praecesit. Sed vanum est in religionis causa vetustatis nomine commendare, quod aliquando non fuit, & tandem hominum ingenio & opera excogitatum est. Nec consuetudo, quae apud quosdam obrepsit (vt D. Cypriani verbis vtamur) impedire debet, quò minus veritas praevaleat & vincat. Nam consuetudo sine veritate, vetustas erroris est. Propter quod, relicto errore, sequamur veritatem: & ad primum vetustatis omnis terminum vel initium respiciamus, & quid tunc à Deo institutum & traditum sit, consyderemus. Inueniemus vero illic Christum Iesum tradi & fidem, qua huic nitimur. Nec vnquam mutata est haec fidei & salutis ratio, vtvt pro temporum varietate ceremoniae & ritus sacri variarint. Quicquid igitur ab hac discrepat, vt nouum & commentitium fugiamus. Quae enim obstinatio (vt idem Cyprianus ait) quaeue praesumptio est, humanam traditionem diuinae dispositioni anteponere, nec animaduertere indignari & irasci Deum, quoties diuina praecepta soluit & praeterit humana traditio, &c. Sed de hoc in iis, quae modo sequuntur, plura dicemus.
units.tr: We are further admonished that errors cannot be defended by any antiquity, custom, or prescription of long time, since many errors have existed of old, and those which exist today were foretold by the oracles of the prophets, and the Holy Spirit has long since condemned both. But if we think that several centuries are enough to defend any doctrine or religion introduced by men, then by the same reasoning we would approve heathenism and that whole chaos of gentile idolatry, which preceded by many centuries all the errors of our age. But it is vain to commend in a matter of religion, under the name of antiquity, something that did not always exist and was at last devised by human cleverness and labour. Nor should custom, which has crept in among some people (to use the words of St. Cyprian), prevent truth from prevailing and conquering. For custom without truth is the antiquity of error. Therefore, let us put error aside and follow the truth; let us look back to the first beginning or origin of all antiquity, and consider what was then instituted and handed down by God. We shall indeed find there that Christ Jesus is delivered, and the faith on which we rest. And this manner of faith and salvation has never changed, although ceremonies and sacred rites have varied with the variety of times. Whatever therefore differs from this, let us flee it as new and invented. For what obstinacy (as the same Cyprian says) or what presumption is it to prefer human tradition to the divine ordinance, and not to notice that God is indignant and angry whenever human tradition breaks and passes over divine precepts, and so on? But we shall speak more about this in what follows.

units.la: Praeceptum Apostoli est: Ne credatis cuiuis spiritui, sed probate spiritus, an ex Deo sint. Plana sunt verba, & quorsum tendant, supra dictum est. Arguuntur autem & conuincuntur illis duo hominum genera, quae hodie passim obuia sunt. Primum eorum est, qui quaecunque vel ab ipsis vel ab alijs, quorum authoritate nituntur, decretum ac constitutum fuerit, ab omnibus sine examinatione aliqua recipi volunt. Est illis iustae & sufficientis rationis loco propria voluntas, vel paucorum quorundam authoritas. Adimunt autem tam ecclesijs quàm singulis fidelibus, quod à Deo non datum modo, sed singulari etiam praecepto iniunctum est, libertatem nimirum iudicandi de doctrinis. Probant sic, quo spiritu agantur. De antichristo legimus, quòd regnum suum humana authoritate & prudentia stabiliturus sit. At Christus ouibus suis hoc proprium esse dicit, vt inter veri & falsi pastoris vocem discernere, & hanc quidem fugere, illam vero sequi possint. Ioan.10. Vult ergo vt de voce, quae in ecclesia sonat, oues iudicent. Et Paulus prophetarum spiritus prophetis subijci, & iudicium penes sedentes esse dicit. 1.Corinth.14. Idem se ipsum, imò & angelos, huic censurae subijcit, & anathema haberi vult omnes, quicunque nouum euangelium docere audent. Gal.1. Quae ergo vaesania est, hodie postulare vt quiduis temere oblatum, reclamante etiam conscientia & deserto Dei verbo, homines amplectantur? Est haec plusquam gygantea audacia, quam Deus, ad quem ecclesiae gubernacula pertinent, inultam non dimittet. Secundum genus eorum est, qui quamuis doctrinam temere vel probant vel improbant, priusquam prout dignum erat, examinata fuerit. Differunt hi animis & voluntatibus. Priores enim ea facilitate morum praediti sunt, vt indignum putent, propter dogmata fidei cum quoquam altercari. Simpliciter ergo credunt, id est, temerarij & leues omne id recipiunt quod docetur, persuasi nimirum, omnem erroris culpam in docente solo haerere. Alteri vero morosi & suarum opinionum pertinaces assertores, illico clamant, quicquid cum his pugnare vident, ne vel ipsi vel maiores ipsorum errauisse videantur. Sed ad vtrosque pertinet quod Ioannes dicit: Probate spiritus. Et vt leuitatis est, cuiuis doctrinae credere: ita inexcusabilis est morositas & pertinacia, quamuis doctrinam damnare & reijcere, non adhibito prius fidei & spiritus iudicio, qui in scripturis loquitur. Medium ergo teneamus ô fratres, & priores sibi dictum putent illud Apostoli: Non amplius simus pueri, qui fluctuemus, & circumferamur quouis vento doctrinae, &c. Ephes.4. Alteri vero ad se pertinere cogitent, quod idem Apostolus 1.Thess.5. ait: Spiritum ne extinguatis, prophetias ne aspernemini. Omnia probate, quod bonum est tenete.
units.tr: The precept of the Apostle is: "Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are from God." The words are plain, and what they aim at was said above. Two kinds of men, which are commonly met with today, are charged and convicted by these words. The first kind are those who wish that whatever decree or constitution has been laid down, either by themselves or by others on whose authority they rely, be received by all without any examination. They put their own will, or the authority of a few, in place of a just and sufficient reason. But they take away from the churches as much as from individual believers the liberty of judging about doctrines, which God has not only given but also enjoined by a special precept. They approve, that is, in this way: by what spirit men are driven. We read about Antichrist that he will establish his kingdom by human authority and prudence. But Christ says it is the proper mark of his sheep that they can distinguish the voice of the true shepherd from that of the false, and flee the one and follow the other (John 10.). He therefore wishes the sheep to judge concerning the voice that sounds in the Church. And Paul says that the spirits of the prophets are to be subject to the prophets, and that judgment rests with those who sit in judgment (1 Cor. 14.). He himself, and even angels, submits to this scrutiny, and wishes all who dare to teach a new gospel to be held accursed (Gal. 1.). What madness, then, is it today to demand that men embrace whatever is rashly offered, even while conscience protests and the Word of God is forsaken? This is more than gigantic audacity, and God, to whom the governance of the Church belongs, will not let it go unpunished. The second kind are those who, although they either approve or reject a doctrine rashly, do so before it has been examined as it ought to be. These differ in their minds and wills. For the former are endowed with such ease of disposition that they think it unworthy to dispute with anyone about the dogmas of faith. Therefore they believe simply, that is, the rash and light-minded receive everything that is taught, persuaded that all the fault of error clings to the teacher alone. The others, however, are peevish and stubborn asserters of their own opinions, and at once they cry out against whatever they see opposed to them, lest they themselves or their forefathers should seem to have erred. But what John says applies to both: "Test the spirits." And just as it is a mark of lightness to believe any doctrine whatever, so peevishness and stubbornness are inexcusable, when a doctrine is condemned and rejected without first applying the judgment of faith and of the Spirit who speaks in the Scriptures. Let us therefore, brothers, hold the middle course, and let the former consider that saying of the Apostle: "Let us no longer be children, tossed about and carried round by every wind of doctrine," and so on (Eph. 4.). And let the others consider that what the same Apostle says in 1 Thess. 5. pertains to them: "Do not quench the Spirit; do not despise prophesyings. Test all things; hold fast what is good."

units.la: Quid vero spectandū in probatione vel dijudicatione doctrinarū? Oportet enim certi aliquid habere, quod in doctrinis deprehésum, illas vel recipiendas vel damnandas esse, doceat. Ostendit hoc vno verbo apostolus: Probate (inquit) spiritus, an ex Deo sint. Breuis sententia pronunciatu, intellectu facilis, sed utinâ tantæ grauitatis esset, ut omnibus, quod hic iubemur, persuaderet. Hic enim scopulus latet, ad quem plerique impingunt, qui per immensum illud opinionum & sectarum nostri seculi pelagus nauigant. Cum enim ad Dei iudicium omnia dogmata referre, & num ex Deo sint, probare debeat, ad hominum potius authoritatem respiciunt. Et alius quidem, num Imperatori vel principibus doctrina aliqua placet, inquirit. Alius num Conciliorum suffragijs confirmata sit. Sunt qui sectatores dogmatum inspiciunt, & ex illorum fortunis vel successu de doctrina, fide & religione iudicant. At non possunt non falli omnes isti, cum omnis homo mendax sit, & exemplis constet, electos quoque Dei cultores nonnunquam in religionis causa hallucinatos fuisse. Prodeat ex horum numero unus atque alter, ut quàm vana sit in fidei & religionis doctrina hominum authoritas, videamus. Et primus quidem Aaron sese offert, Mosis frater natu maior, populi Dei sacerdos ex diuina ordinatione, eruditione, prudentia et fortitudine clarus, & quod omnium est præstantissimum, typus domini & saluatoris nostri Iesu Christi. Quis huius authoritatem contemnat, siquidem alicuius hominis authoritas valere debet? Sed vanam et nullam hanc fuisse, vni cum illud facinus cumprimis atrox & horribile declarat, quo contra Dei præceptum, postulante tota ecclesia (cuius authoritas non minus hic quoque nullius momenti esse debebat) vitulum aureum conflare, & religionis ergo prostituere ausus est. Inspiciant quæso factum hoc, qui ad hominum authoritatem ita obstupescunt, ut summos pontifices & Rom. ecclesiam errare posse neget.
units.tr: What, then, ought to be looked to in testing or judging doctrines? For one must have some fixed standard, by which it may be taught, on finding a doctrine, whether it is to be received or condemned. The apostle shows this in one word: "Test," he says, "the spirits, whether they are from God." It is a brief saying, easy to understand when pronounced, but would that it had such weight that it persuaded everyone of what we are commanded here! For here lies the rock on which most men run aground, who sail across that immense sea of opinions and sects of our age. When they ought to refer all doctrines to the judgment of God and test whether they are from God, they look instead to the authority of men. One inquires whether some doctrine pleases the Emperor or the princes. Another whether it has been confirmed by the votes of Councils. There are those who look at the followers of the doctrines and judge of doctrine, faith and religion from their fortunes or success. But all these cannot help being mistaken, since every man is a liar, and examples show that even the elect worshippers of God have sometimes gone astray in matters of religion. Let one or another from their number come forward, so that we may see how empty human authority is in the doctrine of faith and religion. And first of all Aaron presents himself, the elder brother of Moses, priest of the people of God by divine ordination, renowned for learning, prudence and courage, and, what is most excellent of all, a type of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. Who would despise his authority, since the authority of any man ought to carry weight? But that this authority was empty and worth nothing is declared chiefly by that most atrocious and horrible deed, in which, against God's precept, at the demand of the whole Church (whose authority here too ought to have been of no less weight), he dared to cast a golden calf and to set it up as a religion. Let those who are so amazed at human authority that they deny that the supreme pontiffs and the Roman Church can err, I beg them, look closely at this deed.

units.la: Habemus hic pontificem summum, cuius primatus, non priuata ambitione occupatus, nec principum huius mundi tyrannide confirmatus, sed ab ipso Deo institutus fuit, ut sacerdotij, quod olim filius Dei obire debebat, typus esset. Habemus hic ecclesiam, quâ ipse Deus suum peculium, suum filium, suum regale sacerdotium, & sacerdotale regnum appellat. Videmus tamen cum ecclesia ipsum errare pontificem: nec leuiter errare, sed in ijs, circa quæ fides, religio & vniuersa hominum salus versatur. Eant ergo, et pontificatum humana authoritate institutum, et ecclesiam, in qua maxima hominum pars aliorum potius quàm Christi nomine insigniri cupit, nobis obijciat, qui humanis traditionibus potius quàm Dei verbo credere volunt. Ne tamen veteris testamenti exempla nihil ad se pertinere putent, aliud producamus, quod contemnere nullo modo possunt, Petri nimirum, sub cuius prætextu ad tantum dominationis fastigium Romana sedes ascendit. Is enim Iudæorum metu siue reuerentia eò adductus fuisse legitur, ut parum syncera simulatione, & Iudæos in errore confirmaret, & gentes Iudaisare cogeret. Quare à Paulo accusatur, qui illi crimen longè grauissimum impingit, nempe quòd non recto pede incederet ad euangelij veritatem. Quid hic respondebunt humanæ authoritatis admiratores? Petrũ ne defendent, & Paulum improbæ proteruitatis accusabunt, qui tantum Apostolum, & primum (ut illi volunt) Romanæ ecclesiæ antistitem, tam inciuiliter tractare ausus sit? Non opinor. Fateantur ergo, omnes homines, si suæ rationis suggestiones & affectus sequi velint, errare posse, imò errare frequenter, & proinde doctrinas omnes hoc gnomone probare discant, an ex Deo sint. Deprehenditur hoc, non ex hominum decretis, sed ex Dei verbo, quod æternum manet & impermutabile. Isa. 40. Matth.5. Frustra ergo nobis hodie patres, Concilia, reges, Imperatores, multorum seculorum consuetudinem obijciunt. Nos cum Apostolo, num ex Deo sit ipsorum doctrina, quærimus. Id si demonstrare velint, Dei verbum proferant oportet: quo si destituuntur, vana erit omnium, quorum testimonijs nituntur, authoritas. Frustra enim qui ratione vincuntur, consuetudine nobis opponunt quasi consuetudo maior sit veritate.
units.tr: We have here a supreme pontiff whose primacy was not seized by private ambition, nor confirmed by the tyranny of the princes of this world, but was instituted by God himself, to be a type of the priesthood which the Son of God was to exercise in time to come. We have here a Church, which God himself calls his own peculiar people, his own Son, his own royal priesthood and sacerdotal kingdom. Yet we see that the pontiff himself errs along with the Church: and not in trifles, but in those matters on which faith, religion and the whole salvation of men depend. Let them therefore go and throw in our faces a pontificate instituted by human authority, and a Church in which the greater part of men desire to be named after others rather than after Christ, those who wish to believe human traditions rather than the Word of God. Yet lest they think the examples of the Old Testament have nothing to do with them, let us bring forward another, which they can by no means despise: that of Peter, under whose pretext the Roman see rose to such a height of lordship. For we read that he was led, through fear or reverence for the Jews, to such a degree that by a not wholly sincere pretence he both confirmed the Jews in error and compelled the Gentiles to Judaize. Therefore he is accused by Paul, who charges him with a crime by far the most serious, namely that he did not walk uprightly toward the truth of the gospel. What will the admirers of human authority answer here? Will they defend Peter, and accuse Paul of shameless arrogance, for daring to treat so great an Apostle, and the first (as they wish) bishop of the Roman Church, so rudely? I do not think so. Let them therefore confess that all men, if they wish to follow the promptings of their own reason and their affections, can err, indeed err often, and so let them learn to test all doctrines by this rule: whether they are from God. This is discerned not from the decrees of men, but from the Word of God, which remains eternal and unchangeable. Isa. 40; Matth. 5. In vain, then, do the Fathers, the Councils, kings and emperors, and the custom of many centuries, now get thrown at us. We, with the Apostle, ask whether their doctrine is from God. If they wish to demonstrate this, they must bring forward the Word of God; and if they lack it, the authority of all those on whose testimonies they lean will be empty. For those who are overcome by reason in vain oppose custom to us, as if custom were greater than truth.

units.la: At dicat aliquis: Audio quid abs me fieri velit Ioannes. Video item necessarium omnino esse, ut probentur dogmata, quæ hodie passim & noua, & multũ inter se pugnantia traduntur. Agnosco etiam sic ea probari debere, ut num ex Deo sint, videamus. Nec aliud est quod magis expetam quàm eam mihi facultatem dari, ut singula probare, & in illis verũ à falso discernere possim. Quid autem faciam, cum rudis rerum sim & illiteratus? Pugnatur undiq; ab ijs, qui & eruditione & rerum experientia præstant, & ego qui nec prima elementa noui, me illis iudicem & censorem interponam? Vel si id facere instituam, quo medio, qua regula, aut instrumento examen illud adhibebo? Hæc & multa alia huius generis hodie à multis dici audimus, & ab ijs quidem, quorum animi à religione non abhorrent. Sed si isti Ioannem audiant, omni dubitatione se mox liberatos, & ad examen doctrinarum instrutissimos videbunt. Sic enim scribit:
units.tr: But someone may say: I hear what John wishes me to do. I see too that it is absolutely necessary that the doctrines which are now everywhere handed down as new, and in many ways at odds with one another, be tested, so that we may see whether they are from God. Nor is there anything I desire more than to be given the ability to test each of them, and to be able to distinguish the true from the false in them. But what shall I do, since I am untrained in these matters and unlettered? Those who excel both in learning and in experience of affairs fight on every side, and shall I, who do not even know the first elements, set myself up as their judge and critic? Or if I should undertake to do so, by what means, by what rule or instrument shall I apply that examination? These and many other things of this kind we hear said today by many, and by those indeed whose minds do not shrink from religion. But if they listen to John, they will see that they are soon freed from all doubt and fully equipped for the examination of doctrines. For he writes thus:

units.la: I I. Per hoc cognoscite spiritum Dei. Omnis spiritus, qui confitetur Iesum Christum in carne uenisse, ex Deo est. Et omnis spiritus, qui non confitetur Iesum Christum in carne uenisse, ex Deo non est, &c. Memorabilis omnino, & diligenti consyderatione dignissimus locus. His enim Canon siue amusis, aut etiam Lydius lapis, ad quem doctrinæ omnes probentur, an aurum diuinæ veritatis referant, aut humanarum traditionum scoria adulterata sint, non monstratur modo, verumetiâ in manus datur, & sic quidem, vt non doctiores modo, sed quotquot in toto orbe terrarum sunt Christiani, nobiles, opulenti, obscuri, pauperes, opifices, agricolæ, vinitores, nautæ, viri, fœminæ, senes & iuuenes, de quacunque doctrina dexteritate summa iudicare, & nū ex Deo fit, videre possint. Omnis spiritus (inquit) qui confitetur Iesum Christum in carnem venisse, ex Deo est. Videamus itaque quid sit fateri Christum in carnem venisse, & vniuersa probationis huius vel censuræ ratio nobis constabit. Voluit autem paucis verbis vniuersa Christi mysteria comprehendere Ioannes. Cum enim Iesum Christum in carnem venisse dicit, vtriusque naturæ, diuinæ nimirum & humanæ, veritatem fatetur. Veniendi verbo illum priusquam veniret, fuisse ostendit. Quòd si fuit priusquam in utero virginis carnem assumeret, Deus fit necesse est. Eodem argumento & ipse Christus suam diuinitatem asserit, dicens: Priusquam Abraham esset, ego sum. Ioan. 8. At carnis vocabulo humanam naturam intelligi manifestius est, quàm vt explicari debeat. Quisquis ergo Iesum Christum in carnem venisse docet, illum & Deum & hominem esse prædicat. At nondum in his tota consistit doctrinæ Christianæ ratio, sed aliud quoq; in hac Apostoli sententia consyderandū erit, causa videlicet, propter quam Dei filius in carnem venerit. Quia enim ipsa est patris sapientia, nihil vtque ab illo frustra factum putabimus, & in carnem venisse non proderit, nisi quare venerit, edocemur. Exponit causam hanc ipse Apostolus alibi, cum inquit: In sua venit, & sui eum non receperunt. Quotquot autem receperunt eum, dedit eis vt liceret filios Dei fieri, videlicet his, qui crediderint in nomē ipsius. Ioan. 1. In carnem ergo Christus venit, vt homines, quos peccati culpa Dei hostes fecerat, Dei filios redderet ac hæredes. Idem ipse testatur cum inquit: Venit filius hominis seruare quod perierat. Matth. 18. Perierat humanum genus. Quare, vt illud saluaret, in carnem venire voluit. Gnomon ergo & canon, ad quem doctrinæ omnes probari debent, Christus Iesus est, qui talis tradi ac doceri debet, qualis in scriptura proponitur: qui nimirum verus Deus ab æterno sit, præfinito autem tempore in mundum à patre missus, carnem veram induerit, vt illa pro nobis in Cruce immolata peccatum omne expiaret, nosque suo merito sanctificatos & iustificatos cum Deo patre reduceret in gratiam, vt huius filij facti, æterna cœlestis regni hæreditate perfruamur. Manant ex doctrina hac quæcunque de fidei & vitæ Christianæ officijs dici possunt. Cum enim docetur, Christum nos eiusdem patris filios, adeoque eiusdem corporis membra fecisse, mutuæ charitatis admonemur, quam quiuis pater inter suos liberos vigere vult. Cum Christi sanguinem pro nobis fusum audimus, vt illius merito pro peccatis nostris satisfieret, non possumus non cogitare, quàm vigilanti innocentiæ studio opus sit, ne tantum Christi beneficium impura viuendi consuetudine prophanemus. Quisquis ergo ex verbo Dei, quod scripturis cōtinetur, Iesum Christum verum Deum & hominem esse docet, & in illo monstrat, quæcunque ad humani generis redemptionem faciunt, ac ex eisdem Christianæ vitæ officia instituit, eius doctrinam ex Deo esse, certò credamus. Quisquis verò, vel Christum aliū fingit, quàm scripturis traditur, vel quę in Christi officio continentur, & ad nostram redemptionem faciunt, in Creaturas transfert, & alibi quàm in vno Christo quærere iubet, eius doctrina ex Deo non est, quacunque tandem hominum auctoritate commendetur. Damnantur itaque hoc Canone omnes veterum hæreses, quæ in Christi naturis impegerunt, dum vel diuinitatem negare, vel humanitati detrahere, vel eandem confundere ausæ sunt. Damnantur item nostri seculi errores & traditiones falsæ, quibus quæ Christus sui corporis & sanguinis merito acquisiuit, vel nobisipsis vendicare, vel apud Creaturas quærere docemur. Et tanta est huius Canonis perspicuitas, vt de hoc dubitare non possit, nisi qui sciens volensq; in errorum laqueos incidere cupit.
units.tr: 1 John 4. By this know the Spirit of God. Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God. And every spirit that does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is not from God, etc. This is altogether a memorable passage, and most worthy of diligent consideration. For by this canon, or touchstone, or indeed the Lydian stone, by which all doctrines are tested, to see whether they bear the gold of divine truth or are adulterated with the dross of human traditions, not only is it shown, but it is actually placed in men's hands; and in such a way that not only the more learned, but all Christians in the whole world, noble and wealthy, obscure and poor, craftsmen, farmers, vinedressers, sailors, men and women, old and young, may be able to judge of any doctrine with the greatest skill, and see whether it is from God. Every spirit, he says, that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God. Let us see, then, what it is to confess that Christ has come in the flesh, and the whole method of this testing or judgment will be made clear to us. John wished to comprehend all the mysteries of Christ in a few words. For when he says that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, he affirms the truth of both natures, namely the divine and the human. By the word "come" he shows that he existed before he came. But if he existed before he took flesh in the womb of the virgin, he must be God. By the same argument Christ himself asserts his divinity, saying: Before Abraham was, I am. John 8. But that by the word "flesh" the human nature is understood is too plain to need explanation. Whoever therefore teaches that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh proclaims him to be both God and man. Yet the whole sum of Christian doctrine does not consist in these alone, but another thing must also be considered in this sentence of the Apostle, namely the cause for which the Son of God came in the flesh. For since it is the wisdom of the Father itself, we shall think that nothing was done by him in vain, and coming in the flesh would profit nothing unless we are taught why he came. The Apostle himself explains this cause elsewhere, when he says: He came to his own, and his own did not receive him. But as many as received him, he gave them the power to become the sons of God, namely to those who believe in his name. John 1. Christ therefore came in the flesh so that he might make men, who by the guilt of sin had made themselves enemies of God, the sons and heirs of God. He himself testifies to the same when he says: The Son of man came to save what was lost. Matth. 18. The human race had perished. Therefore, in order to save it, he willed to come in the flesh. The rule and canon, then, by which all doctrines ought to be tested, is Jesus Christ, who ought to be taught and proclaimed in such a way as he is set forth in Scripture: namely, that he is true God from eternity, who, sent by the Father into the world at a fixed time, put on true flesh, so that by that flesh offered for us on the Cross he might expiate every sin, and, sanctified and justified by his merit, restore us to grace with God the Father, so that, having been made sons of this Son, we might enjoy the eternal inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. From this doctrine flow whatever can be said about the duties of faith and of the Christian life. For when we are taught that Christ has made us sons of the same Father, and so members of the same body, we are reminded of the mutual love which any father wishes to flourish among his own children. When we hear that his blood was shed for us, so that satisfaction might be made for our sins by his merit, we cannot but think how watchful a zeal for innocence is needed, lest we profane so great a benefit of Christ by an impure manner of living. Therefore, whoever teaches from the Word of God, which is contained in the Scriptures, that Jesus Christ is true God and man, and shows in him whatever pertains to the redemption of mankind, and from the same establishes the duties of Christian life, let us firmly believe that his doctrine is from God. But whoever either feigns another Christ than is handed down in the Scriptures, or transfers to creatures what is contained in the office of Christ and pertains to our redemption, and bids us seek it anywhere other than in the one Christ, his doctrine is not from God, however it may be commended by human authority. Thus by this canon all the ancient heresies are condemned, which have assaulted the natures of Christ, whether they dared to deny his divinity, or to detract from his humanity, or to confuse the two. Likewise the errors of our own age are condemned, and the false traditions by which we are taught to claim for ourselves, or to seek among creatures, what Christ acquired by the merit of his body and blood. And so clear is this canon that no one can doubt it, except one who knowingly and willingly desires to fall into the snares of error.

units.la: Examinemus ergo ad hunc quæ hodie in controuersia sunt fidei & religionis dogmata aliquot, vt simplicioribus non Canone modo dijudicandi præscripsisse videamur, sed exemplis quoque monstremus, vt illo vti debeant. Contenditur passim de sacramento altaris, quà domini Cœnam, vel Eucharistiam siue Synaxin dicimus: Sunt qui illic verum Christi corpus & sanguinem pro peccatis viuentium & mortuorum efferri doceant, id quod nos constantissimè pernegamus. Applica igitur Canonem, ipsum scilicet Christum, qualis in scriptura traditur. Videbis autem illi cum Christi naturis pugnare corporalem eius in Sacramento præsentiam. Nec enim in panem, sed in carnem hunc venisse, nec panis, sed carnis substantiam ab illo assumptam esse, scriptura docet. Adhæc verum corpus eidem tribuit, quod & loco certo continetur, quem in cœlis esse, & angeli prædicant, & Symboli apostolici articulis omnes confitemur. Sed & Christi officium applica, & res erit multò absurdior. Christum enim in ara Crucis pro nobis immolatum esse constat, non in Cœna, quam ipse non sacrificium, sed mortis suæ commemorationem vocauit. Simili ratione, Christum à nemine mortalium, sed à seipso immolatum fuisse docemur: vanum ergo, quod illi eum à sacerdote immolari posse contendunt. Præterea Christus in Cruce clamat: Consummatum est, Ioan.19. docens nimirum absolutam & perfectam iam esse omnem nostrae salutis rationem, plenum itaq; & omnibus partibus integrum esse sui sacrificij meritum. Annon igitur huic detrahūt, qui illud iterari oportere docent, & sacrificuli alicuius opera perficiendum esse contendunt, quod ipse Christus in Cruce moriens non plenè praestiterit? Quod si ad officia vitae Christianae respicias, videbis à dilectione Christiana alienum esse, ut Sacramento toti ecclesiae tradito unum tantum communicet, à communione autem tota ecclesia arceatur. Cum dilectione pugnat, quod alteram speciem in vniuersum auferunt. Dilectionis spiritu caret, quod non nisi conducti pro mortuorum peccatis sacrificant. Quid vero ad aedificationem, & vitae institutionem conferant non intellecta verba, & praecipites eorundem demurmurationes, quiuis cordatus facilè intelligit. Quia ergo sacrificium Missae, & naturis in Christo, & eiusdem merito detrahit, adhaec nec dilectioni mutuę, nec vitae puritati seruit, ex Deo non sunt, quicunq; illud in ecclesia praedicant.
units.tr: Let us therefore test by this Canon some of the doctrines of faith and religion that are today in dispute, so that we may seem to have prescribed the Canon for judging not only to the simpler sort, but also to show by examples how they ought to use it. The question is raised everywhere about the sacrament of the altar, which we call the Lord's Supper, or the Eucharist, or the Synaxis. There are those who teach that there the true body and blood of Christ are offered for the sins of the living and the dead, which we most steadfastly deny. Apply, then, the Canon, namely Christ himself as he is delivered in Scripture. You will see that a bodily presence of him in the sacrament fights against the natures of Christ. For Scripture teaches that he came not into bread but into flesh, and that it was not the substance of bread but of flesh that he assumed. Moreover, it ascribes to him a true body, which is contained in a definite place, which both the angels proclaim to be in heaven, and which we all confess in the articles of the Apostles' Creed. But apply also Christ's office, and the matter will be much more absurd. For it is certain that Christ was sacrificed for us on the altar of the Cross, not in the Supper, which he called not a sacrifice but a commemoration of his death. In like manner we are taught that Christ was sacrificed by no mortal, but by himself; it is therefore vain that they contend he can be sacrificed by a priest. Besides, Christ cries on the Cross: "It is finished" (John 19), clearly teaching that the whole plan of our salvation is now complete and perfect, and that the merit of his sacrifice is therefore full and entire in every part. Do not those then detract from this who teach that it must be repeated, and who contend that it must be completed by the work of some little priest, what Christ himself, dying on the Cross, did not fully accomplish? But if you look to the duties of the Christian life, you will see that it is foreign to Christian love that, when the sacrament has been delivered to the whole Church, one part alone should receive it, and the whole Church be debarred from communion. Their taking away altogether the other kind is at odds with love. It lacks the spirit of love that they offer sacrifice only as hired men for the sins of the dead. What they contribute to edification and to the instruction of life, the words they do not understand and their hurried mumblings, anyone of sense easily understands. Therefore, since the sacrifice of the Mass detracts both from the natures in Christ and from the merit of the same, and moreover serves neither mutual love nor purity of life, those who preach it in the Church are not of God.

units.la: Idem in Purgatorij causa patebit, pro quo multi tanquam pro focis et aris depugnant, nec im merito vt ipsis videtur, cum haec Alchymia ipsis quaestuosissima fuerit. Fingunt autem animas de functorum in illum ignem recipi, vt illius flammis excoctae & purgatę in coelos tandem subuolet. Interea Missis & alijs eius generis operibus illarum liberatione procurari posse, docet. Sed quam alienum hoc à Christi officio, cuius sanguine nos à peccatis ablui & purgari audiuimus? 1.Ioan. 1. Nonne huic figmento ipse Christus contradixit, latroni illo ipso die, quo moriebatur, paradisi communionem pollicens? Luc.23. Nec est quod ex singulari exemplo vniuersale dogma concludi possit, negent. Nam quod latroni contigit, omnibus in se credentibus Christus pollicetur, dicens: Amen amen dico vobis, qui sermonem meum audit, & credit ei qui misit me, habet vitam aeternam, & in iudicium non veniet, sed transiuit à morte in vitam. Ioan.5. Non potest igitur ex Deo censeri ea doctrina, quae sanguinis Christi merito nostrae sanctificationis gloriam detrahit.
units.tr: The same will be clear in the case of Purgatory, for which many fight as for hearths and altars, and not without reason, as it seems to them, since this alchemy has been most profitable to them. They pretend, however, that the souls of the dead are received into that fire, so that, purged and refined by its flames, they may at last fly up into heaven. Meanwhile they teach that by Masses and other works of this kind their release can be procured. But how foreign is this to the office of Christ, by whose blood we have heard that we are washed and cleansed from sins? (1 John 1). Did not Christ himself contradict this fiction, promising the thief communion in paradise on that very day on which he was dying? (Luke 23). Nor let them deny that a universal dogma can be concluded from a single example. For what happened to the thief, Christ promises to all who believe in him, saying: "Verily, verily, I say unto you, he who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and shall not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life" (John 5). That doctrine, then, which takes away from the glory of our sanctification by the merit of Christ's blood, cannot be judged to be from God.

units.la: Eadem ratio est doctrinae, quae homines suis operibus iustificari tradit. Quid enim ex hac ali ud concludi potest, quàm Christum non ex parte modo, sed in vniuersum omni nostrae iustificationis laude spoliari? Christus enim otiosus sit ijs, quicunque per legem iustificari volunt. Gal.5. Sed & Petro contradicunt, qui magna authoritate negant, vllum nomen sub caelo hominibus datum esse, per quod saluentur, praeter nomen Iesu. Act.4. Possent hic plures alij articuli produci et dijudicari, sed hos exempli loco allegasse sufficiat. Discant ex his fideles, quo pacto singulos examinare debeant. Temporis angustia monet, vt reliqua quoq; huius loci verba excutiamus.
units.tr: The same reasoning applies to the doctrine which teaches that men are justified by their works. For what else can be concluded from this than that Christ is stripped not only in part but altogether of all the praise of our justification? For "Christ will profit you nothing, if you seek to be justified by the law" (Gal. 5). But they also contradict Peter, who with great authority declares that there is no other name under heaven given to men by which they are saved, besides the name of Jesus (Acts 4). Many other articles could be brought forward here and judged, but it is enough to have alleged these by way of example. Let the faithful learn from these how they ought to examine each one. The shortness of time warns us that we should also go through the remaining words of this passage.

units.la: III. Et hic est ille spiritus Antichristi, de quo audistis, quod venturus sit, & jam nunc in mundo est. Videtur Ioannes haec illis opponere, qui licet doctrinam aliquam cum Christi mysteriis non per omnia conuenire videant, eam tamen, non vt par erat, abominari solent: sed omnia pro indifferentibus habent, vt omnibus commodos sese praebeat. Dicit ergo omnes eos, qui incarnationis Christi mysteriis aliqua ex parte detrahunt, Antichristi spiritu duci & impelli. Et Antichristum ita opponit Christo, vt nihil inter hos medium collocet. Quare necessario nos aut Christi doctrinam sequi, aut Antichristi traditionibus seduci oportet. Dicit aut hoc non ex seipso Ioannes, sed ex Christi sententia desumit, qui ait: Qui non est mecum, aduersum me est: qui non congregat mecum, spargit. Matth.12. Refellunt haec omnes eos, qui hodie nos de indifferentibus duntaxat altercari clamant, & omnes religiones tolerabiles fingunt. At miseri reuera sunt, qui illorum blanditijs decepti, de abominandis Antichristi erroribus nimis leuiter iudicare discunt.
units.tr: III. "And this is that spirit of Antichrist, of which you have heard that he is coming, and now already is in the world" (1 John 4). John seems to set these words against those who, though they see that some doctrine does not agree in all respects with the mysteries of Christ, are nevertheless accustomed to regard it not with the abhorrence it deserves, but count everything as indifferent, so as to show themselves accommodating to all. He therefore says that all those who in some part detract from the mysteries of Christ's incarnation are led and driven by the spirit of Antichrist. And he sets Antichrist against Christ in such a way that he places nothing in between. Wherefore we must necessarily either follow the doctrine of Christ or be seduced by the traditions of Antichrist. John does not say this from himself, but takes it from the sentence of Christ, who says: "He who is not with me is against me; he who does not gather with me scatters" (Matt. 12). These words refute all those who today cry out that we quarrel only about things indifferent, and pretend that all religions are tolerable. But truly wretched are they who, deceived by their flatteries, learn to judge too lightly of the abominable errors of Antichrist.

units.la: Obseruandum praeterea, quod Antichristum vel spiritum huius iam tum, quando haec scribebat, in mundo fuisse dicit. Causa huius dicti est, quod (vt Paulus habet) iam tum operabatur mysterium iniquitatis. 2. Thessal. 2. Licet enim magnus ille Antichristus, de quo prophetae & Christus vaticinati sunt, praefinito demum tempore exurgere debuerit, satan tamen iam olim in primitiua ecclesia illius aduentui praeludere & viam sternere coepit, dum varijs & infinitis haeresibus hominum mentes sic turbauit, vt omne Christi negotium in dubium vocare inciperent, & proinde Antichristi mendacijs ac conatibus facilius cederent. Quae causa est, quod Apostoli toties de magno illo Antichristo vaticinati sunt. Sic enim non nobis modò consulere, sed etiam sui seculi hominibus haereses, quę tum ferebantur, exosas & abominabiles facere voluerunt, si eas ad Antichristi regnum praeparationem satanicam esse intelligerent. Admonemur autem, quàm necesse sit, hodie de Antichristi regno saepius verba facere, quando & illum improbè grassari, & oues Christi adeò stupidas esse videmus, vt illius tyrannidi propter temporaria commoda se sponte subijciant. Nostrum itaque erit ô fratres, fidelem Apostoli admonitionem imis animis recondere, eandéq; vero ipsa sequi, & doctrinis, quas proponi audimus, Canonem hunc apostolicum non ofcitatibus animis applicare, vt constet nobis, quae nam ex Deo sint, & quae Antichristi spiritum referant. Non tamen notitiam horum consequi satis est. Antichristiana enim dogmata totis viribus vitare & fugere, Christi vero constanti fide & amplecti & sequi conuenit. Sic enim fiet, vt è tenebris asserti in luce ambulemus, æternum aliquando victuri cum Christo, cui debetur benedictio, glo-ria, honor & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: It is to be observed besides that he says Antichrist, or the spirit of him, was already in the world at the time when he was writing this. The cause of this saying is that (as Paul has it) the mystery of iniquity was already at work (2 Thess. 2). For although that great Antichrist, of whom the prophets and Christ prophesied, was to arise only at a fixed time, Satan had nevertheless already begun in the primitive Church to preface his coming and to prepare the way, while he so troubled men's minds with various and countless heresies that they began to call the whole business of Christ into doubt, and therefore more readily yielded to the lies and efforts of Antichrist. This is the reason why the Apostles so often prophesied of that great Antichrist. For thus they wished not only to advise us, but also the men of their own age, to make the heresies which were then spreading hateful and abominable, if they understood them to be a satanic preparation for the kingdom of Antichrist. We are reminded, moreover, how necessary it is to speak more often today of the kingdom of Antichrist, since we see him raging wickedly and the sheep of Christ so stupid that they willingly submit themselves to his tyranny for temporary advantages. It will therefore be our task, O brothers, to store deep in our hearts the faithful admonition of the Apostle, and to follow that very admonition, and not to apply this apostolic Canon with careless minds to the doctrines we hear proposed, so that it may be clear to us which of them are from God and which bear the spirit of Antichrist. Yet it is not enough to gain knowledge of these things. It is fitting to avoid and flee antichristian doctrines with all our strength, but to embrace and follow the teaching of Christ with a constant faith. For thus it will come about that, having been rescued from darkness, we walk in the light, and at last shall live forever with Christ, to whom belong blessing, glory, honour and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXIII.
units.tr: HOMILIA XXIII.

units.la: Vos ex Deo estis filioli, & uicistis eos: quoniam maior est qui in uobis est, quàm qui in mundo. Ipsi è mundo sunt: ideo è mundo loquuntur, & mundus eos audit. Nos ex Deo sumus. Qui nouit Deum, audit nos: qui non est ex Deo, non audit nos. Per hoc cognoscimus spiritum veritatis, & spiritum erroris.
units.tr: You are from God, little children, and you have overcome them, because greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world. They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world, and the world hears them. We are from God. Whoever knows God hears us; whoever is not from God does not hear us. By this we know the spirit of truth and the spirit of error.

units.la: VT Deus pro singulari suo in nos amore salutarem æternæ veritatis doctrinam ab ipsa mundi origine reuelare dignatus est, & in ea salutis viam omnibus monstrari voluit: ita humani generis hostis satan hanc ipsam falsis hominum traditionibus semper inficere studuit, & iuxta Christi ac Apostolorum ipsius oracula, quo propius mundi finis instat, eo maiori conatu mendacem doctrinam contra diuini verbi veritatem & prodigijs & aperta vi stabilire studebit. Necessarius ergo est omnibus pijs discretionis & iudicij spiritus, quo doctrinas quasuis probare, falsas à vera discernere, & illas quidem vitare, hac autem ceu veri pastoris vocem, sequi possint.
