Cœpit de hoc circa principium huius capitis agere Apostolus, doces potissimum in doctrinis, num ex Deo sint, spectari debere, simul eius rei infallibilem notam nobis indicans. Cæterum obijciuntur nobis in hac causa remorae & offendicula aliquot, quæ cum pijs multum negotij afferant, firmis rationibus tolli & declinari oportet. Primò etenim, cum Christi & Apostolorum de falsis doctoribus, de Antichristo & felicissimis illius successibus oracula proponuntur, multi timore graui concepto de salute sua dubitare incipiunt, nec fieri posse existimant, vt ipsi rudes & imperiti rerum, tot laqueos & tendiculas impostorum euitare possint. Quæ animi consternatio saluti plurimum obest. Nec enim alacriter pugnat miles, qui victoriæ spem amisit. Deinde plerosq; videmus in doctrinarum dijudicatione humana authoritate duci, eamq; doctrinam pro vera & diuina amplecti, cuius sectatores & multos & in mundo præstantes viderint: eam vero damnare & ceu falsam reijcere, cuius studiosi, vel pauci, vel etiam in hoc seculo miseri ac infelices sunt. Vtrique malo in præsenti Ioannes medetur, & sic locum de spirituum dijudicatione concludit.
units.tr: Just as God, out of his singular love for us, has deigned to reveal the saving doctrine of eternal truth from the very beginning of the world, and has willed that the way of salvation be shown to all, so the enemy of the human race, Satan, has always striven to corrupt this same doctrine with false traditions of men. And according to the oracles of Christ and of his Apostles, the nearer the end of the world draws, the more eagerly he will strive to establish lying doctrine against the truth of the divine Word, both by portents and by open force. Therefore all the godly need the spirit of discernment and judgment, by which they can test any doctrines whatever, distinguish false from true, and avoid the former while following the latter as the voice of the true shepherd. The Apostle began to treat of this near the beginning of this chapter, teaching chiefly that in doctrines we must look at whether they are from God, and at the same time indicating to us the infallible mark of this matter. But in this cause several hindrances and stumbling-blocks are put before us, which cause the godly considerable trouble, and these must be removed and turned aside by firm arguments. First, when the oracles of Christ and the Apostles about false teachers, about Antichrist and his most successful progress, are set forth, many, having conceived a grievous fear, begin to doubt their salvation, and think it impossible that they, being simple and inexperienced in affairs, could avoid so many snares and nets of impostors. This consternation of mind does great harm to salvation. For a soldier who has lost hope of victory does not fight cheerfully. Next, we see that most people, in judging doctrines, are led by human authority, and embrace as true and divine that doctrine whose followers they have seen to be many and eminent in the world, but condemn and reject as false that doctrine whose adherents are few, or even wretched and unhappy in this age. John remedies both evils at present, and in this way concludes the passage about the discernment of spirits.

units.la: I. Vos ex Deo estis filioli, & uicistis eos: quoniam maior est, qui in uobis est, quàm qui in mundo. Ex hortationem habent verba hæc, qua fideles ad constantem contra impostores ac pseudoprophetas pugnam excitat. Animantur autem certa & indubitata victoria spe, quæ semel animis concepta, facit vt nullas Antichristianorum technas subtimescamus, nec vllis eorundem conatibus perterreri possimus. Quis enim hostem, quem se certò victurum esse nouit, metuat? Porrò spem victoriæ tribus rationibus confirmat, quas sigillatim infspexisse non parum iuuabit.
units.tr: I. "You are from God, little children, and you have overcome them, because greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world." These words contain an exhortation by which he stirs the faithful to steadfast fighting against impostors and false prophets. They are encouraged by the hope of certain and undoubted victory, which, once conceived in the mind, makes us fear no snares of the Antichrists and cannot terrify us by any of their attempts. For who would fear an enemy whom he knows he will certainly overcome? Moreover, he confirms the hope of victory by three reasons, which it will not be a little helpful to examine one by one.

units.la: Prima est, quòd eos ex Deo esse dicit, id est, ex eorum numero, qui cœlesti & immortali (vt Petrus ait) semine verbi Dei regenerati, Dei filij facti sunt. Nam Paulus ait: Omnes vos filij Dei estis, eò quòd credidistis Christo Iesu. Galat.3. At patris est, tueri & seruare filios suos. Patris ergo officium fidelis Deus præstabit, nec patietur, vt pseudoprophetarum dolis circumueniantur, qui cunque ex verbo suo renati, ipsum patrem suum agnoscunt. Nec putandum est, Deum deteriorem siue negligentiorem patre esse, quàm nos simus, quibus liberorum salus commendatissima est.
units.tr: The first is that he says they are from God, that is, of the number of those who, having been regenerated by the heavenly and immortal seed (as Peter says) of the Word of God, have become children of God. For Paul says: "You are all children of God, because you have believed in Christ Jesus." Galatians 3. But it belongs to a father to protect and preserve his children. The faithful God will therefore perform the office of a father, and will not allow them to be deceived by the wiles of false prophets, since all who have been born again of his word acknowledge him as their own Father. Nor must we think that God is worse or more negligent a father than we are, who hold the salvation of our children most dear.

units.la: Altera ratio, quæ victoriam pollicetur, est: Et uicistis eos. Ab anteactis argumentatur, quasi dicat: Si cum eo hoste vobis res esset, qui semper vincere, nunquam vero vinci assueuisset, merito vos pugnæ huius euentum formidare deberetis. Sed iam olim isti omnes per vos ipsos deuicti sunt. Primò enim Christus Iesus, qui caput vestrum est, cum illorum principe satana congressus, infelix illud tenebrarum regnum euertit, errorum laqueos contriuit & suos in libertatem asseruit. Deinde cum vos, superstitione posita, Christo nomen dedistis & illius doctrinam estis amplexi, quid aliud fecistis, quàm quòd deuictis pseudoprophetis & Christi aduersarijs, animarum libertatem & salutem inuenistis? Ea ergo fide, qua antea impietatis castra deseruistis, eosq; seducatores, qui tū vos captiuos tenebant, vicistis, eadem & nunc pugnate, & eodem successu vincetis. Fides enim victoria vestra est, quæ totum mundum superat. 1. Ioan. 5.
units.tr: The second reason, which promises victory, is: "And you have overcome them." He argues from past events, as if he said: If you had to do with that enemy who had always been accustomed to conquer and never to be conquered, you would rightly have to dread the outcome of this fight. But all those men were long ago already defeated by you yourselves. For first, Christ Jesus, who is your head, when he engaged with their prince Satan, overthrew that unhappy kingdom of darkness, crushed the snares of error, and asserted his own into liberty. Then, when you, having put aside superstition, gave your name to Christ and embraced his doctrine, what else did you do than, the false prophets and adversaries of Christ having been defeated, find liberty and salvation for your souls? Therefore, with the same faith by which you formerly deserted the camp of impiety and overcame those seducers who then held you captive, fight now as well, and you will conquer with the same success. For your victory is faith, which overcomes the whole world. 1 John 5.

units.la: Additur his tertia ratio: Quoniam maior est, qui in vobis est, quàm qui in mundo. Opponit inter se quæ utrinque habentur præsidia. In illis agit mundi huius princeps, nec alijs quàm mundi præsidijs nituntur, humana nimirum prudentia, ingenij solertia, dolis, consilijs astutissimis, ad hæc principum fauore, populorum applausu, vulgi ignorantia, armis deniq; et aperta vi. Sed quanta sit omnium horum vanitas, facilè patet, si cum eo conferantur, qui vobis adest, qui suo fauore vos prosequitur, qui suo spiritu regit, & suo vos patrocinio protegit. Est is unigenitus Dei filius, Jesus Christus, qui serpentis caput iam olim contriuit, cui omnis potestas data in cœlo & in terra, sub cuius pedibus pulverem lingunt inimici omnes, & pedum ipsius scabellum facti sunt. Matth. 28. Psal. 72. & 110. Is consilia gentium dissipat. Psal. 33. Is in ira & furore suo reges arguit. Psal. 2. Is ecclesiæ suæ indiuulsus dux & protector adest usque in consummationem seculi. Matth. 28. Idem fortis ille & inuictus pastor est, qui ouem aliquam suis manibus eripi minime patitur. Joan. 10. Hic suos, ut quiduis possint, confortat. Philip. 4. Modò igitur velitis vincere impostores, & veritatis lucem inuiolatam retinere, successus deesse non poterit. Quamobrem posito timore inuictos vos præbete Christi milites, nec ullis Antichristi dolis & conatibus succumbetis.
units.tr: To these is added a third reason: "Because greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world." He sets against each other the defenses that each side has. On their side acts the prince of this world, and they rely on nothing but worldly defenses: human prudence, cleverness of mind, trickery, most cunning plans, besides the favour of princes, the applause of peoples, the ignorance of the crowd, and finally arms and open force. But how great the emptiness of all these things is, is easily seen if they are compared with him who is present with you, who favours you with his grace, who rules you by his Spirit, and protects you by his patronage. He is the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, who long ago crushed the head of the serpent, to whom all power is given in heaven and on earth, under whose feet all enemies lick the dust and have become the footstool of his feet. Matthew 28; Psalms 72 and 110. He scatters the counsels of the nations. Psalm 33. In his anger and fury he rebukes kings. Psalm 2. He is the undivided leader and protector of his Church, present even to the end of the age. Matthew 28. He is the same strong and unconquered shepherd, who does not suffer any sheep to be snatched from his hands. John 10. He strengthens his own so that they may be able to do anything. Philippians 4. Therefore, if you now wish to conquer the impostors and to keep the light of truth unviolated, success will not be lacking. Wherefore, laying aside fear, show yourselves unconquered soldiers of Christ, and you will not yield to any tricks and attempts of Antichrist.

units.la: Habent hæc non vulgarem consolationem, quæ generalius quoque accipi, & ad omnia extendi debet, quæ fidelibus negotium facere solent. Nam præter falsam doctrinam triaferè sunt, qui-bus nos satan oppugnat. Vel enim argutis & spinosis disputationibus nos adoritur, quibus veritatem obscurare, & animos nostros in eius cognitione perplexos reddere studet: vel tyrannorum armis vtitur & apertam vim nobis inferre conatur. Quod si neutrum ex his succedat, intestinas pugnas intra animos nostros mouet, quos varijs modis tentat, si quo modo vel confidentem securitatem, vel extremam desperationem nobis insinuare possit. Sed in omnibus istis inuicti stant, qui per Christum filij Dei facti sunt, & huius verbum ac spiritum in se regnantem habent. Si enim coram iudicibus, sapientibus mundi, Concilijs vel scholis, fidei ratio reddèda sit, nullas strophas metuunt, nec ullis fallacijs capiuntur. Nec enim illorum, sed Dei causa agitur, & proinde non ipsi, sed patris cœlestis spiritus in ipsis loquitur. Matth. 10. Mar. 13. Rursum, si tyrannos ad vim conuersos, & ob oculos mortem versari videant, ne sic quidem animo deiici possunt. Norunt enim se Christo niti, contra quem ne portæ quidem inferorum prævalent. Matth. 16. Norunt mundum iam olim cum principe suo à Christo deuictum esse. Ioan. 16. Norunt tyrannos in nuda corpora (nō tamen sine Dei permissu) ius habere, animas vero extra omne periculum positas, sub umbra alarum domini tuto latere. Matth. 10. Intrepidi ergo expectant, quid de ipsis Dei prouidentia iá olim statuerit. Exempla utriusque pugnæ siue certaminis multa extant. Agunt Christi causam coram Hierosolymitano Senatu, coram scribis & sacerdotibus Apostoli, & ita agunt, ut qui modò piscatores fuerant, insolubilibus argumentis omnem illorum solertiam capiant & deuincant. Paulus vbi coram rege Agrippa & Proconsulibus Romanis fidei & doctrinæ suæ rationem reddidit, tandem Romam deductus Cæsari sistitur, ibi quoque intrepidum se præbens tam sanctæ causæ patronum. Legimus impuberes iuuenes & puellas, indoctos & plebeios homines, sæpius cum eruditissimis, & longo usu exercitatis philosophis commissos palmam obtinuisse. Inueniuntur etiam infinita martyrum exempla, quorum fidem non promissiones regum, non minæ, non ante oculos posita suppliciorum instrumenta, non ipsi pœnarum grauissimi cruciatus & diutini dolores vincere potuerunt: imò plures extiterunt, qui tanto quantumvis inhumanos carnifices ante fatigauere, quàm ipsi fatigati sint, & desistiterunt interdum ab inferendis supplicijs tortores, cum ipsi à Christi & fidei confessione minimè desisterent. Quæ res multis pudorem offudit regibus, & tyrannis ignominiosum visum fuit à teneris puellis, ab imbelli puerorum ætate, à mulierculis, & decrepitis senibus vinci. Possunt nostra tempora exemplis multis testari, vera esse quæ dicimus. Cæterum, ut in hisce certaminibus suo spiritu suos suffulcit fidelis dominus: ita nec in ultimo illo ijs deest, quando intra se tentationibus varijs oppugnantur. Permittit quidem ut vacillet interdum fides, quò nostræ infirmitatis admoniti minus confidentes reddamur. Sed tentari non sinit ultra quàm ferre possumus, imò facit cum tentatione euentū, quò possimus sufferre. 1. Cor. 10. Quid ergo hinc aliud colligi debet, quàm verè stabilem & felicem esse piorum conditionem, quos (ut in secunda epistola Joannes verè loquitur) veritas non deserit, sed cum illis manet in æternum, quic; soli, tam mundi quàm omnium quæ in mundo sunt, victores gloriosissimi habentur.
units.tr: These things contain no common consolation, which ought also to be understood more generally and extended to all the things that usually cause trouble for the faithful. For besides false doctrine, there are roughly three ways by which Satan attacks us. For either he assails us with subtle and thorny disputations, by which he strives to obscure the truth and to make our minds perplexed in its knowledge; or he uses the arms of tyrants and tries to inflict open violence upon us. But if neither of these succeeds, he stirs up internal battles within our minds, which he tests in various ways, to see whether in some manner he can insinuate into us either a confident security or utter despair. Yet in all these things those stand unconquered who have become children of God through Christ, and who have the Word and Spirit of him reigning within them. For if the reason of their faith has to be rendered before judges, the wise men of the world, councils or schools, they fear no tricks and are caught by no deceits. For the cause is not theirs but God's, and therefore it is not they themselves but the Spirit of the heavenly Father who speaks in them. Matthew 10; Mark 13. Again, if they see tyrants turned to violence and death hanging before their eyes, they cannot be cast down in spirit even so. For they know that they rest upon Christ, against whom not even the gates of hell prevail. Matthew 16. They know that the world with its prince was long ago overcome by Christ. John 16. They know that tyrants have power over bare bodies (yet not without God's permission), but that souls, placed beyond all danger, lie safe under the shadow of the Lord's wings. Matthew 10. Fearless, therefore, they wait to see what God's providence has long ago decided concerning them. Many examples of both kinds of battle or struggle exist. The Apostles plead the cause of Christ before the Jerusalem senate, before the scribes and priests, and they so act that men who had just been fishermen capture and bind all their cleverness with unanswerable arguments. When Paul gave an account of his faith and doctrine before King Agrippa and the Roman proconsuls, and was at last led to Rome and set before Caesar, he showed himself there too a fearless advocate of so holy a cause. We read that youths and girls not yet of age, and uneducated and common people, have often been matched against the most learned philosophers, practised by long experience, and have won the palm. There are also countless examples of martyrs, whose faith neither the promises of kings, nor threats, nor the instruments of torture placed before their eyes, nor the most severe agonies of punishment and long-lasting pains could overcome. Indeed, there were many who wearied their most inhuman executioners before they themselves were wearied, and the torturers sometimes desisted from inflicting punishments, while the martyrs in no way desisted from the confession of Christ and of the faith. This matter brought shame upon many kings, and it seemed disgraceful to tyrants to be conquered by tender girls, by the unwarlike age of boys, by women, and by decrepit old men. Our own times can testify by many examples that what we say is true. But just as the faithful Lord supports his people with his Spirit in these struggles, so he is not lacking to them in that final one, when they are assailed within themselves by various temptations. He indeed permits faith to waver at times, so that, reminded of our weakness, we may become less confident. But he does not allow us to be tempted beyond what we can bear; indeed, together with the temptation he makes the outcome such that we can endure it. 1 Corinthians 10. What then should be gathered from this, other than that the condition of the godly is truly stable and happy, for whom (as John truly says in his second epistle) the truth does not fail, but remains with them forever, and who alone are held to be most glorious victors both over the world and over all that is in the world?

units.la: Cæterum non oscitanter prætereundum est, quàm caute de nostræ fidei victoria Ioannes lo-quatur. Nec enim simpliciter nos victores esse dicit, sed eius facit mētionem, qui in nobis agit, quæ maior & fortior mundi principe, nobis ad hæc certamina vires suppeditat. Reprimit hoc insolentem nostrarum virium fiduciam, qua vix aliud in salutis negotio perniciosius est, cùm ex nobis idonei non simus ad cogitandum quod bonum est, sed omnia nostra ex Deo sint. 2. Cor. 3. Pugnemus ergo (ut Dauid cum Golia congressurus) in nomine domini, memores, nos thesaurū hunc habere in testaceis vasculis, vt virtutis eminentia fit Dei, & non ex nobis.2.Cor.4.Videamus nūc vt alteri malo, quod de doctrinis minus dextrè iudicare facit, Apostolus medeatur.
units.tr: Moreover, we must not pass over carelessly how cautiously John speaks about the victory of our faith. For he does not simply say that we are the victors, but he makes mention of Him who works in us, who is greater and stronger than the prince of the world, and who supplies us with strength for these struggles. This checks the arrogant confidence in our own powers, than which hardly anything is more harmful in the business of salvation, since we are not fit of ourselves to think anything good, but all our sufficiency is from God. 2 Cor. 3. Let us therefore fight (as David, about to engage Goliath) in the name of the Lord, mindful that we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the excellence of the power may be of God and not of ourselves. 2 Cor. 4. Let us now see how the Apostle heals another evil, namely that which makes men judge doctrines less rightly.

units.la: II. Ipsi è mundo sunt, ideo è mundo loquuntur, et mundus eos audit. Nos ex Deo sumus. Qui nouit Deum, audit nos. Qui non est ex Deo, non audit nos. Illis respondet, qui ex sectatorum numero & temporaria felicitate doctrinas iudicant, quod à multis olim factum legimus, & hodie à plerisque fieri consueuit. Nec enim fieri posse existimant, vt tot ac tam praestantes eruditione & prudentia viri simul errent, vel vt communi errore tot simul nationes & regna implicentur. Mouentur etiam regum maiestate, quos religionis, quam profitentur, tutores & propugnatores esse vident. Nec parum apud illos momenti habet lōgi temporis praescriptio, quae vel sola multis animum addit, quo minus superstitiones, quibus assueuerunt, deserant. E contra absurdum & ridiculum illis videtur pauculos aliquot homines, ignoti antea nominis & nulla authoritate insignes, id hodie demum vi disse, quod tot seculis nemo videre potuerit. Hinc illae voces, quibus suarum partium fautores & propugnatores superbè iactant, nos vero cū execrabili vulgo praecipiti iudicio damnant. Sed quid de his aliud dici potest, quàm quòd fides ipsorum humanę authoritatis fundamento nitatur, non Christo, quem Deus suae ecclesiae petram & pretiosum lapidem fundamenti posuit? Si enim addi uinam authoritatem respiciunt, quid opus est patres, reges, principes, scholas, secula, consuetudines, successus, victorias, & alia eius generis nobis obijcere? Damnantur haec omnia, si cū Dei verbo pugnent, initio Capitis huius, quando spiritus probare iubemur, an ex Deo sint. Hoc ergo quæ rimus, & an à Deo tradita sint, quae illi mordicus retinere & nobis constanter obtrudere studeut. Frustra igitur patres, reges & seculorum multorum consuetudinem obijcitis. Imò sic proprio iudicio vt sorices vosipsos proditis, quòd nimirum diuina authoritate, qua vestra probetis, destitua mini. Sunt tamen simpliciores aliquot, qui ad multitudinem falsae doctrinae & superstitionis sectatorum obstupescunt, & causas mirantur, quae tot homines in errorum laqueos pertrahere potuerint. Hos in praesenti omni dubitatione liberat Ioannes. Confert enim inter se falsos doctores & veritatis ministros, simulq; qui nam & quales vel hos vel illos audiant, docet. Primo autem loco de falsis vel Antichristianis doctoribus agit his verbis:
units.tr: II. They are of the world, therefore they speak of the world, and the world hears them. We are of God. He who knows God hears us. He who is not of God does not hear us. He answers those who judge doctrines by the number of their followers and by temporary prosperity, a thing we read was done by many in former times and is still commonly done by most today. For they think it impossible that so many men, so outstanding in learning and prudence, should err together, or that so many nations and kingdoms should be entangled in a common error. They are also moved by the majesty of kings, whom they see to be the guardians and defenders of the religion they profess. The prescription of long time also carries no little weight with them, which alone adds courage to many not to abandon the superstitions to which they have grown accustomed. On the other hand, it seems absurd and ridiculous to them that a few men, of previously unknown name and distinguished by no authority, should only now have brought forth what no one could see in so many centuries. Hence those voices by which the supporters and defenders of their own party boast proudly, while they condemn us with the detestable judgment of the rabble, rushing to conclusions. But what can be said about these things except that their faith rests on the foundation of human authority, and not on Christ, whom God laid as the cornerstone and precious stone of the foundation of His Church? For if they look to any other authority, what need is there to throw at us the Fathers, kings, princes, schools, centuries, customs, successes, victories, and other things of that kind? All these are condemned if they clash with the Word of God, at the beginning of this chapter, where we are bidden to test the spirits, whether they are of God. Therefore let us inquire into this, and whether those things were handed down by God, which they strive to hold on to with their teeth and to press upon us constantly. In vain, then, do you object to us the Fathers, kings, and the custom of many centuries. Indeed, you betray yourselves, like mice, by your own judgment, in that you are destitute of the divine authority by which you should prove your own things. Yet there are some simpler folk who are astonished at the multitude of followers of false doctrine and superstition, and marvel at the causes that could draw so many men into the snares of errors. John frees these from all doubt in the present case. For he sets false teachers and ministers of the truth side by side, and at the same time teaches who and of what sort those who hear either these or those are. But first he speaks of the false or Antichristian teachers in these words:

units.la: Ipsi è mundo sunt, ideo è mundo loquuntur, & mundus eos audit. E mundo esse nō aliud est, quàm mundo addictum esse, & mundi studijs occupari, quod omnibus qui verbo Christi nōdum regenerati sunt, contingit. At qui tales sunt, è mundo etiā loquuntur, id est, sermonibus suis mundanam sapientiam spirant, deq; rebus sacris simul & prophanis ita differunt, vt mundo placere, & huius applausum referre possint. Sic ergo argumentari vult Apostolus. Quicunque mundi studijs addicti mundana docent, à mundo recipiuntur. (Nam similes facilè inter se conueniunt.) At falsi doctores toti mundum sapiunt, & mundana loquūtur. Quid ergo mirum est, si mundus hos audiat, ijs delectetur, & eos omni studio sequatur? Consentiunt his Christi verba, cùm Apostolis dicit: Si de mundo essetis, mundus quod suum est, diligeret. Quia verò de mundo non estis, sed ego selegi vos de mundo, propterea odit vos mundus. Ioan.15. Eò igitur omnia haec tendunt, vt docet Ioannes, falsam doctrinam sectatorum multitudine adeò non probari posse, vt ea potius argumento sit, falsam & mundanam esse, cum mundus hic non nisi falsam amplecti posit. At quomodo è mundo, id est, mundanae sapientiae thesauro loquantur falsi doctores, facilè cernitur, si quae de Deo & religione tradunt, audias. Fatentur quidem vnanimi consensu omnes homines, vnum quoddam summum & aeternum numen esse, quod toti huius mundi machinae praesit. At quomodo vnus Deus vbiq; locorum praesens esse, omnia penetrare, omnia solus videre, tueri & vno eodemq; tempore multas, easq; diuerfisimas, actiones obire posit, id humanae rationis captum longè superat. Vt ergo huic satisfiat, Deum talem nobis fingunt, quales in mundo Reges & Imperatores videmus, qui vni quidem & summi regnorum suorum domini dicuntur, quia vero non vbiuis locorum praesentes esse, nec omnibus officijs soli sufficere possunt, vicarijs opus habent, quorum administratione cuncta gubernentur. Talem inquam Deum proponunt, quicunque è mundo loquuntur, & humanae sapientiae rationes audiunt. Huic debemus gentilitium Deorum multitudinem, in quorum locum apud Christianos Diui successerunt, quorum alius quidem aquis praeft, alius ignem gubernat, hic morbos immittit & propulsat, & quia morborum seges est innumera, singulis singuli diui praefecti sunt, imò & singulis humani corporis partibus & vrbibus singulis peculiares quosdam diuos & Deos tutelares fuisse vidimus. Et quamuis haec cum Dei aeterni maiestate pugnent, Deumq; nobis otiosum (qualem olim Epicurus fingebat) constituant, quia tamen humanae sapientiae commentum est, audiunt illud & magno cum applausu recipiunt quotquot huic seculo addicti sunt; Doctrinam vero de Deo falsam mox & fides & religio falsa consequuntur. Qui enim ad vnum Deum confugere, & in vnum Deum credere debebant per filium eius Iesum Christum, alia via ingressi, vel Deum plane negligunt, vel saltem per Divos illos suos ad eum se peruenire posse existimant. Hinc fit, ut qui ventris torminibus vexatur, vel ab Erasmo opem petant, vel divinitus hanc per Erasmum sibi conferri postulent. Eadem in alijs est ratio. Et eousq; progressum est humanę prudentię deliriū, ut Deo patri & filio eius Iesu Christo nihil præter nudū divinitatis nomē reliquerit, administratione vero rerū huius mūdi in vniuersū ademerit.
units.tr: They are of the world, therefore they speak of the world, and the world hears them. To be of the world is nothing other than to be given over to the world and occupied with worldly pursuits, which happens to all who have not yet been regenerated by the Word of Christ. But those who are such also speak of the world, that is, their speech breathes worldly wisdom, and they discourse about sacred and profane things alike in such a way that they can please the world and win its applause. Thus the Apostle wishes to argue in this way: whoever, given over to worldly pursuits, teaches worldly things, is received by the world. (For like easily agree among themselves.) But false teachers altogether savor of the world and speak worldly things. What wonder, then, is it if the world hears them, delights in them, and follows them with all eagerness? The words of Christ agree with this, when He says to the apostles: If you were of the world, the world would love its own. But because you are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hates you. John 15. To this, then, all these things tend, as John teaches: that false doctrine cannot be approved by a multitude of followers, so that rather this is an argument that it is false and worldly, since this world can embrace nothing but what is false. But how the false teachers speak from the world, that is, from the treasury of worldly wisdom, is easily seen if you listen to what they teach concerning God and religion. All men indeed agree unanimously that there is some one supreme and eternal divinity which presides over the whole machinery of this world. But how one God can be present in all places, penetrate all things, see all things alone, watch over them, and at one and the same time carry out many and most diverse actions, far surpasses the grasp of human reason. So, to satisfy this, they fashion for us a God such as we see kings and emperors in the world, who indeed are called the one and supreme lords of their kingdoms, but because they cannot be present in every place, nor suffice alone for all duties, they need deputies, by whose administration all things are governed. Such a God, I say, do those propose who speak from the world and listen to the reasons of human wisdom. To this we owe the multitude of pagan gods, in whose place among Christians the saints succeeded: one of whom indeed presides over waters, another governs fire, this one sends and drives away diseases, and since the crop of diseases is innumerable, a particular saint has been set over each single one; and indeed we have seen that particular saints and protective gods existed for each single part of the human body and for each single city. And although these things clash with the majesty of the eternal God and make Him an idle God (such as Epicurus once imagined), yet because they are an invention of human wisdom, all who are devoted to this age hear them and receive them with great applause. But from a false doctrine concerning God, false faith and false religion immediately follow. For those who ought to have fled to the one God and believed in the one God through His Son Jesus Christ, having entered another way, either altogether neglect God or at least think they can come to Him through those saints of theirs. Hence it happens that he who is tormented with pains in the bowels either seeks help from Erasmus or asks that it be conferred on him divinely through Erasmus. The reason is the same in other cases. And the madness of human prudence has advanced so far that it has left to God the Father and to His Son Jesus Christ nothing but the bare name of divinity, while it has taken away from them altogether the government of the affairs of this world.

units.la: Obseruanda hic venit insignis mundi corruptio, qui à prima origine sua falsos potius doc-tores quàm veros audire voluit, & mendacia potius magno pretio redimere, quàm salutarem veritatis doctrinam gratis oblatam amplecti. Exempla eius generis multa extant prophetarum temporibus. In nouo Testamento res clarior est, quàm ut demonstratione opus habeat. Clamat Dei filius alta voce, & quasi expansis brachijs ad se inuitat omnes oneratos & laborantes, ac venientibus ad se requiem gratis pollicetur. In se monstrat famelicis panem vitæ, & sitibundis fontem aquæ viuentis offert. Sed quàm pauci inuenti sunt, qui illum ex animo amplecti & sequi voluerunt? Plerique cæcos cæcorum duces, imò fures & latrones potius sequi maluerunt, quorum ditionibus, & opes ipsorum minuebantur, & opprimebantur plus satis afflictæ conscientiæ. Nec meliorem conditionem Apostoli experti sunt, licet omnibus omnia fierent, quo plures Christo possent lucrifacere. Vulgare enim & apud omnes ferè vsitatum fuit, quòd Corinthijs Paulus exprobrat, dicens: Suffertis, si quis vos in seruitutem adigit, si quis exedit, si quis accipit, si quis attollit se, si quis vos in faciem cædit, &c. 2. Cor.II. Quid verò de nostro seculo, adeoq; nouissimis temporibus in vniuersum, sperari debeat, idem Apostolus non obscurè docet. Erit tempus (inquit) cum sanam doctrinam non sustinebunt, sed iuxta concupiscentias suas coaceruabunt sibi doctores ij quibus pruriunt aures, & à veritate quidem aures auertent, ad fabulas verò conuertentur. 2. Tim.4. Coaceruandi verbo uti voluit Paulus, ut insatiabile in mundo falsæ doctrinæ studium euidentius exprimeret. Poterat unus aliquis impostor multis seducendis sufficere, quod in hæresiarchis olim vidimus. Sed paucis non contenti nouissimi seculi homines, multos & infinitos habere cupient, in quos fortunas suas omnes profundant. Confer cum Pauli vaticinio quæ aliquot seculis in Papatu facta sunt, & rem hanc omnem luce clarius videbis. Siquidem non contenti homines, in templis publicis siue parochijs sacrificulum unum & alterum habere, Sacellanos quotidie nouos instituerunt, nec aliquis tam mediocris fortunæ fuit, quin moriens aliquid legaret, quo superstitionis cultus & otiosorum sacrificulorum numerus augeri posset. Accesserunt his monachorum ordines & monasteria, quæ impostorum eiusmodi plena magnis sumptibus alebantur. In hos ferè omnes tam publicæ quàm priuatæ opes collatæ sunt, nec quisquam se grauari quæstus est. At hodie cùm in opulenta aliqua & ampla ciuitate, octo vel decem veritatis ministri sufficiunt qui non priuatorum hominum opes appetunt, nihil ex ærario sibi numerari postulant, non hortos, non agros, non vineta & villas aliorum sibi vendicant, sed ecclesiarum redditibus, qui olim à principibus pijs & viris religiosis in hunc usum collati sunt, contenti victitant, nemini non nimium videtur, quicquid in illos conferri vident, grauiusq; multis putatur decem verbi ministris vitæ necessaria largiri, quàm olim trecentis sacrificulis, monachis & monialibus omnia quæ luxui & libidini inseruiunt, cumulatim suppeditare. O ingratitudinem non leui supplicio dignam. O dignos homines, qui mendacijs & dolis in interitum abducantur, quibus adeò sordet gratis oblata veritas. Cæterum videamus, quid ex opposito de veritatis ministris & horum sectatoribus dicat Ioannes, de quibus in propria persona loquens, sic pronunciat.
units.tr: Here we come to observe the notable corruption of the world, which from its first origin has preferred to hear false teachers rather than true ones, and to buy back lies at a great price rather than to embrace the saving doctrine of truth offered freely. Many examples of this kind exist in the times of the prophets. In the New Testament the matter is clearer than that it needs demonstration. The Son of God cries out with a loud voice, and, as if with arms outstretched, invites to himself all who are burdened and labouring, and freely promises rest to those who come to him. He shows the bread of life to the hungry, and offers the fountain of living water to the thirsty. But how few have been found who wished to embrace and follow him from the heart? Most preferred to follow blind guides of the blind, or rather thieves and robbers, under whose rule their own resources were diminished, and their already more than sufficiently afflicted consciences were oppressed. Nor did the apostles experience a better condition, although they became all things to all men, so that they might win more to Christ. For what Paul reproaches the Corinthians with was common and almost customary among all, when he says: You suffer it, if anyone brings you into bondage, if anyone devours you, if anyone takes you, if anyone exalts himself, if anyone strikes you on the face, etc. 2 Cor. 11. But what ought to be hoped for in our own age, and in the latest times generally, the same Apostle teaches not obscurely. There will be a time (he says) when they will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own lusts they will heap up for themselves teachers, having itching ears, and they will indeed turn their ears away from the truth, and be turned aside to fables. 2 Tim. 4. Paul wished to use the word "heap up" so that the insatiable zeal for false doctrine in the world might be expressed more clearly. One single impostor could have been enough to seduce many, as we once saw in the heresiarchs. But men of the latest age, not content with few, will desire to have many and countless ones, on whom they may pour out all their fortunes. Compare with Paul's prophecy what has been done for some centuries in the Papacy, and you will see the whole matter clearer than the light. For men, not content to have one or another little priest in public temples or parishes, have instituted new chaplains every day, and no one of even moderate means was there who, dying, did not bequeath something by which the number of superstitious worship and of idle little priests could be increased. To these were added orders of monks and monasteries, which, full of such impostors, were maintained at great expense. Almost all public and private resources were contributed to these, and no one complained of being burdened by the outlay. But today, when in some wealthy and large city eight or ten ministers of the truth suffice, who do not covet the riches of private men, demand nothing to be counted out to them from the treasury, do not claim for themselves gardens, fields, vineyards, and the country houses of others, but live content on the revenues of the churches, which were formerly contributed for this use by pious princes and religious men, it seems to nobody that it is too much, and whatever is seen to be bestowed on them is thought too heavy by many: it is considered more burdensome to supply the necessities of life to ten ministers of the Word than formerly to heap up abundantly for three hundred little priests, monks, and nuns everything that serves luxury and lust. O ingratitude worthy of no light punishment! O men worthy to be led to destruction by lies and deceits, for whom the truth offered freely is so cheap! But let us now see what John says on the opposite side about the ministers of the truth and their followers, speaking of them in his own person, and pronouncing thus.

units.la: Nos ex Deo sumus. Qui nouit Deum, audit nos. Qui non est ex Deo, non audit nos. Videri poterat ar-rogantius de seipso loqui, nisi communem omnium Apostolorum personam sustineret. Respicit autem partim aduocationem ministerij, quam ab ipso Christo habebant: partim ad doctrinæ certitudinem. Quia enim omnium quæ docebant, oculati testes fuerant, de eorundem veritate nullo modo poterant dubitare. Dicit ergo: Quemadmodum illi mundani sunt, & proinde mundanæ sapientiæ verba loquuntur: ita nos per Christum ex Deo regeniti coelestia loquimur, & quæ filius ipse nobis reuelauit, inter homines prædicamus. Rursus, ut illorum figmenta, quia humanæ sapientiæ fœtus sunt, apud homines mundo deditos facilè locum inueniunt: ita quicunq; ex Deo sunt & renati spiritu, vocem patris, quæ per nostrum ministerium sonat, agnoscunt & sequuntur. Quot quot autem ex Deo non sunt, illius vocem nec agnoscere nec ferre possunt, & proinde nos quoq; audire dedignantur. Sunt autem hæc non Ioannis, sed ipsius Christi verba. Is enim in euangelio inquit: Oues meæ vocem meam audiunt, & ego cognosco eas, & sequuntur me, &c. Ioan. 10. Et rursum: Qui ex Deo est, verba Dei audit. Ioan.8. De mundo autem, id est, non renatis & rebellibus, idem testatur, quòd spiritum veritatis non possint recipere. Ioan.14. Omnium ergo, quæ Ioannes dicit, hic scopus & finis est: in doctrinis dijudicandis nō hominum authoritatem respici debere,sed Dei verbum,nec hominum multitudini credendum esse, nec credentium paucitate quenquam offendi debere,cum ea sit mundi conditio, ut mendacij quàm veritatis amantior sit,& Christus electorum suorum numerum paucum & exiguum esse passim doceat. Nam ait: Multi sunt vocati,pauci electi.Matth.22.Et alibi:Introite per arctam portam.Quoniá lata est porta & spaciosa via,quæ abducit in exitium,multiq; sunt qui ingrediuntur per illam. Rursum angusta est porta & stricta via,quæ abducit ad vitam,& pauci sunt,qui inveniunt illam.Matth.7. Hæc si expenderent qui nobis hodie adversantur,certè nec nostrorum paucitatem nobis exprobarét nec tanto fastu Reges,Imperatores, principes seculares & spirituales(ut vocant) scholas,Concilia,patres,gentium multarum consensionem,multorum seculorum consuetudinem,& alia huius farinæ objicerent.
units.tr: We are from God. "He who knows" God hears us; "he who is not" from God does not hear us. This might seem an arrogant way of speaking about himself, were he not speaking in the person of all the Apostles together. He refers partly to the authority of the ministry, which they had from Christ himself, and partly to the certainty of the teaching. For since they had been eyewitnesses of everything they taught, they could in no way doubt its truth. He therefore says: just as those people are worldly, and so speak the words of worldly wisdom, so we, born anew from God through Christ, speak heavenly things and proclaim among men what the Son himself has revealed to us. Again, just as their fictions, being products of human wisdom, easily find a place among men devoted to the world, so all who are from God and born again by the Spirit recognise and follow the voice of the Father, which sounds through our ministry. But all who are not from God can neither recognise nor bear his voice, and therefore they also disdain to hear us. These, however, are not the words of John but of Christ himself. For he says in the Gospel: "My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me," etc. John 10. And again: "He who is of God hears the words of God." John 8. Concerning the world, that is, those not born again and rebellious, he testifies in the same way that they cannot receive the Spirit of truth. John 14. Therefore this is the aim and purpose of all that John says here: in judging doctrines one must look not to the authority of men but to the Word of God; nor must we believe the multitude of men, nor should anyone be troubled by the small number of believers, since such is the condition of the world that it loves falsehood more than truth, and Christ everywhere teaches that the number of his elect is small and scanty. For he says: "Many are called, few are chosen." Matt. 22. And elsewhere: "Enter by the narrow gate. For wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter by it. Narrow is the gate and strait is the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it." Matt. 7. If those who oppose us today would weigh these things, they would certainly neither reproach us with our small number nor, with such pride, object to us kings, emperors, secular and spiritual princes (as they are called), schools, councils, Fathers, the consent of many nations, the custom of many centuries, and other things of this kind.

units.la: Expendenda vero est non oscitanter Apostoli sententia: Qui novit Deum, audit nos. Docet enim obedientiam fidei verum & proprium signum esse filiorum Dei. Ut enim germani patris filij dicuntur, qui præcepta patris audiunt, nec illis improbè reluctantur: ita Dei filij agnoscentur, qui Dei vocem in scripturis & ecclesia sonantem agnoscunt, amplestuntur, & eidè obediunt. Arguit hoc illorum insolentiam, qui pleno ore Christi nomen & fidem in Deum tonant, cum interim à fidei obedientia sint alienissimi. Respondebit illis olim Christus: Non omnis qui dicit mihi, Domine domine, introibit in regnum meum, sed qui fecerit voluntatem patris mei, qui in coelis est. Matth.7. Sed pergamus ad reliqua, quibus locum hunc de doctrinarū dijudicatione concludit.
units.tr: The sentence of the Apostle, "He who knows God hears us," must be weighed carefully and not carelessly. For he teaches that obedience of faith is the true and proper sign of the sons of God. Just as those are called true sons of the father who hear the father's commands and do not wickedly resist them, so those will be recognised as sons of God who recognise, embrace and obey the voice of God sounding in the Scriptures and the Church. This condemns the arrogance of those who proclaim with full mouths the name of Christ and faith in God, while in fact they are most remote from the obedience of faith. Christ will one day answer them: "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of my Father, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven." Matt. 7. But let us go on to the rest, by which he concludes this passage on the judging of doctrines.

units.la: III. Per hoc cognoscimus spiritum veritatis, & spiritum erroris. Conclusione caput huius loci principale repetit. Debent enim verba hæc ad id referri, quod supra dixit: Probate spiritus an ex Deo sint. Quasi dicat: Non est fratres, quòd vel credentium paucitas vos offendat, vel eorum multitudo trahat & alliciat, qui impostores sequi solent. Nec enim hic de hominum, sed solius Dei auctoritate agitur. Hoc ergo videte potius, an doctrinæ ex Deo sint, vel ex hominibus sunt, erroneas falsas, hereticas, & iam olim damnatas esse scitote. Dominus enim inquit: Frustra me colunt docentes doctrinas hominum. Et omnis plantatio, quam non plantavit pater meus cœlestis, eradicabitur. Isa.29. Matth.15. Quòd si ex Deo fuerit, eam toto pectore recipite. Falsum enim & mendax esse non potest, quod ex æternæ veritatis fonte promanat.
units.tr: III. "By this we know the spirit of truth and the spirit of error." Here in the conclusion he repeats the principal point of this passage. For these words must be referred to what he said above: "Test the spirits whether they are from God." As if he said: Brethren, let it not trouble you either that believers are few, or that the multitude of them draws and entices you, as impostors are wont to be followed. For here the question is not of the authority of men, but of God alone. Therefore see rather whether doctrines are from God or from men, and know that those that are erroneous, false, heretical, and already condemned of old are of men. For the Lord says: "In vain do they worship me, teaching the doctrines of men." And "every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up." Isa. 29. Matt. 15. But if a doctrine is from God, receive it with your whole heart. For what flows from the fountain of eternal truth cannot be false or lying.

units.la: Hæc diligenter meditemur ò fratres, & Dei in nos benignitatem agnoscamus, qui doctrinam salutis non modò proponit, sed eandem à falsa discernere docet. Intendamus in hoc studia nostra, ne seducamur. Nec enim post tot tamq; fidas admonitiones aliqua superesit seducti excusatio. Fugiamus quæcunque hominum commenta sapiunt. Sequamur autem Dei vocem, illi credamus juxta hanc instituamus nostra omnia, ne audisse tantùm, sed & totis animis eam imbibisse videamur. Sic enim fiet, ut in cœlis olim regnemus cum eo, cui debetur benedictio, gloria, honor & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Let us meditate on these things diligently, brethren, and acknowledge God's kindness towards us, who not only sets forth the doctrine of salvation but also teaches us to distinguish it from what is false. Let us direct our efforts to this, so that we are not led astray. For after so many and so faithful admonitions, no excuse for being deceived remains. Let us flee whatever tastes of human inventions. But let us follow the voice of God, believe it, and order all our affairs according to it, so that we may seem not merely to have heard it but to have drunk it in with all our souls. For in this way it will come to pass that we reign one day in heaven with him to whom belong blessing, glory, honour and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILIA XXIIII.

units.la: Charissimi, diligamus nos mutuò: quia charitas ex Deo est. Et omnis qui diligit, ex Deo natus est, & cognoscit Deum. Qui non diligit, non novit Deum: quoniam Deus charitas est. In hoc apparuit charitas Dei erga nos, quòd filium suum unigenitum misit De-us in mundum, ut vivamus per eum. In hoc est charitas, non quòd nos dilexerimus Deum, sed quòd ipse dilexerit nos, & misit filium suum, propitiationem pro peccatis nostris. Charissimi, si sic Deus dilexit nos, & nos debemus nos mutuò diligere.
units.tr: Beloved, let us love one another, for love is of God. And everyone who loves is born of God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, for God is love. In this the love of God toward us was made manifest, that God sent his only-begotten Son into the world, so that we might live through him. In this is love: not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as the propitiation for our sins. Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.

units.la: PAulus Apostolus 1. Corinth. 4. ait: Non in sermone est regnum Dei, sed in virtute. Consentiunt his, quæ à Christo dicuntur: Non omnis, qui dicit mihi, Domine domine, introibit in regnum meum, sed qui fecerit voluntatem patris mei, &c, Matth.7. Docet autem utraque sententia non sufficere, si in fidei & salutis nostræ mysteriis probè instituamur, nisi vitam vivamus, quæ fidei in Christū & doctrinæ evangelicæ respondeat. Quæ causa est, quòd Apostoli passim in scriptis suis, nō fidei modò mysteria tradunt, verumetiá sedulò hortantur, ut carnē mortificemus & abnegata omni impietate, innocentiam vitæ & sanctimoniæ studium sectemur. Observat idem Joannes,tum vbique alias,tum in præsenti capite. Postquam enim de doctrina veritatis & dijudicatio ne doctrinarum diligenter disseruit,ne huius cognitionem nobis sufficere putaremus,redit ad di lectionem,de qua capite tertio agere coeperat. De hac autem præcipuè agit, quia in ea vitæ Christianæ cardo potissimum versatur. Christus Iesus enim in dilectione Dei & proximi totam legem & prophetas pendere testatur. Matth. 22. Et Paulus: Nemini quicquam debeatis (inquit) nisi vt vos inuicem diligatis. Nam qui diligit alterum, legem expleuit. Rom. 13. Cæterum de dilectione Ioannes in præsenti sic agit, vt primo dilectionis præceptum proponat, ad cuius obseruatione firmis & solidis rationibus nos exhortatur. Quia verò inter alia Dei exemplum allegauit, illud ita il lustrat postea, vt simul omnem salutis nostræ rationem comprehedat. Postremo, Dei exemplum nobis applicans, locum hunc concludit. Nos singula ordine inspiciamus.
units.tr: The Apostle Paul says in 1 Corinthians 4: "The kingdom of God is not in word but in power." These words agree with what is said by Christ: "Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into my kingdom, but he who does the will of my Father," and so on, Matthew 7. Both sayings teach that it is not enough to be carefully instructed in the mysteries of our faith and salvation unless we also live a life that corresponds to faith in Christ and to the evangelical doctrine. This is why the Apostles, throughout their writings, not only hand down the mysteries of faith but also earnestly exhort us to mortify the flesh, to renounce all ungodliness, and to pursue innocence of life and zeal for holiness. John observes the same thing, both elsewhere everywhere and in the present chapter. For after he had carefully discussed the doctrine of truth and the discernment of doctrines, lest we think that knowledge of these was enough for us, he returns to love, which he had begun to treat in the third chapter. He treats it here especially because the hinge of the Christian life chiefly turns upon it. For Christ Jesus testifies that the whole law and the prophets hang upon love of God and neighbor (Matthew 22). And Paul: "Owe nothing to anyone," he says, "except that you love one another. For he who loves another has fulfilled the law" (Romans 13). Moreover, John in the present passage treats of love in such a way that first he sets forth the precept of love, to whose observance he exhorts us by firm and solid reasons. Since he has in the meantime cited the example of God among other things, he afterwards so illustrates it that at the same time he embraces the whole basis of our salvation. Finally, applying the example of God to us, he concludes this passage. Let us examine each part in order.

units.la: I. Charissimi, diligamus nos mutuò: quia charitas ex Deo est. Et omnis qui diligit, ex Deo natus est, & cognoscit Deum. Qui non diligit, non nouit Deum: quoniam Deus charitas est. Videtur Ioannes satis abrupto saltu ad alterius loci tractationem transfire. Sed non ineptè hæc præcedentibus connecti possunt. Demonstrauit enim, veram doctrinam esse, quæ filium Dei Iesum Christum vnicum mundi saluatorem tradit, & huic acceptam fert omnem nostræ redemptionis & salutis gloriam. Quia autem in Christo in vnum corpus coniungimur, cuius ille caput est, & eiusdem patris filij efficimur per vnum & eundem adoptionis spiritum, fieri nequit, vt charitatis officia non doceat, quisquis in Christi prædicatione legitimè versari voluerit. Præmittit verò paucis verbis comprehensum dilectionis præceptum, cuius obseruatione nobis duabus rationibus grauissimis commendat.
units.tr: I. "Beloved, let us love one another, for love is of God. And everyone who loves is born of God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, for God is love." John seems to pass to the treatment of another passage with a rather abrupt leap. But these words can be connected not unsuitably with what precedes. For he has shown that that is the true doctrine which hands down that the Son of God, Jesus Christ, is the only Savior of the world, and which ascribes to him alone all the glory of our redemption and salvation. Since, moreover, we are joined together in Christ into one body, of which he is the head, and by one and the same spirit of adoption we become children of the same Father, it cannot be that whoever wishes to deal rightly with the preaching of Christ should fail to teach the duties of love. He sets forth first, in a few words, the precept of love, the observance of which he commends to us on two very weighty grounds.

units.la: Primam à causa efficiente, vel etiam natura & ingenio charitatis sumit, dicens: Quia charitas ex Deo est. Decet enim, vt qui Dei cultores & filij haberi volunt, ea studiosè sectentur, quæ ex Deo originem trahunt, & diuina sunt. At quid magis diuinum quàm charitas, & quæ ex hac nascitur beneficentia? Charitatem certè & beneficentiam verbo suo passim præscribit, eandem proprio exemplo commendat, & illius studium spiritus sui operatione in animis hominum accendit: vt non ineptè ab ethnicis olim dictum sit, homines benefaciendo proximè ad Dei naturam accedere. Magna ergo debet esse apud Christianos homines huius argumenti authoritas, ne charitatis rei vere diuinæ, studium intermittant.
units.tr: The first he takes from the efficient cause, or rather from the nature and character of love, saying: "for love is of God." For it is fitting that those who wish to be regarded as worshippers and children of God should eagerly pursue those things which derive their origin from God and are divine. But what is more divine than love, and the beneficence that is born of it? He prescribes love and beneficence throughout his Word, commends the same by his own example, and kindles zeal for it in the hearts of men by the working of his Spirit; so that it was not unfittingly said by the pagans of old that men who do good draw very near to the nature of God. Therefore the authority of this argument ought to be great among Christian men, so that they do not neglect the pursuit of love, which is truly a divine thing.

units.la: Altera ratio ipsius Dei exemplum habet, quo probatur charitati deditos esse oportere quicunque Dei filij dici voluerint. Figuratur autem pulchra antithesi cum ait: Omnis qui diligit, ex Deo natus est, & cognoscit Deum. Qui non diligit, non nouit Deum: quoniam Deus charitas est. Sic autem colligit Apostolus. Quisquis Dei ingenium refert, Deum nouit, & ex Deo natus est. Qui diligit, Dei ingenium refert. Ergo qui diligit, Deum nouit, & ex Deo natus est. Maior certa & indubitata est. Cum enim natura corrupti simus, ex Deo genitum neminem censere possumus, nisi quem Dei ingenio videamus respondere. Minorem probat adiecta sententia: Deus charitas est. E qua absolutè sequitur, Dei ingeniu illis inesse, quicunq; charitatis studiosi sunt. Deu verò charitatem vocat eo sensu, quo & veritas ipsa, & sapientia atq; iustitia dicitur. Quia enim Deus æterna & per se subsistens est essentia, nullis accidentibus grauatur, quæ vel absint interdu, vel adsint. Sed quicquid Deus est, idipsum reuera & essentialiter est, suapte natura, non propter aliunde illi connexum accidens. Quare quia veritatem essentialiter in se habet, non verax modò, sed ipsa veritas dicitur. Eadem sapientiæ & iustitiæ atque charitatis ratio est. Quia enim hæ virtutes Deo naturaliter & essentialiter insunt, merito ipsa sapientia, ipsa iustitia & charitas dicitur. Quòd si Deu imitari oportebat, si vel nostro more charitati studeret, quanto magis nunc charitatem ipsius nos æmulari decet, quæ essentiæ diuinæ ita inest, vt ex illa auferri nullo modo possit. Firma ergo & solida stat Ioannis argumentatio, quæ & penes nos tanti momenti esse debet, vt charitatis studium nunquam in animis nostris restingui patiamur. Cæterum priusquam videamus, quo pacto Apostolus probet, Deum charitatem esse, duo nobis in rationibus istis inspicieda sunt, quorum obseruatio institutioni nostræ plurimum seruire poterit.
units.tr: The second reason is drawn from the example of God himself, by which it is proved that all who wish to be called children of God ought to be devoted to love. He sets this forth with a beautiful antithesis when he says: "Everyone who loves is born of God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, for God is love." The Apostle reasons thus: whoever bears the character of God knows God and is born of God. Whoever loves bears the character of God. Therefore whoever loves knows God and is born of God. The major premise is certain and indubitable: since we are corrupt by nature, we can judge no one to be born of God unless we see him answering to the character of God. The minor premise is proved by the added statement: "God is love." From this it follows absolutely that the character of God is present in those who are zealous for love. Now he calls God love in the same sense in which he is also called truth itself, and wisdom, and righteousness. For since God is an eternal and self-subsisting essence, he is burdened by no accidents which may at one time be absent and at another present. But whatever God is, that he truly and essentially is, by his own nature, not by some accident joined to him from elsewhere. Hence, because he has truth essentially in himself, he is called not merely truthful but truth itself. The same reasoning holds for wisdom, righteousness and love. For since these virtues are inherent in God naturally and essentially, he is rightly called wisdom itself, righteousness itself, and love itself. But if we ought to imitate God, if he were to pursue love even in our manner, how much more does it befit us now to emulate his love, which is so inherent in the divine essence that it can in no way be taken away from it. Therefore John's argument stands firm and solid, and it ought to be of such weight with us that we never allow zeal for love to be extinguished in our hearts. But before we see in what way the Apostle proves that God is love, we must look into two things in these reasons, the observation of which will be of great service to our instruction.

units.la: Primò dicit: Charitas ex Deo est. Quæ verba præter quàm charitatis studium nobis commendant, simul etiam docet, vnde & qua ratione illud assequi possimus. Est hoc cognitu necessarium valde. Multos enim est videre, qui non leuiter de eo conqueruntur, quòd animos suos à charitate nimium alienos esse sentiunt, & viam quærunt, qua ad hanc peruenire liceat. Falluntur autem mi serrimi homines, quòd humanis rationibus hic aliquid profici posse putant, & nō nisi homines doctores audiût. Atqui nihil hic vel videt vel agit nostra ratio. Et quò diutius nostræ carnis dictata audimus, eò maiorem in nobisipsis philautiam deprehendemus, quæ maxima fraternæ charitatis pestis est. Præterea, si omnes omnium philosophorum libros euoluas, fratribus quidem benefaciendum esse audies, sed ita, vt tu tibi proximus sis semper. Vlterius ergo nos ascendere, & ad eum magistrum transire oportet, quem hoc loco Ioannes monstrat. Charitas (inquit) ex Deo est. Deo igitur magistro discetur, & eodem solo authore in nobis accendi poterit. Huius verbo docemur, nos non nobis, sed alijs natos esse. Si enim sibijpsis nati essent singuli homines, frustra à nobis exigerentur officia, quæ parentibus, liberis, magistratibus, populo, seruis, dominis, coniugibus, singulis denique hominibus debemus. Rursum, eodem verbo docemur, ita nos proximo obstrictos esse, vt non modo fortunæ bona, sed vitam quoque, si ita necessitas postulet, pro illius salute deponere debeamus. Nec desunt exempla cultorum Dei, qui ad hunc supremum charitatis gradum ascenderunt. Hac enim vrgente Moses clamat: Aut remitte huic populo ô Deus, aut expunge me de libro tuo, quem scripsisti. Exod.32. Eiusdem affectus verba sunt, quibus Dauides pestem in populo grassante deprecatur, dicens: Ego peccaui, ego iniquè egi: oues autem istæ quid fecerunt? Sit quæso manus tua contra me, & contra domum patris mei 2.Sam.24. Grauius adhuc est, quod charitate suadente Paulus loquitur: Optarim ipse ego anathema esse à Christo pro fratribus meis, &c. Ad Romanos nono. Hæc & plura alia tam præcepta quàm exempla charitatis in Dei schola nobis adi munt. Simul autem & hoc docemur, quòd solius Dei sit cor nouum creare, spiritu principali fulcire, & tales fingere homines, qui præcepta hæc saluberrima obire posint. In horum igitur meditatione nos frequenter versari oportet, nec carnem priuati commodi studiosam, nec humanæ sapientiæ traditiones audire. Accedant ardentes preces, & quotidianos profectus in hoc tam sancto exercitio sentiemus.
units.tr: First he says: "Love is of God." These words, besides commending to us zeal for love, also teach at the same time whence, and by what means, we can attain it. This is very necessary to know. For one can see many who complain not lightly that their minds feel far too estranged from love, and who seek a way by which it may be lawful to reach it. But those most wretched men are mistaken in thinking that anything can be advanced here by human reasons, and they hear only human teachers. Yet our reason neither sees nor does anything here. And the longer we listen to the dictates of our flesh, the more self-love we shall discover in ourselves, which is the greatest plague of brotherly love. Moreover, if you should turn over all the books of all the philosophers, you will hear indeed that one must do good to brothers, but in such a way that you always remain nearest to yourself. It is necessary therefore for us to ascend further and pass over to that Teacher whom John points out in this place. "Love," he says, "is of God." Love is therefore learned from God as teacher, and it can be kindled in us by that same God alone as author. By his word we are taught that we are born not for ourselves but for others. For if individual men were born for themselves, the duties which we owe to parents, children, magistrates, the people, servants, masters, spouses, and finally to each single man, would be demanded of us in vain. Again, by the same word we are taught that we are so bound to our neighbor that we ought to lay down not only our goods of fortune but also our life, if necessity so requires, for his salvation. Nor are there lacking examples of worshippers of God who have risen to this highest degree of love. For under the urging of this love Moses cries out: "Either forgive this people, O God, or blot me out of your book, which you have written" (Exodus 32). These are words of the same affection with which David, when the pestilence was raging among the people, entreats God, saying: "I have sinned, I have done wrong; but these sheep, what have they done? Let your hand, I pray, be against me and against my father's house" (2 Samuel 24). Even weightier is what Paul says, moved by love: "I myself could wish to be anathema from Christ for my brothers," etc. (Romans 9). These and many other precepts as well as examples of love are offered to us in the school of God. At the same time we are taught also that it belongs to God alone to create a new heart, to strengthen it by his principal Spirit, and to form men such that they are able to perform these most wholesome precepts. We ought therefore to dwell frequently in the meditation upon these things, and neither to listen to the flesh, which is eager for private advantage, nor to the traditions of human wisdom. Let ardent prayers be added, and we shall perceive daily progress in this so holy exercise.

units.la: Deinde obseruandum quòd ait: Qui diligit, ex Deo natus est, & nouit Deum. Qui non diligit, non nouit Deum. Docemur, quid de illis iudicari debeat, qui ab omni charitatis studio alieni sunt. Deum non nouerunt, nec ex Deo nati sunt. Impossibile enim est, vt Deum non diligat super omnia, quisquis illius bonitatem immensam, qua omnia moderatur & temperat, cognitam habet. At Deum diligere nemo poterit, nisi qui simul omnia quæ ille in se complectitur, diligit, in quibus vniuersis homine nihil præstantius & excellentius est. Quisquis ergo dilectionem in se habet nullam, Deum nec nouit, nec ex illo natus est. De ea enim Dei notitia loquimur, quæ animum totum hominis in Dei consyderationem rapit, & inde in omnem vitæ nostræ conuersationem diffunditur. Grauior omnino hæc sententia est, quàm multis prima fronte appareat. Quid enim aliud manet eos, qui ex Deo non nati sunt, nisi quod ab hæreditate regni cœlorum excludantur? Siquidem illa ad solos Dei filios pertinet. Atqui leuiculum videri poterat hoc, si Ioannem solum hæc dicentem audiremus, quamuis ne sic quidem tanti Apostoli sententia contemni deberet. Sed eiusdem sententiæ author Christus Iesus est, qui in nouissimo vniuersalis iudicij die ex charitatis operibus eos agnoscet, qui regni sui hæreditate possessuri sunt: & rursum impios æterna infernalis ignis pœna dignos iudicabit, quod charitatis officia neglexerint. Matth.25. Quòd si neglectum charitatis officium pœnas tam horribiles meretur, quid de illis dicemus, qui non contenti neglexisse fratres, simul etiam malefaciunt, qui vsuris & malis artibus inopes circùueniunt, qui aliena furantur, qui victum aliorum violenter rapiunt, qui famam proximi lædunt, qui denique nec corpori nec vitæ fratrum parcunt? Scio quidem improbam hominum huius seculi securitatem, qui in omnibus istis sibi placent. Sed sentient olim, quàm longè alia Christi iudicis sit de istis facinoribus sententia. At omissis his ad Ioannis verba redeamus: qui quoniam Dei exemplo nos ad charitatem adhortatus est, illud pluribus verbis illustratum proponit, vt in huius imitationem feruentiori zelo rapiamur.
units.tr: Next, note what he says: "He who loves is born of God, and knows God. He who does not love does not know God." Here we are taught what should be judged of those who are strangers to all zeal for charity. They do not know God, nor are they born of God. For it is impossible that a man should not love God above all things, if he has known God's boundless goodness, by which all things are governed and ordered. But no one can love God unless he at the same time loves all the things that God embraces in himself, and among all of these nothing is more excellent or outstanding than man. Whoever therefore has no love in himself does not know God, nor is he born of him. For we are speaking of that knowledge of God which draws the whole mind of man into the contemplation of God and from there spreads out into the whole conduct of our life. This statement is certainly weightier than it appears at first sight to many. For what else awaits those who are not born of God, except that they are shut out from the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven? For that inheritance belongs to the sons of God alone. And yet this might seem a trifling matter, if we heard only John saying it; although not even so ought the opinion of so great an Apostle to be despised. But the author of this same statement is Christ Jesus, who on the last day of the universal judgment will acknowledge from their works of charity those who are to possess the inheritance of his kingdom, and again will judge the impious, worthy of the eternal punishment of infernal fire, because they have neglected the duties of charity. (Matt. 25.) If the neglect of a duty of charity deserves such horrible punishments, what shall we say of those who, not content merely to have neglected their brothers, also do wrong, who circumvent the poor by usury and wicked arts, who steal what belongs to others, who violently seize the livelihood of others, who injure the reputation of their neighbour, who in short spare neither the body nor the life of their brothers? I know indeed the wicked security of the men of this age, who take pleasure in all these things. But they will one day feel how far different the sentence of Christ the Judge is concerning these crimes. But, setting these aside, let us return to the words of John: since he has exhorted us to charity by the example of God, he sets this out, illustrated with more words, so that we may be carried away with a more fervent zeal in imitating it.

units.la: II. In hoc apparuit charitas Dei erga nos, quòd filium suum unigenitum misit Deus in mundum, vt viuamus per eum. In hoc est charitas, non quòd nos dilexerimus Deum, sed quòd ipse dilexerit nos, & misit filium suum, propitiationem pro peccatis nostris. Ex operibus Dei argumentum sumit, quo probet illum charitatem esse, id est, omnia sua ex mera charitate facere & instituere ad hominum salutem. At qui infinita propemodum sunt, quæ produci poterant. Quocunque enim oculos vertas, diuinæ charitatis argumenta nobis occurrunt, cùm mundi huius machina, quàta quanta est, propter hominem condita sit. Sed & ipse homo non aliam ob causam conditus legitur, quàm quòd Deus aliquos esse voluit, quos bonorum suorum participes redderet. Nec alia creati hominis causa adduci poterit, cum Deus, qui ab æterno est, etiam priusquam homo esset, nullius rei indigus fuerit vnquam. Similiter diuinæ in nos charitatis argumenta sunt, quòd creaturas omnes hominis imperio subiecit, quòd angelos ministerio electorum suorum destinauit, quòd omnia elementa propter hominis conseruationem occupari vult, quòd Solem oriri finit super bonos & malos, quòd super iustos & iniustos depluit, quòd alit, vestit, protegit, & singulis momentis ex periculis, quorum hic mundus plenus est, etiam ignaros, & sæpe inuitos asserit. At Ioannes, ne ea tantummodo diuinæ beneficentiæ tribuere videretur, quæ multi vel propriæ industriæ, vel aliorum auxilij accepta ferre consueuerunt,eius beneficij meminit, cuius excellentiam nec mens nostra satis æstimare, nec lingua pro dignitate explicare potest. In hoc (inquit) apparuit charitas Dei erga nos, quòd filium suum vnigenitum misit Deus in mundum.Dilectionem satis testari videtur,qui periclitanti manum porrigit,qui fortunæ bonis iuuat,qui pascit,vestit & aliis eiusmodi officijs prosequitur.Sed cum hæc omnia faciat Deus,quasi nihil adhuc fecisset, quod sibi charissimum habebat, & quo nihil est in tota rerum vniuersitate nobilius, ad nos transmittere voluit, videlicet filium suum,nec filium modò,sed vnigenitum filium.Hunc (inquam) in mundum misit,in vallem lachrymarum,in palæstram omnis generis calamitatum,in dolores & aduersa, quæ necessariò sustinent,quicunque in hoc mundo viuunt.Nec ideo misit, vt per hunc diuinæ maiestati aliquid ac cederet, quo illa hucusque caruisset (defectus enim hæc nullos sentit, & vt nihil ipsi decedit, ita non aliquid eidem addi potest) sed vt per ipsius meritum viuamus,qui propter peccata mortis æternæ sententiam sustinebamus.Annon ergo sufficiens hoc syncerae charitatis argumentum? Quis obsecro,dum hæc expendit, Deum charitatem esse dubitabit?
units.tr: II. "In this the love of God was made manifest toward us, that God sent his only-begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him. In this is love: not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son as a propitiation for our sins." From the works of God he takes an argument by which he proves that God is love, that is, that he does all his works and arranges all things for the salvation of men out of pure love. And these are almost infinite in number, which could be brought forward. For wherever you turn your eyes, the proofs of divine love meet us, since the whole machinery of this world, however vast it is, was made on account of man. But man himself too is read of as created for no other reason than that God willed there to be some whom he would make partakers of his goods. Nor can any other cause of the creation of man be adduced, since God, who is from eternity, even before man existed, was never in need of anything. Similarly, these are proofs of divine love toward us: that he has subjected all creatures to the rule of man; that he has appointed angels to the service of his elect; that he wills all the elements to be employed for the preservation of man; that he lets the sun rise on the good and the evil; that he sends rain on the just and the unjust; that he feeds, clothes and protects us, and at every moment rescues us, even when we are unaware and often unwilling, from the dangers with which this world is full. But John, lest he should seem to attribute to divine beneficence only those things which many are accustomed to ascribe to their own industry or the help of others, recalls that benefit whose excellence neither our mind can sufficiently estimate nor our tongue worthily explain. "In this," he says, "the love of God was made manifest toward us, that God sent his only-begotten Son into the world." He who stretches out his hand to one in danger, who helps with the goods of fortune, who feeds, clothes and attends with other such services, seems sufficiently to witness love. But although God does all these things, as if he had not yet done anything, he wished to send to us that which he held most dear and than which nothing in the whole universe of things is more noble: namely his Son, and not only his Son, but his only-begotten Son. Him (I say) he sent into the world, into the valley of tears, into the arena of every kind of calamity, into the sorrows and adversities which of necessity are endured by all who live in this world. Nor did he send him so that anything should accrue to the divine majesty through him, which it had lacked until then (for these things feel no lack, and as nothing is taken from him, so nothing can be added to him), but so that we might live through his merit, we who were undergoing the sentence of eternal death on account of our sins. Is not this then a sufficient proof of sincere love? Who, I beseech you, when he weighs these things, will doubt that God is love?

units.la: Attamen, quia obijci poterant sanctissimorum patrum merita,quasi illi suo erga diuinam maiestatem studio tantum beneficium meruissent,clarius sese explicat Ioannes,vt gratuitum & merum diuinæ bonitatis opus hoc esse demonstret.Nam expositionis loco subijcit: In hoc est charitas,non quòd nos dilexerimus Deum,sed quòd ipse dilexerit nos,& misit filium suum, propitiationem pro peccatis nostris.Agnoscimus quidem sanctorum studia,quibus illos Deo placuisse constat.Eadem tamen tanti fieri non debent,vt illis Dei filium meruisse dicantur. Hunc enim primo parenti tunc temporis promisit Deus, quando nil nisi peccatum & peccati poenam ob oculos sibi versari sentiebat.Trepidantem enim & fugientem à facie Dei vocauit ex gratia,& cum damnationis sententiam subire debuerat,lætam & salutiferam feminis saluifici promissionem audiuit. Facessant ergo procul,qui gratuitum diuinæ bonitatis beneficium extenuant,dum vel sua ipsorum, vel aliorum hominum merita iactare audent.Christus Iesus enim, vt peccatorum nostrorum expiatio fieret,missus est.Peccatores ergo nos fuisse oportet, nisi Christum frustra missum esse, dicere velimus.Quid vero peccatores coram illo merebuntur,qui ab omni macula & labe alienus,peccatores odit,& suo conspectu arcet?
units.tr: Yet, because it could be objected that the merits of the most holy fathers might be cited, as if by their zeal toward the divine majesty they had deserved so great a benefit, John explains himself more clearly, in order to show that this is a free and pure work of divine goodness. For by way of explanation he adds: "In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son as a propitiation for our sins." We do acknowledge the zeal of the saints, by which it is certain that they pleased God. Yet these things ought not to be so esteemed that they can be said to have merited for them the Son of God. For God promised him first to our first parent at that time, when he felt that nothing but sin and the punishment of sin was before his eyes. For trembling and fleeing from the face of God he called him out of grace; and when he ought to have undergone the sentence of condemnation, he heard the joyful and saving promise of the seed of salvation. Let those then depart far away who diminish the free benefit of divine goodness while they dare to boast of their own merits or the merits of other men. For Christ Jesus was sent so that the expiation of our sins might be made. We must therefore have been sinners, unless we wish to say that Christ was sent in vain. But what will sinners merit before him, who is alien to every stain and blemish, hates sinners, and keeps them away from his sight?

units.la: Comprehendit ergo paucis hisce verbis Ioannes vniuersam nostræ salutis rationem, & eandem expeditam & facilem esse docet,licet multi eam superbis de humanæ naturæ viribus & meritis disputationibus intricatissimam reddant. Fateamur nos peccatores esse,& peccati lapsu ita corruptos,vt ex nobis ipsis ne cogitare quidem possimus quod bonum est.2.Corinth.3.Agnoscamus item saluatorem nobis cœlitus datum esse,Iesum Christum, qui peccata nostra in se transtulit,sui corporis & sanguinis beneficio in ara Crucis expiauit,vitam salutemq; nobis acquirens certissimam. Dedit hunc ex mera gratia clemens & misericors Deus, nullis nostris meritis prouocatus. Nam ipso Christo teste,ita dilexit Deus mundum,vt filium suum vnigenitum daret,&c. Ioan.3.Christi vero & bonorum, quæ in hoc nobis parta sunt, participes & consortes reddimur sola fide,quæ & ipsa donum Dei est.Ephes.2.
