Cum enim salutis nostræ negotio peracto in cœlos ascenderit,nec vllis corporeis sensibus apprehendi queat,sola mente per fidem apprehenditur, quæ nos ita illi inserit,vt ipse in nobis maneat,& nos vicissim in illo viuamus.Hinc cum Paulo apostolo fatemur,sola fide iustificari hominem absque operibus legis,eò quod sola fide nos Christo, qui iustitia & sanctificatio à nobis à patre factus est (1. Cor. 1.) communicamus,quò per opera legis peruenire nullo modo potest.Nec eos audimus,qui de Ceremonialibus ista intelligi debere clamitant,cum lex non Ceremonias modò,sed vitæ officia, charitatem, innocentiam, iustitiam & alias virtutes præscribat,quæ solæ opera verè bona in nobis generant. Quòd si verò opera, quæ iuxta diuinæ legis præscriptum fiunt,non iustificat,quæ obsecro audacia est,humanarum traditionum operibus id tribuere, quod legis operibus negatum esse videmus? Num sententiæ olim per prophetam dictæ,& à Christo repetitæ,adeò exigua est penes nos authoritas? Frustra me colunt docentes doctrinas hominum. Sed quia Apostolus salutis nostræ causam hoc loco non ex professo tractare instituit,paucula hæc de illa inseruisse contentus, nobis quoq; hæc dicta sufficiant, & ad loci præsentis conclusionem transeamus.
units.tr: John therefore comprehends in these few words the whole plan of our salvation, and teaches that it is easy and simple, although many make it most intricate by proud disputations concerning the powers and merits of human nature. Let us confess that we are sinners, and so corrupted by the fall of sin that of ourselves we cannot even think what is good. (2 Cor. 3.) Let us also acknowledge that a Saviour has been given to us from heaven, Jesus Christ, who transferred our sins to himself and expiated them on the altar of the Cross by the benefit of his body and blood, acquiring for us life and most certain salvation. This Christ God, gracious and merciful, gave out of pure grace, provoked by none of our merits. For, Christ himself being witness, "God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son," etc. (John 3.) But we are made partakers and sharers of Christ and of the goods that have been gained for us in him by faith alone, which is itself also a gift of God. (Eph. 2.) For when he has ascended into heaven, the business of our salvation having been completed, and he cannot be grasped by any bodily senses, he is grasped by the mind alone through faith, which so inserts us into him that he remains in us and we in turn live in him. Hence with the apostle Paul we confess that man is justified by faith alone, without the works of the law, because by faith alone we are made partakers of Christ, who was made by the Father righteousness and sanctification for us (1 Cor. 1.), whereas by the works of the law he can in no way be reached. Nor do we listen to those who loudly maintain that these things ought to be understood of the ceremonial precepts, since the law prescribes not only ceremonies but also the duties of life, charity, innocence, justice and the other virtues, which alone produce truly good works in us. But if indeed works which are done according to the prescription of the divine law do not justify, what audacity, I beseech you, is it to attribute to the works of human traditions that which we see denied to the works of the law? Is the authority of the sentence once spoken by the prophet, and repeated by Christ, so slight among us? "In vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines that are the precepts of men." But since the Apostle has not undertaken to treat the cause of our salvation professedly in this place, being content to insert these few things about it, let these sayings also suffice for us, and let us pass on to the conclusion of the present passage.

units.la: III. Charissimi,si sic Deus dilexit nos, & nos debemus nos mutuo diligere. Nobis applicat Dei patris exemplum, vt illud ad nos pertinere intelligamus, de quo & ipse Christus admonet,dum charitatis nostræ affectum non ad exemplum publicanorum,sed patris sui formari debere ostendit.Matth.5.Et sanè multos inuenire licet, qui de Dei in nos amore multa splendidè dicunt,in eo autem impingunt,quòd sufficere putant horum cognitionem,nec ad se pertinere,vt Dei bonitatem sibi imitandam proponant.Quibus sententiam hanc occinere oportet,vt quid sui sit officij intelligant. Subest tamen & altior quædam huius præcepti causa, quod nos iuxta Dei exemplū proximos diligere iubet. Hoc enim omnes prætextus eripit, quibus omissa charitatis officia excusa-mus, dum in singulis hominibus caro nostra inuida & maligna aliquid animaduertit, cuius gratia amore nostro & beneficijs indignos censet. Nam quos abs se prorsus alienos & nullo propinqui-tatis gradu sibi coniunctos esse videt eos impunè negligi posse credit. In alijs peccata & vitia sufficientem causam esse existimat, propter quam charitas illis denegetur. Quod si rursus in eos incide-rit, qui aliquando nobis hostes & iniurij fuerunt, mox sibi permissum putat, ut ipsos non deserat modò in angustijs constitutos, verumetiam ius suum summo rigore persequatur. Alios rursum tam sordidos est videre, qui nemini benefaciendum esse credant, nisi à quo maius & vberius beneficium sperare posint. His satis magna causa est negandi postulatam opem, si qui petit, gratiam vel parem vel maiorem referre nequeat. Sunt etiam, qui rebus suis metuunt, ne beneficia in alios conferendo illas minuant, & quia illis vix quicquam satis est, accumulandis potius quàm legitimè dispensandis opibus inuigilant. At omnibus istis medetur vnum hoc Dei exemplum, quod in dilectione imitari debent, quicunque Dei filij censeri volunt. Deus etenim nos dilexit, qui ab ipsius natura & coniunctione eramus alienissimi, imò iniquissimi apostatæ. Quid enim post peccatum ingressum reliqui habet homo, quod ipsum de coniunctione cum Deo aliquid sperare doceat? Qua ratione ergo tu alienum censebis eum, qui licet sanguine iunctus non fit, homo tamen est, eodem parente Adamo tecum progenitus, & eiusdem cum alijs hominibus conditionis socius? ut interim de arctissimo Christianæ fraternitatis vinculo nihil dicamus. Deus item peccatores dilexit, nos inquam, qui in peccatis concepti & geniti figmenta cordis nostri ab ineunte ætate prava & corrupta habemus. Psal.51. Gen.8. Tu ergo cum talis sis Deo iudice, cur fratris vitia tam manifesta notas, ut tuo amore, tua ope, tuo patrocinio indignum putes? An verò maiorem iustitiæ zelum tibi inesse dices, quàm Deo, cuius iudicia omnia sunt iustitia & Veritas? Deus hostes diligere dignatus est, & eos quidem hostes, qui diuinæ maiestatis sedem affectare ausi fuerant, qui suis viribus cœlos conscendere conabantur, qui crudelissimæ mortis filio eius authores fuerunt. Quæ ergo tanta in te esse potest fratris iniuria, quæ illum odio dignum esse probet? Deus inopes & egenos dilexit, à quibus nihil vel petere vel accipere potest, quo opus habeat. Quid enim fontibonorum inexhausto daret omnis boni expers, & damnationis reus homuncio? Quæ ergo dementia est fratrem inopem & opis indigum negligere, qui si omnia fallant, preces habet, quibus pro te apud Deum intercedat, imò Deum habet liberalissimum beneficiorum, quæ in illum conferuntur, remuneratorem. Denique, ea in nos fuit Dei patris liberalitas, ut nô quid ipse habeat, sed quid nobis desit, magna solicitudine inspexisse videatur. Vidit victus indigos: & mox terram, aerem, aquas & animalia omnia nobis ad victum inseruire voluit. Vidit vestitu opus esse: nec mora, ex terra & animalibus illum petere iusit. Vidit propter infinita pericula tutores esse oportere, qui nos defendant: & ne nobis diutius isti deessent, angelos dedit, qui circa nos castra metentur & ab insidijs hostilibus liberent. Et quasi parum fecisset, cum filij sui morte nos opus habere videret, illum cœlitus demissum carne miserabili & mortali vestiri, omne genus malorum subire, esuriem & sitim perpeti, opprobrijs peti, & tandem in ara Crucis post acerbissimos dolores expirare voluit, eiusdem rei spectatorem se præbuit, quam nec Sol hic videre, nec petræ & rudis tellus sine motu, doloris teste, sustinere potuerunt. Tu verò homo auarissime, rem grauem ducis, si pecunijs, si frugibus, si vestitu fratris necessitati subuenire iubearis, quem Deus filij sui corpore cibare, & eiusdem iustitia vestire dignatus est? I nunc & Dei filium te esse iacta, qui tanta liberalitate regni cœlorum thesauros in filio suo nobis profudit, cum tu nummos contempleris in arca, quibus fratri inopia pereunti subuenire poteras, & thesaurum tibi in cœlis immortalem acquirere.
units.tr: III. Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another. He sets before us the example of God the Father, so that we understand it applies to us, as Christ himself also admonishes when he shows that the affection of our love ought to be shaped not after the example of the publicans but after that of his Father. (Matt. 5.) And indeed one may find many who speak splendidly of God's love toward us, yet they stumble at this point: they think it enough to know this, and that it does not pertain to them to set God's goodness before themselves as something to imitate. To such people this sentence must be sung, so that they may understand what their duty is. Yet there is also a deeper reason for this precept, which bids us love our neighbours after the example of God. For it takes away every pretext by which we excuse neglecting the duties of charity, whenever our envious and malicious flesh notices in individual men something on account of which it judges them unworthy of our love and our kindness. For it believes that those whom it sees to be wholly strangers to it, and bound to it by no degree of kinship, may safely be neglected. In others it thinks sins and vices are a sufficient cause for denying them charity. And if again it falls upon those who have at some time been our enemies and wrongdoers, it straightway thinks it has permission not only to abandon them when they are in distress, but even to pursue its right with the utmost rigour. Others again are so mean that they believe no one should be done a kindness except someone from whom they can hope for a greater and richer return. For these people there is reason enough to refuse the help that is asked, if the one who asks cannot repay the favour with an equal or greater one. There are also those who fear that by bestowing benefits on others they will diminish their own goods, and because nothing is ever enough for them, they watch over the accumulation of their wealth rather than its lawful distribution. But one example of God cures all these faults, and all who wish to be counted as sons of God ought to imitate it in love. For God loved us, who were most alien to his nature and fellowship, indeed most unjust apostates. For what does man have left after the entry of sin that could teach him to hope for anything of fellowship with God? By what reasoning, then, will you judge alien the man who, though not joined to you by blood, is nonetheless a man, born of the same parent Adam as you and a partner with other men in the same condition? Not to mention for the moment the closest bond of Christian brotherhood. God also loved sinners, I say us, who were conceived and born in sins and have from our earliest age the thoughts of our hearts evil and corrupt. (Ps. 51; Gen. 8.) Since, then, you are such a person before God the judge, why do you note so plainly your brother's faults that you think him unworthy of your love, your help, and your protection? Or will you say that you have a greater zeal for righteousness than God, whose judgments are all righteousness and truth? God deigned to love enemies, and indeed those enemies who had dared to aspire to the throne of the divine majesty, who tried to climb the heavens by their own strength, who were the authors of the most cruel death of his Son. What, then, can be so great an injury from your brother that would prove him worthy of hatred? God loved the poor and needy, from whom he can neither ask nor receive anything he needs. For what would a little man, lacking every good and guilty of damnation, give to the inexhaustible fount of goods? What madness, then, is it to neglect a brother who is poor and in need of help, when he has, if all else fails, prayers by which he may intercede for you with God, and indeed has God himself as the most generous rewarder of the benefits conferred on him. Finally, the liberality of God the Father toward us was such that he seems to have looked, with great concern, not at what he himself has, but at what we lack. He saw that we lacked food, and at once he willed that the earth, the air, the waters and all animals should serve us for sustenance. He saw that we needed clothing, and without delay he commanded us to seek it from the earth and from animals. He saw that because of infinite dangers we needed guardians to defend us, and so that these would not be wanting to us for long, he gave us angels, who encamp about us and free us from hostile snares. And as if he had done too little, when he saw that we had need of the death of his Son, he willed that this Son, sent down from heaven, should be clothed in wretched and mortal flesh, undergo every kind of evil, suffer hunger and thirst, be assailed with reproaches, and at last expire on the altar of the Cross after the most bitter sufferings; he showed himself a spectator of that very thing which neither this Sun could look upon, nor the rocks and the bare earth could endure without moving, as a witness of grief. But you, most greedy man, do you think it a burdensome thing if you are bidden to relieve your brother's need with money, with produce, with clothing, when God has deigned to feed you with the body of his Son and clothe you with his righteousness? Go now and boast that you are a son of God, when with such great liberality he has poured out in his Son for us the treasures of the kingdom of heaven, while you gaze at coins in your chest, with which you could have helped your brother perishing in poverty, and acquired for yourself an immortal treasure in heaven.

units.la: Hæc & multa alia suo exemplo docet cœlestis pater, cuius charitas erga nos immensa & infinita est. Hanc nos imitari decet, & licet ad eius perfectionem ascendere non possimus, ultima tamen sectemur vestigia, ut ex huius studio ceu infallibili nota, pro veris & germanis Dei filijs agnosci, & tandem cum Iesu Christo, domino & saluatore nostro, in cœlesti patria viuere possimus: cui debetur benedictio, gloria, honor, & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: These things, and many others, the heavenly Father teaches by his example, and his love toward us is immense and infinite. It becomes us to imitate it, and although we cannot ascend to its perfection, let us nevertheless follow its final footprints, so that by the pursuit of this, as by an infallible mark, we may be recognised as true and genuine sons of God, and at last may be able to live with Jesus Christ, our Lord and Saviour, in the heavenly fatherland: to whom belong blessing, glory, honour and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXV.
units.tr: HOMILIA XXV.

units.la: Deum nemo vidit vnquam. Si diligamus nos invicem, Deus in nobis manet, & charitas eius perfecta est in nobis. Ex hoc cognoscimus, quod in eo manemus, & ipse in nobis, quoniā de spi-ritu suo
units.tr: God no one has seen at any time. If we love one another, God abides in us, and his love is perfected in us. By this we know that we abide in him, and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.

units.la: ritu suo dedit nobis. Et nos vidimus & testamur, quod pater misit filium suum, servatorem mundi. Quisquis confessus fuerit, quod Jesus est filius Dei, Deus in eo manet, & ipse in Deo.
units.tr: Of his Spirit he has given us. And we have seen and testify that the Father sent his Son, the Saviour of the world. Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.

units.la: Innatum est homini ex originis peccato philautiae vitium, quod privati commodi perquàm studiosos, à fraterna autem dilectione alienissimos reddit. Non proderit ergo charitatis praeceptum leviter propositisse, sed ad eius observationem crebro & firmis argumentis exhortari oportet, ne quid relinquatur, quod caro, suijpsius amans, posit objicere. Vidit hoc singulari studio Jo-annes Apostolus, qui inter alia Dei patris exemplum adduxit, cuius diligens consyderatio vanos esse docet omnes praetextus, quibus omissa fraternae dilectionis officia multi excusare solent, eo quod Deus à se alienissimos, peccatores indignos, hostes denique & laesae maiestatis reos sic dilexit, ut filium suum unigenitum pro illis traderet. At dum haec proponuntur, alia remora incidit, quae in charitate praestanda tardiores reddit. Sunt enim, qui putant Deo minime serviri, etiamsi opes suas omnes in proximos distribuant, cum nulla sit inter divinam maiestatem & homines peccatores communio & societas. Satius ergo fore arbitrantur, si fortunas suas sibijpsis servent, vel in cultum Dei externum conferant. Sic enim illas in ipsum Deum certius impendi. Caeterum huic opinioni, quae charitati fraternae prorsus inimica, superstitionum vero foecundissima parens est, Joannes in praesenti occurrens, docet, nos per beneficentiam & fraternam dilectionem cum ipso Deo conjungi, & quae in fratres conferuntur, Deum sibi collata putare. Deinde, ne quis hinc opera justitiam stabiliri putaret, Christi & fidei Christianae mysteria attingit, ut constet, de qua charitate nobis loquatur.
units.tr: From the sin of origin there is innate in man the vice of self-love, which makes men very eager for private advantage and most alien from brotherly love. It will therefore not be enough to have set forth the precept of love lightly; one must urge its observance often and with firm arguments, lest anything remain which the flesh, lover of itself, might put forward as an objection. The apostle John saw this with singular zeal. Among other things he adduced the example of God the Father, whose diligent consideration teaches that all the pretexts by which many commonly excuse the omission of the duties of brotherly love are empty: namely, that God so loved those most alien from himself, unworthy sinners, enemies and finally guilty of treason against his majesty, that he delivered his only-begotten Son for them. But while these things are being set forth, another hindrance arises, which makes men slower in exercising love. For there are those who think that God is not served at all, even if they distribute all their goods among their neighbours, since there is no communion or fellowship between the divine majesty and sinful men. They therefore judge it better, if they keep their fortunes for themselves, or contribute them to the external worship of God; for in this way, they think, those goods are more surely spent on God himself. But John, meeting this opinion in the present passage, which is utterly hostile to brotherly love and a most fruitful parent of superstitions, teaches that we are joined to God himself through beneficence and brotherly love, and that what is conferred upon the brethren is regarded by him as conferred on himself. Then, lest anyone should think that righteousness is established by works from this, he touches upon the mysteries of Christ and the Christian faith, so that it may be clear what kind of love he is speaking of to us.

units.la: I. Deum nemo vidit unquam. Si diligamus nos invicem, Deus in nobis manet, & charitas eius perfecta est in nobis. Ex hoc cognoscimus, quod in eo manemus, & ipse in nobis, quoniam de spiritu suo dedit nobis. Est haec prima huius loci pars, quae docet, nos per beneficentiam & fraternam charitatem cum ipso Deo conjungi. Probat hoc argumento ex Dei natura sumpto. Deum nemo vidit unquam. Natu-ra enim invisibilis est & lucem habitat inaccessam. 1. Tim.6. Nemo igitur illi corporaliter appro-pinquare potest, ut fortunas suas illi offerat, aut externis officiis ipsum demereri possit. Ut enim illum nec coram videre, nec accedere possumus, quoad in carne hac mortali agimus: ita nostris bonis & quaecunq; in hoc mundo habentur, minimè indiget, cum spiritus aeternus sit, & ab omni corruptione alienissimus, sibiq; ipsi & omnibus creaturis sufficiat. Falleris igitur quisquis es, qui opibus tuis Deo ita servire instituis, quasi is eis vel opus habeat, vel illas de manibus tuis requi-rat. Nec enim domum sibi aedificari petit, cui thronus est coelum & terra scabellum pedum suorum. Isa.66. Non cibos postulat, qui non esurit: nec potum, qui sitim non vllam patitur. Psal. 50. Vestitu quoq; non indiget, qui nec erubescere opus habet propter peccati conscientiam, nec frigori & tempestatum iniquitati subiacet. Quid ergo de meis opibus faciam, quaeris? Annon meipsum & omnia mea Deo debeo? Debes omnino, & verè hoc fateris. Sed Deo da, quod ille postulat: opes vero & fortunae bona illis distribue, quos ille tuae fidei commissos esse voluit. Joannem itaque audi: Si diligamus nos invicem, Deus in nobis manet, & eius charitas perfecta est in nobis. Non nostris indiget Deus, sed indigent hi, quos ille pro suis agnoscit. Eos si diligamus, & omni prosequamur charitatis officio, Deus in nobis manebit. Sic enim ipsius charitas in nobis perfi-cietur, id est, ea faciemus, quae nos Dei amantes esse testabuntur, adeoq; ipse Deus in se collata pu-tabit, quaecunq; juxta ipsius mandatum suis conferuntur. Consentiunt haec ijs quae filius Dei in evangelio docet, qui in novissimo die suis dicturus est: Quaecunque fecistis uni de fratribus his meis minimis, mihi fecistis. Matth.25. Erant haec diligenter examinanda ijs, qui hodie mirum Dei & Christi amorem simulant, & Judaeorum ingratitudinem detestantur, qui tot modis in Christum injurij fuerunt, in cuius honorem & gloriam omnes suas fortunas unà cum corporibus & animabus suis impendere debebát. Pollicentur autem de se mira, quasi si nunc in terris Christus ageret, omnia sua in illum essent collaturi. Interim verò illum esurire vident in membris suis, nec pascunt. Vident sitientem, nec potum praebent. Nudum algere vident, nec vestiunt: cum ipsi interim non necessaria modo habeant, verumetiam ijs quae luxui serviunt, abundent. Peregrinum hinc inde oberrare conspicantur, nec in domum suam colligunt. Aegrotum, captum & varie aflli-ctum non consolantur, nec ulla tangitur membrorum Christi miseria, sed omnem illam fusq; deq; ferunt, modo illis bene sit. Quid de his aliud dicemus, quàm quòd ex his Apostoli verbis legiti-mè colligitur, in illis nec Deum manere, nec Dei dilectionem in ipsis habere locum? Nec habent quo se excusent, cū idem Christus dicat: Quod non fecistis uni de minimis his, nec mihi fecistis.
units.tr: I. "God no one has seen at any time. If we love one another, God abides in us, and his love is perfected in us. By this we know that we abide in him, and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit." This is the first part of this place, which teaches that we are joined to God himself through beneficence and brotherly love. He proves this by an argument drawn from the nature of God. God no one has seen at any time. For his nature is invisible, and he dwells in light inaccessible (1 Tim. 6). No one therefore can approach him bodily, so as to offer him his fortunes, or be able to merit him by external services. For as we can neither see him face to face nor approach him, so long as we live in this mortal flesh, so he has no need of our goods, nor of whatever is had in this world, since he is eternal spirit and utterly free from all corruption, and suffices to himself and to all creatures. You are mistaken, then, whoever you are, who determine to serve God with your riches as if he had need of them or required them at your hands. For he does not ask for a house to be built for himself, to whom heaven is the throne and earth the footstool of his feet (Isa. 66). He does not ask for food, who does not hunger; nor for drink, who suffers no thirst (Ps. 50). He does not need clothing, who has no need to blush on account of the consciousness of sin, nor is subject to cold and the injuries of the weather. "What then shall I do with my riches?" you ask. Do I not owe myself and all that is mine to God? You certainly owe it, and truly you confess this. But give to God what he asks; distribute your riches and goods to those whom he has willed to be committed to your faith. Hear John, then: If we love one another, God abides in us, and his love is perfected in us. God does not need our things, but those whom he acknowledges as his own need them. If we love them and attend to them with every office of love, God will abide in us. For thus his love will be perfected in us, that is, we will do those things which will testify that we are lovers of God, and God himself will regard as conferred on himself whatever is conferred on his people according to his command. These things agree with what the Son of God teaches in the Gospel, who, on the last day, is going to say to his own: "Whatever you did to one of these my least brethren, you did to me" (Matt. 25). These things ought to have been carefully examined by those who today feign a wondrous love of God and Christ, and detest the ingratitude of the Jews, who in so many ways were injurious to Christ, to whose honour and glory they ought to have devoted all their fortunes together with their bodies and souls. Yet they promise wonders about themselves, as if Christ were now living on earth and they were going to contribute all their goods to him. Meanwhile, however, they see him hungering in his members and do not feed him. They see him thirsting and do not give him drink. They see him naked and shivering and do not clothe him, while they themselves not only have necessities but abound even in those things which serve luxury. They behold the stranger wandering hither and thither and do not take him into their house. They do not console the sick, the captive and the variously afflicted, and no misery of the members of Christ touches them; rather they bear all that lightly, provided it goes well with them. What shall we say of these, except that from the words of the Apostle it is rightly gathered that God does not abide in them, nor does the love of God have a place in them? Nor have they anything by which they can excuse themselves, since Christ himself says: "Because you did not do it to one of these least, you did not do it to me."

units.la: Cæterum, ne quid dubij in animis nostris relinquatur, ipsius spiritus Christi, quem is suis fideli-bus largitur, testimonium adducit, sic nimirum monens, vt vel suos ipsorum animos interroget, in quibus spiritum de hac communione, quæ beneficis cum Deo est, testátem sint audituri. Cum enim Christi spiritus sit, non potest diuersum ab eo testari, quod ipse Christus promisit. Plura de spiritus testimonio supra diximus, quare in præsenti pauca hæc sufficiant. Quia tamé verbis Apo-stoli alia quoq; insunt, quæ nostræ institutioni seruire possunt, ea priusquam ab his discedamus, inspici oportet.
units.tr: Moreover, lest any doubt remain in our minds, he adduces the testimony of the Spirit of Christ himself, whom he bestows on his faithful, thus surely admonishing them to question their own minds, in which they will hear the testimony of this fellowship which exists with God through beneficence. For since it is the Spirit of Christ, it cannot testify anything different from what Christ himself promised. We have said more about the testimony of the Spirit above, so let these few things suffice here. But since other things also lie in the words of the Apostle which can serve our instruction, these must be examined before we depart from them.

units.la: Primùm de vero Dei cultu locus hic nos instruit. Si enim Deus inuisibilis & incorporeus est, non corporeis & externis rebus coli poterit. Inter homines enim sic comparatum videmus, vt se-rui dominorum ingenio sese accommodare studeant, quia non aliter illis placere poterunt. Similiter qui Deo placere volent, ijs studeant oportet, quæ diuinæ naturæ & ingenio conformia sunt. At Deus spiritus est. Spiritu ergo adorari & coli vult. Cuius sententiæ testem & authorem habemus ipsum Christum, qui ab æterno in sinu patris est. Ioannis 4. Nisi ergo animos nostros Deo consecremus, frustra illi aurum & argentum, frustra vestes & cibos dabimus, frustra etiam illi domus & palatia vel templa ædificabimus. Facit huc, quod apud prophetā dicitur: Populus hic ore mihi appropinquat, & labijs honorat me, cor autem eius procul à me abest. Ifa.29. Quòd si labijs & sermone, qui ab homine procedit, frustra Deo appropinquatur, multò minus per ea Deus coli poterit, quæ extra hominem posita sunt. Nec obstat, quod ab ipso Deo externos ritus olim tradi-tos fuisse, & tabernaculum cum templo ad Dei præscriptum ædificatum legimus. Fuerunt enim omnia illa rerum sacrarum signa & sacramenta salutis, non in hunc finem tradita, quòd Deus ex his aliquid vtilitatis aut voluptatis capere posset, sed vt nostræ carnis infirmitas haberet, quo su-stentaretur. Siquidem ea est humani ingenij conditio, vt non nisi externis inhæres spiritualia mi-nus capiat. Quòd si externa, quibus occupetur, nulla occurrant, mox ex seipso fingit, quibus Deū coli posse arbitratur. Et hæc humani ingenij, siue curiositas siue audacia, immensum illud super-stitionum & humanarum traditionum pelagus peperit, cuius fluctibus syncerior religio multis seculis obruta & demersa fuit. Ne qua ergo daretur aliquid simile audendi occasio, nec deesset cari-ni quod in religione ageret, æternæ Dei sapientiæ consilio eiusmodi Ceremoniæ institutæ sunt, quæ & omnem salutis nostræ rationem nobis adumbrarent, & nostri nos admonerent officij, si-mulq; animos nostros in cœlestium rerum consyderationem subueherent. Nec vnquam ea Dei mens fuit, vt externis homine inhærerent, quasi ijs Deus reuera coli possit. Imò quoties spiritua-li cultu neglecto, circa externas ceremonias occupati fuerunt, toties per sanctos Dei ministros ac cusati & grauiter correpti sunt. Exempla eius rei ex veteri testamento infinita adduci poterant, sed legantur quæ Psal.50. Ifa.1. & 58. Mich.6. Hose.6. Amos 5. Ierem.4. & 7. scripta sunt, & verum deprehendes esse, quod modò diximus. Nec alia est noui testamenti ratio. Vt enim paucis ceremonijs nos grauare decreuit dominus, ne ipsius iugum Mosaico durius videretur: ita nec in illis quidem salutem quæri voluit. Instituit verbi ministerium, & verbum audiri vult. Sed non placent auditores, qui auribus illud percipiunt, nisi animis recondant & fructus ferant per fidem & patientiam. Luc.8. Adhæc fatuis architectis eos confert, qui in audiendo verbo occupantur, sed vt illud factis exprimant, minus soliciti sunt, Matth.7. Ita ad preces quidem adhortatur, & peccandi formulam præscribit. Pharifaicam verò tautologiam & inanem precādi strepitum seueritate magna damnat. Matth.6. Sed & sacramenta dedit, fidei & salutis nostræ signacula, Baptismū & Cœnam. At de baptismo Apostolus testatur, quòd non externus is saluet, quo carnis sordes abluuntur, sed certa conscientiæ fiducia, qua Deo per Christum nitimur. 1. Pet.3. Et Paulus eos, qui ad domini mensam accedunt indignè, iudicium sibi manducare docet: quæ sententia infelici Iudæ proditoris exitu, & peste Corinthiacam ecclesiam infestante, non obscurè confirmatur. Ioan.13.1. Corinth.11. Quòd si vero Ceremoniæ diuinitus institutæ, Deo non placent, nec his illi seruiri potest, quid obsecro de eo cultu dicemus, qui totus in Ceremoniarum obseruatione consistit, quæ nec scripturarum, nec veteris ecclesiæ consuetudine approbantur? Nonne hos magis desipere di-cemus? Certè humanas traditiones Dei sententia iam olim iugulatas esse, sæpe dictum est. Quoties ergo vel sacella ædificare, vel vestes Deo consecrare, vel opes in eius cultū conferre, vel cha-meunijs & inutilibus ieiunijs Deum demereri iuberis, semper hæ sententiæ animo tuo obuersen-tur: Deum nemo vidit vnquam. Deus spiritus est, & veri adoratores spiritu & veritate adorant. Quibus & hanc Pauli adde: Corporalis exercitatio paululum habet vtilitatis: at pietas (verus ille & spiritualis cultus) ad omnia vtilis est, vt quæ promissiones habeat vitæ præsentis & futuræ. 1. Tim.4. Noli Deo obtrudere, quæ non petit, & quibus non indiget. Noli saxis & truncis sub religionis prętextu offerre, quod viuis Dei imaginibus & egentibus Christi membris debetur.
units.tr: First, this passage instructs us about the true worship of God. If God is invisible and incorporeal, he cannot be worshipped with corporeal and external things. For among men we see it is so arranged that servants strive to accommodate themselves to the disposition of their masters, since otherwise they cannot please them. Similarly, those who wish to please God ought to strive for those things which are in conformity with the divine nature and disposition. But God is spirit. He wishes therefore to be adored and worshipped in spirit. We have as witness and author of this saying Christ himself, who is from eternity in the bosom of the Father. John 4. Unless therefore we consecrate our souls to God, we shall give him gold and silver in vain, we shall give him garments and food in vain, and in vain we shall build him houses, palaces or temples. To this applies what is said by the prophet: "This people draws near to me with its mouth and honours me with its lips, but its heart is far from me." Isa. 29. But if God is approached in vain with lips and speech which proceed from a man, much less can God be worshipped by those things which are placed outside man. Nor does it stand in the way that we read that external rites were handed down by God himself in former times, and that the tabernacle along with the temple was built according to God's prescription. For all those signs and sacraments of sacred things and of salvation were handed down not for this end, that God might derive some profit or pleasure from them, but so that the weakness of our flesh might have something by which it could be sustained. For such is the condition of the human mind that, unless it cleaves to external things, it grasps spiritual things the less. But if no external things present themselves on which it may be occupied, it straightway fashions for itself those things by which it thinks God can be worshipped. And this curiosity or audacity of the human mind has produced that immense sea of superstitions and human traditions, by whose waves the purer religion was overwhelmed and submerged for many centuries. Therefore, lest any occasion for similar daring be given, and lest there be lacking some reason for acting in religion, by the plan of the eternal wisdom of God such ceremonies were instituted, which both set forth to us every manner of our salvation and admonish us of our duty, and at the same time lift up our minds to the contemplation of heavenly things. Nor was it ever God's intention that men should cleave to external things, as if God could truly be worshipped by them. On the contrary, as often as men, neglecting spiritual worship, were occupied with external ceremonies, so often were they accused and sharply rebuked by the holy ministers of God. Innumerable examples of this matter could be adduced from the Old Testament, but let the passages written in Ps. 50, Isa. 1 and 58, Mic. 6, Hos. 6, Amos 5, Jer. 4 and 7 be read, and you will find true what we have just said. Nor is the reasoning of the New Testament otherwise. For just as the Lord decided to burden us with few ceremonies, lest his yoke seem harsher than the Mosaic, so neither did he wish salvation to be sought in these. He instituted the ministry of the Word, and wills the Word to be heard. But hearers who take it in with their ears do not please him, unless they lay it up in their hearts and bear fruit through faith and patience. Luke 8. Moreover, he compares to foolish builders those who are occupied in hearing the word, but who are less concerned to express it in deeds. Matt. 7. Thus he indeed exhorts to prayer and prescribes a formula of praying, but he condemns with great severity the Pharisaic tautology and the empty noise of praying. Matt. 6. He also gave sacraments, the seals of faith and of our salvation, Baptism and the Supper. But concerning baptism the Apostle testifies that it is not the external thing that saves, by which the filth of the flesh is washed away, but the sure confidence of conscience, by which we rely on God through Christ. 1 Pet. 3. And Paul teaches that those who come unworthily to the Lord's table eat judgment to themselves; which sentence is not obscurely confirmed by the unhappy end of Judas the traitor and by the plague which afflicted the Corinthian church. John 13. 1 Cor. 11. But if ceremonies instituted by God himself do not please God, nor can he be served by them, what, I beseech you, shall we say of that worship which consists wholly in the observance of ceremonies that are approved neither by the Scriptures nor by the custom of the ancient Church? Shall we not say that such people are rather out of their minds? Certainly it has often been said that human traditions were long ago slain by the sentence of God. Therefore, whenever you are bidden either to build shrines, or to consecrate garments to God, or to confer wealth on his worship, or to win God's favour by dull and useless fasts, let these sayings always be before your mind: No one has ever seen God. God is spirit, and those who truly worship him worship in spirit and truth. To these add also this saying of Paul: "Bodily exercise profits a little, but godliness (that true and spiritual worship) is profitable for all things, since it has the promises of the present life and of the life to come." 1 Tim. 4. Do not press upon God what he does not ask for and does not need. Do not, under the pretext of religion, offer to stones and tree-trunks what is owed to the living images of God and to the needy members of Christ.

units.la: Secundò spiritus testimonium adducit Apostolus, quem & Paulus nostræ salutis arrhabo-nem vocat.Ephes.1. Observandum autem diligenter hoc spiritus Christi officium, quod non in nobis modò,verumetiam in alijs,qui nos vident, locum habet. Ut enim anima, quæ & ipsa spiritus est,non modò nos vivere facit,sed & vitæ actiones operatur, ex quibus alij quoque nos vivere agnoscant: ita Christi spiritus facit quidem,ut ipsi vivamus per fidem in conspectu Dei,simul vero illorum operum in nobis causa efficiens & author est,quæ nos vitæ filios & hæredes esse palàm declarant.Siquidem otiosus esse non potest spiritus,quin ea operetur indesinenter,quæ naturæ ipsius conformia sunt. Quamobrem Paulus ut carni,ita & spiritui opera sua propria tribuit.Galat. 5.Servit hoc in eum finem, ut ex hominum operibus de spiritu, quo intrinsecus aguntur,iudicare discamus. Ubi enim opera carnis & impuri mundi regnant,Dei spiritus esse nequit.Ubi verò opera fidei,charitatis,innocentiæ,& quæ eius generis sunt,primatum obtinent, Christi spiritum adesse,dubium non est. Docet hæc ipse Christus, qui pharisæos ex diabolo progenitos esse,& illius spiritu regi probat, quia mendaces & homicidæ sint. Ioan.8.Et alibi,è fructu arborem agnosci dicit.Matth.12.Arguit hoc illorum vanam & superbam gloriationem, qui cum Christum prosi-teantur, ita vivunt, ut spiritum Christi ab illis alienissimum esse,nemo non videat.Quod si quis spiritum Christi non habet,hic non est eius.Rom.8.
units.tr: Secondly, the Apostle adduces the testimony of the Spirit, which Paul also calls the pledge of our salvation. Eph. 1. This office of the Spirit of Christ is to be observed carefully, for it holds a place not only in us but also in others who see us. For just as the soul, which is itself also spirit, not only makes us live but also produces the actions of life, by which others too recognise that we live, so the Spirit of Christ indeed makes us live before God in faith, and at the same time is the efficient cause and author of those works in us which openly declare that we are sons and heirs of life. For the Spirit cannot be idle, but without ceasing performs those things which are in conformity with its own nature. Wherefore Paul ascribes works of his own to the flesh and likewise to the Spirit. Gal. 5. This serves to the end that from men's works we may learn to judge of the Spirit by which they are inwardly moved. For where the works of the flesh and of the impure world reign, the Spirit of God cannot be present. But where works of faith, of charity, of innocence and those of this kind hold the first place, there is no doubt that the Spirit of Christ is present. Christ himself teaches this, who declares that the Pharisees were born of the devil and proves that they are ruled by his spirit, because they are liars and murderers. John 8. And elsewhere he says that the tree is known from its fruit. Matt. 12. This refutes the empty and proud boasting of those who, while they profess Christ, so live that everyone sees the Spirit of Christ to be most alien from them. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his. Rom. 8.

units.la: Porrò cum charitatis opera commendantur, multos videre est,qui ea doctrina operum justitiam stabiliri putant, cui non sine Christi ignominia nostræ redemptionis & salutis gloriam tribuunt. Ne quam ergo occasionem haberent isti homines,Apostolus Christi & fidei in Christum mysteria subiungit,ut sic ostendat, quæ nam illa charitas sit,quæ nos in Dei communionem perducit,& ut hæc merito Christi nihil omnino detrahat.
units.tr: Moreover, when the works of charity are commended, one may see many who think that by this doctrine of works the righteousness of works is established, and who ascribe to it the glory of our redemption and salvation, not without dishonour to Christ. Therefore, lest these people have any occasion, the Apostle adds the mysteries of Christ and of faith in Christ, so as to show what that charity is which brings us into communion with God, and that it takes nothing at all away from the merit of Christ.

units.la: II. Et nos vidimus & testamur, quod pater misit filium suum, servatorem mundi. Quisquis confessus fuerit, quod Jesus est filius Dei, Deus in eo manet, & ipse in Deo. Finis & scopus horum est,de ea charitate loqui Apostolum,quæ ex fide in Christum promanat, & proinde charitatem communionis cum Deo eatenus causam esse, quatenus fidem sibi coniunctam habet, imò quatenus fidei effectus,sive opus est.Patet id ex eo, quòd fidei tribuit hoc ipsum, quod paulò ante charitati dederat.Dixit enim:Si diligamus nos invicem,Deus in nobis manet.Hic verò:Quisquis (inquit) confessus fuerit,quòd Jesus est filius Dei,Deus in eo manet,&c.Aut ergo duas,easque inter se diversas,vias statuere oportet,quibus cum Deo coniungamur (quod cum omni scripturarum veritate & Christi doctrina pugnat) aut fatendum erit, Joannem de ea charitate loqui, quam fides in nobis operatur, & communionem cum Deo charitati propter fidem tribui, non propter opera, quæ ipsi facimus. Et sanè multum refert observasse diligenter coniunctionem fidei in Christum & fraternæ dilectionis, quæ tam arcta est,ut separari nullo modo possint. Quia enim fides Deo uni solidè nititur, per Jesum Christum, fieri non potest, quin singularem Dei bonitatem agnoscat,quam is in filio suo nobis præstitit. At qua ratione hanc agnoscet, ut non eundem diligat? Quin potius fidei proprium est, quòd animum hominis totum cum omnibus, tam internis quàm externis facultatibus,in Dei amorem rapiat.Quis enim non ex animo amet,in quo omnem suam spem repositam esse novit? Atqui amoris consequens est obedientia, quam voluntariam ijs præstamus,quos amore syncero prosequimur.Sed & ea amoris vis est,ut in omnes sese extendat,quos personæ adamatæ coniunctos esse novimus.Quare cum Deus in filio suo omnes homines sibi coniunxerit , & evidentia existant in omnibus illis divini amoris argumenta , quo pacto non diliget homines is,qui Deo fidit,Deum amat,& à Dei præceptis totus pendet, maximè cum dilectionem hanc abs se requiri audiat? Vides ergo naturali coniunctione cohærere inter se fidem & charitatem.Et proprie loquendo,iustificationem & salutem fidei tribui debere, quia per hanc solam Christum,qui nostra iustitia est (1.Cor.1.) apprehendimus. Eadem tamen abusivè tum propter coniunctionem illam arctissimam interdum charitati tribuitur, tum ut intelligamus, scripturas quando de fide loquuntur,non nudam aliquam opinionem commendare,sed vivificum nostri animi assensum, quem Deo sic præbemus, ut eidem obtemperare studeamus in omnibus.Vidit hoc & Paulus,quando inquit: In Christo Jesu nihil quicquam valet,nisi fides per dilectionem operans. Galat.5.Turpissimè ergo falluntur & fallunt, qui per charitatis opera operum justitiam stabiliri docent,cum hæc ipsa non aliter Deo grata sint,nisi quatenus ex fide emanant. Sine fide enim ali quem Deo placere,impossibile est.Heb.11.Et quicquid sine fide fit,peccatum est.Roma.14. Qua de causa & pharisæorum eleemosynæ damnantur, quòd absq; fide , & non propter divini nominis gloriam,sed privati commodi gratia fiebant.Matth.6. Sunt autem singula,quæ hic dicuntur, diligenter excutienda,cùm non parua fidei & salutis nostræ mysteria contineant.
units.tr: II. "And we have seen and testify that the Father sent his Son, the Saviour of the world. Whoever shall confess that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him and he in God." The aim and purpose of these words is that the Apostle is speaking of that charity which springs from faith in Christ, and therefore that charity is the cause of communion with God only so far as it is joined with faith, indeed so far as it is an effect or work of faith. This is clear from the fact that he attributes to faith the very thing which a little before he had given to charity. For he had said: "If we love one another, God abides in us." Here, however, he says: "Whoever (he says) shall confess that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him," etc. Either, therefore, we must set up two ways, and these diverse from one another, by which we are joined to God (which is at odds with all the truth of the Scriptures and with the doctrine of Christ), or it must be admitted that John is speaking of that charity which faith works in us, and that communion with God is ascribed to charity on account of faith, not on account of the works which we ourselves do. And indeed it matters much that we have carefully observed the conjunction of faith in Christ and of brotherly love, which is so close that they cannot in any way be separated. For since faith rests solidly on the one God through Jesus Christ, it cannot but acknowledge the singular goodness of God which he has shown us in his Son. But how will it acknowledge this without loving the same? Indeed it is the proper work of faith that it snatches the whole mind of man, with all its faculties, both inward and outward, into the love of God. For who does not love from the heart him in whom he knows all his hope to be placed? And obedience follows love, which we render willingly to those whom we pursue with sincere love. Moreover, the force of love is such that it extends itself to all whom we know to be joined to the beloved person. Wherefore, since God has joined all men to himself in his Son, and since in all of them there are evident tokens of divine love, how should he not love men who trusts in God, loves God, and depends wholly on God's precepts, especially when he hears that this love is required of him? You see therefore that faith and charity cohere with one another by a natural connection. And properly speaking, justification and salvation ought to be ascribed to faith, because by it alone we apprehend Christ, who is our righteousness (1 Cor. 1). Nevertheless, that same thing is sometimes ascribed to charity abusively, both on account of that very close conjunction, and so that we may understand that the Scriptures, when they speak of faith, do not commend some bare opinion, but a living assent of our mind, which we so give to God that we strive to obey him in all things. Paul saw this too, when he says: "In Christ Jesus nothing avails except faith working through love." Gal. 5. Those therefore are most shamefully mistaken, and mislead others, who teach that the righteousness of works is established by the works of charity, since these very works are pleasing to God only so far as they flow from faith. For without faith it is impossible to please God. Heb. 11. And whatever is done without faith is sin. Rom. 14. For this reason even the alms of the Pharisees are condemned, because they were done without faith, and not for the glory of the divine name, but for the sake of private advantage. Matt. 6. Moreover, each of the things said here must be carefully examined, since they contain no small mysteries of faith and of our salvation.

units.la: Primò ait: Vidimus & testamur, quòd pater misit filium.Coprehendit his officiu Apostolorum, certitudinem quoque, usum & finem euangelicæ prædicationis. Est hic, ut homines agnoscant & intelligant singularem Dei bonitatem, quam in filio suo Iesu Christo nobis exhibuit, & proinde ipsi ut fidelissimo parti confidant. Sunt autem huius certi & fidi testes Apostoli, ad hoc muneris ab ipso Christo destinati, qui non de dubiis & ignotis rebus testimonium ferunt, sed de iis, quarum spectatores præsentes fuerunt, eo quod ab initio cum Dei filio, in terris agenti, conuersati sunt. Ioan.15.Act.1.
units.tr: First, he says: "We have seen and we testify that the Father sent the Son." In these words he takes in the office of the apostles, and also the certainty, use and purpose of the gospel preaching. Here the point is that people should recognise and understand the singular goodness of God, which he has shown us in his Son Jesus Christ, and so trust in him as a most faithful Father. The certain and faithful witnesses of this are the apostles, appointed to this office by Christ himself. They do not bear witness to doubtful and unknown things, but to those things of which they were present as eyewitnesses, because from the beginning they lived with the Son of God while he walked on earth. John 15; Acts 1.

units.la: Deinde: Pater (inquit) misit filium, seruatorem mundi. Cum filium à patre missum dicit, omnia Christi mysteria complectitur. Qui mittitur, priusquam mittatur, sit oportet. Quis enim eum, qui nusquam est, mittere poterit? Quod si Christus, priusquam incarnaretur, fuit, & quidem filius fuit eius, à quo mittebatur, non poterat non Deus esse, patri coæternus & consubstantialis. Et missus dicitur in mundum, ut eum qui Dei filius ante secula à patre genitus est (ut Athanasius fatetur) verum hominem in seculo, id est præfinito tempore, ex matre virgine natum esse intelligamus. Ideo autem missum dicit, ut seruator mundi esset. Voluit mundi vocabulo uti, ut Christum ad omnes homines pertinere, & uniuersalem totius humani generis saluatorem esse agnoscere-mus. Est ea cognitio & utilis & necessaria admodum. Nec enim ipse satan negare potest, Dei filium in mundum venisse, & ea fecisse quæ hominum redemptioni seruiebant. Eo autem multos adducit, ut Christum non ad omnes homines ex æquo pertinere putent, & proinde se quoque ex illorum numero esse suspicantur, quos Christi meritum saluare non posit. Est hic proximus ad desperationem gradus, quæ non alia ratione vitare licet, quam ut Christum uniuersalem totius mundi saluatorem esse intelligas. Constat equidem nō omnes homines salutem consequi: sed id hominum improbitati, diffidentiæ & pertinaciæ ascribi debet, qua sibi ipsis interitum asciscunt, non Christo, quem pater vitæ, non mortis, ministrum & authorem esse voluit. Docet hoc unanimis scripturæ sacræ consensus. Quæcunq; enim in hac de Christo habentur, uniuersalia sunt. Primo omnium parenti Adamo promittitur, ut eum ad omnem Adami posteritatem pertinere sciremus. Gene.3. Abrahamo dicitur: In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes. Gene.22. Sed & ipse Christus omnes ad se inuitat, nec quenquam morosè aut importunè reijcit. Venite ad me (inquit) omnes, qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego refocillabo uos. Matth.11. Si quis sitit, veniat ad me & bibat. Ioan.7. Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut filium suum unigenitum daret: ut omnis qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam. Ioan.3. Præterea à suis discessurus, euangelium in omnem orbem terrarum prædicari vult, uniuersalem promissionem adiungens: Quisquis crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, saluabitur. Mar.16. Viderunt hoc ipsum non obscurè Apostoli, qui & Christum saluatorem omnibus promiscuè prædicauerunt, & diserte testati sunt, personarum respectum coram Deo planè nullum esse. Act.10. Rom.2. Et alibi Paulus diserte inquit: Deus vult omnes homines saluos fieri, & ad agnitionem veritatis peruenire. 1.Tim.2. Et supra Apostolus dixit: Christus dedit semetipsum pro peccatis nostris, non pro nostris autem tantum, sed & pro totius mundi. 1.Ioan.2. Nemo igitur perditionem suam, vel immiti Dei patris rigori, vel meriti Christi imperfectioni ascribat: sed inexhaustam Dei patris bonitatem agnoscamus, veramq; esse firmiter credamus Dei sententiam, quæ apud prophetam extat: Perditio ex te est o Israel, salus autem tua ego sum. Hosee.13. Quòd si cui volupe est æternæ prædestinationis mysteria curiosius rimari, & in Dei abscondita penetrare altius, quàm scripturæ docent, id quidem ei per me licet. Sed haud dubiè magno suo malo experietur, quod sapientissimus regum Solomon dixit: Qui scrutator est maiestatis, opprimetur à gloria. Prouerb.25.
units.tr: Then he says: "The Father sent the Son, the Saviour of the world." When he speaks of the Son as sent by the Father, he embraces all the mysteries of Christ. He who is sent must exist before he is sent; for who could send one who is nowhere? But if Christ existed before he was incarnate, and indeed existed as the Son of him by whom he was sent, he could not but be God, co-eternal and consubstantial with the Father. And he is said to be sent into the world so that we may understand that he who, as the Son of God, was begotten of the Father before the ages (as Athanasius confesses), was born in the world, that is, at a appointed time, as a true man of a virgin mother. He is said to be sent so that he might be the Saviour of the world. He chose to use the word "world" so that we might acknowledge that Christ belongs to all men and is the universal Saviour of the whole human race. This knowledge is very useful and altogether necessary. For even Satan himself cannot deny that the Son of God came into the world and did those things which served the redemption of men. But this leads many to suppose that Christ does not belong equally to all men, and so they suspect that they themselves are among those whom Christ's merit cannot save. This is the step next to despair, which cannot be avoided by any other means than by understanding that Christ is the universal Saviour of the whole world. It is certainly true that not all men obtain salvation; but this must be ascribed to the wickedness, distrust and obstinacy of men, by which they bring destruction upon themselves, and not to Christ, whom the Father of life, not of death, willed to be the minister and author of salvation. The unanimous consent of holy Scripture teaches this. For whatever is said about Christ in it is universal. First of all, the promise is made to our first parent Adam, so that we may know that it pertains to all the posterity of Adam. Gen. 3. It is said to Abraham: "In your seed shall all the nations be blessed." Gen. 22. But Christ himself also invites all to himself, and he rejects no one with peevishness or impatience. "Come to me," he says, "all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you." Matt. 11. "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink." John 7. "God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life." John 3. Moreover, about to depart from his own, he wills that the gospel be preached in the whole world, adding a universal promise: "Whoever believes and is baptised will be saved." Mark 16. The apostles, who both preached Christ the Saviour to all without distinction and plainly testified that there is absolutely no respect of persons before God, saw this very thing not obscurely. Acts 10; Rom. 2. And elsewhere Paul says plainly: "God wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth." 1 Tim. 2. And earlier the apostle said: "Christ gave himself for our sins, not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world." 1 John 2. Therefore let no one ascribe his own perdition either to the harsh rigour of God the Father or to the imperfection of Christ's merit; rather let us acknowledge the inexhaustible goodness of God the Father, and firmly believe that the word of God is true, which stands in the prophet: "Destruction is from you, O Israel; but your salvation is in me." Hos. 13. But if anyone wishes to investigate more curiously the mysteries of eternal predestination and to penetrate into God's hidden things more deeply than the Scriptures teach, that is permitted him by me. But he will undoubtedly learn to his great cost what the wisest of kings, Solomon, said: "He who is a searcher of majesty will be overwhelmed by glory." Prov. 25.

units.la: Postremò modum & viam indicat Apostolus, quæ nos tam Christi quàm salutis in ipso confortes facit. Quisquis confessus fuerit, quod Iesus est filius Dei, Deus in eo manet, & ipse in Deo. Confessionis meminit, non quòd Christum ore profiteri, ad salutem sufficiat (multi enim, quem ore profitentur, vita abnegat. Tit.1. Et ipse ait: Multi dicent mihi in illo die: Domine domine: qui-bus respondebo: Non noui vos. Discedite à me operarij iniquitatis, Matth.7.) sed qualem à nobis fidem Christus requirat, docere vult: solidam nimirum & constantem, cuius nos non pudeat coram mundo hoc prauo & adultero. Mar.8. Quare & Paulus fidei confessionem iungit, dicens: Si confessus fueris ore tuo dominum Iesum, & credideris in corde tuo, quòd Deus illum excitauit à mortuis, saluus eris. Corde enim creditur ad iustitiam, ore autem confessio fit ad salutem. Rom.10. Habent hic quod obseruent delicatuli, qui nostro seculo fidei confessionem inter indifferentia ponunt: fidemque in Christum, si quando illorum commodis seruire potest, magno verborum splendore profitentur: ubi vero in fidei hostes incidunt, egregiè quiduis simulare & dissimulare norunt. Sed sunt illi nec frigidi, nec tepidi, & proinde ex ore domini euomentur in exteriores tenebras. Apoc.3. Quid autem confiteri iubet Apostolus? Quòd Iesus sit filius Dei. Hoc ipsum Petrus in euan-gelio confessus esse legitur. Ioan.6. Matt.16. Continet confessio hæc quæcunq; de filio Dei in scri-pturis habentur. De hoc data promissio, quòd conterere debeat caput serpentis. Gen.3. Idem rex Sionis, id est ecclesiæ Dei, constitutus est ab æterno. Psal.2. Eundem populi sui sacerdotem æter-num pater declarauit: Psal.110. De eodem prædictum, quòd infirmitates nostras perferre, discipli-nam quas nos merueramus sustinere, propter nostras iniquitates vulnerari, & sui notitia nos sal-uare debeat. Isa.53. Denique in filio Dei gratiam & veritatem omnesque salutis thesauros exhibi-tos esse, Apostoli omnes docent. Ioan.1. Col.1. & 2. Acto.4. &c. Quisquis ergo Iesum, qui ex Maria virgine homo natus est, Dei filium esse credit & confitetur, idem hunc unicū & solum totius or-bis saluatorem agnoscit, & ex eorum numero est, quibus propter fidem in Christum æternæ vitæ promissio facta est. Possent hic fusius explicari filij Dei mysteria. Sed quia de his alibi diximus, & nusquam non occurrit plura dicendi locus, paucula hæc modò sufficiant.
units.tr: Lastly, the apostle indicates the manner and way which makes us partakers both of Christ and of salvation in him. "Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God." He mentions confession not because it is enough for salvation to profess Christ with the mouth (for many who profess him with their mouths deny him by their life. Titus 1. And he himself says: "Many will say to me in that day, 'Lord, Lord,' to whom I will answer, 'I never knew you. Depart from me, you workers of iniquity.'" Matt. 7), but he wishes to teach what kind of faith Christ requires of us: namely a solid and constant faith, of which we should not be ashamed before this wicked and adulterous world. Mark 8. Therefore Paul also joins the confession of faith, saying: "If you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." Rom. 10. Here the fastidious, who in our age place the confession of faith among indifferent things, and who profess faith in Christ with great show of words whenever it can serve their advantage, but who, when they fall into the enemies of the faith, know very well how to pretend and dissemble anything, have something to take note of. But they are neither cold nor lukewarm, and therefore they will be spewed out of the Lord's mouth into the outer darkness. Rev. 3. But what does the apostle bid us confess? That Jesus is the Son of God. Peter is read to have confessed this very thing in the gospel. John 6; Matt. 16. This confession contains all that is found in the Scriptures concerning the Son of God. Of him was the promise given that he should bruise the head of the serpent. Gen. 3. The same king of Zion, that is, of the Church of God, was appointed from eternity. Ps. 2. The Father declared him the eternal priest of his people. Ps. 110. Of the same it was foretold that he should bear our infirmities, sustain the chastisement which we had deserved, be wounded for our iniquities, and save us by the knowledge of himself. Isa. 53. Finally, all the apostles teach that in the Son of God grace and truth and all the treasures of salvation have been displayed. John 1; Col. 1 and 2; Acts 4, etc. Therefore whoever believes and confesses that Jesus, who was born a man of the virgin Mary, is the Son of God, also acknowledges him to be the only and sole Saviour of the whole world, and is among those to whom the promise of eternal life has been made on account of faith in Christ. The mysteries of the Son of God could be explained here at greater length. But since we have spoken of these elsewhere, and there is never a lack of occasion to say more, let these few things suffice for now.

units.la: Habuimus in præsentis loci explicatione duo præcipua Christianæ religionis capita, in quibus eos exerceri oportet, qui Christum profiteri & in eo saluari volunt, fidem nimirum & charitatem fraternam. Nostrum est hæc duo sic coniungere, vt nec charitatem simulemus absque fide, nec fide mortua, id est, vana & inani opinione gloriemur. Sic enim fiet, vt in præsentis vitæ curriculo sub umbra alarum Dei tutò degere, & olim in cœlis cum Christo regnare liceat, cui debetur benedictio, gloria, honor & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: In the explanation of this passage we have had two chief heads of the Christian religion, in which those who wish to profess Christ and be saved in him ought to exercise themselves, namely faith and brotherly love. It is our task to join these two in such a way that we neither feign love without faith, nor boast of a dead faith, that is, a vain and empty opinion. For thus it will come about that we may be permitted to live safely under the shadow of God's wings through the course of this present life, and one day to reign in heaven with Christ, to whom belongs blessing, glory, honour and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXVI.
units.tr: HOMILY XXVI.

units.la: Et nos cognouimus & credidimus charitatē, quā habet Deus in nobis. Deus charitas est, & qui manet in charitate, in Deo manet, & deus in eo. In hoc perfecta est charitas nobiscū, ut fiduciā habeamus in die iudicij, quòd sicut ille est, & nos sumus in mundo hoc.
units.tr: And we have known and believed the love which God has in us. God is love, and he who abides in love abides in God, and God in him. In this is love made perfect with us, that we may have confidence in the day of judgment, because as he is, so are we in this world.

units.la: DIuus Apostolus Ioannes de Christiana charitate ea ratione disserit, vt simul fidei in Christum & salutis nostræ mysteria suæ doctrinæ interserat. Vidimus hoc in iis quæ proximè præcesserunt, quibus breuiter & summatim complectitur quæcunque de nostra redemptione dici possunt. Ostendit enim, nobis à Deo patre filium datum esse, saluatorem mundi. Et mundi vocabulo ideo vsus est, vt uniuersalem saluatorem esse intelligeremus, ac salutem in hoc partam ad omnes homines pertinere. Deinde docuit, vt & Christi & salutis consortes fieri possimus, fide scilicet, quam confessionis nomine comprehendit, eam fidem requiri indicans, quæ animis nostris ita insideat, ac eo zelo eosdem incendat, vt nos coram mundo hoc, veritatis inimico, eius pudere non possit. Omnium verò scopus hic est, ne dum charitatē tantis præconijs extolli uidemus, ope-rum iustitiam hinc credamus stabiliri: cum de ea charitate loquatur spiritus sanctus, quæ ex fide oritur, fidem sibi coniunctam habet, & propter fidem Deo tam accepta est, non placitura nimirum Deo, nisi ex fide manaret. Cæterum clarius ista in præsenti patebunt. Primò enim Aposto-lus charitatis originem siue causam efficientem nobis in fide monstrat. Deinde eius notas & fru-ctus excellentissimos proponit, quò ardentius eius studium nobis excitetur.
units.tr: The divine Apostle John discourses on Christian love in such a way that he weaves into his teaching the mysteries of faith in Christ and of our salvation. We saw this in what immediately preceded, where he briefly and summarily embraces whatever can be said about our redemption. For he shows that the Son, the Saviour of the world, has been given to us by God the Father. He used the word "world" so that we might understand that he is the universal Saviour, and that the salvation obtained in him pertains to all men. Then he taught that we may become partakers both of Christ and of salvation, namely by faith, which he comprehends under the name of confession, indicating that the faith required is one that so dwells in our minds and so inflames them with zeal that we are not ashamed of it before this world, the enemy of truth. But the aim of the whole passage is this: that, seeing love extolled with such great praises, we should not believe that the righteousness of works is thereby established. For the Holy Spirit speaks of that love which arises from faith, has faith joined to it, and is so acceptable to God on account of faith that it would certainly not please God unless it flowed from faith. Moreover, these things will become clearer in what follows. For first the Apostle shows us that the origin or efficient cause of love is in faith. Then he sets forth its marks and most excellent fruits, so that our zeal for it may be more ardently stirred up.

units.la: I. Et nos cognouimus & credidimus charitatem, quam habet Deus in nobis. Deus charitas est. Unàm solamque fidem proponit, quæ charitatem in nobis operetur. Probat autem, quod dicit, argumento à Dei natura desumpto. Vera & essentialis charitas ipse Deus est. Charitatem igitur non habebunt, nisi qui diuinæ illius charitatis gustum perceperint. At nos cognouimus & credidimus, id est, fide percipimus charitatem, qua nos Deus prosequitur, nec aliud medium est præter fidem, quo diuinæ charitatis consortes fieri possimus. Eadem ergo sola charitatis fraternæ ignem in nobis accendit. Pertinet huc quod infra dicet: Nos diligimus eum, quia ipse prior dilexit nos. Possunt autem omnia hæc in breuem argumenti formam redigi, hoc pacto: Quicunq; charitatis Dei, qua nos ille prosequitur, consortes facti fuerint, charitatem in se excitari sentient. At diuinæ charitatis consortes facit sola fides. Sola igitur fides charitatis nostræ causa est.
units.tr: I. "And we have known and believed the love which God has in us." God is love. He proposes one thing only, and that alone, faith, as that which works love in us. He proves what he says by an argument drawn from the nature of God. True and essential love is God himself. Therefore those will not have love who have not perceived the taste of that divine love. But we have known and believed, that is, we perceive by faith the love with which God embraces us, and there is no means other than faith by which we can become partakers of divine love. Therefore faith alone kindles in us the fire of brotherly love. To this belongs what he says below: "We love him, because he first loved us." All these things can be reduced to a brief form of argument, thus: Whoever shall have become partakers of the love of God, by which he embraces us, will feel love being stirred up in himself. But faith alone makes us partakers of divine love. Faith alone, therefore, is the cause of our love.

units.la: Sunt hæc nō oscitanter nobis excutienda fratres, eò quòd amplissimarum virtutū fontes, & uniuersam salutis nostræ causam cōprehendunt. Deum siquidē, in quo uno beatitudinis fons & scaturigo est, inuisibilem esse & corporeis sensibus percipi non posse, supra audiuimus. Sola fides animum in cœlos & in lucē illam inaccessam subuehit, & æternū illud ac ineffabile bonum appre-hendere nouit. De ea autē fide loquimur, quæ Christo Iesu nititur. In hoc enim Deus expressam suæ essentiæ & diuinitatis imaginem nobis proposuit, vt in incarnato verbo Dei, ceu in speculo, videremus, quæ nostri captus infirmitas alioqui percipere nequit. At quia Deus sine spiritu suo non est, per quem omnia seruat & vegetat, vbicunque est, quiescere nequit, sed indesinenter operari consueuit. Quid vero aliud operetur suo spiritu Deus, quàm quę ipsius ingenio & naturæ consentanea sunt? Inter quæ, cum primatum teneat charitas, non potest non charitatem in illis operari Deus, quibus per fidem vnitus fuerit. Habent enim illi spiritum Dei, in quo clamant, Abba pater. Ob oculos sibi positum vident exemplum Dei patris, quod non possunt non imitari, siquidem genuini Dei filij haberi velint. Diligit is omnes homines, & Solem suum oriri sinit super bonos & malos, pluuiam mittit iustis & iniustis, denique totum mundum sic dilexit, vt filium suum vnigenitum pro illo in mortem traderet. Matth.5. Ioan.3. Quid igitur in tam illustri & eximio diuinæ charitatis exemplo aliud quàm charitatem fraternam discant fideles? Vident præterea arctissimam vnionem, quæ nobis in Christo Iesu obtigit, qui vt vnum nobis spiritum dedit, ita vnius patris filios, vnius & eiusdem corporis membra, vnius denique regni & patriæ hæredes fecit. Quorum confyderatio spiritus operatione excitata, non potest non charitatis fomites inextinguibiles animis fidelium ingerere. Tenedum vero est in omnibus istis, quod supra attigimus, charitatis scilicet doctrina operum nostrorum iustitiam minimè stabiliri. Nisi enim fide Deum apprehendamus, charitas in nobis erit nulla. At fides esse nequit sine Christo, qui legis & peccati maceria disrupta, nos Deo coniunxit. Christo igitur debetur vniuersa charitatis laus, qui & hanc & quæcunque ex hac promanant laude digna in nobis operatur. Nec hic mihi quispiam vel Decios, vel Curtios, vel Pylades, Orecтes & alios eius farinæ obijciat, quos partim poetæ (quorum authoritas non immerito suspecta est) partim gentilium historici celebrauerunt. Nam vt illos merita laude nemo fraudare debet: ita à Christianæ charitatis genio alienissimos fuisse constat, cum quæcunque fecerunt, non tam propter alios quàm priuatæ vtilitatis causa fecerint. Alij enim patriam quidem seruatam voluerunt, & suo interitu huius salutem redimere. Sed quia vel coniugum, vel liberorum, vel pauculorum aliquot amicorum rationem habuerunt, Christianæ charitatis laude digni non sunt, quæ omnium salutem ex æquo quærit, & ab hostibus quoque manum propulsare studet. Plures tamen ex illis fuerunt, quos honorum & popularis auræ cupiditas, vel nominis & famæ apud posteros studium sic dementauit, vt periculis vitæ sese objicerent: qui licet pro aliorum salute aliquid passi videantur, reuera tamen hoc præconium minimè merentur, cum suam potius, quàm aliorum vtilitatem, quæ sierint. Laude ergo digna sunt facinora quæ secundum Christianæ charitatis regulam fiunt. Hæc autem quia ex fide est, nihil huic aduersum agit, & propter fidem Deo placere consueuit.
units.tr: These things are not to be examined carelessly by us, brethren, because they comprehend the sources of the most ample virtues and the whole cause of our salvation. For we have heard above that God, in whom alone is the fountain and spring of blessedness, is invisible and cannot be perceived by bodily senses. Faith alone lifts the mind into the heavens and into that unapproachable light, and knows how to grasp that eternal and ineffable good. But we speak of that faith which rests on Jesus Christ. For in him God has set before us the express image of his essence and divinity, so that we might see in the incarnate Word of God, as in a mirror, what the weakness of our capacity cannot otherwise perceive. But since God is not without his Spirit, through whom he preserves and quickens all things, wherever he is, he cannot be at rest, but is accustomed to work without ceasing. Now what else does God work by his Spirit than what is consonant with his own disposition and nature? Among these things, since love holds the first place, God cannot but work love in those to whom he is united through faith. For they have the Spirit of God, in whom they cry, "Abba, Father." They see before their eyes the example of God the Father, which they cannot but imitate, if they wish to be counted true sons of God. He loves all men, and lets his sun rise upon the good and the evil, sends rain on the just and the unjust, and finally, "God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for it to death." Matt. 5; John 3. What, then, in so illustrious and remarkable an example of divine love, do the faithful learn but brotherly love? Moreover they see the most intimate union which has fallen to us in Christ Jesus, who, as he has given us one Spirit, so has made us sons of one Father, members of one and the same body, and finally heirs of one kingdom and fatherland. The consideration of these things, stirred up by the working of the Spirit, cannot but cast inextinguishable fuel of love into the hearts of the faithful. But in all these things it must be held, as we touched on above, that the doctrine of love does not establish the righteousness of our works. For unless we apprehend God by faith, there will be no love in us. But faith cannot exist without Christ, who, having broken down the wall of the law and of sin, has joined us to God. To Christ therefore belongs the whole praise of love, since he both works this love in us and whatever flows from it that is worthy of praise. Nor let anyone here object to me the Decii, the Curtii, Pylades, Orestes and others of that kind, whom partly the poets (whose authority is not undeservedly suspect) and partly the historians of the Gentiles have celebrated. For just as no one ought to deprive them of deserved praise, so it is clear that they were very far removed from the spirit of Christian love, since whatever they did, they did not so much for the sake of others as for the sake of private advantage. For some indeed wished their country to be preserved, and by their own death sought to redeem its safety. But since they had regard to their wives, their children, or a few friends, they are not worthy of the praise of Christian love, which seeks the salvation of all alike and strives to ward off the hand even of enemies. Yet there were several among them whom the desire for honours and popular favour, or the zeal for a name and fame among posterity, so maddened that they exposed themselves to the perils of life; and although they seem to have suffered something for the salvation of others, in truth they do not at all deserve this commendation, since they did what they did for their own advantage rather than that of others. Deeds therefore are worthy of praise when they are done according to the rule of Christian love. But since this love is from faith, it does nothing contrary to faith, and is accustomed to please God on account of faith.

units.la: Sunt autem præter hæc in Apostoli verbis duo nobis obseruanda. Primò, quod ijs hęc subijcit, quæ paulò ante de Christo, in mundum propter nos misso, dicta sunt. Sic enim docet, in Christo Dei amorem perspici, quo is nos prosequitur. Nam si nos inspicias, quid aliud præter irarum causas videre poteris? Fatendum tibi cum Dauide erit, quòd in peccato conceptus, & in iniquitate formatus sis. Psal. 51. Negare non poteris Dei pronunciatum, qui humani cordis figmenta ab ineunte ætate praua esse dicit. Gen. 8. In multis etenim omnes labimur, & iustus in die cadit septies. Iac.3. Prou.24. At peccati stipendium mors. Rom.5.&6. Impossibile ergo, vt diuinæ charitatis gustum capiat aliquem, quicunque seipsum & sua opera inspexerit. Quòd si vero fide excitati mentis oculos ad Christum transferamus, ea se offerent ilico, quæ nos de Dei gratia & amore certos facient. Vt enim in nobis peccatum, ita in illo iustitiam nostram videbimus. 2. Cor. 5. In nobis peccati debitum, in illo satisfactio sese ostentat. 1. Cor. 1. In nobis peccati pœna mors, in illo vita & redemptio monstratur. Deniq; vt propter peccata nostra Deum nobis iratum esse cernimus: ita propter hunc coram patre nobis gratiam impetratam esse audimus, ipso cœlitus dicen-te: Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi complacitum est. Matth.3. & 17. Hinc fit, vt cum Paulo ratiocinari possimus: Si cum inimici essemus, reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem filij eius, multo magis reconciliati seruabimur per vitam ipsius. Rom.5. Itē: Qui proprio filio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum, qui fieri potest, vt non & cū eodem omnia nobis donet? Rom. 8. Has consolationes & hæc nostræ fidei axiomata, gaudij & spei plenissima, prorsus ignorat, quicunque extra Christum salutis certitudinem sperant & quærunt. Nemo enim ad patrem venit, nisi per hunc. Ioan.14. Extra eundem ergo salus nulla inueniri poterit. Acto.4. Indignissimi itaq; sunt qui audiantur, imò pestes religionis & humanæ salutis sunt, qui Dei gratiam & diuinæ charitatis thesauros alibi quàm in Christo quærere docent. In illos quadrat quod apud prophetā dicit dominus: Popule mi, qui te dirigunt, seductores sunt, & iter semitarum tuarum deprauant.
units.tr: Moreover, besides these things, two points are to be observed in the words of the Apostle. First, that he subjoins these things to what was said a little before about Christ, sent into the world on our account. For he thus teaches that the love of God, by which he embraces us, is seen in Christ. For if you look at yourself, what else will you be able to see besides the causes of wrath? You must confess with David that you were conceived in sin and formed in iniquity. Ps. 51. You will not be able to deny the pronouncement of God, who says that the imaginations of the human heart are evil from early age. Gen. 8. For in many things we all stumble, and the righteous man falls seven times a day. James 3; Prov. 24. But the wages of sin is death. Rom. 5 and 6. It is impossible, therefore, that anyone who looks upon himself and his own works should taste the divine love. But if, roused by faith, we turn the eyes of the mind to Christ, there will at once present themselves those things which will make us certain of God's grace and love. For as we see sin in ourselves, so in him we shall see our righteousness. 2 Cor. 5. In us is the debt of sin; in him satisfaction shows itself. 1 Cor. 1. In us the punishment of sin is death; in him life and redemption are shown.
