Finally, as we perceive that God is angry with us on account of our sins, so we hear that for his sake grace has been obtained for us before the Father, the Father himself speaking from heaven: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Matt. 3 and 17. Hence it comes about that with Paul we can reason: "If when we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, shall we be saved through his life." Rom. 5. Likewise: "He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not also with him freely give us all things?" Rom. 8. Those who seek and look for certainty of salvation outside Christ are wholly ignorant of these consolations and these axioms of our faith, which are most full of joy and hope. For no one comes to the Father except through him. John 14. Therefore salvation cannot be found outside him. Acts 4. Those, therefore, are most unworthy to be heard, indeed they are the pests of religion and of human salvation, who teach that the grace of God and the treasures of divine love are to be sought anywhere other than in Christ. Of them is what the Lord says through the prophet: "My people, those who lead you are seducers, and they corrupt the course of your paths." Isaiah 3.

units.la: Isaiæ tertio.
units.tr: Isaiah 3.

units.la: Deinde obseruandum est, quod non simpliciter Credendi verbo Apostolus vtitur, sed ait: Et nos cognouimus & credidimus charitatem, &c. Simili ratione Petrus fidei cognitionem iungit, dicens: Nos credimus & cognouimus, quód tu es Christus filius Dei viui. Ioan.6. Nolumus hic de verborum ordine disputare curiosius, licet Petrus credendi vocabulum praemittat, Ioanes verò cognitionem priori loco ponat. Constat equidem nulla oculari demonstratione fidei mysteria tradi, sed animi oculis, spiritu sancto illuminatis, percipi, iuxta illud Christi: Caro & sanguis non reuelauit tibi, sed pater meus, qui in coelis est. Matt.16. Cóstat item sine fide cognitionem diuinae veritatis & bonitatis esse nullam, propheta dicente: Nisi crediderit is, non intelligetis. Isa.7. Sed cum primis hic discimus, fidem non esse sine certa, solida, & infallibili salutis & beatitudinis nostrae cognitione, quatenus nos dum hic viuimus, illa nouisse interest: nec incertis opinionibus exagitari, qui fide Christiana imbuti sunt. Fides enim Christo nititur, qui & petra inuicta, & aeterna veritas est. Matt.16. Ioan.14. Dubitare ergo & fluctuari non possunt animis suis, quotquot Christo innituntur. Adhaec salutis nostrae arrhabonem habemus spiritum sanctum, quem & Christus in se credentibus promisit, & eundem illis dari Apostolorum scripta luculenter affirmant. 2.Corint.1.&5. Eph.1.&c.Procul ergo facessant impij & perniciosi impostores, qui de salute sua & eius certitudine homines dubitare docet: quod non aliud est, quàm desperationis ansam praebere ijs, quos eru diendos & consolandos susceperis. Solent illi quidem eo fuco sui commenti impietatem velare, quòd ardens & indefessum bene agendi studium in animis hominum excitare velint, vt iuxta Paulì doctrinam, in timore & tremore salutem suam operentur. Phil.2. At interim videre nolunt, sed dum Scyllam fugiunt, in Charybdim incidere, & tanti periculi authores fieri sine aliqua causa gravi & iusta. Infinitae enim rationes sunt, quae innocentiae & pietatis studium nobis commendant. Pertinent huc minae & promissiones in scripturis propositae. Eodem referi debent sanctorum omnium exempla, & horrendi impiorum exitus. Momenti plurimum quoq; hic habet Christi sanguis, pro peccatis nostris effusus. Quis enim horum atrocitatem non horreat, qui illa tam pretiosò sacro expiari oportuisse audit? Pasim quoque nos hortatur, monet, excitat & corripit spiritus sanctus in scripturis. Accedunt exempla quotidiana iudiciorum Dei, quibus inobedientiam & impietatem infidelium coercet. Quem haec non mouent, eum tu frustra de salutis suae certitudine dubitare docueris. Quid ergo opus est ea frustra excogitare, quae praesens & incurabile salutis periculum pariunt? Quo enim pharmaco ei medebëris, qui peccatorum conscientia exagitatus, in desperationem vergit? Promissionésne per Christum factas proferes? At per te didicit illis fidem certam non adhibere, sed de veritate illarum dubitare. In idem enim recidit dubitatio de salute, & de Dei promissionibus. Quód si exempla proferas eorú, quibus olim peccata remissa sunt, certe haec quoque ad se pertinere negabit. Quibus ergo rationibus illi persuadebis diuinae bonitatis gratiam, si dogma hoc stare voles, hominem, quoad viuit, salutis suae incertum esse? Est itaque doctrina haec non falsa modo & perniciosa, sed plane diabolica, cuius semina in origine mundi per serpentem sparsit diabolus, quando Euam de Dei erga nos amore & beneuolentia dubitare, & nescio quid de inuido & maligno Dei ingenio suspicari docuit. Huic doctrinae debetur totu illud superstitionum pelagus, quo syncera veritatis doctrina multis seculis inundata delituit. Huic debentur quotquot nouae indies prodeunt salutis consequendae rationes, quas illi excogitant, qui de sua salute nil certi statuere possunt. Huic debemus tot animarum perditionem, quas infelix desperatio in dānationis barathrū demersit. Obturemus ergo aures, ô fratres, quoties funeste illę Syrenes letifera haec carmina occinunt. Apostolos audiamus, qui salute digito monstrant, qui spiritum sanctum eius testem & arrhabonem nobis sistunt, qui Christum eius authorem producunt, & de ijs testantur, quorum testes fuerunt oculati, & quae manibus proprijs contrectarunt. Sed omissis tam infelicibus monstris, ad Ioannem redeamus, qui laetos & felices charitatis fructus paucis verbis comprehensos proponit, dicens:
units.tr: Next we must observe that the Apostle does not simply use the verb "to believe," but says: "And we have known and believed the love," etc. In a similar way Peter joins knowledge to faith, saying: "We believe and have come to know that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God." John 6. We do not wish to dispute too closely about the order of the words, although Peter puts the word "believe" first, while John places knowledge in the first position. It is certain that the mysteries of faith are not handed down by any outward demonstration, but are perceived by the eyes of the mind, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, according to that saying of Christ: "Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven." Matt. 16. It is also certain that without faith there is no knowledge of divine truth and goodness, the prophet saying: "Unless you believe, you will not understand." Isa. 7. But here we chiefly learn that faith is not without a certain, solid and infallible knowledge of our salvation and blessedness, since it matters that we, while we live here, know those things; nor should those who are imbued with the Christian faith be troubled by uncertain opinions. For faith rests on Christ, who is the unconquered rock and eternal truth. Matt. 16. John 14. Therefore those who rest on Christ cannot doubt or waver in their minds, as many as there are who rest on him. Moreover, we have the Holy Spirit as the pledge of our salvation, whom Christ also promised to those who believe in him, and the writings of the Apostles clearly affirm that the same Spirit is given to them. 2 Cor. 1 and 5. Eph. 1, etc. Let the impious and pernicious impostors, who teach men to doubt their own salvation and its certainty, therefore keep far away; for this is nothing other than to offer an occasion of despair to those whom you have undertaken to instruct and console. Those men indeed are wont to veil their impiety with the pretext of their invention, namely that they wish to arouse in the minds of men an ardent and tireless zeal for doing good, so that, according to the teaching of Paul, they may work out their salvation in fear and trembling. Phil. 2. But meanwhile they are unwilling to see that, while fleeing Scylla, they fall into Charybdis, and become the authors of so great a danger without any serious and just cause. For there are countless reasons which commend to us the pursuit of innocence and piety. To this belong the threats and promises set forth in the Scriptures. To the same end must be referred the examples of all the saints and the dreadful ends of the wicked. The blood of Christ, shed for our sins, also has very great weight here. For who would not shudder at the atrocity of these things, who hears that they had to be expiated with so precious a sacrifice? The Holy Spirit also everywhere exhorts, admonishes, stirs up and rebukes us in the Scriptures. Daily examples of God's judgments are added, by which he restrains the disobedience and impiety of unbelievers. Whoever is not moved by these things, you will have taught in vain to doubt the certainty of his salvation. Why then is there need to devise in vain those things which produce a present and incurable danger to salvation? For with what medicine will you heal one who, troubled by the consciousness of his sins, is sliding into despair? Will you bring forward the promises made through Christ? But by your teaching he has learned not to apply firm faith to them, but to doubt their truth. For doubt about salvation and doubt about God's promises fall into the same error. But if you bring forward examples of those to whom sins were forgiven in former times, he will certainly deny that these also pertain to him. By what arguments then will you persuade him of the grace of divine goodness, if you wish this doctrine to stand, that a man, as long as he lives, is uncertain of his salvation? This doctrine, therefore, is not only false and pernicious but plainly diabolical; the devil sowed its seeds at the beginning of the world through the serpent, when he taught Eve to doubt God's love and goodwill toward us, and to suspect I know not what about the envious and malicious disposition of God. To this doctrine is owed that whole sea of superstitions by which the pure doctrine of the truth lay submerged, flooded for many centuries. To this are owed all the new methods of obtaining salvation that appear daily, which those devise who can establish nothing certain about their own salvation. To this we owe the perdition of so many souls, whom unhappy despair has plunged into the abyss of damnation. Let us therefore stop our ears, brothers, whenever those deadly Sirens sing these baleful songs. Let us listen to the Apostles, who point out salvation with their finger, who present the Spirit as its witness and pledge to us, who bring forward Christ as its author, and bear witness to those things of which they were eyewitnesses, and which they handled with their own hands. But leaving aside such unhappy monsters, let us return to John, who sets forth in a few words the joyful and happy fruits of love, saying:

units.la: I I. Qui manet in charitate, in Deo manet, & Deus in eo. In hoc perfecta est charitas nobiscum, ut fiduciam habeamus in die iudicij, quod sicut ille est, & nos sumus in mundo hoc. Magna sunt, & omnem ingenij captum superant, quae pollicetur, nedum vt verbis pro dignitate explicari possint. Quibus si ea conferas, quae philosophorum principes olim suis sectatoribus polliciti sunt, plane nullius momenti esse senties. Licet enim in hoc omnes consenserint, quod beatitudinem & veram huius consequendae rationem promittebant, vanissimae tamen illorum pollicitationes fuerunt, cum veram beatitudinem ipsi ignorarent, & in ijs eam anxiè quaererent, quae ab illa longissimè absunt. At Ioannes noster, qui in sinu domini in vltima Coena recumbens salutaria hausit diuini pectoris mysteria, tria hic nobis pollicetur, quae omnem verae felicitatis rationem absolute comprehendunt, de quibus sigillatim dicere, nec iniucundum erit, nec infrugiferum.
units.tr: II. He who abides in love abides in God, and God in him. In this love is made perfect among us, that we may have confidence in the day of judgment, because as he is, so are we in this world. Great are the things he promises, and they surpass every capacity of mind, not to say that they cannot be explained in words as their worth deserves. If you compare these with what the chief philosophers once promised their followers, you will feel that those promises are of no account at all. For although all of them agreed in promising blessedness and the true way of attaining it, nevertheless their promises were most empty, since they themselves did not know true blessedness, and sought it anxiously in those things which are very far removed from it. But our John, who, reclining in the bosom of the Lord at the last Supper, drank in the saving mysteries of the divine heart, here promises us three things, which fully comprehend the whole way of true happiness, and it will be neither unpleasant nor unprofitable to speak of them one by one.

units.la: Primum, Qui manet (inquit) in charitate, in Deo manet, & Deus in eo. Depédet huius promissionis ratio ex præcedenti sententia. Si enim Deus est charitas, utique in Deo manebit, quisquis in charitate manserit. At qua ratione Deus charitas dicatur, supra dictum est. Comprehenditur autem hac promissione non ratio modò & via, qua felicitate homo assequatur, sed ipsa beatitudo & felicitas. Deus etenim vt summum bonum, ita & omnis boni fons est æternus & inexhaustus, in cuius conspectu satietatem bonorum omnium Dauid esse testatur. Psal.16. Nequiter[?] go fieri, vt nobis quicquam desit eorum, quæ incolumitati nostræ seruiunt, si cum illo coniuncti fuerimus. Ex hoc enim fonte manabunt ad nos abundanter quæcunq; verè bona sunt, & ita manabunt, vt nobis salutaria sint, nec abusu suo noceant, quod in seculi huius filij fieri videmus, qui à religione omni & charitate alieni sunt. In suam enim ipsorum perniciem conuertunt honores, amicitias, opes, corporis integram ualetudinem, sapientiam, fortitudinem, & si quæ alia bona diui nitus concessa habent. At qui per fidem & charitatem in Deo manent, non hæc modò ex diuina liberalitate accipiunt, sed simul spiritum Dei sibi dari sentiunt, qui animos cœlestium bonorum amore incensos in terrenis & perituris rebus hærere non finit, & earundem abusum studiosè prohibet. Sed quia de salutari hac communione cum Deo alibi quoque diximus, paucula hæc in præsenti sufficiant.
units.tr: First, "He who abides," he says, "in love abides in God, and God in him." The reasoning of this promise depends on the preceding sentence. For if God is love, certainly whoever abides in love will abide in God. But in what sense God is called love has been said above. Yet this promise comprehends not only the reasoning and way by which a man attains happiness, but blessedness and happiness itself. For God, as the highest good, is also the eternal and inexhaustible fountain of all good, in whose presence David testifies there is the fullness of all good things. Ps. 16. It cannot happen that anything we need for our well-being should be lacking to us, if we have been joined with him. For from this fountain there will flow to us abundantly all things that are truly good, and they will flow in such a way that they are salutary for us and do not harm us by their misuse, which we see happening among the children of this age, who are alien to all religion and love. For they turn to their own destruction honors, friendships, wealth, the sound health of the body, wisdom, strength, and whatever other goods they have been granted by God. But those who abide in God through faith and love not only receive these things from divine generosity, but at the same time feel the Spirit of God given to them, who does not allow minds inflamed with love of heavenly goods to cling to earthly and perishable things, and diligently prevents their misuse. But since we have also spoken elsewhere about this saving communion with God, these few words will suffice for the present.

units.la: Obseruandum tamen, hac promissione auarorum hominum anxiam solicitudinem reprimi, qua metuunt, ne charitatem exercendo sibijpsis inopiam & egestatem contrahant, vt ab aliorū liberalitate petere cogantur, quæ vitæ conseruandæ necessaria sunt. Vetat enim hoc timere Apostolus, cum nos Deum nobis præsentem, & quasi contubernalem habituros pollicetur. Nam qui fieri posset, vt amicis & filijs suis aliquid deesse pateretur is, qui & inimicos sua beneficetia iuuat, & pecori suum pastum dat, nec pullis coruorum ad se crocitantibus deest? Psal.147. Certè Christus inquit: Quærite primò regnum cœlorum & iustitiam eius, & reliqua omnia vobis adijcientur. Matth.6. Et Dauid hæc verè dici suo exemplo probat, dicens: Iuuenis fui, & nunc senui, nec vidi iustum desertum, aut posteros eius mendicantes panem. Quotidie beneficus est & mutuum dat, & posteri eius optimè habent. Psal.37. Frustra ergo auari ringuntur, dum charitatis studium suis defyderijs obstare putant, & beneficentia in proximum annuos redditus minui ac exhauriri timent: cum non alia vsura fœcundior fit & vberior, quàm quæ in pauperibus Christi alendis & sustentandis exercetur. In hac quisquis copiosè serit, metet etiam copiosissimè.2.Corinth.9.
units.tr: It must be observed, however, that by this promise the anxious solicitude of greedy men is restrained, by which they fear that by exercising love they may bring upon themselves want and poverty, so that they will be forced to beg from the generosity of others the things necessary for sustaining life. For the Apostle forbids them to fear this, when he promises that we shall have God present with us and, as it were, as a fellow dweller. For how could it happen that he would allow anything to be lacking to his friends and children, he who helps even his enemies with his kindness, and gives food to his flock, and does not fail the young ravens that cry out to him? Ps. 147. Certainly Christ says: "Seek first the kingdom of heaven and his righteousness, and all the rest will be added to you." Matt. 6. And David proves by his own example that these words are truly spoken, saying: "I was young, and now am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his descendants begging for bread. Every day he is generous and lends, and his descendants do very well." Ps. 37. In vain, then, do the greedy rage, while they think that zeal for love stands in the way of their desires, and fear that the annual income will be diminished and drained by generosity toward a neighbour: since no usury is more fruitful and richer than that which is practised in feeding and sustaining the poor of Christ. Whoever sows abundantly in this will also reap most abundantly. 2 Cor. 9.

units.la: Secundus charitatis fructus est, fiducia in die iudicij illius vniuersalis, quando irreuocabilis sententia feretur super omnem carnem. Eam verò animi tranquillitatem intelligit, qua intrepidi expectamus Christum iudicem, nec illius iudicij metione miseribiliter, vt impij solent, terremur & excruciamur. Est hoc ingens bonum, quod solum vitam hac nostram spe læta exhilarat, aduersa omnia lenit, & consolationem affert omnibus afflictionibus, quæ incidere possunt, superiorem. Nec tantum bonum Ioannes de suo pollicetur, sed Christi verba respicit, qui in euangelio fatetur, se in die iudicij pro suis agnoscere, & regni sui hæredes facere velle eos, qui charitatis regulam secuti, ipsum in membris suis pascunt, vestiunt, domo excipiunt, inuisunt amicè & consolantur, Matth.25. Cæterum, ne quis per hæc operum iustitiam stabiliri putet, obseruare conuenit, quòd hanc ipsam fiduciam cap.2. Apostolus fidei & perseuerantiæ in agnita veritate tribuit: vnde satis claret, de ea tantum charitate hæc dici, quæ ex fide promanat, fidei coniuncta est, & propter fidem Deo placere solet.
units.tr: The second fruit of charity is confidence in that final, universal day of judgment, when an irrevocable sentence will be pronounced upon all flesh. By this he means that peace of mind by which we await Christ the judge without fear, and are not wretchedly terrified and tormented by the thought of that judgment, as the wicked usually are. This is a great good: it alone gladdens our life with a joyful hope, softens all adversities, and brings consolation that surpasses every affliction that can befall us. Nor does John promise so great a good on his own authority; he has in view the words of Christ, who in the Gospel declares that on the day of judgment he will acknowledge as his own, and will make heirs of his kingdom, those who, following the rule of charity, feed, clothe, receive into their house, visit kindly and comfort him in his members (Matt. 25). Furthermore, lest anyone think that righteousness of works is thereby established, it should be observed that the Apostle in chapter 2 ascribes this same confidence to faith and perseverance in the acknowledged truth. Whence it is plain enough that these things are said only of that charity which springs from faith, is joined to faith, and is wont to please God for the sake of faith.

units.la: Sed confydera hic mihi, quisquis es, ingens piorum & impiorum discrimê. Hi enim, quia pruis operibus toti sunt dediti, & fœdas carnis cupiditates sectantur, lucè odiunt, nec aliud magis horrent quàm aduentû Christi, quo opera sua iniqua & impia, nô modò reuelanda, verumetiâ punienda fore intelligunt. Vellent ergo fugere, si possent, à conspectu domini. Vellent se mòtibus potius obtegi & in tenebris cauernarum & antrorum delitescere, quàm in illo die coram Christo iudice comparere. Sed quia id illis nô licet, ad alias artes conuersi, omnem de die iudicij doctrinam cauillis & dicterijs improbis eludere & Christi aduentum cum fine mundi in dubium vocare nituntur. Aiunt enim: Vbi est pollicitatio aduentus eius? Siquidem ex quo die patres dormierunt, sic omnia permanent ab initio creationis. 2. Pet. 3. Adhæc carnis voluptatibus sese studiosè immergunt, verbum Dei surdis auribus contemnunt, conciones sacras deuitant, ne recurrens crebrò iudicij huius memoria molestiam & curas mordaces afferat. Sed nequicquam hæc omnia faciunt. Quia velint nolint obuersantur sæpius animis illorum cogitationes istæ, & nouos indies metus, dolores, cruciatus omniumque studiorum & conatuum incertitudinem pariunt. At pij vicissim in hoc omnem suę spei fiduciam repositā habent, quòd Christum iudicem venturum esse nouerunt. Eundem enim & impiorum iudicem seuerū, & piorum siue fideliū vindicē atq assertorem fore intelligunt. Credunt enim Christi verbis, qui de die iudicij & signis hunc praecessuris differes ait: His fieri incipientibus, suspicite & attollite capita vestra, quoniam appropinquat redemptio vestra. Luc.21. Quis vero redemptionis diem formidet? Quis huius mentione terreatur? Atqui vere redemptionis dies erit Christi aduentus. Tunc enim finis erit peccatorum. Tunc desinet & abolebitur effrenis mundi impietas. Tunc cessabunt multiariae huius seculi angustiae. Tunc cum capite suo satana in aeternos tenebrarum carceres aeternis catenis astringentur omnes impij, & quotquot terrorem suum posuerunt in terra viuentium. Tunc in coelos recepti fideles, extra omnem instabilis fortunae aleam positi, animabus & corporibus felices, aeternum cum Christo suo capite regnabunt. Horum consyderatio quia piorum mentibus obuersatur, non potest illis grauis esse eius diei mentio, qui tam laetum praebebit nunquam intermoriturę felicitatis initiū. Cupiunt enim dissolui, & esse cum Christo. Phil.1. Et cum Dauide clamant: Vt ceruus rugit ad torrentes aquarum, sic anima mea ad te rugit ô deus. Sitit anima mea deum, Deum viuum. Quando demum veniam, vt appaream in conspectu dei? Psal.42. Imo quoties futuri seculi felicitatem cum praesentis calamitatibus & aerumnis conferunt, non possunt non cum Ioanne nostro dicere: Veni domine Iesu, veni cito. Apoc.22. Haec si expendas diligentius, facile videbis, quid de multis nostri seculi hominibus iudicari debeat, qui vt omne studium terrenis impendunt, ita coelestium nulla cura tanguntur, & ad omnem siue mortis siue nouissimi iudicij mentionem totis animis consternamur. Sed ô excellentiam charitatis & fidei, quae animos in coelestium consyderatione subuehit, & in ijs fiduciam habere docet, quae impijs terrorem & cruciatus horribiles inferunt.
units.tr: But consider here, whoever you are, the vast difference between the godly and the wicked. For the latter, because they are wholly given over to their evil works and pursue the foul desires of the flesh, hate the light, and dread nothing more than the coming of Christ, by which they understand that their unjust and impious works will not only be revealed but also punished. They would therefore flee, if they could, from the sight of the Lord. They would rather wish to be hidden in the darkness of caves and dens than to appear before Christ the judge on that day. But since this is not permitted them, they turn to other arts and strive to mock all teaching about the day of judgment with sneers and wicked jibes, and to call the coming of Christ and the end of the world into doubt. For they say: "Where is the promise of his coming? For since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of creation" (2 Pet. 3). Besides, they immerse themselves eagerly in the pleasures of the flesh, despise the word of God with deaf ears, and shun the holy sermons, lest the frequent recollection of this judgment bring them troublesome and gnawing cares. But they accomplish nothing by all this. For whether they will it or not, these thoughts keep coming back to their minds, and they produce fresh fears, pains and torments every day, and uncertainty in all their pursuits and endeavors. But the godly, on the other hand, have placed all the confidence of their hope in this, that they know Christ is coming as judge. For they understand that he will be both the severe judge of the wicked and the avenger and defender of the godly or faithful. They believe the words of Christ, who, speaking of the day of judgment and the signs that will precede it, says: "When these things begin to happen, look up and lift up your heads, for your redemption draws near" (Luke 21). Who then should fear the day of redemption? Who should be terrified by the mention of it? And yet truly the day of redemption will be the coming of Christ. For then there will be an end of sins. Then the lawless impiety of the world will cease and be abolished. Then the manifold distresses of this age will come to an end. Then all the wicked, together with Satan their head, will be bound with eternal chains in the eternal prisons of darkness, and all who have put their terror upon the land of the living. Then the faithful, received into heaven and placed beyond every hazard of unstable fortune, will reign happily with their head Christ forever, in soul and body. Since the contemplation of these things is ever before the minds of the godly, the mention of that day cannot be grievous to them, for it will bring the joyful beginning of a happiness that never ends. For they desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Phil. 1). And with David they cry: "As the deer pants after the water brooks, so my soul pants after you, O God. My soul thirsts for God, the living God. When shall I come and appear before the face of God?" (Ps. 42). Indeed, as often as they compare the happiness of the age to come with the calamities and miseries of the present, they cannot but say with our John: "Come, Lord Jesus, come quickly" (Rev. 22). If you weigh these things more carefully, you will easily see what ought to be judged of the many people of our age, who devote all their zeal to earthly things, are touched by no care for heavenly things, and are struck with dread in their whole souls at every mention of death or of the last judgment. But O the excellence of charity and of faith, which lifts the minds up to the contemplation of heavenly things and teaches them to have confidence in those things which bring terror and dreadful torments upon the wicked!

units.la: Tertius charitatis fructus est, quod sicut ille est, & nos sumus in hoc mundo. Dei ergo simi-les reddit charitas, & quae ex hac nascitur, beneficentia. Nihil enim tam diuinum est quam multis benefacere, eo quod Deus ut omnia condidit, sic eadem conseruat, & beneficia in Creaturas suas quotidiana confert. Viderunt hoc ethnici, qui eo nomine in Deorum numerum retulerunt eos, qui communis alicuius boni vel inuentores primi, vel authores in aliqua gente fuerant. Quamuis vero illi suis opinionibus decepti circa deorum multitudinem turpissimė errarint, eternae tamen veritatis infallibile oraculum est, nos charitatis studio Dei similes fieri, quoad carnis nostrae infirmitas ferre poterit. Est haec insignis & excellens vere fidelium gloria, quam nulli principes vel reges ullis diuitijs aut victorijs assequi possunt. Debet huius consyderatio nos ad indefessum charitatis studium excitare. Solent enim germani filij parentum virtutes imitari, ut paternae gloriae consortes fiant. Studeamus ergo & nos dei patris bonitatem & charitatem factis nostris exprimere, & sic diuinae gloriae merces ad nos quoque peruenient. Debet hoc ipsum ad alias etiam virtutes, quae in Deo eximiae videntur, applicari, imprimis ad sanctimoniam & puritatem, a cuius studio qui absunt, cum Deo puro & sancto communionem habere non possunt. Psal.15. Isa.33. &c.
units.tr: The third fruit of charity is that, as he is, so are we in this world. Charity, and the beneficence that springs from it, therefore makes us like God. For nothing is so divine as to do good to many, because God, as he created all things, so also preserves them, and bestows daily benefits upon his creatures. The heathen saw this, and for this reason they counted among the gods those who had been either the first discoverers or the authors of some common good among a people. Although those heathen, deceived by their own opinions, erred most shamefully about the multitude of gods, yet the infallible oracle of eternal truth is that we become like God through the study of charity, as far as the weakness of our flesh will allow. This is the distinguished and excellent glory of true believers, which no princes or kings can attain by any riches or victories. The consideration of this ought to stir us up to a tireless zeal for charity. For true sons are wont to imitate the virtues of their parents, so that they become sharers in their fatherly glory. Let us therefore also strive to express in our deeds the goodness and charity of God the Father, and so the reward of divine glory will come to us as well. This same point ought to be applied also to the other virtues that appear especially excellent in God, above all to holiness and purity, from the pursuit of which those who are absent cannot have communion with the pure and holy God (Ps. 15; Isa. 33, etc.).

units.la: Didicimus hucusque, quae verae charitatis in nobis causa sit & origo, fides nimirum, quae Dei charitatem erga nos percipit. Vidimus excellentes charitatis fructus, communionem cum Deo, si fiducia in die iudicij, & diuinae imaginis, quae peccato primi parentis obliterata fuit, restitutionem. Horum itaque memores, fidei nostrae professioni charitatis studium iungamus, ne dum sine hac fidem iactamus, a Christo alieni, charitatem vero sine fide simulantes, hypocritae esse deprehendamur. Dabit sanctum hoc studium, ut & in hoc seculo omni metu & terrore liberati, tandem aeternum cum Christo Iesu regnemus, cui debetur benedictio, gloria, honor & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: We have learned so far what is the cause and origin of true charity in us, namely faith, which perceives God's charity toward us. We have seen the excellent fruits of charity: communion with God, confidence in the day of judgment, and the restoration of the divine image, which was obliterated by the sin of our first parent. Therefore, mindful of these things, let us join the zeal of charity to the profession of our faith, lest, while we boast of faith without it, we be found aliens from Christ, or, while we feign charity without faith, we be found to be hypocrites. This holy zeal will grant that, freed from all fear and terror in this age, we may at last reign eternally with Christ Jesus, to whom be blessing, glory, honor and power forever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXVII.
units.tr: HOMILIA XXVII.

units.la: Timor non est in charitate, sed perfecta charitas foras eijcit timorem: quoniam timor cruciatum habet. Qui autem timet, non est perfectus in charitate. Nos diligimus eum, quoniam ipse prior dilexit nos.
units.tr: Fear is not in love, but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has torment. He who fears is not perfect in love. We love him, because he first loved us.

units.la: Quamuis Deus, qui omnium conditor est & dominus, pro suo in nos iure & imperio voluntatis suae praecepta simpliciter proponere, & a nobis obedientiam magna authoritate exigere possit, patris tamen ingenium potius quam domini seueri & immitis mores imitari vult. Nam vt patres non pro suo duntaxat iure obedientiam flagitat, sed promissis & premijs rudem liberorum aetatem inuitant: ita Deus vna cum praeceptis suis amplissimas omnis generis bonorum promissiones proponit, quo facilius a nobis obedientiam impetret, qui tot tamq; graues sentimus remoras, quae a via salutis reuocant. Sunt qui hoc abunde probare possunt, plurimi loci in Lege per Mosem tradita, maximè tamen Leuit.26.& Deut.28.ca. Præterea prophetas in hoc plurimum versari videmus, quòd tam minis quàm promissionibus in Lege propositis obedientiam à nobis flagitant. Facit idem Christus in euangelio, cuius exemplum Apostoli sedulò imitantur, vt tum alibi, tum in præsenti de charitate Christiana tractatione videre licet. Non contentus enim Ioannes, Christi & præceptum & exemplum proposuisse, splendidis etiam promissionis nos ad charitatis studium allicit, de quibus nuper copiosè dictū est. Quia tamen inter alia charitatem sectantibus fiduciam & tutam spem in die iudicij pollicitus fuerat, quæ maxima felicitatis nostræ, quoad hic viuimus, pars est, ne quid dubij in animis nostris remaneret, eum locū in præsenti plenius explicat. Deinde Christianæ charitatis fontes siue causam efficientem denuo attingit, sic tamen, vt eius mentione charitatis studium commendet.
units.tr: Although God, who is the maker and lord of all things, could by his right over us and the authority of his will simply set forth his precepts and demand obedience from us with great authority, he nonetheless wishes to imitate the disposition of a father rather than the harsh and stern manners of a lord. For just as fathers demand obedience not merely by their own right, but also invite the untutored age of their children with promises and rewards, so God, together with his precepts, sets before us the most ample promises of every kind of good, so that he may more easily obtain obedience from us, who feel so many and such heavy hindrances that call us back from the way of salvation. There are those who can prove this abundantly: very many passages in the Law delivered through Moses, but especially Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28. Moreover, we see the prophets especially occupied in this, that they demand obedience from us by threats as well as by the promises set forth in the Law. Christ does the same in the Gospel, and the Apostles diligently imitate his example, as may be seen both elsewhere and in the present treatment of Christian love. For John, not content to have set forth both the command and the example of Christ, also entices us to the pursuit of love by splendid promises, concerning which we have spoken at length just now. Yet because he had among other things promised confidence and a sure hope on the day of judgment to those who pursue love (which is the greatest part of our happiness, so long as we live here), so that nothing doubtful might remain in our minds, he now explains that passage more fully. Then he touches again on the sources, or efficient cause, of Christian love, yet in such a way that by mentioning it he commends the pursuit of love.

units.la: I. Timor non est in charitate, sed perfecta charitas foras eijcit timorem: quoniam timor cruciatum habet. Qui autem timet, non est perfectus in charitate. Poterat alicui superuacanea videri tam diligens huius rei demonstratio. Sed reuera perquam necessaria est, cum tanto tamque horribili metu impiorum conscientiæ exagitari soleant, quoties de die iudicij cogitare contingit. Est autem observandum, Ioannem hoc loco non de Dei timore loqui, qui à pijs abesse nequit, & iuxta Solomonis sententiam, veræ sapientiæ principium est. Prou.1. Sed eum intelligit, quem ex mortis & extremi iudicij recordatione homines à fide & charitate alieni percipiunt: qui tātus est, vt eos quiescere non sinat, & in desperationem rapiat frequenter, cum nō habeant, quod desperationem suadenti satanæ obijcere possint. Hunc à charitate procul abesse dicit Apostolus, id quod argumento solido & euidenti probat ad hunc modū: Quicunq; charitati studēt, cruciatū vel poenam minimè merentur. At in timore cruciatus est, & quidem tātus interdū, vt ipsam poenā quæ timetur, superet. Ergo qui charitati studēt, à timore isto liberi sunt. Et per consequens, quicūq; huic obnoxij sunt, se in charitate nōdum perfectos esse probat. Euidens & perspicua est huius argumenti veritas. Quia enim Christus charitatis studio amplissima vitæ æternæ præmia pollicetur, & huius sectatores se pro suis agnituru testatur, vtiq; ab omni poena & cruciatu alienissimi sunt. Major tamen erit huius loci perspicuitas, si exempla consyderemus, tam eorum qui in charitatem peccauerunt, quàm illorum qui eius studium solicitè sectati sunt. Primò autem loco pij prodeant, & inter hos quidem Moses fidelis ille in domo Dei seruus. Habet is multa charitatis fraternæ, qua totus flagrauit, testimonia. Nam & scriptura eum omnium hominum manssuetissimum fuisse testatur (Nume.12.) & cum Aegypti delicijs frui posset, cum fratribus tamen suis potius afligi, quàm sine his voluptuari voluit, Exo.2.Heb.11. Adhęc populi tam duri, pertinacis & ingrati quotidianas iniurias, calumnias, conuitia & minas tata longanimitate pertulit, vt nesciam si quis sanctorū illi hac parte conferri queat. Sed quàm excelles in eo est quamq; secura Dei fiducia: Cū enim ad Dei concionantis vocē & tonitru totus populus consternaretur, nec tantę vocis maiestatem ferret, solus ad caliginem illam, alijs inaccessam, appropinquare audet, & cum Deo facie ad faciem colloqui. Exo.20. Nume. 12. Idem cum omnis populus propter idololatriæ peccatum delere meruisset, solus est, qui suam pro illis vitam interponere audet, & flagrans iam diuini furoris incendium restinguit. Num ergo diuini iudicij diem misere & desperabundus timere potuit, qui dicere audet: Nunc igitur remitte peccatum hoc eorum, aut si remittere non vis, expunge me quæso de libro tuo, quem scripsisti. Exo.32. Vides ergo in Mose, charitatis fraternæ studiosò, horribilem illum iudicij extremi terrorem locum non habuisse. Sed ne soli Mosi securitatem hanc concessisse putemus, Dauidem quoq; inspice, quem Deus virum esse dicit iuxta cor suum. 1.Sam.13. Extabunt huius infinita in regē Saulem & vniuersum Israelem beneficia, quæ de ipsius charitate luculenter testari poterāt. Nec in eos modo beneficus fuit, qui officia eius agnoscebant, sed in ingratissimos homines, imo in hostes, quos cum Saule in interitum suū conspirauisse videbat. Nam & Ceilam à Palæstinis oppugnatam liberat, & Saulem in manus suas delapsum cum occidere posset, saluum abire permittit. 1.Sam.23.24.&26. Atqui licet ingratissimos sentiret, qui ipsi ingentia præmia debebant, nō tamen fructu caruit tam ardens charitatis studium. Timore enim mortis et tremendi illius iudicij adeò vacuus fuit, vt sponte ad Dei tribunal prouocare, & causam suā Deo iusto iudici subijcere ausus fuerit. Quis ergo miserum dicet Dauidem, qui tantum causæ suæ inspectorem se habere intellexit, & ab illo de hac iudicari voluit? Legantur Psalmi eius quos in Saulina persecutione compositos reliquit, & inter hos cūprimis 7. & 26. & inuictum animi robur in eo videbis quem tot undiq; premebant pericula. Iungatur duobus hisce electum illud Christi organum, Paulus apostolus, qui charitatis ignem tantum in se se sentit, vt pro Iudæis fratribus suis, anathema à Christo fieri cupiat. Roma. 9. Idem enim hic iudicij metu adeò non consternatur, vt cupiat dissolui & esse cum Christo, simulq; intelligat iustitiæ coronam sibi in cœlis repositam esse, Phil.1.2.Tim.4. Constat ergo verisimum esse, quod Ioannes charitatem horribili illo iudicij metu liberam esse dicit.
units.tr: I. Fear is not in love, but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has torment. He who fears is not perfect in love. This demonstration of so diligent a point might seem superfluous to someone. But in truth it is most necessary, since the consciences of the impious are commonly tormented by such great and such horrible fear whenever it happens that they think about the day of judgment. Yet it must be observed that John in this place is not speaking of the fear of God, which cannot be absent from the godly, and which, according to the saying of Solomon, is the beginning of true wisdom (Prov. 1). Rather he means that fear which men estranged from faith and love perceive from the recollection of death and the final judgment: it is so great that it does not let them rest, and it frequently drives them into despair, since they have nothing with which they can oppose Satan urging despair. The Apostle says that this fear is far removed from love, and he proves it by a solid and evident argument in this way: those who pursue love do not deserve torment or punishment at all. But in fear there is torment, and indeed sometimes so great that it surpasses the very punishment that is feared. Therefore those who pursue love are free from that fear. And consequently, whoever is subject to it proves that he is not yet perfect in love. The truth of this argument is evident and plain. For since Christ promises the most ample rewards of eternal life to the pursuit of love, and testifies that he will acknowledge its followers as his own, they are surely most far removed from all punishment and torment. Yet the clarity of this passage will be greater if we consider examples, both of those who have sinned against love and of those who have diligently pursued its practice. Let the godly come forward first, and among these indeed Moses, that faithful servant in the house of God. He has many testimonies of brotherly love, by which he burned throughout. For Scripture testifies that he was the meekest of all men (Num. 12), and although he could enjoy the delights of Egypt, he preferred to be afflicted with his brothers rather than to take pleasure without them (Exod. 2; Heb. 11). Moreover, he bore the daily injuries, calumnies, reproaches and threats of so hard, obstinate and ungrateful a people with such long-suffering that I do not know whether any of the saints can be compared with him in this respect. But how excellent and how secure his confidence in God was! When the whole people was dismayed at the voice and thunder of God speaking, and could not bear the majesty of so great a voice, he alone dares to approach that darkness, inaccessible to the others, and to speak with God face to face (Exod. 20; Num. 12). Again, when the whole people had deserved to be destroyed on account of the sin of idolatry, he alone is the one who dares to interpose his own life for them, and quenches the blazing fire of divine wrath now kindled. Could he then have feared the day of divine judgment wretchedly and in despair, he who dares to say: "Now therefore forgive this sin of theirs, or if you will not forgive it, blot me, I pray, out of your book, which you have written" (Exod. 32)? You see then that in Moses, a zealous lover of brotherly love, that horrible terror of the final judgment had no place. But lest we think that this security was granted to Moses alone, look also at David, whom God calls a man after his own heart (1 Sam. 13). Innumerable benefits toward King Saul and all Israel, which could clearly bear witness to his love, stand out. Nor was he beneficent only to those who acknowledged his services, but also to the most ungrateful men, indeed to enemies, whom he saw conspiring with Saul for his destruction. For he freed Keilah, attacked by the Philistines, and when he could have killed Saul, who had fallen into his hands, he allowed him to go away unharmed (1 Sam. 23, 24, and 26). Yet although he perceived that they were most ungrateful, who ought to have owed him great rewards, such an ardent pursuit of love did not lack its fruit. For he was so free from fear of death and of that dreadful judgment that he dared of his own accord to summon himself before God's tribunal and to submit his cause to God, the just judge. Who then will call David wretched, since he understood that he had such an overseer of his cause, and wished to be judged by him in this matter? Let his Psalms be read, which he left composed during the persecution by Saul, and among these especially Psalms 7 and 26, and you will see in him an unconquered strength of spirit, though so many dangers pressed on him from every side. Let the chosen instrument of Christ, the Apostle Paul, be joined to these two, who feels within himself so great a fire of love that he desires to be made an anathema from Christ for his Jewish brothers (Rom. 9). For he is not so dismayed by the fear of judgment that he does not desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, while at the same time he understands that the crown of righteousness is laid up for him in heaven (Phil. 1; 2 Tim. 4). It is therefore established that what John says is true: love is free from that horrible fear of judgment.

units.la: Sed opponamus his impiorum exempla, ut ingens illud charitatis bonum clarius elucescat. Atqui inter hos primatum merito tenet primogenitus ille satanæ Cain, qui charitatis igne in animo suo sic restinxit, ut ne fratri quidem uterino parcendum esse putaret, et innocenti illius sanguine manus infelices polluere auderet. Quæ vero illi animo post explosam charitate fuisse legimus? Respondere quidem audet Deo de fratre interroganti, qui omnium impiorum mos est, flagitia nimirum recens commissa negare, et impudenti improbitate correptores repellere. Sed infelix est tantæ audaciæ exitus. Ubi enim se propius urgeri, et tam infandum scelus Dei iudicis oculos ne-quaquam latere videt, horribiles in animo suo conscientiæ æstus sentit, qui infelici et verè miserò desperationis plenam vocem extorquent. Iniquitas mea maior est, quàm ut remittatur. Sed et fugit ecclesiam filiorum Dei, cuius commercium sibi interdictum esse sentit. Idem omnino Saulis tyranni, ab omni charitate alieni, exitus fuisse legitur. Ut primum enim ambitionis æstrum animo illius charitatem expulit, infeuit autem odium et inuidia, omnem simul conscientiæ pacem et tranquillitatem recessisse sentit. Nam satanæ spiritu agitatus, Dauidem regno eijcit, filio proprio mortem intentat, Phytonissam consulit, tandem amisis filijs et cæsa exercitus maxima parte, ipse sibi mortem conscicens vitæ miseræ exitum miseriorem sortitur. 1. Sam.28. et 31. &c. Nec absimilis ab his est Iudæ proditoris conditio. Atqui dies me deficeret, si quæcunque in hanc sententiam adduci possunt exempla, copiosius recensere velim. Quę utinam diligentius paulo expenderent, quos hodie iuuat vindictam ardentius persequi, opes per fraudes et dolos cogerere, et sanguine partas diuitias coaceruare. Licet enim nunc surdæ ipsis aures sint, et omnem monitionem fide indignam esse credant, erit tamen aliquando tempus, quando oppressorum clamores, pupillorum eiulatus, viduarum lachrymæ, peregrinorum gemitus, et horrenda effusi sanguinis facies oculorum ipsorum obuersabuntur, et eos terrores iudicij excitabunt, quos Cainum, Saulem et Iudam olim sensisse modò didicimus.
units.tr: But let us set against these the examples of the impious, so that that great good of love may shine out more clearly. Among these, that firstborn child of Satan, Cain, rightly holds the first place: he so extinguished the fire of love in his mind that he thought he should not spare even his own brother by the same mother, and dared to defile his unhappy hands with the innocent blood of that brother. But what do we read happened to his mind after love was driven out? He indeed dares to answer God when God asks about his brother, as is the custom of all the impious: namely, to deny the crimes just committed, and with shameless wickedness to repel those who rebuke him. But the outcome of such audacity is unhappy. For when he sees that he is pressed more closely, and that God, the judge, by no means fails to see so unspeakable a crime, he feels horrible tumults of conscience in his mind, which wring from him a cry full of unhappy and truly wretched despair: "My iniquity is greater than that it can be forgiven." And he flees from the church of the sons of God, whose fellowship he feels is forbidden to him. Altogether the same outcome of the tyrant Saul, a stranger to all love, is read. For as soon as the goad of ambition drove love out of his mind, and hatred and envy raged in its place, he feels that all peace and tranquillity of conscience had departed at once. For, driven by the spirit of Satan, he drives David from his kingdom, threatens his own son with death, consults a medium, and at last, having lost his sons and with the greater part of his army slain, he, consciously bringing death upon himself, obtains a more wretched end to his miserable life (1 Sam. 28 and 31, etc.). Not unlike these is the condition of Judas the traitor. But the days would fail me if I wished to recount more fully all the examples that can be brought to bear on this point. Would that those who today delight to pursue vengeance more eagerly, to gather wealth by fraud and deceit, and to heap up riches acquired by blood, would weigh these things a little more carefully! For although their ears are now deaf to such things, and they believe that every admonition is unworthy of trust, there will nevertheless come a time when the cries of the oppressed, the wailing of orphans, the tears of widows, the groans of strangers, and the dreadful sight of poured-out blood will rise before their eyes, and will stir up in them those terrors of judgment which we have just learned Cain, Saul and Judas once felt.

units.la: Præterea in Apostoli verbis obseruandum venit, quòd ait: Qui timet, non est perfectus in charitate. Quia vero charitatem ex fide originem ducere et fidei coniunctam esse, iam sæpe dictū est, constat nec in fide et religione perfectos esse, aut quicquam certi habere eos, quicunq; mortis et iudicij extremi metu excruciantur. Fidei siquidem proprium est, conscientiarum pacem afferre, et omnem de salute nostra dubitationem eximere. Est enim (ut Paulus definit) solida et firmi-ter subsistens rerum, quæ sperantur, apprehensio. Heb.11. Nec ita nos fidē[?] Christus docet, ut salutis nostræ incertos et dubios esse velit. Nam in euangelio ait: Qui sitiverit ex aqua, quā ego dabo ei, non sitierit in æternum. Ioan.4. Et rursum: Qui venit ad me, non esuriet: et qui credit in me, non sitiet unquam. Ioan.6. Et alibi omnibus oneratis, ad se venientibus, requiem certam ac verā[?] pollicetur. Matth.11. Agnouerunt hæc sancti omnes, quorum fides in scripturis celebratur, et ea de causa spem inuictā secuti sunt, quæ nullis laboribus siue periculis debilitari et expugnari potuit. Vides igitur et hoc loco, quid de Sophistarum doctrina, quæ in Papistarum ecclesijs spargitur, iudicare debeas. Docent illi et constanter affirmant, hominem quoad hic viuit, de gratia Dei certum fieri non posse. Quòd si incertum tibi est, num in gratia Dei sis, salutem quoque tibi incertam esse oportet, quæ extra gratiam Dei nulla est. Parit hæc de gratia Dei et salute nostra dubitatio perpetuos timores, et indefinentes terrores conscientiæ, quod fateri coguntur, quicunque opinionibus hisce assensum præbent. At ubi timores eiusmodi supersunt, charitas perfecta locum non habet, et proinde nec fides, quæ à charitate separari nequit. Talis ergo hæc doctrina est, quæ fidem euertit, et omnem nostræ salutis rationem in dubium vocat. Sed quia de his in præcedenti Sermone plura diximus, hæc modò sufficiant. Ampleetamur nos Christi doctrinam, et in hac ipsum Christum, qui ut fidei fundamentum est insuperabile, ita charitate ea suos incendit, quę omnibus conscientiarum terroribus pulsis, spem et fiduciam salutis certam ac infallibilem nobis conciliat. Cæterum hinc digressi reliqua etiam huius loci videamus.
units.tr: Furthermore, in the Apostle's words we must observe what he says: "He who fears is not perfect in love." Since it has often been said already that love takes its origin from faith and is joined to faith, it is clear that those who are tormented by fear of death and the last judgment are not perfect either in faith and religion, or have anything certain. For it is the proper work of faith to bring peace to consciences and to remove every doubt about our salvation. For faith is (as Paul defines it) the solid and firm apprehension of things that are hoped for. Heb. 11. Nor does Christ teach us in such a way that he wishes us to be uncertain and doubtful of our salvation. For in the Gospel he says: "Whoever shall drink of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst forever." John 4. And again: "Whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst." John 6. And elsewhere he promises certain and true rest to all who are burdened and come to him. Matt. 11. All the saints, whose faith is celebrated in the Scriptures, have acknowledged these things, and for that reason they followed an unconquered hope, which could be weakened and overcome by no labors or dangers. You see, therefore, also in this place, how you ought to judge the teaching of the Sophists, which is spread in the churches of the Papists. They teach and constantly affirm that a man, as long as he lives here, cannot be made certain of the grace of God. But if you are uncertain whether you are in the grace of God, then your salvation must also be uncertain, since outside the grace of God there is no salvation. This doubt about the grace of God and our salvation produces perpetual fears and unending terrors of conscience, which all those who give their assent to these opinions are forced to confess. But where fears of this kind remain, perfect love has no place, and therefore neither has faith, which cannot be separated from love. This teaching, then, is one that overthrows faith and calls into doubt every ground of our salvation. But since we have said more about these matters in the preceding sermon, let these things suffice for now. Let us embrace the teaching of Christ, and in it Christ himself, who, as the unshakable foundation of faith, so kindles his own with that love which, once all terrors of conscience are driven away, procures for us a certain and infallible hope and confidence of salvation. But having digressed thus far, let us now look at the remaining points of this passage.

units.la: II. Nos diligimus cum, quoniam ipse prior dilexit nos. Denuo fontes et causam efficientem charitatis attingit, quia hoc præsentis loci ratio postulare videbatur. Ita enim inter homines comparatum est, ut quoties magnum alicuius rei fructum vident, mox quærant, unde hæc illi virtus et efficacia. Quare cum eos ostendisset charitatis fructus, qui reuera magni et salutares sunt, non inepte veram charitatis causam repetit, ne quid nobis ipsis imaginemur, quod cū veritate pugnet, et diuinæ gloriæ contrarium fit. Dicit ergo: Nos Deū diligimus, et per dilectionē hanc Deo coniungimur ac unimur, quo fit, ut homines etiam, quos ille diligit, amore prosequamur, eamq; insi tuamus[?] vitæ nostræ rationem, quæ ab omni terrore iudicij et desperationis malo liberet. At tantum bonum nemo putet ex nobis esse, vel nostrae naturae viribus procreari. Altius enim ascendamus oportet, ad Deum scilicet, qui illius in nobis author est. Quia hic nos prior dilexit, & nihil talē cogitantes suo amore praeueniens, eum dilectionis affectum in nobis operatur, vt & ipsum diligamus, & propter ipsum eodem amore proximos nostros complectamur.
units.tr: II. "We love him, because he first loved us." Again he touches on the sources and the efficient cause of love, because the logic of the present passage seemed to require it. For it is the way of men that whenever they see the great fruit of something, they soon ask whence comes this power and efficacy. Therefore, having shown the fruits of love, which are truly great and saving, he not unfittingly traces back the true cause of love, so that we may not imagine anything of our own that conflicts with the truth and is contrary to the glory of God. He says, therefore: We love God, and through this love we are joined and united to God, from which it follows that we also embrace with love the men whom he loves, and we adopt a way of life that frees us from every terror of judgment and the evil of despair. But let no one think that so great a good comes from us, or is produced by the powers of our nature. For we must ascend higher, namely to God, who is its author in us. For he first loved us, and, anticipating us with his love when we were thinking of nothing of the kind, he works in us that affection of love, so that we may both love him and, for his sake, embrace our neighbors with the same love.

units.la: Est hæc Apostoli sententia perquàm memorabilis. Perspicuè enim docet, quod iam sæpe di-ctum est. Charitatis doctrina operum nostrorum iustitiam & proprij meriti fiduciam non stabili-ri, sed euerti potius. Siquidem ad causas efficientes effectus omnes referri debent. At quia charitatis fons non in homine, sed in Deo est, qui nō alio medio q; fide apprehendi potest, stultè & inepte homini tribuitur, quod nō suis viribus & proprio motu operatur. Charitatis verò causas ex Deo esse, multis & solidis argumentis probari poterat. Certè hominis naturam peccato primi parentis sic corruptam & vitiatam esse constat, vt non modò boni in se nihil habeat, sed & bonū diu nitus praescriptum odiat & abominetur, ac legi diuinae nō possit subijci. Primas verò in hac corruptione tenet philautiæ malum, quo homo totus in sui amore rapitur, se solum quærit, sibi sem per proximus est, nulla interim vel diuinae gloriae vel salutis alioru ratione habita. At quid à charitate Christiana tam alienū esse potest, quàm philautię vitium? Vt enim charitatis affectus sunt, mansuetudo, clementia, misericordia, iniuriae acceptae obliuio, facilitas in cōdonandis deliictis, bē neuolentia, benefaciendi studium & quosuis iuuādi voluntas: ita ex philautiae fontibus vitiosis-simis promanare solent, inuidia, odium, simultas, inimicitiae, irae, rixae, conuitia, obtrectationes, ca lumniae, pugnae, cędes, vsurae, doli, imposturae, mendacia, rapinae, furta, simulationes, & quicquid aliud vel auaritia vel ambitione dictante faciunt homines. Quis verò à tanta corruptione nos af-ferit? Num ipsi nos liberare possumus? Minimè. Imò ne volumus quidē liberari, & pauci sunt qui videant, quàm ipsis necessarium sit, vt ex tātis malis liberentur. Solus Deus est, qui sua dilectio-ne miseros nos præuenit, & liberatos vult, quos cōdidit ex gratia. Filium enim suum Iesum Chri-stum, priusquàm mundi fundamenta iacerētur, nobis redemptore & saluatorem constituit, & in illo elegit nos, priusquà conditi aliquà habere potuimus istarum rerū notitiā. Et quia in Christo nos ante mundi constitutione elegit, nullo hoc nostro merito factū fuisse constat. Nec hic mihi aliquis praescientiā Dei objiciat, quasi propter opera & merita, quae nos praeuidit facturos, elegerit. Quia nisi ille elegisset, & sua gratia ornare dignatus esset, iustitia nostra nulla omnino futura erat. Nec enim nos proprio nostrae naturae motu Deū quaerimus, & gratiā nobis in Christo recondita se-ctamur, sed nisi queramur ipsi, nulla salutis cura tāgimur. Nam vt oues errauimus, vnufquisq; in viam suā. Isa. 53. At ouis ea natura est, vt semel à grege seducta, nō ipsa pastore quaerat, sed à pasto-re quaesita & inuenta gregi restituitur. Nec aliā esse nostrae salutis rationē, exempla scripturae plu rima docent. Peccauit primus Adam, & nudū se conspicit. Nū vero ad Deū conuersus sponte ve niam petit, culpam deprecatur, emēdatione promittit & in posterum obedientiae studens, cū Deo in gratiā redire meretur? Nemo opinor hoc dixerit. Quin potius se nudū videns timet, velamen-ta consuit verè ficulnea & nullius momenti, Dei conspectum fugit, eiusdem vocem metuit, & eū se praebet, vt non potuisset non perire, nisi Deus ipsum, quaesitū & inuentum in gratiam recepis-set, & ab aeterno destinati saluatoris promissionibus fuisset cōsolatus. Atqui hæc in primo paren-te fieri voluit Dominus Deus, vt quæ salutis omniū nostrum ratio esset, perspicue cerneremus. Eandem & postea in alijs secutus est. Iudæorum etenim gente hoc ipso modo ex mera gratia ele-git, suum fecit peculiū, cū nihil in ipsis esset, propter quod tales fieri mererentur: quod nemo ne-gabit, qui Ezech. cap. 16. & Pauli ad Rom 9. diligenter perlegerit. Quę gentiū cōditio fuerit, idem Paulus multis in locis docet, clarissimè tamen Ephef. 2. & primis epistolæ ad Rom. capitibus. Ve-rissima ergo est Ioannis sententia, nos Dei dilectionem & quicquid ex hac boni emanat, nō ex no bis ipsis, sed ex Dei gratia habere, qui prior nos diligere dignatus est. Quare stultissimi mortalium sunt, qui suis ipsorum viribus & operibus fidunt. Quid enim habes quod non acceperis? Quòd si accepisti, quid gloriaris quasi non acceperis? 1. Cor. 4.
units.tr: This saying of the Apostle is most memorable. For it teaches clearly what has often been said already: that the doctrine of love does not establish the righteousness of our works or confidence in our own merit, but rather overthrows them. For all effects ought to be referred to their efficient causes. But since the source of love is not in man but in God, who cannot be apprehended by any means other than faith, it is foolish and absurd to attribute to man what he does not accomplish by his own powers and his own motion. That the causes of love are from God could be proved by many solid arguments. It is certain that the nature of man has been so corrupted and vitiated by the sin of the first parent that it not only has nothing good in itself, but also hates and abominates the good prescribed by God, and cannot be subjected to the divine law. Yet the first place in this corruption is held by the evil of self-love, by which the whole man is carried away into love of himself; he seeks only himself, is always near to himself, and meanwhile takes no account either of the glory of God or of the salvation of others. But what can be so alien to Christian love as the vice of self-love? For just as the affections of love are gentleness, clemency, mercy, forgetfulness of injuries received, readiness to pardon offenses, goodwill, zeal for doing good, and a willingness to help anyone at all, so from the most vicious springs of self-love there are wont to flow envy, hatred, rivalry, enmities, angers, quarrels, reproaches, detractions, slanders, fights, murders, usury, frauds, deceits, lies, robberies, thefts, pretenses, and whatever else men do under the dictation of either greed or ambition. But who will free us from so great a corruption? Can we free ourselves? By no means. Indeed we do not even wish to be freed, and there are few who see how necessary it is for them to be freed from such great evils. God alone is the one who anticipates us in miserable condition with his love, and wills that those whom he has created out of grace be made free. For before the foundations of the world were laid, he appointed his Son Jesus Christ to be our redeemer and savior, and in him he chose us before we could have any knowledge of these things, since we had been created. And because he chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, it is clear that this came about by no merit of ours. Nor let anyone object to me the foreknowledge of God, as if he had chosen us on account of the works and merits which he foresaw we would do. For if he had not chosen us, and had not deigned to adorn us with his grace, our righteousness would have been nothing at all. For we do not seek God by any motion of our own nature, and follow the grace hidden for us in Christ; rather, unless we are sought ourselves, we are moved by no care for salvation. For, "we had all gone astray like sheep, each one to his own way." Isa. 53. But a sheep is of such a nature that, once led away from the flock, it does not seek the shepherd itself; rather, having been sought and found by the shepherd, it is restored to the flock. The examples of Scripture teach many times that there is no other way of our salvation. The first Adam sinned, and he sees himself naked. Did he, turned to God, of his own accord seek pardon, beg for his fault, promise amendment, and, studying obedience for the future, deserve to return into favor with God? No one, I think, would say this. Rather, seeing himself naked, he is afraid, sews together coverings truly of fig leaves and of no worth, flees the sight of God, fears his voice, and so conducts himself that he could not have failed to perish, unless God had received him into grace when he had been sought and found, and had comforted him with the promises of the Savior destined from eternity. And yet the Lord God willed this to happen in the first parent, so that we might see clearly what the way of salvation for all of us is. He followed the same course afterwards with others. For from the Jewish people he chose in this same way out of mere grace, he made them his own peculiar people, when there was nothing in them on account of which they might deserve to become such; this no one will deny who has carefully read through Ezekiel chapter 16 and Paul to the Romans chapter 9. What the condition of the Gentiles was, Paul teaches in many places, yet most clearly in Ephesians 2 and the first chapters of the Epistle to the Romans. The saying of John is therefore most true: that we have the love of God, and whatever good flows from it, not from ourselves, but from the grace of God, who first deigned to love us. Therefore the most foolish of mortals are those who trust in their own powers and works. For what do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it? 1 Cor. 4.

units.la: Porrò eadem sententia nostri nos officij admonet Apostolus. Si enim nos, cum corruptis-mi essemus, prior dilexit Deus, & gratiæ suæ filios effecit, decet vtique, vt Deū vicisim diligen-tes, in eius gratia perseuerare studeamus. Communis siquidem sensus docet, vt eos diligamus qui suo nos amore dignos censent & beneficia in nos conferunt. Et quia summa in nos est Dei patris dilectio, nec beneficia vlla maiora sunt, quàm quæ in nos Deus confert, summū quoq; & ardens dilectionis Dei studiū merito à nobis exigitur. Nec enim verbis tantū nos se diligere vult Deus, sed cordis affectū requirit, iuxta illud Christi: Diliges dominū deū tuum ex toto corde tuo, ex to ta anima tua, & ex totis viribus tuis. Matt. 22. Sūt dilectionis huius pulcherrimi fructus, ex quib. facilimè agnosci potest. Primus inter hos est obedietia vera, quę dei præceptis exhibetur. Vt enim qui patres diligunt filij, eorundem iusis obtemperant, ne illorum in se iram aliquo modo provocent: ita qui Deum patrem diligunt, præceptis Dei vnicè student, & ea anxiè cauent propter quę venit ira Dei super filios inobedientiæ. Col.3. Alter fructus est, animi propensio, qua pro Dei patris gloria nihil non amittere, nullos non labores perferre, nihil non periculorum subire parati sumus. Habet enim hoc proprium amor, ut leuia & iucunda reddat, quæcunq; ferenda veniunt, quod in illis cernitur, quorum amor circa homines, aut patriam, aut opes aliaque eius generis versatur. Quoties vitæ pericula subit impudicus amator, mercator auarus, miles ambitiosus. At quàto maiorem diuini amoris vim putabimus, cuius obiectum Deus est, summum illud & æternum bonum, cuius possessores non possunt non esse omnibus modis absoluti & beatissimi. De hac Paulus loquitur: Quis nos separabit à dilectione Dei? Num afflictio? num angustia? num persecutio? num fames? num nuditas? num periculum? num gladius? Quemadmodum scriptum est: Propter te morti tradimur tota die, habiti sumus velut oues mactationi destinatæ. Verum in his omnibus superamus per eum, qui dilexit nos. Rom.8. Debent hæc totis animis recondi, siquidem veri Dei cultores esse & dici volumus. Pericula enim ingētia & infinita fidelibus proposita esse, ipse Christus testatur: quæ nunquam sustinebit caro, nisi animi nostri hac Dei dilectione flagrent. Et exempla hodie multorum sunt, quæ docent, quàm infeliciter euangelio Christi & fide glorientur, qui ab hoc amore adhuc alieni sunt. Sed o pudendam nostri seculi corruptionem. Quid enim de periculis, de Cruce, de persecutionibus, & aliis eius generis malis dicere opus est, quę charitate vinci debebāt? Quot obsecro hodie inuenies, qui diuitias superfluas propter Dei gloriā relinquere velint? Quid diuitias dico? Quàm pauci sunt, qui illicitis voluptatibus renunciare velint, sic postulante Christi gloriam? Malè audit & infamatur Christi doctrina propter morum nostrorum corruptelam. Euangelio multi accepta ferunt, quæ inter huius professores regnant vitia, nempe vsurarias artes, rapinas, dolos, mendacia, blasphemias, fidei & religionis contemptum, scortationem, stupra, adulteria, bellandi rabiem, ebrietatem, & effrenem in rebus quibuslibet intemperantiam. Quotus verò quisq; est, qui vt Dei verbum hac infamiæ nota liberet, & tam atrocem contumeliam à Christi nomine depellat, ab hisce tam corruptis studijs sibi abstinendū esse censeat? Imò pergunt plerique, & in deteriora labuntur indies. Num igitur in his Dei dilectionem regnare, imò aliquam huius scintillam inesse dicemus? Imò quod verè de his dici potest, pudet dicere. Dicam tamen, quia hoc illorū meretur impietas. Tam alieni sunt à Dei & filij ipsius Iesu Christi amore isti homines, vt turpe lucrum ex re qualibet, pocula, scorta, & res quasq; nefandissimas Deo & Christo ipsius præferant. Nisi enim hæc illi præferrent, nunquam certè in his contra Dei voluntatem, eum tanta diuini nominis & verbi contumelia, tam impudenter volutarentur. Et vt exemplo cōstet, quales sint, Iudæis omnino conferri debet hæc improba hominum colluuies, quibus olim Barrabas, homo seditiosus & sanguinarius, Christo Iesu largitore & authore salutis potior erat. Nam & ipsi eadem Christo præferunt, quæ in Barraba homine flagitiosissimo locum habebant. Nostrum est, fratres dilecti, insignem Dei patris amorem, quo nos prosecutus est, digno studio expendere, illius mutuo amore incendi, vt tam sancti studij fructus olim percipere, & omni timore vacui, in dio iudicij comparere possimus coram Christo iudice, cui debetur benedictio, gloria, honor & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, the Apostle reminds us of the same thing as a duty of ours. For if God, when we were corrupt, loved us first and made us sons of his grace, it is surely fitting that we, returning his love, should take care to persevere in his grace. For common sense teaches that we should love those who think us worthy of their affection and who confer benefits upon us. And since the love of God the Father toward us is supreme, and since no benefits are greater than those God bestows on us, the highest and most ardent zeal for loving God is rightly demanded of us. For God does not wish to be loved merely with words; he requires the affection of the heart, according to that saying of Christ: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength." Matt. 22. This love has most beautiful fruits, by which it can very easily be recognised. The first among these is true obedience, which is shown to the commandments of God. For just as sons who love their fathers obey their orders, so as not to provoke their anger against themselves in any way, so those who love God the Father take special care to keep his precepts and carefully guard against those things on account of which the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience. Col. 3. The second fruit is a readiness of mind, by which we are prepared to lose nothing, to endure no labours, and to undergo no dangers for the glory of God the Father. For love has this peculiar property, that it makes light and pleasant whatever must be borne; this is seen in those whose love is set upon men, or upon their country, or upon wealth and other things of that kind. How often does the lustful lover undertake the perils of life, the greedy merchant, the ambitious soldier! How much greater, then, shall we suppose the power of divine love to be, whose object is God, that supreme and eternal good, whose possessors cannot but be in every way free and most blessed! Of this love Paul speaks: "Who shall separate us from the love of God? Shall affliction? or distress? or persecution? or famine? or nakedness? or danger? or the sword? As it is written: For your sake we are killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep appointed for slaughter. But in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us." Rom. 8. These things ought to be laid up in our hearts with our whole souls, since we wish to be, and to be called, true worshippers of God. For Christ himself testifies that great and endless dangers are set before the faithful, which the flesh will never endure unless our minds burn with this love of God. And today there are many examples which show how unhappily those glory in the gospel of Christ and in faith who are still strangers to this love. But, oh, the shameful corruption of our age! For why need one speak of dangers, of the Cross, of persecutions, and other evils of that kind, which ought to be overcome by charity? How many, I beseech you, will you find today who are willing to give up superfluous riches for the glory of God? Why do I say riches? How few are there who are willing to renounce unlawful pleasures, when the glory of Christ demands it? The doctrine of Christ is ill spoken of and defamed on account of the corruption of our morals. Many lay to the gospel the blame for the vices that reign among its professors, namely, usurious arts, robberies, deceits, lies, blasphemies, contempt of faith and religion, whoredom, debauchery, adultery, the rage of war, drunkenness, and unbridled intemperance in all things. But how few are there who would judge that they must abstain from such corrupt pursuits, so as to free the word of God from this mark of infamy and to turn away so atrocious a reproach from the name of Christ? Nay, most people carry on, and slide into worse things every day. Shall we then say that the love of God reigns among these people, or that even a spark of it is present? Nay, what can truly be said of them, I am ashamed to say. Yet I will say it, because their impiety deserves it. These men are so estranged from the love of God and of his Son Jesus Christ, that for any base gain whatever they prefer cups, harlots, and any most abominable things to God and Christ. For if they did not prefer these things, they would certainly never wallow in them so shamelessly, against the will of God, with such great insult to the divine name and word. And to make clear by example what sort of people they are, this wicked crowd of men must be compared altogether with the Jews, to whom Barabbas, a seditious and bloodthirsty man, was once preferred to Jesus Christ, the giver and author of salvation. For these men too prefer to Christ the very things which held a place in that most disgraceful man Barabbas. It is our task, beloved brothers, to weigh with due earnestness the remarkable love of God the Father with which he has embraced us, and to be kindled by his mutual love, so that we may one day receive the fruits of so holy a zeal, and, free from all fear, may appear on the day of judgment before Christ the judge, to whom belong blessing, glory, honour, and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXVIII.
units.tr: Homily XXVIII.

units.la: Si quis dixerit: Diligo Deum: & fratrem suum oderit, mendax est. Qui enim non diligit fratrem suum, quem vidit, Deum quem non vidit, quomodo potest diligere? Et hoc ipsum præceptum habemus ab eo, ut qui diligit Deum, diligat & fratrem suum.
units.tr: If anyone says, "I love God," and hates his brother, he is a liar. For he who does not love his brother whom he has seen, how can he love God whom he has not seen? And we have this commandment from him, that whoever loves God should love his brother also.

units.la: <bl>D</bl>IVus Ioannes, Nos (inquit) diligimus Deum, quia ipse prior dilexit nos. Celebris omnino & verè divina sententia. De quà licet quæ Deus dedit nuper dixerimus, multa tamen dicenda restarent, si quis maiori spiritus virtute afflatus, diuinæ illius dilectionis mysteria pro dignitate expendere posset. Crebrò tamen in animis nostris versari debet, & in omnibus actionibus & institutis nostris occurrere, ne diuinæ dilectionis gloriâ insoleti nostrorum operum fiducia nobis vendicemus, interim tamen Deũ, qui prior nos amauit redamare studeamus. Porrò vt passim Deus, vt ipsum verè diligamus, exigit: ita nemo nō Dei amás & studiosus haberi vult. Iactât Dei dilostionem[?] Turcæ & Mahometistæ omnes. Eadem gloriantur Iudæi, vtcunque à Deo propter incre-dulitatem repudiati sint. Splendidè multa & sanctè de eadem disputant Monachi & totus ille scho-lasticorum coetus. Denique si vel fures, latrones, sicarios, veneficos, prædones, vsurarios, parricidas, periuros, & facinorosissimos quosque interroges, non puto aliquem tam impiè impudentem fore, qui se Dei osorem vel inimicum profiteri velit, sed huius amorem omnes plenis buccis testa-buntur. Contra hos omnes modò sermonem instituit Apostolus, vanam illorum gloriationem arguens. Docet enim hos mendaces esse, & dilectione Dei frustra gloriari, cum fratrum odio ringantur. Nec id simpliciter dicit, sed quod dixit argumentis firmis & solidis probat. Dignus ergo locus hic, qui nostro seculo diligenter inspiciatur, quando passim regnant falsi illi & mendaces dilectionis Dei ostentatores.
units.tr: The divine John says: "We love God, because he first loved us." This is altogether a famous and truly divine saying. Although we have recently spoken on what God has given, much would still remain to be said, if anyone, inspired by greater power of the Spirit, could weigh worthily the mysteries of that divine love. Yet it ought often to dwell in our minds and to meet us in all our actions and undertakings, lest, puffed up by the glory of divine love, we claim for ourselves a presumptuous confidence in our works, while we strive meanwhile to love in return God, who loved us first. Moreover, as God everywhere requires that we truly love him, so no one is willing not to be thought a lover of God and zealous for him. The Turks and all the Mahometans boast of God's love. The Jews glory in the same, however much they have been rejected by God for their unbelief. The monks and that whole company of the schoolmen dispute about it splendidly and piously. Finally, if you question thieves, robbers, assassins, poisoners, plunderers, usurers, parricides, perjurers, and the most wicked of all, I do not think there would be anyone so impudently impious as to wish to profess himself an enemy or hater of God, but all of them with full cheeks testify to his love. Against all these the Apostle now directs his discourse, refuting their vain boasting. For he teaches that these are liars, and that they boast in vain of the love of God while they labour under hatred of their brothers. Nor does he say this simply, but he proves what he has said by firm and solid arguments. This place is therefore worthy to be carefully examined in our age, when those false and lying displayers of the love of God reign everywhere.
