units.la: Si quis dixerit: Diligo Deum, & fratrem suum oderit, mendax est. Est hæc præsentis loci propositio, & summa eorum, quæ dicere instituit. Verba plana sunt & perspicua, quare in rebus, quæ hic continentur, perpendendis nos potius versari oportet.
units.tr: If anyone says, "I love God," and hates his brother, he is a liar. This is the proposition of the present passage and the sum of what he undertakes to say. The words are plain and clear, so it is rather in weighing the matters contained here that we ought to be engaged.

units.la: Primum locum in his obtinet, charitatis Dei & proximi coniunctio. Ita enim has coniunctas esse docet, vt neutra sine altera subsistere possit. Vt enim Deum diligere non possumus, nisi & fratres diligamus: ita nec fratres diligemus unquam, nisi Dei dilectio in nobis ardeat. Siquidem nō de prophano amore Apostolus loquitur, quo & impij interdum afficiuntur, vt non tam amare quàm furere, & prauis cōcupiscentijs æstuare dici possint. Qui amor cū fine plerunq; sortiatur vtriq; parti funestū, nequaquà diuinæ huic & sanctæ dilectioni adnumerari debet, quæ lætissimum æterni gaudij & nunquam intermorituræ felicitatis præmiū diuinitus propositū habet. Coniūgi autem et indissolubiliter cohærere Dei & proximi dilectioné, nō Ioànes modo, sed omnis scriptura vna nimi consensu docet. In lege certè vtraque traditur, & vt in prima Decalogi tabula deus quatuor præceptis modum dilectionis, quàm ipsi debemus, explicat: ita sex alterius tabulæ præcepta, quo pacto proximi dilectionem exercere debeamus, docent. In prophetis passim hoc ipsum cernitur, qui & dei cultum & beneficentiam in proximum studiosè tradunt. In euangelio Christi vocē habemus, cuius authoritas vel sola nobis sufficere debet. Is de summo legis præcepto interrogatus, respondet: Primum omnium præceptum est: Audi Israel, dominus deus noster, dominus vnus est. Et diliges dominum deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, & ex tota anima tua, & ex tota mente tua, & ex totis viribus tuis. Hoc est primum præceptum. Et secundum simile hoc est: Diliges proximum tuum, vt teipsum. Maius his aliud præceptum nō est. Mar.12. Obseruandū in Christi verbis, quòd præceptū de proximi dilectione primo simile esse dicit. Deinde quòd de vno summo & principali præcepto quæsitus, vtriusque dilectionis præcepta profert. Item quòd respōsionem suam concludens, ait: Maius his præceptum non est. Quæ omnia satis docent, charitatem vnam esse, cuius duæ principales actiones sunt, altera qua deum, altera qua proximum amplectimur: quare secundum has, non autem reipsa, diuidi solet. Pertinet huc, quòd & alibi in euangelio Christus non mi-nori studio fraternam dilectionē quàm dei amorem requirit. Vt non temere Ioannes dixerit, Mendaces esse, qui cum fratrum odio laborent, se dei amantes esse gloriantur.
units.tr: The first place among these is held by the conjunction of the love of God and of the neighbour. For he teaches that these are so joined that neither can subsist without the other. For just as we cannot love God unless we also love our brothers, so we shall never love our brothers unless the love of God burns within us. For the Apostle is not speaking of that profane love, by which even the wicked are sometimes affected, so that it may be said less to love than to rage and to seethe with depraved desires. Since that love, for the most part, ends in ruin for both parties, it ought by no means to be counted among this divine and holy love, which has the most joyful reward of eternal joy and a happiness that will never perish, set before it by God. Moreover, that the love of God and of the neighbour cohere inseparably, not John alone but all Scripture teaches with one accord. In the Law both are certainly handed down: as in the first table of the Decalogue God explains by four precepts the manner of love which we owe to himself, so the six precepts of the other table teach in what way we ought to exercise the love of our neighbour. In the Prophets this same thing is seen everywhere, who diligently set forth both the worship of God and beneficence towards the neighbour. In the Gospel of Christ we have a voice, whose authority alone ought to suffice for us. Asked about the chief commandment of the Law, he answers: "The first of all the commandments is: Hear, Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord. And you shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, and with your whole soul, and with your whole mind, and with all your strength. This is the first commandment. And the second, like it, is this: You shall love your neighbour as yourself. There is no other commandment greater than these." Mark 12. Note in Christ's words that he says the commandment of love of neighbour is like the first; then that, being asked about the one supreme and principal commandment, he brings forth the commandments of both loves; and likewise that, concluding his answer, he says: "There is no commandment greater than these." All of which teach sufficiently that charity is one, whose two principal actions are, the one by which we embrace God, the other by which we embrace the neighbour; wherefore it is customarily divided according to these, though not in reality. To this belongs also that Christ, elsewhere in the Gospel, demands brotherly love with no less zeal than the love of God. So it is not rashly that John has said that those are liars who, while labouring under hatred of their brothers, glory that they love God.

units.la: Patet in his & singularis in nos dei amor, & excellētissima hominis dignitas, in quam ille nos subuehere dignatus est. Vt enim deus summum bonum, & reuera solus bonus est. Matth.19.itasolus[?] etiam diligi & amari dignus est. Ea tamē nos dilectione prosequitur, vt nos in eius amoris, qui ipsi debetur, consortium admittat, nosq; in seipso diligi velit, nec se diligi à nobis putet, nisi & proximos diligamus. Procul igitur à nostri amoris peruersitate abest deus. Inter nos quidem sic comparatum esse videmus, vt soli velimus diligi ab ijs, quos magnifacimus: & si quando illorum studia & amorem in alios quoque inclinare videamus, mox æmulationis fomites & inuidiæ scintillas concipimus, quæ tandem horribile pariunt odij & inimicitiarum incendium. At non talis deus est, cui tunc demum nostra placet dilectio, si iuxta ipsius præceptum in fratres deriuetur.
units.tr: In these things there appear both the singular love of God towards us and the most excellent dignity of man, to which he has deigned to raise us. For God is the supreme good, and truly the only good. Matt. 19. Therefore he alone is also worthy to be loved and cherished. Yet he pursues us with such love that he admits us into the fellowship of that love which is due to himself, and he wishes to be loved by us in himself, nor does he think himself loved by us unless we also love our neighbours. Far, therefore, from the perversity of our love is God. Among ourselves we see it so arranged that we wish to be loved alone by those whom we hold in high esteem; and if at any time we see their zeal and love inclined towards others also, straightway we conceive the kindling of rivalry and the sparks of envy, which at length give birth to the dreadful fire of hatred and enmities. But God is not such that he is pleased with our love only if it is derived to the brothers according to his own precept.

units.la: Seruiat hoc tam consolationi quàm institutioni nostræ. Consolari siquidem nos debet tam propensus & beneuolus in nos diuinæ mentis affectus, cuius consyderatio omnes, quæ ab iniquis nobis inferuntur, iniurias leues reddere debet. Quid enim homo illi noceat suo odio, quem dei favor protegit? Cum Dauide ergo dicamus: Dominus mihi adiutor, non timebo quid mihi faciat homo. Psal.118. Item: Dominus lux mea & salus mea, à quo nam timerem? Dominus robur vitæ meæ, à quo expauescerem? Psal.27. Cum Paulo item exclamemus: Si deus nobiscum, quis contra nos? Rom.8. Præterea non graue fit, nos ab hominibus prauis & mortalibus contemni vel negli-gi, cum eam nostri curam deus susceperit, vt seipsum in nobis, tam amari quàm negligi & contemni, æstimet. Cuius rei euidens argumentum est, quòd Christus de nouissimo suo in iudicio ad-uentu differens, iudicij siue sententiæ suæ rationem hanc vnam, tam ergo pios quàm impios, prolaturum se dicit: Quicquid fecistis de his fratribus meis minimis, mihi fecistis. Matth.25.
units.tr: Let this serve both our consolation and our instruction. For indeed the so favourable and benevolent disposition of the divine mind towards us ought to console us, and the consideration of it ought to make light all the injuries that are inflicted upon us by the wicked. For what harm can a man do to one whom the favour of God protects by his hatred? Therefore let us say with David: "The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man may do to me." Ps. 118. Likewise: "The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom then shall I fear? The Lord is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?" Ps. 27. Let us also cry out with Paul: "If God is for us, who is against us?" Rom. 8. Moreover, it is no grievous thing that we are despised or neglected by wicked and mortal men, since God has taken up our care in such a way that he counts himself to be loved and despised and neglected in us. Clear proof of this is that Christ, speaking of his last coming to judgment, says that the one reason of his judgment or sentence will be this, that he will bring it forward for the pious and the impious alike: "Whatever you have done to these my least brothers, you have done to me." Matt. 25.

units.la: Institutioni vero nostrae [illegible, ~2 letters] seruire debent, non in hoc tantum quòd nostri nos efficii admo-nent, verumetiam, quòd nostrae naturae stupendam & exemplo carentem corruptionem produt; Si enim tam mentis quàm corporis oculos ad omnes Creaturas animatas & inanimatas, nullam in tota hac universitate deprehendes, quae non suo officio respondeat; & hominis dignitatem, quam illum Deus donauit, agnoscat. Nam quia hunc rerum dominum & principem constituit Deus, omnes creaturae illi obediunt & inseruiunt. Profert in hominum gratiam omnis generis fruges tellus, nec iniquius fert, si aratro scindatur, rastris & occis distrahatur, aquis rigetur, fossis inter-stinguatur, varijs impraegnetur feminibus, modo homini suo principi alimenta, quae debet, prose-rat. Seruit hominis vitae & incolumitati circumfusus vndiq; aer, nec toties haustus & refusus, vel consumitur, vel defatigatus officium detrectat. Fluunt perennes aquarum fontes, cursu suo inde-fessa pergunt flumina, & mare fluuios tam excipit, quàm refundit, vt hominibus debita obsequia praestent. Non deest nobis ignis, quin multiuariam nostris succurrat necessitatibus. Liberalitate sua nos pascunt arbores, plantae, frutices. Et si altius ascendamus, coelestes orbes in hoc vnum in-cumbere, & ideo perpetuo motu versari videbimus, vt nos per illos iuuemur: legesque ab opifice suo praescriptas tanto studio seruant, vt tot iam annorum centurijs nunquam illis hominibus su-um officium negauisse constet. Imò coelestes spiritus, angelos, electorum ministerio & seruitio in tentos esse, scriptura docet. Hebr.1. Et castra figit angelus domini circu eos, qui timent dominum, & eripit eos. Psalm. 34. Et vt in terras redeamus, brutis animantibus hunc sensum inesse experi-mur, quo hominis dignitatem agnoscunt, eiusdem imperium admittunt, seque illius arbitrio sub-ijci patiuntur. Sic immanis & vasti corporis taurus iugum sponte recipit, stimulos patitur, & ad la-nienam sese tandem abripi sustinet: quem si viribus suis contra hominem vti vellet, nemo facile, nec sine periculo vinceret. Sic equus acer & furens ore fraenum, sessorem tergo recipit, calcaribus vrgetur, & in medios hostes, in gladios, hastas, sagittas, bombardarum tonitrua fertur, & ad mor-tem vsque pro suo sessore depugnat. Sed & immanes ferae, quas natura à quotidiano hominum vsu abalienauit, hominis dignitatem obseruant, profundis syluis & obscuris antris clausae delite-scunt, nec in hominis perniciem ruunt, nisi Deo creatori visum fuerit, illarum opera ingrati & im-morigeri insolentiam punire. Quòd si cum his hominem conferas, prorsus alium videbis. Nec ali-qua fera homini tam iniqua & inimica est, quàm ipse homo. Immemor enim suae non modò digni-tatis, verumetiam natiuitatis, quae illum inermem, infirmum, vagientem, & opis alienae indigum, in lucem profudit, quasi ipse sibi ad omnia sufficiat, fratres contemnit, fastidit, odit, persequitur, & nihil non tentat, quo illos & opprimere & in vniuersum extinguere possit. Et quia armis illum natura nullis instruxit, ipse sibi arma parat, quibus odium suum & rabiem exaturet. Nam & ar-matura ferrea corpus totum contegens squamigeros dracones imitatur. Enses, hastas, tela, & ea quidem omnis generis, excogitauit, quibus & cornua taurorum, & leonum vngues, & aprorum dentes, & quicquid deniq; in feris immane & truculentum est, longe superat. Adde his quòd non pauci & rari inueniuntur, qui humanitatis obliti, in fratrum perniciem ruunt: sed regnat passim tam effera rabies, & eò iam multis seculis progressa est, vt inde sibi summam laudem venentur ho-mines, si collectis agminibus, & instructis aciebus armati congrediantur, & leuissimas ob causas (fortasis ob verbulum temere elapsum, aut conspicutum clypeum) riuos humani sanguinis fun-dant. Hic magni & celebres, Heroumque nomine digni iudicantur, qui in eiusmodi certaminibus se reliquis truculentiores praebuerint. Sed quid dicemus si illorum facta & mores cum Ioannis sententia conferamus? Quòd si illos interroges, quo in Deum sint animo affecti, plenis buccis il-lius amorem iactitabunt. At fratres se odisse, negare nō possunt. Mendaces ergo sunt, quoties Dei amore gloriantur. Aperiamus itaque mentis oculos, vt nostrae naturae peruersitatem agnoscere possimus, ne in illis pergamus gloria & laudem quaerere, quae à Deo alienissimos reddunt, & per-petuae damnationis ignominia perfundunt.
units.tr: Yet these things ought to serve our instruction, not only in that they remind us of our duty, but also in that they reveal the astonishing corruption of our nature, which has no parallel. For if you turn the eyes of your mind as well as of your body to all creatures, animate and inanimate, you will find none in this whole universe that does not answer to its office and acknowledge the dignity of man, which God has bestowed upon him. For because God has appointed man lord and prince of these things, all creatures obey him and serve him. The earth brings forth fruits of every kind for the benefit of men, and it does not take it amiss if it is cut with the plough, broken up with the harrow and the hoe, watered with streams, drained by ditches, and sown with various seeds, provided that it supplies its prince, man, with the food he needs. The air that surrounds us serves the life and health of man on every side, and though it is breathed in and out so many times, it is neither used up nor, wearied, refuses its office. The perennial springs of water flow, the rivers run on without tiring, and the sea receives the rivers as much as it gives them back, so that they render due service to men. Fire is never lacking to us, but comes to the aid of our needs in many ways. Trees, plants and shrubs feed us from their bounty. And if we look higher, we will see that the heavenly bodies bend their efforts to this one end alone, and therefore turn in perpetual motion so that we may be helped by them; and they keep the laws prescribed by their Maker with such diligence that it is established that for many centuries they have never failed in their duty to men. Indeed, Scripture teaches that the heavenly spirits, the angels, are employed in the ministry and service of the elect. Heb. 1. "The angel of the Lord encamps round about those who fear him, and delivers them." Ps. 34. And to return to the earth: we find that brute animals have in them a sense by which they acknowledge the dignity of man, submit to his rule, and allow themselves to be subjected to his will. So the huge and vast bull willingly takes the yoke, bears the goad, and at last allows itself to be led off to the slaughter; yet if it wished to use its strength against man, no one could easily overcome it, and not without danger. So the fierce and spirited horse takes the bit in its mouth and carries its rider on its back, is urged on with spurs, and is borne into the midst of enemies, among swords, spears, arrows and the thunder of cannon, and fights to death for its rider. Even the savage beasts, which nature has removed from daily contact with men, observe the dignity of man: shut up in deep forests and dark caves they hide, and they do not rush to destroy man unless it seems good to God the Creator to punish the ingratitude and disobedience of men by their means. But if you compare man with these, you will see him altogether different. No wild beast is as unjust and hostile to man as man himself. For forgetful not only of his dignity but also of his birth, which poured him into the light helpless, weak, crying, and in need of another's help, he despises, disdains, hates, persecutes his brothers as if he himself were sufficient for everything, and he attempts everything by which he may both oppress them and wipe them out entirely. And since nature has not armed him with any weapons, he prepares weapons for himself, by which he may satisfy his hatred and rage. For he also covers his whole body with iron armor, imitating scaly dragons. He has devised swords, spears, missiles, and these of every kind, by which he far surpasses the horns of bulls, the claws of lions, the tusks of boars, and whatever is monstrous and savage in the wild beasts. Add to these that not a few, but rare, are those who, forgetful of humanity, rush to the destruction of their brothers; rather, such fierce rage reigns everywhere, and has now for many centuries advanced to such a point that men hunt for the highest praise from it, if they march in assembled troops and in drawn-up battle lines, and for the slightest causes (perhaps for a word carelessly uttered, or a shield caught sight of) they pour out streams of human blood. Here the great and famous, those judged worthy of the name of heroes, are those who have shown themselves more savage than the rest in such conflicts. But what shall we say if we compare their deeds and manners with the saying of John? For if you ask them what disposition they have toward God, they boast of his love with full cheeks. But they cannot deny that they hate their brothers. Therefore they are liars whenever they glory in the love of God. Let us therefore open the eyes of our mind, so that we may recognize the perversity of our nature, and not persist in seeking glory and praise in those things which make men most alien from God and drench them with the infamy of everlasting damnation.

units.la: Præterea ad religionis causam hæc Apostoli sententia tràsferri debet. Docet enim omnes cul-tus, quos homines à fraterna dilectione alieni exercent, Deo inuisos & exosos esse, & proinde ijs Dei gratia nullo modo promereri posse. Nam cū Deus ipsa veritas sit, cultores medaces & falsilo-quos vel hypocritas ferre non solet, nec potest. At quicunq; Dei cultum & amorem iactant, cū fra-tres suos oderint, mendaces sunt. Eosdem ergo cum suo cultu Deo placere impossibile est. Est hu-ius argumenti veritas tam firma, solida & perspicua, vt huic contradicere nō possit, nisi qui lucem tenebras dicere audeat. Probatur praeterea exemplis plurimis, quae passim in scriptura proponun-tur. Illorum enim hominum patriarcham dicere possumus Cainum, quem cū Abele sacrificauis-se, sacrificium vero illius Deo displicuisse legimus. Atqui vni & eidem Deo vterque sacrum suum obtulit. Nec verisimile est, Cainum alio ritu rem diuinam fecisse, quàm à patre Adam, vnà cum Abele acceperat. Sed & scriptura in ritu sacrificij, & ipsa re sacrificata nihil reprehendit. In ipso igitur Caino fuisse oportet, quod illius sacrum Deo inuisum faceret. Fuit id animus fide vacuus, & à charitate fraterna alienus, quem postea immani parricidio abunde declarauit. Quare cum odio fraterno inflammatus, Dei amorem & cultum simularet, mendax fuit, & Deus mendacis cultum recipere non potuit. Eodem referri debent, quæ apud prophetas multis in locis habentur. Damnat enim sæpius eas Ceremonias & ea sacrificia Deus, quorum ipse author & institutor fuerat. Dicit enim: Odi & abominor vestras ferias, nec odorabor in cœtibus vestris. Et cum sacrificaueritis mihi holocausta & sacrificia vestra cibaria, non erunt mihi grata: gratulatorium sacrificium pinguium vestrorum non aspiciam. Amos 5. Et rursum alibi: Cum expanderitis manus vestras, abscondam oculos meos à vobis, etiamsi multiplicaueritis orationem, haudquaquam exaudiam. Isa.
units.tr: Moreover, this saying of the Apostle ought to be applied to the cause of religion. For it teaches that all the forms of worship which men practise apart from brotherly love are hateful and odious to God, and that therefore by them men can in no way merit the grace of God. For since God is truth itself, he does not usually tolerate, nor can he tolerate, worshippers who are false, deceitful or hypocritical. But whoever boasts of the worship and love of God while hating his brothers is a liar. It is therefore impossible for such people to please God by their worship. The truth of this argument is so firm, solid and clear that no one can contradict it, unless he dares to call light darkness. It is also proved by very many examples which are set forth throughout Scripture. For we may name Cain as the patriarch of these men, whom we read offered a sacrifice along with Abel, but whose sacrifice displeased God. Yet each of them offered his sacrifice to one and the same God. Nor is it likely that Cain performed the sacred rite in a different manner from that which he had received from his father Adam together with Abel. And Scripture finds no fault either with the manner of the sacrifice or with the thing sacrificed. Therefore the cause must have been in Cain himself, which made his sacrifice hateful to God. It was his spirit, empty of faith and alien from brotherly love, which he afterward declared abundantly by his monstrous murder of his brother. Therefore, since he was inflamed with hatred of his brother and pretended a love and worship of God, he was a liar, and God could not receive the worship of a liar. To the same class belong the things that are found in many places in the prophets. For God often condemns those ceremonies and sacrifices of which he himself was the author and institutor. For he says: "I hate and abhor your feast days, nor will I take delight in your assemblies. And when you offer me burnt offerings and your grain offerings, I will not accept them; I will not look upon the peace offerings of your fatted beasts." Amos 5. And again elsewhere: "When you spread out your hands, I will hide my eyes from you; even if you multiply your prayers, I will by no means hear." Isa. 1.

units.la: 1. Quæ vero causa est, quod & sacrificia & preces (quibus nihil magis gratum habere solet) reijcit? Manus (inquit) vestræ plenæ sunt sanguinum. Item: Beneficentiam volo, & non sacrificium. Hof.6. Debebant hæc totis animis consyderare nostri seculi homines, qui cultum Dei in externis Ceremonijs, ijsque frigidissimis & à Deo minimè traditis, consistere putant. Qui vbi vsuris tantum non sanguinarijs, cauponationibus, impostoris, furtis, rapinis, mercenaria sanguinis effusione, opes immensas coacernauerunt, pro omnibus hisce flagitijs egregiè satisfactum putant, si sacellum aliquod & altare suis impensis extrui curent, si vestes sacras coemant, si Missarum sacrificia & luminarium oblationes perpetuas instituant, & annuis redditibus sacrificulos conducant, qui non intellectas preces pro animarum salute deblaterent. At longè alia Deus requirit, & Zachæum imitari conueniebat, qui dimidium suorum bonorum pauperibus dabat, & si quem defraudauerat, reddebat quadruplum. Luc.19. Sed & stultum est putare, Ceremonijs per nos confictis Deo pro sceleribus tantis satisfieri posse, cum is olim abs se tradita sacra tanto fastidio damnarit, quando à talibus hominibus celebrabantur. Præterea, nemo virum bonum dixerit eum, qui à fure furti partem recipere, & ea accepta illius furtum dissimulare vellet. Et tu Deum tam iniquum putas, qui furtis & rapinis tuis propter lucri & comercij spem ignoscere debeat? Explodamus potius ô fratres tam stultas & impias opiniones. Cogitemus Deum purum, sanctum & incōtaminatum[?], imò ipsam veritate esse, & proinde ab impuris & mendacibus nullo modo coli posse. Veritati ergo & dilectioni fraternæ studeamus, ut placere possit Deo cultus noster. Cæterum, quia Ioannis sententia carnis nostræ iudicio non grauis duntaxat, verumetiam intolerabilis & palam falsa videri solet, non contentus hanc nudis verbis proposuisse, eandem duobus argumentis firmissimis comprobat, quæ modò inspiciemus.
units.tr: But what is the reason that he rejects both sacrifices and prayers, which he is wont to hold most pleasing? "Your hands," he says, "are full of blood." Likewise: "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice." Hos. 6. Men of our own age ought to consider these things with their whole minds, men who think that the worship of God consists in external ceremonies, and those very cold ones and never handed down by God. When they have heaped up immense wealth by usury, which is hardly less than bloody, by trade and fraud, by deceit, theft, robbery, and the shedding of blood for hire, they think they have made ample satisfaction for all these crimes if they take care to have some chapel and altar built at their own expense, if they buy up sacred vestments, if they institute perpetual Masses and offerings of lights, and hire little priests with annual stipends to mutter prayers for the salvation of souls which no one understands. But God requires something quite different, and it became them to imitate Zacchaeus, who gave half of his goods to the poor, and if he had defrauded anyone, restored it fourfold. Luke 19. But it is also foolish to think that God can be satisfied for such great wickedness by ceremonies devised by us, since he once condemned with such disdain the sacred rites handed down by himself, when they were celebrated by such men. Moreover, no one would call a good man one who wished to receive a part of his theft from a thief and, having received it, to overlook his theft. And do you think God so unjust that he should pardon your thefts and robberies on account of the hope of gain and trade? Let us rather, brothers, cast off such foolish and impious opinions. Let us consider God to be pure, holy and undefiled, indeed truth itself, and therefore that he cannot in any way be worshipped by the impure and the liars. Let us therefore labour for truth and brotherly love, so that our worship may be pleasing to God. Furthermore, since the saying of John is wont to seem to our flesh's judgment not only burdensome but intolerable and plainly false, not content to have set it forth in bare words, he confirms the same by two most firm arguments, which we shall now examine.

units.la: I. Qui enim non diligit fratrem suum, quem uidit, Deum quem non uidit, quomodo potest diligere? A comparatis argumentatur Apostolus. Ea est hominum natura, ut ijs quæ sub sensum currunt, magis moueantur, quàm absentibus, quæ animi tantummodo contemplatione assequi aliquo modo possumus. Quare, si quis animo tam immiti & inhumano est præditus, ut fratris conspectu, quem coram videt, & ope sua indigere nouit, non commoueri possit, nunquam ille putàdus erit Deum diligere, qui ut oculis nostris videri nequit, ita nullius opis est indigus. Sed obijciat aliquis: An ergo fieri nequit, ut Deum diligam, licet ab hominum aliquorum dilectione alienus sim? Atqui inter homines imò fratres vterinos, alium quidem amare, aliū verò odisse possum, nec statim sequitur me omnes odisse, si vnum aliquem odio prosequar. Quanto magis igitur Dei amorem retinere possum, licet fratres non perinde diligam? Sed facilis est ad hæc responsio. Comparationis enim siue argumenti vis, quo Ioannes vtitur, ex coniunctione, quæ homini cum Deo est, dependet. Homo enim & primitus ad Dei imaginem conditum, & in eam dignitatem euectum esse cōstat, ut quæcunque Deo debemus externa officia, in illum ex præcepto Dei conferri debeant. At eorum, quos amamus, imagines magni facere & amare solemus. Sic liberi parentum imaginibus non paruum honorem deferunt, & honestæ matronæ coniugum absentium picturas non vulgari amoris affectu venerantur. Quòd si ergo Dei amor animis nostris insederit, non poterimus non amare hominem, qui ad eius similitudinem conditus est, & Dei conditoris memoriam quotidie nobis renouat. Et quicunque eum ita neglexerit, ut nec Dei imago quam refert, nec eiusdem præceptū, quo illum nobis commendauit, nec præsens necessitas, quæ illum opis nostræ indigum reddit, in illo commiserationis affectum excitare queat, næ ille frustra & falsò Dei dilectione se teneri gloriabitur.
units.tr: I. For he who does not love his brother, whom he has seen, how can he love God, whom he has not seen? The Apostle argues from things that are compared. It is human nature to be moved more by things that fall under the senses than by things that are absent, which we can grasp in some way only by contemplation of the mind. Therefore, if anyone is endowed with a mind so hard and inhuman that he cannot be moved by the sight of his brother, whom he sees before him and knows to need his help, he must never be thought to love God, who, since he cannot be seen by our eyes, is in need of no help at all. But someone may object: Is it then impossible for me to love God, if I am estranged from the love of certain men? Yet among men, indeed among full brothers, I may love one and hate another, and it does not follow at once that I hate all if I pursue one with hatred. How much more, then, can I keep the love of God, even if I do not love my brothers equally? But the answer to this is easy. For the force of the comparison or argument that John uses depends on the bond that man has with God. For man was both originally created in the image of God and, as is well established, raised to that dignity, so that whatever external duties we owe to God ought to be paid to him by God's command. But we are accustomed to set great store by, and to love, the images of those whom we love. Thus children show no small honour to the portraits of their parents, and honourable matrons venerate the pictures of absent husbands with no ordinary affection. If therefore the love of God has taken root in our hearts, we cannot fail to love the man who has been made in his likeness, and who daily renews in us the memory of God our Creator. And whoever has so neglected him that neither the image of God which he bears, nor the command by which God has commended him to us, nor the present necessity which makes him in need of our help, can stir up in him a feeling of compassion, he will boast in vain and falsely that he is held by the love of God.

units.la: Est hic obseruatione dignum, quòd hominem ad Dei imaginem factum esse & Dei memoriam in nobis refricare diximus. Arguit hoc illorum stultitiam, qui mutis imaginibus, ex ligno aut lapide, vel etiam præstantiori materia creatis, Dei similitudinem repræsentari posse existimant. Quasi vero Dei imago in hominis corpore & vultu conspiciatur, cum ea potius interioris hominis sit, qui per Christi spiritum renouatus, Dei ingenium & mores refert, quoad carnis nostræ infirmitas patitur. Et ut maximè demus, Dei formam & naturam eiusmodi simulachris exprimi posse, non potest tamen non extremè stultum dici, quòd tantis sumptibus, tot laboribus & molestijs simulachra Dei, quibus non indigent, homines faciunt & fieri curant. Non indigent autem, cum multò præstantiores Dei imagines passim habeant in ijs, qui per Christum regenerati, Christi spiritu viuunt, & Dei non simulachra modò, verùmetiam filij & hæredes sunt. At eò dementiæ peruenerunt homines stultissimi, ut viuas Dei imagines spolient, quò lapideas & ligneas vestire possint, & neglectis illis opes suas in truncos ficulneos & salignos conferant, & in ea re summam pietatis & religionis Christianæ consistere putent. Sed quia de simulachris dicendi locus commodior erit in fine epistolæ, pauca hæc modo sufficiant.
units.tr: Here it is worth noting what we have said: that man was made in the image of God and that he refreshes in us the memory of God. This shows the folly of those who think that the likeness of God can be represented by mute images made of wood or stone, or even of more precious material. As if the image of God were to be seen in the body and face of man, when it is rather of the inner man, who, renewed by the Spirit of Christ, reflects the nature and manners of God, so far as the weakness of our flesh allows. And even if we grant most fully that the form and nature of God can be expressed by such likenesses, it cannot but be called extremely foolish that men make and cause to be made, at such great expense, with so much labour, trouble and bother, images of God, which they do not need. They do not need them, since they have far better images of God everywhere in those who, regenerated through Christ, live by the Spirit of Christ, and are not only the images but also the sons and heirs of God. But men of the greatest folly have come to such madness that they strip the living images of God so that they may clothe stone and wood, and, neglecting the living, they spend their wealth on blocks of fig and willow, and think that the chief point of piety and of Christian religion lies in this. But since there will be a more suitable place to speak of images at the end of the letter, let these few words suffice for now.

units.la: I I. Et hoc ipsum præceptum habemus ab eo, ut qui diligit Deum, diligat & fratrem suum.
units.tr: II. And we have this very commandment from him, that he who loves God should love his brother also.

units.la: Argumento à pronunciatis sumpto probat, quod supra propositi. Allegat autem ipsius Dei authoritatem, quæ utiq; apud Christianos maxima esse debet. Dei (inquit) hoc præceptum est, ne proximi dilectionem ab ea, quæ ipsi debetur, separemus. Ut enim se diligi vult, ita fratres quoq; diligere iubet. Iniquum ergo & summæ audaciæ facinus est, seiungere velle, quæ Deus indissolubi li nexu conjuncta esse voluit. Et quia dilectio Dei vera obedientiæ causa est, falsò Dei dilectione gloriabuntur, quicunq; fratres suos, quos tanto studio sibi divinitus commendatos esse audiunt, diligere neglexerint. Debent huc referri, quæ supra de dei & proximi dilectione dicta sunt.
units.tr: He proves by an argument drawn from what has been declared what he proposed above. He appeals to the authority of God himself, which among Christians ought surely to be the greatest. This commandment, he says, is God's: that we should not separate the love of our neighbour from that which is owed to God himself. For as God wishes to be loved, so he also commands that brothers be loved. It is therefore an unjust and most audacious deed to seek to separate what God has willed to be joined in an indissoluble bond. And since the love of God is the true cause of obedience, those will boast falsely of the love of God who neglect to love their brothers, whom they hear have been commended to them by God with such great care. What has been said above about the love of God and of neighbour must be referred here.

units.la: Habemus autem his verbis breviter comprehensam religionis Christianæ summam, quæ in dei & proximi dilectione consistit. Dei dilectio fidem comprehendit, & voluntatis divinæ studium. Nec enim fieri potest, quin illi fidamus, & in eo spem omnem collocemus, quem ex toto corde super omnia diligimus. Adhæc dilectionis proprium est, ut ijs placere studeat, quos diligit. Proximi vero charitate quæcunq; reliquæ sunt legis implentur, juxta illud Pauli: Nemini quicquam debetis, nisi hoc, ut invicem diligatis. Nam qui diligit alterum, legem expleuit. Siquidem illa: Non adulteraberis, non occides, non furaberis, non falsum testimonium dices, non concupisces, & si quod aliud præceptum, in hoc sermone summatim comprehenditur, nempe: Diliges proximum tuum sicut teipsum. Dilectio proximo malum non operatur. Consummatio itaq; legis est dilectio. Rom. 13. Hæc cum ita sint fratres, quæ stultitia est, circa ea altercari, quæ à Deo nec tradita sunt, nec aliqua parte juvant? Sufficiat nobis Christi jugum, suaue & salutiferum. Diligamus deum ex animo illi nos totos consecremus, & omni fiducia salutis in hunc collocata, eidem seruiamus sicut ille præscripsit. Rursum in deo diligamus, quos ille ad suam imaginem condidit, quos filij sui sanguine redemit, quos suos filios & hæredes constituit. Sic fiet, ut illum in spiritu & veritate colentes, in ipsius conspectu comparere possimus, & æterni regni consortes fieri cum filio dei Jesu Christo, cui debetur benedictio, gloria, honor & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Now in these words we have the sum of the Christian religion briefly comprehended, which consists in the love of God and of neighbour. The love of God embraces faith and the desire to do the divine will. For it cannot be that we should not trust in him and place all our hope in him, whom we love above all things with our whole heart. Moreover, it is the property of love to strive to please those whom it loves. But by love of neighbour all the remaining things of the law are fulfilled, according to that saying of Paul: Owe nothing to anyone, except to love one another. For he who loves another has fulfilled the law. For those commands: You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, you shall not covet, and whatever other commandment there is, are summed up briefly in this saying, namely: You shall love your neighbour as yourself. Love does no wrong to a neighbour. Therefore love is the fulfilling of the law. Rom. 13. Since these things are so, brothers, what folly is it to dispute about those things which have been neither handed down by God nor help in any part? Let us be content with the yoke of Christ, which is sweet and saving. Let us love God from the heart, consecrate ourselves wholly to him, place all our confidence of salvation in him, and serve him just as he has prescribed. Again, in God let us love those whom he has created in his own image, whom he has redeemed with the blood of his Son, and whom he has appointed his sons and heirs. So it will come about that, worshipping him in spirit and truth, we may appear in his sight and become partners of the eternal kingdom with the Son of God, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, glory, honour and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT V. HOMILIA XXIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. HOMILY XXIX.

units.la: Omnis qui credit Jesum esse Christum, ex Deo natus est. Et omnis qui diligit eum qui genuit, diligit & eum qui natus est ex eo. In hoc cognoscimus quòd diligamus filios Dei, cum Deum diligimus, & præcepta eius seruamus. Hæc est enim dilectio Dei, ut præcepta eius seruemus.
units.tr: Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God. And everyone who loves him who begat, loves also him who is born of him. By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God and keep his commandments. For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments.

units.la: JOANNEM Apostolum supra dixisse audiuimus: Hoc est præceptum Dei, ut credamus nomini filij ipsius Jesu Christi, & diligamus nos mutuò, sicut ille præcepit. Comprehendit autem duobus capitibus, Fide nimirum & charitate, omnia hominis officia quæ tam Deo q̄ ꝑximo[?] debemus: in quorum explicatione universa scriptura plurimum versatur & Joan. hucusq; nō vulgari diligentia usus est. Et quia dum hæc ꝓponuntur, homines vel sub fidei prætextu carnis licentiæ studēt, factisq; negant quod ore ꝑfitentur: vel dum operib. charitatis studēt, propriæ iustitiæ meritum stabilire conantur, non temere Apostolus fidem cum charitate coniungit, & hanc ex illa manare docet, ut nec fide mortua falsò gloriemur, nec meritum putemus, quod debitum dici debet. Eodem & præsens locus refertur, in cuius prima parte docet fidem & charitatem res esse inter se coniunctissimas. Deinde notas tradit & signa, ex quibus tam proximi quàm Dei dilectionem agnoscere possumus. Nos de singulis ordine agemus.
units.tr: We have heard that the Apostle John said above: This is the commandment of God, that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another, as he commanded. Now he comprehends, under two heads, namely faith and charity, all the duties of man which we owe both to God and to our neighbour; and in the explanation of these the whole of Scripture is greatly occupied, and John has up to now used no common diligence. And because, while these things are set forth, men either, under the pretext of faith, pursue licence for the flesh and deny by their deeds what they profess with their mouths; or, while they busy themselves with works of charity, they strive to establish the merit of their own righteousness, the Apostle does not rashly join faith with charity, and teaches that the latter flows from the former, so that we may neither boast falsely of a dead faith, nor think that merit is earned which ought rather to be called a debt. The present passage refers to the same matter: in its first part he teaches that faith and charity are most closely bound together. Then he hands down the marks and signs by which we may recognise both love of neighbour and love of God. We shall deal with each in order.

units.la: I. Omnis qui credit Iesum esse Christum, ex Deo natus est. Et omnis qui diligit eum qui genuit, diligit & eum qui natus est ex eo. Habent verba hæc integram fere argumentationem, inversa tamen (ut in orationibus fieri solet) propositionum collocatione. Sic enim argumentatur Apostolus: Omnis qui Diligit Deum, diligit & eos qui ex Deo nati sunt. At omnis qui credit Iesum esse Christum, ex Deo natus est. Ergo omnis qui Deum diligit, eos qui Iesum credunt esse Christum, diligit. Maior, dilectionis ingenio sive natura & communi sensu probatur. Ea enim amoris vis est, ut non in eius persona quiescat quem amamus, sed ad alios quoque, qui ei personæ coniuncti sunt, extenda tur. Nec unquam nostri amantem esse putabimus eum, qui nostros vel liberos vel amicos & servos odio prosequitur. Hinc illa in amicorum amicos & cognatos officia, & quod illorum curâ non inviti suscipimus, qui amicorum literis commendati ad nos veniunt. Imò ita comparatum esse videmus, ut illorum pecudes & canes nobis commendatissimi sint, quos syncero amoris affectu amplectimur. Firma ergo stat Ioannis sententia, Dei filios ab ijs diligi, qui Deû diligunt. At quia Dei filios esse dicit eos, qui credunt in Iesum Christum, non obscurè monet, dilectionis fraternæ verissimam causam & radicem esse fidem, quæ ut divinæ bonitatis consyderatione & exemplo dilectionis ignem in nobis accendit: ita nos quoque tales efficit, quibus fraternus amor ex officio debetur. Nec ideo sequitur, eos tantummodo diligendos esse, qui vera in Christum fide imbuti sunt, cum & planè ignotos scriptura alibi commendet: sed scopus Ioannis est, demonstrare, fidem à charitate nullo modo separari posse, sed hanc illius fructum & comitem esse indivulsum. Unde sequitur, à fide in Christum & dilectione Dei alienissimos esse, quotquot fratres amare dedignantur. Quia verò fidem & charitatem, virtutes Christianorum revera principes et cardinales, coiungit, nostrum erit nō ofcitanter, quæ de utraque dicuntur, inspicere. Et primò quidem fidei mysteria excutiemus.
units.tr: I. Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God. And everyone who loves him who begat, loves also him who is born of him. These words contain an almost complete argument, though with the order of the propositions inverted, as is usual in speeches. For the Apostle argues thus: Everyone who loves God loves also those who are born of God. But everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God. Therefore everyone who loves God loves those who believe that Jesus is the Christ. The major premise is proved by the nature of love, by natural feeling and common sense. For such is the force of love that it does not rest in the person whom we love, but extends also to others who are joined to that person. Nor shall we ever think that one loves us who hates our children, or our friends, or our servants. Hence come those offices towards the friends and kinsfolk of our friends, and why we undertake their cause unwillingly, when they come to us commended by the letters of friends. Indeed we see it to be so ordered that the flocks and dogs of those whom we embrace with sincere affection are most dear to us. Firm therefore stands John's saying, that the children of God are loved by those who love God. But because he calls those who believe in Jesus Christ the children of God, he makes it not obscurely clear that faith is the most true cause and root of brotherly love; faith, which, by the consideration and example of divine goodness, kindles the fire of love in us, and thus also makes us such that brotherly love is owed to us as a duty. Nor does it follow from this that only those who are imbued with true faith in Christ are to be loved, since Scripture elsewhere commends even those who are plainly unknown; but John's aim is to show that faith can in no way be separated from charity, but that charity is its fruit and inseparable companion. Hence it follows that those who disdain to love the brethren are most alien from faith in Christ and from love of God. Since, however, he joins faith and charity, the chief and cardinal virtues of Christians indeed, it will be our task not to look carelessly at what is said of each. And first we shall examine the mysteries of faith.

units.la: Est in his primo loco observandum, quòd fidei obiectum nullum constituit Apostolus, præterquam Iesum Dei filium. Atqui poterat plures fidei articulos constituere, qui passim in scripturis explicantur, quales sunt de trinitate, de gratia Dei, de vita æterna, & aliis rebus eius generis. Sed uno hoc, quo Christus Iesus traditur, contentus est: non quod alios, vel negandos vel negligendos esse, existimet, sed quòd hic omnium primus sit, & reliquos omnes in se continet. Christianæ ergo fidei basis & fundamentum Christus est, sicut ipse, & ex spiritu ipsius Paulus testantur. Matth.16.1.Cor.3. In eius agnitione & confessione necessario convenire debet, quotquot Christiani esse & haberi volunt. Qui hunc tenuerit syncerum & integrum, in reliquis perniciosè errare non poterit, & si quando hallucinetur circa alia, eius tamen error nec incurabilis nec exitialis erit. At qui hic impingens novi & alieni dogmatis author est, & schisma facit inter Christiani nominis professores, pro Christiano haberi nequit, donec ad fundamentum fidei unicum, Iesum Christum, revertatur. Arguuntur itaque Ioannis exemplo, qui novos fidei articulos constituere audent, & ecquidem, qui cum Christo Iesu nihil commune habent, imò cum illius merito & officio manifeste pugnant. Tales sunt, qui Missæ sacrificium, operum nostrorum iustitiam, satisfactiones, merita, divorum invocationem & intercessionem, purgatorii ignem, vota monastica, indulgentias, & quæcunque alia sunt huius farinæ, obtrudunt. At qui ea hodie ita quidam tuentur, & tanta cum obstinacia animorum pro illis depugnant, ut blasphemias in Christum Iesum & horribilem divini nominis ac verbi abusum facilius ferant, quàm ut his, quæ modò commemoravimus, quicquam derogetur. Nobis unus Dei filius, Iesus Christus sufficiat, in quo omnes scientiæ & sapientiæ thesauri dati sunt, qui nobis iustitia, sapientia, sanctificatio, satisfactio & redemptio à patre factus est. Qui denique peccatum fieri voluit, ut nos efficeremur iustitia Dei per illum. 1.Corinth.1.2.Cor.5.
units.tr: In these things the first point to be observed is that the Apostle sets up no object of faith except Jesus, the Son of God. And yet he could have set up several articles of faith, which are explained throughout Scripture, such as those concerning the Trinity, the grace of God, eternal life, and other matters of that kind. But he is content with this one, in which Christ Jesus is set forth: not because he thinks the others are to be denied or neglected, but because this is the first of all and contains all the rest within itself. Christ is therefore the basis and foundation of the Christian faith, as both he himself and Paul, speaking by his Spirit, bear witness. Matt. 16; 1 Cor. 3. In the acknowledgement and confession of him, all who wish to be and be considered Christians must of necessity agree. He who holds this pure and entire will not be able to err pernicious in other things, and if at any time he goes astray concerning other matters, his error will nevertheless be neither incurable nor deadly. But he who, stumbling at this point, is the author of a new and alien doctrine, and makes a schism among those who profess the Christian name, cannot be held a Christian until he returns to the one foundation of faith, Jesus Christ. They are therefore refuted by the example of John, those who dare to set up new articles of faith, and indeed those who have nothing in common with Christ Jesus, but rather clearly clash with his merit and office. Such are those who press upon us the sacrifice of the Mass, the righteousness of our works, satisfactions, merits, the invocation and intercession of the saints, the fire of purgatory, monastic vows, indulgences, and whatever else is of this kind. But some who today so defend these things, and fight for them with such obstinacy of mind, that they more easily bear blasphemies against Christ Jesus and the horrible abuse of the divine name and Word, than that anything should be taken away from those things which we have just mentioned. For us let the one Son of God, Jesus Christ, suffice, in whom are given all the treasures of knowledge and wisdom, who has been made by the Father our righteousness, wisdom, sanctification, satisfaction and redemption. Who finally willed to be made sin, that we might be made the righteousness of God through him. 1 Cor. 1; 2 Cor. 5.

units.la: Cæterum non satis est, Christi nomen in ore habere, & de Christo frequenter multa dicere: sed Christo credere, & ea quidè de illo credere oportet, quæ salutis nostræ causa ipse vel fecit vel passus est. Poterant hæc multis extendi, sed brevi compendio omnia illa Ioannes complectitur, cum dicit: Omnis qui credit Iesum esse Christum, ex Deo natus est. Iesus nomen filio Dei proprium fuisse, supra dictum est. Illud enim in Circumcisione (ut hodie in baptismo fieri consuevit) ipsi inditum fuit. Luc.2. Nec tamen sine mysterio. Quemadmodum enim in ipso salutem propofi-tam habebat humanum genus: ita nomine hoc ipsum testatum esse oportuit. At Christi vox officium denotat, cui ipsum cœlestis pater ab æterno destinarat. Latinis enim unctum sonat, id est, sacerdotem & regem: quia hi soli iuxta legem olim inungi solebant. Iesum ergo Christum esse credit,quicunq; illum & sacerdotem & regem esse agnoscit populi Dei,id est, ecclesiæ, & ab illo speratquæcunq; de uncto illo domini per diuinos homines prophetas spiritus sanctus promisit. Ostendit is illum doctorem fore,quem omnes audire debeant. Deut.18. Act.7. Docuit,eundem ultimâ[?] fore,quam ipsemet in ligno pro peccatis nostris immolaturus esset. Isa.53. Ostendit præterea intercessorem fore & patronum, qui causam nostram coram Deo patre solus fideliter & sufficiêter agat. Quare illum non sacerdotem modo vocat, sed sacerdotium eidem tribuit stabile & æternum. Psal.110. Simili ratione eidem omnia regis officia transcribit. Regnum eius extendit per omnes gentes ad extremos cardines orbis terrarum. Psal.2. Zach.9. Victorem proponit,qui caput serpentis conterat,& suos ex illius tyrannide potenti brachio liberet. Gen.3. Denique in hoc nō leges modo & iudicium (quæ nō postrema regni bene instituti pars sunt) indicat, verumetiâ thesauros cœlestis virtutes & spiritualia dona,quibus suos ditare consuevit. Talé postea plenius depingit euangelij doctrina,quam spiritu Christi dictante,Apostoli ore & scriptis ecclesiæ tradiderunt. Describuntur enim in hac Christi sermones,quibus docuit,& voluntate patris clarissimè interpretatus est. Indicatur, ut ecclesiæ suæ verbi ministerium reliquerit,per quod hodie etiâ inter suos docet & concionatur. Eph.4. Explicatur tota sacrificij Christi ratio. Proponuntur eius preces,quibus pro nobis olim in tercelsit,& promissiones quibus pollicetur hodie quoque patri grata & accepta fore vota nostra, quæ in ipsius nomine offerimus. Præterea demonstratur victoriosus ille & gloriosus rex esse,qui deuicto Satana, peccato & morte, portisque inferorum effractis, omnem potestatem acceperit in cœlo & in terra. Matth.28. Hæc & quæcunque alia sunt in Christo Iesu,agnoscere & firmiter credere oportet eos, quicunq; Christianam fidem profiteri volunt. Nec sufficiet illa simpliciter vel credere vel fateri,nisi illa in solo Christo haberi credas, & eundem unicum humani generis salvatorem esse agnoscas. Nec enim vacillantes vult in religionis & fidei causa animos Christus. Sibi soli nos totos vendicat,sibi soli desponsatos vult,& nefandi adulterij contra Christum reus est,quicunq; salutis fiduciam minima ex parte in creaturas declinare permiserit. Unde Petrus non contentus dixisse, Non est in alio quoquam salus: addit: Nec enim aliud nomen datum est sub cœlo inter homines,in quo oporteat nos saluos fieri. Act.4. Et Paulus, se uni viro Christo Corinthios adiunxisse testatur,nec permittere vult,ut è simplicitate fidei, quæ uni Christo debetur,defle-ctant. 2.Cor.11. Obseruent hæc,qui cum Christi nomine glorientur,extra hunc tamen nouum sacerdotium,noua sacrificia,nouos intercessores,noua ecclesiæ capita,nouos doctores & magistros, denique nouam per omnia salutis rationem comminiscuntur. Agnoscamus nos,extremam & sacrilegam impietatem esse,Iesu Dei filio quicquam detrahere,quod Christi,id est,regis & sacerdo-tis nomine comprehenditur.
units.tr: Moreover, it is not enough to have the name of Christ on the lips and to speak often of Christ at length; but one must believe in Christ, and indeed believe those things concerning him which he himself did or suffered for the sake of our salvation. These things could be extended at length, but John embraces them all in a brief summary when he says: Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God. That Jesus was the proper name of the Son of God has been said above. For that name was given to him at his circumcision (as it is customary to do today at baptism). Luke 2. Nor was this without mystery. For just as in him the salvation of the human race was set forth, so it was fitting that this very name should bear witness to it. But the word Christ denotes the office for which the heavenly Father had destined him from eternity. For in Latin it means anointed, that is, priest and king, because these alone were in former times anointed according to the law. He therefore believes that Jesus is the Christ who acknowledges him to be both priest and king of the people of God, that is, of the Church, and who hopes from him for all those things which the Holy Spirit promised through the divinely inspired prophets concerning that anointed one of the Lord. He showed that he would be the teacher whom all ought to hear. Deut. 18; Acts 7. He taught that he would be the victim, which he himself was to offer on the wood for our sins. Isa. 53. He showed further that he would be intercessor and advocate, who alone faithfully and sufficiently pleads our cause before God the Father. Wherefore he calls him not only priest, but ascribes to him a priesthood that is stable and eternal. Ps. 110. In a similar way he transfers to him all the offices of a king. He extends his kingdom through all nations to the farthest corners of the earth. Ps. 2; Zech. 9. He sets forth a conqueror who will crush the head of the serpent, and by his mighty arm will free his own from the tyranny of that one. Gen. 3. Finally, in this he points out not only laws and judgement (which are no small part of a well-ordered kingdom), but also the treasures of heavenly virtues and the spiritual gifts with which he is accustomed to enrich his own. The gospel doctrine, which the Apostles delivered to the Church by mouth and in writings, under the dictation of the Spirit of Christ, afterwards depicts this more fully. For in it are described the sermons of Christ, by which he taught, and by which he most clearly interpreted the will of the Father. It is pointed out that he left the ministry of the Word to his Church, through which even today he teaches and preaches among his own. Eph. 4. The whole reasoning of the sacrifice of Christ is explained. His prayers are set forth, by which he once interceded for us, and the promises by which he assures us that even today our prayers, which we offer in his name, will be pleasing and acceptable to the Father. Moreover, it is shown that he is that victorious and glorious king, who, having overcome Satan, sin and death, and having broken down the gates of hell, has received all power in heaven and on earth. Matt. 28. These things, and whatever else there is in Jesus Christ, it is necessary that those who wish to profess the Christian faith should acknowledge and firmly believe. Nor will it suffice simply either to believe or to confess these things, unless you believe that they are had in Christ alone, and acknowledge him to be the only Saviour of the human race. For Christ does not want wavering minds in the cause of religion and faith. He claims us wholly for himself, he wants us betrothed to himself alone, and he is guilty of a foul adultery against Christ who has allowed his hope of salvation to turn aside, even in the smallest part, to creatures. Hence Peter, not content with saying, There is no salvation in any other, adds: For there is no other name given under heaven among men, in which we must be saved. Acts 4. And Paul testifies that he had joined the Corinthians to one husband, Christ, and he does not wish them to be turned aside from the simplicity of faith, which is owed to Christ alone. 2 Cor. 11. Let those who glory in the name of Christ, yet outside of him invent a new priesthood, new sacrifices, new intercessors, new heads of the Church, new teachers and masters, and finally a new manner of salvation in every respect, observe these things. Let us acknowledge that it is an extreme and sacrilegious impiety to take away from Jesus, the Son of God, anything that is comprehended in the name of Christ, that is, of king and priest.

units.la: Præterea fructum fidei exponit euangelista,ex quo eius dignitatem æstimare licet. Qui (in-quit) credit Iesum esse Christum,ex Deo natus est. Dei filios facit fides,quæ dignitas omnem mū-di gloriam longè superat. Laudi habetur generis nobilitas. Et sanè nonnihil est, ex bonis parentibus progenitū esse,& domestica habere virtutis exempla quæ imiteris. Sed vana est,& plusquam ventosa nobilitas,nisi ex Deo natus sis. Nicodemo etenim Christus ait: Amen amen dico tibi,nisi quis natus fuerit è supernis,non potest videre regnum Dei. Ioan.3. Quæ ergo utilitas erit posse a-uos & atauos numerare gloria & virtute celebres,nisi cœlestis accedat regeneratio,quę sola regni cœlorum hæredes facit? Apud inferos & Pharaonem & reliquos reges torqueri legimus, qui posuerunt terrorem suum in terra viuentium,nec impijs & à fide alienis superba titulorum ostentatio profuit. Ezech.32. Atqui sola fides Dei filios facit. Christo enim inserit,qui spiritum suum nobis communicat,in quo clamamus Abba pater. Rom.8. Gal.4. Nemo itaq; tanquá ignobilem contemnat eum, qui Deo patre & Christo fratre per fidem gloriari potest. Nemo generis nobilitate efferatur,si se Dei filium esse nondum viderit. Imò licet se eum esse certus sit,nondum tamen datam sibi putet gloriandi materiā. Quia ut carnalis natiuitas nō nostri est vel arbitrij vel potestatis sed parentum beneficium est,ex quibus nascimur: ita ut filij Dei nascamur, nec volentis nec currentis est,sed miserantis Dei. Rom.9. Et non ex sanguinibus,neque ex voluntate carnis,neque ex voluntate viri,sed ex Deo nati censeri debent,quotquot eò dignitatis euehuntur. Ioan.1. Nam & fides,cuius medio tales efficimur,non ex nobis,sed donum Dei est. Ephes.2. Euertit hoc omnem meriti nostri & iustitiæ propriæ gloriationem. Ut enim hæres nascitur filius, non hæres esse me-retur: ita nos hæredes Dei sumus,quia ex Deo nascimur: At ex Deo nascimur per fidem,quæ gratuitum diuinæ liberalitatis munus est. Stultum igitur eo gloriari coram domino, quod ex te nec habes,nec unquam habere poteris nisi donante domino. Porrò ne quis fidem imaginetur mortu-am,quæ impijs licentiæ & scelerum prætextus est,ad alteram huius loci partem transeamus,quæ charitatis mysteria explicat,cuius causam & radicem diximus esse fidem in Christum.
units.tr: Furthermore, the Evangelist sets out the fruit of faith, from which we may judge its worth. "Whoever believes that Jesus is the Christ," he says, "is born of God." Faith makes the sons of God, and this dignity far surpasses all the glory of the world. Nobility of birth is held in praise, and it is certainly something to have been born of good parents and to have domestic examples of virtue that you may imitate. But nobility is empty and worse than windy, unless you are born of God. For Christ said to Nicodemus: "Truly, truly I say to you, unless someone is born from above, he cannot see the kingdom of God" (John 3). What use, then, is it to be able to count grandfathers and great-grandfathers famous for glory and virtue, unless a heavenly regeneration is added, which alone makes heirs of the kingdom of heaven? We read that in hell Pharaoh and the other kings are tormented, who set their terror in the land of the living, and that the proud display of titles profited the wicked and those alienated from faith nothing (Ezekiel 32). Yet faith alone makes the sons of God. For it engrafts us into Christ, who communicates his Spirit to us, by whom we cry, "Abba, Father" (Romans 8; Galatians 4). Therefore let no one despise as ignoble the man who can glory in God the Father and Christ the brother through faith. Let no one be puffed up by the nobility of his birth, if he has not yet seen that he is a son of God. Indeed, even if he is certain that he is one, let him nonetheless think that the material for glorying has not yet been given to him. For just as carnal birth is not of our choosing or power, but is the benefit of the parents from whom we are born, so too we are born as sons of God not by the will of the one who wills or the one who runs, but of God who has mercy (Romans 9). "Not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God," those who are raised to this dignity ought to be counted as born (John 1). For faith too, by means of which we are made such, is not from ourselves but is the gift of God (Ephesians 2). This overturns all glorying in our merit and our own righteousness. For just as a son is born an heir without deserving to be an heir, so we are heirs of God because we are born of God; but we are born of God through faith, which is a free gift of divine liberality. It is foolish, therefore, to glory before the Lord in what you neither have from yourself, nor could ever have, unless the Lord grants it. But lest anyone imagine a dead faith, which becomes a pretext for licence and wickedness for the impious, let us turn to the other part of this passage, which explains the mysteries of love, whose cause and root we have said is faith in Christ.

units.la: Sunt in hac duo expendenda, quæ illi Apostolus tribuit. Primò personarum respectum exclu-dit, qui si admittatur præsentissimum charitatis venenum est. Nam charitatem per se laudabilem esse, & eius studium probari debere, nemo facile negauerit. At si à nobis quoq; exiguntur charitatis officia, mirum quàm ingeniosa sit caro nostra, quæ vix aliquem inuenire potest, quem nostra beneficentia dignum iudicet. Hunc enim propter patriam vel negligi, vel etiam contemni & vexari posse putat, eò quòd natale solum longius à nobis remotum illi contigit, vel ex eo aliqua fortasse iniuria nobis illata est. Alium rursus propter vitæ conditionem nostro amore indignum censet. Denique, dum philautiæ oculus in proximi vitiis obseruandis acutissimè cernit, semper aliquid deprehendere solet, quo omissum dilectionis officium excusare studet. At Joannes omnes eos filios Dei esse docet, qui Jesum Christum nobiscum agnoscunt & fatentur. Quòd si filii Dei sunt, fratres tui sint necesse est, nisi te filium Dei negare velis. Tu verò quis es, qui & fratre & filium Dei negligi posse existimas? Multa equidem in externis sunt, quæ personarum discrimina non obscura inducunt. Sed arctior est nostra, quam in Christo Jesu habemus, coniunctio & fraternitas, quàm ut propter externarum rerum discrimina violari debeant. Siquidem in Christo Jesu non est Judæus neque Græcus, non seruus neque liber, non masculus neque fœmina, non Barbarus, non Scytha, non Germanus, non Gallus, non Hispanus vel Italus, sed omnia in omnibus Christus est. Et omnes nos unum sumus in Christo Jesu. Galat.3. Col.3. Explodamus ergo malignum philautiæ iudicium, & Christi doctrinam audiamus, qui omnes illos nobis proximos esse docet, quos nostra ope, nostro consilio & auxilio indigere videmus. Luc.10.
units.tr: There are two points to be weighed in this, which the Apostle attributes to it. First, he excludes respect of persons, which, if admitted, is the most present poison of love. For no one would easily deny that love is praiseworthy in itself and that its practice ought to be commended. But if the duties of love are demanded of us as well, it is remarkable how ingenious our flesh is, which can scarcely find anyone whom it judges worthy of our kindness. For it thinks that one may be neglected or even despised and harassed on account of his homeland, because his native soil happened to be farther removed from us, or perhaps because some wrong was done to us by him. Again, it judges another unworthy of our love on account of his condition of life. Finally, while the eye of self-love sees most sharply in observing the faults of a neighbour, it is always wont to detect something by which it strives to excuse the duty of love it has left undone. But John teaches that all those are sons of God who acknowledge and confess Jesus Christ along with us. And if they are sons of God, they must needs be your brothers, unless you wish to deny that you are a son of God. But who are you, who think that a brother and a son of God may be neglected? Indeed, there are many external things which introduce distinctions between persons that are not obscure. But the bond and brotherhood we have in Christ Jesus is closer, so that it ought not to be violated on account of the differences of external things. For in Christ Jesus there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, neither male nor female, neither Barbarian, nor Scythian, nor German, nor Gaul, nor Spaniard or Italian, but Christ is all in all. And we are all one in Christ Jesus (Galatians 3; Colossians 3). Let us therefore cast out the malicious judgment of self-love, and let us hear the teaching of Christ, who teaches that those are our neighbours whom we see in need of our help, our counsel and our assistance (Luke 10).

units.la: Deinde quorsum charitas referri debeat, vel quod eius obiectum sit, docet. Omnis (inquit) qui Deum patrem diligit, eos etiam diligit, qui ex Deo nati sunt. Proprium ergo charitatis obiectum, quo mouetur, Deus est. Longè enim à prophano amore, quem in filiis huius seculi est videre, sanctam hanc & diuinam dilectionem, spiritus sanctus remouet & distinguit. Equidem multi sunt, qui & amicas amant, & eos, quorum amicitias sibi vel honori vel utilitati esse norunt, magno studio sectantur, & nihil non officiorum illis exhibent. At quia hæc priuatæ utilitatis siue voluptatis causa faciunt, non proximum, sed seipsos diligere dici debent. Aufer enim amatori potiundæ amicæ spem, vel libidinis voluptatem tollito, & amori illius finem feceris. Aufer honores & emolumentum quod alius ex iis sperat, quos suo fauore prosequitur, & mox languere videbis obsequium, quod paulò ante feruere putabas. Aliud ergo obiectum sanctæ illius & Christianæ dilectionis Joannes monstrat, Deum scilicet, quem quia in omnibus hominibus cernere licet, illius respectu ad omnes amandos incitamur. Constat enim ad Dei imaginem conditum esse hominem. Constat eum, qui fidelis est, Dei esse filium, & Christi fratrem atque cohæredem. Constat eū quoque, qui infidelis est, sub Dei cura & patrocinio agere, & fortasis spes est, illum aliquando in salutis cognitionem peruenturum. Hæc quia fidelis cogitat, ubique videt, quod in ipso amoris sancti flammam incendat. Quamuis enim lucri nihil sperare possit, deq; retributione beneficij planè incertus sit, quia tamen Deo se hoc beneficium debere intelligit, non grauatim confert, quod tamen liberalis remunerator ab ipso postulat. Rursus, si iniuria affectus sit à proximo, non tamen huius memoria charitatis affectum extinguet, si in Deum respiciat, qui atrociores multò iniurias ab omnibus nobis illatas sustinuit & condonauit, imò expiauit effuso in ara Crucis filii sui sanguine. Vides ergo necessarium esse, ut in charitate exercenda alio, quàm ad proximum, mentis nostræ oculos conuertamus. Nisi enim id fiat, proximus nobis idolum, & charitas idololatriæ loco erit. Diuina autem charitas dici merebitur, quæ propter Deū & præceptum eius exercetur. Christiana erit, quà Christi nomine fratribus impendimus. Nec tamen hæc quisquà ita accipiat, quasi misericordiæ affectū à charitate excludamus, qui alienæ miseriæ aspectu commouetur. Qui nisi in sanctis locum inueniat, iam illos stipites & truncos, non homines esse iudicabimus. Sed principalem charitatis causam, quà etiam nulla alia accedente excitatur, urgemus, quæ sola charitatis affectum omni vitio liberat, & per omnia syncerū reddit. At quia tā fides quàm charitas Deo nititur, & in deum unum respicit, non potest non arctissima & indissolubilis esse illarum coniunctio: & proinde firmum & certum consistit, quod Apostolus prima huius loci parte probare instituit.
units.tr: Next, he teaches to what love ought to be referred, or what its object is. "Everyone," he says, "who loves the Father also loves those who are born of God." The proper object of love, by which it is moved, is therefore God. For the Holy Spirit removes and distinguishes this holy and divine affection far from the profane love which is seen in the children of this age. Indeed, there are many who both love their girlfriends and eagerly pursue those whose friendships they know to be either an honour or a benefit to themselves, and they show them every kind of service. But because they do these things for the sake of private advantage or pleasure, they ought to be said to love themselves, not their neighbour. Take away from the lover the hope of obtaining his beloved, or remove the pleasure of lust, and you will have made an end of that love. Take away the honours and the profit which another hopes for from those whom he favours, and soon you will see the obedience which you had thought a little while before was glowing grow faint. John therefore points out another object of that holy and Christian love, namely God, whom, because he can be seen in all men, we are stirred to love all people for his sake. For it is certain that man was made in the image of God. It is certain that the one who is faithful is a son of God, and a brother and co-heir of Christ. It is certain also that the one who is unfaithful lives under God's care and protection, and perhaps there is hope that he will someday come to the knowledge of salvation. Since the faithful man reflects on these things, he sees everywhere what kindles the flame of holy love within him. For although he can hope for no gain and is entirely uncertain about any return for a kindness, yet because he understands that he owes this kindness to God, he gives it without reluctance, which the generous rewarder himself requires of him. Again, if he has been wronged by a neighbour, the memory of this love will not extinguish the affection, if he looks to God, who endured and forgave far more grievous injuries inflicted on us all, and indeed expiated them by pouring out the blood of his Son on the altar of the Cross. You see, therefore, that in exercising love it is necessary for us to turn the eyes of our mind to something other than the neighbour. For unless this is done, the neighbour will be an idol for us, and love will take the place of idolatry. But that will deserve to be called divine love which is exercised for God's sake and at his command. It will be Christian, because we bestow it on our brothers in the name of Christ. Yet let no one take this as if we were excluding from love the feeling of mercy, which is moved by the sight of another's misery. If anyone should fail to find a place for this in the saints, we would judge them to be stumps and blocks, not men. But we press the principal cause of love, which is aroused even when no other cause accompanies it, and which alone frees the affection of love from every vice and makes it pure in all respects. And because both faith and love rest upon God, and look to one God, their union cannot but be most close and indissoluble; and therefore what the Apostle undertook to prove in the first part of this passage stands firm and certain.

units.la: I I. In hoc cognoscimus, quod diligamus filios Dei, cum Deum diligimus, & præcepta eius seruamus. Hæc est enim dilectio Dei, ut præcepta eius seruemus. Poterant hæc priorum expositio videri, sed simul veræ dilectionis notas comprehendunt. Loquitur autem tam de Dei quàm proximi dilectione. Dilectionis proximi notam facit dilectionem Dei. Et ut ante dixit, eum qui Deum diligit, & Dei filios necessariò diligere: ita nunc inverso verborum ordine, ait: In hoc cognoscimus, quòd diligamus filios Dei, si ipsum Deum diligamus. Quia enim philautiæ malo excæcati sumus omnes, fucatus erit omnis, quæ proximo impendimus, amor, nisi cum dei amore coiunctus sit. Obseruandum hoc in amicitijs quærendis, in quibus ut maxima terrenæ felicitatis pars consistit: ita qui in illis admittitur error, frequenter opum & famæ ruinam secum trahit. At frequenter fit juxta illud poetæ, ut Vulgus amicitias utilitate probet. Quare diuitum & potentum huius seculi fauorem plerique affectant. Sed quàm miserè fallantur, multi quotidie experiuntur, licet erroris causam non omnes animaduertant. Proximos syncerè non amat, nisi qui Dei amans fuerit. Quis-quis ergo syncerum & stabilem amicum quæris, eum sectare in quo Dei amorem flagrare sense-ris. Hunc ab omni dolo alienum senties. Hic nec secundis rebus, quæ tibi affluunt, inuidebit: nec ad uersis offendetur. Imò eò plus amoris & officij præstabit, quò maiori necessitate te circumuentum viderit. Quòd si hoc præcepto contempto, eos amicos quæras, qui præsentis alicuius emolu-menti spem faciant, eadem esca tu quoq; decipieris, ut & tuam amicitiam tui similes venentur: sicque illud ethnici poetæ in te locum habebit: Donec eris felix, multos numerabis amicos. Tem-pora si fuerint nubila, solus eris.
units.tr: II. In this we know that we love the children of God when we love God and keep his commandments. For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. These words could seem to be an explanation of what came before, but at the same time they set out the marks of true love. He speaks of love for God and love for neighbour alike. He makes love of God the mark of love of neighbour. And, as he said earlier, that whoever loves God necessarily loves the children of God too, so now, reversing the order of the words, he says: "In this we know that we love the children of God, if we love God himself." For since we are all blinded by the evil of self-love, whatever love we show to our neighbour will be counterfeit unless it is joined with the love of God. This should be noted in seeking friendships, in which the greatest part of earthly happiness consists: so whatever error is admitted into them often drags down wealth and reputation with it. And it often happens, as the poet says, that the crowd tests friendships by their usefulness. Hence most people court the favour of the rich and powerful of this world. But how wretchedly they are deceived, many experience every day, though not all notice the cause of the error. Anyone who does not love his neighbour sincerely unless he loves God will not do so. Whoever, then, you seek as a sincere and steadfast friend, pursue the one in whom you perceive the love of God burning. You will find that he is free from all deceit. He will not envy you when good fortune flows to you, nor will he take offence at adversity. Rather, the more he sees you surrounded by need, the more love and service he will render. But if, despising this precept, you seek those friends who hold out hope of some present advantage, you too will be deceived by the same bait, and those like them will hunt your friendship; and so that saying of the heathen poet will apply to you: "While you are fortunate, you will count many friends; if the times become cloudy, you will be alone."

units.la: Porrò ne quid nobis desit, Dei quoq; amorem quo indicio probare debeamus docet. Hæc est (inquit) dilectio Dei, ut præcepta eius seruemus. Opponit sententiam hanc hypocritis, qui de Deo & dilectione eius multa magno cum verborum splendore disputare consueuerunt. Sed ut regnum Dei non est in sermone, sed in potentia & virtute: ita Dei amor non verbis, sed factis optimè probatur. Videtur autem ex communi hominum sensu & experientia quotidiana desumptum esse, quod Apostolus dicit. Sic enim comparatum videmus, ut filij qui parentū verè amantes sunt, ijsdé obedire studeant: nec unquá persuadebis alicui cordato, eū filium patris amore teneri, qui in obedientia sua patri iugis irarū & doloris causa est. Eadé ratione, quicunq; Dei amore animis suis conceperunt, diuinâ voluntate studiosè obseruant, nec illis graue videri potest, quo Deū delectari norunt. Debent huc referri, quod Christū Jesum dixisse legimus: Si diligitis me, præcepta mea seruate. Item: Qui habet præcepta mea & seruat ea, ille est qui diligit me. Joan.14. Et rursus eodem loco: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum seruabit. Et alibi: Si præcepta mea seruaueritis, manebitis in dilectione mea. Joan.15.
units.tr: Moreover, lest anything be lacking to us, he also teaches by what sign we ought to prove our love of God. "This is," he says, "the love of God, that we keep his commandments." He sets this saying against hypocrites, who are accustomed to dispute much about God and his love with great show of words. But as the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power and virtue, so the love of God is best proved not by words but by deeds. What the apostle says seems to be drawn from common human feeling and daily experience. For we see it is so ordained that children who truly love their parents take care to obey them; nor will you ever persuade any sensible person that a son is held by a father's love when by his disobedience he is a constant cause of anger and grief to his father. By the same reasoning, those who have conceived the love of God in their hearts diligently observe the divine will, nor can it seem burdensome to them what they know delights God. To this must be referred what we read that Jesus Christ said: "If you love me, keep my commandments." Likewise: "He who has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me." John 14. And again in the same place: "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word." And elsewhere: "If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love." John 15.
