units.la: Est autem diligenti obseruatione dignum, quòd Dei dilectionem cum præceptorum Dei obseruatione spiritus sanctus coniungit. Nec enim falsos modò dilectionis Dei iactatores arguit, verumetiam contra superstitiosos hypocritas de vera præceptorum Dei obseruatione nos instituit. Nam sunt, qui egregiè se suo officio functos putent, si externa illa, quæ Deus exigit, magno cum splendore peregerint: ut interim de illis nihil dicam, qui hæc ipsa inuiti faciunt, & non nisi pœnæ metu impulsi. At Deus, quia animum hominis requirit, voluntariam quoq; à nobis obedientiam postulat. Quare de populo Christi illud cumprimis regius Psaltes Dauid testatur, quòd promptus per omnia & spontaneæ voluntatis sectator in Christi cultu futurus sit. Psalm.110. Et Moses cum legem totam summatim colligere instituit, de Dei dilectione non indiligenter mentionem facit, dicens: Audi Israel, Dominus Deus noster Dominus unus est. Diliges itaque dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, & tota anima tua, & pro omni virili tua. Deuteronom.6. Et rursum: Et nunc Israel, quid dominus Deus tuus petit à te, nisi ut timeas dominum Deum tuum, & ut incedas in cunctis vijs eius, diligas eum, & seruias domino Deo tuo toto corde tuo, &c. Vbi gradationem, quam Moses ponit, obseruare operæprecium est. Vult ut Deum timeamus, quod verę sapientiæ principium esse testatur Solomon. Prouerb.1. & 9. Psalmo iii. Timorem sequitur præceptorum obseruatio. Nec enim herum timere dicetur seruus, qui heri præcepta negligit. At ne seruilis putetur timor hic, & non spontanea præceptorum Dei obseruatio, tertius locus dilectioni tribuitur, quæ tandem eum cultum parit, qui totum cor hominis Deo vendicat. Confutantur ita quæ hoc loco omnes cultus extra Dei verbum per homines constituti. Nec enim gratus esse potest Deo cultus, nisi qui cum Dei amore coniunctus fuerit. At hic à præceptorum Dei obseruatione alienus non est, imò huic unicè studet, & hominum traditiones, Dei sententia olim damnatas, cane peius & angue odit.
units.tr: It is, moreover, worthy of careful attention that the Holy Spirit joins the love of God with the observance of God's commandments. For he not only accuses the false boasters of love for God, but also instructs us about the true observance of God's commandments against superstitious hypocrites. For there are some who think they have discharged their duty admirably if they have performed with great show those external things which God requires, not to mention those who do even these things unwillingly and only driven by fear of punishment. But God, since he seeks the heart of man, also demands voluntary obedience from us. Therefore, concerning the people of Christ, the royal psalmist David bears witness above all that they will be ready in all things and followers of Christ's worship of their own free will. Psalm 110. And when Moses set out to gather up the whole law in summary, he did not carelessly mention the love of God, saying: "Hear, Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord. You shall therefore love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your might." Deuteronomy 6. And again: "And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, but that you fear the Lord your God, and walk in all his ways, love him, and serve the Lord your God with all your heart, etc." Here it is worth observing the sequence which Moses sets down. He wills that we fear God, which Solomon testifies is the beginning of true wisdom. Proverbs 1 and 9; Psalm 111. Fear is followed by the observance of the commandments. For a servant is not said to fear his master if he neglects his master's commands. But lest this fear be thought servile, and not a spontaneous observance of God's commandments, a third place is given to love, which at last brings forth that worship which claims the whole heart of man for God. Thereby are refuted all the forms of worship that men have devised outside God's word, which are here set aside. For worship cannot be pleasing to God unless it is joined with the love of God. But such worship is not foreign to the observance of God's commandments; rather, it devotes itself to them alone, and it hates the traditions of men, which God's sentence condemned long ago, worse than a dog or a snake.

units.la: Possent hic de præceptorum Dei obseruatione multa dici. Sed quæ huc faciunt in ijs quæ proximè sequuntur, Joannes subjiciet. Agnoscamus nos coniunctionem arctissimam fidei atque charitatis. Sectemur utriusque studium, & fidem quidem Dilectione, Dilectionem verò præceptorum Dei obseruatione probemus. Sic enim fiet, ut pro veris Dei filijs agnosci possimus, & in cœlis olim viuamus cum filio Dei unigenito, Jesu Christo, cui debetur benedictio, gloria, honor & potestas, in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Much could be said here about the observance of God's commandments. But John will add what pertains to this in the words that immediately follow. Let us acknowledge the very close union of faith and love. Let us pursue the zeal of both, and let us prove faith by love, and love by the observance of God's commandments. For so it will come about that we may be recognised as true children of God, and may one day live in heaven with the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, to whom is due blessing, glory, honour and power, for ever. Amen.

units.la: Et præcepta eius grauia non sunt. Quoniam omne, quod natum est ex Deo, vincit mundum, Et hæc est victoria, quæ vicit mundum, fides nostra. Quis est qui vicit mundum, nisi qui credit, quod Iesus est filius Dei?
units.tr: And his commandments are not grievous. For whatever is born of God overcomes the world, and this is the victory that overcomes the world: our faith. Who is he who overcomes the world, but he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?

units.la: VT Deus in scripturis sanctis passim fidem veram & nō fictum fraternæ charitatis studium à nobis exigit: ita omnes ferè tam fide in Deum vera quàm charitate in fratres gloriari solent, cum tamen paucissimos videre liceat, qui his ex animo & verè studeant. Prudentissimè ergo Ioannes de his sermonem sic instituit, ut utramq; certis ac infallibilibus notis describat, quò veros fidei & charitatis cultores ab hypocritis & vanis ostentatoribus possimus discernere. Et fidei quidem notam fecit ipsam charitatem. Quia enim fide filij Dei efficimur, fieri nequit, quin & erga eum patrem & eius filios, qui nobis fratres sunt, amorem verum animis nostris concipiamus. Charitatem verò synceram ex obseruatione præceptorum dei æstimare docet. Nam amoris proprium est, ut ijs quos amamus, placere summum studium sit. At Deo placere non potest, nisi qui præcepta eius seruare studet, ut multi scripturæ loci & exempla passim obuia probant. Semper ergo ob oculos nobis hæc notę versentur, ut tà alios homines quàm nosipsos dijudicare, & quàtum adhuc nobis in fidei & charitatis studio desit, agnoscere possimus. Cæterū quia in obseruationem præceptorum Dei incidit, inde occasione sumpta, de hac in præsenti diligentius & plenius disserit. Insignis locus, & attenta consyderatione dignissimus. Primò enim, ne nimiæ difficultatis opinio omne in nobis studium frangat, & desperabundi in ipso limine cocidamus, docet, Dei præcepta per se grauia & difficilia non esse. Deinde quibus non grauia sint, indicat. Tandem & organu vel medium describit, per quod omnis, quæ hic incidere potest, difficultas facilimè superatur.
units.tr: As God in the holy Scriptures everywhere demands from us true faith and a zeal for fraternal charity that is not feigned, so almost all men are wont to boast both of faith in God that is true and of charity toward the brethren, although one may see very few who really and sincerely strive for these things. John therefore most prudently arranged his discourse about them so as to describe both by certain and infallible marks, so that we may be able to distinguish the true worshippers of faith and charity from hypocrites and vain pretenders. And indeed he made charity itself the mark of faith: for since we are made children of God through faith, it cannot be but that we also conceive in our hearts a true love both toward the Father and toward his children, who are our brethren. But he teaches that sincere charity is to be judged from the observance of God's commandments. For it is the property of love that the greatest concern is to please those whom we love; but no one can please God unless he earnestly strives to keep his commandments, as many passages of Scripture and examples everywhere at hand prove. Let these marks therefore always be before our eyes, so that we may judge both other men and ourselves, and recognise how much we still lack in the zeal for faith and charity. But since he has come upon the observance of God's commandments, taking occasion from this, he discourses on it at present more diligently and fully. It is a remarkable passage and most worthy of careful consideration. For first, lest the opinion of excessive difficulty crush every zeal in us, and we fall despairing at the very threshold, he teaches that God's commandments are not grievous or difficult in themselves. Next he indicates to whom they are not grievous. Finally he describes the instrument or means by which every difficulty that can arise here is most easily overcome.

units.la: I. Et præcepta eius grauia non sunt. Breuis & perspicua (si verba consyderes) sententia, sed quæ penitius inspici mereatur. Si enim eam ad Carnis nostræ iudicium reuocemus, longè diuersum apparebit. Siquidem Caro, quanta quanta est, corruptioni subiacet. In peccatis cocepti & geniti, peccatorum illecebris delectamur, peccatis seruimus, & iuxta prophetæ sententiam, Aethiopis colorem mutare tam facile est, quàm carnis ingenium aliud fingere. Iere.13. Et Paulus apostolus peccati vim tantam in membris suis se sentire testatur, quam nullis viribus aut consilijs superare possit, quin per eam captiuus ducatur, quò non vult. Rom.7. Quomodo igitur non grauia sunt dei præcepta, quibus ferendis non sufficimus? Hic obseruemus oportet, duplicem esse præceptorum dei consyderationem. Prima est, qua illa ad carnis nostræ infirmitatem & ingenitam corruptionem examinamus. Altera, quæ qualia per se sint, indicat. In priori, nō grauia modò, verùetiam prorsus intolerabilia esse deprehenduntur: quæ tamen si nuda & qualia in seipsis sunt, consyderentur, nihil difficultatis continent. Exemplo aut simili res clarior fiet. Fingamus in medio posita massam aliquam nō magni ponderis. Iubeatur hanc in humeros attollere & auferre aliquis, quem vel natura ineptum & imbecillem genuit, vel morbus diuturnior debilitauit. Nunquam certè, quod iubetur, efficiet, & intolerabile pondus erit illi, quod alius, cui vires sunt integræ, paruo labore sublatum amouebit. Massa hæc reuera est Dei voluntas & eius præcepta, quæ per verbū Dei in scripturis proponuntur. Grauia sunt & intolerabilia, non alia de causa, quàm quòd primæ transgressionis peccato vires nostræ eneruatæ, & caro nostra eò corruptionis adducta est, ut nihil illi & gratius & inuisum magis sit, quàm quod cœlestis vitæ rationem præscribit. Quòd si rem ipsam excutiamus, præcepta hæc non leuia modò, sed & dulcia omnino & suauia esse deprehendentur.
units.tr: I. "And his commandments are not grievous." This is a brief and clear saying (if you consider the words), but one that deserves to be examined more deeply. For if we bring it to the judgement of our flesh, it will appear quite different. Indeed the flesh, however great it is, is subject to corruption. Conceived and born in sins, we take delight in the allurements of sin, we serve sin, and, according to the saying of the prophet, it is as easy for an Ethiopian to change his colour as for the flesh to make itself another nature. Jer. 13. And the apostle Paul testifies that he feels in his members such a power of sin that he cannot overcome it by any strength or counsels, but is led captive by it wherever it will not. Rom. 7. How then are God's commandments not grievous, when we are not sufficient to bear them? Here we must observe that there is a twofold consideration of God's commandments. The first is that by which we examine them in relation to the weakness of our flesh and its innate corruption. The other indicates what they are in themselves. In the former they are found not only grievous but altogether intolerable; yet if they are considered naked and as they are in themselves, they contain no difficulty at all. The matter will become clearer by an example or a similar case. Let us imagine some mass of no great weight placed in the middle. Let someone be ordered to lift it onto his shoulders and carry it away, a man whom nature has made feeble and unfit, or whom a lengthy illness has weakened. Certainly he will never do what he is ordered, and the burden will be intolerable to him, which another, whose strength is intact, would remove with little labour once it was lifted. This mass is truly the will of God and his commandments, which are set forth in Scripture through the word of God. They are grievous and intolerable for no other reason than that, through the sin of the first transgression, our strength has been enfeebled and our flesh has been brought to such corruption that nothing is more pleasing or more hateful to it than what prescribes the rule of heavenly life. But if we examine the matter itself, these commandments will be found not only light but altogether sweet and pleasant.

units.la: Incipiamus autem à doctrina, per quam illa proponuntur. Ita enim comparatum est, ut præcepta omnia multum vel facilitatis vel difficultatis ex methodo & tradendi ratione accipiant. Atqui hæc doctrina & simplex est, & clara, certa atq; perfecta. Simplicitatis argumentum ingens est, quòd & ciuibus & rusticis, doctis & indoctis, viris & mulieribus, imò & pueris illam conuenire posse videmus. Simplicitas hæc de eiusdem perspicuitate luculenter testari solet. Certitudinem nemo negare poterit, cum & certis libris comprehensa sit, & iam à prima usque mundi origine durauerit. Perfectionem verò tantum habet, ut nihil illi vel addi debeat vel adimi, nec permissum est, ut quisquam aliquid in illa mutare audeat. Pertinent huc Christi testimonia, qui se omnia nobis tradidisse dicit, quæcunque à patre acceperat. Ioan.14. Idem scripturas scrutari iubet, & in illis vitam æternam monstrat. Ioannis quinto. Et Paulus, scripturam diuinitus inspiratam & utilem esse fatetur ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem, quæ est in iusti-tia, ut integer sit homo Dei, & ad omne opus bonum apparatus.2. Timoth.3. Cum ergo de doctri-næ præceptorum Dei simplicitate nobis constet, nunc potissima illorum capita, ad quæ referri possunt, consyderemus.
units.tr: Let us begin, however, with the doctrine by which they are set forth. For it is so arranged that all commandments receive much of their ease or difficulty from the method and manner of teaching. Now this doctrine is both simple, and clear, certain and perfect. A great proof of its simplicity is that we see it can suit citizens and rustics, learned and unlearned, men and women, and even children. This simplicity is wont to bear witness brilliantly to its own perspicuity. No one will be able to deny its certainty, since it is contained in certain books and has endured from the very first origin of the world. And it has such perfection that nothing ought to be added to it or taken from it, nor is anyone permitted to dare to change anything in it. To this belong the testimonies of Christ, who says that he has delivered to us all things that he had received from the Father. John 14. He likewise bids us search the Scriptures and shows that in them is eternal life. John 5. And Paul confesses that Scripture is divinely inspired and useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction, which is in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete and equipped for every good work. 2 Tim. 3. Since therefore the simplicity of the doctrine of God's commandments is established for us, let us now consider their principal heads, to which they can be referred.

units.la: Primum & summum in his fides est, quam salutis nostræ fundamentum & causam principa-lem esse, omnes fatentur. At huius unicum obiectum proponitur Deus, in quo bona nobis omnia abunde propo-sita sunt. Et medium, per quod illum fide apprehendimus, Christus esse indicatur, qui nos patri reconciliavit, & viam se esse monstrat, quaad illum perveniri potest. Ioan. 14. Quid vero facilius in fidei negotio tradi & a nobis exigi poterat, quam quod iuxta primi fœderis præce-ptum & Decalogi legem (Gene[?].17.Exod.20.) & totius evangelij doctrinam, uni Deo per filium suum Iesum Christum fidere & huius solius gratiæ niti iubemur? Nonne facilius hoc multo est, quam si hominum dogmata sequi, & multis fictitijs diis animo ambiguo adhærere, atq; innumeros mediatores quærere instituamus? Quisquis ergo de fidei præcepto queri audet, quasi illud gra-ve sit & intolerabile, huic etiam molestum erit, si quis eum Labyrinthos & incertas viarum ambages relinquere, regio autem itinere & plano ad locum propositum tendere iubeat.
units.tr: The first and chief of these is faith, which everyone acknowledges to be the foundation of our salvation and its principal cause. But its one object set before us is God, in whom all good things are abundantly offered to us. And the means by which we apprehend him by faith is indicated to be Christ, who has reconciled us to the Father and shows himself to be the way by which one can come to him. John 14. But what could be taught more easily in the matter of faith, and demanded of us, than that, according to the first precept of the covenant and the law of the Decalogue (Gen. 17; Exod. 20) and the whole doctrine of the gospel, we are commanded to trust in the one God through his Son Jesus Christ, and to rest on this grace alone? Is this not far easier than if we were to set about following the doctrines of men, cleaving with a wavering mind to many fictitious gods, and seeking innumerable mediators? Whoever therefore dares to complain about the precept of faith, as if it were grievous and intolerable, will also be annoyed if someone, bidding him leave the labyrinths and uncertain windings of roads, orders him to make for the appointed place by the royal and level road.

units.la: Secundo præcepto ea, quæ ad Dei cultum & religionem faciunt, comprehendemus, in qui-bus eadem est, quæ in priori, simplicitas. Deus enim cum spiritus sit, spiritu coli vult. Ioannis 4. Quare non cultus exigit vel sumptuosos vel laboriosos valde. Auro siquidem nostro & argento non indiget, ut nec reliquis, quæ per nostri corporis ministerium fieri possunt. Animum requirit, qui ab ipso alienus esse non potest, si fidei præceptum non fuerimus aspernati. Quia tamen nostræ carnis infirmitas externis signis & Ceremonijs adiuuari potest, propter nos paucula, quæ suffice-re poterant, tradidit. Nam cœtus instituit sacros, in quibus verbum ipsius audiamus, preces fun-damus ad patrem, & unanimi consensu quasi iunctis viribus in Deum impressionem faciamus, qui ita se a nobis peti & infestari gaudet: adhæc sacramenta usurpemus, quæ ut nostræ salutis tes-feræ & symbola essent, Christus tradidit, baptismum videlicet & Cœnam dominicam. At quid in omnibus illis est, quod grave videri possit? An molestum erit, Dei vocem audire, ijs qui ex Deo nati sunt? Ioan.8.Num precandi officium grave esse potest, cum tot nos undique circumstent pe-ricula, quæ si nemo iuberet, nos ad preces & numinis invocationem cogunt? Quanta vero in sa-cramentis simplicitas, & quam læta proponuntur sub tam facili simplicitate salutis mysteria? Ba-ptismus aquam habet, quæ paruo paratur, simul tamen ex Dei institutione communionis Chri-stianæ symbolum est, de salute per Christu parta testatur, regenerationis & innovationis (quam in eodem habemus) beneficium obsignat, & nostri nos admonet officij. Cœna domini cum ma-xima frugalitate inæstimabiles salutis thesauros comprehendit, de quibus omnibus alibi locus e-rit copiosius dicendi. Hic fateamur oportet, Christianam religionem, si Dei præceptis insistere velimus, nec sumptuum difficultate, nec Ceremoniarum molestia intolerabilem videri posse.
units.tr: In the second precept we comprehend those things which pertain to the worship and religion of God, in which there is the same simplicity as in the first. For since God is spirit, he wills to be worshipped in spirit. John 4. Therefore he does not demand worship that is very costly or very laborious. For he has no need of our gold and silver, nor of the other things that can be done through the service of our body. He requires the mind, which cannot be alien from him if we have not spurned the precept of faith. Yet because the weakness of our flesh can be helped by external signs and ceremonies, he has handed down, for our sake, a few things which could suffice. For he instituted sacred assemblies, in which we hear his word, pour out prayers to the Father, and with united consent, as with joined strength, make an impression upon God, who rejoices to be sought and assailed by us in this way; besides these, we are to use the sacraments, which Christ delivered so that they might be tokens and symbols of our salvation, namely baptism and the Lord's Supper. But what is there in all these things that could seem grievous? Will it be burdensome to hear the voice of God, for those who are born of God? John 8. Can the duty of praying be grievous, when so many dangers surround us on every side, which, even if no one ordered it, compel us to prayer and the invocation of the divine power? And how great is the simplicity in the sacraments, and how joyful are the mysteries of salvation set forth under so easy a simplicity? Baptism has water, which is prepared at small cost; yet at the same time, by the institution of God, it is a symbol of Christian communion, bears witness to salvation obtained through Christ, seals the benefit of regeneration and renewal (which we have in the same), and reminds us of our duty. The Lord's Supper, with the greatest frugality, contains inestimable treasures of salvation, of which there will be opportunity to speak more fully elsewhere. Here we must confess that the Christian religion, if we are willing to abide by the precepts of God, cannot seem intolerable either because of the difficulty of expense or the burden of ceremonies.

units.la: Tertius præceptorum Dei ordo externam vitæ conversationem continet, quæ duabus re-bus absoluitur, charitate nimirum & puritate vel innocentia. Qui enim hisce studuerit, vitam vi-uet Dei iudicio sanctam & irreprehensibilem. Atqui vulgo videmus nihil esse, quod temporariæ felicitati magis seruiat, quam charitatis & innocentiæ studium, adeo ut sine his vita hæc nec tran-quilla nec felix esse queat. Charitate sublata succedunt odia, liuor, simultates, rixæ, conuitia, pu-gnæ, vulnera, cædes, & infinita alia, quæ singula vitæ nostræ conversationem quouis felle amario rem reddunt. At quam magni labores & quanta pericula eos maneant, qui puritatis & innocentiæ studio abiecto impuritatem & scelera quæuis pro animi sui libidine sectantur, clarius est, quam ut longa demonstratione opus habeat. Quis enim negare audsit[?], hominis intemperantis & ebrij conditionem laboriosiorem esse quam temperantis & sobrij? Nonne castitatis & fidei coniuga-lis studium plus gaudij & voluptatis habet, quam vaga scortandi & adulterandi libido, quæ & morbis grauat, & vitæ pericula non raro nobis conciliat? Similiter, qui sua sorte contentus viuit, multis nominibus præstat auarum usurarium & raptorem, qui alienis opibus inuidet, & suis frui non potest. Denique constat (siquidem verum fateri velimus) Dei præcepta leuia per se esse, & non nisi nostro vitio grauia & intolerabilia censeri. Recte ergo Christus Iesus pronunciat: Iu-gum meum commodum est, & onus meum leue est. Matth. 11.Et regius ille Psaltes Dauid, le-gem domini fauis melle stillantibus dulciorem esse, fatetur, Psal.19.
units.tr: The third order of God's precepts concerns outward conduct in life, and it is completed by two things, namely charity and purity or innocence. For whoever has devoted himself to these lives a life that is holy and blameless in God's judgment. And yet we commonly see that nothing serves temporal happiness more than the pursuit of charity and innocence, so much so that without them this life can be neither peaceful nor happy. When charity is removed, there follow hatred, envy, quarrels, brawling, reproaches, fights, wounds, murders, and countless other things, each of which makes the conduct of our life bitter with any kind of gall. But how great the labours are, and how great the dangers that await those who, having cast aside the pursuit of purity and innocence, follow impurity and every kind of crime at the bidding of their own lust, is clearer than that it needs a long demonstration. For who could deny that the condition of the intemperate and drunken man is more laborious than that of the temperate and sober? Does not the pursuit of chastity and faithful marriage have more joy and pleasure than the wandering lust of whoring and adultery, which both burdens us with diseases and not infrequently brings us into danger of life? Similarly, he who lives content with his lot is in many respects better off than the greedy usurer and robber, who envies the riches of others and cannot enjoy his own. Finally, it is agreed (if we are willing to confess the truth) that God's precepts are light in themselves, and that they are considered heavy and intolerable only through our own fault. Rightly, therefore, Christ Jesus declares: My yoke is easy, and my burden is light (Matth. 11.). And the royal psalmist David confesses that the law of the Lord is sweeter than honey dripping from the honeycomb (Psal. 19.).

units.la: Accedunt tamen his, quæ vel grauissimum onus gestatu leue & commodum reddere pote-rant, præmia videlicet ingentia, quæ Christus suorum præceptorum studiosis pollicetur, & mul-ta Dei patris lenitas. Ut enim æternæ vitæ brauio nos inuitat & trahit Deus, ut carnis affectus o-bedientiæ sanctę zelo superemus: ita si quid infirmitate peccatur, non ita rigidè observat, ut propterea è conspectu suo in æternum repulsos velit. Imò, vt apud prophetam legimus: Viuo ego (inquit) & nolo mortem peccatoris, sed vt conuertatur, & viuat. Ezechiel. 18. Adhæc ipse gratia sua adest nobis, & spiritu suo suffulcit, vt possimus præstare, quæ carni nostræ nimis ardua videntur: vt nihil aliud à nobis postulare videri possit, quàm vt sui spiritus organa, & gratiæ suæ vasa nos præbeamus.
units.tr: Yet there are added to these things, which could have made even the heaviest burden light and pleasant to carry, the great rewards which Christ promises to those who diligently keep his precepts, and the great gentleness of God the Father. For as God invites and draws us with the prize of eternal life, so that by the zeal of holy obedience we may overcome the desires of the flesh, so, if we sin through weakness, he does not observe it so rigidly that he therefore wishes us to be cast out of his sight forever. Indeed, as we read in the prophet: As I live (says he), I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live (Ezech. 18.). Moreover, he himself is present to us by his grace and sustains us by his Spirit, so that we may perform what seems too arduous for our flesh; so that nothing else can seem to be required of us than that we offer ourselves as the instruments of his Spirit and the vessels of his grace.

units.la: Admonet nos locus hic, vt enormem nostri seculi ingratitudinem confyderemus, qua in Dei gratiam & præcepta impiè & turpiter peccamus. Cum enim æternæ vitæ præcepta Deus simplici methodo & dilucidè comprehensa proponat, eaq; per se leuia sint, & spiritus sancti auxilio leuiora reddantur, malunt tamen pleriq; hominum sub dura Antichristi tyrannide intolerabilibus humanarum traditionum sarcinis grauari, quàm leue hoc & suaue Christi iugum, tantis propositis præmijs, sustinere. Confer enim cum his, quæ hucusq; dicta sunt, ea quæ toto Papatu traduntur, & facilè intelligēs, quàm grauis sit in omnibus istis animarum sarcina. Doctrina illorum nec simplex, nec perspicua, nec etiam certa & perfecta est. Nam scripturis minimè contenti patrum traditiones & Conciliorum decreta vnà cum nouis Canonibus inuexerunt, & eam vel Pontificum vel Conciliorum authoritatem esse arroganter iactitant, vt noua & hactenus inaudita non minus constituere posint, quàm olim ipsorum maiores fecisse constat. Quis ergo ijs præceptis securus acquiescet, de quorum certitudine & perfectione dubius esse cogitur? Quòd si autem ipsa præcepta confyderes, maiorem incertitudinem deprehendes, & onus sentires longè grauius. Fides, quæ vni Deo debebatur, in multos Deos vel Diuos distrahitur, imò proprijs operibus & meritis homines confidere docentur. Sed quid Confidere dico? Homines de salute & gratia Dei perpetuò dubitare docent, qui huius doctrinæ præstantissimi antistites sunt. Mediator vnus Christus Iesus ijsdem non sufficit, sed tot mediatores finguntur, quot Diui diuéq; in cœlis sunt: & frequenter fit, vt dubij hæreant homines, quem nam ex tanta turba diligere debeant. In religione sumptuosa & laboriosa sunt omnia. Premuntur hominum traditionibus conscientiæ. Peccata dicuntur esse, quæ Deus licita esse voluit, & pecunia accepta in ijsdem dispensatio aliqua admittitur. Sacramentorum numerus auctus est, & eadem nō sine maximis impensis administrari possunt. Baptismus iam nō modò Christianæ fidei cultoribus & illorum liberis datur, sed idem in res inanimas transfertur, & campanas baptismo initiari maxima habetur religio. E Cœna domini alteram speciem impio ausu abstulerunt & totam in sacrificium conuerterunt. Sumptus in ea vestium ingens, calicum item & aliorum, quæ nouus ille Deus Maozim desiderat. Pœnitentiæ doctrina multis additionibus plané intolerabilis facta est, & obrutum prorsus Christi meritum, quod solum hanc nobis leuem & iucundâ reddere poterat. Excogitatæ satisfactiones, quæ quàm indignæ sint hoc nomine, vel hinc patet, quòd nec eius conscientiæ satisfacere possunt, qui illis operam suam sedulò impendit. Nihil nunc dicam de templorum ornatu, monasteriorum regijs ædificijs, monachorum & sacrificulorum turba, pastagijs, sacrorum nundinatione, indulgentiarum mercibus, casibus reseruatis, & in finitis aliis, quorum tyrannis eousq; progressa est, vt maxima opum huius mundi pars, legitimis hæredibus fraudatis, in eorum manus peruenerit, qui spirituales & clerici dici volunt. Atqui in omnibus illis nulla diuini auxilij promissio, nulla gratiæ Dei spes, sed certa Dei ira & vindicta præsens, quæ omnes eos manet, qui Christi verbo contempto, hominum commentis sese regendos præbent. Imò nec ipsi quidem post hanc vitam præmium certum pollicentur, sed de purgatorij igne nouas fabulas excogitarunt, quæ iam morituris nouos terrores incuterent, & pecunias adhuc plures extorquerent. Et quemadmodum veri Christi cultores tam viui quàm mortui sub domini præsidio conferuantur[?] (Roman. 14.) ita quicunque istis sese manciparunt, & viui & mortui ipsorum tyrannidi & rapacitati subiacent. Et tamen talibus delectatur mundus hic, tales veneratur & suspicit, pro talibus pugnat, & in fratrum viscera intestinis bellis grassatur? O cæcas hominum mentes, ô pectora cæca. O impietatem & ingratitudinem quouis supplicio dignam. Sed hoc ipsum est, quod Christus prædixit: Ego veni nomine patris mei, nec recipitis me: si alius venerit nomine suo, illum recipietis. Ioan. 5. Cæterum omisis his ad propositi loci tractationem reuertamur.
units.tr: This passage admonishes us to consider the enormous ingratitude of our age, by which we sin impiously and shamefully against the grace and precepts of God. For since God sets forth the precepts of eternal life in a simple method and clearly comprehended, and since they are light in themselves and are made lighter by the help of the Holy Spirit, yet most people prefer to be weighed down under the harsh tyranny of Antichrist by the intolerable burdens of human traditions, rather than to bear this light and sweet yoke of Christ, with such great rewards set before them. For compare with what has been said so far what is handed down throughout the whole Papacy, and you will easily understand how heavy this burden of souls is in all those things. Their doctrine is neither simple, nor clear, nor even certain and perfect. For, by no means content with the Scriptures, they have introduced the traditions of the Fathers and the decrees of Councils together with new canons, and they arrogantly boast that these have the authority of Popes or Councils, so that they can establish new things hitherto unheard of no less than their forefathers are known to have done. Who, then, will rest securely in those precepts, about whose certainty and perfection he is forced to be in doubt? But if you consider the precepts themselves, you will find greater uncertainty and feel the burden to be far heavier. Faith, which was owed to the one God, is divided among many gods or saints; indeed, men are taught to trust in their own works and merits. But why do I say trust? They teach men to doubt continually about their salvation and the grace of God, those who are the most outstanding leaders of this doctrine. The one Mediator, Christ Jesus, is not enough for them, but as many mediators are invented as there are saints and gods in heaven; and it often happens that men hesitate in doubt as to whom from so great a crowd they ought to love. In religion everything is costly and laborious. Consciences are burdened by human traditions. Things are said to be sins which God wished to be lawful, and some kind of dispensation for those same things is admitted for money received. The number of sacraments has been increased, and these cannot be administered without very great expense. Baptism is now given not only to the worshippers of the Christian faith and their children, but the same rite is transferred to lifeless things, and it is considered a great religious duty to initiate bells by baptism. From the Lord's Supper they have removed the other kind with impious daring and have turned the whole thing into a sacrifice. The expense in this is enormous, both for vestments and for chalices and other things which that new god Maozim desires. The doctrine of repentance has been made utterly intolerable by many additions, and the merit of Christ, which alone could make this doctrine light and pleasant for us, has been completely buried. Satisfactions have been devised, and how unworthy they are in this name is clear from this, that they cannot satisfy the conscience of those who diligently devote their effort to them. I will say nothing now about the adornment of temples, the royal buildings of monasteries, the crowd of monks and little priests, pasture lands, the trafficking in sacred things, the wares of indulgences, reserved cases, and countless other things, whose tyranny has advanced so far that the greatest part of the wealth of this world, the lawful heirs having been defrauded, has come into the hands of those who wish to be called spiritual and clerics. Yet in all those things there is no promise of divine help, no hope of God's grace, but a certain wrath of God and present vengeance, which awaits all those who, having despised the word of Christ, submit themselves to be governed by the inventions of men. Indeed, they do not even promise a certain reward after this life, but they have devised new fables about the fire of purgatory, which might strike new terrors into those now about to die and extort still more money. And just as the true worshippers of Christ are preserved under the protection of the Lord, both living and dying (Rom. 14.), so whoever has surrendered himself to those men, both living and dead, is subject to their tyranny and rapacity. And yet this world is delighted with such men, venerates and admires such men, fights for such men, and rages with internal wars against the bowels of its brothers? O blind minds of men, O blind hearts! O impiety and ingratitude worthy of any punishment! But this is exactly what Christ foretold: I have come in the name of my Father, and you do not receive me; if another comes in his own name, you will receive him (John 5.). But, leaving these things aside, let us return to the treatment of the passage at hand.

units.la: I I. Quoniam omne quod natum est ex Deo, vincit mundum. Indicat quibus hominibus Dei præcepta gratia nō sint: ijs nimirum, qui ex Deo nati sunt. Additur aut & ratio, qua probat quod dicit, Quia tales mundum vincunt. Argumentatio talis est. Quicunq; mundū vincere norunt, ijs Dei præcepta gratia nō sunt. Quicunq; ex Deo nati sunt, mundū vincunt. Ergo qui ex Deo nati sunt, ijs Dei præcepta gratia non sunt. Maior per se plana est & perspicua. Quia enim in præceptorum Dei obseruatione mundus hic nobis maximè obstaculo est, quicunq; illū vicerit, idem maximam illorū difficultatem superauisse dicetur. Mundum verò hic vocat Ioan. quicquid mundi princeps nobis obijcit, vt per illud in salutis via impediamur: qualia sunt, exemplum mundi, opes, honores, voluptates, carnis studium, affectus, desiderium oculorum, & quæcunq; alia sunt huius generis. Ex Deo nati dicuntur, qui (vt initio huius cap. didicimus) per fidem Jesu Christi filij Dei facti sunt. Constat ergo eos nondum fide renatos nec filios Dei esse, quicunque de præceptorum Dei gratiate conqueruntur.
units.tr: II. Because whatever is born of God overcomes the world. He indicates for which men God's precepts are not grievous: namely, for those who are born of God. But a reason is also added by which he proves what he says, namely, that such men overcome the world. The argument is as follows. Whoever knows how to overcome the world, for them God's precepts are not grievous. Whoever are born of God overcome the world. Therefore those who are born of God, for them God's precepts are not grievous. The major premise is in itself plain and clear. For since in the observance of God's precepts this world is especially an obstacle to us, whoever has overcome it will be said to have overcome the greatest difficulty of them. But John here calls the world whatever the prince of the world sets against us, so that we may be hindered in the way of salvation: such as the example of the world, riches, honours, pleasures, devotion to the flesh, affections, the desire of the eyes, and whatever other things are of this kind. Those are said to be born of God who (as we learned at the beginning of this chapter) have become children of God through faith in Jesus Christ. It is clear, therefore, that whoever complains about the grievousness of God's precepts has not yet been born again by faith, nor is a child of God.

units.la: Præterea obseruatione dignissimum est, quòd qui per fidem filij Dei facti sunt, mundum vincere solent. Hinc enim colligi potest, pro filijs Dei & verè fidelibus haberi non posse eos, qui mundi defyderijs & studijs subiacent. Siquidem ideo nos regenerari scriptura docet, vt mundo & peccatis mortui in posterum viuamus Deo. Col.3. Rom.6. Quò omnia præcepta & omnes adhortationes referri debent, quibus vitæ puritas & sanctimoniæ studium nobis passim commendatur. Cæterum, quia non omnibus constat, quomodo qui ex Deo nati sunt, mundum deuincant, ad huius explicationem Apostolus, quæ sequuntur, subijcit.
units.tr: Moreover, it is most worthy of notice that those who have become sons of God through faith are wont to conquer the world. From this it can be gathered that those who are subject to the desires and pursuits of the world cannot be regarded as sons of God and truly faithful. For Scripture teaches that we are regenerated for this purpose: that, dead to the world and to sins, we may live hereafter to God (Col. 3; Rom. 6). To this all precepts and all exhortations must be referred, by which the purity of life and zeal for holiness are commended to us everywhere. But since it is not clear to everyone how those who are born of God overcome the world, the Apostle adds what follows to explain this.

units.la: III. Et hæc est victoria, quæ vicit mundum, fides nostra. Quis est qui vincit mundum, nisi qui credit quòd Jesus est filius Dei? Paucis verbis rem maximam complectitur, & quæstionem carni difficillimam absoluit. In hoc enim maximè exercentur cogitationes hominum, quibus armis, qua arte, quo modo & quibus consilijs improbos mundi conatus & principis ipsius arma artesque vel eludere vel superare possint. Et multos eo adegit consiliorum inopia & rei difficultas, vt temere susceptis ieiunijs, cilicijs, chameunijs, flagellis item & infinitis alijs id confici posse putaret, quæ res superstitiones peperit propemodum infinitas. At Joanes omnem huius pugnæ victoriam fidei in Jesum Christum tribuit, & fidem in hac nobis vice clypei, galeæ, hastæ, ensis, teliqúe fore dicit, denique sola hac omne istud negotium confici. Nec id temere. Nam fides, vt Christo, qui inuicta petra est, nos superædificat: ita Christi spiritus confortes & participes reddit, qui ad omne opus sanctum facit paratos & verè idoneos. Unde Paulus qui alibi de peccati vi, membris suis inhærente, quæritur, rursum se omnia posse dicit in Christo, qui ipsum confortet. Phil.4. Et exempla passim extant, quibus quanta hæc fidei vis sit, demonstratur. Poterit autem huius loci Commentarius absolutissimus censeri epistolæ ad Hebræos cap.11. Ibi enim producuntur, qui fide animati, rebus secundis bene vti, & quæcunque sunt huius mundi bona ex Dei mandato relinquere potuerunt. Nec enim graue est Abrahamo patrios lares & natale solum deserere, quem ita confortauit fides, vt & filium dilectum, sic postulante Deo, propria manu immolare paratus fit. Expende quales in eo facto paterni animi æstus fuerint, quibus arietibus mentem suam peti senserit, quàm multa quamq; grauia obijcere potuerit caro, quæ à cœpto & debito obedientiæ officio illum reuocaret? At omnia hæc vicit una fides, quæ nouerat Deum promissionibus suis nunquam defuturum, & immolatum quoque Isaacum à mortuis resuscitare posse. Eadem fide antea quoque idem Abraham diutinum illud dilati feminis tædium superare potuit, cum indesinenter in Dei veritatem & potentiam respiceret. Rom.4. Per fidem Moses delicias aulæ & regni honores aspernari potuit. Per fidem omnes sancti tyrannorum minas, edicta, tormenta, egestatem, exilium, infamiam & infinita mortis genera superare, imò spernere potuerunt. Nec est, quòd olim quidem hanc fidei virtutem fuisse putemus, quæ iam tota euanuerit. Viget hodie adhuc eadem fidei vis, & passim in ijs cernitur, quibus nec exulare, nec pauperiem & ignominiam perpeti, nec etiam mori pro Christo graue est. Quomodo enim exilium metuat, qui mansionem & ciuitatem permanentem sibi in cœlis paratam esse, firmiter credit? Joan.14. Phil.3. Cur egestate & inopia terreatur, qui immarcescibiles regni cœlorum thesauros sibi repositos esse intelligit? Denique, nec mors illis terribilis esse potest, qui illam non aliud esse certò norunt, quàm vitæ æternæ & nunquam intermoriturę felicitatis ianuam. Joan.5. Quisquis ergo hæc ita metuit, vt illorum terrore sese superari & à veritatis confessione abduci sinat, idem fateatur, se quid fides sit, prorsus ignorare.
units.tr: III. And this is the victory that has overcome the world, our faith. Who is it that overcomes the world, but he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? In a few words he embraces a very great matter and resolves a question most difficult for the flesh. For it is chiefly on this point that men's thoughts are busied: by what arms, by what skill, in what manner and by what counsels the wicked attempts of the world, and the weapons and arts of the prince himself, might be either eluded or overcome. And the lack of counsel and the difficulty of the thing have driven many to think that this could be accomplished by rashly undertaken fasts, hair shirts, chamois garments, and likewise scourgings and countless other things; and this has produced almost countless superstitions. But John ascribes the whole victory of this struggle to faith in Jesus Christ, and says that faith will be to us in this battle a shield, a helmet, a spear and a sword, and in short that this whole business is accomplished by this alone. Nor is this said rashly. For faith, as it builds us up upon Christ, who is an unconquered rock, so also makes us partakers and sharers of Christ's Spirit, who makes us ready and truly fit for every holy work. Hence Paul, who elsewhere complains of the power of sin dwelling in his members, again says that he can do all things in Christ, who strengthens him (Phil. 4). And examples are everywhere extant by which the great power of this faith is shown. Moreover, the most complete commentary on this passage may be judged to be the eleventh chapter of the Epistle to the Hebrews. For there are brought forward those who, inspired by faith, were able to use prosperity well and to leave behind, at God's command, whatever goods of this world there are. Nor was it a hard thing for Abraham to leave his fatherland and the soil of his birth, he whom faith so strengthened that he was ready, when God demanded it, to sacrifice with his own hand his beloved son. Consider what tides of fatherly feeling there were in him in that deed, by what battering rams he perceived his mind to be assailed, how many and how grave objections the flesh could raise to call him back from the undertaken and due duty of obedience! Yet one faith overcame all these things, which knew that God would never fail his promises, and that he could raise Isaac, though sacrificed, from the dead. By the same faith, earlier, that same Abraham was also able to overcome the long weariness of the delayed seed, while he constantly looked to the truth and power of God (Rom. 4). By faith Moses was able to despise the delights of the court and the honours of the kingdom. By faith all the saints were able, or rather, were able to scorn, the threats, edicts, torments, poverty, exile, infamy and countless kinds of death of tyrants. Nor should we think that this virtue of faith was once present but has now wholly vanished away. The same power of faith flourishes today also, and is seen everywhere in those to whom it is no hard thing to be exiled, to suffer poverty and disgrace, or even to die for Christ. For how should he fear exile who firmly believes that a dwelling and a lasting city are prepared for him in heaven (John 14; Phil. 3)? Why should he be terrified by want and poverty who understands that the imperishable treasures of the kingdom of heaven are laid up for him? Finally, death cannot be terrible to those who know for certain that it is nothing other than the gate to eternal life and to a happiness that never ends (John 5). Whoever therefore fears these things so much that he lets himself be overcome by their terror and drawn away from the confession of the truth, let him confess that he is utterly ignorant of what faith is.

units.la: Porro demolitur locus hic & euertit omnem nostrarum virium & operum fiduciam. Constat enim, salutis nostræ rationem omnem ex victoria hac, quà in præsenti proponit Apostolus, pendere. Nam q hic vincitur, salutis iacturâ faciat oportet. At victoriâ refert ex pugna hac sola fides, vt modò demonstrauimus. Soli ergo fidei salutis nostræ gloria debetur. Quòd si verò fidei ingenium & naturam inquiras, hominis vires & merita procul excludi videbis. Primò etenim fides non ex nobis, sed donum Dei est. Ephef. 2. Deinde, non nostris vel viribus, vel meritis, sed vno Christo & illius merito nititur. Stultum ergo & perniciosum est, quicquâ in salutis negotio, vel nostræ voluntati, vel viribus & factis tribuere. Et sanè summæ consolationis plenum est, quòd nō nostris viribus, sed ipsius Christi & spiritus sancti operatione, pugnam hanc omnem deuincendam esse nouimus. Quæ enim victoriæ spes esse poterat, si nostrarum virium robur requireretur, quod planè nullum esse quotidiani lapsus probant? Fidant huic, qui succumbere, quàm vincere malunt.
units.tr: Furthermore, this passage overthrows and subverts all confidence in our own powers and works. For it is clear that the whole ground of our salvation depends upon this victory, which the Apostle now sets forth. For he who is overcome in this contest must necessarily suffer the loss of salvation. But from this struggle, as we have just shown, faith alone brings away the victory. To faith alone, therefore, the glory of our salvation is due. And if you inquire into the nature and character of faith, you will see that the powers and merits of man are far excluded. For first, faith is not from ourselves but is the gift of God (Eph. 2). Next, it rests not upon our own powers or merits but upon Christ alone and his merit. It is therefore foolish and pernicious to ascribe anything in the business of salvation either to our will, or to our powers and deeds. And indeed it is full of the greatest consolation that we know this whole struggle is to be overcome not by our own powers but by the working of Christ himself and of the Holy Spirit. For what hope of victory could there be, if the strength of our own powers were required, which the daily fall shows to be utterly nothing? Let those trust in this who prefer to yield rather than to conquer.

units.la: Debent hæc totis animis recondi fratres dilecti. Agnoscamus præceptorum Dei facilitatem & commoditatem verè salutarem. Intelligamus,ijs qui ex Deo nati sunt,contra mundum,mun-di principem & illecebras perpetuò pugnandum esse. Nec desperemus de victoria,quæ solius fi-dei est,quoniam qui natura infirmi & impotentes sumus, inuicti reddimur in eo,qui serpentis ca-put iam olim contriuit & omnem potestatem aduersariam subegit, Iesu Christo, cui debetur be-nedictio,gloria,honor & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: These things, dear brothers, ought to be laid up with all our hearts. Let us acknowledge the ease and convenience of God's precepts, which is truly salutary. Let us understand that those who are born of God must always fight against the world, the prince of the world and its allurements. Nor let us despair of the victory, which belongs to faith alone; since we, who by nature are weak and powerless, are made invincible in him who has long ago crushed the head of the serpent and subdued every adverse power, Jesus Christ, to whom be blessing, glory, honour and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXI.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXI.

units.la: Hic est qui venit per aquam & sanguinem, Iesus Christus. Non per aquam solum,sed per aquam & sanguinem.Et spiritus est,qui testificatur:quia spiritus est veritas. Quoniam tres sunt, qui testimonium dant in cœlo, Pater, Verbum & Spiritus sanctus: & hi tres unum sunt.Et tres sunt, qui testimonium dant in terra, Spiritus,& Aqua,& Sanguis: & hi tres in unum conveniunt. Si testimonium hominum accipimus, testimonium Dei maius est. Quoniam hoc est testimonium Dei, quo testificatus est de filio suo.
units.tr: "This is he who came by water and blood, Jesus Christ. Not by water only, but by water and blood. And it is the Spirit who bears witness, because the Spirit is truth. For there are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one. And there are three who bear witness on earth: the Spirit, and the Water, and the Blood; and these three agree in one. If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater, for this is the testimony of God, by which he has testified concerning his Son." [1 John 5.6-9]

units.la: UT Deus humani generis saluti unicè studet: ita satan eiusdem communis & publicus ho-stis,nostræ perditioni nunquâ non inuigilat,& tanquâ leo rugiens obambulare solet,quæ-rens quem deuoret.1. Pet.5.Hinc fit,ut vita hæc nostra perpetuæ militiæ instar sit,dum modò volu-ptatum illecebris,modò propriæ carnis cupiditatibus, & frequenter impiorum ac hostium Dei tyrannide nos diabolus oppugnans, à veritatis ac salutis via abstrahere satagit. Cæterum in pugna hac vincit una & sola fides,quæ Christo nos superædificans,& spiritus Christi confortes red-dens,facit ut in illo posimus omnia: quod in præcedenti Sermone pluribus demonstratum est.
units.tr: As God takes the most single-minded care for the salvation of the human race, so Satan, the common and public enemy of the same race, never ceases to keep watch for our ruin, and is wont to prowl like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour [1 Pet. 5.8]. Hence it comes about that this life of ours is like a perpetual warfare: the devil assails us now with the allurements of pleasures, now with the lusts of our own flesh, and often with the tyranny of the impious and the enemies of God, and he labours to draw us away from the way of truth and salvation. Yet in this battle one thing alone conquers, faith, which, building us up upon Christ and making us partakers of the Spirit of Christ, causes us to be able to do all things in him; this was demonstrated at length in the preceding sermon.

units.la: Porro quia fidei huius fundamentum unicum est, Iesus Christus, nec aliud fundamentum à quoquam poni potest, necessarium fuerit,ut eius cognitionem veram,certam atque solidam assequamur. Quis enim ignoto fidere poterit? Vel quis mundi huius tyrannidem & atroces diaboli assultus sustinebit,& per illius nomen vincet,de cuius potentia,gloria & fide ipse dubitat? Opportunè ergo Ioannes,ubi fide vincendum esse docuit,in præsenti de fidei nostræ obiecto & fundamento,Christo Iesu,agit,certis ac firmis argumentis probans, hunc esse verum Dei filium, qui à patre in carnem missus sit,ut humani generis redemptor ac salvator fieret. Quæ omnia in eũ finem tendut,ut firma & infracta fide per omnes tribulationes & satanæ insultus ipsi nitamur. Multum verò lucis loco huic afferet,si orationis figuram obseruemus,quæ prosopopœia constat pulcherrima. Nam perinde ac si causa Christi in iudicio vel foro ageretur,illam in medium productis te-stibus probat. Deinde de testium illorum authoritate agit,ne quis tantæ rei testimonia contemnere auderet.
units.tr: Moreover, since the foundation of this faith is one only, Jesus Christ, and no other foundation can be laid by anyone, it is necessary that we attain a true, certain and solid knowledge of him. For who can trust in one unknown? Or who will endure the tyranny of this world and the fierce assaults of the devil, and conquer through the name of one whose power, glory and faith he himself doubts? Therefore John rightly, having taught that we must conquer by faith, here treats of the object and foundation of our faith, Jesus Christ, proving by certain and firm arguments that he is the true Son of God, who was sent by the Father into the flesh, that he might become the redeemer and saviour of the human race. All these things tend to this end, that by a firm and unshaken faith we may lean upon him through all tribulations and the assaults of Satan. It will bring much light to this passage if we observe the figure of speech which is a most beautiful prosopopoeia. For just as if the cause of Christ were being pleaded in a court of judgement or a forum, he proves it by bringing forward witnesses. Then he speaks of the authority of those witnesses, lest anyone should dare to despise the testimonies in so great a matter.

units.la: I. Hic est, qui venit per aquam & sanguinem, Iesus Christus. Non per aquam solum,sed per aquam & sanguinem. Et spiritus est qui testificatur : quia spiritus est veritas. Dixerat,per eos mundum vinci, qui credunt quod Iesus Christus sit filius Dei. At quia de hoc dubitatur à multis, talem esse probat. Venisse autem dicit per aquam & sanguinem,id est, aqua & sanguine testificatum & demonstratum esse,quòd is sit,quem olim Deus salvatorem fore promiserat, & quem venturum prædixe-rant prophetæ. Primò igitur testes Christi sistit, aquam & sanguinem:quibus tertio loco coniungit ipsum Veritatis æternæ spiritum. Sed operæpretium est,ut de singulis ordine dicamus.
units.tr: I. "This is he who came by water and blood, Jesus Christ. Not by water only, but by water and blood. And it is the Spirit who bears witness, because the Spirit is truth." He had said that through those who believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God the world is conquered. But since many doubt this, he proves that he is such. He says that he came by water and blood, that is, that it has been attested and demonstrated by water and blood that this is the one whom God long ago promised would be the Saviour, and whom the prophets had foretold would come. First, then, he sets forth the witnesses of Christ, water and blood, to which in the third place he joins the Spirit of eternal truth himself. But it is worth our while to speak of each in order.

units.la: Primus testis Aqua est. Commodissimè autem per aquam Christi baptismum,& quæcunq; in illo acciderunt, intelligimus. Nec temere hunc primo loco Ioannes producit. Quamuis enim multæ in Euangelio actiones sint, quæ Iesum Dei filium, & Christum, id est,mundi promissum salvatorem esse testantur,inter eas tamen baptismus illius facilè primatû obtinet: quia ut per hoc publicè quasi inauguratus est, ita multa simul concurrunt,quæ singula illi testimoniû ferunt. Primo enim Baptistam audimus,eum(inquam)qui in spiritu Eliæ ante faciem domini præcessit,& quo nemo sanctior ex mulieribus natus est, qui digito in Iesum extenso ait: Ecce agnus ille Dei, qui tollit peccatum mundi.Ioan.1.Sequitur mox in ipsa baptismi actione,cœlorum apertio: quæ evidenter testabatur, Iesum hunc esse,cuius merito cœlorū ianuæ,quæ hucusque per peccatum humano generi occlusæ fuerant,recludi & reserari deberent.Accedit his spiritus sancti suffragiū, qui visibili forma super Christi caput delapsus, eum esse docebat, cui olim dictum erat: Unxit te Deus oleo lætitiæ præ omnibus consortibus tuis. Psal.45. Et quasi parua esset omnium horū authoritas, Deus pater proprio ore de filii sui officio testari voluit. Nam cœlitus intonat vocem hac spei, gaudii & consolationis plenissimam: Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi complacitum est. Hæc itaque omnia cum Christi baptismo contineantur, Apostolus huius testimonio illius causam munire voluit, quod nemo aspernari poterit, nisi qui & spiritus sancti & Dei patris suffra-gia contemnere audeat.
units.tr: The first witness is the water. Now we understand by the water most fittingly the baptism of Christ and all that happened in it. Nor does John bring this forward first without reason. For although there are many actions in the Gospel which testify that Jesus is the Son of God and the Christ, that is, the promised Saviour of the world, among them his baptism easily holds the first place, because by it he was, as it were, publicly inaugurated, and many things concur at once, each of which bears witness to him. For first we hear the Baptist, he (I say) who went before the face of the Lord in the spirit of Elijah, and than whom no holier man was born of women, who, pointing his finger at Jesus, said: "Behold that Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world" [John 1.29]. Immediately, in the very act of baptism, follows the opening of the heavens, which clearly testified that this is Jesus, by whose merit the gates of heaven, which until now had been closed to the human race by sin, ought to be unlocked and thrown open. To these is added the testimony of the Holy Spirit, who, descending in visible form upon the head of Christ, taught that he is the one to whom it was said long ago: "God has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows" [Ps. 45.8]. And as if the authority of all these were too small, God the Father wished to bear witness with his own voice concerning the office of his Son. For from heaven there thunders this voice, most full of hope, joy and consolation: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" [Matt. 3.17]. Therefore, since all these things are contained in the baptism of Christ, the Apostle wished to fortify his cause by this testimony, which no one will be able to despise, unless he dares to despise the testimonies of the Holy Spirit and of God the Father.

units.la: Secundum testem Sanguinem facit Apostolus. Comprehendit hic passionis & mortis Christi historiam, in qua sanguinem suum pro mundi peccatis fudit. Nam ut sanguinis effusione salutem nobis peperit: ita in hac ipsa multæ res acciderunt, quæ illum nostrum salvatorem esse testarentur. Huc pertinet quod jam morti vicinus latroni se invocanti vitā & paradysum pollicetur. Maximè tamen eo referri debent præclara illa & stupenda prodigia, quæ in præstantissimis mundi partibus visa sunt. Totus siquidem terrarum orbis ingenti terræmotu concussus est. Sol, non observato naturæ ordine, faciem suam obscura caligine texit, quasi sui conditoris indignæ passionis condolens. Rigidæ & duræ petræ scissæ sunt, & templi velum ex summa parte in imam usque disruptum legimus. Sed & sepulchris apertis quidam resuscitati sunt, clarissimū testimonium ferentes, Iesum Christum esse vitæ & salutis amissæ reparatorem unicum. Et hæc quidem omnia tam potenter & perspicuè facta sunt, ut & vulgi mētes in melius moveretur, & Centurioni quan-tumuis duro, & barbaris militibus voces istæ extorqueretur: Verè hic homo filius Dei erat. Matthæi 27. Marc.15.
units.tr: The Apostle makes the blood the second witness. He here comprehends the history of the passion and death of Christ, in which he shed his blood for the sins of the world. For just as by the effusion of his blood he brought us salvation, so in this very event many things happened which bore witness that he is our Saviour. To this belongs what he promised to the thief who called upon him, already near death, of life and paradise. Yet those famous and wondrous portents, which were seen in the most excellent parts of the world, ought above all to be referred to this. For the whole orb of the earth was shaken by a great earthquake. The sun, the order of nature not being observed, covered its face with dark mist, as if grieving at the unworthy passion of its Creator. The hard and rigid rocks were split, and we read that the veil of the temple was torn from the top to the very bottom. Moreover, with the tombs opened, some were raised, bearing the clearest testimony that Jesus Christ is the one restorer of lost life and salvation. And all these things were done so mightily and so plainly that both the minds of the common people were moved to better things, and those words were wrung even from the centurion, however hard he was, and from the barbarian soldiers: "Truly this man was the Son of God" [Matt. 27.54; Mark 15.39].

units.la: Atqui non oscitanter prætereundum est hoc loco, quod duos hosce testes repetere & repetitione in unum coniungere Ioannes videtur, dum ait: Non per aquam solum, sed per aquá & sanguinem. Sic enim ad memorabilem illam historiā alludit, cuius ipse testis oculatus fuit, quamq; singulari diligentia abs se descriptam nobis reliquit. Ioan.19. Nam cum Christi mortui latus lancea confossum esset, ex eo aquá & sanguinem simul effluxisse testatur. Voluit ea re docere dominus, quis mortis ipsius fructus esset. Aqua sordes eluuntur, & recreantur æstuantes hominū animi. Sanguis olim expiationum typus erat, eò quod sine sanguine peccatorum remissio fieri non posset. Heb.9. Idem animæ vel vitæ sedes esse dicitur, Gene.9. At omnia hæc Christus complectitur[?]:in cuius latere fons ille saluberrimus apertus est, è quo & purificationem veram & expiationem peccatorum cum salute æterna haurire licet. Facit huc Zachariæ oraculum, qui cum de Christi morte & electorum ex Iudæis conversione vaticinatus esset, mox subdit: In die illo aperietur fons domui Dauidis & incolis Ierosolymæ ad peccatum & menstruam immunditiem, id est, ad ablutionem peccati omnis, tam actualis quàm innatæ corruptionis, quæ Originale peccatum dicitur. Zach.13. Christi enim sanguis nos emundat ab omni peccato. 1. Ioan.1. In Christo item vitæ promissio proponitur, quam ipse toties iterat, dum quasi ad fastidium usq; illud suum indesinenter inculcat: Qui credit in me, habet vitam æternam. In eodem solo fons est eius aquæ, quæ & æstuantes conscientias recreat, & semel hausta sitim propulsat in æternum. De hac ipse loquitur: Si quis biberit ex aqua, quam ipse haurit, sitiet iterum: qui verò biberit ex aqua quam ego do, non sitiet in æternum. Ioan.4. Et rursum: Si quis sitit, veniat ad me & bibat. Qui credit in me, flumina aquæ vivæ de eius ventre fluent. Ioan.7.
units.tr: Yet it must not be passed over carelessly in this place that John seems to repeat these two witnesses and to join them together by repetition, when he says: "Not by water only, but by water and blood." For thus he alludes to that memorable history, of which he himself was an eyewitness, and which he has left to us described with singular diligence [John 19.34-35]. For when the side of the dead Christ had been pierced with a spear, he testifies that water and blood flowed out from it at the same time. By this the Lord wished to teach what the fruit of his death was. By water are washed away the filth and refreshed the burning minds of men. Blood was once a type of expiations, because without the shedding of blood there could be no remission of sins [Heb. 9.22]. The same is said to be the seat of the soul or of life [Gen. 9.4]. But Christ embraces all these things, in whose side that most wholesome fountain was opened, from which we may draw both true purification and expiation of sins, together with eternal salvation. The oracle of Zechariah bears on this, who, when he had prophesied concerning the death of Christ and the conversion of the elect from the Jews, immediately adds: "On that day a fountain will be opened to the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem for sin and for uncleanness of menstruation," that is, for the washing away of all sin, both actual and of that innate corruption which is called original sin [Zech. 13.1]. For the blood of Christ cleanses us from all sin [1 John 1.7]. In Christ also the promise of life is set forth, which he repeats so often, while he inculcates that saying of his without ceasing, almost to the point of tedium: "He who believes in me has eternal life" [John 6.47]. In the same source there is a fountain of that water which both refreshes troubled consciences and, once drunk, drives away thirst for ever. Of this he himself speaks: "Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst; but whoever drinks of the water that I give will never thirst for ever" [John 4.13-14]. And again: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, out of his heart will flow rivers of living water" [John 7.37-38].

units.la: Restat tertius & ultimus Christi Iesu testis spiritus. Commendatur huius testimonium à veritate, quæ in teste cumprimis requiritur. Nec enim alia de causa illum de Christo testari dicit, quàm quòd veritas sit. Et ipse Christus in euangelio veritatis spiritum nominare cōsuevit. Ioan. 14. Potest autem testimonium hoc bifariam accipi. Vel enim intelligemus solennem illam spiritus sancti misionem super Apostolos, quę Acto.2. describitur: Vel testimonium spiritus Christi, quod singuli fideles in animis suis sentiunt. Utrumque certè non obscuris indiciis, Iesum Christum Dei filium & mundi redemptorem esse, probat. Nam in misione cœlitus exauditus fragor, nihil nisi cœleste & divinum in hoc negotio agi significabat. Et admirabile illud linguarum donum, quo Apostoli repentè instructi prodierunt, argumento erat, eius discipulos hucusque ipsos fuisse, ad quem totius orbis imperium & omnium gentium iurisdictio pertineret. Accesit his nō contemnenda spiritus operatio, qua effectum est, ut Apostoli non modò intrepidè & prudenter Christi causam agebant, verumetiam ingentem hominum multitudinem Christo lucrifaciebát. Quæ omnia, si cum Apostolorum persona conferas, qui literis nullis antea ornati, nulla dicendi facultate prædití erant, adhæc vitæ genus contemptum & humile sectabantur, & toti metu frigidi latebant, facilè agnosces illos maiorem numinis vim sensisse, quæ res tam arduas aggredi, & tam feliciter in illis versari fecit. Possunt huc referri, quæcunque per Apostolos signa & miracula edita sunt, quibus singulis spiritus hic Christo testimonium ferebat. Sed quia parum consolationis afferre posset, si in solis Apostolis spiritum Christi testè monstrare liceret, tam nostrae saluti quàm causae Christi consultissimum fuit, ut tatus testis omnium fidelium animis insereretur. Quare ut Christus carnem & sanguinem ex nobis assumptū in coelos subuexit, ut illic pignoris loco esset, quo edocti, sciremus quid de nostra carne olim sperari deberet: ta vicissim de suo spiritu nobis largiri voluit, qui animis nostris immissus, salutis nostrae arrhabo esset, nos de gratia patris & regni coelorum haereditate assequenda certiores redderet, & in quo ad Deum clamaremus, Abba pater,2. Cor.1. & 5. Ephe.1. Rom.8. &c. Est haec magna fidei nostrae certitudo, quod non in ijs modò quae extra nos sunt, sed in animis nostris eius veritatem deprehendere possumus. Quae caula fuit, qua sanctissimi Christi cultores olim nullis tormentis & cruciatibus à verae fidei confessione abduci potuerunt. Magna quippe & insuperabilis animorum atque conscientiarum vis est, si certam causam, quam tuentur, cognitionem semel assecutae fuerint, nec se à concepta sententia dimoveri patiuntur, nisi aliud quiddam adhibeatur, quod ipsos animos aliter sentire doceat & persuadeat. At nulla est tanta vspiam hominum sapientia, vel authoritas, nullae tantae hominum vires, nulli tanti cruciatus, qui spiritum vincere & expugnare possint, nisi forte hominum potentiam Dei voluntate & omnipotentia superiorem dicere velimus. Quapropter & Paulus ex spiritus sancti testimonio probat, nihil esse in vniuersa rerum natura, quod fideles à Dei dilectione possit abstrahere. Roman.8.
units.tr: There remains the third and last witness of Jesus Christ, the Spirit. His testimony is commended by its truthfulness, which above all is required in a witness. Indeed, he says that he testifies about Christ for no other reason than that he is the truth. And Christ himself in the Gospel was accustomed to call the Spirit the Spirit of truth (John 14). This testimony, however, can be understood in two ways. Either we shall understand that solemn mission of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles which is described in Acts 2, or the testimony of the Spirit of Christ, which individual faithful people feel in their souls. Both, certainly, prove by no obscure signs that Jesus Christ is the Son of God and the redeemer of the world. For the roar heard from heaven at the mission signified that nothing but what is heavenly and divine was at work in this matter. And that wonderful gift of tongues, with which the Apostles suddenly equipped came forward, was a proof that his disciples had until then been those whose the empire of the whole world and the jurisdiction over all nations belonged to. To these is added the operation of the Spirit, which is not to be despised, by which it was brought about that the Apostles not only pleaded Christ's cause fearlessly and wisely, but also won over a huge multitude of people to Christ. If you compare all these things with the persons of the Apostles, who before were without learning and endowed with no faculty of speaking, who followed a despised and humble way of life, and who all lay hidden in fear and coldness, you will easily recognise that they felt a greater power of the divinity, which made them attempt such difficult tasks and made them so successful in them. To this can be referred whatever signs and miracles were performed through the Apostles, by each of which this Spirit bore witness to Christ. But because it would offer little comfort if the Spirit of Christ could be shown to bear witness only in the Apostles, it was most advantageous both for our salvation and for the cause of Christ that this witness be implanted in the souls of all the faithful. Therefore, just as Christ carried our flesh and blood, which he had taken from us, up into heaven, so that there it might be a pledge, by which, being taught, we might know what ought one day to be hoped for our flesh; so in turn he willed to bestow on us of his own Spirit, who, sent into our souls, would be the earnest of our salvation, would make us more certain of the grace of the Father and of the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven to be obtained, and by whom we cry out to God, "Abba, Father" (2 Cor. 1 and 5; Eph. 1; Rom. 8, etc.). This is a great certainty of our faith, that we can perceive its truth not only in those things which are outside us, but in our own souls. This was the reason why the most holy worshippers of Christ in former times could not be drawn away from the confession of the true faith by any torments or tortures. For there is a great and invincible power in souls and consciences, if they have once attained a sure knowledge of the cause which they defend, and do not allow themselves to be moved from the opinion they have conceived, unless something else is applied which teaches and persuades the souls to feel otherwise. But there is nowhere so great a wisdom or authority of men, nor so great strength of men, nor any torments so great, which could conquer and overcome the Spirit, unless perhaps we wish to say that the power of men is superior to the will and omnipotence of God. Therefore Paul also, from the testimony of the Holy Spirit, proves that there is nothing in the whole nature of things which can separate the faithful from the love of God (Rom. 8).

units.la: Porro priusquam ex hoc loco discedamus, Ioannis exemplum nobis probè consyderādum est, quo docemur, quibus testibus & testimonijs Christi causa & fidei doctrina defendi debeat. Solet hic plurimum peccari nostro seculo, dum in tantis controuersijs plerique ad hominum vel multitudinem vel authoritatem respiciunt. Atqui poterat Ioannes vtramque hoc loco producere in medium. Eiusdem enim cum illo sententiae erant reliqui Apostoli omnes, quorum maior pars, imò forsitan omnes, cum haec scriberentur, non verbis modò, verumetiam proprio sanguine Christo & doctrinae ipsius testimonium tulerant. Erant praeterea innumerae per totum orbem terrarum ecclesiae, quae vnanimi consensu hanc de Christo Iesu doctrinam amplexabantur. Sed nulla hominum authoritate nos Ioannes grauari voluit, vt nobis doctrinam hanc & fidem ideo recipiendam esse contendat, quia à multis alijs iam ante recepta fit. Quia enim diuinum & coeleste est negotium illud omne, diuinis & coelestibus testimonijs confirmari debet, nisi forte Dei veritatem & gloriam ex hominum authoritate pendere dicamus. Quod si obseruarent, qui hodie vel principum maiestati, vel scholarum eruditioni, vel Conciliorum authoritati tantum tribuunt, vt cotrouersias fidei & religionis eiusmodi hominum suffragijs determinari oportere existiment, viderent vtique se toto coelo errare. Extant passim in scripturis, quae de fidei doctrina & veritate nos erudire possunt. Illic habetur causae huius testes veri & fideles. Ibidem iudices sunt, quos nec dona flectunt, nec verborum Labyrinthi irretiunt, nec personarum respectus mouet. Hoc qui audire dedignantur, digni sunt, qui hominum mendacissimorum authoritate inextricabilibus tenebris immersi aeternum pereant. Sed pergamus ad reliqua.
units.tr: Moreover, before we depart from this passage, the example of John must be carefully considered by us, by which we are taught by what witnesses and testimonies the cause of Christ and the doctrine of faith ought to be defended. This is a great fault often committed in our age, while in such great controversies most people look either to the multitude or to the authority of men. And yet John could have brought forward both in this place. For all the other Apostles were of the same opinion as he, most of whom, or perhaps all of them, when these things were written, had borne witness to Christ and his doctrine not only by words but even with their own blood. Moreover, there were countless churches throughout the whole world which embraced this doctrine concerning Jesus Christ with unanimous consent. But John did not wish us to be burdened by any authority of men, so as to contend that this doctrine and faith must be received for the reason that it has already been received by many others. For since that whole matter is divine and heavenly, it ought to be confirmed by divine and heavenly testimonies, unless perhaps we say that the truth and glory of God depend on the authority of men. But if those who today attribute so much to the majesty of princes, or to the learning of schools, or to the authority of councils, that they think controversies of faith and religion ought to be decided by the votes of such men, were to observe this, they would certainly see that they are wandering far from the truth. Throughout the Scriptures there are passages which can teach us about the doctrine and truth of faith. There are found the true and faithful witnesses of this cause. There are the judges whom neither gifts bend, nor the labyrinths of words ensnare, nor respect of persons moves. Those who disdain to hear this are worthy to perish eternally, immersed in inextricable darkness by the authority of the most lying men. But let us proceed to the rest.

units.la: I I. Quoniam tres sunt, qui testimonium dant in coelo, Pater, Verbum & Spiritus sanctus: & hi tres unum sunt. Et tres sunt, qui testimonium dant in terra, Spiritus & Aqua & Sanguis: & hi tres in unum conueniunt. Subiungit his pleniorem testimoniorum, quae praemisit, explicationem, quae comparatione constat. Quamuis sint, qui prius membrum de tribus testibus in coelo, adulterinum esse, & à sciolo in marginem ascriptum, tandem in orationis contextum inrepsisse putent. Mouentur hi quorūdam patrum authoritate, & Cyrilli imprimis, qui cum locum hunc citet, membrum tamen illud omisit. Sed nos Hieronymum sequi malumus, cum saepe accidat, vt in scripturis citandis multa intermedia omittantur, tam à prisci s quàm recentioribus scriptoribus, maximè si quae ad suum institutum non omnino necessaria existiment. Praeterea non video, qua ratione membrum hoc nobis suspectum esse debeat. Nam quod multi tractationem de trinitate hoc loco superuacaneā esse putant, nimis friuolum est, cū illam hic minimè instituat Ioannes, eius tamen mentio causae praesenti maximè conueniat. Sic enim mihi dicere videtur Apostolus: Sicut fides nostra in diuinitatis mysterio tres personas agnoscit: ita tres etiam habemus Iesu Christi testes, plenos authoritatis, & omnino irrefragabiles, qui oculis nostris pasim occurrunt, siue in coelum, siue in terram respicias. In coelis enim sacrosancta & adoranda trinitas sese offert, cuius personae singulae de hoc testantur. Et in terris non spernendae authoritatis sunt, quos modò produximus, Spiritus nimirum, Aqua & Sanguis. Quod si trinitatis testimonia audire libeat, passim illa in scripturis habetur. Pater certè semel atque iterum coelitus pronunciat, Iesum hunc esse suum dilectum filium, cuius intercessione nobis reconciliatus sit. Et cum Iesus se à patre glorificari peteret, patris vox coelitus exaudita audita est. Et illustrauì, & rursus illustrabo. Ioan.12. De filij testimonijs non opus est dicere, cum omnes euangelistæ in ijs recensendis laborent. Vnum hoc admonendum, quòd non eo nomine il la nobis suspecta esse debent, quòd de seipso & propria causa testari videtur. Nec enim solus est, qui testatur, sed ipsius patris testimonio de se prodito consentit. Ioan.8. Spiritus verò sancti testimonium & euidens est & multiplex. Nam & olim per prophetas de Christo & venturis in illum afflictionibus testari solebat, & virtutem suam per Apostolos varie exeruit. Vide i.Pet.i.&2.Pet. i. Vt autem tres personæ, Pater, filius, & spiritus sanctus, vna sunt essentia: sic testimonia, quæ de Christo habentur, in unum omnia conueniunt, illumq; Dei filium ac humani generis redemptorem esse declarant.
