units.tr: II. Since there are three who bear witness in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one. And there are three who bear witness on earth, the Spirit, the Water, and the Blood; and these three agree in one. He adds to these a fuller explanation of the testimonies which he has put forward, which consists in comparison. Although there are some who think that the first member about the three witnesses in heaven is spurious, and was added in the margin by some half-learned person and at last crept into the context of the text. They are moved by the authority of certain Fathers, and above all of Cyril, who, although he cites this passage, nevertheless omitted that clause. But we prefer to follow Jerome, since it often happens that in citing Scripture many intervening words are omitted, both by ancient and by more recent writers, especially if they think them not wholly necessary to their purpose. Besides, I do not see for what reason this clause ought to be suspect to us. For that many think a treatment of the Trinity superfluous in this place is too trifling, since John does not here undertake such a treatment at all, yet the mention of it is most fitting to the present cause. For the Apostle seems to me to say thus: just as our faith recognises three persons in the mystery of the Godhead, so we also have three witnesses of Jesus Christ, full of authority and altogether irrefutable, who meet our eyes everywhere, whether you look to heaven or to earth. For in heaven the most holy and adorable Trinity presents itself, each of whose persons bears witness concerning this. And on earth there are those, just now brought forward, of no despicable authority: the Spirit, namely, the Water and the Blood. But if it is pleasing to hear the testimonies of the Trinity, they are found everywhere in the Scriptures. The Father certainly, once and again, declares from heaven that this Jesus is his beloved Son, through whose intercession he has been reconciled to us. And when Jesus asked to be glorified by the Father, the voice of the Father, heard from heaven, was heard: "I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again" (John 12). There is no need to speak of the testimonies of the Son, since all the evangelists labour in recounting them. This one thing is to be noted, that those testimonies ought not to be suspect to us on this ground, that he seems to testify about himself and his own cause. For he is not alone in bearing witness, but agrees with the testimony of the Father himself, disclosed concerning him (John 8). Moreover, the testimony of the Holy Spirit is both clear and manifold. For he both formerly used to bear witness concerning Christ and the afflictions that were to come upon him through the prophets, and in various ways exercised his power through the Apostles (see 1 Pet. 1 and 2 Pet. 1). And just as the three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, are one essence, so all the testimonies that are had concerning Christ agree together in one, and declare that he is the Son of God and the redeemer of the human race.

units.la: Est vero locus hic singulari obseruatione dignus. Admonet enim quàm graue & atrox flagitium sit, si quis Christo contradicere, & doctrinam eius per Apostolos nobis traditam, negare aut fit. Nam cum huic testimonium ferat sacrosancta Trinitas, fieri non potest, quin illam mendacij accusef, quicunque doctrinam de fide in Christum negare instituit. Atqui hominum authoritas tanti fieri consueuit, vt iuratis testibus falsi crimen impingere, capitale habeatur. Quo ergo supplicio nō dignus censebitur, aut quam veniam mereri poterit, cuius impudens os in ipsam deitatem tale quid pronunciare præsumit? Hoc si nostro seculo expenderent, qui de fide & religione disputationes instituunt, multò religiosiores videremus in sententijs suis dicendis. Sed præstat, vt Ioannem audiamus, qui quæ hucusq; dicta sunt, ad hunc modum concludit.
units.tr: There is indeed a singular point here worth noting. For it warns how grave and atrocious a crime it is, if anyone sets himself against Christ and denies or refuses the teaching of Christ handed down to us by the Apostles. For since the most holy Trinity bears witness to this, it cannot be that whoever undertakes to deny the doctrine of faith in Christ should not be accused of lying. Yet the authority of men is customarily held in such high regard that to charge sworn witnesses with false testimony is regarded as a capital offence. What punishment, then, will such a person be judged not to deserve, or what pardon can he hope to obtain, whose shameless mouth presumes to pronounce such a thing about the Godhead itself? If those who conduct disputations about faith and religion weighed this in our own age, we would see them far more scrupulous in the opinions they express. But it is better that we hear John, who concludes what has been said so far in this manner.

units.la: III. Si testimonium hominum accipimus, testimonium Dei maius est. Quoniam hoc est testimonium Dei, quo testificatus est de filio suo. Videtur ad legem alludere Ioannes, quæ duorum aut trium testimonió fidem habere, & secundum illud iudicare docet. Deut.17. Habent verò non obscuram comparationem verba hæc. Si enim hominibus credendum est in ijs rebus, quæ causas humanas & ciuiles concernunt, quanto magis Deo credere debemus, cuius authoritas maior est, quàm ut cum hominibus aliquo modo conferri debeat? Homines quippe natura mendaces sunt, & multis causis moueri solent, ut falsum potius quàm verum loquantur. Adhæc, ut maximè verum dicere velint, falli tamen possunt, & proinde alios quoq; fallere solent. Solus Deus nec ipse fallitur, cum cordium & renum scrutator sit, nec quenquam fallere vel vult vel potest, quia æterna est veritas. Non temere ergo fit, quòd Dei testimonium humano maius esse dicit Apostolus. Est enim maius, primò propter authoritatem & certitudinem. Nam Dei verbum manet in æternũ, & facilius est terram & cœlum transfire, quàm ut verbo Dei sua desit fides & veritas. Isa.40.Matth.5.&24. Deinde maius est, quia non de ignotis testatur Deus, sed quæ ipsi intus & in cute (si sic loqui licet) notissima sunt: de filio nimirum, qui ab æterno in sinu ipsius est. Præterea, non Dei, sed nostra causa hic agitur. Quid enim ex universo nostræ redemptionis negotio Deus habet, quod ante nō habuerit? Ab æterno iustus, bonus, sapiens, verax, omnipotens & gloriosus est. Nobis dedit filium. Propter nos ille incarnatus est. Propter nos tot passim extant de illo in scripturis testimonia, ut nimirum in ipsum credentes vitam æternam consequamur. Nulla igitur causa est, propter quam, quæ de Christo dicuntur, nobis suspecta esse debeant, quò minus illis fidem adhibeamus.
units.tr: III. If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater. For this is the testimony of God, by which he has borne witness concerning his Son. John seems to allude to the law, which teaches that a matter is to be settled by the testimony of two or three witnesses, and that judgment is to be given accordingly. Deut. 17. These words also offer a not obscure comparison. For if we must believe men in those matters which concern human and civil affairs, how much more ought we to believe God, whose authority is too great to be compared in any way with men? Men, indeed, are by nature liars, and are commonly moved by many causes to speak what is false rather than what is true. Moreover, even when they most wish to speak the truth, they can nevertheless be mistaken, and therefore they are accustomed to deceive others as well. God alone is not himself deceived, since he is the searcher of hearts and reins, nor does he wish or is able to deceive anyone, because his truth is eternal. It is therefore not without reason that the Apostle says the testimony of God is greater than human testimony. It is greater, first, on account of its authority and certainty. For the Word of God remains for ever, and it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for the Word of God to lack its faithfulness and truth. Isa. 40; Matt. 5 and 24. Next, it is greater because God does not bear witness concerning unknown things, but concerning those which are most known to himself within and, if I may so speak, in his very skin: namely concerning the Son, who from eternity is in his bosom. Furthermore, the matter here concerns not God's cause but ours. For what does God gain from the whole business of our redemption that he did not have before? From eternity he is just, good, wise, true, almighty and glorious. He gave us his Son. For our sake he was made flesh. For our sake so many testimonies concerning him are found everywhere in the Scriptures, so that indeed by believing in him we may obtain eternal life. There is therefore no reason why what is said about Christ should be suspect to us, so that we should refrain from giving it credence.

units.la: Docent hæc, quanta sit nostræ fidei in Iesum Christũ dignitas. Nam ut de Christo, qui eius fundamentum est unicum, nihil dicamus, quis nō singularem eius maiestatem videt, quæ tot tàq; præclaris testimonijs muniri meretur? Quasi enim parum fecisset dominus, qui per prophetas & apostolos illam nobis commendauit, ipsius sacrosanctæ Trinitatis publico testimonio eandem dignatus est. Debet id nos nostri officij admonere, quod partim in vitæ sanctimonia versatur, ne impuritate & peccandi licentia nos tanta gloria indignos reddamus: partim verò constantiam & perseuerantiam requirit, ne dum dolores sufferre, & paupertatem Christi nomine perpeti detrectamus, à tanta gratia excidamus infelicissimi. Fidei ergo iungere libeat, sanctimoniæ & innocentiæ studiù, atq; fortibus animis patientia munitis per omne tentationis genus indiuulsi adhærea-mus capiti nostro Iesu Christo, cui debetur benedictio, gloria, honor & potestas in æternũ. Amè[?].
units.tr: These things teach how great is the dignity of our faith in Jesus Christ. For, to say nothing of Christ, who is its one foundation, who does not see his singular majesty, which deserves to be supported by so many and such illustrious testimonies? For as if the Lord had done too little who commended it to us through the prophets and apostles, he has also deigned to confirm it by the public testimony of the most holy Trinity itself. This ought to remind us of our duty, which in part consists in the holiness of life, lest by impurity and licence to sin we render ourselves unworthy of so great a glory; and in part requires constancy and perseverance, lest, while we shrink from suffering pains and from enduring poverty for the name of Christ, we fall away, most unhappy, from so great a grace. Let us therefore be pleased to join faith with zeal for holiness and innocence, and, with spirits strengthened by bravery and patience, let us cling inseparably to our head Jesus Christ through every kind of temptation, to whom be blessing, glory, honour and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXII.
units.tr: HOMILIA XXXII.

units.la: Qui credit in filium Dei, habet testimonium in seipso. Qui nō credit Deo, mendacem fecit eum: quia non credidit in testimoniũ, quod testificatus est Deus de filio suo. Et hoc est testimoniũ, quòd uitâ æternâ dedit nobis deus: & hæc uita in filio eius est. Qui habet filium, habet uitam. Qui nō habet filium Dei, uitam non habet.
units.tr: He who believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. He who does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed the testimony that God has borne concerning his Son. And this is the testimony: that God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. He who has the Son has life; he who does not have the Son of God does not have life.

units.la: VAs illud electionis, Paulus Apostolus, in priori ad Corinth. cap. 3. ait: Fundamentum aliud nemo ponere potest, quàm quod positum est, quod est Iesus Christus. Docet ijs verbis spi-ritus sanctus, salutis nostræ rationem vniuersam ex vnius & solius Christi merito depedere, adeò vt iuxta Petri sententiam, in alio nullo salus sit. Actorū 4. Quare nihil homini tam salutare ac ne-cessarium est, quàm vera & solida Christi cognitio, atque indubitata in eundem fides. Qua causa Ioānes motus, fidem hanc tanto studio & diligentia tradit, nec modò quid credere nos oporteat docet, verumetiam fortissimis argumentis ad credendum impellit & vrget. Vidimus id præceden-tibus, vbi vniuersum Iesu Christi negotium, quo salus nobis parta est, testimonijs locupletissimis confirmat, de quibus quātum dominus dederat, tum dictum est. Cohæret autem illis præsens hic locus, qui fidem in Christum tribus rationibus grauissimis sic commendat, vt eam amplecti no-lentibus nullus excusationis locus superfit. Diligenter ergo in earum consyderatione versemur oportet, si quo modo dignus tantæ rei amor, & zelus salutis iustus in nobis accendatur.
units.tr: Concerning that choice passage, the Apostle Paul in his first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 3, says: "No one can lay another foundation than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ." In these words the Holy Spirit teaches that the whole plan of our salvation depends on the merit of one and only Christ, so that, according to the saying of Peter, there is salvation in no other. Acts 4. Therefore nothing is so salutary and necessary for a man as a true and solid knowledge of Christ, and an undoubting faith in him. Moved by this cause, John delivers this faith with such great zeal and diligence; and he not only teaches what we ought to believe, but also drives and urges us to believe with the strongest arguments. We saw this in the preceding passages, where he confirms the whole business of Jesus Christ, by which salvation has been won for us, with the most abundant testimonies, of which, as much as the Lord had given, has been said. Now this present place, which commends faith in Christ by three very weighty reasons in such a way that for those unwilling to embrace it no room for excuse remains, adheres to those passages. We must therefore dwell diligently on the consideration of them, if in any way a love worthy of so great a matter and a just zeal for salvation may be kindled in us.

units.la: I. Qui credit in filium Dei, habet testimonium in seipso. Argumentum est ab authoritate, quo fidem hanc certam & indubiè veram esse probat. Ponit autem hoc primo loco, quia naturaliter sic affecti sunt homines, quod credendo falli nolunt. Vnde & nimia credulitas vitio vertitur, & animi leuis parumq; constantis signum habetur. Sed & multos hodie est inuenire, qui se fidem in Christum libenter amplexuros pollicentur, modò de eius veritate certi esse posint. Quare Apostolus, nihil hic periculi subesse docet, nec timendum vt fallaris, si in filium Dei credere voles. Nam, qui credit (inquit) in filium Dei, habet testimonium in semetipso. Loquitur autem de testimonio spiritus sancti, quem Christum suis pollicitum esse & dedisse, vt arrhabo salutis sit, sicut iam diximus: nec tamen quidquam obstare debet, quin sæpius idem repetatur. Est enim memorabilis omnino & plena consolationis permutatio, qua Christus hic vti voluit: qui vt ex nobis assumpsit carnem & sanguinem, eaq; in cœlos euecta ad dextram patris collocauit, vt certo nobis constaret, nostra quoque corpora cœlestis gloriæ, iuxta promissionem ipsius, aliquando consortia fore: ita vicissim suum spiritum animis fidelium inserit, quo edocti se ex numero saluādorum esse certo intelligant, nec dubitent Deum patris nomine appellare, quem (nisi hoc spiritu animaretur) caro nostra non posset non timere. Atqui miros in fidelis animo effectus hoc spiritus testimonium operari consueuit. Huius enim opus est constans Dei fiducia, quæ nec secundis rebus loco moueri, nec aduersis frangi potest. Cur enim propter mundi huius fauorem & amicitias à Christo recederet, qui spiritu Christi testante nouit, Deum sibi patris loco esse, sic vt mundi amicitia & patrocinio minimè opus habeat? Cur opum studio Christū negligeret, qui in hoc immor-tales cœlestis regni thesauros sibi repositos esse intelligit? Cur denique voluptatum illecebris animum suum à fide Christi abduci pateretur, qui synceras æternæ vitæ voluptates & omnis amaritudinis expertes delicias in Dei filio nobis partas esse firmiter credit? Similiter nec pauperiem pati recusabit, nec exilij molestias sustinere detrectabit, nec orbus & viduus fieri timebit, quisquis tantum suæ fidei testimonium intra sese sentiet. Imò non vllos cruciatus graues esse putabit, cum illi vita Christus, & mors lucrum sit. Phil. 1. Nesciunt huius testimonij virtutem impij, & proinde Christianos pertinaces suæ opinionis sectatores esse clamitant, & qui optimi ex illis sunt, aliquo misericordiæ affectu tanguntur, quòd nos incertæ persuasionis causa tot periculis peti-ma lisque nunquam finiendis vexari vident. Fidelis autem tanti testis authoritate confirmatus, fallax prophani mundi iudicium facilè spernit.
units.tr: I. He who believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. This is an argument from authority, by which he proves that this faith is certain and indubitably true. He places it first, because men are naturally so disposed that they are unwilling to be deceived by believing. Hence excessive credulity is counted as a fault, and is regarded as a sign of a light and little constant mind. But even today many are to be found who promise that they would gladly embrace faith in Christ, provided they could be certain of its truth. Therefore the Apostle teaches that there is no danger here, nor is there any need to fear being deceived if you are willing to believe in the Son of God. For he who believes (he says) in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. Now he speaks of the testimony of the Holy Spirit, whom Christ promised and gave to his own, to be the pledge of salvation, as we have already said; nor ought anything to stand in the way of this same thing being repeated often. For the exchange which Christ wished to use here is altogether memorable and full of consolation: he who took on flesh and blood from us, and, having raised that flesh into heaven, set it at the right hand of the Father, so that it might be certain to us that our bodies too, according to his promise, will one day be partners in heavenly glory; so in turn he implants his own Spirit into the hearts of the faithful, by whom, taught, they may clearly understand that they are among the number of the saved, and not hesitate to call God by the name of Father, whom (unless our flesh were animated by this Spirit) it could not help but fear. Yet this testimony of the Spirit customarily works wonderful effects in the mind of the believer. For this is the work of a steadfast trust in God, which can neither be moved from its place by prosperous circumstances nor broken by adverse ones. For why would he who, by the testimony of the Spirit of Christ, knows that God is a father to him, so that he has no need of the friendship and protection of the world, recede from Christ for the sake of the world's favour and friendships? Why would he who understands that immortal treasures of the heavenly kingdom are laid up for him neglect Christ out of desire for riches? Why, finally, would he allow his mind to be drawn away from faith in Christ by the allurements of pleasures, who firmly believes that the sincere pleasures of eternal life, free of all bitterness, are won for us in the Son of God? Likewise, whoever feels within himself such a testimony of his faith will not refuse to suffer poverty, nor shrink from enduring the troubles of exile, nor fear becoming bereft or widowed. Indeed, he will think no torments grievous, since for him to live is Christ and to die is gain. Phil. 1. The wicked do not know the power of this testimony, and therefore cry out that Christians are stubborn followers of their opinion; and those of them who are best are moved by some feeling of pity, seeing that we are harassed by so many dangers and endless perils for the sake of an uncertain persuasion. But the believer, confirmed by the authority of so great a witness, easily scorns the deceptive judgment of the profane world.

units.la: Admonet autem locus hic de re omnium maxima, quam nostro seculo diligenter obserua-uisse multum prodest. Si enim fidelis suæ fidei testimonium in semetipso habet, non vtique illud extra se ab aljs quærat oportet. Siquidem ea animi nostri natura est, vt in ijs, quæ certò cognouit, facilè acquiescat, nec aliorum dicta moretur amplius. Vanissimi igitur hominum sunt, qui in fidei & religionis causa hominum authoritatem requirunt, nec ante fidem aliquam amplexandam & retinendam esse putant, quàm hominum testimonio approbata fuerit. Tales sunt, qui vel principum vel doctorum authoritate ducuntur, vel Concilij alicuius determinatione expectant, à qua toti pendent. Quorum fidem si definire velis, eam non Deo, sed hominibus niti dicendum erit. Imò quod turpe dictu est, æternam Dei veritatem hominum mendacissimorū authoritati subijcere audent. Longè aliud ergo est verè fidelium ingenium, qui se Dei filio & æternæ veritatis verbo credidisse norunt, & proinde angelum, si aliam doctrinam proponat, anathema pronunciare audent. Gal. 1. Et sanè admiranda est hominum nostri seculi cæcitas, qui tanti erroris turpitudinem non vident. Quis enim adeò demens est, vt in rebus prophanis, quæ per nos fiunt & gubernantur, quod factum est, hominum authoritate infectū fieri posse dicat? Num ergo in ijs, quæ solius Dei sunt, tantum sibi permittent homines audacissimi, vt quæ ipse de salutis nostræ ratione constituit, humahumana authoritate vel stabiliri vel euerti posse existiment? Deus est, qui salutis thesauros in fi-lio suo conclusit, qui hunc vnum & solum mundi saluatorem esse voluit. Tu vero quis es, qui id vere factum esse, & vere doceri negas? Christus Iesus Dei filius ex Cruce dependens, & iam iam moriturus, clamat, hoc suae mortis merito consummari quaecunque ad nos saluandos pertinent. Quae igitur impudentia est, hoc factum esse negare? Spiritus sanctus in animis fidelium testatur, homines solius Christi merito saluari, & eos qui in hunc credunt, vere iustitiam consequi. Quid ergo opus est fidem hanc in dubium vocare, & humanae authoritatis suffragium exigere? Quid enim haec potest, quod spiritus testimonium in fidelium mentibus non possit plenius & perfectius?
units.tr: This place, moreover, admonishes us concerning a matter of the greatest importance, which it is very useful to have observed diligently in our age. For if the believer has the testimony of his faith in himself, he ought certainly not to seek it outside himself from others. Indeed, such is the nature of our mind that it readily rests in those things which it has known for certain, and does not linger any longer over the words of others. Therefore those men are most foolish who, in matters of faith and religion, require the authority of men, and think that no faith ought to be embraced and retained before it has been approved by the testimony of men. Such are those who are led by the authority of princes or of teachers, or who await the determination of some council, on which they wholly depend. If you wish to define their faith, it must be said that it rests not on God but on men. Indeed, what is shameful to say, they dare to subject the eternal truth of God to the authority of the most mendacious of men. Quite different, therefore, is the disposition of those who truly believe, who know that they have believed in the Son of God and in the word of eternal truth, and therefore dare to pronounce an anathema on an angel, if he should propose another doctrine. Gal. 1. And indeed the blindness of the men of our age is to be wondered at, who do not see the shamefulness of so great an error. For who is so foolish as to say that in profane affairs, which are done and governed by us, what has been done can be made to be undone by the authority of men? Will men, then, be so bold as to think that in those things which belong to God alone they may permit themselves so much as to think that what he himself has decreed concerning the manner of our salvation can be either established or overthrown by human authority? It is God who has enclosed the treasures of salvation in his Son, who willed that this one and only Saviour of the world should be. But who are you, who deny that this has truly been done, and that it is truly taught? Christ Jesus, the Son of God, hanging from the Cross and about to die, cries out that by the merit of his death whatever pertains to our salvation is accomplished. What, then, is the impudence in denying that this has been done? The Holy Spirit testifies in the hearts of the faithful that men are saved by the merit of Christ alone, and that those who believe in him truly obtain righteousness. Why then is there any need to call this faith into doubt, and to seek the support of human authority? For what can this do that the testimony of the Spirit in the minds of the faithful cannot do more fully and more perfectly?

units.la: Praeterea discimus hic quae causa fit, quod quicunque extra Christum salutem quaerunt, a-liudq; constituunt fidei suae fundamentum, quiescere non posint[?]. Qui in filium Dei credit, testimonium habet in seipso. Quisquis ergo fide in filiu Dei destituitur, testimonio tali caret, & proinde quiescere non potest. Exemplis res declarari facile potest. Quisquis animo suo de re aliqua dubitat, suspicionibus non potest non agitari, nec prosunt quatumuis multorum magnorumq; hominum testimonia. Quod si pacatum velis reddere, animi dubiu eximas oportet. Eadem in salutis causa ratio est. Cupiut hanc naturali quodam motu omnes homines, nec nisi hac adepti quiescere possunt. At salutis certos nemo faciet, nisi Christi saluatoris spiritus. Qui cū solis credetibus detur, ijdem soli de salute sua certi sunt, reliqui vero perpetuis vruntur suspicionibus curis & solicitudinibus. Huc referri debent Christi verba, qui in euangelio Samaritidi dicit: Quisquis biberit ex aqua elementali, quam ipse haurit, sitiet iterum. Qui autem biberit ex aqua, quam ego do, non sitiet in aeternum. Ioan.4. Per aquam vero elementalem ea intelligit, quae suis viribus faciunt homines, dum proprijs meritis salutem consequi studentur. Ea animum sitientem & esurientem satiare non possunt, quia nulla Dei promissione confirmantur, nec spiritum dant, qui salutis arrhabo est. Imo his fere quod hydropicis euenire solet, qui aqua, quantumuis largissimè hausta, sitim adeo non restinguunt, vt inflamment potius. Ita hi quo plura faciunt, eo magis perplexi haerent, & subinde vnum hoc deesse sentiunt, quo sitis animarum restinguitur. Nec longè rerum exempla petantur. Teipsum appello, qui olim sub Papatus iugo in hoc totus fuisti, vt salutem & acquires, & de ea certus efficereris. Fateberis oportet te ad eam metam peruenire nunquam potuisse, licet omnia faceres sedulò, quaecunq; illa religio dictabat. Promittebatur in Missae sacrificio pro peccatis tuis satisfactio, & ea spe ad Missam accedebas. At idem mox relegaberis ad Confessionem auricularem, ad ieiunia, ad diuorū inuocationem, ad monastica vota, ad passagia, ad Romanas indulgentias, stationes item Romanas, & infinita alia, quae quotidie noua fingebantur salutis nostrae adminicula. Quod si mortis articulus imminebat, & certa salutis fiducia quàm maximè opus erat, noui exoriebantur inferni terrores & purgatorij metus, quos (quasi nihil in viuis fecisses) nouis pecunijs & anniuersarijs nunquam finiendis redimere oportebat. Nunquam non ergo oculis tuis desperatio obuersabatur, quae multos in extrema senectute sub vitae suae finem monachos fieri coegit, si quo modo horribiles animorum aestus effugere possent. Vera me dicere fatebuntur, quotquot nō leui animo in illa superstitione vixerunt. Quod si nunc cū illis animi dubij terroribus eam fidem conferas, quae Christo illucescente affulsit, quantum inter hanc & vanā illam salutis opinionem interfit, facile senties. Nam praeter Christi vocem in euangelio sonantem, spiritus testimonium audis, quod te de salute amplius dubitare non finit. Cum Paulo enim dicis: Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? Qui proprio filio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum, qui fieri potest, vt non & cum eodem omnia nobis donet? Quis intentabit crimina aduersus electos Dei? Deus est, qui iustificat. Quis ille, qui condemnet? Christus est, qui mortuus est, imo qui & suscitatus est, qui etiam est ad dextram Dei, qui & inter cedit pro nobis. Quis nos separabit à dilectione Dei? &c.Rom.8. Omisis ergo superstitiosis hominum traditionibus Christum audiamus, qui omnes laborantes & oneratos ad se inuitat, qui aquam & panem vitae aeternae nobis pollicetur, & salutis nostrae certi omnem fortunam alacri & laeto animo ridebimus.
units.tr: Furthermore, we learn here the reason why all who seek salvation outside Christ, and set up something else as the foundation of their faith, cannot rest. "He who believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself." Whoever therefore is destitute of faith in the Son of God lacks such testimony, and therefore cannot rest. The matter can easily be made clear by examples. Whoever doubts about some matter in his mind cannot help being troubled by suspicions, nor do the testimonies of many great men help him at all. If you wish to make him calm, you must remove the doubt from his mind. It is the same in the cause of salvation. All men desire this by a certain natural impulse, and they cannot rest unless they obtain it. But no one will make us certain of salvation except the Spirit of Christ the Saviour. Since he is given to believers alone, those alone are certain of their salvation, while the rest live in constant suspicions, cares and anxieties. To this belong the words of Christ, who said to the Samaritan woman in the Gospel: "Whoever drinks of the water of this well, which I draw, will thirst again. But whoever drinks of the water which I give will never thirst." John 4. By the elemental water he means that which men make by their own powers, while they strive to obtain salvation by their own merits. Such water cannot satisfy the thirsting and hungering soul, because it is confirmed by no promise of God, and it does not give the Spirit, who is the pledge of salvation. Indeed, this is nearly what usually happens to dropsy patients: however largely they drink water, they do not quench their thirst at all, but rather inflame it. So these men, the more they do, the more entangled they remain, and they continually feel that one thing is lacking, by which the thirst of souls is quenched. Nor need we seek examples far off. I appeal to yourself, who once, under the yoke of the Papacy, were wholly given to this, that you might both acquire salvation and be made certain of it. You must confess that you could never reach that goal, though you diligently did all that that religion prescribed. Satisfaction for your sins was promised in the sacrifice of the Mass, and in that hope you came to Mass. But soon afterwards you were sent on to auricular confession, to fasts, to the invocation of the saints, to monastic vows, to pilgrimages, to Roman indulgences, to the Roman stations as well, and to countless other aids to our salvation, which were invented daily. And if the hour of death was at hand, when a sure confidence of salvation was most needed, new terrors of hell and fears of purgatory arose, which (as if you had done nothing in your life) you had to redeem with new sums of money and anniversary masses that never ended. Thus despair was never absent from your eyes, which drove many monks in extreme old age, near the end of their lives, to take the cowl, if somehow they might escape the dreadful storms of their souls. All who lived in that superstition not without a serious mind will confess that I speak the truth. But if you now compare that faith, which shone forth when Christ rose, with that faith full of the terrors of a doubting mind, you will easily feel how great the difference is between this faith and that empty opinion of salvation. For besides the voice of Christ sounding in the Gospel, you hear the testimony of the Spirit, which does not allow you to doubt any longer about your salvation. For with Paul you say: "If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how can he not also with him freely give us all things? Who will bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who is he who condemns? It is Christ who died, or rather who was raised, who is also at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us. Who shall separate us from the love of God? etc." Rom. 8. Therefore, setting aside the superstitious traditions of men, let us listen to Christ, who invites all who labour and are burdened to himself, who promises us the water and bread of eternal life, and, certain of our salvation, we shall laugh at every fortune with a willing and joyful mind.

units.la: II, Qui non credit Deo, mendacem fecit eum: quia non credidit in testimonium, quod testificatus est Deus de filio suo. Comprehendit his secundum argumentum, quod fidem in Christum Iesum nobis commendat. Ducitur hoc ex contrarijs, dum ostendit quid sit Deo non credere, qui filium suum nobis saluatorem proponit. Qui non credit Deo (inquit) Deum mendacem fecit. Porrò mendacem facere dixit, pro eo quod est, mendacij insimulare vel accusare. Alioqui enim Deus, qui ipsa & aeterna est veritas, mendax fieri nequit. Imo sit Deus verax, omnis autem homo mendax. Rom. 3. Mendacij autem insimulatur Deus, quando verbis eius fidem habere dedignamur. Inter homines equidem sic comparatum est, vt nō nisi illorū verbis credamus, quos veraces esse, vel scimus, vel salte esse putamus. Et si cui quid narrati fidem adhibere dedignamur, ideo hoc fit, quia leuem & mendacem esse credimus. Eadem ergo ratione, quisquis Deo fidem habet, hoc ipso se Deũ veracem agnoscere testatur. Quisquis autem Deo credere negat, eũdem mendacij insimulat, si non verbis, facto certè, quo fidem illi adhibere detrectat. Nemo autem leuiculum crimen esse arbitre-tur, Deum mendacij insimulare, cum blasphemia fit, qua vix alia atrocior & horribilior excogitari potest. Nā inter virtutes, quæ Deo proprię sunt, veritas nō postremo loco poni debet, eō quòd æternæ Dei essentiæ & incorruptibilitati pulchre respondet. Quisquis ergo Dei veritatem negat, non potest nō in ipsum Deum directè peccasse iudicari, cum id oppugnet, sine quo Deus nec fuit vnquam, nec esse potest. At inter diuinæ veritatis promissiones præcipuæ sunt, quæ Iesum Christum saluatorem & redemptorem humani generis esse docent. Hunc primis parentibus, iam para-dyso eijciendis pollicitus est. Eundem Abrahamo promisit. De hoc denique maxima ex parte scripta sunt, quæcunq; spiritu Dei instigante diuini homines literis mandauerunt. Nisi igitur is saluator & redemptor vnicus est, & nisi in illo conclusi sunt universi salutis nostræ thesauri, fieri non potest, quin mendacissimus sit Deus, qui infelix mortalium genus ab ipsa mundi origine falsis promissis & inani spe lactare voluit. Talem vero suspicantur, quicunque vnico Christo Dei filio nolunt contenti viuere, & salutem alibi quærendo illi fidem habere detrectant. Quam enim aliam causam suæ diffidentiæ prætexent, quàm quòd, ne fallantur, metuunt? Atqui nemo est, qui ab illo se falli metuat, quem veracem esse credit. Nunquam ergo Christum solida fide amplecti detrectabunt, quicunque Deo patri, qui hunc passim saluatorem esse testatur, veritatis gloriam et titulum deferunt. Licet enim omnibus Dei verbis fidem indubitatam inesse intelligant, imprimis tamen ea, quæ de Christo dicuntur, magni facient, quia hæc non simpliciter à Deo dicta, sed tanquam abs teste pronunciata esse, & testimonij instar esse audiunt.
units.tr: II. "He who does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed the testimony which God has given concerning his Son." He brings in this second argument, which commends faith in Christ Jesus to us. It is drawn from the contraries, while he shows what it is not to believe God, who sets forth his own Son to us as Saviour. "He who does not believe God," he says, "has made God a liar." Moreover, by "making a liar" he means accusing or charging with lying. For otherwise God, who is himself eternal truth, cannot be made a liar. Indeed, "let God be true, but every man a liar." Rom. 3. God is accused of lying when we disdain to have faith in his words. Among men it is indeed so arranged that we believe only the words of those whom we know, or at least think, to be truthful. And if we disdain to give credence to anything someone has related, this happens because we believe him to be light and lying. By the same reasoning, whoever has faith in God thereby testifies that he acknowledges God to be true. But whoever refuses to believe God charges him with lying, if not in words, certainly in deed, by which he refuses to give him faith. Nor should anyone think it a trifling crime to accuse God of lying, since it is blasphemy, and hardly any more atrocious and horrible blasphemy can be devised. For among the virtues that belong properly to God, truth must not be placed in the last rank, because it fittingly corresponds to the eternal essence and incorruptibility of God. Whoever therefore denies the truth of God cannot but be judged to have sinned directly against God himself, since he attacks that without which God neither ever was nor can be. Now among the promises of divine truth the chief are those which teach that Jesus Christ is the Saviour and Redeemer of the human race. He promised this to our first parents, even as they were about to be cast out of paradise. He promised the same to Abraham. Finally, most of all, it is about him that all that holy men wrote in books under the inspiration of God's Spirit has been written. Unless, therefore, he is the only Saviour and Redeemer, and unless all the treasures of our salvation are shut up in him, it cannot but be that God is most deceitful, who wished to feed the unhappy race of mortals from the very beginning of the world with false promises and empty hope. Indeed, whoever is unwilling to live content with Christ alone, the Son of God, and who, seeking salvation elsewhere, refuses to have faith in him, suspects him of this. For what other cause will they put forward for their distrust, than that they fear to be deceived? Yet there is no one who fears to be deceived by one whom he believes to be true. Therefore, those who are unwilling to embrace Christ with a firm faith will never do so, if they ascribe the glory and title of truth to God the Father, who everywhere testifies that this man is the Saviour. For although they understand that unquestioned faith is present in all the words of God, nevertheless they will set the highest value on those things which are said about Christ, because they hear that these are not merely spoken by God, but declared as by a witness, and are in the nature of testimony.

units.la: Porrò ex his patet, cur in scripturis sacris tanto studio fides in filium Dei inculcetur, eíque omnis tribuatur iustificatio, salus & vita humani generis: quod multi mirātur, qui quid fides sit, non satis intelligunt, nec etiam intelligere volunt. Atqui causa huius doctrinæ magna & grauis est, æterna nimirum Dei veritas, quam euacuant & mendacij accusant, quotquot fidem in Iesum Christum aspernantur: glorificant autem & colunt, quicunque Iesum Christum saluatorē & redemptorem suum vnicum amplectuntur. Ideo (inquam) fides æternæ vitæ & salutis promissionibus comendatur, diffidentia vero & incredulitas æternæ meretur damnationis supplicia. Concidit autem hoc loco omnis humanarum traditionū iustitia, quā fine fide, & plerūq; contra fidei præceptum homines sectantur. Vt enim ingrata, imò exosa, nobis sunt illorum hominum obse-quia & officia, quos de nobis parum honorificè sentire nouimus: ita Deo grata & accepta esse nō possunt quæcunq; in illius honorē & cultū fiunt, si ab illis fiat, qui Christo Iesu nō credentes, pro missionū Dei veritate suspectā habēt & in dubiū vocāt. Verè ergo Paulus pronunciat: Impossibile est Deo placere absq; fide. Heb. 11. Et rursum alibi, peccatū esse dicit, quicquid sine fide fit. Ro. 14.
units.tr: Furthermore, from these things it is clear why in the holy Scriptures faith in the Son of God is inculcated with such great zeal, and why all justification, salvation and life of the human race is ascribed to him. Many wonder at this, who do not sufficiently understand what faith is, and do not even wish to understand it. Yet the reason for this doctrine is great and weighty, namely the eternal truth of God, which all who spurn faith in Jesus Christ empty and accuse of lying; but those who embrace Jesus Christ as their one Saviour and Redeemer glorify and honour it. Therefore (I say) faith is commended by the promises of eternal life and salvation, while diffidence and unbelief deserve the punishments of eternal damnation. Moreover, at this point every righteousness of human traditions collapses, which men pursue without faith, and mostly against the command of faith. For just as the services and duties of those men are unpleasing and even hateful to us, whom we know think poorly of us, so whatever is done in honour and worship of God cannot be pleasing and acceptable to him if it is done by those who do not believe in Christ Jesus, and hold the truth of God's promises in suspicion and call it into doubt. Therefore Paul rightly pronounces: "It is impossible to please God without faith." Heb. 11. And again elsewhere he says that whatever is done without faith is sin. Rom. 14.

units.la: III. Et hoc est testimonium, quòd vitam æternam dedit nobis Deus: & hæc vita in filio eius est. Qui habet filium, habet vitam. Qui non habet filium Dei, vitam non habet. Est hoc tertium argumentū, quo fidem in Christum nobis commendat Apostolus: Ab vtilitate nimirum & fructu, quem inde ad nos reditu-rum docet. Eò autem tendit, vt demonstret, doctrinæ de Iesu Christo non simpliciter modo credi debere, sed nostri esse officij, vt eam totis animis, ardenti studio & amore complectamur, eò quòd in hac universa nostræ salutis ratio proponatur. Sic enim loqui videtur Ioannes: Non abs re fieri putetis ô fratres, quòd testimonij huius de Christo veritatem & authoritate tantopere vrgeo. Nā præter quòd de Dei gloria hic agitur, quæ omnibus pijs commendatissima esse debet, vestra quoq; hic salus & vita vertitur, quam nisi toti obsurdueritis, non potestis conte-re. Quippe testimonij huius & doctrinæ summa & scopus unicus est, quòd Deus miseris nobis, qui per peccatum morte æterna mulctari merebamur, vitam reddidit & donauit ex gratia. Donauit vero hanc in filio, qui vitæ fons & author est unicus. Eum si fide complectamini, viuetis. Eundem si aspernati fueritis, vitam in vobis habere non poteritis. Quàm chara ergo vobis est vita & salus vestra, tam ardens esse debet in animis vestris studium fidei, quæ sola Christum apprehendere, & homines vitæ in Christo propositæ confortes facere solet.
units.tr: III. And this is the testimony, that God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. He who has the Son has life; he who does not have the Son of God does not have life. This is the third argument by which the Apostle commends faith in Christ to us, namely from the usefulness and fruit which he teaches will return to us from it. His aim is to show that the teaching about Jesus Christ must not merely be believed, but that it is our duty to embrace it with our whole souls, with ardent zeal and love, because in it the whole plan of our salvation is set forth. For John seems to speak thus: Do not think, brothers, that I press so earnestly the truth and authority of this testimony about Christ without reason. For apart from the fact that the glory of God is at stake here, which ought to be most commended to all the godly, your own salvation and life also turn on this, which you cannot neglect unless you have become completely deaf. Indeed, the sum and sole aim of this testimony and doctrine is that God, out of grace, has restored and given life to us miserable people, who by sin deserved to be punished with eternal death. He has given this life in his Son, who is the one fountain and author of life. If you embrace him by faith, you will live; if you have spurned him, you will not be able to have life in yourselves. Therefore, as dear as your life and salvation are to you, so ardent ought your zeal for faith to be in your hearts, for faith alone is accustomed to lay hold of Christ and to make men partakers of the life proposed in Christ.

units.la: Comprehendit paucis his Apostolus omnia, quæ nostræ saluti seruiunt, quæq; nouisse oportet, si eam velimus assequi. Primò, vita nobis à Deo datam esse testatur. Priusquam ergo illa daretur, in nobis non erat aliqua. Nam quod aliquis habet, ab alio ipsi dari nō potest. At quomodo vitam habere ex nobis possemus, qui quanti quanti sumus, peccatis sumus inquinatissimi, quorū stipendium est mors? Rom. 5. Agnouerunt id sancti omnes, quorū voces sunt: Domine, ne intres in iudicium cum seruis tuis. Et in cospectu tuo nō iustificabitur vlla caro. Ite, si iniquitates obseruaue-ris, Domine quis subsistet? Deinde vitā hāc in filio Dei, Iesu Christo esse dicit. Inest aūt huic, non ut nobis vita inesse dicitur, dum mouemur, spiramus & alia facimus, quæ à viuentibus fieri consueuerunt. Sed Christo inest tâquam authori, qui eandem alijs quoque largitur & communicat: & ideo alibi ipsa vita & panis vitæ, vel viuificans esse dicitur. Ioan. 14. Hic ergo quia euangelium prædicat & amplectendum proponit, rectè & merito doctrina vitæ & prædicatio salutis dicitur. Et Paulus hæc ritè considerans dixit: Non me pudet euangelij Iesu Christi: quia potentia Dei est ad salutem omni credenti. Rom. 1. Postremò modum quoque explicat Ioannes, quo nos vita in Christo propositavotiri possumus. Qui habet filium (inquit) vitam habet. Filium Dei verò habent, qui in illum credunt. Quia enim peracto nostræ redemptionis negotio terras reliquit & cœlos conscendit, nec in hoc mundo corpore suo versatur, corporaliter haberi aut apprehendi non potest, nec etiam sic apprehensus prodesset. Ioan. 6. Spirituali igitur modo habetur, fide scilicet, quæ animos nostros supra humanæ rationis captū in cœlos euehit, ut ibi Christū Iesum cū omnibus, quæ in hoc nobis data sunt, apprehendat. Unde fit, ut in Christo maneamus toti, & ipse vicissim maneat in nobis. Sensum hunc ipsius Christi verba tradunt, quæ toties repetit & inculcat: Qui credit in me, habet vitam æternam. Ioan. 5. & 6. Summa igitur salutis nostræ, in eo versatur, ut nos mortis reos esse agnoscamus, vitam verò nobis à Deo patre in filio donatam amplectamur vera fide, quæ nos filio Dei Iesu Christo inserit, & bonorum cœlestiū in ipso facit hæredes.
units.tr: In a few words the Apostle has comprehended all the things that serve our salvation and that we must know if we wish to attain it. First, he testifies that life has been given to us by God. Before it was given, then, we had no life in ourselves. For what someone has, cannot be given to him by another. But how could we have life from ourselves, we who, however many we are, are most defiled by sins, whose wages are death? Rom. 5. All the saints have acknowledged this, whose voices are: Lord, do not enter into judgment with your servants; for in your sight no flesh will be justified. And again: If you, Lord, should mark iniquities, who could stand? Next, he says that this life is in the Son of God, Jesus Christ. It is in him not in the way that life is said to be in us, while we move, breathe and do other things that living beings are accustomed to do; rather, it is in Christ as in its author, who also bestows and communicates the same to others; and so elsewhere he himself is called life and the bread of life, or the one who gives life. John 14. Therefore, since he preaches the gospel and sets it forth to be embraced, it is rightly and deservedly called the doctrine of life and the preaching of salvation. And Paul, considering these things rightly, said: I am not ashamed of the gospel of Jesus Christ, for it is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes. Rom. 1. Lastly, John also explains the manner by which the life proposed to us in Christ can be obtained. He who has the Son, he says, has life. Those, however, have the Son of God who believe in him. For since, having completed the business of our redemption, he left the earth and ascended into heaven, and does not dwell in this world in his body, he cannot be had or laid hold of bodily, nor would he benefit us even if he were so grasped. John 6. He is therefore had in a spiritual manner, namely by faith, which lifts our souls above the grasp of human reason into heaven, so that there it may lay hold of Christ Jesus with all the things that have been given to us in him. Hence it comes about that we remain wholly in Christ, and he in turn remains in us. The words of Christ himself convey this meaning, which he repeats and inculcates so often: He who believes in me has eternal life. John 5 and 6. The sum of our salvation, therefore, consists in this: that we acknowledge ourselves to be guilty of death, and that we embrace with true faith the life given to us in the Son by God the Father, which faith engrafts us into the Son of God Jesus Christ and makes us heirs of heavenly goods in him.

units.la: Est autem hic singulari obseruatione dignum, quòd contrariam quoque sententiam pro suo more, nec sine emphasi, repetit: Qui non habet filium Dei, vitam non habet. Sunt enim qui nô negant saluos fieri eos, qui Christum Iesum vera fide apprehendunt: sed hanc salutis viam unicâ & solam esse, agnoscere nolunt. Imò ut se omnibus tolerabiles reddant, ac homines cômodi habeantur, alios quoq; saluari posse existimât, qui bono aliquo zelo aliâ salutis ratione sectantur. Hos ergo breui sententia Ioannes iugulat, docens vitâ in Christo Iesu sic conclusam esse, ut in solo haberi possit, & vita omni careant, quicunque Christo carent. Vanissima igitur sunt quæcunq; homines vel faciunt vel patiuntur, si Christum non habeant. Quia enim Deus externa specie non ducitur, & eum cultum exigit, qui in spiritu & veritate consistit, corporalis exercitatio nihil iuuat, sed pietas (cuius præcipua pars fides est) præsentis & futuræ vitæ promissiones habet. 1. Tim. 4. Pertinent huc crebri & graues prophetarum sermones, quibus dictante spiritu sancto, Israelitarum sacrificia, festa, libationes, circuncisionem, deniq; ipsum templum cum toto illo Ceremoniarum mundo damnant & reiiciunt. Atqui omnia illa diuinitus præscripta erant. Ad vitam tamen prodesse & Deo placere non poterant, eò quòd sine fide in Christū Iesum, quem iam olim Deus promiserat, peragebantur. Quid ergo de frigidissimis Ceremonijs dicemus, quas humanæ rationis stultitia & superstitio iam aliquot seculis peperit? Num ea saluare poterùt homines, quæ non aliam suę institutionis causam habent, quàm quòd de Christi merito & satisfactione homines dubitare, & quæ huius sunt, sibi vendicare cœperunt? Præterea constat, vitam & salutę nullam esse posse sine peccatorum remissione. Quàm diu enim peccatum inhæret homini, peccati pœnâ, mortem videlicet & damnatione, non effugiet. Atqui peccatorum remissio in solo Christo habetur. Is enim est, qui languores & infirmitates nostras tulit. In hunc cófluere fecit omnes nostras iniquitates dominus. Isa. 53. Ipse torcular calcauit solus, & non est cū ipso aliquis. Isa. 63. Ipse delet transgressiones nostras, ut densas nebulas, & peccata nostra ut nubè, idq; propter se. Isa. 43. & 44. Ipse est agnus ille Dei, qui tollit peccatum mūdi. Ioan. 1. Ipse peccatū, id est, hostia pro peccato factus est, ut nos essemus iustitia Dei per ipsum. 2. Cor. 5. Et supra Ioannem dicentem audiuimus: Sanguis filij Dei emundat nos ab omni peccato. 1. Ioan. 1. In solo igitur Christo vitam & salutem consistere & inueniri constat, & verè Petrus pronunciat, dum negat aliud nomen sub Sole hominibus datum esse, præter nomen Iesu, in quo saluari possint. Act. 4. Cuius sententiam & ipse Dei filius approbat dicens: Nemo venit ad patrem, nisi per me. Ioan. 14.
units.tr: Here, moreover, it is worth special note that he repeats the contrary opinion too, in his usual manner and not without emphasis: he who does not have the Son of God does not have life. For there are some who do not deny that those are saved who lay hold of Jesus Christ by true faith; but they are unwilling to acknowledge that this is the one and only way of salvation. Indeed, in order to make themselves tolerable to all and be regarded as agreeable men, they think that others also can be saved who pursue some other way of salvation with some good zeal. John therefore slays these with a brief sentence, teaching that life is so enclosed in Christ Jesus that it can be had in him alone, and that all who lack Christ lack life. Therefore whatever men either do or suffer is most vain if they do not have Christ. For since God is not moved by outward appearance, and requires that worship which consists in spirit and truth, bodily exercise profits nothing, but godliness (of which the principal part is faith) holds promises of the present and of the future life. 1 Tim. 4. To this pertain the frequent and weighty sayings of the prophets, by which, the Holy Spirit dictating, they condemn and reject the sacrifices, feasts, libations and circumcision of the Israelites, and finally the temple itself with that whole world of ceremonies. Yet all those things had been prescribed by God. Nevertheless, they could not profit for life nor please God, because they were performed without faith in Christ Jesus, whom God had promised long before. What then shall we say of the very cold ceremonies which the folly and superstition of human reason has brought forth for some centuries now? Can those things save men which have no other cause of their institution than that men have begun to doubt the merit and satisfaction of Christ and to claim for themselves what belongs to him? Moreover, it is established that there can be no life or salvation without the remission of sins. For as long as sin clings to a man, he will not escape the penalty of sin, namely death and condemnation. But the remission of sins is found in Christ alone. For he is the one who bore our languors and infirmities. The Lord caused the iniquities of us all to meet in him. Isa. 53. He alone has trodden the winepress, and there is no one with him. Isa. 63. He himself blots out our transgressions like a thick cloud, and our sins like a cloud, and this for his own sake. Isa. 43 and 44. He is that Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. John 1. He himself was made sin, that is, a sacrifice for sin, so that we might become the righteousness of God through him. 2 Cor. 5. And above, we have heard John saying: The blood of the Son of God cleanses us from all sin. 1 John 1. Therefore it is evident that life and salvation consist and are found in Christ alone, and Peter truly declares, when he denies that any other name under heaven has been given to men in which they may be saved, except the name of Jesus. Acts 4. The Son of God himself approves this opinion, saying: No one comes to the Father except through me. John 14.

units.la: Memorabilis ergo locus hic est ô fratres, & dignus quê crebrò meditemur, imò in cuius cósyderatione versemur dies & noctes. Docet enim, fidem in Iesum Christum, non utilem modo & salutarem, sed necessariam esse, eò quòd sine hac saluari non possumus. Docet tutam & infallibilem esse eius veritatem, nec ullum subesse, ne per hàc fallamur, periculum. Adhæc ostendit, quàm atrociter peccent in ipsam Dei maiestatem, quicunque hunc saluatorem amplecti nolunt. Abiecta igitur omni dubitatione, & explosis humanæ superstitionis commentis, totos nos fidei consecremus, quæ sola faciet, ut hic feliciter viuere, & olim cum Dei filio regnare possimus, cui debetur benedictio, gloria, honor & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: This, then, is a memorable passage, brothers, and worthy of being meditated upon often, indeed of being occupied with day and night. For it teaches that faith in Jesus Christ is not only useful and saving but necessary, because without it we cannot be saved. It teaches that his truth is safe and infallible, and that there is no danger lurking in it by which we might be deceived. Besides, it shows how atrociously they sin against the very majesty of God who are unwilling to embrace this Saviour. Therefore, with all doubt set aside and the inventions of human superstition cast away, let us wholly devote ourselves to faith, which alone will make it possible for us to live happily here and one day to reign with the Son of God, to whom belong blessing, glory, honour and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXIII. Hæc scripsi vobis, qui creditis in nomè filij Dei: ut sciatis, quòd
units.tr: HOMILY XXXIII. I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that

units.la: uitam habetis æternam, & ut credatis in nomen filij Dei. Et hæc est fiducia quam habemus apud eum, quòd si quid petierimus secundum voluntatem eius, audit nos. Et si scimus quòd audit nos, quic quid[?] petierimus, scimus quòd habemus petitiones, quas postulaui mus ab eo.
units.tr: you have eternal life, and that you may believe in the name of the Son of God. And this is the confidence we have before him: that if we ask anything according to his will, he hears us. And if we know that he hears us, whatever we ask, we know that we have the petitions that we have asked of him.

units.la: QVamuis homines naturali desyderio felicitatem appetant, ea tamen est nostræ carnis cæcitas & corruptio, ut nec huius rationem ipsi inuenire, nec oblatam ampletati possint. Patet hoc tum alibi, tum in Christi saluatoris nostri negotio. Cum enim Deus in hoc omnes suæ gratiæ thesauros concluserit, inquis uno illo comprehensa sint quæcunq; nostræ saluti inseruiunt, plerique tamen hominum illo contempto vel neglecto, ad sua commenta declinant, & nunquam non impletur illud Christi: Ego veni nomine patris mei, nec recipitis me: alius veniet nomine suo, illum recipietis. Ioan.5. Quæ causa est, cur Apostoli in Christo Iesu tradendo studiū tantum tamq; ardens adhibent, si quo modo homines adduci possint, ut hoc vno contenti, in ipso solo quærant quæ salutis sunt. Idem & Ioannis scopus est in omnibus ijs, quæ hucusque vidimus. Nec aliud agit in epistolæ Epilogo, quem modo orditur, & paucis præcipua doctrinæ suæ capita repetit. Et in præsenti quidem, primò causas commemorat, quæ ipsum ad scribendum impulerunt: Deinde ad fidei fructus exponendos reuersus, de precādi fiducia agit, quæ plurimū mo menti habet ad medendum offendiculis, quæ ex Cruce & aduersis huius seculi Christianis hominibus obijciuntur.
units.tr: Although men by natural desire seek happiness, yet such is the blindness and corruption of our flesh that they can neither discover the way to it themselves nor embrace it when it is offered. This appears both elsewhere and in the business of Christ our Saviour. For although God has enclosed in him alone all the treasures of his grace, so that everything that serves our salvation is comprehended in that one, yet most men, despising or neglecting him, turn aside to their own inventions, and that saying of Christ is never not fulfilled: "I came in my Father's name, and you do not receive me; another will come in his own name, and you will receive him" (John 5). This is why the Apostles apply such great and burning zeal to delivering Christ Jesus, if somehow men might be led to be content with this one alone and seek in him alone the things that pertain to salvation. This is also the aim of John in all the things we have seen so far. Nor does he do anything else in the Epilogue of the epistle, which he now begins, and in a few words he repeats the principal heads of his doctrine. And in the present passage he first recalls the causes which moved him to write, and then, returning to set forth the fruits of faith, he treats of confidence in prayer, which has very great weight in healing the stumbling-blocks that are thrown in the way by the Cross and by the adversities which Christians face in this world.

units.la: I. Hæc scripsi vobis, qui creditis in nomen filij Dei: ut sciatis quòd vitam habetis æternam, & ut credatis in nomen filij Dei. Causæ scribendi duæ fuerunt Apostolo. Prima, ut qui credunt, sciant se habere vitam æternam, id est, de salute sua certi sint & ab omni dubitatione alieni. Nec enim in nuda opinione nostra salus versatur, sed fides, certa & infallibilis est rerum cœlestium & salutis apprehensio: Et magna hæc fidei in Christum laus est, quòd salutis certos facit suos cultores, cum in reliquis religionibus omnia incerta sint & dubia. Altera causa est: Vt credatis in nomen filij Dei. Videtur ineptum esse & superuacaneum quod dicit. Si enim illis scribit, qui credunt, quid opus est scribere ut credant? Sed de perseuerantia fidei loquitur Ioannes, quæ nisi accedat, frustra fide gloriabimur. Qui perseuerauerit in finem, saluus erit, inquit Christus. Matth.24. Et qui postquam manum aratro admouit, respicit à tergo, minimè idoneus est ad regnum Christi possidendum. Lucæ 9. Præterea iustitiæ corona non cuiuis certanti, sed ei datur, qui legitimè certauerit. 2. Timoth. 2. Quia ergo multa quotidie occurrunt, quibus fidem nostram solicitare & euertere conatur salutis nostræ hostis, & magna est in hac retinenda carnis infirmitas, non temere factū putabitur, quòd huius epistolæ antidoto fideles cōfirmare voluit Apostolus. Si enim in re domestica non minor est virtus parta tueri, quàm acquirere: in ecclesia quoq;, quæ Dei domus est, non in hoc modò incumbendū erit verbi ministris, ut nouos Christo acquirant & lucrifaciant discipulos, sed curare simul decet, ne forte elabantur qui ante capti fuerunt. Porro sunt quædā in prima hac præsentis loci parte excutienda paulò diligentius.
units.tr: I. "These things I have written to you, who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life, and that you may believe in the name of the Son of God." The Apostle had two causes for writing. The first is that those who believe may know that they have eternal life, that is, that they may be certain of their salvation and free from all doubt. For our salvation does not rest on mere opinion, but faith is a certain and infallible apprehension of heavenly things and of salvation. And this is the great praise of faith in Christ, that it makes its worshippers certain of salvation, whereas in the other religions all things are uncertain and doubtful. The other cause is: "that you may believe in the name of the Son of God." What he says seems absurd and superfluous. For if he writes to those who believe, what need is there to write that they may believe? But John speaks of the perseverance of faith, which, unless it is added, we shall boast of our faith in vain. "He who perseveres to the end will be saved," says Christ (Matt. 24). And he who, after putting his hand to the plough, looks back, is not at all fit for possessing the kingdom of Christ (Luke 9). Moreover, the crown of righteousness is given not to everyone who contends, but to him who has contended lawfully (2 Tim. 2). Since, therefore, many things meet us every day by which the enemy of our salvation tries to unsettle and overthrow our faith, and the weakness of the flesh in holding fast to it is great, it will not be thought rashly done that the Apostle wished to strengthen the faithful with the antidote of this epistle. For if in domestic affairs preserving what has been gained requires no less courage than acquiring it, then in the Church, which is God's house, it will not be enough for the ministers of the Word to labour only in this, that they win and gain new disciples for Christ, but it is also fitting to take care that those who were captured before do not perhaps slip away. Moreover, there are some things in this first part of the present passage that must be examined a little more carefully.

units.la: Primò, ijs scribit Ioannes, quibus ipse testimoniū fert, quod credant in nomen filij Dei. Quapropter non alieni modo à fide & Christi cognitione doceri & instituì debet, sed institutione adhuc opus habent, qui Christum nouerunt, & illum vera fide amplexi sunt. Cuius ratio est, non si[?] dei nostræ perplexitas & nunquam finienda quæstionū copia, sed quòd (ut modò diximus) aliun de multa accedunt, quæ fidelibus admonitionibus & hortationibus remoueri oportet. Insidiatur nobis indefinenti & indefesso studio diabolus, & ut primum dormiunt homines & de salute sua securiores sunt, bono euangelij semini zizania sua superseminat. Matth.13. Magna est insuper carnis nostræ infirmitas, quæ illius blanditijs facilè cedit. Effrenis quoq; est nostræ rationis temeritas, quæ dum in diuinis sapere vult, multa ex semetipsa statuit, quæ cum veritate ex diametro pugnant. Hinc noua quotidie hæreses, nouos & inextricabiles errores, absurda dogmata, & infinita alia prodire videmus, quæ partim præstigiatores improbi & impostores, partim contētionum auidi & ambitiosi homines, magno cum ecclesiarum malo inuehere consueuerunt. Illiciuntur in horum nassam quotidie simplices, & rapacissimis lupis miseranda præda fiunt. Quid verò de illis dicere attinet, qui dum Cruce tentantur, aut carnis mortificationem, quæ euangelij disciplina traditur, sibi molestiorem & intolerabiliorem sentiunt, longum Vale renunciantes Christo, quem totis animis amplexi videbantur, ad mundum infelicem redeunt, quorum exempla passim non sine summo dolore piorum oculis occurrunt. Hęc igitur non simplicem modò docendi rationem exigūt, qua quid faciat homo, instituatur: sed admonere, hortari, arguere, deniq; tepestiuē & intepestiuē instare oportet, ne à semel recepta salutis ratione homines deflectāt. 2. Tim. 4. Obseruent hęc nostri seculi homines, qui dum aures habent nimiū delicatulas, sufficere putant, si semel instituti salutis suæ rationem vtcunque teneant, & proinde prædicationes verbi quotidianas rem plane superuacaneam, admonitiones verò & increpationes non Christiani pectoris & charitatis ve re, sed animi suspicacis, inuidi & turbarum amantis, vel seditiosi, signa esse. Sed næ illi egregiē, si dijs placet, sapiunt. Si in sermone & inani notitia regnum Dei consisteret, illorum sententia aliquem locum mereretur. Verum cum non ij qui dicunt, Domine domine, ingressuri sint regnum Dei, sed qui faciunt voluntatē patris cœlestis: fateantur oportet, admonitione, redargutione, imò & increpatione opus esse, quoad homines securitate pressi officium suum facere negligunt. Nec multum illorum calumnias morentur fideles ministri, quādo & prophetæ olim turbatores Israelis & viri cōtentionum dicti sunt, nec Christus tanti criminis titulum apud eos effugere potuit, quorum saluti vnicē studebat.
units.tr: First, John writes to those to whom he bears witness that they believe in the name of the Son of God. Therefore, not only must those who are far from faith and the knowledge of Christ be taught and instructed, but those who know Christ and have embraced him in true faith also still need instruction. The reason for this is not the perplexity of our minds and the never-ending supply of questions, but that (as we have just said) many other things arise, which must be removed by faithful admonitions and exhortations. The devil lies in wait for us with unending and tireless zeal, and as soon as men fall asleep and become more careless about their salvation, he sows his tares among the good seed of the gospel (Matt. 13). Moreover, our flesh is very weak and readily yields to its flatteries. Our reason also is unbridled in its rashness, which, while it wishes to be wise in divine things, decides many things by itself that flatly contradict the truth. Hence we see new heresies, new and inextricable errors, absurd doctrines, and countless other things arising every day, which partly wicked deceivers and impostors, partly men greedy for contentions and ambitious, are accustomed to bring in to the great harm of the churches. Simple people are caught in their net every day, and become the pitiable prey of the most ravenous wolves. And what need is there to speak of those who, when they are tried by the Cross, or find the mortification of the flesh, which is taught by the discipline of the gospel, too burdensome and intolerable for them, bid a long farewell to Christ, whom they seemed to have embraced with their whole hearts, and return to the unhappy world? Examples of these meet the eyes of the pious everywhere, not without great grief. These things therefore demand not only a simple method of teaching, by which a man is instructed what he should do, but it is necessary to admonish, exhort, rebuke, and finally to press on in season and out of season, lest men turn aside from the way of salvation once received (2 Tim. 4). Let the men of this age take note of this, who, having ears far too dainty, think it enough, if once instructed, they somehow hold to the way of their salvation, and therefore consider the daily preaching of the Word a plainly superfluous thing, and admonitions and rebukes to be signs not of a Christian heart and true charity, but of a suspicious, envious spirit that loves disturbances, or of a seditious one. But surely they are judging excellently, if it please the gods! If the kingdom of God consisted in talk and empty knowledge, their opinion would deserve some place. But since it is not those who say, "Lord, Lord," who will enter the kingdom of God, but those who do the will of the heavenly Father, they must confess that admonition, refutation, and indeed rebuke are needed, as long as men weighed down by security neglect to do their duty. Nor should faithful ministers much delay over their calumnies, since the prophets of old were also called troublers of Israel and men of contention, and Christ could not escape the title of such a crime among those whose salvation he alone was zealous for.

units.la: Deinde non oscitanter prætereundum est, quōd toties de certitudine salutis nos admonet Apostolus. Licet enim iam ante de hac dicta sint multa, plura tamen vel dicere vel audire non pigeat, ne nostra negligentia spiritus sancti diligentiam damnare videamur. Et sanè, nihil tam necessarium homini dici potest, quàm vt de salute sua certus sit: quia dum in huius ratione quæren da animus fluctuat, satanæ laqueis facillimè capitur, quibus in desperationem attrahi solet. Quæ causa est, quōd & ipse Deus olim multiuariam de hac nos instituere voluit, & tandem filium suū, non saluatorem modò, sed doctore quoq; dedit, ne quid de salute dubij restaret. Sed nec hoc contentus, insuper spiritum animis nostris inserit, qui salutis nostræ arrhabo & pignus fit, & in quo clamemus, Abba pater. Huius testimonium supra quoq; allegauit Apostolus, & nuuc denuo repetit, hanc non postremam suæ prædicationis & scriptionis causam esse, vt certò sciant, se vitam habere æternam. Procul ergo hinc facessant cum pestilenti & planè diabolico suo commento sophistæ Antichristiani, quo homines de salute dubitare docent, dum nobis semper incertum esse dicunt, an simus in charitate & gratia Dei. Nec illorum prætextus admittendus, quo sese excusant, quasi non aliud velint, quàm vt homines securitate omni pulsa, iuxta Apostoli præceptum, salutem suam in timore & tremore operentur. Nec enim nos ij sumus, qui securitate docere, aut timorem Dei animis hominum eximere studeamus. Interim verò nefas & horribilem audaciam esse ducimus, in dubium vocare id, cuius tot extát in sacris literis indicia, & de quo ipse pater cœlitus edita voce testari voluit. Impium & plus quàm sacrilegum facinus esse iudicamus, Deū patrem mendacij insimulare, & de Christi veritate vel minimum dubitare, qui omnibus in se credentibus vitam æternam certò pollicetur. Immane & nulla venia dignum scelus esse censemus, spiritui sancto non fidem adhibere, quem Christus nostræ salutis arrhabonem esse voluit. Præterea non videmus, qua ratione ijs mederi liceat, quorum fides satanicis suggestionibus & peccatorum grauissimorum recordatione tentatur, si persuasum esse debet homini, nos dum hic viuimus, de salute & gratia Dei certos fieri non posse. Quid enim tam necessariū est in ea causa, quàm certo damnationis testimonio non minus certum salutis & absolutionis nostræ testimoniū obijcere posse? Atqui nos peccatores esse, & peccatum morte puniri, satan certo & irrefragabili verbi Dei oraculo probare solet, quādo illud legis objicit: Maledictus, qui nō fecerit omnia, quæ scripta sunt in libro isto: Et dicet omnis populus, Amen. Nisi ergo aliud habeas, quo certò nitaris, teque Christi merito peccatorum sarcina exoneratum, & à damnationis sententia liberum esse, indubitatò credas, fieri nequit, quin in hac tam immani Charybdi fidei & salutis tuæ facias naufragium. Num ergo propter paucorum improbitatem, qui euangelij doctrina securius abutuntur ad carnis licentiam, admittendum erit, vt de Dei veritate dubitemus, spiritus sancti testimonio diffida mus, & alijs circa fidem & salutem periclitandi simus authores?
units.tr: Next, we must not pass over carelessly that the Apostle so often admonishes us about the certainty of salvation. For although many things have already been said about this, yet we should not be weary of saying or hearing more, lest we seem by our negligence to condemn the diligence of the Holy Spirit. And indeed, nothing can be said to man as necessary as that he be certain of his salvation, because while his mind wavers in seeking the ground of this, he is very easily caught in the snares of Satan, by which he is commonly drawn into despair. This is why God himself wished of old to instruct us about it in many ways, and at last gave us his Son, not only as Saviour but also as teacher, so that nothing of doubt about salvation might remain. But not content with this, he further plants the Spirit in our hearts, who becomes the pledge and earnest of our salvation, and by whom we cry, "Abba, Father." The Apostle also cited his testimony above, and now repeats it again, that this is not the least cause of his preaching and writing, that they may know for certain that they have eternal life. Let the Antichristian sophists therefore keep far away from here with their pestilential and plainly diabolical invention, by which they teach men to doubt their salvation, while they say that it is always uncertain to us whether we are in the love and grace of God. Nor is their excuse to be admitted, by which they shield themselves, as if they wished nothing other than that men, with all security driven away, according to the Apostle's precept, should work out their salvation in fear and trembling. For we are not those who seek to teach security, or to remove the fear of God from the hearts of men. Meanwhile, we consider it a crime and a horrible audacity to call into doubt that of which so many signs exist in the sacred letters, and which the Father himself wished to attest by a voice sent from heaven. We judge it an impious and more than sacrilegious deed to accuse God the Father of lying, and to have even the least doubt about the truth of Christ, who promises eternal life with certainty to all who believe in him. We judge it a monstrous crime, deserving no pardon, not to give credit to the Holy Spirit, whom Christ wished to be the earnest of our salvation. Besides, we do not see by what method it is permitted to heal those whose faith is assailed by satanic suggestions and by the recollection of the gravest sins, if it must be held that a man, while he lives here, cannot be made certain of the salvation and grace of God. For what is so necessary in this cause as being able to set against the certain testimony of damnation an equally certain testimony of our salvation and absolution? Yet Satan is accustomed to prove that we are sinners, and that sin is punished by death, by the certain and irrefutable oracle of God's Word, when he objects that law: "Cursed is he who does not do all the things written in this book. And all the people shall say, Amen" (Deut. 27). Unless, therefore, you have something else on which you can firmly rest, and believe without doubt that you are relieved of the burden of your sins by the merit of Christ and free from the sentence of damnation, it cannot but happen that you suffer shipwreck in this so immense Charybdis of your faith and salvation. Shall we then, on account of the wickedness of a few who misuse the doctrine of the gospel too carelessly as a license for the flesh, be obliged to doubt the truth of God, distrust the testimony of the Holy Spirit, and become the authors of danger to others concerning faith and salvation?

units.la: Cæterum tertio loco nobis obseruandum venit, quòd certitudinem salutis nostræ cum fide in filium Dei coniungit. Nam cum dixisset, se hæc in eum finem scripsisse, vt certò sciamus nos habere vitam æternam, mox alteram causam subijciens, fidem commendat, qua credimus in nomen filij Dei. Porrò quid sit credere in nomen filij Dei, supra cap.3. expositum est. Faciunt hoc, qui credunt filium Dei esse Iesum, id est, saluatorem, & esse Christum, id est, vnctum Dei, regem & sacerdotem suæ ecclesiæ, qui regiæ maiestatis iure vtens leges fert, iudicat, asserit, tuetur, & gratiæ suæ thesauris suos liberalissimè ditat: qui item sacerdotij munere fungens, suos perpetuò docet, pro ijsdem orat, & peccata suorum vnico sui corporis sacrificio expiat. Quicunq; talem agno scunt, in nomen eius verè credunt, & in hac fide salutis suæ certitudinem infallibilem. Audiunt enim Christum dicentem,se esse petram illam inuictam, cui portæ inferorum non possint prevalere. Matth.16. Norunt hunc esse fidum illum & fortissimum pastorem,qui manibus suis oves eripi minimè patiatur. Joan.10. Atqui probè animaduertendum est,fidem quæ salutis certos reddit, simpliciter uni Christo inniti, minimeq; ambiguam esse vel ancipitem, quæ homines in utrumq; latus claudicare doceat. Imò nihil à fidei veritate tam alienum est, quàm nostræ salutis & redemptionis gloriam non uni Christo Jesu transcribere. Solus enim est,qui propter nos in mundū veniens carnem mortalem induit. Solus est, in quem humani generis peccata pater cœlestis confluere voluit. Isa.53. Solus torcular illud nostrorum scelerū calcauit. Isa.63. In evangelio denique ad se solum invitat omnes,qui laborant & onerati sunt. Matth.11. In se solo panē & aquam vitæ æternæ esurientibus ac sitientibus monstrat. Joan.6.4. & 7. Et alibi,neminem ad patrem venire testatur,nisi per se. Joan.14. Præterea Apostoli in uno hoc omnè salutem & rationè salutis nobis monstrant. Nota est Petri vox,qui aliud nomen datū esse negat,in quo possimus salui fieri. Act.4. Paulum audimus in nullo alio, quàm in Cruce Christi gloriante. Gal.6. Idè se nihil aliud nouisse ingenuè fatetur,quàm Jesum Christum, & hunc crucifixum pro peccatis nostris. 1.Cor.2. Nihil ergo noui docent hodie, qui salutem in uno Christo monstrant, & huius nos participes fieri docēt per fidem. Hæc enim unanimis omnium prophetarum & apostolorum doctrina est. Hoc ipsum pater cœlestis docet,& spiritus sanctus in omnibus scripturæ sacræ libris constantissimè testatur. Deploranda autem est illorum cœcitas,qui bis miseri sunt,dum & simplicem salutis rationem aspernantur,& nunquam finiendis molestijs sese temere mancipant. Nos Christo contenti esse discamus,& fidei veræ studium sectemur, cuius nouum fructum,& quidem amplissimum, in sequentibus Joannes proponit.
units.tr: Thirdly, we must note that the author joins the certainty of our salvation to faith in the Son of God. For after saying that he wrote these things with the aim that we may know for certain that we have eternal life, he at once adds a second cause, commending faith, by which we believe in the name of the Son of God.
