Now what it is to believe in the name of the Son of God was explained above, in chapter 3. They do this who believe that the Son of God is Jesus, that is, the Saviour, and that he is the Christ, that is, the anointed of God, king and priest of his Church, who, exercising the right of royal majesty, makes laws, judges, asserts and protects, and liberally enriches his people from the treasures of his grace; who likewise, discharging the office of priest, continually teaches his own, prays for them, and expiates their sins by the single sacrifice of his body. Whoever knows him thus truly believes in his name, and in this faith has an infallible certainty of their salvation. For they hear Christ saying that he is that unconquered rock against which the gates of hell cannot prevail (Matt. 16). They know that he is that faithful and most valiant shepherd, who suffers no one to snatch the sheep from his hands (John 10). But it must be carefully observed that the faith which makes men certain of salvation rests simply upon Christ alone, and is by no means doubtful or wavering, such as teaches men to limp toward both sides. Indeed, nothing is so foreign to the truth of faith as not to ascribe the glory of our salvation and redemption to Jesus Christ alone. For he alone came into the world for our sake and put on mortal flesh. He alone is the one upon whom the heavenly Father willed the sins of the human race to be laid (Isa. 53). He alone trod that winepress of our sins (Isa. 63). Finally, in the Gospel he invites all who labour and are burdened to himself alone (Matt. 11). In himself alone he shows bread and water of eternal life to those who hunger and thirst (John 6:4 and 7). And elsewhere he testifies that no one comes to the Father except through him (John 14). Moreover, the Apostles in this one thing show us all salvation and the reason of salvation. Peter's word is well known, who denies that any other name has been given in which we can be saved (Acts 4). We hear Paul glorying in nothing but the Cross of Christ (Gal. 6). Hence he frankly confesses that he knew nothing else than Jesus Christ, and him crucified for our sins (1 Cor. 2). Those who today show salvation in Christ alone, and teach that we become partakers of him through faith, therefore teach nothing new. For this is the unanimous doctrine of all the prophets and apostles. The heavenly Father himself teaches this very thing, and the Holy Spirit testifies most constantly to it in all the books of sacred Scripture. But the blindness of those is to be deplored, who are doubly wretched, since they both despise the simple way of salvation and rashly surrender themselves to endless troubles. Let us learn to be content with Christ, and let us pursue the study of true faith, whose new and indeed most ample fruit John sets forth in what follows.

units.la: I I. Et hæc est fiducia,quam habemus apud eum, quòd si quid petierimus secundum voluntatem eius, audit nos.Et si scimus quòd audit nos, quicquid petierimus, scimus quòd habemus petitiones, quas postulauimus ab eo. Possunt hæc Præoccupationis loco posita videri,qua tacitæ objectioni occurrūt.Cum enim doctrina de fide & salutis nostræ certitudine in Christo traditur,multos offendit,quòd fideles rerum indigos esse,infeliciter agere,crebris infortunijs exerceri, & nunquam non affligi videant.Et quia carnis ingenium est, felicitatem hominum præsenti conditione metiri, salutis certitudinem in Christo videre non potest. Docet ergo Joannes, hæc omnia non obstare, quò minus felices & salutis suæ certi sint, quicunque Christo vera fide adhærent:quia Deum sibi tam propitium habent,ut illorum precibus aures præbeat,& votorum compotes reddat. Si enim inter homines infelix & miser dici non potest,quem potentis & diuitis alicuius viri fauor & patrocinium protegit,licet interdum labores & pericula quorundam inuidorum calumnijs sibi structa sustineat:quantò minus infelices & miseros dicere debemus eos, qui Dei patris fauore utuntur,cuius aures ipsorum precibus semper patent? Est hic ingens fidei nostræ fructus,qui si nihil post hac,vitam esset nobis reliqui,illius studium vel solus nobis commendare poterat. Quid enim tam felix, tam iucundum & tutum, imò tam necessarium homini, quàm in huius vitæ palæstra undique periculorum plena,habere ad quem confugias,cui preces tuas offeras,& de cuius ope & vindice manu certus sis? Possent hic multa de precibus & precandi ratione dici,sed quia nunquam nō eadem copiosius exponendi locus occurrit,ea tantum, quæ Joannes in præsenti proponit,breviter perstringemus : qui licet brevitati studeat, magnificè tamen & splendidè nobis hunc fidei fructum commendat.
units.tr: II. "And this is the confidence which we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will, he hears us. And if we know that he hears us, whatever we ask, we know that we have the petitions which we have asked of him." These words may seem to be placed by way of prevention, meeting an unspoken objection. For when the doctrine of faith and of the certainty of our salvation in Christ is taught, it offends many, who see that the faithful lack things, labour unhappily, are constantly exercised by misfortunes, and are never not afflicted. And since it is the nature of the flesh to measure human happiness by present condition, it cannot see the certainty of salvation in Christ. John therefore teaches that none of these things stands in the way of those who cling to Christ with true faith being happy and certain of their salvation, because they have God so favourable to them that he lends his ears to their prayers and grants them the fulfilment of their desires. For if a man cannot be called unhappy and wretched who is protected by the favour and patronage of some powerful and rich man, although he sometimes endures labours and dangers contrived by the slanders of certain envious persons, how much less ought we to call wretched and miserable those who enjoy the favour of God the Father, whose ears always stand open to their prayers? This is a great fruit of our faith, which, even if nothing else remained to us after this life, could alone commend its pursuit to us. For what is so happy, so pleasant and safe, nay, so necessary to man, as, in the arena of this life, which is everywhere full of dangers, to have someone to flee to, to whom you may offer your prayers, and of whose help and hand as protector you are certain? Much could be said here about prayers and the manner of praying, but since there is always an occasion to set forth the same things more fully, we will only briefly touch upon those things which John proposes at present. Although he aims at brevity, he nevertheless commends this fruit of faith to us in a magnificent and splendid way.

units.la: Primò, hæc (inquit) est fiducia, quam habemus apud eum. Fiduciam & liberam Deum accedendi & precandi potestatem nobis tribuit, quæ profectò cum singulari gloria & laude coniuncta est. Superbiunt nimis gloriosuli, qui principum huius seculi facilitate tam familiariter uti solent, ut ipsis quando lubet ad illos accessus pateat. At q̃ exigua,imò nulla hæc laus est,si cū ea libertate & fiducia conferatur, qua nobis,quotiescunque opus est,in Dei conspectum venire,& necessaria quæque postulare audemus? Nec quisquam putet,Joannem propria confidentia usum,nobis tanti boni gloriam polliceri. Habet enim fiducia hæc rationes,quibus nititur,solidas,certas & omnino infallibiles. Siquidem Deus ipse iubet & constanter præcipit, ut ipsum invocemus: imò non semel testatur,hunc illi gratissimum cultum esse,si in angustijs constituti,ad illius opem fidis precibus cōfugiamus. Psal.50. Quis ergo metuet,ne precibus nostris offendatur Deus,qui ut ipsum precemur,passim iubet? Accedit his,quòd coram suprema Dei maiestate,nō seruorum instar aut hostium, sed ut amici,imò filij,comparemus. Per Christum enim filij Dei facti,adoptionis spiritum accepimus. qui eam animis nostris fiduciam inserit,ut Deum blandissimo patris nomine invocare nobis liceat. Num ergo dubitabimus,an pater tam pius & plenus misericordiæ, filios suos opis indigos & ad se clamantes, audire velit? Vel num nos Deo meliores putabimus, qui liliberorū nostrorū precib.aures facilè solemus accómodare? Matth.7.Quin potius omni metu posito,confidenter ad thronū gratię accedamus per Christū Iesum, qui nobis via ad hunc factus est.
units.tr: First, "this is the confidence," he says, "which we have toward him." He grants us confidence and the free power of approaching and praying to God, which certainly is joined with singular glory and praise. Those vain-glorious men are too proud who are accustomed to use the favour of the princes of this age so familiarly that access to them lies open whenever it pleases them. But how small, indeed how nothing, is this praise, if it is compared with that freedom and confidence by which we dare to come into the sight of God whenever need arises, and to ask for whatever is necessary? Nor should anyone think that John, using his own confidence, promises us the glory of so great a good. For this confidence has reasons on which it rests, solid, certain and altogether infallible. For God himself commands and constantly enjoins that we invoke him; indeed, he testifies more than once that this is most pleasing worship to him, if, being placed in distress, we flee with faithful prayers to his aid (Ps. 50). Who then will fear that God is offended by our prayers, when he commands us everywhere to pray to him? To these things is added that we approach the supreme majesty of God not as slaves or enemies, but as friends, nay, as sons. For having been made sons of God through Christ, we have received the spirit of adoption, who inserts into our minds such confidence that it is permitted us to invoke God by the most endearing name of Father. Shall we then doubt whether a Father so loving and full of mercy is willing to hear his sons, who need help and cry out to him? Or shall we think ourselves better than God, who readily lend our ears to the prayers of our little children? (Matt. 7). Rather, laying aside all fear, let us approach confidently to the throne of grace through Jesus Christ, who has been made the way to it for us.

units.la: Secundò,precandi fiduciæ aliud cóiungit Apostolus,nimirum quòd Deus nos audiat,& votorum cópotes faciat. Sunt enim,qui preces sibi fieri vtcunq; ferunt,sed inexorabiles, perinde faciunt,ac si surdis essent auribus. Et Epicuræi ferè Deum talem fingunt, quem rerū humanarū cu raminimè tangat,sed ad cœli cardines obambulans cœlestia sola gubernet. At scriptura nos à Deo audiri sæpe testatur,& promissiones sunt passim obuiæ,quibus hoc ipsum Deus confirmat.In le ge pollicetur, se exaudire peregrinos, viduas & pupillos ad se clamantes. Exod.22. Monet itè ne debitam mercedem mercenario denegantes illius preces contra nos prouocemus.Deut.24. Alibi docet,se priusquā clamemus,nobis respondere velle.Ifa.65.Christus subinde nos omnia acceptu ros promittit,quæcunq; in ipsius nomine petierimus.Ioan.14.& 16.&c.Exempla sunt item innu mera, quæ Deum promissionibus hisce nunquam defuisse testantur . Clamant ad Deum ex Ae-gypto Israelitæ,& mox exauditis assertorem & vindicem Mosem destinat. Exod.3. Tacitis suspi-rijs &gemitibus diuinam opem Moses ad mare rubrum inuocat,& mox audit:Quid clamas? &c. Exod.14.Idem precibus pijs Dei auxilium contra Amalekitas impetrat.Exod.17. Ad preces Eliæ cœlū aperitur & clauditur.Iac.5.3.Reg.18.Sed quid exemplis opus est, quando ipsi quotidie expe rimur,quanta sit precū piarum efficacia apud dominum? Nec enim quisquâ tam infelix & calami tofus est,qui non fateri cogatur, se multoties per dominum voti sui compotem factum esse.
units.tr: Secondly, the Apostle joins to confidence in prayer another thing, namely that God hears us and makes us possessors of our desires. For there are those who bear it somehow that prayers are made to them, but unyielding, and act as if they had deaf ears. And the Epicureans almost feign such a God as does not at all concern himself with human affairs, but, wandering about the poles of heaven, governs only heavenly things. But Scripture often testifies that we are heard by God, and promises everywhere met with confirm this very thing by God. In the Law he promises that he will hear strangers, widows and orphans who cry out to him (Exod. 22). Likewise he warns that by denying the due reward to the hireling we provoke his prayers against us (Deut. 24). Elsewhere he teaches that he is willing to answer us before we cry out (Isa. 65). Christ repeatedly promises that we shall receive all things whatever we ask in his name (John 14 and 16, etc.). There are likewise innumerable examples which testify that God has never failed these promises. The Israelites cry out to God from Egypt, and presently, their cry being heard, he appoints Moses as their defender and deliverer (Exod. 3). Moses, with silent sighs and groans, invokes the divine help at the Red Sea, and presently hears: "Why do you cry out?" etc. (Exod. 14). By pious prayers he obtains God's help against the Amalekites (Exod. 17). At Elijah's prayers the heaven is opened and shut (James 5; 1 Kings 18). But why is there need of examples, when we ourselves daily experience how great is the efficacy of pious prayers with the Lord? For there is no one so unhappy and afflicted who is not compelled to confess that many times through the Lord he has been made possessor of his desire.

units.la: Est tamen diligenter nobis obseruanda precandi regula,quâ Ioannes & breuem & omnibus numeris absolutâ præscribit.Deum enim in ijs nos exaudire dicit, quæ secundum ipsius volunta tem petimus.Quotquot ergo recte & piè,adhæc cū fructu orare volent, vota sua, adeoq; sese totos,diuinæ voluntati subijciant oportet. Equidè inter homines sic comparatū est,vt eorum volū tati nos accommodemus,quorū opem impetrare cupimus. Quantò magis ergo diuinam voluntatem nos in precibus obseruare conuenit,cuius nisi studiosissimi simus,frustra coram Deo compare bimus? Atqui voluntas Dei,quoad preces,in tribus potissimū versatur. Primò fidem à nobis re- quirit.Nam vt ingratæ nobis sunt eorum preces,quos de nostra beneuolentia dubitare nouimus: ita Deo placere nó possunt, qui inter precandū de ipsius vel volútate vel potétia dubitant. Quare Apostolus cū fide,omni hæsitatione deposita,orare iubet.Iac.1.Fides aut intelligitur,quę Chri sto fundamento inhæret:quia impossibile est, nos quicquam boni de Deo sperare, cū peccatores & morte digni simus,nisi in eū toti recumbamus,cuius merito pater nobis reconciliatus est. Ideo & Christus in suo nomine patrem precari iubet.Ioan.16. Et laudabilis est vetus ille ecclesiæ mos, quæ preces omnes Iesu Christi nomine claudit,ficq; testatur, cuius merito & intercessione confi dat. Secundò in precatione perseuerantia & indefesso studio opus est.Differt enim interdum po stulatam opē dominus,non quòd nos vel negligat,vel perditos velit: sed quòd fidè nostram exer ceri prodest,cuius virtus non nisi in aduersis conspici solet.Alienissima igitur à precibus debet es se temeraria præsumptio,qua Deo & tempus & modum auxilij præscribere quidà audet.Nostrū enim est,dominū expectare,& ipsi permittere omnè iuuandi rationem. Pertinet huc viduę exem plum,quo Christus orandi pertinax studiū nobis cõmendat. Luc.18. Tertium in precibus est, vt ea petamus quæ Deo digna sunt.Quia multos est inuenire,qui ea petunt,quæ nec Deus salua sua bonitate & iustitia dare posset,nec nobis prodessent accepta.Eius generis sunt,cum opes petimus libidinis & luxus irritamenta: cum corporis robur postulamus , quo ad voluptates inhonestas a-butamur:itè cum victorias contra proximum poscimus, quę nos beneficentia vincere & demere ri oportebat.Vt interim nihil de illis dicamus,qui palàm inhonesta & turpia postulare audét,quę à viro et matrona honesta petere puderet.Vbi causa patet,cur multorū preces minus exaudiatur. Sed optimè hic nobis Iesus Christus prospexit,dū breui & dilucida formula cõplexus est,quęcū que nos à Deo petere cõuenit.Huic si accommodemus preces nostras,nunquâ errabimus. Quòd si vero diuini nominis negligentes,& salutis nostræ securi,ea precamur, quæ carnis libidini adlu befcunt,non mirum est,si nec exaudimur à Deo,& insuper grauioribus malis inuoluimur.
units.tr: There is, however, a rule of prayer that we must observe carefully, and John sets it out briefly and complete in every respect. For he says that God hears us in those things which we ask according to his will. Whoever therefore wishes to pray rightly and devoutly, and moreover with profit, must submit his desires, and indeed himself entirely, to the divine will. Certainly among men it is so arranged that we accommodate ourselves to the will of those whose help we wish to obtain. How much more therefore ought we to observe the divine will in our prayers, and unless we are most diligent in this, do we not stand before God in vain? Yet the will of God, as regards prayers, chiefly concerns three things. First, it requires faith from us. For just as the prayers of those whom we know to doubt our goodwill are unwelcome to us, so those who doubt, while praying, either the will or the power of God, cannot please him. Therefore the Apostle bids us pray with faith, all hesitation laid aside. James 1. Faith is understood as that which clings to Christ as its foundation, because it is impossible for us to hope for anything good from God, since we are sinners and worthy of death, unless we lean wholly upon him, by whose merit the Father has been reconciled to us. Therefore Christ also bids us pray to the Father in his name. John 16. And that ancient custom of the Church is praiseworthy, which closes all prayers in the name of Jesus Christ, and so testifies whose merit and intercession it trusts. Second, prayer requires perseverance and tireless zeal. For the Lord sometimes postpones the help asked for, not because he neglects us or wishes us to perish, but because it profits us to exercise our faith, whose power is usually seen only in adversity. Therefore a presumption that prescribes to God both the time and the manner of help, which some dare to do, must be utterly foreign to prayer. For it is ours to wait upon the Lord and to leave to him every method of helping. The example of the widow pertains here, by which Christ commends to us a persistent zeal in prayer. Luke 18. Third, in prayers we ought to ask for those things which are worthy of God. For it is possible to find many who ask for things which God could not give, consistent with his goodness and justice, nor would they profit us if received. Of this kind are the requests when we seek wealth, the incentives of lust and luxury, when we ask for bodily strength by which we may be abused for dishonourable pleasures, and likewise when we ask for victories against our neighbour, which we ought to overcome and remove by beneficence. Not to mention those who openly dare to ask for things dishonest and shameful, which an honest man or woman would be ashamed to ask for. Here the reason is plain why the prayers of many are less heard. But Jesus Christ has provided for us most excellently here, since in a brief and clear formula he has comprehended whatever we ought to ask of God. If we fit our prayers to this, we shall never go wrong. But if, neglectful of the divine name and secure about our salvation, we pray for those things which cling to the lust of the flesh, it is no wonder if we are not heard by God, and moreover are entangled in graver evils.

units.la: Meditemur hæc nostro seculo fratres,quando vndique nos pericula circumstant,quibus non fortunæ modò nostræ & corpora, sed animæ ipsæ petuntur . Oppugnatur variè fidei Christianæ veritas & syncera religio.Instant seductores callidi . Grassantur armis & tyrannide aperti hostes. Hic firmi stemus,& in Christum omni fiducia posita,ardétibus precibus Dei opem imploremus, illius voluntati totos nos permittamus, regni Dei gloriæ studeamus , & hic vnus scopus fit,vt in terris vitam nostram Deo patri approbare,tandemq; carcere hoc liberati in cœlis viuere & regna re possimus cum Iesu Christo,saluatore & redemptore nostro vnico,cui debetur benedictio, glo ria,honor & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Let us consider these things, brethren, in our own age, when dangers surround us on every side, by which not only our fortunes and bodies but our very souls are sought. The truth of the Christian faith and sincere religion is assailed in various ways. Crafty seducers press on. Open enemies rage with arms and tyranny. Here let us stand firm, and, with all confidence placed in Christ, implore the help of God with burning prayers; let us commit ourselves wholly to his will, and strive for the glory of God's kingdom; and let this be our one aim, that we may approve our life to God the Father on earth, and at last, freed from this prison, may live and reign in heaven with Jesus Christ, our only Saviour and Redeemer, to whom belong blessing, glory, honour and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT V. HOMILIA XXXIIII. Si quis uiderit fratrem suum peccare peccatum non ad mortē, petet, & dabit ei uitam, peccantibus non ad mortem. Est peccatum ad mortem: non pro illo dico ut roges. Omnis iniquitas peccatum est: Et est peccatum non ad mortem.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. HOMILY XXXIV. If anyone sees his brother sinning a sin not unto death, he shall ask, and God will give him life for those who sin not unto death. There is a sin unto death: I do not say that you should pray for it. All unrighteousness is sin, and there is a sin not unto death.

units.la: QVemadmodum æterno diuinæ sapientiæ & bonitatis consilio statutum est, vt omnis humani generis iustitia, vita & salus in vno & solo Dei filio Iesu Christo, coprehensa esset, cum nos consortes & participes reddimur per fidem: ita vicissim communis noster hostis satan in hoc totus est, vt fidem nostram euertere, & hac euersa, nos à Christo Iesu vnico saluatore abstrahere posset. Nouit enim, sibi contra nos nihil licere, & vires nostras Dei beneficio plane inuictas esse, quoad Christo nitimur & petræ huic insuperabili inhæremus, contra quam nec portæ inferorum prævalent. Non temere ergo factum putemus, quod Ioannes apostolus tanto studio & dili-gentia in ijs tradendis versatur, quæ fidem in Christum spectant. Nec contentus multis ea hactenus expositsse, Epilogum epistolæ sic contexit, vt paucis repetat, quæcunque fidei perseueranti-am nobis commendare possunt. Commemorat autè præcipuos & maximè salutares fidei in Christum fructus. Inter hos primum locum vita æterna vel beatitudo obtinet, quam Christo teste, vel fide amplecti & seruare, vel diffidentia & Christi contemptu amittere oportet. Mar.16. Secundus fructus, vitæ & salutis huius certitudo est, cuius testimonium in animis nostris experimur, attestante conscientijs nostris spiritu Iesu Christi, quem is suis arrhabone salutis dare consueuit. Nec alia est religio aut persuasio hominum, quæ nos salutis certos reddere possit, nisi sola hæc, eò quod quicunque ex alio fonte biberit, iterum sitiet, &c. Ioan.4. Sequitur hunc fructum tertio loco precandi & quiduis à Deo impetrandi fiducia. Quia enim fide filij Dei efficimur, patet nobis ad patre aditus per Iesum Christum, qui hunc nobis reconciliauit: nec fallit promissione sua, qua ait: Quicquid petieritis patrem nomine meo, dabit vobis. Ioan.16. Sed transeamus ad præsentis loci consyderationem, quo fidei fructus quartus exponitur, quem tertij consequentem dicere licebit.
units.tr: As it was decided by the eternal counsel of divine wisdom and goodness that all the righteousness, life and salvation of the human race should be comprehended in the one and only Son of God, Jesus Christ, so that we become partakers and sharers in it through faith, so in turn our common enemy Satan is wholly intent on this: that he might overthrow our faith and, once it is overthrown, draw us away from Christ Jesus, our only Saviour. For he knows that nothing is permitted him against us, and that our strength is plainly invincible by God's benefit, so long as we lean upon Christ and cling to that unconquerable rock, against which the gates of hell do not prevail. Let us not think it happened by chance that the apostle John labours with such great zeal and diligence in delivering those things which pertain to faith in Christ. Not content to have expounded many of these matters so far, he has woven the epilogue of the letter in such a way that in a few words he repeats whatever can commend to us the perseverance of faith. He recalls, moreover, the chief and most salutary fruits of faith in Christ. Among these the first place is held by eternal life or blessedness, which, with Christ as witness, one must either embrace and keep by faith, or lose through distrust and contempt of Christ. Mark 16. The second fruit is the certainty of this life and salvation, the testimony of which we experience in our hearts, the Spirit of Jesus Christ bearing witness to our consciences, whom he is accustomed to give as the pledge of our salvation. Nor is there any other religion or persuasion of men that can make us certain of salvation, except this alone, because whoever drinks from another source will thirst again, etc. John 4. Following this fruit in the third place is confidence in praying and in obtaining anything whatever from God. For since we are made children of God by faith, the way to the Father lies open to us through Jesus Christ, who has reconciled us to him; nor does he fail in his promise, in which he says: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you. John 16. But let us pass on to the consideration of the present passage, in which the fourth fruit of faith is set forth, which may be called a consequence of the third.

units.la: I. Si quis uiderit fratrem suum peccare peccatum non ad mortem, petet, & dabit ei uitam, peccantibus non ad mortem. Videtur sic mihi dicere velle Apostolus: Magna & inæstimabilis est fidei nostræ dignitas, quòd in necessitate aliqua constituti preces nostras exaudiri scimus, quibus nobis[?]ipsis[?] o-pem & gratiam petimus à Deo patre. Sed maius multò bonum est, quòd non nobis modò, verum etiam alijs prodesse licet. Vt enim Christus Iesus nos pro fratribus orare iubet, ita preces pro illis factas Deus exaudire dignatur. Nec ea modò, quæ præsenti vitæ seruiunt & temporaria bona fratribus nostris impetrare, sed vitam & salutem animarum nostris precibus iuuare atque prouehere possumus. Nam si frater peccet, & in delicto aliquo non mortali volutetur, precando illi vitam & gratiam, vel peccati agnitionem & remissionem impetrare licebit. Si quem ergo nō proprię mo-dò, sed & aliorum salutis cura tangit, si quis beneficetiæ studio tenetur, fidem in Iesum Christum apprehendat, quę faciet, vt in re maxima, animarum videlicet salute fratribus prodesse queat.
units.tr: I. If anyone sees his brother sinning a sin not unto death, he shall ask, and God will give him life for those who sin not unto death. The apostle seems to me to wish to say this: Great and inestimable is the dignity of our faith, that, placed in some need, we know our prayers are heard, by which we seek help and grace for ourselves from God the Father. But it is much greater good that this benefits not only ourselves but also others. For just as Christ Jesus bids us pray for our brethren, so God deigns to hear the prayers offered for them. Nor can we obtain only those things that serve the present life and temporal goods for our brethren, but we can aid and advance the life and salvation of their souls by our prayers. For if a brother sins and wallows in some offence that is not mortal, it will be permitted to obtain for him, by prayer, life and grace, or the acknowledgment and forgiveness of sin. If, therefore, anyone is moved by care not only for himself but also for the salvation of others, if anyone is bound by the zeal of kindness, let him lay hold of faith in Jesus Christ, which will make him able to benefit his brethren in the greatest matter, namely the salvation of souls.

units.la: Ne quis tamen Apostolum temere hæc polliceri putet, prodest exempla videre, quæ passim in scripturis proponuntur. Posset autem hic vnus Moses sufficere, qui non semel Dei iram iustam & iamiam imminentem interitum, ab Israelitica gente fidis precibus auertit. Ad mare rubrum ani-mo ad dominum clamans exauditur, & per medium maris siccum & per omnia tutum transitum impetrat. Exod.14. Rursus durante prælio Amelekitico precibus suis victoriam apud Deum obtinet: & id quidem tam euidêter, vt nemo dubitare posset, quin precibus ipsius victoria deberetur. Quoties enim manibus demissis precádi officium intermittit, Amelekitarum vires crescunt, & victoria penes ipsos stare videtur. Quoties vero ad preces Moses redit, & manibus expansis clamat ad dominum, toties Israelitæ hostibus suis superiores fiunt. Exod.17. Voluit enim ceu oculari demonstratione docere Deus, quàti piorum preces facere soleat. Quid autem de illo dicemus, quòd cum idololatriæ peccato in vniuersum deleri meruisset populus, solus Moses pertinaci precu per seuerantia tanti peccati remissionem illis impetrat? Exod. 32. Pertinet huc Maria, quæ cum contra Mosem peccassef, & lepræ contagio esset infecta, eiusdem precibus pristinæ valetudini restituta esse legitur. Numer.12. Sed longum foret omnia Mosis huc afferre, quare pijs reliqua inuestigan-da permitto. Possunt huc adnumerari, qui per preces iam vita defunctos à mortuis reduxerunt, quod de Elisæo propheta, & Petro Apostolo scripturæ narrant. 4.Reg.4. Acto.9. Sed quid exempla coaceruare opus est, cum solius Christi præceptum sufficiat, qui non pro fratribus modò, verumetiam hostibus orare iubet. Nunquam enim id iuberet, nisi preces illas patri suo gratas & efficaces esse sciuisset.
units.tr: Lest anyone think the apostle promises these things rashly, it is useful to look at the examples which are set forth everywhere in the Scriptures. Yet this one Moses alone could suffice, who more than once, by faithful prayers, turned away from the Israelite nation God's just wrath and the destruction impending at any moment. At the Red Sea, crying out to the Lord in his heart, he is heard, and obtains a dry passage through the midst of the sea, safe in every respect. Exod. 14. Again, while the battle with Amalek was going on, he obtains victory from God by his prayers, and that so plainly that no one could doubt the victory was owed to his prayers. For as often as he let down his hands and ceased the office of praying, the strength of the Amalekites grew, and victory seemed to stand with them. But as often as Moses returned to prayer and cried to the Lord with hands outstretched, so often the Israelites became superior to their enemies. Exod. 17. For God wished to teach, as by an ocular demonstration, how much the prayers of the godly are wont to accomplish. But what shall we say of that, that when the people had deserved to be utterly destroyed for the sin of idolatry, Moses alone, by the steadfast perseverance of his prayer, obtained for them forgiveness of so great a sin? Exod. 32. To this belongs Miriam, who, when she had sinned against Moses and was infected by the contagion of leprosy, is read to have been restored to her former health by his prayers. Num. 12. But it would be long to bring all of Moses' examples here, so I leave the rest for the godly to investigate. Those may be counted here who, by prayer, brought back from the dead those already departed from life, as the Scriptures relate of the prophet Elisha and the apostle Peter. 4 Kings 4. Acts 9. But why is it necessary to heap up examples, when the precept of Christ alone suffices, who bids us pray not only for brethren but even for enemies? For he would never command this unless he had known those prayers to be pleasing and effectual to his Father.

units.la: Inter alia verò nos officij nostri locus hic admonet. Docet enim, Christianorum esse, ut non proprię modo, sed & aliorum salutis curam singuli habeant. Postulat hoc fraternitas, qua per Christum coniuncti sumus, & magis exigit arctior illa communio, quæ nos eiusdem corporis membra facit, idemque officium à singulis requirit, quod singula nostri corporis membra fideliter præstare videmus. Oculi certè non sibi solis vident, sed pro totius corporis salute inuigilant, imò pedibus, ne quando impingant, prospiciunt. Manus non sibi modò laborat, sed labore suo totum corpus alere & tueri satagit. Eadem aliorum membrorum omnium est ratio. Hoc ipsum ergo & nos faciamus, qui corporis Christi membra videri & dici volumus. Vides proximum tuum impegisse in via salutis, & hæsitare circa vitiorum & peccatorum scopulos. Vides eum à via vera exorbitasse, & per auia hinc inde errare. Vides eum peccati magnitudine & pondere pressum ad desperationem inclinare. Hic doctrina, admonitione & consilio opus est, ut misero & periclitanti subveniatur. Præcipit id in Lege Dominus, quando bovem proximi errantem ad suum herum reducere, & asinum ponderi succumbentem sublevare iubet. Exo. 23. Deut. 22. Et Christus fratrem qui peccavit, privatim primò, deinde adhibitis arbitris, tandem & publicè admoneri vult. Matth. 18. Quia verò admonendo & docendo nihil proficitur, nisi Dominus corda illuminet & trahat, & multorum non ea est vel authoritas vel ingenij dexteritas, ut hoc officij aliquo cum fructu præstare possint, preces simul iungendæ sunt, quibus à Deo eam gratiam expetamus, ut peccantem in peccati sui agnitionem perducere, pœnitentiæ veræ studio accendere, & commissa peccata benignus remittere dignetur. Sic Christum pro iis, à quibus crucifigebatur, orasse legimus. Luc. 23. Et exemplum Christi piè secutus est protomartyr Stephanus. Act. 7.
units.tr: Among other things, this passage admonishes us about our duty. For it teaches that it is the part of Christians that each one should have care not only for his own salvation but also for that of others. The fraternity by which we are joined through Christ demands this, and that closer communion which makes us members of the same body requires the same duty from each, which we see each member of our body faithfully performs. The eyes, surely, do not see for themselves alone, but keep watch for the salvation of the whole body; indeed they look out for the feet, lest at any time they stumble. The hand does not labour for itself alone, but by its labour strives to nourish and protect the whole body. The reasoning is the same for all the other members. Therefore let us also do this very thing, we who wish to be seen and called members of the body of Christ. You see your neighbour has stumbled on the way of salvation, and hesitates among the rocks of vices and sins. You see him strayed from the true way, and wandering here and there through trackless places. You see him, pressed by the magnitude and weight of sin, inclined to despair. Here teaching, admonition and counsel are needed, so that help may be given to the wretched and endangered man. The Lord commands this in the Law, when he bids us lead back to its owner the ox of our neighbour that has wandered, and help the ass that is sinking under its burden. Exod. 23. Deut. 22. And Christ wishes that a brother who has sinned be admonished first privately, then with witnesses added, and at last publicly. Matt. 18. But since nothing is gained by admonishing and teaching unless the Lord enlightens and draws hearts, and not many have either the authority or the skill of wit to perform this duty with any fruit, prayers must be joined at the same time, by which we seek from God that grace, that he would deign kindly to lead the sinner to the acknowledgment of his sin, to kindle him with the zeal of true repentance, and to forgive the sins committed. Thus we read that Christ prayed for those by whom he was crucified. Luke 23. And the first martyr Stephen piously followed the example of Christ. Acts 7.

units.la: Nec pro illis modò, quos peccatis iam implicitos videmus, orandum est, verumetiam pro omnibus aliis, qui labi poterant, & sæpe labuntur, nisi Domini gratia illos sustentet. Præterea, quorum lapsus graviores sunt, & reliquis etiam officere possunt, pro iis maiori studio precari convenit. Hinc est quod Paulus pro magistratibus, & omnibus, qui in eminentia constituti sunt, privatim & publicè preces fieri vult. 1. Timoth. 2. cap. Cuius officij Ieremias quoque eos, qui in Babylone iam captivi detinebantur, admonet, Ierem. 29. Et inter veteris ecclesiæ ritus non postremum commemorant ecclesiastici scriptores, quòd in publicis cœtibus pro Imperatorum Romanorum salute, pro imperij diuturnitate, & ipsis etiam inimicis suis orauerint. Nec enim fieri potest, ut sine publico malo rex peccet, & principum libidine fere regnorum incolumitas & pax publica turbari consueuit. Eadem ratione pro ministris verbi & ecclesiæ pastoribus orari debet: nimirum, ut ipsis detur sermo in apertione oris cum libertate, ut nota faciant mysteria evangelij, & loquantur sicut eos loqui oportet. Ad Ephesios 6. capite. Denique, sicut Iesus Christus non pro Apostolis modò, sed omnibus aliis orationem habuit: ita nos illius exemplum imitati, pro omnibus hominibus preces indefinentes fundere, & Deo Patri offerre debemus. Hæc enim sunt vera fidei in Christum exercitia, quæ & Deo placent, & inter homines maximorum bonorum causæ sunt, pœnitentiæ nimirum, emendationis morum, charitatis, concordiæ & pacis, sine quibus vita hæc subsistere nullo modo potest.
units.tr: Nor must we pray only for those whom we see already entangled in sins, but also for all others who could fall and often do fall, unless the grace of the Lord sustains them. Moreover, those whose lapses are more serious, and who can also harm others, it is fitting to pray for with greater zeal. Hence Paul wills that prayers be made privately and publicly for magistrates and for all who are set in high positions. 1 Timothy 2. This duty Jeremiah also enjoins concerning those who were already held captive in Babylon, Jeremiah 29. And among the rites of the ancient Church, the ecclesiastical writers record no small one: that in public assemblies they prayed for the safety of the Roman emperors, for the long duration of the empire, and even for their own enemies. For it cannot happen that a king sins without public harm, and by the lust of princes the safety of kingdoms and public peace are commonly thrown into disorder. By the same reasoning prayer must be made for ministers of the Word and pastors of the Church: namely, that speech may be given them in the opening of the mouth with boldness, so that they may make known the mysteries of the gospel and speak as they ought to speak. Ephesians 6. Finally, just as Jesus Christ prayed not only for the Apostles but for all others, so we, imitating his example, ought to pour out unceasing prayers for all men and offer them to God the Father. For these are the true exercises of faith in Christ, which both please God and are the causes of the greatest goods among men, namely repentance, amendment of morals, charity, concord and peace, without which this life cannot in any way subsist.

units.la: Prodest autem hæc cum nostri sæculi moribus conferre, ut quantum in re cumprimis necessaria hodie peccetur, agnoscamus. At nemo negabit, nos frigidissimos esse in eo studio, in quo nos feruentissimos esse oportebat. Nā quoad hostes & inimicos nostros, quibus à Deo Spiritu Sancto, cordis illuminatione, peccati agnitionem, & gratiam remissionis petere debebamus, contempto hoc nostro officio, plerunque vindictæ studio totos nos impendimus. Et ea est multorum insania, ne quid dicam gravius, ut hoc unum virile & magnanimum putent, si quis ipse sui vindex sit strenuus, nec aliquas sibi illatas iniurias inultas patiatur. Ubi potius Domini præceptum observare conveniebat, dicentis: Mihi vindictam, Ego retribuam. Deut. 32. Nec cogitant homines miserrimi, se dum suum ius animis tam acerbis persequuntur, sibi ipsis quàm maximè nocere. Nec enim dum taxat officium pietatis intermittunt, quod pro hostibus orare iubet, verumetiam preces, quas pro seipsis offerunt, exarmare & irritas facere solent. Siquidem Domino iubente oramus: Remitte nobis debita nostra, sicut & nos remittimus debitoribus nostris. Quę autē (proh dolor) nostra erit infelicitas, si eo iure contra nos uti volet Deus, quo nos in proximum ob leviculam aliquam iniuriam acceptam utimur. Certè, aut vindictæ cupiditatem deponere, & pro fratribus orare oportebit, aut nosipsos orando condemnabimus. Idem malum apparebit, si quales erga eos simus cosyderes, qui nullis nos iniurijs offenderunt, & quibus nullo modo hoc officij, quod modo præceptum est, negari debebat. Grassantur pasim poenæ, quibus mundi huius ingratitudinem & socordiam Deus castigat. Laborant egestate, & fame contabescunt domestici fidei nostrę. Bellorum rumores vbique locorum personant, & multi horribilem bellorum aleam experiuntur. Multi inter hæc mala omnia adhuc vitijs suis indormiunt, & carnis studia plane impœnitentes sectantur. Quis vero interea est, qui aliorum miserijs condoleat, qui cum plorantibus ploret, & lugeat cum lugentibus? Nonne ad omnem alienæ infelicitatis sensum obsurduimus, & dummodo nobis bene sit, securi contemnimus etiam totius vicinię incendium? Quotus vero quisque est, qui peccantes fratres ad moneat, hortetur, reprehendat, & in viam reducat, vel saltem precibus suis diuinæ bonitati & misericordię commendet? Illorum quidem ingens est numerus, qui fratrum vitia soliciti obseruant, accusant maligne, diffamât & calumniose obtrectant: quæ res odiorum, inuidiæ & inimicitiarum grauissimarum causa est maxima. Quòd si vero inspicias, quales in illos simus, quorum curæ publica salus commissa est, magistratus dico & verbi ministros, tam abest, vt iuxta Christi & Apostolorum præcepta illis bene velimus & bene precemur, vt nullum hominum genus nostro seculo plerisq; magis inuisum sit, quàm qui docendo & monendo Dei gloriam & multorum salute pro mouere studient. Quid ergo Dei irati fulmina & nouas quotidie calamitates admiramur, quando nulla est publicæ salutis cura hominibus?
units.tr: It is useful, however, to compare this with the customs of our own age, so that we may acknowledge how much sin is committed today in a matter especially necessary. Yet no one will deny that we are most cold in that zeal in which we ought to be most fervent. For as regards our enemies and adversaries, for whom we ought to ask of God, by the Holy Spirit and the illumination of the heart, the knowledge of sin and the grace of forgiveness, we, having despised this duty of ours, for the most part devote ourselves wholly to the zeal of revenge. And such is the madness of many (not to say anything more severe) that they think this alone manly and great-spirited: if someone is a vigorous avenger of himself and suffers no injury done to him to go unavenged. Yet here it was fitting to observe the Lord's precept, saying: "Vengeance is mine; I will repay." Deuteronomy 32. Nor do these most wretched men consider that, while they pursue their own right with such bitter spirits, they do the greatest harm to themselves. For they not only omit the duty of piety, which bids them pray for their enemies, but they are also wont to disarm and render void the very prayers which they offer for themselves. For we pray at the Lord's command: "Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors." But what (alas) will our unhappiness be, if God wishes to use against us the same right by which we use against a neighbour for some slight injury received? Certainly we must either lay aside the desire for revenge and pray for our brothers, or by praying we shall condemn ourselves. The same evil will appear if you consider how we stand toward those who have offended us with no injuries at all, and to whom this duty just prescribed ought in no way to have been denied. Punishments rage everywhere, with which God chastises the ingratitude and sloth of this world. Our household of faith labours in want and wastes away with hunger. Rumours of wars sound in every place, and many experience the dreadful hazard of war. Amid all these evils, many still slumber in their vices and plainly pursue the desires of the flesh without repentance. But who, meanwhile, is there who grieves at the miseries of others, who weeps with those who weep, and mourns with those who mourn? Have we not grown deaf to every sense of another's misfortune, and, so long as all is well with us, do we not carelessly disregard even the burning of the whole neighbourhood? And how few are there who admonish, exhort and rebuke their erring brothers and bring them back into the way, or at least commend them by their prayers to the divine goodness and mercy? Indeed there is a huge number of those who anxiously watch their brothers' faults, accuse them maliciously, spread reports against them and slander them with calumny: a thing which is the greatest cause of the most grievous hatreds, envies and enmities. But if you look at how we stand toward those to whom the public welfare has been entrusted, I mean the magistrates and ministers of the Word, we are so far from wishing them well and praying well for them, according to the precepts of Christ and the Apostles, that no kind of men is more hateful in our age than those who strive to promote the glory of God and the salvation of many by teaching and admonishing. Why then do we marvel at the thunderbolts of an angry God and the new calamities that daily befall us, when there is no care for the public welfare among men?

units.la: Porrò quia Ioannes pro illis preces nostras exaudiri dixit, qui peccant non ad mortē, idipsum pleniori declaratione opus habet, ne dum nostrę carnis iudicium audimus, in precibus nostris vel nimis temerarij, vel tepidiores simus. Hanc vero ipse Apostolus in sequentibus verbis subijcit.
units.tr: Furthermore, because John said that our prayers are heard for those who sin not unto death, this same point needs a fuller explanation, lest, while we hear the judgement of our own flesh, we be either too rash or too lukewarm in our prayers. The Apostle himself adds this in the following words.

units.la: I I. Est peccatum ad mortem, non pro illo dico ut roges. Ideo (inquit) pro illis preces fidelium efficaces fore dixi, qui peccant non ad mortem, quia peccatum, quod ad mortem vergit, veni-am & remissionem apud Deum nullam habet: pro quo qui precari vellet, operam omnem lude-ret, ea petendo quæ cum Dei iustitia, veritate & æternis decretis pugnant. Hic vero peccati natura & ratio nobis consyderanda venit, quam si perspectam habuerimus, nulla erit huius loci obscu-ritas, quæ multis & magna & offendiculi plena videtur. Paucis autem perstringemus quæ præsenti negotio seruiunt, omissis inutilibus & superuacaneis quorundam distinctionibus, quę rem per se claram obscuriorem reddunt.
units.tr: II. "There is a sin unto death; I do not say that you should pray for it." He says (so it runs) that the prayers of the faithful will be effective for those who sin not unto death, because a sin that tends toward death has no pardon or remission with God. Whoever wished to pray for such a sin would labour in vain, asking for things that fight against the justice, truth and eternal decrees of God. Here, however, the nature and reason of sin come to be considered by us; if we have grasped these, there will be no obscurity in this passage, which seems to many both difficult and full of stumbling-blocks. We shall, however, touch briefly on what serves the present matter, omitting the useless and superfluous distinctions of certain men, which make a matter clear in itself more obscure.

units.la: Peccatum est, quicquid vel facto vel dicto, vel etiam cogitando & concupiscendo, contra legem & verbum Dei committitur. Nolumus enim hic rem altius repetere, vt de natiua hominis corruptione vel originis peccato dicamus, cum in præsenti de actualibus duntaxat Apostolus loquatur. Quia autem Deus legem suam ea conditione proposuit, vt maledictione incurrat & mor-te dignus sit, quisquis non manserit in omnibus, quæ ab ipso præcipiuntur, Deut 27. constat omne peccatum, si per se æstimes, mortale & damnatione dignum esse. Nec probanda est scholasticorum distinctio, qui septem duntaxat fecerunt peccata mortalia, reliqua autem omnia venialia esse dixerunt. Quia enim singula cū lege Dei pugnant, singula etiam mortalia sunt, & propter vnumquod que homo damnari meretur, si iustitiæ suæ rigorem dominus sequi voluerit. Et qui septem mortalia peccata statuerunt, multis eius erroris causa fuerunt, quòd propria iustitia confisi sunt, eò quòd se à septem illis immunes esse putabant. Quòd si vero peccati atrocitatem recte cognita habeamus, & intelligamus, Originalem quoque illam noxam mortalem esse, nedum tristes eius peccatorum fructus, qui inde promanant, omnis intercidit nostræ iustitiæ fiducia, & ad Christum Iesum ardentiori studio cõuertimur, in quo solo venia & remissione peccati propositam habemus.
units.tr: Sin is whatever is committed against the law and Word of God, whether by deed or by word, or even by thinking and desiring. For we do not wish here to go back to the matter from a greater height, so as to speak of the natural corruption of man or original sin, since in the present place the Apostle speaks only of actual sins. But since God has set forth his law on this condition, that whoever does not remain in all things which are commanded by him incurs a curse and is worthy of death (Deuteronomy 27), it is established that every sin, if you judge it by itself, is mortal and worthy of condemnation. Nor is the distinction of the schoolmen to be approved, who made only seven sins mortal and said that all the rest were venial. For since each single sin fights against the law of God, each is also mortal, and on account of each one a man deserves to be condemned, if the Lord will follow the rigour of his justice. And those who laid down seven mortal sins were in many cases the cause of this error, because they trusted in their own righteousness, in that they thought themselves free from those seven. But if we rightly grasp the atrocity of sin, and understand that even that original harm is mortal, not only do the sad fruits of sins which spring from it, but all confidence in our own righteousness perishes, and we turn with more ardent zeal to Jesus Christ, in whom alone we have pardon and remission of sin set before us.

units.la: Quemobrem in hominibus potius peccati discrimen quæri debet, quo fit, vt aliud ad mortem perducat, aliud vero à morte alienum fit: & videbimus vnum idemq; peccatum aliis quidem damnationis & mortis causam esse, in aliis autem veniam mereri, imò etiam in bonum cedere: non quòd apud Deum fit personarum respectus, sed quòd varie affecti sunt erga Deum & legem ipsi us homines. Nam aliter peccant electi Dei & fideles, aliter infelices & peruersi huius mundi filij. Peccant fideles, & quidem grauissimè interdum. Sed peccatum mox vel ipsi agnoscunt, vel Dei verbum quo illud arguitur, admittunt, & ex illo de commisso crimine iudicant. Agnitum fatētur, dolent, & de pœnitentia serio cogitant. Adhæc per fidem ad Christum Iesum cõuertuntur, quem pro peccatis nostris sufficientem victimam esse firmiter credunt. Et si nihilominus peccata illorum digno aliquo supplicio Deus inuisat & corripiat, Dei patris manum & virgam patienter sustinent, totosq; se ipsius voluntati permittunt. Illi ergo, quia tales sunt, ad mortem non peccant. Habent enim Dei verbum, dicentis: Nolo mortem peccatoris, sed vt conuertatur & viuat. Ezech. 18. Habent Christum, qui pro ipsis peccatū factus est, vt ipsi eius merito iustitia Dei fieri possent. 2. Cor. 5. Et rursum cum Paulo intrepidi exclamant: Quis intetabit[?] crimina aduersus electos Dei? Deus est qui iustificat. Quis ille qui condemnet? Rom. 8. At longè alia est impiorum conditio, qui mundo semel addicti, illius seruitio se totos confecrarunt. Hi enim non contenti peccauisse, in peccatis etiam & malitia sua gloriantur, peccati atrocitatem agnoscere nolunt, verbum Dei, quo illa arguitur, odio habent & audire detractant. Accedunt his maiora, quod nec conscientias proprias audiunt, & spiritus sancti inspiratione conuicti, reclamant tamen, & agnitae veritati resistunt. Christi factum & meritum eius contemnunt: & tandem, vbi diabolus post diutinam conscelerationem peccata illis ob oculos statuit, vt ea contemnere non possint amplius, omni fide & consolatione vacui horribiliter desperant. Quicunq; ergo tales sunt, ad mortem peccant, nec aliter peccare possunt (quantumuis leuia sint interdum peccati ipsorum principia) cum & poenitentia & fide in Christum saluatorem careant. Alteri vero ad mortem peccare non possunt, quia per fidem in Christum a lapsu, quantumuis crebro & graui, resurgunt. Exempla sunt passim obuia in Veteri & nouo testamento, quibus res omnis declarari potest plenissime. Peccant Dauid & Saul, pares natione, conditione, & reliquis fere rebus omnibus. Vterque enim Israelita, & vterque ex vili conditione ad regnum diuina bonitate vocatus fuit. Et si peccata per se aestimes, grauius multo & atrocius quod a Dauide commissum fuit, apparebit. Sed longe diuersi sunt animi, quo fit, vt hic veniam impetret, alter infeliciter pereat. Saul enim, licet se contra Dei verbum fecisse negare non possit, culpae tamen suae grauitatem non agnoscit, nec fatetur. Deinde non de Dei, sed sua gloria solicitus est, & cum propheta in gratiam redire cupit, ne coram populo peccati accusatus, seditionem vel defectionem metuere cogatur. Nulla omnino apud hunc Christi mentio, nulla poenitentia, nulla contritio. Nec etiam poenae, quam iusto suo iudicio infert Deus, patiens est. Sed vbi alium diuinitus electum & vocatum audit, qui populi Dei sceptrum suscipiat, Dei iudicio pertinaciter sese opponit, quasi proprijs viribus contra Dei decretū regnum retinere posset. Quia ergo peccati modum nescit aliquem, noua indies peccata veteribus accumulat, vt Dei iudicium & merita poenas effugere possit, ad mortem peccat, quod infelici suo exitu satis testatū reliquit. Cum hoc si Dauidem conferas, longe alium inuenies. Peccat is contra communes Dei leges, quibus adulterium prohibetur, & contra regis officium, dum eius vxorem polluit, cuius famam, fortunas & vitam summa fide & studio tueri debebat: & suae libidinis impetum secutus adulterio iniustam viri optimi caedem adijcit. Sed Domini verbo per prophetam admonitus, non contradicit improbe, non suo honori, non regiae dignitati, non familiae metuit, sed quod Deo ingratus fuerit, quod eius gloria tam parui fecerit, quod illius legem spreuerit, maxime dolet. Se peccasse fatetur. Prophetam amat & colit, non propter praedictam poenam, vt rebellem & seditiosum, odit. Ad Deum conuersus multa se misericordia opus habere fatetur. Ad Christum respicit promissum saluatorem, cuius sanguine culpam suam expiari posse confidit. Et cum poenas exigeret Deus, non audacter nec improbe sese opponit, quamuis causa eius contra filium Absolonem esset iustissima. Sed discalceatus, & aperto capite, sponte urbem exit, conuitia & probra hostium patiens audit, sicq; Deo se castigandum praebet humiliter, cuius mandata & leges superbe contempserat. Eadem ratio inuenietur, si Iudae proditoris facinus & Petri lapsum inter se conferas.
units.tr: Therefore, among men one should rather seek the difference between sins, by which one sin leads to death while another is far from death. We shall see that one and the same sin is indeed a cause of damnation and death in some, but in others earns pardon, and even turns to good. This is not because there is respect of persons with God, but because men themselves are disposed in various ways toward God and his law. For the elect and faithful of God sin in one way, and the unhappy and perverse children of this world sin in another. The faithful do sin, and sometimes very gravely. But either they soon recognise the sin themselves, or they accept the word of God by which it is rebuked, and from it they judge the crime they have committed. Having acknowledged it, they confess it, they grieve, and they think seriously about repentance. Moreover, they turn through faith to Jesus Christ, whom they firmly believe to be the sufficient victim for our sins. And even if God nevertheless visits and chastises their sins with some deserved punishment, they patiently endure the hand and rod of God the Father, and wholly yield themselves to his will. Such people, therefore, because they are such, do not sin unto death. For they have the word of God, which says: "I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live." Ezek. 18. They have Christ, who was made sin for them, so that by his merit they might become the righteousness of God. 2 Cor. 5. And again, with Paul they boldly cry out: "Who shall bring any charge against the elect of God? It is God who justifies. Who is he that condemns?" Rom. 8. But the condition of the wicked is far different, who, once given over to the world, have wholly devoted themselves to its service. For they, not content to have sinned, even glory in their sins and their malice; they refuse to recognise the enormity of sin, they hate the word of God by which it is rebuked, and they reluctantly and unwillingly hear it. To these are added greater things: they do not listen to their own consciences, and though convicted by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, they nevertheless protest and resist the truth once acknowledged. They despise the deed and merit of Christ; and at last, when the devil, after long wickedness, sets their sins before their eyes so that they can no longer despise them, they, empty of all faith and consolation, despair in a horrible way. Whoever, therefore, are such, sin unto death, and they cannot sin otherwise (however slight the beginnings of their sins may sometimes be), since they lack both repentance and faith in Christ the Saviour. Others, indeed, cannot sin unto death, because through faith in Christ they rise again from a fall, however frequent and grave. There are examples everywhere, in the Old and New Testaments, by which the whole matter can be most fully declared. David and Saul sinned, equal in nation, condition, and almost all other respects. For both were Israelites, and both were called from a humble condition to the kingdom by the goodness of God. And if you consider the sins in themselves, what David committed will appear much graver and more atrocious. But their dispositions were far different, and so it happens that the one obtains pardon, while the other unhappily perishes. For Saul, although he cannot deny that he acted against the word of God, does not acknowledge or confess the gravity of his fault. Then he is concerned not for the glory of God but for his own, and he desires to be restored to favour with the prophet, lest, accused of sin before the people, he be compelled to fear sedition or defection. There is no mention of Christ at all in him, no repentance, no contrition. Nor is he patient of the punishment which God, by his just judgment, inflicts. But when he hears that another, divinely chosen and called, is to receive the sceptre of the people of God, he obstinately sets himself against the judgment of God, as if by his own strength he could keep the kingdom against the decree of God. Therefore, since he knows no measure of sin, he daily piles new sins upon old, so that he may escape the judgment and the merited punishments of God; he sins unto death, which he has sufficiently attested to by his unhappy end. If you compare David with this man, you will find him quite different. He sins against the common laws of God, by which adultery is forbidden, and against the duty of a king, while he defiles the wife of a man whose reputation, fortune and life he ought to have guarded with the utmost fidelity and care; and, following the impulse of his lust, he adds to the adultery the unjust slaughter of an excellent man. But admonished by the word of the Lord through the prophet, he does not contradict wickedly, he does not fear for his honour, his royal dignity, or his family; but he grieves most of all that he has been ungrateful to God, that he has valued his glory so lightly, that he has spurned his law. He confesses that he has sinned. He loves and reveres the prophet, and does not hate him as a rebel and seditious man on account of the punishment foretold. Turned to God, he confesses that he has great need of mercy. He looks to Christ, the promised Saviour, by whose blood he trusts his guilt can be expiated. And when God exacted punishment, he did not boldly or wickedly oppose it, although his cause against his son Absalom was most just. But barefoot and with head uncovered, he went out of the city of his own accord, patiently heard the insults and reproaches of his enemies, and so humbly offered himself to be chastised by God, whose commands and laws he had proudly despised. The same reasoning will be found if you compare the crime of Judas the traitor with the fall of Peter.

units.la: Horum diligens consyderatio satis docet, qui coram Deo venia digni sint, & pro quibus orari debeat, quiue incurabiles sint, nec precibus adiuuari possint. Quicunque enim infirmitate lapsi, peccata sua agnoscunt, fatentur, poenitent, & ad Christum conuersi remissionem sperant, hi ex electorum & fidelium numero sunt, qui ad mortem non peccant, imo peccata, vt & omnia alia, illis in bonum cooperantur. Hos nos precibus nostris apud Deum pro virili iuuare, nec vnquam de illis desperare debemus, quoad in Christi corpore, ecclesia videlicet, constantes permanent. Quotquot vero peccata sua agnoscere nolunt, eorundem atrocitatem negant, poenitentiae studium aspernantur, Christi meritum & doctrinam gratiae negligunt, non possunt non ad mortem peccare, quoad tales permanserint. Ideo de talibus apud prophetam dicitur: Tu ne oraueris pro populo isto. Ierem. 7. Item: Si expanderitis manus vestras, auertam oculos meos, &c. Isa. 1. Quicquid enim eiusmodi homines faciunt, simulato animo faciunt, nec serio de Dei gloria sunt soliciti. Quia tamen nostrum non est Dei iudicia altius scrutari, nec scire possumus, num semper incurabiles manent, qui nunc contumaciter peccant, non temere tanquam de desperatis pronunciandum erit, qui semel & iterum admonitiones pias & fideles spreuerunt, sed iuxta charitatis ingenium de omnibus bene sperandum est, nisi manifesta peccati in spiritum sanctum argumenta deprehendamus.
units.tr: A careful consideration of these things teaches sufficiently who are worthy of pardon before God, and for whom one ought to pray, and who are incurable and cannot be helped by prayers. For whoever, fallen through weakness, acknowledges his sins, confesses them, repents, and, turned to Christ, hopes for forgiveness, these belong to the number of the elect and faithful, who do not sin unto death; indeed, their sins, like all other things, work together for good for them. We ought to help these, as far as we can, with our prayers before God, and never despair of them, so long as they remain steadfast in the body of Christ, that is, in the Church. But as many as are unwilling to recognise their sins, deny their enormity, scorn the zeal for repentance, neglect the merit and teaching of grace in Christ, cannot but sin unto death, so long as they remain such. Therefore concerning such people it is said in the prophet: "Do not pray for this people." Jer. 7. Likewise: "If you stretch out your hands, I will hide my eyes from you," etc. Isa. 1. For whatever such people do, they do with a feigned mind, nor are they seriously concerned for the glory of God. Yet since it is not ours to search more deeply into the judgments of God, nor can we know whether those who now sin obstinately always remain incurable, we should not rashly pronounce them desperate, those who have once and again spurned pious and faithful admonitions; but in keeping with the nature of charity we must hope well of all, unless we detect clear signs of sin against the Holy Spirit.

units.la: III. Omnis iniquitas peccatum est. Et est peccatum non ad mortem. Habent haec formulā breuis Conclusionis, qua summatim comprehendit, quae ad peccati cognitionē faciunt. Omnis iniquitas, id est, quicquid praeter officiū vel in Deū vel proximū committitur, peccatū est, & si per se estimē tur, morte & damnatione dignū est. Nec enim aliud est peccati stipendiū q; mors. Rursus tamen in peccatis non desperent fideles : quia ijs qui sunt in Christo, nulla potest esse damnatio. Docent hæc de peccato rectius iudicare, quàm vulgò fieri soleat, dum plerique mortalium pecca-ta aut leuiora esse putant, quàm quibus tam grauiter irasci posse dominus : aut illorum atrocita-tem sic horrent, vt interim Christi iustitiæ & meriti obliuiscantur, ficq; desperent. Nostrum est, peccato nō blandiri, nec eius blanditias admittere. Quàm enim absurdum est, leue putare id quod non nisi filij Dei sanguine expiari potuit : Interim sciamus in Christo nobis omnem satisfactio-nem esse propositam, queq; facit, vt mortem nō inferant, quæ alioqui lethifera essent. Amplectamur ergo viva fide Iesum Christum, quæ hanc in nobis fiduciam parit, vt tâ pro nostris quàm fratrum peccatis Dei gratiam inuocare possimus. Oremus autem Deum patrem misericordiæ, vt omnibus nobis peccati cognitionem, pœnitentiæ studium, fidem veram & stabilem largiri velit, vt carnis carcere exempti, in cœlis cum Christo Iesu, filio suo, regnemus : cui debetur benedictio, gloria, honor & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: III. "All unrighteousness is sin, and there is sin not unto death." These words contain the form of a brief conclusion, by which is summarily comprehended what pertains to the knowledge of sin. All unrighteousness, that is, whatever is committed beyond one's duty either toward God or toward neighbour, is sin, and if it is considered in itself, it is worthy of death and damnation. For the wages of sin is nothing other than death. Yet on the other hand, the faithful should not despair over their sins, because for those who are in Christ there can be no condemnation. These things teach us to judge of sin more rightly than is commonly done, since most mortals either think sins are lighter than that the Lord could be so gravely angered by them, or so dread their enormity that in the meantime they forget the righteousness and merit of Christ, and so despair. It is our task not to flatter sin, nor to admit its flatteries. For how absurd it is to think light that which could be expiated only by the blood of the Son of God! Yet let us know that in Christ the whole satisfaction is set before us, and this makes it so that sins do not bring death, which otherwise would be deadly. Let us therefore embrace Jesus Christ with living faith, which begets in us this confidence, that we may invoke the grace of God both for our own sins and for those of our brothers. Let us pray to God the Father of mercy that he will be pleased to bestow on all of us the knowledge of sin, the zeal for repentance, and a true and steadfast faith, so that, freed from the prison of the flesh, we may reign in heaven with Christ Jesus, his Son, to whom belong blessing, glory, honour and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXV.
units.tr: HOMILIA XXXV.

units.la: Scimus, quòd omnis qui natus est ex Deo, non peccat: sed qui genitus est ex Deo, seruat seipsum, & malus ille non tangit eum. Scimus, quòd ex Deo sumus, & mundus totus in malo constitutus est.
units.tr: We know that everyone who is born of God does not sin; but he who has been begotten of God keeps himself, and that evil one does not touch him. We know that we are of God, and the whole world is set in evil.

units.la: POstquam D.Ioannes hac sua epistola diligenter tradidit fidem in Iesum Christum, eiusdem fidei fructus in Epilogo non minori diligentia commemorat. Scopus verò omnium hic vnus est, vt tot tamq; salutarium fructuum consyderatione animati, forti constantia in fide perseuere-mus, nec vllis tentationibus nos à Christo saluatore patiamur abstrahi. Posuit autem quarto loco eam precandi fiduciam, qua non nobis modò, verumetiam fratribus nostris subuenire, & ijs, qui in peccatum lapsi sunt, apud Deum gratiam & peccati remissionem impetrare possumus. Ibidem vt res postulabat, de peccato quædam dixit, docens omne quidem peccatum per se legis transgressionem esse, & æternæ mortis pœnam mereri : credentibus verò non ad mortem imputari pecca-ta,eò quòd per fidem in Christum ad pœnitentiam conuersi, cum Deo patri reconciliantur. Poterant hæc ab impuris & hostibus veritatis ficaccipi, quasi per euangelij prædicationem & fidem in Christum peccandi licentia plantetur. Cur enim à peccatis abstineat? cur carni molestus sit, & de syderia eius reprimat, qui peccatum sibi exitiale non esse credit? Et nostro seculo, non eos modò audimus, qui euangelij doctrina bonos mores corrumpi & securam quiduis audendi licentiam & impunitatem inuehi clamant : verumetiam phanaticos multos vidimus, qui peccata turpissima committentes, ea tamen nihil ad se pertinere dicebant, eò quòd illa carnis opera essent, cui illi iam olim renunciassent, nec nisi spiritu viuerent. Quasi verò, qui carni renunciauit, nō simul eandem crucifigat & mortificet, vt spiritui Christi & obedientiæ fidei tota subijciatur. Cæterum, quia tam impudens calumniandi audacia Apostolos Christi minimè latere potuit, multi in hoc sunt, vt demonstrent: fide in Christum non peccatorum impunitatem & effrenem licentiam, sed potius iuge & indefinens pœnitentiæ studium, plantari. Quod ipsum & Ioannes in præsenti paucis docet, qui fidei in Christum Iesum quintus fructus est, in cuius consyderatione vtinam sic versarentur, vt ex hoc pro verè fidelibus agnosci possent, qui Christo & fide nunquam non gloriantur.
units.tr: After St John had carefully set out in this letter the faith in Jesus Christ, in the Epilogue he recounts the fruits of that same faith with no less care. The aim of all of this is one: that, animated by the consideration of so many and so great saving fruits, we may persevere in faith with strong constancy, and not allow ourselves to be drawn away from Christ our Saviour by any temptations. He has placed fourth the confidence in prayer by which we are able to help not only ourselves but also our brothers, and to obtain from God grace and forgiveness of sin for those who have fallen into sin. In the same place, as the matter required, he spoke somewhat about sin, teaching that every sin is indeed in itself a transgression of the law and deserves the penalty of eternal death; but that sins are not imputed to unto death for those who believe, since, turned to repentance through faith in Christ, they are reconciled with God the Father. These things could be taken up by the impure and the enemies of the truth as though, through the preaching of the gospel and faith in Christ, a licence to sin were being planted. For why should he abstain from sins? Why should he be harsh to the flesh and restrain its desires, if he who believes sin is not deadly for him? And in our own age we hear not only those who cry out that good morals are corrupted by the doctrine of the gospel, and that a secure licence to dare anything and impunity are being introduced; we have also seen many fanatics who, committing the most shameful sins, nevertheless said that these had nothing to do with them, because they were works of the flesh, to which they had long since renounced, and that they lived only by the Spirit. As if he who has renounced the flesh does not at the same time crucify and mortify it, so that he may be wholly subject to the Spirit of Christ and to the obedience of faith. Moreover, since such shameless boldness in slandering could not escape the notice of the apostles of Christ, many are at pains to show that faith in Christ plants not impunity for sins and unbridled licence, but rather a continual and unceasing zeal for repentance. This very thing John also teaches briefly in the present passage, which is the fifth fruit of faith in Christ Jesus; would that they might so occupy themselves with its consideration that from this they could be recognised as truly faithful, who never cease to glory in Christ and in faith.

units.la: I. Scimus, quòd qui ex Deo natus est, non peccat. Sed qui genitus est ex Deo, seruat seipsum, & malus ille non tangit eum. Cohærent hæc pulchrè præcedentibus. Sic enim dicit: Audiuistis, peccata esse quæ non tendunt ad mortem, qualia sunt quæcunque à verè credentibus per carnis infirmitatem committuntur. At nolim mea hæc quisquam sic accipiat, quasi sub fidei & Christi prætextu impunè peccare possimus. Peccandi enim licentia à fidei ingenio tam aliena est, vt non possint peccare, quicunq; per hanc regeniti, & filij Dei facti sunt. Nam quia Deo patri placere studeant, soliciti & anxij plane se ab omni labe custodiunt, talesq; se præbent, vt improbus ille humani generis hostis satan nihil in illos iuris & imperij obtinere possit. Sed prodest singula quæ ab Apostolo dicuntur, penitius inspicere.
units.tr: I. We know that he who is born of God does not sin. But he who has been begotten of God keeps himself, and that evil one does not touch him. These words fit beautifully with what goes before. For he says thus: You have heard that there are sins which do not tend to death, such as whatever is committed by those who truly believe through the weakness of the flesh. But I would not wish anyone to take my words as though under the pretext of faith and Christ we could sin with impunity. For a licence to sin is so alien to the nature of faith that those who have been born again through it and made sons of God cannot sin. For since they earnestly desire to please God the Father, they clearly guard themselves anxiously and carefully from every stain, and they so conduct themselves that that wicked enemy of the human race, Satan, can obtain no right or rule over them. But it is useful to look more deeply into the individual things the Apostle says.

units.la: De ijs loquitur, qui ex Deo nati sunt: quod non de Creatione, quæ omnibus hominibus, imò etiam brutis & inanimatis ex Deo communis est, sed regenerationis mysterio debet intelligi: iuxta quod soli fideles ex Deo nati & Dei filij esse dicutur. Nam si hominem, qualis sua natura est, consyderes, videbis, omnes nos peccatores esse, & quoad nos, æternæ mortis supplicium mereri. In peccatis enim concipimur & nascimur, sicut de seipso regius ille Psaltes testatur. Psal. 51. Qua corruptione fit, ut & intellectus noster non capiat ea quæ sunt spiritus Dei, & voluntas à Dei voluntate alienissima sit, & vires in nobis nullæ reperiantur, quibus ea exequamur, quæ Deo placent, & quæ per nos fieri postulat. Fateantur hoc oportet, quicunq; in semetipsos paulo altius descenderint, & remoto philautiæ velo cupiditates & actiones suas ad Dei verbum vel legis regulã examinarint. Nec aliquis est, qui suis viribus ab hac corruptione liberari aut alterius ope adiuuari possit. Quia filij Dei non ex sanguinibus, neque ex voluntate carnis, nec etiam ex voluntate viri, sed ex ipso Deo nascuntur. Ioan. 1. Ut enim tuus filius non erit, nisi qui ex te natus fuerit: ita nec Dei filij verè dici possunt, nisi quos ipse Deus, ut tales essent, genuit. Is verò tales per Christum Iesum, filium suum naturalem (si ficloqui licet) & sibi coæternum generat. Siquidem is immortale illud regenerationis semen, verbum scilicet Dei, animis suorum inserit, idemq; spiritus sui gratia & operatione viuificat, quo fit ut fructus sequantur, qui hominem innouatum & planè alium factum esse testentur. Quicunq; enim paulò ante spiritualia non capiebat, verbo & spiritu Christi illuminatus, Deum agnoscit, voluntatem Dei intelligit & tota mente in mysteriorum regni dei consyderatione versatur. Adhæc, qui voluntate habebat à dei voluntate diuersissimâ, mox mutatus ijs oblectatur, & ea velle incipit, quæ deo placere possunt. Idemq; viribus nouis se instructum sentit, ut qui antea totus languebat, & se miserum esse clamabat, nunc omnia possit in Christo Iesu, qui ipsum confortat. Phil. 4. Quia verò Christum Iesum & verbum eius fide ample&timur, fide etiã regenerari dicimur, & filij dei sunt, quicunq; in Christum credunt, iuxta illud Apostoli: Quotquot illum receperunt, dedit eis ut liceret filios dei fieri, videlicet his qui crediderint in nomen ipsius. Ioan. 1. Quæcunq; ergo de filijs dei tâ hic quàm alibi in scripturis dicuntur, de solis credentibus in Christum debent intelligi.
units.tr: He speaks of those who have been born of God; which must be understood not of creation, which is common to all men, indeed also to brute and inanimate things, from God, but of the mystery of regeneration; according to which only the faithful are said to be born of God and to be sons of God. For if you consider man as he is by nature, you will see that we are all sinners, and, as far as we are concerned, deserve the punishment of eternal death. For we are conceived and born in sins, as that royal Psalmist bears witness of himself. Ps. 51. By this corruption it comes about that our understanding does not grasp the things of the Spirit of God, and our will is utterly alienated from the will of God, and no powers are found in us by which we might carry out those things which please God, and which he requires of us. All who have descended a little more deeply into themselves, and, with the veil of self-love removed, have examined their desires and actions by the word of God or the rule of the law, must acknowledge this. Nor is there anyone who can be freed from this corruption by his own strength, or helped by the aid of another. Because the sons of God are born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God himself. John 1. For just as your son will not be yours unless he has been born from you, so also they cannot truly be called sons of God unless God himself has begotten them so that they might be such. He, however, begets them as such through Christ Jesus, his natural Son (if it is permitted so to speak), and co-eternal with himself. For he implants that immortal seed of regeneration, namely the word of God, into the souls of his own, and enlivens the same by the grace and operation of his Spirit; whence it comes about that fruits follow which bear witness that the man has been renewed and has become altogether another person. For he who previously did not grasp spiritual things, being illuminated by the word and Spirit of Christ, acknowledges God, understands the will of God, and with his whole mind occupies himself with the consideration of the mysteries of the kingdom of God. Moreover, he who had a will most opposed to the will of God, being soon changed, takes delight in these things, and begins to will those things which can please God. And he feels himself furnished with new powers, so that he who before was altogether weak, and cried out that he was wretched, can now do all things in Christ Jesus, who strengthens him. Phil. 4. But since we are clothed with Christ Jesus and his word by faith, we are also said to be regenerated by faith; and all who believe in Christ are sons of God, according to that saying of the Apostle: As many as received him, to them he gave the power to become sons of God, namely to those who believe in his name. John 1. Whatever therefore is said here and elsewhere in the Scriptures about the sons of God must be understood of those who believe in Christ alone.

units.la: Quid verò de illis pronunciat? Scimus (inquit) quòd qui ex deo natus est, nõ peccat. At paulò antè scripsit: Si quis viderit fratrem peccâtem, oret pro eo. Et supra Cap. 1. ait: Si dixerimus, nos non habere peccatum, nos ipsos fallimus, & veritas in nobis non est. Item: Si dixerimus, non peccauimus, mendacem facimus Deum, & sermo eius non est in nobis. Num ergo sibijpsi contradicit Apostolus, cum modò fidelem peccare neget? Nequaquam: sed peccandi verbo bifariã utitur.
