Primò enim per peccatum omne illud intelligit, quod contra legem & voluntatem dei, siue dicto siue facto, committitur, & sic omnes nos peccatores esse pronunciat, quia in multis labimur omnes, & iustus quoq; in die cadit septies. Iac. 3. Prouerb. 24. Omnibus ergo nobis & Christo saluatore, & mutuis precibus opus est. Rursum verò peccatum pro deuoto peccandi studio & incurabili licentia sumitur, quæ impios exagitat, & damnationem sempiternã meretur. Hi enim non contenti pec cauisse (ut nuper diximus) in peccatis etiã gloriantur, superbiunt, & gaudent cum malè fecerint. Hoc ab ijs, qui per fidem renati sunt, alienissimum est. Quia enim filij dei sunt, deo patri placere studient. Non possunt ergo illis non displicere, quæcunq; contra eius voluntatem abs se & alijs videt esse commissa. Et ut per carnis infirmitatem quotidie impingunt: ita iugem & indefinentem pœnitentiam exercent, ne peccatorum cœno toti immergantur. Peccare igitur se agnoscunt, sed peccato seruire & viuere non possunt, eò quòd peccato mortui cum Christo ad vitæ nouitatem resurrexerunt. Rom. 6. Constat ergo ex Apostoli verbis, fideles & dei filios non esse, quotquot deuotis animis peccandi studium sectantur & pœnitentiam admittere nolunt.
units.tr: But what does he pronounce about those? We know (he says) that he who is born of God does not sin. Yet a little before he wrote: If anyone sees his brother sinning, let him pray for him. And above, in chapter 1, he says: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. Likewise: If we say that we have not sinned, we make God a liar, and his word is not in us. Does the Apostle then contradict himself, when he now denies that the believer sins? By no means: but he uses the word sin in a twofold way. For first, by sin he understands everything which is committed against the law and the will of God, whether in word or in deed; and thus he declares that we are all sinners, because we all slip in many things, and the righteous man falls seven times a day. James 3. Proverbs 24. Therefore all of us need both Christ the Saviour and mutual prayers. On the other hand, sin is taken for a devoted zeal for sinning and an incurable licence, which harasses the impious and deserves eternal damnation. For these, not content to have sinned (as we said recently), even glory in their sins, pride themselves, and rejoice when they have done evil. This is most alien to those who have been reborn through faith. For since they are sons of God, they earnestly strive to please God the Father. Therefore whatever they see to have been committed by themselves and by others against his will cannot fail to displease them. And as they stumble daily through the weakness of the flesh, so they exercise a continual and unceasing repentance, lest they be wholly immersed in the mire of sins. They therefore acknowledge that they sin, but they cannot serve sin and live in it, because, dead to sin, they have risen with Christ to newness of life. Rom. 6. It is clear therefore from the words of the Apostle that all who pursue the zeal for sinning with devoted minds, and are unwilling to admit repentance, are not faithful and not sons of God.

units.la: Cæterum non contentus ostendisse quid non faciant fideles, simul etiam quid faciant & quibus studijs occupati sint, indicat. Qui ex Deo genitus est (ait) seruat seipsum, & malus ille eum non tangit. Seruat seipsum, id est, custodiam sibi ponit, & in dei timore atque reuerentia sese continet, ne peccandi libidine abreptus, à gratia dei excidat. Quia enim vita hæc perpetuæ militiæ, vel feruentis Oceani & tempestatis instar est, fidelis ceu in specula constitutus, omnes mundi & principis ipsius assultus solicitè obseruat, ne forte ex gradu suo deijciatur, vel hosti tâ improbo aliquid contra se agendi occasionem præbeat. Procul igitur à Dei filijs abest securitas, quæ multos à via salutis transfuersos rapit, & inextricabilibus vitiorum laqueis implicat. Apostoli enim præceptum nunquam non obseruant, qui nos in timore & tremore salutem nostram operari iubet. Phil. 2.
units.tr: Moreover, not content to show what the faithful do not do, he also indicates what they do and with what pursuits they are occupied. "He who has been born of God," he says, "keeps himself, and that evil one does not touch him." He keeps himself: that is, he sets a guard over himself and restrains himself in the fear and reverence of God, lest, carried away by lust for sin, he fall from the grace of God. For this life is like perpetual warfare, or like a raging ocean and storm; the faithful man, as if stationed on a watchtower, carefully observes all the assaults of the world and of its prince himself, lest perhaps he be thrown from his place, or give such a wicked enemy any opportunity to act against him. Far from the sons of God, therefore, is that security which carries many off track from the way of salvation and entangles them in the inextricable snares of vices. For those who obey the precept of the Apostle never fail to observe it, the one who bids us work out our salvation in fear and trembling. Phil. 2.

units.la: Nemo tamen hoc ita accipiat, quasi nostrarum virium sit, nosipsos seruare & custodire quo minus peccemus. Quid enim hic homo faciat, qui in peccato conceptus & natus, peccati legem in membris suis sentit, quæ ipsum, inuito quoq; & multum reluctante spiritu Christi, captiuum ducit? Rom. 7. Miserum certè & deploratum præsidium, si ex nobis dependet nostræ salutis custodia. Non ædificat domum qui laborat, sed dominus qui laboribus illius benedicit. Frustra excubias agunt vigiles, nisi Dominus ciuitatem custodierit. Psalmo 127. Et in salutis negotio tantum sibi aliquis tribuere audebit, quasi hic sibi ipsi sufficiat, seq; ab interitu praeseruare possit? Sciamus ergo, solius Dei esse nostrae salutis custodiam, qui nisi suo spiritu nos ducat, sustineat & regat, ex nobis ipsis nihil nisi peccare possumus. Ideo Christus discipulos patri commendat, dicens: Serua eos per nomen tuum, quos dedisti mihi. Item: Serua eos a malo. Ioan. 17. Eius ergo opem & nos inuocare conuenit, & ab illo petere principalem illum & regium spiritum, qui mundi illecebras calcare, carnis lasciuia coercere, & peccati vires infringere possit. Iungatur precibus ardes verbi Dei studium, quod nobis lucernā fecit Deus, qua in mundi tenebris dirigamur. Interim quicquid boni à nobis prodierit, omne hoc Dei gratiae solidum tribuamus, nec in nobis, sed in illo solo gloriemur.
units.tr: Yet no one should take this as meaning that it lies within our own powers to keep and guard ourselves so that we do not sin. For what can this man do, who, conceived and born in sin, feels the law of sin in his members, which leads him captive, even though the Spirit of Christ is unwilling and strongly resists? Rom. 7. Miserable indeed and desperate would be that protection, if the keeping of our salvation depended on us. "Unless the Lord builds the house, those who labour build it in vain; unless the Lord guards the city, the watchmen keep vigil in vain." Ps. 127. And will anyone dare to ascribe so much to himself in the business of salvation, as if he were sufficient for himself and could preserve himself from perishing? Let us know, therefore, that the keeping of our salvation belongs to God alone, who, unless he leads us by his Spirit, sustains and rules us, we can do nothing from ourselves but sin. Therefore Christ commends his disciples to the Father, saying: "Keep them through your name, those whom you have given me." Likewise: "Keep them from evil." John 17. It is fitting, then, that we also call upon his help and ask of him that principal and kingly Spirit, who can trample down the allurements of the world, restrain the wantonness of the flesh, and break the strength of sin. Let the zeal for the Word of God, which God has made a lamp for us to guide us through the darkness of the world, be joined to our prayers. Meanwhile, whatever good comes forth from us, let us ascribe all of it wholly to the grace of God, and let us glory not in ourselves but in him alone.

units.la: Addit his alterum quoque Apostolus: Et malus ille non tangit eos, id est, non laedit, non sic inuadit, vt perdat. Cupit quidem & illos perdere, quia homicida est, & semper ceu leo rugiens quaerit quem deuoret. Sed vt in Christum Iesum, qui caput nostrum est, nihil iuris habet: ita nec in fideles, qui Christi sumus membra. Nulla enim damnatio his, qui sunt in Iesu Christo. Roman. 8. In Aegypto olim illorum primogenita caedebat vastator angelus, quorum limini sanguis agni aspersus non erat. At quia nobis Christi sanguis aspersus est, & per hunc a peccatorum sordibus abluti sumus, manum in nos extendere non audet hostis ille quantumuis crudelis & improbus. Potest huc referri, quod in Apocalypsi signantur serui Dei nostri, ne illis noceant, quibus nocendi potestas data est. Apocal. 8. Et ij duntaxat damnandi esse dicuntur & plagis subiacent, qui beatiae characterem acceperunt. Apocal. 16. & 19. Hoc ergo soletur nos contra satanae artes & conatus improbos, quod illi nihil contra nos licere scimus, nisi permittente domino, qui cum fidelis sit, non finit nos tentari supra id, quod ferre possumus. 1. Corinth. 10. Resistamus fortes in fide hosti nostro diabolo, & fugiet à nobis. Iac. 4. Idem facere solet, quod Thrasones & Thrasycatarchae, qui vbi se metui sentiunt, horrendum in modum saeuiunt & caelum terrae miscere velle videntur. At vbi in eos incidunt, qui minis eiusmodi assueuerunt, & forti animo iniuriam & insolentiam abs se repellunt, illico perterriti minas intermittunt, & maximos nebulones se esse declarant, qui paulo ante viri videbantur fortissimi. Ita hostis noster satan, licet Christi potentia & merito deuictus sit & exarmatus, vult tamen aliquis videri, & ijs quoq; negotium facere audet, in quos sibi nihil licere novit: quos modo ꝑmissis, modo minis petit. Quod si infirmiores cedat, illorū infirmitate ipse vires colligit, & quotidie ferocior redit. Vbi vero eosdē animis receptis sese fortiter opponere videt et suas artes detectas intelligit, fuga molitur, et in media pugna conatū suū intermittit, q paulo ante victor videbatur. Quoties ergo ille pollicetur, mendacē esse cogita, nec quicquā praestare posse. Quoties minatur, victū esse intelligas, nec illi ius esse, vt illis manus inijciat, quos Christus redemit. Sūt enim in omnipotentis illius pastoris tutela, qui oues suas manibus suis eripi non patitur. Ioan. 10.
units.tr: The Apostle adds to these another point: "And that evil one does not touch them"; that is, he does not harm them, does not attack them so as to destroy them. He indeed desires to destroy them too, because he is a murderer, and always, like a roaring lion, seeks whom he may devour. But just as he has no right over Christ Jesus, who is our Head, so neither has he over the faithful, who are members of Christ. "For there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus." Rom. 8. In Egypt of old the destroying angel struck down the firstborn of those whose doorposts were not sprinkled with the blood of the lamb. But because the blood of Christ has been sprinkled on us, and through him we have been washed from the filth of sins, that enemy, however cruel and wicked he may be, does not dare to lay his hand upon us. This may also be applied to what is signified in the Apocalypse, that the servants of our God are sealed, so that they may not be harmed by those to whom power to harm has been given. Apoc. 8. And those alone are said to be condemned and subject to plagues who have received the mark of the beast. Apoc. 16 and 19. Let this therefore comfort us against the arts and wicked attempts of Satan: we know that he is allowed nothing against us except by the permission of the Lord, who, being faithful, does not allow us to be tempted beyond what we are able to bear. 1 Cor. 10. "Resist your enemy the devil, standing firm in the faith, and he will flee from you." James 4. He does just what the braggarts and boasters do: when they sense that they are feared, they rage in a dreadful manner and seem ready to mix heaven with earth. But when they meet those who are accustomed to such threats, and who with a brave spirit repel the injury and insolence from themselves, at once they, struck with terror, drop their threats and declare themselves the greatest scoundrels, who a little before seemed the bravest of men. So our enemy Satan, although he has been conquered and disarmed by the power and merit of Christ, still wishes to seem something, and dares to trouble even those over whom he knows he has no right; he attacks them now with promises, now with threats. But if they yield at all, he gathers strength from their weakness and returns each day more fierce. Yet when he sees that they have taken courage and are bravely setting themselves against him, and understands that his arts have been detected, he takes to flight and abandons his attempt in the middle of the battle, he who a little before seemed the victor. Whenever he promises, therefore, think that he is a liar and cannot deliver. Whenever he threatens, know that he is beaten, and that he has no right to lay hands on those whom Christ has redeemed. For they are under the protection of that almighty Shepherd, who does not allow his sheep to be snatched from his hands. John 10.

units.la: II. Scimus quod ex Deo sumus, & mundus totus in malo constitutus est. Pertinent haec ad explicationem eorum quę dixit, & occultā habent exhortatiunculā ad innocentiae & sanctimoniae studium. Sunt enim qui facile concedunt, quęcunq; hactenus de fide virtute dixit Apostolus. Fatentur fide nos filios Dei fieri, & ea gratia donari, ne peccemus ad mortē. Haerent autem in eo, quod dubitant num filij Dei sint, & ex eorum numero, quos pater in filio suo Iesu Christo saluare decreuit. Terrentur insuper mundi exemplo, quem per omnia corruptum esse, & damnationi subiacere vident. Metuunt ergo, ne vniuersalis totius mundi corruptio ipsis quoque noceat, & aliquam inijciat salutis ipsorum remoram. Quid enim (inquit) in meam gratiam faceret Deus? Num pauculos nos aliquo priuilegio dignabitur, toto mundo, vt par est, pereunte? Caeterum cogitationibus hisce paucula haec opponit Ioannes, quae vt breuia sunt, ita consolationem singularem & eximiam continent. Scimus (inquit) quod ex Deo sumus, & mundus totus in malo constitutus est. Magna est in Apostoli verbis gravitas, & sancta confidentia. Nec enim se meliu s quiddam sperare, aut opinari dicit: sed Scimus, inquit. Quasi dicat: Dubitent de salute & gratia Dei qui fide carent: metuant mundi consceleratione m, & ignorent salutis viam, quicunque huic coniuncti sunt. Alia longe & potior multo est nostra conditio. Quia enim fide in Christum habemus, per eandem spiritū Christi accepimus, qui in animis nostris de Dei gratia & regni caelorum haereditate nobis testimonium fert, & salutis nostrae arrhabo est. Per hunc instructi, scimus, nos ex Deo natos esse, nec dubitare possumus, cum filio Dei vnigenito iubente ad illum clamemus, Pater noster qui es in caelis, &c. Non moramur ergo infelicem hunc mundum, qui vt totus in malo constitutus est, & suae malitiae poenas aliquando sustinebit: ita nobis nocere non poterit, quos ab eius commercio Christus iam olim seperauit. Ioan. 15.
units.tr: II. "We know that we are from God, and the whole world is set in evil." These things pertain to the explanation of what he has said, and they contain a hidden little exhortation to the zeal for innocence and holiness. For there are some who readily grant whatever the Apostle has said so far about faith and virtue. They confess that by faith we become sons of God, and are given that grace so that we do not sin unto death. But they stick at this, that they doubt whether they are sons of God, and among the number of those whom the Father has decided to save in his Son Jesus Christ. Moreover, they are terrified by the example of the world, which they see to be corrupt in every way and subject to damnation. They fear, therefore, lest the universal corruption of the whole world may harm them too, and place some hindrance to their salvation. "For what," they say, "would God do for my sake? Will he deign to grant a privilege to a few of us, while the whole world, as is fitting, perishes?" But John opposes to these thoughts a few words, which, as they are brief, so they contain an singular and outstanding consolation. "We know," he says, "that we are from God, and the whole world is set in evil." There is great weight and holy confidence in the Apostle's words. For he does not say that he hopes or supposes something better; but "We know," he says. As if he were saying: let those who lack faith doubt about the salvation and grace of God; let them fear the wickedness of the world; let those who are joined to it be ignorant of the way of salvation. Our condition is very different and far better. For since we have faith in Christ, through the same faith we have received the Spirit of Christ, who bears witness to us in our hearts concerning the grace of God and the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven, and is the pledge of our salvation. Taught by him, we know that we have been born of God, nor can we doubt when, at the command of the only-begotten Son of God, we cry out to him: "Our Father, who art in heaven," etc. We therefore do not linger over this unhappy world, which, since it is wholly set in evil, will at some time suffer the punishments of its wickedness; so it cannot harm us, whom Christ has long since separated from its fellowship. John 15.

units.la: Expendamus hic aliquantum nostrae fidei dignitatem, de qua licet multa hucusq; dicta sint, iuuat tamen plura adhuc dicere, imo eadem repetere nō est infrugiferū. Sciunt se ex Deo genitos esse, quicunq; in Christū Iesum credunt, & quia hoc sciunt, nō possunt quicquam illorū ignorare, que ad salutem ipsorum spectant. In Christo enim, qui nobis à patre sapientia factus est, & in quo re positi iacent omnes thesauri sapientiae & scientiae, vident quicquid hominem videre & scire oportet. Confer cum hac certa & infallibili salutis cognitione arrogantem philosophorum sapientiam, quam illi olim professi sunt, & stultissimos videbis fuisse, quos mundus pro veris sapientibus admiratur. Platonicorum princeps Socrates, hoc unum se scire dicit, quod nihil sciat. Quid ergo tot noctes vigi latae profuerunt, quid lectio assidua, quid disputationes crebrae, quid tamdiu exercitatum ingenij acumen, quid labores tam assidui vtilitatis attulerunt, si nihil scit Socrates? Nec est, quod hanc vocem temere elapsam putemus. Verè enim sentiebat se nihil scire eorum, quae hactenus magno studio inquisiuerat. Siquidem constat omnes philosophos in hoc sudauisse, vt summum bonum inuestigarent, & scirent, qua in re hominis felicitas & vera beatitudo consisteret. Haec cum in solo Christo sit, quem & Platonici cum schola sua vniuersa, & Peripatetici adeoq; omnes philosophi ignoraverunt, reuera nihil sciuerunt, & ignorantiam hanc Socrates, qui eius cador[?] fuit, dissimulare noluit. Sed o infelicem, qui pro ea sapientia mortem subeundam esse putauit, quae eum nihil scire fecerat.
units.tr: Let us here weigh somewhat the dignity of our faith. Although many things have been said about it so far, it is still helpful to say more, and indeed it is not unprofitable to repeat the same things. Everyone who believes in Jesus Christ knows that they have been born of God, and because they know this, they cannot be ignorant of anything that concerns their salvation. For in Christ, who has been made for us wisdom from the Father, and in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge lie hidden, they see whatever a man ought to see and know. Compare with this sure and infallible knowledge of salvation the arrogant wisdom of the philosophers, which they once professed, and you will see that those whom the world admires as true sages were most foolish. Socrates, the prince of the Platonists, says that he knows this one thing only: that he knows nothing. What then did so many sleepless nights profit him, what did constant reading, frequent disputations, the keenness of a mind so long trained, what did such unremitting labours bring in usefulness, if Socrates knows nothing? Nor should we think that this word slipped out carelessly. For he truly felt that he knew nothing of those things which he had so eagerly inquired into until then. Indeed, it is well established that all the philosophers laboured hard at this, to search out the highest good and to know in what the happiness and true blessedness of man consists. Since this lies in Christ alone, whom the Platonists with their whole school, and the Peripatetics, and indeed all the philosophers, did not know, they truly knew nothing, and Socrates, who was of their company, was unwilling to disguise this ignorance. But O unhappy man, who thought that he must undergo death for that wisdom which had made him know nothing!

units.la: Quod si philosopho tam celebri fidelem conferas, non quidem aliquem ex doctorum numero, sed opificem aliquem mechanicum, pastorem, rusticum, nautam, imo puerum aliquem in fidei principis institutum, is magna cum securitate & confidentia se scire fatebitur, & vere quidem profitebitur, quod Socrates, quod Plato, quod Aristoteles, Zeno, & quotquot alij vnquam fuerunt, ignorauere. Num ergo stultitia aut leuis praesumptio videbitur, si pro Christo & veritate certo sibi comperta & cognita mortem adeant Christiani homines, cum in philosophis olim tantum valuerit in anis[?] sapientiae persuasio?
units.tr: But if you set beside such a celebrated philosopher a believer, not indeed someone from the number of the learned, but some mechanic, a shepherd, a peasant, a sailor, or even a boy instructed in the first principles of the faith, he will confess with great assurance and confidence that he knows, and he will truly profess what Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Zeno, and as many others as have ever existed did not know. Will it then seem folly or light presumption if Christian men go to death for Christ and for the truth made certain and known to them, when once among the philosophers the persuasion of their own wisdom held such sway?

units.la: Quid vero illud est, quod tam certo sciunt fideles? Duo commemorantur ab Apostolo: nimirum quod ipsi filij Dei sint, & quod mundus hic totus in malo constitutus sit. Si filios Dei se esse norunt, vtiq; de Dei patris pa rocinio[?] et protectione dubitare non possunt. Cur enim filios suos tam clemens pater negligeret, cum iuuare illos & posset & velit? Potest equidem, quia dominus est exercituum, & pro suo nutu omnia administrat. De voluntate eiusdem nemo dubitat, qui filium eius vnigenitum pro nobis in mortem datum esse nouit. Nec est, quod mundi corruptum statum nobis obesse timeamus. Nam solidum stat fundamentum Dei, habens signaculum hoc: Nouit do minus qui sint sui.2.Tim.2.Idem quoq; inter suos & impios huius seculi filios sic discernit, vt paucissimos ex vniuersali aliorum interitu facile liberet, quod exemplis euidentissimis saepe declarauit. Cum enim prophanus Dei & religionis contemptus vniuersum terrarum orbem sic occupauisset, vt vnus Noe inueniretur, qui Deum verum agnosceret, & coleret: vnum illum arcae praesidio cum suis seruat, cum reliqui omnes dignum impietatis supplicium sustinerent. Eodem & Loti historia referri debet, cui incurabilis Sodomaeorum impietas non obfuit, quo minus imminens illis supplicium effugeret. Procul ergo pellendus metus ille, qui ob aliorum impietatem aliquando oboritur. Iustus enim & clemens est dominus, qui pilos capitum nostrorum numeratos habet, gemitus nostros audit, & curam nostri deponit nunquam.
units.tr: But what is that which the faithful know so surely? Two things are recalled by the Apostle: namely, that they themselves are the sons of God, and that this whole world lies in evil. If they know that they are the sons of God, then surely they cannot doubt the care and protection of God the Father. For why would so merciful a Father neglect his own sons, since he both can and is willing to help them? He can, indeed, because he is the Lord of hosts and governs all things at his will. No one doubts his will who knows that he gave his only-begotten Son to death for us. Nor should we fear that the corrupt state of the world will harm us. For the firm foundation of God stands, bearing this seal: The Lord knows those who are his (2 Tim. 2). He likewise distinguishes between his own and the impious sons of this age in such a way that he easily delivers very few out of the universal destruction of the rest, as he has often shown by the most evident examples. For when profane contempt of God and of religion had so occupied the whole orb of the earth that only Noah was found who acknowledged and worshipped the true God, he preserved him with his family by the protection of the ark, while all the others suffered the punishment their impiety deserved. The history of Lot must be cited in the same way, whose impiety, though incurable among the Sodomites, did not prevent him from escaping the punishment hanging over them. Therefore that fear which sometimes arises on account of the impiety of others must be driven far away. For the Lord is just and merciful, who has counted the hairs of our heads, hears our groanings, and never lays aside his care for us.

units.la: Caeterum officij quoq; haec sententia admonet. Si enim ex Deo nos genitos esse scimus, & patre tam sancto gloriamur, vtiq; nostrum erit, vitam tanto patre dignam viuere. Inter homines equidem sic comparatum est, vt viri boni & honesti filios degeneres ferre non possint. Cur ergo Deus ferret eos, qui moribus, vita & ingenio ab ipso diuersi sunt? Sunt autem pauca capita, quibus vitae Christianae institutio comprehendi potest. Primum ex his est, vt Deum, cuius filij facti sumus per fidem, super omnia diligamus ex toto corde nostro & totis viribus. Deut.6. Si enim parentes diligimus, ex quibus in vitam hanc lachrymarum plenam sumus progeniti, cur non maiori dilectione Deus dignus est, qui ad vitam aeternam, & regni sui consortium regenerat? Viuum vero & efficacem amore Deus requirit, cuius certa videri possint signa vel argumenta. Sunt haec, Verbi Dei studium, & praeceptorum eiusdem obedientia. Non potest patris sermone satiari frugi filius, nec vnquam admonitiones patris fastidit. Ita fidele verborum Dei satietas nunquam capit, sed totus ab eius ore dependet, & in lege ipsius dies et noctes meditatur. Psalm.1.19. Coniungit autem verbi studio obedientiam, ne ex eorum numero sit, qui vita abnegent eum, quem ore profitentur. Fugit ergo peccatum omne, cuius eam atrocitatem esse nouit, vt sanguine filij Dei expiari oportuerit. Excitantur autem ad hoc studium vehementer fideles, cum mundum hunc omnem in malo constitutum esse intelligunt. Cur enim huius exemplum sequerentur, quem tam profligatae impietatis esse sciunt? Cur eius amicitiam quaererent & ambirent, quem Deo inuisum esse omnis scriptura testatur? Nec etiam minas mundi timere possunt, cuius principem Iesus Christus tam gloriose & potenter deuicit. Imo hoc unum pulchrum, honestum & laudabile esse existimant, si contra mundum & principem eius Christi auspicijs constanter pugnent. Hæc totis animis recondant, qui fidei & Christi nomine gloriantur. Fide filij Dei efficimur. Horum proprium est, non peccare ad mortem. Lapsi enim resurgunt & Deo viuunt. Amplectamur ergo iugis pœnitentiæ studium, ut & hoc signo pro Dei filijs in extremo iudicij die agnoscamur, & Dei patris hæredes simus cum filio eius unigenito, Iesu Christo, cui debetur benedictio, gloria, honor & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, this saying also admonishes us about duty. For if we know that we have been born of God, and glory in so holy a Father, it will surely be ours to live a life worthy of so great a Father. Among men it is indeed so ordered that good and honest fathers cannot bear degenerate sons. Why then would God bear with those who differ from him in morals, life and disposition? There are, however, a few heads under which the institution of the Christian life can be comprehended. The first of these is that we should love God, whose sons we have become through faith, above all things, with our whole heart and with all our strength (Deut. 6). For if we love our parents, from whom we have been born into this life full of tears, why should God not be loved with a greater love, who regenerates us to eternal life and to fellowship in his kingdom? Moreover, God requires a living and effective love, of which sure signs or proofs can be seen. These are zeal for the Word of God and obedience to his precepts. A thrifty son cannot be sated with his father's speech, nor ever despises his father's admonitions. Thus the faithful never reach satiety of the words of God, but depend wholly on his mouth, and meditate on his law day and night (Ps. 1, 19). He joins obedience to zeal for the Word, lest he be among those who deny by their life him whom they profess with their mouth. He therefore flees every sin, knowing its atrocity to be such that it had to be atoned for by the blood of the Son of God. The faithful are moreover powerfully stirred to this zeal when they understand that this whole world lies in evil. For why would they follow the example of one whom they know to be of so profligate impiety? Why would they seek and court the friendship of one whom all Scripture testifies to be hateful to God? Nor can they fear the threats of the world, whose prince Jesus Christ so gloriously and powerfully overcame. Indeed, they regard it as the one fair, honourable and praiseworthy thing if they fight constantly against the world and its prince under the auspices of Christ. Let those who glory in the faith and in the name of Christ store these things up with their whole soul. By faith we are made sons of God. It is peculiar to these not to sin unto death, for those who have fallen rise again and live to God. Let us therefore embrace the constant pursuit of repentance, so that by this sign too we may be acknowledged as the sons of God on the last day of judgment, and be heirs of God the Father together with his only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, glory, honour and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXVI.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXVI.

units.la: Scimus autem quòd filius Dei uenit, & dedit nobis mentem, ut cognoscamus illum uerum Deum. Et sumus in uero, in filio eius Iesu Christo. Hic est uerus Deus, & uita æterna.
units.tr: We know moreover that the Son of God has come, and has given us an understanding to know him who is the true God. And we are in the true one, in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God, and eternal life.

units.la: Dominus & saluator noster Iesus Christus apud Lucam ait: Nemo, qui manu sua aratro admota respexerit à tergo, aptus est regno Dei. Et alibi eandem sententiam clarius explicans: Qui perseuerauerit (inquit) usque in finem, saluus erit. Matth. 24. Prudenter ergo Ioannes apostolus, ubi fidem in Iesum Christum docuit, ad perseuerantiâ in fide nos hortatur. Et quia tentationes multæ sunt, quibus à fide abduci solemus, diligenti enumeratione fidei fructus præcipu-os recenset, ut eius consyderatione animati, aduersa omnia constanter superemus. Pertinet eodem & præsens hic locus, qui breuem omnium eorum, quæ in Christo Iesu nobis præstita sunt, sum-mam comprehendit. Primo enim promissum humani generis saluatorem venisse docet. Deinde quid is nobis contulerit indicat. Meretur autem rei grauitas, ut singula, quæ dicuntur, diligenti studio excutiamus.
units.tr: Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ says in Luke: "No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God." And elsewhere, explaining the same saying more clearly: "He who endures to the end shall be saved." Matt. 24. Therefore the apostle John, having taught faith in Jesus Christ, prudently exhorts us to perseverance in the faith. And because there are many temptations by which we are usually drawn away from faith, he carefully enumerates the principal fruits of faith, so that, encouraged by the consideration of them, we may constantly overcome all adversities. The present passage also belongs here, since it comprehends in brief the sum of all those things that have been bestowed upon us in Christ Jesus. For first he teaches that the Saviour of the human race has come, as had been promised; then he points out what he has conferred upon us. The weight of the matter, however, deserves that we examine diligently each of the things that are said.

units.la: I. Scimus autem, quòd filius Dei uenit. Breui sententia eos confutat, qui de salute nostra dubi-tant, & alios saluatores præter Christum Iesum expectant. Sic enim dicere videtur: Constat ex omnibus veteris Testamenti libris, Deum à prima mundi origine filiũ suum promisisse, qui constituto tempore ex muliebri sexu homo fieri, & humanũ genus suo merito ex damnationis & mortis tyrannide asserere debeat. Hunc videre & audire desyderauerunt omnes iusti & prophetæ. Huius diem videre exultauit Abraham. Imò in hunc respicere cupierunt angeli. Sed quæ illi præsen-tem cernere & excipere non potuerunt, temporis angustia & mortis necessitate exclusi, eũ nos in mundum venisse, & saluatorem factum esse, scimus. Non igitur cum Iudeis Messiam expectamus alium, nec eos admittimus, qui salutis rationem aliâ nobis monstrant, quàm quæ in Christo Iesu nobis cognita & perspecta est. Expresse autem sciendi verbo utitur, ut & supra. Sic enim fidei & salutis nostræ certitudinem indicat, quæ argumentis multis & efficacissimis probari potest. Pertinent huc promissiones ab ipsa mundi origine factæ, unâ cum typis legalibus & oraculis prophetarum de Christo Iesu universis. Exprimitur his & tempus Messiæ, & locus natiuitatis, vitæ denique cursus, miracula, mors & resurrectio. Quæ si cum ijs conferantur quæ Christus tum fecit tum passus est, nemo tam stupidus & hebes fuerit, qui non hunc ipsum in euangelio describi & monstrari intelligat, quem veteres olim venturum expectarunt, & de quo, instigante ipsos spiritu sancto, locuti sunt. Videt hoc populus Hierosolymitanus, dum de Christo saluatore dubitantibus respondet: Christus cum venerit, num signa plura edet his, quæ hic edidit? Ioan. 7. Et ipse dominus eadem de causa tam Iudæos quàm discipulos suos ad Mosem & prophetas relegat, ut eum saluatorem datum esse intelligant, quem illi venturum prædixerunt. Ioan. 5. Luc. 24. &c. Est tamen & aliud huius fidei & cognitionis testimonium efficacius, illud nimirum, quod spiritus Christi in animis nostris exhibet, qui de Christo saluatore nos ita certos reddit, ut de salute per illum parta nullo modo dubitare possimus, sed in tentatione quauis cum Ioanne libere fateamur: Scimus, quod filius Dei venit, & nobis saluator atq; redemptor factus est. Cæterum licet sententia hæc & breuis & lucida sit, non tamen tam facile præteriri debet, quin quædam in hac diligentius inuestigemus.
units.tr: I. "We know moreover that the Son of God has come." In a brief sentence he refutes those who doubt our salvation and look for other saviours besides Christ Jesus. For he seems to say: It is established from all the books of the Old Testament that God from the very origin of the world promised his Son, who, at the appointed time, was to become man from the female sex and to rescue the human race by his own merit from the tyranny of condemnation and death. All the righteous and the prophets desired to see and hear him. Abraham rejoiced to see his day. Indeed, the angels longed to look into him. But those things which they could not see and receive in person, being shut out by the narrowness of time and the necessity of death, we know: he has come into the world and has been made Saviour. Therefore we do not, with the Jews, expect another Messiah, nor do we admit those who show us a way of salvation other than that which has been made known and clearly seen in Christ Jesus. Now he uses the expression "we know" explicitly, as also above. For thus he indicates the certainty of our faith and salvation, which can be proved by many and most effective arguments. To this belong the promises made from the very origin of the world, together with the legal types and the oracles of the prophets, all concerning Christ Jesus. By these is expressed both the time of the Messiah and the place of his birth, and finally the course of his life, his miracles, his death and resurrection. If these are compared with what Christ both did and suffered, no one would be so stupid and dull as not to understand that the very one whom the ancients long expected to come, and about whom they spoke under the prompting of the Holy Spirit, is described and shown in the Gospel. The people of Jerusalem see this, when, answering those who doubted concerning Christ the Saviour, they say: "When Christ comes, will he do more signs than these which this man has done?" John 7. And the Lord himself, for the same reason, refers both the Jews and his disciples to Moses and the prophets, so that they may understand that he is the Saviour given, whom they foretold would come. John 5; Luke 24, etc. There is, however, another and more effective testimony of this faith and knowledge, namely that which the Spirit of Christ displays in our hearts, who makes us so certain concerning Christ the Saviour that we can in no way doubt the salvation obtained through him, but in any temptation whatever, with John, we freely confess: "We know that the Son of God has come, and has been made our Saviour and Redeemer." Yet although this sentence is both brief and clear, it ought not to be passed over so easily that we do not examine some points in it more carefully.

units.la: Primo loco causa, propter quam Dei filius in mundum venit, consyderanda erit. Confer enim supremam illam & æternam maiestatem filij Dei, quam in sinu patris habuit, priusquam in mundum hunc veniret, cum ea conditione, quam in terris hisce miseram, calamitosam & plenam dolo-ris atq; lachrymarum sustinuit, & mirum videbitur, Dei filium in hanc omnis miseriæ palæstram descendere voluisse. Causam verò ipse in euangelio explicat, dum se medicum venisse dicit eorum qui ægrotant. Matth. 9. Et alibi absque omni verborum inuolucro ait: Filius hominis in mundum venit, ut saluet quod perierat. Matth. decimo octauo. Ad quod dictum Paulus respexisse videtur, cum inquit:Fidelis vel certus sermo,& dignus què modis omnibus amplectamur, quod Christus Jesus venit in mundum,ut peccatores salvos faceret.1.Tim.1.Sed & angelus priusquam Christus è virgine nasceretur,Josepho in somnis hunc ipsum finem indicat,cum de virginis pudicitia dubi tanti dicit:Quod in illa conceptum est,à spiritu sancto profectum est.Pariet autem filium,& voca bis nomen eius Jesum. Is enim salvum faciet populum suum à peccatis suis. Matth.1. Causa ergo unica adventus Christi in carnem est, salus & redemptio humani generis. Quia enim omnes nos peccatores sumus,& peccati noxa capitalis est,quæ damnationis & mortis poenam meretur, Dei filius homo fieri voluit,ut frater noster factus causam nostram susciperet,peccata nostra in se transferre,& eadem sui sanguinis precio expiare posset.Quare quæcunq; de filio Dei,Jesu Christo,vel legimus vel audimus,non eo loco habeamus,quo historiæ clarorum virorum haberi solent:sed in omnibus istis nostræ salutis causam agi intelligamus, quæ propter universalem humani generis corruptionem aliter parari & acquiri non potuit.
units.tr: First, the cause for which the Son of God came into the world must be considered. For compare that supreme and eternal majesty of the Son of God, which he had in the bosom of the Father before he came into this world, with the condition which he endured on these wretched, calamitous earthly shores, full of sorrow and tears, and it will seem wonderful that the Son of God was willing to descend into this arena of every misery. The cause, however, he himself explains in the Gospel, when he says that he has come as a physician to those who are sick. Matt. 9. And elsewhere, without any wrapping of words, he says: "The Son of man has come into the world to save what was lost." Matt. 18. Paul seems to have had this saying in view when he says: "This is a faithful and sure saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners." 1 Tim. 1. Also the angel, before Christ was born of the virgin, indicates this very end to Joseph in a dream, when he, doubting the chastity of the virgin, is told: "What has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. For he will save his people from their sins." Matt. 1. The sole cause, therefore, of the coming of Christ in the flesh is the salvation and redemption of the human race. For since we are all sinners, and sin is a capital offence which deserves the penalty of condemnation and death, the Son of God willed to become man, so that, having become our brother, he might take up our cause, transfer our sins to himself, and be able to expiate them by the price of his own blood. Wherefore whatever we read or hear about the Son of God, Jesus Christ, we should not hold in the place where the histories of famous men are usually held; rather, we should understand that in all those things the cause of our salvation is being treated, which, on account of the universal corruption of the human race, could not be otherwise prepared and acquired.

units.la: Confutantur itaq; hoc loco,quotquot Christum Jesum salvatorem quidem esse fatentur,interim vero aliis quoq; mediis eos salvari posse existimant,qui à fide & cognitione Christi sunt a-lienissimi. Tuentur sententiam hanc multi, eò quòd ad mundi amicitiam acquirendam percommoda est,& cum charitate coniuncta esse videtur. Adhæc multi,cum in Turcis & Judæis vitæ puritatem,disciplinæ publicæ severitatem,& justitiæ studium ardentissimum vident,rem indignam esse existimant,si quis illos propter unius Christi ignorantiam damnatorum numero addicere,& non potius salutem,tantorum operum præmium,illis tribuere velit. Sed hallucinātur omnes illi partim quod operibus nostris salutem tribuunt,& nostris meritis in cœlorum regno aliquem locum deberi putant,partim quòd de æterno Dei consilio nimis ofcitanter pronunciant.Si enim illud petitius inspicerent,& secundum hoc de religione omni & salutis ratione judicarent,mox viderent,non errorem modò,sed blasphemiam & impietatem horribilem esse, si quis unumquenq; in sua fide & religione salvum fieri posse afferat, nec necessarium esse putet,ut unum Jesum Christum omnes amplectantur. Ea enim sententia omnes in Deo virtutes negat & evertit, justitiam dico,bonitatem & misericordiam,veritatem,sapientiam,imò ipsum Deum,qui si has dotes illi adimas,Deus nō erit. Nam si aliis quoq; mediis, extra Christum institutis,homines salvari possunt, superuacaneū est omne hoc Jesu Christi pro nobis incarnati,crucifixi & mortui negotium. Quæ ergo hæc erit Dei justitia,quæ filium unigenitum,obedientissimum, & omni carentem labe atq; macula,temere diris hisce cruciatibus obiecit,& peccata nostra tā horribili supplicio per illum expiari voluit,cum ad illorum expiationem quivis Dei cultus,humani ingenij zelo excogitatus,suf ficeret? Quis item Deum hunc sibi propitium & clementem fore pollicebitur, quē in filio suo tam crudelem & immitem fine omni causa fuisse videt? Præterea verax non erit,qui in verbo suo uni ci salvatoris Christi subinde meminit,si extra hunc infinitæ aliæ salutis viæ inveniri possunt. Similiter sapientiæ laudem omnem amittet Deus,si cum aliæ essent salvandi humani generis rationes,hanc instituere voluit,quæ ut omnium difficillima fuit, ita filium unicum poenis tam horrendis subiecit. Hæc ergo maiori studio & vigilantia expendentes Apostoli, nunquam eò peruenire potuerunt,ut sententiam hanc tam plausibilem proponerent,quę omnes omnium gentiū religiones pro talibus agnoscit,in quibus homines salutem possint consequi. Quæ si vera est,nō Dei modo virtutes euacuat (ut modò demonstrauimus) verumetiam extremæ stultitiæ damnat martyres Christi omnes,qui pro ea fide & religione mortem subire voluerunt,quę non solā servat,& eas tam pertinaciter cum vitæ iactura damnarunt,in quibus perinde,ut Christiana,salvari poterant. Sed absint hęc à Christianis pectoribus procul,quibus tolerabilius multò est,omnes Judęos, Turcas, & quotquot Christiani nominis hostes sunt, damnationi subijcere, quam tam fœda & impia de Deo Opt. Max. cogitare. Valeant ergo cum sua carnali prudentia , qui hominum maiorem quam Dei rationem habere didicerunt.Nos cum Apostolis credamus,& ingenuè fateamur, Dei filium Jesum Christum in mundum venisse, nec aliud nomen sub Sole hominibus datum esse, in quo possint salvi fieri,præter nomen Jesu.Act.4.
units.tr: Therefore in this place are refuted all those who, while confessing that Christ Jesus is indeed the Saviour, nevertheless think that those who are most alien from faith and the knowledge of Christ can be saved also by other means. Many defend this opinion because it is very convenient for gaining the friendship of the world and seems to be joined with charity. Moreover, many, when they see among the Turks and Jews purity of life, severity of public discipline, and a most ardent zeal for justice, judge it an unworthy thing if anyone should wish to assign them to the number of the damned on account of ignorance of Christ alone, and not rather grant them salvation, the reward of so great works. But all those men err, partly because they attribute salvation to our works and think that some place in the kingdom of heaven is owed to our merits, and partly because they pronounce too carelessly concerning the eternal counsel of God. For if they examined it more carefully, and judged on this basis concerning all religion and the way of salvation, they would soon see that it is not only error but blasphemy and horrible impiety to assert that each person can be saved in his own faith and religion, and to think it unnecessary that all should embrace the one Jesus Christ. For that opinion denies and overturns all the virtues of God: I mean justice, goodness and mercy, truth, wisdom, indeed God himself, who, if you take these qualities from him, will not be God. For if men can be saved also by other means, instituted apart from Christ, then this whole undertaking of Jesus Christ, incarnate, crucified and dead for us, is superfluous. What then would be the justice of God, which rashly exposed his only-begotten Son, most obedient and free from every stain and spot, to these dreadful torments, and willed that our sins be expiated through him by so terrible a punishment, when any worship of God devised by the zeal of human ingenuity would suffice for their expiation? Who, again, will promise that God will be propitious and merciful to him, whom he sees to have been so cruel and merciless in his Son, without any cause? Moreover, God will not be truthful, who in his word repeatedly calls to mind the one Saviour Christ, if other infinite ways of salvation can be found apart from him. Likewise God will lose all praise for wisdom, if, when there were other ways of saving the human race, he chose to institute this one, which, as the most difficult of all, subjected his only Son to such horrible punishments. The apostles, weighing these things with greater zeal and vigilance, could never come to the point of proposing this opinion, so plausible, which acknowledges all the religions of all the nations as those in which men can attain salvation. If this were true, it would not only nullify the virtues of God (as we have just shown), but would also condemn as in the extreme of folly all the martyrs of Christ, who were willing to undergo death for that faith and religion, which not only preserves, but for which they, with such stubbornness, condemned the loss of life, although in other religions they could have been saved just as well as Christians. But far from Christian breasts be these thoughts, for it is far more tolerable to subject all Jews, Turks, and as many as are enemies of the Christian name, to damnation, than to think so foul and impious thoughts of God the Best and Greatest. Let those who have learned to have regard for human rather than divine reasoning go on with their carnal prudence. We, with the apostles, let us believe and frankly confess that the Son of God, Jesus Christ, has come into the world, and that no other name under heaven has been given to men in which they can be saved, except the name of Jesus. Acts 4.

units.la: Cæterum non contenti causam,quæ Christum ut in mundum veniret commouit,investigas fe,simul eam quoq; inquiramus,quæ Deum patrem, ut illum mitteret,impulit. Indicat hanc ipse Christus, dum in evangelio ait:Sic Deus dilexit mundum , ut filium suum unigenitum traderet pro mundo,ut omnis qui credit in eum nō pereat,sed habeat vitam æternam.Joan.5. Paterni ergo amoris affectus causa fuit,quæ Deum movit, ut filii sui morte nostram vitam & salutem redimeret. Ut enim grave est pio patri, filium periclitantem videre : ita Deus clementissimus pater illorum universalē interitū ferre non potuit , quos mero suæ gratiæ beneficio primitus creauerat. Et quia inter ipsius bonitatem & justitiam,quæ in hac salutis nostræ causa collidi videbātur, alia via non restabat, præter filij Dei incarnatio & mors, eam inuenit & præuidit ab æterno Dei sapientia, & filium hunc nobis saluatorem prædestinauit ante mundi creationem, ac nouissimis temporibus in carne manifestauit. 1.Pet.1.Eph.1.Horum consyderatio de duobus cognitu perquàm necessarijs nos admonet: Quorum prius est, quòd salutè nobis gratuitò obtigisse videmus: alterum, quòd officij nostri admonemur, quo Deo obstricti sumus. Nam vt supra Ioannes monuit, dilectio Dei in hoc est, non quòd nos priores ipsum dilexerimus, sed ipse dilexit nos, & dedit filium suum pro nobis. Et Paulus nos ante filium datum inimicos Dei fuisse testatur. Rom.5. Quid enim habet homo, si Christum auferas, quo se Dei amicum esse gloriari possit? Nam quia peccatum vndique cernitur, nunquam non & eius pœna sese oculis nostris ingerit. Exemplum huius rei luculentum in primis parentibus habetur: qui cum peccauissent, nihil in semetipsis, præter turpem & pudendam nuditatem inuenire potuerunt, nec profuit carnalis industria, quæ perizomata contexere docebat, sed voce & aduentu domini perterriti, fugam ceperunt, quasi eum vel fugere vel latere possent, cuius oculi omnia vident, & cuius potentia vbiq; præsens est. Et nisi dominus illos reuocans pedem sistere coegisset, fugiendo æternum sibi ipsis interitum asciuissent. Eadem est totius posteritatis Adamicæ conditio. Fugimus à conspectu domini frequenter, & friuolis rebus nostram turpitudinem tegi posse putamus. Sed nequicquam. Vt primum enim diuinæ iustitiæ vox intonat, totis animis consternati, nos & peccatores & modis omnibus infelices esse sentimus. Vt verò primos parentes Deus vocare dignatus est, & saluatorem promisit, qui ex muliere homo nasci debuit: ita passim verbo gratiæ nos vocat, & trementes atq; morte dignos ad se inuitans, æternæ vitæ præmia in se credentibus pollicetur. Vehementer ergo eos falli constat, quicunque suis operibus & propriæ iustitiæ confidunt. Quia enim in vno Iesu salutem contineri omnis scriptura affirmat, is aut ex gratia datus est, nemo nō videt, omnē nostri meriti fiducia ,prfus excludi.
units.tr: Yet we should not be content to inquire into the cause that moved Christ to come into the world; let us also investigate what impelled God the Father to send him. Christ himself indicates this when he says in the gospel: "God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for the world, so that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life." John 5. The cause, then, was the affection of a fatherly love, which moved God to redeem our life and salvation by the death of his Son. For just as it is grievous for a loving father to see his son in peril, so God, the most merciful Father, could not bear the universal ruin of those whom he had first created by the pure benefit of his grace. And since between his goodness and his justice, which seemed to clash in this cause of our salvation, there remained no other way except the incarnation and death of the Son of God, the wisdom of God from eternity found this way and foresaw it, and predestined this Son to be our Saviour before the creation of the world, and at the last times manifested him in the flesh. 1 Pet. 1; Eph. 1. The consideration of these things, concerning two most necessary matters, admonishes us: of which the first is that we see salvation to have come to us freely; the other is that we are reminded of the duty by which we are bound to God. For, as John admonished above, the love of God is in this, not that we first loved him, but that he loved us and gave his Son for us. And Paul testifies that before the giving of the Son we were enemies of God. Rom. 5. For what does a man have, if you take away Christ, by which he could glory that he is a friend of God? For since sin is seen everywhere, its punishment also never ceases to present itself to our eyes. A brilliant example of this is found first of all in our first parents, who, when they had sinned, could find nothing in themselves except a shameful and disgraceful nakedness; nor did carnal industry, which taught them to weave loincloths, help them, but terrified by the voice and coming of the Lord, they took to flight, as if they could flee from or hide from him whose eyes see all things and whose power is present everywhere. And unless the Lord, calling them back, had compelled them to halt, they would have procured eternal ruin for themselves by fleeing. The condition of the whole Adamic posterity is the same. We frequently flee from the sight of the Lord, and we think our shame can be covered by trivial things. But in vain. For as soon as the voice of divine justice thunders, struck with terror in our whole souls, we feel that we are both sinners and wretched in every way. But when God has deigned to call our first parents, and has promised a Saviour, who was to be born of a woman, so he everywhere calls us by the word of grace, inviting us, trembling and worthy of death, to himself, and promises the rewards of eternal life to those who believe in him. It is therefore clear that those are greatly deceived who trust in their own works and their own righteousness. For since all Scripture affirms that salvation is contained in the one Jesus, and that he has been given out of grace, no one fails to see that all confidence in our own merit is wholly excluded.

units.la: Nec tamen doctrinam hanc, quasi bonis operibus inimicā, aliquis aspernari debet & damnare. Licet enim nulla sint nostrorum operum merita, non tamen bonorum operum studium ideo intermitti debet, quod à nobis maximo & optimo iure exigit dominus, pro sua in nos beneficentia. Etenim communis sensus hoc monet, vt nostri amantes redamemus, & gratitudinis officia sedulò præstemus erga eos qui beneficia in nos conferre student. Quapropter cum summę dilectionis & beneficentię opus in nos exercuerit Deus, qui nec filiū negare voluit, cū illo nobis opus esset, quis non intelligit, nostrum esse, vt & ipsi Deum ex toto corde & omnibus viribus diligamus, nec quicquam tanti apud nos fieri patiamur, cuius amor & studium nos ab eius obseruantia abstrahat? Postulatur ergo hic à nobis nostrijpsius abnegatio, vitiorū fuga, carnis mortificatio, vitæ totius innouatio & indesinēs Deo placendi studiū, quę & verè bona opera sunt, & sola Deo placere constat. Hæc qui nec præstat, nec illorum studio vel mediocriter tangitur, fateatur, se Christianæ fidei mysteria nondum, vt par est, cognouisse, & nudo tam egregij tituli splendore gloriari desinat.
units.tr: Yet no one ought to despise and condemn this doctrine as though it were hostile to good works. For although our works have no merit, the zeal for good works ought not on that account to be relinquished, since the Lord demands this from us by the most just and best right, in return for his kindness toward us. For common sense itself advises that we love those who love us and diligently render the duties of gratitude to those who strive to confer benefits upon us. Therefore, since God, who did not even wish to spare his Son, when we had need of him, has exercised a work of the greatest love and kindness toward us, who does not understand that it is our duty also to love God with our whole heart and all our strength, and not to allow anything of such great importance among us whose love and zeal would draw us away from his observance? Therefore there is required of us here the denial of ourselves, the flight from vices, the mortification of the flesh, the renewal of the whole life, and an unceasing zeal to please God; these are truly good works, and it is agreed that they alone please God. Whoever neither performs these nor is moved at all by zeal for them, let him confess that he has not yet, as is fitting, come to know the mysteries of the Christian faith, and let him cease to glory in the bare splendour of so excellent a title.

units.la: II. Et dedit nobis mentem, ut cognoscamus illum verum Deum. Pergit exponere salutares fructus quos sua incarnatione & aduentu suo in mundū Christus nobis contulit. Et in præsenti quidem, per Christū veram sapientiam nobis datā esse docet, qua verum illum Deū cognoscimus. Nam vt solus Deus vera & æterna sapientia est: ita sapiens vocari non meretur, nisi qui huius cognitionem veram habuerit. Quæ quia in Christo offertur, idē nobis (vt Paulus ait) à Deo patre sapientia factus est, & in illo thesauros scientiæ & sapientiæ recoditos habemus. 1.Cor.1.Col.2. Atqui cū primis memorabile est Christi beneficium, quod Apostolus hoc loco commemorat. Constat enim in veri Dei cognitione errasse, quotquot vnquā sine Christo illam inuestigare studuerunt. Notæ sunt philosophorum disputationes, quæ vix immensis voluminibus contineri possunt: quibus tamē omnibus illud Paulinū competit: Cum se putarent sapientes esse, stulti facti sunt. Rom.1. Similiter in Iudæis quoq; eiusdē rei exempla habentur. Quotquot enim in Dei cognitione & cultu sine Christi notitia versati sunt, turpissimē impegerunt, talē Deum fingendo, qui amputati præputij ceremonia, sacrificijs, fuffitibus, aspersionibus, diebus festis, cœtibus splendidis, & alijs eiusmodi rebus delectetur. Qui error prophetarū sermonibus argumentū præbuit, quibus frigidas Ceremoniarum legis obseruationes acerrimè insectati sunt. Deniq;, Deum nemo vidit unquā, sed vni genitus filius, qui est in sinu patris, ipse enarrauit, Ioan.1. Et solus eā Dei cognitione in nobis operatur, in qua ipse vitā æternam cōsistere docet. Ioan.17. Porrò, vt id fiat, diligentius paulò examinā dū erit, vt viā discamus, quā eos tenere conuenit, qui in Dei cognitione cū fructu versari volunt.
units.tr: II. "And he has given us understanding, that we may know the true God." He goes on to set out the saving fruits which Christ has brought to us by his incarnation and his coming into the world. And at present he teaches that through Christ true wisdom has been given to us, by which we know that true God. For just as God alone is true and eternal wisdom, so no one deserves to be called wise unless he has a true knowledge of this wisdom. And since it is offered in Christ, the same one (as Paul says) "has been made wisdom to us from God the Father, and in him we have the treasures of knowledge and wisdom hidden away." 1 Cor. 1; Col. 2. Yet the benefit of Christ which the Apostle here recalls is especially memorable. For it is agreed that all who have ever sought to investigate that knowledge of the true God without Christ have erred. The disputations of the philosophers are well known, which can scarcely be contained in immense volumes; yet to all of them that saying of Paul applies: "Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools." Rom. 1. Similarly, examples of the same thing are found among the Jews also. For all who have been engaged in the knowledge and worship of God without knowledge of Christ have fallen most shamefully, feigning a God who delights in the ceremony of circumcision, in sacrifices, fumigations, sprinklings, festival days, splendid assemblies, and other things of this kind. This error provided the prophets with material for their sermons, in which they most sharply attacked the cold observances of the ceremonies of the law. Finally, "No one has ever seen God, but the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known," John 1. And he alone works in us that knowledge of God in which he teaches that eternal life consists. John 17. Furthermore, so that this may come about, we shall have to examine a little more diligently, so that we may learn the way which those who wish to be engaged in the knowledge of God with profit ought to keep.

units.la: Primò, Christus expressa imago est substantiæ Dei, vt qui hunc videt, simul & patrem videat. Heb.1. Ioan.14. Cum ergo se nobis cognoscendum & fruendum offert Christus, quid aliud facit, quàm quòd copiam facit Deum verum cognoscendi? Facit huc, quod in Christo omnes Dei virtutes luculentissimè cōspiciuntur. Nullum quippe est euidentius diuinę iustitiæ argumentū, quàm quod filij sui morte peccata expiari voluit. Nullum certius bonitatis & misericordiæ Dei signum, quàm quod filium pro mundo, imò pro hostibus, tradere dignatus est. Veritas quoque Dei infallibilis in eo cernitur, quòd promissum saluatorem eo tempore & loco dedit, quo illum erat pollicitus. Sapientia item Dei immensa & inscrutabilis in eo cernitur, quòd eam salutis viam (vt paulò ante dictum est) inter bonitatem & iustitiam inuenire potuit. Similiter & omnipotentiæ Dei inuicta virtus apparet, quòd per filium suum, vili hominis specie amictum, omnem princi-pis huius mundi tyrannidem deuicit. Quid multis? Nihil in Deo est, cuius non viuum exemplar in Christo Iesu videre liceat. Cæterum, quia ea est nostræ carnis cæcitas, & tanta salutis nostræ negligentia, vt pauci hæc obseruent, quæ in Christo proponuntur, non contentus in se hæc declarauisse, doctrinam quoq; adhibet, quæ viuo & æterno Dei verbo de singulis instituit, quæ in Deo cognoscenda sunt. Accedunt doctrinæ sacramenta, quibus maximorum beneficiorum Dei visibilia signa, non oculis modo & auribus, verumetiam manibus percipienda offeruntur. Adde his & spiritum Christi, quem fideles ceu domesticum doctorem in animis suis quotidie audiunt, & per hunc plenissimè docentur omnia ea, quæ ad Dei & salutis cognitionem pertinent. Agnoscamus ergo tam insigne Dei beneficium, in Christo Iesu collatu, et cogitemus solum hunc nobis diuinitus doctorem & magistrum datum esse, cuius verba quisquis affert, audiri meretur. At qui diuer-sum docere audet, aut aliena ab illis, quæ ipse tradidit, fide dignus non est, etiamsi angelus fuerit de cœlo delapsus. Gal. 1. Non est ergo quòd scholas & superbos doctorum titulos, & principum authoritatem nobis obijciant, qui nostræ fidei & doctrinæ contradicunt. Quia enim Christum doctorem in euangelio audimus, omnes eos, qui diuersa & aliena ab hoc afferunt, facilè contemnimus. Scimus enim nobis dictum esse à Deo patre, Hunc audite. Matth. 17. Scimus illum suis dicere: Vnus est magister vester, nempe Christus. Matth. 23. Sed & olim sponsæ Christi, ecclesiæ dictum est. Audi filia, & vide, & inclina aurem tuam, & obliuiscere populi tui, & domus patris tui, &c. Psalmo 45. Facit huc quod passim in scripturis inculcatur, in Christi regno fideles nos homi-num discipulos, sed διδακτοὶ θεοῦ, id est, diuinitùs edocti sunt. Isa. 54. Ierē. 31. Ioan. 6. Et Christus di-fertis verbis ait: Nemo nouit filium, nisi pater: neque patrem quisquam nouit, nisi filius, & cuicun-que voluerit filius reuelare. Matth. 11. Verè ergo sapientes & in Dei cognitione instructi erunt, quicunque Christum doctorem & magistrum amplexati fuerint. Sed videamus alium quoq; fructum, quem Christus in fidelibus suis operari consueuit. Addit enim Ioannes:
units.tr: First, Christ is the express image of the substance of God, so that whoever sees him sees the Father also. Heb. 1; John 14. When therefore Christ offers himself to us to be known and enjoyed, what else does he do than make available to us the opportunity of knowing the true God? He does this because in Christ all the virtues of God are most brilliantly visible. Indeed there is no more evident proof of divine justice than that he willed the sins to be expiated by the death of his Son. No more certain sign of the goodness and mercy of God than that he deigned to deliver his Son for the world, indeed for enemies. The infallible truth of God is also seen in this, that he gave the promised Saviour at the time and place he had promised. Likewise the immense and inscrutable wisdom of God is seen in this, that he was able to find that way of salvation (as was said a little before) between goodness and justice. In the same way the unconquered power of God appears in this, that through his Son, clothed in the lowly appearance of a man, he overcame all the tyranny of the prince of this world. What more is there to say? There is nothing in God whose living example cannot be seen in Christ Jesus. Moreover, since such is the blindness of our flesh, and such our negligence of our salvation, that few observe those things which are set forth in Christ, he, not content to have declared these things in himself, also adds teaching which, by the living and eternal Word of God, establishes about each thing those things which are to be known in God. To these are added the sacraments of the teaching, by which the visible signs of God's greatest benefits are offered to be perceived not only by the eyes and ears but also by the hands. Add to these also the Spirit of Christ, whom the faithful hear every day in their souls as a domestic teacher, and through him they are most fully taught all those things which pertain to the knowledge of God and of salvation. Let us therefore acknowledge so remarkable a benefit of God, conferred in Christ Jesus, and let us consider that he alone has been given to us by God as teacher and master, whose words, whoever brings them, deserves to be heard. But whoever dares to teach otherwise, or whose faith is not worthy of trust in things foreign to those which he himself delivered, even if he should be an angel fallen from heaven. Gal. 1. There is therefore no reason for them to throw in our faces schools, proud titles of teachers, and the authority of princes, who contradict our faith and doctrine. For since we hear Christ as teacher in the gospel, we easily despise all those who bring things different and foreign to him. For we know that it was said to us by God the Father: "Hear him." Matt. 17. We know that he says to his own: "One is your teacher, namely Christ." Matt. 23. But also long ago it was said to the bride of Christ, the Church: "Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father's house, etc." Psalm 45. To this bears on what is everywhere insisted upon in the Scriptures: that in the kingdom of Christ we the faithful are not disciples of men, but διδακτοὶ θεοῦ [taught by God], that is, divinely taught. Isa. 54; Jer. 31; John 6. And Christ says in plain words: "No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him." Matt. 11. Truly, therefore, they will be wise and instructed in the knowledge of God who have embraced Christ as teacher and master. But let us see another fruit also, which Christ is accustomed to work in his faithful. For John adds:

units.la: III. Et sumus in uero, in filio eius Iesu Christo. Hic est uerus Deus, & uita æterna. Comprehen-dit his verbis finem totius euangelij, qui est vt Deo vniamur per Christum Iesum. Videtur autem hunc forti & irrefragabili argumento afferere. Quia enim Christum dicit verum Deum esse, fieri nequit quin vero Deo vniti sint, quicunq; per fidem Christo Iesu sunt insiti. Proponit hunc fidei finem ipse Christus, cum in precatione illa sua ardentissima patri dicit: Rogo vt omnes vnù sint, sicut tu pater in me, & ego in te: vt & ipsi IN NOBIS vnum sint, vt credat mundus, quòd tu me misNOTE: Et ego gloriam, quam dedisti mihi, dedi eis, vt sint vnum, sicut & nos vnum sumus: ego in eis, & tu in me, vt sint consummati in vnum, &c. Ioan. 17. Vnionis vel insitionis huius in Christo finis duplex est. Nam & in hac vita fructus fidei in nobis operatur, & æternæ salutis vel beatitudinis causa est. Christus si quidem vitis est, nos palmites. Et vt palmes non fert fructu, nisi in vite manserit: ita nec nos sine Christo quicquam possumus facere. Ioan. 15. Et Paulus ob eam causam, iam non se viuere dicit, sed Christum in ipso. Galat. 2. At qui Christo sic insiti sunt, vt ipse in illis viuat, illi vero in ipso fructificent, ab eode in altero seculo separari non possunt. Vult enim Christus, vt vbi ipse est, simul etiam sint, quos pater ipsi tradidit, & ideo præcessit, locum nobis in cœlo paraturus. Ioan. 17. & 14.
units.tr: III. And we are in the true one, in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God, and eternal life. In these words he sums up the aim of the whole gospel, which is that we should be united with God through Christ Jesus. He seems to set this out by a strong and unanswerable argument. For since he says that Christ is the true God, it cannot but be that those who are grafted by faith into Christ Jesus are united with the true God. Christ himself sets out this goal of faith, when in that most fervent prayer of his he says to the Father: I ask that they may all be one, as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one IN US, so that the world may believe that you have sent me. And I have given them the glory that you gave me, that they may be one, as we are one: I in them, and you in me, that they may be made perfect in one, etc. John 17. The end of this union or grafting in Christ is twofold. For in this life the fruit of faith works in us, and it is also the cause of eternal salvation and blessedness. Christ is indeed the vine, and we the branches. And just as a branch bears no fruit unless it remains in the vine, so neither can we do anything without Christ. John 15. And Paul, for this reason, says that he no longer lives, but Christ lives in him. Gal. 2. But those who are so grafted into Christ that he lives in them, and they bear fruit in him, cannot be separated from him in the next age. For Christ wills that where he himself is, those also whom the Father has given to him should be with him at the same time; and therefore he went before, to prepare a place for us in heaven. John 17 and 14.

units.la: Arguit locus hic illorum improbitatem, qui cum Christiani haberi velint, minimè tamen in hoc sunt, vt Christo viuant, aut illius spiritum vitæ suæ rectorem ducem q; ferant. Sed toti mundo & carnis cupiditatibus dediti, ea studia sectantur, quæ à regno Christi sunt alienissima. Qua ratione enim Christianus dici poterit, qui à fine Christianismi totus abhorret, dum non in Christo, sed in carne & mundo viuere cocupiscit? Vides ergo, quo sensu Apostolus dixerit mūdi amicitiam esse inimicitiam cum Deo. Iac. 4. Quæ sententia, si animis nostris fixa insideret, ardentius multò in omnibus nobis cerneretur fidei, puritatis & innocentiæ studium. Cogitemus ergo quoties affectibus transfuerfi rapimur, nos per fidem Christo vero Deo insitos esse, & proinde abfur-dissimum fore, si non Christo, sed mundo potius & satanæ viuere studeamus. Pertinet huc Pauli locus, dicentis: An ignoratis, quòd quicunq; baptizati sumus in Christum Iesum, in mortem eius baptizati sumus? Sepulti igitur sumus vnà cum illo per baptismum in morte: vt quemadmodum excitatus est Christus ex mortuis per gloriam patris, ita & nos in nouitate vitæ ambulemus, &c. Rom.6. Et paulò post: Existimate vosipsos mortuos quidem esse peccato, viuentes autem Deo per Christum Iesum dominum nostrum. Et alibi, vitam nostram cum Christo in Deo absconditam esse testatur. Col.3.
units.tr: This passage exposes the wickedness of those who, though they wish to be called Christians, are by no means concerned to live in Christ, or to take his Spirit as the guide and leader of their life. But being wholly given over to the whole world and to the desires of the flesh, they pursue those pursuits which are most alien to the kingdom of Christ. For by what reasoning can someone be called a Christian who shrinks entirely from the end of Christianity, while he desires to live not in Christ but in the flesh and in the world? You see, therefore, in what sense the Apostle said that friendship with the world is enmity with God. James 4. If this saying were fixed and settled in our minds, a far more ardent zeal for faith, purity and innocence would be seen in all of us. Let us therefore consider, whenever we are carried away by distorted affections, that we are grafted by faith into Christ, the true God, and that it would therefore be absurd if we strove to live not for Christ but rather for the world and for Satan. The passage of Paul applies here, where he says: Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were therefore buried together with him through baptism into death, so that just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life, etc. Rom. 6. And a little later: Consider yourselves indeed dead to sin, but alive to God through Christ Jesus our Lord. And elsewhere he testifies that our life is hidden with Christ in God. Col. 3.

units.la: Præterea habemus hic euidens diuinitatis Iesu Christi testimonii, cuius infallibilis est contra omnem Arrianorum impietatem authoritas. Diserte enim & verbis minimè figuratis, Iesum Christum verum Deum & vitam æternam esse dicit. Vbi obseruabis eundem & verum Deum & vitam æternam dici. Si enim verus Deus est, ab æterno, & proinde patri coæternus sit oportet. Sic si vita æterna est, æternus quoq; est quoad essentiam suam, & vt fine caret, sic principium quoque nullum habuit. Facit hoc ad eludendas Arianorū nostri seculi argutias, Seruetanorum dico, qui Christum Deum quidem esse fatentur, sed æternum esse negant, adeoq; Deum fingūt, qui aliquando non fuerit, & vt Deus esset, aliunde acceperit, quando ex virgine natus, aut quando in cœlum assumptus est. At nos Apostoli verbis insistamus, qui & verum Deum, & vitam æternam esse dicit. Neque ex se hoc dicit, sed Christum dicentem audiuerat: Glorifica me pater apud temetipsum gloria, quam habui, priusquàm hic mundus esset apud te. Quisquis ergo vel Dei cultor haberi, vel æterna vita frui volet, hunc amplexetur oportet. Magna est hæc nostrę fidei dignitas, quam Iudęorum & Mahometistarū blasphemijs opponere decet, qui nos nudo homine, eoq; crucifixo, confidere & gloriari clamant. Qui enim carne assumpta verus homo natus est, & in Cruce pependit, idem verus Deus & vita æterna est. Nec Apostolorū modò testimonijs eius diuinitas probatur, sed talem olim prophetæ agnouerunt, & eadem infinitis miraculis declarata est. Nostrum est, Iesum Christum, qui verus Deus & vita æterna est, doctorem & saluatorem agnoscere, & vera fide eidem inseri, vt veri Dei cognitione instructi, fructus illo dignos feramus, & cū illo in cœlis viuamus, cui debetur benedictio, gloria, honor & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, here we have clear testimony to the divinity of Jesus Christ, whose authority is infallible against all the impiety of the Arians. For he plainly, and in words not at all figurative, says that Jesus Christ is the true God and eternal life. Here you will observe that the same one is called both the true God and eternal life. For if he is the true God, he must be from eternity, and therefore co-eternal with the Father. Likewise, if he is eternal life, he is also eternal in his essence, and since he has no end, so he had no beginning either. This serves to rebut the subtleties of the Arians of our own age, I mean the Servetians, who confess that Christ is indeed God but deny that he is eternal, and so imagine a God who once did not exist, and who received from elsewhere the means of being God, namely when he was born of the Virgin, or when he was taken up into heaven. But let us, as Apostles, keep to the words of him who says that he is both the true God and eternal life. Nor does he say this from himself, but he had heard Christ saying: Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had before the world was with you. Whoever therefore wishes to be counted a worshipper of God, or to enjoy eternal life, ought to embrace him. Great is the dignity of this our faith, which it is fitting to set against the blasphemies of the Jews and the Mahometans, who cry out that we trust and glory in a mere man, and that a crucified one. For he who was born a true man by assuming flesh, and hung on the Cross, is also the true God and eternal life. Nor is his divinity proved by the testimonies of the Apostles alone, but the prophets recognised him as such long ago, and the same has been declared by countless miracles. It is our task to acknowledge Jesus Christ, who is the true God and eternal life, as our teacher and Saviour, and to be grafted into him by true faith, so that, instructed by the knowledge of the true God, we may bear fruits worthy of him, and live with him in the heavens, to whom belong blessing, glory, honour and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXVII. Filioli, cauete uobis à simulachris. Amen.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXVII. Little children, beware of idols. Amen.

units.la: Quicunque in salutis causa siue negotio non inutiliter versari volunt, eos & veram Dei cognitione instructos esse, & veram cultus Dei rationem nouisse oportet. Vt enim Deo, quem ignoramus, nos coniungi impossibile est: ita nisi cognitum ritè colamus, inanis & superuacanea erit cognitionis Dei gloriatio. Utrunq; verò habebit, quicunq; Christum Iesum vere amplexus fuerit. Nam & expressa Dei imago est, quæ Dei naturam plenè cognoscendam proponit, & idem diserte monet, vt per fidem illi placere possimus. Quæ causa est, quòd in huius cognitione tradenda tanto studio Ioânes versatur. Cæterum quia à Deo & salute multis rebus abstrahi solemus, eas quoq; non minus notiuisse oportet, vt caueri possint. Dixit ergo tu de falsis doctrinis tum de mundo & huius studijs hucusq; Apostolus, quæ duo hic facilè primatum tenent. Comprehendit falsa doctrina cultus omnes, qui contra Dei verbum nostræ rationis suasu instituuntur, inter quos simulachris omnibus ferè seculis primum locum cesisse constat. Non contentus ergo Ioannes de doctrinis falsis admonuisse, contra peruersum & impium simulachrorum cultum sub finem epistolæ peculiari præcepto nos instruit: quod vt breue est, ita breuitate sua singularem grauitatem tegit. Cuius consyderatio diligens haberi debet, cum plerique Christiani nominis professorum, id pro lusu iocoq; habeant, quod tanto studio spiritus sanctus in scripturis prohibet. Et si verum fateri libeat, constabit nostro seculo tam Iudæos quàm Turcas diuini præcepti maiorem rationem habere, quàm eos qui Christi nomine & fide gloriantur.
units.tr: Whoever wishes to engage usefully in the matter of salvation or its business ought to be both instructed in the true knowledge of God and to know the true manner of worshipping God. For just as it is impossible for us to be joined to God whom we do not know, so unless we worship him duly as known, the boast of knowing God will be empty and superfluous. And whoever has embraced Christ Jesus truly will have both. For he is the express image of God, who sets forth the nature of God to be fully known, and he plainly teaches that we may please God through faith. This is why John labours so eagerly in handing down this knowledge.
