But because we are commonly drawn away from God and salvation by many things, it is no less necessary to know these also, so that they may be guarded against. The Apostle has therefore so far spoken of false doctrines and of the world and its pursuits, which two things here easily hold the first place. False doctrine comprises all the cults that are instituted against the Word of God at the suggestion of our reason, among which it is established that images have held the first place in almost every age. John, therefore, not content to have warned about false doctrines, instructs us near the end of the letter by a particular precept against the perverse and impure worship of images; and this precept, short as it is, conceals its singular weight under its brevity. Careful consideration of it ought to be had, since most of those who profess the Christian name treat as a jest and a game what the Holy Spirit so earnestly forbids in the Scriptures. And if we are willing to confess the truth, it will be clear in our age that the Jews and the Turks have a greater regard for the divine precept than those who boast of the name and faith of Christ.

units.la: Filioli, cauete uobis à simulachris. Filiolos appellat credentes, vt sæpe alias. Vtitur autem hoc nomine (vt in præcedentibus videre licuit) quoties de re graui & obseruatu dignissima admonere vult: quia hoc modo & sui animi beneuolentiam testari potest, & illos sui iuris, quod doctori vt patri in filios est, admonet. Perinde ergo est, ac si dicat: Mementote quæso, me non temere vos monendi prouinciam suscepisse. Per euangelium enim vos genui & Christo despondi virginem intemeratam. Exigit ergo patris officium, vt in posterum quoque vestri curam habeam, & de periculis imminentibus admoneam. Exigit vicissim filiorum officium, vt paterni pectoris affectum agnoscatis, monentem audiatis patienter, & obtemperetis sedulò: maximè, quando non filios modò agnosco, sed filiolorum loco habeo, quos tenerrimo amore totos complector.
units.tr: Little children, beware of idols. He calls believers little children, as he often does elsewhere. He uses this name (as we have been able to see in what precedes) whenever he wishes to admonish about a weighty matter most worthy of observance, because in this way he can both testify to his goodwill of mind and remind them of his authority over them, which a teacher has over his children as a father. It is therefore as if he said: Remember, I beg you, that I have not undertaken the task of warning you rashly. For through the gospel I have begotten you and betrothed you to Christ as a pure virgin. The duty of a father therefore requires that I also have care of you in future and warn you of impending dangers. In turn, the duty of children requires that you recognise the affection of a fatherly heart, that you listen patiently to one who warns you, and that you obey diligently; especially since I not only acknowledge you as sons but hold you in the place of little children, whom I embrace entirely with the tenderest love.

units.la: Quid verò illud est, cuius obseruationem huius tituli mentione commendare voluit? Caue-te vobis (inquit) à simulachris. Exposui hucusq; salutis rationem omnem. Audiuistis in Christo exhiberi veram Dei cognitionem, & in eodem nos cum Deo per fidem coniungi. In his ergo vos manere & solidos stare conuenit, nec committendum est, vt vos securitas opprimat. Instant vndiq; pericula ab ijs, qui falsos cultus vero praeferunt. Solicitat mundi amicitia, ne ea abominem ini,in quibus hic religionem & salutem omnem cōfistere arbitratur. Hinc fit, vt & idolorum tem-pla ingredi, & conuiuijs immolatitijs vesci multis non admodum graue fit, qui hoc sufficere pu-tant, quōd animos vera Dei cognitione habeant instructos. Sed si cognitione dei vera non frustra gloriamini, reipsa testari vos conuenit, vos illum amare, & abhorrere ab omnibus, quæ gloriam ipsius obfuscare solent. Id cum praecipuè imagines & simulachra faciàt, illa vitare & ab ijs ceu pe-ste aliqua cauere oportet, ne vel infirmis fratribus offendiculo fitis, vel consuetudine vulgari de-cepti, Deum imaginibus aut exprimi & effingi, aut saltem aliquo modo coli putetis.
units.tr: But what is that thing which, by mentioning this title, he wished to commend for observance? Beware (he says) of idols. Up to this point I have set out the whole manner of salvation. You have heard that the true knowledge of God is set forth in Christ, and that in him we are joined with God through faith. It is fitting, therefore, that you remain in these things and stand firm, and that security should not be allowed to overwhelm you. Dangers press on every side from those who prefer false cults to the true one. The friendship of the world tempts you not to shun those things in which it judges all religion and all salvation to consist. Hence it comes about that for many, who think it is enough that their minds are instructed in the true knowledge of God, it is no great harm to enter the temples of idols and to eat of sacrificial feasts. But if we do not boast in vain of the true knowledge of God, it is fitting that you show by deed that you love him and abhor all those things which are wont to obscure his glory. Since images and idols especially do this, it is right to avoid them and to beware of them as of some plague, lest you either become a stumbling block to weak brethren, or, deceived by common custom, think that God is expressed and fashioned by images, or at least worshipped in some way through them.

units.la: Porrò, si praecedentia repetamus, videbimus, Ioannem eo ordine vti, quo deus ipse in Deca-logo vti voluit. Illic enim primò omnium de seipso loquitur, quis sit docet, & alienos deos finge-re prohibet. Mox verò praeceptum de imaginibus subijcit, quo omnem cultum falsum explodit. Simili ratione prophetæ, quando de Christo & regno eius vaticinantur, sub quo verum dei cul-tum instaurari oporteat, vbi huius formam tradiderunt, mox de simulachris agunt, & illa tunc excindenda esse docent. Vide Isa.2.40.44.Mich.5.Zach.13. &c. Hos ergo imitans Apostolus, vbi veram veri dei cognitionem in Iesu Christo monstrauit, de simulachris admonēs, nos ad dei praeceptum relegat, vt discamus eum cultum deo offerri debere, quem ipse exigit, fugiendum vero esse, quem olim tam vehementer abominatus est.
units.tr: Moreover, if we go back over what precedes, we shall see that John uses the order which God himself willed to use in the Decalogue. For there first of all he speaks of himself, teaches who he is, and forbids the fashioning of other gods. Soon afterwards he adds the precept concerning images, by which he casts out every false worship. In a similar way the prophets, when they prophesy about Christ and his kingdom, under which the true worship of God ought to be restored, after they have set out its form, at once speak of images and teach that these must then be cut off. See Isa. 2, 40, 44; Mich. 5; Zech. 13, etc. Imitating these, the Apostle, having shown the true knowledge of the true God in Jesus Christ, and warning about images, refers us back to God's precept, so that we may learn that the worship which he himself demands ought to be offered to God, and that the worship which he once so vehemently abominated ought to be shunned.

units.la: Caeterum vt olim Apostolis cum gentilium deorū simulachris certamen fuit, ita cū illis ho-die nobis pugna est, qui verum deum sanctosq; dei cultores, vita defunctos, simulachris coli pof-se & debere contendunt. Qui vbi diuinam legem & quaecunq; ex hac tam prophetæ quàm Apo-stoli monuerunt, allegamus, ea omnia duntaxat de gentilium deorum imaginibus intelligi debe-re clamitant. Et hic quidem egregio, si dijs placet, commento vti consueuerunt. Nam inter idola & simulachra distinguentes, illa quidem prohibita esse fatentur, vtpote in deorum gentilium ho-norem facta, haec verò non item, quia in dei veri & sanctorum ipsius honorem erigantur. At pro-dunt hic suam ignorantiam, ne quid grauius dicamus. Quid enim attinet inter idolum & simula-chrum distinguere, quando non eiusdem linguae voces sunt, quarum tamē significatio est vna & eadem? Aut ergo monstrent aliā Latinam vocem, quae quid idolum sit exprimat, aut simulachrū nobis relinquant, quo idem quod idolo significatur. Vel num negare poterūt, Romanos suis dijs simulachra posuisse, cum id Latini scriptores passim doceant? Perinde itaque faciunt, ac si quis di-cat non scortationem, sed <bl>πορνεία</bl> in scripturis prohiberi.
units.tr: Moreover, just as the Apostles once had a contest with the images of the gods of the Gentiles, so today we have a fight with those who contend that the true God and the holy worshippers of God, departed this life, may and ought to be worshipped by images. When we cite the divine law and all that both the prophets and the Apostles have taught from it, they cry out that all these things are to be understood only of the images of the gods of the Gentiles. And these men are wont to use, forsooth, a remarkable invention. For distinguishing between idols and images, they admit that the former are indeed forbidden, as being made to the honour of the heathen gods, but the latter are not likewise forbidden, because they are erected to the honour of the true God and of his saints. But by this they reveal their ignorance, not to say something more severe. For what is the point of distinguishing between an idol and an image, when they are not words of the same language, though their meaning is one and the same? Either let them show us another Latin word that expresses what an idol is, or let them leave us an image by which the same thing is signified as by idol. Or indeed can they deny that the Romans placed images to their gods, since Latin writers teach this everywhere? They therefore act just as if someone said that not fornication but <bl>πορνεία</bl> is forbidden in the Scriptures.

units.la: Constat praeterea eandem esse idololatriae rationem apud Christianos homines, quę olim a-pud gentiles fuit, siue ipsa simulachra, siue eorum vsum cultūq; consyderes. De gentilium enim simulachris Dauid loquens, ea ad hunc modum describit: Simulachra ipsorum sunt argentea & aurea, opus quod manibus hominis producitur. Os habent, & non loquuntur: oculos habent, & non vident. Aures habent, nec audiunt: nasum habent, nec odorantur: Manus habent, nec palpāt: pedes habent, nec ambulant, neque sonum edunt suo gutture, &c. Psal.115. Quid verò ab his Chri-stianorum simulachra differunt vel materia vel forma, vel etiam actionibus? Sed vt de forma plu-ribus agamus, fingebāt gentiles alium quidem senili, alium verò iuuenili habitu. Alius ceu iratus fulmen librabat aut ensem, alius rursum miti & placido aspectu intuētes alliciebat. Inter deas alię matronalem grauitatem referebant, aliæ lasciuiam & intemperantiam non obscurē loquebantur. Accedebant his & brutorum animalium formae, vt Paulus ad Romanos scribit. Num verò haec omnia in Christianorum templis desyderantur? Sedet senili forma (imò ridicula, vt Augustinus monuit) Deus pater, & filium adhuc cruentum atque lacerum sinu fouet. Insidet humero vel pe-ctori adhaeret spiritus sanctus, adhuc columbae speciem, in qua semel apparuit, referens. At cum idem deus fit, num nos deo volucris formam affingere negabimus? Gladio armatus astat Paulus. Cultro nudato cernitur Barptolemaeus. Equēs cataphractus pugnat Georgius. Imò nullus ferè diuorum inermis fingitur. De diuarum imaginibus pudet dicere, sed res ipsa loquitur, tali ferè eas habitu pingi & sculpi, qualem nemo bonus pater in filia, nec maritus probus in vxore fer-ret. Nec desunt brutorum animalium imagines, cum Vendelino boues oues-que, Antonio porci, Eustachio canes & cerui, Gertrudae mures astent. Quid quōd asinus, quo olim Christus vsus est, simulachrum peculiare meruit? Quid si cultum spectes, in hoc etiam à gentibus nihil differimus. Nam vt illi olim, simulachris sacella & templa extruimus, aras consecramus, eadem vestimus, ad-haec esculenta & poculenta sacrificia vnà cum pecunijs offerimus. Coram illis prosternimur cernui, preces ad illa dirigimus, nec prodest diuum vel diuam inuocauisse, nisi locum, quo peculiariter delectari putatur, nominatim exprimas. Cum ergo eadem fit tam simulachrorum quàm cultus qui ipsis impenditur, ratio apud nos, quae olim gentilibus fuit, minimè putandum est, horum tantummodo simulachra diuinitus prohibita esse, nobis vero licere, vt mutatis dunta-xat Deorum nominibus eadem faciamus, propter quae illi olim damnati sunt. Eo enim grauius à nobis peccatur, quòd veri & æterni Dei gloriam in imagines, quas ille tâtopere abominatur, transferimus, & sanctissimorum hominum, qui sanguine effuso Dei gloriam asserere studuerunt, titulis ad idololatriam & superstitionem abutimur.
units.tr: It is further clear that the manner of idolatry among Christian men is the same as it once was among the Gentiles, whether you consider the images themselves or their use and worship. For David, speaking of the images of the Gentiles, describes them in this manner: Their images are of silver and gold, the work produced by the hands of man. They have mouths, and do not speak; they have eyes, and do not see. They have ears, and do not hear; they have noses, and do not smell. They have hands, and do not feel; they have feet, and do not walk, nor do they make a sound with their throat, etc. Ps. 115. But what do the images of Christians differ from these in material, or in form, or even in their actions? But to speak more fully of form: the Gentiles fashioned one god in the appearance of an old man, and another in the appearance of a young man. One, as if angry, poised a thunderbolt or a sword, while another, on the contrary, with a gentle and placid look, drew people to him. Among the goddesses, some bore the dignity of a matron, while others openly expressed wantonness and intemperance. To these were added the forms of brute animals, as Paul writes to the Romans. Are all these things, then, wanting in the temples of Christians? The Father sits in the form of an old man (indeed a ridiculous one, as Augustine warned), and he cherishes the Son, still bloody and torn, in his bosom. The Holy Spirit sits on a shoulder or clings to the breast, still representing the form of the dove in which he once appeared. And when the same God is made, shall we deny that we attribute the form of a bird to God? Paul stands by, armed with a sword. Bartholomew is seen with his knife drawn. Saint George fights on a mailed horse. Indeed, almost none of the saints is portrayed unarmed. It is shameful to speak of the images of the female saints, but the thing itself speaks: they are painted and carved in such a dress as no good father would tolerate in his daughter, nor any upright husband in his wife. Nor are images of brute animals lacking: oxen and sheep stand with Wendelin, pigs with Anthony, dogs and stags with Eustace, mice with Gertrude. What of the fact that the ass, which Christ once used, has earned a special image? And if you look at the worship, in this too we differ in nothing from the nations. For, just as they once did with their images, we build chapels and temples for them, consecrate altars, clothe them in the same way, and besides offer them food and drink as sacrifices, together with money. We prostrate ourselves with our heads bowed before them, we direct prayers to them, and it avails nothing to have invoked a god or goddess unless you name the place in which he or she is thought to take particular delight. Since, therefore, the case of images and of the worship paid to them is the same among us as it once was among the Gentiles, it must by no means be thought that only the images of those gods were forbidden by God, while we are permitted to do the same things, the names of the gods merely being changed, for which those men were once condemned. For we sin all the more gravely in that we transfer the glory of the true and eternal God to images, which he so greatly abominates, and in that we abuse the titles of the most holy men, who strove to defend the glory of God at the cost of their blood, for idolatry and superstition.

units.la: Porrò, vt clarius constet, quàm fallantur qui simulachris cuiuscunque generis, quę religionis ergò fiunt, patrocinari solent, prodest ipsum Deum in monte Sinai de his concionantem audire, hoc modo: Non facies tibi sculptile, neque similitudinem vllam eorum quę in cœlis sunt sursum, vel in terra deorsum, vel quæ in aquis sub terra sunt. Non adorabis, neque coles. Ego sum dominus Deus tuus fortis, zelotes, visitans iniquitatem patrum in filijs, in terram & quartam generationem, eorum qui oderunt me: & faciens misericordiam in millia, his qui diligunt me, & custodiunt præcepta mea. Sunt huius præcepti partes tres. Prima, ne Deo alicuius Creaturæ imaginem[?] affingamus, prohibet. Secunda, quatenus imagines nec fieri nec factæ ab alijs ferri debeant, docet. Tertia ostendit, causas nobis iustas non vllas esse, propter quas vel alienos Deos fingamus, vel Deo vero cultus illegitimos & prohibitos exhibeamus. In horum omnium cōsyderatione si non ofcitanter versemur, mera somnia esse patebunt, quæcunque hodie pro imaginibus siue simulachris & eorum cultu afferuntur.
units.tr: Moreover, so that it may be clearer how mistaken those are who usually defend images of any kind made for the sake of religion, it is useful to hear God himself preaching about them on Mount Sinai, in this way: "You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of what is in heaven above, or on the earth beneath, or of what is in the waters under the earth. You shall not adore them, nor worship them. I am the Lord your God, a strong God, jealous, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me; and showing mercy to thousands, to those who love me and keep my precepts." This precept has three parts. The first forbids us to fashion an image of any creature for God. The second teaches that images ought neither to be made nor, once made, be brought forward by others. The third shows that there are no just causes for which we may either fashion strange gods or offer to the true God illegitimate and forbidden worship. If we attend to all of these with no careless inattention, it will be plain that whatever is today put forward in defence of images or likenesses and their worship is pure dreams.

units.la: Primùm, ne Deo alicuius creaturæ imago tribuatur, prohiberi diximus. Id nos verè dixisse, totius diuinæ orationis contextus & argumentum probant. Dei enim scopus est, Israelitas in religionis causa instituere. Quare primo præcepto, vt se solum & vnum Deum agnoscant, præcipit. Mox autem secundo de cultu, qui ipsi debetur, admonet, à quo imagines & simulachra procul remoueri vult. De ijs ergo simulachris loquitur, quæ in ipsius honore & cultum ab hominibus ineptis & superstitiosis fingûntur. Docet hoc Moses, verborum Dei interpres fidelissimus, qui legem omnem exponens ait: Locutus est dominus ad vos de medio ignis, & quidem vocem verborum eius audiuistis, simulachrum verò nullum vidistis, præterquam vocem. Cauete ergo accurate quàm chara vobis est anima vestra, ne forte peruerse quid agatis, faciendo scilicet vobis sculptile, simulachrum cuiuscunque figuræ, formam maris aut fœminæ, formam cuiuscunque animantis, quæ est in terra: formam cuiuscunq; volucris pennatæ, quæ volat in cœlo: formam cuiuscunque reptantis super terram: formam cuiuscunque piscis, qui est in aquis sub terra, &c. Deut. 4. Docet hæc euidentissimè, quorsum tam diligens omnium rerum creatarum distributio pertineat, qua Deus in sua lege vtitur, nimirum ne alicuius creaturæ formam ipsi affingere tentemus. Causæ huius præcepti in promptu sunt. Primò enim Deus cum infinitus, immensus & æternus sit, nullaq;[?] hominis vel ratione vel eloquentia comprehendi possit, nullius etiam rei imagine exprimi poterit. Quamcunque ergo formam Dei imaginem esse dixeris, ea quod pollicetur, non præstabit, & proinde mendax erit. Num verò Deus, qui æterna est veritas, mendacio coli poterit? Adde his, quod (vt Paulus docet) qui creaturarum simulachris deum exprimere conantur, Dei immortalis gloriam & veritatem mendacio permutât, & quæ solius Dei sunt, in imaginem mortalis & mi-seræ creaturæ transferunt. At quæ Deo contumelia maior inferetur? Quare Lactantius magna cum authoritate pronunciare ausus est: Non est dubium, quin religio nulla sit, vbicunque simulachrum est. Nec enim mētiuntur modò Deum imagines, verumetiam homines à spirituali cultu auocant, vt qui circa hunc versari debebant, in frigidis Ceremonijs & inepto ipsarum cultu toti occupentur. Quam ob causam cultus ille fornicationis nomen meruit. Quia vt fornicatio legitimo matrimonio infesta est, & coniugij vinculum disrumpit: ita idolorum cultus animam à Deo, cui desponsata esse debebat, abstrahit. Fatebuntur hoc, quicunque prioris superstitionis memoriam, cum ijs quæ olim in simulachrorum cultu fecerunt, in animum reuocarint.
units.tr: First, we said that an image of any creature is forbidden to be attributed to God. That we have spoken truly here is proved by the context and the argument of the whole divine discourse. For God's aim is to instruct the Israelites in the matter of religion. Therefore, in the first precept, he commands that they acknowledge him alone as the one God. Then, in the second, he admonishes them concerning the worship that is due to him, from which he wishes images and likenesses to be removed far away. He therefore speaks of those likenesses that foolish and superstitious men fashion for the honour and worship of God himself. Moses, the most faithful interpreter of God's words, teaches this, who, expounding the whole law, says: "The Lord spoke to you out of the midst of the fire, and indeed you heard the voice of his words, but you saw no likeness, except a voice. Take careful heed, therefore, how dear your soul is to you, lest perhaps you do something perverse, namely by making for yourselves a carved image, a likeness of any figure, the form of a male or female, the form of any animal that is on the earth, the form of any winged bird that flies in the heaven, the form of anything that creeps upon the earth, the form of any fish that is in the waters under the earth, etc." Deut. 4. This very clearly teaches to what end that so careful distribution of all created things, which God uses in his law, pertains: namely, that we should not attempt to attribute to him the form of any creature. The causes of this precept lie ready to hand. For first, since God is infinite, immense and eternal, and cannot be comprehended by any man either by reason or by eloquence, he cannot be expressed by the image of any thing whatever. Therefore, whatever form you say is an image of God, it will not perform what it promises, and so will be a liar. But can God, who is eternal truth, be worshipped by a lie? Add to these that (as Paul teaches) those who try to express God by likenesses of creatures exchange the glory and truth of the immortal God for a lie, and transfer to the image of a mortal and wretched creature what belongs to God alone. But what greater insult could be offered to God? Therefore Lactantius, with great authority, has dared to pronounce: "There is no doubt that there is no religion wherever there is an image." For images not only lie about God, but also call men away from spiritual worship, so that those who ought to be occupied with that are wholly taken up with cold ceremonies and the foolish worship of these things. For this reason that worship has deserved the name of fornication. As fornication is hostile to lawful marriage and breaks the bond of wedlock, so the worship of idols draws the soul away from God, to whom it ought to have been betrothed. All who call to mind the memory of the earlier superstition, together with what they once did in the worship of images, will confess this.

units.la: Sed audio quosdam Christi incarnationem & hominem, quem ille assumpsit, nobis obijcere. Fatentur hi, olim quidem Iudæis interdictum fuisse, ne aliquam Deo imaginem fingerent, qui visibili specie ipsis nunquam apparuerat: nos verò eadem lege nequaquam teneri, qui filium Dei, patri coæternum & expressam eiusdem imaginem, hominem verum factum & in terris versatum fuisse nouimus. Imò ad deuotionem animi & fidem excitandam non parum prodesse putant, si in Cruce pendentis imaginem crebrò videamus. Sed hos etiam vehementer falli, multis rationibus demonstrari potest. Primò equidem falsum est, quòd Iudæis siue patribus in veteri Testamento Deum visibili specie apparuisse negant. Diuersum enim docet vniuersa patriarcharum historia. Et Daniel vidit filij hominis formam, venientis in nubibus cœli. Nouerunt denique omnes sancti, quòd Dei filius incarnari & hominem induere deberet, nec tamen quisquam inuentus est, qui ideo illum hominis imagine exprimere voluerit. Deinde satis constat, non ideo incarnatum fuisse Dei filium, vt imaginum causam & occasionem praeberet, sed vt carnem suam daret pro mundi vita.Ioàh.6.Quod vbi fecit,quasi peracto omni negotio,cuius gratia in mundum venerat, eàdem carnem in coelos subuexit, vt & nos eum mentibus in coelum sublatis sequamur, nec in externis moremur.Idem cultum spiritualem praescribit,cum quo imaginibus commercij nihil esse potest. Officia verò,quę ipsi impenderemus,siquidem praesens esset, in pauperes conferre iubet,quos sibi substituit.Matt.26.&25.Ridiculus ergo error est,Christū effingere,qui ideo carne à nobis abire voluit,vt spiritu inter nos regnare posset.Ioan.14. Nec aliqua allegari potest veteris & primitiuae ecclesiae authoritas,quae imagines eiusmodi defendat. Irenaeus quidè vetustissimus scriptor, de Gnosticis meminit,quòd Christi imagines habuerint,quas cum Pythagorae,Platonis aliorūq; philosophorum imaginibus ad cultum proponebant: idem verò hoc in illis damnat & reprehendit. Notum est quoq; Epiphanij Salaminae Cypri episcopi factum, quod in epistola ad Ioannem Hierosolymitanum episcopum ipse D. Hieronymo interprete sic commemorat: Cum venissem ad villam,quę dicitur Anablatha,vidissemq; ibi praeteriens lucernam ardentem,& interrogassem quis locus esset, didicissemq; esse ecclesiam,& intrassem vt orarem: inueni ibi velum pendens in foribus eiusdem ecclesiae tinctum atque depictum,& habens imaginem QVASI CHRISTI, VEL SANCTI CVIVSDAM, Non enim satis memini cuius imago fuerit.Cum ergo hoc vidissem, IN ECCLESIA CHRISTI, CONTRA AVTHORITATEM SCRIPTVRARVM,hominis pendere imaginem,scidi illud,& magis dedi cõsilium custodibus eiusdem loci,vt pauperem mortuum eo obuoluerent & efferrent. Et paulò post addit: Precor,vt iubeas presbyteros eiusdem loci deinceps praecipere,in ecclesia Christi istiusmodi vela,quae contra religionem nostram veniunt,non appendi.Docent haec, quo sensu veteris ecclesiae doctores praecepta Dei de simulachris intellexerint,cum Epiphanius Christi imagines & cõtra scripturarum authoritatem haberi,& religioni Christianae palam aduersari dicat.Quid verò illum facturum putabimus,si nostri seculi templa imaginibus quasi personis Comicis & Tragicis,vndique stipata vt diffet? Nec est,quòd illos audiamus,qui nos templa sine Christo & diuis habere dicūt. Habemus enim Christum spiritu suo in templis viuis regnantem,qui & suis in nomine suo congregatis iuxta promissionem suam praesens adest.Habemus Diuorum scripta & exempla, quae fideles sedulò euoluunt & sequuntur. Quòd si haec aliquibus minus sufficiunt, nae illi frustra contra scripturarum authoritatem ligneos lapideosq; Christos & diuos templis suis inferrent. Caeterū ad legem domini reuertamur,cuius tractatio à nobis instituta est.
units.tr: But I hear that some object to us the incarnation of Christ and the man whom he assumed. These men admit that it was once forbidden to the Jews to make any image of God, since he had never appeared to them in visible form; but they say that we are by no means bound by the same law, since we know that the Son of God, co-eternal with the Father and the express image of him, was made a true man and lived on the earth. Indeed, they think it contributes not a little to stirring up devotion of mind and faith if we often see the image of him hanging on the Cross. But it can be shown by many arguments that these men too are gravely mistaken. First, it is indeed false that they deny God appeared in visible form to the Jews or fathers in the Old Testament. For the whole history of the patriarchs teaches otherwise. And Daniel saw the form of the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven. Finally, all the saints knew that the Son of God was to be incarnate and put on a man, and yet no one has been found who wished on that account to express him by the image of a man. Next, it is quite clear that the Son of God was not incarnate in order to provide a cause and occasion for images, but to give his flesh for the life of the world. John 6. When he had done this, as if all the business for which he had come into the world were finished, he carried the same flesh up into the heavens, so that we too might follow him with our minds lifted up to heaven, and not dwell on external things. He likewise prescribes spiritual worship, with which there can be no dealings with images. As for the duties that we would render to him, were he present, he commands us to confer them upon the poor, whom he has substituted for himself. Matt. 26 and 25. It is therefore a ridiculous error to portray Christ, who wished to depart from us in the flesh so that he might reign among us in the Spirit. John 14. Nor can any authority of the old and primitive Church be alleged that defends images of this kind. Irenaeus, indeed, a very ancient writer, mentions the Gnostics, that they had images of Christ, which they set forth for worship together with images of Pythagoras, Plato and other philosophers; but he himself condemns and reproves this in them. It is also well known what was done by Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, who, in his letter to John, bishop of Jerusalem, which St. Jerome translated, records it thus: "When I had come to a village called Anablatha, and had seen as I passed a burning lamp there, and had asked what place it was, and had learned that it was a church, and had gone in to pray, I found there a veil hanging at the doors of that church, dyed and painted, and having the image of something like Christ or of some saint—for I do not clearly remember whose image it was. When therefore I had seen this, that a human image was hanging IN THE CHURCH OF CHRIST, AGAINST THE AUTHORITY OF THE SCRIPTURES, I tore it, and rather gave advice to the keepers of that place that they should wrap a poor dead man in it and bury him. And a little later he adds: I pray that you will order the elders of that place henceforth to instruct that veils of this kind, which are opposed to our religion, not be hung in the church of Christ." These things teach in what sense the teachers of the old Church understood God's precepts about images, since Epiphanius says that images of Christ are kept against the authority of the Scriptures and openly oppose the Christian religion. But what shall we think he would do if he saw the temples of our age crowded on every side with images, as if they were comic and tragic personages, so that they might be seen? Nor need we listen to those who say that we have temples without Christ and the saints. For we have Christ reigning in our temples living by his Spirit, who, according to his promise, is present with his own gathered in his name. We have the writings and examples of the saints, which the faithful diligently study and follow. But if these are less than sufficient for some, then indeed they vainly bring wooden and stone Christs and saints into their temples against the authority of the Scriptures. But let us return to the law of the Lord, whose treatment we have undertaken.

units.la: Secunda huius parte docemur, quatenus imagines nec à nobis fieri, nec ab alijs factae ferri vel tolerari debeant.Comprehendit vtrumque paucis verbis, cum ait: Non adorabis,neq; coles. Significat his omnem reuerentiae, honoris & cultus speciem, quae ab hominibus fingi,illisq; impendi potest. Hanc verò omnem quia prohibet,facilè constat,non in eum finem vel vsum illas facere debere,vt à nobis colantur, vel aliquo modo religionis instrumenta sint. Quòd si verò religionis instrumenta esse nō debent,facilè liquet, publica authoritate easdem esse tollendas,si à superstitiosis tales vel fiant, vel pro talibus habeantur. Pertinet huc Ezechiae regis exemplum,qui aeneum serpentem, olim diuino praecepto à Mose factum,demoliri & minutim coterere non est vetritus, vbi illum ab aliquibus stultè religiosis coli vidit. 4. Reg. 18. At si quae vnquam imago defendi debuit, hanc defendi debuisse dicemus. Nec enim carnali zelo contra Dei praeceptum,sed mandate Deo, nec absque sanctae obedientiae studio, fabricata fuit. Num. 21. Adhaec Christi Iesu typus erat,& vniuersum humanae redemptionis mysterium complectebatur, sicut ipse dominus explicat.Ioan.3.Laudatur tamen Ezechias,qui coli coeptam,forti & sancto zelo comminuit.Eant ergo & nos ἀκονομάχους[?] esse clamitent,quibus displicet, quòd è templis nostris imagines eiectę sunt. Hoc nomine equidem multos laudem meruisse scimus, neminem verò ob imagines, vel factas, vel cultas, vel defensas, vnquam Deo placuisse legimus. Docet item communis sensus, nihil in ecclesijs ferri debere, quod vero Dei cultui aduersetur, ex quorum genere imagines esse, su-pra didicimus.
units.tr: This second part teaches us that images must neither be made by us nor brought in and tolerated when made by others. The whole matter is covered in a few words when he says: "You shall not adore, nor worship." He signifies by these words every form of reverence, honour and worship that can be devised by men and paid to those things. Since he forbids all of this, it is easily established that images ought not to be made for the purpose or use of being worshipped by us, or to be any kind of instrument of religion. But if they ought not to be instruments of religion, it is plainly clear that they must be removed by public authority, if superstitious people either make them or regard them as such. To this belongs the example of King Hezekiah, who did not hesitate to demolish and grind into small pieces the bronze serpent, once made by Moses by divine command, when he saw it being worshipped by some foolishly pious people. 4 Kings 18. Yet if any image ever ought to have been defended, we shall say that this one ought to have been defended. For it was made not from carnal zeal against God's command, but by God's command, and not without a desire for holy obedience. Num. 21. Moreover, it was a type of Jesus Christ and embraced the whole mystery of human redemption, as the Lord himself explains. John 3. Nevertheless Hezekiah is praised, because with strong and holy zeal he crushed what had begun to be worshipped. Let them therefore go and cry out that we are ἀκονομάχους [?], those who are displeased that images have been cast out of our churches. We know that many have earned praise for this, but we read that no one has ever pleased God on account of images, whether made, worshipped or defended. Common sense likewise teaches that nothing should be carried into churches that is opposed to the true worship of God, and, as we learned above, images are of that kind.

units.la: Porrò prodeunt hic,qui imaginibus cultum minimè impendi debere fatentur,earundem tamen vsum in ecclesijs non vulgarem & inutilem esse contendūt, quòd vel Dei vel sanctorum operam in memoriam reuocent,& ad bene agendum extimulent: quo nomine à multis libri laicorum dici consueuerunt. At produnt isti crassam ignorantiā, qua excaecati, in quibus cultus Dei potissimum versetur,ignorant. Si enim hoc nouissent, scirent vtiq; in hoc nō postremū locū doctrinae & discēdi studio deberi.Christus enim eos verbi sui amore & studio teneri dicit,qui ex Deo nati sunt.Ioan.8.Et Mariam,quae pedibus suis asidens verbū audiebat, Marthae circa externa officia multū occupatae longè praefert,vtpote quae partem potiorem delegerit.Luc.10.Vt autem discēdi studium in religione primas tenet, ita huic verbum suum destinavit Deus, non imagines, quæ re-ligioni veræ adversantur. Et Moses non obscurè docet, ideo imaginem Dei nullam in monte Ho-reb apparuisse, ut in solum Dei verbū intenti, omnia alia fugiamus, quæ ab huius studio nos avo-care poterant. Deut.4. Et sanè veritatem mendacijs doceri impossibile est. Rectè igitur propheta clamat: Quid proderit sculptile? Quoniam sculpsit illud fictor eius: fusile[?], & doctor mendax? Et tamen fidit eo, fictor scilicet figmento suo, ut faceret idola muta. Væ qui ligno dicit, Euigila: & la-pidi effigiato, Excitare. Ipse ne doceret? En obductus est auro & argéto, nec est flatus in eo. At do-minus in templo sanctitatis suæ: taceat à conspectu eius universa terra. Heb.2. Audiant hæc, qui imagines doctores audire cupiunt. Doctores mendaces has vocat propheta. Et si verum fateri li-beat experientia magistra didicimus, veram Dei cognitionem & cultum nulla alia re tam fuisse corruptam, quàm imaginum usu. Ab eo enim tempore, quo primum in ecclesias irrepserunt, ni-hil non errorum obortum est, & fœcundissima hæc fuit omnis superstitionis & corruptelæ seges. Adde his, quòd non alius simulachrorum cultus est magnificétior, quàm si ab ijs discere velimus, quæ ad salutis negotium spectant. Ut enim doctorem suum is demum verè colit, qui talem agnoscit, quem audire & ex cuius ore discere debeat: non verò is, qui cum caput coram illo aperiat, ge-nu flectat, loco cedat, deducat, tamen pro cordato & sapienti non iudicat, cuius doctrina instituì possit: ita plus colit imagines, qui doctoris titulum illis defert, quàm qui vel cerea incédit, vel alijs eiusmodi officijs illas prosequitur. Firmiter ergo teneamus Dei sententiam, qui eas nec honorari nec coli vult. Et quia nullum in religione locum tenere possunt, templis fidelium eijci, non in-ferri debent.
units.tr: Furthermore, there come forward here those who confess that images must by no means be worshipped, yet they maintain that their use in churches is not common and useless, because they recall to memory the works of God or of the saints and stir us up to do good; for this reason they are commonly called "the books of the laity." But these men betray a gross ignorance, by which, blinded, they do not know where the true worship of God chiefly lies. For if they knew this, they would certainly know that in this a not unimportant place must be given to doctrine and eagerness to learn. Christ says that those who are born of God are held by love and zeal for his word. John 8. And he far prefers Mary, who sat at his feet and heard the word, to Martha, who was busy with many external duties, as one who had chosen the better part. Luke 10. As the eagerness to learn holds the first place in religion, so God has assigned to it his word, not images, which are opposed to the true religion. And Moses teaches clearly that for this reason no image of God appeared on Mount Horeb, so that, intent on God's word alone, we might flee from all other things that could call us away from its study. Deut. 4. And indeed it is impossible for truth to be taught by lies. Rightly therefore the prophet cries out: "What will a graven image profit? For its maker has graven it, a molten image, and a lying teacher? And yet he trusts in it, namely its maker in his own figment, to make dumb idols. Woe to him who says to wood, 'Awake,' and to a fashioned stone, 'Arise.' Will it teach? Behold, it is overlaid with gold and silver, and there is no breath in it. But the Lord is in the temple of his holiness; let all the earth keep silence before him." Hab. 2. Let those who desire images as teachers hear these things. The prophet calls these teachers liars. And if it is permitted to speak the truth, experience, the teacher of life, has taught us that the true knowledge and worship of God has been corrupted by no other thing so much as by the use of images. For from the time when they first crept into the churches, every kind of error has arisen, and this has been the most fruitful seedbed of all superstition and corruption. Add to these points that no worship of images is more magnificent than when we wish to learn from them those things that pertain to the business of salvation. For just as a man truly honours his teacher only when he recognises him as one whom he ought to hear and from whose mouth he ought to learn, and not when he uncovers his head before him, bends his knee, yields his place and escorts him, yet does not judge him to be a wise and sensible man from whose teaching he could be instructed; so he who gives the title of teacher to images honours them more than he who merely burns wax candles before them or pays them other such services. Let us therefore hold firmly to God's judgment, who wills that they be neither honoured nor worshipped. And since they can hold no place in religion, they ought to be cast out of the temples of the faithful, not brought in.

units.la: Sed præstat tertiam quoque præcepti diuiui partem inspexisse, quæ docet, nullam nobis causam satis iustam gravemq; esse, qua moti vel alienos Deos fingamus, vel Deum verum cultibus illicitis veneremur. Dicit enim: Ego sum dominus Deus tuus fortis, zelotes, visitans iniquitatem patrum in filijs, in tertiam & quartam generationem eorum, qui oderunt me: & faciens misericordiam in millia his, qui diligunt me, & custodiunt præcepta mea. Tria his consyderanda proponit dominus. Primò, ego sum (inquit) dominus Deus tuus fortis. Id est, talis tantusq; sum, ut solus tibi sufficere, te iuuare & tueri possim, sicut Abrahæ olim sum pollicitus. Gen.17. Stultû ergo fuerit, si me neglecto, apud alios opem quæras, & aliorum potius quàm mea beneficentia te subleuari posse exististimes. Adhæc cum fortis Deus sim, cuius potentia inuicta est, tuusq; Deus sim, quod multis operibus me declarauisse expertus es, maiorem conuenit mei præcepti apud te authoritatem esse, quàm ut temere illud transgredi libeat. Secundò, se zelotem & indignabundum esse dicit. Sunt enim, quibus nec ingenium neque vires desunt, torpent verò & naturali quadam socordia grauati rerum rationem non habent aliquam, sed susque deque ferunt omnia. Talis verò non sum ego, dicit dominus. Quin potius maritos probos refero, qui quò magis amant cóiuges, eò magis de ipsarum amore & fide soliciti sunt, nec quenquam tam charum habent & intimum, quem in huius amoris consortium admittere possint. Quò fit, ut sæpe satis molesti nimiumq; morosi habeantur. Eodem ingenio & me prædituʀ esse intelligas, nec ullo modo ferre posse, ut cultus, qui mihi debetur, in simulachra muta & mendacia transferatur. Huc facit, quod apud Ifaiam dicit: Ego dominus. Hoc est nomen meum, & gloriam meam alteri non dabo, nec laudem meâ sculptilibus. Ifa.42. Qui locus vel solus doceat, simulachra à Dei cultu quàm longissimè remoueri debere. Sed tertium addit, quo zelotis nomen planius & clarius explicatur: Visitans iniquitatem patrum in filios, in tertiam & quartam generationem eorum, qui oderunt me: & faciens misericordiá in millia his, qui diligunt me, & custodiunt præcepta mea. Testatur his dominus se non zelotem modò esse, qui iniuriam iniquo animo ferat, verumetiam in perfidos cultus sui prophanatores horribili iudicio inuehi, eosq; publica suæ iræ exempla facere. Probant hoc exempla, quæ plurima in scripturis extant. Dauidis domum propter idololatriam à Solomone plantatam miseris modis afflictam esse, & regni maximam partem amisisse, sacra historia docet. Fuit scisma illud toti Israeli cuprimis noxium, tandemq; excidio causam præbuit. Quid Ieroboamo, Baafæ, Achabo & posteris ipsius propter simulachrorum cultum euenerit, nemo ignorat mediocriter in sacris literis versatus. Inter Christianos verò propter impiam de imaginibus concertationem Imperium totû scissum esse constat, & eodem tempore Turcarum tyrannidem radices egisse historici fide digni nô obscurè testantur. Nec desunt nostro seculo exempla, quibus suam contra prophanos imaginum cultus iram deus luculenter testatur: at nobis sensus desunt, qui ad omnem fortunam ita obsurduerunt, ut nihil intelligant. Postquam enim verbi sui synceriorem doctrinam nobis deus restituit, ea verò non eo loco habetur, quo iure haberi debebat, & superstitionem cum immani idolomania pluris faciunt homines, quàm quæ dei verbo tradũtur, nec desunt qui templis, per dei verbum repurgatis, idola denuo inferunt, Turcas suppliciorum suorum magistros excitat dominus Deus exercituum, qui verbi contemptores puniant, templa ab idolorum cultu repurgent, & mendaces Christiani nominis professores funditus excindant. Hæc quia Christi spiritu illuminatus præuidit Ioannes, hac tam graui sententia epistolam suam concludi debere putauit, vt diceret: Filioli, cauete vobis à simulachris.
units.tr: But it is worth while also to have looked at the third part of the divine precept, which teaches that we have no cause sufficiently just and weighty by which, moved, we may either fashion strange gods or venerate the true God with forbidden worship. For he says: "I am the Lord your God, a strong God, a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me; and showing mercy to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments." The Lord sets forth three things here to be considered. First, "I am," he says, "the Lord your God, strong." That is, I am of such a kind and so great that I alone can suffice for you, help you and protect you, just as I once promised Abraham. Gen. 17. It will therefore be foolish, if, neglecting me, you seek help from others and think that you can be supported more by the beneficence of others than by mine. Moreover, since I am a strong God, whose power is unconquered, and your God, which you have experienced me to have declared by many works, it is fitting that the authority of my precept should be greater with you than that you should be pleased to transgress it rashly. Second, he says that he is jealous and indignant. For there are some who lack neither talent nor strength, but who are sluggish and, weighed down by a certain natural sloth, take no account of anything, but bear everything carelessly. But I am not such, says the Lord. Rather I resemble good husbands, who, the more they love their wives, the more anxious they are about their love and fidelity, and who hold no one so dear and intimate that they could admit him to the fellowship of this love. As a result, they are often considered rather troublesome and excessively morose. You should understand that I am disposed in the same way, and that in no way can I bear that the worship which is owed to me should be transferred to dumb and lying images. To this pertains what he says through Isaiah: "I am the Lord. This is my name, and I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to graven images." Isa. 42. This passage alone would teach that images must be removed as far as possible from the worship of God. But he adds a third thing, by which the name of jealous is explained more plainly and clearly: "visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me; and showing mercy to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments." By these words the Lord testifies that he is not only a jealous God, who bears an injury with an unfriendly mind, but that he also rushes upon the faithless profaners of his worship with a dreadful judgment and makes them public examples of his anger. The examples which abound in the Scriptures prove this. Sacred history teaches that the house of David, because of idolatry planted by Solomon, was afflicted in wretched ways and lost the greater part of its kingdom. That schism was most harmful to all Israel and at last provided the cause of its destruction. What happened to Jeroboam, Baasha, Ahab and their descendants on account of the worship of images, no one ignorant of the sacred writings, however slightly versed in them, is unaware. Among Christians, indeed, it is well known that the whole empire was torn apart because of the impious contention over images, and historians worthy of belief bear witness, not obscurely, that at the same time the tyranny of the Turks took root. Nor are there lacking in our own age examples by which God clearly bears witness to his anger against the profane worship of images; but we lack senses that have become so deaf to every fortune that they understand nothing. For after God restored to us the purer doctrine of his word, that doctrine is not held in the place it ought rightly to be held, and men value superstition and monstrous idolatry more than what is delivered by the word of God; nor are there lacking those who bring idols back again into temples that have been cleansed through the word of God. The Lord God of hosts raises up the Turks as masters of his punishments, to punish the despisers of his word, to cleanse the temples from the worship of idols, and to utterly overthrow the lying professors of the Christian name. Because John, enlightened by the Spirit of Christ, foresaw these things, he thought that his letter ought to be concluded with this so grave sentence, so that he might say: "Little children, keep yourselves from idols."

units.la: Debent hæc imis animis recondi ô fratres. Repetamus quæso quæ nobis fuerit sub immani regno tenebrarum conditio, quâdo veri Dei ignorantes, infamem simulachrorum cultum & exitialem superstitionem sectabamur. Cogitemus non temere nobis illuxisse veritatis lucem. Vult Deus, vt relictis erroribus veritatis via incedamus. Est hæc vnica verę beatitudinis ratio, quæ nec fallit, nec incertis ludit ambagibus. Aperiamus ergo mentis oculos. Grati simus Deo saluatori & patri clementissimo. Præstemus illi obedientiâ. Seruiamus eidem in spiritu & veritate. Proue hamus nominis sui gloriam, quoad eius fieri poterit. Curemus ne cui offendiculi authores simus. Et inter mundi huius tribulationes constâti fide & spe expectemus cœlestis regni gloriâ, quæ nobis repositâ est in Christo Iesu, cui debetur benedictio, gloria, honor & potestas in æternũ. Amen.
units.tr: These things ought to be stored deep in our hearts, brothers. Let us recall, I beg you, what our condition was under that monstrous kingdom of darkness, when, ignorant of the true God, we pursued the infamous worship of images and a deadly superstition. Let us consider that the light of truth has not dawned upon us by chance. God wills that, having abandoned errors, we walk the way of truth. This is the only way to true blessedness; it neither deceives nor toys with us through uncertain ambiguities. Let us therefore open the eyes of our minds. Let us be thankful to God, our Saviour and most merciful Father. Let us render him obedience. Let us serve him in spirit and in truth. Let us promote the glory of his name as far as we can. Let us take care that we are never the authors of a stumbling block to anyone. And amid the tribulations of this world, let us await with steadfast faith and hope the glory of the heavenly kingdom, which is laid up for us in Christ Jesus, to whom be blessing, glory, honour and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: IN EPISTOLAM D. IOANNIS APOSTOLI II. RODOLPHI GVALTHERI TIGVRINI HOMILIARVM SYLVAB. HOMILIA I.
units.tr: IN EPISTOLAM D. IOANNIS APOSTOLI II. RODOLPHI GVALTHERI TIGVRINI HOMILIARVM SYLVAB. HOMILIA I.

units.la: SENIOR electæ dominæ & liberis eius, quos ego diligo in veritate: & nō ego solus, sed & omnes qui cognouerunt veritatem, propter veritatem quæ permanet in nobis, & nobiscum erit in æternum. Sit nobiscum gratia, misericordia, pax, à Deo patre, & à domino Iesu Christo, filio patris, in veritate & charitate.
units.tr: The elect lady, the elder, and her children, whom I love in truth: and not I alone, but also all who have known the truth, on account of the truth which abides in us and will be with us forever. Grace, mercy and peace be with us from God the Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, in truth and love.

units.la: VEMADMODVM boni ac fidelis pastoris est, non totos modò greges curare & tueri, verumetiâ singulis ouibus pro virili prospicere: ita ecclesiarũ pastores non communi tantum Christiani gregis cura tangi, sed singularũ salutiinuigilare decet. Exemplũ huius curæ & fidei duobus epistolijs, quæ modò tractabimus, D. Ioânes exhibet: quorum prius fideli cuidam matronæ eiusq; liberis, alterum Caio, fratri haud vulgari inscribitur. Priori matronam hanc & eius liberos ad fidei constantiâ hortatur. Quia, vt priori epistola vidimus, iam tûc[?] passim inueniebâtur, qui fidei doctrinam fœdis & impijs erroribus corrumpebant. Simul verò hortatur, ne inani fidei titulo glorientur, sed huius veritatem Christianæ vel fraternæ charitatis operibus declarent.
units.tr: Just as it is the duty of a good and faithful shepherd not only to care for and watch over whole flocks but also to look out for each individual sheep as far as he can, so the ministers of the churches should be moved not only by the common concern for the Christian flock but also be watchful for the salvation of individuals. John gives an example of this care and faithfulness in the two epistles we are about to treat: the first is addressed to a certain faithful matron and her children, the second to Gaius, a brother of no ordinary kind. In the first he exhorts this matron and her children to constancy in the faith, since, as we saw in the first epistle, there were already people spreading everywhere who corrupted the doctrine of faith with foul and impious errors. At the same time he exhorts them not to glory in an empty title of faith, but to show its truth by works of Christian and brotherly love.

units.la: Admonet nos epistolæ argumentum & exemplum Apostoli, quanto studio in monendis & hortandis fratribus opus sit. Si enim viuentibus adhuc Christi Apostolis, qui doctrinæ Christi rumoq; ab ipso gestarũ oculati testes habebâtur, errorũ zizania per impostores passim spargere ausus est satan, quid de nostro de seculo sperabimus? Imò quæ cura nimia & superuacanea videri poterit, cũ in ecclesia palàm grassentur, quos Christus & Apostoli cauere iusserût? Matt.24.2. Pet.2.1.Tim.4.2.Thess.2.&c. Excitetur ergo ministri, ne quis ipsorũ ignauia pereat. Eorundê laboribus & studio faueant qui Christi oues videri volunt, ne maiore mundi & amicitiæ eius, quàm gloriæ Christi rationem habere videantur. Sed istis præmissis præsentem locũ inspiciamus, qui & Inscriptione epistolæ, & apostolicâ salutationem, siue benedictionem (vt alij vocant) continet.
units.tr: The argument and example of the Apostle's letter remind us how great a zeal is needed in admonishing and exhorting the brethren. For if, while the apostles of Christ were still living, men who were eyewitnesses of the doctrine of Christ and of the things done by him, Satan dared to scatter the tares of error everywhere through impostors, what shall we expect in our own age? Indeed, what care could seem excessive or superfluous, when those whom Christ and the apostles bade us beware of are openly rampant in the Church? (Matt. 24; 2 Pet. 2:1; 2 Tim. 4:2; 2 Thess. 2, etc.) Let the ministers therefore be roused, lest any of them perish through sloth. Let those who wish to be seen as Christ's sheep favour their labours and zeal, lest they seem to have regard for the world and its friendship rather than for the glory of Christ. But, with these things premised, let us look at the passage before us, which contains both the inscription of the letter and the apostolic salutation, or blessing, as others call it.

units.la: I. Senior electæ dominæ & liberis eius, quos ego diligo in veritate, &c. Inscriptio comuni more præmittitur, in qua duo consyderãda veniũt. Primũ, quis epistolij autor sit siue scriptor. Nã præter cõmune morem factũ videmus, vt nomen proprium omissum sit. Non tamen author propterea ignorari potest, cũ & veterum codicũ inscriptiones Ioânis nomen præferât, & tota epistolæ dictio sententiæq; omnes Ioannem loquâtur. Seniorem verò se dicit, quod officij nomen est. Tales enim vocabantur & pastores, & qui cum his ecclesiarum curam administrabant, vt ex alijs scripturæ locis nõ obscurè colligitur. Vide Act.14. Tit.1.cap.& 1.Pet.5.&c. Nec tamè ea erat huius nominis ratio,quod nō nisi prouectæ ætatis homines ad id officij deligeretur,sed quia senili grauitate & pru-detia[?] insignes esse deceat, qui id subire velint: qua ratione & Romanis olim Senatores dicti sunt.
units.tr: I. The elder to the elect lady and her children, whom I love in truth, etc. The inscription is prefixed in the common manner, and two things are to be considered in it. First, who is the author or writer of the epistle. For we see that, contrary to common practice, his proper name has been omitted. Yet the author cannot on that account be unknown, since the inscriptions of the ancient manuscripts carry the name of John, and the whole wording and sense of the letter speaks throughout of John. He calls himself "elder," which is the name of an office. For those who administered the care of the churches with them, as is not obscurely gathered from other passages of Scripture, were called elders as well as ministers. See Acts 14; Titus 1; 1 Pet. 5, etc. Nor was the reason for this name that only men of advanced age were chosen for that office, but that those who wished to take it up ought to be distinguished by the dignity and prudence of age; on the same principle the Romans of old were also called senators.

units.la: Obseruandum hic venit,quo loco ecclesiarum & doctrinæ antistites haberi debeant. Senio-res & patres censeantur. Quia per horum ministerium regenerati filij Dei efficimur,quod Paulus non semel admonet. Et Corinthijs se patrem esse affirmat,quia ipsos per euangelium Christo ge-nerauerit. 1.Corinth.4. Adhæc consilijs & admonitionibus patres sunt, tantoq; maior debet esse illorum authoritas,quanto filiorum Dei generatio carnali,quam ex naturalibus parentibus habe-mus,est præstantior. Quod si nostri seculi mores consyderemus,quo hoc uno nomine ministri contemnuntur,quòd per Verbum Christi homines Deo regenerare studeant,facilè patebit quam fit hæc corruptio,& quòd non immerito horrendis plagis puniuntur,qui verbo corrigi nolùt.
units.tr: Here we must observe in what place the leaders of the churches and of doctrine ought to be regarded: they are to be counted as elders and fathers. For through their ministry we are made children of God born again, as Paul reminds us more than once; and he declares that he is a father to the Corinthians because he begot them to Christ through the gospel (1 Cor. 4). Moreover, they are fathers by their counsels and admonitions, and their authority ought to be as much greater as the begetting of the children of God is more excellent than the carnal birth we have from natural parents. And if we consider the morals of our own age, in which ministers are despised for this one reason alone, that they labour to beget men to God through the Word of Christ, it will easily be seen how great this corruption is, and that those who refuse to be corrected by the word are not undeservedly punished with dreadful blows.

units.la: Alterum Inscriptionis membrum eos,quibus Joannes scribit,indicat. Porrò ut suum nomen (quod illis propter familiaritatem & consuetudinem ignotum esse non poterat) reticuit: ita nec horum expressè ponuntur. Contentus est enim docere,quòd Electæ dominæ scribat,eiusq; liberis. Sunt qui Ecclesiam Christi hoc nomine notari putét. Sed si peculiarem alicuius loci ecclesiam intelligamus,absurdus & parum apostolicus hic titulus videri poterit,cum Apostoli Christianos humilitatis ubique admoneant,nec uspiam titulis superbis inebrient. De universali verò Christi ecclesia (quæ nec loco nec tempore certo continetur,sed per totum orbem dispersa ad mundi consum-mationē usq; durat,indeq; æternum cum Christo regnatura) minus intelligi poterit,tum propter breuitatem,tum quòd pleraq; singulare familiaritatem spirant: maximè verò,quòd aduentu suo & præsens colloquium in fine pollicetur. Verisimilius ergo videtur,fuisse hanc primatem aliquam fœminam,genere & dignitate nobilem,quales nō paucas Christo & Apostolis adhæsisse Lucas author est,cap. 8. Quales item Mariam & Martham Lazari Bethaniensis sorores fuisse constat. Nec temere factum putabimus,quòd mulieres in comitatu suo Christus sustinuit,& eædem scriptis compellant apostoli. Quia enim per mulierem peccatum introiuit in mundum,peculiaria quædam & minimè obscura divinæ gratiæ erga hunc sexum argumenta esse oportuit,ne tentationibus superatæ Christi meritum nihil ad se pertinere putarent. Refer huc quæ Paulus tradit 1.Tim.2.cap. Cæterum nō omnino præter vulgarem consuetudinem huic personarum notationi quædam adjungit Joannes,quæ ut ipsius erga hos amorem testantur,ita ad benevolentiam conciliandam vehementer faciunt.
units.tr: The second part of the inscription indicates those to whom John writes. But just as he has kept silent about his own name (which could not be unknown to them because of familiarity and acquaintance), so the names of these are not expressly stated either. He is content to teach that he writes to the elect lady and to her children. There are those who think that the Church of Christ is signified by this name. But if we understand the church of some particular place, this title may seem absurd and little apostolic, since the apostles everywhere admonish Christians to humility and nowhere intoxicate them with proud titles. Yet of the universal Church of Christ (which is contained neither in a certain place nor in a certain time, but is spread through the whole world and endures until the consummation of the world, and thence will reign forever with Christ) less can be understood, both because of the brevity of the letter and because most of it breathes a singular familiarity, and especially because at the end he promises a visit and a personal conversation. It seems more likely, therefore, that this was some leading woman, noble in birth and rank, of the kind that Luke tells us were not few who attached themselves to Christ and the apostles (Luke 8). It is also established that Mary and Martha, the sisters of Lazarus of Bethany, were of this kind. Nor shall we think it was done rashly that Christ supported women in his company, and that the apostles address the same in their writings. For since sin entered the world through a woman, there had to be certain peculiar and quite evident signs of divine grace toward this sex, lest women overcome by temptation should think that the merit of Christ had nothing to do with them. Refer here to what Paul hands down in 1 Tim. 2. Otherwise, John does not add certain things to this designation of persons beyond the ordinary custom, and these both bear witness to his love for them and very greatly serve to win their goodwill.

units.la: Quos ego diligo in veritate: & non ego solus,sed & omnes qui cognouerunt veritatem,propter veritatem quæ permanet in nobis,& nobiscum erit in æternum. Possunt ex his multa argumenta colligi,quibus persuadeantur,ut scriptum hoc benevoli & attenti excipiant & observent. Primum ab Joannis persona sumitur: Ego vos diligo in veritate,absq; fuco & simulatione. Decet ergo ut de meis scriptis æqua feratis judicia,cum quæ à veris fidisq; amicis proficiscuntur,minimè suspecta esse debeant. Alterum à communi omnium piorum expectatione sumit: Quicunq; veritatem cognoverunt,vos diligunt & nihil non boni de vobis sperat. Ergo ne spem illorum fallatis,etiam atq; etiam pro spicite. Accedit tertium à causis: Propter veritatem vos diligunt pij,quam à vobis coli persuasum habent. Veritatis ergo studium flagrans sectemini,nisi spem bonorum fallere velitis. Interserit his & quartum,quo constantiam in Veritatis studio obiter suadet,dum eam stabilem esse & in æternum permanere dicit. Docent hæc quibus argumentis benevolentia apud pios conciliari possit & debeat,ne ineptis adulationibus & ipsos dementemus,& nos omnibus exhibeamus ridiculos. Insunt verò his quædam observatu digna,quæ nostræ & institutioni & consolationi serviunt.
units.tr: Whom I love in truth: and not I alone, but also all who have known the truth, on account of the truth which abides in us and will be with us forever. Many arguments can be drawn from these words, by which they may be persuaded to receive and observe this writing with goodwill and attention. The first is taken from the person of John: I love you in truth, without deceit and pretence. It is fitting, therefore, that you pass a fair judgment on my writings, since what comes from true and faithful friends ought to be least of all suspect. The second is taken from the common expectation of all the godly: all who have known the truth love you and hope nothing but good of you. Therefore do not disappoint their hope, but take care with all your might. A third is added, from the causes: the godly love you on account of the truth, which they are persuaded is cultivated by you. Therefore follow the zealous pursuit of truth, unless you wish to disappoint the hope of the good. He inserts among these a fourth, by which he incidentally urges constancy in the pursuit of truth, while he says that it is stable and abides forever. These words teach by what arguments goodwill can and ought to be won among the godly, lest we both make fools of ourselves with silly flatteries and render ourselves ridiculous to everyone. Yet there are in these words some things worth observing, which serve both our instruction and our consolation.

units.la: Primum, Quos diligo in Veritate. Exprimit proprium charitatis,à quà simulatio & fucus procul abesse debent. Unde ab Apostolis ἀνυπόκριτον[?] dici consueuit. 1.Tim.1.& 1.Pet.1. De hoc officio in priori epistola admonuit Apostolus,ubi ait: Filioli mei,ne diligamus verbo,neq; lingua,sed opere & veritate. 1.Joan.3. Peccant ergo graviter,qui verbo amorem simulant,reipsa vero nocent,vel saltem clam odiunt: quod hominum genus hodie passim regnat,&c.
units.tr: First: Whom I love in truth. He expresses the proper character of charity, from which pretence and deceit ought to be far away. Hence the apostles are accustomed to call it "unfeigned" (anypokriton). (1 Tim. 1; 1 Pet. 1.) The apostle reminded us of this duty in his earlier letter, where he says: "My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue, but in deed and truth" (1 John 3). Those therefore sin gravely who feign love in word while in reality they do harm, or at least secretly hate; this sort of person today rules everywhere, etc.

units.la: Secundum, Propter Veritatem. Causam verae charitatis sive dilectionis indicat,quæ est ipsa Veritas. Qui propter alias causas diligunt,eorum dilectio stabilis & vera esse nequit. Quia sola ve-ritas æterna est,sola sibi ipsi constat,nec mutatur in horas. Veritatem verò hic intelligimus,quam Christus revelavit,sermonem videlicet patris,de quo ipse testatur,quòd Veritas sit. Joan.17. Propter Dei verbum ergo amandi sunt fideles,non vel lucri vel voluptatis causa. Hinc eos æstima,qui fratres nihil mali meritos hanc unam ob causam odiunt,quòd Veritatis cultores esse vident. Sic testantur,se mundi filios esse,qui Veritatis lucem non fert. Joan.3.
units.tr: Second: On account of the truth. He indicates the cause of true charity or love, which is truth itself. Those who love for other causes cannot have a love that is stable and true, since only eternal truth is eternal, only it is consistent with itself, and it does not change from hour to hour. But here we understand by truth that which Christ revealed, namely the word of the Father, of which he himself testifies that it is truth (John 17). The faithful, therefore, are to be loved on account of the word of God, not for the sake of gain or pleasure. Judge from this those who hate brethren who have deserved no evil for this one reason alone, that they see them to be worshippers of the truth. In this way they testify that they are sons of the world, since they do not bear the light of truth (John 3).

units.la: Tertium, In æternum erit nobiscum Veritas. Consolationis plena est sententia. Sunt qui alio quo Veritatis amore incaluerunt. Sed quia metuunt,ne mundi furor & tyrannorum vis Veritatem illis eripiat,sensim tepescunt & frigescunt. Eos Joannes consolatur,docens Veritatem non fallacem vel perfidam esse, quæ cultores suos deserat. Vt enim per se stabilis & æterna est, ita cum illis perpetuò habitare gaudet, quos sui cognitione semel illuminauit. Et si omnes omnium seculorum historias euoluamus, multos quidem à Veritate perfidè defecisse reperiemus, sed à Ve-ritate vel falsum vel desertum vnquam fuisse neminem videbimus. Quò & Paulus respexisse videtur, cum ecclesiam columnam & stabilimentum Veritatis appellat. 1. Timoth. 3. Cum enim ecclesia non fit, nisi quæ verbo Veritatis collecta est, & eiusdem vinculo continetur, ab eadem Ve-ritas discedit nunquam. Nam & Christi promissionem habet, dicentis: Ego vobiscum ero vsque in consummationem seculi. Facilè ergo illorum sententiam recipimus, qui ecclesiam errare non posse contendunt. Sed non quosuis hoc titulo gloriantes pro ecclesia agnoscimus, nisi in verbo Veritatis se collectos esse, & eodem regi atque gubernari, probent. Deinde de pertinaci & incu-rabili perseueratione in erroribus ea sententia debet intelligi. Sunt enim exempla, quæ ecclesias celeberrimas in multis errauisse docent. At quia eædem Dei verbum retinent, & correctionem admittunt, in erroribus non perseuerant. Qui ergo hodie ecclesiá errare posse negant, & hoc argu-mento omnem correctionē reijciunt, hoc iudicio probant, se ecclesiæ nomine indignissimos esse.
units.tr: Third, "In æternum erit nobiscum Veritas" ("Truth will be with us forever"). The sentence is full of comfort. There are some who have grown warm with a love of Truth, but because they fear that the rage of the world and the force of tyrants may tear Truth away from them, they gradually cool and grow cold. John comforts such people, teaching that Truth is not fickle or faithless, so as to abandon its worshippers. For just as it is stable and eternal in itself, so it delights to dwell forever with those whom it has once illuminated by its knowledge. And if we unroll the histories of all ages, we shall find many who have treacherously fallen away from Truth, but we shall see no one who has ever been false to Truth or deserted by it. Paul seems to have had this in view too, when he calls the Church "the pillar and ground of the truth" (1 Tim. 3). For the Church is nothing other than what has been gathered by the word of Truth and held together by its bond, and so it never departs from Truth. Indeed it also has Christ's promise, who says: "I am with you always, even to the end of the world" (Matt. 28). Therefore we readily accept the opinion of those who maintain that the Church cannot err. But we do not acknowledge as the Church those who glory in this title, unless they prove that they have been gathered in the word of Truth and are ruled and governed by it. Furthermore, that statement must be understood of obstinate and incurable persistence in errors. For there are examples which teach that very famous churches have erred in many things. But because these same churches still hold the word of God and admit correction, they do not persist in their errors. Therefore those who today deny that the Church can err, and by this argument reject all correction, prove by this judgment that they are most unworthy of the name of the Church.

units.la: I I. Sit nobiscum gratia, misericordia, pax, à Deo patre, & à domino Iesu Christo, filio patris, in veri-tate & charitate. Est hæc apostolica salutatio siue benedictio, quam communi exemplo præmit-tit. Peculiare tamen habet hoc, quòd in prima persona loquens, seipsum illis coniūgit, quibus fau-sta hæc imprecatur. Testatur & ea re suum erga illos amorem, vtpote quibus cum omnia commu-nia habere cupiat. Veniunt autem hic obseruanda hæc:
units.tr: II. "May grace, mercy and peace be with you, from God the Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, in truth and love." This is the apostolic greeting or blessing, which he sends in the common manner. Yet he has this peculiarity: speaking in the first person, he joins himself to those for whom he invokes these blessings. By this he also bears witness to his love for them, since he desires to have all things in common with them. Here the following things are to be observed:

units.la: Primò, quæ bona verè expetenda & optanda sint Christianis hominibus. Non ea scilicet, quæ infelix mundus cæco iudicio pro bonis ducit, sed quæ Apostoli spiritu dictante fidelibus precari solent. Primum in his gradum Dei gratia obtinet. Gratia autem pro fauore vsurpatur, quo Deus suos prosequitur. Est hic nostræ felicitatis columen, quia sine hoc infelicissimi sumus, & per hunc omnia Dei dona, quibus indigemus, in nos deriuantur. Imò nisi Deum sibi fauere & propitium esse homo intelligat, horribiles terrores sentiet, nec quicquam illi acceptum & suauę esse poterit. Secundo loco misericordia ponitur, quæ fauoris & gratiæ Dei causa efficiens dici potest. Ideo e- nim nobis fauet Deus bonaque sua confert, quia nostri miseretur. Alioqui si nos spectes, odio po-tius quàm fauore digni erimus. Tertio gradu pax sequitur, quæ tam gratiæ quàm misericordiæ fructus siue effectus habet. Ea enim vox apud Hebræos omnem hominis incolumitatem & feli-citatem complectitur, imprimis verò eam animi tranquillitatem denotat, qua muniti coram Dei iudicio comparere possumus. Hæc (inquam) vera & solida bona sunt, sine quibus homini nihil aliud prodesse poterit. Sed ô cæcas hominum mentes, qui pro his tam parum sunt soliciti.
units.tr: First, what goods are truly to be sought and desired by Christian people: not those which the unhappy world, with its blind judgment, counts as good, but those which the Apostle, under the dictation of the Spirit, is accustomed to pray for the faithful. The first place among these is held by the grace of God. Grace, moreover, is used for the favour with which God regards his own. This is the pillar of our happiness, since without it we are most unhappy, and through it all the gifts of God which we need flow down upon us. Indeed, unless a man understands that God is favourable and propitious to him, he will feel horrible terrors, and nothing can be acceptable or sweet to him. In the second place mercy is set down, which can be called the efficient cause of God's favour and grace. For God favours us and bestows his goods upon us because he has mercy on us. Otherwise, if you look at us, we shall be worthy of hatred rather than favour. In the third degree peace follows, which is the fruit or effect of both grace and mercy. For that word among the Hebrews embraces all the soundness and happiness of a man, but chiefly denotes that tranquillity of mind by which, fortified, we can appear before the judgment of God. These (I say) are the true and solid goods, without which nothing else can profit a man. But O blind minds of men, who are so little concerned about these things!

units.la: Secundò fontem horum ostendit, nempe Deum patrem. Nam omne donum bonum à pa-tre luminum proficiscitur. Iac. 1. Falluntur itaq;, qui hæc extra Deum quærere instituunt. Iere. 2. &c. Consolationis verò plenum est, quod in vno se Deus monstrat, quæ nobis ad salutem sunt ne-cessaria, ne illa per varias ambages quærere cogamur, & ita laboribus vanis defatigemur.
units.tr: Second, he shows the source of these, namely God the Father. For every good gift comes from the Father of lights (James 1). Those therefore are deceived who set about seeking these things outside God (Jer. 2, etc.). Moreover, it is full of consolation that in one God shows himself to us, that the things necessary for our salvation are found there, so that we are not compelled to seek them through various circuits and so wear ourselves out with vain labours.

units.la: Tertiò medium, per quod ista obtinguntur, proponit, Iesum Christum Dei filium. In hoc enim Deo patri complacitum est. Matth. 3. & 17. cap. Quare & hic ad se omnes laborates inuitat (Matt. 11.) & Apostoli in solo hoc omnem vitam atque salutem commonstrant. Act. 4. Ioan. 1. &c.
units.tr: Third, he sets forth the means by which these things are obtained, Jesus Christ, the Son of God. For in him it has pleased God the Father (Matt. 3 and chap. 17). Therefore here too he invites all who labour to himself (Matt. 11), and the Apostles show all life and salvation in this one alone (Acts 4; John 1, etc.).

units.la: Addit quarto loco Veritatis & charitatis mentionem, quibus eorum officia comprehendere videtur, qui bona hæc à Deo per Christum accepere. Illorum enim est constanti fide in agnita Ve-ritate perseuerare, fidemque charitatis operibus testari, ne inani eius titulo glorientur. Sed quia de his plura in sequentibus dicet Apostolus, hæc modò annotauisse sufficiat. Curemus autem & nos, vt cœlestia hæc & æterna bona ardenti fide inquiramus, & oblata amplectamur atque reti-neamus, æternum aliquando regnaturi cum Christo Iesu, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: In the fourth place he adds a mention of truth and love, by which he seems to comprehend the duties of those who have received these goods from God through Christ. For it belongs to them to persevere with constant faith in the truth acknowledged, and to attest their faith by works of love, lest they glory in its empty title. But since the Apostle will say more about these things in what follows, it is enough to have noted these things for now. Let us also take care to seek these heavenly and eternal goods with ardent faith, and to embrace and hold on to them when they are offered, so that we may someday reign eternally with Christ Jesus, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA II.
units.tr: HOMILIA II.

units.la: Gauisus sum ualde, quòd inter liberos tuos inueni, qui in veritate ambulant, sicut præceptum accepimus à patre. Et nuncrogo te domina (non tanquam mandatum nouum scribo tibi, sed quod habuimus ab initio) ut diligamus nos mutuò. Et hæc est charitas, ut ambulemus secundum præceptum eius.
units.tr: I rejoiced greatly that I have found among your children some who walk in the truth, just as we have received the command from the Father. And now I ask you, lady (not as though I were writing a new commandment to you, but one which we have had from the beginning), that we love one another. And this is love: that we walk according to his commandment.

units.la: VT dominus noster Iesus Christus neminem, quantumuis vilem & calamitosum fastidit, sed omnium ordinum hominibus sese benignum offert, adeoq; fruendum propinat: ita Apostolos præceptoris & magistri sui exemplum imitatos, omnium saluti inuigilaffe constat. Cuius studij exemplum Ioannes est, qui & fœminas peculiaribus scriptis instituere, & in officio retinere satagit. Debet vero hoc spiritus sancti studium omnes excitare, ne socordia superati sibijpsis desint. Sed præsentem locum excutere oportet, qui epistolij breuis breue exordium, & mox eiusdem propositionem comprehendit.
units.tr: Just as our Lord Jesus Christ does not disdain anyone, however base and wretched, but offers himself kindly to people of every rank and so makes himself available to be enjoyed, so it is evident that the Apostles, imitating the example of their teacher and master, watched over the salvation of all. John is an example of this concern, who strove both to instruct women by special writings and to keep them in their duty. Indeed, this zeal of the Holy Spirit ought to stir up everyone, so that they do not fail themselves through sloth. But we must examine the present passage, which contains the brief opening of a short letter and, soon afterwards, its proposition.
