units.la: I. Gauisus sum valde, quod inter liberos tuos inueni, qui in veritate ambulant, sicut præceptum accepimus a patre. A gratulatione orditur, qua animi sui erga ipsos affectu plenius exprimit, quæ res beneuolentiæ conciliandæ vehementer prodest. Quis enim eum non amet & monente[?] ferat, quem ita erga se affectum nouit, ut ipsius commodis perinde ut proprijs gaudeat? Hinc frequenter epistolas suas hoc modo Paulus exordiri solet, ut & Deo gratias agat, & ecclesijs, quibus scribit congratuletur propter felicem euangelij ac verae fidei profectum. Insunt autem Apostoli verbis, quæ ad nostram institutionem transferri possunt, & proinde diligentius inspici merentur.
units.tr: I. "I rejoiced greatly that I have found among your children some who walk in the truth, just as we have received the command from the Father." He begins with congratulation, by which he expresses more fully the feeling of his heart towards them, a thing that greatly helps to win goodwill. For who would not love and bear with a person who is known to feel towards him in such a way that he rejoices in his advantages as in his own? Hence Paul is accustomed to begin his letters in this manner, so that he both gives thanks to God and congratulates the churches to which he writes on the happy progress of the gospel and of true faith. Moreover, the Apostle's words contain things that can be applied to our instruction, and therefore deserve to be examined more carefully.

units.la: Gaudet Apostolus, quòd matronæ huius liberos in Veritate ambulare intellexit. Docemur hinc, quibus rebus pij gaudere debeant. Quia enim toti Deo consecrati sunt, maior gaudij causa ijs offerri non potest, quàm cum Dei verbum ac veritatis doctrinam longè lateq; propagari, multosq; Christo lucrifactos in veritatis luce ambulare vident. Eò quòd hoc gloriæ Dei cuprimis seruit, quam omnibus pijs quàm maximè cordi esse decet. Seruit item proximi saluti, quam contemnere nō possunt, qui fide vera Christo capiti connexi sunt, in quo eiusdem corporis membra efficimur. Arguit ergo Ioannis exemplū eorum socordiā & duritiem, qui siccis oculis & sine gemitu horribilem ecclesiarum vastationem, turpemq; ab agnita veritate multorum apostasiam intueri possunt.
units.tr: The Apostle rejoices that he has learned that the children of this matron walk in the truth. We are taught from this what things godly people ought to rejoice in. For since they are wholly consecrated to God, no greater cause of joy can be offered to them than when they see the word of God and the doctrine of truth spread far and wide, and many won to Christ walking in the light of truth. This is because it especially serves the glory of God, which ought to be most dear to all the godly. It also serves the salvation of our neighbour, which cannot be despised by those who are joined by true faith to Christ the head, in whom we are made members of the same body. The example of John therefore condemns the sloth and hardness of those who can look upon the dreadful devastation of the churches, and the shameful apostasy of many from the truth once known, with dry eyes and without a groan.

units.la: Obseruandum quoque, quòd illos in veritate ambulare dicit. Differunt enim veritatem nouiẙse, & in veritate ambulare. Prius etiam hypocritæ interdum habent, & palàm impij. At alterum hoc in solis electis ac verè fidelibus conspicitur, qui veritatis cognitionem totius vitæ conuersatione exprimunt. Non sufficit ergo nuda diuinæ veritatis cognitio, sed in ea ambulare, id est, vitæ omnem iuxta huius præceptiones instituere conuenit, nisi in spiritum sanctum peccare, & ijs adnumerari velimus, quibus in magna illa die dominus dicet: Non noui vos. Discedite à me operarij iniquitatis, &c. Matth.7.
units.tr: It is also to be noted that he says they walk in the truth. For it is one thing to know the truth, and another to walk in the truth. Hypocrites sometimes have the former, and so do openly wicked men. But the latter is seen only in the elect and truly faithful, who express their knowledge of the truth through the whole course of their life. Bare knowledge of divine truth is therefore not enough, but it is fitting to walk in it, that is, to order the whole of life according to its precepts, unless we wish to sin against the Holy Spirit and be counted among those to whom the Lord will say on that great day: "I never knew you. Depart from me, you workers of iniquity," etc. Matthew 7.

units.la: Exprimitur verò & modus siue regula ambulandi in veritate, cum addit: Sicut præceptum accepimus à patre. Quia enim omnis homo mendax, in veritate non ambulabunt, nisi qui Deum audiunt. Is filium suum doctorem dedit, qui in euangelio clamat: Ego sum via, lux & veritas. Ioan. 14. Ego sum lux mundi. Qui me sequitur, non ambulat in tenebris. Ioan. 8. Huius vocem sequuntur, qui oues sunt ad salutem electæ, & alienum non audiunt. Ioan. 10. Iugulantur ergo hic omnes hominum traditiones siue regulæ, ac manifestissimi erroris conuincuntur, qui secundum has vitæ suæ conuersationem & religionem instituunt.
units.tr: And the manner or rule of walking in the truth is also expressed when he adds: "just as we have received the command from the Father." For since every man is a liar, they will not walk in the truth unless they hear God. He gave his Son as teacher, who cries out in the gospel: "I am the way, the light and the truth." John 14. "I am the light of the world. He who follows me does not walk in darkness." John 8. Those who are sheep chosen for salvation follow his voice, and do not hear a stranger. John 10. Therefore all human traditions or rules are overthrown here, and those are convicted of the plainest error who order their manner of life and their religion according to them.

units.la: II. Et nūc rogo te domina (non tanquam mandatum nouum scribo tibi, sed quod habuimus ab initio) ut diligamus nos mutuò, &c. Comprehendit his propositionem siue statū epistolę, qui est: Rogo te, ut diligamus nos mutuò. Mox verò per expositionem docet, qua de dilectione loquatur. Hęc est charitas, ut ambulemus secundum præceptum eius. Et quia in religionis negotio vulgò inuisa sunt, quæcunq; nouitatem redolent, eius suspicione omnem declinat, cum interserit propositioni: Non tanquam mandatum nouum scribo tibi, sed quod habuimus ab initio. Qua ratione etiā in priori epistola non semel ostendit, Christi doctrinam nullo modo nouitatis suspicione grauari debere.
units.tr: II. "And now I ask you, lady (not as though I were writing a new commandment to you, but one which we have had from the beginning), that we love one another, etc." He sets out here the proposition or subject of the letter, which is: "I ask you that we love one another." Soon afterwards he explains by way of elaboration what kind of love he is speaking of: "This is love, that we walk according to his commandment." And because in matters of religion whatever smacks of novelty is commonly hated, he avoids any suspicion of it, when he inserts into the proposition: "not as though I were writing a new commandment to you, but one which we have had from the beginning." For this reason, also in the former letter, he has shown more than once that the doctrine of Christ must in no way be burdened with suspicion of novelty.

units.la: Obseruemus autem, quod de obedientia & perseuerantia in agnita veritate dicturus, à dilectione orditur. Causa huius esse videtur, quòd charitas siue dilectio lex tota perficitur. Rom. 13. Matth.22. Interim tamen admonemur, Deum nō inuitos siue coactos, sed spontaneos cultores requirere. Animum enim sibi vendicat, qui si ipsi consecratus fuerit, voluntas hominis omnesq; aliæ animi facultates à Deo alienæ esse non possunt. Huc pertinet, quòd Dauid Christi subditos siue fideles populum spontanearum voluntatum nominat. Psal. 110.
units.tr: We should observe that when John is about to speak of obedience and perseverance in the acknowledged truth, he begins with love. The reason for this seems to be that love, or charity, is the fulfilling of the whole law (Rom. 13; Matth. 22). Meanwhile we are also reminded that God seeks worshippers who are not unwilling or compelled, but willing. For he claims the soul for himself: if a person has been consecrated to him, the human will and all the other faculties of the soul cannot be alienated from God. To this belongs the fact that David calls Christ's subjects, that is, the faithful, a people of willing wills (Ps. 110).

units.la: Præterea veram dilectionem Apostolus describit, quæ descriptio multas ob causas diligenter notari debet. Gloriantur enim Dei dilectione multi, imò ab hac alienus videri vult nemo. Sed ut fratres non sufficit verbis diligere, nisi & rebus præstemus, quod verba pollicentur: ita Dei dilectione frustra gloriabimur, nisi obedientiæ studio testemur, illius honorem & gloriam nobis cordi esse. Grauis ergo & memorabilis sententia est, cuius Apostolus hic meminit, dicens: Hęc est charitas ut ambulemus secundum præcepta eius. In obedientia igitur et obseruatione præceptorum Dei dilectio versatur, à qua quicunque abhorrent, næ illi in dilectione se nimis frigidos esse docent.
units.tr: Moreover, the Apostle describes true love, and this description ought to be noted carefully for many reasons. Many boast of the love of God; indeed, no one wishes to seem to be alien to it. But just as, with brothers, it is not enough to love in words unless we also do in deeds what our words promise, so we shall boast of the love of God in vain unless we bear witness, by eager obedience, that his honour and glory are dear to our hearts. This is therefore a weighty and memorable saying, which the Apostle here recalls, saying: "This is love, that we walk according to his commandments." Love therefore consists in obedience and in keeping God's commandments; those who shrink from this show that they are far too cold in love.

units.la: Cæterum quærat aliquis, quod nam illud præceptum sit in cuius obseruatione dilectio vera consistit. Hic verò ipse Ioannes consulendus erit, qui in prioris epistolæ cap.3. ait: Hoc est præceptum eius, ut credamus nomini filij eius Iesu Christi, & ut diligamus nos mutuò, sicut dedit præceptum. Vnum ergo præceptum est, sed bipertitum. Requirit enim fidem in filium Dei, qui talis agnoscendus est, qualis nomine ipso prædicatur, nimirum saluator mundi, Rex & sacerdos noster vnicus. Huic quia per fidem inserimur, & in eorum communionem cooptamur, quos ipse pro suis agnoscit, fraterna dilectione carere non possumus, ut sæpe iam dictum est. Et qui plura volet, ex loco supra citato petat. Interim agnoscamus, hoc esse vetus illud adeoque primum præceptū, cuius author ipse Deus est, & ad cuius regulam vita omnis debet institui. Veneremur ergo Dei erga nos propensam voluntatē, qui graui & multiplici præceptorū onere nos grauare noluit. Præstemus illi debitum verae obedientiae officium, ut pro veris filijs agnosci, & cum Iesu Christo viuere possimus, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Furthermore, someone may ask what that commandment is in whose keeping true love consists. Here John himself must be consulted, who in the third chapter of his first epistle says: "This is his commandment, that we should believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and that we should love one another, as he gave us commandment." There is therefore one commandment, but it has two parts. For it requires faith in the Son of God, who must be acknowledged as he is proclaimed by his very name, namely the Saviour of the world, our only King and Priest. Since we are grafted into him by faith and admitted to the fellowship of those whom he acknowledges as his own, we cannot be without brotherly love, as has often been said already. Whoever wishes more let him seek it from the passage cited above. Meanwhile let us recognise that this is that ancient and indeed first commandment, whose author is God himself, and by whose rule every life ought to be ordered. Let us therefore revere God's well-disposed will toward us, who did not wish to burden us with a heavy and manifold load of precepts. Let us render to him the due duty of true obedience, so that we may be acknowledged as true sons and may live with Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA III.
units.tr: Homily III.

units.la: Hoc est præceptum, quemadmodum audistis ab initio, ut in eo ambuletis. Quoniam multi seductores ingressi sunt in mundum, qui non confitentur Iesum Christum venisse in carne, Hic est seductor & Antichristus.
units.tr: This is the commandment, as you have heard from the beginning, that you walk in it. For many deceivers have entered into the world, who do not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. This is the deceiver and the Antichrist.

units.la: Divus Ioannes hoc epistolio de obedientia & perseuerantia in agnita veritate dicturus, nō temere à dilectione exorsus est. Vt enim hæc Legem totam implet:ita quæcunq; propter huius obseruationem nobis aduersa accidunt,leuia reddit. Cæterum in præsenti causam hac omnem fusius explicare incipit.Primò enim quæ de Dei præcepto dixerat, clarius repetit. Deinde præsenti periculo ob oculos posito, docet, se non frustra tantam in ipsis monendis diligen-tiam adhibere.
units.tr: Saint John, about to speak in this little letter on obedience and perseverance in the acknowledged truth, did not begin rashly with love. For just as love fulfils the whole Law, so it makes lighter whatever adversities befall us on account of its observance. Moreover, in the present matter he begins to explain the whole more fully. First, he repeats more clearly what he had said about God's commandment. Then, setting the present danger before their eyes, he teaches that he does not apply such great diligence in warning them for nothing.

units.la: I. Hoc est præceptum, quemadmodum audistis, ut in eo ambuletis. Repetitione docet, de quo nam præcepto loquatur, nimirum non de nouo aliquo & hactenus incognito, sed quod & ipsi ab initio audiuerunt, cum in fide Christi primum instituerentur, & quod ab origine mundi Deus humanæ salutis causa promulgauit. Sic verò rursum nouitatis suspicioni medetur, ut maior sit suæ doctrinæ & admonitionis authoritas.
units.tr: I. This is the commandment, as you have heard, that you walk in it. By repetition he shows what commandment he is speaking of: namely not some new commandment, unknown until now, but one that they too heard from the beginning, when they were first instructed in the faith of Christ, and which God proclaimed from the origin of the world for the sake of human salvation. And in this way again he meets the suspicion of novelty, so that the authority of his teaching and admonition may be greater.

units.la: Admonet verò locus hic, ut inquiramus, quod nam præceptum Deus ab initio proposuerit, & in quo instituendi sunt, qui Christo adduci debent. Est hoc non aliud, quàm fidei præceptum (ut in præcedenti sermone dictum est) quo in filium Dei, unicum verumque humani generis salvatorem credere docemur. Hoc enim in paradiso promulgatum fuisse legimus, quando serpenti dicitur: Ponam inimicitias inter te & mulierem, inter semen tuum & inter semen illius. Ipsum conculcabit tibi caput, & tu conculcabis ipsi calcaneum. Quia enim istis verbis de filio suo vaticinatur Deus, quem semen mulieris ideo vocat, quod absque viri congressu ex intemerata virgine natus est, eumque serpentis, id est, satanæ deiectorem & conculcatorem fore docet, utique simul suam voluntatem primis parentibus declaratam voluit, quæ est, ut in promisso hoc salvatore spem omnem repositam haberent. Non temere ergo Ioannes hoc præceptum ab initio fuisse affirmat. Est hoc ipsum postea multiuariam instauratum illustratumq; euidentius. Huc enim promissiones patriarchis datæ pertinent. Eodem referuntur, quæ Moses de magno illo propheta dixerit, Deut.18. Idem præceptum Dauid promulgat, dicens: Osculamini filium, ne irascatur, & pereatis à via: breui exardescet furor eius. Beati omnes, qui sperant in eum. Psal.2. De eodem ipse Christus loquitur, cum ait: Hæc est voluntas eius qui misit me, ut omnis qui videt filium, & credit in eum, habeat vitam æternam. Ioan.6. Quid verò sit in filium Dei credere, supra attigimus, & ultima Capitis tertij prioris epistolæ Homilia fusius explicatum est.
units.tr: This place, however, urges us to inquire what commandment God set forth from the beginning, and in what those who are to be brought to Christ must be instructed. It is none other than the commandment of faith (as was said in the preceding sermon), by which we are taught to believe in the Son of God, the only and true Saviour of the human race. For we read that this was proclaimed in paradise, when it is said to the serpent: I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. He shall crush your head, and you shall crush his heel. For in these words God prophesies about his Son, whom he calls the seed of the woman because he was born of the inviolate virgin without intercourse with a man, and he teaches that he would cast down and crush the serpent, that is, Satan. Thus at the same time he wished his will to be declared to our first parents: that they should place all their hope in this promised Saviour. It is not without reason, then, that John affirms this commandment was from the beginning. It was afterwards renewed and made clearer in many ways. For the promises given to the patriarchs pertain to this. To the same end refer the things Moses said about that great prophet, Deut. 18. David proclaims the same commandment, saying: Kiss the Son, lest he be angry and you perish from the way; soon his wrath will flare up. Blessed are all who trust in him. Ps. 2. Christ himself speaks of the same, when he says: This is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life. John 6. What it is to believe in the Son of God we touched on above, and it was explained more fully in the homily on the last chapter of the third chapter of the former epistle.

units.la: Obseruanda hic venit fidei Christianæ & doctrinæ euangelicæ dignitas atque vetustas. Est hæc nostro seculo apud plerosque solius nouitatis nomine inuisa. At Christum tradit, & Christo nititur, in quem confidere primo omnium præcepto, quod inter homines promulgatum est, iubemur. Eidem testimonium ferunt Lex & prophetæ. Ioan.5. Luc.24. Nouas ergo fidei & religionis leges sequuntur, qui non vni Christo Iesu omnem nostræ redemptionis & salutis gloriam acceptam ferunt.
units.tr: Here the dignity and antiquity of the Christian faith and of the evangelical doctrine must be noted. In our age this is hated by many under the name of novelty alone. But it hands down Christ and rests on Christ, in whom we are commanded to trust, before all else, by the commandment that has been proclaimed among men. The Law and the prophets bear witness to him. John 5; Luke 24. Therefore those who ascribe the whole glory of our redemption and salvation not to Jesus Christ alone, but follow new laws of faith and religion, are the ones who are mistaken.

units.la: Deinde non oscitanter praetereundum est, quòd tam solicitè, & ad fastidium usque repetit, hoc praecepto ambulandum esse. At ambulandi vox vitae conuersationem comprehendit. Arguit igitur varios fidei Christianae iactatores, qui vita & moribus Christum abnegant, quem ore profitentur. Quia enim animum totum requirit Christus (qui omnium actionum fons est) eaedem cum Christi regula necessario conuenire oportet. Vide Iac.2.cap.
units.tr: Next, it must not be passed over carelessly that he repeats so earnestly, and even to the point of tedium, that we must walk in this commandment. Now the word "walk" embraces the conduct of life. He therefore rebukes the various boasters of the Christian faith who deny Christ by life and manners, whom they profess with the mouth. For since Christ, who is the source of all actions, requires the whole soul, those same actions must necessarily agree with the rule of Christ. See James 2.

units.la: II. Quoniam multi seductores ingressi sunt in mundum, qui non confitentur Iesum Christum uenisse in carne. Hic est seductor & Antichristus. Causas reddit sui studij & diligentiae, quam ostendit super uacaneam non esse, quia undique exurgant seductores, qui saluti ipsorum insidiantur. Quo vero facilius caueri possint, eosdem certis notis insignit, de quibus cum Cap.2.et 4.prioris epistolae mul-ta dixerimus, inde petantur, quae ad huius loci explicationem faciunt.
units.tr: II. For many deceivers have entered into the world, who do not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. This is the deceiver and the Antichrist. He gives the reasons for his care and diligence, which he shows is not in vain, because deceivers arise on every side, who lie in wait for their salvation. So that they may be more easily guarded against, he marks them with certain signs. Since we have said much about these in chapters 2 and 4 of the former epistle, let what serves the explanation of this place be sought from there.

units.la: Est vero diligenter obseruandum spiritus sancti studium, quo de seductoribus nos passim in scripturis admonet. Causa eius diligentiae est, quod ut vera doctrina fidem plantat, nosq; Deo per Christum adducit: sic falsa superstitiones & impietatem seminat, imo occidit. Quo sensu & Christus, falsos doctores, qui extra hunc salutis viam monstrant, latrones nominauit. Ioan.10. Quia ve-ro tantum est falsae doctrinae periculum, toto coelo errant, qui falsos doctores hodie nolunt arguì, nec inutiliter modo laborare, sed tumultuum authores esse clamant, qui fidei admonitionibus illos produnt, & omnibus cognoscendos exhibent. Nam & lupos in ecclesia palam grassari, & eam in ouibus stoliditatem conspicimus, vt tenuis lucri gratia, aut etiām carnis studio, se sponte in illorum fauces & vngues ingerant.
units.tr: Moreover, we must carefully observe the zeal of the Holy Spirit, by which he warns us everywhere in the Scriptures about deceivers. The cause of this diligence is that, as true doctrine plants faith and leads us to God through Christ, so false doctrine sows superstition and impiety, indeed kills. In this sense Christ also called the false teachers, who show a way of salvation other than this one, thieves. John 10. Since the danger of false doctrine is so great, those men err by a whole heaven who today do not want false teachers to be exposed, and who cry out that those who expose them by admonitions of the faith are not merely labouring in vain but are authors of tumults, and who present them to everyone to be recognised. For we see wolves openly prowling in the Church, and such stupidity among the sheep that, for the sake of a little gain or even out of devotion to the flesh, they willingly throw themselves into the jaws and claws of those wolves.

units.la: Agnoscamus ergo fidelem & paternam pro nobis Dei curam. Illius vocem in scripturis propositam audiamus & sequamur. Obseruemus ipsius praecepta, & fugiamus Antichristos, vt in coelis aliquando gaudeamus cum Christo Iesu, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Let us therefore acknowledge God's faithful and fatherly care for us. Let us hear and follow his voice set forth in the Scriptures. Let us observe his commandments and flee the Antichrists, so that we may at some time rejoice in heaven with Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA IIII.
units.tr: HOMILIA IIII.

units.la: Prospicite uobis ipsis, ne perdamus quae operati sumus, sed ut mercedem plenam recipiamus. Omnis qui transgreditur, & non manet in doctrina Christi, Deum non habet. Qui manet in doctrina Christi, hic & patrem & filium habet.
units.tr: Take heed to yourselves, that we lose not the things which we have wrought, but that we receive a full reward. Whoever transgresses, and abides not in the doctrine of Christ, has not God. He who abides in the doctrine of Christ, the same has both the Father and the Son.

units.la: QVemadmodum difficile est, hominem naturali vitio corruptum, veritati & saluti lucrifacere: ita non minus laboriosum est, eundem in veritatis via retinere, eò quòd leuissima qua que occasione ad ingenium redit. Non temere ergo tanta diligentia in illis monendis & hortandis vtitur Apostolus, de quorum fide satis certus esse videbatur. Suasit autem hucusque constantiam duobus praecipue argumentis, inter quae primum offendit, fidei praeceptum antiquissimum esse, & proinde turpissimum fore, si hoc neglecto ad noua & incerta dogmata deflectant. Secundum pericula monstrauit ex falsis doctoribus, propter quos cura & diligenti studio opus fit. Sequuntur in praesenti loco rationes ab vtili desumptae, quibus docet, non hic de re leuicula & nullius momenti, sed animarum salute agi. Singula ergo attentam considerationem merentur.
units.tr: As it is difficult to win over a man corrupted by natural vice to the truth and to salvation, so it is no less laborious to keep him in the way of truth, since the slightest occasion brings him back to his disposition. Therefore the Apostle does not without reason use such great diligence in admonishing and exhorting those whose faith he seemed quite sure of. Hitherto he has urged constancy chiefly by two arguments. Of these, the first points out that the precept of the faith is most ancient, and that it would therefore be most shameful if, neglecting this, they turned aside to new and uncertain doctrines. The second sets forth the dangers arising from false teachers, on account of whom care and diligent attention are needed. In the present passage follow the reasons drawn from profit, by which he teaches that this matter is not one of a trifling and worthless kind, but concerns the salvation of souls. Each of these therefore deserves attentive consideration.

units.la: I. Prospicite uobis ipsis, ne perdamus quae operati sumus, sed ut mercedem plenam recipiamus. Videtur haec summaria ratio ab vtili propositio, quam deinde duobus membris, sibi inuicem oppositis, illustrat. Sensus est: Non sufficit aliquouis progressum esse, nisi (vt Christus ait) in finem usque perseueremus. Qui in medio cursu deficiunt, brauium non assequuntur. Et nemo certans coronatur, nisi legitimè certauerit. 2. Tim.2. Et Christus regno suo non idoneos dicit, qui vbi manum aratro admouerunt, respiciunt à tergo. Luc.9. Mementote (idem inquit) vxoris Lot, cui non pro fuit è Sodomis exiuisse, cum ad easdem rerum reliquarum amore respiceret. Luc.17. Erant haec non ofcitanter expendenda nostri seculi hominibus, quibus agnitam veritatem negare lusus iocusque videtur. Sed perdunt hoc ludo, quod ante lucrati fuerant. Fient nouissima illorum peiora primis. Immo satius esset, illos veritatem nunquam cognouisse. Vide Matth.12. Item 2. Pet.2.cap.
units.tr: I. Take heed to yourselves, that we lose not the things which we have wrought, but that we receive a full reward. This summary reason, put forward from profit, seems to be a proposition which he then illustrates by two members set against each other. The sense is this: it is not enough to have made some progress, unless (as Christ says) we persevere to the end. Those who fail in the middle of the course do not obtain the prize. And no one is crowned who does not strive lawfully. 2 Tim. 2. And Christ says that those who, having put their hand to the plough, look back, are not fit for his kingdom. Luke 9. Remember (he says again) the wife of Lot, to whom it did not avail to have come out of Sodom, when she looked back out of love for the same worldly possessions. Luke 17. These things were not to be weighed carelessly by the people of our age, to whom denying the truth once acknowledged seems a game and a joke. But by this game they lose what they had gained before. Their last state will become worse than the first. Indeed it would be better for them never to have known the truth. See Matth. 12. Likewise 2 Pet. 2, chapter.

units.la: Obseruemus autem, quod salutem & beatitudinem, quae in Christo per fidem obtingit, mercedis vocabulo appellat. Videtur hoc ijs patrocinari, qui merita humanorum operum asserunt. Sic enim argumentantur: Merces debetur operibus, nec datur ex gratia. Beatitudo merces dicitur etiam à Christo, vt Matth.5. Ergo operibus nostris ea debetur, &c. Item à natura Contrariorum similiter concludunt, bonis operibus mercedem & praemium deberi, eò quòd malis poenam mereamur. mur. Sed facilis est vtriusq; argumenti solutio. Nam quoad primū, beatitudo quoad nos mihimè merces est, sed Deus ,p paterna in nos beneuolentia sic illā nominat, vt tanq; ingenui liberi efficacius ad bene operandū trahamur. Inter opera enim & mercedē æquiparatione esse oportet, vt illa huic ex æquo respondeant. At quæcunq; hic siue facimus siue etiā patimur, nullo modo cū gloria regni cœlorum conferri possunt. Rom.8. Isa.64. Adhæc beatitudo hæreditas est, quę non operarijs seruis, sed filijs debetur. Filij Dei verò nascimur ex gratia, & vt ad eā dignitatē perueniamus, non est vel volentis vel currentis, sed miserentis Dei. Ioan.1. Rom.9. Quoad verò alterū argumentum, bonorū & malorum operū contrarietas siue oppositio multis nominibus falsa est. Primò enim mala opera ex hobisipsis facimus, ,pprijs viribus atq; cōsilijs: bona verò non ita. Nam sine me (inquit Christus) nihil potestis facere. Ioan.15. Licet ergo malis operib. pœnæ debeatur, quia nostra sunt, merces tamen bonis nulla debebitur, quia hæc in nobis bonus Dei spiritus operatur, & Deus pro sua clementia suū opus in nobis coronat. Deinde mala opera perfectè & absolutè mala sunt, & nullū peccatum tā leuiculum est, quod nō æterna dānatione mulctari mereatur, si ius suū Deus velit persequi. Deut.27. Bonis verò operibus nunq; nō imperfectio & labes aliqua adhæret: non quidē ex spiritu Dei, ea in nobis operante, sed ex nostræ naturæ corruptione, quę nusquam non conspicitur. Quo fit, vt licet propter mala opera damnari mereamur, propter bona tamen quæ multis modis imperfecta sunt, saluari non merebimur. Et hæc quidem obiter dicta sint. Nunc ad præsentis loci tractationem reuertamur.
units.tr: Let us observe, however, that he calls the salvation and blessedness which comes to us in Christ through faith by the name of reward. This seems to favour those who assert the merits of human works. For they argue thus: reward is owed to works, and is not given from grace. Blessedness is also called a reward by Christ, as in Matth. 5. Therefore it is owed to our works, etc. Likewise, from the nature of contraries, they conclude in similar fashion that a reward and prize are owed to good works, inasmuch as we deserve punishment by evil ones. But the solution of both arguments is easy. For as to the first, blessedness is by no means a reward as far as we are concerned, but God, out of paternal goodwill toward us, so names it in order that we may be drawn more effectively to doing good, as free-born children. For between works and reward there ought to be an equality, so that the one corresponds to the other on equal terms. But whatever we do or even suffer here cannot in any way be compared with the glory of the kingdom of heaven. Rom. 8. Isa. 64. Moreover, blessedness is an inheritance, which is owed not to hired servants but to sons. Now we are born children of God by grace, and to attain that dignity it is not of him who wills or runs, but of God who shows mercy. John 1. Rom. 9. As to the second argument, the contrariety or opposition of good and evil works is false in many respects. For first, we perform evil works of ourselves, by our own strength and counsels; but good works are not so. For without me (says Christ) you can do nothing. John 15. Although therefore punishment is owed to evil works, because they are ours, yet no reward will be owed to good ones, because these are wrought in us by the good Spirit of God, and God, by his clemency, crowns his own work in us. Next, evil works are altogether and absolutely evil, and no sin is so trifling that it does not deserve to be punished with eternal damnation, if God should wish to exact his right. Deut. 27. But good works never lack some imperfection and blemish clinging to them: not indeed from the Spirit of God, who works them in us, but from the corruption of our nature, which is everywhere visible. Hence it comes about that, although we deserve to be condemned on account of evil works, we shall not deserve to be saved on account of good ones, which in many ways are imperfect. But these things have been said in passing; let us now return to the treatment of the present passage.

units.la: II. Omnis qui transgreditur, & non manet in doctrina Christi, Deum non habet. Pœnam minatur horribilem & infelicitatem, qua maior excogitari nō potest. Vt enim qui Deū habent, in eodē omnis boni confortes sunt: ita qui hoc carent, omni bono spoliati genus omne malorū tam in præsenti quàm futuro seculo sustinent. Vera aut & irrefragabilis est sententia. Nemo venit ad patrem (inquit Christus) nisi per me. Ego sum via, lux & veritas. Ioan.14. At quomodo per Christū in patris communione & consortium admittetur, qui eius doctrinā non obseruauerit? Nam idem ille ibidem dicit: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meū seruabit, & pater meus diliget eum, & ad eum veniemus, & mansionem apud eum faciemus. Non temere ergo homines ἄθεοι vel Deo vacui dicuntur, qui Christi doctrinam vel non admittunt, vel receptam denuò abijciunt.
units.tr: II. Whoever transgresses, and abides not in the doctrine of Christ, has not God. He threatens a dreadful punishment and unhappiness, than which a greater cannot be imagined. For just as those who have God are partakers of every good in him, so those who lack him, deprived of every good, endure every kind of evil both in the present and in the future age. The saying is true and unfailing. No one comes to the Father (says Christ) except through me. I am the way, the light and the truth. John 14. But how will someone be admitted through Christ into communion and fellowship with the Father, if he has not kept his teaching? For that same Christ says in the same place: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our abode with him. Not without reason, therefore, are men called atheists, or empty of God, who either do not admit the doctrine of Christ or cast it off again once received.

units.la: III. Qui manet in doctrina Christi, is & patrem & filium habet. Opponit priori sententiæ pro suo more, contrariam, quæ cōsolationis plenissima est. Nam vt modò diximus, qui Deum habet, fontem omnis boni habet, nec ipsi quicquam eorum, quæ saluti seruiunt, deesse potest.
units.tr: III. He who abides in the doctrine of Christ, the same has both the Father and the Son. He sets against the former sentence, in his usual manner, the contrary one, which is most full of consolation. For, as we have just said, whoever has God has the fountain of every good, and nothing that serves salvation can be lacking to him.

units.la: Comprehendit itaq; breui sententia Ioan. quæ omniū gentium philosophi nec infinitis speculationibus peruestigare, nec hamaxiæis (vt dicunt) voluminibus copletti potuerunt: Ratione nimirū verę beatitudinis cōsequendę, quę in vna præceptorū Christi obseruatione versatur. Sūt ea simplicia & perspicua, pleneq; in scripturis tradita. Comprehendunt fide in Christū, quæ verę religionis colophon est, ité charitatis officia & vitæ puritate. In horū verò obseruatione felicitatem sitā esse, & omniū seculorū exempla docent, & spiritus Christi (quē is salutis arrhabonem dit) in fideliū animis cōprobat. Quid ergo nostri seculi calamitates miramur, quę Deū à nobis ab alienatum esse docent, quando paucissimi inueniuntur, qui in Christi doctrina permanēt? Obseruemus hāc, & illius ductu ad Deū reuertamur. Sic.n.fiet, vt Deo ,pte&ore hic tuti degamus inter mundi pericula, & in cœlis olim regnemus cū Christo Iesu, cui debetur benedictio, gloria, honor & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: John has therefore comprehended in a brief sentence what the philosophers of all nations could neither trace out by endless speculations nor fill with volumes, as they say, by the hundred: namely, the way of attaining true blessedness, which consists in the observance of the one precept of Christ alone. These precepts are simple and clear, and are fully delivered in the Scriptures. They comprise faith in Christ, which is the crown of true religion, likewise the duties of love and purity of life. That happiness lies in the observance of these, the examples of all ages teach, and the Spirit of Christ (whom he calls the earnest of salvation) confirms in the hearts of the faithful. Why then do we wonder at the calamities of our age, which show that God has been alienated from us, since very few are found who remain in the doctrine of Christ? Let us observe this, and by his guidance return to God. For thus it will come about that we live safely here among the dangers of the world, and one day reign in heaven with Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, glory, honour and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA V.
units.tr: HOMILY V.

units.la: Si quis uenit ad uos, & hanc doctrinam non affert, eum ne receperitis in domum, nec dixeritis ei Aue. Qui enim dicit illi Aue, communicat operibus eius malis. Cùm multa haberem uobis scribenda, nolui per chartam & atramentum. Sed spero me uenturum ad uos, et præsentem præsentibus locuturum, ut gaudium nostrum sit completum. Salutant te filij sororis tuæ electæ. Amen.
units.tr: If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house, nor say to him, Hail. For whoever says to him, Hail, shares in his evil works. Although I had many things to write to you, I did not wish to do so by paper and ink. But I hope to come to you and speak face to face, so that our joy may be complete. The children of your elect sister greet you. Amen.

units.la: VT syncera verbi Dei doctrina verā Dei cognitione & eā fidē plantat, qua Deo cōiuncti salvamur: ita falsa humanarū traditionū dogmata homines à Deo abstractos dānationis mancipia reddunt. Non temere ergo Ioan. totius scripturæ exemplū secutus, tū alibi, tum in hoc epistolio constantiā in vera fidei doctrina tantopere cōmendat, simulq; monet quid defectores manet. Commodè verò ijs, quæ præcesserunt, hunc locum subijcit quo falsos doctores cauere docet, & & ita tandem scripto huic finem imponit.
units.tr: As the pure doctrine of the Word of God plants the true knowledge of God and the faith by which we are saved, joined to God, so the false doctrines of human traditions make men, separated from God, slaves of damnation. Therefore it is not rashly that John, following the example of all Scripture, both elsewhere and in this little epistle, commends so earnestly constancy in the true doctrine of faith, and at the same time warns what awaits the defectors. He appropriately attaches this passage to what precedes, teaching us to beware of false teachers, and thus at last brings this writing to a close.

units.la: I. Si quis uenit ad uos, & hanc doctrinam non affert, cum ne receperitis in domum, nec dixeritis ei Aue, &c. Est hæc fidelis & paterna admonitio, quam verbis quoq; planis & perspicuis comprehendit. Falsam doctrinā nemo sciēs volensq; facilè admitteret. Interim falsos doctores nō perinde horrent, qui vel de fidei suæ constantia præsumptuosius & arrogantius iudicant, vel mundi amiciti-am aspernari nondū didicerunt. Euenit his, quod prouerbio dicitur: Qui picè contrectat, inquinatur ab ea. Norunt enim falsi doctores venenum suum blanditioquentia velatum per familiaria colloquia sic inspirare simplicibus, vt raro discedant, nisi pestifero falsæ alicuius persuasionis aculeo in animis illorum relicto. Serpit enim (Paulo teste) illorum doctrina, vt Cancer morbus, qui dum minimè putatur, vim suam eosq; extendit, vt incurabilis fiat. Rectè ergo Ioannes huius mali fontem obturare studet, & falsorum doctorum commercijs interdicit. Prodest autem singula verba penitius inspexisse, & ponderasse diligentius.
units.tr: I. If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house, nor say to him, Hail, etc. This is a faithful and fatherly admonition, which he expresses in plain and clear words as well. No one who knows and wishes it would readily admit false doctrine. Yet people do not shrink from false teachers in the same measure, those who judge too presumptuously and arrogantly of the constancy of their own faith, or who have not yet learned to despise the friendship of the world. What is said in the proverb happens to them: He who handles pitch is defiled by it. For false teachers know how to breathe their poison, veiled by flattering speech, into simple people through familiar conversation, in such a way that they seldom depart without leaving behind in their minds the deadly sting of some false persuasion. For their teaching (as Paul testifies) creeps on like a cancer, which, while it is least thought of, spreads its force and grows until it becomes incurable. Rightly, therefore, John takes pains to stop up the source of this evil, and forbids all dealings with false teachers. It is useful, however, to examine each word more closely and to weigh it more carefully.

units.la: Qui hanc doctrinam non affert. Loquitur aūt de doctrina Christi, cuius dignitate ipse Christus præ-dicans ait: Doctrina mea non est mea (siquidē me vt hominem consyderetis) sed patris, qui misit me. Ioan. 7. Finis & scopus huius est, vt homines per Christū, vnicam salutis viā, Deo patri adducantur, & Christi merito se huic recōciliatos esse intelligant. Vnde ad se omnes laborantes & oneratos Christus inuitat. Matth. 11. Eadem verum Dei cultū docet, qui non in frigidis Ceremonijs, sed spiritu & veritate consistit. Ioan. 4. Præcipit item de vitæ Christianæ officijs, quorū regula & amusisis est charitas innocentiæ coniuncta. Quisquis ergo diuersa docuerit, & cum his pugnantia, eum sciamus, Christi doctrinam non afferre, & proinde caueri debere.
units.tr: Who does not bring this doctrine. He speaks of the doctrine of Christ, whose dignity Christ himself proclaimed when he said: My doctrine is not mine (if you regard me as a man) but of the Father who sent me. John 7. The aim and goal of this is that men, through Christ, the only way of salvation, should be brought to God the Father, and understand that they have been reconciled to him by the merit of Christ. Hence Christ invites all who labour and are burdened to himself. Matt. 11. The same doctrine teaches the true worship of God, which consists not in cold ceremonies but in spirit and truth. John 4. It likewise instructs in the duties of the Christian life, whose rule and measure is charity joined with innocence. Whoever therefore teaches different things, and things contrary to these, we should know that he does not bring the doctrine of Christ, and that for this reason he must be avoided.

units.la: Eum ne receperitis in domum, nec dixeritis ei Aue. Prohibet his omne commercium, quocunq; humanitatis & charitatis prætextu velatū. Qui locus eos vehementer arguit, qui commercia cum hominibus Christi charitatis officio excusare studēt. Iubet quidem hostes nostros diligere Christus. Suos verò hostes diligere nusquam iubet. At Christi hostes sunt, quicunq; falsis doctrinis in ecclesia grassantur, & animabus, Christi sanguine redemptis, exitiū struunt. De obstinatis verò hic loquimur. Scimus enim multos ignorantia peccare, qui vtiq; admonendi & docendi sunt. Siqui vero vel doctrinam omnem pertinaciter respuunt, vel veritatem edocti falsa dogmata illi præferunt, eos pro manifestis & iuratis Christi hostibus habere, & omni modo vitare decet, ne & nos cum illis perfidè colludere videamur.
units.tr: Do not receive him into your house, nor say to him, Hail. He forbids every fellowship, veiled under whatever pretext of humanity and charity. This passage strongly rebukes those who seek to excuse their dealings with men under the duty of Christian charity. Christ indeed bids us love our enemies. But he nowhere bids us love his enemies. Yet those are enemies of Christ who rage in the Church with false doctrines and plot ruin for souls redeemed by the blood of Christ. Here, however, we are speaking of the obstinate. For we know that many sin through ignorance, and these at all events must be admonished and taught. But if any either stubbornly reject all doctrine, or, having been taught the truth, prefer false dogmas to it, we ought to regard them as manifest and sworn enemies of Christ, and to avoid them in every way, lest we too seem to collude with them in treachery.

units.la: Qui enim dicit illi Aue, communicat operibus eis malis. Causam fui præcepti reddit, quæ multiplex produci poterat. Nam vt modò diximus, præcipua est, quòd falsis doctrinis facilè inficimur, cūnatu-rali quodam motu nostræ rationis commentis maximè delectemur. Sed cum illis hic agit Ioannes, qui ea fidei constantia sibi præditi videntur, vt nullum erroris periculum sibi metuendum esse existiment. Et vt hoc vobis demus (inquit) grauis tamen adhuc causa est, quæ horū commercia vitare iubet. Quicunq; enim illis dixerit Aue, illorū operibus malis communicat, id est consentire facit erroru, quibus illi impliciti sunt, & reliquos implicare solent, ficq; nec pœnas ipsis destinatas effugiet. Est verò multiplex huius dicti ratio. Primū enim constat, seducto-res ipsos in erroribus suis confirmari, quò minus ab illis recedant, cum ne eos quidem, qui rectius sapere videntur, ab ipsorum consuetudine declinare videant. Deinde res est offendiculi plena. Vt enim olim infirmiores offendebatur, si quē immolatitijs carnibus vesci viderent: ita hodie plurimos offendi cōstat, si quos sibi fidei & pietatis exempla proposuerant, cū ijs frequenter versari viderint, quorum doctrina & religionem erroris accusari sæpius audiuerunt. Erant hæc ijs obseruanda, quibus volupe est in monachorū lustris conuiuari, & qui solius ventris gulæq; studio eorū sestantur amicitias quos doctrinæ Christi acerrimos hostes esse norunt. Quòd verò illi charitatem prætexunt, vanissimum est. Nec enim quisquam Apostolorum est, qui charitatem diligentius commendet & fortius vrgeat, q Ioannes, qui tamē idem huius præcepti author est. Sed epilogū epistolæ videamus.
units.tr: For whoever says to him, Hail, shares in his evil works. He gives the reason for the command, which could be drawn out in many ways. For, as we have just said, the chief reason is that we are easily infected by false doctrines, and by a certain natural impulse we take the greatest delight in the inventions of our own reason. But John here deals with those who seem endowed with such constancy of faith that they think no danger of error need be feared by them. And, he says, even if we grant you this, there is still a serious reason that bids you avoid their fellowship. For whoever says Hail to them shares in their evil works, that is, he causes them to agree with the errors in which they are entangled and which they are wont to entangle others, and so he will not escape the punishments destined for them. Now there are several reasons for this saying. First, it is certain that seducers are confirmed in their errors, so that they depart from them the less, when they see that not even those who seem to think more soundly keep away from their company. Next, the matter is full of stumbling. For just as in former times the weaker were offended if they saw someone eating meat offered to idols, so today it is evident that many are offended if those whom they had set before themselves as examples of faith and piety are often seen in the company of those whose doctrine and religion they have often heard accused of error. These things had to be observed by those who delight to feast in the brothels of monks, and who court the friendship, for the sake of their belly and throat, of those whom they know to be the bitterest enemies of the doctrine of Christ. But that they put forward charity as a pretext is most vain. For there is no one among the Apostles who commends charity more diligently and urges it more strongly than John, who is yet the very author of this command. But let us look at the close of the epistle.

units.la: I I. Cum multa haberem uobis scribenda, nolui per chartam & atramentum. Sed spero me venturum ad uos, & præsentem præsentibus locuturum, ut gaudium nostrum sit completum, &c. Est hæc prior epilogi pars, qua breuitatem fui scripsi excusat. Causam vero huius exponit, quòd sperat se illos breui coram videre posse, quādo pluribus cum ipsis agere possit. Et sanè obseruatione dignissimum est Apostoli studium, qui doctrinam salutis non tam chartis commissam esse, quàm hominum animis infidere voluit. Illud enim nisi fiat, frustra & auditur & legitur verbum, sicut dominus in euangelica seminantis parabola monuit. Luc. 8.
units.tr: II. Although I had many things to write to you, I did not wish to do so by paper and ink. But I hope to come to you and speak face to face, so that our joy may be complete, etc. This is the first part of the closing, in which he excuses the brevity of what he has written. He gives the reason for it, namely that he hopes he may soon be able to see them in person, when he can deal with them at greater length. And indeed the Apostle's zeal is most worthy of observation, for he wished the doctrine of salvation to be committed not so much to pages as to sink into the minds of men. For unless this happens, the word is heard and read in vain, as the Lord warned in the parable of the sower. Luke 8.

units.la: Deinde ex hoc loco videre est, qua de causa Apostoli interdum exteras ecclesias inuiserint: non quidem, vt Circulatorum more, indulgentiarum nundinatione, aut Reliquiarum vana ostentatione pecunias emungerent: sed vt vero gaudio implerent Christianos, cuius gaudij causa erat donum aliquod, spirituale, vel doctrinæ, vel admonitionis, vel consolationis, quod illis non fine se[?] singulari profectu conferebant. Sic Paulus & Barnabas ecclesias obambulasse & confirmauisse leguntur, Acto.14. Nec alia causa Paulo fuit, propter quam Romanos inuisere cupiebat. Rom. 1. Hoc studio si flagrarent, qui hodie Episcopi dici & haberi volunt, felicius multò haberent ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Next, from this passage we may see for what reason the Apostles sometimes visited foreign churches: not indeed, like the vagabond sellers, to drain money by the trade in indulgences or by the empty display of relics, but to fill Christians with true joy, the cause of which joy was some spiritual gift, whether of doctrine, admonition or consolation, which they bestowed on them not without singular profit. Thus Paul and Barnabas are read to have gone through the churches and strengthened them, Acts 14. Nor had Paul any other reason for wishing to visit the Romans. Rom. 1. If those who today wish to be and be called bishops were fired with this zeal, the churches would fare far better.

units.la: Altera epilogi parte salutationes ponuntur, more apostolico. Quo exemplo admonemur sa-lutandi officia, & quæcunque alia ad mutuam amicitiam & benevolentiam conciliandam faciût, ab hominibus Christianis nequaquam aliena esse. Nec enim Stoicos vult esse dominus, quos nullus vel priuatæ vel alienæ rei affectus moueat. Imò si Paulum audias, ἀσπονδοι[?] & affectionibus naturalibus vacui, inter eos numerantur, quos nobis imprimis cauendos spiritus sanctus commonstrat. 2.Tim.3.
units.tr: In the second part of the closing, greetings are given, after the apostolic manner. By this example we are reminded that the duties of greeting, and whatever else serves to win mutual friendship and goodwill, are by no means foreign to Christian men. For the Lord does not wish us to be Stoics, whom no feeling, either for their own affairs or for those of others, moves. Indeed, if you listen to Paul, men without love and without natural affections are numbered among those whom the Holy Spirit above all shows us we must beware of. 2 Tim. 3.

units.la: Docuit igitur breui hoc epistolio, quæcunque ad veræ felicitatis rationem faciunt, Apostolus. Proposuit hanc in obseruatione doctrinæ Christi. Ostendit quid eos maneat, qui ab hac deficiunt. Simul docuit, vt tantum periculum cauere possimus. Meditemur hæc nostro seculo, quando tot tamq; infelicia defectionis exempla extant, & oremus Deum patrem, vt ipsius spiritu animati, persueremus in Christo Jesu, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: In this brief epistle, therefore, the Apostle has taught everything that serves the true account of happiness. He has set this forth in observing the doctrine of Christ. He has shown what awaits those who fall away from it. At the same time he has taught us how we may guard against so great a danger. Let us meditate on these things in our own age, when so many and such unhappy examples of defection stand before us, and let us pray God the Father that, animated by his Spirit, we may persevere in Christ Jesus, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: IN EPISTOLAM D. JOANNIS APOSTOLI III. RODOLPHI GUALTHERI TIGURINI HOMILIARUM SYLVAE. HOMILIA I.
units.tr: ON THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED JOHN THE APOSTLE, III. HOMILIES OF RUDOLPH GWALTHER OF ZURICH. HOMILY I.

units.la: SENIOR Caio dilecto, quem ego diligo in veritate. Dilecte, opto te in omnibus prospere agere & valere, sicut prospere agit anima tua. Gauisus sum enim valde venientibus fratribus & testimonium reddentibus veritati tuæ, sicut tu in veritate ambulas. Maius his gaudium non habeo, quàm ut audiam filios meos in veritate ambulare.
units.tr: THE ELDER to Gaius the beloved, whom I love in truth. Beloved, I pray that you may prosper and be in health in all things, just as your soul prospers. For I rejoiced greatly when the brethren came and bore witness to your truth, just as you walk in the truth. I have no greater joy than to hear that my children walk in the truth.

units.la: UT IMPIOS verbi Dei contemptores, ac oppressores, fidelium, palàm arguì atque increpari oportet: ita pios & fideles cultores publicè cõmendare cumpri-mis vtile est & conueniens. Sic enim & sponte currentibus calcar additur, & alij illorum exemplo ad similium studiorum imitationem excitari solent. Obseruat vtrunq; in præsenti epistolio Ioannes. Scribit enim Caio (quem Corinthium fuisse ex Pauli scriptis constat, 1.Cor.1.Rom.16.) qui fratres. propter fidé Christi sedibus proprijs eiectos, colligebat. Eius studiû magnificè laudat, & vt in eo pergat hortatur. Simul vero immites aliquos & duros, qui tam sancto studio aduersabantur, grauiter reprehendit.
units.tr: Just as the impious despisers and oppressors of the Word of God ought to be openly refuted and rebuked, so it is especially useful and fitting to commend publicly the pious and faithful worshippers. For thus a spur is added to those who already run willingly, and others are wont to be stirred up to imitate such zeal by their example. John observes both in the present little letter. For he writes to Gaius (who, as is clear from the writings of Paul, was a Corinthian; 1 Cor. 1; Rom. 16), who was gathering the brethren who had been driven from their homes for the faith of Christ. He praises his zeal magnificently and urges him to persevere in it. At the same time he sharply rebukes certain harsh and cruel men who opposed so holy a labour.

units.la: Docet nos horum consyderatio, pijs & fidelibus Christi nunquam vel benefactores vel ma-lefactores defore. Quia enim veritatis lucem penes se habent, fieri non potest, quin mundo exosi sint, qui hanc propter opera sua mala ferre non potest. Ioan. 3. Hinc Paulus dixit, persecutionem nemini defuturam, qui in Christo pie vivere instituat. 2.Tim.3. At quia sub divinæ providentiæ tutela & protectione agimus, nunquam etiam benefactores & nutritij, divinitus excitati, deerūt, qualem Caium hunc fuisse legimus, quem Paulus ob singularem in pios beneficentiam totius ecclesiæ hospitem vocat. Rom.16. Possunt huc referri, quæ de Abdia, prophetarum patrono & nutritio, legimus. 3.Reg.18. Et quòd discipuli in ultima Cœna ingenuè fatentur, sibi nihil unquam defuisse, quando sine pera & nùmis à Christo emissi fuerunt, ipso nimirum illis satis liberaliter prospiciente. Luc.22. Petant hinc consolationem, qui Christi nomine exilium & paupertatem sustinent. Non deerit illis, qui volatilia cœli pascit, qui pecoribus pascua præparauit, & escam submittit pullis corvorum, dum ipsum invocant. Matt.6. Psal.147. Sed ad Apostoli verba transeamus.
units.tr: The consideration of these men teaches us that the pious and faithful of Christ will never lack either benefactors or persecutors. For since they hold the light of the truth, it cannot be but that they are hated by the world, which cannot bear it because of their own evil works (John 3). Hence Paul said that persecution would be lacking to no one who resolves to live piously in Christ (2 Tim. 3). But because we live under the protection and safeguard of divine providence, benefactors and nourishers, stirred up by God, will never be lacking either, such as we read this Gaius was, whom Paul, on account of his singular kindness to the pious, calls the host of the whole Church (Rom. 16). What we read of Obadiah, the patron and nourisher of the prophets, may be referred here (1 Kings 18). And what the disciples freely confess at the Last Supper, that nothing had ever been lacking to them when they were sent out without a purse and without money, Christ himself of course providing for them quite generously (Luke 22). Let those who endure exile and poverty for the name of Christ seek consolation here: he who feeds the birds of heaven, who has prepared pastures for the flocks and sends food to the young ravens when they call upon him, will not fail them (Matt. 6; Ps. 147). But let us pass on to the words of the Apostle.

units.la: Senior,Caio dilecto, quem ego diligo in veritate. Est hæc inscriptio epistolæ, quæ vulgari more tum authorem, tum eum cui scribitur denotat. At quia de authore, qui vt in præcedenti epistolio,ita & hic Senioris nomen sibi vsurpat,alibi diximus,nec de Caio plura dici opus est, quà quæ in argumento attigimus,nihil hic nobis dicendum restat. Quid enim ex eo discI debeat, quòd dilectioni veritatem tribuit,alibi exposuimus.
units.tr: Elder, to Gaius the beloved, whom I love in truth. This is the inscription of the letter, which in the common manner designates both the author and the one to whom it is written. But since we have said elsewhere about the author, who, as in the previous letter, here too claims for himself the name of Elder, and since there is no need to say more about Gaius than what we touched on in the argument, nothing further remains for us to say here. What we ought to learn from the fact that he ascribes love to the truth we have set forth elsewhere.

units.la: I I. Dilecte,opto te in omnibus prosperè agere & valere,sicut prosperè agit anima tua. Discedit nō nihil hoc loco à communi & Apostolica benedictionis formula, cum tamen verbis mutatis idem illi precetur,quod alibi per gratiæ & pacis vocabula exprimitur. Optat enim,vt illi sit mens sana in corpore sano:quibus vniuersa hominis felicitas absoluitur. Nec negligendū est,quòd animæ prosperitatem reliquæ fortunæ quasi formam & regulam esse vult. Discimus enim,veram hominis in columnitatem in eo consistere,vt anima bene habeat. Nam vt hæc præstantior hominis pars est: ita eiusdem iactura nullis huius mundi bonis (vt Christus monet) est reparabilis. Matth.16. At habet bene anima, si cum Deo se coniunctam & reconciliatam esse intelligat. Quod quia per solam fidem discit,absque hac veram hominis incolumitatem frustra inquiremus. Eadem verò si affuerit,in reliquis quoq; successus sequetur,quem saluti nostræ vtilem & necessarium fore intellexerit Dei prouidentia. Nam Paulo teste, Pietas tam præsentis quàm futuræ vitæ promissiones habet. 1.Tim.4. Huius quia perquam exigua nobis est ratio hodie, non mirum si omnibus modis miseri & calamitosi esse deprehendimur. Lege Deut.28.Ierem.7.&c.
units.tr: II. Beloved, I pray that you may prosper and be in health in all things, just as your soul prospers. In this place he departs somewhat from the common and apostolic formula of blessing, although with changed words he wishes him the same thing that is expressed elsewhere by the words grace and peace. For he wishes that he may have a sound mind in a sound body, in which the whole happiness of man is completed. Nor is it to be neglected that he wishes the prosperity of the soul to be, as it were, the form and rule of all other fortune. For we learn that the true welfare of man consists in this, that the soul be well. For as this is the more excellent part of man, so its loss cannot be repaired by any goods of this world (as Christ warns; Matt. 16). But the soul is well if it understands itself to be joined and reconciled to God. Since it learns this through faith alone, we shall seek the true soundness of man in vain apart from this. But if this is present, success will follow also in other things, which the providence of God will know to be useful and necessary for our salvation. For, as Paul testifies, godliness has promises both for the present life and for the life to come (1 Tim. 4). Since we today have a very small regard for this, it is no wonder that we are found to be wretched and calamitous in every way. Read Deut. 28; Jer. 7, etc.

units.la: III. Gauisus sum enim valde venientibus fratribus & testimonium reddentibus veritati tuæ. &c. Exorditur à narratione, quæ tota ad beneuolentiæ captationem instituitur, simulq; non caret stimulis, quibus vt in tam sancto studio constanter pergat, monetur. Vt enim animos facile despondemus, si studia nostra minus syncerè æstimari videamus: ita si illa bonis & sanctis probetur, improborū calūnias non grauatim contēnimus. Habent verò hic singulæ personæ, quod obseruari debet.
units.tr: III. For I rejoiced greatly when the brethren came and bore witness to your truth, etc. He begins with a narrative, which is wholly designed to win goodwill, and at the same time it is not without spurs by which he is admonished to persevere constantly in so holy a labour. For just as we easily lose heart if we see our labours valued less than sincerely, so if they are approved by the good and holy, we do not grievously despise the calumnies of the wicked. Each of the persons here has something that ought to be observed.

units.la: Primum fratres producuntur,qui ex Corintho profecti apud Ioannem Caij studium & pietatem prædicarunt. Est hoc charitatis & iustitiæ officium, vt nimirum de fratribus bene sentiamus & loquamur,imprimis verò eorum laudes prædicemus,qui virtutibus suis hoc meruerunt. Et vt in Repub. magnum ad bene agendum incitamentum est,si boni laudem habeant, & vituperiū malitia non contemnendus eiusdem rei in ecclesia fructus est. Nec postremam causam existimo, ob quam nostro seculo pietatis studium passim friget, quòd calumnijs potius quàm laudibus prosequimur eos,quorum labores publicæ vtilitati deseruiunt.
units.tr: First, the brethren are brought forward, who, departing from Corinth, proclaimed to John the zeal and piety of Gaius. This is a duty of charity and justice, namely to think and speak well of the brethren, and above all to proclaim the praises of those who have deserved this by their virtues. And just as in a commonwealth there is a great incitement to good conduct if the good have praise, so the fruit of the same thing in the Church is not to be despised, namely that vice has reproach. Nor do I think it the least cause, on account of which in our age the zeal for piety grows cold everywhere, that we pursue with calumnies rather than with praises those whose labours serve the public benefit.

units.la: Secundò Caius inspiciendus erit,vt quid in illo tantopere prædicatū sit,videamus. Commemoratur autem Veritatis studium. Veritatē ipsum Christum esse,sepe iā diximus. In veritate ergo ambulant,qui omnia sua ad huius præscriptionem instituunt,tā in religionis negotio,q; externa vitæ conuersatione. Et hæc vera est ac nunquā intermoritura hominis Christiani gloria. Arguuntur ergo hic,qui inani cognitione turgentes,non in veritate,sed carnis suæ concupiscentijs ambulant. Christianismū enim [illegible, ~6 letters] exigere, & Christus & Apostoli passim docent. Matth.7. Iac.2. Col.3.
units.tr: Second, Gaius is to be considered, so that we may see what was so greatly praised in him. Now the zeal for truth is commemorated. That the truth itself is Christ, we have often said already. Those therefore walk in the truth who order all their affairs by its rule, both in the business of religion and in the outward conduct of life. And this is the true and never-perishing glory of the Christian man. Those are therefore rebuked here who, puffed up with empty knowledge, walk not in the truth but in the lusts of their flesh. For that Christianity demands deeds, both Christ and the Apostles teach everywhere (Matt. 7; James 2; Col. 3).

units.la: Tertiò,Ioannes de se dicit,Maius his gaudiū non habeo, quàm vt audiā filios meos in veritate ambulare. Est hoc Christiani pectoris specimen, quòd & charitatis & gloriæ Dei studio flagrare cernitur. Gaudet enim ob fratrum salutem,quæ veritatis studio & acquiritur & seruatur. Gaudet item ob Dei gloriam, quæ tum maximè in terris prouehitur, quando veritatis studium hominibus cordi est. Huius gaudij fructus non perit. Qui enim hic gaudent diuinæ gloriæ propagatione, ad eandem studia sua omnia dirigunt, tandemq; in cœlis æterni gaudij erunt consortes. Hinc æstimabis vana mundi huius gaudia, & quanta nobis sit hodie dolendi & lugendi occasio, quando multos à veritate cognita turpiter deficere, paucissimos verò in ea ambulare conspicimus, inter eos quoque,qui huius professione gloriantur. Faxit Deus, ut zelo Dei & gloriæ diuinæ studio ardentes, olim gaudeamus in aduentu Christi Iesu, cui debetur benedictio, gloria, honor & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Third, John speaks of himself: "I have no greater joy than to hear that my children walk in the truth." This is a mark of a Christian heart, that it is seen to burn both with love and with zeal for the glory of God. For he rejoices over the salvation of the brethren, which is both gained and kept by zeal for the truth. He rejoices likewise over the glory of God, which is then especially advanced on earth when zeal for the truth is dear to men. The fruit of this joy does not perish. For those who here rejoice in the propagation of the divine glory direct all their labours to the same end, and at last in heaven will be partakers of eternal joy. From this you will judge the vain joys of this world, and how great is our present occasion for sorrow and mourning, when we see many shamefully falling away from the truth once known, and very few walking in it, and among these even those who boast of its profession. May God grant that, burning with zeal for God and with a desire for the divine glory, we may one day rejoice at the coming of Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, glory, honour and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA II.
units.tr: Homily II.

units.la: Charissime,fideliter agis quicquid operaris in fratres & hospites: qui testimonium reddiderunt charitati tuæ in conspectu ecclesiæ: quos bene ages,si deduxeris dignè Deo. Pro eius enim nomine egressi sunt,nihil accipientes à gentibus. Nos ergo debemus recipere eiusmodi,ut cooperatores simus veritati.
units.tr: Dearest friend, you act faithfully in whatever you do for the brothers and for strangers, who have borne witness to your love in the sight of the Church. You will do well to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God. For they went out for the sake of his name, taking nothing from the Gentiles. We therefore ought to receive such people, so that we may be fellow-workers with the truth.

units.la: DIvus Ioannes breui hoc & sancto epistolio Cai beneficentia, qua in fratres exercebat, prædicare, eundemque ne in tam sancto studio ob quorundam calumnias deficiat, exhortari instituit. Ita verò hanc causam tractat, vt Cai exemplo perfectam hominis Christiani formam copre-hendat. Primò enim illi veritate tribuit, sine cuius cognitione nihil proficitur. Deinde, eum in veritate ambulauisse testatur. Nec enim prodest nuda & inanis veritatis cognitio, nisi reipsa præste-mus, quod recte esse nouimus. At quia inter veritatis & fidei fructus primatu habet Charitas, cuius insigne exemplum Caius præbuit, de hac præsenti loco diligentius disserit. Primò enim Caium laudat propter ea quæ hucusque fecerat. Deinde vt eadem facere pergat, hortatur.
units.tr: The divine John, in this short and holy letter, undertakes to proclaim the beneficence of Gaius, with which he showed kindness to the brothers, and to exhort him not to lose heart in so holy a pursuit because of the slanders of certain people. He treats this matter so as to set before us, in the example of Gaius, the complete form of a Christian man. For first he ascribes truth to him, without whose knowledge nothing is accomplished. Then he bears witness that Gaius walked in the truth. For bare and empty knowledge of the truth profits nothing, unless we actually do what we know to be right. But since love holds first place among the fruits of truth and faith, and Gaius gave a notable example of it, he discusses this in the present passage more fully. First he praises Gaius for what he has done so far; then he exhorts him to continue doing the same.

units.la: Charissime, fideliter agis quicquid operaris in fratres, &c. Paucis illius beneficentiam prædicat, ne quicquam adulationis causa dicere videatur. Debet enim in amicorum officijs prædicandis modus adhiberi, ne dum personam nimis anxiè euehimus, rem ipsam faciamus suspectam. Interim modum & rationem indicat, qua Cai in pios fratres ossi[illegible, ~3 letters] cognouerit. Sunt autem in his non pauca, quæ nostræ institutioni seruiant, si non otiosè consyderentur.
units.tr: Dearest friend, you act faithfully in whatever you do for the brothers, etc. He briefly praises his kindness, lest he seem to say anything out of flattery. For in proclaiming the services of friends a measure ought to be observed, lest, while we exalt the person too anxiously, we make the matter itself suspect. Meanwhile he indicates the manner and method by which Gaius showed kindness to the godly brothers [illegible, about 3 letters]. There are in these words not a few things which serve our instruction, if they are not considered carelessly.

units.la: Primò ipsum Cai opus peculiari nota insignit, dicês: Fideliter agis. Clariora autem sunt Græca, πιστῶς ποιεῖς[?], quod perinde sonat ac si dixisset: Opus fidei facis, & quod homine fide præditû cum primis decet. Est enim propriū fidei opus beneficētia, vt sæpe diximus. Vnde & Paulus fidè dicit per charitatè operari. Gal.5. Quæ causa est, quòd huius studiū tâ Christus q Apostoli passim commendant. Ioan.15. Matth.25.1. Cor.13. &c. Patet ergo ex his, à fide alienissimos esse, quicunque charitatis affectum exuerunt, de quo in priori epistola Cap.3. & 4. copiosè disputatum est.
units.tr: First, he marks Gaius's own work with a special note, saying: "You act faithfully." The Greek is clearer, πιστῶς ποιεῖς[?], which sounds just as if he had said: "You are doing the work of faith," and that is especially fitting for a man endowed with faith. For beneficence is the proper work of faith, as we have often said. Hence Paul also says that faith works through love (Gal. 5). This is why Christ and the apostles everywhere commend this duty (John 15; Matt. 25; 1 Cor. 13, etc.). It is clear therefore from these things that those are most alien from faith who have cast off the affection of love, concerning which the earlier epistle has been discussed at length in chapters 3 and 4.

units.la: Deinde cum fratres nominauisset, in quos ille beneficentiâ exercebat, ijsdē hospites siue peregrinos coniungit. Vnde colligi potest, nationū discrimen et regionum interualla nō obstare, quò minus fratres sint, qui in Christo Iesu per fidem coniunguntur. Vt enim Christi regnū iuxta prophetarum oracula ad omnes gentes, vsq; ad extremos fines orbis terrarum, extenditur: it in eodem non est Iudæus vel Græcus, non Scytha vel Barbarus. Gal.3. Colos.3. Nec vlla tam arcta excogitari potest fraternitas siue coniunctio, quàm ea est, quam fideles in Christo habent. Inter hos enim vnus & idem pater agnoscitur, vnus & idem spiritus habetur, vna & eadem fides est, vna & eadem expectatur hereditas, imò vnius & eiusdem corporis membra sunt, sub vno capite Iesu Christo, qui saluator & dominus est omnium. Vide Eph.4.1. Cor.12. Arguit ergo illorum errorē locus hic, qui propter nationis discrimen eos contemnunt & odio prosequuntur, quos pro fratribus debebant agnoscere. Rectius Caius hic, qui peregrinorum curam cumprimis habēdam esse putauit. Et Apostolus non temere monet, ne hospitalitatis immemores simus, quæ causa fuit, vt quidam inscij angelos, hominum forma velatos, exceperint. Heb.13. &c.
units.tr: Then, having named the brothers to whom he showed kindness, he joins to them the strangers or pilgrims. From this it can be gathered that differences of nation and intervals of regions do not prevent those who are joined in Christ Jesus through faith from being brothers. For just as the kingdom of Christ, according to the oracles of the prophets, extends to all nations, even to the farthest ends of the earth, so in it there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither Scythian nor barbarian (Gal. 3; Col. 3). Nor can any bond of brotherhood or union be devised so close as that which the faithful have in Christ. For among these one and the same Father is acknowledged, one and the same Spirit is possessed, one and the same faith is held, one and the same inheritance is expected; indeed they are members of one and the same body, under one head, Jesus Christ, who is the Savior and Lord of all (see Eph. 4; 1 Cor. 12). This passage therefore refutes the error of those who, on account of national difference, despise and persecute those whom they ought to acknowledge as brothers. Gaius here acts more rightly, since he judged that the care of strangers was especially to be undertaken. And the apostle does not warn us without reason not to forget hospitality, which was the reason why some, unknowingly, entertained angels veiled in human form (Heb. 13, etc.).

units.la: Postremò, fratrum gratitudo consyderanda venit, qui beneficiorum Cai non obliti fuerunt, sed eadem non sine honorifica eius mentione reliquis prædicarunt. Est hoc non postremum iustitiæ officium, ne in benefactores nostros ingrati reperiamur. Et reuera multis nominibus infelices & miseri sunt, qui cum eo loco sint vt aliorum beneficentia opus habeant, ea tamen animi perversitate laborant, vt accepta beneficia nec agnoscere, nec cum eorum laude prædicare norunt, à quibus ea accepere. Est autem hoc hominum genus hodie passim obuiû, & optimi ferè haberi debent, qui beneficiorum omnino obliuiscuntur, cum maxima eorum multitudo sit, qui ea vel malitiosè dissimulant, vel fratres optimè de se meritos calumnijs virulentis traducunt. Quorum tamen non tanta haberi debet ratio, vt propter eos Christianæ charitatis officia pij intermittant. Habent enim remuneratorē fidelissimū, Christū Iesum, qui in suas rationes ascribit, quicquid in suos suo nomine confertur: & non raro in hac vita agentibus gratiam magnam retribuit.
units.tr: Lastly, there comes into consideration the gratitude of the brothers, who did not forget the kindnesses of Gaius, but proclaimed them to the others, not without an honorable mention of him. This is no small duty of justice, that we not be found ungrateful toward our benefactors. And indeed they are wretched and miserable in many ways, who, though they are in such a position that they need the beneficence of others, nevertheless labor under such perversity of mind that they neither acknowledge the benefits they have received, nor know how to proclaim them with praise of those from whom they received them. This kind of person is commonly met with today, and those should be regarded as the best who entirely forget benefits; for the greater number are those who either maliciously conceal them, or with virulent slanders traduce brothers who have deserved very well of them. Yet the pious ought not to give so much regard to such people that they should therefore discontinue the duties of Christian love. For they have a most faithful rewarder, Christ Jesus, who credits to his own account whatever is bestowed on his people in his name, and not infrequently repays great grace to those who act in this life.

units.la: Facit ad huius promissionis confirmationem, quod in præsenti de præmio dicitur quod ex hospitalitate sua Caius reportauerit. Prædicarunt hanc olim fratres in conspectu ecclesiæ. Et hodie per omnem Christi ecclesiam magna omnium piorum approbatione prædicari solet. At quæ homini maior gloria poterat contingere? Expende autem hic quàm insanis studijs mundus hic occupetur, dum gloriam aliquam assequatur, & nominis sui memoriâ ad posteros transmittat? Eius gratia diurnos nocturnosq; labores multi sustinent. Propter hanc bellis omnia turbantur. Huius cupidine inflammato vnus Pellæo iuueni non sufficit orbis. Hęc barbara pyramidum miracula, & tot insana ædificia protulit. Eadem inter amicissimos implacabiles inimicitias excitat. At quanto minori labore & sumptu immortalem gloriam Caius hic noster sibi comparauit? O felices nos, si eadem via ad veram & immortalé gloriam aspiraremus. Faciet verò huc non parum, si quæ dominus iustis & beneficis pollicetur cõsyderemus diligenter. De tali enim spiritus sanctus pronunciat: Spargit ac dat pauperibus. Iustitia eius stabit in æternum, & cornu eius altum erit cum gloria. Psal.112. Et rursum: Frange esurienti panem tuum: afflictos, extorres, egenos domum tuam deducito. Si videris nudum, vestito eum, & à carne tua ne abscondas te. Tunc erūpet velut aurora lux tua, &c. Ifa. 58. Sed ad alterum huius loci partem transfire tempus est.
units.tr: What is said in the present passage about the reward that Gaius obtained from his hospitality serves to confirm this promise. The brothers proclaimed it once in the sight of the Church, and today it is customarily proclaimed throughout the whole Church of Christ with the great approval of all the godly. But what greater glory could fall to a man? Consider here, however, with what mad pursuits this world is occupied, while it seeks some glory and transmits the memory of its name to posterity. For the sake of this, many endure labors by day and by night. For this, all things are thrown into confusion by wars. Inflamed with this desire, one young man of Pella did not find the world sufficient (Alexander). This produced the barbarous wonders of the pyramids and so many mad buildings. The same thing stirs up implacable enmities even among the closest friends. But with how much less labor and expense has this Gaius of ours acquired for himself immortal glory! O happy are we, if we were to aspire by the same road to true and immortal glory! Indeed it will contribute no little if we diligently consider what the Lord promises to the just and the beneficent. For the Holy Spirit declares of such a man: "He has scattered abroad and given to the poor; his righteousness shall endure forever, and his horn shall be exalted with glory" (Ps. 112). And again: "Break your bread to the hungry; bring the afflicted and the homeless into your house; when you see the naked, clothe him, and do not hide yourself from your own flesh. Then your light shall break forth like the dawn, etc." (Isa. 58). But it is time to pass to the other part of this passage.

units.la: I I. Quos bene ages, si deduxeris digne Deo. Pro eius enim nomine egressi sunt, &c.
