Hortatur Caium Apostolus, ut quod sancte coepit, pergat facere, & imprimis eos commendat, qui & hanc epistolam ferebant, & beneficentiae ipsius praecones fuerant. Propositio est: Debes illos deducere ut dignum est, & qualiter deduci debent, qui Dei ministri sunt. At deducendi verbo omne, quod hospitibus impendi potest, officium comprehendit, quod varium est pro personarum, temporis & loci ratione. Ut vero facilius persuadeat, argumentis utitur, quę obiter adduxisse sufficiebat, cum sponte officium faceret. Primum ab honesto sumitur, quia Dei cultores decet, ut fratres sibi commendatos habeant. Deinde ab ipsorum persona & utili hortatur. Propter Dei nomen profectione hac susceperunt, non errones sunt & curiosi rerum alienarum inspectores. Quare sibi factum iudicabit Christus, quicquid in illos collatum fuerit. Matth. 10. Ioan. 13. Tertió. Quia à gentibus nihil acceperunt, ne quam remoram euangelio currenti inijceret, eò magis tibi commendati esse debebunt. Omnium verò grauissima ratio est, quòd addit: Sic cooperatores sumus veritati, cuius prouehendæ studium in Christianis quàm maximè flagrare conuenit. Et hæc vera est diuitiarum huius seculi commendatio, quæ & verum earundē usum docet: ut nimirū in veritatis doctrina insumantur. Quod qui faciunt, piorum ministrorum cooperarij fiūt, & idem olim cum illis præmiū recipient.
units.tr: II. Whom you will do well to send on their way in a manner worthy of God, for they went out for the sake of his name, etc. The apostle exhorts Gaius to continue doing what he has begun in a holy way, and especially commends those who both carried this letter and had been heralds of his beneficence. The proposition is: you ought to send them on their way as is fitting, and in the manner in which those who are ministers of God ought to be sent on their way. Now the word "send on their way" comprehends every duty that can be offered to guests, which varies according to the circumstances of persons, time and place. But so that he may persuade more easily, he uses arguments, which it would have been enough to have touched upon in passing, since he was performing the duty willingly. The first is taken from what is honorable: it becomes those who worship God to have the brothers commended to them. Second, he exhorts them from their own person and advantage: they undertook this journey for the sake of God's name; they are not vagabonds and busybodies inspecting other people's affairs. Therefore Christ will judge whatever has been bestowed on them as done to himself (Matt. 10; John 13). Third, since they received nothing from the Gentiles, so that nothing might put a hindrance in the way of the running gospel, they ought to be all the more commended to you. But the weightiest reason of all is what he adds: "So we are fellow-workers with the truth," and the zeal for advancing this truth ought especially to burn among Christians. And this is the true commendation of the riches of this age, which also teaches their true use: namely, that they be spent on the teaching of the truth. Those who do this become fellow-workers with the godly ministers, and will in time receive the same reward with them.

units.la: Venit hic obseruandum, quibus studijs ac rationibus euangelium in primitiua ecclesia propagatū fit, & ut gratis prædicarint Apostoli. Non enim ideo à stipendijs debitis abstinuerunt, quòd ministrum ea recipere nefas sit: sed quia apud multos non admissi fuissent aliquid petentes, aliun de sumpserunt quæ victui ipsorum erant necessaria. Nec defuerunt viri pij & sancti, qui opes suas in eum usum erogabant, è quorum numero Caium fuisse cernimus. Ita Paulus Corinthijs gratis prædicasse legitur, sed ab alijs accepto stipendio, sicuti ipse fatetur. Vide 2. Cor. 11. & 12. Phil. 4. Quia ergo & Apostoli suam operam & opulentiores suas fortunas ad verbi Dei propagationem liberaliter conferebant, diuinæ gratiæ incrementum deesse non potuit. Cum hoc studio si nostri seculi mores conferas, immanis ingratitudo conspicietur. Non quicquam ab aliquo, siue paupere siue diuite, exigitur, cū ubiq; ferè locorum iam olim principū regumq; liberalitate ecclesijs & verbi ministerio prospectum fit. Tanta tamen tamq; pestilens est hominum cæcitas, ut pauci inueniantur, qui ab alijs collata ministris non inuideant. Ut interim de illis nihil dicamus, qui ecclesiarum bona vel dolosè suffurantur, vel etiam palàm & aperta vi surripiunt. Quid ergo miramur, docendi studio tam parum profici? Emendemur potius, & in commune conferamus vires & consilia nostra ad verbi Dei propagationem, & præmium immortale cum Christo Iesu reportabimus, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: It is worth noting here by what methods and means the gospel was spread in the primitive Church, and that the Apostles preached without payment. They did not hold back from the stipends due to them because it would be wrong for a minister to receive them; rather, because many would not admit them when they asked for something, they obtained from elsewhere what was necessary for their own sustenance. Nor were there lacking pious and holy men who spent their resources on this purpose, and we see that Gaius was one of them. So Paul is read to have preached gratis to the Corinthians, but to have received a stipend from others, as he himself confesses. See 2 Cor. 11 and 12; Phil. 4. Since, therefore, both the Apostles freely contributed their labour and their more ample means to the propagation of the Word of God, the increase of divine grace could not be lacking. If you compare the customs of our own age with this zeal, a monstrous ingratitude will be seen. Nothing is demanded from anyone, whether poor or rich, although almost everywhere in the lands rulers and kings have long since provided for the churches and the ministry of the Word by their generosity. Yet such is the blindness of men, so deadly, that few are found who do not begrudge the goods gathered for the ministers by others. To say nothing for now of those who either craftily steal the goods of the churches or openly seize them by violence. Why, then, do we wonder that so little progress is made in the zeal for teaching? Let us rather amend ourselves, and contribute our strength and counsel in common to the propagation of the Word of God, and we shall win an immortal reward with Christ Jesus, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA III.
units.tr: HOMILIA III.

units.la: Scripsi ecclesiæ, sed qui inter eos primatū affectat, Diotrephes non recipit nos. Propterea si uenero, commemorabo facta illius, quæ facit, verbis malitiosis garriens in nos. Nec his cōtentus, non solum fratres ipse non recipit, uerumetiam uolentes recipere prohibet, & ex ecclesia eicit.
units.tr: I wrote to the church, but Diotrephes, who desires the first place among them, does not receive us. Therefore, if I come, I will call to mind his deeds, which he does, prattling against us with malicious words. And not content with this, he not only does not receive the brethren himself, but also forbids those who wish to receive them and casts them out of the church.

units.la: QUamuis Christianæ charitatis officia erga omnes homines exerceri debeant, imprimis tamen nobis commendati esse debent, qui propter Christi nomen & verbum pelluntur. Ut enim in illis ipse Christus affligitur: ita quod illis bene fit, Christus sibi factum esse æstimat. Non temere ergo Ioānes Caij hospitalitatem laudat, & illius exemplum publicè omnibus imitandum proponit. Cæterum ut Deus passim eos habet, qui pijs nominis sui cultoribus benefaciunt: ita satanæ etiam ubiq; locorum sua organa sunt, per quæ ijsdem negotium faciat & noceat. Eius rei exemplū hoc loco in Diotrephe proponitur, cuius diligens consyderatio non parū prodesse poterit.
units.tr: Although the duties of Christian love ought to be exercised toward all men, they ought nevertheless to be especially commended to us, those who are persecuted for the name and the word of Christ. For just as Christ himself is afflicted in them, so Christ reckons whatever good is done to them as done to himself. It is not without reason, then, that John praises the hospitality of Gaius and sets his example publicly before everyone to imitate. Yet just as God everywhere has those who do good to the godly worshippers of his name, so Satan too has his instruments everywhere, through which he carries on his business with these same people and does them harm. An example of this is set forth in this place in Diotrephes, whose careful consideration may be of no small benefit.

units.la: Scripsi ecclesiæ, &c. Quæ illa ecclesia fuerit, non exprimitur. Sed Corinthiacam fuisse verisimile est, propter Caium, quem Corinthi habitauisse constat, nisi is forte inde pulsus alió migraverit: quod non videtur credibile, cum fortunis adhuc integris fuerit, ut fratribus tam liberaliter posset succurrere. Sed utut ista se habeant, de præsenti causa Ioannes se ecclesiæ scripsisse dicit, & epistolæ argumentum fuisse videtur, quòd Caium ob liberalitatem in fratres commendauit, reliquos ad eius imitationem exhortatus est, & æmulos ipsius tamq; sancti studij hostes increpuit. Quòd vero ea epistola nusquam extat, mirum non est. Noluit enim nos spiritus sanctus nimijs libris grauare, sed paucis ijsq; sufficientibus apostolicæ doctrinæ consensum proponere, quò facilior esset omnium, quæ ad salutis negotium spectant, inuestigatio. Alioqui credibile est, & Paulum plures adhuc, quàm extent, epistolas scripsisse, & Petrum cum alijs in scribendi officio non fuisse tam negligentem, vt binis tantum literis fideles docere & consolari voluerit. At quia paucula illa salutis rationem absolutè comprehendunt, non est quòd amissa scrutemur: imò Dei agnoscamus erga nos paternam curam, qua cauere voluit, ne pluribus impliciti, circa salutem incertiores redderemur.
units.tr: I wrote to the church, etc. What that church was is not stated. But it is likely that it was the Corinthian church, on account of Gaius, who is known to have lived at Corinth, unless perhaps he was driven out from there and migrated elsewhere; this does not seem credible, since he was still in possession of his resources, so that he could help the brethren so generously. But however these things stand, John says that he wrote to the church about the present matter, and the subject of the letter seems to have been that he commended Gaius for his generosity toward the brethren, exhorted the rest to imitate him, and rebuked those who envied him and were enemies of such holy zeal. That this letter nowhere survives is no cause for wonder. For the Holy Spirit did not wish to burden us with too many books, but to set forth the agreement of apostolic doctrine in a few writings, which are sufficient, so that the investigation of all those things which pertain to the business of salvation might be easier. Otherwise it is credible that Paul wrote even more letters than exist, and that Peter, with the others, was not so negligent in the duty of writing as to want to teach and console the faithful with only two letters. But since those few letters comprehend the way of salvation completely, there is no reason for us to search after what has been lost; rather we should acknowledge God's fatherly care for us, by which he willed to take care that we, entangled in many writings, should not become more uncertain about our salvation.

units.la: Interim non sine spiritus instinctu factum putabimus, quòd de præsenti causa toti ecclesiæ scripsit Apostolus. Vt enim ex eo apostolici pectoris industriam agnoscere licet, ita docemur, non sufficere, vt vnus & alter in ecclesia officium faciant, sed vt illorum exemplo plures alij proficiant etiam atq; etiā curandum est. Quem scopum si præfixum sibi habeant ministri, sentient, se officio suo nunquam ita defungi posse, quin plura adhuc ipsis agenda restent.
units.tr: Meanwhile we shall think it done not without the prompting of the Spirit that the Apostle wrote to the whole church about the present matter. For just as from this one may recognise the diligence of the apostolic heart, so we are taught that it is not enough for one or two in the church to perform the duty, but that, by their example, many others should also be made to progress, and this must be attended to again and again. If ministers have this goal set before them, they will feel that they can never so discharge their office that much more does not remain for them to do.

units.la: Est autem cumprimis obseruatione dignum, quod ne Ioanni quidem aduersarius defuit, eti-am ex eorū numero, qui & Christiani & inter hos primi vel antesignani haberi volebant. At quid obsecro non habuit Ioannes, quod illi authoritatem atq; beneuolentiam conciliare poterat? Poterat sanè vnum hoc pijs omnibus sufficere, quod illum Christus singulari amore fuerat prosecutus. Tamè inuenti sunt inter Christiani nominis professores, qui se illi auderet opponere. Est hæc perpetua ecclesiæ sors, vt ij se ministris maximè opponant, quorum erat illorum studijs & laboribus succurrere. Sensit hoc mali Moses, vt Num.16.cap.legitur. Extant & apud prophetas exempla, quæ huc faciunt, vt 3.Reg.22.Ierem.28. Amos 7.&c. Et in Christo ab Iuda discipulo & quæstore prodito, prælusum fuit, quid fidelibus Christi seruis in infelici hoc mundo expectandum sit. Neminem igitur hodie falsorum fratrum insidiæ & subdolæ machinationes offendant. Habemus enim vindicem dominum, cui aliquando graves pœnas exoluent. Quòd si vero domesticis pericu-la instant (quod & Christus monuit, Matth.10.) quid ex mūdo sperabimus, qui totus in malo cō- stitutus est? 1.Ioan.5.Ioan.16. Cæterū videamus, quis & qualis Diotrephes ille fuerit, Caij & Ioan. aduersarius, vt ex hoc omnes iudicemus, q. apostolorū doctrinæ & monitis sese opponere audent.
units.tr: It is, moreover, especially worthy of notice that John did not lack an adversary, even from the number of those who wished to be considered both Christians and, among these, the first or foremost. But what, I beg you, did John lack that could win him authority and goodwill? Surely this alone might have sufficed for all the godly, that Christ had followed him with singular love. Yet there have been found among those who professed the Christian name some who dared to oppose him. This is the perpetual lot of the Church: that those most opposed to the ministers are those whose duty it was to help their studies and labours. Moses felt this evil, as is read in Numbers chapter 16. There are also examples among the prophets which pertain to this: 3 Kings 22; Jeremiah 28; Amos 7, etc. And in Christ, Judas, the disciple and treasurer who betrayed him, was a foreshadowing of what is to be expected by the faithful servants of Christ in this unhappy world. Let no one, therefore, be offended today by the snares and crafty machinations of false brethren. For we have a Lord who avenges, and they will at some time pay heavy penalties. But if dangers threaten from within the household (as Christ also warned, Matthew 10), what shall we hope for from the world, which is wholly set in evil? 1 John 5; John 16. But let us look at what sort of man that Diotrephes was, and what kind, the adversary of Gaius and John, so that from this we may all judge how they dare to set themselves against the doctrine and admonitions of the apostles.

units.la: Principio illum φιλοπρωτευων,id est, primatū affectare vel ambire dicit. Sic vero omnis mali son-tem siue radicem indicat, Ambitionem nimirum, vel immoderatum vanæ gloriæ studium. Qui-cunq; enim hoc flagrant, neminem vel æqualem sibi, nedum superiorem ferre possunt. Et vt reliquis præstantiores habeantur, noua dogmata proferunt, schisma faciunt, omnibusq; se opponūt acriter, quoscunq; virtutibus insignes viderint. Non temere ergo Christus ab Apostolis humilitatis studium tantopere requirit, & eos regni sui capaces fore negat, qui illud sectari noluerint. Vide Matth.18.&20.Ioan.13. Et sanè, si nostra tempora inspiciamus, nullos acerbiores renascentis euangelij hostes inuenire licebit, quàm qui hodie quoq; in ecclesia primatum ambiunt, sibiq; solis omnem in hac potestatem vendicant.
units.tr: In the first place, he calls him philoprōteuōn, that is, one who desires or ambitiously seeks the first place. Thus he indicates the source or root of every evil, namely ambition, or an immoderate zeal for empty glory. For those who burn with this cannot endure anyone even equal to themselves, much less superior. And so that they may be considered more outstanding than the rest, they put forward new doctrines, make schisms, and oppose themselves fiercely to all whom they see distinguished by virtues. It is not without reason, then, that Christ so earnestly requires the pursuit of humility from his Apostles, and denies that those who refuse to pursue it will be fit for his kingdom. See Matthew 18 and 20; John 13. And indeed, if we look at our own times, it will be possible to find no bitterer enemies of the renewed gospel than those who today too seek the primacy in the Church, and claim for themselves alone all the power in it.

units.la: Deinde calumniandi studium Diotrephi tribuit, qui proprius ferè ambitionis fructus est. Quia enim qui tales sunt, emergere non possunt, nisi se superiores deprimant, vbi id nullis honestis rationibus fieri potest, ad calumnias & conuitia cōuerti solent. Ita lupos olim canibus hoc ob iecisse apologus refert, quòd latratu suo improbo inimicitiarum contra oues causam præberent. Et hodie, quicunq; cum veritatis oppressione ad ecclesiarum summam gubernationem enituntur, vel in male occupato primatus fastigio permanere cupiunt, nihil non conuitiorum comminiscun- tur, quibus fideles veritatis ministros omnibus inuisos faciant.
units.tr: Next, Diotrephes shows a zeal for slander, which is almost the peculiar fruit of ambition. For since such people cannot rise up unless they press down their superiors, and when this cannot be done by any honest means, they are wont to turn to calumnies and reproaches. So the fable tells that the wolves once threw this at the dogs, that by their wicked barking they gave cause for enmity against the sheep. And today, whoever strives for the supreme government of the churches by the oppression of the truth, or desires to remain in the primacy wrongly seized, devises every kind of reproach by which they may make the faithful ministers of the truth hateful to all.

units.la: Accedit his vltimo loco, quòd non contentus propria inhumanitate, aliorum quoq; pijs co-natibus obstitit, & per tyrannidem excommunicare ausus est, qui ipsi minus obediebant. Eò demē-tiæ euadit cæca ambitio, vt tandē omnibus intolerabilis fiat. Nisi enim tales pestes circa initia opprimantur, ijs viribus sese armât, vt quosuis facilè opprimere possint, qui se ipsis opponunt. Exempla hodie nimis (proh dolor) multa passim extant. Qui enim ecclesiæ proceres & bonorum ecclesiæ legitimi administratores videri volunt, non contenti, quòd nec ipsi docent sibi comissum gregem, nec pauperibus subueniunt, insuper si quis docere conetur, & opum ecclesiæ vsum verum commonstret, eum & minis prohibent, & excommunicationis fulmine ecclesia eijciunt, imò irreconciliabili odio ad necem vsque persequuntur.
units.tr: Added to these, last of all, is that, not content with his own inhumanity, he also obstructed the pious endeavours of others, and dared through tyranny to excommunicate those who were less obedient to him. Blind ambition descends to such madness that at last it becomes intolerable to all. For unless such pests are suppressed at the beginning, they arm themselves with such strength that they can easily overwhelm whoever opposes them. Today there are, alas, many examples everywhere. For those who wish to be seen as the leaders of the church and the lawful administrators of its goods, not content that they neither teach the flock committed to them nor help the poor, moreover, if anyone tries to teach and shows the true use of the church's resources, they forbid him with threats and cast him out of the church with the thunderbolt of excommunication, indeed they pursue him even to death with irreconcilable hatred.

units.la: Quid verò contra talem tantumq; hostem gessit Apostolus? Num siluit? Num patientia hic vtendum esse putauit? Nequaquam. Sed in præsenti apud Caium, singularem amicum & fratrem de illius improbitate conqueritur. Simul verò minatur, quòd coràm vniuersa ecclesia eius malitiam arguere & accusare velit. Hoc ergo pastoris fidi officium est, vt ecclesiæ pestes palàm arguat, & suq;
units.tr: But what did the Apostle do against so great and so powerful an enemy? Did he keep silent? Did he think that patience should be used here? By no means. But in the present letter, to Gaius, his singular friend and brother, he complains of the other's wickedness. At the same time he threatens that he wishes to argue against and accuse that malice openly before the whole church. This, therefore, is the duty of a faithful pastor: to expose the church's pests openly, and

units.la: fidei commissos ab illis cauere doceat. Hoc olim prophetas fecisse legimus, vt videre est Isa.56. Ie-rem.23. Ezech.34. &c. In eodem officio acerrimè & Christus versatus est, perfectissimū alioqui (vt & aliarum virtutum) mansuetudinis exemplum. Matth.15. & 23. Ioan.2. & 10. &c. Et Apostoli non modò sui seculi impostores arguendos putarunt, verumetiā de venturis magna diligentia nos mo-nuerunt, vt illorum scripta passim testantur. Frustra ergo hodie à verbi ministris patientia exigi-tur, quando non vnus Diotrephes ecclesiam turbat. Nisi enim illorum conatibus resistatur, breui omnem ecclesiae doctrinam corruere cernemus. Faueamus ergo fidelium ministrorum laboribus quibus tales oppugnant, & in hoc simus omnes, vt simplicē doctrinae euangelicae regulā secuti in coelis viuamus cū Iesu Christo, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternū. Amen.
units.tr: to teach those committed to him to beware of them. We read that the prophets did this of old, as may be seen in Isaiah 56, Jeremiah 23, Ezekiel 34, etc. In the same office Christ too was most fiercely engaged, otherwise a most perfect example of gentleness (as of the other virtues). Matthew 15 and 23; John 2 and 10, etc. And the Apostles thought that not only the impostors of their own age should be exposed, but also with great diligence they warned us about those to come, as their writings everywhere attest. It is vain, therefore, to demand patience today from the ministers of the Word, when it is not one Diotrephes alone who disturbs the church. For unless resistance is offered to their attempts, we shall soon see the whole doctrine of the church collapse. Let us therefore favour the labours of the faithful ministers by which they assail such men, and let us all be intent on this: that, following the simple rule of evangelical doctrine, we may live in heaven with Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA IIII.
units.tr: HOMILIA IIII.

units.la: Dilecte, ne æmuleris quod malum est, sed quod bonū est. Qui bene facit, ex Deo est: qui autem male facit, non vidit Deum. Demetrio testimonium redditum est ab omnibus, & ab ipsa veritate: sed & nos testimonium perhibemus, & scitis testimonium nostrum verum esse. Multa habebam, quae scriberem: sed nolo per atramentum & calamum scribere tibi. Spero autem me protinus visurum te, & praesentes coram loquemur. Pax tibi. Salutant te amici. Saluta amicos nominatim.
units.tr: Beloved, do not emulate what is evil, but what is good. He who does good is of God; but he who does evil has not seen God. Demetrius has testimony given him by all, and by the truth itself; and we also bear witness, and you know that our testimony is true. I had many things to write to you, but I do not wish to write to you with ink and pen. I hope, however, to see you shortly, and we shall speak face to face. Peace be with you. The friends greet you. Greet the friends by name.

units.la: DIui [?] Ioannis institutum est, & Caij erga fratres exules beneficentiam commendare, & illius exemplum omnibus pijs imitandum proponere. Id vt maiori cum fructu faciat, duo exempla sibi inuicem opponit. Vt enim Caium magnificè laudat: ita Diotrephis inhumanitatem & insolentiam reprehendit, vt constet, perpetuam infamiam eos manere, qui immiti & superbo animo fratres contemnunt & negligunt. Caeterum, quia impij & praefracti saepe diuturnis successibus vtuntur, quae res pios plurimum offendit, Apostolus priusquam epistolae finem imponat, huic etiam offendiculo medetur.
units.tr: The purpose of the divine John is to commend Gaius's kindness toward the brethren who are exiles, and to set his example before all the godly for imitation. So that he may do this with greater profit, he sets two examples over against each other. For as he praises Gaius magnificently, so he rebukes the inhumanity and insolence of Diotrephes, so that it is clear that those who scorn and neglect the brethren with a harsh and proud spirit remain in perpetual infamy. Moreover, because the wicked and obstinate often enjoy lasting success, a thing that greatly offends the godly, the Apostle, before he brings the letter to a close, also remedies this stumbling block.

units.la: I. Dilecte, ne æmuleris quod malum est, sed quod bonum est. Qui bene facit, ex Deo est, &c. Communi & generali praecepto Caium instruit, & praecepti sui rationem reddit grauem admodum. Praeceptum est, Ne æmuleris malum, sed bonum. Sic vero dicere videtur: Scio molestum esse pijs, si quando impios feliciter agere & impunè quiduis tentare videant. Ea enim res plurimos vexauit, quorum exempla in scripturis quoq; proponuntur, vt Psal.73. Ierem.12. Malach.3. &c. At Christi cultorem ea aemulatio minimè decet, quem felicitas & haereditas in coelis aeterna manet, cū impio rū fortuna planè vitrea fit & incerta, vt Dauides egregiè docuit, Psal.37. Prodest vero praeceptum hoc diligenter expendisse, quando nostro seculo plurimi ad hunc lapidem offendunt.
units.tr: I. Beloved, do not emulate what is evil, but what is good. He who does good is of God, etc. He instructs Gaius with a common and general precept, and gives a very weighty reason for his precept. The precept is: Do not emulate evil, but good. Yet he seems to say this: I know it is troublesome to the godly when they see the wicked prospering and able to attempt whatever they like with impunity. For this has troubled many, whose examples are also set forth in the Scriptures, as in Psalm 73, Jeremiah 12, Malachi 3, etc. But emulation of this kind is by no means fitting for a worshipper of Christ, whom happiness and an eternal inheritance in heaven await, whereas the fortune of the wicked is plainly fragile and uncertain, as David taught excellently in Psalm 37. Indeed, it is useful to have weighed this precept carefully, since in our age very many stumble at this stone.

units.la: Principiò, bonum aemulari iubet, non malum. Bonus est solus Deus, vt Christus in euangelio monuit. Matth.19. Hinc vero bonum dicitur, quod Dei ingenio atq; voluntati conuenit: malum autem, quodcunq; ab hac discrepat. Est haec perpetua & infallibilis boni & mali discernendi regula, quam nisi obseruemus, bonum videbitur, quod reuera malum atque noxium est, & è contra malum dicemus, quod reipsa bonum est. Huc Dei praeceptū referri debet, quo per Mosem vetat, ne faciamus quod nobis bonum videtur, sed quod ipse fieri iussit. Num.15.
units.tr: First, he bids us emulate what is good, not what is evil. God alone is good, as Christ admonished in the Gospel, Matthew 19. Now a thing is called good when it agrees with the nature and will of God; but evil is whatever differs from this. This is the perpetual and infallible rule for distinguishing good and evil, and unless we observe it, we shall see as good what is in truth evil and harmful, and on the contrary we shall call evil what is in fact good. To this should be referred the precept of God, by which through Moses he forbids us to do what seems good to us, but what he himself has commanded us to do. Numbers 15.

units.la: Deinde aemulandi verbo vsus est, quo ardens flagransq; animi studium denotatur. Nec enim sufficit, bonum nouisse, nisi bene agendi studio incensi in ijs toti occupemur, quae Deo pro bonis probari nouimus. Tales vero efficit huius aemulationis studium, vt nec malum vel specie mali patienter ferre, nec bene agendo satiari possimus. Vno igitur verbo tepidos illos arguit Ioannes, qui cum euangelicae doctrinae studium & fidem in Christum profiteantur, patienter tamen ferre possunt quae ipsius gloriae derogant. Faciunt hoc hodie multi ex ministrorum numero, qui vt se omnibus commodos praebeant, grauissima quoq; vitia magnatum vel ignaui dissimulant, vel perfidi nimis etiam excusant.
units.tr: Next, he has used the word "emulate," by which an ardent and burning zeal of the mind is denoted. For it is not enough to know what is good, unless we, kindled with the desire of acting well, are wholly occupied in those things which we know to be approved by God as good. The zeal of this emulation makes us such that we can neither bear evil patiently, even in the appearance of evil, nor be satisfied with doing good. Therefore John rebukes with one word those lukewarm men who, while they profess zeal for the evangelical doctrine and faith in Christ, can nevertheless patiently bear the things that detract from his glory. Many of the number of ministers do this today: in order to show themselves agreeable to all, they either overlook, through laziness, or excuse, even too much, through treachery, the most grievous vices of the great.

units.la: Sed & rationem huius praecepti videre oportet, quae bimembris est, & ex Dei natura sumitur. Qui Dei ingenium referunt, ex Deo nati sunt. Dei vero ingenium est, bonum, sanctum & immaculatum esse. Quisquis ergo bonus & sanctus esse studuerit, ex Deo natus esse iure cēsebitur. E contra, qui malè agendo delectantur, à Dei ingenio alienissimi sunt, & proinde Deum viderū nunquam. Tanta est enim illius summi boni præstantia, vt toti in eius amorem rapiantur, quicūq; eius cognitionem habent aliquam. Docet locus hic, quid de palàm flagitiosis iudicemus, qui (vt Solomon ait) gaudent cum malè fecerunt, & cum Idumæo Doeg in malitia gloriantur. Volunt & ipsi ex Deo nati videri, sed reuera ex diabolo sunt, siquidem Apostolum, imò ipsum Christum eadem dicentem audire velimus. Ioan. 8.
units.tr: But we must also see the reason for this precept, which has two parts and is drawn from the nature of God. Those who reproduce the nature of God are born of God. Now the nature of God is to be good, holy and spotless. Whoever therefore has striven to be good and holy will rightly be judged to be born of God. On the contrary, those who delight in acting wickedly are most alien from the nature of God, and therefore have never seen God. For so great is the excellence of that highest good that all who have any knowledge of him are drawn wholly into love of him. This passage teaches what we should judge concerning those who openly live in shameful vice, who (as Solomon says) rejoice when they have done evil, and boast in malice with Doeg the Edomite. They wish also to seem born of God, but in truth they are of the devil, since, if we wish to hear the Apostle, or rather Christ himself, saying the same thing, John 8.

units.la: II. Demetrio testimonium redditum est ab omnibus, &c. Videtur Demetrij exemplum Diotre-phi opponere Apostolus, vt eius consyderatione Caius animatus ab incoeptis minus deficiat. Plurimum enim in rebus arduis momenti habet, si non solos nos esse intelligamus, quorum humeris omne onus & periculum incubat. Ostendit ergo Ioannes, Caio nō soli hanc impositam esse prouinciam, nec propter Diotrephen esse desperandum, cum Demetrium simili studio flagrantem excitarit bonus Dei spiritus, qui tantum iam profecerit, vt nemo non ipsius fidei & pietati testimonium ferat.
units.tr: II. Demetrius has testimony given him by all, etc. The Apostle seems to set the example of Demetrius over against Diotrephes, so that Gaius, encouraged by considering it, may be less inclined to give up what he has begun. For it carries great weight in difficult affairs if we understand that we are not alone, upon whose shoulders every burden and danger lies. John therefore shows that this task has not been laid on Gaius alone, nor should he despair on account of Diotrephes, since the good Spirit of God has roused Demetrius, burning with a similar zeal, who has already advanced so far that nobody fails to bear witness to his faith and piety.

units.la: Sunt in his duo præcipuè obseruanda. Primum quidem, quòd tanta diligentia de Demetrij pietate testimonium fert Ioannes. Suo enim exemplo docet, ne in testimonijs ferendis leuiores simus, & vt fratrum innocentiam & famam omni studio tueamur. Deinde verò, quòd Deus passim suos habet, quos hostium suorum improbitati opponat. Et hi quidem plerunque maiori in numero sunt, quàm quisquam sperare ausit. Ita Caio Demetrius accedit. Et Elias cū se solum superesse putaret ex cultorum Dei grege, audit adhuc septem millia relicta esse eorum, qui genua sua coram Baal nunquam flexerint. Debet hoc nos consolari in rebus arduis & persecutionum fluctibus. Deus etenim causæ suæ semper patronos dabit & aduocatos, & si nos officium fecerimus, laborum etiam & periculorum socios excitabit. Sic Iosepho Arimathæensi socius accedit Nicodemus, cum ille Christi corpus ad sepulturæ honorem sibi dari perijsset. Et quàdo maximè instant pericula, ex occultis discipulis quotidie prodeunt, qui prius à fide alieni videbantur. Errant ergo turpissimè, qui vt suam ignauiam excusent, alios omnes accusant, quasi solis ipsis Dei gloria cordi sit, quam tamen perfidè negligunt, & ab impijs obrui patiuntur.
units.tr: Two things are to be especially observed here. The first is that John bears witness to the piety of Demetrius with such great care. By his own example he teaches us not to be too hasty in bearing witness, and to guard the innocence and good name of the brethren with every effort. The second is that God everywhere has his own people, whom he sets against the wickedness of his enemies. And these are for the most part in greater numbers than anyone dares to hope. So Demetrius joins Gaius. And when Elijah thought that he alone was left of the flock of God's worshippers, he hears that seven thousand remain who have never bowed their knees before Baal. This ought to console us in difficult matters and in the waves of persecutions. For God will always give patrons and advocates to his cause, and if we do our duty, he will also raise up companions in labours and dangers. So Nicodemus joins Joseph of Arimathea, when the latter had been at a loss how to obtain the body of Christ for burial honour. And when dangers press hardest, daily there come forth from among the secret disciples those who previously seemed alien to the faith. They therefore err most shamefully who, to excuse their own sloth, accuse all others, as if only they themselves cared for the glory of God, which yet they faithlessly neglect, and allow to be overwhelmed by the wicked.

units.la: III. Multa habebam quæ scriberem, &c. Est hæc epistolæ Conclusio, qua & breuitatem excusat, & salutationes pro more subiungit. Quia verò eadem dicit, quæ in præcedentis fine dixerat, inde petantur, quæ huic loco explicando seruiunt. Noluit Apostolus calamo & atramēto, sed Caij animo rem hanc omnem commendare. Studeamus & nos, vt Christianæ charitatis & beneficentiæ præcepta non calamo tantum in chartis descripta, sed Dei digito animis nostris impressa habeamus. Sic enim fiet, vt tota vita Christum loquatur, nosque eius curriculum emensi, cœlorum gaudijs fruamur. Domino & saluatori nostro Iesu Christo debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: III. I had many things which I would write, etc. This is the conclusion of the letter, by which he both excuses its brevity and adds greetings according to custom. But since he says the same things that he had said at the end of the previous one, let us seek from there what serves to explain this passage. The Apostle did not wish to commend this whole matter with pen and ink, but to Gaius's mind. Let us also strive that the precepts of Christian charity and beneficence be held not only described on paper with a pen, but impressed on our hearts by the finger of God. For thus it will come about that our whole life speaks Christ, and that, having run his course, we enjoy the joys of heaven. To our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: FINIS
units.tr: FINIS

units.la: CHRISTIANO LECTORI.
units.tr: TO THE CHRISTIAN READER.

units.la: QUONIAM Apostolos in scriptis suis hoc unum prae cæteris quaesivisse constat, ut & Christi Jesu doctrinam ecclesiis simplicem ac incorruptam traderent, & fidelibus in ea constanter perseverandi authores essent: non alienum ab instituto nostro putavi, si vetustissimorum patrum traditiones sive sententias de fide Christiana, quas illi apostolicas esse crediderunt, nostris in Joannis epistolas Homiliis subiicerem. Ex iis enim videre licebit, quanta apud hos fuerit olim Apostolicae doctrinae authoritas, & quid illis responderi debeat, qui sub plausibili patrum nomine novos fidei articulos obtrudunt, & salutis rationem monstrant, quam & Apostolos & prophetas ignoravisse, satis constat. Tu vero, Christiane Lector, omnibus his ita fruere, ut agnitam veritatem retinere, & in salutis via per Apostolos tradita constanter ingredi pergas. Vale.
units.tr: Since the Apostles, as is clear, sought above all else in their writings to hand on the teaching of Christ Jesus to the churches simple and uncorrupted, and to be the authors for the faithful of constant perseverance in it, I thought it not out of keeping with my purpose to append to my homilies on the Epistles of John the traditions or opinions of the most ancient Fathers concerning the Christian faith, which they believed to be apostolic. For from them it will be possible to see how great the authority of apostolic teaching was among them in former times, and what ought to be answered to those who, under the plausible name of the Fathers, thrust upon us new articles of faith and show a way of salvation which, as is well established, neither the Apostles nor the prophets knew. As for you, Christian reader, enjoy all these things in such a way that you may keep the truth you have acknowledged and continue to walk constantly in the way of salvation handed down through the Apostles. Farewell.

units.la: D. CYPRIANUS MARTYR DE SYMBOLO Apostolicae fidei hæc tradit.
units.tr: BLESSED CYPRIAN THE MARTYR ON THE CREED OF THE APOSTLES HANDS DOWN THE FOLLOWING.

units.la: Tradunt maiores nostri, quòd post ascensionem domini, cum per adventum spiritus sancti supra singulos quosque Apostolos igneæ linguæ sedissent, ut loquelis diversis variisq; loquerentur, per quod eis nulla gens extera, nulla linguæ barbaries inaccessa videretur & invia, præceptum eis à domino datum hoc, ad prædicandum Dei verbum, ad singulas quemque proficisci regiones. Discessuri itaque ab invicem, normam sibi prius futuræ prædicationis in cōmune constituunt: ne forte alii alió abducti, diversum aliquid his, qui ad fidem Christi invitabantur, exponerent. Omnes igitur in uno positi, & spiritu sancto repleti, breve istud futuræ sibi (ut diximus) prædicationis indicium, in unum conferendo quod sentiebat unusquisque, componunt, atq; hæc credentibus dandam esse regulam, statuunt. Symbolum autem hoc multis & iustissimis ex causis appellari voluerunt. Symbolum enim Græcè & indicium dici potest, & collatio: hoc est, quod plures in unum conferunt. Id enim fecerunt Apostoli in his sermonibus, in unum conferendo, quod unusquisque sensit. Indicium verò vel signum idcirco dicitur, quia in illo tempore (sicut Paulus Apostolus dicit, & in Actibus Apostolorum refertur) multi ex circumeuntibus Judæis simulabant se esse Apostolos Christi, & lucri alicuius, vel ventris gratia, ad prædicandum proficiscebantur, nominantes quidem Christum, sed non integris traditionum lineis nunciantes. Idcirco istud indicium posuerunt, per quod agnosceretur is, qui Christum verè secundum apostolicas regulas prædicaret. Denique & in bellis civilibus hoc observari ferunt, quoniam & armorum habitus par, & sonus vocis idem & mos unus est, atq; eadem instituta bellandi: ne qua doli surreptio fiat, symbola distincta unusquisq; dux suis militibus tradit, quæ Latinè Signa vel Indicia nominantur: ut si forte occurrerit quis, de quo dubitetur, interrogatus Symbolum prodat, si sit hostis vel socius. Idcirco denique hæc non scribi chartulis aut membranis, sed requiri in credentium cordibus tradiderunt: ut certum esset hæc neminem ex lectione (quæ interdum peervenire etiá ad infideles solet) sed ex Apostolorum traditione didicisse. Hæc Cyprianus.
units.tr: Our forebears hand down that after the ascension of the Lord, when through the coming of the Holy Spirit tongues of fire had settled upon each of the Apostles so that they spoke in diverse languages, by which no foreign nation or barbarous tongue seemed to them inaccessible or impassable, the Lord gave them this command: to set out for the proclamation of the word of God, each to his own regions. Therefore, about to part from one another, they first agreed in common upon a rule for their future preaching, lest perhaps, drawn off in different directions, some should set forth something different from the others to those who were being invited to the faith of Christ. So all of them, gathered together and filled with the Holy Spirit, composed this brief indication of their future preaching (as we have said) by bringing together into one what each of them thought, and they decreed that this should be given as a rule to believers. They wished this symbol to be called by many very just reasons. For "symbolum" in Greek can mean both a sign and a collection, that is, what many bring together into one. For the Apostles did this in these addresses, bringing together into one what each of them thought. It is called an indication or sign, moreover, because at that time (as the Apostle Paul says, and as is related in the Acts of the Apostles) many of the Jews who went about pretended that they were Apostles of Christ, and set out to preach for the sake of some gain or their bellies, naming Christ indeed, but not announcing him by the unbroken lines of tradition. Therefore they set up this sign, by which he who truly preached Christ according to the apostolic rules might be recognised. Finally, they report that this is also observed in civil wars: since the dress of arms is alike, the sound of the voice the same, the custom one, and the methods of fighting identical, so that no deceit may steal in, each commander hands to his own soldiers distinct symbols, which in Latin are called signs or indications; so that if perhaps someone comes upon them about whom there is doubt, being questioned, he may reveal the symbol, whether he is enemy or ally. Hence finally they handed down that these things should not be written on little papers or parchments, but sought in the hearts of believers, so that it might be certain that no one had learned them from reading (which sometimes comes even into the hands of unbelievers), but from the tradition of the Apostles. Thus Cyprian.

units.la: SYMBOLUM APOSTOLORUM, QUOD VETERES (ut Cyprianus non obscurè fatetur & Irenæus infra evidentius testabitur.) Traditionis nomine intellexerunt, hoc est:
units.tr: THE CREED OF THE APOSTLES, WHICH THE ANCIENTS (as Cyprian does not obscurely confess, and Irenaeus will bear witness more clearly below) understood under the name of tradition, that is:

units.la: Credo in Deum, patrem omnipotentem, creatorem cœli & terræ. Et in Jesum Christum, filium eius unicum, Dominum nostrum. Qui conceptus est de spiritu sancto: natus ex Maria virgine: passus sub Pontio Pilato, crucifixus, mortuus & sepultus est. Descendit ad inferos. Tertia die resurrexit à mortuis. Ascendit ad cœlos. Sedet ad dexteram Dei patris omnipotentis: Inde ventuventūrus ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos. Credo in spiritum sanctum. Sanctam ecclesiam catholicam, sanctorum communionem. Peccatorum remissionem. Carnis huius resurrectionem, & vitam aeternam. Amen.
units.tr: I believe in God the Father almighty, Creator of heaven and earth. And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord. Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried. He descended into hell. On the third day he rose again from the dead. He ascended into heaven. He sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty; from there he will come to judge the living and the dead. I believe in the Holy Spirit. The holy catholic Church, the communion of saints. The forgiveness of sins. The resurrection of this flesh, and life everlasting. Amen.

units.la: IRENAEVS SIMILITER APOSTOLICAE FIDEI ET DOCTRINAE SVMMAM lib.1.Cap.2.contra Valent.sic comprehendit.
units.tr: IRENAEUS LIKEWISE, A SUMMARY OF THE APOSTOLIC FAITH AND TEACHING, Book 1, chapter 2, against Valentinus, comprehends thus.

units.la: Ecclesia per vniuersum orbem vsque ad fines terrae dispersa, ab Apostolis & ipsorum discipulis eam accepit fidem, quae est in vnum Deum, patrem omnipotentem, qui fecit cœlum & terram, mare & omnia quae in eis sunt. Et in vnum Iesum Christum, filium Dei, incarnatum pro nostra salute. Et in spiritum sanctum, qui per prophetas praedicauit dispensationis mysterium & aduentum, & ex virgine natiuitatem, & passionem, & resurrectionem ex mortuis, & in carne ad cœlos ascensionem dilecti Iesu Christi domini nostri: & ipsius è cœlis in gloria patris aduentum ad instauranda omnia, & resuscitandam omnem humani generis carnem, vt Christo Iesu domino nostro, & Deo & saluatori & regi iuxta voluntatem patris inuisibilis, omne genu flectatur cœlestium & terrestrium ac infernorum, & omnis lingua confiteatur ipsi, & iudicium iustum in omnibus faciat: & spiritualia quidem nequitiei, & angelos transgressores ac desertores factos, & impios ac iniustos, & iniquos & blasphemos homines in aeternum ignem mittat: iustis vero & sanctis, & qui mandata eius seruarunt, & in dilectione eius permanserunt, partim ab initio, partim ex poenitentia, vitam largitus incorruptibilitatem donet, & gloriam aeternam tribuat, &c.
units.tr: The Church, scattered throughout the whole world even to the ends of the earth, received from the Apostles and their disciples this faith: in one God, the Father almighty, who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them; and in one Jesus Christ, the Son of God, made flesh for our salvation; and in the Holy Spirit, who through the prophets proclaimed the mystery of the dispensation and the coming, and the birth from the Virgin, and the passion, and the resurrection from the dead, and the ascension in the flesh into heaven of the beloved Jesus Christ our Lord, and his coming from heaven in the glory of the Father to restore all things and to raise up all the flesh of the human race; so that to Christ Jesus our Lord, and God and Saviour and King, according to the will of the invisible Father, every knee of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth may bow, and every tongue may confess him, and he may execute just judgment upon all; and he will send the spiritual powers of wickedness and the angels who transgressed and became deserters, and the impious and unjust and wicked and blasphemous men, into eternal fire; but to the just and holy, who have kept his commandments and remained in his love, some from the beginning, others after repentance, he will grant life, bestow incorruptibility, and give eternal glory, etc.

units.la: IDEM LIBRO III. CAP. IIII. OSTENDIT HANC IPSAM fidem, esse traditionem illam Apostolicam, quae fidelibus per totum orbem praescripta paßim obseruetur.
units.tr: The same author, Book III, chapter 4, shows that this very faith is that Apostolic tradition which is observed everywhere, prescribed to the faithful throughout the whole world.

units.la: Quid autem si neque Apostoli quidem scripturas reliquissent nobis, nonne oportebat ordinem sequi traditionis, quam tradiderunt ijs, quibus committebant ecclesias, cui ordinationi assentiunt multae gentes barbarorum, eorum qui in Christum credunt, sine chartae aut atramento scriptam habentes per spiritum in cordibus suis salutem, & veterem traditionem diligenter custodientes: in vnum Deum credentes, fabricatorem cœli & terrae, & omnium quae in eis sunt, per Christum Iesum, Dei filium. Qui propter eminentissimam erga figmentum[?] suum dilectionem, eam quae esset ex virgine generatione suscitauit, ipse per se homine adunans Deo, & passus sub Pontio Pilato, & resurgens, & in claritate receptus, in gloria venturus saluator eorum, qui saluantur: & iudex eorum, qui iudicantur, & mittes in ignem aeternum transfiguratores veritatis & contemptores patris sui, & aduentus eius. Hanc fidem, qui sine literis crediderunt, quantum ad sermonem nostrum, Barbari sunt. Quantum autem ad sententiam, & consuetudinem, & cōuersationem, propter fidem per quam sapientissimi sunt, & placent Deo, cōuersantes in omni iustitia & castitate & sapientia, &c.
units.tr: But what if the Apostles had not even left Scriptures to us? Ought we not still to follow the order of the tradition which they handed down to those to whom they committed the churches? Many nations of barbarians, who believe in Christ, assent to this order: they have salvation written in their hearts by the Spirit, without paper or ink, and they diligently keep the ancient tradition, believing in one God, the maker of heaven and earth and of all that is in them, through Christ Jesus, the Son of God. Out of his most excellent love for his handiwork [figmentum?], he brought about the generation from the virgin; he himself, by himself, joining man to God, suffered under Pontius Pilate, rose again, was received in glory, and will come in glory as the saviour of those who are saved and the judge of those who are judged, sending into eternal fire the transgressors of the truth and the despisers of his Father and of his coming. Those who have believed this faith without letters are barbarians so far as our speech is concerned; but as regards their opinion, their custom and their conduct, they are most wise and pleasing to God, because of the faith by which they live in all righteousness, chastity and wisdom, and so on.

units.la: TERTVLLIANVS DE PRAESCRIPTIONIBVS HAERETICORVM, fidei orthodoxae & catholicae Regulam exponit his verbis:
units.tr: TERTULLIAN, IN HIS BOOK ON THE PRESCRIPTIONS AGAINST HERETICS, SETS OUT THE RULE OF ORTHODOX AND CATHOLIC FAITH IN THESE WORDS:

units.la: Regula est fidei, vt iam hinc quid credamus profiteamur: illa scilicet, qua creditur, vnum omnino Deum esse, nec alium praeter mundi Creatorem: qui vniuersa de nihilo produxerit per verbum suum primo omnium emissum. Id verbum Filius eius appellatum, in nomine Dei varie visum patriarchis, in prophetis semper auditum, postremo delatum ex spiritu patris Dei & virtute in virginem Mariam, carnem factum in vtero eius & ex ea natum, egisse Iesum Christum: exinde praedicasse nouam legem, & nouam promissionem regni cœlorum, virtutes fecisse, sedisse ad dexteram patris, fixum cruci tertia die resurrexisse: in cœlos ereptum sedere ad dexteram patris: misisse vicariam[?] vim spiritus sancti, qui credentes agat: venturum cum claritate ad sumendos sanctos in vitae aeternae & promissorum cœlestium fructum: & ad prophanos iudicandos igni perpetuo, facta vtriusque partis resuscitatione cum carnis restitutione. Haec Regula à Christo (vt probabitur) instituta, nullas habet apud nos quaestiones, nisi quas haereses inferunt, & quae haereticos faciunt.
units.tr: The rule of faith is this, so that from here we may now profess what we believe: namely, that there is absolutely one God, and no other besides the Creator of the world, who brought forth all things out of nothing through his Word, sent forth first of all. This Word, called his Son, was seen in various ways by the patriarchs in the name of God, was always heard by the prophets, and at last, sent down from the Spirit of God the Father and by his power into the virgin Mary, was made flesh in her womb and was born of her. He then lived as Jesus Christ; afterwards he preached a new law and a new promise of the kingdom of heaven, performed miracles, was crucified, and on the third day rose again. Taken up into the heavens, he sits at the right hand of the Father. He sent in his place the power of the Holy Spirit, to guide believers. He will come with glory to take the saints into the fruition of eternal life and the heavenly promises, and to judge the profane with everlasting fire, after the resurrection of both parts with the restoration of the flesh. This rule, instituted by Christ (as will be proved), has no questions among us except those which heresies bring in and which make men heretics.

units.la: SYMBOLVM BEATI ATHANASII EPISCOPI Alexandrini.
units.tr: THE CREED OF ST ATHANASIUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA

units.la: Quicunque vult saluus esse, ante omnia opus est, vt teneat catholicā fidem, quam nisi quis integram inuiolatamq; seruauerit, absque dubio in aeternum peribit.
units.tr: Whoever wishes to be saved must, above all things, hold the Catholic faith; unless a person keeps this whole and inviolate, he will without doubt perish eternally.

units.la: Fides autem catholica haec est, vt vnum Deum in trinitate, & trinitate in vnitate veneremur: neque confundentes personas, neque substantiam separantes. Alia est enim persona patris, alia filij, alia spiritus sancti: sed patris & filij & spiritus sancti una est diuinitas, æqualis gloria, coæterna maiestas.
units.tr: Now the Catholic faith is this: that we worship one God in Trinity, and Trinity in Unity; neither confusing the persons nor dividing the substance. For the person of the Father is one, the person of the Son another, and the person of the Holy Spirit another; but the Godhead of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit is one, their glory equal, their majesty co-eternal.

units.la: Qualis pater, talis filius, talis spiritus sanctus. Increatus pater, increatus filius, increatus spiritus sanctus. Immensus pater, immensus filius, immensus spiritus sanctus. Aeternus pater, æternus filius, æternus spiritus sanctus. Et tamen non tres æterni, sed unus æternus: sicut non tres increati, nec tres immensi, sed unus increatus, & unus immensus.
units.tr: Such as the Father is, such is the Son, and such is the Holy Spirit. The Father is uncreated, the Son uncreated, the Holy Spirit uncreated. The Father is immeasurable, the Son immeasurable, the Holy Spirit immeasurable. The Father is eternal, the Son eternal, the Holy Spirit eternal. And yet they are not three eternals, but one eternal; just as there are not three uncreated nor three immeasurable, but one uncreated and one immeasurable.

units.la: Similiter omnipotens pater, omnipotens filius, omnipotens spiritus sanctus. Et tamen non tres omnipotentes, sed unus omnipotens. Ita Deus pater, Deus filius, Deus spiritus sanctus. Et tamen non tres Dij, sed unus est Deus. Ita dominus pater, dominus filius, dominus spiritus sanctus. Et tamen non tres domini, sed unus est dominus.
units.tr: Likewise the Father is almighty, the Son almighty, the Holy Spirit almighty; and yet they are not three almighties, but one almighty. So the Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God; and yet they are not three Gods, but there is one God. So the Father is Lord, the Son is Lord, the Holy Spirit is Lord; and yet they are not three Lords, but there is one Lord.

units.la: Quia sicut sigillatim unamquamque personam Deum aut dominum confiteri Christiana veritate compellimur: ita tres Deos aut dominos dicere catholica religione prohibemur.
units.tr: For just as the Christian truth compels us to confess each person separately as God and Lord, so the Catholic religion forbids us to say that there are three Gods or three Lords.

units.la: Pater à nullo est factus, nec creatus, nec genitus. Filius à patre solo est, non factus, nec creatus, sed genitus. Spiritus sanctus à patre & filio, nó factus nec creatus, nec genitus, sed procedēs. Vnus ergo pater, nó tres patres. Vnus filius, nó tres filij. Vnus spiritus sanctus, nó tres spiritus sancti.
units.tr: The Father is made by no one, neither created nor begotten. The Son is from the Father alone: not made, nor created, but begotten. The Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son: not made, nor created, nor begotten, but proceeding. There is therefore one Father, not three Fathers; one Son, not three Sons; one Holy Spirit, not three Holy Spirits.

units.la: Et in hac trinitate nihil prius nec posterius, nihil maius aut minus: sed totæ tres personæ coæternæ sibi sunt & coæquales. Ita vt per omnia (sicut iam dictum est) & vnitas in trinitate, & trinitas in vnitate veneranda sit. Qui vult ergo saluus esse, ita de trinitate sentiat.
units.tr: And in this Trinity nothing is before or after, nothing greater or less; but the three persons are wholly co-eternal and co-equal with one another. So that in all things, as has already been said, both the Unity in Trinity and the Trinity in Unity is to be worshipped. Therefore whoever wishes to be saved must think thus concerning the Trinity.

units.la: Sed necessarium est ad æternam salutem, vt incarnationem quoque domini nostri Iesu Christi fideliter credat. Est ergo fides recta, vt credamus & confiteamur, quia dominus noster Iesus Christus, Dei filius, Deus & homo est.
units.tr: But it is necessary to eternal salvation that a person also faithfully believe in the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. The right faith, then, is that we believe and confess that our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is God and man.

units.la: Deus est ex substantia patris ante secula genitus: & homo ex substantia matris in seculo natus. Perfectus Deus, perfectus homo, ex anima rationali & humana carne subsistens. Aequalis patri secundum diuinitatem, minor patre secundum humanitatem.
units.tr: He is God, of the substance of the Father, begotten before the ages; and he is man, of the substance of his mother, born in the world: perfect God, perfect man, subsisting of a rational soul and human flesh; equal to the Father according to his Godhead, less than the Father according to his manhood.

units.la: Qui licet Deus sit & homo, nó duo tamē, sed unus est Christus. Unus autem, nó cōuersione diuinitatis in carnē, sed assumptione humanitatis in Deū. Unus omnino, nó cōfusione substātię, sed unitate psonę. Nā sicut anima rationalis & caro, unus est homo: ita deus & homo, unus est Christus.
units.tr: Although he is God and man, yet they are not two, but one Christ. He is one, not by conversion of the Godhead into flesh, but by the taking up of the manhood into God; one altogether, not by confusion of substance, but by unity of person. For just as the rational soul and flesh make one man, so God and man are one Christ.

units.la: Qui passus est pro salute nostra, descendit ad inferos, tertia die resurrexit à mortuis. Ascendit ad cœlos: sedet ad dextram Dei patris omnipotentis: inde venturus est iudicare viuos & mortuos.
units.tr: Who suffered for our salvation, descended into hell, rose again from the dead on the third day. He ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the almighty Father; from there he will come to judge the living and the dead.

units.la: Ad cuius aduentum omnes homines resurgent cum corporibus suis, & reddituri sunt de factis proprijs rationem. Et qui bona egerūt, ibunt in vitam æternam: qui vero mala, in igne æternū.
units.tr: At his coming all men will rise again with their bodies, and they will give account of their own deeds. Those who have done good will go into eternal life; those who have done evil, into eternal fire.

units.la: Hæc est fides Catholica, quam nisi quisq; fideliter firmiterq; crediderit, saluus esse nó poterit.
units.tr: This is the Catholic faith; unless a person believes it faithfully and firmly, he cannot be saved.

units.la: SYMBOLVM B. DAMASI EPISCOPI ROMANI.
units.tr: THE SYMBOL OF SAINT DAMASUS, BISHOP OF ROME.

units.la: CREDIMUS in unum Deum, patrem omnipotentem: & in unum Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, Dei filium: & in spiritum sanctum. Deum, non tres Deos: sed patre, filio & spiritu sancto, unum Deū colimus & confitemur: non sic unum Deū, quasi solitariū, nec eundem qui ipse sibi pater sit, ipse & filius: sed patre esse, qui genuit: & filiū esse, qui genitus sit: spiritū vero sanctū non genitū neq; ingenitum, non creatū neq; factū, sed de patre filioq; procedente, patri & filio coæternū & coæqualem & cooperatorē: quia scriptum est: Verbo domini cœli firmati sunt, id est à filio Dei, & spiritu oris eius omnis virtus eorū. Et alibi: Emitte spiritū tuū, & creabuntur, & renouabis faciem terræ. Ideoq; in nomine patris & filij & spiritus sancti unū confitemur Deū, quod nomen est potestatis, nõn proprietatis. Proprium nomen est patri, Pater: & proprium nomen est filio, Filius: & proprium nomen spiritui sancto, Spiritus sanctus. In hac trinitate unū Deum colimus, quia ex uno patre quod est, unius cū patre naturę est, unius substantiæ & unius potestatis. Pater filium genuit, non voluntate nec necessitate, sed natura. Filius vltimo tempore ad nos salvandos & ad implendas scripturas descendit à patre, qui nunquā desijt esse cū patre. Et cœceptus est de spiritu sancto, & natus ex virgine: carnem & animā & sensum, hoc est, perfectū suscepit hominem, nec amisit quod erat, sed cœpit esse quod non erat: ita tamen, vt perfectus in suis sit, & verus in nostris. Nam qui Deus erat, homo natus est: & qui homo natus est, operatur vt Deus: & qui operatur vt Deus, vt homo moritur: & qui vt homo moritur, vt Deus resurgit. Qui deuicto mortis imperio, cum ea carne, qua natus & passus & mortuus fuerat & resurrexit, ascendit ad patrem, sedetq; ad dextram eius in gloria, quam semper habuit & habet. In huius morte & sanguine credimus emūdatos nos, & ab eo resuscitandos die nouissimo in hac carne, qua nūc viuimus. Et habemus spem, nos cōsecuturos prēmiū boni meriti, aut poenā pro peccatis æterni supplicij. Hæc lege, hæc crede, hæc retine, huic fidei animā tuam subiuga, & vitā consequeris & prēmiū à Christo.
units.tr: We believe in one God, the Father almighty; and in one Lord our Jesus Christ, the Son of God; and in the Holy Spirit. We worship and confess one God, not three Gods: with the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, we worship and confess one God. We do not understand this one God as solitary, nor as the same person who is himself both Father and Son. Rather, he is the Father, who begot, and the Son, who was begotten; but the Holy Spirit is neither begotten nor unbegotten, neither created nor made, but proceeds from the Father and the Son, coeternal and coequal with the Father and the Son, and their fellow worker. For it is written: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were established," that is, by the Son of God, "and all their power by the breath of his mouth." And elsewhere: "Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth." Therefore, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, we confess one God; this is a name of power, not of property. "Father" is the proper name of the Father; "Son" is the proper name of the Son; and "Holy Spirit" is the proper name of the Holy Spirit. In this Trinity we worship one God, because from the one Father, what is, is of one nature with the Father, of one substance and one power. The Father begot the Son, not by will nor by necessity, but by nature. At the last time the Son came down from the Father, who never ceased to be with the Father, to save us and to fulfil the Scriptures. He was conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin; he took on flesh, soul and understanding, that is, he took on a perfect man, and did not lose what he was, but began to be what he was not: yet in such a way that he is perfect in his own and true in ours. For he who was God was born a man, and he who was born a man works as God, and he who works as God dies as a man, and he who dies as a man rises again as God. Having overcome the power of death, with that flesh in which he was born, suffered, died and rose, he ascended to the Father and sits at his right hand in glory, which he always had and has. We believe that we are cleansed by his death and blood, and that we shall be raised by him on the last day in this flesh in which we now live. And we have the hope of obtaining the reward of good merit, or the punishment of eternal torment for sins. Read these things, believe these things, hold fast to these things; subject your soul to this faith, and you shall obtain life and the reward from Christ.

units.la: Age, ad utilitatem legentium breviter incarnationis unigeniti causam, & recessus sui ad patrem grandem utilitatem perstringamus. Homo igitur factus est, ut ab interitu, quem pri-sca maledictio intulerat, nos liberaret. Et quoniam nulla divinae naturae ad peccadum inclinatio est, omnes nos per ipsam carnem assumpsit. In ipso enim omnes sumus ea ratione, qua homo est. Assumpsit igitur nos, ut terrena haec umbra, id est, carnis passiones & peccati legem, quae in mem-bra hominum irruperat, extingueret: adde, & naturam nostram sanctificaret, & dux ad pietatem & optimae disciplinae viuendi humano generi fieret. Et hęc quidem homo factus effecit. Sed non solum voluit ab interitu & a peccato nos liberare, verum etiam ad ipsos coelos reducere, ac summi boni participes facere, in angelorum consortio numeratos: & quemadmodum per resurrectio-nem suam mortem destruxit, sic coram ipso patre collocaret. Ea recte intelligens Paulus, dicit: Non enim in sancta manu facta introiuit Christus, in exemplaria verorum, sed in ipsum coelum, ut appareat vultui Dei pro nobis. Audis, quia cum sit semper cum patre propter identitatem substantiæ, non pro seipso, sed pro nobis patri apparet. Ita cum ipse sit primitiæ generis nostri, quando in coelum cum carne ascendit, coram patre (ut modo dixi) nos constituit. Et sicut quamuis secundum naturam vita sit, mortuus tamen propter nos fuit. Ita etiamsi patrem semper videat ipse, ab eoque videatur, nunc tamen, id est, posteaquam homo factus est, apparuisse illi, non propter se, sed propter nos ut homo dicitur. Quasi ergo deficere hoc dispensationi videbatur, ut in ipsos etiam coelos ascenderemus in Christo primo, ut in primitijs. Præcursor enim ille ascendit, ut Paulus dicit, & sic in quantum homo, Pontifex & intercedes pro nobis, & paracletus & propitiatio pro peccatis nostris: in quantum vero Deus & dominus, natura cum patre simul sedet, quæ tamen gloria etiam ad nos transit secundum Paulum, qui de patre scribit, quia & conresuscitavit, & consedere nos fecit in coelestibus in Christo. Cum ergo omnia, quæ in terris ut ab homine facienda fuerunt, perfecerit, restabat ut iam ad patrem ascenderet. Idcirco ait: Expedit vobis ut ego vadā. Nam nisi abiero, paracletus non veniet ad vos. Opus enim erat participes nos naturae suae fieri, & in novam inauditamque vitam transformari: quod aliter quam participatione spiritus sancti fieri non poterat. Commodissima vero adventus spiritus opportunitas post Christi ad coelos reditu fuit. Oportebat autem spiritum venire, ut illum habetes libere clamemus, Abba pater, & ad virtutem redacti, tam adversus diabolum quam adversus persecutiones hominum fortes efficeremur. Quod autem præsentia spiritus ad novam vitam omnes, in quibus habitat, transformantur, non est difficile è scripturis ostendere. Dicit enim Samuel ad Saulem: Et insiliet in te spiritus domini, & converteris in alium virum. Et Paulus: Nos vero (inquit) omnes reuelata facie gloriam Domini speculantes, in eandem imaginem transformamur, à claritate in claritatem, tanquam à domini spiritu. Vides quia ad aliam, sicuti vult spiritus, imaginem nos ut domini reformat, nempe qui facile à terrenis ad coelestia nostros transponit animos. Quod in discipulis factum fuisse inueniemus: per spiritum sanè ad eam fortitudinem ab humana ignauia reducti sunt, ut nec ulla pericula timerent, & Christo inseparabiliter inhærerent. Expediebat igitur verè discipulis (ut sal-vator dicit) in cœlum ipsum abire. Tempus enim iam aduentus spiritus erat.
units.tr: Come now, for the benefit of the readers, let us briefly set out the cause of the only-begotten Son's incarnation and his return to the Father, which is of great use. Man, therefore, was made so that he might free us from the destruction which the ancient curse had brought upon us. And since there is no inclination in the divine nature toward sin, he took us up through the flesh itself. For in him we are all, by that reason by which he is man. He took us up, therefore, so that he might extinguish that earthly shadow, that is, the passions of the flesh and the law of sin, which had burst into the members of men; and besides, that he might sanctify our nature and become a guide to piety and to the best discipline of living for the human race. And indeed, having been made man, he accomplished these things. But he did not only will to free us from destruction and from sin, but also to lead us back to the heavens themselves, and to make us sharers of the highest good, numbered in the fellowship of the angels; and just as through his resurrection he destroyed death, so he would place us before the Father himself. Paul, understanding these things rightly, says: "For Christ did not enter into a holy place made with hands, a copy of the true one, but into heaven itself, to appear now in the presence of God for us." You hear that, since he is always with the Father on account of the identity of substance, he appears before the Father not for himself, but for us. Thus, since he is the firstfruits of our race, when he ascended into heaven with the flesh, he placed us before the Father (as I have just said). And just as, although he is life according to nature, he nevertheless died on our account, so also, although he himself always sees the Father and is seen by him, yet now, that is, after he was made man, he is said to have appeared to him not for himself, but for us, as man. It seemed, then, as if this arrangement would be lacking, unless we also ascended into the heavens themselves in Christ the first, as in the firstfruits. For that forerunner ascended, as Paul says, and so in so far as he is man, he is High Priest and intercessor for us, and Advocate and propitiation for our sins; but in so far as he is God and Lord, he sits together with the Father by nature; which glory nevertheless passes also to us, according to Paul, who writes of the Father that he both raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ. Therefore, when he had completed all those things which had to be done on earth by him as man, it remained that he should now ascend to the Father. Hence he says: "It is expedient for you that I go away. For unless I go away, the Advocate will not come to you." For it was necessary that we be made partakers of his nature and be transformed into a new and unheard-of life, which could not be done otherwise than by participation in the Holy Spirit. Indeed, the most fitting opportunity for the coming of the Spirit was after Christ's return to the heavens. Now it was necessary for the Spirit to come, so that, having him, we might freely cry, "Abba, Father," and, brought back to strength, we might be made brave both against the devil and against the persecutions of men. That by the presence of the Spirit all those in whom he dwells are transformed into a new life is not difficult to show from the Scriptures. For Samuel says to Saul: "And the Spirit of the Lord will leap upon you, and you will be turned into another man." And Paul: "But we all (he says), with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord." You see that he reforms us, as the Lord's Spirit, into another image, to which he wills, namely, him who easily transposes our minds from earthly things to heavenly ones. We shall find that this happened in the disciples: they were indeed led by the Spirit from human cowardice to such a strength that they feared no dangers and adhered inseparably to Christ. It was therefore truly expedient for the disciples (as the Savior says) to depart into heaven itself. For the time of the Spirit's coming had now arrived.
